why_others_wrong.E: The Na+/K+ ATPase is basolateral and maintains the sodium gradient that drives SGLT1, but it does not transport glucose itself.

exam_trap: GLUT2 (option B) tempts because it is the main enterocyte glucose transporter, but it sits on the basolateral membrane and is not sodium-dependent.
takeaway: Gut lumen → SGLT1 → enterocyte; basolateral exit → GLUT2.
thinking: Sodium-dependent glucose uptake on the brush border ↓ secondary active transport driven by the sodium gradient ↓ apical co-transporter for glucose and galactose ↓ SGLT1
pearl: Oral rehydration solutions exploit SGLT1 sodium-glucose co-transport, which remains functional in secretory diarrhoea such as cholera, so added glucose enhances sodium and water absorption.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: Colonic water absorption
stem: A patient has extensive colonic disease and develops increased stool water losses. Which physiological function of the colon has been impaired?
correct_answer: B. Absorption of water and electrolytes
why_correct: The colon plays an important role in recovering water and electrolytes from intestinal contents.

why_others_wrong.A: Protein digestion occurs mainly in the stomach and small intestine, so colonic disease would not impair it or explain watery stool.
why_others_wrong.C: Bile is produced by hepatocytes in the liver, not by the colon.
why_others_wrong.D: Intrinsic factor is secreted by gastric parietal cells and is unrelated to colonic function.
why_others_wrong.E: Pancreatic enzymes are activated in the duodenum by enteropeptidase, not in the colon.

exam_trap: Most nutrient absorption occurs in the small intestine, but the colon remains important for fluid and electrolyte handling.
takeaway: Colon = water and electrolyte recovery.
thinking: Extensive colonic disease with watery stool ↓ the colon recovers water and electrolytes from ileal effluent ↓ that recovery is lost ↓ Absorption of water and electrolytes
pearl: Patients with an ileostomy have lost the colonic absorptive reserve, so a high stoma output can rapidly cause dehydration, hyponatraemia and hypomagnesaemia.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: Portal circulation
stem: Which vessel carries nutrient-rich blood from the gastrointestinal tract to the liver?
why_correct: Venous blood from much of the gastrointestinal tract, spleen and associated organs reaches the liver through the portal venous system.

why_others_wrong.A: The hepatic artery delivers oxygenated systemic arterial blood to the liver, not nutrient-rich venous blood from the gut.
why_others_wrong.B: The hepatic veins drain blood out of the liver into the inferior vena cava rather than carrying blood from the gut to the liver.
why_others_wrong.D: The inferior vena cava returns systemic venous blood, including hepatic venous outflow, to the right atrium after the liver.
why_others_wrong.E: The splenic artery supplies the spleen, pancreas and part of the stomach; it is arterial and does not carry absorbed nutrients to the liver.

exam_trap: Candidates pick the hepatic vein (option B) by name association, but the hepatic veins drain blood out of the liver into the inferior vena cava, not from gut to liver.
takeaway: Gut → portal vein → liver → systemic circulation.
thinking: Nutrient-rich venous blood from the gut ↓ drains via the superior mesenteric and splenic veins ↓ these unite to form the vessel entering the porta hepatis ↓ Portal vein
pearl: In portal hypertension, portosystemic collaterals open at the gastro-oesophageal junction, the rectum and the umbilicus, explaining variceal bleeding and caput medusae.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: Hepatic synthetic function
stem: A patient with severe chronic liver disease develops hypoalbuminaemia. Which hepatic function is impaired?
why_correct: The liver synthesises albumin and many plasma proteins, including several coagulation factors.

why_others_wrong.A: Urea is made by the liver but filtered by the kidney; the liver does not filter urea, and this would not explain hypoalbuminaemia.
why_others_wrong.C: Insulin is secreted by pancreatic beta cells, not the liver, and has no direct link to low albumin.
why_others_wrong.D: Bile salts are reabsorbed in the terminal ileum and taken back up by hepatocytes, but this enterohepatic recycling does not determine plasma albumin concentration.
why_others_wrong.E: Ammonium excretion is a renal function and does not account for reduced albumin in liver disease.

exam_trap: Low albumin can also occur through other mechanisms, including inflammation, renal loss and gastrointestinal loss. In severe liver disease, impaired hepatic synthesis is an important mechanism.
takeaway: Liver = major plasma protein synthesis.
thinking: Severe chronic liver disease ↓ reduced functioning hepatocyte mass ↓ the liver is the site of albumin synthesis ↓ Albumin synthesis
pearl: Albumin has a half-life of around three weeks, so it reflects chronic synthetic function, whereas the prothrombin time or INR changes within days and is the better marker in acute liver failure.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: Urea cycle
stem: A patient with severe hepatic dysfunction develops hyperammonaemia. Which hepatic metabolic process is directly impaired?

options.C: Conversion of lactate to pyruvate only
options.D: Conversion of cholesterol to bile salts
options.E: Conversion of fatty acids to triglycerides

correct_answer: A. Conversion of ammonia to urea
why_correct: The liver converts toxic ammonia into urea through the urea cycle. Severe hepatic dysfunction can therefore contribute to hyperammonaemia.

why_others_wrong.B: Glycogen synthesis stores glucose and its impairment affects glucose homeostasis, not ammonia clearance.
why_others_wrong.C: Lactate to pyruvate conversion feeds gluconeogenesis in the Cori cycle and does not detoxify ammonia.
why_others_wrong.D: Conversion of cholesterol to bile salts supports fat digestion and does not remove ammonia.
why_others_wrong.E: Triglyceride synthesis from fatty acids is part of lipid storage and does not affect ammonia handling.

exam_trap: Do not confuse the urea cycle with renal excretion. The kidney excretes urea, but hepatic conversion of ammonia to urea occurs first.
takeaway: Liver converts ammonia → urea; kidney excretes urea.
thinking: Hepatic dysfunction with hyperammonaemia ↓ ammonia comes from protein metabolism and gut bacteria ↓ the liver detoxifies it through the urea cycle ↓ Conversion of ammonia to urea
pearl: Lactulose treats hepatic encephalopathy by acidifying colonic contents, trapping ammonia as ammonium and speeding its faecal loss; rifaximin is added to reduce ammonia-producing gut bacteria.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: Insulin and glucose uptake
stem: Following a carbohydrate-rich meal, insulin secretion increases. Which tissue demonstrates insulin-stimulated translocation of GLUT4 to the cell membrane?
why_correct: Insulin promotes GLUT4 translocation particularly in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue, increasing glucose uptake.

why_others_wrong.B: Enterocytes absorb glucose via apical SGLT1 and basolateral GLUT2, neither of which depends on insulin-stimulated GLUT4 translocation.
why_others_wrong.C: Hepatocytes take up glucose through GLUT2, which is not insulin-dependent, and the liver is not the only tissue relevant here.
why_others_wrong.D: Red blood cells rely on GLUT1 for insulin-independent glucose uptake.
why_others_wrong.E: Glomerular endothelium does not use insulin-stimulated GLUT4 translocation for glucose uptake.

exam_trap: The liver uses GLUT2, which is not dependent on insulin-mediated GLUT4 translocation.
takeaway: Insulin → GLUT4 → skeletal muscle/adipose glucose uptake.
thinking: Insulin rises after a carbohydrate meal ↓ GLUT4 is the insulin-responsive glucose transporter ↓ it is moved from vesicles to the membrane in muscle and fat ↓ Skeletal muscle
pearl: Muscle contraction also translocates GLUT4 independently of insulin, which is why physical activity improves glucose control in insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: Glucagon
stem: During fasting, which hormone is most important in promoting hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis?
why_correct: Glucagon rises during fasting and promotes hepatic glucose production through glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.

why_others_wrong.A: Insulin dominates in the fed state and suppresses glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, the opposite of the fasting response.
why_others_wrong.C: Calcitonin lowers serum calcium by inhibiting osteoclasts and has no major role in hepatic glucose production.
why_others_wrong.D: Aldosterone regulates sodium and potassium balance through the kidney and does not drive hepatic glucose output.
why_others_wrong.E: ADH regulates water reabsorption and vascular tone and is not a key hormone in fasting glucose production.

exam_trap: Insulin (option A) is chosen as the main glucose hormone, but it dominates the fed state and suppresses the glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis that fasting requires.
takeaway: Fed state → insulin; fasting state → glucagon.
thinking: Fasting state ↓ insulin falls and alpha cells release the counter-regulatory hormone ↓ the liver mobilises glycogen and makes new glucose ↓ Glucagon
pearl: Intramuscular glucagon can treat severe hypoglycaemia when intravenous access is unavailable, but it is ineffective when hepatic glycogen is depleted, as in starvation or alcohol excess.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: Early fasting
stem: A healthy adult stops eating but continues to drink water. During the early fasting period, which process becomes increasingly important for maintaining blood glucose?

options.E: Increased glucose uptake by adipose tissue

why_correct: During early fasting, hepatic glycogen stores are mobilised to maintain blood glucose. As fasting continues, gluconeogenesis becomes increasingly important.

why_others_wrong.B: Once eating stops there is no dietary glucose to absorb, so intestinal absorption cannot maintain blood glucose.
why_others_wrong.C: Insulin secretion falls during fasting, allowing glucagon to promote hepatic glucose output.
why_others_wrong.D: Glycogen synthesis is a fed-state process; in fasting glycogen is broken down rather than built.
why_others_wrong.E: Adipose glucose uptake is insulin-dependent and falls during fasting, sparing glucose for the brain.

exam_trap: Do not apply the metabolic pattern of prolonged starvation to the first few hours of fasting.
takeaway: Early fasting → glycogenolysis; prolonged fasting → increasing gluconeogenesis and ketogenesis.
thinking: Early fasting with no dietary glucose ↓ insulin falls and glucagon rises ↓ the liver first breaks down its stored glycogen ↓ gluconeogenesis takes over later ↓ Hepatic glycogenolysis
pearl: Preoperative carbohydrate loading drinks, used in enhanced recovery pathways, aim to bring patients to surgery in a fed metabolic state and reduce postoperative insulin resistance.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: Prolonged starvation
stem: During prolonged starvation, which fuel becomes increasingly important for the brain?
why_correct: During prolonged starvation, increased hepatic ketogenesis provides ketone bodies that can be used by the brain, reducing its dependence on glucose and helping conserve body protein.

why_others_wrong.A: Long-chain free fatty acids cross the blood–brain barrier poorly, so the brain cannot use them directly as a major fuel.
why_others_wrong.C: Hepatic glycogen stores are exhausted within about a day and cannot supply the brain during prolonged starvation.
why_others_wrong.D: Lactate can be used by neurons in some circumstances, but it is not the main alternative cerebral fuel in prolonged starvation.
why_others_wrong.E: Amino acids feed hepatic gluconeogenesis early in starvation, but ketone use increases later to spare body protein.

exam_trap: The brain cannot simply switch to using circulating free fatty acids as its principal alternative fuel because long-chain fatty acids cross the blood–brain barrier poorly.
takeaway: Prolonged starvation → hepatic ketogenesis → increased cerebral ketone utilisation.
thinking: Prolonged starvation ↓ hepatic glycogen is exhausted and low insulin drives lipolysis ↓ the liver converts fatty acids into ketone bodies ↓ the brain adapts to use them, sparing protein ↓ Ketone bodies
pearl: Refeeding a starved patient too quickly can cause refeeding syndrome with hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia, so NICE advises cautious introduction of nutrition in those at high risk.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Refeeding syndrome
stem: A severely malnourished patient has had negligible nutritional intake for 12 days. Nutrition is restarted rapidly. Two days later the patient develops weakness, oedema and cardiac instability. Which biochemical abnormality is classically associated with refeeding syndrome?
why_correct: Refeeding increases insulin secretion and drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium intracellularly. Hypophosphataemia is a characteristic biochemical feature of refeeding syndrome. NICE identifies prolonged poor intake and low phosphate, potassium or magnesium among important risk features and recommends cautious introduction of nutrition in high-risk patients.

why_others_wrong.A: Phosphate is driven into cells by the insulin surge of refeeding, so serum phosphate falls rather than rises.
why_others_wrong.C: Hypercalcaemia is not a recognised feature of refeeding syndrome, which is characterised by falling phosphate, potassium and magnesium.
why_others_wrong.D: Magnesium shifts intracellularly with refeeding, so hypomagnesaemia rather than hypermagnesaemia is expected.
why_others_wrong.E: Insulin drives potassium into cells after feeding restarts, so refeeding typically causes hypokalaemia rather than hyperkalaemia.

exam_trap: Hyperkalaemia and hyperphosphataemia are tempting because weakness and arrhythmia suggest electrolyte excess, but refeeding drives these ions into cells, producing low serum levels.
takeaway: Refeeding → insulin surge → intracellular phosphate shift → hypophosphataemia.
source: NICE CG32 (2017).
thinking: Prolonged starvation followed by rapid refeeding ↓ insulin surge drives glucose and electrolytes into cells ↓ phosphate, potassium and magnesium fall ↓ Hypophosphataemia
pearl: In patients at high risk of refeeding syndrome, NICE advises starting nutrition at a low energy level and increasing slowly, with thiamine before feeding and close monitoring of phosphate, potassium and magnesium.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: Lactate
stem: During severe tissue hypoperfusion, anaerobic glycolysis increases. What is the principal immediate metabolic fate of pyruvate under these conditions?

options.C: Conversion to ketone bodies in skeletal muscle

why_correct: When oxidative metabolism is insufficient, pyruvate is converted to lactate, allowing regeneration of NAD+ and continued glycolysis.

why_others_wrong.B: Urea is formed from ammonia in the hepatic urea cycle and is not a product of pyruvate metabolism.
why_others_wrong.C: Ketone bodies are made from acetyl-CoA in hepatic mitochondria, not from pyruvate in skeletal muscle during hypoperfusion.
why_others_wrong.D: Bilirubin is derived from haem breakdown and is unrelated to glycolysis.
why_others_wrong.E: Cholesterol synthesis is an energy-consuming process from acetyl-CoA and is not the immediate fate of pyruvate under anaerobic conditions.

exam_trap: An elevated lactate is a marker of disturbed metabolism/perfusion but is not synonymous with hypoxia in every clinical circumstance.
takeaway: Pyruvate + impaired oxidative metabolism → lactate.
thinking: Severe hypoperfusion limits oxygen delivery ↓ oxidative phosphorylation cannot accept pyruvate ↓ lactate dehydrogenase reduces pyruvate and regenerates NAD+ ↓ Conversion to lactate
pearl: Serial lactate measurement guides resuscitation in sepsis and trauma, and a raised lactate with pain out of proportion to the signs should prompt consideration of mesenteric ischaemia.

subject: Physiology
title: Anion gap
stem: A patient has the following results: Na+ = 140 mmol/L Cl− = 104 mmol/L HCO3− = 16 mmol/L What is the approximate anion gap using the conventional formula Na+ − (Cl− + HCO3−)?
why_correct: Anion gap = 140 − (104 + 16) = 140 − 120 = 20 mmol/L. This indicates an increased anion gap in the appropriate clinical context.

why_others_wrong.A: 8 mmol/L does not match the arithmetic: 140 − (104 + 16) = 20, not 8.
why_others_wrong.B: 12 mmol/L underestimates the correct subtraction; the values given yield 20, not 12.
why_others_wrong.D: 28 mmol/L overstates the result of the calculation, which correctly gives 20 mmol/L.
why_others_wrong.E: 36 mmol/L is far higher than the value obtained from the stated formula and figures.

exam_trap: Candidates choosing B (12 mmol/L) may recall a typical normal anion gap instead of calculating; the values given yield 140 minus 120, which is 20 mmol/L.
takeaway: Anion gap = Na+ − (Cl− + HCO3−).
thinking: Anion gap = Na − (Cl + HCO3) ↓ chloride plus bicarbonate = 104 + 16 = 120 ↓ 140 − 120 = 20 ↓ higher than a typical normal gap ↓ 20 mmol/L
pearl: A raised anion gap metabolic acidosis in a surgical patient should prompt a search for lactic acidosis from hypoperfusion or ischaemic bowel, ketoacidosis, renal failure or toxins.

subject: Physiology
title: Compensation for metabolic acidosis
stem: A patient develops an acute metabolic acidosis. Which physiological response occurs most rapidly to compensate?
why_correct: Respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis occurs rapidly through increased ventilation, reducing PaCO2. Renal compensation takes longer.

why_others_wrong.A: Increased renal bicarbonate generation is a renal compensatory mechanism that develops over hours to days, not the most rapid response.
why_others_wrong.B: Increased renal ammonium excretion is also part of the slower renal compensation for acidosis, not the immediate response.
why_others_wrong.D: Increased erythropoiesis is a chronic adaptive response to hypoxia, not an acid-base compensatory mechanism.
why_others_wrong.E: Aldosterone secretion influences sodium and potassium handling and is not the primary rapid mechanism compensating for metabolic acidosis; ventilatory changes occur first.

exam_trap: Candidates choosing A or B pick genuine compensatory mechanisms, but renal bicarbonate generation and ammonium excretion take hours to days; ventilation responds within minutes.
takeaway: Metabolic acidosis → hyperventilation → ↓PaCO2.
thinking: Acute metabolic acidosis ↓ chemoreceptors are stimulated by rising hydrogen ion concentration ↓ ventilation increases within minutes, lowering PaCO2 ↓ renal bicarbonate generation takes hours to days ↓ Increased alveolar ventilation
pearl: Respiratory compensation does not fully normalise the pH, so a normal pH with a low bicarbonate and low PaCO2 should raise suspicion of a mixed acid-base disorder.

subject: Physiology
title: Respiratory acidosis
stem: A patient develops hypoventilation from severe opioid toxicity. Which primary acid–base disturbance is expected?
why_correct: Hypoventilation causes carbon dioxide retention. Increased PaCO2 produces respiratory acidosis.

why_others_wrong.A: Metabolic acidosis arises from excess acid production or bicarbonate loss, not from hypoventilation and CO2 retention.
why_others_wrong.B: Metabolic alkalosis results from acid loss or bicarbonate gain and is unrelated to CO2 retention from hypoventilation.
why_others_wrong.D: Respiratory alkalosis results from hyperventilation and CO2 loss, the opposite of the hypoventilation described here.
why_others_wrong.E: Hypoventilation causes CO2 retention and acidosis, not any form of alkalosis.

exam_trap: Candidates may choose metabolic acidosis (A) because overdose suggests a poisoning picture, but the primary problem here is CO2 retention from hypoventilation.
takeaway: Hypoventilation → CO2 retention → respiratory acidosis.
thinking: Opioid toxicity depresses the respiratory centre ↓ hypoventilation ↓ CO2 is retained and PaCO2 rises ↓ more carbonic acid lowers the pH ↓ Respiratory acidosis
pearl: Opioid-induced respiratory depression is reversed with titrated naloxone, but its short duration of action means repeated doses or an infusion may be needed after long-acting opioids.

subject: Physiology
title: Respiratory alkalosis
stem: A patient is acutely hyperventilating because of severe anxiety. Which initial biochemical change is expected?

options.C: Increased bicarbonate due to immediate renal compensation
options.D: Increased lactate as the primary acid–base change
options.E: Increased chloride as the primary event

why_correct: Acute hyperventilation removes CO2 from the blood, producing respiratory alkalosis.

why_others_wrong.A: Hyperventilation removes CO2 from the blood, so PaCO2 falls rather than rises.
why_others_wrong.C: Renal compensation by altering bicarbonate takes days to develop and does not explain the immediate biochemical change of acute hyperventilation.
why_others_wrong.D: Lactate is not the primary driver of the acid-base change in simple anxiety-related hyperventilation, which is a straightforward respiratory event.
why_others_wrong.E: Chloride shifts may occur secondarily but are not the primary, initial biochemical change in acute hyperventilation.

exam_trap: Renal compensation occurs over a longer period and does not explain the immediate fall in PaCO2.
takeaway: Hyperventilation → ↓CO2 → respiratory alkalosis.
thinking: Anxiety-driven acute hyperventilation ↓ CO2 is removed faster than it is produced ↓ PaCO2 falls immediately ↓ renal compensation lags by days ↓ Reduced PaCO2
pearl: Acute respiratory alkalosis increases calcium binding to albumin and lowers ionised calcium, explaining the perioral tingling and carpopedal spasm seen during hyperventilation.

subject: Physiology
title: Bicarbonate and carbon dioxide
stem: Which pair forms the principal extracellular buffer system involved in regulation of blood pH?
why_correct: The bicarbonate/CO2 buffer system is central to extracellular acid–base regulation. The lungs regulate CO2 while the kidneys regulate bicarbonate and acid excretion.

why_others_wrong.A: Sodium and chloride are the major extracellular electrolytes but do not function as the principal buffer pair regulating blood pH.
why_others_wrong.C: Phosphate is an important intracellular and urinary buffer, but potassium and phosphate together are not the principal extracellular buffer system for blood pH.
why_others_wrong.D: Calcium and albumin are not recognised as the primary buffer pair for extracellular pH regulation.
why_others_wrong.E: Lactate and pyruvate form a metabolic redox couple related to cellular energy metabolism, not a pH-buffering system.

exam_trap: Candidates choosing C know phosphate is a buffer, but it acts mainly intracellularly and in urine; the dominant extracellular buffer pair is bicarbonate with carbon dioxide.
takeaway: Lungs control CO2; kidneys control bicarbonate and net acid excretion.
thinking: Principal extracellular buffer ↓ carbonic acid–bicarbonate equilibrium catalysed by carbonic anhydrase ↓ open system: lungs set CO2, kidneys set bicarbonate ↓ Bicarbonate and carbon dioxide
pearl: Because CO2 can be exhaled, the bicarbonate system buffers far more effectively in vivo than its chemistry alone predicts, and pH depends on the ratio of bicarbonate to PaCO2 rather than on either value alone.

subject: Physiology
title: Fever
stem: A patient develops fever during an acute infection. Which physiological change best explains the development of the raised temperature?

options.B: A raised hypothalamic temperature set point
options.D: Permanent increase in basal metabolic rate
options.E: Direct heating of the blood by inflammatory cells

correct_answer: B. A raised hypothalamic temperature set point
why_correct: Endogenous pyrogens and inflammatory mediators can increase the hypothalamic set point. The body then activates mechanisms such as vasoconstriction and shivering to raise core temperature toward the new set point.

why_others_wrong.A: Destruction of the hypothalamus would impair coordinated thermoregulation altogether rather than produce the regulated rise in temperature seen in fever.
why_others_wrong.C: Vasoconstriction is one of the mechanisms actively used to raise body temperature toward a new set point during fever, not a failure that causes it.
why_others_wrong.D: Fever reflects a temporary, regulated resetting of the hypothalamic set point, not a permanent change in basal metabolic rate.
why_others_wrong.E: Fever arises because circulating pyrogens reset the hypothalamic set point, triggering heat-generating and heat-conserving mechanisms; inflammatory cells do not directly heat the blood.

exam_trap: Fever is regulated elevation of the set point; hyperthermia is different because the set point is not necessarily raised.
takeaway: Fever = raised hypothalamic set point.
thinking: Fever during infection ↓ pyrogenic cytokines such as IL-1, IL-6 and TNF are released ↓ prostaglandin E2 raises the hypothalamic set point ↓ vasoconstriction and shivering raise temperature to the new set point ↓ A raised hypothalamic temperature set point
pearl: Antipyretics such as paracetamol lower the raised set point, which is why they are ineffective in heat stroke or malignant hyperthermia, where the set point is not raised.

subject: Physiology
title: Heat loss
stem: A patient in a hot environment is sweating heavily. Which mechanism allows sweat to reduce core temperature?
why_correct: Evaporation of sweat from the skin removes heat from the body.

why_others_wrong.A: Conduction refers to heat transfer through direct contact and is not the mechanism by which sweating cools the body.
why_others_wrong.B: Radiation is heat loss via infrared emission from the body surface, unrelated to the cooling effect of sweat.
why_others_wrong.D: Vasoconstriction reduces skin blood flow and heat loss, the opposite of what is needed to dissipate heat during sweating.
why_others_wrong.E: Shivering is a heat-generating response used in cold exposure, not a mechanism relevant to cooling via sweat evaporation.

exam_trap: Candidates may choose radiation (B), the main route of heat loss at rest in a cool room, but sweat cools only by evaporation, which becomes ineffective in high humidity.
takeaway: Sweat cools principally through evaporation.
thinking: Heavy sweating in a hot environment ↓ when ambient temperature approaches skin temperature, radiation and conduction fail ↓ heat is removed as the latent heat of vaporising sweat ↓ Evaporation
pearl: Open abdominal or thoracic cavities lose considerable heat through evaporation and radiation, so warmed fluids, forced-air warming and limited exposure help prevent perioperative hypothermia.

subject: Physiology
title: Shivering
stem: A patient exposed to cold develops involuntary rhythmic skeletal muscle contractions. What is the principal physiological purpose?
why_correct: Shivering consists of involuntary skeletal muscle activity that increases metabolic heat production.

why_others_wrong.A: Shivering increases, rather than reduces, metabolic heat production through repeated muscle contraction.
why_others_wrong.C: Shivering generates heat through muscle activity; it does not promote sweating or evaporative heat loss.
why_others_wrong.D: Cold exposure increases sympathetic activity as part of the thermoregulatory response, rather than reducing it.
why_others_wrong.E: Shivering is a thermogenic skeletal muscle response and has no direct role in gastrointestinal absorption.

exam_trap: Candidates choosing D forget that cold increases sympathetic activity, causing cutaneous vasoconstriction; shivering adds heat production rather than reducing sympathetic tone.
takeaway: Cold → shivering → increased heat production.
thinking: Cold exposure ↓ hypothalamus triggers involuntary rhythmic skeletal muscle contraction ↓ muscle activity generates metabolic heat ↓ Increase heat production
pearl: Postoperative shivering can markedly increase oxygen consumption, which matters in patients with limited cardiac reserve, so active warming is preferable to allowing patients to rewarm by shivering.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Nitrogen balance
stem: A patient with severe sepsis has prolonged catabolic illness and is losing skeletal muscle despite adequate fluid resuscitation. Which metabolic state is most likely?
why_correct: During severe catabolic illness, protein breakdown can exceed protein synthesis, resulting in net nitrogen loss and muscle wasting.

why_others_wrong.A: Positive nitrogen balance means protein synthesis exceeds breakdown, as in recovery or growth, not in a patient actively losing skeletal muscle.
why_others_wrong.C: Zero nitrogen balance reflects equilibrium between intake and losses, which does not fit progressive muscle wasting during sepsis.
why_others_wrong.D: In severe catabolic illness protein breakdown exceeds synthesis, the reverse of what this option describes.
why_others_wrong.E: Sepsis increases proteolysis to supply amino acids for gluconeogenesis and acute phase proteins, rather than suppressing it.

exam_trap: "Nutrition provided" does not automatically mean positive nitrogen balance. Severe inflammation, infection and physiological stress can drive substantial catabolism.
takeaway: Catabolic surgical illness → protein breakdown > synthesis → negative nitrogen balance.
source: [GH14]; NICE CG32, Nutrition support for adults.
thinking: Severe sepsis is a prolonged catabolic state ↓ proteolysis supplies amino acids for gluconeogenesis and acute phase proteins ↓ breakdown exceeds synthesis with net nitrogen loss ↓ Negative nitrogen balance
pearl: Nitrogen balance can be estimated from urinary urea nitrogen against protein intake; in severe catabolic illness feeding attenuates but rarely abolishes muscle loss, so early mobilisation also matters.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Acute inflammation
stem: A patient develops an acutely inflamed wound. Which leukocyte is normally the predominant cell during the early phase of acute inflammation?
why_correct: Neutrophils are typically the predominant early inflammatory leukocytes in acute inflammation. Monocytes subsequently migrate into tissues and differentiate into macrophages.

why_others_wrong.B: Plasma cells are antibody-secreting cells seen in established chronic, antigen-driven infiltrates; they are not the predominant early cell in acute inflammation.
why_others_wrong.C: Lymphocytes are characteristic of chronic inflammation and adaptive immunity, appearing over a longer time course than the immediate neutrophilic response of acute inflammation.
why_others_wrong.D: Macrophages, derived from migrating monocytes, become prominent later in the inflammatory response as it evolves, not during the earliest phase.
why_others_wrong.E: Eosinophils are recruited predominantly in parasitic infection and allergic reactions rather than being the predominant leukocyte of a typical early acute inflammatory response.

exam_trap: Macrophages are important later in the inflammatory response and in tissue repair, but they are not normally the first predominant leukocyte in acute inflammation.
takeaway: Acute inflammation → neutrophils early → macrophages later.
thinking: Acutely inflamed wound ↓ early phase ↓ neutrophils emigrate first from post-capillary venules ↓ Neutrophil
pearl: Neutrophils predominate for roughly the first day and are replaced by monocyte-derived macrophages over the next one to two days; macrophages are essential for normal progression to the proliferative phase.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Histamine
stem: A patient develops immediate local swelling and erythema following tissue injury. Which mediator is particularly important in producing early vasodilatation and increased vascular permeability?
why_correct: Histamine released principally from mast cells contributes to vasodilatation and increased vascular permeability during the early inflammatory response.

why_others_wrong.B: Insulin is a metabolic hormone regulating glucose uptake and is not a mediator released at sites of injury to cause acute inflammatory vascular changes.
why_others_wrong.C: Albumin is a plasma protein that escapes into tissue as a consequence of increased vascular permeability; it does not itself trigger the vascular change.
why_others_wrong.D: Haemoglobin is confined within red blood cells for oxygen transport and has no mediator function in the vascular response to injury.
why_others_wrong.E: Erythropoietin stimulates erythrocyte production in bone marrow and has no role in the acute vascular changes of local inflammation.

exam_trap: Candidates choose albumin (C) because swelling contains protein-rich fluid, but albumin leaks out as a result of increased permeability; histamine produces the early vascular change.
takeaway: Histamine → early vascular changes of inflammation.
thinking: Immediate swelling and erythema after injury ↓ mast cell degranulation ↓ histamine causes arteriolar dilatation and venular leakage ↓ Histamine
pearl: Mast cell degranulation also explains the immediate local response to some anaesthetic drugs and the wheal of a positive skin prick test.

subject: Immunology
title: Complement
stem: A patient has activation of the complement system during an acute bacterial infection. Which complement component is an important opsonin?
why_correct: C3b binds to microbial surfaces and facilitates recognition and phagocytosis by phagocytes.

why_others_wrong.A: C1 is the recognition complex that starts the classical pathway by binding antibody; it does not coat microbes to promote phagocytosis.
why_others_wrong.C: C5 is cleaved later into C5a, a chemotactic anaphylatoxin, and C5b, which seeds the membrane attack complex; it is not the classic opsonin.
why_others_wrong.D: C7 is a terminal component that helps anchor the membrane attack complex into the target membrane rather than tagging microbes for phagocytes.
why_others_wrong.E: C9 polymerises to form the pore of the membrane attack complex, causing lysis rather than opsonisation.

exam_trap: C5a is strongly associated with chemotaxis and inflammatory signalling; C3b is the classic complement opsonin.
takeaway: C3b = opsonisation.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Complement activated in bacterial infection ↓ question asks for an opsonin ↓ C3 cleavage yields C3b, which coats microbial surfaces ↓ phagocytes bind C3b via complement receptors ↓ C3b
pearl: C3 sits at the convergence of all three pathways, so C3 deficiency produces severe recurrent pyogenic infection, whereas loss of C5-C9 mainly predisposes to Neisseria.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Chronic inflammation
stem: A patient has a chronic inflammatory condition with a tissue infiltrate predominantly composed of macrophages and lymphocytes. Which description best fits the process?
why_correct: Chronic inflammation is characterised by persistent inflammatory cell infiltration, particularly macrophages and lymphocytes, together with ongoing tissue injury and repair.

why_others_wrong.A: Acute inflammation is characterised by an early neutrophilic infiltrate and vascular changes over hours to days, not the macrophage/lymphocyte-predominant picture described, which reflects a persistent chronic process.
why_others_wrong.C: Immediate hypersensitivity is an IgE/mast-cell-mediated reaction occurring within minutes of antigen exposure, not a description of a persistent tissue infiltrate of macrophages and lymphocytes.
why_others_wrong.D: Haemostasis refers to the clotting response that stops bleeding immediately after injury; it does not describe a cellular infiltrate of macrophages and lymphocytes.
why_others_wrong.E: Primary intention healing describes closure of a clean, apposed surgical wound, a mechanism of repair rather than a description of an inflammatory cell infiltrate.

exam_trap: Candidates choose acute inflammation (A) because the condition is described as inflammatory, but acute inflammation is neutrophil-rich; macrophages and lymphocytes indicate a chronic process.
takeaway: Chronic inflammation → macrophages + lymphocytes + ongoing tissue injury/repair.
thinking: Persistent inflammatory condition ↓ infiltrate of macrophages and lymphocytes ↓ simultaneous tissue destruction and repair ↓ Chronic inflammation
pearl: Chronic inflammation is characterised by concurrent tissue destruction, attempted repair with fibrosis and angiogenesis, as seen in chronic cholecystitis or Crohn strictures.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Granuloma
stem: A patient with persistent intracellular infection develops discrete collections of activated macrophages with surrounding lymphocytes. What pathological structure is most likely?
why_correct: A granuloma is an organised collection of activated macrophages, often with surrounding lymphocytes, formed in response to persistent inflammatory stimuli.

why_others_wrong.A: An abscess is a localised collection of neutrophils and liquefactive pus from acute pyogenic infection, not an organised aggregate of macrophages seen with persistent intracellular pathogens.
why_others_wrong.C: A haematoma is a localised collection of extravasated blood, not an immune-cell aggregate formed in response to a persistent infective stimulus.
why_others_wrong.D: A seroma is a collection of serous fluid, typically postoperative, and does not represent an organised macrophage/lymphocyte response to infection.
why_others_wrong.E: A keloid is an abnormal fibroproliferative scar that extends beyond the original wound margins, unrelated to macrophage aggregation against intracellular infection.

exam_trap: Candidates choose abscess (A) because both are localised infective collections, but an abscess is neutrophil-rich pus; organised activated macrophages define a granuloma.
takeaway: Persistent stimulus → macrophage aggregation → granuloma.
thinking: Persistent intracellular infection ↓ discrete collections of activated macrophages ↓ surrounding rim of lymphocytes ↓ Granuloma
pearl: Granulomas are caseating in tuberculosis but non-caseating in sarcoidosis and Crohn disease, so the presence of caseation on biopsy helps narrow the differential.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Caseous necrosis
stem: A biopsy from a chronic granulomatous lesion shows soft, friable, cheese-like necrotic material. Which type of necrosis is classically associated with this appearance?
why_correct: Caseous necrosis is classically associated with granulomatous infections such as tuberculosis.

why_others_wrong.A: Coagulative necrosis preserves the basic outline of dead tissue architecture (as in ischaemic infarcts of solid organs), producing a firm rather than soft, cheese-like appearance.
why_others_wrong.B: Liquefactive necrosis produces a soft, liquefied mass from enzymatic digestion (classically seen in brain infarcts or pyogenic abscesses), not the friable cheese-like material of caseation.
why_others_wrong.D: Fat necrosis produces chalky white deposits from saponification of fat (as in acute pancreatitis), a different gross appearance from the cheese-like material described.
why_others_wrong.E: Fibrinoid necrosis is a microscopic pattern seen in blood vessel walls in immune-mediated vasculitis, not a gross cheese-like necrotic mass.

exam_trap: Do not automatically select liquefactive necrosis whenever necrotic tissue is described as soft. The "cheese-like" description is a classic clue to caseous necrosis.
takeaway: Caseous necrosis → think granulomatous infection, classically tuberculosis.
thinking: Chronic granulomatous lesion ↓ soft, friable, cheese-like necrotic material ↓ caseation ↓ Caseous
pearl: Caseous necrosis combines features of coagulative and liquefactive necrosis, and on histology appears as amorphous pink granular debris without preserved tissue outlines.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Coagulative necrosis
stem: A patient develops an infarction of the kidney. Which type of necrosis is most characteristic of the resulting tissue injury?
why_correct: Ischaemic infarction of most solid organs produces coagulative necrosis, with preservation of the basic tissue architecture for a period despite cell death.

why_others_wrong.A: Liquefactive necrosis, with enzymatic digestion and loss of tissue architecture, is characteristic of the brain and of pyogenic abscesses, not typical ischaemic injury in a solid organ like the kidney.
why_others_wrong.B: Caseous necrosis is the classic pattern of granulomatous infections such as tuberculosis, not of simple ischaemic infarction.
why_others_wrong.D: Fat necrosis results from lipase-mediated destruction of adipose tissue, as in acute pancreatitis, not from arterial occlusion in the kidney.
why_others_wrong.E: Fibrinoid necrosis is seen in vessel walls in immune-mediated vasculitic processes, not as the pattern of a renal infarct.

exam_trap: Candidates choose liquefactive necrosis (A) remembering that infarcts can liquefy, but that is specific to the brain; renal and other solid-organ infarcts show coagulative necrosis.
takeaway: Solid-organ infarction → coagulative necrosis; brain infarction → liquefactive necrosis.
thinking: Renal infarct ↓ ischaemic solid organ ↓ proteins denatured so architecture briefly preserved ↓ Coagulative
pearl: Renal and splenic infarcts are typically wedge-shaped pale infarcts with the base at the capsule, reflecting end-arterial supply.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Apoptosis
stem: Which statement best describes apoptosis?

options.A: It invariably causes extensive surrounding inflammation
options.E: It occurs only in malignant cells

correct_answer: C. It involves programmed cell death
why_correct: Apoptosis is regulated programmed cell death that removes unwanted or damaged cells with relatively little surrounding inflammation.

why_others_wrong.A: Apoptosis is characterised by minimal surrounding inflammation because the cell membrane remains intact and apoptotic bodies are cleared by phagocytes without spilling their contents, unlike necrosis.
why_others_wrong.B: Apoptosis is a tightly regulated, programmed process, the opposite of the uncontrolled tissue destruction seen in necrosis.
why_others_wrong.D: Apoptosis occurs in many physiological and pathological contexts (development, immune regulation, DNA damage) and is not limited to, nor an invariable consequence of, severe ischaemia.
why_others_wrong.E: Apoptosis is a normal physiological process occurring throughout the body (e.g., in development and cell turnover), not a phenomenon restricted to malignant cells.

exam_trap: Candidates choose always follows severe ischaemia (D), but severe ischaemia mainly causes necrosis; apoptosis is also physiological and not confined to malignant cells (E).
takeaway: Apoptosis = regulated cell deletion, usually with limited inflammation.
thinking: Apoptosis ↓ regulated programmed cell death ↓ apoptotic bodies cleared with little inflammation ↓ It involves programmed cell death
pearl: Apoptosis is physiological in embryological remodelling, such as separation of digits and canalisation of the gut, and failure of apoptosis contributes to tumour development.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Reversible cell injury
stem: A cell exposed to a temporary reduction in oxygen develops cellular swelling but recovers after restoration of perfusion. What does this represent?
why_correct: Cellular swelling is a classic early manifestation of reversible cell injury. If the insult is removed before irreversible mitochondrial and membrane damage develops, the cell can recover.

why_others_wrong.A: Irreversible cell injury involves severe mitochondrial and membrane damage that persists or progresses to cell death even after the insult is removed, unlike the recovery described here.
why_others_wrong.C: Apoptosis is an active, programmed form of cell death rather than a transient swelling that resolves with restoration of perfusion.
why_others_wrong.D: Caseous necrosis is an irreversible, granulomatous pattern of cell death with cheese-like gross appearance, not a description of transient reversible swelling.
why_others_wrong.E: Metastasis refers to the spread of malignant cells to distant sites and has no relevance to a transient hypoxic cellular change.

exam_trap: Candidates choose irreversible injury (A) because swelling sounds damaging, but recovery after restoring perfusion means the insult stopped before membrane and mitochondrial damage.
takeaway: Early injury + removal of insult → potentially reversible cellular damage.
thinking: Temporary reduction in oxygen ↓ ion pump failure causes cell swelling ↓ recovery after reperfusion ↓ Reversible cell injury
pearl: Cell swelling (hydropic change) and fatty change are the two classic light microscopic features of reversible injury, both reflecting impaired ATP-dependent processes.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Wound healing: proliferative phase
stem: Which cell is principally responsible for producing new collagen during the proliferative phase of wound healing?
why_correct: Fibroblasts migrate into the wound and synthesise extracellular matrix, including collagen, during the proliferative phase.

why_others_wrong.A: Neutrophils are the dominant leukocyte of the early inflammatory phase, focused on debridement and pathogen clearance, not on collagen synthesis.
why_others_wrong.C: Platelets act in the initial haemostatic phase and release growth factors that help recruit fibroblasts, but they do not themselves lay down collagen.
why_others_wrong.D: Red blood cells are oxygen carriers with no biosynthetic role in extracellular matrix production during healing.
why_others_wrong.E: Osteoclasts are bone-resorbing cells of monocyte lineage and play no role in soft-tissue collagen synthesis during wound healing.

exam_trap: Candidates choose platelets (C) because they release growth factors early in healing, but platelets recruit fibroblasts rather than making collagen; fibroblasts produce the new collagen.
takeaway: Fibroblast → collagen and extracellular matrix production.
thinking: Proliferative phase ↓ new collagen production ↓ fibroblasts recruited by platelet and macrophage growth factors ↓ Fibroblast
pearl: Corticosteroids inhibit fibroblast proliferation and collagen synthesis as well as inflammation, which is why patients on long-term steroids have a higher risk of wound dehiscence.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Collagen maturation
stem: A patient has impaired hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues in newly synthesised collagen. Which nutrient deficiency is classically associated with impaired collagen maturation and poor wound healing?
why_correct: Vitamin C is required for hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues during collagen synthesis. Deficiency impairs collagen maturation and wound healing.

why_others_wrong.A: Vitamin A supports epithelial differentiation and immune function but is not the vitamin classically linked to defective collagen cross-linking and hydroxylation seen with deficiency.
why_others_wrong.B: Vitamin B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia and neurological disease through impaired DNA synthesis and myelin maintenance, not defective collagen hydroxylation.
why_others_wrong.D: Vitamin D primarily governs calcium and phosphate homeostasis and bone mineralisation, not the proline/lysine hydroxylation steps of collagen synthesis.
why_others_wrong.E: Vitamin K is needed for gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors, a coagulation-related function unconnected to collagen cross-linking.

exam_trap: Vitamin A tempts because it supports wound healing and epithelial repair, but proline and lysine hydroxylation in collagen synthesis specifically requires vitamin C.
takeaway: Vitamin C → collagen hydroxylation → normal wound healing.
thinking: Impaired hydroxylation of proline and lysine ↓ prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases need ascorbate as a cofactor ↓ unstable collagen triple helix ↓ poor wound healing ↓ Vitamin C
pearl: Scurvy causes perifollicular haemorrhages, gum bleeding and poor wound healing, so wound breakdown in a malnourished patient should prompt assessment of vitamin C status.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Wound healing and oxygen
stem: A patient with peripheral vascular disease has a poorly healing lower-limb wound. Which factor is most directly impaired by reduced tissue perfusion?
correct_answer: A. Oxygen delivery to the wound
why_correct: Adequate oxygen delivery is essential for cellular metabolism, collagen synthesis, fibroblast function and host defence during wound healing.

why_others_wrong.B: Intrinsic factor is produced by gastric parietal cells for vitamin B12 absorption and is unrelated to limb tissue perfusion or wound oxygen delivery.
why_others_wrong.C: Bile salt recycling occurs via the enterohepatic circulation in the gut and liver and has no connection to peripheral limb perfusion or wound healing.
why_others_wrong.D: Cerebrospinal fluid production occurs in the choroid plexus of the brain and is entirely unrelated to peripheral vascular disease or wound oxygenation.
why_others_wrong.E: Thyroid hormone synthesis occurs in the thyroid gland via iodine uptake and is not directly affected by reduced peripheral tissue perfusion.

exam_trap: Candidates may be distracted by unrelated physiological options (B-E), but reduced perfusion most directly lowers wound oxygen delivery, impairing collagen synthesis and bacterial killing.
takeaway: Poor perfusion → poor oxygen delivery → impaired wound healing.
thinking: Peripheral vascular disease ↓ reduced tissue perfusion ↓ less oxygen reaching the wound ↓ Oxygen delivery to the wound
pearl: An ankle-brachial pressure index should be checked before applying compression to a lower-limb ulcer, as compression on an ischaemic limb can cause tissue necrosis.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Wound healing: primary intention
stem: A clean surgical incision is closed immediately with accurately opposed wound edges. What type of healing is this?
why_correct: Primary intention occurs when clean wound edges are directly approximated, producing relatively little granulation tissue and a smaller scar.

why_others_wrong.A: Secondary intention describes healing of a wound left open to close by granulation, contraction and epithelialisation, the opposite of an immediately closed, opposed incision.
why_others_wrong.B: Tertiary intention (delayed primary closure) involves leaving a wound open initially before later surgical closure, not the immediate apposition described here.
why_others_wrong.D: Granulomatous healing is not a recognised wound-healing classification; granulomas form around persistent inflammatory stimuli, not standard surgical wound closure.
why_others_wrong.E: Fibrotic necrosis is not a standard wound-healing term and does not describe closure of a clean incision.

exam_trap: A contaminated or infected wound deliberately left open to heal by granulation is not primary intention.
takeaway: Clean, closely apposed wound → primary intention.
thinking: Clean surgical incision ↓ edges accurately apposed immediately ↓ minimal granulation tissue ↓ Primary intention
pearl: Wounds closed by primary intention are usually sealed by epithelium within about 48 hours, which is why many clean incisions can have the dressing removed and get wet after this time.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Wound healing: secondary intention
stem: A large contaminated wound is left open and gradually fills with granulation tissue before contracting and epithelialising. Which process is occurring?
why_correct: Secondary intention occurs when wound edges cannot be directly approximated. Healing involves granulation tissue formation, contraction and epithelialisation, usually producing a larger scar.

why_others_wrong.A: Primary intention applies to clean wounds with directly apposed edges producing minimal granulation tissue, the opposite of a large open contaminated wound healing by granulation.
why_others_wrong.C: Immediate regeneration is not how wound healing occurs after tissue loss; large defects heal through the granulation, contraction and epithelialisation sequence, not instantaneous restoration of normal tissue.
why_others_wrong.D: Apoptosis is a form of programmed single-cell death, not a description of the tissue-level process of granulation, contraction and epithelialisation.
why_others_wrong.E: Caseous healing is not a recognised healing process; caseous necrosis refers to a pattern of cell death in granulomatous infection, unrelated to secondary-intention wound closure.

exam_trap: Candidates choose primary intention (A) because the wound eventually heals, but primary intention requires apposed edges; healing by granulation and contraction is secondary intention.
takeaway: Open wound → granulation + contraction + larger scar = secondary intention.
thinking: Large contaminated wound left open ↓ fills with granulation tissue ↓ contraction and epithelialisation ↓ Secondary intention
pearl: Topical negative pressure dressings are often used for large open wounds healing by secondary intention, as they remove exudate and promote granulation.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Myofibroblasts
stem: Which cell is particularly important in wound contraction?
why_correct: Myofibroblasts possess contractile properties and contribute significantly to wound contraction.

why_others_wrong.B: Neutrophils function in debridement and pathogen clearance during early inflammation; they lack the contractile actin-myosin apparatus that drives wound contraction.
why_others_wrong.C: Eosinophils are associated with parasitic and allergic responses and have no recognised contractile role in wound healing.
why_others_wrong.D: Osteoblasts are bone-forming cells responsible for depositing bone matrix, unrelated to soft-tissue wound contraction.
why_others_wrong.E: Chondrocytes are cartilage-forming cells maintaining cartilage matrix, with no role in contracting a healing skin or soft-tissue wound.

exam_trap: Candidates choose neutrophils (B) as an early wound cell, but they lack the contractile apparatus; myofibroblasts with smooth muscle actin drive wound contraction.
takeaway: Myofibroblast → wound contraction.
thinking: Wound contraction ↓ specialised fibroblasts with smooth muscle actin ↓ pull the wound edges inwards ↓ Myofibroblast
pearl: Excessive myofibroblast-driven contraction across a joint or flexural surface can cause a contracture, which may need release and skin grafting or flap reconstruction.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Hypertrophic scar
stem: A patient develops a raised scar after surgery that remains confined to the original wound boundaries. Which diagnosis is most appropriate?
why_correct: A hypertrophic scar is raised but remains within the original wound boundaries. A keloid extends beyond them.

why_others_wrong.A: A keloid scar characteristically extends beyond the original wound margins into surrounding normal tissue, which distinguishes it from the confined hypertrophic scar described here.
why_others_wrong.C: A desmoid tumour is a locally aggressive fibromatosis arising in deep soft tissue, not a raised scar confined to a surgical wound.
why_others_wrong.D: Fibrosarcoma is a malignant tumour of fibroblastic origin, an entirely different process from a benign reactive scar.
why_others_wrong.E: A granuloma is an organised collection of activated macrophages responding to a persistent stimulus, not a raised fibrous scar confined to a wound.

exam_trap: Candidates choose keloid (A) because both are raised scars, but keloids extend beyond the original wound margins; a raised scar confined to the wound is hypertrophic.
takeaway: Hypertrophic scar = stays within wound; keloid = extends beyond wound.
thinking: Raised scar after surgery ↓ confined to the original wound boundaries ↓ excess collagen without extension ↓ Hypertrophic scar
pearl: Hypertrophic scars often improve with time and pressure or silicone therapy, whereas keloids frequently recur after simple excision.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Metastatic spread
stem: A patient with a malignant solid tumour develops tumour deposits in the liver. Which route commonly allows tumour cells from many abdominal and gastrointestinal primaries to reach the liver?
why_correct: Tumour cells from organs draining into the portal venous system can reach the liver through portal venous blood.

why_others_wrong.B: The pulmonary artery carries systemic venous blood to the lungs, so it explains lung metastases rather than delivery of abdominal tumour cells to the liver.
why_others_wrong.C: The thoracic duct drains lymph into the left subclavian vein and does not route abdominal visceral blood to the liver as the portal vein does.
why_others_wrong.D: The coronary circulation supplies the myocardium and has no role in carrying tumour cells from gastrointestinal organs to the liver.
why_others_wrong.E: The cerebral venous system drains the brain into the internal jugular veins and does not connect abdominal organs to the liver.

exam_trap: The thoracic duct tempts as a route for abdominal tumour, but it carries lymph to the left subclavian vein; gut tumour cells reach the liver through portal venous blood.
takeaway: Many GI/abdominal tumours → portal venous drainage → liver metastases.
thinking: Liver deposits from an abdominal or gastrointestinal primary ↓ venous blood from the gut drains through the portal vein ↓ the liver is the first capillary bed these tumour cells meet ↓ Portal venous circulation
pearl: Because colorectal liver metastases arrive via the portal system, isolated resectable liver deposits can be treated with curative-intent hepatectomy, unlike most other patterns of metastatic disease.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Tumour grading
stem: A histopathology report describes a tumour as "high grade". What does grading primarily assess?
correct_answer: B. Histological differentiation and biological aggressiveness
why_correct: Tumour grade reflects histological characteristics such as differentiation and mitotic activity and provides information about tumour biology.

why_others_wrong.A: Anatomical spread is described by stage, not grade, which reflects how the tumour looks and behaves histologically.
why_others_wrong.C: Distant metastasis is the M component of stage, whereas a high grade describes poor differentiation and high mitotic activity.
why_others_wrong.D: Patient age is a clinical characteristic that may affect prognosis but is not assessed by histological tumour grading.
why_others_wrong.E: Margin status describes whether tumour reaches the resection edge (the R classification) and is reported separately from grade.

exam_trap: Anatomical spread and distant metastases describe stage, not grade; candidates conflate the two because both appear on the same histopathology report.
takeaway: Grade = tumour biology; stage = anatomical extent.
thinking: 'High grade' on a histopathology report ↓ grade is assigned by looking down the microscope ↓ it reflects differentiation and mitotic activity ↓ high grade = poorly differentiated, more aggressive ↓ Histological differentiation and biological aggressiveness
pearl: Grade can add prognostic information independent of stage; breast carcinoma grading, for example, combines tubule formation, nuclear pleomorphism and mitotic count into an overall grade of 1 to 3.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Tumour suppressor genes
stem: Loss of function of a tumour suppressor gene generally contributes to cancer development by:

options.A: Increasing the removal of abnormal cells
options.B: Removing a restraint on cell proliferation

correct_answer: B. Removing a restraint on cell proliferation
why_correct: Tumour suppressor genes normally help regulate cell proliferation, DNA integrity and/or cell survival. Loss of their function can facilitate uncontrolled growth.

why_others_wrong.A: Loss of tumour suppressor function reduces, rather than increases, elimination of abnormal cells, for example by impairing p53-mediated apoptosis.
why_others_wrong.C: Tumour suppressor loss permits unchecked DNA replication and division; preventing replication entirely would halt tumour growth.
why_others_wrong.D: Many tumour suppressors promote apoptosis, so their loss typically reduces apoptosis and allows damaged cells to survive.
why_others_wrong.E: Tumour suppressor loss tends to favour rather than block angiogenesis, and no single mechanism blocks angiogenesis in all tumours.

exam_trap: Increased apoptosis and increased removal of abnormal cells describe what intact tumour suppressors do; candidates who miss the word 'loss' choose them, but loss reduces these effects.
takeaway: Tumour suppressor loss → loss of growth restraint.
thinking: Tumour suppressors act as brakes on the cell cycle ↓ loss of function removes the brake ↓ damaged cells keep dividing and escape elimination ↓ Removing a restraint on cell proliferation
pearl: Because both alleles usually need to be lost, inherited tumour suppressor mutations such as APC, BRCA1/2 and RB1 cause dominantly inherited cancer predisposition despite acting recessively at the cellular level.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Oncogenes
stem: Activation of an oncogene most directly promotes malignant transformation by:

options.B: Promoting inappropriate cellular growth or survival
options.D: Increasing DNA repair in all circumstances

correct_answer: B. Promoting inappropriate cellular growth or survival
why_correct: Oncogenes arise from altered or abnormally activated genes that promote proliferation or survival.

why_others_wrong.A: Oncogene activation drives proliferation; permanent inhibition of proliferation is closer to the effect of intact tumour suppressors or senescence.
why_others_wrong.C: Oncogenic signalling such as RAS activation tends to promote angiogenesis, for example through VEGF, rather than preventing it.
why_others_wrong.D: Oncogene activation does not enhance DNA repair; defective repair is more typically linked to loss of caretaker genes such as BRCA1 and BRCA2.
why_others_wrong.E: Oncogenic signalling usually impairs normal differentiation and favours a proliferative, less differentiated state.

exam_trap: Permanently inhibiting proliferation describes intact tumour suppressors or senescence; candidates who swap the two gene classes choose it, but an activated oncogene drives growth.
takeaway: Oncogene activation → inappropriate growth/survival signalling.
thinking: Proto-oncogenes drive normal growth signalling ↓ activation = gain of function ↓ excess or unregulated growth and survival signals ↓ Promoting inappropriate cellular growth or survival
pearl: Activated oncogenes can be drug targets: HER2-amplified breast cancer is treated with trastuzumab and BCR-ABL-positive chronic myeloid leukaemia with imatinib.

subject: Immunology
title: Hypersensitivity type I
stem: A patient develops urticaria, bronchospasm and hypotension within minutes of exposure to an allergen. Which immunological mechanism is most characteristic?
why_correct: Immediate hypersensitivity reactions are mediated by allergen-specific IgE bound to mast cells and basophils. Cross-linking triggers mediator release.

why_others_wrong.B: Immune-complex (type III) disease develops over hours to days as complexes deposit and activate complement, not within minutes of allergen exposure.
why_others_wrong.C: T-cell-mediated (type IV) reactions take 48-72 hours to develop, far too slow for urticaria, bronchospasm and hypotension within minutes.
why_others_wrong.D: Complement deficiency predisposes to infection or immune-complex disease; it does not cause acute allergen-triggered anaphylaxis.
why_others_wrong.E: Autoantibody destruction of red cells is a type II process causing haemolytic anaemia, not immediate urticaria, bronchospasm and hypotension.

exam_trap: T-cell-mediated delayed hypersensitivity tempts candidates who group all allergy together, but type IV reactions take 48-72 hours; urticaria, bronchospasm and hypotension within minutes are IgE-mediated.
takeaway: Immediate allergy/anaphylaxis → IgE + mast-cell mediator release.
source: Roitt's Essential Immunology, 13th ed.; Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Urticaria, bronchospasm and hypotension ↓ onset within minutes of allergen exposure ↓ immediate (type I) hypersensitivity ↓ allergen cross-links IgE on mast cells and basophils ↓ IgE-mediated hypersensitivity
pearl: In suspected perioperative anaphylaxis, serial mast-cell tryptase samples (at the time of reaction and after recovery) help confirm mast-cell degranulation, and the patient should be referred for allergy testing.

subject: Immunology
title: Autoimmune disease
stem: Which immunological failure most directly permits development of autoimmune disease?
why_correct: Autoimmunity occurs when immune responses are directed against self-antigens because mechanisms maintaining self-tolerance have failed.

why_others_wrong.B: Increased oxygen delivery is a physiological change unrelated to immune recognition of self-antigens and does not cause autoimmunity.
why_others_wrong.C: Increased erythropoiesis is a marrow response to hypoxia or blood loss, not a failure of immune tolerance.
why_others_wrong.D: Increased platelet production is a haematological change and does not allow lymphocytes to attack self-antigens.
why_others_wrong.E: Reduced gastric acid secretion can result from autoimmune gastritis but is a consequence, not the immunological failure that permits autoimmunity.

exam_trap: Reduced gastric acid tempts candidates who recall pernicious anaemia, but achlorhydria is a consequence of autoimmune gastritis, not the tolerance failure that allows autoimmunity.
takeaway: Autoimmunity = immune response against self → failure of tolerance.
source: Roitt's Essential Immunology, 13th ed.; Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Autoimmune disease = immune attack on self-antigens ↓ self-reactive lymphocytes are normally deleted or controlled ↓ failure of central or peripheral tolerance lets them act ↓ Loss of self-tolerance
pearl: Self-tolerance is maintained centrally (thymic and marrow deletion) and peripherally (anergy, regulatory T cells); defects in FOXP3 or AIRE produce multi-organ autoimmunity.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Anaemia: microcytosis
stem: A patient has fatigue. Blood results show a low haemoglobin, low MCV and low MCH. Which diagnosis is most consistent with this red-cell pattern?

options.B: Acute blood loss before physiological compensation

why_correct: Iron deficiency classically produces a microcytic, hypochromic anaemia.

why_others_wrong.B: Immediately after acute blood loss the Hb and red-cell indices are often still normal because cells and plasma are lost together, so microcytosis is not expected.
why_others_wrong.C: Vitamin B12 deficiency impairs DNA synthesis and produces a macrocytic, megaloblastic anaemia with a raised MCV rather than a low one.
why_others_wrong.D: Folate deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia with a high MCV, the opposite of the low MCV and MCH shown here.
why_others_wrong.E: Aplastic anaemia results from marrow failure and usually gives a normocytic or mildly macrocytic anaemia with pancytopenia, not a microcytic hypochromic picture.

exam_trap: Vitamin B12 and folate deficiency characteristically produce macrocytosis rather than microcytosis.
takeaway: Iron deficiency → microcytic/hypochromic anaemia.
source: [HEH7].
thinking: Low haemoglobin ↓ low MCV = microcytic ↓ low MCH = hypochromic ↓ commonest microcytic hypochromic anaemia ↓ Iron-deficiency anaemia
pearl: In adults, unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia should prompt investigation for gastrointestinal blood loss, including colorectal and gastric cancer.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Anaemia: macrocytosis
stem: A patient has anaemia with a markedly increased MCV. Which deficiency is classically associated with megaloblastic macrocytic anaemia?
why_correct: Vitamin B12 deficiency can cause megaloblastic macrocytic anaemia due to impaired DNA synthesis. Folate deficiency produces a similar megaloblastic pattern.

why_others_wrong.A: Iron deficiency causes a microcytic hypochromic anaemia with a low MCV, not megaloblastic macrocytosis.
why_others_wrong.C: Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy with perifollicular haemorrhage and poor wound healing rather than a megaloblastic anaemia.
why_others_wrong.D: Vitamin K deficiency reduces functional factors II, VII, IX and X and causes bleeding, not a raised MCV.
why_others_wrong.E: Calcium deficiency affects bone, nerve and muscle function and plays no part in DNA synthesis for red-cell production.

exam_trap: Do not assume that every macrocytic anaemia is due to B12 deficiency; alcohol excess, liver disease, hypothyroidism and other causes can also produce macrocytosis.
takeaway: B12/folate deficiency → impaired DNA synthesis → megaloblastic macrocytosis.
source: [HEH7].
thinking: Anaemia with a markedly raised MCV ↓ megaloblastic change = impaired DNA synthesis ↓ B12 and folate are both needed for DNA synthesis ↓ Vitamin B12
pearl: After total gastrectomy or terminal ileal resection, loss of intrinsic factor or of the absorptive site causes B12 deficiency, so these patients need lifelong parenteral B12 replacement.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Platelet function
stem: A patient has a normal platelet count, but platelet function testing is abnormal. Which bleeding pattern is most characteristic of this primary haemostatic defect?

options.E: Delayed bleeding several days after surgery only

why_correct: Primary haemostasis depends principally on platelet plug formation. Platelet disorders typically produce mucocutaneous bleeding such as petechiae, epistaxis and gum bleeding. By contrast, coagulation-factor disorders more typically cause deep tissue bleeding and haemarthroses.

why_others_wrong.A: Deep muscle haematomas are typical of coagulation-factor deficiencies such as haemophilia rather than platelet defects.
why_others_wrong.B: Haemarthroses are the hallmark of severe factor VIII or IX deficiency, a secondary haemostatic defect, not a platelet disorder.
why_others_wrong.D: Retroperitoneal bleeding is a deep-tissue bleed more characteristic of coagulation-factor disorders or anticoagulation than of platelet dysfunction.
why_others_wrong.E: Delayed post-operative bleeding suggests a defect in fibrin formation or stabilisation, such as factor XIII deficiency, whereas platelet defects bleed immediately.

exam_trap: Use the bleeding phenotype: Platelets → mucocutaneous. Coagulation factors → deep tissue/joint bleeding.
takeaway: Mucosal bleeding + petechiae → think platelet/primary haemostasis problem.
source: [HEH7].
thinking: Normal platelet count but abnormal platelet function ↓ primary haemostasis defect ↓ platelet plug fails in small vessels ↓ mucocutaneous bleeding ↓ Mucosal bleeding and petechiae
pearl: Aspirin and clopidogrel cause acquired platelet dysfunction and are a common reason for excess mucosal and surgical oozing in patients with normal platelet counts.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Extrinsic coagulation pathway
stem: A patient has an isolated prolonged prothrombin time (PT) with a normal activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT). Which pathway is most specifically being assessed by the PT?
why_correct: The PT primarily assesses the extrinsic and common coagulation pathways and is particularly sensitive to factor VII.

why_others_wrong.A: The intrinsic pathway is assessed by the APTT, which is normal in this patient.
why_others_wrong.C: The fibrinolytic pathway is assessed by tests such as D-dimer or fibrin degradation products, not by the PT.
why_others_wrong.D: Platelet adhesion depends on von Willebrand factor and GPIb and is not measured by the PT, which is performed on platelet-poor plasma.
why_others_wrong.E: The complement pathway is part of innate immunity and is not measured by the PT, which tests tissue factor-initiated clotting.

exam_trap: Candidates choose the intrinsic pathway by mixing up the two tests; the intrinsic pathway is measured by the APTT, which is normal here, whereas the PT reflects factor VII.
takeaway: PT → extrinsic + common pathway. APTT → intrinsic + common pathway.
source: [HEH7].
thinking: Isolated prolonged PT with a normal APTT ↓ the PT is initiated by tissue factor ↓ factor VII is the only factor tested by the PT alone ↓ Extrinsic pathway
pearl: Factor VII has the shortest half-life of the vitamin K-dependent factors, so the PT/INR is the first test to rise with warfarin, early vitamin K deficiency or acute liver failure.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Activated partial thromboplastin time
stem: A patient has an isolated prolonged APTT with a normal PT. Which group of coagulation factors is being assessed predominantly?
correct_answer: B. Intrinsic and common pathway factors
why_correct: APTT assesses the intrinsic and common coagulation pathways.

why_others_wrong.A: Extrinsic pathway factors, particularly factor VII, are assessed by the PT, which is normal here.
why_others_wrong.C: Platelet receptors are not tested by the APTT, which is performed on platelet-poor plasma and measures clotting factors.
why_others_wrong.D: Fibrinolytic factors such as plasminogen are not assessed by the APTT, which measures fibrin formation rather than breakdown.
why_others_wrong.E: Red-cell membrane proteins such as spectrin relate to haemolytic disorders and are not measured by any clotting time.

exam_trap: Extrinsic pathway factors only is the swap-the-tests error; the extrinsic pathway is assessed by the PT, which is normal here, so the defect lies in intrinsic or common factors.
takeaway: APTT → intrinsic + common pathway.
source: [HEH7].
thinking: Isolated prolonged APTT with a normal PT ↓ extrinsic factor VII is intact ↓ the defect lies in intrinsic factors VIII, IX, XI or XII or the common pathway ↓ Intrinsic and common pathway factors
pearl: An unexpected isolated prolonged APTT before surgery should prompt a mixing study: correction suggests a factor deficiency such as haemophilia, whereas failure to correct suggests an inhibitor such as lupus anticoagulant, which is prothrombotic rather than a bleeding risk.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Fibrinogen
stem: During coagulation, fibrinogen is converted into fibrin. Which enzyme catalyses this conversion?
why_correct: Thrombin converts soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin, which forms the structural framework of the clot.

why_others_wrong.A: Plasmin degrades fibrin during fibrinolysis rather than forming it from fibrinogen.
why_others_wrong.C: Factor VIIa complexes with tissue factor to activate factors IX and X, initiating coagulation, but it does not cleave fibrinogen.
why_others_wrong.D: Activated protein C is an anticoagulant that inactivates factors Va and VIIIa and does not convert fibrinogen to fibrin.
why_others_wrong.E: Antithrombin inhibits thrombin and factor Xa, opposing rather than catalysing fibrin formation.

exam_trap: Plasmin is chosen because it also acts on fibrin, but it degrades fibrin during fibrinolysis; thrombin is the enzyme that converts fibrinogen to fibrin.
takeaway: Thrombin → fibrinogen → fibrin.
source: [HEH7].
thinking: Fibrinogen to fibrin is the final step of the common pathway ↓ prothrombinase converts prothrombin to the active enzyme ↓ that enzyme cleaves fibrinogen into fibrin monomers ↓ Thrombin
pearl: In massive haemorrhage fibrinogen is often the first clotting factor to fall to critical levels, so it is monitored and replaced with cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Factor XIII
stem: A patient has delayed bleeding after minor surgery and poor wound healing, despite a normal PT and APTT. Which coagulation abnormality should be considered?
why_correct: Factor XIII stabilises fibrin by cross-linking fibrin strands. Because it acts after the fibrin clot has formed, routine PT and APTT may be normal in factor XIII deficiency.

why_others_wrong.A: Factor VII deficiency prolongs the PT because factor VII is specifically tested by the extrinsic pathway assay.
why_others_wrong.B: Factor VIII deficiency, as in haemophilia A, prolongs the APTT and so would not be consistent with normal routine tests.
why_others_wrong.D: Factor X lies in the common pathway, so its deficiency prolongs both the PT and the APTT.
why_others_wrong.E: Factor V is a common-pathway cofactor, and its deficiency prolongs both the PT and the APTT.

exam_trap: Factor VIII deficiency tempts for surgical bleeding, but haemophilia A prolongs the APTT; normal PT and APTT with delayed bleeding and poor healing points to factor XIII.
takeaway: Factor XIII = fibrin stabilisation; deficiency can have normal PT/APTT.
source: [HEH7].
thinking: Delayed bleeding after minor surgery with poor wound healing ↓ PT and APTT are both normal ↓ the clot forms but is unstable ↓ fibrin cross-linking defect ↓ Factor XIII deficiency
pearl: Congenital factor XIII deficiency classically presents with bleeding from the umbilical stump in the neonate; a specific factor XIII assay is needed because the standard clotting screen is normal.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Vitamin K-dependent coagulation factors
stem: Which group consists predominantly of vitamin K-dependent coagulation factors?
correct_answer: A. II, VII, IX and X
why_correct: Factors II, VII, IX and X are vitamin K dependent. Protein C and protein S are also vitamin K-dependent anticoagulant proteins.

why_others_wrong.B: Fibrinogen and factors V, VIII and XIII do not undergo vitamin K-dependent gamma-carboxylation.
why_others_wrong.C: Tissue factor and factors V, XI and XII are not vitamin K dependent, so this group does not fit.
why_others_wrong.D: Although factor IX is vitamin K dependent, factors VIII, XI and XII are not, so this group is not predominantly vitamin K dependent.
why_others_wrong.E: Factor II is vitamin K dependent, but fibrinogen and factors V and VIII are not, so this set is not predominantly vitamin K dependent.

exam_trap: The VIII, IX, XI and XII group tempts because it contains factor IX, but factor VIII is not vitamin K dependent; only II, VII, IX and X are.
takeaway: Vitamin K → II, VII, IX, X + proteins C and S.
source: [HEH7].
thinking: Vitamin K is the cofactor for gamma-carboxylation ↓ the procoagulants modified are II, VII, IX and X ↓ fibrinogen and factors V, VIII and XIII are not ↓ II, VII, IX and X
pearl: For urgent warfarin reversal in major bleeding, UK practice gives intravenous vitamin K plus prothrombin complex concentrate, which replaces factors II, VII, IX and X immediately.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Disseminated intravascular coagulation
stem: A critically ill patient develops widespread bleeding. Blood tests show prolonged PT and APTT, thrombocytopenia and a markedly reduced fibrinogen concentration. Which diagnosis best explains this pattern?
