why_correct: DIC involves widespread activation of coagulation, consumption of platelets and coagulation factors, and secondary fibrinolysis. Patients can therefore develop both thrombosis and bleeding.

why_others_wrong.A: Haemophilia A prolongs the APTT but leaves the PT, platelet count and fibrinogen normal, so it cannot explain this combined picture.
why_others_wrong.C: Immune thrombocytopenia lowers the platelet count but does not prolong clotting times or consume fibrinogen.
why_others_wrong.D: Vitamin B12 deficiency may cause cytopenias but does not produce prolonged PT and APTT with low fibrinogen and widespread bleeding.
why_others_wrong.E: Factor XIII deficiency gives normal PT, APTT, platelets and fibrinogen, unlike the consumptive pattern described here.

exam_trap: DIC is a systemic consumptive process rather than an isolated platelet disorder.
takeaway: DIC → consumption of platelets/factors → thrombosis + bleeding.
source: [HEH7].
thinking: Critically ill patient with widespread bleeding ↓ prolonged PT and APTT, low platelets and markedly low fibrinogen ↓ simultaneous consumption of platelets and clotting factors ↓ Disseminated intravascular coagulation
pearl: Management of DIC centres on treating the trigger, such as sepsis, major trauma or obstetric emergencies, with blood components reserved for patients who are bleeding or need invasive procedures.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: D-dimer
stem: Which substance is measured by the D-dimer test?
why_correct: D-dimer is generated when cross-linked fibrin is broken down by fibrinolysis.

why_others_wrong.A: Intact fibrinogen is measured by the Clauss fibrinogen assay, whereas D-dimer reflects breakdown of fibrin that has already been cross-linked.
why_others_wrong.C: Platelet membrane glycoproteins such as GPIIb/IIIa are assessed by flow cytometry, not by the D-dimer test.
why_others_wrong.D: Free haemoglobin is a marker of intravascular haemolysis and is unrelated to fibrin degradation.
why_others_wrong.E: Factor VIII concentration is measured by a specific factor assay and is not what the D-dimer test detects.

exam_trap: Intact fibrinogen tempts because D-dimer relates to fibrin, but breakdown of fibrinogen alone does not generate D-dimer; it comes only from factor XIII cross-linked fibrin.
takeaway: D-dimer = breakdown product of cross-linked fibrin.
source: NICE NG158, Venous thromboembolic diseases; updated 2023.
thinking: Factor XIII cross-links fibrin within the clot ↓ plasmin cleaves this cross-linked fibrin ↓ the fragments released include D-dimer ↓ Cross-linked fibrin degradation products
pearl: D-dimer is sensitive but non-specific: a negative result helps exclude venous thromboembolism when clinical probability is low, but it is raised after surgery, trauma, in malignancy and in pregnancy, limiting its value post-operatively.

subject: Major trauma & fluids
title: Acute haemorrhage
stem: A patient develops sudden major blood loss. Which physiological response occurs early to help maintain arterial pressure?
why_correct: Acute blood loss reduces effective circulating volume and arterial pressure. Baroreceptor-mediated sympathetic activation increases heart rate, contractility and peripheral vasoconstriction.

why_others_wrong.A: Baroreceptor unloading after sudden blood loss increases sympathetic outflow, so a reduction in sympathetic activity would worsen the fall in arterial pressure.
why_others_wrong.B: Vagal activity is withdrawn after acute haemorrhage to allow tachycardia; increased vagal tone would slow the heart and lower pressure.
why_others_wrong.D: Erythropoiesis increases red-cell mass over days to weeks, too slowly to support arterial pressure in the early phase of haemorrhage.
why_others_wrong.E: Hepatic albumin synthesis takes days to restore plasma proteins and does not contribute to the immediate maintenance of arterial pressure.

exam_trap: Immediate increases in erythrocyte mass or albumin synthesis sound restorative, but both take days; the early defence of arterial pressure is the sympathetic baroreceptor reflex.
takeaway: Acute blood loss → sympathetic response first; haematological replacement is later.
thinking: Sudden major blood loss ↓ arterial pressure falls and baroreceptors are unloaded ↓ a rapid neural reflex acts within seconds ↓ red-cell and albumin replacement take days ↓ Increased sympathetic activity
pearl: Over the following hours interstitial fluid moves into the capillaries (transcapillary refill) and dilutes the blood, which is why haemoglobin can be near normal immediately after acute haemorrhage.

subject: Major trauma & fluids
title: Hypovolaemic shock
stem: Which finding is most characteristic of significant hypovolaemic shock?

options.E: Increased venous capacitance with no compensatory response

why_correct: Sympathetic activation causes peripheral vasoconstriction in an attempt to preserve arterial pressure and perfusion of vital organs.

why_others_wrong.A: Hypovolaemic shock typically causes cool, pale peripheries and tachycardia; warm peripheries with bradycardia suggest neurogenic shock.
why_others_wrong.B: Significant hypovolaemia increases sympathetic tone through baroreceptor unloading, producing tachycardia and vasoconstriction rather than reduced tone.
why_others_wrong.D: Renal vasoconstriction and increased ADH and aldosterone reduce urine output in hypovolaemic shock, making oliguria the expected finding.
why_others_wrong.E: Hypovolaemia provokes venoconstriction that reduces venous capacitance, along with strong compensatory sympathetic responses, so this describes the opposite.

exam_trap: Warm peripheries with bradycardia may be chosen as a shock picture, but that pattern indicates neurogenic shock from loss of sympathetic tone, not hypovolaemia.
takeaway: Hypovolaemia → sympathetic vasoconstriction → preservation of central perfusion.
thinking: Significant hypovolaemic shock ↓ baroreceptor unloading raises sympathetic tone ↓ skin and splanchnic vessels constrict to protect heart and brain ↓ cool, pale peripheries and oliguria ↓ Peripheral vasoconstriction
pearl: Prolonged capillary refill, cool peripheries and falling urine output are early signs of hypoperfusion; an adult urine output below about 0.5 ml/kg/h is a commonly used marker of inadequate renal perfusion.

subject: Major trauma & fluids
title: Cardiogenic shock
stem: A patient develops profound hypotension following extensive myocardial infarction. Cardiac output is markedly reduced despite adequate circulating volume. Which type of shock is most appropriate?
why_correct: Cardiogenic shock occurs when the heart cannot generate sufficient cardiac output to maintain tissue perfusion, despite adequate intravascular volume.

why_others_wrong.A: Hypovolaemic shock follows loss of circulating volume, whereas this stem states that volume is adequate and the problem is pump failure after infarction.
why_others_wrong.C: Obstructive shock results from mechanical impediment to filling or outflow, such as tamponade or massive pulmonary embolism, not from infarcted myocardium failing to contract.
why_others_wrong.D: Neurogenic shock follows spinal cord injury with loss of sympathetic tone, causing vasodilatation and bradycardia, and does not fit an extensive myocardial infarction.
why_others_wrong.E: Distributive shock is driven by vasodilatation and maldistribution of flow, as in sepsis or anaphylaxis, rather than by a primary fall in cardiac output.

exam_trap: Obstructive shock is the usual wrong pick because it also lowers cardiac output, but it results from tamponade or massive pulmonary embolism, not from infarcted myocardium.
takeaway: Pump failure + inadequate cardiac output → cardiogenic shock.
thinking: Extensive myocardial infarction ↓ cardiac output markedly reduced ↓ circulating volume adequate, so not hypovolaemia ↓ primary pump failure ↓ Cardiogenic shock
pearl: Cardiogenic shock typically shows high filling pressures, pulmonary oedema and raised systemic vascular resistance, so large fluid volumes can worsen it, unlike hypovolaemic shock.

subject: Major trauma & fluids
title: Obstructive shock
stem: A trauma patient develops sudden hypotension, distended neck veins and severe respiratory compromise. Which category of shock should be considered?
why_correct: Obstructive shock results from mechanical obstruction to cardiac filling or output. Important causes include massive pulmonary embolism and cardiac tamponade; tension pneumothorax can also produce obstructive physiology.

why_others_wrong.A: Hypovolaemia causes collapsed rather than distended neck veins, so raised venous pressure with respiratory compromise points to an obstructive cause such as tension pneumothorax.
why_others_wrong.B: Cardiogenic shock reflects primary pump failure, whereas sudden post-traumatic distended neck veins with respiratory compromise suggest an external obstruction such as tension pneumothorax.
why_others_wrong.D: Endocrine causes such as adrenal insufficiency do not explain sudden distended neck veins and severe respiratory compromise after trauma.
why_others_wrong.E: Anaemia alone does not cause sudden hypotension with raised jugular venous pressure and respiratory distress in a trauma patient.

exam_trap: Hypovolaemic shock is the reflex answer in trauma, but hypovolaemia causes collapsed neck veins; distension with respiratory compromise indicates obstructive shock such as tension pneumothorax.
takeaway: Mechanical obstruction to circulation → obstructive shock.
thinking: Trauma with sudden hypotension ↓ distended neck veins mean raised venous pressure, not volume loss ↓ severe respiratory compromise suggests tension pneumothorax ↓ mechanical impediment to cardiac filling ↓ Obstructive
pearl: Neck veins may be flat in tension pneumothorax or tamponade if the patient is also bleeding, so obstructive causes must still be considered in a shocked trauma patient without distended neck veins.

subject: Major trauma & fluids
title: Septic shock physiology
stem: A patient with severe infection becomes hypotensive despite apparently adequate intravascular volume. Which haemodynamic abnormality is particularly characteristic of early distributive septic shock?

options.D: Increased blood viscosity as the primary mechanism

why_correct: Sepsis can cause profound vasodilatation and reduced systemic vascular resistance, producing distributive shock.

why_others_wrong.A: A markedly raised systemic vascular resistance is typical of hypovolaemic or cardiogenic shock, whereas early septic shock is driven by vasodilatation.
why_others_wrong.C: Cardiac output is usually preserved or even raised in early septic shock; complete absence of output is cardiac arrest, not a feature of sepsis.
why_others_wrong.D: Blood viscosity is not the primary mechanism of septic shock, which results mainly from inflammatory vasodilatation and capillary leak.
why_others_wrong.E: Mechanical obstruction of venous return describes obstructive shock such as tension pneumothorax or tamponade, not the vasodilatation of sepsis.

exam_trap: Markedly increased systemic vascular resistance fits hypovolaemic or cardiogenic shock; early septic shock is distributive, with vasodilatation and often preserved or raised cardiac output.
takeaway: Septic/distributive shock → vasodilatation → ↓SVR.
thinking: Severe infection with hypotension despite adequate volume ↓ inflammatory mediators and nitric oxide cause vasodilatation ↓ capillary leak and maldistribution of flow ↓ distributive shock pattern ↓ Reduced systemic vascular resistance
pearl: Early septic shock often presents with warm peripheries and a bounding pulse; noradrenaline is the usual first-line vasopressor when hypotension persists after fluid resuscitation.

subject: Major trauma & fluids
title: Oxygen delivery
stem: Which equation best describes systemic oxygen delivery?
correct_answer: A. Cardiac output × arterial oxygen content
why_correct: Systemic oxygen delivery (DO2) depends principally on cardiac output and arterial oxygen content.

why_others_wrong.B: Venous oxygen content reflects what remains after tissue extraction, and heart rate alone ignores stroke volume, so this does not describe oxygen delivery.
why_others_wrong.C: Oxygen delivery uses total cardiac output and arterial oxygen content; stroke volume and venous saturation describe neither the full flow nor the oxygen supplied.
why_others_wrong.D: Blood pressure and respiratory rate are clinical observations that do not quantify flow or oxygen content, so their product has no physiological meaning here.
why_others_wrong.E: Carbon dioxide content relates to elimination of metabolic waste, not to the oxygen carried to the tissues, so it does not define oxygen delivery.

exam_trap: Heart rate × venous oxygen content is tempting, but venous content reflects what remains after extraction; delivery uses total cardiac output and arterial oxygen content.
takeaway: DO2 = cardiac output × arterial oxygen content.
thinking: Oxygen delivery = blood flow × oxygen carried per unit of blood ↓ blood flow is cardiac output ↓ oxygen carried to tissues is arterial, not venous, content ↓ Cardiac output × arterial oxygen content
pearl: Arterial oxygen content is dominated by haemoglobin-bound oxygen (about 1.34 ml per gram of saturated haemoglobin), with dissolved oxygen contributing very little, so anaemia reduces delivery much more than a modest fall in PaO2.

subject: Major trauma & fluids
title: Blood transfusion: red cells
stem: A stable adult undergoing elective surgery has anaemia but no active bleeding or acute coronary syndrome. According to NICE transfusion guidance, what restrictive haemoglobin threshold is generally considered for red-cell transfusion?
why_correct: NICE NG24 recommends a restrictive red-cell transfusion threshold of 70 g/L for patients who require transfusion and do not have major haemorrhage or acute coronary syndrome, with a post-transfusion target of 70–90 g/L.

why_others_wrong.A: A threshold of 50 g/L is lower than the NICE restrictive threshold of 70 g/L for stable adults without major haemorrhage or acute coronary syndrome.
why_others_wrong.B: A threshold of 60 g/L is lower than the 70 g/L restrictive threshold NICE recommends for stable adults without major haemorrhage or acute coronary syndrome.
why_others_wrong.D: A threshold of 90 g/L is the upper end of the NICE post-transfusion target range and is not the restrictive trigger for starting transfusion.
why_others_wrong.E: A threshold of 110 g/L lies within the normal range and would expose a stable, non-bleeding patient to unnecessary transfusion risks.

exam_trap: Candidates choose 90 g/L, confusing the upper end of the 70–90 g/L post-transfusion target with the restrictive 70 g/L trigger for starting transfusion.
takeaway: Stable adult, no major haemorrhage/ACS → restrictive RBC threshold around 70 g/L.
source: NICE NG24.
thinking: Stable adult for elective surgery ↓ no active bleeding or acute coronary syndrome ↓ NICE NG24 restrictive strategy applies ↓ transfuse below 70 g/L, aiming for 70–90 g/L afterwards ↓ 70 g/L
pearl: NICE uses a higher threshold of 80 g/L (target 80–100 g/L) in acute coronary syndrome, while major haemorrhage is managed by protocol rather than a haemoglobin trigger.

subject: Major trauma & fluids
title: Single-unit transfusion
stem: A stable adult with no active bleeding is judged to need a red-cell transfusion. What does NICE recommend considering?

options.C: Give two units regardless of response

correct_answer: B. Give one unit and reassess
why_correct: NICE recommends considering single-unit red-cell transfusion in adults who are not actively bleeding, followed by clinical reassessment and haemoglobin measurement before giving further units if needed.

why_others_wrong.A: Automatically giving four units ignores the NICE single-unit approach and risks circulatory overload and unnecessary exposure in a patient who is not bleeding.
why_others_wrong.C: Giving two units regardless of response removes the reassessment step that NICE recommends after each unit in adults without active bleeding.
why_others_wrong.D: NICE recommends checking the haemoglobin and reassessing clinically after each unit, so avoiding reassessment contradicts the guidance.
why_others_wrong.E: Platelets are indicated for thrombocytopenia or platelet dysfunction with bleeding or procedural risk, not routinely alongside red cells in a stable non-bleeding patient.

exam_trap: Two units regardless of response feels routine, but NICE advises one unit followed by clinical reassessment and a haemoglobin check in adults who are not actively bleeding.
takeaway: No active bleeding → one unit → reassess → further blood only if required.
source: NICE NG24.
thinking: Stable adult, not actively bleeding ↓ red-cell transfusion judged necessary ↓ NICE favours single-unit transfusion ↓ recheck haemoglobin and reassess before more blood ↓ Give one unit and reassess
pearl: Single-unit transfusion reduces donor exposure and the risk of transfusion-associated circulatory overload, especially in older or low-body-weight patients and those with cardiac or renal impairment.

subject: Major trauma & fluids
title: Fresh frozen plasma
stem: A patient is actively bleeding and has a significant coagulation abnormality. Which blood component provides multiple coagulation factors?
why_correct: Fresh frozen plasma contains multiple coagulation factors and may be considered in clinically significant bleeding when coagulation tests are abnormal. NICE advises against using FFP simply to correct abnormal coagulation tests in patients who are not bleeding and are not undergoing an invasive procedure with significant bleeding risk.

why_others_wrong.A: Red cells restore oxygen-carrying capacity but contain negligible coagulation factors, so they do not correct a coagulopathy.
why_others_wrong.B: Platelets correct thrombocytopenia or platelet dysfunction but do not supply the broad range of soluble coagulation factors found in plasma.
why_others_wrong.D: Albumin is a colloid for volume or protein replacement and contains no clinically useful coagulation factors.
why_others_wrong.E: Cryoprecipitate is concentrated mainly for fibrinogen, factor VIII, von Willebrand factor and factor XIII, so it lacks the full range of factors found in fresh frozen plasma.

exam_trap: Cryoprecipitate only is tempting because it contains clotting factors, but it is concentrated for fibrinogen, factor VIII, von Willebrand factor and factor XIII, not the full range in plasma.
takeaway: FFP → multiple coagulation factors; use requires clinical context.
source: NICE NG24.
thinking: Active bleeding with significant coagulopathy ↓ needs replacement of many soluble clotting factors ↓ red cells, platelets and albumin lack them ↓ cryoprecipitate is concentrated mainly for fibrinogen ↓ Fresh frozen plasma
pearl: For warfarin-related bleeding, prothrombin complex concentrate is preferred to FFP because it replaces factors II, VII, IX and X faster and in a far smaller volume.

subject: Major trauma & fluids
title: Cryoprecipitate
stem: A patient with major bleeding has a critically low fibrinogen concentration. Which blood component is particularly rich in fibrinogen?
why_correct: Cryoprecipitate contains concentrated fibrinogen along with other proteins including factor VIII, von Willebrand factor and factor XIII. NICE recommends considering cryoprecipitate in clinically significant bleeding when fibrinogen is below 1.5 g/L in patients without major haemorrhage; major haemorrhage protocols require separate consideration.

why_others_wrong.A: Red cells are given to restore oxygen-carrying capacity and contain negligible fibrinogen, so they cannot correct a low fibrinogen level.
why_others_wrong.B: Platelets address low platelet count or function and are not a concentrated source of fibrinogen.
why_others_wrong.C: Fresh frozen plasma contains fibrinogen but at a much lower concentration, so large volumes would be needed to raise a critically low fibrinogen level.
why_others_wrong.E: Albumin is used for volume or protein replacement and contains no clinically useful fibrinogen.

exam_trap: Fresh frozen plasma is the common wrong pick because it contains fibrinogen, but at a much lower concentration, so large volumes would be needed to correct critical hypofibrinogenaemia.
takeaway: Low fibrinogen + clinically significant bleeding → consider cryoprecipitate.
source: NICE NG24.
thinking: Major bleeding with critically low fibrinogen ↓ needs concentrated fibrinogen replacement ↓ FFP contains fibrinogen but is too dilute ↓ cryoprecipitate concentrates fibrinogen, factor VIII, von Willebrand factor and factor XIII ↓ Cryoprecipitate
pearl: Fibrinogen is typically the first clotting factor to fall to critical levels in major haemorrhage, so it should be checked early by laboratory or viscoelastic testing.

subject: Major trauma & fluids
title: Platelet transfusion
stem: A patient with thrombocytopenia requires surgery with a substantial risk of bleeding. Which platelet count is the commonly used NICE threshold below which prophylactic platelet transfusion is considered for invasive procedures or surgery?
why_correct: NICE recommends considering prophylactic platelet transfusion to raise the platelet count above 50 × 10⁹/L for patients undergoing invasive procedures or surgery, with higher thresholds for certain critical sites.

why_others_wrong.A: A count of 10 × 10⁹/L is the NICE prophylactic threshold for patients who are not bleeding and not having a procedure, not the target for surgery or invasive procedures.
why_others_wrong.B: A count of 20 × 10⁹/L is below the level NICE recommends for surgery or invasive procedures, where the target is above 50 × 10⁹/L.
why_others_wrong.C: A count of 30 × 10⁹/L is a threshold NICE applies to some clinically significant bleeding, not the prophylactic target for surgery with bleeding risk.
why_others_wrong.E: A count of 150 × 10⁹/L is the lower limit of normal and far exceeds any NICE prophylactic transfusion threshold for surgery.

exam_trap: Candidates pick 10 × 10⁹/L, which is the NICE prophylactic threshold for patients who are not bleeding and not having a procedure, not the level for surgery.
takeaway: Surgery/invasive procedure → commonly target platelets >50 × 10⁹/L; critical sites may require higher.
source: NICE NG24.
thinking: Thrombocytopenia ↓ surgery with substantial bleeding risk ↓ prophylactic platelet transfusion considered ↓ NICE: raise the count above 50 × 10⁹/L, higher for critical sites ↓ 50 × 10⁹/L
pearl: NICE advises a higher threshold of 100 × 10⁹/L for surgery at critical sites such as neurosurgery or the posterior segment of the eye.

subject: Major trauma & fluids
title: Transfusion reaction
stem: A patient develops fever, chills, back pain and hypotension shortly after starting a blood transfusion. Which complication is most likely?
why_correct: Acute haemolysis after transfusion is a medical emergency. Fever, rigors, pain, hypotension and haemoglobinuria can occur. The transfusion should be stopped and the patient assessed and managed urgently according to the local transfusion-reaction protocol.

why_others_wrong.A: Iron deficiency develops over weeks and does not cause acute fever, rigors, back pain and hypotension shortly after a transfusion.
why_others_wrong.C: Chronic anaemia is a long-standing state and cannot explain an abrupt febrile, hypotensive reaction occurring during or soon after transfusion.
why_others_wrong.D: Dilutional anaemia follows large-volume fluid or product replacement and does not produce fever, back pain and hypotension.
why_others_wrong.E: Physiological haemodilution is a benign fall in haematocrit and does not account for the acute systemic features of a transfusion reaction.

exam_trap: Delayed iron deficiency, chronic anaemia and haemodilution are slow or benign processes; fever, back pain and hypotension soon after starting blood indicate acute haemolysis.
takeaway: Suspected acute haemolytic reaction → stop transfusion + urgent assessment.
source: NICE NG24; British Society for Haematology (BSH) guidelines on the management of acute transfusion reactions.
thinking: Fever, chills, back pain and hypotension ↓ shortly after starting a transfusion ↓ intravascular destruction of incompatible red cells ↓ usually ABO incompatibility from an identification error ↓ Acute haemolytic transfusion reaction
pearl: Most ABO-incompatible transfusions result from patient identification errors at sampling or administration, so the bedside identity check is the key preventive step.

subject: Genetics
title: Autosomal dominant inheritance
stem: A man is heterozygous for a pathogenic variant causing an autosomal dominant disorder. His partner is unaffected and does not carry the variant. What is the approximate probability that each of their children will inherit the variant?
why_correct: In a typical autosomal dominant disorder, a heterozygous affected parent has one normal and one pathogenic allele. Each pregnancy has an independent 50% probability of inheriting the pathogenic allele.

why_others_wrong.A: A 0% risk would apply only if neither parent carried the variant, but here one parent is heterozygous and can pass on the pathogenic allele.
why_others_wrong.B: A 10% figure has no basis in Mendelian segregation; a heterozygous parent transmits one of two alleles with equal probability at each meiosis.
why_others_wrong.C: A 25% risk is the chance of an affected child when both parents are carriers of an autosomal recessive variant, not one heterozygous parent with a dominant variant.
why_others_wrong.E: A 100% risk would require the affected parent to be homozygous for the variant, whereas a heterozygous parent passes the normal allele half the time.

exam_trap: The probability applies independently to each pregnancy; previous unaffected children do not alter the probability for the next pregnancy.
takeaway: Heterozygous autosomal dominant × unaffected → 50% risk per pregnancy.
source: [TTG8].
thinking: Autosomal dominant disorder, father heterozygous ↓ mother does not carry the variant ↓ each child receives one of the father's two alleles at random ↓ half the chance of receiving the pathogenic allele ↓ 50%
pearl: Reduced penetrance and variable expressivity are common in dominant disorders, so a child who inherits the variant may be mildly affected or appear unaffected, as in some inherited cancer syndromes.

subject: Genetics
title: Autosomal recessive inheritance
stem: Two unaffected parents are known carriers of the same autosomal recessive pathogenic variant. What is the probability that a child will be affected?
why_correct: For two heterozygous carriers, each pregnancy has: 25% affected, 50% carrier, 25% unaffected non-carrier.

why_others_wrong.A: A 0% risk would apply if at least one parent were a non-carrier, but two carrier parents can each pass on the pathogenic allele.
why_others_wrong.B: A 10% figure does not arise from Mendelian segregation; each carrier transmits the variant with a probability of one half.
why_others_wrong.D: A 50% probability is the chance that a child of two carriers will be an unaffected carrier, not the chance of being affected.
why_others_wrong.E: A 100% risk would require both parents to be homozygous affected; two heterozygous carriers produce an affected child in one in four pregnancies.

exam_trap: Candidates choose 50% by confusing the chance of an unaffected carrier child with the chance of an affected child; the affected risk is one in four.
takeaway: Carrier × carrier → 25% affected per pregnancy.
source: [TTG8].
thinking: Both parents unaffected carriers of the same recessive variant ↓ each passes the pathogenic allele with probability one half ↓ affected child needs two pathogenic alleles ↓ 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4 ↓ 25%
pearl: An unaffected sibling of an affected child has a two-thirds chance of being a carrier, because the affected genotype has already been excluded from that sibling.

subject: Genetics
title: X-linked recessive inheritance
stem: A woman is a carrier of an X-linked recessive disorder and the father is unaffected. What is the probability that an individual son will inherit the pathogenic X chromosome from his mother?
why_correct: A son receives his X chromosome from his mother and Y chromosome from his father. A carrier mother has a 50% probability of passing the pathogenic X chromosome to each son.

why_others_wrong.A: A 0% risk would apply to sons of an affected father, who pass on the Y chromosome, but a carrier mother gives each son one of her two X chromosomes.
why_others_wrong.B: A 25% figure is the chance that any child of unknown sex is an affected son; for a son specifically, the probability of receiving the pathogenic X is one half.
why_others_wrong.D: A 75% figure has no basis here, as the mother transmits either her normal or her pathogenic X chromosome with equal probability.
why_others_wrong.E: A 100% risk would require the mother to have two pathogenic X chromosomes, whereas a heterozygous carrier also has a normal X to pass on.

exam_trap: Do not confuse "probability that a son is affected" with the probability that any child is affected.
takeaway: Carrier mother → each son has a 50% chance of inheriting the affected X.
source: [TTG8].
thinking: Son receives X from mother and Y from father ↓ carrier mother has one normal and one pathogenic X ↓ each X passed with equal probability ↓ 50%
pearl: Haemophilia A and B are X-linked recessive conditions of surgical relevance; a carrier mother has a 50% chance of an affected son and a 50% chance of a carrier daughter.

subject: Genetics
title: Penetrance
stem: A pathogenic genetic variant is present in several family members, but not every carrier develops the associated disease. Which term describes this phenomenon?
why_correct: Penetrance refers to the proportion of individuals carrying a particular genotype who express the associated phenotype. If not all carriers manifest the condition, penetrance is incomplete.

why_others_wrong.A: Complete penetrance means every carrier of the variant expresses the phenotype, the opposite of this family in which some carriers remain unaffected.
why_others_wrong.C: Codominance describes both alleles of a heterozygote being fully expressed, as in the AB blood group, and does not explain unaffected carriers.
why_others_wrong.D: Anticipation is earlier onset or increasing severity in successive generations, usually due to repeat expansion, rather than carriers who never develop disease.
why_others_wrong.E: Variable expressivity describes differing severity among affected carriers, whereas here some carriers show no disease at all, which is incomplete penetrance.

exam_trap: Variable expressivity is the usual wrong choice; it describes differing severity among affected carriers, whereas unaffected carriers indicate incomplete penetrance.
takeaway: Penetrance = whether the phenotype appears.
source: [TTG8].
thinking: Pathogenic variant present in several relatives ↓ some carriers never develop the disease ↓ proportion of carriers expressing the phenotype is below 100% ↓ Incomplete penetrance
pearl: Incomplete penetrance explains apparently skipped generations in dominant pedigrees, so an unaffected relative may still carry and transmit a high-risk variant such as BRCA1 or BRCA2.

subject: Genetics
title: Variable expressivity
stem: Two people carry the same pathogenic variant and both have the associated disorder, but one has mild disease while the other has severe disease. Which concept best describes this?
why_correct: Variable expressivity means that individuals with the same disease-associated genotype can manifest different degrees or patterns of phenotype.

why_others_wrong.A: Incomplete penetrance means some carriers show no phenotype at all, whereas here both carriers are affected and differ only in severity.
why_others_wrong.C: Nondisjunction is failure of chromosomes to separate during cell division, causing aneuploidy, and does not explain differing severity from the same variant.
why_others_wrong.D: Anticipation describes earlier onset or greater severity in successive generations, not variation in severity between two people with the same variant.
why_others_wrong.E: Homozygosity means carrying two identical alleles; the stem describes the same variant producing different severity, which is expressivity rather than zygosity.

exam_trap: Incomplete penetrance is the common wrong answer, but it describes carriers with no phenotype; here both carriers are affected and differ only in severity.
takeaway: Penetrance = whether disease appears. Expressivity = how strongly/differently it appears.
source: [TTG8].
thinking: Same pathogenic variant in two people ↓ both are affected ↓ they differ only in severity ↓ Variable expressivity
pearl: Neurofibromatosis type 1 is a classic example of variable expressivity, ranging from a few cafe-au-lait macules to extensive plexiform neurofibromas within one family.

subject: Statistics & evidence-based medicine
title: Sensitivity
stem: A diagnostic test is used to identify a disease. Of 100 patients who truly have the disease, 90 have a positive test. What is the sensitivity?
why_correct: Sensitivity = true positives / all people who actually have the disease. 90 / 100 = 90%. NICE defines sensitivity as the probability that the test is positive in a person who has the condition.

why_others_wrong.A: 10% is the false-negative proportion (10 of the 100 diseased patients testing negative), which is the complement of sensitivity, not sensitivity itself.
why_others_wrong.B: 50% has no basis in these figures; it would require only 50 of the 100 diseased patients to test positive, not the 90 reported.
why_others_wrong.C: 80% does not follow from 90 true positives out of 100 with disease; it would need a slip such as subtracting the 10 false negatives from 90.
why_others_wrong.E: 100% would mean every diseased patient tested positive, but 10 of the 100 had a false-negative result.

exam_trap: Candidates who pick 10% have calculated the false-negative proportion, the complement of sensitivity, rather than the proportion of diseased patients who test positive.
takeaway: Sensitivity asks: "Of those who HAVE disease, how many test positive?"
source: [CEBM].
thinking: 100 patients truly have the disease ↓ sensitivity = true positives / all with disease ↓ 90 / 100 test positive ↓ 90%
pearl: A highly sensitive test has few false negatives, so a negative result helps rule disease out (SnNout); this is why screening and rule-out tests prioritise sensitivity.

subject: Statistics & evidence-based medicine
title: Specificity
stem: A diagnostic test is used in 200 patients who do not have a disease. Of these, 180 test negative. What is the specificity?
why_correct: Specificity = true negatives / all people who do not have the disease. 180 / 200 = 90%. NICE defines specificity as the probability that a test is negative in a person who does not have the condition.

why_others_wrong.A: 10% is the false-positive proportion (20 of the 200 disease-free patients testing positive), which is the complement of specificity, not specificity itself.
why_others_wrong.B: 20% treats the count of 20 false positives as if it were a percentage, or divides it by 100 instead of by the 200 disease-free patients.
why_others_wrong.C: 80% does not follow from 180 true negatives out of 200; it would need a slip such as subtracting the 20 false positives again from 180.
why_others_wrong.E: 100% would require all 200 disease-free patients to test negative, but 20 of them had a false-positive result.

exam_trap: Choosing 10% gives the false-positive proportion among disease-free patients, while 20% is the raw count of false positives mistaken for a percentage.
takeaway: Specificity asks: "Of those who DON'T have disease, how many test negative?"
source: [CEBM].
thinking: 200 patients without the disease ↓ specificity = true negatives / all without disease ↓ 180 / 200 test negative ↓ 90%
pearl: A highly specific test has few false positives, so a positive result helps rule disease in (SpPin); confirmatory tests are chosen for high specificity.

subject: Statistics & evidence-based medicine
title: Positive predictive value
stem: A disease has a low prevalence in the population. A diagnostic test has high sensitivity and specificity, but many positive results are false positives. Which measure is particularly affected by the low prevalence?
why_correct: Positive predictive value is the proportion of positive test results that represent true disease. It depends strongly on disease prevalence. When prevalence falls, PPV can fall even when sensitivity and specificity remain unchanged. NICE distinguishes predictive values from sensitivity and specificity and notes the importance of prevalence when applying diagnostic-test results.

why_others_wrong.B: Sensitivity is calculated within people who have the disease, so it is largely independent of prevalence and would not explain the excess of false positives.
why_others_wrong.C: Specificity is calculated within people without the disease, so it is largely independent of prevalence; the stem states it remains high.
why_others_wrong.D: Relative risk compares outcome risk between exposed and unexposed groups; it is not a measure of how a diagnostic test performs.
why_others_wrong.E: A hazard ratio compares event rates over time in survival analysis and has no role in describing diagnostic test accuracy.

exam_trap: Candidates often blame sensitivity or specificity, but both are calculated within disease-status groups and are largely independent of prevalence; only predictive values shift with prevalence.
takeaway: PPV depends heavily on prevalence.
source: [CEBM].
thinking: Sensitivity and specificity remain high ↓ yet many positives are false ↓ low prevalence means false positives outnumber true positives ↓ PPV depends on prevalence ↓ Positive predictive value
pearl: Predictive values cannot be transferred between settings: a test validated in a high-prevalence specialist clinic will have a lower PPV when used for screening in primary care.

subject: Statistics & evidence-based medicine
title: Positive likelihood ratio
stem: A diagnostic test has a positive likelihood ratio (LR+) substantially greater than 1. What does this indicate?

options.A: A positive result makes the disease less likely
options.B: A positive result has no diagnostic information
options.C: A positive result increases the probability of disease

correct_answer: C. A positive result increases the probability of disease
why_correct: An LR+ greater than 1 indicates that a positive result is more likely in people with the disease than in those without it and therefore increases the post-test probability of disease. NICE describes LR+ as indicating how much more likely a positive finding is in people with the condition than people without it.

why_others_wrong.A: A positive result makes disease less likely when LR+ is below 1; a value substantially above 1 moves the post-test probability upwards.
why_others_wrong.B: An LR+ of exactly 1 carries no diagnostic information because a positive result is equally likely with or without disease; this test is well above 1.
why_others_wrong.D: A high LR+ depends on the ratio of sensitivity to the false-positive rate and can be achieved with sensitivity well below 100%.
why_others_wrong.E: Likelihood ratios are derived from sensitivity and specificity and do not depend on, or require, any particular disease prevalence.

exam_trap: Some assume a strong LR+ requires perfect sensitivity or a set prevalence, but it reflects the ratio of sensitivity to the false-positive rate and is independent of prevalence.
takeaway: LR+ >1 → positive result moves probability upward.
source: [CEBM].
thinking: LR+ = sensitivity / (1 − specificity) ↓ LR+ above 1 means a positive result is commoner in disease ↓ pre-test odds multiplied by LR+ give post-test odds ↓ A positive result increases the probability of disease
pearl: As a rule of thumb, an LR+ above 10 produces a large, often conclusive rise in post-test probability, whereas values between 1 and 2 change it very little.

subject: Research methods & screening
title: Randomised controlled trial
stem: Researchers want to determine whether a new peri-operative intervention causes better patient outcomes than standard care. Patients are randomly allocated to receive either the new intervention or standard care. What study design is this?
why_correct: Random allocation of participants to intervention and comparison groups characterises a randomised controlled trial. Randomisation aims to reduce confounding and create groups that are comparable at baseline, although the quality of a trial also depends on factors such as allocation concealment, blinding where appropriate, follow-up and analysis.

why_others_wrong.A: A case-control study selects people by outcome status and looks back at past exposures; here the investigators assign the intervention themselves.
why_others_wrong.B: A cross-sectional study measures exposure and outcome at a single point in time without allocating any intervention to participants.
why_others_wrong.D: An ecological study compares aggregate population-level data rather than randomly allocating individual patients to intervention or standard care.
why_others_wrong.E: A case report describes one or a few individual patients and involves no comparison group or random allocation.

exam_trap: Candidates sometimes choose case-control because outcomes are compared between groups, but a case-control study selects by outcome and never assigns the intervention, unlike random allocation here.
takeaway: Random allocation + intervention/comparator → RCT.
source: [RCSEng] candidate information; evidence-based practice and research domains. Updated January 2020.
thinking: Investigators allocate the intervention themselves ↓ allocation is by chance ↓ new intervention compared with standard care ↓ Randomised controlled trial
pearl: Randomisation balances both known and unknown confounders only if allocation is concealed; poorly concealed or small trials can still show baseline imbalance by chance.

subject: Research methods & screening
title: Incidence
stem: A surgical department records 30 new cases of a particular complication among 1,000 patients at risk during a defined 12-month period. Which epidemiological measure is being described?
why_correct: Incidence describes the occurrence of new cases in a defined population over a specified period.

why_others_wrong.A: Prevalence counts all existing cases at a point or over a period, whereas the stem describes new cases arising among people at risk.
why_others_wrong.C: Case fatality is the proportion of people with a condition who die from it; the stem reports new complications, not deaths.
why_others_wrong.D: An odds ratio compares the odds of an outcome between two groups, but the stem describes a single group with no comparison.
why_others_wrong.E: Positive predictive value is the proportion of positive test results that are true positives, which is a diagnostic test measure, not an occurrence rate.

exam_trap: Prevalence refers to existing cases at a particular point or over a specified period, rather than specifically new cases.
takeaway: Incidence = new cases over time.
source: [CEBM].
thinking: 30 new cases counted ↓ among 1,000 people at risk ↓ over a defined 12-month period ↓ new cases per population at risk per time ↓ Incidence
pearl: Prevalence is approximately incidence multiplied by average disease duration, so a chronic condition with low incidence can still have a high prevalence.

subject: Research methods & screening
title: Prevalence
stem: A survey assesses 5,000 people on a single day and finds that 250 currently have a particular disease. Which epidemiological measure is most directly represented?
why_correct: Point prevalence describes the proportion of a population with a condition at a particular point in time.

why_others_wrong.A: Incidence counts new cases arising over a period of follow-up, whereas this single-day survey records existing cases at one moment.
why_others_wrong.C: Relative risk compares the risk of an outcome between exposed and unexposed groups; the stem gives one population with no exposure comparison.
why_others_wrong.D: Case fatality rate is the proportion of people with the disease who die from it, and no deaths are reported in the survey.
why_others_wrong.E: A hazard ratio compares event rates over time between groups in survival analysis, which requires follow-up rather than a single-day snapshot.

exam_trap: Candidates pick incidence because a number of cases is given, but incidence needs new cases over a follow-up period, whereas a single-day survey counts existing cases.
takeaway: Prevalence = existing disease burden at a specified time.
source: [CEBM].
thinking: Single day survey ↓ counts people who currently have the disease ↓ existing cases at one moment ↓ Point prevalence
pearl: Cross-sectional surveys measure prevalence, not incidence; to measure incidence you need a disease-free population followed over time.

subject: Statistics & evidence-based medicine
title: Relative risk
stem: A cohort study reports the following outcome rates: Treatment group: 10% Control group: 20% What is the relative risk of the outcome with treatment?
why_correct: Relative risk = risk in exposed/intervention group ÷ risk in control group. RR = 0.10 / 0.20 = 0.5. An RR of 0.5 means the observed risk in the treatment group is half that in the control group.

why_others_wrong.A: 0.25 has no standard derivation from 10% and 20%; it resembles squaring the correct ratio of 0.5 rather than dividing the two risks once.
why_others_wrong.C: A relative risk of 1 means equal risk in both groups, but the treatment group risk of 10% is half the control risk of 20%.
why_others_wrong.D: 2 is the inverted ratio, control risk divided by treatment risk (0.20 / 0.10), rather than treatment risk divided by control risk.
why_others_wrong.E: 10 is the absolute risk difference of 10 percentage points (20% minus 10%), which is the absolute risk reduction, not a ratio.

exam_trap: Candidates pick 2 by dividing control risk by treatment risk, or 10 by quoting the absolute difference in percentage points, which is the absolute risk reduction rather than a ratio.
takeaway: RR = EER / CER.
source: [GRP6].
thinking: Treatment group risk 10% ↓ control group risk 20% ↓ RR = treatment risk / control risk ↓ 0.10 / 0.20 ↓ 0.5
pearl: Relative risk is the natural measure from cohort studies and trials because they measure incidence directly; an RR below 1 indicates a protective effect.

subject: Statistics & evidence-based medicine
title: Absolute risk reduction
stem: A trial reports a complication rate of 15% in the control group and 9% in the intervention group. What is the absolute risk reduction?
why_correct: ARR = control event rate − experimental event rate. ARR = 15% − 9% = 6%.

why_others_wrong.A: 3% is half the true difference, as if the 6-percentage-point gap between 15% and 9% had been divided by two.
why_others_wrong.C: 9% is simply the complication rate in the intervention group, not the difference between control and intervention rates.
why_others_wrong.D: 15% is simply the control group complication rate, not the difference between control and intervention rates.
why_others_wrong.E: 60% is the relative risk expressed as a percentage (9 / 15 = 0.6); the corresponding relative risk reduction would be 40%, and neither is an absolute difference.

exam_trap: Choosing 60% confuses the ratio of the two rates (the relative risk) with the absolute difference; the ARR is simply 15% minus 9%.
takeaway: ARR tells you the absolute difference in event rates.
source: [GRP6].
thinking: Control event rate 15% ↓ intervention event rate 9% ↓ ARR = CER − EER ↓ 6%
pearl: The absolute risk reduction depends on baseline risk, so the same relative benefit gives a larger ARR, and a smaller NNT, in high-risk surgical patients.

subject: Statistics & evidence-based medicine
title: Number needed to treat
stem: A treatment reduces an adverse outcome from 20% to 10%. What is the approximate number needed to treat?
why_correct: ARR = 0.20 − 0.10 = 0.10. NNT = 1 / ARR = 1 / 0.10 = 10. Oxford CEBM defines NNT as the number of patients who need treatment to prevent one additional adverse outcome and gives NNT = 1/ARR.

why_others_wrong.A: 2 is the ratio of the two event rates (0.20 / 0.10), the reciprocal of the relative risk, rather than the reciprocal of the absolute risk reduction.
why_others_wrong.B: 5 is 1 divided by the control event rate of 0.20, rather than 1 divided by the absolute risk reduction of 0.10.
why_others_wrong.D: 20 is 1 divided by 0.05, which would correspond to a 5-percentage-point reduction; here the absolute reduction is 10 percentage points.
why_others_wrong.E: 100 results from treating the 10-percentage-point reduction as 0.01 (1%) before taking the reciprocal, a decimal-place error.

exam_trap: Candidates choosing 2 take the reciprocal of the relative risk, and those choosing 5 invert the control rate; NNT must be calculated as 1 divided by the absolute risk reduction.
takeaway: NNT = 1 / ARR.
source: [GRP6].
thinking: Adverse outcome falls from 20% to 10% ↓ ARR = 0.20 − 0.10 = 0.10 ↓ NNT = 1 / ARR ↓ 10
pearl: An NNT should always be quoted with its time frame and comparator, because the same intervention will have a different NNT over one year than over five.

subject: Statistics & evidence-based medicine
title: Number needed to harm
stem: A new treatment increases an adverse event from 4% to 9%. What is the approximate number needed to harm?
why_correct: Absolute risk increase = 9% − 4% = 5% = 0.05. NNH = 1 / 0.05 = 20.

why_others_wrong.A: 5 is the absolute risk increase in percentage points (9% minus 4%) left unconverted; the number needed to harm is its reciprocal, 1 / 0.05.
why_others_wrong.B: 10 would require an absolute risk increase of 10 percentage points; it approximates 1 divided by the 9% treated-group risk rather than the 5-point difference.
why_others_wrong.C: 15 would require an absolute risk increase of about 6.7 percentage points, whereas the rise from 4% to 9% is 5 percentage points.
why_others_wrong.E: 25 is 1 divided by the baseline risk of 0.04, rather than 1 divided by the absolute risk increase of 0.05.

exam_trap: Choosing 5 leaves the absolute risk increase in percentage points unconverted, and 25 inverts the baseline risk; the NNH is the reciprocal of the 0.05 increase.
takeaway: NNH = 1 / absolute risk increase.
source: [GRP6].
thinking: Adverse event rises from 4% to 9% ↓ absolute risk increase = 5% = 0.05 ↓ NNH = 1 / ARI ↓ 20
pearl: Comparing NNT with NNH for the same treatment is a practical way to weigh benefit against harm when counselling patients before surgery or starting a drug.

subject: Statistics & evidence-based medicine
title: Odds ratio
stem: A case-control study investigates an exposure associated with postoperative infection. Which effect measure is particularly appropriate for a case-control study?

options.C: Absolute risk in the exposed cohort

why_correct: Case-control studies begin with outcome status and look retrospectively at exposure. The odds ratio is the standard association measure used in this design.

why_others_wrong.B: Incidence cannot be estimated in a conventional case-control study because the investigator fixes the numbers of cases and controls rather than following a population.
why_others_wrong.C: Absolute risk in an exposed cohort requires following exposed people forward in time, which a case-control design does not do.
why_others_wrong.D: The number needed to treat is derived from an absolute risk reduction in a trial or cohort, which a case-control study cannot supply.
why_others_wrong.E: Case fatality describes the proportion of cases who die and does not compare exposure between cases and controls.

exam_trap: Relative risk is naturally calculated from incidence in cohort studies; it cannot generally be calculated directly from a conventional case-control study because the investigator fixes the numbers of cases and controls.
takeaway: Case-control → odds ratio.
source: [GRP6].
thinking: Case-control study starts from outcome status ↓ numbers of cases and controls are fixed by the investigator ↓ incidence and absolute risk cannot be measured ↓ compare odds of exposure ↓ Odds ratio
pearl: When the outcome is rare, the odds ratio from a case-control study gives a good approximation of the relative risk (the rare disease assumption).

subject: Research methods & screening
title: Cohort study
stem: Researchers identify patients exposed to a particular occupational risk and follow them for 10 years to compare the incidence of cancer with that in an unexposed group. What study design is this?
why_correct: Participants are classified according to exposure and followed over time to observe outcomes.

why_others_wrong.A: A case-control study starts from people with and without the outcome and looks back at exposure, the reverse of following exposed workers forward.
why_others_wrong.B: A cross-sectional study measures exposure and outcome at one time point and would not follow participants for 10 years to capture new cancers.
why_others_wrong.D: A case report describes individual patients without a defined exposed and unexposed group followed over time.
why_others_wrong.E: An ecological study uses aggregate population data, whereas here individual exposed and unexposed participants are followed and compared.

exam_trap: Case-control is a common wrong choice because exposure and cancer are compared, but case-control starts from the outcome and looks back, not forward from exposure.
takeaway: Exposure first → follow forward → cohort study.
source: [CEBM].
thinking: Groups defined by exposure ↓ exposed and unexposed workers followed forward ↓ incidence of cancer compared ↓ Cohort
pearl: Cohort studies can calculate incidence and relative risk directly and can study several outcomes from one exposure, but are slow and inefficient for rare outcomes.

subject: Research methods & screening
title: Case-control study
stem: Researchers identify 300 patients with a rare postoperative complication and 600 patients without it. Previous exposure to a suspected risk factor is then compared between the two groups. What study design is being used?
why_correct: Participants are selected according to outcome status and previous exposures are compared.

why_others_wrong.A: A cohort study starts from exposure status and follows people forward to see who develops the outcome, rather than selecting by complication status.
why_others_wrong.C: A randomised controlled trial allocates an intervention to participants, whereas here the researchers only compare previous exposures between groups.
why_others_wrong.D: A cross-sectional study samples a population at one time point, not deliberately chosen groups of people with and without the complication.
why_others_wrong.E: An ecological study analyses group-level data, whereas this design compares individual patients' previous exposures between cases and controls.

exam_trap: Candidates choose cohort because two groups are compared, but a cohort is defined by exposure; here groups are defined by having the complication, which makes it case-control.
takeaway: Outcome first → look back for exposure → case-control.
source: [CEBM].
thinking: Participants selected by outcome (complication present or absent) ↓ past exposure then compared ↓ outcome first, looking back ↓ Case-control
pearl: Case-control studies are efficient for rare outcomes and produce an odds ratio, which approximates the relative risk when the outcome is rare; they cannot directly measure incidence.

subject: Research methods & screening
title: Cross-sectional study
stem: Researchers measure smoking status and prevalence of chronic respiratory disease in 20,000 people during one survey period. Which study design is this?
why_correct: Exposure and outcome are measured at approximately the same point in time.

why_others_wrong.B: A cohort study follows people over time from exposure to outcome, whereas here both are measured during a single survey period.
why_others_wrong.C: A case-control study selects participants by disease status and looks back at exposure, rather than surveying a whole population at once.
why_others_wrong.D: A randomised controlled trial allocates an intervention, but smoking status here is observed and not assigned by the investigators.
why_others_wrong.E: A prospective interventional study delivers an intervention and follows participants forward, neither of which happens in a one-off survey.

exam_trap: A cross-sectional study can identify associations but generally cannot establish the temporal sequence needed to demonstrate causation.
takeaway: Exposure + outcome measured at one time → cross-sectional study.
source: [CEBM].
thinking: Smoking and respiratory disease measured together ↓ single survey period ↓ no follow-up and no allocation ↓ Cross-sectional
pearl: Because exposure and outcome are measured simultaneously, cross-sectional studies suffer reverse causation problems, for example people with lung disease may already have stopped smoking.

subject: Research methods & screening
title: Selection bias
stem: A study investigating postoperative complications recruits participants only from a specialist private hospital, while the target population is intended to represent all NHS surgical patients. Which problem could this introduce?
why_correct: The recruited population may systematically differ from the intended target population, affecting the validity and generalisability of the results.

why_others_wrong.B: Recall bias concerns inaccurate or differential remembering of past exposures, which is unrelated to recruiting from an unrepresentative hospital.
why_others_wrong.C: Observer bias arises when assessors' expectations influence how outcomes are measured, not from who is recruited into the study.
why_others_wrong.D: Lead-time bias is a screening phenomenon in which earlier diagnosis lengthens apparent survival, which has no bearing on where participants are recruited.
why_others_wrong.E: Publication bias concerns which completed studies reach print, not how participants within a single study were chosen.

exam_trap: Observer or recall bias may be chosen because the study involves complications, but neither relates to an unrepresentative recruitment site, which is the defining feature of selection bias.
takeaway: Who gets into the study matters → selection bias.
source: [CEBM].
thinking: Participants recruited from a private specialist hospital only ↓ target population is all NHS surgical patients ↓ recruited sample differs systematically from target ↓ Selection bias
pearl: Selection bias cannot be corrected by enlarging the sample; a bigger unrepresentative sample just gives a more precise wrong answer.

subject: Research methods & screening
title: Recall bias
stem: In a case-control study, patients with a disease are asked to remember exposures from 15 years earlier. Patients with the disease provide much more detailed exposure histories than controls. Which bias is particularly concerning?
why_correct: Participants may remember or report previous exposures differently depending on whether they have the outcome.

why_others_wrong.B: Lead-time bias arises when screening brings diagnosis forward and inflates survival, which is unrelated to how participants remember past exposures.
why_others_wrong.C: Publication bias concerns selective publication of studies with positive results, not differences in how cases and controls report exposure.
why_others_wrong.D: Attrition bias results from unequal loss to follow-up, which is not a feature of a retrospective exposure interview in a case-control study.
why_others_wrong.E: Spectrum bias affects diagnostic accuracy estimates when the tested population is unrepresentative, not the reporting of historical exposures.

exam_trap: Attrition bias is sometimes chosen because data are incomplete, but attrition means loss to follow-up; here every participant is interviewed and cases simply remember differently.
takeaway: Retrospective self-report + different memory between groups → recall bias.
source: [CEBM].
thinking: Case-control design with exposures 15 years ago ↓ cases search their memory harder than controls ↓ differential reporting of exposure ↓ Recall bias
pearl: Recall bias is reduced by using contemporaneous records (for example prescription or occupational records) rather than self-report, or by choosing controls with a different illness.

subject: Research methods & screening
title: Confounding
stem: A study finds that coffee consumption is associated with cardiovascular disease. Further analysis shows that smoking is much more common among coffee drinkers and is independently associated with cardiovascular disease. What statistical problem might smoking represent?
why_correct: A confounder is associated with both the exposure and outcome and can distort the apparent relationship between them.

why_others_wrong.B: Randomisation is a method used in trials to distribute confounders evenly between groups, not a problem that distorts an observed association.
why_others_wrong.C: Blinding prevents knowledge of allocation influencing behaviour or assessment and does not describe a third factor linked to exposure and outcome.
why_others_wrong.D: Precision refers to the random error around an estimate, whereas smoking here introduces systematic distortion of the coffee association.
why_others_wrong.E: External validity concerns whether results apply to other populations, whereas smoking here distorts the association within the study itself.

exam_trap: Candidates may choose external validity because the association seems untrustworthy, but smoking distorts the association within this study itself, which is confounding, not a generalisability problem.
takeaway: Confounder = third factor distorting exposure–outcome relationship.
source: [CEBM].
thinking: Smoking linked to coffee drinking (exposure) ↓ smoking independently causes cardiovascular disease (outcome) ↓ not on the causal pathway ↓ distorts the coffee association ↓ Confounding
pearl: Confounding can be handled at the design stage by randomisation, restriction or matching, and at analysis by stratification or multivariable adjustment; only randomisation deals with unknown confounders.

subject: Statistics & evidence-based medicine
title: Effect modification
stem: A treatment appears highly effective in younger patients but has little effect in older patients, and this difference persists after appropriate analysis. Which concept describes a genuine difference in treatment effect between subgroups?
why_correct: Effect modification occurs when the effect of an exposure or intervention genuinely differs according to the level of another variable.

why_others_wrong.A: Confounding is a distortion of an association by a third variable that should be controlled away, whereas here the subgroup difference is genuine and persists after analysis.
why_others_wrong.C: Recall bias arises when participants remember past exposures differently according to outcome status, typically in case-control studies, not in comparing treatment effects by age.
why_others_wrong.D: Selection bias results from systematic differences in how participants enter or remain in a study, not from a real variation in treatment effect across age groups.
why_others_wrong.E: Measurement error is inaccuracy in recording variables; it would not produce a genuine, persisting difference in effect between younger and older patients.

exam_trap: Confounding is a distortion that should be controlled; effect modification can represent a real difference that should be reported rather than simply eliminated.
takeaway: Different true effects in subgroups → effect modification.
source: [CEBM].
thinking: Treatment effect differs by age ↓ difference persists after appropriate analysis ↓ not a distortion to be removed ↓ the effect genuinely varies by subgroup ↓ Effect modification
pearl: Subgroup effects should be prespecified and tested formally for interaction; unplanned subgroup analyses frequently produce spurious differences by chance.

subject: Research methods & screening
title: Allocation concealment
stem: In a randomised trial, the investigator enrolling the next participant can see which treatment allocation will be assigned before deciding whether to enrol them. What important methodological protection has been compromised?
why_correct: Allocation concealment prevents those recruiting participants from knowing the upcoming assignment and selectively influencing recruitment.

why_others_wrong.B: Blinding of outcome assessors protects outcome measurement after allocation, whereas the problem here arises before enrolment when the recruiter sees the next assignment.
why_others_wrong.C: Intention-to-treat analysis concerns analysing participants in their randomised groups and does not govern foreknowledge of allocation at recruitment.
why_others_wrong.D: External validity concerns generalising results to other populations, not the recruiter's ability to foresee and influence treatment allocation.
why_others_wrong.E: Publishing the protocol improves transparency about planned methods but does not stop a recruiter seeing the upcoming allocation.

exam_trap: Allocation concealment occurs before/during enrolment. Blinding generally concerns knowledge of treatment after allocation.
takeaway: Conceal the next allocation from recruiters → reduce selection bias.
source: [CEBM].
thinking: Recruiter can see the next allocation ↓ can choose whether to enrol the patient ↓ problem arises before enrolment ↓ Allocation concealment
pearl: Allocation concealment is possible in every trial, even surgical trials where blinding is impossible, using central telephone or web randomisation or sealed opaque sequentially numbered envelopes.

subject: Research methods & screening
title: Blinding
stem: In a clinical trial, participants and investigators are unaware of which treatment each participant receives. What methodological feature is being described?
why_correct: Blinding prevents knowledge of treatment assignment from influencing participant behaviour, treatment delivery or outcome assessment, depending on who is blinded.

why_others_wrong.A: Randomisation is the chance-based allocation of participants to groups; it does not by itself stop participants or investigators knowing the treatment received.
why_others_wrong.C: Allocation concealment hides the upcoming assignment from recruiters until enrolment, whereas the stem describes concealing treatment after allocation.
why_others_wrong.D: Stratification balances important prognostic factors during randomisation and does not keep participants or investigators unaware of treatment.
why_others_wrong.E: Intention-to-treat analysis keeps participants in their randomised groups at analysis and says nothing about whether treatment is concealed.

exam_trap: Allocation concealment is the commonest wrong pick; it hides the upcoming assignment before enrolment, whereas blinding hides the treatment received after allocation.
takeaway: Not knowing treatment allocation → blinding.
source: [CEBM].
thinking: Participants unaware of their treatment ↓ investigators also unaware ↓ knowledge concealed after allocation ↓ Blinding
pearl: In surgical trials the surgeon usually cannot be blinded, but patients and outcome assessors often can be, for example with identical dressings over different incisions.

subject: Research methods & screening
title: Intention-to-treat analysis
stem: In a randomised controlled trial, several participants assigned to the intervention stop taking it and switch to standard treatment. For the primary analysis, they remain analysed in their originally allocated group. What principle is being used?
why_correct: Intention-to-treat analysis retains participants in the groups to which they were originally randomised, regardless of adherence or treatment changes, preserving the benefits of randomisation.

why_others_wrong.A: Per-protocol analysis includes only participants who adhered to their allocated treatment, so those who switched would be excluded rather than retained.
why_others_wrong.C: As-treated analysis groups participants by the treatment actually received, which would move the switchers into the standard treatment group.
why_others_wrong.D: Subgroup analysis examines effects within particular participant categories and does not describe how non-adherent participants are handled.
why_others_wrong.E: Interim analysis is a planned look at accumulating data before the trial ends, not a rule for which group switchers are analysed in.

exam_trap: As-treated analysis is a tempting choice because switchers did receive standard care, but it regroups by treatment actually received, breaking randomisation; analysing by original allocation is intention to treat.
takeaway: Analyse according to original allocation → intention to treat.
source: [CEBM].
thinking: Participants switch from the intervention to standard treatment ↓ still analysed in originally allocated group ↓ preserves randomisation ↓ Intention-to-treat analysis
pearl: Intention-to-treat tends to dilute differences towards the null, which makes it conservative for superiority trials; non-inferiority trials usually report per-protocol analysis alongside it.

subject: Research methods & screening
title: Attrition bias
stem: A randomised trial begins with equal groups, but 30% of participants in the intervention arm are lost to follow-up compared with 5% in the control arm. What problem is most concerning?
why_correct: Unequal loss to follow-up can distort the comparison between groups, particularly if losses are related to treatment or outcome.

why_others_wrong.B: Recall bias concerns differential memory of past exposures, typically in case-control studies, not unequal loss to follow-up in a trial.
why_others_wrong.C: Lead-time bias is an artefact of earlier diagnosis in screening, not a consequence of participants dropping out of trial arms.
why_others_wrong.D: Spectrum bias affects diagnostic accuracy studies with unrepresentative populations and does not describe differential dropout between randomised groups.
why_others_wrong.E: Publication bias concerns selective publication of whole studies, not missing outcome data within one trial.

exam_trap: Recall bias is sometimes chosen because data are incomplete, but recall bias concerns memory of past exposures; 30% versus 5% loss to follow-up after randomisation is attrition bias.
takeaway: Unequal loss to follow-up → attrition bias.
source: [CEBM].
thinking: Equal groups at randomisation ↓ 30% versus 5% lost to follow-up ↓ unequal dropout may relate to treatment or outcome ↓ Attrition bias
pearl: Losses above about one-fifth, or losses that differ between arms, should prompt sensitivity analyses such as worst-case imputation to test whether conclusions hold.

subject: Research methods & screening
title: Publication bias
stem: A systematic review finds mainly positive studies supporting an intervention, but investigators suspect that several negative studies were never published. What form of bias is this?
why_correct: Studies with positive or statistically significant findings may be more likely to be published than studies with negative or inconclusive results. CEBM identifies funnel plots as one method used to explore whether results in a systematic review may have been affected by publication bias.

why_others_wrong.B: Recall bias arises from differential remembering of past exposures by participants, not from unpublished studies missing from a review.
why_others_wrong.C: Selection bias within a cohort concerns how participants enter a single study, whereas the concern here is which studies reach the literature.
why_others_wrong.D: Measurement bias results from systematic error in how exposures or outcomes are measured within a study, not from non-publication of negative studies.
why_others_wrong.E: Spectrum bias affects diagnostic accuracy when the tested population is unrepresentative and does not explain missing negative studies in a review.

exam_trap: Selection bias within a cohort is a distractor because studies were selectively available, but that term describes participant entry into one study, not missing studies in the literature.
takeaway: Missing negative studies → publication bias.
source: [CEBM].
thinking: Systematic review finds mostly positive studies ↓ negative studies suspected never published ↓ selective publication of results ↓ Publication bias
pearl: A funnel plot of effect size against study precision that is asymmetrical suggests small negative studies are missing; prospective trial registration helps reduce publication bias.

subject: Statistics & evidence-based medicine
title: P value
stem: A trial reports p = 0.03 for the difference between two treatments. Which interpretation is most accurate?

options.A: There is a 3% probability that the null hypothesis is true
options.B: There is a 97% probability that the treatment works
options.C: If the null hypothesis were true, results at least this extreme would have a probability of approximately 3%
options.D: The treatment effect is clinically important
options.E: The result is free from bias

correct_answer: C. If the null hypothesis were true, results at least this extreme would have a probability of approximately 3%
why_correct: A p-value describes the probability of observing a result at least as extreme as the observed result under the assumption that the null hypothesis is true. It does NOT give the probability that the null hypothesis is true or that the treatment is effective. CEBM explicitly warns against interpreting a p-value as the probability that a result is right or wrong.

why_others_wrong.A: The p-value is calculated assuming the null hypothesis is true, so it cannot give the probability that the null hypothesis itself is true.
why_others_wrong.B: A p-value of 0.03 does not translate into a 97% probability that the treatment works; that is a posterior probability a p-value does not provide.
why_others_wrong.D: A p-value says nothing about the size of the effect, so clinical importance must be judged from the effect estimate and its confidence interval.
why_others_wrong.E: A small p-value reflects random error only and offers no protection against systematic error such as selection bias or confounding.

exam_trap: The commonest error is choosing that there is a 3% probability the null hypothesis is true; a p-value assumes the null is true and cannot give its probability.
takeaway: p-value ≠ probability that the hypothesis is true.
source: [CEBM].
thinking: p = 0.03 ↓ p-value is calculated assuming the null hypothesis is true ↓ it is the probability of data at least this extreme under the null ↓ If the null hypothesis were true, results at least this extreme would have a probability of approximately 3%
pearl: The 0.05 cut-off is an arbitrary convention; testing many outcomes or subgroups inflates the chance of at least one false-positive result unless corrections for multiple comparisons are made.

subject: Statistics & evidence-based medicine
title: Statistical versus clinical significance
stem: A trial finds a statistically significant reduction in hospital stay of 0.1 days with a new intervention. The p-value is <0.001. Which statement is most appropriate?

options.A: The intervention must be clinically important
options.B: Statistical significance automatically establishes clinical importance
options.C: The result may be statistically significant without representing a clinically important benefit
options.D: The result proves absence of bias
options.E: The intervention should automatically replace standard care

correct_answer: C. The result may be statistically significant without representing a clinically important benefit
why_correct: Statistical significance does not determine whether the magnitude of an effect is clinically meaningful. The clinical importance of an effect must be interpreted in context, including its size, confidence interval, harms, costs and patient relevance; a 0.1-day reduction in stay is unlikely to matter to patients however small the p-value.

why_others_wrong.A: A 0.1-day reduction in stay is very small, and a tiny p-value does not make such a modest effect clinically important.
why_others_wrong.B: Statistical significance reflects how unlikely the result is under the null hypothesis, not whether the size of the effect matters to patients.
why_others_wrong.D: A p-value addresses random error only; it cannot show that a study is free from bias in design or conduct.
why_others_wrong.E: Replacing standard care depends on effect size, harms, costs and patient relevance, not on statistical significance of a 0.1-day difference.

exam_trap: Candidates impressed by p <0.001 may choose that the intervention must be clinically important, but a tiny p-value cannot turn a 0.1-day benefit into a meaningful one.
takeaway: Statistically significant ≠ clinically important.
source: [CEBM].
thinking: Stay reduced by only 0.1 days ↓ p <0.001 shows the result is unlikely by chance ↓ significance does not measure effect size ↓ The result may be statistically significant without representing a clinically important benefit
pearl: Trials should be powered on a minimal clinically important difference agreed in advance, so that a significant result is also one that matters to patients.

subject: Statistics & evidence-based medicine
title: Confidence interval
stem: A trial reports a relative risk of 0.80 with a 95% confidence interval of 0.60–1.10. Which conclusion is most appropriate regarding statistical significance at the conventional 5% level?

options.C: The confidence interval includes the null value, so statistical significance is not demonstrated
options.D: The treatment definitely has no effect
options.E: The treatment definitely reduces risk by 20%

correct_answer: C. The confidence interval includes the null value, so statistical significance is not demonstrated
why_correct: For a ratio measure such as relative risk, the null value is 1. Because the 95% CI crosses 1, the result is not statistically significant at the conventional 5% level.

why_others_wrong.A: A statistically significant benefit would need the whole 95% interval below 1, but the upper limit of 1.10 crosses the null value.
why_others_wrong.B: Statistically significant harm would need the whole 95% interval above 1, but most of the interval, including the point estimate of 0.80, lies below 1.
why_others_wrong.D: An interval from 0.60 to 1.10 includes important benefit as well as no effect, so lack of significance does not demonstrate absence of effect.
why_others_wrong.E: The point estimate of 0.80 suggests a 20% relative reduction, but the interval is compatible with values from a 40% reduction to a 10% increase.

exam_trap: Do not say the treatment "has no effect". The study may simply be insufficiently precise to exclude clinically important effects.
takeaway: RR/OR/HR → null value = 1.
source: [CEBM].
thinking: Ratio measure, so the null value is 1 ↓ 95% CI 0.60 to 1.10 crosses 1 ↓ not significant at the 5% level ↓ The confidence interval includes the null value, so statistical significance is not demonstrated
