pearl: If the 95% confidence interval for a ratio excludes 1, the corresponding two-sided p-value is below 0.05, so the interval conveys both significance and the plausible size of effect.

subject: Statistics & evidence-based medicine
topic: Confidence interval for an absolute difference
title: Confidence interval for an absolute difference
stem: A trial reports an absolute reduction in complications of 4%, with a 95% confidence interval from −1% to 9%. What does this indicate?

options.C: The confidence interval includes no difference, so a statistically significant benefit is not demonstrated
options.D: The treatment has exactly a 4% benefit in every patient

correct_answer: C. The confidence interval includes no difference, so a statistically significant benefit is not demonstrated
why_correct: For an absolute difference, the null value is 0. Because the CI spans zero, the data are compatible with benefit, no difference and a small degree of harm.

why_others_wrong.A: The interval extends down to minus 1%, which includes no difference and slight harm, so a definite reduction is not established.
why_others_wrong.B: Most of the interval, and the point estimate of 4%, lies on the side of benefit, so the data do not show that complications increase.
why_others_wrong.D: A 4% absolute reduction is an average group-level estimate with uncertainty; it does not mean every patient gains exactly the same benefit.
why_others_wrong.E: Equivalence requires the interval to lie within prespecified equivalence margins, and an interval stretching to a 9% benefit does not demonstrate that.

exam_trap: Candidates focus on the 4% point estimate and choose a definite reduction, ignoring that the interval reaches minus 1% and therefore includes zero, the null value for a difference.
takeaway: Difference measure → null = 0. Ratio measure → null = 1.
source: [CEBM].
thinking: Absolute difference, so the null value is 0 ↓ 95% CI −1% to 9% spans zero ↓ compatible with benefit, no difference or slight harm ↓ The confidence interval includes no difference, so a statistically significant benefit is not demonstrated
pearl: Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence: a wide interval like this calls for a larger or pooled study rather than a conclusion that the treatment is ineffective.

subject: Statistics & evidence-based medicine
title: Precision
stem: Two studies estimate the effect of the same treatment. Study A: RR 0.80 (95% CI 0.78–0.82) Study B: RR 0.80 (95% CI 0.50–1.30) Which study provides the more precise estimate?

options.D: Precision cannot be assessed from a confidence interval

why_correct: Study A has a much narrower confidence interval and therefore provides a more precise estimate of the effect. CEBM notes that a wide confidence interval indicates greater uncertainty around the estimated effect.

why_others_wrong.B: Study B has a much wider interval (0.50 to 1.30), indicating greater uncertainty and therefore less precision, despite the same point estimate.
why_others_wrong.C: Identical point estimates do not mean equal precision; precision is reflected in interval width, which differs greatly between the studies.
why_others_wrong.D: The width of a confidence interval is the standard way of judging precision, so it can be assessed directly from these figures.
why_others_wrong.E: Both studies report a point estimate of RR 0.80 with a confidence interval, so each clearly provides an estimate.

exam_trap: Some assume identical point estimates mean equal precision, but precision is shown by interval width, and Study B's 0.50 to 1.30 interval is very wide.
takeaway: Narrow CI → greater precision. Wide CI → greater uncertainty.
source: [CEBM].
thinking: Same point estimate RR 0.80 in both studies ↓ precision is judged by confidence interval width ↓ Study A interval 0.78 to 0.82 is far narrower ↓ Study A
pearl: Confidence interval width narrows mainly with larger sample size and more events, which is why large multicentre trials and meta-analyses give more precise estimates.

subject: Statistics & evidence-based medicine
title: Type I error
stem: A researcher concludes that a new treatment is effective when, in reality, there is no true treatment effect. What type of statistical error has occurred?
why_correct: A Type I error is a false-positive conclusion: rejecting the null hypothesis when it is actually true.

why_others_wrong.B: A Type II error is the opposite: failing to detect a treatment effect that truly exists, a false-negative conclusion.
why_others_wrong.C: Selection bias is a systematic error in how participants are chosen or retained, not a false-positive error of hypothesis testing.
why_others_wrong.D: Recall bias is differential recollection of past exposures by participants and is not a category of statistical inference error.
why_others_wrong.E: Confounding is distortion of an association by a third variable; it can produce a spurious finding but is not itself a Type I or II error.

exam_trap: Candidates often swap the two errors; a Type II error is missing a real effect, whereas concluding an effect exists when none does is a Type I error.
takeaway: Type I = false positive.
source: [CEBM].
thinking: Concludes treatment works ↓ in reality there is no effect ↓ null hypothesis wrongly rejected ↓ false positive ↓ Type I error
pearl: The probability of a Type I error is set by the significance level alpha, conventionally 0.05, and rises with multiple testing unless a correction is applied.

subject: Statistics & evidence-based medicine
title: Type II error
stem: A study fails to detect a genuine treatment effect. Which statistical error may have occurred?
why_correct: A Type II error is a false-negative conclusion: failing to reject the null hypothesis when a real effect exists.

why_others_wrong.A: A Type I error is a false-positive conclusion, finding an effect that does not exist, which is the reverse of this scenario.
why_others_wrong.C: Publication bias concerns which studies get published across a body of evidence, not an error within a single study's hypothesis test.
why_others_wrong.D: Recall bias arises from inaccurate participant recollection of exposures and is not a statistical error in failing to detect an effect.
why_others_wrong.E: Spectrum bias affects diagnostic accuracy estimates when the study population does not reflect the clinical case mix, not treatment-effect testing.

exam_trap: Type I error is the tempting swap, but it is a false-positive finding; failing to detect a real effect is a false negative, a Type II error.
takeaway: Type II = false negative.
source: [CEBM].
thinking: A genuine treatment effect exists ↓ the study fails to detect it ↓ null hypothesis wrongly retained ↓ false negative ↓ Type II error
pearl: Type II errors are most often due to an underpowered study; power equals 1 minus beta, and trials are conventionally designed for 80-90% power.

subject: Statistics & evidence-based medicine
title: Statistical power
stem: Which change generally increases the statistical power of a clinical study, assuming other factors remain appropriate?

options.E: Increased variability without increasing sample size

why_correct: Increasing sample size generally reduces random error and increases the ability of a study to detect a true effect.

why_others_wrong.A: A smaller sample increases random error and widens confidence intervals, reducing power to detect a true effect.
why_others_wrong.C: Greater measurement error adds noise to the outcome, increasing variability and reducing the power of the study.
why_others_wrong.D: Greater loss to follow-up reduces the effective sample size and may introduce bias, lowering rather than raising power.
why_others_wrong.E: Increased variability in the outcome with no increase in sample size makes a true difference harder to detect, lowering power.

exam_trap: Loss to follow-up is sometimes thought harmless once recruitment is complete, but it shrinks the analysed sample and can introduce attrition bias, lowering power.
takeaway: More participants generally → greater statistical power.
source: [CEBM].
thinking: Power = ability to detect a true effect ↓ random error falls as sample size rises ↓ smaller samples, more noise or loss to follow-up reduce power ↓ Larger sample size
pearl: Besides sample size, power rises with a larger true effect, lower outcome variability and a less stringent alpha; these are the inputs of a sample-size calculation.

subject: Research methods & screening
title: Audit cycle
stem: A surgical department discovers that only 65% of eligible patients received VTE assessment within the locally agreed standard. The team introduces a change in practice and subsequently measures compliance again. What part of the audit cycle is the repeat measurement?
why_correct: Clinical audit involves measuring current practice against a defined standard, implementing improvement where necessary, and then repeating measurement to determine whether practice has improved.

why_others_wrong.A: Identifying the topic is the first stage of the audit cycle, completed before the initial 65% compliance measurement was made.
why_others_wrong.B: Setting the standard defines the expected level of care and precedes data collection, rather than following the introduced change.
why_others_wrong.C: Implementing change is the step that came before the repeat measurement; the new measurement tests whether that change worked.
why_others_wrong.E: Writing a research hypothesis belongs to research, whereas audit measures practice against an agreed standard and does not test a hypothesis.

exam_trap: Implementing change is sometimes chosen because it immediately precedes the second measurement, but the repeat measurement itself is re-audit, which tests whether the change worked.
takeaway: Measure → compare with standard → change → re-measure = audit cycle.
source: [RCSEng] MRCS candidate information: clinical audit and governance.
thinking: VTE assessment compliance measured against a standard ↓ change in practice introduced ↓ compliance measured again ↓ closes the audit loop ↓ Re-audit
pearl: An audit is only complete when the loop is closed; a single measurement without re-audit after change does not show whether care has improved.

subject: Research methods & screening
title: Audit versus research
stem: A surgical team measures whether current practice meets an established national standard and introduces changes if compliance is poor. What is the primary purpose?

options.B: Determine whether current practice meets a predefined standard
options.D: Establish disease incidence in the population

correct_answer: B. Determine whether current practice meets a predefined standard
why_correct: Clinical audit evaluates current practice against agreed standards and aims to improve quality. Research primarily seeks to generate new knowledge.

why_others_wrong.A: Generating new generalisable knowledge is the primary aim of research, whereas this team is checking practice against an established standard.
why_others_wrong.C: A randomised experiment allocates participants to compare interventions, which is research rather than measuring compliance with a standard.
why_others_wrong.D: Establishing disease incidence is an epidemiological research or surveillance aim, not the purpose of checking compliance with a national standard.
why_others_wrong.E: A laboratory experiment tests hypotheses under controlled conditions, whereas audit evaluates routine clinical practice against a standard.

exam_trap: An audit may generate useful information, but its defining purpose is improvement against a standard rather than discovery of entirely new knowledge.
takeaway: Audit = "Are we doing what we should?" Research = "What new knowledge can we generate?"
source: [RCSEng], MRCS candidate information: clinical audit and research.
thinking: Practice measured against an established national standard ↓ changes made if compliance is poor ↓ quality improvement, not new knowledge ↓ Determine whether current practice meets a predefined standard
pearl: Audit does not usually require research ethics committee approval because it measures existing care against a standard without allocating patients to new interventions.

subject: Research methods & screening
title: Systematic review
stem: Researchers identify all relevant studies addressing a focused clinical question using a predefined search strategy and explicit inclusion criteria. They critically appraise the studies and synthesise their findings. What type of evidence synthesis is this?
why_correct: A systematic review uses a predefined and reproducible approach to identify, select and critically appraise relevant evidence addressing a focused question. A meta-analysis may additionally statistically combine results from individual studies when appropriate, but not every systematic review contains a meta-analysis.

why_others_wrong.A: A case report describes one or a few individual patients and does not systematically search for and appraise all relevant studies.
why_others_wrong.B: A narrative opinion summarises evidence selectively without a predefined search strategy or explicit inclusion criteria, so it is open to bias.
why_others_wrong.D: A cross-sectional survey collects primary data from participants at one time point, rather than synthesising the findings of existing studies.
why_others_wrong.E: A case-control study is a primary observational design comparing exposures between cases and controls, not a synthesis of published studies.

exam_trap: Candidates may hesitate because a meta-analysis is not mentioned, but a systematic review does not need statistical pooling; a narrative opinion lacks the predefined search and inclusion criteria.
takeaway: Systematic review = systematic identification + selection + appraisal + synthesis of evidence.
source: [CEBM].
thinking: Focused question ↓ predefined search strategy and explicit inclusion criteria ↓ studies critically appraised and synthesised ↓ Systematic review
pearl: A meta-analysis pools results statistically and displays them in a forest plot; heterogeneity between studies is assessed with measures such as the I-squared statistic.

subject: Research methods & screening
title: Qualitative versus quantitative research
stem: A surgical team wants to explore why some patients decline elective colorectal cancer surgery despite being offered the same information. Which research approach is most appropriate if the primary aim is to understand patients’ experiences and reasons in depth?
why_correct: Qualitative research explores experiences, perceptions, beliefs, attitudes and reasons, typically collecting data through in-depth interviews or focus groups and analysing it with methods such as thematic analysis.

why_others_wrong.A: A randomised controlled trial measures the effect of an intervention on outcomes, not patients' experiences and reasons for declining surgery.
why_others_wrong.C: A case-control study tests associations between past exposures and an outcome numerically and cannot explore patients' reasons in depth.
why_others_wrong.D: A cohort study follows groups over time to measure associations with outcomes, rather than exploring individual perceptions and decision-making.
why_others_wrong.E: An ecological study analyses population-level aggregate data and cannot capture individual patients' experiences or reasons for their choices.

exam_trap: Candidates pick a randomised controlled trial or cohort study as stronger evidence, but those measure outcomes numerically; exploring reasons and experiences in depth requires qualitative methods.
takeaway: “Why?” and “What is the experience?” → think qualitative research.
source: RCS England, MRCS Candidate Information Pack, research and evidence-based practice content, January 2020.
thinking: Aim is to understand why patients decline surgery ↓ experiences and reasons explored in depth ↓ interviews or focus groups, not numbers ↓ Qualitative research
pearl: Qualitative studies use purposive rather than random sampling and continue recruiting until thematic saturation, when new interviews stop producing new themes.

subject: Statistics & evidence-based medicine
title: Null hypothesis
stem: A randomised trial compares two postoperative analgesic regimens. The investigators state that there is no difference in mean postoperative pain score between the two groups. What does this statement represent?
why_correct: The null hypothesis generally states that there is no difference or no association between the groups being compared.

why_others_wrong.A: The alternative hypothesis states that a difference in mean pain score does exist between the regimens, the opposite of this statement.
why_others_wrong.C: A Type II error is a mistaken conclusion after testing, failing to detect a true difference, not a statement made before analysis.
why_others_wrong.D: A confidence interval is a range of plausible values for an estimated effect, not a statement of no difference between groups.
why_others_wrong.E: Effect modification describes a treatment effect that varies across subgroups, not a formal statement of no difference.

exam_trap: Candidates sometimes choose the alternative hypothesis, but that states a difference exists; a statement of no difference between regimens is the null hypothesis.
takeaway: Null hypothesis = “no difference/no association.”
source: [CEBM].
thinking: Statement of no difference in mean pain score ↓ made before testing ↓ the formal hypothesis tested statistically ↓ Null hypothesis
pearl: Hypothesis tests aim to reject the null; failure to reject it does not prove the two regimens are equivalent, which requires a specifically designed equivalence trial.

subject: Research methods & screening
title: Primary outcome
stem: A randomised trial is designed to determine whether a new surgical dressing reduces surgical-site infection. The protocol specifies surgical-site infection at 30 days as the main outcome used to determine the trial's principal conclusion. What is this outcome?
why_correct: The primary outcome is the prespecified main outcome used to address the principal research question.

why_others_wrong.A: A surrogate outcome is a biomarker substituting for a patient-important outcome, whereas surgical-site infection is itself a clinical outcome.
why_others_wrong.B: A secondary outcome is prespecified but supplementary; the stem states this outcome determines the trial's principal conclusion.
why_others_wrong.D: A composite confounder is not a recognised outcome type; confounders are third factors distorting associations, not the trial's main endpoint.
why_others_wrong.E: An exploratory variable is examined to generate hypotheses, not prespecified as the main outcome answering the principal research question.

exam_trap: Do not choose an outcome because it is clinically interesting after seeing the results. Primary outcomes should be specified in advance.
takeaway: Primary outcome = the trial's prespecified principal endpoint.
source: [GRP6].
thinking: Main outcome specified in the protocol ↓ used to determine the principal conclusion ↓ prespecified main endpoint ↓ Primary outcome
pearl: The sample size calculation is based on the primary outcome, so a trial is often underpowered for its secondary outcomes and these should be interpreted cautiously.

subject: Research methods & screening
title: Surrogate endpoint
stem: A cardiovascular trial assesses whether a drug reduces LDL cholesterol but does not directly assess myocardial infarction, stroke or cardiovascular mortality. LDL cholesterol is being used as what type of endpoint?
why_correct: A surrogate endpoint is a biological or laboratory measure used as a substitute for a clinically meaningful outcome.

why_others_wrong.A: A hard clinical endpoint is a patient-important event such as myocardial infarction or death, which the stem states this trial does not assess.
why_others_wrong.C: A composite endpoint combines several clinical events into one measure, whereas LDL cholesterol is a single laboratory marker.
why_others_wrong.D: A safety endpoint captures adverse effects of treatment, whereas LDL cholesterol here is used to judge the drug's efficacy.
why_others_wrong.E: A patient-reported endpoint is reported directly by patients, such as symptoms or quality of life, not a measured blood lipid level.

exam_trap: A surrogate improving does not automatically prove that patients have better clinical outcomes.
takeaway: Biomarker used instead of a patient-important outcome → surrogate endpoint.
source: [GRP6].
thinking: LDL cholesterol measured ↓ clinical events not directly assessed ↓ laboratory marker substitutes for a patient-important outcome ↓ Surrogate endpoint
pearl: Surrogate endpoints can mislead: some drugs improve a biomarker such as an arrhythmia count or lipid level yet fail to reduce, or even increase, clinical events.

subject: Research methods & screening
title: Composite endpoint
stem: A trial defines its primary endpoint as the first occurrence of myocardial infarction, stroke or cardiovascular death. What type of endpoint is this?
why_correct: A composite endpoint combines two or more individual outcomes into a single outcome measure.

why_others_wrong.A: A surrogate endpoint is a biomarker standing in for clinical events, whereas myocardial infarction, stroke and death are clinical events themselves.
why_others_wrong.C: A continuous endpoint is measured on a numerical scale, whereas first occurrence of these events is a binary or time-to-event outcome.
why_others_wrong.D: A laboratory endpoint is a blood or tissue measurement, whereas the stem lists clinical events rather than test results.
why_others_wrong.E: Per-protocol describes an analysis population of adherent participants, not a type of endpoint combining several outcomes.

exam_trap: A statistically significant composite result does not necessarily mean that every component is significantly affected.
takeaway: Several clinically defined events combined into one endpoint = composite endpoint.
source: [GRP6].
thinking: Myocardial infarction, stroke or cardiovascular death ↓ first occurrence of any one counts ↓ several clinical events combined into one measure ↓ Composite endpoint
pearl: Composite endpoints increase event rates and therefore statistical power, but the overall effect may be driven by the least serious component, so each component should be reported separately.

subject: Statistics & evidence-based medicine
topic: Sample size and clinically important difference
title: Sample size and clinically important difference
stem: Investigators are planning a randomised trial. Which factor generally influences the sample size required when comparing two treatment groups?

options.A: The number of investigators on the trial team
options.B: The expected variability and clinically important difference
options.D: The journal planned for publication of the results

correct_answer: B. The expected variability and clinically important difference
why_correct: Sample-size calculations depend on factors including the anticipated effect size or clinically important difference, variability, desired power and significance level.

why_others_wrong.A: The number of investigators affects workload and logistics, not the number of participants needed, which depends on effect size, variability, power and significance level.
why_others_wrong.C: Recruitment rate determines how long the trial takes to reach its target, not the target sample size itself, which is set by effect size, variability, power and alpha.
why_others_wrong.D: Where the results will be published has no bearing on the number of participants needed to detect a clinically important difference.
why_others_wrong.E: Being single-centre does not of itself determine the required number; the core inputs are expected difference, variability, power and significance level.

exam_trap: A statistically significant difference is not the same as a clinically important difference.
takeaway: Smaller expected differences generally require larger samples to detect reliably.
source: [GRP6].
thinking: Planning a two-group trial ↓ sample size depends on effect size, variability, power and significance level ↓ smaller differences or more variable outcomes need more participants ↓ logistics and publication plans do not change the number needed ↓ The expected variability and clinically important difference
pearl: Because sample size varies with the inverse square of the effect size, halving the difference to be detected roughly quadruples the number of participants needed.

subject: Research methods & screening
title: Stratified randomisation
stem: A multicentre trial is concerned that an important prognostic factor, such as tumour stage, may become unevenly distributed between treatment groups. Which randomisation strategy can help ensure balance for that factor?
why_correct: Stratified randomisation separates participants into predefined strata based on important characteristics and randomises within those strata.

why_others_wrong.B: Historical control allocation compares new patients with past patients, which increases rather than reduces imbalance and involves no randomisation.
why_others_wrong.C: Convenience sampling recruits whoever is readily available and concerns sampling, not balanced allocation of a prognostic factor between arms.
why_others_wrong.D: Case matching after treatment is a retrospective observational adjustment, not a randomisation strategy that ensures balance at allocation.
why_others_wrong.E: Ecological allocation is not a recognised randomisation method and would not balance tumour stage between individual treatment groups.

exam_trap: Stratification is performed as part of the allocation strategy; it is not the same as retrospectively adjusting an observational study.
takeaway: Important prognostic factor → consider stratification during randomisation.
source: [GRP6].
thinking: Concern about uneven distribution of tumour stage ↓ prognostic factor must be balanced ↓ randomise separately within strata of that factor ↓ Stratified randomisation
pearl: Block randomisation within strata is commonly used in multicentre trials to keep group sizes balanced at each centre; minimisation is an alternative when there are many factors.

subject: Research methods & screening
title: Crossover trial
stem: Patients with a stable chronic condition are randomly allocated to treatment A or treatment B and subsequently receive the alternative treatment after a defined period. Each participant therefore receives both interventions. What type of design is this?
why_correct: In a crossover trial, participants receive more than one intervention sequentially, allowing each participant to act as their own comparator.

why_others_wrong.A: In a parallel-group trial each participant receives one intervention only, whereas here every participant receives both treatments in sequence.
why_others_wrong.C: A case-control study is observational and compares past exposures between people with and without an outcome, with no allocated treatments.
why_others_wrong.D: An ecological study analyses aggregate population data and does not give individual participants sequential interventions.
why_others_wrong.E: A diagnostic accuracy study compares a test with a reference standard, rather than comparing two treatments within the same participants.

exam_trap: Crossover designs are unsuitable when the first intervention has a lasting effect that could influence the subsequent treatment period.
takeaway: Same patient receives A and B sequentially → crossover trial.
source: [GRP6].
thinking: Stable chronic condition ↓ randomised to A or B then switched ↓ each participant receives both treatments ↓ participant acts as own control ↓ Crossover trial
pearl: A washout period between treatments limits carry-over effects; crossover designs suit stable chronic conditions but not curable diseases or treatments with lasting effects.

subject: Research methods & screening
title: Cluster randomised trial
stem: A study randomises entire general practices to either an educational intervention or usual care rather than randomising individual patients. What type of trial is this?
why_correct: The unit of randomisation is a group or cluster, such as a practice, hospital or geographical area, rather than an individual participant.

why_others_wrong.A: A crossover trial gives each participant both interventions in sequence, whereas here each practice receives one arm without switching.
why_others_wrong.C: A case-control study is observational and selects by outcome status, whereas here practices are randomly allocated to an intervention.
why_others_wrong.D: A case series describes a group of patients with a condition or treatment and has no randomised comparison group.
why_others_wrong.E: A diagnostic cohort study evaluates test accuracy against a reference standard, not the effect of an educational intervention allocated to practices.

exam_trap: The individual patients may provide the outcome data, but the allocation occurred at cluster level.
takeaway: Randomised by practice/hospital/group → cluster randomised trial.
source: [GRP6].
thinking: Whole general practices randomised ↓ unit of allocation is a group, not an individual ↓ educational intervention suits group delivery ↓ Cluster randomised trial
pearl: Patients within one cluster tend to be similar, so cluster trials need a larger sample size, adjusted using the intracluster correlation coefficient, and analysis must account for clustering.

subject: Research methods & screening
title: Non-inferiority trial
stem: A new surgical technique is expected to be cheaper and quicker than the standard technique. Investigators want to determine whether its clinical effectiveness is not unacceptably worse than the standard technique. What type of trial is most appropriate?
why_correct: A non-inferiority trial tests whether a new intervention is not worse than the comparator by more than a prespecified clinically acceptable margin.

why_others_wrong.A: A superiority trial seeks to show the new technique is better, whereas the aim here is to show it is not unacceptably worse.
why_others_wrong.C: A case-control study is observational and cannot provide a prespecified margin-based comparison of two surgical techniques.
why_others_wrong.D: A diagnostic accuracy study assesses how well a test identifies disease, not whether a treatment's effectiveness is acceptably close to standard.
why_others_wrong.E: An ecological study uses aggregate population data and cannot compare clinical effectiveness between individually treated patients.

exam_trap: Candidates pick a superiority trial because a new technique is being tested, but the aim here is to show it is not unacceptably worse, which needs a prespecified non-inferiority margin.
takeaway: New treatment expected to have other advantages but must not be clinically unacceptably worse → non-inferiority design.
source: [GRP6].
thinking: New technique is cheaper and quicker ↓ aim is to show it is not unacceptably worse ↓ prespecified non-inferiority margin ↓ Non-inferiority trial
pearl: Non-inferiority is shown when the confidence interval for the difference lies entirely within the prespecified margin; a non-significant superiority trial cannot be used to claim non-inferiority.

subject: Research methods & screening
title: Screening versus diagnosis
stem: Which statement best describes screening?

options.A: It is performed only after symptoms develop
options.B: It identifies apparently healthy people who may have an increased chance of a condition
options.C: It always establishes a definitive diagnosis
options.E: It is only appropriate for hospital inpatients

correct_answer: B. It identifies apparently healthy people who may have an increased chance of a condition
why_correct: The UK National Screening Committee defines screening as identifying apparently healthy people who may have an increased chance of disease or another condition, followed by further assessment where appropriate.

why_others_wrong.A: Testing after symptoms develop is diagnostic assessment; screening is offered to apparently healthy people before symptoms appear.
why_others_wrong.C: Screening identifies people at increased chance of a condition, and a positive result usually needs further diagnostic testing to confirm disease.
why_others_wrong.D: Screening tests produce false-positive results, which are a recognised harm of screening programmes rather than something screening removes.
why_others_wrong.E: Population screening is typically offered to apparently healthy people in the community, not restricted to hospital inpatients.

exam_trap: Candidates choose the option that screening establishes a diagnosis, but a positive screen only indicates increased chance; confirmation needs diagnostic testing, and false positives are an accepted harm.
takeaway: Screening identifies increased chance; diagnostic testing establishes or excludes disease.
source: [UKNSC], Principles of screening, updated 11 July 2025.
thinking: Screening targets apparently healthy people ↓ identifies increased chance of a condition ↓ positive result needs further diagnostic assessment ↓ Identifies apparently healthy people who may have an increased chance of a condition
pearl: Screening tests prioritise high sensitivity, accepting some false positives, because positives are followed by more specific diagnostic tests such as colonoscopy after a positive faecal immunochemical test.

subject: Research methods & screening
title: Appropriate screening programme
stem: Which feature would support consideration of a population screening programme?

options.A: The disease has no effective intervention
options.D: Screening causes substantial harm with no measurable benefit
options.E: No diagnostic pathway exists after a positive result

why_correct: UK NSC criteria require evidence that earlier intervention at a presymptomatic stage provides better outcomes than usual care, together with an appropriate test, diagnostic pathway and treatment.

why_others_wrong.A: Without an effective intervention, early detection cannot improve outcomes, so this argues against rather than for a screening programme.
why_others_wrong.B: An unreliable test would produce misleading results, whereas UK NSC criteria require a simple, safe, precise and validated screening test.
why_others_wrong.D: Screening is justified when benefits outweigh harms; substantial harm with no measurable benefit is a clear reason not to screen.
why_others_wrong.E: UK NSC criteria require an agreed diagnostic pathway for people who screen positive, so its absence argues against screening.

exam_trap: Candidates may pick 'the disease has no effective intervention' thinking serious untreatable disease merits screening, but without effective treatment earlier detection cannot improve outcomes, which is the core UK NSC requirement.
takeaway: Screening needs a complete pathway: condition → test → diagnosis → effective intervention → overall benefit.
source: [UKNSC], criteria for population screening, updated 29 September 2022.
thinking: UK NSC criteria for screening ↓ need a reliable test, diagnostic pathway and effective treatment ↓ benefit must come from earlier detection ↓ Earlier detection improves outcomes
pearl: The UK NSC criteria build on classic WHO screening principles: an important condition, a recognisable latent stage, an acceptable test and an effective treatment.

subject: Research methods & screening
title: Lead-time bias
stem: A screening programme detects cancer earlier. Patients subsequently appear to survive for longer from the date of diagnosis, but mortality has not changed. Which bias could explain this apparent improvement?
why_correct: Earlier diagnosis can increase measured survival time from diagnosis without actually delaying death. Example: Without screening: Diagnosis at year 8 → death at year 10 = 2-year measured survival. With screening: Diagnosis at year 6 → death at year 10 = 4-year measured survival. The patient has not lived longer, but measured survival after diagnosis has increased.

why_others_wrong.A: Recall bias concerns inaccurate remembering of past exposures, not an apparent survival gain produced by diagnosing cancer earlier.
why_others_wrong.C: Selection bias arises from unrepresentative study populations, whereas the stem describes an earlier diagnosis date with unchanged time of death.
why_others_wrong.D: Observer bias occurs when assessors' expectations influence measurement, which does not explain longer survival from diagnosis with unchanged mortality.
why_others_wrong.E: Publication bias concerns selective publication of studies and does not explain why survival from diagnosis lengthens after screening.

exam_trap: Selection bias is a tempting pick because screened people may be healthier, but here death time is unchanged and only diagnosis moved earlier, the hallmark of lead-time bias.
takeaway: Earlier diagnosis + unchanged death time → lead-time bias.
source: [UKNSC] guidance discusses lead-time bias in interpretation of screening outcomes; NHS screening standards updated 2025.
thinking: Screening diagnoses cancer earlier ↓ survival from diagnosis lengthens ↓ time of death and mortality unchanged ↓ survival clock simply started earlier ↓ Lead-time bias
pearl: Screening benefit should be judged by disease-specific mortality in randomised trials rather than survival from diagnosis, which is inflated by lead-time and length-time bias.

subject: Research methods & screening
title: Length-time bias
stem: A cancer screening programme disproportionately detects slow-growing tumours, which naturally have a better prognosis than rapidly growing tumours. What phenomenon can contribute to this apparent improvement in outcomes?
why_correct: Slow-growing tumours generally have a longer preclinical detectable period and are therefore more likely to be identified by periodic screening.

why_others_wrong.A: Lead-time bias concerns bringing the date of diagnosis forward, whereas the stem describes preferential detection of slow-growing tumours.
why_others_wrong.C: Recall bias concerns differential remembering of past exposures and has nothing to do with which tumours periodic screening detects.
why_others_wrong.D: Attrition bias results from unequal loss to follow-up, not from the growth rate of the tumours that screening tends to pick up.
why_others_wrong.E: Performance bias arises from differences in care between trial groups other than the intervention, not from the biology of screen-detected tumours.

exam_trap: Lead-time bias concerns advancing the time of diagnosis; length-time bias concerns preferential detection of slower-growing disease.
takeaway: Slow-growing disease is more likely to enter the screening window → length-time bias.
source: UK government screening methodology describes length-time bias as a source of apparent improvement in survival.
thinking: Screening programme detects tumours periodically ↓ slow-growing tumours have a longer preclinical detectable phase ↓ screening preferentially catches indolent disease ↓ prognosis looks better ↓ Length-time bias
pearl: Interval cancers, those presenting between screening rounds, tend to be faster-growing and more aggressive, which is the clinical counterpart of length-time bias.

subject: Research methods & screening
title: Overdiagnosis
stem: A screening programme detects a tumour that would never have caused symptoms or affected the patient's health during their lifetime. What is this phenomenon called?
why_correct: Overdiagnosis is detection of a condition that would not have caused clinically important disease during the person's lifetime.

why_others_wrong.A: A false negative is a missed condition that is present, whereas here a real tumour was detected but would not have caused harm.
why_others_wrong.B: Lead-time bias is an apparent survival gain from earlier diagnosis of disease that would have progressed, not detection of harmless disease.
why_others_wrong.D: Recall bias concerns inaccurate remembering of past exposures and does not describe detecting a tumour that would never have caused symptoms.
why_others_wrong.E: Under-treatment means failing to treat significant disease adequately, whereas overdiagnosis leads towards unnecessary treatment of harmless disease.

exam_trap: Overdiagnosis is different from a false-positive result: the detected abnormality is real, but it would not have caused harm.
takeaway: Real disease that would never have caused harm → overdiagnosis.
source: [UKNSC]: criteria for appraising the viability, effectiveness and appropriateness of a screening programme.
thinking: Real tumour detected by screening ↓ would never have caused symptoms in the patient's lifetime ↓ not a false positive ↓ Overdiagnosis
pearl: Overdiagnosis is a recognised problem in prostate cancer screening with PSA, where many low-risk tumours are now managed with active surveillance rather than radical treatment.

subject: Research methods & screening
title: Harm from screening
stem: Which is a recognised potential harm of a screening programme?

options.E: Prevention of every future case of disease

why_correct: Screening can produce false-positive results, false reassurance, overdiagnosis, overtreatment and unnecessary follow-up.

why_others_wrong.B: Screening cannot guarantee reduced mortality, and a mortality benefit would be a hoped-for benefit rather than a potential harm.
why_others_wrong.C: Screening often generates additional investigations after positive results, so it tends to increase rather than eliminate unnecessary tests.
why_others_wrong.D: Screening introduces uncertainty through false positives, false negatives and borderline findings, rather than removing all diagnostic uncertainty.
why_others_wrong.E: Screening cannot prevent every future case, and preventing disease would be a benefit rather than a recognised harm.

exam_trap: A screening programme must be judged on the whole pathway, including its harms, rather than only the number of diseases detected.
takeaway: Screening can help and harm; benefit must outweigh harm.
source: [UKNSC], Principles of screening, updated 11 July 2025.
thinking: Question asks for a harm of screening ↓ other options are benefits or impossible claims ↓ positive screens in people without disease ↓ False-positive results
pearl: False positives cause anxiety and invasive follow-up investigations with their own complications, such as bleeding or perforation after colonoscopy in bowel screening.

subject: Research methods & screening
title: Informed choice in screening
stem: A healthy person is invited to participate in a screening programme. Which approach is most consistent with UK National Screening Committee principles?

options.B: The patient should receive balanced information about benefits and harms before deciding
options.C: The clinician should conceal false-positive rates to encourage attendance
options.D: A positive screen should be described as a confirmed diagnosis
options.E: Declining screening should automatically result in removal from routine care

correct_answer: B. The patient should receive balanced information about benefits and harms before deciding
why_correct: The UK NSC describes personal informed choice as a decision based on accessible, accurate, evidence-based information about the benefits and risks of screening.

why_others_wrong.A: UK NSC principles support personal informed choice, so participation in screening is voluntary rather than compulsory.
why_others_wrong.C: Concealing false-positive rates undermines informed choice; the UK NSC requires accurate information about both benefits and harms.
why_others_wrong.D: A positive screening result indicates increased chance of a condition and usually needs further diagnostic testing, so it is not a confirmed diagnosis.
why_others_wrong.E: Declining screening is a legitimate informed choice and should not affect access to routine clinical care.

exam_trap: High uptake is not a justification for withholding information about potential harms.
takeaway: Screening invitation → evidence-based information → personal informed choice.
source: [UKNSC], Informed choice, updated 11 July 2025.
thinking: Healthy person invited to screening ↓ UK NSC supports personal informed choice ↓ requires balanced information on benefits and harms ↓ Balanced information about benefits and harms before deciding
pearl: UK screening invitations are accompanied by standardised information leaflets explaining false positives, false negatives and overdiagnosis so that attendance is a genuine choice rather than an expectation.

subject: Statistics & evidence-based medicine
title: Forest plot
stem: In a meta-analysis, individual studies are represented by squares with horizontal lines, while the pooled estimate is represented by a diamond. What type of figure is being described?
why_correct: Forest plots display effect estimates and their confidence intervals for individual studies and often a pooled estimate.

why_others_wrong.A: A Kaplan-Meier curve plots the proportion surviving over time as a stepped line, without study squares or a pooled diamond.
why_others_wrong.C: A funnel plot shows each study's effect against its size or precision to look for publication bias, not squares with a pooled diamond.
why_others_wrong.D: A ROC curve plots sensitivity against 1 minus specificity across thresholds for a diagnostic test, not meta-analysis results.
why_others_wrong.E: A scatter plot shows the relationship between two continuous variables as points, not study estimates with intervals and a pooled diamond.

exam_trap: The horizontal line usually represents the confidence interval, not the range of raw patient measurements.
takeaway: Squares + horizontal confidence intervals + pooled diamond → forest plot.
source: Standard evidence-based medicine methodology; MRCS evidence-based practice syllabus.
thinking: Individual studies shown as squares with horizontal lines ↓ lines are confidence intervals ↓ pooled estimate shown as a diamond ↓ Forest plot
pearl: In a forest plot the size of each square reflects the study's weight in the meta-analysis, and the width of the diamond shows the confidence interval of the pooled estimate.

subject: Statistics & evidence-based medicine
title: Heterogeneity in meta-analysis
stem: A meta-analysis combines several studies, but the study results vary substantially in their direction or magnitude of effect. What does this suggest?
why_correct: Heterogeneity refers to differences between studies that may arise from differences in populations, interventions, outcomes, methodology or other factors.

why_others_wrong.B: Blinding conceals treatment allocation from participants or assessors within a trial; it does not describe variation in results between studies.
why_others_wrong.C: Allocation concealment prevents foreknowledge of the next assignment during randomisation and does not describe between-study differences.
why_others_wrong.D: Randomisation is the allocation method within a trial; it does not describe inconsistency of effects across studies in a meta-analysis.
why_others_wrong.E: External validity concerns applying results to other populations, not variation in effect size or direction between the included studies.

exam_trap: External validity may tempt, but it concerns applying results to other populations; inconsistent effects between the pooled studies are described as heterogeneity.
takeaway: Studies differ materially → assess heterogeneity before interpreting the pooled estimate.
source: Evidence-based medicine and systematic-review methodology; MRCS evidence-based practice syllabus.
thinking: Several studies combined in a meta-analysis ↓ results vary in direction or magnitude ↓ variation beyond chance between studies ↓ Heterogeneity
pearl: Substantial heterogeneity is usually handled with a random-effects model and explored by subgroup or sensitivity analysis, rather than relying on a single fixed-effect pooled estimate.

subject: Statistics & evidence-based medicine
title: I² statistic
stem: A meta-analysis reports an I² statistic of 0%. What does this indicate?

options.B: No observed variability exists between the studies
options.C: No observed statistical heterogeneity is detected
options.E: The pooled estimate is statistically significant

correct_answer: C. No observed statistical heterogeneity is detected
why_correct: I² estimates the proportion of observed variability in effect estimates that is attributable to heterogeneity rather than sampling error. An I² of 0% indicates no observed statistical heterogeneity by this measure.

why_others_wrong.A: I-squared is a statistical measure of between-study heterogeneity and says nothing about whether participants were blinded.
why_others_wrong.B: An I-squared of 0% means variability is no greater than expected by chance, not that study results are identical with no variability at all.
why_others_wrong.D: I-squared describes consistency between studies, not effect size, so a value of 0% does not indicate an ineffective treatment.
why_others_wrong.E: Statistical significance of the pooled estimate is judged from its confidence interval or p-value, not from the heterogeneity statistic.

exam_trap: Candidates often choose no observed variability, but I² of 0% means variation is no more than expected by chance, not that study results are identical.
takeaway: I² assesses heterogeneity, not treatment efficacy.
source: Standard meta-analysis methodology; MRCS evidence-based practice syllabus.
thinking: I² = proportion of variability due to heterogeneity rather than chance ↓ I² of 0% ↓ variability no greater than chance ↓ No observed statistical heterogeneity is detected
pearl: I² values around 25%, 50% and 75% are conventionally described as low, moderate and high heterogeneity, and I² is imprecise when only a few studies are pooled.

subject: Research methods & screening
title: Internal validity
stem: A trial is well randomised, has minimal loss to follow-up and uses appropriate outcome measurement. The investigators are primarily assessing whether the study's results are likely to be valid for the participants actually studied. What concept is being assessed?
why_correct: Internal validity concerns whether the study has been conducted sufficiently well to provide a trustworthy estimate for the population actually studied.

why_others_wrong.B: External validity concerns whether results apply to populations beyond those studied, whereas the stem asks about validity for the participants actually studied.
why_others_wrong.C: Generalisability is essentially external validity, concerning application to other populations rather than trustworthiness within the trial itself.
why_others_wrong.D: Cost-effectiveness compares costs with health outcomes and is an economic question, not an assessment of the trial's methodological quality.
why_others_wrong.E: Ecological validity concerns how closely study conditions resemble real-world settings, not whether randomisation and follow-up make results trustworthy.

exam_trap: External validity and generalisability attract candidates because the trial seems high quality, but both concern other populations; trustworthiness for the participants actually studied is internal validity.
takeaway: “Is the study result trustworthy in its own participants?” → internal validity.
source: MRCS evidence-based practice and critical-appraisal principles.
thinking: Well randomised with minimal loss to follow-up ↓ appropriate outcome measurement ↓ question is about trustworthiness in the participants studied ↓ Internal validity
pearl: Internal validity is a prerequisite for external validity: a biased trial gives an untrustworthy result that cannot be generalised to anyone, however representative its population.

subject: Statistics & evidence-based medicine
title: External validity
stem: A clinical trial is methodologically rigorous but only included highly selected young patients. Investigators question whether its findings apply to elderly patients with multiple comorbidities. Which concept is being questioned?
why_correct: External validity concerns whether study findings can reasonably be generalised to other populations, settings or clinical circumstances.

why_others_wrong.A: Internal validity concerns whether the trial's result is free from bias within its own participants, and the stem describes it as methodologically rigorous.
why_others_wrong.C: Randomisation protects against confounding within the trial; it does not address whether findings extend to elderly comorbid patients.
why_others_wrong.D: Allocation concealment prevents selection bias at enrolment and is part of internal validity, not generalisability to other populations.
why_others_wrong.E: Statistical power concerns the ability to detect a true effect in the studied sample, not whether results transfer to a different population.

exam_trap: A highly controlled trial may have excellent internal validity but limited generalisability.
takeaway: “Can I apply this result to my patient?” → external validity.
source: MRCS evidence-based practice and critical-appraisal principles.
thinking: Methodologically rigorous trial ↓ highly selected young participants ↓ question is whether results apply to elderly comorbid patients ↓ generalisability ↓ External validity
pearl: Strict trial inclusion criteria often exclude older and frail surgical patients, so registries and pragmatic trials are used to check whether results hold in routine practice.

subject: Statistics & evidence-based medicine
title: Statistical versus clinical significance
stem: A very large trial finds that a new postoperative intervention reduces mean pain by 0.2 points on a 10-point scale with p<0.001. Which statement is most appropriate?

options.A: The result is statistically significant, but its clinical importance may be limited
options.B: The result cannot be statistically significant
options.C: Statistical significance proves the effect is clinically important
options.D: The treatment must replace standard care

correct_answer: A. The result is statistically significant, but its clinical importance may be limited
why_correct: A small difference can become statistically significant in a large sample. Clinical importance depends on the magnitude of benefit and its relevance to patients.

why_others_wrong.B: With p below 0.001 the result is statistically significant; a very large sample can make even a small difference significant.
why_others_wrong.C: Statistical significance shows the result is unlikely under the null hypothesis, not that a 0.2-point pain reduction matters to patients.
why_others_wrong.D: Changing practice needs a clinically meaningful benefit weighed against harms and costs, not merely a significant but small difference.
why_others_wrong.E: The p-value reflects sample size and random error; clinical importance is judged from the magnitude of the effect.

exam_trap: Choosing that statistical significance proves clinical importance ignores effect size; a very large trial can make a 0.2-point pain difference highly significant yet clinically trivial.
takeaway: Statistical significance ≠ clinical significance.
source: Greenhalgh, How to Read a Paper, 6th edition (2019), chapter on statistics for the non-statistician; CEBM (Oxford), Statistical significance vs clinical significance.
thinking: 0.2-point reduction on a 10-point scale ↓ p <0.001 because the trial is very large ↓ large samples make small effects significant ↓ The result is statistically significant, but its clinical importance may be limited
pearl: For pain scores the minimal clinically important difference is usually well above 0.2 points on a 10-point scale, so this effect is unlikely to be noticed by patients.

subject: Statistics & evidence-based medicine
title: Absolute versus relative effect
stem: A treatment reduces an event rate from 10% to 8%. Which statement correctly describes the absolute risk reduction?
why_correct: ARR = control event rate − treatment event rate = 10% − 8% = 2 percentage points. The relative risk reduction is 20%.

why_others_wrong.A: 0.2% misplaces the decimal: the relative reduction of 0.2 has been written as a percentage, whereas the absolute fall is 0.02, or 2 percentage points.
why_others_wrong.C: 20 percentage points would mean a fall from 10% to minus 10%; the 20 figure is the relative reduction mislabelled as absolute.
why_others_wrong.D: 20% is the relative risk reduction (2 divided by 10), not the absolute difference between the two event rates.
why_others_wrong.E: 80% is the relative risk (8 divided by 10) expressed as a percentage, not the absolute reduction in event rate.

exam_trap: Do not confuse a 20% relative reduction with a 2 percentage-point absolute reduction.
takeaway: 10% → 8% = ARR 2 percentage points; RRR 20%.
source: CEBM (Oxford), Explanation of the EBM glossary: absolute risk reduction, relative risk reduction and NNT; Greenhalgh, How to Read a Paper, 6th edition (2019).
thinking: Event rate falls from 10% to 8% ↓ ARR = 10% − 8% ↓ the 20% figure is the relative reduction ↓ 2 percentage points
pearl: Relative risk reductions sound more impressive than absolute ones, so patient information and consent discussions should present absolute risks wherever possible.

subject: Statistics & evidence-based medicine
title: Relative risk interpretation
stem: A trial reports a relative risk of 0.75 for postoperative infection in the intervention group compared with controls. Which interpretation is correct?

options.A: The intervention group has 75% more infections
options.B: The risk in the intervention group is 75% of the control risk
options.E: The intervention reduces risk by 75 percentage points

correct_answer: B. The risk in the intervention group is 75% of the control risk
why_correct: RR = risk in intervention group / risk in control group. RR 0.75 means the intervention group's risk is 75% of the control risk, corresponding to a relative risk reduction of 25%.

why_others_wrong.A: A relative risk of 0.75 is below 1, indicating fewer infections; 75% more infections would correspond to a relative risk of 1.75.
why_others_wrong.C: A relative risk is a ratio of two risks and does not give the absolute infection risk in either group.
why_others_wrong.D: The number needed to treat requires the absolute risk reduction, which cannot be derived from the relative risk alone.
why_others_wrong.E: A relative risk of 0.75 corresponds to a 25% relative reduction, not a reduction of 75 percentage points in absolute risk.

exam_trap: Candidates who choose a 75-point reduction read the RR as the size of the benefit; RR 0.75 means risk is 75% of control, a 25% relative reduction.
takeaway: RR below 1 → lower relative risk in the intervention group.
source: CEBM (Oxford), Explanation of the EBM glossary: absolute risk reduction, relative risk reduction and NNT; Greenhalgh, How to Read a Paper, 6th edition (2019).
thinking: RR 0.75 for infection ↓ RR = intervention risk / control risk ↓ intervention risk is 0.75 times control risk ↓ equivalent to a 25% relative risk reduction ↓ The risk in the intervention group is 75% of the control risk
pearl: The relative risk reduction is 1 minus RR, so RR 0.75 is a 25% relative reduction; the absolute benefit still depends on the baseline infection rate.

subject: Research methods & screening
title: Generalisability and eligibility criteria
stem: A trial excludes patients with renal impairment, advanced age and multiple comorbidities. Which issue should a clinician consider most carefully before applying its findings to a frail older patient with renal impairment?
why_correct: The patient differs substantially from the population studied, raising concerns about generalisability.

why_others_wrong.B: Allocation concealment protects internal validity at recruitment and does not address whether excluded patient groups can apply the findings.
why_others_wrong.C: Blinding reduces bias in delivering and assessing treatment within the trial but does not resolve differences between trial participants and this patient.
why_others_wrong.D: Random sequence generation affects internal validity through fair allocation, not the applicability of findings to patients the trial excluded.
why_others_wrong.E: Type I error is a false-positive statistical conclusion within the trial, not the mismatch between the trial population and a frail older patient.

exam_trap: A statistically convincing trial can still have limited applicability to a particular patient.
takeaway: Compare your patient with the trial population before applying the result.
source: MRCS evidence-based practice and critical-appraisal principles.
thinking: Trial excluded older, renally impaired, comorbid patients ↓ your patient is frail with renal impairment ↓ patient differs from the trial population ↓ applicability is the issue ↓ External validity
pearl: Before applying trial evidence, compare your patient with the eligibility criteria and baseline characteristics table; frail and multimorbid patients are commonly under-represented in surgical trials.

subject: Research methods & screening
title: Research consent
stem: A competent adult is invited to participate in a clinical research study. Which statement best describes valid research consent?

options.A: It must be obtained under pressure to ensure recruitment
options.B: It should be voluntary and informed
options.C: It is valid if the patient signs without reading the information
options.E: It is unnecessary if the research is scientifically important

correct_answer: B. It should be voluntary and informed
why_correct: UK research policy requires explicit consent, where consent is sought, to be voluntary and informed. Participants who refuse or withdraw should not face reprisal.

why_others_wrong.A: Consent obtained under pressure is not voluntary and is therefore not valid, regardless of any recruitment targets.
why_others_wrong.C: Signing without reading the information means the participant is not informed, so a signature alone does not make consent valid.
why_others_wrong.D: Research participants can withdraw consent at any time without reprisal, as participation is voluntary.
why_others_wrong.E: Scientific importance does not override the requirement for consent from a competent adult; ethical review protects participants' rights.

exam_trap: A signed form alone does not make consent ethically valid if the participant has not been appropriately informed.
takeaway: Research consent = informed + voluntary + appropriately documented.
source: [HRA], UK Policy Framework for Health and Social Care Research; HRA consent guidance, updated 2026.
thinking: Competent adult invited to research ↓ consent must be free of pressure ↓ must understand the information ↓ Voluntary and informed
pearl: Research participants should be told they may withdraw at any time without giving a reason and without their routine clinical care being affected.

subject: Research methods & screening
title: Research Ethics Committee
stem: A research team proposes a study involving human participants. Which body has the role of reviewing the ethical acceptability of relevant health and social care research proposals in the UK?

options.D: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence

why_correct: Research Ethics Committees review research proposals and give an opinion on their ethical acceptability, with the aim of safeguarding participants' rights, safety, dignity and wellbeing.

why_others_wrong.B: The General Medical Council regulates doctors' registration and professional standards, not the ethical review of individual research proposals.
why_others_wrong.C: The Care Quality Commission inspects and regulates health and social care services, not the ethical acceptability of research studies.
why_others_wrong.D: NICE produces clinical and technology appraisal guidance on what care should be recommended, not ethical opinions on research proposals.
why_others_wrong.E: A Royal College examination board sets and runs professional examinations and has no role in the ethical review of research.

exam_trap: An REC is not responsible for deciding whether a treatment should be recommended clinically.
takeaway: Human research → appropriate research governance and ethical review.
source: [HRA], Research Ethics Committees overview, updated 7 May 2026.
thinking: Proposed study with human participants ↓ needs independent ethical review ↓ body that protects participants' rights, safety and wellbeing ↓ Research Ethics Committee
pearl: In England, NHS research needs both a favourable REC opinion and Health Research Authority approval; clinical audit and service evaluation do not normally need REC review.

subject: Research methods & screening
title: Participant withdrawal
stem: A participant who previously consented to a research study informs the research team that they no longer wish to participate. What is the most appropriate general principle?

options.A: Participation must continue because consent was originally signed
options.B: The participant's decision to withdraw should be respected
options.C: Withdrawal should result in loss of routine clinical care
options.D: The investigator should conceal the withdrawal
options.E: The participant must provide a medical reason

correct_answer: B. The participant's decision to withdraw should be respected
why_correct: Research participation is voluntary. UK research policy states that where consent is refused or withdrawn, this should occur without reprisal.

why_others_wrong.A: Signing a consent form does not bind a participant to continue, since research consent can be withdrawn at any time.
why_others_wrong.C: Withdrawal from research should occur without reprisal, so it must not affect the participant's access to appropriate routine clinical care.
why_others_wrong.D: Concealing a withdrawal would be dishonest and could lead to data being used against the participant's wishes, contrary to research governance.
why_others_wrong.E: Participants are not required to give a reason, medical or otherwise, for withdrawing from a voluntary research study.

exam_trap: Some candidates think a signed consent form commits the participant to continue, but research consent can be withdrawn at any time, without giving a reason or losing routine care.
takeaway: Research participation is voluntary; withdrawal should not result in punishment or loss of appropriate care.
source: [HRA], UK Policy Framework for Health and Social Care Research (2017, updated 2022).
thinking: Participant previously consented ↓ now wishes to stop ↓ research participation is voluntary ↓ no reason needed and no reprisal ↓ The decision to withdraw should be respected
pearl: When a participant withdraws, the team should clarify whether they also want data already collected to be withdrawn, as the consent form often addresses retention of existing data.

subject: Research methods & screening
title: Research Ethics and equipoise
stem: A randomised trial is proposed comparing two accepted surgical strategies. The investigators genuinely do not know which strategy produces better patient outcomes. What ethical concept describes this state of genuine uncertainty?
why_correct: Clinical equipoise describes genuine uncertainty within the relevant clinical community about which intervention is preferable. It provides an important ethical basis for randomised comparison of alternative treatments.

why_others_wrong.B: Confounding is a third factor distorting an association between exposure and outcome, not an ethical justification for randomising patients.
why_others_wrong.C: Selection bias arises from systematic differences in who enters or is analysed in a study, not from uncertainty about which treatment is better.
why_others_wrong.D: Attrition is loss of participants during follow-up, which is a methodological issue rather than the ethical basis for a trial.
why_others_wrong.E: Publication bias concerns selective reporting of completed studies, not the genuine uncertainty that justifies starting a randomised comparison.

exam_trap: The individual investigator does not need to believe that both treatments are identical; the key issue is genuine uncertainty about which is superior.
takeaway: Genuine clinical uncertainty between treatments → equipoise.
source: Research ethics principles and standard clinical-trial methodology; MRCS evidence-based practice syllabus.
thinking: Two accepted surgical strategies compared ↓ investigators genuinely do not know which is better ↓ ethical basis for randomising patients ↓ Equipoise
pearl: Clinical equipoise refers to uncertainty in the expert community, not just the individual surgeon, and trials should be stopped early if accumulating data clearly resolve that uncertainty.

subject: Statistics & evidence-based medicine
title: Quality-adjusted life year
stem: A new treatment gives a patient an additional year of life at a health-related quality of life utility of 0.8. Approximately how many QALYs does this represent?
why_correct: A QALY combines length of life with quality of life. QALYs = years of life × utility = 1 × 0.8 = 0.8 QALYs.

why_others_wrong.A: 0.2 is the shortfall from full health (1 minus 0.8), not the QALYs gained from one year lived at a utility of 0.8.
why_others_wrong.B: 0.5 does not follow from one year multiplied by a utility of 0.8 and has no basis in the figures given.
why_others_wrong.D: 1.0 counts the extra year as if lived in full health, ignoring the utility weight of 0.8.
why_others_wrong.E: 1.8 adds the year of life and the utility together instead of multiplying them.

exam_trap: Choosing 1.0 counts the year as full health, and 1.8 adds years and utility; QALYs are found by multiplying years of life by the utility weight.
takeaway: QALY = quantity of life × quality of life.
source: NICE Health Technology Evaluations: The Manual (process and methods guide PMG36, January 2022).
thinking: One extra year of life ↓ utility of 0.8 ↓ QALYs = years × utility ↓ 1 × 0.8 ↓ 0.8
pearl: QALYs let interventions for different conditions be compared on a common scale, which is how NICE judges cost-effectiveness using cost per QALY gained.

subject: Statistics & evidence-based medicine
title: Incremental cost-effectiveness ratio
stem: A new treatment costs £30,000 more per patient than standard treatment and provides an additional 1.5 QALYs. What is the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio?
why_correct: ICER = incremental cost ÷ incremental health benefit = £30,000 ÷ 1.5 = £20,000 per QALY gained.

why_others_wrong.A: £10,000/QALY divides £30,000 by 3, as if the QALY gain were double the stated 1.5.
why_others_wrong.B: £15,000/QALY divides £30,000 by 2, as if the QALY gain were rounded up from 1.5 to 2, instead of dividing by the actual 1.5.
why_others_wrong.D: £30,000/QALY ignores the QALY gain altogether, treating the incremental cost as if it bought exactly one QALY.
why_others_wrong.E: £45,000/QALY multiplies the £30,000 extra cost by 1.5 QALYs instead of dividing by them.

exam_trap: The ICER uses the incremental difference between the interventions, not the total treatment cost.
takeaway: ICER = extra cost ÷ extra benefit.
source: NICE health technology evaluation methodology.
thinking: Extra cost £30,000 per patient ↓ extra benefit 1.5 QALYs ↓ ICER = incremental cost / incremental QALYs ↓ £20,000/QALY
pearl: An ICER is only meaningful against the relevant current comparator; choosing an inappropriate comparator can make a new technology look falsely cost-effective.

subject: Statistics & evidence-based medicine
title: NICE cost-effectiveness range
stem: When considering cost-effectiveness in NICE technology evaluation methodology, which range is commonly used when discussing the acceptability of interventions in terms of cost per QALY?
why_correct: From April 2026 NICE uses £25,000 and £35,000 per QALY as its reference values in technology evaluation (previously £20,000 and £30,000). Decisions are not determined by the ICER alone and may consider uncertainty and other relevant factors.

why_others_wrong.A: £100 to £500 per QALY is far below the reference values NICE uses; interventions this cheap per QALY are rarely the subject of threshold debate.
why_others_wrong.B: £1,000 to £5,000 per QALY is well below NICE reference values and does not reflect the range used in its technology evaluation methodology.
why_others_wrong.C: £5,000 to £10,000 per QALY would generally be regarded as highly cost-effective but is not the range NICE uses as its reference values.
why_others_wrong.E: £100,000 to £200,000 per QALY is far above NICE's reference range of £25,000 to £35,000 and would generally not be considered cost-effective.

exam_trap: Do not describe £35,000/QALY as an absolute automatic rejection threshold, and note the range rose from £20,000–£30,000 in April 2026.
takeaway: NICE cost-effectiveness decisions are not simply “above £35k = reject.”
source: NICE health technology evaluations manual.
thinking: NICE judges cost per QALY gained ↓ reference values used in technology evaluation ↓ range raised from £20,000-£30,000 in April 2026 ↓ £25,000–£35,000/QALY
pearl: NICE decisions also weigh uncertainty in the estimates, innovation and severity of the condition, so an ICER above the range does not automatically mean rejection.

subject: Statistics & evidence-based medicine
title: Opportunity cost
stem: An NHS organisation uses limited resources to fund a new treatment. As a result, resources are unavailable for another potentially beneficial treatment. What economic concept describes the benefit forgone from the alternative use?
why_correct: Opportunity cost is the benefit lost when resources are used for one option rather than the next best alternative.

why_others_wrong.A: Marginal utility is the additional benefit from consuming one more unit of something, not the benefit given up from the next best alternative.
why_others_wrong.C: Relative risk is an epidemiological ratio comparing outcome risk between groups and is not an economic concept.
why_others_wrong.D: Economies of scale describe falling cost per unit as output increases, not the benefit forgone by choosing one use of resources.
why_others_wrong.E: External validity concerns generalising study findings to other populations and has no bearing on resource allocation trade-offs.

exam_trap: Opportunity cost is not the price paid for the chosen treatment, and marginal utility describes the extra benefit of one more unit rather than the benefit forgone.
takeaway: Limited resources → choosing A means giving up benefits from another option → opportunity cost.
source: NICE Health Technology Evaluations: The Manual (process and methods guide PMG36, January 2022).
thinking: Limited NHS resources ↓ funding one treatment removes funding from another ↓ the benefit given up from the next best use ↓ Opportunity cost
pearl: Opportunity cost is the reason cost-effectiveness thresholds exist: funding an expensive treatment displaces health gains elsewhere in the NHS budget.

subject: Statistics & evidence-based medicine
title: Dominated intervention
stem: Treatment A costs more than treatment B and produces fewer QALYs. What is the economic relationship between the two treatments?
why_correct: An intervention is dominated when another option is both less costly and more effective. Here, B is cheaper and produces more QALYs, so B dominates A.

why_others_wrong.A: Treatment A is both more expensive and less effective, so it is the dominated option rather than the dominant one.
why_others_wrong.C: Cost-neutral would require the two treatments to cost the same, but A costs more than B.
why_others_wrong.D: They differ in both cost and QALYs, so they cannot be considered equivalent.
why_others_wrong.E: Comparing costs and QALYs is exactly what allows a dominance judgement, and here it clearly favours B.

exam_trap: Candidates sometimes reverse the term and say A dominates B; the dominant option is the one that is both cheaper and more effective, here B.
takeaway: Cheaper + better → dominates.
source: NICE economic-evaluation methodology.
thinking: Treatment A costs more ↓ treatment A produces fewer QALYs ↓ B is cheaper and more effective ↓ B dominates A
pearl: When one option dominates, no ICER needs calculating; ICERs are only informative when the more effective option also costs more.

subject: Statistics & evidence-based medicine
title: Sensitivity versus specificity trade-off
stem: A diagnostic test threshold is changed so that more patients are classified as positive. Which change is generally expected?
correct_answer: B. Sensitivity increases and specificity decreases
why_correct: Lowering the threshold generally captures more people with disease, increasing sensitivity, but also classifies more people without disease as positive, reducing specificity.

why_others_wrong.A: Classifying more patients as positive detects more true cases and more false positives, which raises sensitivity and lowers specificity, the reverse of this.
why_others_wrong.C: Moving a single threshold creates a trade-off; both measures cannot generally rise together without an improvement in the test itself.
why_others_wrong.D: Classifying more patients as positive increases the number of diseased patients detected, so sensitivity is expected to rise rather than fall.
why_others_wrong.E: Changing the positivity threshold alters which patients are labelled positive, so sensitivity and specificity are expected to change.

exam_trap: Candidates sometimes reverse the direction and choose falling sensitivity; labelling more patients positive captures more true cases but also more false positives, so specificity drops.
takeaway: More permissive positive threshold → usually ↑ sensitivity, ↓ specificity.
source: NICE diagnostic-test methodology.
thinking: Threshold changed so more patients test positive ↓ more true cases detected, so sensitivity rises ↓ more disease-free patients labelled positive ↓ specificity falls ↓ Sensitivity increases and specificity decreases
pearl: This trade-off is why rule-out tests in surgery, such as D-dimer for venous thromboembolism, use low cut-offs that maximise sensitivity at the cost of many false positives.

subject: Statistics & evidence-based medicine
title: ROC curve
stem: A researcher wants to assess the performance of a diagnostic test across a range of possible thresholds. Which graphical method is most appropriate?
why_correct: A receiver operating characteristic curve illustrates the trade-off between sensitivity and specificity across different diagnostic thresholds.

why_others_wrong.A: A Kaplan-Meier curve estimates survival over time and does not show diagnostic performance across thresholds.
why_others_wrong.B: A forest plot displays effect estimates and confidence intervals from studies in a meta-analysis, not test performance by threshold.
why_others_wrong.D: A funnel plot plots study effect against precision to explore publication bias; it does not evaluate diagnostic thresholds.
why_others_wrong.E: A Bland-Altman plot assesses agreement between two measurement methods, not the sensitivity-specificity trade-off across cut-offs.

exam_trap: Bland-Altman plots may tempt because they also assess tests, but they measure agreement between two methods, not sensitivity-specificity trade-off across thresholds.
takeaway: Diagnostic threshold performance → ROC curve.
source: NICE diagnostic accuracy methodology includes ROC curves and area under the ROC curve as measures of diagnostic-test accuracy.
