exam_trap: Candidates choosing X-linked dominant inheritance focus on the mother; affected fathers transmit X-linked dominant traits to all daughters, whereas mitochondrial disease passes only via mothers.
takeaway: Mitochondrial DNA → maternal transmission.
source: Standard medical genetics; MRCS Applied Basic Science syllabus.
thinking: Pathogenic mitochondrial DNA variant ↓ mitochondria come from the oocyte cytoplasm ↓ sperm mitochondria are normally eliminated ↓ Maternal inheritance
pearl: Heteroplasmy, the mixture of normal and mutant mitochondrial DNA within cells, explains why severity varies widely among children of the same affected mother.

subject: Immunology
topic: Antigen presentation via MHC class I
title: Antigen presentation via MHC class I
stem: MHC class I molecules primarily present endogenous intracellular peptides to which cells?
why_correct: MHC class I presents intracellular peptides to CD8 cytotoxic T lymphocytes.

why_others_wrong.B: CD4 T cells recognise peptides presented on MHC class II, which are mainly derived from extracellular antigen.
why_others_wrong.C: B cells recognise native antigen through their surface immunoglobulin and are not the cells that read MHC class I peptides.
why_others_wrong.D: Neutrophils are innate phagocytes without T-cell receptors, so they do not recognise peptide presented on MHC class I.
why_others_wrong.E: Eosinophils are innate granulocytes involved in helminth and allergic responses and do not recognise MHC-peptide complexes.

exam_trap: MHC class II is classically associated with presentation to CD4 T helper cells.
takeaway: MHC I → intracellular antigen → CD8.
source: Standard immunology; MRCS Applied Basic Science syllabus.
thinking: MHC class I ↓ expressed on all nucleated cells ↓ loaded with endogenous cytosolic peptides ↓ recognised by the CD8 co-receptor on cytotoxic T cells ↓ CD8 T cells
pearl: The rule of eights helps recall: MHC class I x CD8 = 8 and MHC class II x CD4 = 8.

subject: Immunology
title: MHC class II
stem: MHC class II molecules primarily present extracellularly derived antigen to which cells?
why_correct: Professional antigen-presenting cells process extracellular antigens and present peptide fragments via MHC class II to CD4 T cells.

why_others_wrong.A: CD8 T cells recognise peptides on MHC class I, which are mainly derived from intracellular (endogenous) proteins.
why_others_wrong.C: Red blood cells have no antigen receptors and do not recognise peptide presented on MHC molecules.
why_others_wrong.D: Platelets are anucleate cell fragments involved in haemostasis and do not act as responders to MHC class II presentation.
why_others_wrong.E: Neutrophils are innate phagocytes lacking T-cell receptors, so they do not recognise peptide on MHC class II.

exam_trap: Candidates who mix up the two pathways choose CD8 T cells, but CD8 reads MHC class I carrying intracellular peptide, whereas class II-presented extracellular antigen goes to CD4 cells.
takeaway: MHC II → extracellular antigen → CD4.
source: Standard immunology; MRCS Applied Basic Science syllabus.
thinking: MHC class II ↓ expressed by professional antigen-presenting cells ↓ presents peptides from endocytosed extracellular antigen ↓ recognised by the CD4 co-receptor on helper T cells ↓ CD4 T cells
pearl: HIV binds CD4 on helper T cells, so falling CD4 counts weaken MHC class II-driven help and predispose to opportunistic infection.

subject: Immunology
title: Complement membrane attack complex
stem: Which complement complex directly forms pores in susceptible target cell membranes?
why_correct: The terminal complement pathway forms the membrane attack complex, which creates membrane pores.

why_others_wrong.A: The C1 complex initiates the classical pathway by binding antibody; it does not insert into membranes to form pores.
why_others_wrong.B: C3 convertase cleaves C3 into C3a and C3b in the amplification step and does not itself create membrane pores.
why_others_wrong.C: C5a is a soluble anaphylatoxin and chemoattractant for neutrophils; the pore is formed by C5b with C6-C9.
why_others_wrong.E: C-reactive protein is an acute-phase protein that can bind microbes and activate the classical pathway, but it does not form pores.

exam_trap: Do not pick C5a because it shares a number with C5b; C5a is a soluble chemoattractant, while C5b with C6 to C9 forms the pore.
takeaway: MAC → membrane pores.
source: Standard immunology; MRCS Applied Basic Science syllabus.
thinking: Pore formation in target membranes ↓ terminal complement pathway ↓ C5b recruits C6, C7, C8 and polymerised C9 ↓ Membrane attack complex
pearl: Gram-negative organisms such as Neisseria are particularly susceptible to MAC lysis, which is why eculizumab (anti-C5) therapy requires meningococcal vaccination.

subject: Immunology
title: IgA
stem: Which immunoglobulin is particularly important in mucosal secretions?
why_correct: Secretory IgA is an important component of mucosal immune defence, including the respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts.

why_others_wrong.B: IgD is found mainly as a surface receptor on naive B cells and is present in very low concentration in secretions.
why_others_wrong.C: IgE is present at low levels and is mainly bound to mast cells, mediating type I hypersensitivity and helminth defence rather than mucosal secretion.
why_others_wrong.D: IgG is the predominant serum immunoglobulin, but secretory defence at mucosal surfaces is dominated by dimeric IgA.
why_others_wrong.E: IgM is the first antibody of a primary response and mainly intravascular; it contributes little to mucosal secretions compared with IgA.

exam_trap: IgE is associated particularly with type I hypersensitivity and helminth responses, not the principal mucosal secretory immunoglobulin.
takeaway: Mucosal immunity → think IgA.
source: Standard immunology; MRCS Applied Basic Science syllabus.
thinking: Antibody of mucosal secretions ↓ secreted across epithelium as a dimer bound to secretory component ↓ protects respiratory and gastrointestinal surfaces ↓ IgA
pearl: Selective IgA deficiency is the commonest primary immunodeficiency; affected patients can form anti-IgA antibodies and react to IgA-containing blood products.

subject: Immunology
title: IgE and mast cells
stem: Which immunoglobulin is classically involved in immediate type I hypersensitivity through interaction with mast cells?
why_correct: IgE binds high-affinity Fcε receptors on mast cells and basophils. Cross-linking can trigger mediator release.

why_others_wrong.A: IgA is the main mucosal secretory antibody and does not sensitise mast cells for immediate hypersensitivity.
why_others_wrong.B: IgD mainly serves as an antigen receptor on naive B cells and has no established role in mast-cell-mediated allergy.
why_others_wrong.D: IgG4 is associated with chronic antigen exposure and can act as a blocking antibody after allergen immunotherapy, not as the mast-cell sensitiser.
why_others_wrong.E: IgM is the first antibody of the primary response and activates complement well, but it does not bind high-affinity Fc receptors on mast cells.

exam_trap: IgG4 tempts candidates who link it with allergy, but it acts as a blocking antibody after immunotherapy; only IgE arms mast cells for immediate hypersensitivity.
takeaway: Type I hypersensitivity → IgE + mast cells.
source: Standard immunology; MRCS Applied Basic Science syllabus.
thinking: Immediate type I hypersensitivity ↓ antibody bound to high-affinity Fc receptors on mast cells ↓ allergen cross-linking triggers degranulation ↓ IgE
pearl: Raised total and specific IgE support atopy, while mast-cell tryptase rather than IgE is the marker used to confirm an acute anaphylactic episode.

subject: Immunology
title: Neutrophils in bacterial infection
stem: Which leukocyte is particularly important in the early innate immune response to many acute bacterial infections?
why_correct: Neutrophils are rapid innate immune responders that migrate toward sites of acute inflammation and can phagocytose and kill microorganisms.

why_others_wrong.B: Eosinophils are mainly involved in helminth infections and allergic inflammation rather than the early response to acute bacterial infection.
why_others_wrong.C: Plasma cells are terminally differentiated B cells of the adaptive response that secrete antibody and take days to appear.
why_others_wrong.D: Memory B cells provide faster responses on re-exposure but are part of adaptive immunity, not the early innate responders.
why_others_wrong.E: Megakaryocytes are bone marrow cells that produce platelets and do not migrate to sites of infection to kill bacteria.

exam_trap: Memory B cells and plasma cells belong to the adaptive response and take days to act; eosinophils target helminths, so the early bacterial responder is the neutrophil.
takeaway: Acute bacterial inflammation → neutrophils are key early responders.
source: Standard immunology/pathology; MRCS Applied Basic Science syllabus.
thinking: Early innate response to acute bacterial infection ↓ cell recruited within hours to inflamed tissue ↓ phagocytoses and kills bacteria ↓ Neutrophil
pearl: Neutrophils are the predominant cell in pus and in acute appendicitis on histology; persistent neutrophilia after surgery should prompt a search for a collection or anastomotic leak.

subject: Microbiology & surgical infection
title: Biofilm
stem: Why can bacterial biofilms make some infections difficult to eradicate?

options.B: They can provide a protected community with altered bacterial physiology and reduced susceptibility to antimicrobial and host responses
options.D: They occur only in the bloodstream
options.E: They make bacteria incapable of adhesion

correct_answer: B. They can provide a protected community with altered bacterial physiology and reduced susceptibility to antimicrobial and host responses
why_correct: Biofilms are structured microbial communities attached to surfaces and embedded within an extracellular matrix. They are important in infections involving implanted devices and other surfaces.

why_others_wrong.A: Bacteria within biofilms continue to replicate, although often more slowly; slow growth reduces antibiotic efficacy rather than stopping replication entirely.
why_others_wrong.C: Biofilms are typically bacterial or fungal communities, not purely viral, and their significance in surgery lies in bacterial device infection.
why_others_wrong.D: Biofilms form on surfaces such as prostheses, catheters and chronic wounds rather than being confined to the bloodstream.
why_others_wrong.E: Adhesion to a surface is the first step in biofilm formation, so biofilms enhance rather than abolish bacterial attachment.

exam_trap: Biofilm-associated reduced antimicrobial susceptibility is not simply the same as genetically determined antibiotic resistance.
takeaway: Device-associated persistent infection → think biofilm.
source: Standard microbiology and surgical infection principles; MRCS Applied Basic Science syllabus.
thinking: Biofilm = surface-attached community in an extracellular matrix ↓ bacteria grow slowly with altered physiology ↓ matrix shields them from antibiotics and phagocytes ↓ They can provide a protected community with altered bacterial physiology and reduced susceptibility to antimicrobial and host responses
pearl: Because biofilm on an implant is rarely eradicated by antibiotics alone, established prosthetic or device infection often needs removal or exchange of the device as well as antimicrobial therapy.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Functional residual capacity
stem: Which lung volume represents the amount of air remaining in the lungs at the end of a normal, passive expiration?
why_correct: Functional residual capacity (FRC) is the volume remaining in the lungs at the end of normal expiration. FRC = expiratory reserve volume + residual volume.

why_others_wrong.A: Residual volume is the air remaining after a maximal forced expiration, not after a normal passive expiration.
why_others_wrong.C: Inspiratory reserve volume is the extra air that can be inhaled above a normal tidal breath; it does not describe the resting end-expiratory volume.
why_others_wrong.D: Vital capacity is the maximum volume that can be exhaled after a maximal inspiration, not a volume present at the end of quiet breathing.
why_others_wrong.E: Total lung capacity is the volume in the lungs at maximal inspiration, not at the end of a normal passive expiration.

exam_trap: Residual volume is the air remaining after maximal forced expiration, not normal expiration.
takeaway: End of quiet expiration → FRC.
source: Standard respiratory physiology; MRCS Applied Basic Science syllabus.
thinking: End of a normal passive expiration ↓ elastic recoil of lung and chest wall balance ↓ remaining volume = expiratory reserve volume + residual volume ↓ Functional residual capacity
pearl: FRC acts as the oxygen reservoir during apnoea, which is why preoxygenation before induction prolongs the safe apnoea time, especially in patients with a low FRC.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Closing capacity
stem: What happens when closing capacity exceeds functional residual capacity?

options.A: Small airways are more likely to close during normal tidal breathing
options.E: Diffusion becomes independent of lung volume

correct_answer: A. Small airways are more likely to close during normal tidal breathing
why_correct: If closing capacity rises above FRC, dependent small airways may close during normal expiration, causing ventilation-perfusion mismatch and impaired oxygenation. This is more likely with increasing age and can be worsened perioperatively.

why_others_wrong.B: Airway closure impairs effective ventilation of the affected units; it does not necessarily increase overall alveolar ventilation.
why_others_wrong.C: Closing capacity exceeding FRC has no bearing on residual volume becoming zero, which is not a physiologically meaningful outcome.
why_others_wrong.D: Airway closure represents increased local obstruction, so airway resistance would rise in that region, not fall to zero.
why_others_wrong.E: Diffusion capacity remains volume dependent; airway closure does not make gas diffusion independent of lung volume.

exam_trap: Residual volume becomes zero tempts candidates who confuse closing capacity with residual volume; closing capacity is closing volume plus residual volume, and airway closure above FRC traps gas rather than emptying the lung.
takeaway: Closing capacity > FRC → airway closure during tidal breathing.
source: Standard respiratory physiology; perioperative physiology principles.
thinking: Closing capacity = volume at which dependent small airways begin to close ↓ normally lies below FRC ↓ if it exceeds FRC, closure occurs during tidal breathing ↓ Small airways are more likely to close during normal tidal breathing
pearl: Closing capacity rises with age and smoking and reaches FRC in the supine position in later middle age, contributing to postoperative hypoxaemia in older patients.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Functional residual capacity after anaesthesia
stem: What commonly happens to functional residual capacity following induction of general anaesthesia?

options.C: It becomes equal to total lung capacity
options.E: It is unaffected in all patients

why_correct: General anaesthesia reduces FRC, partly because of changes in respiratory muscle tone and chest-wall/lung mechanics. A reduction in FRC can promote dependent airway closure and worsen ventilation-perfusion mismatch.

why_others_wrong.A: FRC typically falls, not rises substantially, after induction of general anaesthesia due to changes in respiratory muscle tone and chest wall mechanics.
why_others_wrong.C: FRC becoming equal to total lung capacity is physiologically implausible; FRC is normally much smaller than TLC and anaesthesia reduces it further.
why_others_wrong.D: FRC does not fall to zero; some lung volume always remains, even though the functional reserve is reduced.
why_others_wrong.E: A fall in FRC under general anaesthesia is a near-universal finding, so stating it is unaffected in all patients is incorrect.

exam_trap: A fall in FRC does not mean the lungs have lost all residual volume.
takeaway: General anaesthesia → ↓ FRC → greater risk of airway closure/atelectasis.
source: Standard anaesthetic and respiratory physiology.
thinking: Induction of general anaesthesia ↓ loss of inspiratory muscle tone and cranial shift of the diaphragm ↓ FRC falls, especially supine ↓ It decreases
pearl: The fall in FRC under anaesthesia promotes atelectasis in dependent lung regions, which can be limited by PEEP and recruitment manoeuvres.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Lung compliance
stem: Which statement best describes lung compliance?

options.A: Change in pressure divided by change in volume
options.B: Change in volume divided by change in pressure

correct_answer: B. Change in volume divided by change in pressure
why_correct: Compliance describes the ease with which the respiratory system changes volume in response to a pressure change. Compliance = ΔV / ΔP.

why_others_wrong.A: Pressure divided by volume describes elastance, the inverse of compliance, not compliance itself.
why_others_wrong.C: Airflow divided by resistance does not correctly represent flow-resistance relationships (flow equals pressure divided by resistance) and is not the definition of compliance.
why_others_wrong.D: Pressure divided by oxygen saturation is not a recognised physiological formula and has no relevance to lung mechanics.
why_others_wrong.E: Oxygen content divided by haemoglobin relates to gas carriage, not to the mechanical volume-pressure relationship that defines compliance.

exam_trap: Elastance is the inverse concept: the tendency to return to the resting configuration.
takeaway: Compliance = ΔV/ΔP.
source: Standard respiratory physiology.
thinking: Compliance = ease of inflation ↓ expressed as volume change per unit pressure change ↓ its inverse is elastance ↓ Change in volume divided by change in pressure
pearl: Static compliance in a ventilated patient is calculated from tidal volume divided by plateau pressure minus PEEP, and a falling value can signal worsening lung injury or pneumothorax.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Pulmonary fibrosis and compliance
stem: A patient with pulmonary fibrosis has stiff lungs. Which change would be expected?

options.E: Increased residual volume as the defining feature

why_correct: Fibrotic lung tissue is stiff and requires greater pressure to produce a given change in volume.

why_others_wrong.A: Increased compliance would mean the lungs expand more easily for a given pressure, which is the opposite of the stiffness seen in fibrosis.
why_others_wrong.C: The premise explicitly states the lungs are stiff, which is itself a change in elastic properties, contradicting 'no change'.
why_others_wrong.D: Pulmonary fibrosis is a restrictive parenchymal process; it does not abolish airway resistance, which is a separate mechanical property.
why_others_wrong.E: Fibrosis classically causes reduced lung volumes (a restrictive pattern), not an increase in residual volume as its defining feature.

exam_trap: Increased residual volume is chosen because it signals lung disease, but it reflects air trapping in obstruction; fibrosis characteristically reduces compliance and lung volumes.
takeaway: Fibrosis → stiff lungs → ↓ compliance.
source: Standard respiratory physiology/pathophysiology.
thinking: Pulmonary fibrosis makes the lungs stiff ↓ more pressure is needed for a given volume change ↓ volume per unit pressure falls ↓ Reduced lung compliance
pearl: Restrictive disease reduces lung volumes with a preserved or raised FEV1/FVC ratio and a reduced gas transfer, distinguishing parenchymal fibrosis from chest wall restriction.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Emphysema and compliance
stem: Which mechanical change is characteristic of emphysema?
why_correct: Destruction of elastic tissue reduces elastic recoil and makes the lungs more compliant.

why_others_wrong.A: Emphysema is characterised by loss of elastic tissue, which increases rather than reduces lung compliance.
why_others_wrong.C: Emphysema is typically associated with air trapping and an increased, not absent, residual volume.
why_others_wrong.D: Destruction of elastic tissue in emphysema reduces elastic recoil rather than increasing it.
why_others_wrong.E: Emphysema is associated with increased airway resistance and expiratory flow limitation, not the complete absence of airway resistance.

exam_trap: Increased compliance does not mean improved respiratory function. Reduced elastic recoil contributes to expiratory airflow limitation.
takeaway: Emphysema → ↑ compliance + ↓ elastic recoil.
source: Standard respiratory physiology/pathophysiology.
thinking: Emphysema destroys alveolar walls and elastic tissue ↓ elastic recoil falls ↓ lungs distend more for a given pressure ↓ Increased lung compliance
pearl: Loss of elastic recoil removes the radial traction that holds small airways open, which is why emphysema causes expiratory airway collapse and air trapping.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Airway resistance
stem: Where is the greatest proportion of total airway resistance normally generated?
why_correct: Most airway resistance is generated in medium-sized bronchi, where total cross-sectional area is still small and flow is fast and often turbulent. The small bronchioles are narrow individually but lie in parallel in huge numbers, so their combined resistance is low.

why_others_wrong.A: Although individual small bronchioles are narrow, their large combined cross-sectional area (arranged in parallel) means they contribute relatively little to total resistance.
why_others_wrong.C: The alveoli are the site of gas exchange, not conducting airway structures that generate airflow resistance.
why_others_wrong.D: Pulmonary capillaries are part of the vascular circulation and contribute to vascular, not airway, resistance.
why_others_wrong.E: The pleural space has no airflow through it and is not a site that generates airway resistance.

exam_trap: The narrowest individual airway is not necessarily the site of greatest total resistance.
takeaway: Total airway resistance is influenced strongly by medium-sized conducting airways.
source: Standard respiratory physiology.
thinking: Resistance depends on the combined cross-sectional area at each generation ↓ small bronchioles are narrow but numerous and in parallel ↓ medium bronchi have small total area and fast, often turbulent flow ↓ Medium-sized airways
pearl: Because small airways contribute little to total resistance, early small-airway disease can be present before spirometry becomes abnormal, the so-called quiet zone of the lung.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Poiseuille's relationship
stem: If the radius of a cylindrical airway is reduced by half, what happens to laminar flow resistance, assuming all other factors remain constant?
why_correct: For laminar flow, resistance is inversely proportional to the fourth power of radius: R ∝ 1/r⁴. Halving the radius therefore increases resistance by: 1/(0.5⁴) = 16.

why_others_wrong.A: Halving the radius increases resistance according to Poiseuille's relationship; resistance does not fall, as this option states.
why_others_wrong.B: A simple doubling underestimates the effect; because resistance is inversely proportional to the fourth power of radius, the true increase is far greater than two-fold.
why_others_wrong.C: A four-fold increase would apply if resistance varied with the inverse square of radius, but Poiseuille's relationship is to the fourth power, giving a much larger increase.
why_others_wrong.E: Resistance is highly sensitive to airway radius under Poiseuille's relationship, so it cannot remain unchanged when radius is halved.

exam_trap: The 4-fold option catches candidates who square the radius change; laminar resistance varies with the fourth power, so halving the radius raises it about 16-fold.
takeaway: Small decrease in airway radius → very large increase in resistance.
source: Standard respiratory physiology.
thinking: Laminar flow obeys Poiseuille relationship ↓ resistance is proportional to 1/r to the fourth power ↓ halving radius gives 2 to the fourth = 16 ↓ It increases approximately 16-fold
pearl: The same fourth-power relationship explains why a short, wide-bore cannula delivers fluid far faster than a long, narrow central line.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Work of breathing
stem: Which situation increases the elastic work of breathing?
why_correct: Stiff lungs require greater pressure generation to produce a given volume change, increasing elastic work.

why_others_wrong.B: Reduced elastic recoil makes the lungs easier to inflate (increases compliance), which would decrease, not increase, elastic work.
why_others_wrong.C: Reduced airway resistance lowers resistive work of breathing, not elastic work, which relates to lung/chest wall stiffness.
why_others_wrong.D: Increased airway diameter reduces resistive work of breathing and does not affect the elastic properties driving elastic work.
why_others_wrong.E: Reduced respiratory rate alone does not change the underlying elastic properties of the lung that determine elastic work.

exam_trap: Airway obstruction primarily increases resistive work, whereas restrictive stiffness increases elastic work.
takeaway: Stiff lungs → ↑ elastic work.
thinking: Elastic work overcomes lung and chest wall recoil ↓ stiffer lungs need more pressure for each tidal volume ↓ reduced elastic recoil would make inflation easier ↓ Increased lung stiffness
pearl: Patients with stiff lungs reduce elastic work by breathing rapidly and shallowly, whereas those with airflow obstruction tend to breathe slowly and deeply to reduce resistive work.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: V/Q mismatch and hypoxaemia
stem: Which mechanism is a common cause of hypoxaemia in patients with lung disease?
why_correct: Uneven matching of ventilation and pulmonary perfusion is a major mechanism of hypoxaemia in many pulmonary disorders.

why_others_wrong.B: Increased haemoglobin concentration alone would tend to raise arterial oxygen content and carrying capacity, not cause hypoxaemia.
why_others_wrong.C: Increased inspired oxygen concentration raises alveolar and arterial PO2, correcting rather than causing hypoxaemia.
why_others_wrong.D: Increased cardiac output alone generally improves overall oxygen delivery and is not a recognised cause of hypoxaemia.
why_others_wrong.E: Increased plasma albumin affects oncotic pressure and fluid balance, not gas exchange, and is not a cause of hypoxaemia.

exam_trap: V/Q mismatch is distinct from a true anatomical right-to-left shunt, although both can cause hypoxaemia.
takeaway: Many pulmonary diseases → V/Q mismatch → hypoxaemia.
source: Standard respiratory physiology.
thinking: Lung disease causing hypoxaemia ↓ uneven ventilation and perfusion across lung units ↓ low V/Q units deliver poorly oxygenated blood ↓ Ventilation-perfusion mismatch
pearl: Hypoxaemia from V/Q mismatch usually improves with supplemental oxygen, whereas true shunt responds poorly, a useful bedside distinction.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Dead space ventilation
stem: A patient has a large proportion of each breath ventilating alveoli that receive little or no pulmonary blood flow. What happens to physiological dead-space ventilation?

options.E: It becomes identical to shunt fraction

why_correct: Ventilation of areas with little or no perfusion contributes to dead-space ventilation.

why_others_wrong.B: Dead-space ventilation would decrease only if more of each breath reached well-perfused alveoli; here, more ventilation is going to poorly perfused units, so it increases.
why_others_wrong.C: Dead-space ventilation becoming zero is physiologically implausible given that a large proportion of ventilation is going to poorly perfused alveoli.
why_others_wrong.D: Dead-space ventilation is directly affected by mismatched ventilation and perfusion, so it cannot be described as unaffected in this scenario.
why_others_wrong.E: Dead space (wasted ventilation) and shunt (wasted perfusion) are distinct physiological concepts and are not identical, even though both cause impaired gas exchange.

exam_trap: Dead space is wasted ventilation; shunt represents perfusion of poorly or non-ventilated regions.
takeaway: Ventilation without adequate perfusion → dead space.
source: Standard respiratory physiology.
thinking: Large fraction of each breath goes to poorly perfused alveoli ↓ that ventilation takes no part in gas exchange ↓ wasted ventilation is dead space ↓ It increases
pearl: Physiological dead space can be estimated from the difference between arterial and mixed expired CO2, and it normally amounts to roughly a third of tidal volume.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Systemic versus pulmonary vascular response
stem: Which vascular response distinguishes pulmonary circulation from most systemic vascular beds?

options.B: Alveolar hypoxia always causes pulmonary vasodilation
options.C: Carbon dioxide has no effect on pulmonary vessels
options.D: Pulmonary vessels never respond to oxygen

correct_answer: A. Alveolar hypoxia causes pulmonary vasoconstriction
why_correct: Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction is an important mechanism for matching perfusion to ventilation.

why_others_wrong.B: Alveolar hypoxia causes pulmonary vasoconstriction (hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction), not vasodilation, which distinguishes it from the response of most systemic vascular beds.
why_others_wrong.C: Carbon dioxide and the acidosis it produces also contribute to pulmonary vasoconstriction, so it is incorrect to say CO2 has no effect on pulmonary vessels.
why_others_wrong.D: Pulmonary vessels do respond to oxygen tension, most notably through hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, contradicting this option.
why_others_wrong.E: The pulmonary circulation is a low-resistance system, but it is not a zero-resistance system, and this statement does not address the described vascular response.

exam_trap: Option B tempts candidates who apply the systemic rule to the lungs; alveolar hypoxia constricts pulmonary arterioles rather than dilating them.
takeaway: Systemic hypoxia often dilates vessels; alveolar hypoxia constricts pulmonary arterioles.
source: Standard cardiovascular/respiratory physiology.
thinking: Most systemic beds dilate in response to tissue hypoxia ↓ pulmonary arterioles behave differently ↓ alveolar hypoxia constricts local pulmonary vessels ↓ Alveolar hypoxia causes pulmonary vasoconstriction
pearl: Chronic global alveolar hypoxia, as in COPD or high altitude, causes widespread hypoxic vasoconstriction, pulmonary hypertension and eventually right heart failure.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Fluid assessment
stem: According to NICE guidance for adult hospital patients requiring IV fluids, which approach should be used when initially assessing fluid status?

options.B: ABCDE assessment combined with clinical context and trends

correct_answer: B. ABCDE assessment combined with clinical context and trends
why_correct: NICE recommends assessing fluid status using an ABCDE approach alongside clinical examination, trends and relevant context.

why_others_wrong.A: Blood pressure can be maintained by compensation until late hypovolaemia, so it is unreliable as the sole measure of fluid status.
why_others_wrong.C: Serum sodium reflects water balance relative to sodium rather than total fluid volume, so it cannot assess fluid status alone.
why_others_wrong.D: Urine colour is influenced by concentration, drugs and diet and is too crude to establish volume status on its own.
why_others_wrong.E: Body weight trends are useful but a single weight alone cannot distinguish hypovolaemia, overload or redistribution.

exam_trap: Blood pressure alone is the commonest wrong choice, but compensatory vasoconstriction can preserve it until hypovolaemia is advanced, so trends and full assessment are needed.
takeaway: Fluid assessment = clinical picture + trends + investigations, not one number.
source: NICE CG174, Intravenous fluid therapy in adults in hospital.
thinking: NICE guidance on intravenous fluids for adults ↓ no single parameter reliably defines volume status ↓ structured ABCDE assessment with context and trends ↓ ABCDE assessment combined with clinical context and trends
pearl: NICE lists indicators of need for fluid resuscitation including systolic blood pressure below 100 mmHg, heart rate above 90, capillary refill over 2 seconds, respiratory rate above 20 and a NEWS of 5 or more.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: IV fluid prescription
stem: When prescribing intravenous fluids for an adult inpatient, which information should be explicitly specified?
correct_answer: C. Fluid type, rate and volume
why_correct: NICE recommends that IV fluid prescriptions specify the type of fluid and the rate and volume to be administered.

why_others_wrong.A: Specifying the fluid type without rate and volume leaves administration open to interpretation and risks under- or over-infusion.
why_others_wrong.B: A rate alone does not state what fluid is given or the total volume, both of which NICE expects on the prescription.
why_others_wrong.D: The cannula brand is irrelevant to the fluid prescription, which must state type, rate and volume.
why_others_wrong.E: Blood group is relevant to transfusion, not to prescribing crystalloid or colloid intravenous fluids.

exam_trap: Fluid type only or rate only each seem sufficient at a glance, but a safe prescription must state type, rate and volume so the infusion cannot be misinterpreted.
takeaway: IV prescription → what fluid + how fast + how much.
source: NICE CG174, recommendation 1.5.11.
thinking: An IV fluid prescription must be unambiguous ↓ the prescriber states what fluid is given ↓ and how fast and how much ↓ Fluid type, rate and volume
pearl: NICE recommends that patients on IV fluids have an IV fluid management plan reviewed at least daily, with fluid balance charts, weight and electrolyte monitoring.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Maintenance fluid versus resuscitation
stem: A stable postoperative patient is unable to drink but has no evidence of shock or major ongoing losses. What category of IV-fluid therapy is most relevant?
why_correct: Maintenance therapy provides the patient's expected physiological fluid and electrolyte requirements when these cannot be met orally or enterally.

why_others_wrong.A: Fluid resuscitation is for hypovolaemia or shock, which this stable patient without major losses does not have.
why_others_wrong.C: Massive transfusion is for major haemorrhage, which is absent in a stable patient simply unable to drink.
why_others_wrong.D: Plasma exchange removes plasma constituents in specific immunological or haematological conditions and is not a form of fluid maintenance.
why_others_wrong.E: Hypertonic solutions are used in specific situations such as raised intracranial pressure or severe symptomatic hyponatraemia, not routine postoperative needs.

exam_trap: Fluid resuscitation is tempting for any postoperative patient on IV fluids, but it is reserved for hypovolaemia or shock, which this stable patient does not have.
takeaway: No shock + cannot maintain intake → think maintenance.
source: NICE CG174.
thinking: Stable patient with no shock or major losses ↓ cannot meet needs orally ↓ requires normal daily water and electrolyte requirements ↓ Routine maintenance
pearl: NICE routine maintenance is roughly 25-30 ml/kg/day of water with about 1 mmol/kg/day each of sodium, potassium and chloride and 50-100 g/day of glucose to limit starvation ketosis.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Ongoing abnormal losses
stem: A patient has a high-output stoma with ongoing fluid and electrolyte losses. Which principle is most appropriate?

options.A: Give standard maintenance fluid only and ignore the losses
options.B: Assess and replace ongoing abnormal losses in addition to maintenance requirements
options.E: Use glucose alone regardless of the composition of losses

correct_answer: B. Assess and replace ongoing abnormal losses in addition to maintenance requirements
why_correct: NICE separates routine maintenance from replacement of ongoing abnormal losses. Examples include gastrointestinal losses, stoma losses, fistula losses and ongoing urinary losses.

why_others_wrong.A: Standard maintenance covers normal daily needs and does not account for the extra fluid and electrolytes lost through a high-output stoma.
why_others_wrong.C: Stopping fluids in a patient with ongoing stoma losses would rapidly cause dehydration, electrolyte depletion and acute kidney injury.
why_others_wrong.D: Stoma output is electrolyte-rich fluid, not blood, so it should be replaced with appropriate crystalloid rather than blood products.
why_others_wrong.E: Glucose solutions contain no sodium, whereas stoma losses are sodium-rich, so replacement should match the composition of the losses.

exam_trap: Standard maintenance alone is chosen by candidates who assume routine fluids cover everything, but maintenance does not replace the extra electrolyte-rich losses from a high-output stoma.
takeaway: Maintenance ≠ replacement of abnormal losses.
source: NICE CG174.
thinking: High-output stoma with ongoing losses ↓ maintenance covers only normal daily needs ↓ extra losses must be estimated and replaced with matching fluid ↓ Assess and replace ongoing abnormal losses in addition to maintenance requirements
pearl: High-output stoma losses are sodium-rich, so management includes restricting hypotonic oral fluids, using an oral rehydration solution and antimotility agents such as loperamide, with monitoring of sodium and magnesium.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Enteral route for maintenance
stem: A patient requires prolonged fluid and nutritional support but has a functioning gastrointestinal tract. Which principle is generally preferred when feasible?

options.A: Long-term IV maintenance regardless of gastrointestinal function
options.B: Oral or enteral provision where appropriate

correct_answer: B. Oral or enteral provision where appropriate
why_correct: NICE recommends assessing whether fluid and electrolyte needs can be met orally or enterally before prescribing IV maintenance.

why_others_wrong.A: Relying on long-term IV maintenance ignores a functioning gut, which NICE advises using orally or enterally where appropriate.
why_others_wrong.C: Withholding fluids from a patient who needs prolonged support would lead to dehydration and malnutrition.
why_others_wrong.D: Permanent IV fluids carry line infection and thrombosis risks and are unnecessary when the gastrointestinal tract works.
why_others_wrong.E: Blood products are given for specific deficits such as anaemia or coagulopathy and are not a source of maintenance fluid or nutrition.

exam_trap: Long-term IV maintenance is tempting when access is already in place, but with a working gut the oral or enteral route is preferred and avoids line complications.
takeaway: Functional gut → use oral/enteral routes when clinically appropriate.
source: NICE CG174.
thinking: Prolonged support needed ↓ gastrointestinal tract is functioning ↓ oral or enteral route is safer and more physiological than IV ↓ Oral or enteral provision where appropriate
pearl: Enteral feeding helps maintain gut mucosal integrity and avoids the catheter-related sepsis and metabolic complications of parenteral nutrition, so if the gut works, use it.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Fluid overload
stem: A postoperative patient develops increasing peripheral oedema, rising weight and pulmonary crackles while receiving IV fluids. What should this prompt?

options.A: Automatic increase in IV fluid rate
options.B: Reassessment for fluid excess and review of ongoing fluid prescriptions
options.D: Ignoring the findings because oedema is expected after surgery

correct_answer: B. Reassessment for fluid excess and review of ongoing fluid prescriptions
why_correct: NICE emphasises repeated clinical and laboratory assessment and recognition of fluid excess.

why_others_wrong.A: Oedema, weight gain and crackles suggest fluid excess, so increasing the infusion rate would worsen overload.
why_others_wrong.C: Giving more crystalloid to a patient showing signs of fluid excess risks pulmonary oedema and further harm.
why_others_wrong.D: Rising weight and pulmonary crackles are not simply expected postoperative findings and need reassessment of fluid balance.
why_others_wrong.E: Transfusion addresses anaemia or bleeding and would add volume in a patient already showing signs of overload.

exam_trap: Options A and C, giving more fluid, appeal if oedema is misread as intravascular depletion, but rising weight and crackles indicate fluid excess requiring review, not more fluid.
takeaway: New oedema/crackles + IV fluids → reassess balance before giving more.
source: NICE CG174.
thinking: Patient receiving IV fluids ↓ new oedema, weight gain and pulmonary crackles ↓ signs of fluid excess ↓ stop and reassess before giving more ↓ Reassessment for fluid excess and review of ongoing fluid prescriptions
pearl: Postoperative fluid overload is associated with pulmonary complications, gut oedema with prolonged ileus and impaired anastomotic healing, which is why enhanced recovery pathways avoid excessive positive fluid balance.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Perioperative hypothermia
stem: Why is perioperative hypothermia clinically important?

options.B: It can affect coagulation, drug metabolism and postoperative recovery
options.E: It increases oxygen delivery in every patient

correct_answer: B. It can affect coagulation, drug metabolism and postoperative recovery
why_correct: Hypothermia can impair coagulation, alter pharmacokinetics and contribute to adverse perioperative outcomes.

why_others_wrong.A: Hypothermia has recognised consequences including coagulopathy, altered drug handling, wound infection and cardiac events.
why_others_wrong.C: Hypothermia affects many systems, not just glucose, and it does not consistently cause hyperglycaemia.
why_others_wrong.D: Perioperative hypothermia is associated with increased surgical site infection through vasoconstriction and impaired immune function.
why_others_wrong.E: Hypothermia shifts the oxyhaemoglobin curve to the left and may reduce tissue oxygen delivery, and shivering raises demand.

exam_trap: Option D tempts candidates who link cooling with reduced metabolism, but hypothermia actually increases surgical site infection through vasoconstriction and impaired immune function.
takeaway: Hypothermia → think coagulation + drug handling + recovery.
source: Standard perioperative physiology and UK perioperative-care principles.
thinking: Perioperative hypothermia ↓ impairs clotting enzyme and platelet function ↓ slows drug metabolism and prolongs anaesthetic effects ↓ increases wound infection and delays recovery ↓ It can affect coagulation, drug metabolism and postoperative recovery
pearl: NICE guidance on inadvertent perioperative hypothermia recommends measuring temperature before induction and warming patients with forced-air devices and warmed fluids during longer procedures.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Shivering and oxygen consumption
stem: A patient develops significant postoperative shivering. Which physiological effect may occur?
why_correct: Shivering is an involuntary thermogenic response involving skeletal-muscle activity and can substantially increase metabolic and oxygen requirements.

why_others_wrong.B: Shivering increases metabolic activity to generate heat, so metabolism rises rather than stopping.
why_others_wrong.C: Shivering consists of involuntary skeletal muscle contraction, so muscle activity increases rather than falls.
why_others_wrong.D: The rise in oxygen consumption from shivering increases cardiac output and myocardial workload, which can be hazardous in cardiac patients.
why_others_wrong.E: Shivering is a thermogenic response whose purpose is to increase heat production, not eliminate it.

exam_trap: Option D appeals to candidates who see shivering as a harmless reflex, but the increased oxygen demand raises cardiac output and myocardial workload rather than reducing it.
takeaway: Shivering → ↑ metabolic demand → ↑ oxygen consumption.
source: Standard thermoregulatory physiology.
thinking: Significant postoperative shivering ↓ involuntary skeletal muscle contraction generates heat ↓ metabolic rate rises ↓ Increased oxygen consumption
pearl: The rise in oxygen demand from shivering can precipitate myocardial ischaemia in patients with coronary disease; active warming and drugs such as pethidine can reduce it.

subject: Physiology
title: Thyroid hormone
stem: Which thyroid hormone is biologically more active at the tissue level?
why_correct: T3 has greater biological activity than T4. Much circulating T3 is generated by peripheral conversion of T4.

why_others_wrong.A: T4 is secreted in far greater quantity by the thyroid but is less biologically active at the tissue level than T3.
why_others_wrong.C: Reverse T3 is a largely biologically inactive metabolite formed from T4, not the more active hormone.
why_others_wrong.D: Thyroglobulin is an intrathyroidal storage/precursor protein, not a circulating hormone acting on peripheral tissue.
why_others_wrong.E: TSH is a pituitary hormone that stimulates the thyroid gland; it is not itself a thyroid hormone acting at peripheral tissue receptors.

exam_trap: The thyroid gland secretes predominantly T4, but T3 is the more biologically active hormone.
takeaway: T4 = major circulating precursor; T3 = greater biological activity.
source: Standard endocrine physiology.
thinking: Tissue-level activity ↓ the thyroid secretes mainly T4 ↓ peripheral deiodinases convert T4 to T3 ↓ T3 binds the nuclear receptor with higher affinity ↓ T3
pearl: In severe illness and after major surgery, peripheral conversion shifts towards reverse T3, giving a low T3 with often normal TSH (sick euthyroid syndrome) that usually needs no thyroid treatment.

subject: Physiology
title: Thyroid-stimulating hormone
stem: Which pituitary hormone stimulates thyroid hormone production by the thyroid gland?
why_correct: TSH from the anterior pituitary stimulates thyroid follicular cells to synthesise and release thyroid hormones. The hypothalamus-pituitary-thyroid axis operates through negative feedback.

why_others_wrong.A: ACTH stimulates the adrenal cortex to produce cortisol, not thyroid hormone.
why_others_wrong.C: FSH acts on the gonads to stimulate follicular development and is unrelated to thyroid hormone synthesis.
why_others_wrong.D: LH acts on the gonads to trigger ovulation or testosterone production and has no role in thyroid hormone synthesis.
why_others_wrong.E: Growth hormone promotes somatic growth and IGF-1 production; it does not stimulate thyroid hormone synthesis.

exam_trap: Candidates may select ACTH (A) because it is another pituitary stimulating hormone, but ACTH targets the adrenal cortex; only TSH acts directly on thyroid follicular cells.
takeaway: Hypothalamus TRH → pituitary TSH → thyroid T3/T4.
source: Standard endocrine physiology.
thinking: Thyroid hormone production ↓ hypothalamic TRH acts on the anterior pituitary ↓ thyrotrophs secrete TSH ↓ TSH acts on receptors of thyroid follicular cells ↓ TSH
pearl: In autoimmune hyperthyroidism, autoantibodies stimulate the TSH receptor directly, so thyroid hormone levels are high while pituitary TSH is suppressed.

subject: Physiology
title: Thyroid hormone and metabolism
stem: Which effect is associated with thyroid hormone?
correct_answer: B. Increase in basal metabolic rate
why_correct: Thyroid hormones increase metabolic activity and oxygen consumption in many tissues and contribute to thermogenesis.

why_others_wrong.A: This is the opposite effect: thyroid hormone increases, rather than reduces, basal metabolic activity.
why_others_wrong.C: Thyroid hormone actually potentiates (upregulates) tissue responsiveness to catecholamines rather than inhibiting their effects.
why_others_wrong.D: Thyroid hormone increases, rather than suppresses, mitochondrial oxidative activity as part of raising metabolic rate.
why_others_wrong.E: Thyroid hormone promotes thermogenesis and heat production; it does not eliminate it.

exam_trap: Candidates choosing C miss that thyroid hormone enhances beta-adrenergic responsiveness, which is why beta-blockers rapidly control tachycardia and tremor in thyrotoxicosis.
takeaway: Thyroid hormone → ↑ metabolic activity and thermogenesis.
source: Standard endocrine physiology.
thinking: Thyroid hormone acts on nuclear receptors in most tissues ↓ increases Na+/K+-ATPase activity and mitochondrial oxygen consumption ↓ raises thermogenesis ↓ Increase in basal metabolic rate
pearl: Uncontrolled hyperthyroidism risks thyroid storm at surgery, so patients are rendered euthyroid with antithyroid drugs, with beta-blockade for symptoms, before thyroidectomy.

subject: Physiology
title: Growth hormone and glucose
stem: Which metabolic effect is associated with growth hormone?

options.A: Increased insulin sensitivity in all tissues
options.B: Promotion of lipolysis and reduced peripheral glucose uptake

correct_answer: B. Promotion of lipolysis and reduced peripheral glucose uptake
why_correct: Growth hormone has anti-insulin effects on glucose metabolism and promotes lipolysis.

why_others_wrong.A: This is the opposite of GH's action: growth hormone reduces peripheral insulin sensitivity (a diabetogenic, anti-insulin effect), rather than increasing it universally.
why_others_wrong.C: Growth hormone promotes lipolysis rather than suppressing it.
why_others_wrong.D: Growth hormone is a distinct peptide hormone acting through its own receptor and IGF-1 pathway; it is not converted into insulin.
why_others_wrong.E: As part of its anti-insulin, diabetogenic action, growth hormone tends to increase rather than eliminate hepatic glucose output.

exam_trap: Growth hormone is not simply an anabolic hormone; its metabolic actions include diabetogenic effects.
takeaway: GH → growth effects + lipolysis + anti-insulin metabolic effects.
source: Standard endocrine physiology.
thinking: Growth hormone has direct metabolic actions ↓ it is counter-regulatory to insulin ↓ promotes lipolysis and reduces peripheral glucose uptake ↓ increases hepatic glucose output ↓ Promotion of lipolysis and reduced peripheral glucose uptake
pearl: Because of these anti-insulin effects, acromegaly is often complicated by impaired glucose tolerance or diabetes, which frequently improves after successful trans-sphenoidal pituitary surgery.

subject: Physiology
title: Cortisol and stress
stem: Which effect of cortisol is particularly relevant during physiological stress?

options.B: Complete suppression of vascular responsiveness to catecholamines

why_correct: Cortisol supports the stress response partly by promoting gluconeogenesis and modifying protein and lipid metabolism. It also contributes to maintenance of vascular responsiveness to catecholamines.

why_others_wrong.B: Cortisol supports and permits vascular responsiveness to catecholamines rather than suppressing it, which is particularly important during stress.
why_others_wrong.C: Cortisol promotes, rather than eliminates, protein catabolism to provide substrate for gluconeogenesis.
why_others_wrong.D: Cortisol promotes lipolysis rather than permanently inhibiting it.
why_others_wrong.E: Cortisol modulates and dampens immune activity but does not completely blockade it.

exam_trap: Candidates may choose B, but cortisol permits rather than suppresses vascular responsiveness to catecholamines; its key metabolic stress action listed here is promotion of gluconeogenesis.
takeaway: Stress + cortisol → glucose availability + vascular support + immune modulation.
source: Standard endocrine physiology.
thinking: Physiological stress ↓ cortisol secretion rises ↓ promotes gluconeogenesis and mobilises protein and fat ↓ also permits vascular responsiveness to catecholamines ↓ Promotion of gluconeogenesis
pearl: The cortisol surge after major surgery contributes to postoperative hyperglycaemia and catabolism, so blood glucose is worth monitoring perioperatively even in patients without diabetes.

subject: Physiology
title: Adrenal insufficiency and cortisol
stem: A patient with severe adrenal insufficiency becomes acutely unwell during physiological stress. Why can inadequate cortisol be particularly dangerous?

options.B: Cortisol supports vascular responsiveness and metabolic adaptation to stress
options.C: Cortisol is only required for digestion
options.E: Cortisol is required only during sleep

correct_answer: B. Cortisol supports vascular responsiveness and metabolic adaptation to stress
why_correct: During major physiological stress, increased cortisol availability supports vascular tone and metabolic responses. Adrenal insufficiency can therefore become clinically critical during acute illness.

why_others_wrong.A: Cortisol requirement actually increases, not disappears, during physiological stress, which is why its deficiency becomes dangerous.
why_others_wrong.C: Cortisol has broad metabolic and cardiovascular actions and is not limited to a role in digestion.
why_others_wrong.D: Calcium regulation is governed primarily by PTH and vitamin D, not cortisol, so this does not explain the danger of adrenal insufficiency during stress.
why_others_wrong.E: Cortisol follows a diurnal rhythm but is also essential during acute physiological stress, not only during sleep.

exam_trap: Candidates drawn to D confuse adrenal and calcium physiology; calcium is governed by PTH and vitamin D, whereas cortisol deficiency causes catecholamine-resistant hypotension under stress.
takeaway: Stress → increased cortisol requirement.
source: Standard endocrine physiology and perioperative medicine.
thinking: Severe adrenal insufficiency with acute stress ↓ cortisol requirement rises during illness ↓ cortisol maintains vascular tone and glucose supply ↓ deficiency causes hypotension and hypoglycaemia ↓ Cortisol supports vascular responsiveness and metabolic adaptation to stress
pearl: Suspected adrenal crisis is treated with immediate intravenous hydrocortisone and fluid resuscitation, without waiting for confirmatory cortisol results.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Oxygen delivery and haemoglobin
stem: Which change would most directly reduce arterial oxygen content in an otherwise stable patient?
why_correct: Most oxygen in arterial blood is carried bound to haemoglobin. A major reduction in haemoglobin concentration therefore substantially reduces arterial oxygen content even if oxygen saturation is normal.

why_others_wrong.B: Mild isolated tachycardia does not itself reduce oxygen-carrying capacity and may even be a compensatory response to reduced delivery.
why_others_wrong.C: Increased plasma sodium concentration has no direct role in the oxygen-carrying capacity of arterial blood.
why_others_wrong.D: Increased albumin affects plasma oncotic pressure, not the amount of oxygen carried by haemoglobin.
why_others_wrong.E: Increased body temperature shifts the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve rightward, aiding oxygen unloading at tissues, but it does not itself reduce arterial oxygen content.

exam_trap: A normal SpO₂ does not guarantee normal oxygen delivery when haemoglobin concentration is severely reduced.
takeaway: Normal saturation + severe anaemia ≠ normal oxygen content.
source: Standard cardiovascular/respiratory physiology; MRCS Applied Basic Science syllabus.
thinking: Arterial O2 content is dominated by Hb-bound oxygen ↓ content = Hb x saturation x carrying constant + small dissolved fraction ↓ severe anaemia lowers Hb directly ↓ Severe anaemia
pearl: Carbon monoxide poisoning also reduces oxygen content with a misleadingly normal pulse oximeter reading, because standard oximeters cannot distinguish carboxyhaemoglobin.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Surgical stress response
stem: Which hormonal change is characteristic of the physiological response to major surgery?
correct_answer: C. Increased catecholamine and cortisol activity
why_correct: Major surgery produces a neuroendocrine stress response involving catecholamines, cortisol, glucagon and inflammatory mediators. This promotes mobilisation of energy substrates and cardiovascular adaptation.

why_others_wrong.A: Sympathetic activation after major surgery increases catecholamine release rather than reducing it.
why_others_wrong.B: Cortisol secretion rises after major surgery through ACTH stimulation, as part of the neuroendocrine stress response.
why_others_wrong.D: Glucagon secretion increases after surgery and contributes to gluconeogenesis and hyperglycaemia.
why_others_wrong.E: Surgery triggers release of cytokines such as IL-6, so inflammatory mediators are increased rather than inhibited.

exam_trap: Option B tempts candidates who recall that steroids suppress inflammation, but cortisol secretion rises after major surgery as part of the stress response rather than falling.
takeaway: Major surgery → stress hormones + inflammation + catabolism.
source: Standard surgical physiology; MRCS Principles of Surgery in General.
thinking: Major surgery triggers the neuroendocrine stress response ↓ sympathetic activation releases catecholamines ↓ hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis raises cortisol ↓ Increased catecholamine and cortisol activity
pearl: The magnitude of the stress response is broadly proportional to the extent of tissue injury, one reason minimally invasive surgery and regional anaesthesia are associated with a smaller metabolic response.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Postoperative insulin resistance
stem: Why can blood glucose rise after major surgery even in a patient without pre-existing diabetes?

options.A: Surgery always destroys pancreatic beta cells
options.B: The stress response can produce postoperative insulin resistance

correct_answer: B. The stress response can produce postoperative insulin resistance
why_correct: Catecholamines, cortisol, growth hormone and inflammatory mediators contribute to insulin resistance and increased hepatic glucose availability during surgical stress.

why_others_wrong.A: Surgery does not destroy beta cells; the hyperglycaemia is driven by counter-regulatory hormones and insulin resistance.
why_others_wrong.C: Glucagon rises rather than disappears after surgery and contributes to increased hepatic glucose output.
why_others_wrong.D: Cortisol is a counter-regulatory hormone that raises blood glucose by promoting gluconeogenesis and insulin resistance.
why_others_wrong.E: Insulin continues to be secreted after surgery; the problem is reduced tissue sensitivity to it, not absent secretion.

exam_trap: Option E appeals to those who equate hyperglycaemia with insulin deficiency, but after surgery insulin is still secreted; the problem is reduced tissue sensitivity to it.
takeaway: Surgery → stress response → insulin resistance + hyperglycaemia.
source: Standard perioperative physiology.
thinking: Non-diabetic patient with postoperative hyperglycaemia ↓ counter-regulatory hormones rise after surgery ↓ peripheral insulin resistance and increased hepatic glucose output ↓ The stress response can produce postoperative insulin resistance
pearl: Preoperative carbohydrate loading drinks within enhanced recovery pathways are used to reduce postoperative insulin resistance in non-diabetic patients.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Catabolism after major surgery
stem: Which metabolic change commonly occurs after major surgery?

options.A: Positive nitrogen balance without nutritional support
options.D: Permanent suppression of hepatic glucose production

why_correct: The postoperative stress response promotes catabolism, including breakdown of protein to provide substrates for gluconeogenesis and tissue repair.

why_others_wrong.A: Without nutritional support the catabolic response after major surgery produces negative, not positive, nitrogen balance.
why_others_wrong.C: Catecholamines and cortisol stimulate lipolysis after surgery to mobilise fatty acids as an energy source.
why_others_wrong.D: Hepatic glucose production increases after surgery through glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis rather than being suppressed.
why_others_wrong.E: Energy requirements generally increase after major surgery because of tissue repair and the hypermetabolic stress response.

exam_trap: Option A tempts candidates who assume rest conserves protein, but without nutritional support the stress response produces negative nitrogen balance, not positive.
takeaway: Major surgery → catabolic state → nitrogen loss unless recovery/nutrition counteract it.
source: Standard surgical metabolism.
thinking: Major surgery provokes a catabolic stress response ↓ cortisol, catecholamines and glucagon mobilise substrates ↓ muscle protein is broken down for gluconeogenesis ↓ Increased protein catabolism
pearl: Postoperative catabolism can be blunted but not abolished by enhanced recovery measures such as minimally invasive surgery, regional anaesthesia, early feeding and early mobilisation.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Malnutrition and wound healing
stem: Which nutritional problem can impair collagen synthesis and wound healing?
why_correct: Adequate protein and energy availability are important for immune function, fibroblast activity and collagen production.

why_others_wrong.B: Mild isolated hyperchloraemia is an electrolyte finding, not a nutritional deficiency, and does not impair collagen synthesis.
why_others_wrong.C: Adequate water intake supports tissue perfusion and does not impair collagen synthesis or wound healing.
why_others_wrong.D: Normal iron stores support oxygen delivery and collagen hydroxylation, so they would not impair healing.
why_others_wrong.E: Normal vitamin intake, including vitamin C, supports collagen formation rather than impairing it.

exam_trap: Normal iron stores may tempt because iron is a cofactor for collagen hydroxylation, but adequate iron supports healing; it is protein deficiency that limits fibroblast collagen synthesis.
takeaway: Poor nutrition → impaired immunity + impaired collagen formation + poorer healing.
source: NICE CG32, Nutrition support for adults.
thinking: Wound healing needs collagen synthesis by fibroblasts ↓ collagen production requires amino acid substrate and energy ↓ protein deficiency limits fibroblast activity and immunity ↓ Protein deficiency
pearl: Vitamin C is a cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase in collagen cross-linking, so scurvy causes poor wound healing and breakdown of previously healed scars.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Malnutrition screening
stem: Which combination is particularly relevant when screening an adult surgical patient for malnutrition?

options.B: Blood group and pulse rate only

correct_answer: A. BMI and unintentional weight loss
why_correct: NICE recommends that nutritional screening considers BMI, percentage unintentional weight loss and the duration/reduction of nutritional intake.

why_others_wrong.B: Blood group and pulse rate are not nutritional indicators and form no part of recognised malnutrition screening tools such as MUST.
why_others_wrong.C: Height alone cannot identify malnutrition without weight, BMI and recent weight loss.
why_others_wrong.D: Serum sodium reflects water and electrolyte balance, not nutritional status, and is not part of nutritional screening.
why_others_wrong.E: Age is a risk factor for malnutrition but cannot on its own identify patients who are malnourished.

exam_trap: Height alone or age alone may seem relevant, but neither identifies malnutrition; screening needs BMI combined with unintentional weight loss and intake history.
takeaway: Nutrition screen → BMI + weight loss + intake history.
source: NICE CG32, current recommendations.
thinking: Screening for malnutrition in a surgical adult ↓ nutritional status is captured by body mass and its recent change ↓ MUST combines BMI, unplanned weight loss and acute illness effect on intake ↓ BMI and unintentional weight loss
pearl: The Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool scores BMI, percentage unplanned weight loss over 3-6 months and an acute disease effect on intake; NICE advises screening all hospital inpatients on admission.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Enteral nutrition
stem: A malnourished postoperative patient cannot safely maintain oral intake but has a functioning gastrointestinal tract. Which route is generally preferred when appropriate?
why_correct: NICE recommends considering enteral tube feeding for patients who are malnourished or at risk, have inadequate or unsafe oral intake and have a functional, accessible gastrointestinal tract.

why_others_wrong.B: Crystalloid provides water and electrolytes but negligible nutrition, so it cannot treat malnutrition.
why_others_wrong.C: Blood transfusion corrects anaemia or blood loss and provides no meaningful nutritional support.
why_others_wrong.D: A malnourished patient unable to maintain oral intake needs nutritional support; withholding it worsens healing and recovery.
why_others_wrong.E: Intramuscular feeding is not a route for delivering nutrition; the options are oral, enteral or parenteral.

exam_trap: Long-term intravenous crystalloid may tempt because it keeps the patient hydrated, but it provides water and electrolytes only and cannot correct malnutrition.
takeaway: If the gut works and oral intake is inadequate → think enteral.
source: NICE CG32.
thinking: Malnourished patient unable to eat safely ↓ gastrointestinal tract is functioning ↓ use the gut via a feeding tube ↓ Enteral feeding
pearl: Nasogastric tube position must be confirmed before first use, usually by aspirate pH of 5.5 or below or by chest X-ray; feeding into a misplaced tube is an NHS never event.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Early postoperative oral intake
stem: A patient has undergone abdominal surgery, can swallow safely and has no specific concern about gastrointestinal function or integrity. What does NICE recommend considering?

options.A: Avoiding oral intake for several weeks
options.E: Oral intake only after bowel sounds return

correct_answer: B. Some oral intake within 24 hours
why_correct: NICE recommends considering some oral intake within 24 hours after abdominal surgery in patients who can swallow safely and have no specific concern about gut function or integrity.

why_others_wrong.A: Prolonged avoidance of oral intake is unnecessary after uncomplicated abdominal surgery and delays recovery.
why_others_wrong.C: Parenteral nutrition is for patients whose gut cannot be used, not for someone who can swallow safely with a functioning gut.
why_others_wrong.D: Nasogastric feeding is unnecessary in a patient who can swallow safely, and permanent tube feeding is not indicated.
why_others_wrong.E: Bowel sounds are not a prerequisite for starting oral intake, and waiting for them delays early feeding.

exam_trap: Option E is the classic trap: waiting for bowel sounds is traditional practice, but NICE does not require it before starting oral intake after abdominal surgery.
takeaway: Uncomplicated abdominal surgery + safe swallowing + functioning gut → early oral intake can be considered.
source: NICE CG32.
thinking: Uncomplicated abdominal surgery ↓ safe swallow with no concern about gut function ↓ NICE advises early oral intake ↓ Some oral intake within 24 hours
pearl: Early oral feeding after colorectal surgery is a core enhanced recovery element and has not been shown to increase anastomotic leak, while it is associated with faster return of gut function.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Refeeding syndrome
stem: A severely malnourished patient starts nutritional support and subsequently develops profound hypophosphataemia. What complication should be considered?
why_correct: Reintroduction of nutrition after prolonged undernutrition can produce marked metabolic shifts, particularly involving phosphate, potassium and magnesium.

why_others_wrong.B: Hyperthyroidism causes weight loss and tachycardia but does not explain profound hypophosphataemia after nutrition is restarted.
why_others_wrong.C: Primary polycythaemia is a myeloproliferative disorder with raised red cell mass and is unrelated to refeeding electrolyte shifts.
why_others_wrong.D: Acute appendicitis is a surgical inflammatory condition and has no link with hypophosphataemia after feeding a malnourished patient.
why_others_wrong.E: Iron deficiency causes anaemia but does not account for a profound fall in phosphate when nutrition is reintroduced.

exam_trap: Hyperthyroidism may tempt as a cause of weight loss and tachycardia, but only refeeding explains a profound phosphate fall immediately after nutrition is reintroduced.
takeaway: Malnutrition + feeding + falling phosphate → think refeeding syndrome.
source: NICE CG32; refeeding-risk recommendations.
thinking: Severely malnourished patient ↓ nutrition restarted ↓ profound hypophosphataemia follows ↓ Refeeding syndrome
pearl: Hypophosphataemia in refeeding depletes ATP and 2,3-DPG, which can cause respiratory muscle weakness, cardiac failure, arrhythmias, confusion and rhabdomyolysis.

subject: Microbiology & surgical infection
title: Surgical site infection prevention
stem: Which principle is appropriate when preventing surgical site infection?

options.A: Antibiotics can compensate for poor surgical technique
options.B: Appropriate aseptic technique and perioperative measures are important
options.C: Every surgical wound requires prolonged postoperative antibiotics
options.E: Hand hygiene is irrelevant in theatre

correct_answer: B. Appropriate aseptic technique and perioperative measures are important
why_correct: Prevention of surgical site infection is multifactorial and includes appropriate aseptic technique, patient preparation, antibiotic prophylaxis where indicated and good perioperative practice.

why_others_wrong.A: Antibiotic prophylaxis supplements but cannot compensate for poor technique, devitalised tissue or contamination; SSI prevention depends on a bundle of measures.
why_others_wrong.C: Most clean wounds do not need prolonged antibiotics; unnecessary courses add resistance, C. difficile risk and side effects without reducing SSI.
why_others_wrong.D: NICE recommends antiseptic skin preparation of the operative site, so omitting it would increase the risk of surgical site infection.
why_others_wrong.E: Hand hygiene and surgical hand antisepsis are core theatre infection-control measures and are fundamental to preventing SSI.

exam_trap: Candidates may choose 'antibiotics can compensate for poor surgical technique', but prophylaxis only supplements asepsis and tissue handling; devitalised tissue and contamination still cause infection.
takeaway: SSI prevention = bundle, not antibiotics alone.
source: NICE NG125.
thinking: SSI prevention is multifactorial ↓ asepsis, skin preparation, hand hygiene and physiological optimisation ↓ antibiotics only supplement good technique ↓ Appropriate aseptic technique and perioperative measures are important
pearl: Gentle tissue handling, careful haemostasis, avoiding dead space and removing devitalised tissue reduce surgical-site infection independently of antibiotic prophylaxis.

subject: Microbiology & surgical infection
title: Surgical antibiotic prophylaxis
stem: What is the principal purpose of prophylactic antibiotics given around an operation?

options.A: To sterilise the entire patient's body
options.B: To reduce the risk of surgical site infection when indicated
options.E: To eliminate all postoperative bacterial colonisation

correct_answer: B. To reduce the risk of surgical site infection when indicated
why_correct: Antimicrobial prophylaxis is used for selected procedures where reducing microbial contamination can reduce surgical site infection.

why_others_wrong.A: Prophylaxis cannot and is not intended to sterilise the body; it aims to lower bacterial numbers at the operative site during surgery.
why_others_wrong.C: Postoperative fever has many non-infective causes, and established infection is managed with treatment courses, not prophylaxis.
why_others_wrong.D: Antibiotics do not replace drainage or removal of an infected source; source control remains essential when there is established infection.
why_others_wrong.E: Bacterial colonisation of skin and gut persists after surgery; prophylaxis only reduces the risk of wound infection rather than eradicating colonisation.

exam_trap: Replacing surgical source control is a common misconception; prophylaxis prevents wound infection, whereas established infection needs treatment courses plus drainage or removal of the source.
takeaway: Prophylaxis = prevention, not treatment.
source: NICE NG125.
thinking: Prophylaxis is given before contamination occurs ↓ aim is to lower bacterial load at the operative site ↓ only for operations where it is indicated ↓ To reduce the risk of surgical site infection when indicated
pearl: Prophylaxis is usually a single dose before incision; continuing antibiotics after surgery needs a separate treatment indication, otherwise it adds resistance and adverse effects without benefit.

subject: Microbiology & surgical infection
title: Surgical infection and source control
stem: A patient has an intra-abdominal abscess with systemic illness. Which principle is central to definitive management?

options.C: Delaying all intervention until fever resolves
options.D: Giving fluids without treating the source

why_correct: An established abscess or other infected collection may require drainage or operative intervention in addition to appropriate antimicrobial therapy.

why_others_wrong.B: An established abscess is poorly penetrated by antibiotics, so antibiotics alone often fail without drainage; small collections are sometimes managed medically, but not in every case.
why_others_wrong.C: Waiting for fever to settle delays definitive treatment; fever often persists until the collection has been drained.
why_others_wrong.D: Fluid resuscitation is important but is supportive only; without source control the septic focus persists.
why_others_wrong.E: Imaging such as CT is usually needed to confirm and localise the collection and to plan percutaneous or surgical drainage.

exam_trap: Antibiotics alone in every case is the trap; small abscesses may settle medically, but an established collection with systemic illness usually needs drainage as definitive treatment.
takeaway: Surgical sepsis → antibiotics + resuscitation + source control where required.
source: Standard surgical infection principles; NICE antimicrobial and surgical infection guidance.
thinking: Intra-abdominal abscess with systemic illness ↓ walled-off pus is poorly penetrated by antibiotics ↓ drainage, percutaneous or operative, removes the septic focus ↓ Source control
pearl: Many intra-abdominal abscesses can be drained percutaneously under CT or ultrasound guidance, with laparotomy reserved for inaccessible or multiloculated collections or ongoing contamination such as an anastomotic leak.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Wound dehiscence
stem: A patient develops sudden serosanguineous discharge from a laparotomy wound several days after surgery. What complication should be considered?
why_correct: Sudden serosanguineous discharge from a recent abdominal wound can precede or accompany fascial dehiscence.

why_others_wrong.B: A keloid is a raised scar extending beyond the wound margins that develops over weeks to months, not an acute discharge presenting days after a laparotomy.
why_others_wrong.C: A chronic hypertrophic scar is a long-term raised scar confined to the wound, unrelated to an acute serosanguineous discharge in the early postoperative period.
why_others_wrong.D: Primary skin closure describes the surgical technique of apposing wound edges at the time of operation; it is not a postoperative complication or diagnosis to explain new discharge.
why_others_wrong.E: Immediate complete wound healing would not present with new serosanguineous discharge several days after surgery; that finding is concerning for a complication rather than uneventful healing.

exam_trap: Do not dismiss sudden “pink” wound discharge as normal postoperative ooze when it occurs in the appropriate timeframe.
takeaway: Sudden serosanguineous wound discharge → think fascial dehiscence.
source: Standard postoperative surgical principles.
thinking: Laparotomy several days ago ↓ sudden pink serosanguineous discharge ↓ fluid tracking through a fascial defect ↓ Wound dehiscence
pearl: Fascial dehiscence classically occurs around days 5-8 after laparotomy, and risk factors include obesity, malnutrition, steroids, infection and raised intra-abdominal pressure.

subject: Acute abdomen & GI surgery
title: Incisional hernia
stem: What is an incisional hernia?

options.A: Herniation through a previous abdominal surgical incision
options.B: Herniation through the oesophageal hiatus only

correct_answer: A. Herniation through a previous abdominal surgical incision
why_correct: An incisional hernia develops through weakness at a previous operative incision. Risk factors include impaired healing, wound infection, obesity and increased intra-abdominal pressure.

why_others_wrong.B: Herniation through the oesophageal hiatus is a hiatus hernia, which involves a natural diaphragmatic opening rather than a previous operative incision.
why_others_wrong.C: A congenital inguinal defect, such as a patent processus vaginalis, underlies an indirect inguinal hernia, whereas an incisional hernia is acquired at a surgical scar.
why_others_wrong.D: A femoral hernia passes through the femoral canal below the inguinal ligament, a natural anatomical weakness unrelated to any previous incision.
why_others_wrong.E: Diaphragmatic rupture follows trauma and allows abdominal contents into the chest; it is not a hernia through an abdominal wall surgical incision.

exam_trap: Candidates may pick a congenital inguinal defect or a femoral hernia because both are common, but these pass through natural weaknesses, whereas an incisional hernia is acquired at a surgical scar.
takeaway: Previous abdominal incision + later abdominal wall bulge → incisional hernia.
source: Standard general surgical principles.
thinking: Defined by site of herniation ↓ hiatus, inguinal and femoral hernias use natural openings ↓ incisional hernia emerges through a failed operative wound ↓ Herniation through a previous abdominal surgical incision
pearl: Midline laparotomy closure with a small-bite technique using a slowly absorbable continuous suture reduces incisional hernia rates, and wound infection is one of the strongest modifiable risk factors.

subject: Acute abdomen & GI surgery
title: Postoperative ileus
stem: Which feature is characteristic of postoperative ileus?

options.A: Functional reduction in intestinal motility without a mechanical obstruction
options.B: Always caused by an obstructing tumour
options.C: Always associated with a strangulated hernia
