correct_answer: A. Functional reduction in intestinal motility without a mechanical obstruction
why_correct: Postoperative ileus is a transient impairment of gastrointestinal motility following surgery and other systemic insults.

why_others_wrong.B: Postoperative ileus is a functional motility disturbance with no mechanical cause, so an obstructing tumour describes mechanical obstruction rather than ileus.
why_others_wrong.C: A strangulated hernia causes mechanical obstruction with compromised blood supply, whereas postoperative ileus is a transient functional hypomotility without a mechanical cause.
why_others_wrong.D: Perforation is not part of postoperative ileus, which is a transient reduction in motility that usually resolves with supportive care.
why_others_wrong.E: Postoperative ileus involves reduced and uncoordinated gut motility, the opposite of increased coordinated peristalsis.

exam_trap: Choosing an obstructing tumour or strangulated hernia confuses ileus with mechanical obstruction; ileus is functional, with no physical blockage and no transition point on imaging.
takeaway: Postoperative distension + reduced bowel function → consider ileus, but exclude mechanical obstruction when indicated.
source: Standard postoperative surgical principles.
thinking: Postoperative ileus = transient hypomotility after surgery ↓ no mechanical blockage is present ↓ options citing tumour, strangulation or perforation describe mechanical or complicated pathology ↓ Functional reduction in intestinal motility without a mechanical obstruction
pearl: Opioids, electrolyte disturbance (especially low potassium or magnesium) and intra-abdominal sepsis prolong ileus, so persistent ileus should prompt a search for a leak or collection rather than simply waiting.

subject: Acute abdomen & GI surgery
title: Anastomotic leak
stem: Which postoperative finding should raise concern for an anastomotic leak after gastrointestinal surgery?
why_correct: Anastomotic leakage can present with systemic deterioration, abdominal pain, fever, tachycardia, inflammatory response or other signs of intra-abdominal sepsis.

why_others_wrong.B: Normal recovery with improving observations is reassuring and argues against a leak, which typically causes unexplained deterioration or signs of sepsis.
why_others_wrong.C: Return of appetite on its own suggests recovering gut function and does not raise concern for a leak, although it does not exclude one.
why_others_wrong.D: Independent mobilisation reflects good postoperative progress rather than the unexplained systemic deterioration that should prompt consideration of a leak.
why_others_wrong.E: A normal wound says little about the anastomosis inside the abdomen, so it neither suggests nor excludes a leak.

exam_trap: A normal wound appearance is falsely reassuring: it reflects only the skin and fascia and gives no information about the integrity of the anastomosis inside the abdomen.
takeaway: Unexpected postoperative deterioration after GI anastomosis → consider leak and sepsis.
source: Standard postoperative surgical principles.
thinking: GI anastomosis in the postoperative period ↓ leak causes intra-abdominal contamination and sepsis ↓ early sign is often unexplained tachycardia, fever or general deterioration ↓ New unexplained systemic deterioration
pearl: Persistent tachycardia or a failure to progress after bowel surgery should prompt early CT with contrast rather than attributing it to pain or dehydration, as delayed diagnosis of a leak increases mortality.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Postoperative pulmonary atelectasis
stem: What is atelectasis?

options.A: Collapse or incomplete expansion of alveolar units

correct_answer: A. Collapse or incomplete expansion of alveolar units
why_correct: Atelectasis involves loss of aeration in part of the lung and is common in the postoperative setting, particularly when ventilation is impaired.

why_others_wrong.B: Pulmonary artery thrombosis describes a vascular occlusion, as in pulmonary embolism, not collapse of alveoli.
why_others_wrong.C: Pleural infection is empyema or parapneumonic effusion in the pleural space, not loss of alveolar aeration.
why_others_wrong.D: Bronchial carcinoma is a malignancy that can cause distal collapse, but it is not the definition of atelectasis.
why_others_wrong.E: Atelectasis reduces ventilation of the affected alveoli, the opposite of increased alveolar ventilation.

exam_trap: Bronchial carcinoma is tempting because it can cause distal collapse, but it is one cause; atelectasis itself means collapse or incomplete expansion of alveoli, not pneumonia.
takeaway: Postoperative reduced aeration/collapse → atelectasis.
source: Standard respiratory and perioperative medicine.
thinking: Loss of aeration in lung tissue ↓ alveoli collapse or fail to expand ↓ common after anaesthesia and abdominal surgery ↓ Collapse or incomplete expansion of alveolar units
pearl: Postoperative atelectasis typically causes low-grade fever and hypoxia in the first 48 hours and is prevented by good analgesia, early mobilisation and breathing exercises.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Postoperative pneumonia
stem: Which factor increases the risk of postoperative chest infection?
correct_answer: A. Impaired cough and poor mobilisation
why_correct: Pain, sedation, immobility and impaired respiratory mechanics can reduce effective secretion clearance and ventilation.

why_others_wrong.B: Early mobilisation improves lung expansion and secretion clearance, so it reduces rather than increases chest infection risk.
why_others_wrong.C: Effective analgesia allows deep breathing and coughing, lowering the risk of postoperative chest infection.
why_others_wrong.D: Physiotherapy helps clear secretions and re-expand collapsed lung, reducing the risk of chest infection.
why_others_wrong.E: Appropriate hydration keeps secretions less viscous and easier to clear, so it does not increase infection risk.

exam_trap: Option C appeals to candidates who fear opioid-induced respiratory depression, but effective analgesia enables deep breathing and coughing and lowers chest infection risk.
takeaway: Postoperative chest risk → pain + immobility + poor secretion clearance.
source: Standard perioperative respiratory principles.
thinking: Postoperative pain, sedation and immobility ↓ shallow breathing and an ineffective cough ↓ secretions are retained ↓ infection develops in poorly ventilated lung ↓ Impaired cough and poor mobilisation
pearl: Upper abdominal and thoracic incisions carry the highest risk of postoperative pulmonary complications, because pain limits deep breathing and coughing; epidural analgesia can reduce this.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Postoperative urinary retention
stem: Which factor can contribute to postoperative urinary retention?
why_correct: Anaesthetic agents, opioids, pain and perioperative autonomic changes can impair bladder emptying.

why_others_wrong.B: Early mobilisation tends to help bladder emptying rather than cause retention, so increased mobility by itself is not a recognised contributor.
why_others_wrong.C: Intact bladder sensation allows the patient to perceive fullness and void, whereas retention is favoured by blunted sensation from anaesthesia or opioids.
why_others_wrong.D: Higher oral intake increases urine production but does not impair detrusor function or sphincter relaxation, so on its own it does not cause retention.
why_others_wrong.E: Retention results from perioperative disturbance of autonomic control of the bladder, so normal autonomic function would support rather than impair voiding.

exam_trap: Increased oral intake may be chosen because it fills the bladder, but higher urine volume alone does not impair detrusor function; anaesthesia and opioids do.
takeaway: Postoperative inability to void → consider retention, especially after anaesthesia/opioids.
source: Standard perioperative physiology.
thinking: Postoperative inability to void ↓ anaesthetic agents and opioids reduce bladder sensation and detrusor contractility ↓ autonomic disturbance impairs sphincter relaxation ↓ Anaesthesia and opioid analgesia
pearl: A bladder scan can confirm retention after surgery; spinal anaesthesia, hernia and anorectal surgery, older age and large intraoperative fluid volumes are recognised risk factors.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Postoperative delirium
stem: Which statement about postoperative delirium is correct?

options.A: It is always caused by dementia
options.B: It is an acute disturbance in attention and cognition with a fluctuating course

correct_answer: B. It is an acute disturbance in attention and cognition with a fluctuating course
why_correct: Delirium is an acute neuropsychiatric syndrome characterised particularly by impaired attention and fluctuating cognition.

why_others_wrong.A: Dementia is a major risk factor for postoperative delirium, but delirium commonly occurs without dementia and has many precipitants such as infection, drugs and hypoxia.
why_others_wrong.C: Depression is a mood disorder without the acute onset, inattention and fluctuating consciousness that define delirium, although hypoactive delirium can be mistaken for it.
why_others_wrong.D: Delirium is often reversible when the precipitating causes are identified and treated, although some patients have persisting cognitive decline afterwards.
why_others_wrong.E: Postoperative delirium is common after many operations, particularly emergency and orthopaedic surgery in older patients such as hip fracture repair, not just neurosurgery.

exam_trap: Option A tempts because dementia is the strongest risk factor, but delirium often occurs without dementia and is defined by acute, fluctuating inattention, not by its cause.
takeaway: Acute + fluctuating + impaired attention → think delirium.
source: Standard perioperative medicine; NICE delirium guidance.
thinking: Acute onset ↓ impaired attention ↓ fluctuating course ↓ Acute disturbance in attention and cognition with a fluctuating course
pearl: Hypoactive delirium is common in older surgical patients and easily missed; the 4AT is a quick bedside screening tool, and treatment centres on identifying precipitants such as infection, drugs, pain and urinary retention.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: VTE risk assessment
stem: According to NICE, what should happen to a surgical patient's VTE and bleeding risk assessment when their clinical condition changes?

options.D: VTE prophylaxis should automatically continue unchanged

why_correct: NICE recommends reassessing surgical and trauma patients for VTE and bleeding risk when their clinical condition changes.

why_others_wrong.A: NICE treats VTE and bleeding risk assessment as dynamic, so leaving it unrevisited after a change in clinical condition could miss a new risk or contraindication.
why_others_wrong.C: The surgeon's age has no bearing on thrombosis or bleeding risk; reassessment concerns the patient's own risk factors and clinical state.
why_others_wrong.D: Continuing prophylaxis unchanged without review ignores that new bleeding risk or reduced VTE risk may alter whether prophylaxis is still appropriate.
why_others_wrong.E: NICE requires VTE risk to be weighed against bleeding risk, so ignoring bleeding risk could lead to harmful anticoagulation after a clinical change.

exam_trap: Option D tempts because continuing an existing plan feels safe, but a change in condition may create a contraindication to prophylaxis, so reassessment is required.
takeaway: Clinical condition changes → reassess VTE + bleeding risk.
source: NICE NG89, VTE prevention.
thinking: Clinical condition of a surgical patient changes ↓ VTE and bleeding risks may both alter ↓ NICE treats assessment as dynamic ↓ It should be reassessed
pearl: NICE recommends assessing VTE and bleeding risk on admission, at the first consultant review and whenever the clinical condition changes, for example after a return to theatre or new bleeding.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Mechanical VTE prophylaxis
stem: A patient undergoing abdominal surgery is at increased risk of VTE. Which mechanical intervention is recommended by NICE on admission?

options.A: Anti-embolism stockings or intermittent pneumatic compression

correct_answer: A. Anti-embolism stockings or intermittent pneumatic compression
why_correct: NICE recommends mechanical VTE prophylaxis on admission for patients undergoing abdominal surgery who are at increased risk.

why_others_wrong.B: Therapeutic warfarin treats established thrombosis and carries significant bleeding risk; it is not a mechanical measure or routine prophylaxis for abdominal surgery.
why_others_wrong.C: Withholding prophylaxis from an abdominal surgery patient at increased VTE risk contradicts NICE, which recommends mechanical prophylaxis on admission.
why_others_wrong.D: Starting compression only after discharge misses the in-hospital period of highest risk, whereas NICE advises mechanical prophylaxis from admission.
why_others_wrong.E: Aspirin is a pharmacological agent, not a mechanical intervention, and is not recommended by NICE as routine VTE prophylaxis for all abdominal surgery.

exam_trap: Aspirin is tempting as a familiar antithrombotic, but it is pharmacological rather than mechanical and is not NICE routine prophylaxis for abdominal surgery.
takeaway: Abdominal surgery + increased VTE risk → mechanical prophylaxis on admission.
source: NICE NG89.
thinking: Abdominal surgery with increased VTE risk ↓ NICE starts prophylaxis from admission ↓ mechanical options are stockings or intermittent pneumatic compression ↓ Anti-embolism stockings or intermittent pneumatic compression
pearl: Anti-embolism stockings are contraindicated in significant peripheral arterial disease, peripheral neuropathy and fragile skin, so ankle-brachial pressure index and skin checks matter before fitting them.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: VTE prophylaxis and bleeding risk
stem: A surgical patient has a high risk of VTE but also a high risk of major bleeding. What principle should guide pharmacological prophylaxis?

options.A: Give pharmacological prophylaxis regardless of bleeding risk
options.B: Balance VTE risk against bleeding risk
options.E: Use the same prophylaxis for every patient

correct_answer: B. Balance VTE risk against bleeding risk
why_correct: NICE specifically recommends balancing individual VTE risk against bleeding risk when deciding whether to offer pharmacological prophylaxis.

why_others_wrong.A: Giving pharmacological prophylaxis regardless of bleeding risk could cause major haemorrhage in this high-bleeding-risk patient; NICE requires the two risks to be weighed.
why_others_wrong.C: This patient's VTE risk is high, so ignoring it would leave a serious and preventable thrombotic risk unaddressed, for example by omitting mechanical prophylaxis.
why_others_wrong.D: Therapeutic anticoagulation is treatment for established thrombosis and would greatly increase haemorrhage in a patient already at high bleeding risk.
why_others_wrong.E: A uniform regimen ignores individual risk; NICE bases the decision on each patient's balance of VTE and bleeding risk.

exam_trap: Option D tempts candidates who equate high VTE risk with full anticoagulation, but therapeutic dosing treats established thrombosis and greatly increases bleeding in this patient.
takeaway: VTE prophylaxis = VTE risk versus bleeding risk.
source: NICE NG89.
thinking: High VTE risk ↓ and high bleeding risk ↓ pharmacological prophylaxis must weigh both risks ↓ mechanical methods may be used while bleeding risk persists ↓ Balance VTE risk against bleeding risk
pearl: When bleeding risk makes pharmacological prophylaxis unsafe, mechanical methods can be used and the decision reviewed regularly so that low molecular weight heparin can start once bleeding risk falls.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Early mobilisation
stem: Which postoperative measure helps reduce venous thromboembolic risk?
correct_answer: A. Early mobilisation where clinically appropriate
why_correct: NICE recommends encouraging patients to mobilise as soon as possible and avoiding unnecessary dehydration.

why_others_wrong.B: Unnecessary bed rest promotes venous stasis in the legs, increasing rather than reducing the risk of DVT and pulmonary embolism.
why_others_wrong.C: Dehydration raises blood viscosity and favours thrombosis, which is why NICE advises avoiding it after surgery.
why_others_wrong.D: Immobilising both legs removes the calf muscle pump and increases venous stasis, raising the risk of deep vein thrombosis.
why_others_wrong.E: Physiotherapy supports mobilisation and chest recovery, so avoiding it would delay mobility and increase VTE and pulmonary risk.

exam_trap: Mobilisation is part of VTE prevention but does not replace risk-based mechanical or pharmacological prophylaxis when indicated.
takeaway: Postoperative VTE prevention → mobilise + hydrate appropriately + risk-assess.
source: NICE NG89.
thinking: Postoperative venous stasis promotes thrombosis ↓ calf muscle pump empties the deep veins ↓ walking restores venous flow ↓ Early mobilisation where clinically appropriate
pearl: Venous stasis, endothelial injury and hypercoagulability all coexist after major surgery, which is why mobilisation is combined with risk-based mechanical or pharmacological prophylaxis rather than used alone.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Postoperative fever
stem: A patient develops a fever shortly after surgery. Which principle is most appropriate?

options.B: Assess the patient clinically and consider the timing, likely causes and severity
options.E: Assume an anastomotic leak in every patient

correct_answer: B. Assess the patient clinically and consider the timing, likely causes and severity
why_correct: Postoperative fever has multiple possible causes, including inflammatory response, pulmonary complications, urinary infection, wound infection, intra-abdominal sepsis, drug reactions and thromboembolic disease.

why_others_wrong.A: Early postoperative fever has many causes, including the inflammatory response to surgery and atelectasis, and wound infection typically presents later, around days 5 to 7.
why_others_wrong.C: Antibiotics without assessment may treat a non-infective cause, delay the correct diagnosis and promote resistance and Clostridioides difficile infection.
why_others_wrong.D: Fever may be the first sign of a serious complication such as pneumonia, a leak or VTE, so it warrants clinical assessment rather than being ignored.
why_others_wrong.E: An anastomotic leak is one possible cause, typically later and after bowel surgery, and assuming it in everyone ignores the many more common causes.

exam_trap: Option A tempts as the most familiar cause, but wound infection usually presents around days 5 to 7; early fever more often reflects the inflammatory response or atelectasis.
takeaway: Postoperative fever → assess, don't automatically label it “wound infection.”
source: Standard postoperative assessment principles.
thinking: Fever soon after surgery ↓ causes vary with timing, from inflammatory response and atelectasis to infection, leak and VTE ↓ history, examination and targeted tests identify the source ↓ Assess the patient clinically and consider the timing, likely causes and severity
pearl: A useful framework for postoperative fever is to check the chest, wound, urine, lines, drains and legs, and to consider drug reactions and intra-abdominal collections when fever appears later.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Surgical drain
stem: What is an important principle when deciding whether a surgical drain should remain in place?

options.A: It should remain indefinitely once inserted
options.B: Its ongoing indication and output should be reviewed
options.D: A drain prevents all anastomotic leaks

correct_answer: B. Its ongoing indication and output should be reviewed
why_correct: Drains can provide therapeutic or diagnostic benefits but can also introduce infection, cause discomfort and occasionally damage tissues. Their indication and output should therefore be reviewed.

why_others_wrong.A: Drains carry risks of infection, discomfort and tissue damage, so leaving one indefinitely without reviewing its indication exposes the patient to avoidable harm.
why_others_wrong.C: A drain is a foreign body and potential route for bacteria, so it can introduce rather than eliminate postoperative infection.
why_others_wrong.D: A drain may help detect or control a leak but cannot prevent one, since leak depends on anastomotic technique, blood supply and tension.
why_others_wrong.E: Most drains are removed once output falls or their purpose is fulfilled, so removal is frequently appropriate after review.

exam_trap: Option D appeals to candidates who see a drain as protective, but a drain can only detect or control a leak; it cannot prevent anastomotic breakdown.
takeaway: Drain present → know why it is there + review whether it is still needed.
source: Standard surgical postoperative principles.
thinking: A drain is a foreign body with benefits and risks ↓ it can introduce infection and cause discomfort ↓ need and output should be reviewed regularly ↓ Its ongoing indication and output should be reviewed
pearl: Routine prophylactic drainage has not been shown to reduce complications after many operations, such as uncomplicated cholecystectomy or colonic anastomosis, so drains are increasingly used selectively.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Surgical drains and output
stem: A patient has a drain following abdominal surgery. Which change is most concerning?

options.A: Unexpected change in volume or character of drainage
options.B: Stable low output consistent with the planned postoperative course

correct_answer: A. Unexpected change in volume or character of drainage
why_correct: Sudden changes such as enteric, bilious, faeculent, purulent or haemorrhagic output can indicate a postoperative complication depending on the operation and clinical context.

why_others_wrong.B: A stable low output that matches the expected course is reassuring and does not suggest haemorrhage, leak or collection.
why_others_wrong.C: A gradual fall in output is the expected pattern as tissues settle and often supports planning drain removal.
why_others_wrong.D: Serous drainage when expected is a normal finding, unlike a sudden switch to bilious, enteric, purulent or bloody fluid.
why_others_wrong.E: An unchanged, stable clinical condition is reassuring and is not in itself a sign of a postoperative complication.

exam_trap: Stable low output may worry candidates who expect a drain to keep draining, but low output on the expected course is reassuring; an unexpected change in volume or character is the warning sign.
takeaway: Drain output = diagnostic information, not just fluid to empty.
source: Standard postoperative surgical principles.
thinking: Drain after abdominal surgery ↓ expected output falls gradually and stays serous ↓ a sudden change in volume or appearance suggests bleeding, leak or infection ↓ Unexpected change in volume or character of drainage
pearl: A drain can be falsely reassuring: it may block or be positioned away from a collection, so a deteriorating patient needs assessment and imaging even when drain output looks normal.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Surgical oncology: margin
stem: In oncological surgery, what does an R0 resection generally indicate?

options.C: No residual tumour is identified after resection

correct_answer: C. No residual tumour is identified after resection
why_correct: An R0 resection indicates that no residual tumour is identified following resection. R1 generally indicates microscopic residual disease, while R2 indicates macroscopic residual disease.

why_others_wrong.A: Macroscopic residual tumour after resection is classified as R2, not R0.
why_others_wrong.B: Microscopic residual tumour, such as tumour at the resection margin, is classified as R1 rather than R0.
why_others_wrong.D: The R classification describes residual disease after resection and says nothing about whether a biopsy was taken beforehand.
why_others_wrong.E: An abandoned operation would leave tumour in place, which is the opposite of an R0 resection with no residual disease.

exam_trap: Candidates confuse the suffixes and pick microscopic residual tumour, but that is R1; R2 is macroscopic residue, and only R0 means no residual tumour is identified.
takeaway: R0 = no residual tumour identified.
source: [RCPath]: standards and datasets for cancer resection reporting.
thinking: The R classification describes residual tumour after resection ↓ R2 = macroscopic residue; R1 = microscopic residue ↓ R0 = no residual tumour identified ↓ No residual tumour is identified after resection
pearl: In rectal cancer the circumferential resection margin is a key quality measure, and tumour close to or involving the mesorectal fascia on pre-operative MRI is a reason to consider neoadjuvant treatment.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Surgical oncology: lymph-node staging
stem: What does the “N” component of TNM staging describe?
why_correct: TNM: T = primary tumour extent, N = regional lymph-node involvement, M = distant metastasis.

why_others_wrong.A: Primary tumour size and local extent are described by the T component, not N.
why_others_wrong.C: Distant metastases are described by the M component of TNM staging.
why_others_wrong.D: Nutritional status is a patient factor relevant to fitness for treatment but is not part of TNM staging.
why_others_wrong.E: Histological grade describes differentiation and is recorded separately from TNM stage.

exam_trap: Distant metastases tempts candidates who equate any nodal spread with M disease; N describes regional node involvement only, and histological grade is not part of TNM.
takeaway: TNM → T tumour, N nodes, M metastases.
source: Standard surgical oncology principles.
thinking: TNM = tumour, nodes, metastasis ↓ T describes the primary tumour and M distant spread ↓ N records regional lymph-node involvement ↓ Regional lymph-node involvement
pearl: Involved nodes outside the regional drainage basin are classed as distant metastasis (M1) rather than N disease, which moves a cancer from potentially curable to metastatic stage.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Cancer and multidisciplinary care
stem: What is the principal purpose of a multidisciplinary team (MDT) discussion in cancer care?

options.A: To allow one clinician to make every treatment decision without discussion
options.B: To integrate relevant specialist perspectives when developing an individualised management plan
options.C: To eliminate the need for patient involvement

correct_answer: B. To integrate relevant specialist perspectives when developing an individualised management plan
why_correct: Cancer management frequently requires coordinated input from surgery, oncology, radiology, pathology and other relevant disciplines.

why_others_wrong.A: An MDT exists precisely to bring several specialists together, so decisions by one clinician without discussion defeat its purpose.
why_others_wrong.C: MDT recommendations are discussed with the patient, and informed consent and shared decision-making remain essential.
why_others_wrong.D: No process can guarantee cure; the MDT aims to recommend the most appropriate evidence-based plan for the individual.
why_others_wrong.E: Histopathologists are core MDT members, and the MDT relies on histology for diagnosis rather than replacing it.

exam_trap: MDT discussion does not remove the need for informed patient involvement and shared decision-making.
takeaway: Cancer MDT → integrate expertise + formulate a patient-specific plan.
source: Standard UK multidisciplinary cancer-care principles.
thinking: Cancer care involves surgery, oncology, radiology and pathology ↓ the MDT brings these perspectives together ↓ recommendations are then discussed with the patient for a shared decision ↓ To integrate relevant specialist perspectives when developing an individualised management plan
pearl: In the UK new cancer diagnoses are discussed at a specialist MDT, and the clinical nurse specialist is a core member who supports the patient through treatment decisions.

subject: Acute abdomen & GI surgery
title: ACUTE APPENDICITIS
stem: A 22-year-old man develops central abdominal pain that later localises to the right iliac fossa. He has anorexia, nausea and a low-grade fever. Which pathological process most commonly initiates acute appendicitis?

options.D: Ischaemia caused by superior mesenteric artery thrombosis
options.E: Direct spread from the sigmoid colon

correct_answer: B. Luminal obstruction of the appendix
why_correct: Luminal obstruction, commonly by lymphoid hyperplasia or a faecolith, can cause mucus accumulation, increased intraluminal pressure, venous congestion, bacterial proliferation and progressive inflammation.

why_others_wrong.A: Haematogenous bacterial seeding is not the usual trigger; bacterial proliferation in appendicitis follows luminal obstruction and rising intraluminal pressure.
why_others_wrong.C: Appendicitis is not a primary autoimmune process; it usually begins with obstruction of the lumen by lymphoid hyperplasia or a faecolith.
why_others_wrong.D: Superior mesenteric artery thrombosis causes widespread midgut ischaemia, whereas appendiceal ischaemia in appendicitis is a late consequence of distension after luminal obstruction.
why_others_wrong.E: Appendicitis does not arise by direct spread from the sigmoid colon; the initiating event is obstruction of the appendiceal lumen itself.

exam_trap: Ischaemia from superior mesenteric artery thrombosis is chosen because appendicitis can end in gangrene, but appendiceal ischaemia follows luminal obstruction and distension rather than initiating it.
takeaway: Appendicitis usually begins with appendiceal luminal obstruction → distension → inflammation → possible ischaemia and perforation.
source: Standard surgical pathology and MRCS syllabus knowledge; Intercollegiate MRCS syllabus, current examination framework.
thinking: Periumbilical pain migrating to the right iliac fossa with anorexia and fever ↓ acute appendicitis ↓ lumen blocked by lymphoid hyperplasia or a faecolith ↓ mucus build-up, rising pressure, venous congestion and bacterial overgrowth ↓ Luminal obstruction of the appendix
pearl: Early pain is periumbilical because visceral afferents from the midgut appendix enter the cord at about T10; it shifts to the right iliac fossa once the inflamed appendix irritates the somatically innervated parietal peritoneum.

subject: Acute abdomen & GI surgery
title: PERFORATED PEPTIC ULCER
stem: A patient develops sudden severe epigastric pain followed by generalised abdominal pain and guarding. An erect chest radiograph demonstrates free subdiaphragmatic gas. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Sudden severe abdominal pain with peritonism and free intraperitoneal gas strongly suggests perforation of a hollow viscus. A perforated gastric or duodenal ulcer is a classic cause.

why_others_wrong.A: Acute pancreatitis causes severe epigastric pain but does not usually produce free subdiaphragmatic gas, which indicates a perforated hollow viscus.
why_others_wrong.C: Acute cholecystitis causes right upper quadrant pain with a positive Murphy sign and does not produce free intraperitoneal gas unless the gallbladder perforates, which is uncommon.
why_others_wrong.D: Small bowel obstruction presents with colicky pain, vomiting and distension, and free subdiaphragmatic gas would suggest a complicating perforation rather than simple obstruction.
why_others_wrong.E: Mesenteric infarction typically causes pain out of proportion to examination, and free gas appears only late if necrotic bowel perforates, making it less likely than a perforated ulcer here.

exam_trap: Acute pancreatitis also causes sudden epigastric pain with peritonism, but it does not produce free subdiaphragmatic gas, which points to a perforated hollow viscus.
takeaway: Sudden pain + peritonism + free intraperitoneal gas = perforated hollow viscus until proven otherwise.
source: Standard MRCS acute abdomen knowledge; Intercollegiate MRCS syllabus.
thinking: Sudden severe epigastric pain ↓ rapid generalised peritonism ↓ free subdiaphragmatic gas = perforated hollow viscus ↓ Perforated peptic ulcer
pearl: An erect chest radiograph misses a proportion of perforations, so CT is the more sensitive test when clinical suspicion remains high; NSAID use and Helicobacter pylori are key risk factors to address after repair.

subject: Acute abdomen & GI surgery
title: SMALL BOWEL OBSTRUCTION
stem: A man with a previous laparotomy presents with colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, abdominal distension and failure to pass flatus. What is the most likely cause of his small bowel obstruction?
why_correct: Postoperative adhesions are a major cause of small bowel obstruction in adults.

why_others_wrong.A: Colorectal carcinoma is a common cause of large bowel obstruction, but after a previous laparotomy adhesions are the leading cause of small bowel obstruction.
why_others_wrong.C: Crohn disease can cause small bowel strictures, but nothing in the stem suggests it and adhesions are far commoner after a previous laparotomy.
why_others_wrong.D: Volvulus in adults mainly affects the sigmoid colon or caecum and is a much less common cause of small bowel obstruction than postoperative adhesions.
why_others_wrong.E: Intussusception is a rare cause of small bowel obstruction in adults, usually with a lead point, whereas adhesions are typical after previous laparotomy.

exam_trap: Colorectal carcinoma is picked because obstruction suggests malignancy, but it typically causes large bowel obstruction; after a previous laparotomy, adhesions are the leading cause of small bowel obstruction.
takeaway: Previous abdominal surgery + small bowel obstruction = adhesions are a key diagnosis.
source: Standard MRCS surgical knowledge; Intercollegiate MRCS syllabus.
thinking: Previous laparotomy ↓ colicky pain, vomiting, distension and failure to pass flatus ↓ mechanical small bowel obstruction ↓ commonest cause after abdominal surgery is fibrous bands ↓ Adhesions
pearl: Adhesional small bowel obstruction without signs of strangulation is usually managed first with nasogastric decompression and intravenous fluids, and a water-soluble contrast study helps predict which patients will settle without surgery.

subject: Acute abdomen & GI surgery
title: STRANGULATED BOWEL
stem: A patient with bowel obstruction develops continuous severe abdominal pain, fever, tachycardia and increasing tenderness. What complication should be suspected?
why_correct: A transition from intermittent colicky pain to continuous severe pain with systemic deterioration raises concern for compromised bowel blood supply.

why_others_wrong.A: Simple constipation does not cause fever, tachycardia and increasing tenderness, which in bowel obstruction point to compromised bowel perfusion.
why_others_wrong.C: Functional ileus causes distension with reduced motility but not the progression to continuous severe pain, fever and tachycardia that suggests strangulation.
why_others_wrong.D: Uncomplicated adhesional obstruction usually produces colicky pain without systemic toxicity; continuous pain with fever and tachycardia suggests the bowel has become ischaemic.
why_others_wrong.E: Gastroenteritis causes diarrhoea and vomiting with diffuse cramps, not the change from colicky to continuous pain with rising tenderness in a known obstruction.

exam_trap: Candidates may choose uncomplicated adhesions because adhesions cause most obstructions, but continuous pain with fever and tachycardia signals ischaemia requiring urgent surgery.
takeaway: Obstruction + continuous pain + systemic deterioration = think strangulation/ischaemia.
source: Standard MRCS acute surgical abdomen knowledge.
thinking: Known bowel obstruction ↓ pain changes from colicky to continuous ↓ fever, tachycardia and increasing tenderness ↓ compromised blood supply to the bowel ↓ Strangulation with bowel ischaemia
pearl: A rising lactate, leucocytosis and features such as reduced bowel wall enhancement on CT support strangulation, but a normal lactate does not exclude it, so clinical signs should drive the decision to operate.

subject: Acute abdomen & GI surgery
title: CLOSED-LOOP OBSTRUCTION
stem: A patient has a bowel obstruction caused by obstruction at two points along the same bowel segment. Why is this particularly dangerous?

options.C: The isolated segment can rapidly become distended and ischaemic

correct_answer: C. The isolated segment can rapidly become distended and ischaemic
why_correct: A closed-loop obstruction traps bowel between two points of obstruction. Increasing pressure can impair venous drainage followed by arterial inflow, producing strangulation and necrosis.

why_others_wrong.A: Closed-loop obstruction does not typically cause diarrhoea; its danger lies in rapid distension of the trapped segment leading to ischaemia.
why_others_wrong.B: Stasis in a trapped segment promotes rather than prevents bacterial overgrowth, which adds to the risk once the bowel wall becomes ischaemic.
why_others_wrong.D: Closed-loop obstruction is a surgical emergency that tends to progress to strangulation rather than resolve spontaneously.
why_others_wrong.E: Closed-loop obstruction can affect any segment of bowel, for example a volvulus or an obstructing colonic lesion with a competent ileocaecal valve, not just the stomach.

exam_trap: Assuming closed-loop obstruction can be managed like simple obstruction is wrong; the trapped segment cannot decompress, so strangulation develops early and urgent surgery is needed.
takeaway: Closed loop = trapped bowel + rising pressure + high risk of strangulation.
source: Standard MRCS surgical knowledge.
thinking: Obstruction at two points along one segment ↓ closed loop with no proximal decompression ↓ pressure rises rapidly in the trapped loop ↓ venous then arterial compromise ↓ The isolated segment can rapidly become distended and ischaemic
pearl: Large bowel obstruction with a competent ileocaecal valve behaves as a closed loop, and caecal tenderness or marked caecal distension warns of impending caecal perforation.

subject: Acute abdomen & GI surgery
title: LARGE BOWEL OBSTRUCTION
stem: Which symptom pattern is most characteristic of a large bowel obstruction?

options.A: Early profuse vomiting with minimal distension
options.B: Marked abdominal distension with altered bowel habit and later vomiting

correct_answer: B. Marked abdominal distension with altered bowel habit and later vomiting
why_correct: Large bowel obstruction commonly produces progressive distension, constipation/obstipation and abdominal pain. Vomiting may occur later than in small bowel obstruction.

why_others_wrong.A: Early profuse vomiting with little distension is typical of proximal small bowel obstruction, whereas large bowel obstruction causes marked distension with later vomiting.
why_others_wrong.C: Haematemesis indicates bleeding from the upper gastrointestinal tract and is not a feature of large bowel obstruction.
why_others_wrong.D: Isolated epigastric pain suggests upper gastrointestinal or pancreatic pathology rather than the progressive distension and obstipation of large bowel obstruction.
why_others_wrong.E: Painless jaundice suggests an obstructing lesion of the bile duct or pancreatic head, not large bowel obstruction.

exam_trap: Early profuse vomiting with minimal distension is tempting as a classic obstruction picture, but it describes proximal small bowel obstruction rather than large bowel obstruction.
takeaway: Large bowel obstruction commonly produces prominent distension and obstipation.
source: Standard MRCS surgical knowledge.
thinking: Large bowel obstruction is distal ↓ colon distends greatly before vomiting ↓ obstipation and altered bowel habit dominate ↓ vomiting appears late ↓ Marked abdominal distension with altered bowel habit and later vomiting
pearl: Colorectal cancer is the commonest cause of large bowel obstruction in the UK, followed by volvulus and diverticular stricture, and pseudo-obstruction must be excluded with CT before laparotomy.

subject: Acute abdomen & GI surgery
title: LEFT-SIDED COLORECTAL OBSTRUCTION
stem: A patient presents with acute left-sided large bowel obstruction caused by a colorectal tumour. Which treatment may be considered in selected patients?
why_correct: NICE recommends considering stenting for acute left-sided large bowel obstruction when treatment is intended to be palliative. For potentially curative treatment, either stenting or emergency surgery may be considered depending on the circumstances.

why_others_wrong.A: Appendicectomy treats appendicitis and has no role in relieving a malignant obstruction of the left colon.
why_others_wrong.C: ERCP is used to decompress an obstructed biliary or pancreatic duct, not to relieve an obstructing colorectal tumour.
why_others_wrong.D: Percutaneous nephrostomy drains an obstructed kidney and does not treat large bowel obstruction, although a pelvic tumour can sometimes obstruct the ureters as well.
why_others_wrong.E: Splenectomy has no role in treating left-sided colorectal obstruction; the options are colonic stenting or emergency surgery depending on intent and circumstances.

exam_trap: Do not treat colonic stenting as mandatory in every obstructing colorectal cancer.
takeaway: Acute left-sided malignant obstruction → consider stent versus emergency surgery according to intent and clinical circumstances.
source: NICE NG151, Colorectal cancer, current recommendations.
thinking: Acute large bowel obstruction ↓ left-sided colorectal tumour ↓ endoscopic decompression is possible ↓ self-expanding metal stent is an option, especially with palliative intent ↓ Colonic stenting
pearl: A stent can act as a bridge to elective resection, converting an emergency operation into a planned one, but stent perforation is a recognised risk and stents are less suitable for right-sided or very low rectal tumours.

subject: Acute abdomen & GI surgery
title: SIGMOID VOLVULUS
stem: An elderly patient presents with massive abdominal distension, constipation and colicky abdominal pain. Imaging demonstrates a markedly dilated loop of sigmoid colon with a characteristic coffee-bean appearance. What is the diagnosis?
why_correct: Sigmoid volvulus occurs when the sigmoid colon twists around its mesenteric attachment, causing large bowel obstruction and potentially bowel ischaemia.

why_others_wrong.A: Caecal carcinoma causes right-sided obstruction and does not produce a twisted, massively dilated sigmoid loop with a coffee-bean appearance.
why_others_wrong.C: Small bowel obstruction shows multiple central dilated loops with valvulae conniventes, not a single hugely dilated sigmoid loop.
why_others_wrong.D: Toxic megacolon occurs with severe colitis and systemic toxicity, typically dilating the transverse colon, rather than a twisted sigmoid loop in an elderly, constipated patient.
why_others_wrong.E: Ileus causes diffuse gaseous dilatation of small and large bowel without a single twisted loop producing the coffee-bean sign.

exam_trap: Toxic megacolon also causes massive colonic dilatation, but it occurs with severe colitis and systemic toxicity, typically involving the transverse colon, not a twisted sigmoid loop.
takeaway: Massive colonic dilatation + coffee-bean appearance = sigmoid volvulus.
source: Standard MRCS radiological and surgical knowledge.
thinking: Elderly patient with massive distension and constipation ↓ single hugely dilated sigmoid loop ↓ coffee-bean sign ↓ Sigmoid volvulus
pearl: Without peritonitis or ischaemia, first-line management is endoscopic decompression with a flatus tube, but recurrence is common, so elective sigmoid resection is often considered in fit patients.

subject: Acute abdomen & GI surgery
title: CAECAL VOLVULUS
stem: Which segment of bowel is twisted in caecal volvulus?
why_correct: Caecal volvulus involves abnormal mobility of the caecum, allowing it to twist, often with the terminal ileum and ascending colon.

why_others_wrong.A: The sigmoid colon twists in sigmoid volvulus, a separate entity from caecal volvulus, which involves a mobile caecum.
why_others_wrong.B: The rectum is largely fixed in the pelvis and extraperitoneal in its lower part, so it does not twist in caecal volvulus.
why_others_wrong.D: Transverse colon volvulus is a rare separate entity, whereas caecal volvulus involves the mobile caecum with the ascending colon and often the terminal ileum.
why_others_wrong.E: The terminal ileum is often drawn into caecal volvulus but is not the only segment; the defining feature is twisting of a mobile caecum and ascending colon.

exam_trap: Candidates reflexly choose sigmoid colon because sigmoid volvulus is commoner, but caecal volvulus involves a mobile caecum and ascending colon, often with the terminal ileum.
takeaway: Sigmoid volvulus and caecal volvulus are distinct anatomical entities.
source: Standard MRCS surgical knowledge.
thinking: Caecal volvulus ↓ requires an abnormally mobile caecum ↓ twist involves the caecum and ascending colon ↓ terminal ileum often drawn in ↓ Caecum and ascending colon
pearl: Unlike sigmoid volvulus, caecal volvulus is rarely suitable for endoscopic decompression and is usually treated surgically, often by right hemicolectomy.

subject: Acute abdomen & GI surgery
title: INCARCERATED VERSUS STRANGULATED HERNIA
stem: A groin hernia cannot be reduced but the patient has no evidence of bowel ischaemia. Which term best describes the hernia?
why_correct: An incarcerated hernia is irreducible. Strangulation specifically implies compromised blood supply to the herniated contents.

why_others_wrong.A: A reducible hernia can be pushed back into the abdomen, whereas this hernia cannot be reduced.
why_others_wrong.C: Strangulation requires compromised blood supply to the hernia contents, and this patient has no evidence of ischaemia despite irreducibility.
why_others_wrong.D: Recurrent describes a hernia returning after previous repair, which says nothing about whether it can be reduced.
why_others_wrong.E: A sliding hernia has part of a viscus forming the wall of the sac; it describes sac anatomy rather than an irreducible hernia without ischaemia.

exam_trap: Choosing strangulated equates irreducibility with ischaemia; strangulation requires compromised blood supply, which this patient does not have despite the hernia being irreducible.
takeaway: Incarcerated = irreducible. Strangulated = compromised blood supply.
source: Standard MRCS surgical knowledge.
thinking: Hernia cannot be reduced ↓ irreducible = incarcerated ↓ no evidence of ischaemia ↓ strangulation therefore not established ↓ Incarcerated
pearl: Femoral hernias have a narrow, rigid neck and the highest risk of strangulation among groin hernias, so they are repaired promptly rather than managed expectantly.

subject: Acute abdomen & GI surgery
title: STRANGULATED HERNIA
stem: A patient with an irreducible hernia develops severe pain, tenderness, tachycardia and systemic toxicity. What complication must be assumed until excluded?
why_correct: Pain and systemic deterioration in an irreducible hernia suggest compromised bowel or other herniated tissue.

why_others_wrong.A: Simple incarceration means irreducibility without ischaemia, so severe pain, tachycardia and systemic toxicity should prompt assumption of strangulation instead.
why_others_wrong.C: A hydrocele is a painless fluid collection around the testis that transilluminates and does not cause systemic toxicity.
why_others_wrong.D: A lipoma is a benign fatty lump that is usually painless and does not produce tachycardia or systemic toxicity.
why_others_wrong.E: A varicocele is a dilated pampiniform plexus, often described as a bag of worms, and does not cause acute systemic deterioration.

exam_trap: Simple incarceration is tempting because the hernia is irreducible, but severe pain, tachycardia and systemic toxicity indicate ischaemic contents and strangulation must be assumed.
takeaway: Painful irreducible hernia + systemic deterioration = emergency assessment for strangulation.
source: Standard MRCS surgical knowledge.
thinking: Irreducible hernia ↓ new severe pain and local tenderness ↓ tachycardia and systemic toxicity ↓ compromised blood supply to the contents ↓ Strangulation
pearl: Forceful reduction of a suspected strangulated hernia risks returning ischaemic bowel to the abdomen or reduction en masse, where the sac is pushed back with its constricting neck intact, so emergency exploration is needed instead.

subject: Acute abdomen & GI surgery
title: ACUTE MESENTERIC ISCHAEMIA
stem: A patient with atrial fibrillation develops sudden severe abdominal pain but initially has relatively little abdominal tenderness. What diagnosis should be strongly considered?
why_correct: Acute mesenteric ischaemia can initially produce severe abdominal pain out of proportion to physical findings. Embolic arterial occlusion is an important cause, particularly in patients with atrial fibrillation.

why_others_wrong.B: Acute cholecystitis usually produces right upper quadrant tenderness with a positive Murphy sign, not severe pain with little tenderness in a patient with atrial fibrillation.
why_others_wrong.C: Appendicitis typically has localised right iliac fossa tenderness, whereas pain out of proportion to examination with atrial fibrillation suggests embolic mesenteric ischaemia.
why_others_wrong.D: Diverticular disease usually presents with left iliac fossa pain and tenderness, and atrial fibrillation offers no link to it.
why_others_wrong.E: Uncomplicated peptic ulcer disease causes dyspeptic epigastric pain rather than sudden severe pain in a patient with an embolic source such as atrial fibrillation.

exam_trap: A relatively benign abdomen does not exclude life-threatening bowel ischaemia early in the disease.
takeaway: Pain out of proportion to examination = think mesenteric ischaemia.
source: Standard MRCS acute vascular and abdominal surgery knowledge.
thinking: Atrial fibrillation = embolic source ↓ sudden severe abdominal pain ↓ little tenderness: pain out of proportion to examination ↓ superior mesenteric artery embolus ↓ Acute mesenteric ischaemia
pearl: CT angiography is the investigation of choice for suspected acute mesenteric ischaemia, and a raised lactate is a late and non-specific finding that should not be awaited before imaging.

subject: Acute abdomen & GI surgery
title: CHRONIC MESENTERIC ISCHAEMIA
stem: A patient develops recurrent abdominal pain after meals and has progressively reduced food intake because eating provokes symptoms. What diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Chronic mesenteric arterial insufficiency can cause postprandial abdominal pain and food avoidance, sometimes producing weight loss.

why_others_wrong.B: Acute appendicitis is a single acute illness with right iliac fossa pain, not recurrent postprandial pain causing food avoidance.
why_others_wrong.C: Haemorrhoids cause bright red rectal bleeding or perianal discomfort, not abdominal pain after meals with reduced food intake.
why_others_wrong.D: Acute cholecystitis causes persistent right upper quadrant pain with fever, not recurrent pain after every meal with progressive food avoidance.
why_others_wrong.E: Small bowel volvulus is an acute obstructive emergency with colicky pain and vomiting, not a recurring pattern of postprandial pain.

exam_trap: Acute cholecystitis is tempting because pain follows meals, but it causes persistent right upper quadrant pain with fever rather than recurrent postprandial pain with food avoidance.
takeaway: Postprandial pain + food avoidance + weight loss = consider chronic mesenteric ischaemia.
source: Standard MRCS vascular surgery knowledge.
thinking: Recurrent pain after meals ↓ patient avoids food ("food fear") ↓ gut cannot increase blood flow to meet postprandial demand ↓ Chronic mesenteric ischaemia
pearl: Chronic mesenteric ischaemia is usually atherosclerotic and generally involves more than one mesenteric vessel because of the rich collateral circulation; endovascular stenting is now commonly the first-line revascularisation.

subject: Acute abdomen & GI surgery
title: DIVERTICULITIS
stem: A patient presents with left lower abdominal pain, fever and altered bowel habit. Examination demonstrates localised left iliac fossa tenderness. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Left lower abdominal pain with systemic inflammatory features is a classic presentation of acute diverticulitis. Potential complications include abscess, perforation, fistula and obstruction.

why_others_wrong.B: Acute appendicitis typically causes right iliac fossa pain and tenderness, not localised left iliac fossa tenderness.
why_others_wrong.C: Acute pancreatitis causes epigastric pain radiating to the back, not localised left iliac fossa tenderness with altered bowel habit.
why_others_wrong.D: Testicular torsion causes acute scrotal pain in a young male and would not explain fever, altered bowel habit and left iliac fossa tenderness.
why_others_wrong.E: Biliary colic causes episodic right upper quadrant or epigastric pain without fever, not left lower abdominal pain with inflammatory features.

exam_trap: Do not assume every left iliac fossa pain is diverticulitis; urinary, gynaecological and colorectal pathology can mimic it.
takeaway: Left iliac fossa pain + inflammatory features → diverticulitis is a key diagnosis.
source: Standard MRCS colorectal surgery knowledge.
thinking: Left lower abdominal pain ↓ fever and altered bowel habit ↓ localised left iliac fossa tenderness ↓ Acute diverticulitis
pearl: CT is used to confirm complicated diverticulitis, and a pericolic abscess can often be managed with antibiotics and percutaneous drainage rather than surgery.

subject: Acute abdomen & GI surgery
title: DIVERTICULAR BLEEDING
stem: A patient develops sudden, painless, large-volume fresh rectal bleeding. Which colonic condition is a common cause of significant lower gastrointestinal bleeding?
why_correct: Diverticular bleeding can arise from erosion of vessels associated with diverticula and may be substantial and painless.

why_others_wrong.B: Acute appendicitis causes abdominal pain and fever and is not a recognised cause of large-volume painless rectal bleeding.
why_others_wrong.C: An anal fissure causes painful defaecation with small amounts of bright blood on the paper, not sudden large-volume painless bleeding.
why_others_wrong.D: Small bowel volvulus presents as an acute obstruction with pain and vomiting, not painless fresh rectal bleeding.
why_others_wrong.E: Cholecystitis is a gallbladder inflammatory condition causing right upper quadrant pain and does not cause lower gastrointestinal bleeding.

exam_trap: Do not assume that all rectal bleeding associated with diverticular disease is caused by diverticulitis; diverticular bleeding is often painless.
takeaway: Painless significant fresh rectal bleeding → consider diverticular bleeding.
source: Standard MRCS colorectal knowledge.
thinking: Sudden painless large-volume fresh rectal bleeding ↓ colonic source ↓ eroded vasa recta at the neck of a diverticulum ↓ Diverticular disease
pearl: Most diverticular bleeds stop spontaneously; in persistent haemodynamically significant bleeding, CT angiography localises the source to guide colonoscopic or radiological (embolisation) therapy before surgery is considered.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: COLORECTAL CANCER AND IRON-DEFICIENCY ANAEMIA
stem: A 68-year-old man develops unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia. Which diagnosis must be considered?
why_correct: Occult gastrointestinal blood loss from colorectal cancer can present as iron-deficiency anaemia, particularly in older adults.

why_others_wrong.B: Acute pancreatitis presents with severe epigastric pain and raised amylase or lipase, not with occult blood loss causing iron deficiency.
why_others_wrong.C: Gallstones alone do not cause chronic gastrointestinal blood loss and are not an explanation for unexplained iron deficiency in an older man.
why_others_wrong.D: An inguinal hernia presents as a groin swelling and does not cause chronic occult blood loss or iron-deficiency anaemia.
why_others_wrong.E: Haemorrhoids cause visible bright red bleeding and should not be assumed to explain unexplained iron deficiency in an older adult without excluding colorectal cancer.

exam_trap: Do not dismiss iron deficiency as dietary without considering gastrointestinal blood loss when clinically appropriate.
takeaway: Unexplained iron deficiency in an older adult = investigate for gastrointestinal blood loss, including colorectal cancer.
source: NICE NG12/NICE NG151; current UK colorectal cancer guidance.
thinking: 68-year-old man ↓ unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia ↓ occult gastrointestinal blood loss until proven otherwise ↓ right-sided colon cancers often present this way without bowel symptoms ↓ Colorectal cancer
pearl: Iron-deficiency anaemia in older adults warrants urgent investigation of both the lower and upper gastrointestinal tract, because either may be the source of occult bleeding.

subject: Genetics
title: Genetics: familial adenomatous polyposis
stem: A patient has hundreds of adenomatous colorectal polyps and a strong family history of colorectal cancer. Which gene is classically associated with familial adenomatous polyposis?
why_correct: Familial adenomatous polyposis is classically caused by pathogenic variants in the APC tumour suppressor gene. Without appropriate management, colorectal cancer risk is extremely high.

why_others_wrong.B: BRCA1 is a tumour suppressor associated mainly with hereditary breast and ovarian cancer, not with hundreds of adenomatous colorectal polyps.
why_others_wrong.C: RET gain-of-function variants cause multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 with medullary thyroid carcinoma and phaeochromocytoma, not adenomatous polyposis.
why_others_wrong.D: MEN1 variants cause multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1, with parathyroid, pituitary and pancreatic endocrine tumours rather than colorectal polyposis.
why_others_wrong.E: VHL variants cause von Hippel-Lindau disease, with haemangioblastomas, renal cell carcinoma and phaeochromocytoma, not hundreds of colorectal adenomas.

exam_trap: RET or MEN1 may be chosen as familiar inherited cancer genes, but they cause endocrine neoplasia syndromes; hundreds of colorectal adenomas point to APC.
takeaway: Hundreds of adenomatous polyps + inherited colorectal cancer syndrome = APC/FAP.
source: Standard MRCS genetics and colorectal surgery knowledge.
thinking: Hundreds of adenomatous colorectal polyps ↓ strong family history of colorectal cancer ↓ familial adenomatous polyposis ↓ germline tumour suppressor defect in the Wnt pathway ↓ APC
pearl: Classical FAP is managed with endoscopic surveillance from adolescence and prophylactic colectomy, usually in early adulthood; patients also need upper GI surveillance for duodenal adenomas.

subject: Genetics
title: Genetics: Lynch syndrome
stem: Which molecular abnormality is classically associated with Lynch syndrome?
why_correct: Lynch syndrome is associated with inherited defects in DNA mismatch repair genes, producing microsatellite instability in affected tumours.

why_others_wrong.B: CFTR mutations cause cystic fibrosis through defective chloride transport, not an inherited colorectal cancer syndrome driven by mismatch repair failure.
why_others_wrong.C: APC loss underlies familial adenomatous polyposis; Lynch syndrome is caused by germline mismatch repair gene defects, and no single abnormality occurs in every case.
why_others_wrong.D: RET activation is the basis of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 and some thyroid cancers, not Lynch syndrome.
why_others_wrong.E: Mitochondrial DNA deletions cause maternally inherited mitochondrial disorders, not the nuclear mismatch repair defect that underlies Lynch syndrome.

exam_trap: FAP produces numerous adenomatous polyps; Lynch syndrome does not characteristically produce hundreds of colorectal polyps.
takeaway: Lynch = mismatch repair deficiency + inherited colorectal and other cancer susceptibility.
source: Standard MRCS genetics and colorectal oncology knowledge.
thinking: Lynch syndrome ↓ germline defect in a DNA mismatch repair gene ↓ replication errors persist in repetitive sequences ↓ microsatellite instability in tumours ↓ DNA mismatch repair deficiency
pearl: In the UK, NICE recommends testing all newly diagnosed colorectal and endometrial cancers for mismatch repair deficiency or microsatellite instability to identify possible Lynch syndrome.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: RECTAL CANCER
stem: Which imaging modality is particularly important for local staging of rectal cancer?
why_correct: Pelvic MRI provides detailed assessment of the rectal tumour and surrounding structures and is central to local staging and treatment planning.

why_others_wrong.B: A plain abdominal radiograph may show obstruction but cannot define rectal wall invasion, the mesorectal fascia or nodal status.
why_others_wrong.C: Non-contrast head CT images the brain and has no role in local staging of a pelvic tumour.
why_others_wrong.D: A chest radiograph looks for thoracic disease and cannot assess local rectal tumour extent; CT is preferred for distant staging.
why_others_wrong.E: Thyroid ultrasound is unrelated to rectal cancer and gives no information about local tumour extent in the pelvis.

exam_trap: Chest radiograph alone attracts candidates who confuse local with distant staging, but it cannot assess the pelvis; local rectal staging needs MRI, and distant staging uses CT.
takeaway: Rectal cancer → pelvic MRI is central to local staging.
source: NICE NG151, Colorectal cancer.
thinking: Local staging of rectal cancer ↓ need depth of invasion, mesorectal fascia and nodal status ↓ pelvic MRI gives high-resolution soft-tissue detail ↓ MRI pelvis
pearl: MRI predicts threat to the circumferential resection margin and extramural vascular invasion, which guide neoadjuvant therapy; CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis is used separately for distant staging.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: COLORECTAL CANCER MDT
stem: A patient has newly diagnosed colorectal cancer. Why is multidisciplinary team discussion important?

options.B: To integrate surgical, oncological, radiological and pathological assessment
options.C: To avoid discussing treatment options with the patient
options.D: To determine treatment using only the CT scan

correct_answer: B. To integrate surgical, oncological, radiological and pathological assessment
why_correct: Cancer management often requires integration of pathology, imaging, surgical options, systemic treatment, radiotherapy and patient factors.

why_others_wrong.A: MDT discussion informs treatment recommendations, but valid informed consent must still be obtained from the patient.
why_others_wrong.C: The MDT plan is a recommendation that is discussed with the patient, who remains central to treatment decisions.
why_others_wrong.D: Colorectal cancer management combines CT with histology, MRI for rectal tumours, clinical findings and patient factors, not a single scan.
why_others_wrong.E: Histological confirmation is a core part of MDT assessment, and the pathologist is a key team member.

exam_trap: 'To replace informed consent' attracts candidates who see the MDT as the decision-maker, but its plan is a recommendation and valid consent must still be obtained from the patient.
takeaway: Cancer MDT = coordinated multidisciplinary assessment and treatment planning.
source: NICE NG151; current colorectal cancer guidance.
thinking: Newly diagnosed colorectal cancer ↓ treatment depends on histology, imaging, surgical options and oncology ↓ the MDT combines these assessments into a recommendation ↓ To integrate surgical, oncological, radiological and pathological assessment
pearl: An MDT plan made in the patient's absence is a recommendation, not a decision; it must be discussed with the patient, who may choose differently after an informed discussion.

subject: Acute abdomen & GI surgery
title: ACUTE CHOLECYSTITIS
stem: A patient develops persistent right upper quadrant pain, fever and a positive Murphy sign. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Acute inflammation of the gallbladder commonly presents with persistent right upper quadrant pain, systemic inflammatory features and local tenderness.

why_others_wrong.B: Acute appendicitis causes right iliac fossa pain, and a positive Murphy sign points to gallbladder inflammation instead.
why_others_wrong.C: Acute diverticulitis usually causes left iliac fossa pain and tenderness, not right upper quadrant pain with a positive Murphy sign.
why_others_wrong.D: Mesenteric ischaemia typically causes severe pain out of proportion to examination, not localised right upper quadrant tenderness with a Murphy sign.
why_others_wrong.E: Small bowel obstruction causes colicky pain, vomiting and distension rather than persistent right upper quadrant pain with a positive Murphy sign.

exam_trap: Biliary colic is typically transient; persistent pain with systemic inflammation suggests cholecystitis.
takeaway: Persistent RUQ pain + inflammatory features = acute cholecystitis.
source: NICE CG188, Gallstone disease.
thinking: Persistent right upper quadrant pain ↓ fever = inflammatory response ↓ positive Murphy sign = gallbladder tenderness ↓ Acute cholecystitis
pearl: Ultrasound is the first-line imaging, showing gallstones, wall thickening and pericholecystic fluid, and NICE advises laparoscopic cholecystectomy within one week of diagnosis for acute cholecystitis.

subject: Hepatobiliary surgery
title: MANAGEMENT OF ACUTE CHOLECYSTITIS
stem: A patient has confirmed acute cholecystitis and is suitable for surgery. What does NICE recommend?

options.A: Routine delayed cholecystectomy after several years
options.E: No treatment if gallstones are present

why_correct: NICE recommends early laparoscopic cholecystectomy for acute cholecystitis, with the guideline specifying that it should be carried out within 1 week of diagnosis.

why_others_wrong.A: Delaying cholecystectomy for years leaves the patient exposed to recurrent cholecystitis, pancreatitis and duct stones; NICE advises surgery within 1 week of diagnosis for fit patients.
why_others_wrong.C: Total gastrectomy removes the stomach for gastric malignancy and has no role in treating inflammation of the gallbladder.
why_others_wrong.D: ERCP is reserved for common bile duct stones or cholangitis needing duct clearance, not as routine treatment for uncomplicated acute cholecystitis.
why_others_wrong.E: Untreated acute cholecystitis risks empyema, gangrene and perforation, and a patient fit for surgery should be offered early laparoscopic cholecystectomy.

exam_trap: ERCP is primarily used when the common bile duct requires clearance, not as routine treatment for uncomplicated acute cholecystitis.
takeaway: Acute cholecystitis → early laparoscopic cholecystectomy when appropriate.
source: NICE CG188, Gallstone disease.
thinking: Confirmed acute cholecystitis in a patient fit for surgery ↓ delay leaves the patient exposed to recurrent attacks, pancreatitis and duct stones ↓ NICE advises laparoscopic cholecystectomy within 1 week of diagnosis ↓ Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy
pearl: For a patient too unwell or frail for surgery whose cholecystitis fails to settle or progresses to empyema, percutaneous cholecystostomy gives source control as a bridge or alternative to cholecystectomy.

subject: Hepatobiliary surgery
title: ASCENDING CHOLANGITIS
stem: A patient has fever, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain. Blood tests show cholestatic liver dysfunction. What diagnosis should be suspected?
why_correct: Ascending cholangitis results from infection of an obstructed biliary tree, commonly associated with common bile duct stones.

why_others_wrong.B: Acute appendicitis typically causes periumbilical pain migrating to the right iliac fossa, and does not explain jaundice with a cholestatic liver picture.
why_others_wrong.C: Acute diverticulitis usually causes left iliac fossa pain and fever in older adults, without jaundice or cholestatic liver tests.
why_others_wrong.D: Mesenteric ischaemia presents with severe pain out of proportion to signs and raised lactate, not the fever, jaundice and cholestasis of biliary infection.
why_others_wrong.E: An incisional hernia is a bulge at a previous scar and would not produce fever, jaundice and cholestatic liver dysfunction.

exam_trap: Candidates swayed by fever and right-sided pain may pick appendicitis or mesenteric ischaemia, but neither explains jaundice with a cholestatic picture, which points to infection of an obstructed biliary tree.
takeaway: Cholangitis = infected obstructed biliary system → antibiotics + assessment for biliary drainage/source control.
source: Standard MRCS hepatobiliary surgery knowledge; NICE CG188.
thinking: Fever + jaundice + right upper quadrant pain ↓ cholestatic liver tests point to an obstructed biliary tree ↓ infection above an obstruction, usually a common bile duct stone ↓ Ascending cholangitis
pearl: Hypotension and confusion added to the classic triad signal severe cholangitis; these patients need resuscitation, intravenous antibiotics and urgent biliary drainage, usually by ERCP, with percutaneous transhepatic drainage if ERCP fails.

subject: Hepatobiliary surgery
title: COMMON BILE DUCT STONES
stem: A patient with symptomatic gallstone disease is found to have a common bile duct stone. Which intervention can be used to clear the bile duct?
why_correct: ERCP can be used for endoscopic clearance of common bile duct stones. NICE recommends bile duct clearance surgically at the time of laparoscopic cholecystectomy or by ERCP before or at the time of laparoscopic cholecystectomy.

why_others_wrong.B: Appendicectomy removes the appendix and has no access to, or effect on, a stone lodged in the common bile duct.
why_others_wrong.C: Colonoscopy examines the colon and terminal ileum and cannot cannulate the ampulla to clear the bile duct, which needs a side-viewing duodenoscope.
why_others_wrong.D: Nephrostomy drains an obstructed kidney through the renal pelvis and does not address biliary tract obstruction.
why_others_wrong.E: Splenectomy removes the spleen for trauma or haematological disease and plays no part in bile duct stone clearance.

exam_trap: A stone confined to the gallbladder does not automatically require ERCP.
takeaway: CBD stone → establish a strategy for duct clearance; ERCP is an important endoscopic option.
source: NICE CG188, Gallstone disease.
thinking: Symptomatic gallstones with a common bile duct stone ↓ the duct must be cleared as well as the gallbladder dealt with ↓ endoscopic access through the ampulla allows sphincterotomy and stone extraction ↓ ERCP
pearl: Post-ERCP pancreatitis is the most common serious complication of ERCP, alongside bleeding after sphincterotomy, duodenal perforation and cholangitis, which is why diagnostic ERCP has been replaced by MRCP or EUS.

subject: Acute abdomen & GI surgery
title: ACUTE PANCREATITIS
stem: Which combination best supports a diagnosis of acute pancreatitis?

options.A: Epigastric pain plus compatible pancreatic enzyme elevation (amylase/lipase more than 3x the upper limit of normal) and/or characteristic imaging

correct_answer: A. Epigastric pain plus compatible pancreatic enzyme elevation (amylase/lipase more than 3x the upper limit of normal) and/or characteristic imaging
why_correct: Acute pancreatitis is diagnosed using the overall clinical, biochemical and imaging picture. The classic presentation is acute upper abdominal/epigastric pain, often radiating to the back, with elevated pancreatic enzymes. Per the revised Atlanta classification, biochemical support for the diagnosis requires amylase or lipase more than 3x the upper limit of normal.

why_others_wrong.B: Right iliac fossa pain suggests appendicitis or other local pathology and on its own gives no clinical or biochemical support for pancreatitis.
why_others_wrong.C: Painless jaundice suggests malignant biliary obstruction, such as a pancreatic head cancer, rather than acute pancreatitis, which is typically painful.
why_others_wrong.D: Fresh rectal bleeding points to a lower gastrointestinal source and does not support a diagnosis of acute pancreatitis.
why_others_wrong.E: Dysuria suggests urinary tract pathology and does not meet any of the clinical, biochemical or imaging criteria for acute pancreatitis.

exam_trap: An elevated lipase/amylase result should be interpreted in clinical context rather than treated as a diagnosis in isolation; note that the diagnostic threshold is more than 3x the upper limit of normal, not any elevation.
takeaway: Acute pancreatitis = compatible clinical picture + biochemical and/or imaging evidence.
source: Standard MRCS acute surgical knowledge.
thinking: Pancreatitis diagnosis needs two of three criteria ↓ characteristic epigastric pain ↓ amylase or lipase more than 3x upper limit of normal ↓ or typical imaging findings ↓ Epigastric pain plus compatible pancreatic enzyme elevation and/or characteristic imaging
pearl: Enzyme levels do not correlate with severity; severity is judged by organ failure, and early CT is not needed when the diagnosis is clear, because necrosis may not be visible until about 72 hours.

subject: Hepatobiliary surgery
title: PANCREATIC HEAD CANCER
stem: A patient develops progressive painless obstructive jaundice and weight loss. Imaging shows a mass in the head of the pancreas. Which additional finding may occur because of biliary obstruction?

options.C: Fresh rectal bleeding as the defining feature

correct_answer: A. Dark urine and pale stools
why_correct: Obstruction of bile flow reduces bilirubin delivery to the intestine, producing pale stools, while conjugated bilirubin can appear in urine.

why_others_wrong.B: Haemoptysis arises from the respiratory tract and is not a consequence of obstruction of bile flow by a pancreatic head mass.
why_others_wrong.C: Fresh rectal bleeding points to a distal colorectal or anal source and is not a feature of biliary obstruction.
why_others_wrong.D: Diabetes insipidus results from deficient or ineffective antidiuretic hormone and is unrelated to biliary obstruction, although pancreatic cancer may cause diabetes mellitus.
why_others_wrong.E: Unilateral leg oedema suggests deep vein thrombosis, a recognised paraneoplastic association, but it is not caused by obstruction of the bile duct.

exam_trap: Do not assume all jaundice is hepatocellular; obstructive and hepatocellular patterns differ.
takeaway: Painless progressive obstructive jaundice + weight loss → pancreatic head malignancy is an important consideration.
source: Standard MRCS hepatobiliary and pancreatic surgery knowledge.
thinking: Painless progressive jaundice + weight loss + pancreatic head mass ↓ the tumour obstructs the distal common bile duct ↓ conjugated bilirubin cannot reach the gut and spills into the urine instead ↓ Dark urine and pale stools
pearl: A palpable, non-tender gallbladder in a jaundiced patient suggests malignant distal obstruction rather than stones, because a chronically inflamed stone-bearing gallbladder is usually fibrosed and does not distend.

subject: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care
title: PERIPHERAL ARTERIAL DISEASE
stem: A patient has exertional calf pain that reliably occurs after walking a certain distance and settles with rest. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Intermittent claudication is exertional limb muscle pain caused by inadequate arterial blood flow, typically relieved by rest. NICE recommends assessment including symptoms, examination of pulses and ankle-brachial pressure index.

why_others_wrong.B: Acute limb ischaemia is a sudden-onset emergency with pain at rest, pallor and pulselessness, not predictable pain that appears at a set walking distance and eases with rest.
why_others_wrong.C: Cellulitis causes a spreading red, warm, tender area of skin with constant pain, not muscle pain that is reproducibly triggered by walking and relieved by rest.
why_others_wrong.D: Deep vein thrombosis produces persistent unilateral calf swelling and tenderness that does not come on reliably at a fixed walking distance and settle within minutes of rest.
why_others_wrong.E: Chronic exertional compartment syndrome can cause exercise-related leg pain, but it usually affects young athletes, and the classic picture of reproducible calf pain at a set distance in a vascular patient is claudication.

exam_trap: Candidates choose compartment syndrome because it also causes exercise-related leg pain, but reproducible calf pain at a fixed distance that settles with rest is classic arterial claudication.
takeaway: Predictable exertional limb pain relieved by rest = intermittent claudication.
source: NICE CG147, Peripheral arterial disease.
thinking: Exertional calf pain ↓ comes on reliably at a set distance ↓ settles with rest ↓ inadequate arterial supply to exercising muscle ↓ Intermittent claudication
pearl: The level of claudication helps localise disease: calf pain suggests superficial femoral or popliteal disease, while buttock and thigh claudication suggests aortoiliac disease.

subject: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care
title: ANKLE-BRACHIAL PRESSURE INDEX
stem: How is the ankle-brachial pressure index calculated?

options.A: Lowest ankle systolic pressure ÷ lowest arm systolic pressure
options.B: Highest ankle systolic pressure ÷ highest arm systolic pressure
options.C: Highest arm pressure ÷ highest ankle pressure
options.E: Diastolic ankle pressure ÷ systolic arm pressure

correct_answer: B. Highest ankle systolic pressure ÷ highest arm systolic pressure
why_correct: NICE specifies calculating ABPI using the highest ankle pressure divided by the highest arm pressure, with Doppler measurement preferred.

why_others_wrong.A: NICE specifies the highest, not the lowest, ankle and arm systolic pressures, so using the lowest values departs from the recommended method.
why_others_wrong.C: This inverts the ratio; the ankle pressure is the numerator and the brachial pressure the denominator, so reversing them gives a meaningless index.
why_others_wrong.D: Mean arterial pressure divided by heart rate is not a recognised vascular index and says nothing about the ankle-to-arm pressure gradient that ABPI measures.
why_others_wrong.E: ABPI compares systolic pressures at both sites; using an ankle diastolic pressure would systematically underestimate the index and misclassify patients.

exam_trap: Candidates choose the lowest pressures or invert the ratio; NICE uses the highest ankle pressure divided by the highest arm pressure, with ankle pressure as numerator.
takeaway: ABPI = highest ankle systolic pressure / highest brachial systolic pressure.
source: NICE CG147, Peripheral arterial disease.
thinking: ABPI compares ankle with arm systolic pressure ↓ use Doppler for accuracy ↓ numerator is the highest ankle systolic pressure ↓ denominator is the highest brachial systolic pressure ↓ Highest ankle systolic pressure ÷ highest arm systolic pressure
