pearl: An ABPI below 0.9 supports peripheral arterial disease, while a value above about 1.3 suggests incompressible calcified vessels, as in diabetes or chronic kidney disease, and needs further assessment.

subject: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care
title: ABDOMINAL AORTIC ANEURYSM
stem: A 72-year-old man presents with sudden abdominal and back pain, hypotension and collapse. What vascular emergency should be considered immediately?
why_correct: NICE specifically advises considering ruptured AAA in people with new abdominal and/or back pain, cardiovascular collapse or loss of consciousness, particularly when risk factors are present.

why_others_wrong.B: Chronic venous insufficiency causes leg oedema, skin changes and ulceration over months to years, not sudden abdominal and back pain with collapse.
why_others_wrong.C: Intermittent claudication is chronic exertional leg pain relieved by rest and does not cause acute abdominal pain, hypotension or collapse.
why_others_wrong.D: Varicose veins are dilated superficial leg veins causing aching or cosmetic concern, with no link to sudden abdominal pain and cardiovascular collapse.
why_others_wrong.E: An uncomplicated inguinal hernia is a reducible groin swelling and would not explain back pain, hypotension and collapse in an older man.

exam_trap: Do not wait for the classic triad of abdominal pain, hypotension and a palpable pulsatile mass.
takeaway: Sudden abdominal/back pain + collapse in an at-risk patient = ruptured AAA until excluded.
source: NICE NG156.
thinking: 72-year-old man ↓ sudden abdominal and back pain ↓ hypotension and collapse ↓ ruptured AAA must be considered first ↓ Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm
pearl: In suspected ruptured AAA, permissive hypotension is used to limit further bleeding, and a haemodynamically unstable patient with a known aneurysm goes straight to theatre or for endovascular repair.

subject: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care
title: AAA REPAIR THRESHOLD
stem: An otherwise suitable patient is found to have an asymptomatic abdominal aortic aneurysm measuring 5.6 cm on ultrasound. Which statement is consistent with NICE guidance?

options.A: Repair should never be considered for an asymptomatic AAA
options.B: Repair should be considered because the aneurysm is at or above the NICE threshold
options.E: The finding is treated as peripheral arterial disease

correct_answer: B. Repair should be considered because the aneurysm is at or above the NICE threshold
why_correct: NICE recommends considering repair of an asymptomatic AAA when it is 5.5 cm or larger, measured using the specified ultrasound methodology. Symptomatic aneurysms and rapidly expanding aneurysms are also indications for consideration of repair.

why_others_wrong.A: NICE recommends considering repair of an asymptomatic AAA at 5.5 cm or larger, so a blanket statement that repair is never considered contradicts the guidance.
why_others_wrong.C: An abdominal aortic aneurysm is a degenerative dilatation of the aorta, not a malignancy, so chemotherapy has no role in its management.
why_others_wrong.D: ERCP is an endoscopic procedure for biliary and pancreatic duct disease and plays no part in assessing or treating an aortic aneurysm.
why_others_wrong.E: Although both share atherosclerotic risk factors, an AAA is managed on its own size-based pathway with surveillance or repair, not as peripheral arterial disease.

exam_trap: Do not confuse the threshold for considering repair with a statement that every patient must automatically undergo surgery; individual circumstances and shared decision-making remain important.
takeaway: Asymptomatic AAA ≥5.5 cm → consider repair and refer for specialist vascular assessment.
source: NICE NG156.
thinking: Asymptomatic AAA of 5.6 cm ↓ fit for intervention ↓ NICE threshold for considering repair is 5.5 cm ↓ refer for specialist vascular assessment ↓ Repair should be considered because the aneurysm is at or above the NICE threshold
pearl: Aneurysms of 4.0 cm or more growing by over 1 cm a year, and any symptomatic aneurysm, also warrant referral for consideration of repair; after endovascular repair, lifelong imaging surveillance for endoleak is needed.

subject: Breast surgery
title: BREAST CANCER: AXILLARY ASSESSMENT
stem: A woman has a newly diagnosed invasive breast cancer. Which investigation is recommended as part of pretreatment assessment of the axilla?
why_correct: NICE recommends pretreatment ultrasound assessment of the axilla in people being investigated for early and locally advanced invasive breast cancer. If abnormal nodes are identified, ultrasound-guided needle sampling should be performed.

why_others_wrong.A: Brain imaging is not part of axillary staging and is reserved for patients with neurological symptoms suggesting metastatic disease.
why_others_wrong.C: PET-CT is not recommended routinely for early breast cancer; axillary ultrasound is the standard first test for the nodes.
why_others_wrong.D: Diagnostic laparoscopy plays no part in staging breast cancer and cannot assess the axillary lymph nodes.
why_others_wrong.E: Bone marrow biopsy is not a staging test for early breast cancer and gives no information about axillary nodal status.

exam_trap: PET-CT (C) sounds more thorough, but it is not routine for early breast cancer; NICE recommends axillary ultrasound, with needle sampling of any abnormal node, before treatment.
takeaway: Invasive breast cancer → assess the axilla with ultrasound.
source: NICE NG101; updated recommendations reviewed through 2025.
thinking: Newly diagnosed invasive breast cancer ↓ nodal status guides axillary surgery and adjuvant treatment ↓ the axilla is imaged before any surgery ↓ abnormal nodes are then sampled under ultrasound guidance ↓ Axillary ultrasound
pearl: A normal axillary ultrasound does not exclude low-volume nodal disease, so patients with a radiologically normal axilla still proceed to sentinel lymph node biopsy for surgical staging.

subject: Breast surgery
title: BREAST CANCER: SENTINEL NODE BIOPSY
stem: A patient has invasive breast cancer with no evidence of axillary lymph-node involvement on ultrasound. What is the usual surgical method for axillary staging?
why_correct: NICE recommends sentinel lymph node biopsy rather than axillary lymph-node clearance for axillary staging in invasive breast cancer when there is no evidence of nodal involvement on ultrasound, or when ultrasound-guided needle biopsy is negative.

why_others_wrong.A: Axillary clearance is a therapeutic procedure with higher lymphoedema risk and is not used for staging when ultrasound shows no nodal involvement.
why_others_wrong.C: Thyroidectomy has no role in breast cancer staging; the thyroid is not part of the lymphatic drainage of the breast.
why_others_wrong.D: PET-CT is not a routine staging tool for early breast cancer and PET-guided node excision is not a standard axillary staging operation.
why_others_wrong.E: A normal axillary ultrasound does not exclude micrometastases, so surgical staging with sentinel node biopsy is still needed to guide treatment.

exam_trap: Candidates choose routine axillary clearance (A), but in an ultrasound-negative axilla clearance adds lymphoedema and nerve morbidity without staging benefit; sentinel node biopsy is the standard.
takeaway: Clinically node-negative invasive breast cancer → SLNB is the key axillary staging procedure.
source: NICE NG101.
thinking: Invasive cancer with an ultrasound-normal axilla ↓ occult micrometastases remain possible, so staging is still needed ↓ minimally invasive surgical staging is preferred over clearance ↓ Sentinel lymph node biopsy
pearl: The sentinel node is usually localised with a radioisotope combined with blue dye or an alternative tracer; blue dye carries a small risk of anaphylaxis and can cause prolonged skin staining.

subject: Breast surgery
title: DCIS AND SENTINEL NODE BIOPSY
stem: A patient has ductal carcinoma in situ and is undergoing breast-conserving surgery. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Sentinel node biopsy is mandatory in every case
options.B: Sentinel node biopsy is never appropriate
options.C: Sentinel node biopsy is not routinely performed unless there is high risk of invasive disease
options.E: The axilla must always be biopsied with CT guidance

correct_answer: C. Sentinel node biopsy is not routinely performed unless there is high risk of invasive disease
why_correct: NICE advises against routine SLNB for DCIS treated with breast-conserving surgery unless there is high risk of invasive disease, such as a palpable mass or extensive microcalcifications.

why_others_wrong.A: NICE advises against routine sentinel node biopsy for DCIS treated by breast-conserving surgery, because pure in situ disease should not spread to lymph nodes.
why_others_wrong.B: Sentinel node biopsy is appropriate for DCIS when invasive disease is likely, such as with a palpable mass or extensive microcalcifications.
why_others_wrong.D: Axillary clearance is not indicated for DCIS, which is non-invasive, and would add morbidity such as lymphoedema without benefit.
why_others_wrong.E: CT-guided axillary biopsy is not a standard technique; axillary assessment in breast disease uses ultrasound and ultrasound-guided sampling.

exam_trap: Candidates pick A by applying the mastectomy rule; after breast conservation the lymphatics stay intact for later mapping, so SLNB is reserved for those at high risk of invasion.
takeaway: DCIS + breast-conserving surgery → no routine SLNB unless specific high-risk features exist.
source: NICE NG101.
thinking: DCIS is non-invasive, with an intact basement membrane ↓ pure DCIS should not spread to lymph nodes ↓ breast is conserved, so later sentinel mapping remains possible ↓ SLNB only if invasion is likely, such as a palpable mass or extensive microcalcification ↓ Sentinel node biopsy is not routinely performed unless there is high risk of invasive disease
pearl: If the excision specimen unexpectedly shows invasive cancer, sentinel node biopsy can still be done as a second procedure because the breast and its lymphatic drainage remain intact.

subject: Breast surgery
title: DCIS AND MASTECTOMY
stem: A patient with extensive DCIS is undergoing mastectomy. Which axillary procedure should be offered?
why_correct: NICE recommends offering SLNB to people undergoing mastectomy for DCIS because subsequent sentinel-node assessment may not be feasible after the breast has been removed.

why_others_wrong.A: Omitting axillary assessment risks missing occult invasion, and sentinel node mapping is unreliable once the breast has been removed.
why_others_wrong.C: Bilateral axillary clearance is not indicated for DCIS; the contralateral axilla has no role and ipsilateral clearance would be overtreatment.
why_others_wrong.D: PET-guided axillary biopsy is not a standard staging method; sentinel node biopsy is the recommended procedure at mastectomy for DCIS.
why_others_wrong.E: Axillary radiotherapy is a treatment for proven nodal disease, not a staging procedure, and would be overtreatment for DCIS.

exam_trap: Candidates choose no axillary assessment (A) because DCIS is non-invasive, but after mastectomy sentinel mapping is no longer feasible, so SLNB is offered at the same operation.
takeaway: DCIS + mastectomy → offer SLNB.
source: NICE NG101.
thinking: Extensive DCIS treated by mastectomy ↓ occult invasive disease may be found in the specimen ↓ removing the breast destroys the lymphatic pathway needed for later sentinel mapping ↓ so the axilla is staged at the same operation ↓ Sentinel lymph node biopsy
pearl: Extensive or high-grade DCIS carries a higher chance of hidden invasion, which is why the mastectomy specimen is sampled thoroughly and the axilla is staged at the same sitting.

subject: Breast surgery
title: BREAST MRI
stem: A patient has biopsy-proven invasive breast cancer. Clinical examination, mammography and ultrasound clearly define the extent of disease. Which statement about breast MRI is most accurate?

options.A: MRI is routinely mandatory before every breast operation
options.B: MRI is never useful in breast cancer
options.C: MRI is not routinely required when conventional assessment adequately defines the disease
options.E: MRI replaces mammography in all patients

correct_answer: C. MRI is not routinely required when conventional assessment adequately defines the disease
why_correct: NICE does not recommend routine breast MRI as part of preoperative assessment for biopsy-proven invasive breast cancer or DCIS. MRI has selected indications, including uncertainty about disease extent or difficult mammographic assessment.

why_others_wrong.A: NICE does not recommend routine preoperative breast MRI, so it is not mandatory when conventional assessment already defines the disease.
why_others_wrong.B: MRI has recognised selective uses, such as unclear disease extent, dense breasts limiting mammography and assessing tumour size in lobular cancer.
why_others_wrong.D: MRI cannot provide a histological diagnosis; core biopsy is still needed to confirm malignancy and determine receptor status.
why_others_wrong.E: Mammography remains a core part of breast assessment and screening; MRI is a supplementary problem-solving test for selected patients.

exam_trap: Candidates choosing A assume more imaging means better staging, but NICE does not recommend routine preoperative MRI when conventional assessment already defines the disease.
takeaway: Breast MRI = selective problem-solving investigation, not routine imaging for every breast cancer.
source: NICE NG101.
thinking: Biopsy-proven invasive cancer ↓ examination, mammography and ultrasound already define the extent ↓ routine MRI adds false positives and delay without clear benefit ↓ MRI is kept for selected indications ↓ MRI is not routinely required when conventional assessment adequately defines the disease
pearl: Breast MRI is highly sensitive but less specific, so routine use generates extra biopsies and can push patients towards mastectomy; it is most useful for lobular cancer, dense breasts and an occult primary presenting with axillary nodes.

subject: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care
title: THYROID NODULE: INITIAL IMAGING
stem: A patient is found to have a thyroid nodule requiring investigation for malignancy. What is the recommended initial diagnostic imaging test?

options.C: Greyscale ultrasound using an established grading system

correct_answer: C. Greyscale ultrasound using an established grading system
why_correct: NICE recommends greyscale ultrasound with an established system for grading ultrasound appearance as the initial diagnostic test when investigating thyroid nodules for malignancy.

why_others_wrong.A: CT chest is not the first test for a thyroid nodule; it may later stage known cancer or assess retrosternal extension but does not grade nodule malignancy risk.
why_others_wrong.B: PET-CT is not used to investigate a thyroid nodule for malignancy; incidental PET-avid thyroid lesions themselves need ultrasound assessment.
why_others_wrong.D: MRI brain has no role in assessing a thyroid nodule and would not evaluate its ultrasound features or malignancy risk.
why_others_wrong.E: A plain radiograph may show tracheal deviation from a large goitre but cannot characterise a nodule or grade its risk of malignancy.

exam_trap: Candidates choose CT chest or PET-CT because they sound thorough, but neither grades a thyroid nodule; greyscale ultrasound with an established grading system comes first.
takeaway: Thyroid nodule → ultrasound first.
source: NICE NG230, Thyroid cancer: assessment and management.
thinking: Thyroid nodule needing malignancy assessment ↓ first test should characterise the nodule ↓ greyscale ultrasound with a grading system ↓ stratifies need for cytology ↓ Greyscale ultrasound using an established grading system
pearl: Ultrasound features that raise suspicion of thyroid cancer include microcalcification, irregular margins, marked hypoechogenicity and a taller-than-wide shape.

subject: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care
title: THYROID NODULE: FNAC
stem: A thyroid nodule has an ultrasound appearance that reaches the threshold for cytological assessment. What should be offered?

options.B: Immediate total thyroidectomy in every case

why_correct: NICE recommends FNAC for thyroid nodules meeting the threshold based on an established ultrasound grading system. Ultrasound guidance should be used when performing FNAC.

why_others_wrong.B: Total thyroidectomy is not performed on every nodule on the basis of ultrasound alone; cytology is obtained first to guide whether and how much surgery is needed.
why_others_wrong.C: ERCP examines the biliary and pancreatic ducts and has no role in sampling a thyroid nodule.
why_others_wrong.D: Colonoscopy investigates the large bowel and is irrelevant to the cytological assessment of a thyroid nodule.
why_others_wrong.E: Bone marrow biopsy assesses haematological disease and would not provide cytology from the thyroid nodule that met the ultrasound threshold.

exam_trap: Not every thyroid nodule requires FNAC; ultrasound risk stratification helps determine which nodules require sampling.
takeaway: Thyroid ultrasound risk assessment → FNAC when the threshold is met.
source: NICE NG230.
thinking: Thyroid nodule ↓ ultrasound appearance meets the cytology threshold ↓ tissue sampling needed before surgery ↓ ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration ↓ Fine-needle aspiration cytology
pearl: UK thyroid cytology is reported using Thy categories from Thy1 (non-diagnostic) to Thy5 (malignant), and a non-diagnostic sample is usually repeated under ultrasound guidance.

subject: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care
title: FOLLICULAR THYROID NEOPLASM
stem: A thyroid FNAC result is reported as Thy3f, suggesting a follicular neoplasm. Which management option may be considered?
why_correct: NICE recommends considering diagnostic hemithyroidectomy for Thy3f cytology, which suggests a follicular neoplasm.

why_others_wrong.B: A Thy3f result is indeterminate and many lesions prove benign follicular adenomas, so chemotherapy is not indicated and differentiated thyroid cancer is not treated this way.
why_others_wrong.C: ERCP is a biliary and pancreatic procedure and has no role in managing an indeterminate thyroid cytology result.
why_others_wrong.D: Axillary clearance treats nodal breast cancer; thyroid malignancy spreads to cervical, not axillary, nodes.
why_others_wrong.E: Appendicectomy is unrelated to thyroid disease and would not help distinguish follicular adenoma from carcinoma.

exam_trap: Cytology cannot reliably distinguish follicular adenoma from follicular carcinoma because capsular or vascular invasion requires histological assessment.
takeaway: Follicular-pattern thyroid lesion → remember that invasion is a histological diagnosis.
source: NICE NG230.
thinking: FNAC reported as Thy3f ↓ follicular neoplasm suspected ↓ adenoma and carcinoma differ only by capsular or vascular invasion ↓ needs histology of the whole lesion ↓ Diagnostic hemithyroidectomy
pearl: If diagnostic hemithyroidectomy confirms follicular carcinoma, completion thyroidectomy may then be needed, which carries a further risk to the contralateral recurrent laryngeal nerve.

subject: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care
title: THYROID CANCER: CALCITONIN
stem: A patient has a thyroid nodule. Which statement regarding calcitonin testing is correct?

options.A: It should be measured routinely in every thyroid nodule
options.C: It should be considered when medullary thyroid cancer is suspected

correct_answer: C. It should be considered when medullary thyroid cancer is suspected
why_correct: NICE advises against routine calcitonin testing for thyroid nodules unless there is a reason to suspect medullary thyroid cancer, such as a relevant family history or suspicious ultrasound appearance.

why_others_wrong.A: NICE advises against routine calcitonin measurement in every thyroid nodule and reserves it for when medullary thyroid cancer is suspected.
why_others_wrong.B: Calcitonin is useful when medullary thyroid cancer is suspected, for example with a family history of MEN2, so ruling it out entirely is wrong.
why_others_wrong.D: Calcitonin is a tumour marker for medullary carcinoma and cannot replace ultrasound, which remains the initial test for grading any thyroid nodule.
why_others_wrong.E: Calcitonin is secreted by parafollicular C cells and relates to medullary carcinoma, whereas papillary cancer arises from follicular cells and is diagnosed cytologically.

exam_trap: Calcitonin is associated particularly with medullary thyroid carcinoma, not as a universal thyroid-nodule marker.
takeaway: Suspected medullary thyroid cancer → calcitonin becomes relevant.
source: NICE NG230.
thinking: Thyroid nodule ↓ calcitonin is a C-cell marker ↓ routine testing not recommended ↓ use when medullary thyroid cancer is suspected ↓ It should be considered when medullary thyroid cancer is suspected
pearl: Before surgery for medullary thyroid carcinoma, phaeochromocytoma must be excluded with plasma or urine metanephrines because of the MEN2 association.

subject: Urology
title: PROSTATE CANCER: FIRST-LINE MRI
stem: A man has suspected clinically localised prostate cancer. According to NICE, what is the first-line investigation?
why_correct: NICE recommends multiparametric MRI as the first-line investigation for people with suspected clinically localised prostate cancer.

why_others_wrong.A: A bone scan is a staging test for metastatic disease in higher-risk confirmed cancer, not the first-line investigation for suspected localised prostate cancer.
why_others_wrong.C: Diagnostic laparoscopy has no role in diagnosing prostate cancer; the prostate is assessed by imaging and targeted biopsy, not by peritoneal inspection.
why_others_wrong.D: CT colonography images the colon for colorectal neoplasia and gives no useful assessment of the prostate gland.
why_others_wrong.E: PET-CT, such as PSMA PET, is reserved for selected staging or recurrence questions and is not recommended routinely as the first-line test for suspected localised disease.

exam_trap: Candidates choose PET-CT or bone scan because they sound comprehensive, but these are staging tools for confirmed disease; suspected localised cancer starts with multiparametric MRI.
takeaway: Suspected clinically localised prostate cancer → mpMRI first.
source: NICE NG131, Prostate cancer: diagnosis and management.
thinking: Suspected clinically localised prostate cancer ↓ need to detect and localise significant tumour before biopsy ↓ NICE places imaging of the gland first ↓ multiparametric MRI guides whether and where to biopsy ↓ Multiparametric MRI
pearl: Prostate MRI is ideally performed before biopsy because post-biopsy haemorrhage degrades image quality; staging tests such as bone scan are reserved for confirmed higher-risk disease.

subject: Urology
title: PROSTATE MRI AND BIOPSY
stem: A patient's prostate MRI has a Likert score of 4. What is the next investigation recommended by NICE?

options.C: Immediate radical prostatectomy without tissue diagnosis

why_correct: NICE recommends MRI-influenced prostate biopsy for people whose multiparametric MRI has a Likert score of 3 or more.

why_others_wrong.A: A Likert score of 4 indicates a lesion likely to be clinically significant cancer, so stopping investigation would miss disease that NICE says should be biopsied.
why_others_wrong.C: Radical prostatectomy is not performed without histological confirmation, grading and staging, because MRI alone cannot establish a cancer diagnosis.
why_others_wrong.D: Colonoscopy investigates the large bowel and does not provide tissue from a suspicious prostate lesion.
why_others_wrong.E: TURBT is resection of a bladder tumour and has no role in obtaining a diagnosis from an MRI-detected prostate lesion.

exam_trap: Candidates are tempted by radical prostatectomy because a Likert 4 lesion looks like cancer, but MRI cannot provide histology, grade or risk group, so biopsy comes first.
takeaway: Prostate mpMRI Likert ≥3 → MRI-influenced biopsy.
source: NICE NG131.
thinking: Likert score of 4 on prostate MRI ↓ significant cancer is likely ↓ NICE threshold for biopsy is a score of 3 or more ↓ tissue diagnosis is needed before treatment ↓ MRI-influenced prostate biopsy
pearl: MRI-influenced biopsy is increasingly performed transperineally under local anaesthetic, which carries a lower infection risk than the transrectal route.

subject: Urology
title: LOW-RISK PROSTATE MRI
stem: A patient with suspected clinically localised prostate cancer has a multiparametric MRI Likert score of 2. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: Biopsy is mandatory in every patient
options.C: Biopsy may be omitted after discussion of risks and benefits and shared decision-making

correct_answer: C. Biopsy may be omitted after discussion of risks and benefits and shared decision-making
why_correct: NICE allows consideration of omitting biopsy in people with Likert 1 or 2, provided risks and benefits are discussed and a shared decision is reached.

why_others_wrong.A: NICE allows biopsy to be omitted after shared decision-making when the Likert score is 1 or 2, so biopsy is not mandatory for every patient.
why_others_wrong.B: A low Likert score does not exclude significant cancer, and biopsy can still be offered if the patient or clinical risk factors favour it.
why_others_wrong.D: Radical prostatectomy requires a histological diagnosis of cancer, which has not been made in a patient with a low-suspicion MRI.
why_others_wrong.E: Chemotherapy is used for selected advanced or metastatic prostate cancer, not for a patient without any tissue diagnosis and a low-suspicion MRI.

exam_trap: Candidates choose 'biopsy is mandatory' from old PSA-driven pathways, or 'biopsy can never be performed'; NICE allows either route after shared decision-making for Likert 1 or 2.
takeaway: Low-risk MRI can support biopsy avoidance in selected patients, but shared decision-making remains important.
source: NICE NG131.
thinking: Suspected localised prostate cancer ↓ MRI Likert score of 2 indicates low suspicion ↓ NICE permits omitting biopsy in this group ↓ only after discussing risks and benefits with the patient ↓ Biopsy may be omitted after discussion of risks and benefits and shared decision-making
pearl: Factors such as PSA density, family history and patient preference influence whether biopsy is still offered after a low-suspicion MRI.

subject: Urology
title: ACUTE URINARY RETENTION
stem: An elderly man with lower urinary tract symptoms develops painful inability to pass urine with a palpable distended bladder. What is the immediate treatment?
why_correct: Acute urinary retention requires prompt bladder decompression, usually with urethral catheterisation unless contraindicated or unsuccessful.

why_others_wrong.B: Nephrectomy removes a kidney and plays no part in relieving bladder outflow obstruction causing acute retention.
why_others_wrong.C: ERCP investigates and treats biliary and pancreatic duct disease and is irrelevant to a distended, obstructed bladder.
why_others_wrong.D: Colonoscopy examines the large bowel and would neither relieve the retention nor address its likely prostatic cause.
why_others_wrong.E: Bladder tumour resection is not the treatment for retention, and any later outflow surgery follows, rather than replaces, initial bladder decompression.

exam_trap: Candidates who jump to definitive outflow surgery forget that the bladder must be decompressed first; resection or other procedures follow initial catheterisation, never replace it.
takeaway: Painful retention + palpable bladder → decompress first, investigate cause second.
source: Standard MRCS urological surgery knowledge.
thinking: Elderly man with LUTS ↓ painful inability to void ↓ palpable distended bladder ↓ acute urinary retention needs immediate decompression ↓ Urinary catheterisation
pearl: If urethral catheterisation fails or is contraindicated, for example after recent urethral surgery or suspected urethral injury, suprapubic catheterisation is used, and the residual volume drained should be recorded.

subject: Urology
title: TESTICULAR TORSION
stem: A 17-year-old develops sudden severe unilateral scrotal pain and nausea. The affected testis is high-riding. What is the priority?

options.B: Emergency surgical assessment for testicular torsion

correct_answer: B. Emergency surgical assessment for testicular torsion
why_correct: Testicular torsion is a time-critical surgical emergency. Delay can result in testicular ischaemia and infarction.

why_others_wrong.A: Sudden severe scrotal pain with a high-riding testis suggests torsion, and outpatient review would allow irreversible testicular infarction within hours.
why_others_wrong.C: Antibiotics treat epididymo-orchitis, which is usually more gradual in onset, and would delay the surgical exploration needed to salvage a torted testis.
why_others_wrong.D: Delaying imaging for weeks is unsafe when torsion is suspected, and exploration should not wait for ultrasound where the clinical picture is typical.
why_others_wrong.E: Colonoscopy examines the large bowel and has no role in the assessment of acute scrotal pain.

exam_trap: Do not delay scrotal exploration for ultrasound or blood tests; raised inflammatory markers or preserved Doppler flow do not exclude torsion.
takeaway: Sudden severe testicular pain in an adolescent = torsion until proven otherwise.
source: Standard MRCS urology knowledge.
thinking: Adolescent with sudden severe unilateral scrotal pain ↓ nausea and a high-riding testis ↓ classic features of testicular torsion ↓ testicular viability is time-dependent ↓ Emergency surgical assessment for testicular torsion
pearl: At exploration for torsion, the contralateral testis is also fixed because the bell-clapper anomaly that predisposes to torsion is usually bilateral.

subject: Urology
title: RENAL COLIC
stem: A patient develops sudden severe flank pain radiating towards the groin with microscopic haematuria. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Renal/ureteric colic classically causes severe flank pain that may radiate towards the groin and is commonly associated with haematuria.

why_others_wrong.B: Appendicitis typically causes periumbilical pain migrating to the right iliac fossa with peritonism, not colicky flank-to-groin pain with haematuria.
why_others_wrong.C: Acute cholecystitis causes right upper quadrant pain with fever and a positive Murphy sign rather than flank pain radiating to the groin.
why_others_wrong.D: Diverticulitis usually produces constant left iliac fossa pain with fever and tenderness, not severe colicky loin-to-groin pain with haematuria.
why_others_wrong.E: An inguinal hernia presents as a groin swelling, which may become painful if obstructed, but does not cause flank pain radiating downwards with haematuria.

exam_trap: Candidates choose appendicitis or diverticulitis because both cause abdominal pain, but sudden flank pain radiating to the groin with microscopic haematuria is the pattern of ureteric colic.
takeaway: Flank-to-groin colicky pain + haematuria = ureteric stone.
source: NICE NG118
thinking: Sudden severe flank pain ↓ radiating towards the groin ↓ microscopic haematuria ↓ pattern of ureteric colic ↓ Ureteric stone
pearl: Non-contrast CT of the kidneys, ureters and bladder is the standard imaging for suspected renal colic in adults, and NSAIDs are first-line analgesia when not contraindicated.

subject: Urology
title: OBSTRUCTED INFECTED KIDNEY
stem: A patient has fever, rigors, flank pain and imaging demonstrates an obstructed urinary system due to a ureteric stone. What is the key management principle?

options.B: Urgent urinary drainage is required alongside treatment of infection
options.D: Immediate elective stone surgery only after several months
options.E: No treatment if creatinine is normal

correct_answer: B. Urgent urinary drainage is required alongside treatment of infection
why_correct: An infected obstructed urinary tract can deteriorate rapidly. Antibiotics treat infection, but source control requires decompression of the obstructed system.

why_others_wrong.A: Antibiotics cannot adequately penetrate an obstructed, infected collecting system, so without drainage the patient may progress to urosepsis.
why_others_wrong.C: The obstruction is the source of the sepsis, and leaving it untreated risks septic shock and loss of the kidney.
why_others_wrong.D: Definitive stone treatment is deferred until infection settles, but the system must be decompressed urgently first rather than left obstructed for months.
why_others_wrong.E: A normal creatinine often just reflects a functioning contralateral kidney, and an infected obstructed system still needs urgent drainage to control sepsis.

exam_trap: Candidates choose antibiotics alone because the problem looks like infection, but an obstructed infected system needs urgent drainage or the patient can progress to septic shock.
takeaway: Infected + obstructed urinary system = antibiotics + urgent drainage/source control.
source: Standard MRCS urological emergency knowledge.
thinking: Fever and rigors with flank pain ↓ imaging shows obstruction from a ureteric stone ↓ infected obstructed kidney behaves like an abscess ↓ antibiotics need source control by drainage ↓ Urgent urinary drainage is required alongside treatment of infection
pearl: Decompression is by percutaneous nephrostomy or retrograde ureteric stent; definitive stone treatment is deferred until sepsis has resolved because manipulating an infected stone risks bacteraemia.

subject: Major trauma & fluids
title: MAJOR TRAUMA: AIRWAY
stem: A patient with major trauma cannot maintain their airway or ventilation. What is the definitive method of securing the airway according to NICE?

options.B: Drug-assisted rapid sequence induction and intubation

correct_answer: B. Drug-assisted rapid sequence induction and intubation
why_correct: NICE recommends drug-assisted RSI and intubation as the definitive airway method in major trauma patients who cannot maintain their airway and/or ventilation.

why_others_wrong.A: Oxygen by mask supports oxygenation but does not protect or secure an airway that the patient cannot maintain, nor provide ventilation.
why_others_wrong.C: A nasogastric tube decompresses the stomach and does nothing to secure the airway; it may also be hazardous in suspected base-of-skull fracture.
why_others_wrong.D: Observation leaves a patient who cannot maintain their airway or ventilation at immediate risk of hypoxia and aspiration.
why_others_wrong.E: Airway and breathing threats are treated before imaging, so delaying airway control for CT would risk hypoxic injury or arrest.

exam_trap: Immediate CT before airway management appeals as information gathering, but airway and breathing threats are treated before imaging; delay risks hypoxic brain injury or arrest.
takeaway: Major trauma + failed airway/ventilation → definitive airway control with RSI.
source: NICE NG39, Major trauma: assessment and initial management.
thinking: Major trauma ↓ cannot maintain airway or ventilation ↓ needs a protected airway plus controlled ventilation ↓ NICE definitive method is drug-assisted RSI ↓ Drug-assisted rapid sequence induction and intubation
pearl: Manual in-line stabilisation of the cervical spine is maintained during intubation in major trauma, and the front of a cervical collar may be opened to allow laryngoscopy.

subject: Major trauma & fluids
title: TENSION PNEUMOTHORAX
stem: A trauma patient develops severe respiratory compromise and haemodynamic instability with clinical features of tension pneumothorax. What should happen?
correct_answer: B. Perform chest decompression before imaging
why_correct: NICE recommends chest decompression before imaging in tension pneumothorax when there is haemodynamic instability or severe respiratory compromise. In hospital, NICE recommends open thoracostomy followed by chest drain where appropriate expertise is available.

why_others_wrong.A: Waiting for CT delays life-saving decompression in a patient already showing haemodynamic instability and severe respiratory compromise from tension physiology.
why_others_wrong.C: Oral antibiotics have no role in treating the raised intrathoracic pressure of a tension pneumothorax, which requires urgent decompression.
why_others_wrong.D: Spirometry is a lung-function test for chronic disease and has no place in an unstable trauma patient with suspected tension pneumothorax.
why_others_wrong.E: Observation allows tension physiology to progress to cardiovascular collapse and cardiac arrest, so immediate decompression is needed.

exam_trap: Waiting for CT before decompression is the classic wrong choice; tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis and an unstable patient may arrest before imaging is complete.
takeaway: Tension physiology + instability/severe respiratory compromise → decompress before imaging.
source: NICE NG39.
thinking: Trauma with clinical features of tension pneumothorax ↓ haemodynamic instability and severe respiratory compromise ↓ clinical diagnosis needing immediate treatment ↓ NICE: decompress before imaging ↓ Perform chest decompression before imaging
pearl: In hospital, open thoracostomy followed by a chest drain is preferred, especially in ventilated patients; needle decompression is temporising and can fail because of chest-wall thickness or catheter kinking.

subject: Major trauma & fluids
title: MAJOR TRAUMA: EXTERNAL HAEMORRHAGE
stem: A patient has life-threatening bleeding from a traumatic limb wound. Direct pressure fails to control the haemorrhage. What should be considered?
why_correct: NICE recommends a tourniquet for major limb trauma when direct pressure has failed to control life-threatening haemorrhage.

why_others_wrong.B: A plaster cast immobilises a fracture but cannot control life-threatening arterial bleeding and would hide the wound from view.
why_others_wrong.C: Observation is inappropriate when direct pressure has failed and the bleeding is life-threatening, as exsanguination can occur within minutes.
why_others_wrong.D: Oral iron replenishes iron stores over weeks and has no role in stopping active haemorrhage.
why_others_wrong.E: Compression stockings are used for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis and cannot generate enough pressure to stop arterial limb bleeding.

exam_trap: A tourniquet is not the first step for every minor bleeding wound; direct pressure is recommended initially.
takeaway: Life-threatening limb haemorrhage + failed direct pressure → tourniquet.
source: NICE NG39.
thinking: Life-threatening limb bleeding ↓ direct pressure has failed ↓ arterial inflow must be occluded proximally ↓ NICE recommends a tourniquet in major limb trauma ↓ Tourniquet
pearl: The time of tourniquet application should be recorded, and if one tourniquet fails to stop bleeding a second can be applied just proximal to the first.

subject: Major trauma & fluids
title: MAJOR TRAUMA: TRANEXAMIC ACID
stem: A patient has major trauma with active or suspected active bleeding. What does NICE recommend regarding intravenous tranexamic acid?

options.A: Give it as soon as possible
options.D: Give it only after definitive surgery
options.E: Give it only if the haemoglobin is normal

correct_answer: A. Give it as soon as possible
why_correct: NICE recommends intravenous tranexamic acid as soon as possible in patients with major trauma and active or suspected active bleeding. NICE also advises against giving it more than 3 hours after injury unless there is evidence of hyperfibrinolysis.

why_others_wrong.B: Tranexamic acid is most effective when given early, and NICE advises against starting it more than 3 hours after injury unless hyperfibrinolysis is shown.
why_others_wrong.C: NICE recommends intravenous tranexamic acid for major trauma with active or suspected active bleeding, so avoiding it entirely contradicts the guidance.
why_others_wrong.D: Waiting until after definitive surgery would delay antifibrinolytic treatment well beyond the early window in which it reduces death from bleeding.
why_others_wrong.E: Haemoglobin may be normal early in haemorrhage, and NICE bases tranexamic acid use on active or suspected bleeding rather than a haemoglobin value.

exam_trap: Giving it only after 48 hours or after definitive surgery misses the early window; NICE advises against starting it beyond 3 hours unless hyperfibrinolysis is shown.
takeaway: Major trauma + active/suspected bleeding → early IV tranexamic acid.
source: NICE NG39.
thinking: Major trauma ↓ active or suspected active bleeding ↓ tranexamic acid inhibits fibrinolysis ↓ benefit is greatest early; avoid after 3 hours unless hyperfibrinolysis ↓ Give it as soon as possible
pearl: Tranexamic acid is a lysine analogue that blocks plasminogen binding to fibrin; it does not replace clotting factors, so it complements rather than replaces blood-component resuscitation.

subject: Major trauma & fluids
title: MAJOR TRAUMA: PELVIC BLEEDING
stem: A patient sustains blunt high-energy pelvic trauma and active bleeding from a pelvic fracture is suspected. What immediate mechanical intervention is recommended?
why_correct: NICE recommends applying a purpose-made pelvic binder when active bleeding is suspected from a pelvic fracture following blunt high-energy trauma.

why_others_wrong.B: A knee immobiliser stabilises the knee and has no effect on pelvic volume or bleeding from a pelvic fracture.
why_others_wrong.C: A cervical collar may be needed for spinal protection but does nothing to control haemorrhage from a pelvic fracture.
why_others_wrong.D: Abdominal massage could disturb clot and worsen bleeding, and it provides no pelvic stabilisation.
why_others_wrong.E: Mobilising a patient with a suspected unstable pelvic fracture could displace fragments and increase haemorrhage.

exam_trap: A cervical collar may be needed for spinal protection but does nothing for pelvic haemorrhage; the binder is applied to control bleeding, not merely to immobilise.
takeaway: High-energy pelvic trauma + suspected active bleeding → pelvic binder.
source: NICE NG39 and NG37.
thinking: Blunt high-energy pelvic trauma ↓ suspected active bleeding from the fracture ↓ reducing pelvic volume and stabilising fragments aids tamponade ↓ purpose-made pelvic binder ↓ Pelvic binder
pearl: A pelvic binder is centred over the greater trochanters, not the iliac crests; placing it too high is ineffective and can widen the fracture.

subject: Major trauma & fluids
title: PELVIC FRACTURE AND INTERVENTIONAL RADIOLOGY
stem: A patient has active arterial pelvic haemorrhage but does not require immediate laparotomy for another abdominal injury. Which treatment is recommended as first-line invasive management?
why_correct: NICE recommends interventional radiology for active arterial pelvic bleeding when emergency laparotomy is not required for abdominal injuries.

why_others_wrong.B: Elective colonoscopy investigates the colonic lumen and cannot identify or treat active arterial bleeding from a pelvic fracture.
why_others_wrong.C: Appendicectomy treats appendicitis and has no role in controlling arterial haemorrhage from pelvic trauma.
why_others_wrong.D: ERCP investigates and treats biliary and pancreatic duct disease, not pelvic arterial bleeding.
why_others_wrong.E: Nephrectomy removes a kidney and does not address bleeding from pelvic arteries.

exam_trap: The presence of pelvic bleeding does not automatically mean laparotomy is the definitive haemorrhage-control procedure.
takeaway: Active arterial pelvic bleeding without need for laparotomy → interventional radiology.
source: NICE NG37/NG39.
thinking: Active arterial pelvic haemorrhage ↓ no immediate laparotomy needed for another injury ↓ arterial bleeding can be targeted angiographically ↓ NICE first-line invasive option ↓ Interventional radiology
pearl: Most pelvic fracture bleeding is venous or from fracture surfaces; if a patient remains unstable and interventional radiology is not immediately available, pre-peritoneal pelvic packing with external fixation is an alternative.

subject: Major trauma & fluids
title: MAJOR TRAUMA: TRANSPORT DESTINATION
stem: Where should patients with major trauma usually be managed?
why_correct: NICE states that the optimal destination for patients with major trauma is usually a major trauma centre, although regional trauma-network arrangements may determine exceptions.

why_others_wrong.B: An outpatient clinic lacks the resuscitation, imaging, surgical and critical care facilities needed for a patient with major trauma.
why_others_wrong.C: A community pharmacy provides medicines and advice and cannot assess or treat life-threatening injuries.
why_others_wrong.D: Rehabilitation follows resuscitation, assessment and definitive treatment of injuries, so sending a patient there first would miss life-threatening injuries.
why_others_wrong.E: A GP surgery lacks the emergency, imaging and surgical capability required for major trauma, which is managed within a trauma network.

exam_trap: Do not interpret "major trauma centre" as meaning every patient must bypass all local emergency care regardless of circumstances.
takeaway: Major trauma → major trauma centre is generally the definitive trauma destination.
source: NICE NG39.
thinking: Major trauma ↓ needs immediate resuscitation, imaging, surgery and critical care ↓ these are concentrated within regional trauma networks ↓ usual definitive destination ↓ Major trauma centre
pearl: Within a trauma network, a local trauma unit may first stabilise a patient with an immediately life-threatening problem, such as an unmanageable airway, before transfer to the major trauma centre.

subject: Major trauma & fluids
title: MAJOR TRAUMA: WHOLE-BODY CT
stem: An adult has blunt major trauma with suspected multiple injuries and is haemodynamically suitable for CT. What imaging strategy does NICE recommend?
why_correct: NICE recommends whole-body CT in adults aged 16 or over with blunt major trauma and suspected multiple injuries.

why_others_wrong.B: MRI of every region is slow, difficult with resuscitation equipment and unsuitable for rapid assessment of multiple injuries in blunt major trauma.
why_others_wrong.C: Ultrasound can detect free fluid but misses many solid-organ, bony, retroperitoneal and thoracic injuries, so it cannot replace whole-body CT here.
why_others_wrong.D: Plain radiographs miss many significant injuries in blunt multiple trauma, which is why NICE recommends whole-body CT for suspected multiple injuries.
why_others_wrong.E: Omitting imaging in suspected multiple injuries after blunt major trauma would risk missing life-threatening injuries.

exam_trap: The recommendation is for the specified major-trauma population; it should not be extrapolated to every minor trauma presentation.
takeaway: Adult blunt major trauma + suspected multiple injuries → whole-body CT when appropriate.
source: NICE NG39/NG37.
thinking: Adult with blunt major trauma ↓ suspected multiple injuries ↓ haemodynamically suitable for CT ↓ one comprehensive scan rather than piecemeal imaging ↓ Whole-body CT
pearl: NICE defines whole-body CT as vertex to mid-thigh, so injured limbs beyond that range need separate imaging.

subject: Major trauma & fluids
title: MAJOR TRAUMA: NEGATIVE FAST
stem: A haemodynamically stable trauma patient has a negative FAST scan. Which statement is correct?

options.A: A negative FAST excludes all intra-abdominal bleeding
options.B: A negative FAST excludes retroperitoneal bleeding
options.C: A negative FAST does not exclude intra-abdominal or retroperitoneal haemorrhage
options.D: No further assessment is ever required
options.E: The patient must have no significant injury

correct_answer: C. A negative FAST does not exclude intra-abdominal or retroperitoneal haemorrhage
why_correct: NICE explicitly states that a negative FAST does not exclude intraperitoneal or retroperitoneal haemorrhage.

why_others_wrong.A: FAST detects free intraperitoneal fluid above a certain volume and can miss smaller bleeds and solid-organ injuries, so a negative result does not exclude bleeding.
why_others_wrong.B: FAST assesses the retroperitoneum poorly, so a negative scan cannot exclude retroperitoneal haemorrhage from renal, pelvic or major vessel injury.
why_others_wrong.D: A negative FAST is one limited test, and further clinical assessment, repeat examination or CT may still be needed.
why_others_wrong.E: Significant injuries such as hollow-viscus, retroperitoneal or skeletal trauma may coexist with a negative FAST.

exam_trap: A negative FAST excluding retroperitoneal bleeding is the classic error; FAST barely images the retroperitoneum, so renal, pelvic and major-vessel haemorrhage can be missed.
takeaway: Negative FAST ≠ no bleeding.
source: NICE NG39.
thinking: Stable trauma patient with negative FAST ↓ FAST detects only free intraperitoneal fluid above a threshold volume ↓ retroperitoneum, solid organs and hollow viscera are poorly assessed ↓ a negative scan cannot rule out bleeding ↓ A negative FAST does not exclude intra-abdominal or retroperitoneal haemorrhage
pearl: FAST is most useful in the unstable patient, where a positive scan supports immediate laparotomy; a stable patient with suspected abdominal injury should still proceed to CT despite a negative FAST.

subject: Major trauma & fluids
title: MAJOR TRAUMA: DAMAGE CONTROL SURGERY
stem: A patient with major trauma remains haemodynamically unstable despite volume resuscitation. Which surgical strategy does NICE recommend?
why_correct: NICE recommends damage control surgery in patients with haemodynamic instability who are not responding to volume resuscitation.

why_others_wrong.B: Prolonged definitive reconstruction in an unstable patient worsens acidosis, hypothermia and coagulopathy, so NICE recommends damage control surgery instead.
why_others_wrong.C: Delaying surgery for 72 hours would leave uncontrolled haemorrhage in a patient who is not responding to volume resuscitation.
why_others_wrong.D: Colonoscopy is a diagnostic luminal procedure and has no role in controlling haemorrhage in an unstable trauma patient.
why_others_wrong.E: Persistent instability despite resuscitation usually means ongoing bleeding that needs prompt surgical or radiological control rather than no intervention.

exam_trap: The aim is rapid control of life-threatening injury rather than prolonged definitive reconstruction in a physiologically unstable patient.
takeaway: Unstable despite resuscitation → damage control rather than prolonged definitive surgery.
source: NICE NG39.
thinking: Major trauma ↓ unstable despite volume resuscitation ↓ prolonged surgery would worsen acidosis, hypothermia and coagulopathy ↓ control bleeding and contamination quickly, then resuscitate ↓ Damage control surgery
pearl: Damage control surgery has three phases: abbreviated surgery for haemorrhage and contamination control, physiological restoration in intensive care, then planned return for definitive repair.

subject: Major trauma & fluids
title: MAJOR TRAUMA: DEFINITIVE SURGERY
stem: A patient with major trauma has a normal haemodynamic status. Which surgical approach is recommended when surgery is required?

options.B: Damage control surgery in every case

why_correct: NICE recommends definitive surgery for patients whose haemodynamic status is normal.

why_others_wrong.B: Damage control surgery is reserved for physiological instability, so a haemodynamically normal patient can usually undergo definitive surgery instead.
why_others_wrong.C: The stem specifies that surgery is required, and NICE supports definitive surgery when haemodynamic status is normal.
why_others_wrong.D: Diagnostic colonoscopy investigates the colonic lumen and is not the surgical approach for major trauma injuries.
why_others_wrong.E: Rehabilitation follows treatment of injuries, so transferring a patient who needs surgery there would leave injuries untreated.

exam_trap: Damage control is driven by physiological instability, not simply by the fact that the patient has multiple injuries.
takeaway: Stable physiology → definitive surgery can be undertaken when indicated.
source: NICE NG39.
thinking: Major trauma needing surgery ↓ haemodynamic status normal ↓ no physiological exhaustion from acidosis, hypothermia or coagulopathy ↓ patient can tolerate a complete operation ↓ Definitive surgery
pearl: Physiology can deteriorate during an operation, so a planned definitive procedure may be converted to damage control if the patient becomes acidotic, hypothermic or coagulopathic.

subject: Vascular & fracture complications
title: COMPARTMENT SYNDROME
stem: A patient with a high-energy limb injury develops severe escalating pain, particularly with passive stretch of the affected muscles. What diagnosis must be considered?
why_correct: Acute compartment syndrome is caused by increased pressure within a closed fascial compartment, compromising tissue perfusion. Severe pain, particularly pain on passive stretch, is an important clinical warning sign.

why_others_wrong.B: Simple bruising causes localised tenderness but not severe escalating pain after high-energy trauma that is markedly worsened by passive muscle stretch.
why_others_wrong.C: Chronic venous insufficiency develops over months to years with oedema and skin changes, and does not present acutely after limb trauma with pain on passive stretch.
why_others_wrong.D: Cellulitis produces spreading erythema, warmth and systemic features of infection rather than escalating pain provoked by passive stretch after a high-energy injury.
why_others_wrong.E: Osteoarthritis is a chronic degenerative joint condition with mechanical pain and stiffness, unrelated to acute escalating pain after a high-energy limb injury.

exam_trap: Candidates choose cellulitis or simple bruising and wait for absent pulses, but escalating pain on passive stretch after high-energy trauma is compartment syndrome until excluded.
takeaway: Severe escalating pain + pain on passive stretch after limb trauma → compartment syndrome until excluded.
source: NICE NG37, Complex fractures: assessment and management.
thinking: High-energy limb injury ↓ severe escalating pain ↓ pain on passive stretch of compartment muscles ↓ raised pressure in a closed fascial compartment ↓ Acute compartment syndrome
pearl: Circumferential dressings and casts should be fully split to skin when compartment syndrome is suspected, and the limb kept at heart level rather than elevated, as elevation further reduces perfusion pressure.

subject: Vascular & fracture complications
title: OPEN FRACTURE
stem: A patient sustains an open long-bone fracture. Which management principle is important?

options.B: Give prophylactic antibiotics as soon as possible
options.C: Close the wound immediately in the emergency department regardless of contamination

correct_answer: B. Give prophylactic antibiotics as soon as possible
why_correct: NICE recommends prophylactic antibiotic treatment for open fractures as soon as possible, preferably within 1 hour of injury.

why_others_wrong.A: Delaying antibiotics until definitive surgery increases the risk of deep infection; NICE and BOAST advise giving them as soon as possible, ideally within 1 hour of injury.
why_others_wrong.C: Primary closure of a contaminated open fracture wound in the emergency department traps contamination; BOAST advises photographing it and applying a saline-soaked dressing until formal surgical debridement.
why_others_wrong.D: The soft-tissue injury determines infection risk, need for debridement and plastic surgical coverage, which is why open fractures need joint orthoplastic management.
why_others_wrong.E: Oral analgesia alone ignores the need for early intravenous antibiotics, tetanus cover, splintage, surgical debridement and definitive fixation with soft-tissue cover.

exam_trap: Candidates choose immediate wound closure in the emergency department to protect the bone, but closing a contaminated open fracture traps contamination; it needs a dressing and formal debridement.
takeaway: Open fracture → early antibiotics + urgent specialist orthoplastic management.
source: NICE NG37/NG40.
thinking: Open long-bone fracture ↓ contaminated wound with high infection risk ↓ prophylactic antibiotics reduce deep infection ↓ given as soon as possible, ideally within 1 hour ↓ Give prophylactic antibiotics as soon as possible
pearl: Open fractures need tetanus prophylaxis according to immunisation status, and wound photography before dressing so the wound need not be repeatedly exposed before debridement.

subject: Major trauma & fluids
title: MAJOR TRAUMA: ACTIVE BLEEDING AND FLUIDS
stem: A patient with major trauma has active bleeding. Which approach is consistent with NICE hospital guidance?

options.A: Large-volume crystalloid replacement as the sole strategy
options.B: Rapid haemorrhage control with restrictive volume resuscitation
options.C: Delay haemorrhage control until normal haemoglobin is achieved
options.E: Wait for CT before treating haemorrhage

correct_answer: B. Rapid haemorrhage control with restrictive volume resuscitation
why_correct: NICE recommends a restrictive approach to volume resuscitation in active bleeding until definitive early control of bleeding is achieved. In hospital, NICE advises against using crystalloids for patients with active bleeding and recommends blood-component-based resuscitation.

why_others_wrong.A: Large-volume crystalloid dilutes clotting factors, worsens coagulopathy and hypothermia, and NICE advises against crystalloid in hospital for patients with active bleeding.
why_others_wrong.C: Haemorrhage control is the priority, and haemoglobin cannot be normalised while bleeding continues, so waiting would allow further blood loss.
why_others_wrong.D: Oral fluids cannot restore circulating volume in major haemorrhage and are unsafe in a patient who may need urgent anaesthesia and surgery.
why_others_wrong.E: Haemorrhage control and blood-component resuscitation should not be delayed for imaging, and unstable patients may need immediate surgery or radiological intervention.

exam_trap: The goal is not to normalise the blood pressure with large volumes before haemorrhage control.
takeaway: Major haemorrhage → control bleeding early + avoid unnecessary crystalloid loading.
source: NICE NG39, Major trauma: assessment and initial management.
thinking: Major trauma with active bleeding ↓ the problem is uncontrolled haemorrhage ↓ large crystalloid volumes dilute clotting factors and may disrupt clot ↓ restrict volume until bleeding is controlled ↓ Rapid haemorrhage control with restrictive volume resuscitation
pearl: Permissive hypotension is generally avoided in traumatic brain injury, where maintaining cerebral perfusion pressure takes priority.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: PREOPERATIVE CHEST X-RAY
stem: A healthy 45-year-old patient is scheduled for uncomplicated elective surgery. There are no respiratory or cardiac symptoms. Which statement about routine preoperative chest X-ray is correct?

options.A: It should be performed in every patient
options.B: It should routinely replace clinical assessment
options.C: It should not be routinely offered
options.D: It is mandatory before general anaesthesia
options.E: It is required before every abdominal operation

correct_answer: C. It should not be routinely offered
why_correct: NICE recommends against routine preoperative chest X-rays. Testing should be guided by the patient's clinical circumstances and type of surgery.

why_others_wrong.A: NICE recommends against routine preoperative chest X-rays, and this healthy 45-year-old with no cardiorespiratory symptoms has no indication for one.
why_others_wrong.B: Investigations support rather than replace history and examination, and a chest X-ray would not substitute for clinical assessment of this patient.
why_others_wrong.D: General anaesthesia does not in itself require a chest X-ray; testing is guided by symptoms, comorbidity and type of surgery.
why_others_wrong.E: Abdominal surgery does not automatically require a chest X-ray; NICE advises against routine preoperative chest imaging in patients like this.

exam_trap: Option D tempts candidates who link general anaesthesia with lung imaging, but anaesthesia alone is not an indication; NICE advises against routine preoperative chest X-ray.
takeaway: Routine elective surgery ≠ routine chest X-ray.
source: NICE NG45, Routine preoperative tests for elective surgery.
thinking: Healthy 45-year-old ↓ no cardiorespiratory symptoms ↓ uncomplicated elective surgery ↓ NICE advises against routine preoperative chest X-ray ↓ It should not be routinely offered
pearl: NICE guidance on routine preoperative tests bases testing on ASA grade and surgical grade; unnecessary tests generate incidental findings that can delay surgery without improving outcomes.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: PREOPERATIVE ECHOCARDIOGRAPHY
stem: A patient is being assessed before surgery and has a cardiac murmur associated with exertional breathlessness. What investigation may be appropriate?
why_correct: NICE recommends considering resting echocardiography in a patient with a heart murmur plus cardiac symptoms such as breathlessness, syncope or chest pain, or with signs or symptoms of heart failure.

why_others_wrong.A: A chest X-ray cannot assess valve function or ventricular performance, so it would not clarify the cause of a murmur with exertional breathlessness.
why_others_wrong.C: Colonoscopy examines the large bowel and has no role in evaluating a cardiac murmur or breathlessness.
why_others_wrong.D: Abdominal ultrasound images abdominal organs and cannot assess heart valves or ventricular function.
why_others_wrong.E: D-dimer is used to help exclude venous thromboembolism and gives no information about valvular or structural heart disease.

exam_trap: Option A tempts as a quick cardiopulmonary test, but a chest X-ray cannot assess valve function; a murmur with symptoms needs echocardiography.
takeaway: Murmur + cardiac symptoms → consider echo.
source: NICE NG45.
thinking: Heart murmur ↓ plus exertional breathlessness ↓ possible significant valve disease or ventricular dysfunction ↓ NICE advises considering resting echo ↓ Resting echocardiography
pearl: Undiagnosed severe aortic stenosis is important before anaesthesia, because vasodilatation from induction or neuraxial block can cause profound hypotension with a fixed cardiac output.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: PREOPERATIVE ECG
stem: A 70-year-old patient with ASA grade 2 status is being assessed before major surgery. Which investigation is NICE guidance consistent with offering?
why_correct: NICE recommends an ECG for people having major or complex surgery who are ASA grade 2 or 3/4. For ASA 1 patients aged over 65, ECG should be considered if there is no ECG result from the previous 12 months.

why_others_wrong.B: NICE advises against routine preoperative chest X-rays, and a chest X-ray alone would not provide the cardiac assessment recommended here.
why_others_wrong.C: Echocardiography is reserved for specific indications such as a murmur with cardiac symptoms or suspected heart failure, not every surgical patient.
why_others_wrong.D: Arterial blood gas analysis is not a routine preoperative test and is reserved for specific respiratory or metabolic concerns.
why_others_wrong.E: NICE does not recommend routine preoperative lung function testing; spirometry is targeted to particular respiratory problems.

exam_trap: Routine echocardiography in every patient may appeal to those wanting thorough cardiac assessment, but NICE reserves echo for specific indications; the routine test here is an ECG.
takeaway: Major or complex surgery + ASA 2 or above → offer a preoperative ECG (NICE NG45).
source: NICE NG45.
thinking: 70-year-old, ASA grade 2 ↓ major surgery ↓ NICE advises offering an ECG for ASA 2 or higher before major surgery ↓ ECG
pearl: A preoperative ECG gives a baseline for comparison if postoperative chest pain, arrhythmia or myocardial injury occurs, and may reveal unrecognised atrial fibrillation or conduction disease.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: PREOPERATIVE HbA1c
stem: A patient with diabetes is being assessed for elective surgery. Their HbA1c was last measured 8 months ago. What does NICE recommend?

options.A: No further HbA1c measurement is ever required
options.C: Perform an oral glucose tolerance test instead
options.D: Perform a glucose tolerance test immediately before anaesthesia

why_correct: NICE recommends offering HbA1c testing to people with diabetes having surgery if they have not been tested within the previous 3 months.

why_others_wrong.A: NICE recommends HbA1c testing if none has been done in the previous 3 months, so an 8-month-old result needs repeating.
why_others_wrong.C: An oral glucose tolerance test is a diagnostic test for diabetes, whereas this patient already has diabetes and needs assessment of recent control.
why_others_wrong.D: A glucose tolerance test just before anaesthesia is impractical, would disrupt fasting and does not reflect longer-term control as HbA1c does.
why_others_wrong.E: An outdated HbA1c prompts testing and optimisation where needed, not permanent cancellation of all surgery.

exam_trap: Option C tempts because it sounds like a glucose test, but an oral glucose tolerance test diagnoses diabetes; this patient already has diabetes and needs an up-to-date HbA1c.
takeaway: Diabetes + surgery + no HbA1c within 3 months → offer HbA1c.
source: NICE NG45.
thinking: Patient with diabetes before elective surgery ↓ HbA1c should be within the last 3 months ↓ last result was 8 months ago ↓ Offer HbA1c testing
pearl: A markedly raised preoperative HbA1c is associated with more postoperative infections and complications, and many centres use it to prompt referral for optimisation of glycaemic control before elective surgery.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: PREOPERATIVE URINE TESTING
stem: A patient without urinary symptoms is undergoing elective surgery. Which statement about routine urine dipstick testing is correct?

options.C: It should not routinely be offered
options.D: It replaces clinical assessment for UTI
options.E: It is required before every operation

correct_answer: C. It should not routinely be offered
why_correct: NICE recommends against routine urine dipstick testing before surgery. Urine microscopy and culture may be considered when the presence of a UTI would influence the decision to operate.

why_others_wrong.A: NICE recommends against routine urine dipstick testing before surgery, so it is not mandatory for this asymptomatic patient.
why_others_wrong.B: Routine dipstick testing in asymptomatic patients is not recommended by NICE and may detect clinically irrelevant bacteriuria.
why_others_wrong.D: A dipstick is an adjunct to clinical assessment, and microscopy and culture are used when a UTI would influence the decision to operate.
why_others_wrong.E: Urine testing is not required before every operation; it is reserved for patients in whom urinary infection would change management.

exam_trap: Option B tempts candidates who equate thoroughness with safety, but routine dipstick testing in asymptomatic patients is not recommended and may detect irrelevant bacteriuria.
takeaway: No urinary indication → no routine preoperative urine dipstick.
source: NICE NG45.
thinking: Asymptomatic patient ↓ elective surgery ↓ NICE advises against routine preoperative urine dipstick ↓ test only if UTI would change the decision to operate ↓ It should not routinely be offered
pearl: Treating asymptomatic bacteriuria is generally not recommended outside specific situations such as pregnancy and some urological procedures, because it promotes antimicrobial resistance without benefit.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: PREGNANCY AND ELECTIVE SURGERY
stem: A woman of childbearing potential is due to undergo surgery. What should happen on the day of surgery?

options.A: Pregnancy status should never be discussed
options.B: She should sensitively be asked whether there is any possibility she could be pregnant
options.C: Pregnancy testing is mandatory regardless of circumstances
options.E: Only the patient's partner should be asked

correct_answer: B. She should sensitively be asked whether there is any possibility she could be pregnant
why_correct: NICE recommends sensitively asking women of childbearing potential on the day of surgery whether there is any possibility of pregnancy and discussing fetal risks of anaesthesia and the procedure where relevant.

why_others_wrong.A: Pregnancy status matters because anaesthesia and surgery may carry fetal risks, so NICE advises that it is discussed sensitively on the day of surgery.
why_others_wrong.C: NICE does not make testing mandatory regardless of circumstances; testing is offered with consent when there is any possibility of pregnancy.
why_others_wrong.D: The possibility of pregnancy prompts discussion and possibly testing, not automatic cancellation of the operation.
why_others_wrong.E: The patient herself should be asked, confidentially and sensitively; asking her partner instead would breach her autonomy and confidentiality.

exam_trap: Option C tempts as the safest approach, but NICE does not make testing mandatory regardless of circumstances; testing is offered with consent when pregnancy is possible.
takeaway: Before surgery → sensitively establish whether pregnancy is possible and discuss testing appropriately.
source: NICE NG45.
thinking: Woman of childbearing potential ↓ day of surgery ↓ anaesthesia and surgery may carry fetal risks ↓ ask sensitively and offer testing with consent ↓ She should sensitively be asked whether there is any possibility she could be pregnant
pearl: If pregnancy is possible, a urine pregnancy test is offered with consent; in a young woman with abdominal pain, ectopic pregnancy must also be excluded before attributing symptoms to another surgical cause.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: PREOPERATIVE ANAEMIA
stem: A patient scheduled for major elective surgery is found to have iron-deficiency anaemia. Which principle is most appropriate?

options.A: Ignore it because surgery is already booked
options.B: Identify and manage the anaemia where appropriate before surgery
options.C: Give erythropoietin routinely to every surgical patient

correct_answer: B. Identify and manage the anaemia where appropriate before surgery
why_correct: Preoperative anaemia is associated with poorer postoperative outcomes and should prompt assessment and appropriate management. NICE recommends oral iron for iron-deficiency anaemia before and after surgery, with IV iron considered in selected circumstances.

why_others_wrong.A: Preoperative anaemia is linked with poorer outcomes and more transfusion, so it should be investigated and treated rather than ignored because of a booking.
why_others_wrong.C: Erythropoietin is not routine for surgical patients and would not correct iron deficiency, which is treated with oral or intravenous iron.
why_others_wrong.D: Transfusion is not the first-line response to iron-deficiency anaemia before elective surgery; iron replacement is preferred where time allows.
why_others_wrong.E: Anaemia is a modifiable risk factor to be optimised, not a reason to cancel all future surgery.

exam_trap: Option D tempts as a quick fix, but transfusion carries risks and is not first line for iron deficiency; iron replacement is preferred where time allows before elective surgery.
takeaway: Elective surgery + anaemia → diagnose the cause and optimise where possible.
source: NICE NG24.
thinking: Major elective surgery ↓ iron-deficiency anaemia found ↓ anaemia is a modifiable risk factor ↓ investigate the cause and replace iron before surgery ↓ Identify and manage the anaemia where appropriate before surgery
pearl: Unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia in an adult should prompt investigation for gastrointestinal blood loss, including colorectal and gastric cancer, rather than iron replacement alone.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: TRANEXAMIC ACID IN SURGERY
stem: An adult is undergoing major surgery where expected blood loss is greater than 500 mL. Which treatment should be considered?
why_correct: NICE recommends offering tranexamic acid to adults undergoing surgery where at least moderate blood loss, defined in the guideline as greater than 500 mL, is expected.

why_others_wrong.B: Recombinant factor VIIa is not a routine blood-conservation measure and carries thrombotic risk, being reserved for specific refractory bleeding situations.
why_others_wrong.C: Prophylactic platelet transfusion is not routine in a patient without thrombocytopenia or platelet dysfunction and does not reduce surgical blood loss.
why_others_wrong.D: Fresh frozen plasma is given for clinically significant coagulopathy or major haemorrhage, not routinely to prevent expected surgical blood loss.
why_others_wrong.E: With expected blood loss over 500 mL, NICE recommends tranexamic acid, so omitting any blood-conservation strategy is inappropriate.

exam_trap: Routine FFP or platelets may appeal as ways of preventing bleeding, but without a coagulopathy or thrombocytopenia they add transfusion risk; tranexamic acid is the recommended measure.
takeaway: Expected surgical blood loss over 500 mL in an adult: offer tranexamic acid.
source: NICE NG24.
thinking: Adult major surgery ↓ expected blood loss over 500 mL ↓ NICE recommends antifibrinolytic prophylaxis ↓ Tranexamic acid
pearl: Tranexamic acid inhibits plasminogen activation and so reduces fibrinolysis; it is also given early in major trauma haemorrhage, where benefit is greatest when given within 3 hours of injury.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: CELL SALVAGE
stem: A patient is expected to lose a very large volume of blood during complex surgery. Which blood-conservation strategy may be considered?

options.A: Intraoperative cell salvage with tranexamic acid
options.B: Routine cell salvage alone in every operation

correct_answer: A. Intraoperative cell salvage with tranexamic acid
why_correct: NICE recommends considering intraoperative cell salvage with tranexamic acid when very high blood loss is expected.

why_others_wrong.B: Cell salvage is not needed in every operation, and NICE advises against routinely using it without tranexamic acid.
why_others_wrong.C: Very high expected blood loss is exactly the setting in which blood-conservation measures such as cell salvage with tranexamic acid are advised.
why_others_wrong.D: Prophylactic FFP before incision in the absence of coagulopathy is not recommended and exposes the patient to transfusion risks without benefit.
why_others_wrong.E: Prophylactic platelet transfusion without thrombocytopenia is not a blood-conservation strategy and adds transfusion risk.

exam_trap: Option B tempts because cell salvage sounds universally beneficial, but NICE advises against routine cell salvage without tranexamic acid and reserves it for very high expected blood loss.
takeaway: Very high expected blood loss → consider cell salvage + TXA.
source: NICE NG24.
thinking: Very high expected blood loss ↓ NICE advises considering intraoperative cell salvage ↓ combined with tranexamic acid ↓ Intraoperative cell salvage with tranexamic acid
pearl: Cell salvage is often acceptable to Jehovah's Witness patients who decline allogeneic blood, particularly if the circuit remains continuous with the circulation; this should be discussed individually before surgery.

subject: Microbiology & surgical infection
title: SURGICAL SITE INFECTION: HAIR REMOVAL
stem: Hair needs to be removed from the operative field before surgery. Which method is recommended?

options.B: Electric clippers with a single-use head on the day of surgery

correct_answer: B. Electric clippers with a single-use head on the day of surgery
why_correct: NICE advises against routine hair removal. If hair must be removed, electric clippers with a single-use head should be used on the day of surgery. Razors increase SSI risk.

why_others_wrong.A: Razor shaving causes skin microabrasions that become colonised, and NICE advises against razors because they increase SSI risk, particularly when done days before.
why_others_wrong.C: Depilatory creams can cause skin reactions and NICE does not recommend routine hair removal, so using them in every patient is inappropriate.
why_others_wrong.D: Waxing is not a recommended method; it traumatises the skin and is not part of NICE guidance for preoperative hair removal.
why_others_wrong.E: Timing matters: when hair removal is needed NICE recommends clippers on the day of surgery to minimise bacterial colonisation of the skin.

exam_trap: Razor shaving several days beforehand reflects traditional practice that candidates still choose, but razor microabrasions become colonised and raise SSI risk; clippers on the day are recommended.
takeaway: Hair removal only when necessary → clippers, on the day, not a razor.
source: NICE NG125, Surgical site infections.
thinking: Hair removal only if necessary ↓ razors cause microabrasions that become colonised ↓ electric clippers with a single-use head are preferred ↓ performed on the day of surgery ↓ Electric clippers with a single-use head on the day of surgery
pearl: Microscopic skin nicks from razors become colonised with bacteria, so the longer the interval between shaving and incision, the greater the infection risk; clipping on the day avoids both problems.

subject: Microbiology & surgical infection
title: SURGICAL SITE INFECTION: SKIN PREPARATION
stem: During preparation of the surgical site with an alcohol-based antiseptic, diathermy will be used. What is important?

options.A: Allow the preparation to pool beneath the patient
options.B: Allow the preparation to dry by evaporation and avoid pooling
options.D: Cover the wet solution with a drape immediately

correct_answer: B. Allow the preparation to dry by evaporation and avoid pooling
why_correct: NICE specifically advises allowing antiseptic skin preparations to dry by evaporation and avoiding pooling of alcohol-based preparations when diathermy is used.

why_others_wrong.A: Pooled alcohol-based preparation beneath the patient is a fire hazard with diathermy and can also cause chemical skin injury, so pooling must be avoided.
why_others_wrong.C: Igniting the solution would cause a surgical fire and burns; alcohol preparations must be dry before any ignition source is used.
why_others_wrong.D: Draping over wet alcohol preparation traps flammable vapour beneath the drapes, increasing fire risk when diathermy is used.
why_others_wrong.E: Adding alcohol during diathermy introduces fresh flammable fuel next to an ignition source and creates a high fire risk.

exam_trap: Covering the wet solution with a drape immediately seems efficient, but it traps flammable alcohol vapour beneath the drapes, where diathermy sparks can ignite it.
takeaway: Alcohol-based skin prep + diathermy → dry completely and prevent pooling.
source: NICE NG125.
thinking: Alcohol-based skin preparation is flammable ↓ diathermy is an ignition source ↓ preparation must dry by evaporation without pooling ↓ Allow the preparation to dry by evaporation and avoid pooling
