pearl: Theatre fires need fuel (alcohol preparation, drapes), an ignition source (diathermy, laser) and an oxidiser (oxygen-enriched air), so risk is highest in head and neck surgery with open oxygen delivery.

subject: Microbiology & surgical infection
title: SURGICAL SITE INFECTION: WOUND IRRIGATION
stem: Which statement about routine wound irrigation to prevent surgical site infection is correct?

options.B: It is mandatory after every contaminated operation
options.C: NICE does not recommend wound irrigation specifically to reduce SSI

correct_answer: C. NICE does not recommend wound irrigation specifically to reduce SSI
why_correct: NICE recommends against using wound irrigation specifically to reduce the risk of surgical site infection.

why_others_wrong.A: NICE recommends against wound irrigation specifically to reduce SSI, so it is not something that should always be performed for that purpose.
why_others_wrong.B: NICE does not mandate irrigation after contaminated surgery for SSI reduction; any irrigation is a clinical judgement rather than a requirement.
why_others_wrong.D: Irrigation is not a substitute for antibiotic prophylaxis, which is recommended for clean-contaminated and contaminated operations.
why_others_wrong.E: Irrigation cannot replace preoperative antiseptic skin preparation, which remains a recommended SSI-prevention measure.

exam_trap: Irrigation may have other clinical roles; this question asks specifically about routine SSI prevention.
takeaway: Do not confuse "may be used clinically" with "recommended routinely to prevent SSI."
source: NICE NG125.
thinking: Question asks about irrigation specifically to reduce SSI ↓ NICE recommends against wound irrigation for this purpose ↓ irrigation does not replace prophylaxis or skin antisepsis ↓ NICE does not recommend wound irrigation specifically to reduce SSI
pearl: NICE similarly advises against using topical antimicrobial agents on surgical wounds healing by primary intention to reduce the risk of surgical site infection.

subject: Microbiology & surgical infection
title: SURGICAL SITE INFECTION: INTRACAVITY LAVAGE
stem: Which statement is consistent with NICE guidance regarding intracavity lavage?

options.A: It should routinely be used to prevent SSI
options.C: It should not be used specifically to reduce SSI risk
options.D: It is mandatory after every abdominal operation
options.E: It is required after every anastomosis

correct_answer: C. It should not be used specifically to reduce SSI risk
why_correct: NICE advises against intracavity lavage for the specific purpose of reducing surgical site infection.

why_others_wrong.A: NICE advises against intracavity lavage specifically to reduce SSI, so routine use for prevention is not supported.
why_others_wrong.B: Lavage does not replace antibiotic prophylaxis, which is recommended for clean-contaminated and contaminated operations.
why_others_wrong.D: Lavage is not mandatory after abdominal surgery; NICE advises against it for the specific aim of reducing SSI.
why_others_wrong.E: Creation of an anastomosis does not in itself require lavage, and NICE does not recommend lavage to reduce SSI risk.

exam_trap: Do not confuse lavage with source control of an established intra-abdominal infection.
takeaway: Established contamination/source control is different from routine lavage as SSI prevention.
source: NICE NG125.
thinking: Lavage as a routine SSI-prevention measure ↓ NICE advises against intracavity lavage for this aim ↓ this differs from washing out established contamination ↓ It should not be used specifically to reduce SSI risk
pearl: In established peritonitis, removal of pus and contaminated material at laparotomy is part of source control, which is a different indication from routine lavage to prevent wound infection.

subject: Microbiology & surgical infection
title: SURGICAL SITE INFECTION: PATIENT TEMPERATURE
stem: Which perioperative physiological abnormality should be actively avoided because NICE recommends maintaining patient temperature appropriately?
why_correct: NICE recommends maintaining patient temperature in line with its guidance on prevention and management of hypothermia during surgery.

why_others_wrong.B: Normothermia is the goal of perioperative temperature management, so it is the state to maintain rather than an abnormality to avoid.
why_others_wrong.C: Normal oxygenation is a target NICE recommends maintaining and is not a physiological abnormality.
why_others_wrong.D: Adequate perfusion supports oxygen delivery to the wound and is desirable rather than something to avoid.
why_others_wrong.E: Appropriate glucose management is part of good perioperative care and is not an abnormality to avoid.

exam_trap: Do not think of temperature as an anaesthetic issue only; maintaining physiological homeostasis is part of SSI prevention.
takeaway: During surgery → maintain normothermia.
source: NICE NG125.
thinking: NICE SSI guidance includes temperature management ↓ hypothermia causes vasoconstriction and poor tissue oxygenation ↓ normothermia must be maintained ↓ Hypothermia
pearl: Inadvertent perioperative hypothermia also impairs coagulation, increases blood loss and raises the risk of cardiac events, so active warming is used for longer or higher-risk procedures.

subject: Microbiology & surgical infection
title: SURGICAL SITE INFECTION: BLOOD GLUCOSE
stem: Which statement is correct regarding insulin in patients without diabetes undergoing surgery?

options.A: Routine insulin should be given to all patients to prevent SSI
options.B: Insulin should never be used under any circumstances
options.C: NICE does not recommend routine insulin in people without diabetes solely to optimise postoperative glucose and reduce SSI

correct_answer: C. NICE does not recommend routine insulin in people without diabetes solely to optimise postoperative glucose and reduce SSI
why_correct: NICE specifically advises against routinely giving insulin to patients without diabetes for this purpose.

why_others_wrong.A: NICE advises against routinely giving insulin to people without diabetes to optimise postoperative glucose for SSI prevention.
why_others_wrong.B: Insulin may be needed clinically, for example for significant hyperglycaemia, so a blanket prohibition is incorrect; NICE only advises against routine use for SSI prevention.
why_others_wrong.D: Hyperglycaemia impairs immune function and is associated with higher infection risk, so inducing it would be harmful.
why_others_wrong.E: Glucose monitoring is not prohibited; clinically significant hyperglycaemia should still be detected and managed.

exam_trap: Candidates who know hyperglycaemia raises infection risk choose routine insulin for all patients, but NICE advises against routine insulin in non-diabetic patients solely to prevent SSI.
takeaway: Do not give routine insulin to non-diabetic surgical patients solely as an SSI-prevention strategy.
source: NICE NG125.
thinking: Patient without diabetes undergoing surgery ↓ NICE advises against routine insulin solely to lower glucose for SSI prevention ↓ clinically significant hyperglycaemia is still detected and treated ↓ NICE does not recommend routine insulin in people without diabetes solely to optimise postoperative glucose and reduce SSI
pearl: In people with diabetes, poor perioperative glycaemic control is associated with wound infection, so elective surgery is planned around optimising control beforehand.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: VTE RISK ASSESSMENT
stem: A patient is admitted for emergency abdominal surgery. What should happen regarding VTE risk?

options.A: VTE risk is assessed only after discharge
options.B: VTE and bleeding risk should be assessed as soon as possible

correct_answer: B. VTE and bleeding risk should be assessed as soon as possible
why_correct: NICE recommends assessing all surgical and trauma patients for VTE and bleeding risk as soon as possible after admission or by first consultant review.

why_others_wrong.A: Assessment is needed as soon as possible after admission so that prophylaxis can be started while the patient is at highest risk, not after discharge.
why_others_wrong.C: Age is one of several VTE risk factors, and decisions also depend on the surgery, comorbidities, mobility and bleeding risk.
why_others_wrong.D: NICE requires bleeding risk to be assessed alongside VTE risk before deciding on pharmacological prophylaxis.
why_others_wrong.E: Pharmacological prophylaxis is given according to the balance of VTE and bleeding risk, not automatically to every patient.

exam_trap: Option E tempts as a simple rule, but pharmacological prophylaxis is given only after weighing VTE against bleeding risk, not automatically to every patient.
takeaway: Every surgical admission → assess both thrombosis and bleeding risk.
source: NICE NG89, VTE prevention.
thinking: Emergency abdominal surgical admission ↓ NICE requires prompt risk assessment ↓ both VTE and bleeding risk are assessed ↓ As soon as possible after admission or by first consultant review ↓ VTE and bleeding risk should be assessed as soon as possible
pearl: Low molecular weight heparin is the usual pharmacological prophylaxis after abdominal surgery, and extended prophylaxis for 28 days is recommended after major abdominal or pelvic cancer surgery.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: ABDOMINAL SURGERY: MECHANICAL VTE PROPHYLAXIS
stem: A patient is admitted for abdominal surgery and is at increased risk of VTE. When should mechanical VTE prophylaxis be started?

options.E: Only if the patient becomes hypotensive

why_correct: NICE recommends mechanical VTE prophylaxis on admission for people undergoing abdominal surgery. Options include anti-embolism stockings or intermittent pneumatic compression, according to the patient's circumstances.

why_others_wrong.B: Delaying mechanical prophylaxis until discharge leaves the patient unprotected during the in-hospital period when VTE risk is high.
why_others_wrong.C: Six weeks after surgery is far too late; NICE advises mechanical prophylaxis from admission to cover the perioperative period.
why_others_wrong.D: Prophylaxis aims to prevent thrombosis, so waiting for a DVT to develop defeats its purpose and would then require treatment rather than prevention.
why_others_wrong.E: Hypotension is not a trigger for mechanical VTE prophylaxis; the decision is based on VTE risk assessment at admission.

exam_trap: Option D appeals to those who confuse prophylaxis with treatment; mechanical prophylaxis is started on admission to prevent thrombosis, not after a DVT has developed.
takeaway: Abdominal surgery + increased VTE risk → mechanical prophylaxis from admission.
source: NICE NG89.
thinking: Abdominal surgery with increased VTE risk ↓ risk begins before the operation and continues afterwards ↓ NICE starts mechanical prophylaxis at admission ↓ On admission
pearl: Mechanical prophylaxis is generally continued until the patient no longer has significantly reduced mobility relative to their normal state.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: MAJOR ABDOMINAL CANCER SURGERY
stem: A patient undergoes major abdominal cancer surgery. The risk of VTE remains significant after discharge. What duration of pharmacological prophylaxis should be considered?
why_correct: NICE recommends considering extending pharmacological VTE prophylaxis to 28 days after major cancer surgery in the abdomen.

why_others_wrong.A: Twenty-four hours is far shorter than the extended period recommended after major abdominal cancer surgery, when VTE risk persists after discharge.
why_others_wrong.B: Three days does not cover the prolonged post-discharge risk after major abdominal cancer surgery, for which NICE advises extended prophylaxis.
why_others_wrong.C: A fixed 7-day course falls short of the extended prophylaxis to 28 days that NICE advises considering after major abdominal cancer surgery.
why_others_wrong.E: Lifelong anticoagulation is not prophylaxis after surgery and would expose the patient to long-term bleeding risk without indication.

exam_trap: Option C tempts because 7 days is a common standard course, but after major abdominal cancer surgery NICE advises considering extended prophylaxis to 28 days.
takeaway: Major abdominal cancer surgery → consider extended prophylaxis to 28 days.
source: NICE NG89.
thinking: Major abdominal cancer surgery ↓ malignancy and major surgery both raise VTE risk ↓ risk persists for weeks after discharge ↓ NICE advises considering extended prophylaxis ↓ Up to 28 days postoperatively
pearl: Extended prophylaxis is usually given as daily subcutaneous low molecular weight heparin, so patients or carers are taught self-injection before discharge.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: ELECTIVE SURGERY AND OESTROGEN
stem: A patient taking an oestrogen-containing combined oral contraceptive is planning elective surgery. What does NICE advise?

options.B: Consider stopping it 4 weeks before elective surgery and provide alternative contraception if stopped

correct_answer: B. Consider stopping it 4 weeks before elective surgery and provide alternative contraception if stopped
why_correct: NICE advises people to consider stopping oestrogen-containing oral contraceptives or HRT 4 weeks before elective surgery, with alternative contraception advice where appropriate.

why_others_wrong.A: Oestrogen-containing contraceptives increase VTE risk, so NICE advises considering stopping them before elective surgery rather than continuing without assessment.
why_others_wrong.C: The advice relates to the perioperative period only; permanent discontinuation is not required and can be restarted when appropriate.
why_others_wrong.D: Therapeutic anticoagulation is not a substitute for contraception and would add bleeding risk without indication.
why_others_wrong.E: Stopping after surgery does not reduce perioperative VTE risk; NICE suggests considering stopping it 4 weeks before elective surgery.

exam_trap: Option E appeals as a way to avoid an unplanned pregnancy before surgery, but stopping afterwards does not reduce perioperative VTE risk; the advice is about 4 weeks beforehand.
takeaway: Oestrogen-containing therapy + elective surgery → consider VTE implications and the 4-week recommendation.
source: NICE NG89.
thinking: Oestrogen-containing combined pill ↓ oestrogen increases thrombotic risk ↓ elective surgery adds a further VTE risk ↓ NICE advises considering stopping it 4 weeks before ↓ Consider stopping it 4 weeks before elective surgery and provide alternative contraception if stopped
pearl: Progestogen-only contraception does not carry the same VTE risk as oestrogen-containing methods, so it can be offered as an alternative when the combined pill is stopped before surgery.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: SPINAL SURGERY AND VTE
stem: A patient undergoes elective spinal surgery. Which mechanical prophylaxis is recommended on admission?

options.A: Anti-embolism stockings or intermittent pneumatic compression
options.E: Aspirin in every patient regardless of risk

correct_answer: A. Anti-embolism stockings or intermittent pneumatic compression
why_correct: NICE recommends mechanical VTE prophylaxis on admission for elective spinal surgery. Pharmacological prophylaxis requires consideration of VTE risk, bleeding risk and surgical factors.

why_others_wrong.B: Therapeutic-dose anticoagulation treats established VTE and could cause a spinal haematoma with serious neurological consequences.
why_others_wrong.C: Thrombolysis is used for established clot such as massive pulmonary embolism and would be highly dangerous around spinal surgery.
why_others_wrong.D: Omitting prophylaxis entirely ignores VTE risk, whereas NICE recommends mechanical prophylaxis on admission for elective spinal surgery.
why_others_wrong.E: Aspirin is pharmacological rather than mechanical, and giving it regardless of risk ignores the individual bleeding considerations after spinal surgery.

exam_trap: Aspirin in every patient may tempt as a low-risk option, but it is pharmacological rather than mechanical and ignores individual bleeding risk after spinal surgery.
takeaway: Elective spinal surgery → mechanical prophylaxis on admission; pharmacological prophylaxis is risk-dependent.
source: NICE NG89.
thinking: Elective spinal surgery ↓ a spinal haematoma could compress the cord ↓ NICE starts mechanical prophylaxis on admission ↓ Anti-embolism stockings or intermittent pneumatic compression
pearl: New leg weakness, numbness or sphincter disturbance after spinal surgery or neuraxial anaesthesia may indicate an epidural haematoma, which needs urgent MRI and decompression.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: CRANIAL SURGERY AND ANTICOAGULATION
stem: A patient has undergone cranial surgery. When pharmacological VTE prophylaxis is appropriate, when does NICE generally recommend starting LMWH?

options.A: Immediately before skin incision in every patient

why_correct: NICE recommends considering LMWH 24–48 hours after cranial surgery when VTE risk outweighs bleeding risk, with duration determined according to the guideline.

why_others_wrong.A: Starting LMWH before incision would increase the risk of intracranial haemorrhage, where even small bleeds can be devastating.
why_others_wrong.C: Starting LMWH a week before surgery has no rationale and would raise intraoperative and postoperative intracranial bleeding risk.
why_others_wrong.D: Waiting until discharge leaves the patient without pharmacological protection during the in-hospital period when VTE risk is high.
why_others_wrong.E: Prophylaxis aims to prevent thrombosis, so waiting for a confirmed DVT would turn prevention into treatment.

exam_trap: Option A tempts because preoperative LMWH is routine for some operations, but in cranial surgery it would increase intracranial haemorrhage risk; LMWH is considered 24-48 hours after surgery.
takeaway: Cranial surgery → mechanical prophylaxis early; LMWH requires careful bleeding-risk assessment.
source: NICE NG89.
thinking: Cranial surgery ↓ even a small postoperative intracranial bleed can be devastating ↓ pharmacological prophylaxis is delayed until early haemostasis is secure ↓ NICE suggests considering LMWH 24-48 hours after surgery ↓ 24-48 hours after surgery
pearl: Mechanical prophylaxis is used from admission in neurosurgical patients, and the timing of any pharmacological prophylaxis is usually agreed with the neurosurgical team.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: INTRACRANIAL HAEMORRHAGE AND VTE PROPHYLAXIS
stem: A patient has an intracranial haemorrhage. What is the appropriate principle regarding pharmacological VTE prophylaxis?

options.B: Do not offer pharmacological prophylaxis until the lesion has been secured or the condition has stabilised

correct_answer: B. Do not offer pharmacological prophylaxis until the lesion has been secured or the condition has stabilised
why_correct: NICE specifically advises against pharmacological VTE prophylaxis in intracranial haemorrhage until the lesion has been secured or the condition has stabilised.

why_others_wrong.A: Immediate LMWH could extend an unsecured or unstable intracranial bleed, which is why NICE advises delaying pharmacological prophylaxis.
why_others_wrong.C: Therapeutic anticoagulation in active intracranial haemorrhage carries a high risk of haematoma expansion and is not VTE prophylaxis.
why_others_wrong.D: Thrombolysis is contraindicated in intracranial haemorrhage because it would promote further bleeding.
why_others_wrong.E: Warfarin is not used for VTE prophylaxis here and would risk expanding the intracranial haemorrhage.

exam_trap: Option A tempts because immobile neurological patients have high VTE risk, but immediate LMWH could expand an unsecured bleed; pharmacological prophylaxis must wait.
takeaway: Intracranial haemorrhage → stabilise/secure bleeding before pharmacological VTE prophylaxis.
source: NICE NG89.
thinking: Intracranial haemorrhage ↓ anticoagulants risk haematoma expansion ↓ pharmacological prophylaxis waits until the lesion is secured or the condition stable ↓ Do not offer pharmacological prophylaxis until the lesion has been secured or the condition has stabilised
pearl: In acute intracranial haemorrhage, intermittent pneumatic compression can be used from admission to reduce VTE risk while pharmacological prophylaxis is withheld.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Anaesthetic monitoring: capnography
stem: During general anaesthesia, which monitoring method provides continuous information about exhaled carbon dioxide?
why_correct: Capnography measures exhaled CO₂ and provides information about ventilation and airway integrity.

why_others_wrong.A: Pulse oximetry measures oxygen saturation of haemoglobin, reflecting oxygenation, not exhaled carbon dioxide or ventilation.
why_others_wrong.C: ECG monitors the heart's electrical activity and provides no information about exhaled gases.
why_others_wrong.D: Non-invasive blood pressure measures arterial pressure and gives no continuous information about exhaled carbon dioxide.
why_others_wrong.E: A temperature probe measures body temperature and has no role in monitoring exhaled carbon dioxide.

exam_trap: Pulse oximetry is chosen as the most familiar monitor, but it reports haemoglobin oxygen saturation and gives no direct information about exhaled carbon dioxide.
takeaway: SpO₂ = oxygenation. Capnography = ventilation/expired CO₂.
source: Standard MRCS anaesthesia and physiology knowledge.
thinking: Need continuous exhaled CO2 information ↓ infrared analysis of expired gas ↓ displayed as a waveform and end-tidal value ↓ Capnography
pearl: Loss of the capnography trace may indicate oesophageal intubation, circuit disconnection or cardiac arrest, so it is checked continuously during anaesthesia.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Anaesthetic monitoring: end-tidal CO2 and intubation
stem: Immediately after attempted tracheal intubation, which monitoring finding provides strong evidence that the tube is in the trachea and that pulmonary gas exchange is occurring?
why_correct: Continuous waveform capnography provides objective confirmation of exhaled CO₂ and is an essential method for confirming tracheal intubation in an appropriately ventilated patient.

why_others_wrong.B: Pulse rate alone does not confirm that the tube is located in the trachea or that gas exchange is occurring.
why_others_wrong.C: Blood pressure alone gives no information about airway placement or ventilation, so it cannot confirm correct tube position.
why_others_wrong.D: Skin colour alone is a late, nonspecific sign of oxygenation problems and does not reliably confirm tracheal placement.
why_others_wrong.E: A chest X-ray taken before any ventilation cannot demonstrate ongoing gas exchange and is not an immediate or continuous monitoring method.

exam_trap: Chest movement and auscultation are useful but should not replace objective capnography.
takeaway: After intubation → confirm and continuously monitor with waveform capnography.
source: [AoA]: guidelines for capnography.
thinking: Tube placement must be confirmed immediately ↓ exhaled CO2 appears only if the tube ventilates perfused lungs ↓ a sustained waveform over several breaths confirms tracheal placement ↓ Persistent waveform capnography
pearl: A flat capnography trace after intubation should be assumed to mean oesophageal intubation until proven otherwise, even in cardiac arrest, where some CO2 trace is still expected with effective CPR.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Anaesthetic monitoring: pulse oximetry limitation
stem: A patient receiving supplemental oxygen has a normal oxygen saturation but is becoming progressively drowsy and hypoventilating. Which statement is correct?

options.C: Hypercapnia can occur despite apparently normal SpO₂

correct_answer: C. Hypercapnia can occur despite apparently normal SpO₂
why_correct: Supplemental oxygen can maintain oxygen saturation despite inadequate ventilation and rising CO₂.

why_others_wrong.A: A normal SpO2 does not exclude ventilatory failure, since supplemental oxygen can maintain saturation even as CO2 rises from hypoventilation.
why_others_wrong.B: Pulse oximetry measures haemoglobin oxygen saturation only; it does not directly measure PaCO2.
why_others_wrong.D: SpO2 reflects arterial oxygen saturation, not cardiac output, so this statement misattributes what the device measures.
why_others_wrong.E: Capnography measures end-tidal carbon dioxide, which helps detect hypoventilation and rising CO2, so it is directly relevant here.

exam_trap: Option A is chosen by candidates who equate a good saturation with adequate breathing; supplemental oxygen can mask rising CO2 from hypoventilation.
takeaway: Normal SpO₂ does not guarantee adequate ventilation.
source: Standard MRCS anaesthesia and respiratory physiology knowledge.
thinking: Drowsy, hypoventilating patient on supplemental oxygen ↓ oxygen keeps SpO2 normal ↓ PaCO2 still rises with hypoventilation ↓ Hypercapnia can occur despite apparently normal SpO2
pearl: Arterial or venous blood gas analysis, or capnography, is needed to detect hypercapnia; pulse oximetry alone can falsely reassure in a patient receiving oxygen.

subject: Pharmacology
title: MALIGNANT HYPERTHERMIA
stem: During general anaesthesia, a patient develops rapidly increasing end-tidal CO₂, tachycardia, muscle rigidity and rapidly rising temperature. What diagnosis should be suspected?
why_correct: Rapidly increasing CO₂ production, tachycardia, muscle rigidity and hyperthermia during anaesthesia are classic warning features of malignant hyperthermia.

why_others_wrong.B: Simple postoperative fever develops more gradually and is not accompanied by the rapid rise in end-tidal CO2, tachycardia and muscle rigidity seen here.
why_others_wrong.C: Hypoglycaemia does not typically cause muscle rigidity or a rapid rise in end-tidal CO2 during anaesthesia.
why_others_wrong.D: Pulmonary embolism can cause tachycardia and hypoxia but does not characteristically cause muscle rigidity and rapidly rising temperature.
why_others_wrong.E: Acute appendicitis is a localised abdominal pathology and does not explain intraoperative rigidity, hypercapnia and hyperthermia.

exam_trap: The earliest and most important clue may be rapidly rising end-tidal CO₂ rather than fever.
takeaway: Anaesthesia + rising ETCO₂ + rigidity + hyperthermia → malignant hyperthermia emergency.
source: Standard MRCS anaesthesia knowledge.
thinking: General anaesthesia ↓ rapidly rising end-tidal CO2, tachycardia and muscle rigidity ↓ uncontrolled skeletal muscle hypermetabolism ↓ rapidly rising temperature ↓ Malignant hyperthermia
pearl: Treatment is to stop volatile agents, hyperventilate with 100% oxygen, give intravenous dantrolene and actively cool; the patient and relatives are referred for specialist testing because susceptibility is inherited.

subject: Pharmacology
title: MALIGNANT HYPERTHERMIA: TRIGGER
stem: Which class of anaesthetic drug is classically associated with triggering malignant hyperthermia?
why_correct: Volatile anaesthetic agents are established triggers of malignant hyperthermia. Succinylcholine is also a recognised trigger, although it is not an inhalational agent.

why_others_wrong.B: Local anaesthetics are not recognised triggers of malignant hyperthermia; the reaction is specific to volatile agents and suxamethonium.
why_others_wrong.C: Paracetamol has no association with triggering malignant hyperthermia.
why_others_wrong.D: Opioids are not implicated as triggers of malignant hyperthermia.
why_others_wrong.E: Antibiotics are not recognised triggers of malignant hyperthermia; the susceptibility relates specifically to anaesthetic agents.

exam_trap: Local anaesthetics or opioids may be chosen by candidates who suspect any anaesthetic drug, but only volatile agents and succinylcholine trigger malignant hyperthermia; dantrolene is the treatment.
takeaway: Malignant hyperthermia triggers → volatile anaesthetics and succinylcholine.
source: Standard MRCS anaesthesia knowledge.
thinking: Malignant hyperthermia is a pharmacogenetic disorder of skeletal muscle calcium release ↓ triggered by specific anaesthetic agents ↓ volatile inhalational agents and succinylcholine are the recognised triggers ↓ Volatile inhalational anaesthetics
pearl: A susceptible patient can be anaesthetised safely with a trigger-free technique such as total intravenous anaesthesia with propofol, a non-depolarising muscle relaxant and a vapour-free anaesthetic machine.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: SEPSIS: NEWS2 HIGH-RISK CATEGORY
stem: A 68-year-old patient with suspected infection has a NEWS2 score of 8. According to current NICE guidance, how should this patient be classified?

options.A: Very low risk of severe illness or death from sepsis
options.E: No sepsis risk can be assigned

why_correct: NICE defines a person aged 16 or over with suspected or confirmed infection and a NEWS2 score of 7 or above as being at high risk of severe illness or death from sepsis.

why_others_wrong.A: A NEWS2 score of 8 with suspected infection meets the NICE high-risk threshold of 7 or more, so it cannot be very low risk.
why_others_wrong.B: Low risk applies to much lower NEWS2 scores, whereas a score of 8 meets the high-risk threshold.
why_others_wrong.C: Moderate risk corresponds to a NEWS2 score of 5 or 6, whereas this patient's score of 8 exceeds that range.
why_others_wrong.E: NICE uses NEWS2 to stratify sepsis risk in people aged 16 or over, so a risk category can be assigned to this patient.

exam_trap: Option C tempts candidates unsure of the thresholds, but moderate risk covers NEWS2 of 5 or 6; a score of 8 meets the high-risk threshold of 7 or more.
takeaway: NEWS2 ≥7 + suspected infection → high-risk sepsis pathway.
source: NICE NG253, Suspected sepsis, current recommendations.
thinking: Suspected infection in an adult ↓ NEWS2 of 8 ↓ NICE high-risk threshold is 7 or more ↓ High risk
pearl: NEWS2 scores respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, supplemental oxygen, systolic blood pressure, pulse, level of consciousness or new confusion, and temperature.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: SEPSIS: MODERATE-RISK NEWS2
stem: A patient with suspected infection has a NEWS2 score of 5. There are no additional features suggesting a higher risk category. Which classification applies?

options.E: Sepsis cannot be assessed using NEWS2

why_correct: NICE defines suspected or confirmed infection with NEWS2 of 5 or 6 as moderate risk, unless other clinical factors require management as a higher-risk patient.

why_others_wrong.A: Very low risk does not fit a NEWS2 of 5, which falls in the moderate-risk band.
why_others_wrong.B: Low-risk scores are below 5, so a NEWS2 of 5 places this patient in the moderate category.
why_others_wrong.D: High risk requires a NEWS2 of 7 or above or other high-risk features, which this patient does not have.
why_others_wrong.E: NICE uses NEWS2 to stratify sepsis risk in adults with suspected infection, so the score can be used here.

exam_trap: Option D tempts candidates who treat any NEWS2 of 5 as urgent, but high risk requires a score of 7 or more or additional high-risk features, which are absent here.
takeaway: NEWS2 5–6 → moderate-risk pathway, subject to clinical judgement.
source: NICE NG253.
thinking: Suspected infection ↓ NEWS2 of 5 ↓ no additional high-risk features ↓ NICE moderate band is NEWS2 5 or 6 ↓ Moderate risk
pearl: A moderate-risk patient should be reassessed for evidence of hypoperfusion, such as a raised lactate or acute kidney injury, which would move them into the high-risk pathway.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: SEPSIS: HIGH-RISK ANTIBIOTIC TIMING
stem: A patient aged 16 or over is assessed in the emergency department with suspected infection and a NEWS2 score of 8. No antibiotics have yet been given. When should broad-spectrum IV antibiotics be given according to NICE?

options.A: Within 1 hour of calculating the NEWS2 score
options.E: Only if the patient becomes hypotensive

correct_answer: A. Within 1 hour of calculating the NEWS2 score
why_correct: For adults at high risk of severe illness or death from sepsis, NICE recommends broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 hour of calculating the initial NEWS2 score.

why_others_wrong.B: A 6-hour window is permitted for low-risk patients, whereas this high-risk patient needs antibiotics within 1 hour.
why_others_wrong.C: Waiting for microbiology would delay treatment by many hours, whereas cultures should be taken without delaying antibiotics in high-risk patients.
why_others_wrong.D: Deferring antibiotics to the following day in a high-risk septic patient risks progression to septic shock and death.
why_others_wrong.E: Hypotension is not required to start antibiotics; a NEWS2 of 8 with suspected infection already mandates treatment within 1 hour.

exam_trap: Option C appeals to those wanting targeted therapy, but waiting for microbiology delays treatment for many hours; cultures are taken without delaying antibiotics.
takeaway: High-risk sepsis → IV broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour.
source: NICE NG253.
thinking: Adult with suspected infection ↓ NEWS2 of 8 means high risk ↓ NICE target is IV broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour ↓ Within 1 hour of calculating the NEWS2 score
pearl: Blood cultures should be taken before antibiotics where possible, but in a high-risk patient sampling must not delay antibiotic administration beyond the 1-hour target.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: SEPSIS: MODERATE-RISK ANTIBIOTIC TIMING
stem: A patient with suspected infection has a NEWS2 score of 5 and is assessed as moderate risk. There is diagnostic uncertainty and no evidence of hypoperfusion. What does NICE allow the clinician to consider?

options.A: Deferring broad-spectrum antibiotics for up to 3 hours while clarifying the diagnosis
options.C: Waiting for blood cultures to become positive

correct_answer: A. Deferring broad-spectrum antibiotics for up to 3 hours while clarifying the diagnosis
why_correct: For moderate-risk patients, NICE allows a clinician with appropriate acute-care competencies to consider deferring broad-spectrum antibiotics for up to 3 hours to gather information for a more specific diagnosis and discuss the case with a senior decision maker. Once the decision to give antibiotics is made, administration should not be delayed further.

why_others_wrong.B: The permitted deferral is up to 3 hours for diagnostic clarification, not an automatic 24-hour delay in a moderate-risk patient.
why_others_wrong.C: Blood culture results take a day or more, so waiting for positivity would exceed the 3-hour window NICE allows.
why_others_wrong.D: Antibiotic timing depends on sepsis risk, not on surgery; making them conditional on an operation is not part of the NICE approach.
why_others_wrong.E: Deferral is for diagnostic clarification only, and antibiotics should be given promptly once a decision to treat is made.

exam_trap: Option C tempts because culture-directed treatment sounds rational, but blood cultures take a day or more; the permitted deferral is a maximum of 3 hours for diagnostic clarification.
takeaway: Moderate risk → diagnostic clarification may occur within the permitted window, but once antibiotics are indicated, give them promptly.
source: NICE NG253.
thinking: Suspected infection with moderate risk ↓ diagnostic uncertainty ↓ no hypoperfusion ↓ NICE permits deferral of up to 3 hours to clarify the diagnosis ↓ Deferring broad-spectrum antibiotics for up to 3 hours while clarifying the diagnosis
pearl: The reason for deferral is antimicrobial stewardship: a more specific diagnosis allows narrower, targeted antibiotics, but the patient should be reassessed throughout and escalated if hypoperfusion develops.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: SEPSIS: LOW-RISK ANTIBIOTIC TIMING
stem: A patient with suspected infection has a NEWS2 score of 3 and is assessed as low risk. What does NICE allow a clinician to consider?

options.A: Deferring broad-spectrum antibiotics for up to 6 hours while seeking a more specific diagnosis
options.D: Antibiotics only if a blood culture is positive

correct_answer: A. Deferring broad-spectrum antibiotics for up to 6 hours while seeking a more specific diagnosis
why_correct: For adults assessed as low risk, NICE allows consideration of deferring broad-spectrum antibiotics for up to 6 hours while obtaining more diagnostic information. If antibiotics are decided upon, they should not then be delayed.

why_others_wrong.B: A 15-minute mandatory deadline is not part of NICE guidance and is stricter than even the 1-hour target for high-risk patients.
why_others_wrong.C: NICE allows deferral for up to 6 hours in low-risk patients, not several days, and reassessment continues meanwhile.
why_others_wrong.D: Waiting for a positive blood culture would delay indicated treatment well beyond the 6-hour window.
why_others_wrong.E: Low-risk patients still need reassessment, as their condition may deteriorate and move them into a higher risk category.

exam_trap: Option E appeals to candidates who equate low risk with safety, but low-risk patients still need reassessment because they can deteriorate into a higher risk category.
takeaway: Low-risk sepsis assessment → diagnostic clarification may be prioritised, with reassessment.
source: NICE NG253.
thinking: Suspected infection with low risk ↓ NEWS2 of 3 ↓ NICE permits deferral of up to 6 hours ↓ continue reassessment meanwhile ↓ Deferring broad-spectrum antibiotics for up to 6 hours while seeking a more specific diagnosis
pearl: The 1, 3 and 6 hour antibiotic windows for high, moderate and low sepsis risk reflect a stewardship-based approach that matches urgency to the risk of deterioration.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: SEPSIS: LACTATE
stem: A patient with suspected infection is assessed as moderate risk and has a venous lactate of 3.2 mmol/L. How should this affect management?
why_correct: NICE states that a moderate-risk patient with evidence of hypoperfusion, such as lactate above 2 mmol/L or evidence of acute kidney injury, should be treated as high risk.

why_others_wrong.B: A lactate above 2 mmol/L indicates possible hypoperfusion, which upgrades this patient to high risk and makes discharge unsafe.
why_others_wrong.C: NICE uses lactate above 2 mmol/L as evidence of hypoperfusion, so ignoring a value of 3.2 would under-treat this patient.
why_others_wrong.D: The raised lactate moves the patient up to the high-risk category, not down to very low risk.
why_others_wrong.E: Although liver disease can impair lactate clearance, in suspected sepsis a raised lactate is treated as evidence of hypoperfusion.

exam_trap: Option C or E may tempt candidates who regard lactate as non-specific, but in suspected sepsis a lactate above 2 mmol/L is treated as hypoperfusion and upgrades the patient to high risk.
takeaway: Moderate-risk sepsis + lactate >2 mmol/L → manage as high risk.
source: NICE NG253, amended 2025.
thinking: Moderate-risk suspected sepsis ↓ lactate 3.2 mmol/L exceeds 2 mmol/L ↓ suggests tissue hypoperfusion ↓ NICE upgrades such patients to high risk ↓ Treat as high risk
pearl: Lactate in sepsis reflects inadequate tissue perfusion and stress-related glycolysis; serial measurements help judge the response to fluid resuscitation, and a persistently high level is a poor prognostic sign.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: SEPSIS: BLOOD CULTURES
stem: A hospital patient has suspected sepsis and antibiotics are about to be administered. What does NICE recommend regarding microbiological sampling?

options.A: Take appropriate microbiological and blood samples before antimicrobials
options.B: Always wait for culture results before giving antibiotics
options.D: Take cultures only after antibiotic treatment has finished
options.E: Take only a urine sample in every patient

correct_answer: A. Take appropriate microbiological and blood samples before antimicrobials
why_correct: NICE recommends taking microbiological and blood samples before giving an antimicrobial when possible, while ensuring treatment is not inappropriately delayed in patients who require urgent antibiotics.

why_others_wrong.B: Culture results take a day or more, and waiting for them would dangerously delay antibiotics in suspected sepsis.
why_others_wrong.C: Omitting cultures loses the chance to identify the organism and tailor or narrow antimicrobial therapy later.
why_others_wrong.D: Cultures taken after a course of antibiotics are much less likely to grow the causative organism and are too late to guide treatment.
why_others_wrong.E: Sampling is guided by the suspected source, so a urine sample alone would miss blood cultures and other relevant specimens.

exam_trap: Option B tempts candidates who want targeted therapy from the start, but culture results take a day or more, and waiting for them would dangerously delay antibiotics in sepsis.
takeaway: Cultures before antibiotics where feasible — but never create dangerous treatment delay.
source: NICE NG253.
thinking: Suspected sepsis with antibiotics imminent ↓ microbiology guides later targeted therapy ↓ cultures become less reliable once antibiotics are given ↓ sample first unless this dangerously delays treatment ↓ Take appropriate microbiological and blood samples before antimicrobials
pearl: Microbiology results allow antibiotics to be narrowed or stopped at review, and NICE antimicrobial stewardship guidance advises reviewing the prescription and the need for IV therapy within 48-72 hours.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: SEPSIS: SOURCE CONTROL
stem: A patient has sepsis caused by an infected obstructed biliary system. Antibiotics are started, but the obstruction remains. What additional principle is essential?

options.C: Avoid intervention because antibiotics always provide definitive treatment
options.E: Wait for the infection to resolve spontaneously

why_correct: NICE sepsis guidance emphasises finding and controlling the source of infection. In an infected obstructed system, definitive treatment may require drainage or another source-control procedure.

why_others_wrong.B: Stopping antibiotics would leave the patient's ongoing cholangitis and sepsis untreated while the obstruction persists.
why_others_wrong.C: Antibiotics alone often cannot clear infection behind an obstruction, so drainage or another source-control procedure is usually required.
why_others_wrong.D: Antipyretics only reduce fever and do nothing to treat the infection or relieve the biliary obstruction.
why_others_wrong.E: An infected obstructed biliary system is unlikely to resolve spontaneously and may progress to septic shock without decompression.

exam_trap: Option C tempts because antibiotics are started promptly, but infection behind an obstruction persists until the biliary tree is decompressed; source control is essential.
takeaway: Sepsis = antimicrobial treatment + identify and control the source.
source: NICE NG253.
thinking: Sepsis from an infected obstructed biliary tree ↓ antibiotics cannot reliably clear infection behind an obstruction ↓ the obstruction must be drained ↓ Source identification and control
pearl: Acute cholangitis with obstruction is usually decompressed by ERCP with stone extraction or stenting; percutaneous transhepatic drainage is an alternative when ERCP fails or is not possible.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: AKI: RENAL REPLACEMENT THERAPY
stem: A patient with acute kidney injury develops persistent severe hyperkalaemia despite appropriate medical treatment. What should happen?

options.E: Give routine loop diuretics solely to treat AKI

correct_answer: A. Immediately discuss renal replacement therapy
why_correct: NICE recommends immediate referral/discussion for renal replacement therapy when hyperkalaemia is not responding to medical management.

why_others_wrong.B: Low-dose dopamine does not protect or improve renal function in AKI and does nothing to remove potassium, so NICE advises against it.
why_others_wrong.C: Waiting for spontaneous recovery leaves life-threatening hyperkalaemia untreated when medical measures have already failed, risking arrhythmia and cardiac arrest.
why_others_wrong.D: Potassium must be monitored closely in refractory hyperkalaemia; stopping monitoring removes the means of detecting a dangerous rise.
why_others_wrong.E: Loop diuretics are not recommended to treat AKI itself and will not reliably correct hyperkalaemia that has failed medical treatment.

exam_trap: Low-dose dopamine may appeal as a renal protective measure, but it does not improve kidney function or remove potassium, and NICE advises against it in AKI.
takeaway: AKI + refractory hyperkalaemia → urgent RRT discussion.
source: NICE NG148, Acute kidney injury.
thinking: AKI with severe hyperkalaemia ↓ medical measures have failed ↓ refractory hyperkalaemia is an indication for renal replacement therapy ↓ Immediately discuss renal replacement therapy
pearl: Calcium gluconate stabilises the myocardium and insulin with glucose shifts potassium into cells, but only dialysis or other removal methods reduce total body potassium.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: AKI: REFRACTORY ACIDOSIS
stem: A patient with AKI develops severe metabolic acidosis that does not respond to appropriate medical treatment. Which intervention should be considered urgently?
why_correct: NICE lists metabolic acidosis that does not respond to medical management as an indication for immediate referral for renal replacement therapy.

why_others_wrong.B: Low-dose dopamine has no proven renal benefit in AKI and does not correct metabolic acidosis, so NICE advises against its use.
why_others_wrong.C: Fluid status still needs ongoing assessment in a deteriorating patient with AKI; abandoning it does nothing for the refractory acidosis.
why_others_wrong.D: Oral iron treats iron deficiency anaemia and has no role in correcting severe metabolic acidosis in AKI.
why_others_wrong.E: Elective colonoscopy is an irrelevant investigation that would delay urgent treatment of refractory acidosis.

exam_trap: Routine low-dose dopamine is a recurring distractor, but it has no proven renal benefit and does not correct acidosis; refractory acidosis in AKI needs renal replacement therapy.
takeaway: AKI + refractory metabolic acidosis → urgent RRT assessment.
source: NICE NG148.
thinking: AKI with severe metabolic acidosis ↓ not responding to medical treatment ↓ refractory acidosis is a NICE indication for renal replacement therapy ↓ Renal replacement therapy
pearl: The classic indications for urgent dialysis in AKI are refractory hyperkalaemia, acidosis and fluid overload or pulmonary oedema, uraemic complications such as pericarditis or encephalopathy, and certain dialysable toxins.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: AKI: URAEMIC COMPLICATIONS
stem: A patient with severe AKI develops uraemic pericarditis despite medical management. What is the appropriate next step?
correct_answer: A. Discuss urgent renal replacement therapy
why_correct: NICE specifically lists symptoms or complications of uraemia, including pericarditis and encephalopathy, as indications for immediate RRT when not responding to medical treatment.

why_others_wrong.B: Uraemic pericarditis is a serious complication that can progress to effusion and tamponade, so discharge would be unsafe.
why_others_wrong.C: Dopamine does not improve renal function in AKI and does not clear the uraemic toxins causing the pericarditis.
why_others_wrong.D: Uraemic pericarditis despite medical treatment is a recognised indication for immediate renal replacement therapy, so ignoring it is unsafe.
why_others_wrong.E: Uraemic pericarditis is caused by retained toxins rather than infection, so antibiotics alone would not treat it.

exam_trap: Option E tempts because pericarditis sounds infective, but uraemic pericarditis is caused by retained toxins, so antibiotics do not help; it needs renal replacement therapy.
takeaway: AKI + uraemic complication → urgent RRT discussion.
source: NICE NG148.
thinking: Severe AKI ↓ uraemic pericarditis despite medical management ↓ complication of retained uraemic toxins ↓ an indication for urgent renal replacement therapy ↓ Discuss urgent renal replacement therapy
pearl: Uraemic pericarditis can produce a pericardial effusion and tamponade, and anticoagulation during dialysis should be used cautiously because of the risk of haemorrhagic effusion.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: AKI: PULMONARY OEDEMA
stem: A patient with AKI develops pulmonary oedema that does not respond adequately to medical treatment. What should be considered?
why_correct: NICE lists fluid overload and pulmonary oedema that do not respond to medical management as indications for immediate RRT referral.

why_others_wrong.B: Dopamine has no proven renal benefit in AKI and will not remove the excess fluid causing refractory pulmonary oedema.
why_others_wrong.C: Pulmonary oedema that does not respond to medical treatment is life-threatening and needs urgent renal replacement therapy assessment, not inaction.
why_others_wrong.D: Elective surgery is irrelevant here and would add physiological stress to a patient with refractory fluid overload.
why_others_wrong.E: Oral fluid loading would worsen fluid overload and pulmonary oedema in a patient whose kidneys cannot excrete the excess.

exam_trap: Routine dopamine is offered as a tempting renal support, but it neither improves function nor removes fluid; refractory pulmonary oedema in AKI needs renal replacement therapy.
takeaway: AKI + refractory pulmonary oedema → urgent RRT assessment.
source: NICE NG148.
thinking: AKI with pulmonary oedema ↓ inadequate response to medical treatment ↓ the kidneys cannot excrete the excess fluid ↓ fluid must be removed by renal replacement therapy ↓ Renal replacement therapy
pearl: In refractory fluid overload, ultrafiltration by haemodialysis or continuous haemofiltration removes fluid directly, while non-invasive ventilation may support oxygenation during the transfer to renal care.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: AKI: LOOP DIURETICS
stem: Which statement about loop diuretics in acute kidney injury is correct?

options.A: They should routinely be given to reverse AKI
options.B: They should never be used in a patient with AKI
options.C: They may be considered for fluid overload/oedema in selected circumstances
options.D: They replace renal replacement therapy in all cases

correct_answer: C. They may be considered for fluid overload/oedema in selected circumstances
why_correct: NICE does not recommend routine loop diuretics to treat AKI itself. They may be considered for fluid overload or oedema while awaiting RRT or while renal function is recovering.

why_others_wrong.A: NICE advises against routine loop diuretics to treat AKI; increasing urine output does not reverse the underlying kidney injury.
why_others_wrong.B: Loop diuretics may be considered for fluid overload or oedema in AKI, for example while awaiting RRT, so they are not absolutely contraindicated.
why_others_wrong.D: Loop diuretics cannot replace renal replacement therapy when indications such as refractory hyperkalaemia or acidosis are present.
why_others_wrong.E: Loop diuretics act on the thick ascending limb to increase natriuresis; they do not directly improve renal perfusion or reverse AKI.

exam_trap: Option A tempts because restoring urine output looks like recovery, but diuretics do not reverse AKI; option B is too absolute, since they can help selected fluid overload.
takeaway: Loop diuretics treat selected fluid overload — they do not "cure" AKI.
source: NICE NG148.
thinking: Loop diuretics in AKI ↓ they increase urine output but do not reverse the injury ↓ NICE advises against routine use to treat AKI ↓ may be considered for fluid overload while awaiting RRT or during recovery ↓ They may be considered for fluid overload/oedema in selected circumstances
pearl: Before giving diuretics in postoperative oliguria, hypovolaemia must be excluded, because diuresis in a fluid-depleted patient worsens renal perfusion.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: AKI: ISOLATED CREATININE
stem: A patient has AKI with a markedly elevated creatinine but no refractory hyperkalaemia, acidosis, uraemic complication, fluid overload or pulmonary oedema. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: RRT is automatically required because of the creatinine value alone
options.B: RRT decisions should consider the whole clinical picture
options.C: Dialysis is mandatory whenever creatinine exceeds a fixed value

correct_answer: B. RRT decisions should consider the whole clinical picture
why_correct: NICE explicitly advises basing the decision to start RRT on the overall condition rather than an isolated urea, creatinine or potassium value.

why_others_wrong.A: NICE advises basing the decision to start RRT on the overall clinical condition, not on an isolated creatinine value.
why_others_wrong.C: There is no fixed creatinine threshold that mandates dialysis; the decision depends on complications and the whole clinical picture.
why_others_wrong.D: Creatinine remains important for staging AKI and tracking its course, even though it does not alone decide the need for RRT.
why_others_wrong.E: RRT may still become necessary if complications develop or the patient deteriorates, so it should not be ruled out.

exam_trap: Options A and C tempt candidates who memorise a single creatinine cut-off, but there is no fixed creatinine threshold that by itself mandates renal replacement therapy.
takeaway: RRT is a clinical decision, not a creatinine-triggered reflex.
source: NICE NG148.
thinking: Markedly raised creatinine in AKI ↓ no refractory hyperkalaemia, acidosis, uraemic complication or fluid overload ↓ NICE bases RRT on the overall clinical condition, not one value ↓ RRT decisions should consider the whole clinical picture
pearl: Many patients with severe AKI recover renal function with treatment of the cause and supportive care alone; obstruction should be excluded early with ultrasound when the cause is unclear.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: PRESSURE ULCER PREVENTION: REPOSITIONING
stem: A hospitalised adult is assessed as being at high risk of developing a pressure ulcer but can reposition independently. What should be encouraged?

options.E: Routine IV fluids regardless of hydration

why_correct: NICE recommends frequent repositioning for adults at risk of pressure ulcers. For those at high risk, repositioning should occur frequently, with a documented frequency and assistance where needed.

why_others_wrong.B: Bed rest without repositioning allows sustained pressure over bony prominences, which is how pressure ulcers develop.
why_others_wrong.C: NICE recommends against skin massage or rubbing to prevent pressure ulcers because it can damage vulnerable tissue.
why_others_wrong.D: Avoiding movement increases sustained pressure and ischaemia, raising rather than reducing pressure-ulcer risk in a patient able to move.
why_others_wrong.E: Routine IV fluids regardless of hydration status do not relieve pressure and risk fluid overload; hydration should be assessed individually.

exam_trap: Option C may appeal as stimulating circulation, but NICE advises against skin massage or rubbing because it can damage vulnerable tissue; repositioning relieves pressure.
takeaway: Pressure-risk patient → regular repositioning + appropriate equipment.
source: NICE CG179, Pressure ulcers.
thinking: High pressure-ulcer risk ↓ patient can move independently ↓ sustained pressure causes tissue ischaemia ↓ Regular repositioning
pearl: NICE advises adults at risk of pressure ulcers to change position at least every 6 hours, and at least every 4 hours if at high risk, with help and equipment if they cannot do so independently.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: PRESSURE ULCERS: SKIN MASSAGE
stem: Which intervention should NOT be offered to adults specifically to prevent pressure ulcers?
why_correct: NICE specifically recommends against skin massage or rubbing to prevent pressure ulcers.

why_others_wrong.A: Repositioning redistributes pressure and is a core NICE-recommended measure for preventing pressure ulcers.
why_others_wrong.B: Pressure-redistributing equipment such as high-specification foam mattresses is recommended by NICE for at-risk adults.
why_others_wrong.D: Risk assessment identifies patients at risk and guides preventive care, so it should be offered.
why_others_wrong.E: Nutritional assessment is part of recommended pressure-ulcer prevention, allowing malnutrition to be identified and managed.

exam_trap: Candidates who read the question as asking for a recommended measure may pick repositioning; massage feels helpful but is specifically not recommended for prevention.
takeaway: Do not massage/rub pressure-prone skin as a prevention strategy.
source: NICE CG179.
thinking: Question asks which intervention should NOT be offered ↓ repositioning, equipment, risk and nutritional assessment are all recommended ↓ rubbing can damage vulnerable skin ↓ Skin massage or rubbing
pearl: The heels and sacrum are the commonest pressure ulcer sites in hospital; for adults at high risk of heel ulcers, NICE advises offloading the heels with appropriate devices.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: PRESSURE ULCERS: MATTRESS
stem: A hospitalised adult is assessed as being at high risk of developing a pressure ulcer. Which equipment should be used?
why_correct: NICE recommends a high-specification foam mattress for adults admitted to secondary care who are assessed as being at high risk of pressure ulcer development.

why_others_wrong.B: An ordinary chair cushion alone does not provide adequate pressure redistribution in bed for a high-risk inpatient.
why_others_wrong.C: Omitting pressure redistribution leaves a high-risk patient exposed to sustained pressure, contrary to NICE advice.
why_others_wrong.D: Water restriction is not pressure-relieving equipment and dehydration may impair tissue health and increase ulcer risk.
why_others_wrong.E: A plaster cast creates pressure points and is itself a cause of pressure injury, not a preventive measure.

exam_trap: An ordinary chair cushion may look like pressure-relief equipment, but it does not redistribute pressure in bed; NICE recommends a high-specification foam mattress.
takeaway: High pressure-ulcer risk in hospital → high-specification foam mattress + repositioning plan.
source: NICE CG179.
thinking: Adult inpatient at high pressure-ulcer risk ↓ pressure must be redistributed while in bed ↓ NICE recommends a high-specification foam mattress ↓ High-specification foam mattress
pearl: If a high-specification foam mattress is not sufficient, for example in patients who cannot be repositioned, a dynamic alternating-pressure support surface may be considered.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: PRESSURE ULCERS: NUTRITION
stem: An adult has adequate nutritional intake but is at risk of developing a pressure ulcer. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Nutritional supplements should automatically be prescribed solely to prevent pressure ulcers
options.B: Nutritional supplements should not be offered specifically for pressure-ulcer prevention when nutritional intake is adequate
options.E: The patient should be kept fasting

correct_answer: B. Nutritional supplements should not be offered specifically for pressure-ulcer prevention when nutritional intake is adequate
why_correct: NICE advises against nutritional supplements specifically for pressure-ulcer prevention in adults whose nutritional intake is adequate.

why_others_wrong.A: NICE advises against prescribing nutritional supplements solely to prevent pressure ulcers when a patient's intake is already adequate.
why_others_wrong.C: Parenteral nutrition is reserved for patients who cannot be fed adequately via the gut and is not indicated with adequate oral intake.
why_others_wrong.D: IV fluids are not needed for pressure-ulcer prevention in a patient who is eating and drinking adequately.
why_others_wrong.E: Keeping the patient fasting would compromise nutrition and tissue health, increasing rather than reducing pressure-ulcer risk.

exam_trap: Option A tempts because nutrition aids healing, but NICE advises against supplements solely to prevent pressure ulcers when intake is already adequate.
takeaway: Assess nutrition properly; do not prescribe supplements automatically simply because pressure-ulcer risk exists.
source: NICE CG179.
thinking: Adult at pressure-ulcer risk ↓ nutritional intake is adequate ↓ supplements add no benefit for prevention in well-nourished patients ↓ Nutritional supplements should not be offered specifically for pressure-ulcer prevention when nutritional intake is adequate
pearl: In contrast, adults who already have a pressure ulcer and are malnourished or at risk of malnutrition should receive nutritional assessment and supplements as part of their wound management.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: POSTOPERATIVE ACUTE RESPIRATORY FAILURE
stem: A postoperative patient becomes acutely breathless, hypoxic and increasingly fatigued. What is the most appropriate initial principle?

options.A: Assess airway, breathing and circulation and identify the cause
options.E: Delay assessment until the following day

correct_answer: A. Assess airway, breathing and circulation and identify the cause
why_correct: Postoperative respiratory deterioration has multiple potentially life-threatening causes, including airway obstruction, aspiration, pneumonia, pulmonary oedema, pulmonary embolism and pneumothorax.

why_others_wrong.B: Assuming atelectasis without assessment risks missing life-threatening causes such as pulmonary embolism, aspiration or pneumothorax.
why_others_wrong.C: Sedatives depress respiratory drive and could precipitate respiratory arrest in an already hypoxic, fatiguing patient.
why_others_wrong.D: Oxygen saturation is a key measure of hypoxia and guides oxygen therapy and escalation, so it must be monitored.
why_others_wrong.E: A hypoxic, tiring patient may be approaching respiratory failure and needs immediate assessment, not a delay until the next day.

exam_trap: Option B tempts because atelectasis is the commonest postoperative chest problem, but assuming it without assessment risks missing PE, aspiration, pulmonary oedema or pneumothorax.
takeaway: Postoperative hypoxia = ABC assessment + identify the cause.
source: [RCUK], ABCDE approach to the acutely ill patient.
thinking: Acute breathlessness, hypoxia and fatigue after surgery ↓ fatigue signals impending respiratory failure ↓ causes range from atelectasis to PE, aspiration and pneumothorax ↓ systematic ABC assessment and diagnosis ↓ Assess airway, breathing and circulation and identify the cause
pearl: A rising PaCO2 in a tiring postoperative patient indicates ventilatory failure; it needs early critical care input and may require non-invasive or invasive ventilation.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: POSTOPERATIVE PULMONARY OEDEMA
stem: A postoperative patient develops acute severe breathlessness, bilateral crackles and hypoxia shortly after receiving a large fluid load. Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Acute pulmonary oedema can occur after fluid overload or cardiac dysfunction and causes breathlessness, hypoxia and bilateral pulmonary crackles.

why_others_wrong.B: Atelectasis typically causes basal reduced air entry and mild hypoxia, not acute severe breathlessness with bilateral crackles after a large fluid load.
why_others_wrong.C: Appendicitis is an abdominal condition presenting with pain and fever, not acute hypoxia with bilateral chest crackles.
why_others_wrong.D: Testicular torsion causes acute scrotal pain and does not explain bilateral crackles and hypoxia.
why_others_wrong.E: An incisional hernia is a late abdominal wall defect and would not cause acute breathlessness or pulmonary crackles.

exam_trap: Option B tempts as the commonest postoperative respiratory problem, but atelectasis gives basal changes and mild hypoxia, not bilateral crackles after a large fluid load.
takeaway: Acute postoperative hypoxia + bilateral crackles + fluid excess → consider pulmonary oedema.
source: [AoA] guidance, perioperative fluid management.
thinking: Acute severe breathlessness and hypoxia ↓ bilateral crackles ↓ after a large fluid load ↓ fluid overload causing acute pulmonary oedema ↓ Pulmonary oedema
pearl: Older patients and those with impaired left ventricular function are at highest risk of iatrogenic fluid overload, so postoperative fluids should be reviewed against weight, balance charts and examination.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: POSTOPERATIVE ASPIRATION
stem: A patient aspirates gastric contents during induction of anaesthesia and subsequently develops respiratory distress. What pulmonary complication is of particular concern?
why_correct: Aspiration of gastric contents can cause chemical pneumonitis and may be followed by bacterial pneumonia.

why_others_wrong.B: Emphysema is a chronic destructive lung disease, typically smoking-related, that does not develop acutely after aspiration.
why_others_wrong.C: Smoking-related pulmonary fibrosis develops over years and is unrelated to an acute aspiration event at induction.
why_others_wrong.D: Primary lung cancer is a chronic neoplastic process and not an acute complication of aspirating gastric contents.
why_others_wrong.E: Mesothelioma is a pleural malignancy linked to asbestos exposure decades earlier, not to perioperative aspiration.

exam_trap: Chronic options such as emphysema or smoking-related fibrosis appeal as familiar lung diseases, but only aspiration pneumonitis or pneumonia arises acutely after induction.
takeaway: Aspiration → assess respiratory compromise and distinguish chemical injury from subsequent infection.
source: [AoA] guidance, pulmonary aspiration during anaesthesia.
thinking: Gastric contents aspirated at induction ↓ acid causes chemical injury to the airways and alveoli ↓ secondary bacterial infection may follow ↓ Aspiration pneumonitis/pneumonia
pearl: Rapid sequence induction with preoxygenation and cricoid pressure is used in patients at high aspiration risk, such as those with bowel obstruction, a full stomach or pregnancy; the right lower lobe is most often affected when aspiration occurs upright.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: POSTOPERATIVE PNEUMOTHORAX
stem: A patient develops sudden unilateral pleuritic chest pain, respiratory distress and markedly reduced breath sounds after central venous access. What complication should be considered?
why_correct: Pneumothorax is a recognised complication of procedures involving the thorax, including central venous access depending on the site and technique.

why_others_wrong.B: Acute cholecystitis causes right upper quadrant pain and fever, not unilateral pleuritic pain with reduced breath sounds after line insertion.
why_others_wrong.C: Diverticulitis presents with left iliac fossa pain and fever and does not explain reduced breath sounds after central venous access.
why_others_wrong.D: Urinary retention causes suprapubic discomfort and cannot account for sudden respiratory distress and absent breath sounds.
why_others_wrong.E: Ileus causes abdominal distension and vomiting and does not explain acute unilateral chest signs after a thoracic procedure.

exam_trap: The abdominal options are clearly unrelated, but candidates may overlook tension pneumothorax; if haemodynamic compromise develops, decompression must not wait for imaging.
takeaway: Post-procedure acute unilateral respiratory deterioration → consider pneumothorax.
source: [AoA] guidance, safe vascular/central venous access.
thinking: Sudden unilateral pleuritic pain and respiratory distress ↓ markedly reduced breath sounds on one side ↓ immediately after central venous access ↓ pleural puncture during cannulation ↓ Iatrogenic pneumothorax
pearl: Ultrasound-guided central venous cannulation, as recommended by NICE, reduces pneumothorax and arterial puncture; the subclavian approach carries a higher pneumothorax risk than the internal jugular, so a chest X-ray is usually checked after insertion.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: POSTOPERATIVE MYOCARDIAL INJURY
stem: An older patient develops unexplained tachycardia and mild hypotension after major surgery. Which serious complication should remain in the differential even without typical chest pain?
why_correct: Older and postoperative patients may have atypical or silent myocardial ischaemia. Unexplained haemodynamic or physiological deterioration should prompt consideration of cardiac causes.

why_others_wrong.B: Constipation does not explain new tachycardia and hypotension, and attributing deterioration to it risks missing silent myocardial injury.
why_others_wrong.C: An incisional hernia is a late wound complication and does not cause unexplained haemodynamic instability after surgery.
why_others_wrong.D: Simple wound bruising is a minor local finding that would not explain tachycardia and hypotension.
why_others_wrong.E: Haemorrhoids are a minor anorectal condition and do not account for unexplained postoperative haemodynamic deterioration.

exam_trap: Constipation may be offered as a benign explanation, but unexplained tachycardia and hypotension after major surgery must prompt consideration of silent myocardial injury even without chest pain.
takeaway: Unexplained postoperative deterioration → keep silent/atypical MI in the differential even with no chest pain.
source: [AoA] guidance, perioperative myocardial injury.
thinking: Older patient after major surgery ↓ unexplained tachycardia and hypotension ↓ postoperative ischaemia is often silent, masked by analgesia ↓ check ECG and troponin ↓ Myocardial infarction/myocardial injury
pearl: Most perioperative myocardial infarctions occur within the first few postoperative days and many are painless; myocardial injury after non-cardiac surgery, detected by troponin, is associated with increased 30-day mortality.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: POSTOPERATIVE ACUTE KIDNEY INJURY: DRUGS
stem: A postoperative patient develops AKI. Which medication group can contribute to kidney injury and should be reviewed?
why_correct: NSAIDs can reduce renal prostaglandin-mediated vasodilation and may precipitate or worsen AKI, particularly in susceptible patients.

why_others_wrong.B: Simple emollients are topical skin products with negligible systemic absorption and do not cause kidney injury.
why_others_wrong.C: Topical moisturisers act on the skin surface and are not recognised nephrotoxins requiring review in AKI.
why_others_wrong.D: Saline nasal spray is a harmless local preparation with no meaningful effect on renal function.
why_others_wrong.E: Topical barrier creams protect the skin locally and do not contribute to acute kidney injury.

exam_trap: Topical preparations such as emollients or barrier creams may seem worth reviewing as medicines, but their systemic absorption is negligible; NSAIDs impair prostaglandin-mediated afferent arteriolar dilatation and can precipitate AKI.
takeaway: AKI → review potentially nephrotoxic medicines, including NSAIDs.
source: NICE NG180, acute kidney injury.
thinking: Postoperative AKI ↓ NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandin-mediated afferent arteriolar vasodilatation ↓ glomerular perfusion falls, especially if hypovolaemic ↓ NSAIDs
pearl: Drug review in AKI covers nephrotoxins such as NSAIDs, aminoglycosides and iodinated contrast, drugs that reduce renal perfusion such as ACE inhibitors, ARBs and diuretics, and renally cleared drugs such as metformin that accumulate and cause harm.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: RENAL TRANSPLANT: REJECTION
stem: A kidney transplant recipient develops worsening renal function without another obvious explanation. Which complication should be considered?
why_correct: NHS Blood and Transplant states that rejection may first be detected through deterioration in transplant function and blood-test abnormalities. Diagnosis may require transplant biopsy.

why_others_wrong.B: Acute appendicitis presents with abdominal pain and fever and would not typically cause isolated deterioration in graft function.
why_others_wrong.C: Diverticular bleeding causes rectal bleeding and does not explain worsening renal function in a transplant recipient.
why_others_wrong.D: Gallstone ileus causes small bowel obstruction and is not a cause of unexplained kidney graft dysfunction.
why_others_wrong.E: An inguinal hernia is an abdominal wall problem and does not cause worsening transplant renal function.

exam_trap: Do not assume every rise in creatinine after transplant is rejection; other causes include obstruction, vascular complications, drug toxicity and infection.
takeaway: Transplant dysfunction → consider rejection, but investigate the differential.
source: [NHSBT]: guidance on transplant rejection and post-transplant graft dysfunction.
thinking: Kidney transplant recipient ↓ worsening graft function ↓ no other obvious cause ↓ rejection often presents first as rising creatinine ↓ Acute rejection
pearl: Transplant renal biopsy is the definitive test for rejection; an ultrasound with Doppler is usually performed first to exclude obstruction, collections and renal artery or vein thrombosis.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: RENAL TRANSPLANT: IMMUNOSUPPRESSION
stem: Why are immunosuppressive medicines required after kidney transplantation?

options.A: To prevent the recipient's immune system attacking the transplanted kidney
options.E: To eliminate the need for follow-up

correct_answer: A. To prevent the recipient's immune system attacking the transplanted kidney
why_correct: Immunosuppressants reduce the immune response responsible for graft rejection. NHS Blood and Transplant emphasises that these medicines are essential after transplantation but increase susceptibility to infection.

why_others_wrong.B: Immunosuppressants do not stimulate red-cell production; that is the role of erythropoietin, and some agents can suppress the marrow.
why_others_wrong.C: Immunosuppressive drugs have no role in dissolving renal stones; their purpose is to prevent graft rejection.
why_others_wrong.D: Immunosuppression increases rather than prevents infection risk by lowering the recipient's immune defences.
why_others_wrong.E: Transplant recipients need lifelong follow-up, including drug-level monitoring and surveillance for rejection and infection.

exam_trap: Option D tempts candidates who confuse immune modulation with protection, but immunosuppression lowers defences and increases infection risk rather than preventing infections.
takeaway: Transplant immunosuppression = protect the graft, but at the cost of increased infection susceptibility.
source: [NHSBT]: Organ and Tissue Donation and Transplantation guidelines.
thinking: Transplanted kidney carries foreign HLA antigens ↓ recipient T cells and antibodies recognise them ↓ immunosuppression dampens this response ↓ To prevent the recipient's immune system attacking the transplanted kidney
pearl: Long-term immunosuppression increases the risk of opportunistic infection and malignancy, particularly skin cancers and post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder, so recipients need regular skin surveillance.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: RENAL TRANSPLANT: TACROLIMUS TOXICITY
stem: A kidney transplant recipient develops worsening renal function while receiving tacrolimus. Which adverse effect should be considered?
why_correct: NHS Blood and Transplant identifies impaired kidney function as a potential adverse effect of high tacrolimus exposure and notes that blood tests are required to ensure appropriate dosing.

why_others_wrong.B: A rising creatinine after transplantation does not automatically mean rejection; tacrolimus toxicity, obstruction and infection must also be considered.
why_others_wrong.C: Appendicitis is an unrelated abdominal condition and would not explain declining graft function during tacrolimus therapy.
why_others_wrong.D: Iron deficiency causes anaemia and does not explain worsening renal function in a patient on tacrolimus.
why_others_wrong.E: Diverticulitis presents with abdominal pain and fever and is not a cause of calcineurin-related graft dysfunction.

exam_trap: Option B tempts because rejection is the first concern after transplant, but rising creatinine is not automatically rejection; calcineurin inhibitor toxicity must be excluded with drug levels.
takeaway: Transplant + rising creatinine → distinguish rejection from drug toxicity and other causes.
source: [NHSBT]: Organ and Tissue Donation and Transplantation guidelines; [BNF].
thinking: Kidney transplant recipient on tacrolimus ↓ rising creatinine ↓ calcineurin inhibitors cause dose-related afferent vasoconstriction and nephrotoxicity ↓ check trough drug level ↓ Tacrolimus nephrotoxicity
pearl: Tacrolimus is metabolised by CYP3A4, so inhibitors such as clarithromycin and azole antifungals can raise levels to toxic ranges; trough monitoring is routine after transplantation.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: LIVER TRANSPLANT: REJECTION
stem: A liver transplant recipient develops worsening liver function tests and new jaundice. Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: NHS Blood and Transplant notes that liver rejection is often first detected through abnormal liver blood tests and may occasionally present with jaundice. Diagnosis usually requires liver biopsy.

why_others_wrong.B: Acute appendicitis presents with abdominal pain and would not explain new jaundice and deranged liver tests after liver transplant.
why_others_wrong.C: A femoral hernia causes a groin lump and possible obstruction but not graft dysfunction with jaundice.
why_others_wrong.D: Renal colic causes loin-to-groin pain from a ureteric stone and does not affect liver function tests.
why_others_wrong.E: Diverticulosis is usually asymptomatic colonic outpouching and does not cause jaundice or abnormal graft function.

exam_trap: Not every abnormal liver test after transplantation is rejection; biliary, vascular, infective and drug-related complications also require consideration.
takeaway: Liver transplant dysfunction → consider rejection and investigate graft-specific complications.
source: [NHSBT]: Organ and Tissue Donation and Transplantation guidelines.
thinking: Liver transplant recipient ↓ rising liver enzymes and new jaundice ↓ graft dysfunction ↓ rejection is a key cause, confirmed by biopsy ↓ Liver graft rejection
pearl: Hepatic artery thrombosis is a serious early complication after liver transplantation that can cause graft failure and biliary necrosis, so Doppler ultrasound is an early investigation for graft dysfunction.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: LIVER TRANSPLANT: IMMUNOSUPPRESSION AND INFECTION
stem: Why are transplant recipients particularly susceptible to infection?

options.D: All infections are caused by rejection
options.E: Transplant recipients have no infection risk after discharge

correct_answer: A. Immunosuppressive treatment reduces immune function
