why_correct: NHS Blood and Transplant explains that immunosuppressive medicines lower immune responses and consequently increase susceptibility to infection.

why_others_wrong.B: Transplanted organs can become infected, and graft infections are an important complication in immunosuppressed recipients.
why_others_wrong.C: Immunosuppressants reduce rather than increase immune cell function, and some agents also lower neutrophil counts.
why_others_wrong.D: Infections arise mainly from reduced immune defences, not from rejection, so fever should prompt a search for infection.
why_others_wrong.E: Infection risk persists for as long as immunosuppression continues, so it does not end at discharge.

exam_trap: Option D appeals if fever is attributed to rejection, but infections arise from reduced immune defences, so a febrile recipient needs a search for infection first.
takeaway: Transplant + immunosuppression → maintain a low threshold for investigating infection.
source: [NHSBT]: Organ and Tissue Donation and Transplantation guidelines.
thinking: Transplant recipients take long-term immunosuppression ↓ these drugs suppress T-cell and other immune responses ↓ defences against bacterial, viral and fungal pathogens fall ↓ Immunosuppressive treatment reduces immune function
pearl: Opportunistic infections such as cytomegalovirus and Pneumocystis are most frequent in the first months after transplantation, which is why prophylaxis such as co-trimoxazole and valganciclovir is commonly given.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: TRANSPLANT: POSITIVE CROSS-MATCH
stem: A potential kidney donor-recipient pair has a strongly positive cross-match indicating antibodies that would attack the donor kidney. What does this imply?

options.B: The transplant should not proceed because of the risk of immediate rejection
options.E: It proves the donor has an infection

correct_answer: B. The transplant should not proceed because of the risk of immediate rejection
why_correct: NHS Blood and Transplant explains that a positive cross-match indicates antibodies capable of attacking the donor kidney and means the transplant cannot proceed because of the risk of immediate rejection.

why_others_wrong.A: A strongly positive cross-match indicates donor-specific antibodies that would attack the kidney, so proceeding routinely risks immediate rejection.
why_others_wrong.C: Appendicectomy is irrelevant to cross-match results and does not remove antibodies directed against the donor kidney.
why_others_wrong.D: A cross-match is performed before transplantation to predict antibody-mediated rejection; it does not diagnose chronic rejection in an existing graft.
why_others_wrong.E: A positive cross-match reflects recipient antibodies against donor antigens, not infection in the donor.

exam_trap: Option D tempts those who link antibodies with chronic rejection, but a cross-match is a pre-transplant test predicting immediate rejection, not a diagnosis in an existing graft.
takeaway: Positive cross-match → donor-specific antibodies create a major transplantation barrier.
source: [NHSBT]: Organ and Tissue Donation and Transplantation guidelines.
thinking: Strongly positive cross-match ↓ recipient has preformed antibodies against donor antigens ↓ these would bind graft endothelium on reperfusion ↓ risk of immediate antibody-mediated rejection ↓ The transplant should not proceed because of the risk of immediate rejection
pearl: Preformed donor-specific antibodies cause hyperacute rejection, with graft thrombosis within minutes to hours of reperfusion; sensitisation commonly follows previous transplants, pregnancy or blood transfusion.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss
stem: A 52-year-old man develops sudden unilateral hearing loss over the last 24 hours. Otoscopy is normal and there is no evidence of external or middle-ear disease. What is the most appropriate next step?
why_correct: Sudden hearing loss developing over 3 days or less within the preceding 30 days, when not explained by external or middle-ear disease, requires immediate referral so that the patient is seen within 24 hours.

why_others_wrong.A: A routine audiology referral would delay assessment of sudden hearing loss with a normal ear, which needs immediate referral so the patient is seen within 24 hours.
why_others_wrong.B: Waiting 4 weeks loses the early window for assessing and treating sudden sensorineural loss, which needs specialist review within 24 hours.
why_others_wrong.D: Oral antibiotics treat bacterial ear infection, but normal otoscopy with no middle-ear disease points to a sensorineural cause that antibiotics will not help.
why_others_wrong.E: Tympanostomy tubes ventilate a middle ear with effusion, whereas this ear is normal on otoscopy and the loss is presumed sensorineural.

exam_trap: Do not treat sudden sensorineural hearing loss as simple earwax or otitis media when otoscopy is normal.
takeaway: Sudden hearing loss + normal ear → think sensorineural → urgent ENT assessment.
source: NICE NG98, updated October 2023.
thinking: Sudden unilateral hearing loss over 24 hours ↓ normal otoscopy with no external or middle-ear cause ↓ presumed sudden sensorineural loss within the 30-day window ↓ must be seen within 24 hours ↓ Immediate specialist assessment
pearl: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss is usually treated with oral or intratympanic corticosteroids, which seem to work best when started early, so delayed referral can lose the treatment window.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
topic: Sudden hearing loss occurring more than 30 days ago
title: Sudden hearing loss occurring more than 30 days ago
stem: A 61-year-old woman reports sudden unilateral hearing loss that began 6 weeks ago. Otoscopy does not identify an external or middle-ear cause. What is the appropriate referral timeframe?
correct_answer: C. Urgent specialist assessment within 2 weeks
why_correct: Sudden hearing loss developing more than 30 days previously should be referred urgently for assessment within 2 weeks.

why_others_wrong.A: An emergency 1-hour referral is not a hearing-loss pathway timeframe; sudden loss that began more than 30 days ago needs specialist review within 2 weeks.
why_others_wrong.B: The 24-hour pathway is for sudden loss that began within the preceding 30 days, whereas this loss started 6 weeks ago.
why_others_wrong.D: Waiting 6 months is too long for unexplained sudden unilateral loss, which still needs urgent assessment within 2 weeks to look for a retrocochlear or other serious cause.
why_others_wrong.E: Unexplained sudden unilateral hearing loss still needs specialist assessment even after 30 days, because causes such as vestibular schwannoma must be excluded.

exam_trap: The 24-hour pathway applies when sudden loss occurred within the preceding 30 days.
takeaway: Sudden ≤3 days + within 30 days → 24 hours. Older sudden loss → within 2 weeks.
source: NICE NG98, updated October 2023.
thinking: Sudden-onset unilateral hearing loss ↓ onset 6 weeks ago, so more than 30 days previously ↓ outside the 24-hour pathway window ↓ urgent referral to be seen within 2 weeks ↓ Urgent specialist assessment within 2 weeks
pearl: Vestibular schwannoma can present with sudden as well as gradual hearing loss, so unexplained unilateral sensorineural loss should lead to MRI of the internal auditory meati whatever its tempo.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Rapidly progressive hearing loss
stem: A 47-year-old patient has progressive hearing loss that has worsened substantially over 6 weeks. There is no acute external or middle-ear cause. What is the appropriate management?
correct_answer: C. Urgent ENT or audiovestibular referral
why_correct: Rapid worsening over 4–90 days warrants urgent specialist assessment, generally within 2 weeks.

why_others_wrong.A: Reassurance alone ignores rapid deterioration over weeks, which is a red flag needing urgent specialist assessment within about 2 weeks.
why_others_wrong.B: A 12-month review suits slowly progressive age-related loss, not hearing that has worsened substantially over 6 weeks.
why_others_wrong.D: Oral antibiotics treat bacterial ear infection, but there is no acute external or middle-ear cause here to explain the loss.
why_others_wrong.E: Ear irrigation removes impacted wax, and there is no external-ear cause here to account for rapidly progressive loss.

exam_trap: Routine review in 12 months (B) tempts candidates who treat this as age-related hearing loss, but substantial worsening over weeks is a red flag needing urgent referral.
takeaway: Rapid hearing deterioration over weeks → urgent specialist assessment.
source: NICE NG98, updated October 2023.
thinking: Hearing loss worsening substantially over 6 weeks ↓ rapid progression over weeks, not slow age-related decline ↓ no acute external or middle-ear cause ↓ urgent specialist referral, generally within 2 weeks ↓ Urgent ENT or audiovestibular referral
pearl: Rapidly progressive sensorineural loss has a differential that includes autoimmune inner-ear disease, retrocochlear tumour and infection such as syphilis, which is why audiometry and MRI-based specialist work-up are needed.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Hearing loss with facial weakness
stem: A 70-year-old man develops unilateral hearing loss accompanied by ipsilateral facial drooping and altered facial sensation. What is the appropriate action?
why_correct: Acquired unilateral hearing loss with ipsilateral altered sensation or facial droop requires immediate assessment within 24 hours. Stroke should also be considered where clinically appropriate.

why_others_wrong.A: A routine audiology referral is inappropriate when hearing loss comes with ipsilateral facial droop and altered sensation, which need immediate assessment within 24 hours.
why_others_wrong.B: Ear irrigation removes wax and would do nothing for new facial weakness and sensory change suggesting a neurological or cerebellopontine angle cause.
why_others_wrong.D: Reassurance risks missing stroke or a skull-base lesion, as focal neurological signs with hearing loss need immediate assessment.
why_others_wrong.E: Fitting a hearing aid without investigation would miss the cause of loss accompanied by focal neurological signs, which needs immediate specialist assessment.

exam_trap: Do not assume that all facial weakness accompanying hearing loss is uncomplicated Bell's palsy.
takeaway: Hearing loss + focal neurological signs = immediate assessment.
source: NICE NG98, updated October 2023.
thinking: Unilateral hearing loss ↓ plus ipsilateral facial droop and altered facial sensation ↓ focal neurological signs suggest stroke or a cerebellopontine angle lesion ↓ needs assessment within 24 hours ↓ Immediate specialist assessment
pearl: A cerebellopontine angle tumour can involve the trigeminal nerve, with a reduced corneal reflex often an early sign, and the facial nerve, in addition to the vestibulocochlear nerve.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
topic: Immunocompromised patient with otalgia and otorrhoea
title: Immunocompromised patient with otalgia and otorrhoea
stem: A 64-year-old immunocompromised patient has severe ear pain and purulent discharge. Symptoms have not improved after 72 hours of treatment. What is the appropriate next step?
why_correct: Immunocompromised adults with otalgia and otorrhoea that has not responded to treatment within 72 hours require immediate ENT assessment because of the risk of serious invasive external-ear infection.

why_others_wrong.A: Routine audiology does not address the risk of necrotising otitis externa in an immunocompromised patient whose painful discharging ear has failed 72 hours of treatment.
why_others_wrong.C: Ear syringing is inappropriate in an infected, painful ear and delays the immediate ENT assessment needed to exclude invasive external-ear infection.
why_others_wrong.D: Reassurance is unsafe because persistent severe otalgia and otorrhoea in an immunocompromised patient may be necrotising otitis externa spreading to the skull base.
why_others_wrong.E: Withholding further assessment ignores the red flag of treatment failure in an immunocompromised patient, who needs immediate ENT review.

exam_trap: Persistent severe otalgia in an immunocompromised patient is not routine otitis externa.
takeaway: Immunocompromised + persistent otalgia/otorrhoea = urgent ENT safety signal.
source: NICE NG98, updated October 2023.
thinking: Immunocompromised patient ↓ severe otalgia with purulent otorrhoea ↓ no response after 72 hours of treatment ↓ risk of necrotising otitis externa spreading to the skull base ↓ Immediate ENT referral
pearl: Necrotising otitis externa classically affects older people with diabetes, is usually caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa and may show granulation tissue on the canal floor; a facial nerve palsy indicates skull-base spread.

subject: ENT: head & neck
topic: Unilateral middle-ear effusion and nasopharyngeal malignancy
title: Unilateral middle-ear effusion and nasopharyngeal malignancy
stem: A 48-year-old man of Chinese ethnicity develops persistent unilateral middle-ear effusion without a recent upper respiratory tract infection. What diagnosis must particularly be considered?
why_correct: Persistent middle-ear effusion without an upper respiratory tract infection in adults of Chinese or South-East Asian family origin warrants consideration of nasopharyngeal malignancy and ENT assessment.

why_others_wrong.A: Ménière's disease causes episodic vertigo, fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus and aural fullness, and does not produce a persistent middle-ear effusion.
why_others_wrong.C: Otosclerosis causes progressive conductive hearing loss from stapes fixation with a normal tympanic membrane, not a middle-ear effusion.
why_others_wrong.D: Presbycusis is age-related bilateral symmetrical sensorineural hearing loss and would not explain a unilateral effusion in a 48-year-old.
why_others_wrong.E: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo causes brief positional vertigo from displaced otoconia and has no association with middle-ear fluid.

exam_trap: Candidates offered ear-related options such as Ménière's disease or otosclerosis forget that a persistent adult unilateral effusion with no URTI needs the nasopharynx examined for a tumour.
takeaway: Adult unilateral effusion without URTI → look for a nasopharyngeal cause.
source: NICE NG98, updated October 2023.
thinking: Adult with persistent unilateral middle-ear effusion ↓ no preceding upper respiratory tract infection ↓ Chinese ethnicity raises the risk of nasopharyngeal cancer ↓ a nasopharyngeal tumour can block the Eustachian tube orifice ↓ Nasopharyngeal carcinoma
pearl: Examination of an adult with a unilateral effusion must include endoscopic inspection of the postnasal space; nasopharyngeal carcinoma is strongly associated with Epstein-Barr virus and often presents first with a painless upper cervical node.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss
stem: An adult has sensorineural hearing loss with an asymmetry of 15 dB at two adjacent frequencies on pure-tone audiometry. Which investigation should be considered?

options.B: MRI of the internal auditory meati

correct_answer: B. MRI of the internal auditory meati
why_correct: NICE recommends considering MRI of the internal auditory meati for sensorineural hearing loss without localising signs when there is an asymmetry of 15 dB or more at any two adjacent test frequencies.

why_others_wrong.A: CT chest does not image the internal auditory meatus or cerebellopontine angle, where a vestibular schwannoma would cause asymmetric sensorineural loss.
why_others_wrong.C: Carotid Doppler assesses extracranial carotid stenosis and does not look for the retrocochlear lesion suggested by asymmetric sensorineural loss.
why_others_wrong.D: CT abdomen has no role in investigating asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss, where the concern is a retrocochlear lesion such as vestibular schwannoma.
why_others_wrong.E: Lumbar puncture samples cerebrospinal fluid for infection or inflammation and cannot show a structural lesion in the internal auditory meatus.

exam_trap: Carotid Doppler (C) tempts candidates thinking of a vascular cause, but asymmetric sensorineural loss points to a retrocochlear lesion that only MRI of the internal auditory meati will show.
takeaway: Asymmetric SNHL → think retrocochlear pathology → MRI IAM.
source: NICE NG98, updated October 2023.
thinking: Sensorineural loss on pure-tone audiometry ↓ 15 dB asymmetry at two adjacent frequencies ↓ meets the NICE threshold for suspected retrocochlear pathology ↓ vestibular schwannoma must be excluded ↓ MRI of the internal auditory meati
pearl: Gadolinium-enhanced or high-resolution T2-weighted MRI is the investigation of choice for vestibular schwannoma, and small tumours are often managed with surveillance scanning rather than immediate surgery or radiosurgery.

subject: ENT: head & neck
title: Bell's palsy pattern
stem: A 36-year-old woman develops sudden unilateral facial weakness. There are no other neurological abnormalities. Which finding most strongly supports a lower motor neurone facial palsy?

options.C: Inability to close the ipsilateral eye

correct_answer: C. Inability to close the ipsilateral eye
why_correct: A lower motor neurone facial palsy affects the entire ipsilateral face, including forehead movement and eye closure.

why_others_wrong.A: Forehead sparing points to an upper motor neurone lesion because the upper face has bilateral cortical innervation.
why_others_wrong.B: Weakness confined to the mouth is typical of an upper motor neurone lesion; a lower motor neurone palsy affects the whole side of the face.
why_others_wrong.D: Contralateral limb weakness suggests a central lesion such as a stroke, and the stem states there are no other neurological abnormalities.
why_others_wrong.E: Tongue deviation reflects hypoglossal nerve dysfunction and tells you nothing about whether a facial palsy is of lower motor neurone type.

exam_trap: Candidates pick forehead sparing (A), but that indicates an upper motor neurone lesion; a lower motor neurone palsy involves the forehead and eye closure.
takeaway: LMN VII → whole side of face. UMN lesion → forehead relatively spared.
thinking: Unilateral facial weakness with no other neurological signs ↓ the upper face has bilateral cortical supply, so forehead and eye closure are relatively spared in UMN lesions ↓ weakness of the upper face, including eye closure, places the lesion in the facial nerve or its nucleus ↓ Inability to close the ipsilateral eye
pearl: For Bell's palsy presenting within 72 hours, oral prednisolone is recommended, and incomplete eye closure needs eye protection with lubricants and taping at night to prevent corneal injury.

subject: ENT: head & neck
title: Eye protection in Bell's palsy
stem: A patient with uncomplicated Bell's palsy cannot fully close the affected eye. What is an important component of management?
why_correct: Incomplete eye closure exposes the cornea to drying and injury. NICE specifically recommends advising adults with Bell's palsy about eye care.

why_others_wrong.B: Permanent patching for 6 months is not advised; eye care involves lubricants and taping or protecting the eye closed at night, with review if symptoms develop.
why_others_wrong.C: Facial nerve surgery has no role in the initial management of uncomplicated Bell's palsy, most of which recovers spontaneously.
why_others_wrong.D: Ear irrigation treats wax or debris in the ear canal and does nothing to protect the exposed cornea.
why_others_wrong.E: Avoiding facial movement does not protect the cornea and is not part of Bell's palsy management; the problem is incomplete eye closure.

exam_trap: Option B looks protective, but prolonged patching is not advised; the real priority is lubrication and night-time taping to prevent exposure keratitis, not immobilising the eye.
takeaway: Bell's palsy + incomplete eye closure → protect the cornea.
source: NICE NG127, 2019.
thinking: Bell's palsy with incomplete eye closure ↓ the cornea is exposed and dries ↓ risk of exposure keratitis and corneal ulceration ↓ lubricating drops by day, ointment and taping at night ↓ Eye protection
pearl: Advise urgent review for a red or painful eye in Bell's palsy because exposure keratitis can progress to ulceration; oral prednisolone started within 72 hours of onset improves facial recovery.

subject: ENT: head & neck
title: Uncomplicated Bell's palsy referral
stem: A 42-year-old patient has an isolated unilateral lower motor neurone facial palsy involving the forehead and eye closure. There is no middle-ear disease or other neurological abnormality. What does NICE recommend regarding routine specialist referral?

options.B: Routine ENT referral for every patient

why_correct: NICE advises that uncomplicated Bell's palsy without evidence of another medical condition does not routinely require specialist referral.

why_others_wrong.A: Neurosurgical referral is not needed for an isolated lower motor neurone facial palsy with no other neurological signs or structural cause.
why_others_wrong.B: NICE does not advise ENT referral for every patient; ENT review is reserved for atypical features, ear disease or failure to improve.
why_others_wrong.D: Imaging is kept for atypical features, other neurological signs or failure to recover, not performed immediately in every uncomplicated case.
why_others_wrong.E: Lumbar puncture has no place in uncomplicated Bell's palsy and would be considered only if features suggested meningitis or another central cause.

exam_trap: Do not automatically convert every classic Bell's palsy presentation into a neurological referral.
takeaway: Classic isolated Bell's palsy → can usually be managed without routine specialist referral.
source: NICE NG127, 2019.
thinking: Isolated lower motor neurone facial palsy involving forehead and eye closure ↓ no ear disease and no other neurological signs ↓ this is uncomplicated Bell's palsy ↓ NICE advises no routine specialist referral ↓ Do not routinely refer
pearl: Refer if there is no improvement after about 3 weeks, or if there are atypical features such as bilateral palsy, a parotid mass, vesicles in the ear canal or other cranial nerve signs, because these suggest another cause.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Tinnitus with sudden hearing loss
stem: A patient develops tinnitus together with sudden unilateral hearing loss over the previous 48 hours. What is the appropriate management?
why_correct: Tinnitus accompanied by sudden hearing loss developing over 3 days or less within the previous 30 days requires referral for assessment within 24 hours.

why_others_wrong.A: Routine audiology in 6 months is far too slow when tinnitus comes with sudden hearing loss in the past 48 hours, which needs assessment within 24 hours.
why_others_wrong.B: Reassurance alone misses the accompanying sudden hearing loss, which is the urgent feature and needs assessment within 24 hours.
why_others_wrong.D: Sudden unilateral hearing loss with tinnitus needs urgent specialist assessment, including audiometry and later imaging to look for a retrocochlear cause.
why_others_wrong.E: CT abdomen has no role in tinnitus or sudden hearing loss; the priority is urgent ear and hearing assessment within 24 hours.

exam_trap: The tinnitus itself is not the main emergency; the associated sudden hearing loss is.
takeaway: Tinnitus + sudden hearing loss → urgent hearing-loss pathway.
source: NICE NG155, 2020; NICE NG98, updated October 2023.
thinking: Tinnitus with sudden unilateral hearing loss ↓ onset within the last 48 hours ↓ the sudden loss within 30 days drives the urgency, not the tinnitus ↓ refer for assessment within 24 hours ↓ Assessment within 24 hours
pearl: Tinnitus commonly accompanies sudden sensorineural hearing loss; treat the hearing loss as the index problem, with urgent audiometry to confirm a sensorineural pattern and later MRI to exclude a retrocochlear cause.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Tinnitus with acute neurological symptoms
stem: A patient presents with tinnitus accompanied by sudden facial weakness. What is the appropriate approach?
why_correct: Tinnitus associated with sudden significant neurological symptoms such as facial weakness requires immediate assessment, with stroke considered where appropriate.

why_others_wrong.A: A routine tinnitus clinic referral is inappropriate because sudden facial weakness is an acute neurological sign that needs immediate assessment.
why_others_wrong.C: Reassurance risks missing a stroke or other neurological cause, as tinnitus with sudden facial weakness needs immediate assessment.
why_others_wrong.D: Fitting a hearing aid does not address sudden facial weakness, which needs immediate assessment for stroke or another neurological cause.
why_others_wrong.E: Wax drops treat impacted cerumen and do nothing for a new facial weakness that needs immediate assessment.

exam_trap: Routine tinnitus clinic referral (A) tempts candidates who focus on the tinnitus, but sudden facial weakness is an acute neurological deficit that needs immediate assessment.
takeaway: Tinnitus + acute neurological deficit = emergency assessment.
source: NICE NG155, 2020.
thinking: Tinnitus ↓ with sudden facial weakness ↓ acute focal neurological deficit ↓ stroke or another neurological cause must be considered ↓ Immediate specialist assessment
pearl: Facial weakness that spares the forehead suggests an upper motor neurone cause such as stroke, whereas weakness of the whole half-face suggests a lower motor neurone lesion of the facial nerve.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Unilateral non-pulsatile tinnitus
stem: A 55-year-old man has persistent unilateral non-pulsatile tinnitus but no neurological, audiological or otological abnormality. Which investigation should be considered?

options.A: MRI of the internal auditory meati

correct_answer: A. MRI of the internal auditory meati
why_correct: NICE recommends considering MRI of the internal auditory meati for unilateral or asymmetrical non-pulsatile tinnitus even when no associated signs are present.

why_others_wrong.B: CT abdomen does not image the internal auditory meatus, where a vestibular schwannoma could cause unilateral tinnitus.
why_others_wrong.C: An EEG records cortical electrical activity for seizures and cannot show a retrocochlear lesion such as vestibular schwannoma.
why_others_wrong.D: Carotid endarterectomy is an operation for symptomatic carotid stenosis, not an investigation, and has no place in unilateral non-pulsatile tinnitus.
why_others_wrong.E: NICE recommends considering MRI for unilateral non-pulsatile tinnitus even without other signs, because it may be the first sign of a vestibular schwannoma.

exam_trap: Candidates pick 'no assessment is ever indicated' (E) because examination is normal, but unilateral non-pulsatile tinnitus alone can signal vestibular schwannoma and justifies considering MRI.
takeaway: Persistent unilateral tinnitus → consider MRI IAM.
source: NICE NG155, 2020.
thinking: Persistent unilateral non-pulsatile tinnitus ↓ no neurological, audiological or otological abnormality ↓ asymmetric tinnitus alone may be the first sign of vestibular schwannoma ↓ NICE: consider imaging the internal auditory meati ↓ MRI of the internal auditory meati
pearl: Vestibular schwannoma arises from the Schwann cells of the vestibular nerve, and bilateral tumours suggest neurofibromatosis type 2.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Pulsatile tinnitus
stem: A 59-year-old patient describes persistent tinnitus synchronised with the heartbeat. What is the appropriate investigation principle?

options.E: MRI is contraindicated in all tinnitus

why_correct: NICE recommends imaging for pulsatile tinnitus because vascular and other structural causes may be present.

why_others_wrong.A: Pulsatile tinnitus may reflect a vascular or structural cause such as a dural arteriovenous fistula or glomus tumour, so NICE recommends imaging.
why_others_wrong.C: Antibiotics treat infection and do not address the vascular or structural lesions that commonly underlie pulsatile tinnitus.
why_others_wrong.D: Ear irrigation removes wax and cannot explain or treat tinnitus that pulses with the heartbeat, which needs imaging for a vascular cause.
why_others_wrong.E: MRI is not contraindicated in tinnitus; it is widely used to assess unilateral tinnitus, and MR angiography can help assess pulsatile tinnitus.

exam_trap: Choosing no imaging (A) wrongly applies the rule for symmetrical non-pulsatile tinnitus; tinnitus synchronised with the pulse needs imaging to look for a vascular or structural cause.
takeaway: Pulsatile tinnitus → image for an underlying structural/vascular cause.
source: NICE NG155, 2020.
thinking: Tinnitus synchronised with the heartbeat ↓ pulsatile tinnitus ↓ suggests a vascular or structural cause ↓ NICE recommends imaging ↓ Offer imaging
pearl: Causes of pulsatile tinnitus include dural arteriovenous fistula, glomus (paraganglioma) tumours, carotid stenosis or dissection and idiopathic intracranial hypertension; a red mass behind the eardrum suggests a glomus tumour.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Symmetrical non-pulsatile tinnitus
stem: A 50-year-old patient has bilateral symmetrical non-pulsatile tinnitus with no neurological, audiological, otological or head-and-neck signs. What does NICE recommend regarding imaging?

options.D: Do not offer imaging solely for the tinnitus

correct_answer: D. Do not offer imaging solely for the tinnitus
why_correct: NICE advises against imaging for symmetrical non-pulsatile tinnitus when there are no associated signs or symptoms.

why_others_wrong.A: NICE advises against imaging for symmetrical non-pulsatile tinnitus without associated signs, as the yield is very low.
why_others_wrong.B: CT is not recommended for uncomplicated symmetrical tinnitus and would add radiation exposure with little chance of finding a cause.
why_others_wrong.C: Angiography looks for vascular causes relevant to pulsatile tinnitus, not bilateral symmetrical non-pulsatile tinnitus without red flags.
why_others_wrong.E: There is no surgical target in uncomplicated symmetrical tinnitus, which is managed with information, support and treatment of any hearing loss.

exam_trap: MRI for everyone (A) is chosen by candidates who over-apply the unilateral tinnitus rule; symmetrical non-pulsatile tinnitus without associated signs does not need imaging.
takeaway: Symmetrical non-pulsatile tinnitus + no red flags → no routine imaging.
source: NICE NG155, 2020.
thinking: Bilateral symmetrical tinnitus ↓ non-pulsatile ↓ no neurological, audiological, otological or head-and-neck signs ↓ imaging has a very low yield ↓ Do not offer imaging solely for the tinnitus
pearl: Uncomplicated tinnitus is managed with information and reassurance, hearing assessment with amplification of any hearing loss, sound therapy and psychological approaches such as CBT when it causes distress.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Acute sinusitis and antibiotics
stem: A 28-year-old patient has facial pressure, nasal discharge and congestion for 7 days. There are no red flags and the patient is not systemically very unwell. What is the most appropriate antimicrobial approach?

options.C: Do not offer an antibiotic prescription routinely

correct_answer: C. Do not offer an antibiotic prescription routinely
why_correct: NICE advises against antibiotic prescribing for acute sinusitis when symptoms have been present for around 10 days or less in the absence of features requiring another approach.

why_others_wrong.A: NICE advises against antibiotics for acute sinusitis lasting 10 days or less without red flags, because it is usually viral and self-limiting.
why_others_wrong.B: IV antibiotics are for serious complications such as orbital or intracranial spread, not uncomplicated sinusitis in a patient who is not systemically very unwell.
why_others_wrong.D: Long-term prophylactic antibiotics have no role in an acute, usually viral, self-limiting sinusitis of 7 days' duration.
why_others_wrong.E: Emergency sinus surgery is for complications such as orbital abscess, not uncomplicated acute sinusitis without red flags.

exam_trap: Purulent discharge tempts candidates towards immediate broad-spectrum antibiotics (A), but sinusitis lasting 10 days or less without red flags is usually viral and settles without them.
takeaway: Acute sinusitis ≤10 days → usually supportive management, not antibiotics.
source: NICE NG79, 2017.
thinking: Facial pressure, nasal discharge and congestion for 7 days ↓ no red flags and not systemically very unwell ↓ acute sinusitis of 10 days or less is usually viral and self-limiting ↓ no routine antibiotic prescription ↓ Do not offer an antibiotic prescription routinely
pearl: If symptoms last around 10 days or more without improvement, NICE suggests considering a high-dose nasal corticosteroid for 14 days in people aged 12 or over, or a back-up antibiotic for those more likely to have bacterial infection.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Expected duration of acute sinusitis
stem: A patient with uncomplicated acute sinusitis asks how long symptoms usually last. Which timeframe should be given?
why_correct: NICE advises that the usual course of acute sinusitis is approximately 2–3 weeks.

why_others_wrong.A: Acute sinusitis rarely settles within 24 hours; NICE advises that symptoms usually last around 2 to 3 weeks.
why_others_wrong.B: Two to three days is too short and may lead patients to think treatment has failed, when the usual course is around 2 to 3 weeks.
why_others_wrong.D: Symptoms lasting around 3 months fall into the chronic rhinosinusitis range (12 weeks or more) rather than the usual acute course.
why_others_wrong.E: A year-long course would suggest chronic rhinosinusitis or another diagnosis, not uncomplicated acute sinusitis, which usually lasts 2 to 3 weeks.

exam_trap: Candidates choose 2–3 days (B) expecting a quick recovery, but acute sinusitis usually lasts 2–3 weeks, so persisting symptoms after a week do not mean treatment failure.
takeaway: Acute sinusitis commonly lasts 2–3 weeks.
source: NICE NG79, 2017.
thinking: Uncomplicated acute sinusitis ↓ usually viral and self-limiting ↓ but symptoms resolve slowly ↓ NICE: usual course about 2–3 weeks ↓ Usually 2–3 weeks
pearl: Symptoms lasting 12 weeks or more define chronic rhinosinusitis, and unilateral symptoms or blood-stained discharge should prompt specialist assessment to exclude a sinonasal tumour.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Sinusitis with orbital complication
stem: A patient with acute sinusitis develops severe periorbital swelling, visual disturbance and worsening systemic illness. What is the most appropriate action?
why_correct: Orbital or intracranial complications of sinusitis are serious and require hospital assessment.

why_others_wrong.A: A review in a month is dangerous when periorbital swelling and visual disturbance suggest orbital spread that can threaten sight within hours.
why_others_wrong.B: Visual disturbance, periorbital swelling and systemic deterioration are features of complicated sinusitis, not uncomplicated disease.
why_others_wrong.D: Reassurance could miss orbital cellulitis, subperiosteal abscess or intracranial spread, which need urgent hospital assessment.
why_others_wrong.E: Decongestants do not treat orbital complications, and long-term use risks rebound congestion; this patient needs urgent hospital care.

exam_trap: Visual symptoms in a patient with sinusitis are a complication warning sign.
takeaway: Sinusitis + orbital/neurological features → think complication, not routine sinusitis.
source: NICE NG79 (2017); urgent hospital referral is standard practice for suspected orbital or intracranial complications.
thinking: Acute sinusitis ↓ severe periorbital swelling and visual disturbance ↓ worsening systemic illness ↓ orbital or intracranial complication ↓ Urgent hospital assessment
pearl: Orbital complications usually arise from the ethmoid sinuses through the thin lamina papyracea; reduced acuity or colour vision, ophthalmoplegia or proptosis suggests post-septal infection or abscess needing urgent CT.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Persistent unexplained hoarseness
stem: A 49-year-old smoker has persistent unexplained hoarseness. What is the appropriate NICE pathway?
why_correct: NICE recommends considering a suspected cancer pathway referral for laryngeal cancer in people aged 45 years or over with persistent unexplained hoarseness.

why_others_wrong.A: Waiting 12 months could delay diagnosis of laryngeal cancer in a smoker over 45 with persistent unexplained hoarseness.
why_others_wrong.C: Antibiotics treat bacterial infection and would not address a possible laryngeal cancer causing persistent hoarseness in a smoker over 45.
why_others_wrong.D: Speech therapy can help voice disorders once the larynx has been examined, but starting it before assessment risks missing laryngeal cancer.
why_others_wrong.E: Persistent unexplained hoarseness at 45 or over meets NICE criteria for considering a suspected cancer referral, so it cannot be left uninvestigated.

exam_trap: Do not dismiss persistent hoarseness as simple laryngitis in an older adult.
takeaway: Age 45 or over + persistent unexplained hoarseness → consider a suspected cancer pathway referral.
source: NICE NG12, updated 2025.
thinking: 49-year-old smoker ↓ persistent unexplained hoarseness ↓ age 45 or over meets the NICE threshold ↓ possible laryngeal cancer ↓ Suspected cancer pathway referral
pearl: Glottic cancer presents early with hoarseness and the vocal cords have sparse lymphatic drainage, so it metastasises to nodes late and carries a better prognosis than supraglottic cancer.

subject: ENT: head & neck
topic: Unexplained neck lump and laryngeal cancer
title: Unexplained neck lump and laryngeal cancer
stem: A 57-year-old adult presents with a persistent unexplained neck lump. Which diagnosis should be considered in the NICE head-and-neck cancer pathway?
why_correct: NICE recommends considering a suspected cancer pathway referral for laryngeal cancer in people aged 45 years or over with an unexplained neck lump.

why_others_wrong.B: Appendicitis is an acute abdominal condition and has no link to a persistent unexplained neck lump.
why_others_wrong.C: Renal cell carcinoma can rarely metastasise to the neck, but it is not the diagnosis the NICE head-and-neck pathway targets for a neck lump.
why_others_wrong.D: Osteoarthritis is a degenerative joint disease and does not present as a persistent unexplained neck lump.
why_others_wrong.E: Peptic ulcer disease causes epigastric pain and bleeding, not a neck lump, and is not part of the head-and-neck cancer pathway.

exam_trap: Option C (renal cell carcinoma) tempts because it can rarely metastasise to the neck, but the NICE head-and-neck pathway targets laryngeal cancer in adults aged 45 or over.
takeaway: Adult unexplained neck lump → investigate for head-and-neck malignancy.
source: NICE NG12, updated 2025.
thinking: Adult aged 45 or over ↓ persistent unexplained neck lump ↓ NICE suspected cancer criteria for laryngeal cancer include an unexplained neck lump or persistent hoarseness ↓ Laryngeal cancer
pearl: In an adult, a persistent lateral neck lump is metastatic squamous cell carcinoma until proven otherwise; the primary is most often in the upper aerodigestive tract, so the full head and neck must be examined.

subject: ENT: head & neck
title: Persistent oral ulcer
stem: A 61-year-old patient has an unexplained oral ulcer that has persisted for 4 weeks. What is the appropriate management?
why_correct: NICE recommends considering a suspected cancer pathway referral for unexplained oral ulceration lasting more than 3 weeks.

why_others_wrong.A: Reassurance alone is unsafe because an unexplained oral ulcer persisting beyond 3 weeks meets the NICE threshold for suspected oral cancer referral.
why_others_wrong.C: Prolonged antibiotics would delay diagnosis of a possible malignancy and are not a treatment for unexplained persistent oral ulceration.
why_others_wrong.D: Review in a year would allow a possible oral cancer to progress; this ulcer has already exceeded the 3-week threshold for urgent referral.
why_others_wrong.E: An ulcer persisting for 4 weeks needs examination and referral for possible cancer, not withholding further assessment.

exam_trap: Candidates choosing reassurance or prolonged antibiotics forget that persistence beyond 3 weeks is the red flag that converts a benign-looking ulcer into a suspected cancer referral.
takeaway: Unexplained oral ulcer >3 weeks → investigate for oral cancer.
source: NICE NG12, updated 2025.
thinking: Oral ulcer lasting 4 weeks ↓ unexplained and not healing ↓ NICE threshold for possible oral cancer is ulceration persisting more than 3 weeks ↓ Suspected cancer pathway referral
pearl: Most oral squamous cell carcinomas arise on the lateral border of the tongue or the floor of the mouth; smoking and alcohol act synergistically as the main risk factors.

subject: ENT: head & neck
title: Persistent oral cavity lump
stem: A patient presents with an unexplained lump in the oral cavity. Which professional should provide urgent assessment for possible oral cancer when the lesion has not yet been assessed by a dentist?
why_correct: NICE recommends urgent assessment by a dentist for an unexplained lump on the lip or in the oral cavity.

why_others_wrong.A: A cardiologist has no role in assessing oral cavity lesions for possible malignancy.
why_others_wrong.C: A gastroenterologist manages the gastrointestinal tract and is not the professional NICE names for assessing an unexplained oral lump.
why_others_wrong.D: A neurologist assesses nervous system disorders and is not involved in urgent assessment of an oral cavity lump.
why_others_wrong.E: A physiotherapist provides rehabilitation and does not examine or assess oral lesions for suspected cancer.

exam_trap: Do not confuse this with the separate suspected cancer pathway recommendation when a dentist has already assessed the lesion as suspicious.
takeaway: Unexplained oral/lip lump → urgent dental assessment.
source: NICE NG12, updated 2025.
thinking: Unexplained lump in the oral cavity ↓ not yet assessed by a dentist ↓ NICE recommends urgent dental assessment for possible oral cancer ↓ Dentist
pearl: If the dentist judges an oral lump or patch suspicious of cancer, NICE advises a suspected cancer pathway referral; GPs still refer directly for unexplained oral ulceration lasting more than 3 weeks or a persistent unexplained neck lump.

subject: ENT: head & neck
title: Red and white oral lesion
stem: A 58-year-old patient has a persistent red-and-white patch in the oral cavity. What is the appropriate principle?

options.D: Assume it is candidiasis without examination

why_correct: NICE identifies red or red-and-white oral patches consistent with erythroplakia or erythroleukoplakia as lesions requiring urgent assessment for possible oral cancer.

why_others_wrong.A: Absence of pain does not make a red-and-white patch benign; erythroplakia and erythroleukoplakia carry a significant risk of malignancy and need urgent assessment.
why_others_wrong.C: Topical antibiotics do not treat erythroplakia or erythroleukoplakia and indefinite use would delay diagnosis of a potentially malignant lesion.
why_others_wrong.D: Assuming candidiasis without examination risks missing erythroplakia or early oral cancer, which the persistence of the patch should raise.
why_others_wrong.E: A persistent red-and-white patch is a potentially malignant lesion that needs urgent assessment, so it cannot be left without follow-up.

exam_trap: Option D (assume candidiasis) catches candidates because thrush can look red and white, but a persistent patch must be assessed for erythroleukoplakia, not treated blind.
takeaway: Persistent red/white oral lesion → cancer pathway awareness.
source: NICE NG12, updated 2025.
thinking: Persistent red-and-white oral patch ↓ consistent with erythroleukoplakia ↓ red oral lesions carry the highest malignant potential ↓ NICE: urgent assessment for possible oral cancer ↓ Arrange appropriate urgent assessment
pearl: Erythroplakia carries a much higher risk of dysplasia or carcinoma than homogeneous leukoplakia, so any red component in a persistent oral patch increases concern and warrants biopsy.

subject: ENT: head & neck
title: Unexplained thyroid lump
stem: A 45-year-old woman is found to have an unexplained thyroid lump. What is the appropriate NICE recommendation?

options.B: Suspected cancer pathway referral should be considered

correct_answer: B. Suspected cancer pathway referral should be considered
why_correct: NICE recommends considering a suspected cancer pathway referral for an unexplained thyroid lump.

why_others_wrong.A: Being euthyroid does not exclude thyroid cancer, as most thyroid malignancies present with normal thyroid function.
why_others_wrong.C: Antibiotics have no role in an unexplained thyroid lump without features of infection and would delay assessment for cancer.
why_others_wrong.D: Thyroidectomy is not performed in primary care and surgery is decided only after specialist assessment with ultrasound and cytology.
why_others_wrong.E: NICE advises considering a suspected cancer pathway referral for an unexplained thyroid lump, so leaving it unassessed is inappropriate.

exam_trap: Option A (ignore if euthyroid) traps candidates who equate normal thyroid function with benign disease; most thyroid cancers present as a lump with normal thyroid function.
takeaway: Thyroid lump ≠ benign simply because TSH is normal.
source: NICE NG12, updated 2025.
thinking: Unexplained thyroid lump ↓ thyroid function does not distinguish benign from malignant ↓ NICE: consider a suspected cancer pathway referral ↓ Suspected cancer pathway referral should be considered
pearl: Assessment of a thyroid nodule is a triple assessment: clinical examination, ultrasound graded by U-score, and ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration cytology reported by Thy category.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
topic: Otitis media with effusion in a child
title: Otitis media with effusion in a child
stem: A 6-year-old child has suspected otitis media with effusion and hearing difficulties. Which investigation forms part of the formal assessment?
why_correct: NICE recommends formal assessment of suspected OME including clinical examination, hearing testing and tympanometry.

why_others_wrong.A: Colonoscopy examines the large bowel and has no role in assessing middle-ear effusion or hearing in a child.
why_others_wrong.C: Lumbar puncture samples cerebrospinal fluid for suspected meningitis and has no role in assessing uncomplicated glue ear.
why_others_wrong.D: CT abdomen does not assess the middle ear; OME is assessed with otoscopy, hearing testing and tympanometry.
why_others_wrong.E: Echocardiography images the heart and has no part in assessing middle-ear effusion or hearing.

exam_trap: OME is primarily an assessment and hearing problem, not automatically an acute infection.
takeaway: Suspected glue ear → otoscopy + hearing assessment + tympanometry.
source: NICE NG233, Otitis media with effusion in under 12s, 2023.
thinking: 6-year-old with suspected OME ↓ hearing difficulties ↓ formal assessment = examination, hearing testing and tympanometry ↓ tympanometry measures middle-ear compliance ↓ Tympanometry
pearl: A flat (type B) tympanogram with a normal ear canal volume indicates middle-ear effusion, whereas a flat trace with a large canal volume suggests a perforation or a patent grommet.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Antibiotics for glue ear
stem: A 5-year-old child has uncomplicated otitis media with effusion without evidence of acute infection. Which of the following should NOT be offered specifically for OME?
why_correct: NICE specifically recommends not offering antibiotics to treat OME.

why_others_wrong.A: Hearing assessment is a core part of OME management because it guides whether monitoring, hearing support or surgery is needed.
why_others_wrong.B: Supportive listening strategies, such as reducing background noise and facing the child when speaking, are recommended to help while OME resolves.
why_others_wrong.D: Auto-inflation can be considered in children with OME who are able to cooperate, so it is an appropriate option.
why_others_wrong.E: Discussing how hearing loss affects speech, learning and behaviour is part of recommended shared decision-making in OME.

exam_trap: Candidates may hesitate over auto-inflation (D), but it is a recommended option; antibiotics are the treatment NICE specifically advises against for OME.
takeaway: Glue ear ≠ acute otitis media → antibiotics are not routine treatment.
source: NICE NG233, 2023.
thinking: Uncomplicated OME without acute infection ↓ middle-ear fluid is not a bacterial infection to treat ↓ management is hearing assessment, support and observation, with auto-inflation or grommets in selected cases ↓ NICE advises not offering antibiotics ↓ Antibiotics
pearl: OME often resolves spontaneously, so NICE advises a period of active observation of about 3 months before considering grommets for persistent bilateral OME with hearing loss.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
topic: Steroids for otitis media with effusion
title: Steroids for otitis media with effusion
stem: A child has persistent OME-related hearing loss. Which of the following should NOT be offered for OME or OME-related hearing loss?

options.D: Consideration of grommets in appropriate cases

why_correct: NICE recommends against oral or nasal corticosteroids for OME or OME-related hearing loss.

why_others_wrong.B: Hearing support is recommended for OME-related hearing loss and is not a pharmacological treatment.
why_others_wrong.C: Audiological assessment is a recommended part of OME management and is an investigation rather than a drug treatment.
why_others_wrong.D: Grommets can be considered for persistent OME-related hearing loss and are a surgical option rather than a pharmacological one.
why_others_wrong.E: Changing the listening environment is a recommended supportive measure for OME-related hearing loss, not a drug treatment.

exam_trap: Candidates may think grommets (D) are excessive, but they are a recognised option for persistent hearing loss; oral or nasal steroids are not recommended.
takeaway: OME → no routine oral/nasal steroids.
source: NICE NG233, 2023.
thinking: Persistent OME-related hearing loss ↓ management is audiology, hearing support, listening strategies and grommets if criteria are met ↓ steroids give no lasting benefit in OME ↓ NICE advises against oral or nasal corticosteroids ↓ Oral corticosteroids
pearl: In children with trisomy 21, NICE advises hearing aids rather than grommets as the usual treatment for persistent OME with hearing loss.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Grommets and OME-related hearing loss
stem: A 7-year-old child has confirmed OME associated with hearing loss despite appropriate assessment and supportive management. Which intervention can be considered?
why_correct: NICE recommends considering grommets for children with OME-related hearing loss, with benefits and risks discussed as part of shared decision-making.

why_others_wrong.B: NICE recommends against antibiotics for OME, as the effusion is not an acute bacterial infection and long-term use adds harm without lasting benefit.
why_others_wrong.C: NICE advises against corticosteroids for OME, and long-term systemic steroids would expose a child to significant adverse effects without benefit.
why_others_wrong.D: Cochlear implantation is for severe to profound sensorineural loss, whereas OME causes a conductive loss that is usually mild to moderate and reversible.
why_others_wrong.E: Treatment options, including their benefits and risks, should be discussed with the family as part of shared decision-making.

exam_trap: Long-term antibiotics (B) tempt candidates as a medical alternative, but antibiotics are not recommended for OME; persistent OME with hearing loss is the indication for considering grommets.
takeaway: OME + hearing loss → grommets may be considered after appropriate assessment.
source: NICE NG233, 2023.
thinking: Confirmed OME in a 7-year-old ↓ associated hearing loss ↓ persists despite assessment and supportive management ↓ NICE: consider grommets with shared decision-making ↓ Grommet insertion
pearl: Grommets usually extrude spontaneously within about a year; common complications include otorrhoea and tympanic membrane changes such as tympanosclerosis or a persistent perforation.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: OME without hearing loss
stem: A 4-year-old child has OME confirmed on assessment but has no hearing loss. What is the most appropriate management principle?

options.C: Reassurance and no treatment specifically for OME

correct_answer: C. Reassurance and no treatment specifically for OME
why_correct: NICE advises that children with OME without hearing loss should generally be reassured because OME often resolves spontaneously and no treatment is necessary.

why_others_wrong.A: Grommets are considered for OME with hearing loss; without hearing loss, the effusion often resolves on its own and surgery is not needed.
why_others_wrong.B: Adenoidectomy is considered as an adjunct when grommets are planned, not as an immediate procedure for OME without hearing loss.
why_others_wrong.D: NICE advises against antibiotics for OME, which is non-infective middle-ear fluid that usually resolves spontaneously.
why_others_wrong.E: NICE advises against oral corticosteroids for OME, and a child without hearing loss usually needs reassurance only.

exam_trap: Immediate grommet insertion (A) tempts candidates who equate middle-ear fluid with surgery, but grommets are considered for OME with hearing loss, not fluid alone.
takeaway: OME without hearing loss → usually observe and support, not operate.
source: NICE NG233, 2023.
thinking: OME confirmed in a 4-year-old ↓ no hearing loss ↓ OME often resolves spontaneously ↓ surgery is reserved for hearing loss and drugs are not recommended ↓ Reassurance and no treatment specifically for OME
pearl: Children with Down syndrome or cleft palate are at high risk of persistent OME and need closer hearing surveillance; in Down syndrome, hearing aids are usually preferred to grommets.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: OME and adenoidectomy
stem: A child with OME-related hearing loss is being considered for grommet insertion. Which additional procedure should be considered when planning grommets, provided there is no abnormality of the palate?
why_correct: NICE recommends considering adjuvant adenoidectomy when planning grommets for OME, unless assessment indicates an abnormality with the palate.

why_others_wrong.A: Tonsillectomy is not recommended alongside grommets for OME; the recommended adjunct is adenoidectomy, since adenoids affect Eustachian tube function.
why_others_wrong.C: Total laryngectomy removes the larynx for advanced laryngeal cancer and has no relevance to glue ear.
why_others_wrong.D: Mastoidectomy is for chronic ear disease such as cholesteatoma or complicated mastoiditis, not a routine addition to grommets for OME.
why_others_wrong.E: Cochlear implantation treats severe to profound sensorineural loss, whereas OME causes a conductive loss that grommets address.

exam_trap: This is a conditional recommendation, not an instruction to perform adenoidectomy in every child with OME.
takeaway: OME + planned grommets → consider adenoidectomy, but assess the palate first.
source: NICE NG233, 2023.
thinking: OME with hearing loss ↓ grommets being planned ↓ adenoids contribute to Eustachian tube dysfunction ↓ palate assessed and normal ↓ Adjuvant adenoidectomy
pearl: Adenoidectomy is avoided in children with a cleft or submucous cleft palate because loss of adenoid tissue can cause velopharyngeal insufficiency and hypernasal speech; a bifid uvula is a clue to a submucous cleft.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo
stem: A 63-year-old woman develops brief episodes of rotational vertigo whenever she turns over in bed. Each episode lasts less than a minute. She has no hearing loss or neurological deficit. What is the most appropriate diagnostic bedside test?
why_correct: Transient rotational vertigo triggered by head movement is characteristic of BPPV. NICE recommends the Hallpike manoeuvre when performed by someone trained and experienced in its use.

why_others_wrong.A: Romberg's test assesses proprioceptive and vestibular balance in general but does not provoke the positional nystagmus that confirms BPPV.
why_others_wrong.C: Weber's test uses a tuning fork to lateralise hearing loss and is not useful here, as she has no hearing loss and the problem is positional vertigo.
why_others_wrong.D: Rinne's test compares air and bone conduction to detect conductive loss and does not test the posterior canal involved in BPPV.
why_others_wrong.E: Caloric testing is a laboratory test of horizontal canal function, not the bedside test for typical posterior canal BPPV.

exam_trap: Candidates choose the Rinne or Weber test (C, D) because vertigo seems to be an ear problem, but tuning-fork tests assess hearing and cannot provoke the positional nystagmus of BPPV.
takeaway: Brief positional vertigo → Hallpike.
source: NICE NG127, updated October 2023.
thinking: Brief rotational vertigo on turning over in bed ↓ episodes under a minute, no hearing loss or neurological deficit ↓ BPPV, usually of the posterior canal ↓ provoke positional nystagmus at the bedside ↓ Hallpike manoeuvre
pearl: A positive test gives torsional, upbeating nystagmus towards the lowermost ear after a short latency, fatiguing within about a minute; atypical or non-fatiguing nystagmus should raise concern for a central cause.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Treatment of BPPV
stem: A patient has typical BPPV confirmed by a trained clinician. There is no cervical-spine instability. Which treatment should be offered?
why_correct: NICE recommends a canalith repositioning manoeuvre such as the Epley manoeuvre when BPPV is diagnosed and the patient has no unstable cervical spine disease.

why_others_wrong.A: BPPV is caused by displaced otoconia in a semicircular canal, not infection, so antibiotics have no role.
why_others_wrong.C: Cochlear implantation is for severe to profound sensorineural hearing loss and plays no part in treating BPPV.
why_others_wrong.D: Steroids do not move displaced otoconia; typical BPPV is treated with a repositioning manoeuvre such as the Epley.
why_others_wrong.E: Mastoidectomy is for chronic middle-ear and mastoid disease such as cholesteatoma and does not treat BPPV.

exam_trap: The Epley manoeuvre is treatment for BPPV; it is not a general treatment for all vertigo.
takeaway: Confirmed BPPV → reposition the displaced canaliths.
source: NICE NG127, updated October 2023.
thinking: Typical BPPV confirmed by a trained clinician ↓ displaced otoconia in a semicircular canal ↓ no unstable cervical spine disease ↓ move the debris back out of the canal ↓ Canalith repositioning manoeuvre
pearl: Vestibular suppressant drugs are not recommended for BPPV; recurrence is common, and repeat repositioning remains effective.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: BPPV and unstable cervical spine
stem: A patient has classic positional vertigo, but also has unstable cervical spine disease. What is the appropriate approach?

options.A: Perform a forceful Epley manoeuvre regardless
options.B: Perform Hallpike and Epley repeatedly at home
options.C: Refer according to the local pathway

correct_answer: C. Refer according to the local pathway
why_correct: NICE advises referral when a trained clinician is not available to perform the manoeuvre or when the patient has unstable cervical spine disease.

why_others_wrong.A: An Epley manoeuvre involves significant neck rotation and extension, so performing it forcefully with an unstable cervical spine risks neurological injury.
why_others_wrong.B: Repeated home manoeuvres still involve the neck movements that are unsafe with unstable cervical spine disease, and they are not supervised.
why_others_wrong.D: BPPV is a mechanical problem caused by displaced otoconia, not infection, so antibiotics have no role.
why_others_wrong.E: Mastoid surgery treats chronic ear disease and is not a treatment for BPPV, even when neck disease rules out standard manoeuvres.

exam_trap: A correct manoeuvre can still be inappropriate when there is a significant cervical-spine contraindication.
takeaway: BPPV + unstable neck → do not force the manoeuvre.
source: NICE NG127, updated October 2023.
thinking: Classic positional vertigo ↓ unstable cervical spine disease ↓ repositioning needs neck rotation and extension ↓ contraindication, so refer via the local pathway ↓ Refer according to the local pathway
pearl: When neck movement is unsafe or restricted, specialist services can use modified repositioning techniques, such as on a tilting table, or vestibular rehabilitation instead of the standard manoeuvre.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Acute vestibular syndrome
stem: A 58-year-old develops sudden persistent vertigo, nausea, vomiting and gait unsteadiness. There is no obvious benign positional trigger. Which clinical assessment can help distinguish a peripheral vestibular disorder from a central cause when performed by an appropriately trained clinician?
why_correct: NICE recommends HINTS for adults with sudden-onset acute vestibular syndrome when a healthcare professional with appropriate training and experience is available.

why_others_wrong.B: Rinne's test detects conductive hearing loss and cannot separate peripheral vestibular disease from posterior-circulation stroke.
why_others_wrong.C: Weber's test lateralises hearing loss and does not assess the eye movement signs needed to tell central from peripheral vertigo.
why_others_wrong.D: A Snellen chart measures visual acuity and does not help localise the cause of acute vestibular syndrome.
why_others_wrong.E: The whispered voice test is a crude hearing screen and cannot distinguish a peripheral vestibular disorder from a central cause.

exam_trap: Candidates apply HINTS to any dizziness, but it is valid only in continuous acute vestibular syndrome, performed by a trained clinician; Rinne and Weber tests (B, C) assess hearing only.
takeaway: Acute vestibular syndrome → HINTS only in trained hands.
source: NICE NG127, updated October 2023.
thinking: Sudden persistent vertigo, nausea, vomiting and gait unsteadiness ↓ no benign positional trigger ↓ acute vestibular syndrome: peripheral versus central cause ↓ trained bedside eye-movement examination ↓ HINTS examination
pearl: HINTS stands for head impulse, nystagmus and test of skew; in trained hands it is more sensitive than early MRI for detecting posterior-circulation stroke in acute vestibular syndrome.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: HINTS suggesting stroke
stem: A trained clinician performs HINTS in a patient with acute vestibular syndrome. The patient has a normal head-impulse test, direction-changing nystagmus and skew deviation. What should happen next?
why_correct: These are central neurological signs on HINTS and NICE recommends immediate neuroimaging.

why_others_wrong.A: A normal head impulse with direction-changing nystagmus and skew deviation suggests posterior-circulation stroke, so routine ENT review would dangerously delay imaging.
why_others_wrong.B: These are central signs on HINTS, and reassurance could miss a posterior-circulation stroke that needs immediate neuroimaging.
why_others_wrong.D: The Epley manoeuvre treats BPPV, which causes brief positional attacks, not persistent vertigo with central HINTS signs.
why_others_wrong.E: Ear irrigation removes wax and has no role when HINTS findings point to a central cause such as stroke.

exam_trap: A normal head impulse test in this context is concerning rather than reassuring.
takeaway: Normal head impulse + direction-changing nystagmus/skew → think stroke.
source: NICE NG127, updated October 2023.
thinking: Acute vestibular syndrome ↓ normal head impulse test ↓ direction-changing nystagmus and skew deviation ↓ central pattern suggesting posterior-circulation stroke ↓ Immediate neuroimaging
pearl: The reassuring peripheral pattern is an abnormal head impulse with a corrective saccade, unidirectional horizontal nystagmus and no skew; any single central feature should be treated as stroke until proven otherwise.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: HINTS unavailable
stem: A patient has sudden-onset acute vestibular syndrome. No clinician trained in HINTS is available, and BPPV or postural hypotension does not explain the presentation. What is the appropriate management?

options.B: Immediate referral through the stroke pathway

correct_answer: B. Immediate referral through the stroke pathway
why_correct: NICE recommends immediate referral to exclude posterior-circulation stroke when trained HINTS assessment is unavailable and the presentation is not explained by BPPV or postural hypotension.

why_others_wrong.A: Discharge is unsafe because posterior-circulation stroke cannot be excluded without trained HINTS assessment in acute vestibular syndrome.
why_others_wrong.C: Routine audiology does not assess for stroke, which must be excluded urgently when acute vestibular syndrome is not explained by BPPV or postural hypotension.
why_others_wrong.D: There is nothing to suggest infection, and antibiotics would delay urgent assessment for posterior-circulation stroke.
why_others_wrong.E: Ear irrigation removes wax and does nothing to exclude posterior-circulation stroke in acute vestibular syndrome.

exam_trap: Candidates discharge with reassurance (A) when HINTS cannot be performed, but without a trained assessment stroke has not been excluded, so immediate stroke-pathway referral is needed.
takeaway: Acute vestibular syndrome + no trained HINTS clinician → urgent stroke assessment.
source: NICE NG127, updated October 2023.
thinking: Sudden-onset acute vestibular syndrome ↓ no clinician trained in HINTS ↓ not explained by BPPV or postural hypotension ↓ posterior-circulation stroke cannot be excluded ↓ Immediate referral through the stroke pathway
pearl: Posterior-circulation strokes are easily missed because limb power may be normal and early CT is insensitive in the posterior fossa; inability to sit or walk unaided is an important red flag.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Vestibular migraine
stem: A 31-year-old woman has recurrent episodes of dizziness lasting several hours. She has a history of recurrent migraine headaches. Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: NICE advises clinicians to consider vestibular migraine in adults with recurrent episodes lasting 5 minutes to 72 hours and a history of recurrent headache.

why_others_wrong.B: Acute mastoiditis presents with post-auricular pain, swelling and fever after otitis media, not recurrent dizzy spells in someone with migraine.
why_others_wrong.C: Otosclerosis mainly causes progressive conductive hearing loss, not recurrent episodes of dizziness lasting hours with a migraine history.
why_others_wrong.D: Cholesteatoma usually presents with foul-smelling discharge and conductive hearing loss rather than recurrent episodic dizziness linked to migraine.
why_others_wrong.E: Acute otitis media causes ear pain and fever, usually in children, and does not explain recurrent dizzy spells in an adult with migraine.

exam_trap: Vestibular migraine can occur even when headache is not present during every vertigo episode.
takeaway: Recurrent vertigo 5 min–72 h + migraine history → vestibular migraine.
source: NICE NG127, updated October 2023.
thinking: Recurrent dizziness lasting several hours ↓ episodes within the 5 minutes to 72 hours range ↓ history of recurrent migraine headaches ↓ nothing in the stem suggests ear infection or progressive hearing loss ↓ Vestibular migraine
pearl: Vestibular migraine is a common cause of recurrent spontaneous vertigo and can mimic Ménière's disease, but hearing loss is usually absent or mild and does not progress.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Dizziness after head injury
stem: A patient develops brief recurrent positional vertigo several days after a head injury. Which diagnosis should be considered?

options.E: Acoustic neuroma as the only possibility

why_correct: NICE notes that BPPV is common after head injury.

why_others_wrong.B: Ménière's disease causes attacks lasting minutes to hours with fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus and fullness, not brief positional vertigo after head injury.
why_others_wrong.C: Otosclerosis causes progressive conductive hearing loss and is not linked to brief positional vertigo after head trauma.
why_others_wrong.D: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma may present with unilateral glue ear, nasal obstruction or neck lumps, not brief positional vertigo after a head injury.
why_others_wrong.E: Vestibular schwannoma typically causes gradual unilateral hearing loss and tinnitus, not brief positional vertigo that starts after head injury.

exam_trap: Head trauma can precipitate BPPV; the positional nature and brief attacks remain important.
takeaway: Head injury + brief positional vertigo → BPPV is a classic association.
source: NICE NG127, updated October 2023.
thinking: Brief recurrent positional vertigo ↓ starting days after a head injury ↓ trauma can dislodge otoconia into a semicircular canal ↓ BPPV is common after head injury ↓ BPPV
pearl: Post-traumatic BPPV is more often bilateral or multi-canal than idiopathic BPPV and may need repeated repositioning; vertigo with hearing loss after head trauma should raise concern for a temporal bone fracture.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Sudden dizziness with new deafness
stem: A patient develops sudden severe vertigo with new unilateral deafness and marked unsteadiness. What is the safest initial approach?

options.B: Immediate assessment for a central neurological cause

correct_answer: B. Immediate assessment for a central neurological cause
why_correct: NICE identifies sudden-onset dizziness with new-onset deafness or other focal neurological features as requiring immediate referral when BPPV or postural hypotension does not account for the presentation.

why_others_wrong.A: BPPV causes brief positional attacks without hearing loss, so it cannot explain sudden severe vertigo with new unilateral deafness.
why_others_wrong.C: Waiting 6 months ignores new deafness with acute vertigo, which can indicate posterior-circulation stroke and needs immediate assessment.
why_others_wrong.D: Ear syringing removes wax and does not address sudden vertigo with new deafness, where a central cause must be excluded first.
why_others_wrong.E: Reassurance is unsafe because new deafness with acute dizziness and marked unsteadiness is a red flag for a central neurological cause.

exam_trap: Candidates assume BPPV (A) or another benign peripheral cause, but new deafness with acute vertigo and marked unsteadiness can be a posterior-circulation stroke needing immediate assessment.
takeaway: Acute dizziness + new deafness → exclude posterior circulation pathology.
source: NICE NG127, updated October 2023.
thinking: Sudden severe vertigo ↓ new unilateral deafness and marked unsteadiness ↓ BPPV does not cause hearing loss or persistent imbalance ↓ focal red flags mean a central cause must be excluded ↓ Immediate assessment for a central neurological cause
pearl: Occlusion of the anterior inferior cerebellar artery, which gives rise to the labyrinthine artery in most people, can cause acute vertigo with sudden deafness, so hearing loss does not guarantee a peripheral cause.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Acute otitis media: expected course
stem: A 4-year-old child has uncomplicated acute otitis media. Which statement about the natural history is most accurate?

options.B: Most children improve within about 3 days

correct_answer: B. Most children improve within about 3 days
why_correct: NICE states that symptoms usually last about 3 days, although they can persist for up to 1 week, and most children improve without antibiotics.

why_others_wrong.A: Acute otitis media is usually self-limiting, with symptoms lasting about 3 days and up to about a week, not several months.
why_others_wrong.C: Most children with uncomplicated acute otitis media improve without antibiotics, so NICE supports no, back-up or immediate prescribing depending on the situation.
why_others_wrong.D: Mastoiditis is a rare complication of acute otitis media, not an expected part of its natural history.
why_others_wrong.E: Uncomplicated acute otitis media usually settles with analgesia and does not need surgery.

exam_trap: Candidates choose 'all children require antibiotics' (C) by assuming AOM is always bacterial, but most children improve within about 3 days without antibiotics.
takeaway: AOM → usually self-limiting; most improve within ~3 days.
source: NICE NG91, updated March 2022.
thinking: 4-year-old with uncomplicated AOM ↓ usually self-limiting ↓ symptoms last about 3 days, up to a week ↓ most improve without antibiotics ↓ Most children improve within about 3 days
pearl: The commonest bacterial causes of AOM are Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae and Moraxella catarrhalis; when an antibiotic is needed, amoxicillin is the usual first choice in the UK.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Acute otitis media and analgesia
stem: A child with acute otitis media has significant ear pain. Which treatment should be offered for symptom control?
why_correct: NICE recommends regular paracetamol or ibuprofen for pain in children with acute otitis media.

why_others_wrong.B: Oral steroids are not recommended for acute otitis media and would expose the child to side effects without helping the pain.
why_others_wrong.C: Anticoagulation prevents thrombosis and has no role in the pain of acute otitis media.
why_others_wrong.D: Grommets are for persistent OME with hearing loss or recurrent infection, not immediate symptom control in a single episode.
why_others_wrong.E: Antihistamines do not help acute otitis media symptoms, so they are not a routine treatment.

exam_trap: Candidates jump to antibiotics or grommets (D) and forget analgesia, yet regular paracetamol or ibuprofen is core symptom treatment whether or not an antibiotic is prescribed.
takeaway: AOM management starts with pain control.
source: NICE NG91, updated March 2022.
thinking: Child with AOM ↓ significant ear pain ↓ symptom control comes first ↓ NICE: regular paracetamol or ibuprofen ↓ Regular paracetamol or ibuprofen
pearl: NICE also allows anaesthetic-analgesic ear drops to be considered for pain when an immediate oral antibiotic is not given and there is no eardrum perforation or otorrhoea.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Acute otitis media: antihistamines
stem: A parent asks whether an antihistamine will speed recovery from acute otitis media. What should be explained?

options.B: They reduce the need for analgesia
options.C: Evidence suggests they do not help symptoms

correct_answer: C. Evidence suggests they do not help symptoms
why_correct: NICE advises explaining that decongestants and antihistamines do not help symptoms of acute otitis media.

why_others_wrong.A: Antihistamines do not cure acute otitis media; NICE advises they do not help symptoms, and the condition is usually self-limiting.
why_others_wrong.B: Antihistamines do not relieve ear pain, so they do not reduce the need for analgesia such as paracetamol or ibuprofen.
why_others_wrong.D: There is no evidence that antihistamines prevent mastoiditis, which is a rare complication of acute otitis media.
why_others_wrong.E: Antihistamines are not recommended in acute otitis media, so they are not a step that must come before antibiotics.

exam_trap: Candidates assume antihistamines help because the nose is often blocked, but NICE states antihistamines and decongestants do not improve acute otitis media symptoms.
takeaway: AOM → antihistamines/decongestants do not improve symptoms.
source: NICE NG91, updated March 2022.
thinking: Parent asks about antihistamines ↓ AOM is a middle-ear infection, not an allergic process ↓ NICE: antihistamines and decongestants do not help symptoms ↓ explain this and focus on analgesia ↓ Evidence suggests they do not help symptoms
pearl: AOM often follows a viral upper respiratory infection causing Eustachian tube dysfunction, and young children are prone because their Eustachian tubes are shorter and more horizontal.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Acute otitis media: otorrhoea
stem: A 3-year-old child has acute otitis media with otorrhoea. Which statement is correct?

options.B: This group may be more likely to benefit from antibiotics

correct_answer: B. This group may be more likely to benefit from antibiotics
why_correct: NICE identifies children of any age with otorrhoea as a group that may be more likely to benefit from antibiotic treatment, while still allowing clinical judgement regarding no, back-up or immediate antibiotics.

why_others_wrong.A: NICE identifies children with otorrhoea as more likely to benefit from antibiotics, so antibiotics can be considered.
why_others_wrong.C: Mastoidectomy is for complications such as coalescent mastoiditis or cholesteatoma, not otorrhoea from a perforated eardrum in acute otitis media.
why_others_wrong.D: Otorrhoea in acute otitis media usually reflects a small perforation releasing pus and does not on its own point to cholesteatoma.
why_others_wrong.E: Pain relief with paracetamol or ibuprofen is recommended for acute otitis media whether or not there is discharge.

exam_trap: Otorrhoea increases the likelihood of benefit but does not mean every child automatically requires immediate antibiotics.
takeaway: AOM + otorrhoea → antibiotic benefit is more plausible, but assess individually.
source: NICE NG91, updated March 2022.
thinking: 3-year-old with AOM ↓ otorrhoea means the drum has perforated and is discharging ↓ NICE: children with otorrhoea are more likely to benefit from antibiotics ↓ still individual judgement on no, back-up or immediate antibiotic ↓ This group may be more likely to benefit from antibiotics
pearl: Perforation in AOM often relieves the pain as pus drains, and most such perforations heal spontaneously; persistent discharge or a perforation that fails to heal needs ENT review.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
topic: Bilateral AOM in a young child
title: Bilateral AOM in a young child
stem: A 20-month-old child has acute otitis media affecting both ears and is otherwise clinically stable. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Bilateral disease is irrelevant to management
options.B: Children under 2 with bilateral infection may be more likely to benefit from antibiotics

correct_answer: B. Children under 2 with bilateral infection may be more likely to benefit from antibiotics
why_correct: NICE identifies children under 2 years with bilateral acute otitis media as a group more likely to benefit from antibiotics.
