why_others_wrong.A: Bilateral disease matters because NICE identifies children under 2 with bilateral acute otitis media as more likely to benefit from antibiotics.
why_others_wrong.C: Uncomplicated bilateral acute otitis media in a stable child is managed medically, and surgery is not routinely needed.
why_others_wrong.D: Antibiotics are not contraindicated; a child under 2 with bilateral infection is in a group more likely to benefit from them.
why_others_wrong.E: Mastoidectomy is for complications such as coalescent mastoiditis, not first-line treatment of uncomplicated bilateral acute otitis media.

exam_trap: Candidates choose 'bilateral disease is irrelevant' (A), missing that NICE identifies children under 2 with bilateral AOM as more likely to benefit from antibiotics.
takeaway: AOM under 2 + bilateral → consider greater likelihood of antibiotic benefit.
source: NICE NG91, updated March 2022.
thinking: 20-month-old child ↓ AOM affecting both ears ↓ under 2 years with bilateral infection ↓ NICE group more likely to benefit from antibiotics ↓ Children under 2 with bilateral infection may be more likely to benefit from antibiotics
pearl: Children who are systemically very unwell or at high risk of complications should receive an immediate antibiotic, with amoxicillin the usual first choice in the UK.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Acute otitis media with mastoiditis
stem: A child with acute otitis media develops post-auricular swelling and tenderness with systemic deterioration. What is the appropriate management?
why_correct: NICE recommends hospital referral when acute otitis media is associated with acute complications including mastoiditis.

why_others_wrong.A: Post-auricular swelling and tenderness with systemic deterioration suggest mastoiditis, which needs hospital referral rather than community follow-up.
why_others_wrong.C: Reassurance is unsafe because mastoiditis can progress to subperiosteal abscess or intracranial spread without hospital treatment.
why_others_wrong.D: Wax treatment has no role here; post-auricular swelling in an unwell child with otitis media suggests mastoiditis needing hospital care.
why_others_wrong.E: Suspected mastoiditis is an acute complication of otitis media that needs hospital assessment, usually with IV antibiotics and sometimes imaging.

exam_trap: Candidates treat this as ordinary AOM with community follow-up (A), but post-auricular swelling with systemic deterioration indicates mastoiditis, which needs hospital referral.
takeaway: AOM + mastoiditis → hospital.
source: NICE NG91, updated March 2022.
thinking: Child with AOM ↓ post-auricular swelling and tenderness ↓ systemic deterioration ↓ acute mastoiditis ↓ Hospital referral
pearl: Acute mastoiditis classically pushes the pinna forwards and outwards; complications include subperiosteal abscess, facial palsy, sigmoid sinus thrombosis and intracranial abscess, so imaging is often needed.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
topic: Acute otitis media with facial paralysis
title: Acute otitis media with facial paralysis
stem: A child with acute otitis media develops ipsilateral facial nerve paralysis. What should happen?

options.C: Treat only with topical ear drops

why_correct: Facial nerve paralysis is listed by NICE as an acute complication of AOM requiring hospital referral.

why_others_wrong.A: Facial nerve paralysis is an acute complication of otitis media needing hospital referral, not a review in 6 months.
why_others_wrong.C: Topical drops alone do not treat facial nerve involvement from acute otitis media, which needs hospital assessment and management.
why_others_wrong.D: A hearing aid does not address facial nerve paralysis, which signals complicated otitis media needing hospital referral.
why_others_wrong.E: Facial paralysis complicating otitis media needs hospital assessment, which may include imaging and specialist ENT management.

exam_trap: Facial paralysis is a complication, not a routine feature of uncomplicated AOM.
takeaway: AOM + facial palsy = complicated disease → hospital.
source: NICE NG91, updated March 2022.
thinking: Child with AOM ↓ ipsilateral facial nerve paralysis ↓ facial nerve runs through the middle ear ↓ acute complication of AOM ↓ Hospital referral
pearl: The tympanic segment of the facial nerve lies in the medial wall of the middle ear, where its bony canal is often dehiscent, so otitis media can cause a lower motor neurone palsy that usually recovers when the infection is treated.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Acute otitis media with meningitis
stem: A child with acute otitis media develops fever, neck stiffness and reduced consciousness. What is the most appropriate action?
why_correct: Meningitis is a serious complication associated with acute otitis media and requires emergency hospital management.

why_others_wrong.A: Fever, neck stiffness and reduced consciousness suggest meningitis, which needs emergency hospital care rather than a routine ENT referral.
why_others_wrong.C: Antihistamines do not treat meningitis, and any delay in emergency treatment worsens outcomes.
why_others_wrong.D: Ear irrigation is irrelevant and delays emergency care when a child with otitis media shows signs of meningitis.
why_others_wrong.E: Observation at home is unsafe because suspected meningitis with reduced consciousness needs emergency hospital management.

exam_trap: Do not anchor on the ear infection when systemic neurological deterioration develops.
takeaway: AOM + meningism/reduced consciousness → emergency management.
source: NICE NG91, updated March 2022.
thinking: Child with AOM ↓ fever, neck stiffness and reduced consciousness ↓ suspected meningitis as an intracranial complication ↓ emergency hospital management ↓ Hospital emergency management
pearl: Otogenic intracranial complications include meningitis, brain abscess (often temporal lobe or cerebellar) and sigmoid sinus thrombosis, and pneumococcus is a common cause of otogenic meningitis.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Acute otitis media review
stem: A child with acute otitis media is being managed without an immediate antibiotic prescription. When should the family seek further medical assessment?

options.B: If symptoms worsen rapidly or significantly, fail to start improving after 3 days, or the child becomes systemically very unwell
options.C: Only if hearing loss persists for 1 year

correct_answer: B. If symptoms worsen rapidly or significantly, fail to start improving after 3 days, or the child becomes systemically very unwell
why_correct: NICE gives these safety-netting criteria when an antibiotic is not prescribed immediately.

why_others_wrong.A: Waiting 6 months would miss complications; families should seek help if the child worsens, fails to improve after 3 days or becomes very unwell.
why_others_wrong.C: Waiting a year for persistent hearing loss ignores acute warning signs such as rapid worsening or systemic illness that need prompt review.
why_others_wrong.D: Waiting for a second episode ignores deterioration during the current episode, which is what safety-netting advice is meant to catch.
why_others_wrong.E: Safety-netting is needed when antibiotics are not given immediately, because some children worsen or develop complications.

exam_trap: Candidates may think no antibiotic means no follow-up (E), but withholding antibiotics needs explicit safety-netting about worsening, no improvement after 3 days or systemic illness.
takeaway: No immediate antibiotic → explicit 3-day/worsening/systemic safety-net.
source: NICE NG91, updated March 2022.
thinking: AOM managed without an immediate antibiotic ↓ explicit safety-netting is needed ↓ NICE triggers: rapid or significant worsening, no improvement after 3 days, systemic illness ↓ Seek assessment if symptoms worsen rapidly or significantly, fail to start improving after 3 days, or the child becomes systemically very unwell
pearl: A back-up antibiotic prescription lets families start treatment only if symptoms fail to improve or worsen, reducing antibiotic use while keeping a route to treatment.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Adult persistent otorrhoea
stem: An adult has recurrent ear discharge despite appropriate treatment. The ear canal and tympanic membrane appear abnormal. What is the appropriate next step?
why_correct: Discharge that recurs despite treatment, together with an abnormal ear canal and eardrum, suggests chronic ear disease such as cholesteatoma and warrants ENT assessment.

why_others_wrong.A: Recurrent discharge despite treatment with an abnormal ear canal and eardrum may indicate chronic ear disease such as cholesteatoma, so it needs ENT assessment.
why_others_wrong.C: A cardiovascular review does not address persistent otorrhoea with abnormal ear findings, which needs ENT assessment.
why_others_wrong.D: Antihistamines do not treat chronic ear discharge or the underlying middle-ear or ear-canal disease suggested here.
why_others_wrong.E: An abnormal canal and eardrum with recurrent discharge needs specialist examination, often with microscopy, to find the cause.

exam_trap: Candidates keep repeating medical treatment such as antihistamines (D), but discharge recurring despite treatment with an abnormal canal and eardrum suggests cholesteatoma and needs ENT assessment.
takeaway: Persistent/recurrent otorrhoea → ENT assessment.
source: NICE NG98, updated October 2023.
thinking: Adult with recurrent ear discharge ↓ persists despite appropriate treatment ↓ abnormal ear canal and tympanic membrane ↓ possible chronic ear disease such as cholesteatoma ↓ ENT referral
pearl: Cholesteatoma typically causes painless, foul-smelling discharge and conductive loss with an attic retraction or crust; untreated it erodes the ossicles and can cause facial palsy, labyrinthine fistula or intracranial infection.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Adult persistent ear pain
stem: An adult has ear pain lasting 10 days despite first-line treatment. There is no obvious acute infection explaining the persistence. What is the appropriate management?
why_correct: Ear pain lasting 1 week or more despite first-line treatment, with no acute cause found, needs ENT assessment, because persistent otalgia may be referred from head and neck disease.

why_others_wrong.A: Ear pain persisting for over a week despite first-line treatment needs further assessment, as it may be referred pain from head and neck pathology.
why_others_wrong.C: Repeated irrigation is not an investigation or treatment for persistent unexplained otalgia and risks trauma to the ear canal.
why_others_wrong.D: Waiting 2 years risks missing serious causes, including head and neck cancer presenting as referred otalgia.
why_others_wrong.E: A hearing aid does not address pain and would leave the cause of persistent otalgia uninvestigated.

exam_trap: Candidates reassure or keep irrigating (A, C) because no ear infection is found, but persistent unexplained otalgia may be referred pain from head and neck cancer.
takeaway: Persistent otalgia despite treatment → investigate the cause.
source: NICE NG98, updated October 2023.
thinking: Adult ear pain for 10 days ↓ failed first-line treatment ↓ no acute infection to explain it ↓ consider referred otalgia from head and neck disease ↓ ENT referral
pearl: Referred otalgia travels via the trigeminal, glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves and upper cervical nerves, so persistent ear pain with a normal ear should prompt examination of the oropharynx, larynx and hypopharynx for cancer.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Abnormal tympanic membrane
stem: An adult has hearing loss and an abnormal tympanic membrane with a visible polypoid growth. What is the appropriate management?
why_correct: NICE lists abnormal appearance of the outer ear or eardrum, including polyp formation and abnormal bony or skin growths, as indications to consider ENT referral.

why_others_wrong.A: A polypoid growth on the eardrum may indicate chronic suppurative otitis media, cholesteatoma or, rarely, a tumour, so reassurance is unsafe.
why_others_wrong.C: Fitting a hearing aid without ENT assessment would leave the polyp and any underlying chronic ear disease undiagnosed.
why_others_wrong.D: Indefinite antibiotics do not diagnose or treat a polyp or possible cholesteatoma and risk resistance; ENT assessment is needed.
why_others_wrong.E: A polypoid growth on the eardrum needs specialist assessment to find the cause, so it cannot be left without follow-up.

exam_trap: A polyp in the ear canal or middle-ear region can represent significant chronic ear disease.
takeaway: Abnormal TM/polyp → ENT, not simple hearing-aid management.
source: NICE NG98, updated October 2023.
thinking: Adult with hearing loss ↓ abnormal tympanic membrane ↓ visible polypoid growth ↓ suggests chronic suppurative otitis media, cholesteatoma or tumour ↓ ENT referral
pearl: An aural polyp is often granulation tissue overlying cholesteatoma, so it should not be avulsed blindly because it may be attached to the ossicles or an exposed facial nerve.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Middle-ear effusion after URTI
stem: An adult develops a middle-ear effusion during an upper respiratory tract infection. It resolves as the infection improves. Which statement is most appropriate?

options.B: Persistent effusion after the infection would warrant further assessment

correct_answer: B. Persistent effusion after the infection would warrant further assessment
why_correct: NICE specifically highlights middle-ear effusion in the absence of an acute URTI, or that persists after an acute URTI, as a reason to consider ENT referral.

why_others_wrong.A: An effusion that clears as the URTI settles is explained by transient Eustachian tube dysfunction; nasopharyngeal carcinoma becomes a concern when effusion is unilateral, persistent or unexplained.
why_others_wrong.C: Cochlear implantation is for severe-to-profound sensorineural loss unhelped by hearing aids, not a self-limiting conductive effusion that has already resolved.
why_others_wrong.D: A post-viral effusion that resolves with the infection needs no antibiotics, let alone a long course; persistence prompts assessment rather than prolonged antimicrobials.
why_others_wrong.E: Otoscopic examination is part of assessing any ear symptom, and a persistent adult effusion needs examination of the postnasal space to exclude a nasopharyngeal lesion.

exam_trap: Candidates choose nasopharyngeal carcinoma (A) for any adult effusion, but an effusion that clears with a URTI is benign; persistence or absence of an infective cause is the warning sign.
takeaway: Adult effusion + no/persistent URTI → investigate.
source: NICE NG98, updated October 2023.
thinking: Adult middle-ear effusion during a URTI ↓ resolves as the infection improves ↓ explained by transient Eustachian tube dysfunction ↓ effusion persisting after, or without, a URTI would need assessment ↓ Persistent effusion after the infection would warrant further assessment
pearl: Persistent unilateral middle-ear effusion in an adult is a classic presentation of nasopharyngeal carcinoma obstructing the Eustachian tube opening, so the postnasal space should be examined endoscopically.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Recurrent vertigo and hearing loss
stem: An adult has recurrent episodes of vertigo with fluctuating hearing loss that are not associated with an upper respiratory infection. What is the appropriate next step?
why_correct: NICE recommends considering referral for diagnostic investigation where hearing loss fluctuates without an associated URTI, particularly when accompanied by recurrent vertigo.

why_others_wrong.A: Fluctuating hearing loss with recurrent vertigo points to inner-ear disease such as Ménière's disease, so dismissing the hearing symptoms risks missing a treatable or serious cause.
why_others_wrong.C: Ear syringing removes wax, which causes a steady conductive loss and does not explain episodic vertigo with fluctuating hearing.
why_others_wrong.D: Tonsillectomy treats recurrent tonsillitis or obstructive tonsils and has no role in episodic vestibular and cochlear symptoms.
why_others_wrong.E: There is no infection here, as the episodes are unrelated to URTI, so antibiotics would not address the likely inner-ear cause.

exam_trap: Fluctuating hearing loss plus vertigo suggests inner-ear pathology rather than simple conductive disease.
takeaway: Fluctuating hearing loss + recurrent vertigo → audiovestibular/ENT assessment.
source: NICE NG98, updated October 2023.
thinking: Recurrent episodes of vertigo ↓ fluctuating hearing loss ↓ not related to URTI ↓ suggests inner-ear disease such as Ménière's disease ↓ Specialist ENT/audiovestibular assessment
pearl: Ménière's disease typically causes vertigo attacks lasting 20 minutes to 12 hours with fluctuating low-frequency sensorineural loss, tinnitus and aural fullness, reflecting endolymphatic hydrops.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Tinnitus with recurrent vertigo
stem: A patient has persistent tinnitus associated with recurrent episodes of vertigo. What is the appropriate principle?

options.C: Treat as impacted wax without examination

why_correct: NICE identifies persistent tinnitus associated with vestibular symptoms and recurrent/persistent vertigo as requiring assessment according to the relevant pathway.

why_others_wrong.A: Tinnitus accompanied by recurrent vertigo suggests vestibular or otological pathology, such as Ménière's disease or a vestibular schwannoma, which needs further assessment.
why_others_wrong.C: Wax cannot be diagnosed without otoscopy, and impacted wax would not explain recurrent episodes of vertigo.
why_others_wrong.D: Nothing in the stem suggests infection, and antibiotics do not treat the likely vestibular or inner-ear cause of these symptoms.
why_others_wrong.E: Laryngectomy is major surgery for laryngeal cancer and bears no relation to tinnitus or vertigo, which arise from the ear and vestibular system.

exam_trap: Candidates treat this as isolated benign tinnitus needing no action (A), but tinnitus with recurrent vertigo suggests vestibular or otological disease needing specialist assessment.
takeaway: Tinnitus + recurrent vertigo → investigate the vestibular/otological cause.
source: NICE NG155, 2020; NICE NG98, updated 2023.
thinking: Persistent tinnitus ↓ recurrent episodes of vertigo ↓ vestibular symptoms broaden the differential beyond benign tinnitus ↓ needs pathway assessment for an otological or vestibular cause ↓ Consider specialist assessment
pearl: Assessment of tinnitus with vertigo includes otoscopy and pure-tone audiometry, with MRI of the internal auditory meati when symptoms are unilateral or asymmetric to exclude vestibular schwannoma.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Distressing tinnitus
stem: A patient with tinnitus remains severely distressed despite initial tinnitus support, and the distress is preventing normal daily activities. What does NICE recommend?
why_correct: NICE recommends referral for assessment and management within 2 weeks when tinnitus causes significant distress affecting mental wellbeing despite initial support.

why_others_wrong.A: NICE treats significant tinnitus-related distress as a reason for expedited referral, because the psychological impact is the main driver of disability and can include risk to mental health.
why_others_wrong.C: A five-year review would leave someone whose daily life is already disrupted without help; NICE advises assessment within 2 weeks when distress persists despite initial support.
why_others_wrong.D: Mastoidectomy treats mastoid disease such as cholesteatoma and does nothing for distress caused by tinnitus.
why_others_wrong.E: There is no infection to treat, and antibiotics have no effect on tinnitus or the distress it causes.

exam_trap: The referral criterion is significant persistent distress, not merely the existence of tinnitus.
takeaway: Tinnitus causing major persistent distress → expedited assessment.
source: NICE NG155, 2020.
thinking: Tinnitus ↓ severe distress despite initial tinnitus support ↓ distress preventing normal daily activities ↓ NICE: referral for assessment within 2 weeks ↓ Assessment within 2 weeks
pearl: Tinnitus distress is closely linked with anxiety, depression and insomnia, so a mental health risk assessment is part of the review, and anyone at risk of suicide needs immediate crisis referral.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: OME reassessment
stem: A child has bilateral OME with associated hearing loss and is managed initially without surgery. When should hearing be reassessed?

options.E: Only when the child becomes an adult

why_correct: NICE recommends reassessing hearing after 3 months in children with bilateral OME and hearing loss.

why_others_wrong.A: One week is too early to judge, because OME often resolves spontaneously over weeks to months; NICE sets the review at 3 months.
why_others_wrong.B: One month allows too little time for the natural resolution of OME; NICE sets the reassessment at 3 months.
why_others_wrong.D: Waiting a year would leave a child with bilateral hearing loss unmonitored through a critical period for speech, language and learning.
why_others_wrong.E: Delaying review until adulthood would ignore the effect of hearing loss on development and schooling; NICE advises reassessment at 3 months.

exam_trap: Do not confuse this with the approach to children who have OME without hearing loss.
takeaway: Bilateral OME + hearing loss → reassess at 3 months.
source: NICE NG233, 2023.
thinking: Bilateral OME ↓ associated hearing loss ↓ managed initially without surgery ↓ many effusions resolve within months ↓ 3 months
pearl: If bilateral OME with hearing loss persists at reassessment, options include grommets, with or without adjuvant adenoidectomy, or hearing aids, chosen with the family.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Unilateral OME with hearing loss
stem: A child has unilateral OME associated with hearing loss. Which is the appropriate initial reassessment strategy?
correct_answer: B. Consider hearing reassessment after 3 months
why_correct: NICE recommends considering reassessment of hearing after 3 months for unilateral OME with hearing loss.

why_others_wrong.A: Unilateral OME with hearing loss still warrants monitoring, and NICE advises considering hearing reassessment after 3 months.
why_others_wrong.C: Cochlear implantation is for severe-to-profound sensorineural loss, not a conductive loss from middle-ear fluid that often resolves on its own.
why_others_wrong.D: NICE advises against antibiotics for OME, because any benefit is small and short-lived and does not outweigh side effects and antimicrobial resistance.
why_others_wrong.E: Tonsillectomy does not treat OME; if surgery is needed, grommets with or without adenoidectomy are the relevant options.

exam_trap: The recommendation differs from bilateral OME but still centres on monitoring hearing and impact.
takeaway: Unilateral OME + hearing loss → consider 3-month reassessment.
source: NICE NG233, 2023.
thinking: Unilateral OME ↓ associated hearing loss ↓ one normal ear usually limits the impact ↓ NICE: consider reassessing hearing after 3 months ↓ Consider hearing reassessment after 3 months
pearl: Decisions in OME depend on the impact on speech, language, learning and behaviour, not only the audiogram, so these should be reviewed alongside the hearing test.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: OME and hearing aids
stem: A child has persistent OME-related hearing loss. The family does not want surgery. Which non-surgical option can be considered?
why_correct: NICE recommends considering air-conduction hearing aids or bone-conduction devices for children with OME-related hearing loss.

why_others_wrong.B: Long-term antibiotics are not recommended for OME, as any benefit is small and short-lived and they add resistance and side effects.
why_others_wrong.C: Oral corticosteroids have no lasting benefit in OME and carry systemic side effects, so NICE does not recommend them.
why_others_wrong.D: Decongestants do not speed the resolution of OME and are not recommended for its treatment.
why_others_wrong.E: Proton-pump inhibitors target acid reflux and are not a treatment for OME-related hearing loss.

exam_trap: Hearing support can be an alternative to surgical treatment depending on the individual child and circumstances.
takeaway: OME-related hearing loss → hearing support is a legitimate treatment option.
source: NICE NG233, 2023.
thinking: Persistent OME-related hearing loss ↓ family declines surgery ↓ antibiotics, steroids and decongestants are not recommended ↓ NICE: consider air- or bone-conduction hearing aids ↓ Hearing aid
pearl: Hearing aids for OME are usually temporary because the effusion tends to resolve, and they are often preferred in children with Down syndrome, whose narrow ear canals make grommets difficult.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: OME and adenoid hypertrophy
stem: A child has recurrent OME and symptoms suggesting adenoid hypertrophy. Which anatomical structure is particularly relevant to the pathophysiology of Eustachian tube dysfunction?
correct_answer: B. Adenoid tissue in the nasopharynx
why_correct: Adenoid hypertrophy is associated with OME and can contribute to Eustachian tube dysfunction.

why_others_wrong.A: The palatine tonsils sit in the oropharynx away from the Eustachian tube openings, so on their own they do not explain Eustachian tube dysfunction.
why_others_wrong.C: The thyroid cartilage forms the laryngeal framework in the neck and plays no part in Eustachian tube function.
why_others_wrong.D: The epiglottis guards the laryngeal inlet during swallowing and is far from the nasopharyngeal openings of the Eustachian tubes.
why_others_wrong.E: The vocal cords lie within the larynx and have no anatomical relationship to the Eustachian tube or the middle ear.

exam_trap: Candidates choose the palatine tonsil (A) because tonsils and adenoids are often removed together, but only adenoid tissue in the nasopharynx lies next to the Eustachian tube openings.
takeaway: OME + nasal obstruction/snoring → think adenoids.
source: NICE NG233, 2023.
thinking: Recurrent OME ↓ symptoms of adenoid hypertrophy ↓ adenoids sit in the nasopharynx beside the Eustachian tube openings ↓ obstruction and infection impair tube function ↓ Adenoid tissue in the nasopharynx
pearl: The Eustachian tube opens on the lateral nasopharyngeal wall, bordered above and behind by the cartilaginous torus tubarius; the pharyngeal recess behind the torus is the commonest site of origin of nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

subject: ENT: head & neck
title: Facial numbness with facial pain
stem: A 67-year-old patient develops persistent unilateral facial pain accompanied by persistent facial numbness. What is the appropriate management?

options.B: Neuroimaging using a suspected cancer pathway

correct_answer: B. Neuroimaging using a suspected cancer pathway
why_correct: NICE NG127 recommends referring adults with facial pain associated with persistent facial numbness or other abnormal neurological signs for neuroimaging using a suspected cancer pathway referral, because a structural lesion such as a skull-base or trigeminal tumour must be excluded.

why_others_wrong.A: Persistent facial numbness with facial pain is a neurological red flag, so reassurance and discharge could miss a structural lesion.
why_others_wrong.C: Ear irrigation removes wax or debris from the ear canal and does not address unilateral facial pain with sensory loss.
why_others_wrong.D: A dental review alone would not investigate the persistent facial numbness, which points to trigeminal or skull-base pathology needing urgent neuroimaging.
why_others_wrong.E: Antihistamines treat allergic symptoms and have no role in facial pain accompanied by persistent numbness.

exam_trap: Option D (dental review) appeals because facial pain is often dental, but persistent numbness is a neurological red flag that needs neuroimaging, not dental assessment alone.
takeaway: Facial pain + persistent numbness → investigate for significant structural/neurological disease.
source: NICE NG127, updated October 2023.
thinking: Persistent unilateral facial pain ↓ plus persistent facial numbness ↓ sensory loss is a neurological sign suggesting a structural lesion ↓ skull-base or trigeminal tumour must be excluded ↓ Neuroimaging using a suspected cancer pathway
pearl: Classic trigeminal neuralgia causes brief electric-shock pain with a normal sensory examination; fixed sensory loss in the trigeminal territory suggests a secondary cause such as a tumour or demyelination.

subject: ENT: head & neck
title: Submandibular salivary gland stone
stem: A 42-year-old man develops recurrent painful swelling beneath the jaw whenever he eats. The swelling settles between meals. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Salivary stones commonly obstruct the submandibular gland/duct and classically cause pain and swelling associated with meals because salivary flow increases.

why_others_wrong.A: A parotid tumour usually presents as a painless persistent swelling in front of the ear, not a submandibular swelling that comes and goes with meals.
why_others_wrong.C: Thyroid carcinoma causes a midline or paramedian lower neck lump that does not swell and settle with eating.
why_others_wrong.D: A branchial cyst is a persistent lateral neck swelling anterior to sternocleidomastoid and does not fluctuate with meals.
why_others_wrong.E: Lymphoma causes persistent, usually painless lymphadenopathy rather than recurrent meal-related swelling that settles between meals.

exam_trap: Option A (parotid tumour) and option E (lymphoma) cause persistent swellings; only duct obstruction gives swelling that comes with meals and settles between them.
takeaway: Painful gland swelling at mealtimes → think salivary stone.
source: NHS.uk: "Salivary gland stones" patient information page; [BL27].
thinking: Recurrent painful swelling beneath the jaw ↓ triggered by eating ↓ settles between meals ↓ salivary flow building up behind an obstructed duct ↓ Submandibular sialolithiasis
pearl: Most salivary stones occur in the submandibular gland because its saliva is more alkaline and mucinous and the submandibular duct runs upward against gravity.

subject: ENT: head & neck
title: Salivary gland stone: initial conservative treatment
stem: A patient has a small symptomatic salivary gland stone without systemic infection. Which measure can help promote salivary flow?

options.B: Sugar-free chewing gum or a sugar-free lozenge

correct_answer: B. Sugar-free chewing gum or a sugar-free lozenge
why_correct: Increasing salivary flow can help a small stone pass. Hydration, gentle gland massage and sialogogues such as sugar-free gum or sweets can be used.

why_others_wrong.A: Fluid restriction reduces salivary flow and makes stone impaction and infection more likely; hydration is advised instead.
why_others_wrong.C: Corticosteroids do not help a stone pass and long-term use carries significant adverse effects without benefit here.
why_others_wrong.D: Anticoagulation has no role in salivary stones and would add bleeding risk without any benefit.
why_others_wrong.E: Gland excision is reserved for recurrent or refractory disease after conservative or less invasive measures, not a small uncomplicated stone.

exam_trap: Option E (immediate gland excision) is chosen by candidates who jump to surgery; small uncomplicated stones are managed conservatively first, with excision kept for refractory or recurrent disease.
takeaway: Small salivary stone → hydrate + stimulate saliva + gentle massage.
source: NHS.uk: "Salivary gland stones" patient information page; [BL27].
thinking: Small symptomatic salivary stone ↓ no systemic infection ↓ goal is to increase salivary flow to flush the stone ↓ sialogogues, hydration and gland massage ↓ Sugar-free chewing gum or a sugar-free lozenge
pearl: Stones that fail to pass may be removed through an intraoral duct incision if palpable near the duct opening, or by sialendoscopy, keeping gland excision for recurrent or refractory disease.

subject: ENT: head & neck
title: Salivary stone with infection
stem: A patient with a known salivary gland stone develops increasing gland swelling, erythema, purulent discharge and fever. What complication has developed?
why_correct: Obstruction of salivary flow by a stone can predispose to infection of the gland.

why_others_wrong.B: Cholesteatoma is a keratinising squamous lesion of the middle ear and has no relationship to a salivary stone.
why_others_wrong.C: Ménière's disease is an inner-ear disorder causing episodic vertigo and hearing loss, not an inflamed discharging salivary gland.
why_others_wrong.D: Otosclerosis causes conductive hearing loss from stapes fixation and does not cause gland swelling, pus or fever.
why_others_wrong.E: Vocal-cord paralysis results from recurrent laryngeal nerve injury and is not a complication of an obstructed, infected salivary gland.

exam_trap: The stone explains the obstruction; fever, erythema and purulent discharge indicate superimposed infection.
takeaway: Obstruction + fever/pus → infected salivary gland.
source: NHS.uk: "Salivary gland stones" patient information page; [BL27].
thinking: Known salivary stone ↓ increasing swelling, erythema and purulent discharge ↓ fever indicates infection ↓ stasis behind the obstruction allows bacterial infection ↓ Acute sialadenitis
pearl: Acute bacterial sialadenitis is most often due to Staphylococcus aureus; treatment is hydration, sialogogues, massage and antibiotics, with drainage if an abscess forms.

subject: Anatomy
title: Parotid duct location
stem: A surgeon is examining the oral cavity of a patient with suspected parotid duct obstruction. Where does the parotid duct normally open?

options.C: At the tip of the tongue

correct_answer: B. Opposite the upper second molar
why_correct: The parotid duct crosses the masseter, turns medially and opens into the oral cavity opposite the upper second molar.

why_others_wrong.A: The floor of the mouth behind the lower incisors is where the submandibular duct opens at the sublingual papilla, not the parotid duct.
why_others_wrong.C: No major salivary duct opens at the tip of the tongue; this is not an anatomical duct orifice.
why_others_wrong.D: The tonsillar fossa houses the palatine tonsil and has no associated salivary duct opening.
why_others_wrong.E: The vallecula is a mucosal recess between the tongue base and epiglottis relevant to laryngoscopy, not a site of salivary duct drainage.

exam_trap: Candidates choose behind the lower central incisor, but that is where the submandibular duct opens at the sublingual papilla; the parotid duct opens opposite the upper second molar.
takeaway: Parotid duct → opposite upper second molar.
source: Standard surgical anatomy; NHS Greater Glasgow and Clyde ENT referral guidance, reviewed 2025.
thinking: Parotid duct crosses masseter ↓ pierces buccinator ↓ opens on the buccal mucosa ↓ Opposite the upper second molar
pearl: The parotid duct runs along the middle third of a line from the tragus to the mid-upper lip, so deep cheek lacerations along this line should prompt exploration for duct and buccal branch facial nerve injury.

subject: ENT: head & neck
title: Submandibular duct location
stem: A patient has a suspected submandibular duct stone. Where should the clinician inspect the oral cavity?

options.B: Floor of the mouth beside the lingual frenulum
options.C: Buccal mucosa opposite the upper second molar

correct_answer: B. Floor of the mouth beside the lingual frenulum
why_correct: Wharton's duct opens in the floor of the mouth beside the lingual frenulum.

why_others_wrong.A: The hard palate has minor salivary glands but no major duct opening, so it is not where Wharton's duct is inspected.
why_others_wrong.C: The buccal mucosa opposite the upper second molar is where the parotid (Stensen's) duct opens, not the submandibular duct.
why_others_wrong.D: The posterior pharyngeal wall has no major salivary duct opening and is not relevant to a submandibular stone.
why_others_wrong.E: The vallecula lies between the tongue base and epiglottis and does not contain the submandibular duct opening.

exam_trap: Option C (buccal mucosa opposite the upper second molar) is the opening of the parotid duct, so candidates who mix up the two ducts pick it.
takeaway: Submandibular duct → floor of mouth.
source: Standard surgical anatomy; NHS Greater Glasgow and Clyde ENT guidance, reviewed 2025.
thinking: Suspected submandibular duct stone ↓ Wharton's duct runs forward in the floor of the mouth ↓ opens on the sublingual papilla beside the lingual frenulum ↓ Floor of the mouth beside the lingual frenulum
pearl: Bimanual palpation of the floor of the mouth, with one finger inside the mouth and the other under the jaw, can detect a stone along Wharton's duct; the lingual nerve loops under the duct and is at risk during stone removal.

subject: ENT: head & neck
title: Parotid swelling and facial nerve
stem: A 59-year-old patient has a persistent unilateral parotid mass. Which nerve is particularly important when assessing a parotid lesion?
why_correct: The facial nerve passes through the parotid gland and divides into its terminal branches within the gland. Facial weakness in association with a parotid mass is therefore an important clinical finding.

why_others_wrong.B: The phrenic nerve runs on scalenus anterior in the lower neck to supply the diaphragm and has no relationship to the parotid gland.
why_others_wrong.C: The hypoglossal nerve lies in the submandibular region and supplies the tongue muscles; it does not pass through the parotid.
why_others_wrong.D: The femoral nerve supplies the anterior thigh and is anatomically unrelated to the parotid region.
why_others_wrong.E: The median nerve is an upper-limb nerve and has no role in assessing a parotid mass.

exam_trap: The facial nerve does not provide the parasympathetic secretomotor supply to the parotid; that pathway involves CN IX.
takeaway: Parotid mass → always assess facial nerve function.
source: Standard head-and-neck surgical anatomy; NICE NG36
thinking: Persistent parotid mass ↓ facial nerve runs through the parotid ↓ divides into its terminal branches within the gland ↓ facial nerve function must be documented ↓ Facial nerve
pearl: Most parotid tumours are benign, the commonest being pleomorphic adenoma; superficial parotidectomy starts by identifying the facial nerve trunk using landmarks such as the tragal pointer.

subject: ENT: head & neck
title: Facial weakness with parotid mass
stem: A patient with a longstanding parotid mass develops new ipsilateral facial weakness. Which interpretation is most concerning?

options.A: This proves the lesion is benign
options.B: Facial nerve dysfunction is a concerning feature requiring specialist assessment
options.E: It is diagnostic of Bell's palsy

correct_answer: B. Facial nerve dysfunction is a concerning feature requiring specialist assessment
why_correct: A parotid mass associated with facial nerve dysfunction raises concern for malignant or locally invasive disease.

why_others_wrong.A: New facial weakness with a parotid mass suggests nerve invasion, which raises rather than removes concern for malignancy.
why_others_wrong.C: A salivary stone causes meal-related obstructive swelling and does not cause facial nerve weakness, so this finding cannot confirm a stone.
why_others_wrong.D: Facial nerve involvement is a feature strongly associated with malignant parotid tumours and cannot be used to exclude malignancy.
why_others_wrong.E: Bell's palsy is a diagnosis of exclusion and should not be made when facial weakness accompanies a structural parotid lesion.

exam_trap: Do not diagnose Bell's palsy when facial weakness occurs in the setting of a structural parotid lesion.
takeaway: Parotid mass + facial weakness → red flag for malignancy/invasion.
source: Standard head-and-neck oncology practice; NICE NG36; NICE NG12(urgent referral criteria for suspected head and neck cancer).
thinking: Longstanding parotid mass ↓ new ipsilateral facial weakness ↓ benign tumours rarely cause facial palsy ↓ nerve involvement suggests malignant infiltration ↓ Facial nerve dysfunction is a concerning feature requiring specialist assessment
pearl: Other features suggesting a malignant parotid tumour include rapid growth, pain, fixation to skin or deep tissues, and cervical lymphadenopathy.

subject: ENT: head & neck
title: Neck lump investigation
stem: An adult has a persistent unexplained neck lump suspicious for an upper aerodigestive tract malignancy. Which investigation can be used to obtain cytology while reducing the risk associated with blind sampling?
why_correct: NICE recommends considering ultrasound guidance when performing FNA or core biopsy of a neck lump suspected to represent upper aerodigestive tract cancer.

why_others_wrong.B: Laparotomy explores the abdomen and would not sample a neck lump or help diagnose upper aerodigestive tract cancer.
why_others_wrong.C: Lumbar puncture samples cerebrospinal fluid and provides no cytology from a neck lump.
why_others_wrong.D: Bone marrow biopsy is used for haematological disease and does not sample a suspected metastatic neck node.
why_others_wrong.E: Colonoscopy examines the large bowel and is irrelevant to diagnosing a suspected upper aerodigestive tract malignancy.

exam_trap: An unexplained adult neck lump should not simply be excised without an appropriate diagnostic pathway.
takeaway: Suspicious neck lump → imaging + appropriately guided tissue sampling.
source: NICE NG36 (2016).
thinking: Persistent neck lump suspicious for upper aerodigestive tract cancer ↓ cytology is needed before any open procedure ↓ ultrasound guidance improves targeting and yield ↓ Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration
pearl: If cytology is inconclusive, core biopsy is preferred to open excision because open biopsy of a metastatic squamous node can seed tumour and complicate later neck dissection.

subject: ENT: head & neck
topic: Unknown primary with metastatic cervical SCC
title: Unknown primary with metastatic cervical SCC
stem: A patient has cervical lymph-node metastases confirmed as squamous cell carcinoma, but no primary tumour is identified clinically. Which imaging investigation may be used to search for an occult upper aerodigestive tract primary?
why_correct: NICE recommends offering FDG PET-CT as the first investigation to identify the primary site when metastatic nodal squamous cell carcinoma is suspected to arise from the upper aerodigestive tract.

why_others_wrong.B: A plain abdominal radiograph assesses bowel gas and obstruction and cannot localise an occult head-and-neck primary.
why_others_wrong.C: A DEXA scan measures bone mineral density and plays no part in searching for a primary tumour.
why_others_wrong.D: Renal ultrasound images the kidneys and would not detect an occult upper aerodigestive tract primary.
why_others_wrong.E: Echocardiography assesses cardiac structure and function and has no role in finding the source of metastatic cervical squamous cell carcinoma.

exam_trap: Candidates expecting conventional imaging may hesitate, but the occult-primary pathway starts with FDG PET-CT to direct targeted biopsy, not with plain radiographs or imaging of other organs.
takeaway: Cervical metastatic SCC + unknown primary → PET-CT can search for the occult primary.
source: NICE NG36 (2016).
thinking: Metastatic squamous cell carcinoma in cervical nodes ↓ no primary found clinically ↓ needs whole-body functional imaging ↓ NICE recommends FDG PET-CT as the first investigation ↓ FDG PET-CT
pearl: PET-CT is best done before panendoscopy and biopsies, because biopsy-related inflammation can cause false-positive uptake; the commonest occult primary sites are the tonsil and tongue base.

subject: ENT: head & neck
title: Thyroid swelling with airway compromise
stem: A patient with a large thyroid swelling develops stridor and increasing difficulty breathing. What is the appropriate response?

options.B: Immediate airway assessment and emergency management

correct_answer: B. Immediate airway assessment and emergency management
why_correct: Stridor from a thyroid swelling indicates potential airway compromise.

why_others_wrong.A: Stridor signals impending airway obstruction, so a routine clinic referral would dangerously delay emergency airway management.
why_others_wrong.C: Reassurance is unsafe when a thyroid swelling is causing stridor and worsening breathlessness, as the airway is at risk.
why_others_wrong.D: Antibiotics do not relieve compression of the airway by a large thyroid swelling and would not address the emergency.
why_others_wrong.E: Review in 6 months ignores the immediate risk to the airway that stridor from a neck mass represents.

exam_trap: The presence of a thyroid mass does not make the airway problem less urgent.
takeaway: Neck mass + stridor → airway emergency.
source: NICE NG12 (updated 2025).
thinking: Large thyroid swelling ↓ new stridor and increasing breathlessness ↓ stridor signals critical narrowing of the upper airway ↓ Immediate airway assessment and emergency management
pearl: Airway management in a large goitre needs senior anaesthetic and surgical input, often with awake fibreoptic intubation and a surgical airway team ready, because tracheal compression or deviation makes standard intubation hazardous.

subject: ENT: head & neck
title: Vocal-cord paralysis
stem: A patient develops unilateral vocal-cord paralysis after thyroid surgery. Which nerve has most likely been injured?
why_correct: The recurrent laryngeal nerves supply most intrinsic muscles of the larynx and are vulnerable during thyroid surgery.

why_others_wrong.B: The optic nerve serves vision and is not at risk in thyroid surgery or involved in vocal-cord movement.
why_others_wrong.C: The facial nerve supplies the muscles of facial expression and has no role in laryngeal function.
why_others_wrong.D: Accessory nerve injury weakens trapezius and sternocleidomastoid, typically after posterior triangle surgery, and does not paralyse a vocal cord.
why_others_wrong.E: The greater auricular nerve is sensory to the ear and angle of the jaw and has no motor supply to the larynx.

exam_trap: External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve injury primarily affects pitch rather than producing the classic unilateral vocal-cord paralysis.
takeaway: Thyroid surgery + vocal-cord palsy → recurrent laryngeal nerve.
source: Standard surgical anatomy and thyroid-surgery principles.
thinking: Unilateral vocal-cord paralysis ↓ after thyroid surgery ↓ recurrent laryngeal nerve runs in the tracheo-oesophageal groove near the inferior thyroid artery ↓ supplies all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid ↓ Recurrent laryngeal nerve
pearl: Pre- and postoperative laryngoscopy is used to document vocal-cord function; on the right side the nerve may rarely be non-recurrent, arising directly from the vagus in the neck.

subject: ENT: head & neck
title: Bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury
stem: A patient develops bilateral vocal-cord paralysis following neck surgery. Which complication is most concerning?
why_correct: Bilateral vocal-cord paralysis can leave the cords close to the midline and significantly narrow the airway.

why_others_wrong.B: Diarrhoea is not a consequence of laryngeal nerve injury and is not the concern with bilateral vocal-cord paralysis.
why_others_wrong.C: Renal failure is not caused by vocal-cord paralysis; the immediate danger lies in the narrowed glottic airway.
why_others_wrong.D: Visual loss is unrelated to recurrent laryngeal nerve injury and is not a complication of bilateral cord palsy.
why_others_wrong.E: Lower-limb weakness reflects spinal or peripheral nerve pathology, not injury to the laryngeal nerves during neck surgery.

exam_trap: Bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury can produce a more serious airway problem than unilateral palsy.
takeaway: Bilateral RLN palsy → think airway.
source: Standard surgical anatomy and postoperative airway management principles.
thinking: Bilateral vocal-cord paralysis ↓ after neck surgery ↓ both cords lie near the midline ↓ glottic aperture narrows, causing stridor and distress ↓ Airway obstruction
pearl: Bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy often shows soon after extubation as stridor with a relatively good voice, and may need reintubation or tracheostomy.

subject: Anatomy
topic: External branch of superior laryngeal nerve
title: External branch of superior laryngeal nerve
stem: A professional singer develops difficulty producing high-pitched sounds after thyroid surgery. Which nerve is most likely to have been injured?

options.A: External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve

correct_answer: A. External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
why_correct: The external branch supplies the cricothyroid muscle, which tenses and lengthens the vocal cords and contributes to production of high-pitched sounds.

why_others_wrong.B: The hypoglossal nerve supplies the intrinsic and most extrinsic tongue muscles; it has no role in laryngeal pitch control.
why_others_wrong.C: The facial nerve supplies the muscles of facial expression and is unrelated to laryngeal function.
why_others_wrong.D: The glossopharyngeal nerve supplies pharyngeal sensation, stylopharyngeus and posterior tongue taste, not the cricothyroid muscle.
why_others_wrong.E: The greater occipital nerve provides cutaneous sensation to the posterior scalp and has no laryngeal function.

exam_trap: Do not automatically attribute every post-thyroid voice problem to recurrent laryngeal nerve injury.
takeaway: Loss of high pitch after thyroid surgery → external SLN.
source: Standard surgical anatomy.
thinking: Singer loses high-pitched voice ↓ pitch rises when the cricothyroid tenses the vocal cords ↓ cricothyroid is the only intrinsic muscle not supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve ↓ its nerve runs close to the superior thyroid vessels ↓ External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
pearl: The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve runs close to the superior thyroid artery near the upper pole, so the upper pole vessels should be ligated close to the gland during thyroidectomy.

subject: Anatomy
title: Laryngeal cartilage
stem: Which laryngeal cartilage forms the main anterior and lateral framework of the larynx and is commonly known as the "Adam's apple"?
why_correct: The thyroid cartilage forms the largest cartilage of the laryngeal skeleton and creates the laryngeal prominence.

why_others_wrong.A: The cricoid cartilage is the signet-ring-shaped complete ring below the thyroid cartilage; it does not form the anterior laryngeal prominence.
why_others_wrong.C: The arytenoid cartilages are small paired cartilages sitting atop the cricoid lamina posteriorly, not the anterior/lateral framework forming the Adam's apple.
why_others_wrong.D: The corniculate cartilages are tiny cartilages capping the arytenoids within the aryepiglottic folds, not the main laryngeal framework.
why_others_wrong.E: The cuneiform cartilages are small supportive cartilages within the aryepiglottic folds, not the structure forming the laryngeal prominence.

exam_trap: Cricoid may tempt because it is also palpable in the anterior neck, but it is the signet-ring cartilage below the thyroid cartilage and does not form the laryngeal prominence.
takeaway: Adam's apple = thyroid cartilage.
source: Standard surgical anatomy.
thinking: Laryngeal prominence in the anterior neck ↓ two laminae meet in the midline anteriorly ↓ largest laryngeal cartilage ↓ Thyroid
pearl: The thyroid cartilage laminae meet at a more acute angle in men, making the laryngeal prominence more obvious, and the vocal cords attach at the inner aspect of this angle.

subject: Anatomy
title: Cricoid cartilage
stem: Which statement about the cricoid cartilage is correct?

options.A: It is an incomplete anterior ring
options.B: It is the only complete cartilaginous ring of the airway
options.E: It is part of the hyoid bone

correct_answer: B. It is the only complete cartilaginous ring of the airway
why_correct: The cricoid forms a complete ring around the airway.

why_others_wrong.A: This describes the tracheal rings, which are incomplete (C-shaped, open posteriorly); the cricoid cartilage is distinctively complete all the way round.
why_others_wrong.C: The epiglottis is a separate elastic cartilage superior to the laryngeal inlet, not formed by the cricoid.
why_others_wrong.D: The vocal cords/ligaments attach anteriorly to the thyroid cartilage and posteriorly to the arytenoid cartilages, not to the cricoid.
why_others_wrong.E: The hyoid is an independent U-shaped bone suspended above the larynx; it is not part of the cricoid cartilage.

exam_trap: Candidates choose an incomplete anterior ring by confusing the cricoid with tracheal rings; tracheal rings are C-shaped and open posteriorly, whereas the cricoid is complete.
takeaway: Cricoid = complete airway ring.
source: Standard surgical anatomy.
thinking: Cricoid cartilage ↓ signet-ring shape: narrow anteriorly, broad lamina posteriorly ↓ encircles the airway completely ↓ tracheal rings are open posteriorly ↓ It is the only complete cartilaginous ring of the airway
pearl: Because the cricoid is a complete ring, prolonged intubation or a high tracheostomy can cause subglottic stenosis at this level, which is why tracheostomy avoids the first tracheal ring and cricoid.

subject: Anatomy
title: Cricothyroid membrane
stem: In an emergency airway procedure, which structure lies between the thyroid and cricoid cartilages?
why_correct: The cricothyroid membrane lies between the thyroid cartilage and cricoid cartilage and is an important anatomical landmark for emergency front-of-neck access.

why_others_wrong.B: The thyrohyoid membrane connects the thyroid cartilage to the hyoid bone superiorly, not the interval between thyroid and cricoid cartilages.
why_others_wrong.C: The vocal ligament runs within the larynx from the thyroid cartilage to the arytenoid cartilages, not externally between the thyroid and cricoid cartilages.
why_others_wrong.D: The pharyngobasilar fascia attaches the pharyngeal wall to the skull base and has no relation to the cricothyroid space.
why_others_wrong.E: The buccopharyngeal fascia overlies the pharyngeal constrictor muscles and is unrelated to the interval between thyroid and cricoid cartilages.

exam_trap: The thyrohyoid membrane is tempting as another laryngeal membrane, but it lies above the thyroid cartilage, joining it to the hyoid, not between the thyroid and cricoid.
takeaway: Thyroid → cricothyroid membrane → cricoid.
source: Standard surgical anatomy.
thinking: Emergency front-of-neck access ↓ gap between thyroid cartilage above and cricoid below ↓ spanned by a membrane ↓ Cricothyroid membrane
pearl: Surgical cricothyroidotomy using a scalpel, bougie and tube is the recommended rescue technique in a "can't intubate, can't oxygenate" situation; the membrane is identified by palpation (laryngeal handshake).

subject: Anatomy
title: Laryngeal inlet
stem: Which structure forms the anterior boundary of the laryngeal inlet?
why_correct: The epiglottis forms the anterior boundary of the laryngeal inlet.

why_others_wrong.B: The cricoid cartilage lies inferiorly at the subglottic level, well below the laryngeal inlet, not forming its anterior boundary.
why_others_wrong.C: The arytenoid cartilages sit posteriorly and contribute to the posterolateral margins near the inlet, not its anterior boundary.
why_others_wrong.D: The vocal ligaments lie at the level of the true vocal folds, below the laryngeal inlet, not bounding it.
why_others_wrong.E: The hyoid body lies superior to the larynx, connected via the thyrohyoid membrane, and does not itself form a boundary of the inlet.

exam_trap: Arytenoid cartilage is tempting because it forms part of the inlet margin, but the arytenoids lie posteriorly; the epiglottis forms the anterior boundary of the laryngeal inlet.
takeaway: Laryngeal inlet → epiglottis anteriorly.
source: Standard surgical anatomy.
thinking: Laryngeal inlet opens into the laryngopharynx ↓ bounded laterally by the aryepiglottic folds ↓ posteriorly by the arytenoids and interarytenoid fold ↓ anteriorly by the upper edge of the epiglottis ↓ Epiglottis
pearl: During direct laryngoscopy a curved blade tip sits in the vallecula and lifts the epiglottis indirectly via the hyoepiglottic ligament to expose the inlet.

subject: Anatomy
topic: Sensory supply above the vocal cords
title: Sensory supply above the vocal cords
stem: Which nerve carries sensation from the larynx above the vocal cords?

options.A: Internal branch of superior laryngeal nerve

correct_answer: A. Internal branch of superior laryngeal nerve
why_correct: The internal laryngeal nerve, a branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, supplies sensation above the vocal folds.

why_others_wrong.B: The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies sensation below the vocal folds, the opposite territory to that described.
why_others_wrong.C: The hypoglossal nerve is a motor nerve to the tongue musculature and carries no laryngeal sensory fibres.
why_others_wrong.D: The facial nerve supplies facial muscles and taste to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, not laryngeal mucosa.
why_others_wrong.E: The glossopharyngeal nerve supplies sensation to the oropharynx and posterior tongue, not the larynx above the vocal folds.

exam_trap: The recurrent laryngeal nerve is the main distractor, but it carries sensation below the vocal folds; the internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve supplies above them.
takeaway: Above cords = internal SLN; below cords = RLN.
source: Standard surgical anatomy.
thinking: Sensation from the larynx ↓ vocal folds divide two sensory territories ↓ above the folds = internal laryngeal nerve, piercing the thyrohyoid membrane ↓ Internal branch of superior laryngeal nerve
pearl: The internal laryngeal nerve mediates the cough reflex from the supraglottis, so its injury or anaesthesia increases aspiration risk; it can be blocked near the thyrohyoid membrane for awake intubation.

subject: Anatomy
topic: Laryngeal sensation below the vocal cords
title: Laryngeal sensation below the vocal cords
stem: Which nerve carries sensory fibres from the larynx below the vocal cords?
why_correct: The recurrent laryngeal nerve provides sensation below the vocal folds as well as motor supply to most intrinsic laryngeal muscles.

why_others_wrong.B: The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve supplies sensation above the vocal folds, the opposite territory to that described.
why_others_wrong.C: The facial nerve supplies facial expression muscles and anterior tongue taste, with no laryngeal sensory role.
why_others_wrong.D: The hypoglossal nerve is a motor nerve to tongue musculature and carries no laryngeal sensory fibres.
why_others_wrong.E: The greater auricular nerve provides cutaneous sensation over the parotid gland and ear region, unrelated to laryngeal mucosa.

exam_trap: Candidates choose the internal superior laryngeal nerve because it is the sensory nerve of the larynx, but it supplies only above the vocal folds; below them is the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
takeaway: Below cords = recurrent laryngeal nerve.
source: Standard surgical anatomy.
thinking: Sensation from the larynx below the vocal folds ↓ subglottic mucosa and trachea ↓ supplied by the nerve that also supplies most intrinsic laryngeal muscles ↓ Recurrent laryngeal nerve
pearl: Unilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy causes hoarseness and a weak cough, whereas bilateral palsy after thyroidectomy can leave both cords near the midline, causing stridor and airway obstruction.

subject: ENT: head & neck
title: Laryngeal cancer: early glottic disease
stem: A patient has a newly diagnosed T1a squamous-cell carcinoma of the glottic larynx. Which treatment does NICE recommend?
why_correct: NICE recommends transoral laser microsurgery for newly diagnosed T1a squamous-cell carcinoma of the glottic larynx.

why_others_wrong.B: Oesophagectomy treats oesophageal cancer and has no role in managing a small glottic laryngeal tumour.
why_others_wrong.C: Neck dissection alone does not treat the primary glottic tumour, and T1a glottic cancer rarely involves the neck nodes.
why_others_wrong.D: Total laryngectomy is not appropriate for T1a glottic cancer, which is managed with voice-preserving treatment.
why_others_wrong.E: Antibiotics have no therapeutic role in squamous cell carcinoma of the larynx.

exam_trap: Candidates choose total laryngectomy (D) for any laryngeal cancer, but T1a glottic tumours are treated with voice-preserving transoral laser microsurgery.
takeaway: T1a glottic SCC → transoral laser microsurgery.
source: NICE NG36 (2016).
thinking: T1a glottic SCC is confined to one vocal cord ↓ early glottic cancer has a low risk of nodal spread ↓ treatment should preserve the larynx and voice ↓ NICE recommends transoral laser microsurgery ↓ Transoral laser microsurgery
pearl: Glottic cancers present early with hoarseness and rarely spread to nodes because the vocal cords have sparse lymphatics, which is why outcomes for early glottic tumours are good.

subject: ENT: head & neck
title: Early glottic cancer T1b–T2
stem: A patient has T1b–T2 squamous-cell carcinoma of the glottic larynx. Which treatment options does NICE recognise?
correct_answer: A. Transoral laser microsurgery or radiotherapy
why_correct: NICE recommends a choice between transoral laser microsurgery and radiotherapy for T1b–T2 glottic squamous-cell carcinoma.

why_others_wrong.B: Antibiotics and observation do not treat laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma and would allow the tumour to progress.
why_others_wrong.C: Total laryngectomy is not the standard for T1b to T2 glottic cancer, where organ-preserving options such as laser surgery or radiotherapy are recommended.
why_others_wrong.D: Thyroidectomy does not treat laryngeal cancer, and chemotherapy alone is not a recommended primary treatment for early glottic disease.
why_others_wrong.E: Withholding treatment is not appropriate for T1b to T2 glottic cancer, which has good cure rates with laser surgery or radiotherapy.

exam_trap: The treatment choice depends on tumour and patient factors rather than one universal operation.
takeaway: Early glottic SCC → organ-preserving treatment options exist.
source: NICE NG36 (2016).
thinking: T1b to T2 glottic squamous cell carcinoma ↓ still early-stage disease ↓ organ-preserving options give good cure rates ↓ NICE: choice of laser microsurgery or radiotherapy ↓ Transoral laser microsurgery or radiotherapy
pearl: Hoarseness is an early symptom of glottic cancer because even a small cord lesion disturbs vibration, which is why glottic tumours tend to present earlier than supraglottic ones.

subject: ENT: head & neck
topic: Advanced laryngeal cancer and treatment choice
title: Advanced laryngeal cancer and treatment choice
stem: A patient has T3 squamous-cell carcinoma of the larynx. Which treatment options are recognised by NICE?

options.A: Radiotherapy with concomitant chemotherapy or surgery with adjuvant radiotherapy ± chemotherapy

correct_answer: A. Radiotherapy with concomitant chemotherapy or surgery with adjuvant radiotherapy ± chemotherapy
why_correct: For T3 laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma NICE recommends discussing both organ-preserving radiotherapy with concomitant chemotherapy and primary surgery with adjuvant radiotherapy with or without chemotherapy.

why_others_wrong.B: Antibiotics do not treat laryngeal carcinoma and would allow a T3 tumour to progress and threaten the airway.
why_others_wrong.C: Observation is not appropriate for T3 laryngeal cancer, which needs curative-intent treatment planned by the MDT.
why_others_wrong.D: Tonsillectomy removes the palatine tonsils and does not treat a laryngeal primary.
why_others_wrong.E: Ear surgery has no role in the treatment of laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma.

exam_trap: Treatment decisions in advanced laryngeal cancer involve both oncological control and preservation of airway, swallowing and voice.
takeaway: T3 laryngeal SCC → multidisciplinary organ-preservation versus surgical strategy.
source: NICE NG36 (2016).
thinking: T3 laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma ↓ locally advanced disease ↓ balance oncological control against voice and swallowing ↓ NICE: chemoradiotherapy or surgery with adjuvant treatment ↓ Radiotherapy with concomitant chemotherapy or surgery with adjuvant radiotherapy ± chemotherapy
pearl: After total laryngectomy the patient breathes through a permanent end tracheostome, and voice can be restored with a tracheo-oesophageal puncture and voice prosthesis.

subject: ENT: head & neck
topic: Neck node metastasis in head-and-neck SCC
title: Neck node metastasis in head-and-neck SCC
stem: A patient has a small oral cavity squamous-cell carcinoma with a clinically N0 neck. Which principle applies to early oral cavity cancer?

options.A: The neck can never require treatment
options.B: Surgical management of the neck should be offered

correct_answer: B. Surgical management of the neck should be offered
why_correct: NICE recommends surgical management of the neck for early T1–T2, N0 oral cavity cancer.

why_others_wrong.A: Early oral cavity cancer carries a meaningful risk of occult nodal metastasis, so the clinically N0 neck frequently needs treatment.
why_others_wrong.C: Antibiotics have no effect on nodal metastases from squamous cell carcinoma.
why_others_wrong.D: Neck dissection is not prohibited; elective neck dissection is one of the recommended ways to manage the N0 neck in early oral cancer.
why_others_wrong.E: Chest imaging stages distant disease but does not address the risk of occult cervical nodal metastasis.

exam_trap: A clinically negative neck does not necessarily mean there is no risk of occult nodal metastasis.
takeaway: Early oral SCC → consider management of the clinically N0 neck.
source: NICE NG36 (2016).
thinking: Small oral cavity squamous cell carcinoma ↓ clinically N0 neck ↓ significant risk of occult nodal metastasis ↓ NICE recommends surgical management of the neck ↓ Surgical management of the neck should be offered
pearl: Tumour depth of invasion is a key predictor of occult nodal spread in oral cancer, which is why the clinically negative neck is not simply left untreated.

subject: ENT: head & neck
topic: Sentinel node biopsy in oral cancer
title: Sentinel node biopsy in oral cancer
stem: A patient has T1–T2 N0 oral cavity cancer and is being considered for surgical management of the neck. Which alternative to elective neck dissection does NICE recognise in suitable patients?
why_correct: NICE recommends sentinel lymph-node biopsy as an alternative to elective neck dissection for suitable patients with early T1–T2 N0 oral cavity cancer, unless cervical access is already required for another reason such as free-flap reconstruction.

why_others_wrong.B: Lumbar puncture samples cerebrospinal fluid and plays no part in staging the neck in oral cavity cancer.
why_others_wrong.C: Bone marrow aspiration is used for haematological disease and does not assess cervical lymph nodes.
why_others_wrong.D: Carotid stenting treats carotid stenosis and is unrelated to nodal staging in oral cancer.
why_others_wrong.E: Omitting nodal assessment ignores the risk of occult metastasis, which is why NICE recommends surgical management of the N0 neck.

exam_trap: This is specific to selected early oral cavity cancer, not all head-and-neck cancers.
takeaway: Early oral SCC, N0 → sentinel node biopsy can replace elective neck dissection in selected patients.
source: NICE NG36 (2016).
thinking: T1 to T2 N0 oral cavity cancer ↓ surgical management of the neck is planned ↓ a staging alternative avoids elective neck dissection ↓ not used when the neck is opened anyway for free-flap reconstruction ↓ Sentinel lymph-node biopsy
pearl: A positive sentinel node is followed by a completion neck dissection, whereas a negative sentinel node spares the patient the shoulder dysfunction and scarring of an elective neck dissection.

subject: ENT: head & neck
title: Head-and-neck cancer MDT
stem: A patient has newly diagnosed upper aerodigestive tract squamous-cell carcinoma. Where should definitive treatment planning occur?
why_correct: Head-and-neck cancers require coordinated assessment and treatment planning involving appropriate surgical, oncological, radiological, pathological and supportive disciplines.

why_others_wrong.A: Primary care has a role in referral and support, but definitive treatment planning for head-and-neck cancer is not done there.
why_others_wrong.C: The emergency department manages acute presentations such as airway compromise but does not plan definitive cancer treatment.
why_others_wrong.D: A community pharmacy has no role in planning definitive treatment for head-and-neck malignancy.
why_others_wrong.E: Head-and-neck cancer care needs surgical, oncological, radiological, pathological and supportive input, so multidisciplinary discussion is expected.

exam_trap: Candidates may see option A (primary care) as reasonable, but primary care only refers and supports; definitive treatment decisions are made by the specialist head-and-neck MDT.
takeaway: Head-and-neck cancer → MDT planning.
source: NICE head-and-neck cancer service guidance; NICE NG36.
thinking: Newly diagnosed upper aerodigestive tract squamous cell carcinoma ↓ treatment affects airway, voice, swallowing and appearance ↓ needs surgical, oncological, radiological and pathological input ↓ Multidisciplinary head-and-neck cancer team
pearl: The head and neck team also includes restorative dentistry, speech and language therapy and dietetics; dental assessment before radiotherapy reduces the risk of osteoradionecrosis.

subject: ENT: head & neck
topic: Persistent unilateral throat pain with otalgia
title: Persistent unilateral throat pain with otalgia
stem: A 58-year-old patient has persistent unilateral throat pain for more than 4 weeks and referred unilateral ear pain. Otoscopy is normal. What should be considered?
why_correct: Referred otalgia with normal otoscopy can arise from pathology in the pharynx, larynx or other head-and-neck structures. Persistent unilateral symptoms are a red flag.

why_others_wrong.B: Otitis externa would produce abnormal otoscopy with canal inflammation, which is absent here, and would not explain persistent throat pain.
why_others_wrong.C: Ménière's disease causes episodic vertigo, fluctuating hearing loss and tinnitus, not throat pain with referred otalgia.
why_others_wrong.D: Otosclerosis causes painless conductive hearing loss and does not explain unilateral throat pain or otalgia.
why_others_wrong.E: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo causes brief positional vertigo and is not associated with throat pain or ear pain.

exam_trap: Option B (otitis externa) appeals because of the ear pain, but normal otoscopy means the pain is referred, so the throat and larynx must be examined.
takeaway: Normal ear + persistent unilateral otalgia → examine the throat/head and neck.
source: NICE NG12 and head-and-neck cancer referral framework.
thinking: Persistent unilateral throat pain over 4 weeks ↓ referred ear pain with normal otoscopy ↓ ear and pharynx share glossopharyngeal and vagal sensory supply ↓ pharyngeal or laryngeal lesion must be excluded ↓ Head-and-neck malignancy
pearl: Referred otalgia arises because the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves supply both the ear and the pharynx or larynx, so tonsil, tongue-base or hypopharyngeal tumours can present as ear pain.

subject: ENT: head & neck
title: Neck lump: avoid blind excision
stem: An adult presents with an unexplained cervical lymph-node mass suspicious for metastatic head-and-neck cancer. Which approach should generally be avoided as the initial diagnostic procedure?

options.C: Unplanned open excision of the neck mass

correct_answer: C. Unplanned open excision of the neck mass
why_correct: A persistent adult neck lump may represent metastatic malignancy. Diagnostic evaluation should be appropriately planned, often using imaging and needle sampling rather than simply excising the node without establishing the diagnostic pathway.

why_others_wrong.A: Specialist assessment is the appropriate first step for a suspicious neck mass, not something to avoid.
why_others_wrong.B: Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration is a recommended way to obtain cytology from a suspicious neck lump before any excision.
why_others_wrong.D: Imaging is an appropriate part of the diagnostic work-up, helping characterise the node and look for a primary tumour.
why_others_wrong.E: Assessment of the upper aerodigestive tract is needed to search for the primary site, so it should be done rather than avoided.

exam_trap: An apparently isolated lymph node may be the first manifestation of a head-and-neck primary.
takeaway: Adult neck lump → investigate systematically before excision.
source: NICE NG36 (2016).
thinking: Adult neck lump suspicious for metastatic cancer ↓ diagnosis should be planned ↓ imaging and needle sampling come first ↓ open excision can seed tumour and compromise later neck dissection ↓ Unplanned open excision of the neck mass
pearl: If open biopsy is truly needed after inconclusive needle sampling, it should be done by the head and neck team with the incision planned so it can be incorporated into a later neck dissection.

subject: ENT: head & neck
title: Dysphagia with head-and-neck symptoms
stem: A 64-year-old smoker develops progressive dysphagia accompanied by persistent hoarseness and an unexplained neck lump. What is the most appropriate overall approach?

options.A: Treat reflux for several months without investigation

correct_answer: B. Urgent assessment for head-and-neck malignancy
why_correct: The combination of progressive swallowing difficulty, persistent hoarseness and an unexplained neck lump is concerning for upper aerodigestive tract malignancy.

why_others_wrong.A: Treating reflux for months without investigation would delay diagnosis when dysphagia, hoarseness and a neck lump together suggest malignancy.
why_others_wrong.C: Audiology assesses hearing and does not address progressive dysphagia, hoarseness or a neck lump.
why_others_wrong.D: Ear irrigation treats ear canal wax and has no bearing on these upper aerodigestive tract red flags.
why_others_wrong.E: Reassurance is unsafe in a smoker with several converging red flags for head-and-neck cancer.

exam_trap: Multiple converging red flags should increase urgency rather than being treated as separate minor symptoms.
takeaway: Progressive dysphagia + hoarseness + neck lump → cancer pathway.
source: NICE NG12 (updated 2025).
thinking: Smoker aged 64 ↓ progressive dysphagia, persistent hoarseness and a neck lump ↓ several converging red flags ↓ upper aerodigestive tract malignancy is likely ↓ Urgent assessment for head-and-neck malignancy
pearl: Smoking and alcohol multiply the risk of upper aerodigestive tract cancer, and a patient with one primary is at higher risk of a second primary, which is why the whole tract is examined.

subject: ENT: head & neck
title: Trismus and oral malignancy
stem: A 60-year-old patient develops persistent trismus associated with an unexplained oral lesion. Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Persistent trismus associated with oral or oropharyngeal pathology can indicate infiltrative head-and-neck disease and warrants appropriate assessment.

why_others_wrong.B: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo causes brief positional vertigo and does not cause trismus or an oral lesion.
why_others_wrong.C: Otosclerosis causes conductive hearing loss and has no association with trismus or oral lesions.
why_others_wrong.D: Otitis externa causes ear canal pain and discharge, not persistent trismus with an unexplained oral lesion.
why_others_wrong.E: Ménière's disease is an inner-ear disorder with episodic vertigo and does not restrict mouth opening.

exam_trap: Candidates may put persistent trismus down to temporomandibular joint dysfunction or a dental infection, but trismus with an unexplained oral lesion suggests tumour infiltrating the pterygoid muscles and needs urgent assessment.
takeaway: Persistent trismus + suspicious oral lesion → investigate malignancy.
source: NICE NG36 (2016); NICE NG12 (updated 2025).
thinking: Persistent trismus ↓ with an unexplained oral lesion ↓ suggests tumour infiltration of the pterygoid muscles or masticator space ↓ Oral/head-and-neck malignancy
pearl: New trismus in a patient with oral or oropharyngeal cancer suggests tumour involvement of the pterygoid muscles, and trismus can also develop later as a late effect of radiotherapy.

subject: ENT: head & neck
title: Neck lump and occult primary
stem: A patient has a cervical lymph-node biopsy showing metastatic squamous-cell carcinoma, but clinical examination does not identify a primary tumour. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: The lymph node should simply be excised and no further investigation undertaken
options.B: The upper aerodigestive tract should be systematically investigated for an occult primary
options.D: The primary tumour must be in the colon

correct_answer: B. The upper aerodigestive tract should be systematically investigated for an occult primary
why_correct: Metastatic cervical squamous-cell carcinoma may arise from an occult upper aerodigestive tract primary. NICE recommends a structured diagnostic pathway, including FDG PET-CT in appropriate patients and subsequent targeted assessment when the primary remains unidentified.

why_others_wrong.A: Excising the node without further investigation leaves the primary untreated and ignores the need for a structured occult-primary work-up.
why_others_wrong.C: Squamous cell carcinoma on biopsy is an epithelial cancer, so the diagnosis cannot be lymphoma.
why_others_wrong.D: Metastatic squamous cell carcinoma in cervical nodes most often arises from the upper aerodigestive tract, not the colon, which usually produces adenocarcinoma.
why_others_wrong.E: Imaging, particularly FDG PET-CT, is central to finding an occult primary, so it is clearly useful here.

exam_trap: Cervical metastatic SCC is not itself the primary diagnosis; the primary site must be sought.
takeaway: Cervical metastatic SCC + unknown primary → structured head-and-neck occult-primary work-up.
source: NICE NG36 (2016).
thinking: Cervical node shows metastatic squamous cell carcinoma ↓ no primary on clinical examination ↓ likely occult upper aerodigestive tract primary ↓ structured work-up with PET-CT and targeted assessment ↓ The upper aerodigestive tract should be systematically investigated for an occult primary
pearl: When PET-CT does not localise the primary, panendoscopy with tonsillectomy and tongue-base sampling is used to find it, as many occult primaries are HPV-associated oropharyngeal cancers.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Acute sore throat: natural history
stem: A 24-year-old patient presents with an uncomplicated acute sore throat. There are no features suggesting a serious complication. Which statement is most accurate?

options.B: Symptoms commonly last around 1 week and usually resolve without antibiotics

correct_answer: B. Symptoms commonly last around 1 week and usually resolve without antibiotics
