why_correct: Acute sore throat, including pharyngitis and tonsillitis, is usually self-limiting. NICE states that symptoms can last around 1 week and most people recover without antibiotics.

why_others_wrong.A: Most acute sore throats are viral or self-limiting, so antibiotics help only a minority, identified with tools such as FeverPAIN or Centor.
why_others_wrong.C: Uncomplicated acute sore throat usually settles within about a week; symptoms lasting 4 to 6 weeks would need a different explanation.
why_others_wrong.D: Tonsillectomy is reserved for recurrent, severe, documented tonsillitis and is not indicated for a single uncomplicated episode.
why_others_wrong.E: IV antibiotics are for complicated or severe infection, such as a quinsy or inability to swallow, not an uncomplicated sore throat.

exam_trap: Candidates choose 'most cases require antibiotics' (A), but most acute sore throats settle within about a week without them and only selected patients benefit.
takeaway: Acute sore throat → usually self-limiting.
source: NICE NG84, 2018.
thinking: Uncomplicated acute sore throat in a young adult ↓ no features of a serious complication ↓ usually viral or self-limiting ↓ symptoms last around 1 week, most recover without antibiotics ↓ Symptoms commonly last around 1 week and usually resolve without antibiotics
pearl: Red flags in sore throat include trismus, drooling, unilateral peritonsillar swelling with uvular deviation, stridor and inability to swallow fluids, which need same-day hospital assessment.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: FeverPAIN
stem: Which clinical scoring system can help identify adults and children who are more likely to benefit from antibiotics for acute sore throat?
why_correct: NICE recommends FeverPAIN or Centor criteria to identify people with acute sore throat who are more likely to benefit from antibiotics.

why_others_wrong.A: The Wells score estimates the pretest probability of deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism, not bacterial sore throat.
why_others_wrong.C: CHA2DS2-VASc estimates stroke risk in atrial fibrillation to guide anticoagulation and has no role in sore throat.
why_others_wrong.D: CURB-65 grades the severity of community-acquired pneumonia, not the likelihood of benefit from antibiotics in sore throat.
why_others_wrong.E: The Glasgow-Blatchford score assesses the risk from upper gastrointestinal bleeding and is unrelated to throat infection.

exam_trap: FeverPAIN is for acute sore throat; it is not a general sepsis score.
takeaway: Sore throat antibiotic decision → FeverPAIN or Centor.
source: NICE NG84, 2018.
thinking: Acute sore throat ↓ need a score predicting benefit from antibiotics ↓ NICE endorses FeverPAIN or Centor criteria ↓ other options score VTE, stroke in AF, pneumonia and GI bleeding ↓ FeverPAIN
pearl: FeverPAIN scores fever, purulence, attending within 3 days, severely inflamed tonsils and no cough or coryza; higher scores mean antibiotics are more likely to help, with phenoxymethylpenicillin first choice.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Acute sore throat and dehydration
stem: A 9-year-old child with acute tonsillitis is unable to drink adequately and is becoming dehydrated. What is the most important immediate management priority?
why_correct: In acute throat infection, inability to maintain hydration is a clinically important complication requiring active management.

why_others_wrong.A: Tonsillectomy is not an acute treatment for a dehydrated child; the immediate need is fluid resuscitation and supportive care.
why_others_wrong.C: Long-term prophylactic antibiotics do nothing for the child's current fluid deficit and are not standard in recurrent tonsillitis.
why_others_wrong.D: A hearing assessment does not address the immediate physiological problem of dehydration from painful swallowing.
why_others_wrong.E: Nasal surgery is irrelevant to acute tonsillitis and does not correct the child's dehydration.

exam_trap: Candidates focus on the infection and choose tonsillectomy (A), but in a dehydrated child the immediate priority is assessing and correcting fluid status, not definitive surgery.
takeaway: Sore throat + inability to drink → think hydration and systemic status first.
source: NICE NG84, 2018; general paediatric acute-care principles.
thinking: Child with acute tonsillitis ↓ unable to drink adequately ↓ becoming dehydrated ↓ physiological compromise takes priority over the infection itself ↓ Assess and treat dehydration
pearl: Inability to swallow in tonsillitis may also signal a peritonsillar abscess, suggested by trismus, a muffled voice and uvular deviation, which needs drainage and intravenous antibiotics.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Antibiotics and acute sore throat
stem: A patient with uncomplicated acute sore throat asks why antibiotics are not automatically prescribed. What is the best explanation?

options.A: Antibiotics are never effective against bacteria
options.B: Most sore throats resolve without antibiotics and antibiotics provide limited benefit for many patients

correct_answer: B. Most sore throats resolve without antibiotics and antibiotics provide limited benefit for many patients
why_correct: NICE emphasises the self-limiting nature of acute sore throat and recommends using clinical scoring to identify patients more likely to benefit from antibiotics.

why_others_wrong.A: Antibiotics do kill susceptible bacteria; the reason for withholding them is that most sore throats are viral or self-limiting and the benefit is small.
why_others_wrong.C: Antibiotics carry risks such as side effects and resistance, but they are not harmful to everyone, and NICE supports them for selected patients.
why_others_wrong.D: Most acute sore throats are viral, with some bacterial, mainly streptococcal; fungal throat infection is uncommon and mostly seen in immunosuppressed patients.
why_others_wrong.E: Antibiotics treat the current infection at most and do not prevent future episodes of sore throat.

exam_trap: Avoid the false dichotomy that either every sore throat needs antibiotics or antibiotics are never appropriate.
takeaway: Antibiotics are selective, not automatic, in acute sore throat.
source: NICE NG84, 2018.
thinking: Uncomplicated acute sore throat ↓ most are viral or self-limiting ↓ antibiotics give only a modest benefit for most ↓ scoring identifies those more likely to benefit ↓ Most sore throats resolve without antibiotics and antibiotics provide limited benefit for many patients
pearl: Amoxicillin should be avoided when glandular fever is possible because it commonly causes a widespread maculopapular rash in Epstein-Barr virus infection.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Tonsillectomy for recurrent tonsillitis
stem: A patient has recurrent, severe, documented episodes of acute tonsillitis that substantially interfere with normal activities despite appropriate medical management. Which intervention may be considered after specialist assessment?
why_correct: Recurrent, clinically significant tonsillitis is an established indication for considering tonsillectomy after appropriate specialist assessment.

why_others_wrong.B: Cochlear implantation restores hearing in severe-to-profound sensorineural loss and has nothing to do with recurrent tonsillitis.
why_others_wrong.C: Mastoidectomy treats mastoid and middle-ear disease such as cholesteatoma, not infection of the palatine tonsils.
why_others_wrong.D: Tympanoplasty repairs the tympanic membrane or ossicular chain and does not treat tonsillitis.
why_others_wrong.E: Thyroidectomy removes the thyroid gland and is unrelated to recurrent throat infection.

exam_trap: The indication is recurrent clinically significant disease, not simply having large tonsils.
takeaway: Recurrent disabling tonsillitis → consider tonsillectomy.
source: [SIGN117]: Management of Sore Throat and Indications for Tonsillectomy; [ENTUK] guidance on tonsillectomy, which set out recurrent acute or chronic tonsillitis as an indication for tonsillectomy.
thinking: Recurrent, severe, documented tonsillitis ↓ substantially interferes with normal activities ↓ despite appropriate medical management ↓ established indication after specialist assessment ↓ Tonsillectomy
pearl: Widely used UK criteria for tonsillectomy are 7 or more well-documented episodes in 1 year, 5 or more a year for 2 years, or 3 or more a year for 3 years.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Tonsillectomy and obstructive symptoms
stem: A child has markedly enlarged tonsils causing obstructive breathing during sleep. Which operation may be considered?
why_correct: Enlarged tonsils and adenoids are important causes of paediatric obstructive sleep apnoea. Children with symptoms of sleep apnoea should be referred for specialist assessment.

why_others_wrong.B: Tympanoplasty repairs the eardrum and does not relieve airway obstruction from enlarged tonsils.
why_others_wrong.C: Parotidectomy removes the parotid gland, usually for a tumour, and does nothing for obstructive breathing during sleep.
why_others_wrong.D: The obstruction here comes from the tonsils, so septoplasty alone would leave the main pharyngeal obstruction untreated.
why_others_wrong.E: Cochlear implantation treats severe sensorineural hearing loss and has no role in paediatric sleep-disordered breathing.

exam_trap: Septoplasty alone (D) tempts candidates thinking of nasal obstruction, but in this child the enlarged tonsils are the obstructing lesion, so adenotonsillar surgery is considered.
takeaway: Child + obstructive sleep symptoms + enlarged tonsils/adenoids → ENT assessment.
thinking: Child with markedly enlarged tonsils ↓ obstructive breathing during sleep ↓ adenotonsillar hypertrophy is a major cause of paediatric OSA ↓ removing the obstruction treats it ↓ Tonsillectomy/adenotonsillar surgery
pearl: Very young children and those with severe OSA or significant comorbidity have a higher risk of respiratory complications after adenotonsillectomy and may need surgery where paediatric high-dependency care is available.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Paediatric obstructive sleep apnoea
stem: A 7-year-old child snores loudly and has witnessed pauses in breathing during sleep. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.B: Referral to ENT or paediatric respiratory services
options.E: No investigation unless daytime sleepiness develops

correct_answer: B. Referral to ENT or paediatric respiratory services
why_correct: NICE recommends referral of children with symptoms of sleep apnoea to ENT or paediatric respiratory services.

why_others_wrong.A: Witnessed apnoeas go beyond simple snoring and suggest obstructive sleep apnoea, which NICE says needs specialist referral rather than reassurance.
why_others_wrong.C: There is no infection, and antibiotics do not treat obstructive sleep apnoea caused by tonsil and adenoid enlargement.
why_others_wrong.D: Ear irrigation removes wax from the ear canal and has no role in a child with snoring and apnoeas.
why_others_wrong.E: Children with sleep apnoea often have behavioural or learning problems rather than obvious sleepiness, and NICE does not require daytime sleepiness before referral.

exam_trap: Waiting for daytime sleepiness (E) applies adult thinking, but children with sleep apnoea more often show behavioural or learning problems, and referral does not require sleepiness.
takeaway: Child with witnessed apnoea → specialist assessment.
thinking: 7-year-old with loud snoring ↓ witnessed pauses in breathing during sleep ↓ suggests obstructive sleep apnoea, not simple snoring ↓ NICE: refer to ENT or paediatric respiratory services ↓ Referral to ENT or paediatric respiratory services
pearl: Untreated paediatric OSA can cause poor growth, behavioural and attention problems and poor school performance, and severe disease can lead to pulmonary hypertension.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Adult OSAHS: when to suspect
stem: Which combination most strongly suggests obstructive sleep apnoea/hypopnoea syndrome in an adult?
why_correct: NICE recommends assessing adults for OSAHS when they have two or more suggestive features, including snoring, witnessed apnoeas, unrefreshing sleep, waking headaches and excessive daytime sleepiness.

why_others_wrong.B: Isolated anosmia points to olfactory or sinonasal disease, not obstructive sleep apnoea.
why_others_wrong.C: Tinnitus and hearing loss are otological symptoms and are not features of OSAHS.
why_others_wrong.D: Recurrent epistaxis arises from nasal mucosal vessels and does not suggest upper airway collapse during sleep.
why_others_wrong.E: Dysphagia alone suggests oesophageal or pharyngeal swallowing pathology rather than sleep-disordered breathing.

exam_trap: Candidates may label OSAHS from snoring alone, but NICE advises assessment when two or more suggestive features are present, such as snoring with witnessed apnoeas.
takeaway: Snoring + witnessed apnoea → think OSAHS.
source: NICE NG202, 2021.
thinking: Adult with possible sleep-disordered breathing ↓ NICE: assess when two or more suggestive features are present ↓ snoring with witnessed apnoeas are core features ↓ other options are unrelated ENT symptoms ↓ Snoring and witnessed apnoeas
pearl: Risk factors for OSAHS include obesity, a large neck circumference, retrognathia and alcohol or sedative use; sleepiness questionnaires support assessment but cannot diagnose the condition.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: OSAHS diagnostic investigation
stem: An adult has suspected OSAHS based on clinical assessment. Which investigation does NICE recommend?
why_correct: NICE recommends offering home respiratory polygraphy to people with suspected OSAHS.

why_others_wrong.B: CT head does not assess breathing during sleep and has no routine place in the diagnosis of OSAHS.
why_others_wrong.C: Bronchoscopy examines the lower airways and does not measure sleep-related apnoeas or hypopnoeas.
why_others_wrong.D: Echocardiography may assess cardiac consequences in selected patients but cannot diagnose OSAHS.
why_others_wrong.E: Colonoscopy examines the large bowel and is unrelated to the investigation of sleep apnoea.

exam_trap: Do not assume that full inpatient polysomnography is required for every patient.
takeaway: Suspected adult OSAHS → home respiratory polygraphy.
source: NICE NG202, 2021.
thinking: Adult with clinically suspected OSAHS ↓ diagnosis needs measurement of breathing during sleep ↓ NICE first-line test is home respiratory polygraphy ↓ CT, bronchoscopy and echocardiography do not measure apnoeas ↓ Home respiratory polygraphy
pearl: Severity is graded by the apnoea-hypopnoea index, and moderate to severe OSAHS is usually treated with CPAP; undiagnosed OSAHS increases perioperative risk with opioids and sedation.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: OSAHS and negative oximetry
stem: A patient has significant symptoms strongly suggestive of OSAHS, but home oximetry is negative. What is the appropriate next investigation?
correct_answer: B. Consider respiratory polygraphy or polysomnography
why_correct: NICE recommends considering respiratory polygraphy or polysomnography when oximetry is negative but significant symptoms persist.

why_others_wrong.A: Oximetry can miss OSAHS, particularly with hypopnoeas or arousals without desaturation, so strong symptoms justify further testing.
why_others_wrong.C: Surgery before a diagnosis is confirmed is inappropriate, and nothing in the stem describes large obstructive tonsils.
why_others_wrong.D: There is no infection, and antibiotics neither investigate nor treat suspected OSAHS.
why_others_wrong.E: CT abdomen plays no part in the diagnosis of sleep-disordered breathing.

exam_trap: Candidates stop investigating (A) after normal oximetry, but oximetry can miss hypopnoeas and arousals without desaturation, so persistent significant symptoms justify polygraphy or polysomnography.
takeaway: High clinical suspicion + negative oximetry → further sleep investigation.
source: NICE NG202, 2021.
thinking: Strong clinical suspicion of OSAHS ↓ home oximetry negative ↓ oximetry can miss events without desaturation ↓ NICE: consider respiratory polygraphy or polysomnography ↓ Consider respiratory polygraphy or polysomnography
pearl: Oximetry can be falsely negative in younger, slimmer people who arouse before desaturating and falsely positive in lung disease, so it is less reliable than respiratory polygraphy.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Adult moderate/severe OSAHS
stem: An adult is diagnosed with symptomatic moderate-to-severe OSAHS. Which treatment is recommended?
why_correct: NICE recommends fixed-level CPAP, alongside lifestyle advice, for adults with moderate or severe OSAHS.

why_others_wrong.B: OSAHS is mechanical upper airway collapse during sleep, not an infection, so antibiotics have no role.
why_others_wrong.C: Tonsillectomy is considered only in selected adults with large obstructive tonsils and a BMI below 35; CPAP is the standard treatment for moderate-to-severe OSAHS.
why_others_wrong.D: Supplemental oxygen may correct desaturation but does not prevent airway collapse or the arousals that fragment sleep.
why_others_wrong.E: Untreated moderate-to-severe OSAHS causes daytime sleepiness, road traffic accident risk and cardiovascular complications, so treatment is recommended.

exam_trap: Oxygen alone (D) tempts candidates focused on desaturation, but it does not prevent airway collapse or arousals; fixed-level CPAP treats the obstruction itself.
takeaway: Moderate/severe symptomatic OSAHS → CPAP.
source: NICE NG202, 2021; NICE TA139 updated 2021.
thinking: Adult with symptomatic OSAHS ↓ moderate-to-severe on sleep study ↓ upper airway collapses during sleep ↓ positive pressure splints the airway open ↓ Fixed-level CPAP
pearl: Mandibular advancement splints are an option for mild OSAHS or for people who cannot tolerate CPAP, and everyone should be advised on weight loss and avoiding alcohol and sedatives.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Tonsillectomy in adult OSAHS
stem: An adult has OSAHS, very large obstructive tonsils and a BMI of 31 kg/m². Which surgical treatment can be considered?
why_correct: NICE recommends considering tonsillectomy for people with OSAHS who have large obstructive tonsils and BMI below 35 kg/m².

why_others_wrong.B: Total laryngectomy removes the larynx for cancer and would be a grossly disproportionate and irrelevant treatment for OSAHS.
why_others_wrong.C: Mastoidectomy treats ear disease and does nothing for pharyngeal obstruction during sleep.
why_others_wrong.D: Parotidectomy removes the parotid gland and does not affect the upper airway obstruction caused by large tonsils.
why_others_wrong.E: Septal cautery treats anterior epistaxis and would not relieve obstruction from large tonsils.

exam_trap: This is a selected surgical group; CPAP remains a major treatment for moderate/severe OSAHS.
takeaway: OSAHS + large obstructive tonsils + BMI <35 → consider tonsillectomy.
source: NICE NG202, 2021.
thinking: Adult with OSAHS ↓ very large obstructive tonsils ↓ BMI 31, below the NICE threshold of 35 ↓ removing obstructing tissue can relieve the obstruction ↓ Tonsillectomy
pearl: In adults, an asymmetrically enlarging tonsil should raise concern for lymphoma or squamous cell carcinoma and is often removed for histology.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: OSAHS and driving risk
stem: A professional driver has suspected OSAHS with significant daytime sleepiness. What should happen?

options.A: Routine assessment without regard to occupation
options.B: Prioritised assessment because vigilance-critical work increases risk

correct_answer: B. Prioritised assessment because vigilance-critical work increases risk
why_correct: NICE recommends rapid assessment for suspected OSAHS in people whose occupation requires critical vigilance, including vocational drivers.

why_others_wrong.A: NICE says occupation matters: a vocational driver with sleepiness is a safety risk to themselves and others, so assessment should be expedited.
why_others_wrong.C: Reassurance ignores significant sleepiness in a safety-critical job and delays diagnosis of a treatable condition.
why_others_wrong.D: Surgery is not a first step before OSAHS is confirmed and severity assessed, and nothing in the stem suggests obstructive tonsils.
why_others_wrong.E: Waiting for hypertension to develop would leave a sleepy professional driver unassessed; the driving risk alone justifies urgent assessment.

exam_trap: Candidates choose routine assessment (A) on clinical grounds alone, but NICE expedites assessment for vocational drivers because sleepiness endangers the patient and the public.
takeaway: Suspected OSAHS + safety-critical occupation → prioritise assessment.
source: NICE NG202, 2021.
thinking: Suspected OSAHS ↓ significant daytime sleepiness ↓ professional driver in vigilance-critical work ↓ NICE: expedite assessment ↓ Prioritised assessment because vigilance-critical work increases risk
pearl: In the UK, drivers with moderate or severe OSAHS causing excessive sleepiness must not drive and must notify the DVLA until symptoms are controlled, usually with CPAP.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Post-traumatic anosmia
stem: A patient loses their sense of smell immediately after a head injury. There are no other neurological abnormalities. What does NICE recommend?

options.A: Routine neurological referral solely for anosmia
options.C: Do not routinely refer solely for post-traumatic loss of smell

correct_answer: C. Do not routinely refer solely for post-traumatic loss of smell
why_correct: NICE states that isolated loss of smell immediately after head injury does not routinely require neurological referral.

why_others_wrong.A: NICE advises against routine neurological referral when loss of smell after head injury is the only finding and the neurological examination is normal.
why_others_wrong.B: Brain biopsy is an invasive procedure with no role in isolated post-traumatic anosmia, which usually reflects shearing of the olfactory fibres.
why_others_wrong.D: Tonsillectomy has no bearing on smell loss caused by head injury.
why_others_wrong.E: Post-traumatic anosmia is caused by olfactory nerve injury, not infection, so a prolonged antibiotic course would not help.

exam_trap: Post-traumatic anosmia is common and can be persistent; it does not automatically indicate major intracranial injury.
takeaway: Isolated post-traumatic anosmia → usually no routine neurology referral.
thinking: Loss of smell immediately after head injury ↓ no other neurological abnormality ↓ olfactory fibres shear at the cribriform plate ↓ NICE: no routine neurological referral for this alone ↓ Do not routinely refer solely for post-traumatic loss of smell
pearl: Olfactory training, with repeated daily sniffing of a set of strong odours, is a low-risk treatment used for post-traumatic and post-viral smell loss.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Persistent unexplained anosmia
stem: An adult has unexplained loss of smell lasting 5 months. There is no obvious rhinological cause. What should be considered?
why_correct: NICE recommends considering neuroimaging for unexplained loss of smell or taste lasting more than 3 months.

why_others_wrong.B: Tonsillectomy does not investigate or treat loss of smell and has no connection to the olfactory pathway.
why_others_wrong.C: Unexplained smell loss beyond 3 months warrants consideration of neuroimaging to exclude an intracranial or skull-base cause.
why_others_wrong.D: Ear irrigation removes wax from the ear canal and has no connection to olfaction.
why_others_wrong.E: There is no infective cause described, and antibiotics would not investigate or correct unexplained anosmia.

exam_trap: The recommendation applies to unexplained persistent symptoms, not every episode of transient anosmia.
takeaway: Unexplained anosmia >3 months → consider neuroimaging.
thinking: Unexplained loss of smell ↓ lasting 5 months, beyond 3 months ↓ no rhinological cause ↓ consider an intracranial or skull-base cause ↓ Neuroimaging
pearl: Olfactory groove meningioma can present with slowly progressive anosmia that patients often fail to notice, followed later by frontal lobe personality change and visual loss.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Olfactory hallucinations
stem: A patient reports brief, repetitive episodes of smelling burning rubber when no such smell is present. The episodes are stereotyped and recurrent. What neurological condition should be considered?
why_correct: NICE recommends neurological assessment for transient, repetitive smell or taste hallucinations because they can represent focal seizures.

why_others_wrong.B: BPPV causes brief positional vertigo from displaced otoconia and does not produce olfactory hallucinations.
why_others_wrong.C: Otitis externa causes ear pain, itching and discharge, not stereotyped episodes of phantom smells.
why_others_wrong.D: Ménière's disease causes episodic vertigo, fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus and aural fullness rather than olfactory hallucinations.
why_others_wrong.E: Otosclerosis causes progressive conductive hearing loss from stapes fixation and has no link to smell disturbance.

exam_trap: A smell hallucination is different from simple loss or distortion of smell.
takeaway: Stereotyped olfactory hallucinations → think focal seizure.
thinking: Brief, repetitive smell of burning rubber ↓ no smell actually present: an olfactory hallucination ↓ stereotyped and recurrent episodes ↓ suggests focal seizures from the mesial temporal lobe ↓ Temporal-lobe epilepsy
pearl: Olfactory auras arise from the uncus and amygdala of the mesial temporal lobe, so MRI should look for a structural cause such as a tumour or hippocampal sclerosis.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Septal haematoma after nasal trauma
stem: A 19-year-old sustains a nasal injury. Examination reveals a soft, fluctuant swelling of the nasal septum with bilateral nasal obstruction. What is the most appropriate management?
why_correct: A septal haematoma can compromise the blood supply to septal cartilage and lead to cartilage necrosis, deformity and infection if untreated.

why_others_wrong.B: A six-month wait would allow cartilage necrosis, abscess and saddle-nose deformity to develop; a septal haematoma needs same-day drainage.
why_others_wrong.C: Reassurance misses a surgical emergency, as untreated septal haematoma threatens the septal cartilage.
why_others_wrong.D: A steroid spray treats mucosal inflammation and cannot evacuate blood collected under the septal perichondrium.
why_others_wrong.E: Without drainage, a septal haematoma can progress to abscess, septal perforation and saddle deformity.

exam_trap: Candidates offer reassurance or a steroid spray (C, D) assuming simple soft-tissue swelling, but a fluctuant septal swelling after trauma is a haematoma needing same-day drainage.
takeaway: Nasal trauma + fluctuant septal swelling → septal haematoma → urgent ENT.
source: NHS GGC ENT guidance, reviewed May 2025.
thinking: Nasal injury ↓ soft, fluctuant septal swelling ↓ bilateral nasal obstruction ↓ septal haematoma threatening the cartilage ↓ Same-day ENT assessment
pearl: Septal haematoma is treated by incision and drainage followed by packing or quilting sutures to prevent reaccumulation; in children, resulting cartilage loss can impair midfacial growth.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Why septal haematoma matters
stem: Why must a septal haematoma be treated promptly?

options.B: It can compromise septal cartilage and cause deformity

correct_answer: B. It can compromise septal cartilage and cause deformity
why_correct: Blood beneath the septal mucosa can interrupt cartilage nutrition. Untreated haematoma can lead to cartilage destruction, septal perforation, deformity and potentially infection.

why_others_wrong.A: A septal haematoma affects the nasal septum, not the cochlea or auditory nerve, so it does not cause sensorineural deafness.
why_others_wrong.C: Infection can spread intracranially in rare cases, but meningitis is not inevitable; the main risk is septal cartilage necrosis.
why_others_wrong.D: The retina is unrelated to the nasal septum, and septal haematoma does not cause retinal detachment.
why_others_wrong.E: A haematoma is a collection of blood, not a neoplasm, and it has no malignant potential.

exam_trap: The problem is not simply the volume of blood; it is the effect on cartilage viability.
takeaway: Septal haematoma → cartilage ischaemia → deformity if untreated.
source: NHS GGC ENT guidance, reviewed 2025.
thinking: Septal haematoma ↓ blood separates cartilage from its perichondrium ↓ cartilage relies on the perichondrium for nutrition ↓ ischaemic necrosis, perforation and saddle deformity ↓ It can compromise septal cartilage and cause deformity
pearl: An untreated haematoma can become a septal abscess, which rarely spreads to the cavernous sinus through valveless facial and ophthalmic veins.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Nasal fracture imaging
stem: A patient has an isolated uncomplicated suspected nasal fracture with no neurological or other facial injuries. Which statement is most accurate?

options.D: CT head is mandatory in every case

correct_answer: B. Clinical assessment usually determines management
why_correct: Plain nasal radiographs have limited value and are generally not required for uncomplicated nasal fractures; management is guided primarily by clinical findings.

why_others_wrong.A: Nasal bone X-rays correlate poorly with clinical deformity and do not change management, so they are not routinely needed.
why_others_wrong.C: MRI adds nothing to the management of an uncomplicated nasal fracture and is not indicated.
why_others_wrong.D: CT head is guided by head injury criteria, and this stem states there are no neurological or other facial injuries.
why_others_wrong.E: Bone scintigraphy has no role in diagnosing or managing an acute nasal fracture.

exam_trap: Candidates request a plain nasal X-ray (A) to confirm the fracture, but radiographs do not change management; deformity and septal haematoma are assessed clinically.
takeaway: Simple nasal fracture → clinical assessment, not routine X-ray.
source: NHS hospital ENT guidance, current UK practice.
thinking: Isolated uncomplicated suspected nasal fracture ↓ no neurological or other facial injury ↓ nasal X-rays correlate poorly with deformity ↓ management decided clinically ↓ Clinical assessment usually determines management
pearl: Swelling often hides deformity, so patients are usually reassessed after about a week, with closed manipulation, if needed, best done within about 2 weeks of injury.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Nasal fracture with clear rhinorrhoea
stem: A patient sustains a significant facial injury and subsequently develops persistent unilateral clear watery nasal discharge. What should be considered?
why_correct: Clear unilateral rhinorrhoea following significant head/facial trauma raises concern for a skull-base injury with CSF leakage.

why_others_wrong.B: Allergic rhinitis usually causes bilateral rhinorrhoea with sneezing and itching, and would not explain a unilateral watery leak starting after significant trauma.
why_others_wrong.C: Otitis externa affects the external ear canal and does not produce nasal discharge.
why_others_wrong.D: BPPV causes positional vertigo and has no link to clear nasal discharge.
why_others_wrong.E: Salivary gland obstruction causes swelling and pain of the gland at mealtimes, not watery rhinorrhoea.

exam_trap: Allergic rhinitis (B) tempts candidates because the discharge is clear and watery, but a unilateral leak after significant trauma suggests a skull-base fracture with CSF rhinorrhoea.
takeaway: Head trauma + clear unilateral rhinorrhoea → think CSF leak.
source: NHS nasal-trauma guidance; current UK emergency practice.
thinking: Significant facial injury ↓ persistent unilateral clear watery nasal discharge ↓ possible anterior skull-base fracture ↓ CSF leaking into the nose ↓ CSF rhinorrhoea
pearl: Beta-2 transferrin testing of the fluid confirms CSF, whereas glucose testing is unreliable, and a persistent leak carries a risk of meningitis.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Nasal foreign body
stem: A 4-year-old child has unilateral foul-smelling purulent nasal discharge. What diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Unilateral foul-smelling nasal discharge in a child is a classic presentation of a retained nasal foreign body.

why_others_wrong.B: Allergic rhinitis causes bilateral clear watery discharge with sneezing, not unilateral purulent, foul-smelling discharge.
why_others_wrong.C: Otosclerosis is a middle-ear disorder causing conductive hearing loss in adults and does not cause nasal discharge.
why_others_wrong.D: Ménière's disease is an inner-ear disorder causing vertigo and fluctuating hearing loss, with no nasal symptoms.
why_others_wrong.E: Thyroid carcinoma presents as a neck lump and does not cause foul-smelling nasal discharge in a young child.

exam_trap: Bilateral watery symptoms are more typical of rhinitis; unilateral offensive discharge should trigger consideration of a foreign body.
takeaway: Child + unilateral offensive nasal discharge → foreign body until assessed.
source: Standard paediatric ENT clinical practice.
thinking: 4-year-old child ↓ unilateral nasal discharge ↓ foul-smelling and purulent ↓ retained object causing local infection ↓ Nasal foreign body
pearl: Anterior nasal foreign bodies in a cooperative child can often be removed with positive-pressure techniques, such as a parent blowing into the mouth while the clear nostril is occluded, or with a hook under good light.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Button battery in the nose
stem: A child has inserted a button battery into one nostril. What is the appropriate management?
why_correct: Button batteries can rapidly cause local tissue injury through electrical and chemical mechanisms and require urgent removal.

why_others_wrong.A: A button battery in the nose will not pass spontaneously, and it can cause liquefactive necrosis and septal perforation within hours.
why_others_wrong.C: A steroid spray does nothing to stop the ongoing electrical and chemical tissue injury caused by a battery.
why_others_wrong.D: Delaying a week would allow severe mucosal burns, septal perforation and necrosis; removal must be immediate.
why_others_wrong.E: Antihistamines treat allergic symptoms and do nothing to remove the battery or limit the tissue damage.

exam_trap: Candidates choose routine review (D) as for an inert bead, but a button battery causes electrical and chemical necrosis within hours and needs emergency removal.
takeaway: Button battery in nose/ear → emergency removal.
source: UK paediatric ENT emergency practice.
thinking: Button battery in a nostril ↓ electrical current and chemical injury to the mucosa ↓ damage begins within hours ↓ cannot wait for spontaneous passage ↓ Emergency removal
pearl: After removal of a button battery, follow-up is needed because septal perforation, stenosis or adhesions can develop even when early damage looks limited.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Nasal foreign body: failed removal
stem: A child has a nasal foreign body that cannot be safely removed in the emergency department. What is the safest next step?

options.D: Give antibiotics and ignore the object

why_correct: Repeated blind attempts can push the foreign body posteriorly or cause mucosal trauma and aspiration. Unsuccessful removal should prompt appropriate specialist management.

why_others_wrong.A: Repeated blind attempts can push the object posteriorly, risk aspiration and cause bleeding and mucosal trauma.
why_others_wrong.C: A retained foreign body causes infection, mucosal damage and aspiration risk, so it needs removal rather than being left.
why_others_wrong.D: Antibiotics may reduce secondary infection but leave the object in place, so the cause of the problem remains.
why_others_wrong.E: Packing the nose would push the object further back and make removal harder, with a risk of aspiration.

exam_trap: Candidates persist with repeated blind instrumentation (A), but each failed attempt can push the object posteriorly, risking aspiration and mucosal trauma; specialist removal is safer.
takeaway: Failed safe removal → stop, refer, don't repeatedly traumatise the nose.
source: Standard paediatric ENT emergency practice.
thinking: Child with a nasal foreign body ↓ cannot be removed safely in the emergency department ↓ further blind attempts risk posterior displacement and aspiration ↓ escalate to ENT with proper equipment or anaesthesia ↓ Specialist ENT assessment/removal
pearl: A posteriorly displaced nasal foreign body can enter the airway, so specialist removal in an uncooperative child is often done under general anaesthesia with a protected airway.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Foreign body aspiration risk
stem: A child has a small object lodged in the posterior nasal cavity and begins coughing suddenly during attempted removal. What is the immediate concern?
correct_answer: A. Aspiration into the lower airway
why_correct: Manipulation of a nasal foreign body can dislodge it posteriorly, creating an aspiration risk.

why_others_wrong.B: Ménière's disease is an inner-ear condition with no connection to sudden coughing during nasal instrumentation.
why_others_wrong.C: Otosclerosis is a chronic cause of conductive hearing loss and does not explain acute coughing during removal.
why_others_wrong.D: Thyroid storm is a hyperthyroid emergency with fever and tachycardia and has no link to a nasal foreign body.
why_others_wrong.E: Acute pancreatitis presents with epigastric pain and is unrelated to airway events during foreign body removal.

exam_trap: The airway must be considered during any attempted removal of a foreign body.
takeaway: Nasal foreign body + coughing during removal → think aspiration.
source: Standard paediatric ENT emergency practice.
thinking: Small object in the posterior nasal cavity ↓ sudden coughing during attempted removal ↓ object may have been dislodged into the nasopharynx ↓ it can pass into the larynx and bronchi ↓ Aspiration into the lower airway
pearl: Inhaled foreign bodies more often enter the right main bronchus because it is wider and more vertical, although in young children either side can be affected.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Septal deviation
stem: A patient has chronic unilateral nasal obstruction following previous nasal trauma. Examination demonstrates a deviated nasal septum. Which structure is primarily responsible for the anatomical obstruction?
why_correct: A deviated nasal septum can narrow one nasal passage and produce chronic unilateral obstruction.

why_others_wrong.B: The tympanic membrane lies in the ear and cannot obstruct the nasal airway.
why_others_wrong.C: The epiglottis sits at the laryngeal inlet and plays no part in nasal obstruction.
why_others_wrong.D: The arytenoid cartilages move the vocal cords in the larynx and do not affect nasal patency.
why_others_wrong.E: The parotid duct opens into the mouth opposite the upper second molar and has no role in nasal airflow.

exam_trap: Candidates may blame mucosal rhinitis, but chronic unilateral obstruction after trauma with a visible deviation is structural, arising from the nasal septum, not the ear or larynx.
takeaway: Persistent unilateral obstruction after trauma → assess the septum.
source: Standard ENT anatomy and clinical practice.
thinking: Chronic unilateral nasal obstruction ↓ previous nasal trauma ↓ deviated septum on examination ↓ the deviation narrows one nasal passage ↓ Nasal septum
pearl: Septoplasty is the operation for symptomatic septal deviation, and its complications include septal haematoma, perforation and saddle deformity if too much supporting cartilage is removed.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Nasal obstruction and rhinitis
stem: A patient has bilateral nasal obstruction, sneezing and clear watery rhinorrhoea that varies with exposure to house dust. What diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Bilateral fluctuating obstruction, sneezing and clear rhinorrhoea associated with an environmental trigger are characteristic of allergic rhinitis.

why_others_wrong.B: A septal haematoma follows nasal trauma and causes a fluctuant septal swelling, not trigger-related sneezing and watery rhinorrhoea.
why_others_wrong.C: CSF rhinorrhoea is usually unilateral and follows trauma or surgery; it does not come with sneezing or vary with dust exposure.
why_others_wrong.D: A nasal foreign body typically causes unilateral foul-smelling purulent discharge, not bilateral watery symptoms with sneezing.
why_others_wrong.E: Cholesteatoma is a middle-ear disease causing ear discharge and hearing loss, not nasal symptoms.

exam_trap: This pattern differs from unilateral foul-smelling discharge caused by a foreign body.
takeaway: Sneezing + clear watery bilateral rhinorrhoea + trigger → allergic rhinitis.
source: Standard UK ENT/primary-care practice.
thinking: Bilateral nasal obstruction ↓ sneezing and clear watery rhinorrhoea ↓ symptoms vary with house dust exposure ↓ IgE-mediated response to an allergen ↓ Allergic rhinitis
pearl: Allergic rhinitis can be confirmed with skin prick testing or specific IgE and is managed with allergen avoidance, antihistamines and intranasal corticosteroids, with immunotherapy in selected cases.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Nasal corticosteroid for allergic rhinitis
stem: A patient with persistent allergic rhinitis has troublesome nasal congestion. Which treatment is appropriate?
why_correct: Intranasal corticosteroids are an established treatment for allergic rhinitis, particularly where nasal congestion is prominent.

why_others_wrong.B: Allergic rhinitis is an IgE-mediated inflammatory condition, not an infection, so antibiotics have no role.
why_others_wrong.C: Septoplasty corrects a structural septal deviation and does not treat the mucosal inflammation of allergic rhinitis.
why_others_wrong.D: Tonsillectomy treats tonsillar disease and has no effect on nasal congestion from allergic rhinitis.
why_others_wrong.E: Mastoidectomy treats ear disease and is unrelated to the treatment of allergic rhinitis.

exam_trap: Treatment should target the inflammatory nasal disease rather than proceeding directly to surgery.
takeaway: Allergic rhinitis + congestion → intranasal corticosteroid is a core treatment.
source: NICE/UK allergic-rhinitis clinical practice.
thinking: Persistent allergic rhinitis ↓ congestion is the dominant symptom ↓ the problem is mucosal inflammation, not structure ↓ intranasal steroid reduces inflammation and congestion ↓ Intranasal corticosteroid
pearl: Intranasal corticosteroids take several days to reach full effect, so regular use and correct technique matter, while topical decongestants should be limited to a few days to avoid rhinitis medicamentosa.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Nasal obstruction and sleep apnoea
stem: An adult with suspected OSAHS also has significant chronic nasal congestion. What underlying condition should be assessed?
why_correct: NICE recommends assessing people with OSAHS and nasal congestion for underlying allergic or vasomotor rhinitis.

why_others_wrong.B: Otosclerosis causes conductive hearing loss and does not produce nasal congestion or affect the airway during sleep.
why_others_wrong.C: A salivary stone causes meal-related gland swelling and pain, not chronic nasal congestion.
why_others_wrong.D: Cholesteatoma is a destructive middle-ear lesion and does not explain nasal congestion.
why_others_wrong.E: A parotid tumour presents as a facial or preauricular mass and is not a cause of chronic nasal congestion.

exam_trap: Nasal congestion may contribute to sleep-related symptoms but does not itself establish OSAHS.
takeaway: OSAHS + nasal congestion → assess for rhinitis.
source: NICE NG202, 2021.
thinking: Suspected OSAHS ↓ significant chronic nasal congestion ↓ nasal obstruction can worsen sleep-disordered breathing ↓ NICE: assess for allergic or vasomotor rhinitis ↓ Rhinitis
pearl: Treating nasal congestion matters in OSAHS because nasal obstruction can reduce tolerance of CPAP, and humidification or mask changes may also help.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Vasomotor rhinitis with OSAHS
stem: A patient with OSAHS has persistent nasal congestion. Assessment suggests vasomotor rather than allergic rhinitis. Which treatment does NICE recommend initially?
why_correct: NICE recommends topical nasal corticosteroids for vasomotor rhinitis in people with OSAHS.

why_others_wrong.B: Vasomotor rhinitis is non-infective, so long-term antibiotics would add side effects and resistance without benefit.
why_others_wrong.C: Tonsillectomy is considered only in selected OSAHS patients with large obstructive tonsils and does not treat vasomotor nasal congestion.
why_others_wrong.D: Anticoagulation treats or prevents thrombosis and has no role in nasal congestion or OSAHS.
why_others_wrong.E: Mastoidectomy treats ear disease and is unrelated to vasomotor rhinitis.

exam_trap: Candidates assume nasal steroids are only for allergic rhinitis, but NICE recommends a topical nasal corticosteroid for vasomotor rhinitis in OSAHS; tonsillectomy (C) does not treat it.
takeaway: OSAHS + vasomotor rhinitis → topical nasal steroid.
source: NICE NG202, 2021.
thinking: OSAHS ↓ persistent nasal congestion ↓ vasomotor rather than allergic rhinitis ↓ NICE initial treatment: topical nasal corticosteroid ↓ Topical nasal corticosteroid
pearl: Vasomotor (non-allergic) rhinitis is triggered by irritants, temperature change or alcohol rather than allergens, and an ipratropium nasal spray helps when watery rhinorrhoea dominates.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Post-tonsillectomy haemorrhage
stem: A patient presents to the emergency department 8 days after tonsillectomy with fresh oral bleeding. What is the most appropriate initial approach?

options.B: Treat as a potentially significant postoperative haemorrhage and urgently involve ENT/anaesthetic teams
options.D: Perform blind throat packing in the waiting room

correct_answer: B. Treat as a potentially significant postoperative haemorrhage and urgently involve ENT/anaesthetic teams
why_correct: Post-tonsillectomy haemorrhage can rapidly become life-threatening. The patient requires urgent airway, circulation and bleeding assessment with early senior ENT and anaesthetic involvement.

why_others_wrong.A: Secondary post-tonsillectomy bleeding around days 5 to 10 can suddenly become torrential, so fresh bleeding should not be dismissed even if the patient looks stable.
why_others_wrong.C: Antihistamines do nothing to control bleeding from the tonsillar bed or to protect the airway.
why_others_wrong.D: Blind packing outside a resuscitation setting risks airway obstruction and aspiration; the patient needs resuscitation with urgent ENT and anaesthetic input.
why_others_wrong.E: Fresh bleeding after tonsillectomy is a potential airway and haemorrhage emergency, not something for a routine clinic appointment.

exam_trap: Candidates reassure and discharge (A) because the patient looks stable, but a small bleed can herald torrential post-tonsillectomy haemorrhage, so urgent ENT and anaesthetic involvement is needed.
takeaway: Post-tonsillectomy bleeding = airway/haemorrhage emergency.
source: [ENTUK]: post-tonsillectomy haemorrhage guidance, and UK ENT emergency practice, which recognise haemorrhage as a significant complication of tonsillectomy.
thinking: 8 days after tonsillectomy ↓ fresh oral bleeding ↓ secondary post-tonsillectomy haemorrhage ↓ can become torrential with airway risk ↓ Treat as a potentially significant postoperative haemorrhage and urgently involve ENT/anaesthetic teams
pearl: Primary haemorrhage occurs within 24 hours of surgery and secondary haemorrhage usually at 5 to 10 days; initial care includes sitting up, IV access, group and save and senior review, with return to theatre if bleeding continues.

subject: Hand trauma
title: Hand trauma: FDP laceration
stem: A 28-year-old man sustains a deep laceration across the palmar aspect of his right index finger. He cannot actively flex the distal interphalangeal joint. Which structure is most likely completely divided?
why_correct: Flexor digitorum profundus inserts onto the distal phalanx and is responsible for flexion of the distal interphalangeal joint. Isolated inability to flex the DIP joint therefore strongly suggests FDP disruption.

why_others_wrong.A: Flexor digitorum superficialis inserts on the middle phalanx and flexes the PIP joint, so its division alone would leave DIP flexion intact through profundus.
why_others_wrong.C: Extensor digitorum runs on the dorsum and extends the finger; a palmar laceration with loss of DIP flexion points to a flexor, not an extensor, injury.
why_others_wrong.D: The lumbrical flexes the MCP joint and extends the interphalangeal joints, so its injury would not abolish active DIP flexion.
why_others_wrong.E: The first dorsal interosseous abducts the index finger at the MCP joint and plays no part in flexing the DIP joint.

exam_trap: Do not equate inability to flex the finger generally with FDP injury. Test the DIP joint specifically with the PIP joint stabilised.
takeaway: DIP flexion = FDP.
source: [BSSH], Flexor Tendon Injury.
thinking: Deep palmar laceration of the index finger ↓ cannot actively flex the DIP joint ↓ FDP is the only tendon that flexes the finger DIP joint ↓ Flexor digitorum profundus
pearl: Divided flexor tendons in the fingers are normally repaired primarily by a hand surgeon within days of injury, because delay allows the proximal end to retract and the muscle to shorten.

subject: Hand trauma
title: Hand trauma: FDS vs FDP testing
stem: A patient has a laceration across the palmar aspect of the middle finger. With the other fingers held in extension, active flexion of the proximal interphalangeal joint is absent, but isolated distal interphalangeal flexion is preserved. Which structure is most likely injured?
why_correct: FDS flexes the PIP joint. During isolated testing, the other fingers are held extended to reduce FDP contribution through the common muscle-tendon unit.

why_others_wrong.A: Profundus is the tendon that flexes the DIP joint, and isolated DIP flexion is preserved here, so profundus is intact.
why_others_wrong.C: Extensor digitorum is a dorsal extensor; a palmar laceration causing loss of PIP flexion reflects a flexor tendon injury.
why_others_wrong.D: Flexor pollicis longus flexes the thumb interphalangeal joint and has no action on the middle finger.
why_others_wrong.E: The lumbricals flex the MCP joints and extend the interphalangeal joints, so they do not produce PIP flexion.

exam_trap: FDP flexes the DIP joint and also contributes to PIP and overall finger flexion, so FDS must be tested at the PIP joint with the other fingers held extended.
takeaway: PIP flexion = FDS; DIP flexion = FDP.
source: [BSSH], Flexor Tendon Injury.
thinking: Palmar laceration of the middle finger ↓ other fingers held extended to block FDP ↓ no active PIP flexion ↓ isolated DIP flexion preserved, so FDP intact ↓ Flexor digitorum superficialis
pearl: In the little finger, FDS is absent or weak in a proportion of people, so a negative superficialis test there must be interpreted with caution and compared with the other hand.

subject: Hand trauma
title: Hand trauma: tendon injury assessment
stem: A patient with a deep finger laceration has loss of active finger flexion. What additional examination is essential before deciding on management?
why_correct: Tendons, digital nerves and vessels lie close together. A penetrating hand injury may damage more than one structure. Sensation, capillary refill and vascular status must therefore be documented.

why_others_wrong.A: Blood pressure is part of general observations but says nothing about the digital nerves and vessels that lie beside the flexor tendons in the finger.
why_others_wrong.B: Capillary glucose may matter in a diabetic patient but does not assess the digital nerve and vascular injury that commonly accompanies a deep flexor laceration.
why_others_wrong.D: Abdominal examination has no bearing on an isolated finger laceration; the priority is local nerve and vascular assessment of the injured digit.
why_others_wrong.E: Visual acuity is irrelevant to a finger wound; the key extra assessment is sensation and perfusion of the digit distal to the injury.

exam_trap: A normal capillary refill does not exclude a digital nerve injury, so candidates who stop after checking perfusion miss nerve damage that needs repair.
takeaway: Every significant hand wound requires assessment of tendon, nerve and vascular function.
source: [BSSH] Hand Injuries / Flexor and Extensor Tendon Injury resources.
thinking: Deep finger laceration ↓ tendons run alongside digital nerves and arteries ↓ one wound can injure all three ↓ Neurovascular assessment
pearl: Digital nerve sensation should be tested before any local anaesthetic block, because sensory loss cannot be assessed once the digit is anaesthetised.

subject: Hand trauma
title: Hand trauma: extensor tendon (DIP)
stem: A patient sustains a laceration over the dorsal aspect of the finger and cannot actively extend the distal interphalangeal joint. Which injury is most likely?
why_correct: Loss of active DIP extension is characteristic of disruption of the terminal extensor mechanism.

why_others_wrong.A: Profundus injury causes loss of active DIP flexion after a palmar wound, not loss of DIP extension after a dorsal wound.
why_others_wrong.B: Superficialis injury causes loss of PIP flexion from a palmar wound and does not affect active DIP extension.
why_others_wrong.D: A boutonniere injury follows central slip disruption over the PIP joint and causes loss of PIP extension, not DIP extension.
why_others_wrong.E: Trigger finger is a stenosing tenosynovitis at the A1 pulley causing catching in flexion, not a traumatic loss of DIP extension.

exam_trap: Boutonniere injury is the usual wrong choice; it follows central slip disruption over the PIP joint and causes loss of PIP, not DIP, extension.
takeaway: DIP extension failure = think mallet injury.
source: [BSSH], Extensor Tendon Injury.
thinking: Dorsal finger laceration ↓ loss of active DIP extension ↓ terminal extensor mechanism inserts on the distal phalanx ↓ Mallet finger
pearl: An open mallet injury from a laceration is usually explored and repaired, whereas closed mallet injuries are usually treated with continuous extension splintage of the DIP joint.

subject: Hand trauma
title: Hand trauma: central slip injury
stem: A patient develops inability to actively extend the proximal interphalangeal joint after a forceful injury to the finger. Which tendon structure is most likely affected?

options.A: Central slip of the extensor mechanism

correct_answer: A. Central slip of the extensor mechanism
why_correct: The central slip contributes to extension of the PIP joint. Injury can produce a boutonnière deformity.

why_others_wrong.B: Profundus is a flexor that flexes the DIP joint, so its injury causes loss of flexion rather than loss of PIP extension.
why_others_wrong.C: Superficialis flexes the PIP joint, so its injury would impair PIP flexion, not active PIP extension.
why_others_wrong.D: The terminal extensor tendon inserts on the distal phalanx; its disruption causes a mallet finger with loss of DIP, not PIP, extension.
why_others_wrong.E: The A1 pulley is part of the flexor sheath at the MCP joint and is involved in trigger finger, not in PIP extension.

exam_trap: Do not confuse PIP extension failure with mallet finger, which affects the DIP joint.
takeaway: PIP extension failure after injury → consider central-slip injury.
source: [BSSH], Boutonnière Injury.
thinking: Forceful finger injury ↓ loss of active PIP extension ↓ central slip inserts on the base of the middle phalanx ↓ Central slip of the extensor mechanism
pearl: An untreated central slip injury can progress to a boutonniere deformity as the lateral bands slip volar to the PIP axis, flexing the PIP and hyperextending the DIP joint.

subject: Hand trauma
title: Hand trauma: extensor tendon repair
stem: A patient with a clean dorsal finger laceration cannot fully extend the finger. What is the most appropriate next principle?

options.A: Assume the wound is superficial because the skin wound is small
options.B: Assess extensor tendon function and neurovascular status
options.E: Apply a plaster and ignore tendon function

correct_answer: B. Assess extensor tendon function and neurovascular status
why_correct: Extensor tendons lie immediately beneath the skin and may be divided by relatively small wounds.

why_others_wrong.A: Extensor tendons lie just beneath the thin dorsal skin, so a small wound with loss of extension can still hide a complete tendon division.
why_others_wrong.C: Discharging without examination risks missing a divided extensor tendon or digital nerve injury in a patient who already has loss of extension.
why_others_wrong.D: Testing sensation alone assesses the digital nerves but ignores the extensor tendon, which is the structure suggested by the loss of extension.
why_others_wrong.E: Splinting without assessing tendon function may leave a divided extensor tendon unrepaired; the level and extent of injury must be established first.

exam_trap: Option A is the classic error: a small dorsal skin wound can still hide a complete extensor tendon division, so function must be tested.
takeaway: Small dorsal wound + loss of extension = tendon injury until proven otherwise.
source: [BSSH], Extensor Tendon Injury.
thinking: Clean dorsal finger laceration ↓ cannot fully extend the finger ↓ extensor tendons lie just beneath thin dorsal skin ↓ Assess extensor tendon function and neurovascular status
pearl: Dorsal wounds over the MCP joint after a punch should be treated as a possible human bite (fight bite) with exploration and antibiotics, because joint infection is common.

subject: Hand trauma
title: Hand trauma: juncturae tendinum
stem: A patient with an extensor tendon laceration can partially extend the finger despite a suspected complete tendon injury. Which anatomical feature can produce misleading preserved extension?
why_correct: The juncturae tendinum can transmit extensor force between neighbouring tendons, potentially allowing some extension despite disruption of an individual extensor tendon.

why_others_wrong.A: The annular ligament of the radius encircles the radial head at the proximal radioulnar joint and has no connection with the extensor tendons of the hand.
why_others_wrong.C: The flexor retinaculum roofs the carpal tunnel on the palmar side of the wrist and does not link the extensor tendons.
why_others_wrong.D: The palmar aponeurosis is a palmar fascial sheet involved in Dupuytren disease and does not connect the dorsal extensor tendons.
why_others_wrong.E: The A1 pulley is a flexor sheath pulley at the MCP joint and cannot transmit extension across a divided extensor tendon.

exam_trap: Candidates may pick the A1 pulley (E) or another palmar structure, but only the dorsal juncturae tendinum link extensor tendons and can mask a divided tendon.
takeaway: Extensor testing must be performed carefully and individually.
source: [BSSH], Extensor Tendon Injuries in the Hand, professional guidance.
thinking: Suspected complete extensor tendon laceration ↓ yet partial finger extension is preserved ↓ juncturae tendinum link adjacent extensor digitorum tendons on the dorsum of the hand ↓ force from neighbouring tendons can extend the finger ↓ Juncturae tendinum
pearl: Testing each finger with the neighbouring fingers held flexed reduces the influence of the juncturae, and a dorsal laceration over a tendon should be explored if function is in doubt.

subject: Hand trauma
title: Hand trauma: ulnar nerve laceration
stem: A patient sustains a sharp laceration to the wrist. There is reduced sensation over the little finger and ulnar half of the ring finger. Which nerve is most likely injured?
why_correct: The ulnar nerve supplies palmar sensation to the little finger and ulnar half of the ring finger; its dorsal cutaneous branch arises proximal to the wrist, so a wrist laceration usually spares dorsal sensation.

why_others_wrong.A: The median nerve supplies the thumb, index, middle and radial half of the ring finger, not the little finger and ulnar half of the ring finger.
why_others_wrong.B: The radial nerve at the wrist supplies dorsal skin over the radial side of the hand, not the palmar little and ring fingers.
why_others_wrong.D: The musculocutaneous nerve ends as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm and does not supply the fingers.
why_others_wrong.E: The axillary nerve supplies skin over the lateral shoulder and would not be injured by a wrist laceration.

exam_trap: Do not diagnose a median nerve injury simply because the wound is at the wrist; map the sensory deficit.
takeaway: Map sensory loss anatomically rather than by wound location.
source: Applied surgical anatomy; [BSSH] hand-trauma assessment guidance.
thinking: Sharp wrist laceration ↓ sensory loss over the little finger and ulnar half of the ring finger ↓ that is ulnar nerve territory ↓ Ulnar
pearl: Ulnar nerve injury at the wrist weakens the interossei and ulnar lumbricals, causing ulnar clawing, and paralysis of adductor pollicis weakens key pinch.

subject: Hand trauma
title: Hand trauma: vascular assessment
stem: A patient with a penetrating hand injury has absent capillary refill in a digit. What is the priority?

options.A: Ignore the finding if sensation is intact
options.D: Routine outpatient review in several weeks

why_correct: Absent or severely impaired digital perfusion may represent arterial injury and threatens tissue viability.

why_others_wrong.A: Intact sensation does not exclude arterial injury, and an absent capillary refill in a digit indicates a threat to tissue viability.
why_others_wrong.C: Physiotherapy has no place while the digit is poorly perfused; restoring blood supply takes priority over rehabilitation.
why_others_wrong.D: Delaying review for weeks in a digit with absent capillary refill risks loss of the finger, which needs same-day surgical assessment.
why_others_wrong.E: Analgesia treats pain but does nothing for a possible digital arterial injury that may need urgent exploration and repair.

exam_trap: Option A tempts candidates reassured by intact sensation, but nerves and arteries can be injured independently, so absent capillary refill needs urgent surgical assessment.
takeaway: Hand trauma + compromised perfusion = urgent surgical/vascular assessment.
source: [BSSH] Standards of Care in Hand Trauma: Revascularisation Management.
thinking: Penetrating hand injury ↓ absent capillary refill in a digit ↓ possible digital arterial injury ↓ tissue viability threatened ↓ Urgent vascular assessment
pearl: A digit with absent perfusion after a laceration may need urgent exploration and microvascular repair, and warm ischaemia time strongly influences whether the digit can be saved.

subject: Hand trauma
title: Hand trauma: functional assessment
stem: A patient sustains a deep laceration across the palm. Which combination represents the most appropriate initial functional assessment?
correct_answer: D. Tendon, neurological and vascular assessment
why_correct: Hand injuries may involve skin, tendons, nerves, vessels, bones and joints. A structured assessment must therefore evaluate all relevant structures.

why_others_wrong.A: Assessing tendon function alone could miss digital nerve or vessel injury, which often accompanies a deep palmar laceration.
why_others_wrong.B: Testing sensation alone checks the nerves but misses tendon division and vascular compromise in a deep palmar wound.
why_others_wrong.C: Vascular status alone does not reveal tendon or nerve injury; normal perfusion can coexist with divided tendons and nerves.
why_others_wrong.E: A pain score does not identify which structures are damaged and cannot replace a structured tendon, nerve and vascular examination.

exam_trap: A visible tendon injury should not stop the examiner from checking nerves and vessels.
takeaway: Think T-N-V: tendon, nerve, vascular.
source: [BSSH] Hand Injuries; BSSH Standards of Care in Hand Trauma.
thinking: Deep palmar laceration ↓ tendons, nerves and vessels lie together ↓ any combination may be divided ↓ Tendon, neurological and vascular assessment
pearl: Hand wounds should be explored under good lighting and a bloodless field, usually with a tourniquet, because blind examination in the emergency department often underestimates injury.

subject: Hand trauma
title: Hand trauma: flexor sheath infection
stem: A patient develops severe finger pain, swelling and tenderness after a penetrating injury. The finger is held in slight flexion and passive extension is extremely painful. What diagnosis should be suspected?
why_correct: The combination is characteristic of pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis. Kanavel's signs include fusiform swelling, tenderness along the flexor sheath, a flexed resting posture and pain on passive extension.

why_others_wrong.A: Trigger finger causes catching or locking at the A1 pulley without the acute swelling, sheath tenderness and pain on passive extension seen after penetrating injury.
why_others_wrong.C: Osteoarthritis is a chronic degenerative joint condition and would not produce acute swelling and severe pain on passive extension after a penetrating wound.
why_others_wrong.D: Dupuytren disease is a painless progressive palmar fibrosis causing flexion contracture, not an acutely painful swollen finger after a wound.
why_others_wrong.E: Simple bruising would not typically cause a flexed posture with severe pain on passive extension, which suggests infection within the flexor sheath.

exam_trap: Trigger finger tempts candidates because both involve the flexor sheath, but triggering causes catching without acute swelling or severe pain on passive extension.
takeaway: Kanavel signs → urgent hand-surgical assessment.
source: [BSSH], Flexor Sheath Infection standard.
thinking: Recent penetrating finger injury ↓ severe pain, swelling and tenderness ↓ finger held in slight flexion with severe pain on passive extension ↓ pattern of Kanavel signs ↓ Flexor sheath infection
pearl: Staphylococcus aureus is the commonest organism in pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis, but a mixed or unusual flora should be considered after bites or gardening injuries.

subject: Hand trauma
title: Hand trauma: flexor tenosynovitis management
stem: What is the appropriate management principle for suspected pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis?

options.C: Elevation, splintage, IV antibiotics and urgent hand-surgical referral

correct_answer: C. Elevation, splintage, IV antibiotics and urgent hand-surgical referral
why_correct: Flexor sheath infection can rapidly compromise tendon function and generally requires urgent specialist management. BSSH notes that most patients require urgent surgical washout.

why_others_wrong.A: Routine outpatient review is too slow for a closed-space infection that can destroy the flexor tendon within hours to days.
why_others_wrong.B: Massage and mobilisation may spread infection and do not treat pus within the flexor sheath, which needs antibiotics and often surgical washout.
why_others_wrong.D: Steroid injection is used for non-infective trigger finger and would worsen a bacterial flexor sheath infection.
why_others_wrong.E: Oral analgesia alone leaves the infection untreated; the condition needs IV antibiotics, splintage and urgent hand-surgical input.

exam_trap: Routine review or oral analgesia alone tempts candidates who wait for obvious pus; suspected flexor sheath infection needs IV antibiotics and urgent hand-surgical referral.
takeaway: Flexor sheath infection is a surgical infection, not a routine minor hand infection.
source: [BSSH], Flexor Sheath Infection standard.
thinking: Suspected pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis ↓ closed-space infection can destroy the tendon ↓ needs IV antibiotics, elevation, splintage ↓ most need urgent surgical washout ↓ Elevation, splintage, IV antibiotics and urgent hand-surgical referral
pearl: Delayed treatment of flexor sheath infection can lead to tendon necrosis, adhesions, a stiff finger and sometimes amputation, which is why early surgical input matters.

subject: Hand trauma
title: Hand trauma: Kanavel signs
stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the classic Kanavel signs?
why_correct: The classic Kanavel signs are fusiform swelling, tenderness along the flexor tendon sheath, pain on passive extension and a flexed resting posture.

why_others_wrong.A: Fusiform swelling of the whole digit is one of the classic Kanavel signs of flexor sheath infection.
why_others_wrong.B: Tenderness along the course of the flexor tendon sheath is one of the classic Kanavel signs.
why_others_wrong.C: Pain on passive extension of the finger is one of the classic Kanavel signs and is traditionally regarded as an early and important finding.
why_others_wrong.D: A partially flexed resting posture of the finger is one of the classic Kanavel signs.

exam_trap: Candidates who see a serious vascular finding assume it must be a sign of sheath infection, but loss of the radial pulse is not a Kanavel sign.
takeaway: Kanavel = swelling + sheath tenderness + passive-extension pain + flexed posture.
source: [BSSH], Flexor Sheath Infection standard.
thinking: Recall the four Kanavel signs ↓ fusiform swelling, sheath tenderness, passive-extension pain, flexed posture ↓ loss of a radial pulse is not among them ↓ Loss of radial pulse
pearl: Pain on passive extension is often regarded as the earliest and most sensitive Kanavel sign, but the absence of one sign does not exclude infection.

subject: Hand trauma
title: Hand trauma: flexor sheath infection risk
stem: A patient has a penetrating hand wound sustained while gardening. What complication should particularly be considered if there is progressive pain, swelling and reduced finger movement?
why_correct: Penetrating injuries can introduce bacteria into the flexor sheath, producing a potentially destructive infection.

why_others_wrong.B: Trigger finger is a stenosing tenosynovitis at the A1 pulley causing catching or locking, not progressive pain and swelling after a penetrating wound.
why_others_wrong.C: Dupuytren disease is a painless, slowly progressive palmar fibrosis and is not caused by a penetrating wound.
why_others_wrong.D: Carpal tunnel syndrome causes median nerve sensory symptoms and thenar weakness rather than rapidly progressive pain and swelling after a puncture wound.
why_others_wrong.E: Complex regional pain syndrome develops over weeks with disproportionate pain and vasomotor changes, and should not be considered until deep infection has been excluded after a penetrating wound.

exam_trap: Candidates choose complex regional pain syndrome (E), but it develops over weeks; escalating pain and swelling after a penetrating wound means infection until proven otherwise.
takeaway: Penetrating hand injury + escalating pain/swelling = actively exclude deep infection.
source: [BSSH], Flexor Sheath Infection standard.
thinking: Penetrating hand wound while gardening ↓ contamination can inoculate the flexor sheath ↓ progressive pain, swelling and reduced finger movement ↓ suggest deep infection tracking along the sheath ↓ Flexor sheath infection
pearl: Puncture wounds over the volar finger creases are particularly risky because the flexor sheath lies just beneath the thin skin there.

subject: Hand trauma
title: Hand trauma: tendon injury imaging
stem: A patient cuts the palm with glass and has reduced finger movement. Which investigation may be particularly useful in addition to clinical tendon examination?
why_correct: Radiography may identify retained glass or associated bony/joint injury. Clinical examination remains essential for tendon function.

why_others_wrong.B: Nerve conduction studies do not help acutely, because a divided nerve continues to conduct distally for several days; digital nerve injury is diagnosed clinically and confirmed at exploration.
why_others_wrong.C: MRI of the cervical spine assesses radiculopathy and cannot show retained glass or bony injury in a palmar wound.
why_others_wrong.D: Bone scintigraphy shows bone turnover and has no role in detecting retained glass or acute structural injury after a laceration.
why_others_wrong.E: Serum creatine kinase reflects muscle damage and gives no information about retained glass, bony injury or tendon continuity in the hand.

exam_trap: Candidates choose nerve conduction studies (B), but a divided nerve still conducts distally for several days; acute nerve injury is diagnosed clinically and at exploration.
takeaway: Glass injury → think retained foreign body and associated structural injury.
source: [BSSH], Flexor Tendon Injury.
thinking: Palm cut with glass ↓ reduced finger movement needs clinical tendon assessment ↓ most glass is radio-opaque ↓ X-ray detects retained fragments and bony injury ↓ Plain radiograph
pearl: Most glass fragments are visible on plain radiographs, whereas wood and many plastics are radiolucent and may need ultrasound to detect them.

subject: Hand trauma
title: Hand trauma: mallet finger
stem: A patient has a closed injury causing a drooping fingertip and inability to actively extend the DIP joint. What is the usual initial management principle?

options.C: Buddy strapping with early active mobilisation

why_correct: Closed extensor injuries such as mallet finger are commonly managed with appropriate splintage and hand-surgical/therapy follow-up.

why_others_wrong.A: Closed soft-tissue mallet injuries are usually treated without surgery; operative fixation is reserved for selected cases such as a large bony fragment with joint subluxation.
why_others_wrong.C: Buddy strapping allows DIP flexion, which separates the tendon ends; the DIP joint must be held continuously in extension for healing.
why_others_wrong.D: Steroid injection into the tendon would weaken it and does not restore continuity of the terminal extensor mechanism.
why_others_wrong.E: Leaving a mallet finger untreated risks a permanent extensor lag or swan-neck deformity, whereas continuous extension splintage usually gives a good result.

exam_trap: Candidates choose urgent open repair (A), but most closed mallet injuries heal with continuous extension splintage; surgery is for selected bony injuries with subluxation.
takeaway: Closed extensor injury → identify the tendon level and consider splintage.
source: [BSSH], Extensor Tendon Injury.
thinking: Closed injury with a drooping fingertip ↓ unable to actively extend the DIP joint ↓ terminal extensor tendon disrupted (mallet finger) ↓ continuous extension splintage of the DIP joint ↓ Finger splintage
pearl: The DIP joint must be held continuously in extension, usually for 6-8 weeks; any flexion during that period disrupts healing, while the PIP joint is left free to move.

subject: Hand trauma
title: Hand trauma: postoperative tendon rehab
stem: A patient undergoes flexor tendon repair. Which postoperative principle is particularly important for functional recovery?

options.E: Avoid all movement for six months

why_correct: After flexor tendon repair, controlled rehabilitation is crucial to promote tendon gliding while protecting the repair.

why_others_wrong.A: Prolonged complete immobilisation promotes adhesions and stiffness, so repairs are usually followed by early protected mobilisation under a hand therapist.
why_others_wrong.C: Unrestricted gripping loads the repair beyond its early strength and risks rupture, so loading is increased gradually over several weeks.
why_others_wrong.D: Forceful passive stretching stresses the healing repair and risks gapping or rupture rather than promoting safe tendon glide.
why_others_wrong.E: Avoiding all movement for six months would cause severe adhesions and stiffness; controlled movement begins early after repair.

exam_trap: More immobilisation is not necessarily better; excessive immobilisation can contribute to adhesions and stiffness.
takeaway: Flexor tendon repair = repair + splinting + carefully controlled rehabilitation.
source: [BSSH], Flexor Tendon Injury.
thinking: Flexor tendon repair ↓ immobilisation causes adhesions ↓ unrestricted loading risks rupture ↓ balance needed under a hand therapist ↓ Protected hand therapy
pearl: Most flexor tendon repairs are protected in a dorsal blocking splint with early controlled active motion supervised by a hand therapist, aiming to limit adhesions while protecting the repair.

subject: Hand trauma
title: Hand trauma: tendon re-rupture
stem: A patient notices a sudden “ping” followed by loss of finger flexion several weeks after flexor tendon repair. What complication should be suspected?
why_correct: A sudden change in active movement after tendon repair, particularly with a reported “ping”, raises concern for repair failure.

why_others_wrong.B: Adhesions cause a gradual loss of active flexion, with passive movement better than active, not an abrupt loss after a felt ping.
why_others_wrong.C: Carpal tunnel syndrome causes median nerve sensory symptoms and thenar weakness, not an abrupt loss of flexion after a felt ping.
why_others_wrong.D: Complex regional pain syndrome causes disproportionate pain, swelling and stiffness developing gradually, not a sudden loss of flexion after a ping.
why_others_wrong.E: A digital nerve neuroma causes localised pain and tingling at the scar, not loss of active finger flexion.

exam_trap: Candidates attribute the loss to tendon adhesions (B), but adhesions cause gradual stiffness; a sudden ping with loss of active flexion means rupture.
takeaway: Sudden loss of tendon function after repair → urgent specialist review.
source: [BSSH], Flexor Tendon Injury.
thinking: Flexor tendon repair several weeks ago ↓ sudden ping felt ↓ abrupt loss of active flexion ↓ the repair has failed ↓ Tendon repair rupture
pearl: Suspected rupture needs prompt hand-surgical review, because early re-repair is easier before the tendon ends retract and the sheath scars.

subject: Hand trauma
title: Hand trauma: active movement testing
stem: A patient has a suspected flexor tendon injury. Why is active movement particularly important when examining the hand?
correct_answer: A. It directly tests tendon continuity
why_correct: Active movement tests whether the musculotendinous unit can transmit force across the injured area.

why_others_wrong.B: Bone density is measured with DEXA scanning, not by asking the patient to move the finger.
why_others_wrong.C: Active movement tests the musculotendinous unit and cannot diagnose infection on its own.
why_others_wrong.D: Active movement says nothing about perfusion; vascular injury is assessed with capillary refill, colour, temperature and pulses.
why_others_wrong.E: Sensation is tested separately with light touch or two-point discrimination and is not measured by active movement.

exam_trap: Candidates relying on passive movement miss complete divisions, because the joint still moves passively; only active movement tests tendon continuity.
takeaway: Compare active and passive movement in suspected tendon injury.
