source: [BSSH], Flexor Tendon Injury.
thinking: Suspected flexor tendon injury ↓ active movement requires force transmitted across the injury ↓ passive movement can be normal despite division ↓ Active movement directly tests tendon continuity
pearl: Observing the resting cascade of the fingers is a useful passive sign: a finger lying more extended than its neighbours suggests a divided flexor tendon.

subject: Hand trauma
title: Hand trauma: combined injury referral
stem: A patient has a severe hand injury with suspected tendon, nerve and vascular damage. Which specialist service is most appropriate for definitive assessment?
why_correct: Complex hand trauma frequently requires specialist assessment because several structures may be injured simultaneously and functional outcome depends on appropriate management.

why_others_wrong.A: Dermatology manages skin disease and does not repair divided tendons, nerves or vessels in the hand.
why_others_wrong.C: Vascular surgeons manage larger limb vessels; injured digital and palmar vessels with associated tendon and nerve damage need microsurgical repair by a hand surgery service.
why_others_wrong.D: Hand therapy is vital after repair, but physiotherapy cannot provide the exploration and repair this injury needs.
why_others_wrong.E: Neurology manages medical nerve disorders and does not explore or repair traumatic nerve injuries in the hand.

exam_trap: Candidates choose vascular surgery (C) because of vessel injury, but small hand vessels with tendon and nerve damage need microsurgical repair by a hand surgery service.
takeaway: Complex hand injury → early specialist hand-surgery involvement.
source: [BSSH] Hand Injury Triage and Standards of Care.
thinking: Severe hand injury ↓ suspected tendon, nerve and vascular damage together ↓ needs exploration and microsurgical repair ↓ a hand surgery service provides combined reconstruction ↓ Hand surgery service
pearl: A digit with vascular compromise needs urgent revascularisation, and nerve and tendon repairs are usually performed at the same operation, followed by structured hand therapy.

subject: Major trauma & fluids
title: Major trauma: suspected spinal injury
stem: A patient falls from a height and has neck pain with reduced sensation in both hands. What is the immediate principle?

options.B: Protect the cervical spine while assessment proceeds
options.C: Sit the patient upright and rotate the neck
options.E: Discharge if blood pressure is normal

correct_answer: B. Protect the cervical spine while assessment proceeds
why_correct: Possible spinal injury requires cervical-spine protection while the patient undergoes structured trauma assessment.

why_others_wrong.A: Active neck movement could displace an unstable fracture and worsen cord injury in a patient with neck pain and neurological symptoms.
why_others_wrong.C: Sitting the patient up and rotating the neck moves a potentially unstable cervical spine and risks further neurological damage.
why_others_wrong.D: Massaging the neck applies force to a possibly injured spine and delays proper assessment and imaging.
why_others_wrong.E: Normal blood pressure does not exclude spinal injury, and hand sensory loss after a fall from height needs imaging before discharge.

exam_trap: A normal blood pressure does not make discharge safe; bilateral hand sensory loss after a fall from height signals possible cord injury needing spinal protection and imaging.
takeaway: Trauma + neurological symptoms + neck pain = protect the cervical spine.
source: NICE NG41, Spinal injury: assessment and initial management (2016).
thinking: Fall from height ↓ neck pain with reduced sensation in both hands ↓ possible cervical cord injury with an unstable spine ↓ immobilise while structured assessment continues ↓ Protect the cervical spine while assessment proceeds
pearl: Bilateral hand symptoms after neck trauma, with arms more affected than legs, can indicate central cord syndrome, which often follows hyperextension in older people with cervical spondylosis.

subject: Major trauma & fluids
title: Major trauma: spinal injury red flags
stem: During assessment of suspected spinal injury, which neurological feature increases concern for spinal injury?
why_correct: Motor weakness is an important neurological indicator of possible spinal injury.

why_others_wrong.A: An isolated mild headache is non-specific and is not a neurological indicator of spinal cord or nerve root injury.
why_others_wrong.C: Mild thirst is non-specific and has no relationship to spinal cord or nerve root injury.
why_others_wrong.D: Abdominal bloating is not a recognised neurological red flag for spinal injury, although ileus can follow cord injury.
why_others_wrong.E: Isolated ankle swelling suggests local soft-tissue or bony injury rather than a neurological sign of spinal injury.

exam_trap: Abdominal bloating can follow cord injury through ileus, but it is not a neurological red flag; subtle hand or foot weakness is the feature that raises concern.
takeaway: Trauma + weakness or altered sensation → actively assess for spinal injury.
source: NICE NG41, Spinal injury: assessment and initial management (2016).
thinking: Suspected spinal injury ↓ look for neurological deficit below the injured level ↓ motor weakness in hands or feet suggests cord or root involvement ↓ other options are not neurological signs ↓ Hand or foot weakness
pearl: Priapism, diaphragmatic breathing and hypotension with bradycardia are further clues to cervical or high thoracic cord injury in an unconscious patient.

subject: Major trauma & fluids
title: Major trauma: skull-base fracture imaging
stem: A patient with major facial trauma has a complex skull-base fracture and develops neurological symptoms suggesting posterior circulation involvement. Which imaging may be required to assess vascular injury?

options.A: CT or MR angiography of the neck vessels

correct_answer: A. CT or MR angiography of the neck vessels
why_correct: NICE recommends CT or MRI angiography when there is suspicion of vascular injury, including certain high-risk fractures and posterior circulation syndromes.

why_others_wrong.B: A plain abdominal radiograph images the abdomen and cannot demonstrate vertebral or carotid artery injury in the neck.
why_others_wrong.C: Gallbladder ultrasound assesses biliary disease and has no relevance to suspected cervical vascular injury.
why_others_wrong.D: A DEXA scan measures bone mineral density and cannot assess acute vascular injury.
why_others_wrong.E: Mammography images breast tissue and has no role in evaluating traumatic cervical vessel injury.

exam_trap: A normal initial neurological examination does not eliminate the possibility of traumatic vascular injury when high-risk features are present.
takeaway: High-risk cervical/facial trauma + vascular concern → consider CT/MR angiography.
source: NICE NG232, Head injury: assessment and early management, recommendation 1.6.10 (2023).
thinking: Major facial trauma with complex skull-base fracture ↓ neurological symptoms of posterior circulation involvement ↓ possible vertebral or carotid artery injury ↓ vascular imaging of the neck needed ↓ CT or MR angiography of the neck vessels
pearl: Blunt cerebrovascular injury is easily missed because neurological signs may be delayed; fractures involving the foramen transversarium or carotid canal are recognised high-risk patterns.

subject: Major trauma & fluids
title: Major trauma: cervical ligamentous injury imaging
stem: A patient with head injury requires assessment for possible cervical ligamentous injury after CT imaging. Which modality may be considered for ligamentous or disc injury?
why_correct: MRI can assess ligamentous and disc injuries suggested by CT or clinical findings.

why_others_wrong.B: A plain abdominal X-ray does not image the cervical spine and cannot show ligamentous or disc injury.
why_others_wrong.C: DEXA measures bone mineral density and cannot demonstrate acute ligamentous or disc injury in the neck.
why_others_wrong.D: Mammography is a breast imaging technique and has no role in assessing cervical soft-tissue injury.
why_others_wrong.E: Echocardiography assesses cardiac structure and function and cannot evaluate the cervical ligaments or intervertebral discs.

exam_trap: CT is excellent for bony injury but does not provide the same assessment of soft-tissue structures.
takeaway: Bone injury → CT; suspected ligamentous/disc injury → MRI may add information.
source: NICE NG232, Head injury: assessment and early management (2023).
thinking: Head-injured patient already imaged with CT ↓ concern for ligamentous or disc injury ↓ CT is excellent for bone but limited for soft tissue ↓ MRI shows ligaments, discs and cord ↓ MRI
pearl: MRI is also indicated when neurological signs are referable to the cervical spine, as it shows cord compression, contusion and haematoma that CT cannot.

subject: Major trauma & fluids
title: Major trauma: fluid resuscitation principle
stem: A patient with major trauma has active haemorrhage in hospital. Which fluid replacement principle is recommended by NICE?

options.A: Large-volume crystalloid replacement as the default
options.B: Blood components according to a major haemorrhage protocol
options.E: No resuscitation until CT is completed

correct_answer: B. Blood components according to a major haemorrhage protocol
why_correct: For patients with active bleeding in hospital, NICE advises against crystalloid fluid replacement and recommends blood-component resuscitation according to the major haemorrhage approach.

why_others_wrong.A: NICE advises against crystalloid volume replacement in active in-hospital bleeding because it dilutes clotting factors and worsens coagulopathy, acidosis and hypothermia.
why_others_wrong.C: Oral water provides no meaningful circulating volume, oxygen-carrying capacity or clotting factors and is inappropriate in a shocked, actively bleeding patient.
why_others_wrong.D: Dextrose is distributed largely outside the circulation once the glucose is metabolised, so it neither restores intravascular volume nor corrects coagulopathy.
why_others_wrong.E: Resuscitation with blood components and haemorrhage control must start immediately; delaying it until CT is complete risks exsanguination.

exam_trap: Large-volume crystalloid as the default is the familiar but wrong answer; NICE advises against crystalloid in active in-hospital bleeding because it dilutes clotting factors.
takeaway: Active major bleeding → haemorrhage control + blood-component resuscitation.
source: NICE NG39, Major trauma: assessment and initial management (2016).
thinking: Major trauma in hospital ↓ active haemorrhage ↓ crystalloid dilutes clotting factors and worsens coagulopathy ↓ replace lost blood with blood components ↓ Blood components according to a major haemorrhage protocol
pearl: Hypothermia, acidosis and coagulopathy reinforce each other in bleeding trauma patients, so warming the patient and all blood products is part of haemorrhage management.

subject: Major trauma & fluids
title: Major trauma: massive transfusion ratio
stem: According to NICE major-trauma guidance, what plasma:red-cell ratio is recommended for adults with active bleeding in hospital?
why_correct: NICE recommends a ratio of 1 unit of plasma to 1 unit of red cells for adults aged 16 or over when replacing fluid volume in active bleeding.

why_others_wrong.A: A 1:4 plasma to red-cell ratio gives too little plasma, so clotting factors are diluted and trauma-induced coagulopathy is left uncorrected.
why_others_wrong.B: A 1:2 ratio still under-replaces plasma compared with the 1:1 ratio NICE recommends for adults with active bleeding.
why_others_wrong.D: Giving twice as much plasma as red cells is not recommended and would under-replace oxygen-carrying capacity while adding volume.
why_others_wrong.E: A 4:1 plasma-heavy ratio has no role in major-haemorrhage protocols and would provide inadequate red cells for oxygen delivery.

exam_trap: Candidates choose 1:2 from older red-cell-heavy protocols, but this under-replaces plasma; NICE recommends a 1:1 plasma to red-cell ratio for adults with active bleeding.
takeaway: Adult major trauma with active bleeding: NICE recommends plasma and red cells in a 1:1 ratio, not crystalloid.
source: NICE NG39, Major trauma: assessment and initial management, recommendation 1.5.24 (2016).
thinking: Adult major trauma in hospital ↓ active bleeding ↓ plasma must be replaced alongside red cells to prevent coagulopathy ↓ NICE: 1 unit of plasma per unit of red cells ↓ 1:1
pearl: Once bleeding is controlled, NICE moves from fixed-ratio resuscitation to transfusion guided by laboratory or near-patient viscoelastic coagulation testing.

subject: Major trauma & fluids
title: Major trauma: sepsis fluid bolus
stem: A haemodynamically unstable patient with suspected sepsis requires IV fluid resuscitation. Under current NICE adult sepsis guidance, what is the initial crystalloid bolus?
why_correct: Current NICE NG253 recommends an initial 250 ml isotonic crystalloid bolus, ideally over 10–15 minutes, with reassessment after each bolus.

why_others_wrong.A: A 50 ml bolus is too small to produce a measurable haemodynamic response in an unstable adult with suspected sepsis.
why_others_wrong.B: A 100 ml bolus is below the 250 ml volume NICE NG253 specifies for the initial crystalloid bolus in adults.
why_others_wrong.D: A 1 litre bolus exceeds the current 250 ml initial volume and approaches the 1,000 ml total NICE sets before senior review, risking fluid overload.
why_others_wrong.E: A 2 litre fixed bolus far exceeds current NICE sepsis guidance, which uses small 250 ml boluses with reassessment to avoid fluid overload.

exam_trap: Do not automatically use the older “500 ml bolus” rule from general adult IV-fluid guidance when answering a current sepsis-specific question.
takeaway: Current sepsis guidance: 250 ml → reassess → further 250 ml boluses if needed.
source: NICE NG253, Managing suspected sepsis (2025).
thinking: Suspected sepsis with haemodynamic instability ↓ IV crystalloid resuscitation required ↓ current NICE sepsis guidance uses small boluses ↓ 250 ml over 10–15 minutes with reassessment after each ↓ 250 ml
pearl: Small repeated boluses with reassessment limit fluid overload; persistent hypotension or a high lactate despite fluid should prompt early critical care review for vasopressor support.

subject: Major trauma & fluids
title: Major trauma: sepsis fluid reassessment
stem: A patient receiving IV fluid resuscitation for suspected sepsis has received 250 ml. What should happen next?
why_correct: NICE recommends reassessment after each 250 ml bolus. Further boluses depend on the patient's response and clinical context.

why_others_wrong.A: An automatic 2 litre prescription ignores the reassess-after-each-bolus principle and risks fluid overload in a patient who may already have responded.
why_others_wrong.C: Monitoring must continue during resuscitation, as the response to each bolus determines whether further fluid, escalation or vasopressors are needed.
why_others_wrong.D: Routine furosemide has no place in early sepsis resuscitation and would worsen hypovolaemia unless there is clear evidence of fluid overload.
why_others_wrong.E: A patient still receiving resuscitation fluid for suspected sepsis is not safe for discharge and needs ongoing assessment and treatment.

exam_trap: Automatically prescribing another 2 litres ignores the bolus-then-reassess principle and risks fluid overload, especially in older patients or those with cardiac or renal impairment.
takeaway: Bolus → reassess → decide.
source: NICE NG253, Managing suspected sepsis (2025).
thinking: Suspected sepsis ↓ first 250 ml bolus given ↓ the response determines the next step ↓ NICE: reassess after each bolus ↓ Reassess the patient
pearl: Reassessment covers heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate, capillary refill, mental state, urine output and lactate, and looks for overload such as new crackles or rising oxygen requirement.

subject: Major trauma & fluids
title: Fluid therapy: maintenance framework
stem: A stable adult in hospital requires IV fluids but is not in shock and has no major ongoing losses. Which framework should guide the prescription?

options.B: The 5 Rs: resuscitation, routine maintenance, replacement, redistribution and reassessment

correct_answer: B. The 5 Rs: resuscitation, routine maintenance, replacement, redistribution and reassessment
why_correct: NICE adult IV-fluid guidance uses the 5 Rs to structure fluid assessment and prescribing.

why_others_wrong.A: This patient is stable and not in shock, so a resuscitation-only approach misses the maintenance and replacement needs that the 5 Rs address.
why_others_wrong.C: Antibiotic stewardship governs antimicrobial prescribing and says nothing about the volume, type or electrolyte content of IV fluids.
why_others_wrong.D: A transfusion protocol applies to blood-component replacement, not to routine IV fluid prescribing in a stable patient without major losses.
why_others_wrong.E: A variable-rate insulin infusion manages hyperglycaemia and does not provide a structure for assessing water and electrolyte needs.

exam_trap: Resuscitation only is tempting because it is the first R, but this patient is not shocked; maintenance and replacement needs must be assessed using all five Rs.
takeaway: First identify the purpose of the fluid: resuscitation, maintenance, replacement or redistribution, then reassess.
source: NICE CG174, Intravenous fluid therapy in adults in hospital (2013).
thinking: Stable adult needing IV fluids ↓ not shocked and no major ongoing losses ↓ first define the purpose of the fluid ↓ NICE adult IV-fluid guidance structures this ↓ The 5 Rs: resuscitation, routine maintenance, replacement, redistribution and reassessment
pearl: NICE routine maintenance for adults is roughly 25–30 ml/kg/day of water, about 1 mmol/kg/day each of sodium, potassium and chloride, and 50–100 g/day of glucose.

subject: Major trauma & fluids
title: MRCS Part B: examination domains
stem: A surgical trainee is asked which major domains are tested in the current MRCS Part B examination. Which answer is most accurate?

options.C: Anatomy and surgical pathology, applied surgical science and critical care, and clinical/procedural/communication skills

correct_answer: C. Anatomy and surgical pathology, applied surgical science and critical care, and clinical/procedural/communication skills
why_correct: The RCS describes Part B as a clinical practical examination covering applied knowledge and applied skills. This includes anatomy and surgical pathology, applied surgical science and critical care, communication, history taking and clinical/procedural skills.

why_others_wrong.A: Part B tests far more than anatomy, including applied surgical science, critical care, communication and clinical and procedural skills.
why_others_wrong.B: Part B assesses applied knowledge and clinical and communication skills as well as procedural skills, not operative technique alone.
why_others_wrong.D: Pharmacology appears within applied surgical science and critical care but is not the sole domain of the Part B examination.
why_others_wrong.E: Written multiple-choice papers form Part A; Part B is an OSCE-style clinical practical examination.

exam_trap: Written MCQs only describes Part A; candidates confuse the two parts, whereas Part B is a clinical practical examination testing applied knowledge and skills.
takeaway: Build Part A knowledge so that it remains clinically transferable to Part B.
source: [RCSEng], MRCS examination syllabus and guidance.
thinking: Question concerns MRCS Part B ↓ Part B is an OSCE-style clinical practical examination ↓ it tests applied knowledge and applied skills ↓ knowledge: anatomy and pathology, applied science and critical care; skills: clinical, procedural and communication ↓ Anatomy and surgical pathology, applied surgical science and critical care, and clinical/procedural/communication skills
pearl: Part B stations commonly combine anatomy with surgical pathology, and critical care physiology with clinical decisions, so Part A basic science is best learned in a clinically applied way.

subject: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care
title: Vascular: intermittent claudication
stem: A 67-year-old man has calf pain after walking 150 metres that settles after several minutes of rest. His foot is warm and there is no tissue loss. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Reproducible exertional muscle pain relieved by rest is characteristic of intermittent claudication due to peripheral arterial disease.

why_others_wrong.A: Acute limb ischaemia presents suddenly with a cold, pale, pulseless limb, whereas this foot is warm and the pain is predictable and relieved by rest.
why_others_wrong.C: Critical limb ischaemia implies rest pain, ulceration or gangrene, and this patient has pain only on walking with no tissue loss.
why_others_wrong.D: Deep-vein thrombosis causes persistent calf swelling and tenderness rather than pain that reliably appears at 150 metres and settles within minutes of stopping.
why_others_wrong.E: Acute compartment syndrome follows trauma or reperfusion with severe pain on passive stretch, not reproducible exertional pain in a 67-year-old man.

exam_trap: Do not call all lower-limb pain in a smoker “critical ischaemia”. Critical limb ischaemia implies substantially more severe disease, often with rest pain or tissue loss.
takeaway: Exertional reproducible pain → claudication.
source: NICE CG147, Peripheral arterial disease: diagnosis and management (2012).
thinking: 67-year-old man ↓ calf pain at 150 metres ↓ settles after a few minutes of rest ↓ warm foot without tissue loss ↓ Intermittent claudication
pearl: Most patients with intermittent claudication remain stable, but they carry high cardiovascular risk, so antiplatelet and statin therapy and smoking cessation are central to management.

subject: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care
title: Vascular: ankle-brachial pressure index
stem: A patient is being assessed for suspected peripheral arterial disease. Which bedside measurement is recommended as part of the assessment?
why_correct: NICE recommends measuring the ankle–brachial pressure index in people with suspected peripheral arterial disease.

why_others_wrong.B: Central venous pressure reflects right atrial filling and fluid status and gives no information on arterial perfusion of the legs.
why_others_wrong.C: Peak expiratory flow rate assesses airway obstruction in asthma or COPD and has no role in diagnosing peripheral arterial disease.
why_others_wrong.D: The Glasgow Coma Scale grades conscious level and is irrelevant to assessing lower-limb arterial disease.
why_others_wrong.E: Pulmonary artery pressure is estimated by echocardiography or right heart catheterisation to assess pulmonary hypertension and says nothing about lower-limb arterial perfusion.

exam_trap: Candidates choose central venous pressure because it is a pressure measurement, but it reflects right heart filling; arterial disease in the legs is assessed with ABPI.
takeaway: Suspected PAD → pulses + ABPI.
source: NICE CG147, Peripheral arterial disease, recommendations 1.3.1-1.3.3 (2012).
thinking: Suspected peripheral arterial disease ↓ bedside assessment of arterial perfusion ↓ compare ankle with arm systolic pressure ↓ ABPI recommended by NICE ↓ Ankle–brachial pressure index
pearl: Toe pressures or toe-brachial index are used when ankle vessels are incompressible, because digital arteries are less often calcified.

subject: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care
title: Vascular: ABPI in diabetes
stem: A patient with diabetes has exertional leg pain and a foot ulcer. His ankle–brachial pressure index is apparently normal. What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.D: The patient cannot have arterial disease because he has diabetes
options.E: ABPI proves the ulcer is neuropathic

why_correct: NICE specifically advises that PAD should not be excluded in people with diabetes on the basis of a normal or raised ABPI alone.

why_others_wrong.A: Medial arterial calcification in diabetes can make vessels incompressible and falsely normalise ABPI, so a normal reading does not exclude PAD here.
why_others_wrong.C: A normal-looking ABPI does not establish a venous cause; with exertional leg pain the ulcer may still be arterial or neuroischaemic and needs further assessment.
why_others_wrong.D: Diabetes increases rather than protects against peripheral arterial disease, which is common and often more distal in people with diabetes.
why_others_wrong.E: ABPI assesses arterial perfusion and cannot prove neuropathy; a diabetic foot ulcer is frequently neuroischaemic and PAD must still be sought.

exam_trap: Diabetes can cause arterial calcification, which may make ankle pressures misleadingly high.
takeaway: Diabetes + suspicious symptoms → normal ABPI does not automatically exclude PAD.
source: NICE CG147, Peripheral arterial disease, recommendation 1.3.4 (2012).
thinking: Diabetes with exertional leg pain and foot ulcer ↓ ABPI appears normal ↓ medial arterial calcification makes vessels incompressible ↓ ankle pressure falsely high ↓ PAD remains possible
pearl: In diabetes, peripheral arterial disease tends to affect the tibial and peroneal arteries below the knee, often with neuropathy masking claudication symptoms.

subject: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care
title: Vascular: revascularisation imaging
stem: A patient with PAD is being considered for revascularisation. What is the recommended first-line imaging modality?
why_correct: NICE recommends duplex ultrasound as first-line imaging for people with PAD in whom revascularisation is being considered.

why_others_wrong.A: Plain radiography may show vessel calcification but cannot map stenoses or occlusions to plan revascularisation.
why_others_wrong.C: CT brain images the head and plays no part in planning lower-limb revascularisation for peripheral arterial disease.
why_others_wrong.D: MRI spine may help if neurogenic claudication is suspected but does not image the leg arteries needed to plan revascularisation.
why_others_wrong.E: Echocardiography assesses cardiac structure and function and may inform fitness for surgery, but it does not image peripheral arterial lesions.

exam_trap: Candidates choose echocardiography as a preoperative fitness test or plain radiography for calcification, but neither maps leg arterial lesions; duplex ultrasound is first-line.
takeaway: PAD requiring revascularisation → duplex first.
source: NICE CG147, Peripheral arterial disease, recommendation 1.4.1 (2012).
thinking: PAD being considered for revascularisation ↓ first imaging should map lesions noninvasively ↓ duplex ultrasound shows stenosis and flow ↓ contrast imaging follows if needed ↓ Duplex ultrasound
pearl: NICE advises contrast-enhanced MR angiography for patients needing further imaging after duplex, with CT angiography if MRA is contraindicated or not tolerated.

subject: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care
title: Vascular: claudication conservative treatment
stem: A patient with intermittent claudication has received risk-factor advice but remains significantly limited by symptoms. What conservative treatment should be offered?
why_correct: NICE recommends a supervised exercise programme for people with intermittent claudication.

why_others_wrong.A: Bed rest reduces walking distance and promotes deconditioning, whereas regular structured exercise improves collateral development and walking capacity in claudication.
why_others_wrong.C: Long-term opioids are not a treatment for claudication, which settles with rest, and they carry dependence risks without improving walking distance.
why_others_wrong.D: Claudication without tissue loss carries a low risk of limb loss, so major amputation is not indicated as treatment.
why_others_wrong.E: Thrombolysis is used for selected acute limb ischaemia due to thrombosis, not for stable chronic claudication.

exam_trap: Candidates choose bed rest to avoid pain, but rest causes deconditioning; supervised exercise to the point of claudication improves walking distance in intermittent claudication.
takeaway: Claudication → risk-factor modification + supervised exercise.
source: NICE CG147, Peripheral arterial disease, recommendation 1.5.1 (2012).
thinking: Intermittent claudication ↓ risk-factor advice already given ↓ symptoms still limiting ↓ NICE recommends a supervised exercise programme ↓ Supervised exercise programme
pearl: Naftidrofuryl oxalate may be considered for claudication when supervised exercise has not improved symptoms and the patient prefers not to have revascularisation.

subject: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care
title: Vascular: critical limb ischaemia
stem: A patient has severe peripheral arterial disease with ischaemic tissue loss. Which statement is most appropriate?

options.A: Major amputation should automatically be first-line treatment

correct_answer: B. Vascular multidisciplinary assessment is required
why_correct: NICE recommends assessment by a vascular multidisciplinary team before treatment decisions in critical limb ischaemia.

why_others_wrong.A: Major amputation is generally considered after vascular MDT assessment finds revascularisation unsuitable or unsuccessful, not as an automatic first step.
why_others_wrong.C: Revascularisation is a key treatment option in critical limb ischaemia with tissue loss, so saying it is never needed is wrong.
why_others_wrong.D: Supervised exercise is for intermittent claudication; ischaemic tissue loss signals a threatened limb that needs specialist assessment for revascularisation.
why_others_wrong.E: ABPI and further imaging help assess disease severity and plan treatment, so they remain part of the work-up in severe PAD.

exam_trap: Candidates choose amputation as first-line because tissue loss sounds advanced, but many limbs can be salvaged; vascular MDT assessment for revascularisation comes first.
takeaway: Threatened limb → involve vascular specialists and consider revascularisation.
source: NICE CG147, Peripheral arterial disease, recommendation 1.6.1 (2012).
thinking: Severe PAD with ischaemic tissue loss ↓ chronic limb-threatening ischaemia ↓ options include revascularisation or amputation ↓ NICE requires vascular MDT assessment ↓ Vascular multidisciplinary assessment is required
pearl: Critical limb ischaemia is defined by ischaemic rest pain, ulceration or gangrene attributable to proven arterial disease, and carries a high risk of amputation and cardiovascular death.

subject: Vascular & fracture complications
title: Fracture: vascular injury after alignment
stem: A patient sustains a complex tibial fracture and has persistent clinical signs of vascular injury after fracture alignment. What is the appropriate principle?
why_correct: NICE recommends immediate surgical exploration when hard signs of vascular injury persist after necessary restoration of limb alignment and joint reduction.

why_others_wrong.A: Observing a limb with persistent hard signs of vascular injury allows warm ischaemia time to accumulate; BOAST advises revascularisation within 3 to 4 hours.
why_others_wrong.C: Discharging a patient with persistent hard signs of vascular injury risks irreversible ischaemia and limb loss, which requires immediate surgical exploration.
why_others_wrong.D: Routine outpatient angiography would impose a delay of days on a limb-threatening emergency when hard signs persist after restoring alignment.
why_others_wrong.E: Compression stockings are used for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis and would further compromise perfusion in a limb with arterial injury.

exam_trap: Candidates choose observation or delayed angiography, but persistent hard signs after realignment mean ongoing ischaemia that needs immediate exploration, not monitoring.
takeaway: Hard vascular signs after major limb trauma → urgent exploration.
source: NICE NG37, Fractures (complex): assessment and management, recommendation 1.2.3 (2016).
thinking: Complex tibial fracture ↓ persistent signs of vascular injury ↓ alignment already restored ↓ limb-threatening arterial injury ↓ Immediate surgical exploration
pearl: Knee dislocations and fractures around the knee carry a particular risk of popliteal artery injury because the artery is tethered at the adductor hiatus and soleal arch.

subject: Vascular & fracture complications
title: Fracture: devascularised limb management
stem: A patient with a complex fracture has a cold, pulseless limb. Which investigation should NOT delay revascularisation when a limb is clearly devascularised?
why_correct: NICE states that revascularisation should not be delayed for angiography in people with complex fractures and a devascularised limb.

why_others_wrong.B: A full blood count can be taken alongside resuscitation and theatre preparation, and is not the investigation NICE singles out as delaying revascularisation.
why_others_wrong.C: Group and save is part of preparation for surgery and is sent in parallel, rather than being the imaging study that NICE warns against waiting for.
why_others_wrong.D: An ECG is quick and done in parallel with resuscitation, and is not the investigation that NICE warns may delay limb revascularisation.
why_others_wrong.E: Urea and electrolytes are sent alongside other bloods during resuscitation and do not hold up surgery the way formal angiography can.

exam_trap: Candidates pick routine blood tests such as FBC or U&E as delaying factors, but these are sent in parallel; NICE specifically warns against delaying revascularisation for angiography.
takeaway: Clearly devascularised limb → restore perfusion urgently.
source: NICE NG37, Fractures (complex): assessment and management, recommendation 1.2.5 (2016).
thinking: Complex fracture with cold pulseless limb ↓ limb clearly devascularised ↓ ischaemia time determines limb survival ↓ formal imaging must not delay revascularisation ↓ Angiography
pearl: On-table angiography in theatre can define the injury without the delay of transfer to radiology when the limb is clearly ischaemic.

subject: Vascular & fracture complications
title: Fracture: compartment syndrome vigilance
stem: A patient sustains a tibial fracture. Which complication requires continued vigilance during the first 48 hours after injury or fixation?
why_correct: NICE recommends maintaining awareness of compartment syndrome for 48 hours following tibial fracture or fixation, with regular assessment and documentation.

why_others_wrong.B: Cataract is a lens opacity related to age, diabetes or steroids and is not a recognised early complication of a tibial fracture or its fixation.
why_others_wrong.C: Chronic liver disease develops over years from alcohol, viral hepatitis or fatty liver and has no link to the first 48 hours after a tibial fracture.
why_others_wrong.D: Peptic ulcer disease is not a specific complication of tibial fracture; although NSAIDs and stress may contribute, it does not need serial limb monitoring.
why_others_wrong.E: Otitis media is a middle ear infection, mainly in children, and has no relationship to tibial fracture or its fixation.

exam_trap: Candidates may believe that once a fracture is fixed compartment syndrome is no longer a risk, but it can develop after fixation and needs monitoring for 48 hours.
takeaway: Tibial fracture → serial compartment assessment.
source: NICE NG37, Fractures (complex): assessment and management, recommendation 1.2.7 (2016).
thinking: Tibial fracture ↓ high-risk injury for compartment syndrome ↓ risk persists after injury and after fixation ↓ NICE advises 48 hours of vigilance ↓ Compartment syndrome
pearl: Regional anaesthetic blocks and patient-controlled analgesia may mask the pain of compartment syndrome, so increasing analgesic requirement should prompt reassessment.

subject: Vascular & fracture complications
title: Fracture: compartment syndrome recognition
stem: A patient with suspected acute compartment syndrome has escalating pain, particularly with passive stretch of the affected muscles. What is the key concern?

options.B: Raised compartment pressure threatening muscle and nerve viability

correct_answer: B. Raised compartment pressure threatening muscle and nerve viability
why_correct: Acute compartment syndrome is caused by increased pressure within a closed fascial compartment, compromising microvascular perfusion and potentially causing irreversible muscle and nerve injury.

why_others_wrong.A: Escalating pain that is worse on passive stretch is a warning sign of compartment syndrome and should not be dismissed as benign postoperative pain.
why_others_wrong.C: Venous eczema is a chronic skin manifestation of venous hypertension and does not cause acute escalating pain on passive muscle stretch.
why_others_wrong.D: Chronic osteoarthritis causes longstanding joint pain and stiffness and does not explain acute escalating pain in a muscle compartment.
why_others_wrong.E: Cellulitis causes spreading skin erythema and warmth, and attributing these symptoms to cellulitis alone risks missing raised compartment pressure.

exam_trap: Candidates dismiss escalating pain as benign postoperative pain, but pain out of proportion and worsened by passive stretch signals raised compartment pressure.
takeaway: Severe escalating pain + pain on passive stretch → compartment syndrome until excluded.
source: NICE NG37, Fractures (complex): assessment and management, compartment-syndrome recommendations (2016).
thinking: Suspected acute compartment syndrome ↓ escalating pain on passive stretch ↓ raised pressure in closed fascial space ↓ threatens muscle and nerve viability ↓ Raised compartment pressure threatening muscle and nerve viability
pearl: Untreated compartment syndrome leads to muscle necrosis and fibrosis, causing ischaemic flexion contracture in the forearm and claw toes or foot drop in the leg.

subject: Breast surgery
title: Breast: new lump referral pathway
stem: A 42-year-old woman has a new unexplained breast lump. Which investigation pathway is most appropriate?

options.A: Ignore the lump if it is painless
options.B: Assessment through a breast diagnostic pathway

correct_answer: B. Assessment through a breast diagnostic pathway
why_correct: An unexplained breast lump in an adult requires appropriate breast assessment. NICE recommends suspected-cancer referral for an unexplained breast lump in people aged 30 and over.

why_others_wrong.A: Painless lumps can be malignant and many cancers present without pain, so a painless lump still needs assessment.
why_others_wrong.C: Prolonged antibiotics would delay diagnosis of a possible cancer; an unexplained lump in a woman aged 30 or over warrants suspected-cancer referral.
why_others_wrong.D: A breast lump is a breast problem, not a neurological one, and needs assessment through the breast diagnostic pathway.
why_others_wrong.E: Clinical examination is the first element of triple assessment and is needed to characterise any new breast lump.

exam_trap: Candidates may reassure for a painless lump (A), but absence of pain is not reassuring; many breast cancers are painless and a new unexplained lump at 42 needs urgent assessment.
takeaway: New unexplained breast lump in an adult → investigate.
source: NICE NG12, suspected breast cancer recommendations (updated 2025).
thinking: Woman aged 42 with a new unexplained breast lump ↓ NICE suspected-cancer referral applies from age 30 ↓ assessment needs examination, imaging and tissue sampling ↓ Assessment through a breast diagnostic pathway
pearl: For people under 30 with an unexplained breast lump, NICE suggests considering non-urgent referral; from age 30 upwards the suspected-cancer pathway is used.

subject: Breast surgery
title: Breast: unilateral nipple discharge
stem: A 55-year-old woman has unilateral spontaneous nipple discharge. What is the most appropriate approach?

options.E: Ignore if there is no fever

why_correct: NICE identifies unilateral nipple discharge in people aged 50 and over as a feature warranting suspected-cancer-pathway referral.

why_others_wrong.A: Unilateral nipple discharge in a woman aged 50 or over meets NICE criteria for suspected-cancer referral, so reassurance without assessment is unsafe.
why_others_wrong.C: Indefinite antibiotics would not investigate the cause and could delay diagnosis of an underlying papilloma or carcinoma.
why_others_wrong.D: Mastectomy without a diagnosis is inappropriate; the discharge must first be assessed with examination, imaging and tissue diagnosis where needed.
why_others_wrong.E: Fever is irrelevant here; the concern is malignancy, and unilateral spontaneous discharge at this age needs assessment regardless of temperature.

exam_trap: Candidates may reassure (A) because no lump is felt, but unilateral spontaneous discharge in a woman aged 50 or over is itself a NICE suspected-cancer referral criterion.
takeaway: Unilateral concerning nipple change/discharge in an older woman → breast assessment.
source: NICE NG12, recommendation 1.4.1 (updated 2025).
thinking: Woman aged 55 ↓ spontaneous discharge from one nipple ↓ NICE suspected-cancer criterion: aged 50 or over with unilateral nipple discharge ↓ needs examination, imaging and tissue diagnosis as required ↓ Urgent breast assessment
pearl: Bloodstained single-duct discharge is most often caused by an intraduct papilloma, but carcinoma must be excluded; persistent single-duct discharge with normal imaging may need microdochectomy for diagnosis.

subject: Breast surgery
title: Breast: triple assessment
stem: A 48-year-old woman has a suspicious breast lump. Which combination best represents the principle of triple assessment?

options.B: Clinical assessment, imaging and tissue diagnosis when indicated
options.C: Blood pressure, urinalysis and CT brain

correct_answer: B. Clinical assessment, imaging and tissue diagnosis when indicated
why_correct: Breast diagnosis commonly uses clinical assessment, appropriate imaging and pathological assessment of tissue when required.

why_others_wrong.A: ECG and chest X-ray may form part of anaesthetic work-up but include neither breast imaging nor tissue diagnosis.
why_others_wrong.C: Blood pressure, urinalysis and brain CT are unrelated to diagnosing a breast lump and omit clinical breast assessment and pathology.
why_others_wrong.D: Mammography alone is only the imaging component and cannot confirm the diagnosis without clinical assessment and tissue sampling.
why_others_wrong.E: MRI alone is a single, selectively used imaging test and cannot replace clinical examination or histological diagnosis.

exam_trap: Candidates choosing mammography alone (D) forget that a normal mammogram does not exclude cancer; a lump needs clinical, imaging and pathological findings that agree before reassurance.
takeaway: Breast lump → triple-assessment concept.
source: Standard UK breast-surgical diagnostic practice; NICE NG12 (updated 2025).
thinking: Suspicious breast lump ↓ triple assessment combines three independent components ↓ clinical history and examination ↓ imaging plus tissue diagnosis ↓ Clinical assessment, imaging and tissue diagnosis when indicated
pearl: Triple assessment results must be concordant; if any one component is suspicious or the three disagree, further sampling or multidisciplinary review is needed rather than reassurance.

subject: Breast surgery
title: Breast: axillary lymphadenopathy
stem: A woman with breast cancer in the upper outer quadrant has hard, enlarged regional lymph nodes on examination. Which anatomical route best explains this regional spread?
why_correct: The axillary nodes are a major regional lymphatic basin for breast cancer, making axillary examination and staging clinically important.

why_others_wrong.B: Portal venous drainage carries blood from the gut to the liver and is not the route by which breast cancer reaches axillary nodes.
why_others_wrong.C: Caval drainage describes systemic venous return, not the lymphatic route that explains spread to the axillary nodes.
why_others_wrong.D: Mesenteric drainage serves the bowel, not the breast, so it does not explain axillary lymphadenopathy in breast cancer.
why_others_wrong.E: Pelvic lymphatics drain the pelvic organs and lower limbs; the breast drains mainly to axillary and internal mammary nodes.

exam_trap: Candidates may pick caval drainage (C) by confusing haematogenous with lymphatic spread; enlarged regional nodes reflect axillary lymphatic drainage of the breast.
takeaway: Breast cancer → think lymphatic drainage and axillary staging.
source: Applied surgical anatomy; Gray's Anatomy, 42nd ed.
thinking: Upper outer quadrant breast cancer ↓ hard enlarged regional nodes suggest lymphatic metastasis ↓ the upper outer quadrant and axillary tail drain to the axilla ↓ portal, caval and mesenteric routes are venous or gut pathways ↓ Axillary lymphatic drainage
pearl: Axillary nodes are described by level relative to pectoralis minor: level I lateral to, level II behind and level III medial to the muscle, which guides axillary surgery and staging.

subject: Urology
title: Urology: painless visible haematuria
stem: A man presents with painless visible haematuria without evidence of urinary infection. He is 52 years old. What is the most appropriate next principle?

options.B: Urgent urological assessment for possible malignancy
options.E: Ignore if renal function is normal

correct_answer: B. Urgent urological assessment for possible malignancy
why_correct: NICE recommends suspected-cancer-pathway referral for unexplained visible haematuria in adults aged 45 and over when it is not attributable to UTI or persists/recurs after successful treatment.

why_others_wrong.A: At 52, unexplained visible haematuria meets the NICE threshold for a suspected-cancer referral, so permanent reassurance could miss a bladder or renal tumour.
why_others_wrong.C: Steroids have no role in unexplained painless visible haematuria, which needs investigation for urological malignancy rather than empirical immunosuppression.
why_others_wrong.D: Renal colic is typically painful, and labelling painless haematuria as a stone without assessment risks missing urothelial or renal cancer.
why_others_wrong.E: Normal renal function does not exclude a bladder, upper tract or renal tumour, so it gives no reason to stop investigating.

exam_trap: Candidates choose to ignore the haematuria because renal function is normal, but bladder and renal tumours often leave creatinine unchanged; painless visible haematuria needs urgent assessment.
takeaway: Unexplained visible haematuria at 45 or over → suspected-cancer pathway referral.
source: NICE NG12, urological cancer recommendations (updated 2025).
thinking: Man aged 52 ↓ painless visible haematuria ↓ no urinary infection to explain it ↓ meets the age threshold for suspected urological cancer ↓ Urgent urological assessment for possible malignancy
pearl: Haematuria investigation typically combines flexible cystoscopy to assess the bladder with upper tract imaging, often CT urography, to look for renal and upper tract urothelial tumours.

subject: Urology
title: Urology: LUTS and prostate assessment
stem: A man has lower urinary tract symptoms including hesitancy, weak stream and nocturia. Which assessment may be appropriate when prostate cancer is being considered?
correct_answer: A. PSA and digital rectal examination
why_correct: NICE recommends considering PSA testing and digital rectal examination in men with relevant lower urinary tract symptoms, erectile dysfunction or visible haematuria when assessing for prostate cancer.

why_others_wrong.B: An EEG records cerebral electrical activity for seizure disorders and gives no information about the prostate.
why_others_wrong.C: Spirometry assesses lung function and has no part in evaluating lower urinary tract symptoms or possible prostate cancer.
why_others_wrong.D: Colonoscopy examines the large bowel and does not assess the prostate, which is evaluated clinically by examination and PSA.
why_others_wrong.E: The ankle-brachial pressure index assesses peripheral arterial disease in the legs and is unrelated to prostate assessment.

exam_trap: Candidates may reject PSA and DRE because LUTS are usually benign, but in men with relevant symptoms NICE advises considering both when prostate cancer is a concern.
takeaway: LUTS with cancer concern → consider PSA and DRE.
source: NICE NG12, recommendation 1.6.2 (updated 2025).
thinking: Man with hesitancy, weak stream and nocturia ↓ prostate cancer is being considered ↓ assessment includes digital rectal examination ↓ and PSA after counselling ↓ PSA and digital rectal examination
pearl: PSA can be falsely raised by urinary infection, recent ejaculation, vigorous exercise, catheterisation and retention, so testing is timed to avoid these.

subject: Urology
title: Urology: malignant-feeling prostate
stem: A man has a prostate that feels malignant on digital rectal examination. What is the appropriate next principle?

options.C: Treat empirically with antibiotics for six months

why_correct: NICE recommends suspected-cancer-pathway referral when the prostate feels malignant on DRE.

why_others_wrong.A: NICE recommends suspected-cancer referral for a malignant-feeling prostate on its own, so an unknown PSA gives no grounds for reassurance.
why_others_wrong.C: Prolonged empirical antibiotics would treat presumed prostatitis but delay the urgent assessment needed for a gland that feels malignant.
why_others_wrong.D: A hard, irregular or nodular prostate is a recognised sign of cancer, so ignoring it risks missing treatable disease.
why_others_wrong.E: Waiting five years to re-examine would allow any cancer to progress, when the finding warrants referral on a suspected-cancer pathway.

exam_trap: Candidates choose reassurance while awaiting PSA, but a malignant-feeling prostate meets the suspected-cancer referral criterion regardless of the PSA value.
takeaway: Malignant-feeling prostate → suspected-cancer pathway referral.
source: NICE NG12, recommendation 1.6.1 (updated 2025).
thinking: Prostate feels malignant on DRE ↓ hard, irregular or nodular gland ↓ NICE criterion for referral on its own ↓ PSA result is not required first ↓ Suspected-cancer referral
pearl: Prostate cancer arises mostly in the peripheral zone, which lies posteriorly against the rectum, which is why DRE can detect it.

subject: Urology
title: Urology: post-biopsy sepsis
stem: A man develops fever and rigors after a transrectal prostate biopsy. What serious complication must be considered?
why_correct: Prostate biopsy can introduce infection. NICE notes sepsis as an important serious complication of transrectal biopsy.

why_others_wrong.B: A cataract is a gradual lens opacity causing visual loss and is not a complication of prostate biopsy or a cause of fever and rigors.
why_others_wrong.C: Migraine is a primary headache disorder and would not explain fever and rigors developing after a transrectal biopsy.
why_others_wrong.D: Appendicitis is unrelated to prostate biopsy, whereas rectal bacteria introduced by a transrectal needle readily explain fever and rigors.
why_others_wrong.E: Chronic venous insufficiency causes long-standing leg oedema and skin changes, not an acute febrile illness after a urological procedure.

exam_trap: Candidates may dismiss post-biopsy fever as a minor reaction, but fever with rigors after transrectal biopsy should be treated as possible sepsis with urgent sepsis assessment.
takeaway: Fever or rigors after prostate biopsy → urgent sepsis assessment.
source: NICE NG131, Prostate cancer: diagnosis and management (2019, updated 2021).
thinking: Fever and rigors ↓ after transrectal prostate biopsy ↓ needle passes through rectal wall ↓ bacteraemia from rectal flora ↓ Sepsis
pearl: The transperineal route avoids passing the needle through the rectum and has a lower risk of post-biopsy infection, which is one reason for its increasing use.

subject: Paediatric surgery
title: Paediatric surgery: pyloric stenosis
stem: An infant under 2 months develops progressively worsening projectile vomiting after feeds. What diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: NICE identifies frequent forceful/projectile vomiting in infants up to 2 months as a red flag for hypertrophic pyloric stenosis and recommends same-day specialist assessment for progressively worsening or forceful vomiting.

why_others_wrong.B: Appendicitis is rare in the first two months of life and presents with fever, pain and peritonism rather than progressive projectile vomiting straight after feeds.
why_others_wrong.C: Crohn disease is a chronic inflammatory bowel condition of older children and adults, causing diarrhoea, pain and growth failure rather than projectile vomiting in a young infant.
why_others_wrong.D: Diverticular disease is an acquired colonic condition of older adults and has no place in the differential of projectile vomiting in an infant under two months.
why_others_wrong.E: Peptic ulcer disease of the adult type does not explain progressively forceful vomiting after every feed in a young infant, which points to gastric outlet obstruction.

exam_trap: Candidates who pick adult peptic ulcer disease (E) look for a mucosal cause, but progressive projectile vomiting at this age reflects outlet obstruction from pyloric muscle hypertrophy.
takeaway: Young infant + progressive projectile vomiting → pyloric stenosis.
source: NICE NG1, Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease in children and young people: diagnosis and management, recommendations 1.1.5 and 1.1.19 (2015).
thinking: Infant under 2 months ↓ progressively worsening projectile vomiting after feeds ↓ forceful, worsening vomiting suggests gastric outlet obstruction ↓ typical age for hypertrophy of the pyloric muscle ↓ Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis
pearl: Repeated loss of gastric acid causes a hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, which must be corrected with intravenous fluids before pyloromyotomy because uncorrected alkalosis increases anaesthetic risk, including postoperative apnoea.

subject: Paediatric surgery
title: Paediatric surgery: green vomit
stem: An infant presents with green vomit. What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.B: Possible intestinal obstruction requiring urgent specialist assessment

correct_answer: B. Possible intestinal obstruction requiring urgent specialist assessment
why_correct: Bilious vomiting in an infant is a red flag for possible intestinal obstruction, including malrotation with volvulus.

why_others_wrong.A: Physiological reflux produces effortless, milky posseting; green bile-stained vomit is a red flag for obstruction distal to the ampulla and is not reassuring reflux.
why_others_wrong.C: Teething does not cause vomiting of bile, and attributing green vomit to it risks missing malrotation with volvulus, where delay can cost the midgut.
why_others_wrong.D: Lactose intolerance causes loose stools, wind and bloating after milk feeds; it does not produce bile-stained vomiting, which suggests mechanical obstruction.
why_others_wrong.E: Viral rhinitis may cause mucus-streaked posseting but not green bilious vomit, which must be treated as possible intestinal obstruction until proven otherwise.

exam_trap: Candidates choose physiological reflux (A) because infant vomiting is common, but reflux is milky and effortless; green bile-stained vomit means obstruction until proven otherwise.
takeaway: Infant + bilious vomiting = obstruction until proven otherwise.
source: NICE NG1, Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease in children and young people: diagnosis and management, recommendations on red-flag vomiting (2015).
thinking: Infant with green vomit ↓ green colour means bile ↓ bile enters distal to the ampulla, so any obstruction lies beyond it ↓ malrotation with volvulus must be excluded urgently ↓ Possible intestinal obstruction requiring urgent specialist assessment
pearl: Midgut volvulus can cause ischaemia of the entire midgut within hours, and a well-looking infant with a soft abdomen does not exclude it.

subject: Paediatric surgery
title: Paediatric surgery: bilious vomiting
stem: An infant has unexplained bile-stained vomiting. Which investigation does NICE recommend urgently?
correct_answer: A. Same-day upper GI contrast study
why_correct: NICE recommends an urgent same-day upper GI contrast study for infants with unexplained bile-stained vomiting to exclude serious obstruction such as midgut volvulus.

why_others_wrong.B: Colonoscopy assesses the large bowel electively and cannot show the duodenojejunal flexure position or a midgut volvulus, which is the urgent concern with bilious vomiting.
why_others_wrong.C: A DEXA scan measures bone mineral density and has no role in the acute assessment of an infant with possible intestinal obstruction.
why_others_wrong.D: MRI of the knee is irrelevant to bile-stained vomiting; the priority is same-day imaging of the upper gastrointestinal tract to exclude malrotation.
why_others_wrong.E: An outpatient ECG does not investigate the bowel, and deferring to an outpatient pathway is unsafe when midgut volvulus needs excluding the same day.

exam_trap: Candidates may accept an outpatient pathway (E) for a well-looking infant, but unexplained bilious vomiting needs same-day contrast imaging to exclude midgut volvulus.
takeaway: Bilious vomiting in an infant → urgent assessment for malrotation/volvulus.
source: NICE NG1, Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease in children and young people: diagnosis and management, recommendation 1.1.16 (2015).
thinking: Infant with unexplained bile-stained vomiting ↓ main concern is malrotation with midgut volvulus ↓ the duodenojejunal flexure position must be shown ↓ urgent same-day upper GI contrast study ↓ Same-day upper GI contrast study
pearl: On upper GI contrast the normal duodenojejunal flexure lies to the left of the spine at about the level of the duodenal bulb; a low or right-sided flexure indicates malrotation needing urgent surgical review.

subject: Burns & paediatric fluids
title: Paediatric surgery: non-accidental burn pattern
stem: A child has a scald injury involving both buttocks and the perineum with a sharply demarcated distribution. What should this pattern raise concern about?

options.B: Accidental spill of a hot drink
options.C: Accidental contact with a hot radiator

why_correct: NICE identifies sharply demarcated burns, forced-immersion patterns and burns involving areas such as the buttocks and perineum as patterns that should raise concern about maltreatment.

why_others_wrong.B: An accidental spill produces an irregular flow or splash pattern of variable depth, usually on the face, chest or arms, not a sharply demarcated burn of the buttocks and perineum.
why_others_wrong.C: A contact burn takes the shape of the hot object on a single surface and does not produce a sharply demarcated immersion pattern over the buttocks and perineum.
why_others_wrong.D: A viral exanthem is a widespread blanching rash with systemic features, not a localised thermal injury with a sharply demarcated edge over the buttocks and perineum.
why_others_wrong.E: Psoriasis causes chronic scaly plaques, typically on extensor surfaces, and does not mimic an acute scald with a sharply demarcated immersion-type distribution.

exam_trap: Candidates accept an accidental spill (B), but spills leave irregular splash marks of varying depth; sharp-edged buttock and perineal scalds suggest forced immersion.
takeaway: Suspicious burn pattern → safeguarding assessment.
source: NICE CG89, Child maltreatment: when to suspect maltreatment in under 18s (2009, updated 2017).
thinking: Scald involving both buttocks and the perineum ↓ sharply demarcated edges suggest forced immersion ↓ spills give irregular splash patterns; contact burns mirror the object ↓ the pattern raises safeguarding concern ↓ Child maltreatment
pearl: Forced immersion scalds typically show symmetrical, sharply demarcated glove, stocking or buttock patterns without splash marks, sometimes sparing the skin pressed against the cooler bath base or flexural creases.

subject: Burns & paediatric fluids
title: Paediatric surgery: forced-immersion burn
stem: A child has a burn injury with a pattern resembling forced immersion. What is the most appropriate response?

options.B: Ignore the pattern if the burn is small

correct_answer: A. Document and assess safeguarding concerns
why_correct: A suspicious burn pattern should trigger consideration of maltreatment and appropriate safeguarding assessment.

why_others_wrong.B: Burn size does not reduce safeguarding concern; a forced-immersion pattern is suspicious because of its mechanism, even when the area involved is small.
why_others_wrong.C: Discharging without assessment would leave a child with a suspicious immersion pattern at risk of further harm and misses the need for safeguarding review.
why_others_wrong.D: Analgesia is part of burn care, but managing pain alone ignores the forced-immersion pattern that should prompt documentation and safeguarding assessment.
why_others_wrong.E: Assuming accidental injury ignores a pattern recognised by NICE as suggestive of maltreatment; the explanation must be checked against the burn pattern and development.

exam_trap: Candidates may treat a small burn with analgesia alone (D), but burn size does not lessen concern; a forced-immersion pattern demands documentation and safeguarding assessment.
takeaway: Burn pattern + unsuitable explanation → safeguarding.
source: NICE CG89, Child maltreatment, thermal injuries recommendations (2009, updated 2017).
thinking: Burn with a forced-immersion pattern ↓ mechanism suggests deliberate injury regardless of burn size ↓ findings must be recorded and acted on ↓ Document and assess safeguarding concerns
pearl: Documentation should include a body map or photographs, the explanation given and whether it fits the child's developmental stage, with referral following local safeguarding procedures.

subject: Burns & paediatric fluids
title: Burns: TBSA estimation
stem: In a major burn, which method is used to estimate the percentage of total body surface area burned, particularly in children?
why_correct: The Lund and Browder method is used to estimate burn total body surface area and accounts for changing body proportions with age.

why_others_wrong.B: The Glasgow Coma Scale grades conscious level after injury and gives no measure of the percentage of body surface area burned.
why_others_wrong.C: The Wells score estimates the clinical probability of deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism and has no role in estimating burn extent.
why_others_wrong.D: CHA2DS2-VASc estimates stroke risk in atrial fibrillation to guide anticoagulation and is unrelated to measuring burned body surface area.
why_others_wrong.E: The Apgar score assesses a newborn's condition at one and five minutes after birth and does not estimate total body surface area burned.

exam_trap: The listed scores are unrelated; the real pitfall is using the adult rule of nines in a child, which misestimates burn size because head and limb proportions change with age.
takeaway: Burn TBSA → Lund and Browder, particularly important in children.
source: NICE MIB58, Mersey Burns for calculating fluid resuscitation in adults and children with severe burns (2016).
thinking: Need to estimate percentage TBSA burned ↓ children have proportionally larger heads and smaller legs than adults ↓ a chart that adjusts body-part percentages for age is needed ↓ Lund and Browder chart
pearl: Simple erythema without blistering is excluded from TBSA estimates, and the patient's palm including fingers (roughly 1% TBSA) is useful for estimating small or patchy burns.

subject: Burns & paediatric fluids
title: Paediatric fluids: shock bolus
stem: A child requires IV fluid resuscitation for shock unrelated to diabetic ketoacidosis. Which initial bolus does current NICE paediatric IV-fluid guidance recommend?
why_correct: NICE recommends glucose-free crystalloids containing sodium 131–154 mmol/L, with a 10 ml/kg bolus over less than 10 minutes for children and young people requiring IV fluid resuscitation, with reassessment and adjustment for comorbidities.

why_others_wrong.A: A 1 ml/kg bolus is far too small to restore circulating volume in a shocked child and is not a recommended resuscitation volume in NICE guidance.
why_others_wrong.B: A 5 ml/kg bolus is smaller than the standard NICE resuscitation dose, which is 10 ml/kg of glucose-free isotonic crystalloid over less than 10 minutes.
why_others_wrong.D: A 50 ml/kg bolus risks fluid overload; NICE advises 10 ml/kg boluses with reassessment and paediatric intensive care advice if 40-60 ml/kg or more is needed.
why_others_wrong.E: A 100 ml/kg bolus is roughly a full day's maintenance in a small child given at once and would cause dangerous fluid overload.

exam_trap: Candidates may reach for a large volume such as 50 ml/kg (D), but that approaches the 40-60 ml/kg total at which NICE advises seeking critical care advice; the single resuscitation bolus is 10 ml/kg over less than 10 minutes.
takeaway: Paediatric fluid resuscitation → weight-based prescription.
source: NICE NG29, Intravenous fluid therapy in children and young people in hospital, recommendation 1.3.1 (2015).
thinking: Child needs IV fluid resuscitation, not for DKA ↓ NICE: glucose-free crystalloid with sodium 131–154 mmol/L ↓ bolus of 10 ml/kg over less than 10 minutes ↓ reassess after each bolus ↓ 10 ml/kg
pearl: Diabetic ketoacidosis is excluded from the standard algorithm because it has its own more cautious fluid guidance, reflecting the risk of cerebral oedema in children.

subject: Burns & paediatric fluids
title: Paediatric fluids: bolus volume calculation
stem: A child weighing 20 kg requires IV fluid resuscitation under the standard NICE paediatric algorithm. What volume corresponds to the initial 10 ml/kg bolus?
why_correct: 10 ml/kg × 20 kg = 200 ml.

why_others_wrong.A: 20 ml corresponds to 1 ml/kg in a 20 kg child, a tenth of the 200 ml produced by the 10 ml/kg bolus.
why_others_wrong.B: 50 ml equals 2.5 ml/kg in a 20 kg child, which does not match the 10 ml/kg NICE bolus of 200 ml.
why_others_wrong.C: 100 ml is 5 ml/kg in a 20 kg child, half of the 200 ml delivered by a 10 ml/kg bolus.
why_others_wrong.E: 500 ml is an adult-style fixed bolus and equals 25 ml/kg for a 20 kg child, well above the 10 ml/kg dose.

exam_trap: Candidates may pick 500 ml (E) from adult fixed-bolus habits, or 100 ml (C) by using 5 ml/kg; 10 ml/kg in a 20 kg child is 200 ml.
takeaway: Always calculate paediatric resuscitation by weight.
source: NICE NG29, Intravenous fluid therapy in children and young people, recommendation 1.3.1 (2015).
thinking: Bolus is prescribed per kilogram ↓ NICE resuscitation bolus is 10 ml/kg ↓ 10 ml/kg × 20 kg ↓ 200 ml
pearl: When a child's weight is unknown in an emergency, an age-based estimate or length-based tape allows weight-based fluid and drug doses to be given without delay.

subject: Burns & paediatric fluids
title: Burns: extent assessment
stem: An adult with a significant burn requires formal assessment of burn extent before fluid resuscitation calculations. Which measurement is most important?
correct_answer: A. Total body surface area burned
why_correct: Burn resuscitation calculations depend on burn size and patient characteristics. Accurate TBSA assessment is therefore fundamental.

why_others_wrong.B: Height alone does not describe how much skin is burned; burn fluid formulas such as Parkland use percentage TBSA together with body weight.
why_others_wrong.C: BMI describes body habitus rather than burn extent, and burn resuscitation formulas use burned TBSA with weight, not BMI.
why_others_wrong.D: Head circumference is a paediatric growth measure and plays no part in estimating the extent of an adult burn or its fluid requirement.
why_others_wrong.E: Mid-arm circumference is a nutritional assessment tool and gives no information about the percentage of body surface area burned.

exam_trap: Height (B) and BMI (C) tempt because they relate to body size, but burn resuscitation formulas use the percentage TBSA burned with body weight, so TBSA must be measured first.
takeaway: Significant burn → determine TBSA accurately before formal fluid calculation.
source: NICE MIB58, Mersey Burns for calculating fluid resuscitation in adults and children with severe burns (2016).
thinking: Significant adult burn ↓ burn fluid formulas use percentage TBSA burned and body weight ↓ TBSA must therefore be estimated accurately first ↓ Total body surface area burned
pearl: Erythema alone is excluded from TBSA and overestimation of burn size is common, risking fluid overload; resuscitation is then titrated to urine output rather than fixed to the formula.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Fluid therapy: adult maintenance water
stem: A patient requires IV fluids for routine maintenance rather than resuscitation. Which adult daily water requirement is recommended initially by NICE?
why_correct: NICE recommends an initial routine-maintenance prescription of approximately 25–30 ml/kg/day of water, with adjustment for clinical circumstances.

why_others_wrong.A: 5-10 ml/kg/day is far below adult maintenance needs and would lead to dehydration if used as the routine prescription.
why_others_wrong.B: 10-15 ml/kg/day is roughly half the NICE starting figure of 25-30 ml/kg/day and would underhydrate most adults.
why_others_wrong.D: 50-60 ml/kg/day is about double adult maintenance needs and would risk fluid overload and hyponatraemia.
why_others_wrong.E: 100 ml/kg/day is closer to the first-10-kg requirement used in paediatric calculations and would grossly overload an adult.

exam_trap: Option E tempts candidates who recall the paediatric figure of 100 ml/kg/day for the first 10 kg, but adult maintenance is about 25-30 ml/kg/day.
takeaway: Adult maintenance ≠ resuscitation.
source: NICE CG174, Intravenous fluid therapy in adults in hospital, recommendation 1.4.1 (2013).
thinking: Routine maintenance, not resuscitation ↓ NICE gives a weight-based starting figure for adults ↓ about 25-30 ml/kg/day of water ↓ 25-30 ml/kg/day
pearl: For a 70 kg adult, 25-30 ml/kg/day equals roughly 1.75-2.1 litres a day; obese patients should be prescribed according to ideal body weight, and lower volumes used in older, frail or cardiac patients.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Fluid therapy: hyperchloraemic acidosis
stem: A hospitalised adult receiving IV fluids has been prescribed sodium chloride 0.9% for several days and develops hyperchloraemia with acidaemia. What should be considered?

options.A: Reassess the IV-fluid prescription and acid–base status
options.B: Automatically increase the sodium chloride concentration

correct_answer: A. Reassess the IV-fluid prescription and acid–base status
why_correct: NICE recommends monitoring chloride in patients receiving fluids with chloride concentrations above 120 mmol/L and reassessing the fluid prescription and acid–base status if hyperchloraemia or acidaemia develops.

why_others_wrong.B: Giving more sodium chloride would increase the chloride load and worsen the hyperchloraemic acidosis.
why_others_wrong.C: Hyperchloraemia with acidaemia is a recognised complication of sodium chloride 0.9% and should prompt reassessment, not be disregarded.
why_others_wrong.D: Patients on IV fluids need ongoing monitoring of electrolytes and acid-base status, particularly once a complication has appeared.
why_others_wrong.E: Routine potassium does not address hyperchloraemic acidosis and should be prescribed according to measured levels and needs.

exam_trap: Option E may tempt because potassium is often added to maintenance fluids, but it does not correct hyperchloraemic acidosis; the fluid choice and acid-base status need reassessment.
takeaway: IV fluids are drugs: prescribe, monitor and reassess.
source: NICE CG174, Intravenous fluid therapy in adults in hospital, recommendation 1.2.5 (2013).
thinking: Several days of sodium chloride 0.9% ↓ chloride 154 mmol/L is well above plasma levels ↓ chloride load causes hyperchloraemic acidosis ↓ NICE advises reassessing fluids and acid-base status ↓ Reassess the IV-fluid prescription and acid–base status
pearl: Balanced crystalloids such as compound sodium lactate contain less chloride than 0.9% saline and are often preferred for large-volume resuscitation to avoid hyperchloraemic acidosis.

subject: Cardiothoracic surgery
title: Cardiothoracic surgery: tension pneumothorax
stem: A 29-year-old patient develops severe respiratory distress and hypotension following major blunt chest trauma. There is markedly reduced air entry on one side and the trachea appears deviated. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
why_correct: A tension pneumothorax is a clinical emergency. In a patient with suspected tension pneumothorax who has haemodynamic instability or severe respiratory compromise, decompression should not be delayed for imaging.

why_others_wrong.A: CT takes this hypotensive, severely distressed patient away from resuscitation, and NICE advises decompressing suspected tension pneumothorax before imaging when the patient is unstable.
why_others_wrong.B: A chest X-ray would only confirm what the clinical signs already show, and waiting for it delays decompression while tension physiology causes cardiovascular collapse.
why_others_wrong.D: eFAST may support the diagnosis, but a scan alone treats nothing; this unstable patient with clinical signs of tension needs the chest decompressed straight away.
why_others_wrong.E: Bronchoscopy assesses the airways for injury or obstruction and has no role in relieving the rising intrapleural pressure that is causing this patient's shock.

exam_trap: Do not choose CT or chest X-ray simply because imaging would confirm the diagnosis.
takeaway: Tension pneumothorax with instability or severe respiratory compromise → decompress before imaging.
source: NICE NG39, Major trauma: assessment and initial management, recommendations 1.3.4 and 1.4.1. Current guidance accessed 2026.
thinking: Blunt chest trauma with severe respiratory distress and hypotension ↓ unilateral reduced air entry with tracheal deviation ↓ clinical tension pneumothorax causing obstructive shock ↓ imaging would only delay life-saving treatment ↓ Immediate chest decompression
pearl: Tracheal deviation is a late and unreliable sign, so hypotension with unilateral absent breath sounds is enough to act; needle decompression is only a temporising measure and must be followed by a chest drain.

subject: Cardiothoracic surgery
title: Cardiothoracic surgery: open pneumothorax
stem: A patient has a penetrating chest wound with an audible sucking sound and respiratory distress. What is the appropriate immediate treatment of the open chest wound?

options.C: Perform immediate thoracotomy in all cases
options.D: Insert a central venous catheter through the wound
options.E: Apply a circumferential pressure bandage around the entire chest

correct_answer: B. Apply a simple occlusive dressing
why_correct: NICE recommends covering an open pneumothorax with a simple occlusive dressing and observing for development of tension pneumothorax.

why_others_wrong.A: Leaving a sucking chest wound open lets air continue to enter the pleural space with each breath, worsening lung collapse and respiratory distress.
why_others_wrong.C: Thoracotomy is reserved for specific indications such as massive haemorrhage or traumatic arrest, not as routine first treatment for every open pneumothorax.
why_others_wrong.D: Central venous access is placed through intact skin at standard sites for vascular access and does nothing to seal a penetrating chest wall defect.
why_others_wrong.E: A tight circumferential bandage restricts chest wall movement and ventilation without reliably sealing the wound, and could worsen respiratory compromise.

exam_trap: Candidates pick the circumferential pressure bandage, which restricts ventilation without sealing the wound, or thoracotomy, which is reserved for massive haemorrhage or arrest rather than every open wound.
takeaway: Open pneumothorax → simple occlusive dressing and watch for tension.
source: NICE NG39, recommendation 1.3.7. Current guidance accessed 2026.
thinking: Penetrating chest wound with an audible sucking sound ↓ open pneumothorax: air enters the pleura through the chest wall defect ↓ seal the defect to stop air entry ↓ observe closely for conversion to tension ↓ Apply a simple occlusive dressing
pearl: If the patient deteriorates after the wound is sealed, suspect tension and release the dressing or decompress; definitive care is a chest drain inserted away from the wound, with later closure of the defect.

subject: Cardiothoracic surgery
title: Cardiothoracic surgery: efast limitation
stem: A trauma patient has severe chest pain and respiratory distress. An eFAST examination does not demonstrate a pneumothorax. Which statement is most accurate?

options.B: A CT scan is mandatory before any treatment
options.C: A negative chest eFAST does not exclude pneumothorax
options.D: Pneumothorax is excluded if oxygen saturation is normal
options.E: A normal chest X-ray is required before clinical treatment

correct_answer: C. A negative chest eFAST does not exclude pneumothorax
why_correct: NICE specifically states that a negative chest eFAST does not exclude pneumothorax.

why_others_wrong.A: eFAST can miss a pneumothorax, so a negative scan in a patient with severe chest pain and respiratory distress does not rule the diagnosis out.
why_others_wrong.B: Treatment of life-threatening chest injury is guided by the clinical picture and physiology, and a critically unwell patient should not wait for CT before intervention.
why_others_wrong.D: Normal oxygen saturation does not exclude a pneumothorax, particularly early or with supplemental oxygen, so it cannot compensate for a limited negative eFAST.
why_others_wrong.E: Clinical treatment of suspected serious chest injury is not conditional on a chest X-ray, and a normal film can itself miss a small or anterior pneumothorax.

exam_trap: Option A tempts candidates who treat a negative eFAST as a rule-out test, but operator skill, body habitus and surgical emphysema limit its sensitivity for pneumothorax.
takeaway: Negative eFAST ≠ no pneumothorax.
source: NICE NG39, recommendation 1.3.3. Current guidance accessed 2026.
thinking: Trauma patient with severe chest pain and respiratory distress ↓ eFAST reports no pneumothorax ↓ ultrasound accuracy is limited by operator, body habitus and surgical emphysema ↓ a negative screen cannot override high clinical suspicion ↓ A negative chest eFAST does not exclude pneumothorax
pearl: Ultrasound diagnosis of pneumothorax relies on loss of lung sliding, which surgical emphysema and obesity can obscure; a deteriorating patient with clinical signs is treated on clinical grounds, not on a reassuring scan.

subject: Cardiothoracic surgery
title: Cardiothoracic surgery: chest trauma imaging
stem: A haemodynamically stable adult has significant blunt chest trauma but no severe respiratory compromise and responds to initial resuscitation. Which imaging strategy should be considered?
why_correct: For adults with suspected chest trauma without severe respiratory compromise who are responding to resuscitation or have normal haemodynamic status, NICE recommends considering immediate CT.
