why_others_wrong.B: Significant blunt chest trauma carries a real risk of occult injury to the lungs, great vessels and ribs, so omitting imaging in this patient would be unsafe.
why_others_wrong.C: Immediate thoracotomy is for patients in extremis, such as traumatic arrest or massive haemorrhage, not a stable adult who is responding to resuscitation.
why_others_wrong.D: Pericardiocentesis is a treatment for suspected tamponade in a compromised patient and is not a diagnostic imaging strategy for a stable chest trauma patient.
why_others_wrong.E: MRI is slow, requires the patient to be away from the resuscitation area for long periods and is not a first-line imaging test in acute chest trauma.

exam_trap: Candidates choose no imaging because the patient looks stable, but significant blunt chest trauma needs CT to find occult injury; thoracotomy and pericardiocentesis belong to the unstable patient.
takeaway: Stable significant chest trauma → CT may be appropriate.
source: NICE NG39, recommendation 1.4.5. Current guidance accessed 2026.
thinking: Significant blunt chest trauma ↓ haemodynamically stable, responding to resuscitation, no severe respiratory compromise ↓ occult thoracic injury is still likely ↓ stable enough to be scanned safely ↓ Immediate CT
pearl: A supine chest X-ray misses many pneumothoraces, rib fractures and mediastinal injuries that CT detects; contrast CT also assesses for blunt aortic injury, which may be suggested by a widened mediastinum on plain film.

subject: Trauma & orthopaedics
title: Trauma & orthopaedics: open fracture antibiotics
stem: A patient sustains an open tibial fracture. He is haemodynamically stable and is being transferred to a trauma centre. When should prophylactic intravenous antibiotics be given?

options.C: As soon as possible, preferably within 1 hour

correct_answer: C. As soon as possible, preferably within 1 hour
why_correct: For open fractures, NICE recommends prophylactic IV antibiotics as soon as possible and preferably within 1 hour of injury, without delaying transport.

why_others_wrong.A: Waiting for wound excision in theatre delays antibiotics by hours, whereas infection risk is reduced when they are given as soon as possible after an open fracture.
why_others_wrong.B: Fracture fixation happens later, often at the trauma centre, and antibiotics should already have been given within an hour of injury rather than postponed until then.
why_others_wrong.D: The antibiotics are prophylaxis against contamination of the open wound, so they are started immediately rather than held back until signs of infection such as fever appear.
why_others_wrong.E: Microbiology results take days and early wound cultures predict infection poorly, so waiting for them would leave the contaminated fracture unprotected in the critical early period.

exam_trap: Candidates pick wound excision or fixation because antibiotics feel like a theatre step, but delaying them until definitive surgery increases deep infection after open fracture.
takeaway: Open fracture → early IV antibiotics, ideally within 1 hour of injury.
source: NICE NG37, recommendation 1.1.10. Current guidance accessed 2026.
thinking: Open tibial fracture, stable, awaiting transfer ↓ contaminated wound with high deep-infection risk ↓ prophylaxis works best when started early ↓ do not wait for theatre, fixation or cultures ↓ As soon as possible, preferably within 1 hour
pearl: Open fracture care also includes tetanus cover, photographing the wound before applying a saline-soaked dressing, and joint orthoplastic debridement at a specialist centre, so the dressing is not repeatedly lifted in the emergency department.

subject: Trauma & orthopaedics
title: Trauma & orthopaedics: open fracture prehospital management
stem: What should NOT routinely be performed in the prehospital setting for an open long-bone fracture?
correct_answer: D. Irrigation of the open fracture
why_correct: NICE advises against irrigating open fractures of the long bones, hindfoot or midfoot in the prehospital setting.

why_others_wrong.A: Covering the wound with a saline-soaked dressing is recommended prehospital care, protecting it from further contamination and drying until formal debridement.
why_others_wrong.B: An occlusive layer over the saline-soaked dressing is recommended to limit further contamination during transfer, so it is done rather than avoided.
why_others_wrong.C: Early intravenous antibiotics, ideally within an hour of injury, are recommended for open fractures and should be started prehospital where available rather than withheld.
why_others_wrong.E: Splinting restores alignment, reduces pain and bleeding and protects the soft tissues, so it is a standard prehospital step for an open long-bone fracture.

exam_trap: Candidates assume washing the wound immediately is good first aid, but prehospital irrigation of open long-bone fractures is not recommended and can drive contamination deeper.
takeaway: Open fracture prehospital: cover with saline-soaked dressing, splint, antibiotics; do not irrigate.
source: NICE NG37, recommendation 1.1.8. Current guidance accessed 2026.
thinking: Open long-bone fracture in the prehospital setting ↓ aim is to limit further contamination and stabilise ↓ cover, splint and give antibiotics where available ↓ irrigation is deferred to formal debridement in hospital ↓ Irrigation of the open fracture
pearl: Formal wound excision and lavage of an open fracture are done in theatre by combined orthopaedic and plastic surgical teams; gross contamination can be removed prehospital but wounds are not washed out at the roadside.

subject: Trauma & orthopaedics
title: Trauma & orthopaedics: devascularised limb
stem: A patient has a complex long-bone fracture with a clearly devascularised limb after initial alignment. What is the recommended first surgical intervention?
why_correct: NICE recommends using a vascular shunt as the first surgical intervention in a devascularised limb following long-bone fracture, before skeletal stabilisation and definitive vascular reconstruction.

why_others_wrong.A: Definitive internal fixation takes time while the limb remains ischaemic, so flow is restored with a shunt first and definitive fixation follows afterwards.
why_others_wrong.B: CT angiography is a diagnostic test rather than a surgical intervention and would delay reperfusion when the limb is already clearly devascularised.
why_others_wrong.D: Fasciotomy is often needed alongside revascularisation to prevent reperfusion compartment syndrome, but on its own it does not restore arterial flow to the limb.
why_others_wrong.E: Delaying reconstruction leaves the limb ischaemic, and warm ischaemia beyond a few hours risks muscle necrosis and amputation, so flow must be restored first.

exam_trap: Candidates choose CT angiography or definitive fixation first, but a clearly devascularised limb needs flow restored by shunt before imaging or definitive skeletal work.
takeaway: Devascularised limb after fracture → shunt first, then stabilise and reconstruct.
source: NICE NG37, recommendation 1.2.4. Current guidance accessed 2026.
thinking: Long-bone fracture with a clearly devascularised limb ↓ warm ischaemia time is the limiting factor ↓ temporary shunt restores flow quickly ↓ skeletal stabilisation and definitive vascular repair follow ↓ Vascular shunt
pearl: A temporary intravascular shunt lets the orthopaedic surgeon stabilise the fracture without disrupting a fresh vascular repair, and fasciotomies are commonly performed at the same sitting to prevent reperfusion compartment syndrome.

subject: Trauma & orthopaedics
title: Trauma & orthopaedics: hard signs of vascular injury
stem: A patient with a complex limb fracture has persistent hard signs of vascular injury after limb alignment has been restored. What is the appropriate management?
why_correct: Persistent hard signs of vascular injury warrant immediate surgical exploration after necessary restoration of limb alignment or joint reduction.

why_others_wrong.A: Observation lets ischaemia progress; persistent hard signs such as pulsatile bleeding, an expanding haematoma or absent pulses after realignment need immediate exploration.
why_others_wrong.B: A Doppler study may add information, but relying on it alone delays treatment, and an equivocal result should not override convincing clinical hard signs.
why_others_wrong.D: Outpatient review is inappropriate for a limb-threatening arterial injury, which needs emergency surgical management without delay.
why_others_wrong.E: Compartment pressure measurement assesses compartment syndrome, not arterial injury, and waiting for it would delay the exploration that persistent hard signs require.

exam_trap: Candidates choose Doppler ultrasound to confirm the injury, but persistent hard signs after realignment mandate exploration and an equivocal Doppler must not delay it.
takeaway: Persistent hard signs of vascular injury → immediate exploration.
source: NICE NG37, recommendation 1.2.3. Current guidance accessed 2026.
thinking: Complex limb fracture with persistent hard signs ↓ alignment already restored and signs persist ↓ hard signs indicate a significant arterial injury ↓ delay risks limb loss ↓ Immediate surgical exploration
pearl: Hard signs of arterial injury include pulsatile bleeding, an expanding or pulsatile haematoma, absent distal pulses, a bruit or thrill and signs of distal ischaemia; soft signs alone usually prompt imaging rather than exploration.

subject: Plastic surgery
title: Plastic surgery: open fracture management
stem: A patient has a high-energy open tibial fracture requiring definitive fixation and soft-tissue coverage. Which team approach is recommended?
why_correct: NICE recommends that wound excision, fixation and cover of open long-bone, hindfoot or midfoot fractures should be performed concurrently by consultant orthopaedic and plastic surgeons using a combined orthoplastic approach.

why_others_wrong.A: Orthopaedic fixation alone neglects the soft-tissue cover that NICE requires to be planned and performed concurrently with consultant plastic surgeons.
why_others_wrong.B: Plastic surgeons alone cannot provide definitive skeletal stabilisation; NICE advises joint excision, fixation and cover by orthopaedic and plastic consultants together.
why_others_wrong.D: Vascular surgeons are involved when there is limb ischaemia, but they do not lead fixation or soft-tissue reconstruction of an open tibial fracture.
why_others_wrong.E: Rehabilitation is essential after definitive surgery but does not deliver wound excision, fixation or flap cover of the open fracture.

exam_trap: Option A tempts because fixation seems an orthopaedic task, but fixing bone without concurrent plastic surgical planning delays cover and raises the risk of deep infection and non-union.
takeaway: Complex open fracture → combined orthoplastic team.
source: NICE NG37, recommendation 1.2.27. Current guidance accessed 2026.
thinking: High-energy open tibial fracture ↓ needs both skeletal stabilisation and soft-tissue cover ↓ NICE: excision, fixation and cover done together by consultant orthopaedic and plastic surgeons ↓ Combined orthoplastic approach
pearl: NICE advises that open fractures are managed in a specialist centre with orthoplastic facilities, and that definitive soft-tissue cover is performed within 72 hours of injury if it cannot be achieved at the first debridement.

subject: Plastic surgery
title: Plastic surgery: open fracture excision timing
stem: A highly contaminated open fracture of the lower limb arrives at a trauma centre. When should wound excision be performed?
why_correct: NICE recommends immediate wound excision for highly contaminated open fractures.

why_others_wrong.B: A 48-hour delay is outside every NICE window; even non-contaminated high-energy injuries should be excised within 12 hours and others within 24 hours.
why_others_wrong.C: Oral antibiotics cannot sterilise a grossly contaminated wound; prompt intravenous antibiotics are given, but surgical excision of the contamination must not be deferred.
why_others_wrong.D: Leaving contaminated tissue until fracture union would invite deep infection and osteomyelitis, preventing union rather than protecting it.
why_others_wrong.E: A highly contaminated open fracture is a surgical emergency requiring theatre on arrival, not assessment at a routine outpatient appointment.

exam_trap: Do not apply the 12-hour or 24-hour windows indiscriminately to highly contaminated injuries.
takeaway: Highly contaminated open fracture → immediate wound excision.
source: NICE NG37, recommendation 1.2.28. Current guidance accessed 2026.
thinking: Highly contaminated open fracture ↓ contamination drives the risk of deep infection ↓ NICE sets excision timing by contamination and energy ↓ highly contaminated wounds are excised immediately ↓ Immediately
pearl: NICE timing for wound excision is immediate for highly contaminated wounds, within 12 hours for other high-energy injuries and within 24 hours for other open fractures, with intravenous antibiotics started as soon as possible.

subject: Urology
title: Urology: psa alone
stem: A man has a raised PSA level but no other assessment has yet been performed. Which statement is most appropriate?

options.C: MRI and clinical assessment should contribute to the decision about biopsy

correct_answer: C. MRI and clinical assessment should contribute to the decision about biopsy
why_correct: NICE specifically states not to automatically offer prostate biopsy on the basis of serum PSA alone.

why_others_wrong.A: NICE advises against offering biopsy on the basis of serum PSA alone, because MRI and clinical assessment should first refine the risk.
why_others_wrong.B: PSA can rise with benign enlargement, infection, retention or instrumentation, so it indicates risk and cannot establish cancer without histology.
why_others_wrong.D: A raised PSA is a useful risk marker that should prompt further assessment, not be disregarded.
why_others_wrong.E: Radical treatment requires histological confirmation and staging, neither of which is available from a raised PSA alone.

exam_trap: Candidates choose 'PSA alone mandates biopsy' from older pathways, but NICE advises against biopsy on PSA alone; MRI and clinical assessment should inform the decision.
takeaway: PSA is a risk marker, not a histological diagnosis.
source: NICE NG131, recommendation 1.2.6. Current guidance accessed 2026.
thinking: Raised PSA with no other assessment ↓ PSA is a risk marker, not a diagnosis ↓ NICE: do not offer biopsy on PSA alone ↓ MRI and clinical assessment refine risk first ↓ MRI and clinical assessment should contribute to the decision about biopsy
pearl: Free-to-total PSA ratio and PSA density (PSA divided by prostate volume) help distinguish benign enlargement from cancer when PSA is mildly raised.

subject: Urology
title: Urology: negative biopsy + suspicious mri
stem: A patient has a negative prostate biopsy but an MRI Likert score of 3 or more. What should be considered?

options.C: Discuss the possibility of significant disease in an MDT meeting

correct_answer: C. Discuss the possibility of significant disease in an MDT meeting
why_correct: NICE recommends MDT discussion regarding the possibility of significant disease, with a view to repeating biopsy.

why_others_wrong.A: A Likert score of 3 or more after a negative biopsy raises concern that the biopsy missed the lesion, so the MRI finding should not be disregarded.
why_others_wrong.B: Permanent discharge ignores the residual risk of significant cancer suggested by the MRI, which NICE says merits MDT review.
why_others_wrong.D: Chemotherapy is used for selected advanced prostate cancer and cannot be started when biopsy has not confirmed any cancer.
why_others_wrong.E: Cystectomy removes the bladder for bladder malignancy and has no role in unresolved suspicion of prostate cancer.

exam_trap: Candidates choose discharge because the biopsy was negative, but a suspicious MRI after a negative biopsy raises concern of a missed lesion and needs MDT review.
takeaway: Negative biopsy does not always end the investigation if MRI is suspicious.
source: NICE NG131, recommendation 1.2.10. Current guidance accessed 2026.
thinking: Negative prostate biopsy ↓ but MRI Likert score of 3 or more ↓ the biopsy may have missed the lesion ↓ NICE advises MDT discussion with a view to repeat biopsy ↓ Discuss the possibility of significant disease in an MDT meeting
pearl: Discordance between imaging and pathology is a recurring reason for MDT review across surgical oncology, including breast and prostate pathways.

subject: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care
title: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care: lower-limb immobilisation
stem: A patient has a lower-limb injury requiring prolonged immobilisation. Which intervention may be considered when VTE risk outweighs bleeding risk?
why_correct: NICE recommends considering pharmacological VTE prophylaxis with LMWH or fondaparinux sodium for lower-limb immobilisation when VTE risk outweighs bleeding risk.

why_others_wrong.A: NICE does not recommend aspirin for all patients with lower-limb immobilisation; prophylaxis follows individual VTE and bleeding risk assessment, using LMWH or fondaparinux.
why_others_wrong.C: Warfarin is not a recommended routine prophylactic agent for lower-limb immobilisation, needs INR monitoring and would not be given to everyone.
why_others_wrong.D: NICE requires VTE and bleeding risk assessment, which determines whether prophylaxis is appropriate, so skipping assessment is unsafe.
why_others_wrong.E: Therapeutic-dose anticoagulation treats established VTE; for immobilisation the aim is prophylactic dosing, and treatment doses would raise bleeding risk unnecessarily.

exam_trap: Candidates choose therapeutic anticoagulation for maximum protection, but prophylaxis uses prophylactic doses of LMWH or fondaparinux; treatment doses add bleeding risk without indication.
takeaway: Immobilised lower limb with VTE risk greater than bleeding risk → consider LMWH or fondaparinux.
source: NICE NG89, recommendation 1.11.1. Current guidance accessed 2026.
thinking: Lower-limb immobilisation ↓ individual VTE and bleeding risk assessment ↓ if VTE risk outweighs bleeding risk ↓ consider pharmacological prophylaxis ↓ LMWH or fondaparinux sodium
pearl: VTE prophylaxis for lower-limb immobilisation is usually continued for the duration of immobilisation and stopped when the cast or brace is removed.

subject: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care
title: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care: hip fracture vte prophylaxis
stem: A patient undergoes surgery for a fragility fracture of the proximal femur. For how long should VTE prophylaxis generally be offered when VTE risk outweighs bleeding risk?
why_correct: NICE recommends VTE prophylaxis for a month following fragility fractures of the pelvis, hip or proximal femur when the VTE risk outweighs bleeding risk.

why_others_wrong.A: Twenty-four hours is far too short, as VTE risk after hip fracture surgery persists for weeks and NICE recommends prophylaxis for a month.
why_others_wrong.B: Three days would stop prophylaxis while the patient is still at high VTE risk, well short of the one month NICE recommends.
why_others_wrong.C: Seven days is below the one month NICE recommends after fragility fractures of the pelvis, hip or proximal femur.
why_others_wrong.E: Six months exceeds recommended prophylaxis and approaches treatment duration for established VTE, adding bleeding risk without clear benefit.

exam_trap: Candidates choose 7 days, matching typical inpatient stays, but NICE recommends prophylaxis for a month after fragility fractures of the pelvis, hip or proximal femur.
takeaway: Hip or proximal femur fragility fracture → one month of VTE prophylaxis.
source: NICE NG89, recommendation 1.11.2. Current guidance accessed 2026.
thinking: Fragility fracture of the proximal femur ↓ high and prolonged VTE risk ↓ VTE risk outweighs bleeding risk ↓ NICE advises extended prophylaxis ↓ 1 month
pearl: If hip fracture surgery is delayed, LMWH may be given before surgery, but the last prophylactic dose must be at least 12 hours before a spinal anaesthetic, so dosing is coordinated with the anaesthetic plan.

subject: Neurosurgery
title: Neurosurgery: neurological localisation
stem: A patient develops sudden unilateral weakness affecting the face, arm and leg. Which broad anatomical location is most likely?
why_correct: A face-arm-leg pattern involving one side of the body suggests a central lesion rather than an isolated peripheral nerve or muscle disorder.

why_others_wrong.A: A single peripheral nerve supplies a limited territory and cannot produce weakness of the face, arm and leg together on one side.
why_others_wrong.B: Weakness of one muscle would affect a single movement, not the whole hemibody pattern of face, arm and leg described here.
why_others_wrong.D: Neuromuscular junction disorders cause fatigable, usually bilateral and often ocular or bulbar weakness, not sudden unilateral face, arm and leg weakness.
why_others_wrong.E: A tendon injury causes loss of one specific movement from mechanical failure, not neurological weakness spanning the face, arm and leg.

exam_trap: Candidates choosing neuromuscular junction (D) overlook that myasthenic weakness is fatigable and usually bilateral, ocular or bulbar, never a sudden one-sided face, arm and leg deficit.
takeaway: Face + arm + leg on one side → think central lesion.
source: MRCS Applied Basic Sciences / Principles of Surgery framework; RCS England MRCS Part A. Current examination information accessed 2026.
thinking: Sudden weakness of the face, arm and leg ↓ all on one side of the body ↓ no single nerve, muscle or junction serves that whole territory ↓ the pathways for all three converge only within the central nervous system ↓ Central nervous system lesion
pearl: Sudden unilateral face, arm and leg weakness should be treated as a possible stroke, and urgent brain imaging is needed because thrombolysis and thrombectomy are time-dependent treatments.

subject: Neurosurgery
title: Neurosurgery: cauda equina localisation
stem: A patient develops bilateral leg symptoms, saddle sensory disturbance and new bladder dysfunction. Which anatomical structure is most directly implicated?
why_correct: The combination of saddle sensory disturbance and bladder dysfunction with lower-limb neurological symptoms is characteristic of cauda equina involvement.

why_others_wrong.A: Brachial plexus lesions affect one upper limb and do not cause saddle anaesthesia, bladder dysfunction or bilateral leg symptoms.
why_others_wrong.C: The median nerve supplies part of the forearm and hand, so it cannot explain saddle sensory loss, bladder dysfunction or leg symptoms.
why_others_wrong.D: Cerebellar lesions cause ataxia and incoordination rather than saddle sensory loss and bladder dysfunction from sacral root compression.
why_others_wrong.E: The phrenic nerve (C3 to C5) supplies the diaphragm, and injury causes diaphragmatic paralysis, not saddle anaesthesia or bladder dysfunction.

exam_trap: Candidates distracted by bilateral leg symptoms may choose cerebellum (D), but ataxia never explains saddle anaesthesia; sacral sensory loss with bladder change points to the cauda equina.
takeaway: Saddle sensory change + bladder dysfunction → cauda equina red flag.
source: RCS England surgical curriculum framework and MRCS Part A applied surgical knowledge. Current examination information accessed 2026.
thinking: Bilateral leg symptoms ↓ saddle sensory disturbance in the sacral dermatomes ↓ new bladder dysfunction ↓ compression of the lumbosacral nerve roots below the conus ↓ Cauda equina
pearl: Suspected cauda equina syndrome needs emergency MRI of the lumbosacral spine and same-day spinal surgical referral; outcomes are better when decompression is performed before painless urinary retention develops.

subject: Neurosurgery
title: Neurosurgery: head injury
stem: Following significant head trauma, a patient develops worsening neurological function. What principle should guide the initial assessment?

options.B: Delay neurological assessment until pain settles
options.C: Assess systematically for life-threatening trauma and neurological deterioration
options.E: Discharge if the first GCS is normal

correct_answer: C. Assess systematically for life-threatening trauma and neurological deterioration
why_correct: Significant head injury requires structured assessment and recognition of deterioration rather than reliance on a single initial examination.

why_others_wrong.A: Worsening neurology after significant head trauma must be presumed to reflect intracranial injury until proven otherwise, not attributed to psychological causes.
why_others_wrong.B: Neurological assessment and GCS monitoring must start immediately; waiting for pain to settle risks missing an expanding haematoma needing urgent intervention.
why_others_wrong.D: Deteriorating neurology after significant head injury needs urgent CT head, not outpatient MRI, to identify lesions requiring immediate neurosurgical treatment.
why_others_wrong.E: A single normal GCS does not exclude later deterioration; this patient is already worsening and needs imaging, repeated observations and reassessment.

exam_trap: Option E tempts candidates who trust a single normal GCS, but expanding haematomas cause later deterioration, so serial observations and reassessment remain essential after head injury.
takeaway: Head injury → reassess if the clinical state changes.
source: NICE head-injury guidance framework; current NICE guidance accessed 2026.
thinking: Significant head trauma ↓ neurological function is worsening ↓ possible expanding intracranial haematoma and coexisting injuries ↓ structured ATLS-style primary survey with serial GCS and pupil checks ↓ Assess systematically for life-threatening trauma and neurological deterioration
pearl: A fall in GCS of two or more points or a new unequal pupil should prompt urgent senior review and immediate CT head, and the cervical spine should be protected because it is often injured alongside significant head trauma.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: ENT: nasal foreign body
stem: A 4-year-old child has a bead visible in the anterior part of the right nasal cavity. The child is calm and cooperative, and there is no bleeding or respiratory distress. What is the most appropriate first approach to removal?

options.A: Push the bead backwards into the nasopharynx so it can be swallowed
options.B: Positive-pressure technique, with a parent blowing into the child's mouth while the clear nostril is occluded
options.D: Nasal steroid spray and review in 1 week

correct_answer: B. Positive-pressure technique, with a parent blowing into the child's mouth while the clear nostril is occluded
why_correct: For a visible anterior nasal foreign body in a cooperative child, a positive-pressure technique is simple, non-invasive and often successful, and it avoids the risks of instrumentation; instrument removal or specialist referral follows if it fails.

why_others_wrong.A: Pushing the object backwards risks it entering the airway and being aspirated.
why_others_wrong.C: General anaesthesia is reserved for failed simpler attempts, posterior objects or uncooperative children, not a first approach in a calm child with an anterior object.
why_others_wrong.D: A retained foreign body will not resolve with a steroid spray and will cause infection and mucosal damage if left.
why_others_wrong.E: Packing would push the object further back and make removal harder, with a risk of aspiration.

exam_trap: Candidates jump to general anaesthesia (C), but a visible anterior foreign body in a cooperative child should first be tried with a simple positive-pressure technique.
takeaway: Anterior nasal foreign body + cooperative child → try positive pressure first.
source: NICE NG127 neurological/ENT recognition framework and standard UK ENT practice; current guidance accessed 2026.
thinking: Visible anterior nasal foreign body ↓ calm, cooperative child with no bleeding or distress ↓ use the simplest non-invasive method first ↓ positive pressure via the mouth with the clear nostril occluded ↓ Positive-pressure technique, with a parent blowing into the child's mouth while the clear nostril is occluded
pearl: A button battery in the nose is an emergency needing urgent removal, because it causes rapid liquefactive necrosis and septal perforation.

subject: Oral & maxillofacial surgery
title: Oral & maxillofacial surgery: facial trauma
stem: A patient has major facial trauma following a high-speed collision. Which initial priority remains fundamental?
correct_answer: B. Airway and life-threatening trauma assessment
why_correct: Major facial trauma may compromise the airway and can coexist with significant head and cervical injuries.

why_others_wrong.A: Cosmetic reconstruction is a later definitive step; delaying airway assessment in major facial trauma risks death from obstruction or missed life-threatening injury.
why_others_wrong.C: Dental restoration is an elective, late concern and has no place in the initial resuscitation of a patient with major facial trauma.
why_others_wrong.D: Imaging such as facial CT follows primary survey and stabilisation, and relying on it alone ignores the immediate airway, breathing and circulation priorities.
why_others_wrong.E: Neurological assessment forms part of the primary survey, and deliberately delaying it risks missing a significant head injury that often coexists with facial trauma.

exam_trap: Candidates drawn to facial CT (D) forget that imaging follows the primary survey; a compromised airway kills before any facial fracture pattern is defined.
takeaway: Facial trauma → airway first, then definitive facial assessment.
source: NICE NG39 major trauma framework; current guidance accessed 2026.
thinking: High-speed collision with major facial trauma ↓ blood, swelling and mobile fractures can obstruct the airway ↓ head and cervical spine injuries often coexist ↓ trauma priorities start with airway and cervical spine control ↓ Airway and life-threatening trauma assessment
pearl: Bilateral anterior mandibular fractures can remove support for the tongue and cause airway obstruction, and nasal tubes are avoided when a skull base fracture is suspected.

subject: Paediatric surgery
title: Paediatric surgery: congenital inguinal hernia
stem: A 6-month-old infant has an intermittent reducible groin swelling that becomes more obvious when crying. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: An intermittent groin swelling that becomes prominent with crying is typical of an inguinal hernia in an infant.

why_others_wrong.A: A hydrocele of the cord is a smooth, non-reducible cystic swelling that transilluminates and does not come and go with crying as described here.
why_others_wrong.C: Femoral hernias are very uncommon in infants and lie below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, whereas this intermittent groin bulge fits a patent processus vaginalis.
why_others_wrong.D: A testicular tumour is a firm, painless swelling of the testis itself that does not reduce or enlarge with crying.
why_others_wrong.E: An undescended testis gives an empty hemiscrotum with a palpable or impalpable testis in the groin, not an intermittent reducible bulge that increases with crying.

exam_trap: Candidates choose hydrocele of the cord (A), but an encysted hydrocele is irreducible and transilluminates, unlike a swelling that comes and goes with crying.
takeaway: Infant + intermittent groin bulge → think inguinal hernia.
source: RCS England paediatric surgery curriculum overview; current information accessed 2026.
thinking: 6-month-old with a groin swelling ↓ intermittent and reducible ↓ more obvious with crying as intra-abdominal pressure rises ↓ a patent processus vaginalis lets abdominal contents into the canal ↓ Congenital inguinal hernia
pearl: Paediatric inguinal hernias are indirect and are treated by herniotomy (ligation of the sac at the deep ring) without mesh; an irreducible hernia in an infant needs prompt reduction and early repair.

subject: Paediatric surgery
title: Paediatric surgery: gastroschisis
stem: A newborn has bowel loops protruding through a defect in the anterior abdominal wall without a covering sac. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Gastroschisis is an anterior abdominal wall defect through which bowel protrudes without a protective covering sac.

why_others_wrong.A: An omphalocele is a midline umbilical defect in which the herniated viscera are contained within a covering membrane, unlike the uncovered bowel described here.
why_others_wrong.C: Hirschsprung disease is an aganglionic motility disorder presenting with delayed meconium and distension; it does not cause bowel to lie outside the abdominal wall.
why_others_wrong.D: Pyloric stenosis is an acquired gastric outlet obstruction presenting at a few weeks old with projectile vomiting, not a congenital abdominal wall defect at birth.
why_others_wrong.E: A Meckel diverticulum is a remnant of the vitellointestinal duct within the abdomen and does not produce exposed bowel through the abdominal wall.

exam_trap: The presence or absence of a covering sac helps distinguish gastroschisis from omphalocele.
takeaway: Bowel outside abdomen + no sac → gastroschisis.
source: Royal College of Surgeons England paediatric surgery overview; current information accessed 2026.
thinking: Newborn with bowel loops outside the abdomen ↓ anterior abdominal wall defect ↓ no covering sac ↓ Gastroschisis
pearl: Gastroschisis is usually an isolated anomaly associated with young maternal age, whereas omphalocele is strongly associated with chromosomal and cardiac anomalies and needs a full anomaly screen.

subject: Urology
title: Urology: undescended testis
stem: A 2-year-old boy has a persistently undescended testis. Which specialty area is primarily responsible for assessment and management?
why_correct: Undescended testes are an important paediatric surgical/urological condition requiring appropriate assessment and management.

why_others_wrong.A: Dermatology manages skin disease, whereas an undescended testis needs surgical assessment and usually orchidopexy.
why_others_wrong.C: Neurosurgery deals with the brain and spinal cord and has no role in managing testicular maldescent.
why_others_wrong.D: Vascular surgery treats arterial and venous disease and does not manage undescended testes.
why_others_wrong.E: Cardiothoracic surgery treats heart and chest disease and is unrelated to the assessment of a child with cryptorchidism.

exam_trap: Candidates may treat an undescended testis as cosmetic, but it carries fertility and malignancy implications and needs paediatric surgical or urological management.
takeaway: Persistent undescended testis → paediatric surgical or urological assessment.
source: Royal College of Surgeons England paediatric surgery overview; current information accessed 2026.
thinking: Boy aged 2 ↓ persistently undescended testis ↓ risks include infertility, malignancy and torsion ↓ needs surgical assessment and orchidopexy ↓ Paediatric/urological surgery
pearl: Orchidopexy is ideally performed between 6 and 12 months of age to optimise fertility; it makes the testis easier to examine but does not fully remove the raised malignancy risk.

subject: Plastic surgery
title: Plastic surgery: burn tbsa
stem: A child sustains a significant scald injury. Which tool is particularly useful for estimating the percentage of total body surface area burned in children?
why_correct: The Lund and Browder chart accounts for age-related differences in body proportions and is therefore useful for estimating burn surface area in children.

why_others_wrong.A: The Glasgow Coma Scale grades conscious level after head injury or other insults and gives no estimate of the body surface area burned.
why_others_wrong.C: The APGAR score assesses a newborn's condition in the first minutes after delivery and has no role in sizing a burn.
why_others_wrong.D: The Child-Pugh score grades the severity of chronic liver disease and is unrelated to estimating burn surface area.
why_others_wrong.E: The Wells score estimates the pre-test probability of deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism, not the extent of a scald.

exam_trap: The Glasgow Coma Scale and APGAR score (options A and C) are familiar scoring tools that tempt under pressure, but neither sizes a burn; only the Lund and Browder chart adjusts for a child's body proportions.
takeaway: Child burns → Lund and Browder chart.
source: UK/NICE burn-care framework; current guidance accessed 2026.
thinking: Child with a scald ↓ children have proportionally larger heads and smaller legs than adults ↓ the adult rule of nines misestimates the burned area ↓ the Lund and Browder chart adjusts for age ↓ Lund and Browder chart
pearl: Simple erythema is excluded from TBSA estimation, and the patient's palm including the fingers approximates 1% TBSA, which is useful for small or patchy burns.

subject: Plastic surgery
title: Plastic surgery: burn depth
stem: A burn has a dry, white, leathery appearance and is relatively insensate. Which depth is most consistent with this description?
why_correct: Deep/full-thickness burns may appear white, brown or charred, have a leathery texture and lose sensation because of destruction of cutaneous nerve endings.

why_others_wrong.A: A superficial epidermal burn is red, painful and blanches with brisk capillary refill; it is not dry, white, leathery or insensate.
why_others_wrong.B: Superficial partial-thickness burns are pink, moist, blistered and very painful because dermal nerve endings are preserved, unlike this insensate leathery burn.
why_others_wrong.D: Simple erythema reflects epidermal injury with intact sensation and would be painful and red rather than white, leathery and numb.
why_others_wrong.E: A mid-dermal burn is dark pink with sluggish capillary refill and some preserved sensation, so it is not dry, white, leathery and insensate.

exam_trap: Severe burns may be less painful than superficial burns because sensory nerves have been destroyed.
takeaway: Leathery + pale/charred + insensate → deep burn.
source: UK burn-care principles; current guidance accessed 2026.
thinking: Dry, white, leathery burn ↓ insensate because dermal nerve endings are destroyed ↓ superficial and partial-thickness burns are moist or pink and painful ↓ Deep/full-thickness burn
pearl: Circumferential full-thickness burns of a limb or the chest can compromise perfusion or ventilation and may need escharotomy; full-thickness burns generally need excision and grafting because they cannot heal from dermal elements.

subject: Cardiothoracic surgery
title: Cardiothoracic surgery: cardiac tamponade
stem: A patient develops hypotension, tachycardia, raised jugular venous pressure and muffled heart sounds following penetrating chest trauma. Which diagnosis should be suspected?
why_correct: The combination of hypotension, elevated venous pressure and muffled heart sounds is classically associated with cardiac tamponade.

why_others_wrong.A: Tension pneumothorax can cause hypotension and raised JVP, but it gives unilateral absent breath sounds and hyper-resonance rather than muffled heart sounds.
why_others_wrong.C: Massive pulmonary embolism can cause shock and raised JVP, but it is not the expected consequence of penetrating chest trauma and does not muffle the heart sounds.
why_others_wrong.D: A simple haemothorax causes reduced breath sounds and dullness on the affected side, and blood loss would lower rather than raise the jugular venous pressure.
why_others_wrong.E: Flail chest is a mechanical chest wall injury from blunt trauma seen as paradoxical movement, not a cause of raised JVP with muffled heart sounds.

exam_trap: Tension pneumothorax (A) also causes hypotension with raised JVP, but it gives unilateral absent breath sounds and hyper-resonance rather than muffled heart sounds.
takeaway: Hypotension + raised JVP + muffled heart sounds → think tamponade.
source: MRCS applied surgical science / major trauma principles; NICE NG39, current guidance accessed 2026.
thinking: Penetrating chest trauma ↓ hypotension and tachycardia with raised JVP ↓ muffled heart sounds point to fluid around the heart ↓ classic triad of obstructive shock from the pericardium ↓ Cardiac tamponade
pearl: Pulsus paradoxus and a pericardial effusion on FAST support tamponade; after penetrating trauma the definitive treatment is surgical decompression, with pericardiocentesis only a temporising bridge.

subject: Cardiothoracic surgery
title: Cardiothoracic surgery: massive haemothorax
stem: A patient with major thoracic trauma is hypotensive with severe respiratory distress. Imaging demonstrates a large pleural blood collection. Which immediate physiological problem is most important?

options.B: Combined respiratory compromise and major blood loss

correct_answer: B. Combined respiratory compromise and major blood loss
why_correct: A major haemothorax can impair ventilation while simultaneously causing significant intrathoracic blood loss.

why_others_wrong.A: Hypoxaemia is only part of the picture; a large haemothorax also represents major intrathoracic haemorrhage, which explains this patient's hypotension.
why_others_wrong.C: Stress hyperglycaemia may occur after trauma but is not the immediate life-threatening problem in a hypotensive patient with a large pleural blood collection.
why_others_wrong.D: Urinary retention is irrelevant to the immediate physiology here, where the threats are impaired ventilation and major blood loss into the chest.
why_others_wrong.E: Raised intracranial pressure relates to head injury, and nothing in this thoracic trauma scenario suggests it is the dominant immediate problem.

exam_trap: Isolated hypoxaemia (A) tempts candidates who see only a lung problem, but a large haemothorax is also major haemorrhage, which explains the hypotension and needs blood replacement.
takeaway: Major haemothorax = chest problem + haemorrhage problem.
source: NICE NG39, Major trauma: assessment and initial management. Current guidance accessed 2026.
thinking: Major thoracic trauma with hypotension and severe respiratory distress ↓ imaging shows a large pleural blood collection ↓ blood compresses the lung and is lost from the circulation ↓ massive haemothorax causes both ventilatory failure and shock ↓ Combined respiratory compromise and major blood loss
pearl: Treat with blood product resuscitation and a large-bore chest drain; immediate drainage of about 1500 mL, or continuing loss of around 200 mL per hour, is the traditional ATLS trigger for thoracotomy.

subject: Cardiothoracic surgery
title: Cardiothoracic surgery: flail chest
stem: A patient sustains multiple adjacent rib fractures at multiple points. A segment of the chest wall moves paradoxically during respiration. What is this finding called?
why_correct: A flail segment results from multiple rib fractures creating a mechanically unstable portion of the chest wall.

why_others_wrong.A: An open pneumothorax is a penetrating chest wall defect that sucks air into the pleural space, not a segment of ribs moving paradoxically after multiple fractures.
why_others_wrong.C: Tension pneumothorax is a build-up of pleural air causing mediastinal shift and shock, not a mechanically unstable segment of chest wall.
why_others_wrong.D: Pulmonary embolism is an intravascular clot in the pulmonary arteries and does not cause a chest wall segment to move paradoxically with breathing.
why_others_wrong.E: A simple rib fracture keeps the chest wall mechanically stable, whereas paradoxical movement needs adjacent ribs each broken in more than one place.

exam_trap: Candidates may pick simple rib fracture (E), but a flail segment needs two or more adjacent ribs each broken in two or more places, producing paradoxical movement.
takeaway: Multiple adjacent rib fractures + paradoxical movement → flail chest.
source: NICE NG39; current guidance accessed 2026.
thinking: Multiple adjacent ribs each fractured in more than one place ↓ a free-floating segment of chest wall ↓ it moves inwards on inspiration and outwards on expiration ↓ paradoxical movement of an unstable segment ↓ Flail chest
pearl: The main threat in flail chest is often the underlying pulmonary contusion, so management centres on good analgesia (often regional), oxygenation and careful fluid balance, with surgical rib fixation in selected patients.

subject: Cardiothoracic surgery
title: Cardiothoracic surgery: pericardium
stem: Which layer of the pericardium lies directly on the external surface of the heart?
why_correct: The visceral layer of the serous pericardium lies directly on the heart and is also called the epicardium.

why_others_wrong.A: The parietal serous pericardium lines the inner surface of the fibrous pericardium rather than lying on the heart itself, so it is not the layer applied to the heart surface.
why_others_wrong.C: The endocardium is the innermost layer lining the heart chambers and valves, on the opposite side of the myocardium from the pericardium.
why_others_wrong.D: The myocardium is the muscular wall of the heart itself, lying deep to the epicardium, not a covering between the heart and the pericardial sac.
why_others_wrong.E: The pleura surrounds the lungs and lies outside the fibrous pericardium laterally, so it does not sit between the heart and its fibrous sac.

exam_trap: Parietal pericardium (A) is the usual wrong pick: it lines the inner surface of the fibrous sac, whereas the visceral layer, the epicardium, lies on the heart itself.
takeaway: Visceral pericardium = epicardium = on the heart.
source: Standard surgical anatomy / MRCS Applied Basic Sciences curriculum.
thinking: Layer directly on the surface of the heart ↓ pericardium = outer fibrous sac plus a two-layered serous pericardium ↓ parietal serous layer lines the inside of the fibrous sac ↓ visceral serous layer adheres to the myocardium as the epicardium ↓ Visceral pericardium
pearl: The pericardial cavity is the potential space between the parietal and visceral serous layers; because the fibrous pericardium is inelastic, even a modest but rapid collection of blood can cause tamponade.

subject: Cardiothoracic surgery
title: Cardiothoracic surgery: coronary artery
stem: The sinoatrial node is most commonly supplied by a branch of which coronary artery?

options.E: Left main stem in all individuals

why_correct: The sinoatrial nodal artery most commonly arises from the right coronary artery, although anatomical variation occurs.

why_others_wrong.A: The left anterior descending artery supplies the anterior interventricular septum and anterior left ventricle, not typically the sinoatrial node.
why_others_wrong.C: The circumflex artery gives the sinoatrial nodal artery in a minority of people, so stating it supplies the node in all individuals ignores the usual RCA origin.
why_others_wrong.D: The posterior interventricular artery runs in the posterior interventricular groove and supplies the inferior septum, not the sinoatrial node in the right atrium.
why_others_wrong.E: The left main stem divides into the anterior descending and circumflex arteries and does not supply the sinoatrial node in all individuals.

exam_trap: Circumflex (C) tempts candidates who recall that it can supply the sinoatrial node, but it does so only in a minority, and the word "all" makes the option wrong.
takeaway: SA node → most commonly RCA.
source: Standard surgical anatomy / MRCS Applied Basic Sciences curriculum.
thinking: Sinoatrial node in the right atrium near the superior vena cava ↓ supplied by the sinoatrial nodal artery ↓ this arises from the RCA in most people and from the circumflex in a minority ↓ options claiming "all individuals" ignore this variation ↓ Right coronary artery
pearl: Because the RCA usually supplies both the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes, inferior myocardial infarction from RCA occlusion is commonly complicated by sinus bradycardia and heart block.

subject: Neurosurgery
title: Neurosurgery: epidural haematoma
stem: A patient has a head injury followed by a brief loss of consciousness, a lucid interval and then neurological deterioration. Which lesion is classically associated with this pattern?
why_correct: An epidural haematoma classically results from traumatic arterial bleeding and may present with a lucid interval followed by deterioration.

why_others_wrong.A: Traumatic subarachnoid blood usually causes headache and meningism but does not classically produce a lucid interval followed by rapid deterioration.
why_others_wrong.C: A chronic subdural haematoma develops over weeks with fluctuating confusion, usually in older patients, rather than a short lucid interval after trauma.
why_others_wrong.D: A cerebellar tumour causes gradually progressive ataxia and raised pressure symptoms, not deterioration following a lucid interval after head injury.
why_others_wrong.E: Meningitis presents with fever, headache and neck stiffness from infection, not a traumatic loss of consciousness followed by a lucid interval.

exam_trap: Chronic subdural haematoma tempts because it also causes delayed deterioration after head injury, but it evolves over weeks with fluctuating confusion; a lucid interval of hours followed by rapid decline suggests an extradural haematoma.
takeaway: Head trauma + lucid interval + deterioration → epidural haematoma.
source: NICE NG232, Head injury: assessment and early management; current guidance accessed 2026.
thinking: Head injury with brief loss of consciousness ↓ lucid interval ↓ then deterioration as an arterial bleed expands ↓ blood collects between skull and dura, usually from the middle meningeal artery ↓ Epidural haematoma
pearl: On CT an extradural haematoma is biconvex (lentiform) and does not cross suture lines because the dura is firmly attached at the sutures, whereas a subdural haematoma is crescentic and can cross them.

subject: Neurosurgery
title: Neurosurgery: subdural haematoma
stem: Which vessel is classically torn in an acute subdural haematoma?
why_correct: Subdural haematomas classically result from tearing of bridging veins crossing from the cerebral surface to the dural venous sinuses.

why_others_wrong.A: The middle meningeal artery is the classic source of an extradural haematoma, which lies between the skull and the dura, not in the subdural space.
why_others_wrong.C: Internal carotid artery injury causes dissection, aneurysm or carotid-cavernous fistula rather than a subdural collection.
why_others_wrong.D: The superior sagittal sinus receives bridging veins, but it is tearing of those veins as they cross the subdural space that classically causes the haematoma.
why_others_wrong.E: The ophthalmic artery runs within the orbit with the optic nerve and is not a source of a subdural haematoma.

exam_trap: Candidates choose middle meningeal artery (A) by reflex, but that arterial source produces an extradural haematoma between skull and dura, not a collection in the subdural space.
takeaway: Subdural = bridging veins.
source: Standard neurosurgical anatomy; NICE NG232.
thinking: Acute subdural haematoma ↓ blood lies between the dura and the arachnoid ↓ veins crossing this space from the cortex to the dural sinuses are vulnerable to shearing ↓ Bridging vein
pearl: Acute subdural haematomas often accompany significant underlying brain injury, so outcomes are generally worse than for extradurals; cerebral atrophy in older people and in alcohol misuse stretches bridging veins and raises the risk.

subject: Neurosurgery
title: Neurosurgery: subarachnoid haemorrhage
stem: A patient develops a sudden, maximal-at-onset severe headache described as the worst headache of their life. Which diagnosis must be considered?
why_correct: A thunderclap headache is a classic presentation of subarachnoid haemorrhage and requires urgent assessment.

why_others_wrong.A: Tension headache is gradual, band-like and of mild to moderate severity, not a sudden maximal-at-onset worst-ever headache.
why_others_wrong.C: Cluster headache causes recurrent unilateral orbital pain with autonomic features, and a thunderclap headache must not be assumed benign before haemorrhage is excluded.
why_others_wrong.D: A chronic subdural haematoma causes insidious headache and confusion over weeks, not a sudden explosive headache at maximum intensity.
why_others_wrong.E: Trigeminal neuralgia causes brief electric shock-like facial pain in a trigeminal distribution, not a sustained sudden severe headache.

exam_trap: Candidates may choose cluster headache (C) because the pain is severe, but cluster attacks are recurrent orbital episodes with autonomic features, not a single maximal-onset thunderclap.
takeaway: Thunderclap headache → exclude SAH.
source: NICE NG228, Stroke and transient ischaemic attack in over 16s; current guidance accessed 2026.
thinking: Sudden headache, maximal at onset ↓ worst headache of life, a thunderclap pattern ↓ classic for bleeding into the subarachnoid space, usually from an aneurysm ↓ Subarachnoid haemorrhage
pearl: Non-contrast CT is most sensitive in the first hours after onset; if CT is normal and suspicion remains, lumbar puncture is delayed until at least 12 hours after onset to detect xanthochromia.

subject: Neurosurgery
title: Neurosurgery: cerebrospinal fluid
stem: Where is most cerebrospinal fluid produced?
why_correct: Most CSF is produced by the choroid plexus within the ventricular system.

why_others_wrong.A: The dural venous sinuses receive CSF absorbed through arachnoid granulations; they drain CSF rather than produce it.
why_others_wrong.C: Arachnoid granulations are the main site of CSF absorption into the venous sinuses, not its production.
why_others_wrong.D: The pituitary gland is an endocrine gland in the sella turcica and does not produce cerebrospinal fluid.
why_others_wrong.E: The cerebral cortex contributes little, if any, CSF; most is secreted by the choroid plexus within the ventricles.

exam_trap: Candidates who choose arachnoid granulations (C) confuse production with absorption; the granulations return CSF to the dural venous sinuses rather than secreting it.
takeaway: CSF production → choroid plexus.
source: Standard anatomy and physiology; MRCS Applied Basic Sciences curriculum.
thinking: Question asks where CSF is produced ↓ specialised secretory epithelium lines vascular tufts within the ventricles ↓ arachnoid granulations absorb rather than produce CSF ↓ Choroid plexus
pearl: Total CSF volume is far smaller than the amount produced each day, so CSF turns over several times daily and any outflow obstruction, such as aqueduct stenosis, rapidly causes hydrocephalus.

subject: Neurosurgery
title: Neurosurgery: csf absorption
stem: CSF is principally returned to the venous circulation through which structures?
why_correct: Arachnoid granulations project into the dural venous sinuses and provide a major route for CSF absorption.

why_others_wrong.A: The choroid plexuses produce most of the CSF within the ventricles; they are not the main route by which it is absorbed.
why_others_wrong.C: Dural arteries supply the meninges with arterial blood and are not a route for CSF to reach the venous circulation.
why_others_wrong.D: The lateral ventricles contain the choroid plexus and circulate CSF, but they do not return it to the venous system.
why_others_wrong.E: Pituitary veins drain the pituitary gland into the cavernous sinus and play no principal role in CSF absorption.

exam_trap: Choroid plexus (A) is the reflex answer to any CSF question, but it produces CSF; the question asks which structures return it to the venous circulation.
takeaway: Produce CSF → choroid plexus. Absorb CSF → arachnoid granulations.
source: Standard anatomy and physiology.
thinking: Question asks how CSF returns to the venous circulation ↓ CSF flows from the ventricles into the subarachnoid space ↓ arachnoid villi project into the dural venous sinuses, especially the superior sagittal sinus ↓ Arachnoid granulations
pearl: Impaired absorption at the granulations, for example after subarachnoid haemorrhage or meningitis, causes communicating hydrocephalus, whereas a block within the ventricular system causes obstructive (non-communicating) hydrocephalus.

subject: Urology
title: Urology: testicular tumour
stem: A young adult has a painless unilateral testicular mass. Which investigation is the appropriate initial imaging test?
why_correct: Scrotal ultrasound is the key initial imaging investigation for a suspected testicular mass.

why_others_wrong.A: CT brain is not the initial test for a testicular mass and is reserved for selected patients with suspected cerebral metastases.
why_others_wrong.C: MRI of the pelvis may help in equivocal cases, but it is not the routine first-line imaging, which is scrotal ultrasound.
why_others_wrong.D: A plain abdominal radiograph cannot characterise a testicular lesion and has no role in its initial assessment.
why_others_wrong.E: A bone scan is not part of the initial work-up of a testicular mass; staging after diagnosis uses CT and tumour markers.

exam_trap: Candidates choose CT or bone scan as staging tests, but staging follows diagnosis; the first imaging for a testicular lump is scrotal ultrasound.
takeaway: Painless testicular mass → scrotal ultrasound.
source: NICE NG12, Suspected cancer: recognition and referral; current guidance accessed 2026.
thinking: Young adult ↓ painless unilateral testicular mass ↓ suspected germ cell tumour ↓ high-frequency scrotal ultrasound characterises it ↓ Ultrasound of the scrotum
pearl: Suspected testicular cancer is treated by radical inguinal orchidectomy; a scrotal approach or scrotal biopsy is avoided because it can alter lymphatic spread to the inguinal nodes.

subject: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care
title: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care: acute limb ischaemia
stem: A patient develops sudden severe leg pain with pallor, paraesthesia and absent distal pulses. Which diagnosis should be assumed until proven otherwise?
why_correct: The sudden onset of pain, pallor, sensory disturbance and absent pulses indicates acute arterial compromise.

why_others_wrong.A: Chronic venous insufficiency causes gradual swelling, skin changes and ulceration, with preserved pulses and no sudden pallor or paraesthesia.
why_others_wrong.C: Cellulitis causes red, warm, swollen skin with fever, whereas this limb is pale and pulseless with sensory loss.
why_others_wrong.D: Varicose veins cause aching and visible dilated superficial veins but do not abolish distal pulses or produce sudden pallor and paraesthesia.
why_others_wrong.E: Chronic lymphoedema develops gradually with non-pitting swelling and preserved arterial pulses, unlike this sudden pale, pulseless limb.

exam_trap: Candidates choose cellulitis or venous disease because of leg pain, but a pale, pulseless limb with sudden paraesthesia indicates arterial occlusion, not inflammation or venous pathology.
takeaway: Sudden pain, pallor, paraesthesia and pulselessness → acute limb ischaemia.
source: European Society for Vascular Surgery acute limb-ischaemia principles; current surgical practice accessed 2026.
thinking: Sudden severe leg pain ↓ pallor and paraesthesia ↓ absent distal pulses ↓ acute arterial occlusion ↓ Acute limb ischaemia
pearl: Embolic acute limb ischaemia is often treated by embolectomy, whereas thrombosis on chronic disease may need thrombolysis, angioplasty or bypass; heparin is started early unless contraindicated.

subject: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care
title: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care: acute limb ischaemia — neurological deficit
stem: A patient with acute limb ischaemia develops rapidly progressive motor weakness. What does this indicate?

options.E: Isolated neuropathy unrelated to the vascular problem

correct_answer: B. Threatened limb requiring urgent revascularisation
why_correct: Motor deficit is a major marker of limb threat in acute limb ischaemia.

why_others_wrong.A: Motor loss indicates immediately threatened muscle and nerve viability, so observation would risk irreversible ischaemia and limb loss.
why_others_wrong.C: Chronic venous disease does not cause acute motor weakness; here the weakness reflects ischaemic nerve and muscle injury.
why_others_wrong.D: Cellulitis is a skin infection and does not explain progressive motor weakness in an acutely ischaemic limb.
why_others_wrong.E: In acute limb ischaemia, new motor weakness reflects ischaemic nerve and muscle injury, so attributing it to an unrelated neuropathy delays revascularisation.

exam_trap: Candidates attribute new weakness to an unrelated neuropathy, but in acute limb ischaemia motor deficit marks an immediately threatened limb needing urgent revascularisation.
takeaway: Acute ischaemia with motor deficit → urgent revascularisation.
source: European Society for Vascular Surgery acute limb-ischaemia guidance/principles.
thinking: Acute limb ischaemia ↓ rapidly progressive motor weakness ↓ muscle and nerve viability threatened ↓ limb is immediately threatened ↓ Threatened limb requiring urgent revascularisation
pearl: After revascularisation of a severely ischaemic limb, reperfusion can cause compartment syndrome, hyperkalaemia and myoglobinuria, so fasciotomy may be required.

subject: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care
title: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care: abdominal aortic aneurysm
stem: A 72-year-old man develops sudden severe abdominal and back pain with hypotension. A pulsatile abdominal mass is present. What diagnosis should be considered immediately?
why_correct: Pain, hypotension and a pulsatile abdominal mass constitute a classic presentation of ruptured AAA.

why_others_wrong.B: Acute pancreatitis can cause epigastric pain radiating to the back, but a pulsatile mass with hypotension in a 72-year-old man points to aneurysm rupture.
why_others_wrong.C: Renal colic causes loin-to-groin pain, and a ruptured AAA is a recognised mimic, so it should not be assumed when there is shock and a pulsatile mass.
why_others_wrong.D: Bowel obstruction presents with colicky pain, distension, vomiting and absolute constipation rather than a pulsatile mass with sudden back pain.
why_others_wrong.E: Diverticulitis causes left iliac fossa pain and fever, typically without sudden collapse or a pulsatile abdominal mass.

exam_trap: Do not wait for complete imaging confirmation in a shocked patient with a compelling clinical presentation.
takeaway: Pain, shock and a pulsatile mass → ruptured AAA.
source: NICE NG156, Abdominal aortic aneurysm: diagnosis and management; current guidance accessed 2026.
thinking: 72-year-old man ↓ sudden abdominal and back pain ↓ hypotension ↓ pulsatile abdominal mass ↓ Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm
pearl: The NHS AAA screening programme offers a single ultrasound to men in the year they turn 65, as men are affected much more often than women.

subject: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care
title: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care: carotid stenosis
stem: A patient has a recent transient ischaemic attack attributable to severe ipsilateral carotid stenosis. What is the key principle of management?

options.B: Urgent specialist assessment for possible carotid intervention

correct_answer: B. Urgent specialist assessment for possible carotid intervention
why_correct: Symptomatic significant carotid stenosis may benefit from carotid endarterectomy when appropriately selected, and assessment should be undertaken urgently.

why_others_wrong.A: Symptomatic significant carotid stenosis carries a high early risk of stroke, so ignoring it forgoes the benefit of timely endarterectomy.
why_others_wrong.C: Carotid atherosclerotic stenosis is not infective, so antibiotics have no role in preventing further ischaemic events.
why_others_wrong.D: Stroke risk after a carotid-territory TIA is highest in the first days, so NICE advises assessment within a week and endarterectomy within two weeks of symptoms.
why_others_wrong.E: Amputation treats limb ischaemia and has no relevance to transient cerebral ischaemia from carotid stenosis.

exam_trap: Candidates treat carotid stenosis as a chronic risk factor to review later, but after a recent TIA the benefit of endarterectomy is greatest within two weeks.
takeaway: Recent carotid-territory TIA or stroke with significant stenosis → urgent vascular assessment.
source: NICE NG128, Stroke and transient ischaemic attack in over 16s; current guidance accessed 2026.
thinking: Recent TIA ↓ severe ipsilateral carotid stenosis ↓ stroke risk highest in the first days ↓ endarterectomy benefit falls with delay ↓ Urgent specialist assessment for possible carotid intervention
pearl: Carotid endarterectomy can injure the hypoglossal nerve, causing tongue deviation to the side of the injury, and the marginal mandibular and vagus nerves are also at risk.

subject: Paediatric surgery
title: Paediatric surgery: hirschsprung disease
stem: A newborn develops marked abdominal distension and fails to pass meconium in the expected early neonatal period. Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Failure to pass meconium with abdominal distension is an important presentation of Hirschsprung disease.

why_others_wrong.B: Pyloric stenosis presents at around 2 to 8 weeks with non-bilious projectile vomiting, not with failure to pass meconium and distension in the first days of life.
why_others_wrong.C: Gastro-oesophageal reflux causes effortless posseting or vomiting in a feeding infant, not abdominal distension with failure to pass meconium.
why_others_wrong.D: Testicular torsion causes an acutely painful, swollen scrotum and does not explain abdominal distension or failure to pass meconium.
why_others_wrong.E: Intussusception usually affects infants from a few months of age with colicky pain and bloody stool, and is not a cause of delayed passage of meconium in a newborn.

exam_trap: Pyloric stenosis typically presents later with non-bilious projectile vomiting rather than neonatal failure to pass meconium.
takeaway: Delayed meconium + distension → think Hirschsprung.
source: Standard paediatric surgical principles / RCS paediatric surgery curriculum.
thinking: Newborn with marked abdominal distension ↓ fails to pass meconium in the expected early period ↓ functional distal bowel obstruction ↓ aganglionic distal bowel cannot relax ↓ Hirschsprung disease
pearl: Diagnosis is confirmed by rectal suction biopsy showing absent ganglion cells, and Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis, with fever, distension and explosive foul stools, is its most dangerous complication.

subject: Paediatric surgery
title: Paediatric surgery: intussusception
stem: A young child develops intermittent severe abdominal pain, drawing up the legs and episodic distress. Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Intermittent colicky abdominal pain with episodes of distress is characteristic of intussusception.

why_others_wrong.B: Pyloric stenosis causes projectile non-bilious vomiting in young infants rather than episodic severe colicky pain with drawing up of the legs.
why_others_wrong.C: An inguinal hernia produces a groin swelling and, if incarcerated, a tender irreducible lump; episodic colic without a groin finding points to intussusception.
why_others_wrong.D: Hirschsprung disease typically presents with delayed meconium, chronic constipation and distension rather than discrete bouts of severe pain with intervening calm.
why_others_wrong.E: Appendicitis gives constant, progressive pain with fever and localised tenderness, not intermittent paroxysms of distress, and it is not the diagnosis in every child with abdominal pain.

exam_trap: Appendicitis tempts as the commonest childhood surgical emergency, but its pain is constant and progressive; paroxysms of colic with drawing up of the legs and calm between episodes suggest intussusception.
takeaway: Episodic colicky pain in a child → consider intussusception.
source: NICE NG1, Diarrhoea and vomiting caused by gastroenteritis in under 5s; paediatric surgical principles. Current guidance accessed 2026.
thinking: Young child ↓ intermittent severe abdominal pain ↓ drawing up the legs with episodic distress ↓ telescoping bowel causes colicky obstruction ↓ Intussusception
pearl: Most infant cases are ileocolic and idiopathic, often following a viral illness with lymphoid hyperplasia; in older children a pathological lead point such as a Meckel diverticulum or polyp is more likely.

subject: Paediatric surgery
title: Paediatric surgery: intussusception — imaging
stem: A clinically stable child has suspected intussusception. Which imaging modality is particularly useful?
why_correct: Ultrasound is highly useful in suspected intussusception and can demonstrate characteristic bowel-within-bowel appearances.

why_others_wrong.B: A chest radiograph does not image the bowel loops in question and cannot show the target or bowel-within-bowel sign of intussusception.
why_others_wrong.C: CT of the brain is irrelevant to an intra-abdominal bowel obstruction and would expose the child to radiation without diagnostic benefit.
why_others_wrong.D: MRI of the spine does not assess the bowel, and the child needs a rapid bedside test such as ultrasound rather than a lengthy scan needing sedation.
why_others_wrong.E: A bone scan detects skeletal pathology such as infection or metastases and has no role in diagnosing intussusception.

exam_trap: Do not automatically expose a child to CT when ultrasound can provide the relevant diagnostic information.
takeaway: Child + suspected intussusception → ultrasound.
source: UK paediatric surgical practice; current guidance accessed 2026.
thinking: Clinically stable child ↓ suspected intussusception ↓ needs fast, radiation-free bowel imaging ↓ ultrasound shows a target or bowel-within-bowel appearance ↓ Ultrasound
pearl: In a stable child without peritonitis, ultrasound diagnosis is usually followed by image-guided air enema reduction; peritonitis or perforation requires surgery instead.

subject: Paediatric surgery
title: Paediatric surgery: omphalocele
stem: A newborn has abdominal viscera protruding through a midline umbilical defect and covered by a membrane. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: An omphalocele is a midline abdominal-wall defect at the umbilicus with herniated viscera contained within a covering sac.

why_others_wrong.A: Gastroschisis is usually a defect to the right of the umbilicus with bowel exposed and no covering membrane, whereas here the viscera are membrane-covered and midline.
why_others_wrong.C: Pyloric stenosis is an acquired gastric outlet obstruction presenting weeks after birth with projectile vomiting, not a congenital umbilical defect.
why_others_wrong.D: Hirschsprung disease is a disorder of enteric ganglion cells causing obstruction and delayed meconium, not herniation of viscera through the abdominal wall.
why_others_wrong.E: Intussusception is telescoping of bowel within the abdomen in older infants and does not produce viscera protruding through an umbilical defect.

exam_trap: Candidates pick gastroschisis (A) because both are abdominal wall defects, but gastroschisis is paraumbilical with uncovered bowel; a membrane-covered midline sac is omphalocele.
takeaway: Midline + umbilical defect + covering sac → omphalocele.
source: Standard paediatric surgical anatomy.
thinking: Newborn with viscera protruding ↓ midline defect at the umbilicus ↓ contents covered by a membrane ↓ failed return of the midgut from the umbilical cord ↓ Omphalocele
pearl: An omphalocele may contain liver as well as bowel and is associated with chromosomal anomalies and cardiac defects, so echocardiography and genetic testing form part of the work-up.

subject: Plastic surgery
title: Plastic surgery: skin graft take
stem: Which process is responsible for the earliest survival of a newly applied skin graft?
why_correct: Initially, a skin graft survives by diffusion of nutrients and oxygen from the recipient wound bed before vascular connections become established.

why_others_wrong.A: Revascularisation by inosculation and capillary ingrowth begins after roughly 48 hours, so it is not the mechanism that sustains the graft first.
why_others_wrong.C: Bone formation plays no part in skin graft take, which depends on nutrient diffusion and then revascularisation from the wound bed.
why_others_wrong.D: Lymphatic connections are re-established later and help clear graft oedema, but they do not provide the initial nutrition that keeps the graft alive.
why_others_wrong.E: Nerve regeneration into a graft is slow, occurring over months, and affects later sensation rather than early survival of the graft.

exam_trap: Revascularisation is important but is not the earliest mechanism of graft survival.
takeaway: Early graft survival → plasmatic imbibition, then inosculation and revascularisation.
source: Standard plastic-surgery physiology / MRCS Applied Basic Sciences.
thinking: A newly applied graft has no blood supply ↓ for about the first 48 hours nutrients and oxygen diffuse from the wound bed ↓ this is plasmatic imbibition ↓ inosculation and capillary ingrowth follow ↓ Plasmatic imbibition
pearl: Thin split-thickness grafts take more reliably than thick or full-thickness grafts because diffusion can sustain the thinner tissue until revascularisation, but they undergo more secondary contraction as they mature.

subject: Plastic surgery
title: Plastic surgery: skin graft failure
stem: Which factor is most likely to prevent successful skin-graft take?
why_correct: A collection of blood or fluid between the graft and wound bed prevents intimate contact and interferes with graft nutrition and vascularisation.

why_others_wrong.A: A well-vascularised bed supplies the diffusion and capillary ingrowth a graft needs, so it promotes take rather than preventing it.
why_others_wrong.C: Immobilisation prevents shear between graft and bed, protecting the fragile early vascular connections and so favouring successful take.
why_others_wrong.D: Close contact between graft and bed is exactly what allows plasmatic imbibition and inosculation, so it supports rather than prevents take.
why_others_wrong.E: Proper wound-bed preparation, with debridement and control of infection, improves the chance of take rather than causing failure.

exam_trap: The other options all favour take; candidates who misread 'prevent' may pick one, but haematoma, seroma, shear and infection are the classic causes of graft failure.
takeaway: Haematoma under a graft → poor take.
source: Standard plastic-surgery graft principles.
thinking: Graft take needs close contact with a vascularised bed ↓ a haematoma separates graft from bed ↓ it blocks imbibition and capillary ingrowth ↓ Haematoma beneath the graft
pearl: Meshing or pie-crusting the graft and using tie-over or negative pressure dressings help prevent fluid collection and shear, which with infection are the commonest causes of graft loss.

subject: Plastic surgery
title: Plastic surgery: split-thickness graft
stem: Which feature distinguishes a split-thickness skin graft from a full-thickness skin graft?

options.B: It contains epidermis and part of the dermis
options.C: It contains the entire dermis and subcutaneous fat

correct_answer: B. It contains epidermis and part of the dermis
why_correct: A split-thickness graft contains the epidermis and a variable proportion of the dermis.

why_others_wrong.A: A graft of epidermis alone is not a standard split-thickness graft, which carries a variable portion of the dermis as well as the epidermis.
why_others_wrong.C: Taking the entire dermis defines a full-thickness graft, and subcutaneous fat is normally removed because it impairs graft take.
why_others_wrong.D: Muscle is not part of any skin graft; tissue carrying muscle with its own blood supply is a muscle or musculocutaneous flap.
why_others_wrong.E: Fascia alone is not skin and cannot resurface a wound as a skin graft; fascial tissue is transferred as a fascial graft or flap.

exam_trap: Option A is the near miss: a split-thickness graft is not epidermis alone; it always includes a variable part of the dermis, whereas a full-thickness graft contains all of it.
takeaway: Split-thickness = epidermis + partial dermis.
source: Standard plastic-surgery anatomy.
thinking: Skin grafts are classified by how much dermis they carry ↓ a full-thickness graft includes the entire dermis ↓ a split-thickness graft includes the epidermis and only part of the dermis ↓ It contains epidermis and part of the dermis
pearl: Split-thickness donor sites heal by re-epithelialisation from retained adnexal structures and can be reharvested, whereas full-thickness donor sites must be closed directly.

subject: Anatomy
title: ENT: recurrent laryngeal nerve
stem: Which muscle of the larynx is NOT supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve?
why_correct: The cricothyroid is supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve. The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies the other intrinsic laryngeal muscles.

why_others_wrong.A: The posterior cricoarytenoid, despite being the sole abductor of the vocal cords, is still supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve like the other intrinsic muscles (aside from cricothyroid).
why_others_wrong.B: The lateral cricoarytenoid, an adductor of the vocal cords, is supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
why_others_wrong.C: The thyroarytenoid muscle is supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
why_others_wrong.E: The vocalis muscle, part of the thyroarytenoid complex, is also supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

exam_trap: The posterior cricoarytenoid is supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve despite being the only muscle that abducts the vocal cords.
takeaway: Cricothyroid → external superior laryngeal nerve.
source: Standard head-and-neck surgical anatomy.
thinking: Intrinsic laryngeal muscles ↓ all supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve except one ↓ cricothyroid lies on the external surface of the larynx ↓ supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve ↓ Cricothyroid
pearl: The posterior cricoarytenoid is the only vocal cord abductor, so bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury removes abduction and can produce life-threatening stridor needing tracheostomy.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: ENT: superior laryngeal nerve
stem: Damage to the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve is most likely to impair which function?
correct_answer: B. Tensioning of the vocal cords
why_correct: The external branch supplies the cricothyroid muscle, which increases vocal-cord tension and contributes to production of higher-pitched sounds.

why_others_wrong.A: Vocal-cord abduction depends on the posterior cricoarytenoid, which is supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve, not the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve.
why_others_wrong.C: Tongue protrusion depends on genioglossus, which is supplied by the hypoglossal nerve.
why_others_wrong.D: Shoulder elevation is performed by trapezius, which is supplied by the spinal accessory nerve.
why_others_wrong.E: The muscles of facial expression are supplied by the facial nerve, not the vagal branches to the larynx.
