exam_trap: Vocal-cord abduction (A) tempts candidates who confuse laryngeal nerves, but abduction is by posterior cricoarytenoid, supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve; the external branch supplies only cricothyroid.
takeaway: External SLN → cricothyroid → high-pitched voice.
source: Standard head-and-neck surgical anatomy.
thinking: External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve ↓ supplies cricothyroid ↓ cricothyroid tilts the thyroid cartilage, lengthening the cords ↓ increased tension raises pitch ↓ Tensioning of the vocal cords
pearl: The external branch runs with the superior thyroid artery, so the artery is ligated close to the upper pole during thyroidectomy; injury causes loss of high pitch and voice fatigue.

subject: Oral & maxillofacial surgery
title: Oral & maxillofacial surgery: mandibular nerve
stem: Which nerve carries the major motor supply to the muscles of mastication?
why_correct: The mandibular division (V3) is the only trigeminal division carrying motor fibres, supplying the muscles of mastication and several other muscles.

why_others_wrong.A: The ophthalmic division (V1) is purely sensory, supplying the forehead, upper eyelid and cornea, and carries no motor fibres to the masticatory muscles.
why_others_wrong.B: The maxillary division (V2) is purely sensory, supplying the midface, upper teeth and palate, and does not innervate the muscles of mastication.
why_others_wrong.D: The facial nerve supplies the muscles of facial expression, not the muscles of mastication, and it is not a division of the trigeminal nerve.
why_others_wrong.E: The glossopharyngeal nerve supplies stylopharyngeus and posterior tongue sensation and taste; it is a separate cranial nerve, not a trigeminal division.

exam_trap: The facial nerve tempts because it supplies muscles of the face, but it innervates the muscles of facial expression, not masseter, temporalis or the pterygoids.
takeaway: V3 carries both sensory and motor fibres; V1 and V2 are purely sensory.
source: Standard cranial nerve anatomy.
thinking: Muscles of mastication ↓ first pharyngeal arch derivatives ↓ supplied by the trigeminal nerve ↓ only V3 carries motor fibres ↓ Mandibular division
pearl: V3 also supplies mylohyoid, the anterior belly of digastric, tensor tympani and tensor veli palatini; with a V3 motor lesion the jaw deviates towards the affected side on opening.

subject: Oral & maxillofacial surgery
title: Oral & maxillofacial surgery: facial nerve
stem: A patient undergoes parotid surgery. Which nerve is particularly important because it traverses the parotid gland and divides within it?
why_correct: The facial nerve enters the parotid gland and divides into its major terminal branches within the gland. It does not provide the gland's secretomotor supply.

why_others_wrong.A: The hypoglossal nerve runs deep to the posterior belly of digastric towards the tongue and is relevant in submandibular, not parotid, surgery.
why_others_wrong.C: The vagus nerve descends within the carotid sheath deep in the neck and does not traverse or divide within the parotid gland.
why_others_wrong.D: The accessory nerve crosses the posterior triangle to supply sternocleidomastoid and trapezius and does not pass through the parotid gland.
why_others_wrong.E: The phrenic nerve descends on scalenus anterior in the root of the neck to the diaphragm and has no relationship to the parotid gland.

exam_trap: Candidates choosing hypoglossal nerve (A) mix up salivary gland operations; the hypoglossal is at risk in submandibular gland excision, whereas the facial nerve traverses the parotid.
takeaway: Parotid surgery → protect the facial nerve.
source: Standard head-and-neck surgical anatomy.
thinking: Parotid surgery ↓ one nerve runs through the substance of the gland ↓ it divides into its terminal branches within the gland, between superficial and deep parts ↓ injury causes ipsilateral facial weakness ↓ Facial nerve
pearl: At parotidectomy the facial nerve trunk is identified near its exit from the stylomastoid foramen using landmarks such as the tragal pointer and the posterior belly of digastric.

subject: Oral & maxillofacial surgery
title: Oral & maxillofacial surgery: parotid secretomotor supply
stem: Parasympathetic secretomotor fibres to the parotid gland ultimately travel through which nerve?
why_correct: Preganglionic parasympathetic fibres originate with the glossopharyngeal nerve, synapse in the otic ganglion and postganglionic fibres reach the parotid via the auriculotemporal nerve.

why_others_wrong.A: The facial nerve passes through the parotid and divides within it but does not carry its secretomotor fibres, which come from the glossopharyngeal nerve via the otic ganglion.
why_others_wrong.C: The hypoglossal nerve is a motor nerve to the tongue muscles and carries no parasympathetic secretomotor fibres to the parotid gland.
why_others_wrong.D: The phrenic nerve arises from C3 to C5 to supply the diaphragm and has no role in the autonomic supply of the salivary glands.
why_others_wrong.E: The greater occipital nerve is a sensory branch of the C2 dorsal ramus supplying the posterior scalp and carries no parotid secretomotor fibres.

exam_trap: The facial nerve is intimately related to the parotid but is not its parasympathetic secretomotor nerve.
takeaway: Parotid secretomotor → CN IX → otic ganglion → auriculotemporal nerve.
source: Standard head-and-neck anatomy / MRCS Applied Basic Sciences.
thinking: Parotid secretomotor supply is parasympathetic ↓ preganglionic fibres leave with the glossopharyngeal nerve via the lesser petrosal nerve ↓ they synapse in the otic ganglion ↓ postganglionic fibres travel with the auriculotemporal nerve to the gland ↓ Auriculotemporal nerve
pearl: After parotidectomy, regenerating auriculotemporal secretomotor fibres can grow into the sweat glands of the overlying skin, causing gustatory sweating and flushing on eating.

subject: Cardiothoracic surgery
title: Cardiothoracic surgery: aortic dissection
stem: A 58-year-old patient develops sudden severe chest pain radiating to the back. There is a difference in blood pressure between the arms. Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Abrupt severe chest or back pain with a pulse or blood-pressure differential is a classic warning pattern for acute aortic dissection.

why_others_wrong.A: Stable angina is exertional, predictable chest tightness relieved by rest, not abrupt tearing pain to the back with an inter-arm blood pressure difference.
why_others_wrong.C: Pleurisy gives sharp pain on breathing or coughing and does not explain a sudden severe onset with an inter-arm blood pressure differential.
why_others_wrong.D: Pericarditis causes positional pain eased by sitting forward, and does not produce an inter-arm blood pressure difference suggesting arch branch involvement.
why_others_wrong.E: Gastro-oesophageal reflux causes burning retrosternal discomfort related to meals and posture, not sudden severe back pain with unequal arm pressures.

exam_trap: Stable angina (A) or reflux (E) may be chosen for chest pain, but neither causes abrupt severe pain radiating to the back with a blood pressure difference between the arms.
takeaway: Sudden chest/back pain + pulse/BP difference → think aortic dissection.
source: NICE NG39, Major trauma framework; standard cardiothoracic surgical principles. Current guidance accessed 2026.
thinking: Sudden severe chest pain radiating to the back ↓ blood pressure differs between the arms ↓ implies involvement of the aortic arch branches ↓ abrupt pain plus a pulse or pressure deficit is the dissection pattern ↓ Acute aortic dissection
pearl: CT angiography is the usual diagnostic test; Stanford type A dissection involving the ascending aorta needs emergency surgery, whereas uncomplicated type B is usually managed medically with blood pressure and heart rate control.

subject: Cardiothoracic surgery
title: Cardiothoracic surgery: aortic dissection — ascending aorta
stem: A patient is diagnosed with an acute dissection involving the ascending aorta. Which complication is particularly feared?
why_correct: An ascending aortic dissection can rupture into the pericardial space, causing haemopericardium and tamponade.

why_others_wrong.A: Appendicitis is an intra-abdominal inflammatory condition with no mechanistic link to a dissection of the ascending aorta.
why_others_wrong.C: Acute cholecystitis is gallbladder inflammation, usually from gallstones, and is not a recognised complication of ascending aortic dissection.
why_others_wrong.D: Tension pneumothorax arises from air in the pleural space, whereas ascending dissection threatens rupture into the pericardium, coronary occlusion and aortic regurgitation.
why_others_wrong.E: Renal colic is caused by ureteric stones; dissection can compromise renal perfusion, but that follows distal extension rather than being the feared ascending complication.

exam_trap: Tension pneumothorax (D) appears alongside other chest emergencies, but ascending dissection threatens the pericardium rather than the pleura, so the feared complication is haemopericardium with tamponade.
takeaway: Ascending aortic dissection → think tamponade.
source: Standard cardiothoracic surgical anatomy and pathology.
thinking: Acute dissection involving the ascending aorta ↓ the ascending aorta lies within the pericardial reflection ↓ rupture or leakage into the pericardium causes haemopericardium ↓ rapid accumulation in the inelastic sac compresses the heart ↓ Cardiac tamponade
pearl: Ascending dissection can also extend into the aortic root to cause acute aortic regurgitation or coronary occlusion, most often of the right coronary ostium, which is why type A dissection is a surgical emergency.

subject: Cardiothoracic surgery
title: Cardiothoracic surgery: pulmonary venous return
stem: Which chamber receives oxygenated blood returning from the lungs?
why_correct: Pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium.

why_others_wrong.A: The right atrium receives deoxygenated systemic blood from the venae cavae and coronary sinus, not oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins.
why_others_wrong.B: The right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood into the pulmonary trunk towards the lungs rather than receiving blood returning from them.
why_others_wrong.D: The left ventricle receives oxygenated blood from the left atrium through the mitral valve, so it is the second, not the first, chamber reached.
why_others_wrong.E: The coronary sinus is a vein that drains deoxygenated blood from the myocardium into the right atrium, not a chamber receiving pulmonary venous return.

exam_trap: Left ventricle (D) is chosen by candidates who jump straight to the systemic pump, but pulmonary venous blood enters the left atrium first and then crosses the mitral valve.
takeaway: Pulmonary veins → left atrium.
source: Standard cardiovascular anatomy.
thinking: Oxygenated blood returning from the lungs ↓ carried by the pulmonary veins ↓ the pulmonary veins drain into the posterior left atrium ↓ blood then passes through the mitral valve to the left ventricle ↓ Left atrium
pearl: The pulmonary vein ostia in the left atrium are the usual source of the ectopic triggers of atrial fibrillation, which is why pulmonary vein isolation is the basis of catheter ablation.

subject: Cardiothoracic surgery
title: Cardiothoracic surgery: coronary dominance
stem: In a right-dominant coronary circulation, the posterior interventricular artery usually arises from which artery?
why_correct: Coronary dominance is determined by which coronary artery gives rise to the posterior interventricular artery. In most people this is the RCA.

why_others_wrong.A: The left main stem is a short trunk that divides into the anterior descending and circumflex arteries and does not directly give the posterior interventricular artery.
why_others_wrong.C: The left anterior descending artery runs in the anterior interventricular groove; it may wrap around the apex but does not form the posterior interventricular artery.
why_others_wrong.D: The circumflex artery gives the posterior interventricular artery in a left-dominant circulation, which is the opposite of the right-dominant pattern described.
why_others_wrong.E: The internal thoracic artery is a branch of the subclavian supplying the anterior chest wall; it is used as a bypass graft but is not a native coronary branch.

exam_trap: Circumflex (D) catches candidates who confuse the patterns: it gives the posterior interventricular artery only in a left-dominant circulation, the opposite of the one described.
takeaway: Right-dominant circulation → PDA from RCA.
source: Standard cardiac anatomy.
thinking: Dominance is defined by which artery gives the posterior interventricular artery ↓ right dominance is the commonest pattern ↓ the RCA runs in the coronary sulcus to the crux of the heart ↓ there it turns down the posterior interventricular groove ↓ Right coronary artery
pearl: In a left-dominant circulation the circumflex gives the posterior interventricular artery, so the left coronary system then supplies the whole interventricular septum and a left main stem occlusion is especially catastrophic.

subject: Cardiothoracic surgery
title: Cardiothoracic surgery: internal thoracic artery
stem: The internal thoracic artery is commonly used as a conduit in coronary artery bypass surgery. Which artery does it arise from?
why_correct: The internal thoracic artery arises from the first part of the subclavian artery.

why_others_wrong.A: The axillary artery begins at the lateral border of the first rib, beyond the origin of the internal thoracic artery, and supplies the shoulder and upper limb.
why_others_wrong.C: The brachial artery is the continuation of the axillary artery in the arm and gives no branches to the anterior chest wall.
why_others_wrong.D: The common carotid artery ascends in the neck and divides into the internal and external carotids without giving a thoracic branch.
why_others_wrong.E: The vertebral artery also arises from the first part of the subclavian, but it ascends through the cervical transverse foramina to supply the brain rather than the chest wall.

exam_trap: Vertebral artery (E) also arises from the first part of the subclavian, so candidates confuse the branches; it ascends to the brain rather than descending onto the anterior chest wall.
takeaway: Internal thoracic artery → subclavian.
source: Standard thoracic vascular anatomy.
thinking: Arterial conduit for coronary artery bypass ↓ internal thoracic artery runs behind the costal cartilages just lateral to the sternum ↓ traced back to the root of the neck ↓ it arises from the first part of the subclavian artery ↓ Subclavian artery
pearl: The left internal thoracic artery grafted to the left anterior descending artery has excellent long-term patency; its terminal branches are the musculophrenic and superior epigastric arteries.

subject: Neurosurgery
title: Neurosurgery: brainstem localisation
stem: A patient has ipsilateral cranial nerve findings with contralateral limb weakness. What anatomical region should be considered?
why_correct: "Crossed" neurological signs, with cranial nerve deficits on one side and limb motor/sensory findings on the opposite side, strongly suggest a brainstem lesion.

why_others_wrong.A: A cortical lesion produces cranial and limb signs on the same side, contralateral to the lesion, rather than the crossed pattern described.
why_others_wrong.C: A peripheral nerve lesion cannot cause both cranial nerve signs and contralateral limb weakness, which need a lesion involving crossing central pathways.
why_others_wrong.D: Neuromuscular junction disease causes fatigable, often symmetrical weakness without crossed cranial nerve and contralateral limb signs.
why_others_wrong.E: Primary muscle disease causes mostly proximal symmetrical weakness and cannot produce ipsilateral cranial nerve with contralateral limb findings.

exam_trap: Candidates choosing cerebral cortex (A) forget that a hemispheric lesion gives face and limb signs on the same side of the body, not a crossed pattern.
takeaway: Crossed cranial + limb signs → think brainstem.
source: Standard neuroanatomy / MRCS Applied Basic Sciences.
thinking: Cranial nerve signs on one side ↓ limb weakness on the opposite side ↓ cranial nerve nuclei lie beside corticospinal fibres that have not yet decussated ↓ a single lesion there produces crossed signs ↓ Brainstem
pearl: The cranial nerve involved localises the level of the lesion: a third nerve palsy points to the midbrain, sixth or seventh nerve palsies to the pons, and lower cranial nerve signs to the medulla.

subject: Neurosurgery
title: Neurosurgery: internal capsule
stem: A small lesion produces contralateral weakness affecting the face, arm and leg. Which structure is particularly likely to be involved?
why_correct: The internal capsule contains densely packed descending corticospinal and corticobulbar fibres, so a small lesion can produce substantial contralateral motor deficit.

why_others_wrong.B: Cerebellar vermis lesions cause truncal and gait ataxia, not contralateral weakness of the face, arm and leg.
why_others_wrong.C: The hippocampus is involved in memory, and a small lesion there causes memory impairment rather than contralateral motor weakness.
why_others_wrong.D: An optic chiasm lesion causes a bitemporal hemianopia, not weakness, because it carries visual fibres rather than motor tracts.
why_others_wrong.E: A medullary lesion would typically give crossed signs with lower cranial nerve involvement, and it lies below the level of the facial nucleus.

exam_trap: Candidates choosing medulla (E) miss that face weakness requires a lesion above the facial nucleus in the pons; medullary lesions give crossed lower cranial nerve signs instead.
takeaway: Small lesion + face/arm/leg weakness → internal capsule.
source: Standard neuroanatomy.
thinking: Small lesion ↓ contralateral weakness of face, arm and leg together ↓ corticobulbar and corticospinal fibres are tightly packed in the genu and posterior limb ↓ a single small infarct damages them all ↓ Internal capsule
pearl: Lacunar infarcts from occlusion of small penetrating lenticulostriate arteries commonly cause a pure motor stroke at the internal capsule, whereas the same deficit from the cortex would need a large infarct across MCA and ACA territories.

subject: Neurosurgery
title: Neurosurgery: cerebellar lesion
stem: Which finding is most characteristic of a cerebellar lesion?

options.B: Complete loss of pain sensation bilaterally
options.E: Pure lower motor neurone facial palsy

why_correct: Cerebellar dysfunction typically produces ipsilateral coordination abnormalities, including limb ataxia.

why_others_wrong.B: Bilateral loss of pain sensation suggests a spinal cord or peripheral sensory lesion, as the cerebellum coordinates movement rather than conveying pain.
why_others_wrong.C: Aphasia arises from dominant cerebral hemisphere language areas, whereas cerebellar lesions cause dysarthria and incoordination, not isolated aphasia.
why_others_wrong.D: A bitemporal hemianopia indicates optic chiasm compression, typically by a pituitary mass, and is unrelated to cerebellar function.
why_others_wrong.E: A lower motor neurone facial palsy arises from the facial nerve or its nucleus, not from the cerebellum, whose lesions cause ataxia.

exam_trap: Candidates may pick isolated aphasia (C) by confusing speech disorders; cerebellar disease causes slurred, scanning dysarthria, while aphasia is a dominant-hemisphere language deficit.
takeaway: Cerebellar lesion → ipsilateral ataxia.
source: Standard neuroanatomy.
thinking: Cerebellum coordinates movement ↓ its pathways cross twice, so each hemisphere controls the same side of the body ↓ damage causes incoordination, intention tremor and dysdiadochokinesia ↓ Ipsilateral limb ataxia
pearl: Midline vermis lesions cause truncal and gait ataxia with relatively preserved limb coordination, whereas hemisphere lesions cause ipsilateral limb ataxia; posterior fossa masses can also cause obstructive hydrocephalus.

subject: Neurosurgery
title: Neurosurgery: optic chiasm
stem: A patient develops loss of temporal visual fields in both eyes. Which structure is most likely affected?
why_correct: The nasal retinal fibres cross at the optic chiasm. Damage therefore affects the temporal visual fields of both eyes.

why_others_wrong.A: An optic nerve lesion causes visual loss in one eye only, not loss of the temporal fields in both eyes.
why_others_wrong.C: An optic tract lesion, behind the chiasm, causes a contralateral homonymous hemianopia rather than bitemporal field loss.
why_others_wrong.D: A lateral geniculate body lesion causes a contralateral homonymous field defect, not loss of both temporal fields.
why_others_wrong.E: A visual cortex lesion causes a contralateral homonymous hemianopia, often with macular sparing, rather than a bitemporal defect.

exam_trap: Candidates choosing optic tract (C) forget that lesions behind the chiasm cause a contralateral homonymous hemianopia, not loss of the temporal field in each eye.
takeaway: Bitemporal hemianopia → optic chiasm.
source: Standard neuroanatomy.
thinking: Loss of the temporal fields in both eyes ↓ temporal fields are seen by the nasal retina of each eye ↓ nasal retinal fibres cross at the chiasm ↓ a midline lesion there damages both crossing sets ↓ Optic chiasm
pearl: Compression from below by a pituitary adenoma classically affects the upper temporal quadrants first, whereas compression from above, for example by a craniopharyngioma, tends to affect the lower temporal quadrants first.

subject: Neurosurgery
title: Neurosurgery: pituitary tumour
stem: A patient with a pituitary-region mass develops bitemporal hemianopia. Why does this visual-field defect occur?

options.B: Compression of the optic nerve only

correct_answer: A. Compression of the optic chiasm
why_correct: The optic chiasm lies superior to the pituitary gland and can be compressed by an enlarging sellar mass.

why_others_wrong.B: Compression of one optic nerve would cause visual loss in that eye only, not bitemporal hemianopia from crossing nasal fibres.
why_others_wrong.C: The facial nerve controls facial expression and runs nowhere near the sella, so its compression cannot cause a visual-field defect.
why_others_wrong.D: The auditory cortex in the temporal lobe processes hearing and is not involved in the visual pathway.
why_others_wrong.E: The cerebellum sits in the posterior fossa and controls coordination; it does not carry visual fibres or cause bitemporal hemianopia.

exam_trap: Candidates choosing optic nerve compression (B) forget that a single nerve lesion causes monocular loss; only damage to the crossing fibres at the chiasm explains bitemporal defects.
takeaway: Pituitary mass + bitemporal field loss → chiasm compression.
source: Standard neuroanatomy.
thinking: Pituitary-region mass ↓ expands upwards out of the sella ↓ the optic chiasm lies directly above the gland ↓ crossing nasal fibres are compressed, giving bitemporal hemianopia ↓ Compression of the optic chiasm
pearl: Sudden headache, visual loss and ophthalmoplegia in a patient with a pituitary mass suggests pituitary apoplexy, which needs urgent steroid replacement and neurosurgical input; lateral extension into the cavernous sinus can affect nerves III, IV and VI.

subject: Urology
title: Urology: bladder cancer
stem: A 68-year-old smoker develops painless visible haematuria. Which diagnosis requires urgent consideration?
why_correct: Visible haematuria, particularly painless haematuria in an older adult, is a major presenting feature of urinary tract malignancy.

why_others_wrong.B: Dehydration may concentrate urine but does not cause frank blood, so attributing painless visible haematuria to it risks missing a tumour.
why_others_wrong.C: Appendicitis presents with abdominal pain and fever, not painless visible haematuria in an older smoker.
why_others_wrong.D: An inguinal hernia presents as a groin swelling and is not a cause of painless visible haematuria.
why_others_wrong.E: Renal trauma can cause haematuria but needs a history of injury, which is absent here, and is usually painful.

exam_trap: Candidates attribute haematuria to dehydration or assume painless bleeding is benign, but painless visible haematuria in an older smoker is bladder cancer until proven otherwise.
takeaway: Painless visible haematuria → think urothelial malignancy.
source: NICE NG12, Suspected cancer: recognition and referral. Current guidance accessed 2026.
thinking: 68-year-old smoker ↓ painless visible haematuria ↓ smoking is the main bladder cancer risk factor ↓ urothelial malignancy must be excluded ↓ Bladder cancer
pearl: Most bladder cancers are urothelial carcinomas, and occupational exposure to aromatic amines in dye, rubber and leather industries is a recognised risk factor alongside smoking.

subject: Urology
title: Urology: bladder cancer — risk factor
stem: Which exposure is a major established risk factor for urothelial bladder cancer?
why_correct: Tobacco exposure is an important established risk factor for bladder cancer.

why_others_wrong.B: Regular exercise is not a recognised risk factor for bladder cancer and is generally associated with better health outcomes.
why_others_wrong.C: A high-fibre diet is not an established cause of urothelial cancer, unlike tobacco smoking and occupational aromatic amine exposure.
why_others_wrong.D: Good hydration dilutes urinary carcinogens and is not a risk factor for bladder cancer.
why_others_wrong.E: Short-term paracetamol use is not linked to urothelial cancer, unlike historical heavy phenacetin analgesic use.

exam_trap: Candidates may be distracted by analgesic use, but historical phenacetin abuse, not short-term paracetamol, is linked to urothelial cancer; smoking is the major factor.
takeaway: Smoking is the major bladder cancer risk factor.
source: NICE NG12; standard urological oncology principles.
thinking: Risk factor for urothelial bladder cancer ↓ carcinogens are excreted in urine ↓ prolonged contact with urothelium ↓ tobacco smoking is the major established cause ↓ Cigarette smoking
pearl: Chronic schistosomiasis (Schistosoma haematobium) infection predisposes to squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder, as do long-term indwelling catheters and chronic bladder stones.

subject: Urology
title: Urology: benign prostatic enlargement
stem: A man develops progressive hesitancy, weak urinary stream and incomplete bladder emptying. Which condition is most likely?
why_correct: Progressive lower urinary tract symptoms in an older man are commonly associated with benign prostatic enlargement.

why_others_wrong.B: Testicular torsion causes sudden severe scrotal pain, not progressive voiding symptoms such as hesitancy and a weak stream.
why_others_wrong.C: Renal cell carcinoma may cause haematuria, flank pain or a mass but does not obstruct bladder outflow to produce these voiding symptoms.
why_others_wrong.D: Epididymitis causes a painful, swollen epididymis, sometimes with dysuria, rather than progressive hesitancy, weak stream and incomplete emptying.
why_others_wrong.E: A ureteric stone causes acute colicky flank pain, and distal stones can cause frequency, but not a progressive weak stream and hesitancy.

exam_trap: Candidates choose a ureteric stone because distal stones cause urinary frequency, but gradual hesitancy, weak stream and incomplete emptying indicate prostatic outflow obstruction.
takeaway: Older man with obstructive LUTS → think BPE, while assessing for cancer.
source: NICE CG97, Lower urinary tract symptoms in men. Current guidance accessed 2026.
thinking: Older man ↓ progressive hesitancy and weak stream ↓ incomplete bladder emptying ↓ bladder outflow obstruction from prostatic enlargement ↓ Benign prostatic enlargement
pearl: Alpha-blockers relax prostatic smooth muscle for rapid symptom relief, whereas 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors shrink the gland over months and reduce PSA by about half.

subject: Urology
title: Urology: renal cell carcinoma
stem: Which presentation is classically associated with renal cell carcinoma?
why_correct: Haematuria is an important presenting feature of renal malignancy, although the classic triad is uncommon.

why_others_wrong.B: Bilateral ankle sprain is a musculoskeletal injury with no association with renal cell carcinoma.
why_others_wrong.C: Isolated dysphagia points to oesophageal or pharyngeal disease rather than a renal tumour.
why_others_wrong.D: Acute tonsillitis is an upper respiratory infection and is not a presentation of renal cell carcinoma.
why_others_wrong.E: Testicular torsion is an acute scrotal emergency, whereas renal cell carcinoma may instead cause a left varicocele via renal vein involvement.

exam_trap: Candidates wait for the full triad of haematuria, flank pain and mass, but this occurs in a minority; isolated haematuria warrants investigation for renal cancer.
takeaway: Renal malignancy can present with haematuria alone.
source: NICE NG12, Suspected cancer: recognition and referral.
thinking: Renal cell carcinoma presentations ↓ classic triad of haematuria, loin pain and mass is uncommon ↓ haematuria is the commonest presenting symptom ↓ many tumours are found incidentally on imaging ↓ Painless haematuria
pearl: Renal cell carcinoma tends to grow into the renal vein and IVC, and paraneoplastic effects include polycythaemia from erythropoietin and hypercalcaemia from PTH-related peptide.

subject: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care
title: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care: venous leg ulcer
stem: A patient has a chronic ulcer around the medial gaiter area with oedema and skin pigmentation. Which underlying condition is most likely?
why_correct: Venous ulcers commonly occur in the gaiter region and are associated with oedema and chronic venous skin changes.

why_others_wrong.B: Acute arterial embolism causes a sudden, pale, painful, pulseless limb rather than a chronic gaiter ulcer with oedema and pigmentation.
why_others_wrong.C: Compartment syndrome is an acute rise in muscle compartment pressure, usually after trauma, and does not produce a chronic gaiter ulcer.
why_others_wrong.D: Acute lymphangitis produces red streaks tracking proximally with fever, not a chronic medial gaiter ulcer with pigmentation.
why_others_wrong.E: A sarcoma may rarely ulcerate, but a chronic medial gaiter ulcer with oedema and pigmentation is typical of venous disease; atypical or non-healing ulcers warrant biopsy.

exam_trap: Candidates consider a sarcoma or lymphatic cause, but a medial gaiter ulcer with oedema and pigmentation is typical of venous disease; atypical or non-healing ulcers need biopsy.
takeaway: Gaiter ulcer with oedema and skin changes → venous disease.
source: NICE CG168, Varicose veins; standard vascular principles.
thinking: Chronic ulcer in the medial gaiter area ↓ surrounding oedema ↓ skin pigmentation ↓ features of venous hypertension ↓ Chronic venous insufficiency
pearl: Before compression bandaging for a venous ulcer, ABPI must be measured to exclude significant arterial disease, as compression can cause ischaemic injury.

subject: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care
title: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care: arterial leg ulcer
stem: Which feature favours an arterial rather than venous ulcer?

options.C: Distal foot/toe location with reduced perfusion

correct_answer: C. Distal foot/toe location with reduced perfusion
why_correct: Arterial ulcers often occur distally, particularly over pressure points and toes, and are associated with evidence of poor arterial perfusion.

why_others_wrong.A: The medial gaiter area is the classic site for venous ulcers, so this location favours a venous rather than arterial cause.
why_others_wrong.B: Dependent oedema reflects raised venous pressure and is typical of venous ulceration rather than arterial insufficiency.
why_others_wrong.D: Haemosiderin pigmentation results from red cell leakage in venous hypertension and points to a venous ulcer.
why_others_wrong.E: Lipodermatosclerosis is a fibrotic skin change of chronic venous hypertension and favours a venous ulcer.

exam_trap: Candidates choose haemosiderin pigmentation or lipodermatosclerosis as general chronic ulcer features, but both point to venous disease; distal location with poor perfusion favours arterial ulcer.
takeaway: Distal ulcer with poor perfusion → think arterial.
source: NICE CG147 / UK vascular practice.
thinking: Arterial versus venous ulcer ↓ arterial ulcers occur distally over pressure points and toes ↓ with signs of poor perfusion ↓ venous features are oedema and pigmentation ↓ Distal foot/toe location with reduced perfusion
pearl: Arterial ulcers are typically painful, worse on elevation and eased by hanging the leg down, with a punched-out appearance and pale base.

subject: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care
title: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care: deep vein thrombosis
stem: A patient develops unilateral calf swelling and pain following prolonged immobilisation. Which investigation is commonly used when DVT is suspected?
why_correct: Compression duplex ultrasonography is a key investigation in suspected lower-limb DVT.

why_others_wrong.B: A plain skull X-ray has no role in investigating suspected leg DVT.
why_others_wrong.C: Echocardiography may show right heart strain in pulmonary embolism but cannot visualise a calf or thigh vein thrombus.
why_others_wrong.D: Colonoscopy may later look for occult malignancy but does not diagnose deep vein thrombosis.
why_others_wrong.E: MRI brain images the head and has no role in assessing unilateral calf swelling for DVT.

exam_trap: Candidates choose echocardiography because it can detect PE effects, but it cannot visualise a leg thrombus; suspected DVT is imaged with compression duplex ultrasound.
takeaway: Suspected lower-limb DVT → duplex ultrasound.
source: NICE NG158, Venous thromboembolic diseases: diagnosis and management. Current guidance accessed 2026.
thinking: Unilateral calf swelling and pain ↓ after prolonged immobilisation ↓ suspected DVT ↓ compression duplex ultrasound images the deep veins ↓ Duplex ultrasound
pearl: A negative proximal leg vein ultrasound in a DVT-likely patient with a positive D-dimer is usually repeated about a week later, as NICE recommends.

subject: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care
title: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care: pulmonary embolism
stem: A patient develops sudden dyspnoea and pleuritic chest pain after recent surgery. Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Recent surgery is an important VTE risk factor, and sudden breathlessness with pleuritic chest pain should raise concern for PE.

why_others_wrong.B: A chronic venous ulcer is a slow-healing leg wound and cannot explain sudden breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain after surgery.
why_others_wrong.C: Stable angina causes exertional central chest tightness relieved by rest, not sudden pleuritic pain with dyspnoea after surgery.
why_others_wrong.D: Carpal tunnel syndrome is median nerve compression causing hand paraesthesia and has no link to breathlessness or chest pain.
why_others_wrong.E: Otitis externa is an ear canal infection and would not cause sudden dyspnoea or pleuritic chest pain.

exam_trap: Candidates choose stable angina for chest pain, but sudden pleuritic pain with dyspnoea after surgery points to PE rather than exertional ischaemic pain.
takeaway: Postoperative sudden dyspnoea with pleuritic pain → consider PE.
source: NICE NG158. Current guidance accessed 2026.
thinking: Recent surgery ↓ sudden dyspnoea ↓ pleuritic chest pain ↓ postoperative VTE risk ↓ Pulmonary embolism
pearl: Suspected PE is assessed with a two-level clinical probability score, and CTPA is the usual first imaging, with V/Q scanning as an alternative when contrast is contraindicated.

subject: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care
title: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care: chronic venous disease
stem: Which physiological abnormality most directly contributes to venous hypertension in chronic venous insufficiency?
why_correct: Failure of venous valves permits reflux and contributes to sustained venous hypertension, particularly when standing.

why_others_wrong.A: Arterial vasospasm reduces arterial inflow, as in Raynaud's, and does not raise venous pressure in the leg.
why_others_wrong.C: Reduced cardiac output does not explain chronic venous hypertension, which in chronic venous insufficiency results from valvular reflux.
why_others_wrong.D: Increased lymphatic drainage would reduce tissue oedema; lymphatic failure, not increased flow, contributes to swelling.
why_others_wrong.E: Hyperventilation alters blood carbon dioxide and pH but has no effect on lower-limb venous valve function or venous pressure.

exam_trap: Candidates choose reduced cardiac output, but chronic venous hypertension in the legs results from valvular reflux, not low cardiac output.
takeaway: Venous valve failure → reflux → venous hypertension.
source: Standard vascular physiology.
thinking: Chronic venous insufficiency ↓ valves fail to prevent reflux ↓ standing column of blood is not interrupted ↓ sustained ambulatory venous hypertension ↓ Venous valve incompetence
pearl: The calf muscle pump normally lowers venous pressure during walking; valve incompetence or deep vein damage after DVT means ambulatory venous pressure stays high.

subject: Trauma & orthopaedics
title: Trauma & orthopaedics: fat embolism syndrome
stem: A young adult with a major long-bone fracture develops hypoxaemia, neurological symptoms and a petechial rash several days later. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: The classic syndrome involves respiratory dysfunction, neurological disturbance and petechial rash after major long-bone trauma.

why_others_wrong.B: Appendicitis causes abdominal pain and fever and does not explain hypoxaemia, confusion and petechiae arising days after a long-bone fracture.
why_others_wrong.C: Compartment syndrome causes severe local limb pain and pain on passive stretch, not respiratory failure, neurological disturbance or a petechial rash.
why_others_wrong.D: Cellulitis produces localised spreading erythema, warmth and fever, not systemic hypoxaemia, altered consciousness and petechiae over the upper body and conjunctivae.
why_others_wrong.E: Atelectasis can cause mild hypoxaemia but does not explain the neurological symptoms or petechial rash, and the stem does not describe a postoperative patient.

exam_trap: Candidates choose postoperative atelectasis because of the hypoxaemia, but atelectasis does not explain confusion and a petechial rash after a long-bone fracture.
takeaway: Long-bone fracture + hypoxaemia + neurology + petechiae → fat embolism syndrome.
source: Standard trauma and orthopaedic principles.
thinking: Major long-bone fracture ↓ respiratory, neurological and petechial features ↓ appearing after a latent interval of days ↓ classic triad of fat embolism syndrome ↓ Fat embolism syndrome
pearl: Petechiae in fat embolism syndrome classically appear over the axillae, upper chest, neck and conjunctivae; early fixation of long-bone fractures reduces the risk, and treatment is supportive.

subject: Trauma & orthopaedics
title: Trauma & orthopaedics: scaphoid fracture
stem: A patient falls onto an outstretched hand and develops tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox. Which fracture should be suspected?
why_correct: Anatomical snuffbox tenderness following a fall onto an outstretched hand is a classic clinical clue to scaphoid injury.

why_others_wrong.B: Olecranon fractures usually follow a direct blow or fall onto the point of the elbow and cause posterior elbow tenderness, not snuffbox tenderness.
why_others_wrong.C: A clavicle fracture can follow a fall on the outstretched hand, but it causes tenderness and deformity over the clavicle rather than in the anatomical snuffbox.
why_others_wrong.D: Patellar fractures result from a direct blow to the knee or forceful quadriceps contraction and are unrelated to tenderness at the wrist.
why_others_wrong.E: Tibial plateau fractures follow axial or varus-valgus loading of the knee and cause knee pain and swelling, so they do not fit a wrist injury.

exam_trap: Candidates are reassured by a normal first radiograph, but occult scaphoid fractures are common and missing one risks non-union and avascular necrosis.
takeaway: Snuffbox tenderness after a fall on the outstretched hand → scaphoid fracture until proven otherwise.
source: Standard UK orthopaedic practice.
thinking: Fall onto an outstretched hand ↓ tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox ↓ the scaphoid forms the floor of the snuffbox ↓ suspect scaphoid fracture ↓ Scaphoid fracture
pearl: If initial scaphoid radiographs are normal but clinical suspicion remains, the wrist is immobilised and further imaging, typically MRI, is arranged rather than discharging the patient.

subject: Trauma & orthopaedics
title: Trauma & orthopaedics: scaphoid blood supply
stem: Why is a proximal scaphoid fracture at risk of avascular necrosis?

options.A: The proximal pole has a relatively poor direct blood supply
options.B: It receives no arterial supply at all
options.C: It is supplied exclusively by the ulnar artery
options.E: It is covered by cartilage only

correct_answer: A. The proximal pole has a relatively poor direct blood supply
why_correct: Much of the scaphoid's vascular supply enters distally and travels towards the proximal pole, making proximal injuries vulnerable to disruption of blood flow.

why_others_wrong.B: The proximal pole is not entirely without arterial supply; it receives retrograde flow through intraosseous vessels entering distally, which a fracture can interrupt.
why_others_wrong.C: The scaphoid is supplied mainly by branches of the radial artery entering dorsally and distally, not by the ulnar artery.
why_others_wrong.D: The scaphoid contains cancellous bone and marrow like other carpal bones; its necrosis risk comes from the retrograde blood supply, not absent marrow.
why_others_wrong.E: Extensive articular cartilage limits where vessels can enter, but the proximal pole is still bone whose supply arrives retrogradely from distal entry points.

exam_trap: Candidates choose 'no arterial supply at all', but the proximal pole is supplied retrogradely from distal entry vessels; it is vulnerable, not avascular.
takeaway: Proximal scaphoid fracture → avascular necrosis risk from retrograde blood supply.
source: Standard orthopaedic anatomy.
thinking: Proximal scaphoid fracture ↓ vessels enter the scaphoid dorsally and distally ↓ proximal pole receives retrograde intraosseous flow ↓ fracture interrupts that supply ↓ The proximal pole has a relatively poor direct blood supply
pearl: The more proximal the scaphoid fracture, the higher the risk of non-union and avascular necrosis, which is why proximal pole fractures are often considered for early internal fixation.

subject: Trauma & orthopaedics
title: Trauma & orthopaedics: femoral neck fracture
stem: Which complication is particularly associated with intracapsular fracture of the femoral neck?

options.A: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head

correct_answer: A. Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
why_correct: Intracapsular fractures can disrupt the retinacular vessels supplying the femoral head.

why_others_wrong.B: Appendicitis is an intra-abdominal inflammatory condition unrelated to hip fracture and has no link with the blood supply of the femoral head.
why_others_wrong.C: Carpal tunnel syndrome is median nerve compression at the wrist and is not a complication of a femoral neck fracture.
why_others_wrong.D: Tension pneumothorax follows chest trauma or thoracic procedures, not an isolated intracapsular hip fracture.
why_others_wrong.E: Facial nerve palsy relates to temporal bone, parotid or intracranial pathology and has no connection with a femoral neck fracture.

exam_trap: Candidates who think of all hip fractures together miss that avascular necrosis is specific to intracapsular fractures, which disrupt the retinacular vessels running up the femoral neck.
takeaway: Intracapsular femoral neck fracture → AVN risk.
source: Standard orthopaedic anatomy and trauma principles.
thinking: Intracapsular femoral neck fracture ↓ retinacular vessels run along the neck inside the capsule ↓ displacement tears these vessels ↓ femoral head loses its main supply ↓ Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
pearl: Displaced intracapsular hip fractures in older patients are usually managed with hemiarthroplasty or total hip replacement, whereas extracapsular fractures, where head blood supply is preserved, are fixed with a sliding hip screw or nail.

subject: Plastic surgery
title: Plastic surgery: keloid scar
stem: Which feature distinguishes a keloid from a hypertrophic scar?

options.A: It remains confined to the original wound
options.B: It extends beyond the original wound margins

correct_answer: B. It extends beyond the original wound margins
why_correct: Keloid scars characteristically extend beyond the boundaries of the original injury, whereas hypertrophic scars remain within them.

why_others_wrong.A: Staying within the original wound is the hallmark of a hypertrophic scar, so it describes the opposite of a keloid.
why_others_wrong.C: Keloids rarely regress and often recur after excision; it is hypertrophic scars that tend to settle spontaneously over time.
why_others_wrong.D: Keloids consist of excess, disorganised thick collagen bundles, so a lack of collagen is the reverse of their histology.
why_others_wrong.E: Keloids follow many minor injuries such as ear piercing, acne or surgical wounds, so they are not restricted to burns.

exam_trap: Option A describes a hypertrophic scar; candidates swap the two, but only a keloid spreads beyond the original wound.
takeaway: Beyond the original wound margins → keloid.
source: Standard plastic-surgery principles.
thinking: Keloid versus hypertrophic scar ↓ a hypertrophic scar stays within the original wound margins ↓ a keloid invades the surrounding normal skin ↓ It extends beyond the original wound margins
pearl: Keloids are commoner in darker skin and on the earlobes, sternum and shoulders; excision alone has a high recurrence rate, so it is combined with intralesional steroid, pressure or radiotherapy.

subject: Plastic surgery
title: Plastic surgery: hypertrophic scar
stem: A raised scar remains within the original wound margins and develops after a burn. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Hypertrophic scars are raised but remain within the original wound boundaries.

why_others_wrong.A: A keloid grows beyond the original wound margins, whereas this raised burn scar stays within them, which points to a hypertrophic scar.
why_others_wrong.C: Basal cell carcinoma is a pearly nodule with telangiectasia arising on sun-exposed skin, not a raised scar confined to a burn wound.
why_others_wrong.D: Melanoma is a pigmented lesion with irregular shape and colour, not a raised scar limited to the margins of a previous burn.
why_others_wrong.E: An abscess is a painful, fluctuant collection of pus with signs of infection rather than a firm raised scar following a burn.

exam_trap: Keloid (option A) tempts because burns scar heavily, but keloids extend beyond the wound edge; a raised scar confined to the burn margins is hypertrophic.
takeaway: Raised scar within the wound margins → hypertrophic scar.
source: Standard plastic-surgery principles.
thinking: Raised scar after a burn ↓ it remains within the original wound margins ↓ hypertrophic scars respect the wound boundary; keloids do not ↓ Hypertrophic scar
pearl: Hypertrophic burn scars are prevented and treated with pressure garments, silicone gel and massage, and often soften and flatten as the scar matures.

subject: Plastic surgery
title: Plastic surgery: melanoma
stem: Which feature of a pigmented lesion is particularly concerning for melanoma?
why_correct: Asymmetry is one of the established clinical warning features used when assessing pigmented lesions.

why_others_wrong.A: Symmetry of shape is a reassuring feature of a benign naevus; it is asymmetry and irregular outline that raise concern for melanoma.
why_others_wrong.B: Uniform colour suggests a benign naevus, whereas irregular or multiple colours within a lesion are a warning sign of melanoma.
why_others_wrong.D: A lesion unchanged over many years is reassuring, since change in size, shape or colour is a major warning feature of melanoma.
why_others_wrong.E: A small uniform macule lacks the asymmetry, colour variation and large diameter that make a pigmented lesion suspicious for melanoma.

exam_trap: Symmetry, uniform colour and long-term stability (options A, B and D) are all reassuring features; asymmetry with an irregular outline and change over time raise concern.
takeaway: Asymmetry, irregular border, colour variation, large diameter or change → think melanoma.
source: NICE NG14, Melanoma: assessment and management.
thinking: Pigmented lesion assessed for melanoma ↓ ABCDE: asymmetry, border irregularity, colour variation, diameter, evolution ↓ benign naevi are symmetrical, uniform and stable ↓ Irregular asymmetry
pearl: Suspicious pigmented lesions are referred on the suspected cancer pathway and removed by excision biopsy with a narrow margin rather than shave or punch biopsy, so that tumour thickness can be measured accurately.

subject: Plastic surgery
title: Plastic surgery: basal cell carcinoma
stem: Which description is most characteristic of a basal cell carcinoma?
correct_answer: A. Pearly lesion with possible ulceration
why_correct: Basal cell carcinoma commonly appears as a pearly or translucent lesion and may ulcerate.

why_others_wrong.B: A rapidly spreading petechial rash suggests meningococcal sepsis or a bleeding disorder, not a slowly growing basal cell carcinoma.
why_others_wrong.C: A deep abscess cavity is a collection of pus from infection, whereas basal cell carcinoma is a slow-growing pearly skin tumour.
why_others_wrong.D: Acute blistering after trauma reflects a friction or thermal injury, not the slow-growing pearly lesion of basal cell carcinoma.
why_others_wrong.E: Basal cell carcinoma very rarely metastasises, so an isolated fluctuant lymph node is not its presentation and suggests infection instead.

exam_trap: Option E tempts candidates who expect skin cancer to spread to nodes, but basal cell carcinoma very rarely metastasises; it is a slow, locally destructive pearly lesion that may ulcerate.
takeaway: Pearly, ulcerating skin lesion → consider BCC.
source: NICE NG14 / standard dermatological surgical principles.
thinking: Slow-growing skin tumour ↓ pearly, translucent appearance ↓ may ulcerate centrally (rodent ulcer) ↓ Pearly lesion with possible ulceration
pearl: Margin-controlled micrographic surgery is preferred for high-risk facial BCCs, such as recurrent, ill-defined or morphoeic lesions near the eyes, nose or ears, to maximise clearance while preserving tissue.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Physiology: conductive hearing loss
stem: A patient has conductive hearing loss. Where is the underlying pathology most likely to be located?
why_correct: Conductive hearing loss results from impaired transmission of sound through the external or middle ear.

why_others_wrong.B: Damage to the cochlear nerve causes sensorineural hearing loss, not conductive loss.
why_others_wrong.C: Cerebellar lesions cause ataxia and incoordination, not failure of sound conduction through the ear.
why_others_wrong.D: The visual cortex processes vision and plays no part in conducting sound.
why_others_wrong.E: The optic nerve carries visual information and has no role in hearing.

exam_trap: Cochlear nerve only (B) tempts candidates who link any hearing loss to nerve damage, but cochlear or nerve lesions cause sensorineural, not conductive, hearing loss.
takeaway: Conductive = external/middle ear.
source: Standard ENT physiology and anatomy.
thinking: Conductive hearing loss ↓ failure of sound transmission to the cochlea ↓ conducting pathway is canal, eardrum and ossicles ↓ lesion in the external or middle ear ↓ External or middle ear
pearl: In conductive loss, bone conduction is better than air conduction on the affected side and a midline tuning fork lateralises to the affected ear; in sensorineural loss it lateralises to the better ear.

subject: ENT: ear, throat, sleep & nose
title: Physiology: sensorineural hearing loss
stem: Which structure is most directly involved in sensorineural hearing loss?
correct_answer: C. Cochlea or auditory nerve pathway
why_correct: Sensorineural hearing loss results from dysfunction of the cochlea, auditory nerve or more central auditory pathways.

why_others_wrong.A: Pathology confined to the external auditory canal, such as wax or otitis externa, causes conductive rather than sensorineural loss.
why_others_wrong.B: A tympanic membrane perforation or scarring impairs sound transmission and causes conductive hearing loss.
why_others_wrong.D: Eustachian tube dysfunction causes middle-ear pressure problems and effusion, producing conductive hearing loss.
why_others_wrong.E: The pinna collects sound, and its abnormalities affect conduction rather than cochlear or neural function.

exam_trap: The tympanic membrane (B) or Eustachian tube (D) tempt candidates, but lesions there impair sound transmission and cause conductive rather than sensorineural hearing loss.
takeaway: Sensorineural = cochlea/auditory pathway.
source: Standard ENT physiology and anatomy.
thinking: Sensorineural hearing loss ↓ sound reaches the inner ear normally ↓ fault lies in transduction or neural transmission ↓ cochlea, auditory nerve or central pathway ↓ Cochlea or auditory nerve pathway
pearl: Presbycusis, the commonest cause of sensorineural loss, affects high frequencies first, giving a down-sloping audiogram and difficulty hearing speech in background noise.

subject: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care
title: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care: primary hyperparathyroidism
stem: A patient has recurrent renal stones, hypercalcaemia and an inappropriately elevated parathyroid hormone concentration. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Primary hyperparathyroidism causes excessive PTH secretion, typically resulting in hypercalcaemia and increased renal calcium excretion.

why_others_wrong.B: Primary hypothyroidism raises TSH and lowers thyroxine and does not produce hypercalcaemia with an elevated PTH.
why_others_wrong.C: Addison disease can occasionally raise calcium, but PTH is appropriately suppressed and hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia dominate.
why_others_wrong.D: SIADH causes euvolaemic hyponatraemia from excess ADH and does not raise calcium or PTH.
why_others_wrong.E: Hypercalcaemia can cause nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and polyuria, but diabetes insipidus does not cause hypercalcaemia with raised PTH and stones.

exam_trap: Candidates choose diabetes insipidus because hypercalcaemia causes polyuria, but raised calcium with an unsuppressed PTH points to primary hyperparathyroidism.
takeaway: High calcium with inappropriately high PTH → primary hyperparathyroidism.
source: Standard endocrine physiology; MRCS Applied Basic Sciences curriculum.
thinking: Recurrent renal stones ↓ hypercalcaemia ↓ PTH inappropriately elevated ↓ autonomous parathyroid secretion ↓ Primary hyperparathyroidism
pearl: Most primary hyperparathyroidism is due to a single parathyroid adenoma, localised before surgery with ultrasound and sestamibi scanning to allow focused parathyroidectomy.

subject: Physiology
title: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care: pth effect on phosphate
stem: Which renal effect of parathyroid hormone contributes to the hypophosphataemia of primary hyperparathyroidism?

options.D: Complete inhibition of renal calcium reabsorption

correct_answer: B. Reduced proximal tubular phosphate reabsorption
why_correct: PTH decreases proximal tubular phosphate reabsorption, increasing urinary phosphate excretion.

why_others_wrong.A: This is the opposite renal effect: increased proximal phosphate reabsorption would tend to cause hyperphosphataemia, not the hypophosphataemia described.
why_others_wrong.C: PTH's indirect effect via increased calcitriol formation would tend to increase intestinal phosphate absorption, which would not account for the hypophosphataemia seen with PTH excess; the dominant effect is renal phosphate wasting.
why_others_wrong.D: PTH increases, rather than inhibits, renal calcium reabsorption; this option misstates its calcium effect.
why_others_wrong.E: Increased distal sodium excretion is not the mechanism responsible for PTH-associated phosphate wasting, which occurs via reduced proximal tubular phosphate reabsorption.

exam_trap: Candidates choosing C remember that PTH increases calcitriol and gut phosphate absorption, but that would raise phosphate; renal phosphate wasting dominates and lowers it.
takeaway: PTH → phosphate wasting.
source: Standard renal/endocrine physiology.
thinking: Primary hyperparathyroidism ↓ excess PTH acts on the proximal tubule ↓ phosphate reabsorption falls ↓ urinary phosphate loss causes hypophosphataemia ↓ Reduced proximal tubular phosphate reabsorption
pearl: Primary hyperparathyroidism typically shows high calcium, low phosphate and a raised or inappropriately normal PTH; a single adenoma is the usual cause and is localised before surgery with ultrasound and sestamibi imaging.

subject: ENT: head & neck
title: ENT: thyroid nerve anatomy
stem: During thyroid surgery, injury to the recurrent laryngeal nerve is most likely to cause:

options.E: Loss of taste from the posterior tongue

why_correct: The recurrent laryngeal nerves supply almost all intrinsic muscles of the larynx and are therefore critical to normal vocal-cord movement.

why_others_wrong.A: General sensation from the anterior tongue is carried by the lingual nerve, not the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
why_others_wrong.C: Loss of shoulder elevation follows accessory nerve injury to trapezius, not recurrent laryngeal nerve injury.
why_others_wrong.D: Facial sensation is supplied by the trigeminal nerve, which is not at risk during thyroid surgery.
why_others_wrong.E: Taste from the posterior third of the tongue is carried by the glossopharyngeal nerve, not the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

exam_trap: The cricothyroid is supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve.
takeaway: Thyroid surgery + recurrent laryngeal nerve injury → voice change from vocal-cord dysfunction.
source: Standard head-and-neck surgical anatomy.
thinking: Thyroid surgery ↓ recurrent laryngeal nerve at risk near the inferior thyroid artery ↓ supplies almost all intrinsic laryngeal muscles ↓ Vocal-cord dysfunction
pearl: Unilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury causes hoarseness and a weak cough, and if the paralysed cord rests away from the midline it may also cause aspiration.

subject: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care
title: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care: superior laryngeal nerve
stem: Following thyroid surgery, a professional singer notices difficulty producing high-pitched sounds but has relatively preserved ordinary speech. Which nerve injury is most likely?

options.B: External branch of superior laryngeal nerve

correct_answer: B. External branch of superior laryngeal nerve
why_correct: The external branch supplies the cricothyroid, which increases vocal-cord tension and is important for high-pitched phonation.

why_others_wrong.A: Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury paralyses most intrinsic laryngeal muscles, causing hoarseness or a weak breathy voice rather than isolated loss of high pitch.
why_others_wrong.C: The hypoglossal nerve supplies the tongue muscles, so injury causes tongue deviation and dysarthria rather than loss of vocal pitch.
why_others_wrong.D: The glossopharyngeal nerve supplies posterior tongue sensation and stylopharyngeus and does not control vocal-cord tension.
why_others_wrong.E: The phrenic nerve supplies the diaphragm, so injury causes hemidiaphragm paralysis and breathlessness rather than a pitch problem.

exam_trap: Candidates choose the recurrent laryngeal nerve as the classic thyroid surgery injury, but it causes hoarseness; isolated loss of high pitch indicates external superior laryngeal nerve injury.
takeaway: High-pitched voice problem after thyroid surgery → external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve.
source: Standard surgical anatomy.
thinking: Singer after thyroid surgery ↓ loss of high-pitched notes ↓ ordinary speech largely preserved ↓ cricothyroid tenses the vocal cords ↓ External branch of superior laryngeal nerve
pearl: The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve runs close to the superior thyroid vessels, so they are ligated close to the upper pole of the gland to protect it.

subject: Anatomy
title: ENT: thyroid blood supply
stem: The superior thyroid artery is usually a branch of which vessel?

options.E: Common carotid artery directly in every case

why_correct: The superior thyroid artery usually arises from the external carotid artery close to its origin.

why_others_wrong.B: The internal carotid artery gives off essentially no branches in the neck and does not supply the thyroid gland.
why_others_wrong.C: The subclavian artery gives rise to the inferior thyroid artery via the thyrocervical trunk, not the superior thyroid artery.
why_others_wrong.D: The vertebral artery supplies the posterior cerebral circulation and has no role in thyroid blood supply.
why_others_wrong.E: The superior thyroid artery arises from the external carotid artery (or occasionally near the carotid bifurcation), not consistently as a direct branch of the common carotid artery.

exam_trap: The inferior thyroid artery is associated with the thyrocervical trunk of the subclavian artery.
takeaway: Superior thyroid → external carotid.
source: Standard neck anatomy.
thinking: Superior thyroid artery ↓ first anterior branch of the external carotid ↓ arises just above the carotid bifurcation ↓ inferior thyroid arises from the thyrocervical trunk ↓ External carotid artery
pearl: Ligating the superior thyroid pedicle close to the upper pole protects the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, which runs with the artery.

subject: Anatomy
title: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care: thyroid embryology
stem: The thyroid descends embryologically from the foramen caecum towards its final position in the neck. Which structure represents the embryological tract of this descent?
why_correct: The thyroid begins at the foramen caecum and descends through the thyroglossal duct.

why_others_wrong.B: The vitelline duct connects the embryonic midgut to the yolk sac and its persistence causes a Meckel diverticulum, unrelated to thyroid descent.
why_others_wrong.C: The urachus connects the bladder to the allantois; its remnant is the median umbilical ligament, unrelated to thyroid embryology.
why_others_wrong.D: The omphalomesenteric artery accompanies the vitelline duct and relates to midgut, not thyroid, development.
why_others_wrong.E: The neural tube gives rise to the central nervous system and has no relation to thyroid descent.

exam_trap: The vitelline duct is a tempting embryological duct remnant, but it connects midgut to yolk sac; the thyroid descends through the thyroglossal duct from the foramen caecum.
takeaway: Thyroid descent → thyroglossal duct.
source: Standard embryology.
thinking: Thyroid starts at the foramen caecum ↓ descends anterior to the hyoid and larynx ↓ its path is an epithelial tract ↓ tract normally involutes ↓ Thyroglossal duct
pearl: Persistence of the lower end of the tract forms the pyramidal lobe, present in a significant proportion of people, and failure of descent results in a lingual thyroid at the tongue base.

subject: ENT: head & neck
title: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care: thyroglossal cyst
stem: A young adult has a painless midline neck swelling that moves upwards when they protrude their tongue. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Thyroglossal cysts are typically midline and characteristically move with swallowing or tongue protrusion because of their embryological relationship with the tongue base.

why_others_wrong.A: A branchial cyst is a lateral swelling at the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid, at the junction of its upper and middle thirds, and does not move with tongue protrusion.
why_others_wrong.C: A parotid tumour lies in front of or below the ear, not in the midline, and does not move with the tongue.
why_others_wrong.D: A carotid aneurysm is a lateral pulsatile swelling and has no attachment to the tongue base.
why_others_wrong.E: Lymphoma causes lymphadenopathy, which is usually lateral and does not rise with tongue protrusion.

exam_trap: Candidates choosing branchial cyst (option A) miss that a branchial cyst is lateral; only a thyroglossal cyst is midline and rises with tongue protrusion.
takeaway: Midline neck mass + moves with tongue protrusion → thyroglossal cyst.
source: Standard head-and-neck surgery.
thinking: Painless midline neck swelling ↓ rises on tongue protrusion ↓ attached to the thyroglossal tract from the foramen caecum ↓ Thyroglossal cyst
pearl: Thyroglossal cysts are excised together with the central part of the hyoid bone and the tract up towards the tongue base, because simple cyst excision has a high recurrence rate.

subject: Anatomy
title: Colorectal surgery: appendix
stem: Which artery is the principal arterial supply to the appendix?
why_correct: The appendicular artery usually arises from the ileocolic artery and travels in the mesoappendix.

why_others_wrong.A: The left colic artery is a branch of the inferior mesenteric artery supplying the descending colon, not the appendix.
why_others_wrong.C: The middle colic artery, a branch of the superior mesenteric artery, supplies the transverse colon, not the appendix.
why_others_wrong.D: The superior rectal artery is the terminal continuation of the IMA supplying the upper rectum, not the appendix.
why_others_wrong.E: The inferior mesenteric artery supplies hindgut derivatives (descending colon to upper rectum); the appendix is a midgut structure supplied via the ileocolic/SMA system, not the IMA.

exam_trap: The inferior mesenteric artery may tempt because of the appendix's low pelvic position, but the appendix is midgut, supplied by the appendicular branch of the ileocolic artery.
takeaway: Appendix → appendicular artery → ileocolic system.
source: Standard abdominal surgical anatomy.
thinking: Appendix is a midgut structure ↓ supplied via the SMA ↓ ileocolic artery gives the appendicular artery ↓ runs in the mesoappendix ↓ Appendicular artery
pearl: The appendicular artery is an end artery, so thrombosis in appendicitis leads to gangrene and perforation; at appendicectomy it is ligated within the mesoappendix.

subject: Anatomy
title: Colorectal surgery: appendix location
stem: McBurney point is located approximately between which anatomical landmarks?

options.A: Umbilicus and left anterior superior iliac spine
options.B: Umbilicus and right anterior superior iliac spine

correct_answer: B. Umbilicus and right anterior superior iliac spine
why_correct: McBurney point is classically described along the line between the umbilicus and right ASIS, approximately one-third of the distance from the ASIS.

why_others_wrong.A: The umbilicus to left ASIS describes the wrong side; the appendix and McBurney point are right-sided structures.
why_others_wrong.C: The xiphisternum-to-umbilicus line describes the midline epigastric axis, not the McBurney point, which lies laterally in the right iliac fossa.
why_others_wrong.D: Pubic symphysis to left ASIS is both the wrong side and the wrong pair of landmarks for McBurney's point.
why_others_wrong.E: Right costal margin to umbilicus describes a different abdominal reference line, not the umbilicus-to-right-ASIS line used for McBurney's point.

exam_trap: The exact position of the appendix is variable; McBurney point is a clinical surface landmark rather than an exact anatomical location.
takeaway: McBurney point lies one-third of the way along the line from the right anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus.
source: Standard surface anatomy.
thinking: Surface marking of the appendix base ↓ right iliac fossa ↓ line from the right ASIS to the umbilicus ↓ point one-third of the way from the ASIS ↓ Umbilicus and right anterior superior iliac spine
pearl: McBurney point approximates the base of the appendix, which is relatively constant where the taeniae coli converge on the caecum, whereas the tip position is variable (retrocaecal is commonest).

subject: Acute abdomen & GI surgery
title: Colorectal surgery: appendicitis pain
stem: Why may pain from early acute appendicitis initially be felt around the umbilicus before localising to the right iliac fossa?

options.A: Direct irritation of the sciatic nerve
options.B: Visceral afferent pain followed by parietal peritoneal irritation

correct_answer: B. Visceral afferent pain followed by parietal peritoneal irritation
why_correct: Early appendiceal inflammation produces poorly localised visceral pain. As inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum, pain becomes more localised.

why_others_wrong.A: The sciatic nerve supplies the posterior thigh and leg and has no role in the shift of appendiceal pain from the umbilicus to the right iliac fossa.
why_others_wrong.C: Renal nerves are not primarily involved; the periumbilical pain comes from midgut visceral afferents entering around the T10 segment.
why_others_wrong.D: Femoral nerve compression causes anterior thigh symptoms and does not explain the migration of pain that reflects visceral then parietal peritoneal involvement.
why_others_wrong.E: Obturator nerve paralysis would cause weakness of hip adduction, whereas a pelvic appendix may cause pain on the obturator test without paralysis.

exam_trap: Obturator nerve paralysis is tempting because the obturator sign is linked to appendicitis, but a pelvic appendix irritates obturator internus; it causes pain, not nerve paralysis.
takeaway: Visceral pain is poorly localised to the periumbilical region; parietal peritoneal irritation localises pain to the right iliac fossa.
source: Standard surgical physiology and anatomy.
thinking: Early appendicitis distends the viscus ↓ visceral afferents from midgut enter around T10 ↓ pain felt vaguely at the umbilicus ↓ inflammation reaches parietal peritoneum with somatic innervation ↓ Visceral afferent pain followed by parietal peritoneal irritation
pearl: Atypical appendix positions change the parietal signs: a retrocaecal appendix may cause flank pain and a positive psoas sign, while a pelvic appendix may cause suprapubic pain, urinary frequency or a positive obturator sign.

subject: Anatomy
title: Colorectal surgery: colon blood supply
stem: Which artery primarily supplies the descending colon?
why_correct: The inferior mesenteric artery gives rise to the left colic and sigmoid arteries supplying the descending and sigmoid colon.

why_others_wrong.A: The superior mesenteric artery supplies midgut derivatives (up to the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon), not the descending colon.
why_others_wrong.C: The coeliac trunk supplies foregut structures such as the stomach, liver and spleen, not the colon.
why_others_wrong.D: The internal iliac artery supplies pelvic viscera, not the descending colon.
why_others_wrong.E: The renal artery supplies the kidney and has no role in colonic blood supply.

exam_trap: Superior mesenteric artery is tempting because it supplies much of the colon, but its territory ends at the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon; the descending colon is hindgut supplied by the IMA.
takeaway: Descending colon → IMA territory.
source: Standard abdominal vascular anatomy.
thinking: Descending colon is hindgut ↓ hindgut supplied by the IMA ↓ via the left colic artery ↓ Inferior mesenteric artery
pearl: The IMA arises at about L3 and is divided in left-sided and rectal cancer resections; high ligation at its origin improves lymph node yield, relying on the marginal artery for colonic perfusion.

subject: Anatomy
title: Colorectal surgery: rectal blood supply
stem: Which artery is the principal continuation of the inferior mesenteric arterial supply to the rectum?
why_correct: The superior rectal artery is the terminal branch of the inferior mesenteric artery and supplies the upper rectum.

why_others_wrong.B: The inferior rectal artery arises from the internal pudendal artery and supplies the lower anal canal, not a continuation of the IMA.
why_others_wrong.C: The middle rectal artery arises from the internal iliac artery, not from the inferior mesenteric artery.
why_others_wrong.D: The obturator artery supplies the pelvic wall and medial thigh muscles, unrelated to rectal blood supply.
why_others_wrong.E: The internal pudendal artery supplies perineal structures (including branches to the lower anal canal) but is not itself the terminal continuation of the IMA.

exam_trap: Middle rectal artery may tempt because it also supplies the rectum, but it arises from the internal iliac; only the superior rectal artery continues the inferior mesenteric artery.
takeaway: IMA → superior rectal artery.
source: Standard pelvic vascular anatomy.
thinking: IMA terminal continuation ↓ crosses the left common iliac vessels ↓ becomes the superior rectal artery ↓ supplies the upper rectum ↓ Superior rectal artery
pearl: The rectum has a triple arterial supply (superior, middle and inferior rectal arteries), but in anterior resection the remaining rectal stump depends largely on the middle and inferior rectal vessels once the superior rectal is divided.

subject: Anatomy
title: Colorectal surgery: portal-systemic anastomosis
stem: Which venous territory contributes to the portal-systemic anastomosis at the rectum?

options.A: Superior rectal and middle/inferior rectal venous territories

correct_answer: A. Superior rectal and middle/inferior rectal venous territories
why_correct: The superior rectal vein drains into the portal system, while middle and inferior rectal veins drain into the systemic circulation.

why_others_wrong.B: The renal and gonadal veins are unrelated systemic veins and play no part in the rectal portosystemic anastomosis.
why_others_wrong.C: The femoral and popliteal veins drain the lower limb and are unrelated to the rectal venous plexus.
why_others_wrong.D: Hepatic and splenic arteries are arterial, not venous, structures and are not the basis of a portosystemic venous anastomosis.
why_others_wrong.E: The pulmonary veins drain the lungs into the left atrium and have no connection to the rectal venous plexus.

exam_trap: Hepatic and splenic arteries may tempt because they relate to the portal circulation, but they are arterial; portosystemic anastomoses are between portal and systemic veins.
takeaway: Rectum = portal + systemic venous connection.
source: Standard pelvic and portal-systemic anatomy.
thinking: Portosystemic anastomosis at the rectum ↓ superior rectal vein drains to the IMV and portal system ↓ middle and inferior rectal veins drain to systemic iliac veins ↓ they meet in the rectal venous plexus ↓ Superior rectal and middle/inferior rectal venous territories
pearl: Rectal varices from portal hypertension are distinct from haemorrhoids, which are vascular cushions, and portal hypertension does not increase the incidence of haemorrhoids.

subject: Anatomy
title: Colorectal surgery: colorectal cancer — lymphatic spread
stem: A tumour in the ascending colon most directly drains initially towards lymph nodes associated with which artery?
why_correct: The ascending colon is derived from the midgut and its lymphatic drainage follows the superior mesenteric vascular territory.

why_others_wrong.B: The inferior mesenteric artery supplies hindgut structures such as the descending and sigmoid colon, not the midgut-derived ascending colon.
why_others_wrong.C: The coeliac trunk supplies foregut structures, unrelated to the ascending colon's lymphatic territory.
why_others_wrong.D: The internal iliac artery supplies pelvic structures, not the ascending colon.
why_others_wrong.E: The inferior epigastric artery supplies the anterior abdominal wall and has no relation to colonic lymphatic drainage.

exam_trap: Inferior mesenteric artery may tempt because the IMA is linked with colorectal cancer, but the ascending colon is midgut and drains along SMA branches.
takeaway: Ascending colon → SMA lymphatic territory.
source: Standard colorectal anatomy.
thinking: Ascending colon is midgut ↓ lymph drains along its arteries ↓ ileocolic and right colic vessels ↓ which arise from the SMA ↓ Superior mesenteric artery
pearl: A right hemicolectomy for cancer removes the ileocolic and right colic vessels with their mesentery, ligated close to their origin from the SMA, to clear the draining lymph nodes.

subject: Anatomy
title: Hepatobiliary surgery: portal triad
stem: Which structures are contained within the hepatoduodenal ligament?

options.A: Portal vein, hepatic artery and bile duct
options.C: Splenic artery, pancreatic duct and portal vein
options.D: Cystic artery, renal artery and bile duct
options.E: Common iliac artery, portal vein and ureter

correct_answer: A. Portal vein, hepatic artery and bile duct
why_correct: The hepatoduodenal ligament contains the main components of the portal triad.

why_others_wrong.B: The hepatic veins, IVC and aorta lie posteriorly and drain/supply the liver from a different route; they are not contents of the hepatoduodenal ligament.
why_others_wrong.C: The splenic artery and pancreatic duct lie within the pancreas and splenorenal ligament region, not within the hepatoduodenal ligament.
why_others_wrong.D: The renal artery is a retroperitoneal branch of the aorta that never enters the hepatoduodenal ligament, so this combination is not the portal triad.
why_others_wrong.E: The common iliac artery and ureter are pelvic/retroperitoneal structures with no relation to the hepatoduodenal ligament.

exam_trap: Hepatic veins, IVC and aorta may tempt as major liver vessels, but the hepatic veins drain directly into the IVC behind the liver and none lie in the hepatoduodenal ligament.
takeaway: Portal triad = bile duct + hepatic artery + portal vein.
source: Standard hepatobiliary anatomy.
thinking: Hepatoduodenal ligament is the free edge of the lesser omentum ↓ it forms the anterior wall of the epiploic foramen ↓ contains common bile duct, hepatic artery and portal vein ↓ Portal vein, hepatic artery and bile duct
pearl: Within the hepatoduodenal ligament the bile duct lies to the right, the hepatic artery to the left and the portal vein posterior to both, which guides dissection in cholecystectomy and liver surgery.

subject: Hepatobiliary surgery
title: Hepatobiliary surgery: pringle manoeuvre
stem: What is temporarily compressed during the Pringle manoeuvre?
why_correct: Compression of the hepatoduodenal ligament occludes inflow through the hepatic artery and portal vein.

why_others_wrong.B: The splenorenal ligament carries the splenic vessels and pancreatic tail and is divided when mobilising the spleen, not compressed to control liver inflow.
