exam_trap: Candidates choose a vascular network because fibrocartilage seems tougher, but both cartilage types are largely avascular; the distinguishing feature is abundant type I collagen.
takeaway: Fibrocartilage → type I collagen + tensile strength.
source: Gray's Basic Anatomy, 3rd ed.; RCS England MRCS preparation resources. Accessed September 2026.
thinking: Compare fibrocartilage with hyaline cartilage ↓ both are avascular and lack a basement membrane ↓ hyaline matrix is predominantly type II collagen ↓ fibrocartilage adds dense type I collagen bundles ↓ Abundant type I collagen bundles
pearl: Microfracture of an articular cartilage defect produces repair tissue that is predominantly fibrocartilage, which is mechanically inferior to native hyaline cartilage and wears less well.

subject: Anatomy
title: Histology: Bone
stem: Which cell is primarily responsible for producing osteoid?
why_correct: Osteoblasts synthesise osteoid, the organic component of bone matrix, which subsequently undergoes mineralisation.

why_others_wrong.A: Osteoclasts are multinucleate cells of monocyte lineage that resorb bone rather than lay down osteoid.
why_others_wrong.C: Osteocytes are mature osteoblasts trapped in lacunae that maintain and sense bone but produce little new osteoid.
why_others_wrong.D: Chondroblasts produce cartilage matrix containing type II collagen, not osteoid.
why_others_wrong.E: Fibrocytes are inactive fibroblasts in connective tissue and do not form bone matrix.

exam_trap: Osteocyte may tempt as the main bone cell, but osteocytes are trapped osteoblasts that maintain bone; active osteoid production is by osteoblasts, while osteoclasts resorb bone.
takeaway: Osteoblast → osteoid formation. Osteoclast → bone resorption.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.; RCS-listed MRCS preparation resource. Accessed September 2026.
thinking: Osteoid is unmineralised bone matrix ↓ laid down by bone-forming cells ↓ later mineralised ↓ Osteoblast
pearl: In osteomalacia, osteoid is produced normally but fails to mineralise because of vitamin D deficiency, leaving excess unmineralised osteoid on bone surfaces.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Physiology: Venous Return
stem: Which change would generally increase venous return to the right atrium?

options.E: Increased intrathoracic pressure during positive-pressure ventilation

why_correct: Contraction of skeletal muscles compresses veins and promotes venous blood movement towards the heart, particularly in the lower limbs. Venous valves help maintain directional flow.

why_others_wrong.A: Reduced blood volume lowers the filling pressure of the venous system and so would reduce, not increase, venous return.
why_others_wrong.B: Increased venous capacitance allows more blood to pool in the veins, reducing the pressure gradient driving blood back to the heart and so reducing venous return.
why_others_wrong.D: Severe venodilation similarly increases venous pooling and capacitance, lowering the pressure gradient for venous return rather than raising it.
why_others_wrong.E: Positive-pressure ventilation raises intrathoracic and right atrial pressure, which opposes the pressure gradient from peripheral veins to the right atrium and reduces venous return.

exam_trap: Positive-pressure ventilation is chosen because it involves increased thoracic pressure, but raised intrathoracic pressure impedes, rather than aids, venous return.
takeaway: Skeletal-muscle pump → venous return ↑.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.; RCS England lists this among MRCS preparation resources. Accessed September 2026.
thinking: Venous return depends on the gradient from peripheral veins to the right atrium ↓ skeletal muscle contraction squeezes deep veins ↓ venous valves keep flow towards the heart ↓ Skeletal-muscle pump activity
pearl: Immobility after surgery removes the calf muscle pump, contributing to venous stasis and deep vein thrombosis, which is why early mobilisation and mechanical prophylaxis are used.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Physiology: Afterload
stem: For the left ventricle, which factor most directly represents an increase in afterload?
why_correct: Afterload represents the load against which the ventricle must eject blood. For the left ventricle, increased aortic pressure/systemic vascular resistance increases the load against which it contracts.

why_others_wrong.A: Reduced systemic vascular resistance lowers the resistance the left ventricle ejects against, decreasing afterload rather than increasing it.
why_others_wrong.C: Increased venous return raises ventricular filling and therefore preload, not the resistance to ejection that defines afterload.
why_others_wrong.D: An isolated rise in end-diastolic volume reflects greater filling (preload), not the load faced during ejection.
why_others_wrong.E: Reduced arterial pressure would lower, not raise, the resistance the left ventricle must overcome during ejection.

exam_trap: Increased venous return and end-diastolic volume tempt because they alter output, but both reflect filling and therefore preload, not afterload.
takeaway: LV afterload → think arterial pressure/systemic vascular resistance.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.; RCS-listed MRCS preparation resource. Accessed September 2026.
thinking: Afterload = load opposing left ventricular ejection ↓ the ventricle ejects against aortic pressure ↓ higher aortic pressure means higher afterload ↓ Increased aortic pressure
pearl: Aortic stenosis raises the pressure the left ventricle must generate even when systemic arterial pressure is normal, so it imposes a fixed afterload upstream of the aorta.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Physiology: Preload
stem: Which variable most closely reflects left ventricular preload immediately before ventricular contraction?
why_correct: Preload reflects myocardial fibre stretch at the end of diastole. Clinically, ventricular end-diastolic volume is commonly used as a useful representation of preload.

why_others_wrong.B: End-systolic volume is the volume remaining after ejection is complete, reflecting emptying rather than the filling that determines preload.
why_others_wrong.C: Systemic vascular resistance is a determinant of afterload (the resistance to ejection), not of ventricular filling before contraction.
why_others_wrong.D: Mean arterial pressure reflects the pressure the ventricle must eject against (afterload-related), not the degree of diastolic filling.
why_others_wrong.E: Ejection fraction measures the proportion of end-diastolic volume ejected during systole, a marker of systolic performance rather than preload itself.

exam_trap: End-systolic volume is chosen because it is also a ventricular volume, but it is measured after ejection and reflects emptying, not preload.
takeaway: Preload → ventricular filling/stretch before contraction.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.; RCS-listed MRCS resource. Accessed September 2026.
thinking: Preload = fibre stretch just before contraction ↓ stretch is set by end-diastolic filling ↓ end-diastolic volume reflects this best ↓ End-diastolic volume
pearl: Ejection fraction is stroke volume divided by end-diastolic volume, so it describes systolic performance and can be normal despite a small, underfilled ventricle.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Physiology: Frank–Starling Mechanism
stem: Within physiological limits, an increase in ventricular filling generally produces which immediate effect?
why_correct: The Frank–Starling mechanism describes the increase in force of ventricular contraction produced by increased myocardial fibre stretch within physiological limits.

why_others_wrong.A: This is the opposite of the Frank–Starling relationship, in which greater filling produces a stronger, not weaker, contraction.
why_others_wrong.C: Increased filling within physiological limits enhances contraction; it does not abolish it.
why_others_wrong.D: The premise is increased ventricular filling, which stretches myocardial fibres further, not reduces the degree of stretch.
why_others_wrong.E: Increased filling by definition raises end-diastolic volume; it does not reduce it.

exam_trap: This is an intrinsic property of cardiac muscle and is not the same as sympathetic stimulation.
takeaway: More filling → greater stretch → stronger contraction.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.; RCS-listed MRCS resource. Accessed September 2026.
thinking: Increased ventricular filling ↓ greater sarcomere stretch improves actin-myosin overlap and calcium sensitivity ↓ force of contraction rises ↓ Increased force of contraction
pearl: The Frank-Starling mechanism keeps right and left ventricular outputs matched beat to beat, preventing blood accumulating in either circulation.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Physiology: Systemic Vascular Resistance
stem: Which vascular bed contributes most substantially to systemic vascular resistance?
why_correct: Arterioles are major resistance vessels. Their smooth-muscle tone can substantially alter vascular resistance and therefore influence arterial pressure and tissue blood flow.

why_others_wrong.B: Large veins are highly compliant, low-resistance capacitance vessels; they store blood rather than generating substantial resistance.
why_others_wrong.C: Capillaries have an enormous total cross-sectional area, giving each vessel very low individual resistance and only a small contribution to total systemic resistance.
why_others_wrong.D: Large arteries are wide, low-resistance conduit vessels that mainly transmit pulsatile flow rather than regulate resistance.
why_others_wrong.E: Venules, like veins generally, are low-resistance vessels involved in collecting blood rather than generating systemic vascular resistance.

exam_trap: Capillaries are chosen because they are the narrowest vessels, but their enormous total cross-sectional area in parallel keeps their combined resistance low.
takeaway: Arterioles = major resistance vessels.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.; RCS-listed MRCS preparation resource. Accessed September 2026.
thinking: Systemic vascular resistance asked ↓ resistance rises steeply as radius falls ↓ arterioles have thick smooth muscle and narrow lumens ↓ Arterioles
pearl: The largest pressure drop in the systemic circulation occurs across the arterioles, which is where local metabolic and sympathetic control of flow is exerted.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Respiratory Physiology: Surfactant
stem: What is the principal physiological effect of pulmonary surfactant?
why_correct: Pulmonary surfactant reduces surface tension at the air-liquid interface within alveoli, improving alveolar stability and reducing the work required to inflate the lungs.

why_others_wrong.A: Surfactant lowers, rather than raises, surface tension at the alveolar air-liquid interface.
why_others_wrong.C: Surfactant acts on surface tension at the alveolar lining, not as a barrier to gas diffusion across the membrane.
why_others_wrong.D: Surfactant helps keep alveoli and small airways open, so if anything it lowers rather than raises airway resistance.
why_others_wrong.E: Surfactant affects alveolar surface tension, not pleural pressure, which is governed by the balance of chest wall and lung recoil forces.

exam_trap: Surfactant is protective against alveolar collapse; it does not increase surface tension.
takeaway: Surfactant → surface tension ↓ → alveolar stability ↑.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.; RCS-listed MRCS preparation resource. Accessed September 2026.
thinking: Surfactant lines the alveolar air-liquid interface ↓ it reduces surface tension ↓ small alveoli stay open and compliance increases ↓ Reduces alveolar surface tension
pearl: Antenatal corticosteroids are given before preterm delivery to accelerate surfactant production and reduce neonatal respiratory distress syndrome.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Respiratory Physiology: Dead Space
stem: Which situation would most directly increase physiological dead space?

options.A: Complete airway obstruction with no ventilation
options.B: Ventilated alveoli with markedly reduced pulmonary perfusion
options.C: Increased pulmonary blood flow to normally ventilated alveoli

correct_answer: B. Ventilated alveoli with markedly reduced pulmonary perfusion
why_correct: Dead space represents ventilation that does not participate effectively in gas exchange. Ventilated alveoli with little or no perfusion contribute to alveolar dead space.

why_others_wrong.A: A completely unventilated alveolus that is still perfused represents shunt (perfusion without effective ventilation), the opposite pattern to dead space.
why_others_wrong.C: Increased blood flow to already well-ventilated alveoli improves ventilation-perfusion matching rather than creating dead space.
why_others_wrong.D: Reduced anatomical airway length would shorten, not lengthen, the conducting airway component of dead space.
why_others_wrong.E: Increased alveolar perfusion improves matching with ventilation and so reduces, rather than increases, the dead-space effect.

exam_trap: Complete airway obstruction is chosen because gas exchange fails, but a perfused unventilated alveolus represents shunt, the opposite of dead space.
takeaway: Ventilation without effective perfusion → dead space.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.; RCS-listed MRCS preparation resource. Accessed September 2026.
thinking: Physiological dead space = ventilation not taking part in gas exchange ↓ need ventilated alveoli with poor perfusion ↓ option B describes exactly this ↓ Ventilated alveoli with markedly reduced pulmonary perfusion
pearl: Low cardiac output and high airway pressures during positive-pressure ventilation both reduce perfusion of ventilated alveoli and therefore increase alveolar dead space.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Physiology: Oxygen Content
stem: Which component contributes most to the oxygen content of arterial blood under normal circumstances?
why_correct: Most oxygen in arterial blood is carried bound to haemoglobin. Only a small proportion is dissolved in plasma.

why_others_wrong.A: Oxygen dissolved in plasma contributes only a small fraction of total arterial oxygen content compared with haemoglobin-bound oxygen.
why_others_wrong.C: Bicarbonate is the principal transport form for carbon dioxide, not a carrier of oxygen.
why_others_wrong.D: Carbon dioxide bound to protein relates to CO2 transport, not to the oxygen content of arterial blood, and albumin is not a major CO2 carrier either (that role belongs mainly to haemoglobin and bicarbonate).
why_others_wrong.E: Plasma sodium is an electrolyte with no role in carrying oxygen in the blood.

exam_trap: A normal PaO₂ does not necessarily guarantee normal oxygen content if haemoglobin concentration is severely reduced.
takeaway: Arterial oxygen content is dominated by haemoglobin-bound oxygen.
thinking: Arterial oxygen content components ↓ Hb-bound O2 is about 1.34 mL per gram at full saturation ↓ dissolved O2 is only about 0.03 mL per litre per mmHg ↓ Oxygen bound to haemoglobin
pearl: Hyperbaric oxygen therapy works by greatly increasing dissolved oxygen, because once haemoglobin is fully saturated, extra inspired oxygen at normal pressure adds very little to content.

subject: Physiology
title: Renal Physiology: Glomerular Filtration
stem: Which Starling force normally favours filtration of fluid from glomerular capillaries into Bowman's space?

options.D: Bowman's space oncotic pressure of equal magnitude

why_correct: The relatively high hydrostatic pressure within glomerular capillaries drives filtration into Bowman's space.

why_others_wrong.A: Bowman's space hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid back toward the capillary, opposing filtration rather than favouring it.
why_others_wrong.B: Plasma oncotic pressure draws fluid back into the capillary, opposing filtration rather than promoting it.
why_others_wrong.D: Bowman's space is normally virtually protein-free, so its oncotic pressure is negligible, not equal in magnitude to plasma oncotic pressure.
why_others_wrong.E: Renal venous pressure is not one of the Starling forces acting directly across the glomerular capillary wall.

exam_trap: Candidates choosing A or B pick forces that oppose filtration; only glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure drives fluid into Bowman's space, and Bowman's oncotic pressure is negligible.
takeaway: Glomerular filtration is driven principally by high glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.; RCS-listed MRCS preparation resource. Accessed September 2026.
thinking: Starling forces at the glomerulus ↓ capillary hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid out ↓ plasma oncotic and Bowman's space hydrostatic pressures oppose filtration ↓ Bowman's space oncotic pressure is negligible ↓ Glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure
pearl: Angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole to maintain glomerular hydrostatic pressure when perfusion falls, which is why ACE inhibitors and ARBs can precipitate acute kidney injury in hypovolaemia.

subject: Physiology
title: Renal Physiology: Potassium Secretion
stem: Which nephron region is particularly important for regulated potassium secretion?
correct_answer: C. Distal nephron and collecting duct
why_correct: Potassium balance is regulated substantially by secretion from principal cells in the distal nephron and collecting duct. Aldosterone promotes potassium secretion in this region.

why_others_wrong.A: The glomerulus is the site of filtration only and has no tubular secretory function for potassium.
why_others_wrong.B: The proximal tubule reabsorbs most filtered potassium passively but is not the site of regulated secretion.
why_others_wrong.D: The thin descending limb is not a site of regulated potassium secretion; aldosterone-responsive secretion occurs in principal cells of the distal nephron.
why_others_wrong.E: Bowman's capsule is a filtration structure and has no secretory function.

exam_trap: Candidates choosing the proximal tubule (B) recall that most filtered potassium is reabsorbed there, but the regulated secretion that sets potassium balance occurs in distal principal cells.
takeaway: Final potassium regulation → distal nephron/collecting duct.
thinking: Regulated potassium secretion ↓ principal cells of the distal nephron and collecting duct ↓ aldosterone increases ENaC and ROMK activity ↓ higher distal flow also increases secretion ↓ Distal nephron and collecting duct
pearl: Potassium-sparing diuretics and ACE inhibitors both reduce distal potassium secretion, so hyperkalaemia is a recognised risk when they are combined, particularly with renal impairment.

subject: Physiology
title: Renal Physiology: Urea
stem: Which process contributes to the renal medullary concentration gradient by allowing urea to accumulate in the inner medulla?

options.C: Urea synthesis in the collecting duct

why_correct: Urea recycling contributes to the high osmolality of the inner renal medulla. This supports water reabsorption and the kidney's ability to concentrate urine.

why_others_wrong.B: Urea is in fact recycled and partially reabsorbed, especially in the inner medullary collecting duct; complete absence of reabsorption would prevent the accumulation described.
why_others_wrong.C: Urea is produced by the hepatic urea cycle, not synthesised within the collecting duct.
why_others_wrong.D: Glomerular destruction is a pathological process unrelated to the physiological urea-recycling mechanism.
why_others_wrong.E: Sodium is filtered rather than secreted into Bowman's space, and this has no bearing on urea recycling.

exam_trap: Urea is not simply a waste product that is completely eliminated on its first passage through the nephron.
takeaway: Urea recycling helps build the medullary osmotic gradient.
thinking: Inner medullary osmolality ↓ ADH increases urea permeability of the inner medullary collecting duct ↓ urea enters the interstitium and recycles into the loop ↓ adds to the gradient generated by NaCl transport ↓ Urea recycling
pearl: Protein-malnourished patients generate less urea and have reduced maximal urinary concentrating ability, illustrating how much urea contributes to the medullary gradient.

subject: Physiology
title: Endocrinology: Calcium Regulation
stem: Which hormone is released by thyroid parafollicular C cells?
why_correct: Thyroid parafollicular C cells secrete calcitonin. Calcitonin generally acts to reduce plasma calcium, although its physiological importance in adult calcium homeostasis is limited compared with PTH and vitamin D.

why_others_wrong.B: Parathyroid hormone is released by the parathyroid glands, not thyroid C cells, and it raises rather than lowers plasma calcium.
why_others_wrong.C: Aldosterone is an adrenal cortex mineralocorticoid with no role in calcium regulation.
why_others_wrong.D: Cortisol is an adrenal glucocorticoid unrelated to calcium homeostasis via C cells.
why_others_wrong.E: Calcitriol is the active form of vitamin D produced via renal (and hepatic) hydroxylation, not a secretion of thyroid C cells.

exam_trap: Candidates choosing parathyroid hormone (B) confuse thyroid C cells with parathyroid chief cells; PTH raises calcium, whereas C-cell calcitonin tends to lower it.
takeaway: C cells → calcitonin.
thinking: Parafollicular C cells of the thyroid ↓ derived from the neural crest ↓ secrete calcitonin in response to high calcium ↓ PTH comes from parathyroid chief cells ↓ Calcitonin
pearl: Medullary thyroid carcinoma arises from C cells, so calcitonin is its tumour marker; it may be familial with RET mutations as part of MEN 2.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: Endocrinology: Insulin Secretion
stem: Which pancreatic cell type secretes insulin?
why_correct: Pancreatic β-cells within the islets of Langerhans produce insulin.

why_others_wrong.A: Alpha cells in the islets secrete glucagon, which raises blood glucose and opposes insulin.
why_others_wrong.C: Delta cells secrete somatostatin, which inhibits both insulin and glucagon release.
why_others_wrong.D: PP cells secrete pancreatic polypeptide, which regulates pancreatic exocrine secretion and appetite, not insulin.
why_others_wrong.E: Acinar cells form the exocrine pancreas and secrete digestive enzymes rather than insulin.

exam_trap: Alpha cells (option A) are a common slip because they are also islet cells, but they secrete glucagon; insulin comes from the beta cells.
takeaway: Beta → insulin. Alpha → glucagon. Delta → somatostatin.
thinking: Insulin is an endocrine hormone ↓ made in the islets of Langerhans ↓ by the islet beta cells ↓ Beta cell
pearl: Insulinoma presents with fasting hypoglycaemia and inappropriately high insulin and C-peptide; most are benign and solitary, so enucleation is often curative.

subject: Pharmacology
title: Pharmacology: Receptor Efficacy
stem: A partial agonist is administered in the presence of a full agonist acting at the same receptor. What can happen?

options.A: The partial agonist may reduce the overall response
options.B: The partial agonist must always increase the maximal response
options.C: The partial agonist has no receptor affinity
options.D: The partial agonist irreversibly destroys the receptor
options.E: The partial agonist cannot bind to the same receptor

correct_answer: A. The partial agonist may reduce the overall response
why_correct: A partial agonist has receptor affinity but produces a lower maximal response than a full agonist. In the presence of a full agonist, it can compete for receptor occupancy and thereby reduce the overall response.

why_others_wrong.B: A partial agonist has lower intrinsic efficacy than a full agonist, so when it occupies receptors in the presence of a full agonist it tends to reduce, not increase, the maximal response achievable.
why_others_wrong.C: A partial agonist does bind the receptor with affinity; its defining feature is producing a submaximal response despite that binding, not an absence of affinity.
why_others_wrong.D: Partial agonists act via reversible receptor binding and typical receptor pharmacology; they do not irreversibly destroy receptors, unlike some irreversible antagonists.
why_others_wrong.E: A partial agonist binds the same receptor as the full agonist (that is what allows it to compete for occupancy); it is not excluded from that receptor.

exam_trap: 'The partial agonist must always increase the maximal response' tempts candidates who think adding any agonist adds effect, but a partial agonist displacing a full agonist lowers the overall response.
takeaway: Partial agonist alone = agonist; in presence of full agonist = can behave functionally as an antagonist.
thinking: Partial agonist has receptor affinity but lower intrinsic efficacy ↓ in the presence of a full agonist it competes for the same receptors ↓ receptors occupied by the partial agonist give a smaller response ↓ The partial agonist may reduce the overall response
pearl: Buprenorphine is a partial mu-opioid agonist with high receptor affinity, so it can blunt the effect of full agonists such as morphine and can precipitate withdrawal in opioid-dependent patients.

subject: Pharmacology
title: Pharmacology: Irreversible Antagonism
stem: Which finding best characterises an irreversible antagonist?

options.A: Its effect can always be overcome by increasing agonist concentration
options.B: It permanently or very persistently reduces receptor availability
options.E: It acts only by increasing drug clearance

correct_answer: B. It permanently or very persistently reduces receptor availability
why_correct: An irreversible antagonist, commonly through covalent receptor binding, reduces the number of receptors available to the agonist. Increasing agonist concentration may not restore the original maximum response.

why_others_wrong.A: Overcoming antagonism by raising agonist concentration is characteristic of reversible competitive antagonism, not irreversible antagonism, where the maximal response may not be restored.
why_others_wrong.C: An irreversible antagonist reduces available functional receptors and thus tends to reduce achievable response, rather than increasing agonist potency.
why_others_wrong.D: An irreversible antagonist does have receptor affinity (often forming a covalent bond); the defining feature is the persistence of binding, not an absence of affinity.
why_others_wrong.E: Irreversible antagonism acts directly at the receptor level, reducing receptor availability, rather than acting through altered drug clearance.

exam_trap: 'Its effect can always be overcome by increasing agonist concentration' is chosen by candidates who confuse antagonist types, but surmountability defines reversible competitive antagonism, not irreversible antagonism.
takeaway: Irreversible antagonist → receptor availability ↓ → maximal response may fall.
thinking: Irreversible antagonist typically binds covalently ↓ receptors are effectively removed until new ones are made ↓ adding more agonist cannot reclaim those receptors ↓ It permanently or very persistently reduces receptor availability
pearl: Phenoxybenzamine, an irreversible alpha-blocker, is used preoperatively in phaeochromocytoma; its effect persists until new receptors are synthesised, which can contribute to postoperative hypotension after tumour removal.

subject: Pharmacology
title: Pharmacology: Therapeutic Index
stem: Which statement best describes the therapeutic index?

options.A: Ratio relating toxic and effective doses
options.C: Fraction of drug bound to albumin
options.E: Time required to reach steady state

correct_answer: A. Ratio relating toxic and effective doses
why_correct: The therapeutic index provides an indication of the margin between doses producing desired and toxic effects. A narrow therapeutic index indicates a relatively small margin between effective and toxic exposure.

why_others_wrong.B: Percentage of orally absorbed drug describes bioavailability, not therapeutic index.
why_others_wrong.C: Fraction of drug bound to albumin describes plasma protein binding, a separate pharmacokinetic property from therapeutic index.
why_others_wrong.D: Rate of renal drug excretion relates to clearance, not to the margin between effective and toxic doses described by therapeutic index.
why_others_wrong.E: Time required to reach steady state is governed by half-life, not by the ratio between toxic and effective doses that defines therapeutic index.

exam_trap: Time required to reach steady state is tempting for candidates who confuse pharmacokinetic terms, but that depends on half-life; therapeutic index compares toxic and effective doses.
takeaway: Therapeutic index compares toxic and effective doses; a narrow therapeutic index means a small margin between benefit and toxicity.
thinking: Therapeutic index defined ↓ compares the dose producing toxicity with the dose producing the desired effect ↓ a ratio, classically TD50 divided by ED50 ↓ Ratio relating toxic and effective doses
pearl: A drug's therapeutic index does not tell you about individual susceptibility; renal impairment, interactions or hypoalbuminaemia can push a patient into toxicity even with standard doses of a narrow-index drug.

subject: Pharmacology
title: Pharmacology: Pharmacodynamic Tolerance
stem: A patient requires progressively higher doses of a drug to achieve the same effect. What phenomenon is being described?
why_correct: Tolerance refers to a reduced response to a drug after repeated exposure, resulting in the need for a higher dose to produce a similar effect.

why_others_wrong.A: Potentiation describes one drug enhancing the effect of another when combined, not a reduced response to the same drug over time.
why_others_wrong.C: An idiosyncratic reaction is an unpredictable, often genetically determined abnormal response to a drug, not a dose-related reduction in effect with repeated use.
why_others_wrong.D: First-pass metabolism refers to hepatic drug breakdown after oral absorption and does not describe a need for escalating doses over time.
why_others_wrong.E: Bioavailability refers to the fraction of an administered dose reaching systemic circulation, not to a diminishing response with repeated dosing.

exam_trap: Potentiation may be chosen because it also concerns altered drug effect, but it means one drug enhancing another; a falling response to the same drug over time is tolerance.
takeaway: Same drug → progressively less effect → tolerance.
thinking: Same drug given repeatedly ↓ progressively higher doses needed for the same effect ↓ reduced response after repeated exposure ↓ Tolerance
pearl: Tolerance is distinct from dependence and addiction; patients on long-term opioids before surgery often need higher postoperative doses and early specialist pain team input.

subject: Microbiology & surgical infection
title: Microbiology: Gram Staining
stem: Which component primarily determines the ability of bacteria to retain crystal violet during Gram staining?

options.A: Thickness and structure of the peptidoglycan layer

correct_answer: A. Thickness and structure of the peptidoglycan layer
why_correct: Gram-positive bacteria have a thick peptidoglycan cell wall that retains the crystal-violet/iodine complex during the decolourisation step. Gram-negative bacteria have a thinner peptidoglycan layer and an outer membrane.

why_others_wrong.B: Bacteria are prokaryotes and lack a nucleus, so a eukaryotic nucleus plays no part in Gram staining.
why_others_wrong.C: Bacteria do not have mitochondria; Gram stain retention depends on the cell envelope.
why_others_wrong.D: Viral capsids are not stained by the Gram method and are irrelevant to bacterial crystal violet retention.
why_others_wrong.E: Ergosterol is a fungal membrane sterol and has no role in the bacterial Gram reaction.

exam_trap: Candidates who drift to eukaryotic or fungal structures miss that Gram staining depends on the bacterial cell envelope; thick peptidoglycan retains crystal violet after decolourisation.
takeaway: Gram-positive → thick peptidoglycan.
thinking: Crystal violet-iodine complex forms in the cell wall ↓ alcohol or acetone decolourisation follows ↓ thick peptidoglycan retains the dye; thin layer plus outer membrane loses it ↓ Thickness and structure of the peptidoglycan layer
pearl: Mycobacteria stain poorly with the Gram method because of their mycolic acid-rich wall and are identified with acid-fast stains instead.

subject: Microbiology & surgical infection
title: Microbiology: Gram-Negative Outer Membrane
stem: Which component is characteristic of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria?

options.B: Teichoic acid as the defining outer-membrane component

why_correct: Gram-negative bacteria possess an outer membrane containing lipopolysaccharide (LPS). Lipid A is responsible for the endotoxin activity of LPS.

why_others_wrong.B: Teichoic acids are found in the thick peptidoglycan wall of Gram-positive bacteria, which have no outer membrane.
why_others_wrong.C: Chitin is a structural polysaccharide of fungal cell walls and arthropod exoskeletons, not a bacterial component.
why_others_wrong.D: Ergosterol is the principal sterol of fungal cell membranes; bacterial membranes generally lack sterols.
why_others_wrong.E: Cellulose is the main structural polymer of plant cell walls and is not a component of the Gram-negative outer membrane.

exam_trap: Teichoic acid is the trap, but it is a Gram-positive cell-wall component; Gram-positive bacteria have no outer membrane, whereas the Gram-negative outer membrane contains LPS.
takeaway: Gram-negative outer membrane → LPS.
thinking: Gram-negative envelope ↓ thin peptidoglycan plus an outer membrane ↓ outer leaflet of the membrane contains lipopolysaccharide ↓ Lipopolysaccharide
pearl: The outer membrane acts as a permeability barrier, which is why Gram-negative organisms are intrinsically resistant to large molecules such as vancomycin.

subject: Microbiology & surgical infection
title: Microbiology: Fungi
stem: Which structural component is characteristic of the fungal cell wall?
why_correct: Fungal cell walls contain chitin and other polysaccharides. Fungal cell membranes contain ergosterol.

why_others_wrong.A: Peptidoglycan is the characteristic cell-wall polymer of bacteria and is absent from fungal cell walls.
why_others_wrong.C: Lipopolysaccharide is a component of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria, not of fungi.
why_others_wrong.D: Mycolic acids are long-chain fatty acids characteristic of mycobacterial cell walls, not a fungal wall component.
why_others_wrong.E: Keratin is a structural protein of human skin, hair and nails that dermatophytes digest, not a component of the fungal wall.

exam_trap: Peptidoglycan is chosen by candidates thinking of cell walls generally, but it is bacterial; fungal walls are built from chitin and glucans, with ergosterol in the membrane.
takeaway: Fungal wall → chitin. Fungal membrane → ergosterol.
thinking: Fungal cell wall ↓ built from polysaccharides including chitin and glucans ↓ peptidoglycan is bacterial; ergosterol sits in the fungal membrane ↓ Chitin
pearl: Echinocandins such as caspofungin inhibit fungal cell-wall glucan synthesis, whereas azoles and amphotericin act on membrane ergosterol.

subject: Microbiology & surgical infection
title: Microbiology: Viruses
stem: Which structure is present in all viruses?
why_correct: Viruses contain genetic material enclosed within a protein capsid. Some viruses also possess a lipid envelope, but not all do.

why_others_wrong.A: A lipid envelope, derived from host membranes, is present in only some viruses; non-enveloped viruses such as norovirus lack one.
why_others_wrong.C: Peptidoglycan cell walls are a bacterial feature; viruses are acellular and have no cell wall.
why_others_wrong.D: Viruses have no organelles such as mitochondria and rely on host-cell metabolism for energy.
why_others_wrong.E: Viruses lack their own ribosomes and use host-cell ribosomes to translate viral proteins.

exam_trap: Lipid envelope is the tempting option, but only some viruses are enveloped; non-enveloped viruses such as norovirus lack it, whereas every virus has a protein capsid.
takeaway: All viruses → nucleic acid + protein capsid. Envelope → only some viruses.
thinking: Virus = nucleic acid genome in a protein coat ↓ the capsid is present in every virus ↓ a lipid envelope is present only in some ↓ Protein capsid
pearl: Non-enveloped viruses such as norovirus are more resistant to alcohol hand rub than enveloped viruses, so soap-and-water handwashing is preferred during outbreaks.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Surgical Science: Wound Oxygenation
stem: Which factor is most likely to impair wound healing by reducing tissue oxygen delivery?
why_correct: Oxygen delivery depends on cardiac output, haemoglobin concentration and arterial oxygen content. Severe anaemia can therefore reduce oxygen delivery even when measured oxygen saturation is normal.

why_others_wrong.A: Adequate tissue perfusion supports, rather than impairs, oxygen delivery to a healing wound, so it would not be the factor that reduces oxygenation.
why_others_wrong.C: A normal oxygen saturation reflects the proportion of available haemoglobin that is oxygenated; it does not by itself impair oxygen delivery and can even coexist with reduced total oxygen delivery if haemoglobin is very low.
why_others_wrong.D: A good local vascular supply promotes oxygen delivery to tissue and would support, not impair, wound healing.
why_others_wrong.E: Adequate nutritional intake supports the substrates needed for healing (such as protein and vitamin C) but does not itself determine tissue oxygen delivery.

exam_trap: Oxygen saturation measures the proportion of haemoglobin saturated, not the total amount of haemoglobin available to carry oxygen.
takeaway: Normal SpO₂ does not exclude impaired oxygen delivery when haemoglobin is very low.
thinking: Wound oxygen delivery ↓ depends on cardiac output, haemoglobin and saturation ↓ severe anaemia lowers oxygen content ↓ Severe anaemia
pearl: Pre-operative anaemia should be identified and treated before elective surgery, for example with iron for iron deficiency, because it reduces tissue oxygen delivery and is associated with worse post-operative outcomes.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Surgical Science: Wound Tensile Strength
stem: After a surgical wound has healed, which statement about its tensile strength is most accurate?

options.A: It immediately returns to 100% of normal tissue strength
options.B: It never develops any tensile strength
options.C: Tensile strength gradually increases during remodelling but remains below that of uninjured tissue
options.D: Tensile strength is determined entirely by the first 24 hours
options.E: Tensile strength depends only on wound length

correct_answer: C. Tensile strength gradually increases during remodelling but remains below that of uninjured tissue
why_correct: Healing tissue progressively gains strength as collagen is deposited, reorganised and remodelled. Even mature scar tissue does not generally regain the full tensile strength of uninjured tissue.

why_others_wrong.A: Tensile strength does not return immediately to 100% of normal after healing; it increases gradually over weeks to months during collagen remodelling and typically remains below baseline strength.
why_others_wrong.B: A healed wound does develop measurable tensile strength through collagen deposition and remodelling; it is inaccurate to say it never develops any strength.
why_others_wrong.D: Tensile strength continues to increase for many months as collagen is remodelled; it is not fixed or determined entirely within the first 24 hours.
why_others_wrong.E: Tensile strength depends on the quality and organisation of collagen deposition and remodelling, not simply on the physical length of the wound.

exam_trap: A wound that looks healed externally is not necessarily mechanically equivalent to uninjured tissue.
takeaway: Scar strength increases over time but does not return completely to normal.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.; RCS England lists this as an MRCS preparation resource. Accessed September 2026.
thinking: Healed surgical wound ↓ collagen remodelled for months ↓ scar strength rises but stays below normal ↓ Tensile strength gradually increases during remodelling but remains below that of uninjured tissue
pearl: Mass closure of the abdominal fascia with a suture length to wound length ratio of at least 4:1 reduces incisional hernia, reflecting the importance of suture support while the fascia heals.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Cardiorespiratory physiology: endothelial function
stem: A healthy artery is exposed to increased laminar blood flow. Which endothelial mediator is most directly responsible for promoting vasodilatation in response to this stimulus?
why_correct: Increased shear stress stimulates endothelial nitric oxide production. Nitric oxide diffuses into vascular smooth muscle and activates guanylate cyclase, increasing cyclic GMP and causing relaxation. Endothelin-1 and thromboxane A2 are vasoconstrictor/pro-thrombotic mediators.

why_others_wrong.A: Endothelin-1 is a potent endothelium-derived vasoconstrictor, the opposite of the vasodilator response produced by shear stress.
why_others_wrong.C: Thromboxane A2 is a platelet-derived vasoconstrictor and pro-thrombotic mediator, not the endothelial mediator released in response to increased shear stress.
why_others_wrong.D: Angiotensin II is a systemic vasoconstrictor generated via the renin-angiotensin system, not an endothelial shear-stress-induced mediator.
why_others_wrong.E: Vasopressin is a posterior pituitary hormone that causes vasoconstriction, unrelated to flow-mediated endothelial vasodilatation.

exam_trap: Do not confuse endothelial nitric oxide with platelet-derived thromboxane A2. Their vascular effects are broadly opposite.
takeaway: Shear stress → endothelial NO → smooth-muscle relaxation → vasodilatation.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.; RCS England recommended MRCS preparation resource list, accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Increased laminar flow raises endothelial shear stress ↓ shear activates endothelial nitric oxide synthase ↓ NO diffuses to smooth muscle and raises cyclic GMP ↓ smooth muscle relaxes ↓ Nitric oxide
pearl: Glyceryl trinitrate and sodium nitroprusside act by releasing NO, and phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors prolong cGMP action, which is why combining them can cause profound hypotension.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Pathology: oncology & haematology: platelet adhesion
stem: A patient has a defect affecting platelet adhesion to exposed subendothelial collagen. Which molecule normally provides the key bridge between the injured vessel wall and platelet glycoprotein Ib?
why_correct: von Willebrand factor binds exposed subendothelial structures and platelet glycoprotein Ib/IX, allowing initial platelet adhesion. It also carries and stabilises factor VIII in plasma.

why_others_wrong.A: Fibrinogen bridges activated platelets via GPIIb/IIIa during aggregation rather than linking subendothelial collagen to GPIb during adhesion.
why_others_wrong.C: Factor VII initiates the extrinsic coagulation pathway with tissue factor and is not a platelet adhesion molecule.
why_others_wrong.D: Protein C is a vitamin K-dependent anticoagulant that inactivates factors Va and VIIIa and does not mediate platelet adhesion.
why_others_wrong.E: Plasminogen is the precursor of plasmin in fibrinolysis and has no bridging role between the vessel wall and platelet GPIb.

exam_trap: Fibrinogen is important for platelet aggregation by linking activated platelets through glycoprotein IIb/IIIa. It is not the principal molecule responsible for initial GPIb-mediated adhesion.
takeaway: Initial platelet adhesion = vWF + platelet GPIb.
source: Merck Manual Professional, Overview of Hemostasis; updated/current page accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Defective platelet adhesion to subendothelial collagen ↓ the bridge links the vessel wall to platelet GPIb ↓ von Willebrand factor binds both collagen and GPIb ↓ von Willebrand factor
pearl: von Willebrand factor also carries and protects factor VIII, so severe von Willebrand disease can prolong the APTT as well as cause mucocutaneous bleeding.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Pathology: oncology & haematology: platelet-inhibitory endothelium
stem: Which pair of endothelial mediators normally acts to inhibit platelet aggregation and maintain blood fluidity in an intact vessel?
why_correct: Intact endothelial cells produce nitric oxide and prostacyclin (PGI2), which inhibit platelet aggregation and promote vasodilatation. Endothelial disruption removes this antithrombotic environment.

why_others_wrong.A: Thromboxane A2 and ADP are released by activated platelets and promote, rather than inhibit, platelet aggregation.
why_others_wrong.C: Endothelin is a vasoconstrictor and thromboxane A2 a pro-aggregatory platelet product, so neither maintains blood fluidity.
why_others_wrong.D: ADP and serotonin are released from platelet granules and amplify platelet activation and aggregation.
why_others_wrong.E: Histamine and bradykinin mainly increase vascular permeability and vasodilatation in inflammation and are not the principal endothelial platelet inhibitors.

exam_trap: Thromboxane A2 is produced by activated platelets and promotes platelet aggregation and vasoconstriction.
takeaway: Healthy endothelium is actively antithrombotic.
source: Merck Manual Professional, Overview of Hemostasis; accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Intact endothelium keeps blood fluid ↓ it releases platelet-inhibitory vasodilators ↓ nitric oxide raises platelet cGMP; prostacyclin raises platelet cAMP ↓ Nitric oxide and prostacyclin
pearl: Low-dose aspirin exploits this balance: it irreversibly blocks platelet thromboxane A2 production, while nucleated endothelial cells can make new cyclo-oxygenase and continue producing prostacyclin.

subject: Immunology
title: Microbiology & surgical infection: complement activation
stem: A bacterial surface activates complement without the involvement of antibody. Which pathway is most directly involved?
why_correct: The alternative pathway can be activated directly on microbial surfaces and does not require antibody. The classical pathway is classically associated with antigen-antibody complexes, while the lectin pathway recognises microbial carbohydrate patterns.

why_others_wrong.A: The classical pathway is mainly triggered when C1q binds antigen-bound IgG or IgM, so it is the antibody-associated route rather than direct surface activation.
why_others_wrong.C: The intrinsic pathway is part of the coagulation cascade initiated by contact activation of factor XII, not complement.
why_others_wrong.D: The extrinsic pathway is the tissue factor-driven arm of coagulation and has no role in complement activation on bacteria.
why_others_wrong.E: The fibrinolytic pathway breaks down fibrin clots through plasmin and does not activate complement.

exam_trap: "Classical" does not mean "first-line." The alternative pathway is an important component of innate immunity.
takeaway: Alternative pathway = antibody-independent complement activation on microbial surfaces.
source: MSD Manual Professional, Complement System; accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Complement activated on a bacterial surface ↓ no antibody involved ↓ classical pathway needs antibody-bound C1q ↓ spontaneous C3 hydrolysis is stabilised on microbial surfaces ↓ Alternative pathway
pearl: The alternative pathway amplifies all complement activation because every C3b deposited can form more C3 convertase (C3bBb), stabilised by properdin.

subject: Immunology
title: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing: lectin pathway
stem: The lectin pathway of complement is activated when mannose-binding lectin recognises carbohydrate structures on a microorganism. Which statement is correct?

options.D: It begins with C1q binding to antibody

why_correct: Mannose-binding lectin recognises carbohydrate groups such as mannose on microbial surfaces. The pathway subsequently generates a C3 convertase and converges with the other complement pathways.

why_others_wrong.A: The lectin pathway is triggered by mannose-binding lectin recognising microbial sugars, so it does not require IgM.
why_others_wrong.B: IgG-dependent activation describes the classical pathway; the lectin pathway proceeds without antibody.
why_others_wrong.D: C1q binding to antibody initiates the classical pathway, whereas the lectin pathway starts with mannose-binding lectin and its associated serine proteases.
why_others_wrong.E: The lectin pathway generates a C3 convertase and converges on C3 cleavage, so it does not bypass C3.

exam_trap: Option D tempts candidates because C1q and MBL are structurally similar, but C1q binding to antibody starts the classical pathway; the lectin pathway needs no antibody.
takeaway: Lectin pathway = microbial carbohydrate recognition without antibody.
source: MSD Manual Professional, Complement System; accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Mannose-binding lectin binds microbial carbohydrate ↓ MBL-associated serine proteases cleave C4 and C2 ↓ no antibody is needed ↓ pathway converges on C3 convertase ↓ It is antibody-independent
pearl: MBL is an acute-phase protein made by the liver, and MBL deficiency is common and usually mild, becoming relevant mainly in infancy or with other immune defects.

subject: Immunology
title: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing: complement convertase
stem: Which complement component is cleaved at the point where the classical, lectin and alternative pathways converge, releasing an anaphylatoxin and generating the principal opsonin?
why_correct: All three complement activation pathways converge on C3 cleavage. C3 is split into C3a and C3b. C3b contributes to opsonisation and formation of C5 convertase.

why_others_wrong.A: C1 is the initiating recognition complex of the classical pathway and acts upstream, before C3 convertase is formed.
why_others_wrong.B: C2 is cleaved by C1s (or MASP-2) and its fragment helps form the classical and lectin C3 convertase, rather than being its substrate.
why_others_wrong.D: C5 is cleaved by C5 convertase at a later stage, after C3b has been generated and incorporated into that enzyme.
why_others_wrong.E: C9 is the final terminal component that polymerises to form the membrane attack complex pore and is not cleaved by C3 convertase.

exam_trap: Candidates choose C5 (D) because C5a is a potent anaphylatoxin, but C5 is cleaved later; the convergence point generating the C3b opsonin is C3.
takeaway: Three pathways → C3 convertase → C3a + C3b.
source: MSD Manual Professional, Complement System; accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Classical, lectin and alternative pathways ↓ each forms a C3 convertase ↓ C3 is cleaved into C3a and C3b ↓ C3a is an anaphylatoxin and C3b the main opsonin ↓ C3
pearl: Deficiency of the terminal components C5-C9 predisposes to recurrent Neisseria infection, whereas C3 deficiency causes severe recurrent pyogenic infections because opsonisation fails.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing: hereditary angioedema
stem: A patient has recurrent episodes of non-urticarial facial and airway swelling. A complement investigation suggests C1 inhibitor deficiency. Which mediator is particularly important in the resulting oedema?
why_correct: C1 inhibitor regulates both complement and the kallikrein-kinin system. Deficiency or dysfunction increases bradykinin generation, producing increased vascular permeability and angioedema.

why_others_wrong.A: Histamine is the principal mediator of classic mast-cell/IgE-driven urticarial angioedema, which is a different, non-C1-inhibitor-dependent mechanism from hereditary angioedema.
why_others_wrong.C: Serotonin is involved in vascular tone and smooth muscle contraction in other contexts but is not the key mediator implicated in bradykinin-driven hereditary angioedema.
why_others_wrong.D: Thromboxane A2 promotes platelet aggregation and vasoconstriction and is not the mediator responsible for the oedema of C1 inhibitor deficiency.
why_others_wrong.E: Leukotriene B4 is chiefly a neutrophil chemoattractant involved in acute inflammation, not the mediator driving bradykinin-related hereditary angioedema.

exam_trap: Candidates choose histamine (A), the mediator of allergic urticaria and angioedema, but C1 inhibitor deficiency causes non-urticarial bradykinin-mediated swelling.
takeaway: C1 inhibitor deficiency → increased bradykinin → angioedema.
source: MSD Manual Professional, Hereditary and Acquired C1 Inhibitor Deficiency/Dysfunction; accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Recurrent non-urticarial swelling of face and airway ↓ C1 inhibitor deficiency ↓ unchecked kallikrein generates bradykinin ↓ Bradykinin
pearl: Hereditary angioedema does not respond reliably to adrenaline, antihistamines or steroids; acute attacks are treated with C1 inhibitor concentrate or a bradykinin receptor antagonist such as icatibant.

subject: Immunology
title: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing: phagocyte oxidative burst
stem: A child has recurrent deep abscesses caused by catalase-positive organisms. A neutrophil oxidative burst assay is abnormal. Which cellular enzyme is most likely defective?
why_correct: Chronic granulomatous disease results from defective NADPH oxidase activity, impairing generation of reactive oxygen species within phagocytes. Recurrent infections with catalase-producing organisms are characteristic.

why_others_wrong.A: Myeloperoxidase deficiency impairs hypochlorous acid formation but is usually mild, and the oxidative burst itself remains intact.
why_others_wrong.C: Cyclooxygenase-2 produces prostaglandins in inflammation and has no role in generating the phagocyte respiratory burst.
why_others_wrong.D: Superoxide dismutase converts superoxide to hydrogen peroxide downstream; the respiratory burst failure in chronic granulomatous disease lies upstream in superoxide generation.
why_others_wrong.E: Nitric oxide synthase generates nitric oxide and is not the enzyme tested by the neutrophil oxidative burst assay.

exam_trap: Myeloperoxidase deficiency affects conversion of hydrogen peroxide to hypochlorous acid but is not the classic defect in chronic granulomatous disease.
takeaway: CGD = defective NADPH oxidase → defective oxidative killing.
source: MSD Manual Professional, Chronic Granulomatous Disease; updated April 2026.
thinking: Recurrent deep abscesses with catalase-positive organisms ↓ abnormal oxidative burst assay ↓ phagocytes cannot generate superoxide ↓ chronic granulomatous disease ↓ NADPH oxidase
pearl: The dihydrorhodamine flow cytometry test has largely replaced the nitroblue tetrazolium test for diagnosing chronic granulomatous disease.

subject: Immunology
title: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing: chronic granulomatous disease
stem: Which organism is particularly associated with serious infection in chronic granulomatous disease?

options.D: Candida limited to mucosal surfaces only

why_correct: CGD predisposes to recurrent bacterial and fungal infections, particularly with catalase-producing organisms. Aspergillus is an important cause of serious disease.

why_others_wrong.B: Giardia is a luminal intestinal parasite associated with antibody deficiencies such as low IgA, not phagocyte killing defects.
why_others_wrong.C: Plasmodium falciparum is transmitted by mosquitoes and infects red cells; its severity is not linked to defective NADPH oxidase.
why_others_wrong.D: Candida confined to mucosal surfaces suggests a T-cell or Th17 defect, whereas chronic granulomatous disease predisposes to deep, invasive infections.
why_others_wrong.E: Enterobius vermicularis is a common threadworm infection in healthy children and is not associated with chronic granulomatous disease.

exam_trap: Candida limited to mucosal surfaces tempts because fungi are relevant in CGD, but mucosal candidiasis points to a T-cell or Th17 defect; chronic granulomatous disease causes invasive Aspergillus infection.
takeaway: CGD should trigger recognition of catalase-positive pathogens, especially Aspergillus.
source: MSD Manual Professional, Chronic Granulomatous Disease; updated April 2026.
thinking: Chronic granulomatous disease ↓ phagocytes lack the NADPH oxidase respiratory burst ↓ catalase-positive organisms destroy their own hydrogen peroxide ↓ invasive fungal infection is a leading cause of death ↓ Aspergillus species
pearl: Typical catalase-positive pathogens in chronic granulomatous disease include Staphylococcus aureus, Serratia, Burkholderia cepacia, Nocardia and Aspergillus; patients take prophylactic co-trimoxazole and itraconazole.

subject: Major trauma & fluids
title: Transfusion: taco
stem: A patient develops acute breathlessness and pulmonary oedema during a blood transfusion. He is hypertensive with a raised JVP. Which diagnosis is most consistent with these findings?
why_correct: Transfusion-associated circulatory overload results from excessive intravascular volume relative to cardiovascular reserve. Hypertension and raised JVP favour circulatory overload.

why_others_wrong.A: TRALI causes non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, typically with hypotension and without raised JVP, so the hypertension and venous distension here point away from it.
why_others_wrong.C: An acute haemolytic reaction presents with fever, rigors, loin pain, hypotension and haemoglobinuria rather than hypertension with volume overload.
why_others_wrong.D: A delayed haemolytic reaction occurs days after transfusion with anaemia, jaundice and a positive DAT, not acute pulmonary oedema during transfusion.
why_others_wrong.E: A febrile non-haemolytic reaction causes fever and rigors without pulmonary oedema, hypertension or a raised JVP.

exam_trap: TRALI also causes acute hypoxaemic respiratory distress and pulmonary oedema, but is not primarily a hydrostatic volume-overload syndrome.
takeaway: Transfusion + pulmonary oedema + hypertension/raised JVP → think TACO.
source: UK Transfusion Guidelines, Acute Transfusion Reactions; accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Breathlessness and pulmonary oedema during transfusion ↓ hypertension and raised JVP ↓ hydrostatic volume overload ↓ TRALI usually has hypotension without raised JVP ↓ TACO
pearl: Risk factors for TACO include older age, low body weight, heart failure, renal impairment and rapid or large-volume transfusion; pre-transfusion risk assessment and single-unit transfusion reduce it.

subject: Major trauma & fluids
title: Transfusion: trali
stem: A patient develops acute hypoxaemia and bilateral pulmonary infiltrates shortly after transfusion. There is no evidence of circulatory overload. Which complication is most likely?
why_correct: Transfusion-related acute lung injury presents with acute respiratory deterioration and pulmonary oedema that is not primarily explained by circulatory overload.

why_others_wrong.A: TACO is a hydrostatic volume-overload syndrome with raised JVP and hypertension, which the stem specifically excludes.
why_others_wrong.C: A delayed haemolytic reaction causes anaemia and jaundice days later, not acute hypoxaemia with bilateral infiltrates shortly after transfusion.
why_others_wrong.D: Iron overload develops over many transfusions and causes organ damage such as cardiomyopathy and liver disease, not acute lung injury.
why_others_wrong.E: Transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease presents about one to two weeks after transfusion with fever, rash, diarrhoea, liver dysfunction and pancytopenia.

exam_trap: Both TRALI and TACO can produce acute pulmonary oedema after transfusion. The distinction depends on the clinical context and evidence of volume overload.
takeaway: Acute post-transfusion respiratory failure without evidence of overload → consider TRALI.
source: NICE NG24 Transfusion; acute transfusion reaction material; accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Acute hypoxaemia with bilateral infiltrates ↓ shortly after transfusion ↓ no circulatory overload, so not TACO ↓ immune-mediated lung injury from donor antibodies ↓ TRALI
pearl: TRALI is classically linked to donor anti-HLA or anti-neutrophil antibodies, which is why UK plasma for transfusion is sourced preferentially from male donors.

subject: Major trauma & fluids
title: Major trauma & fluids: transfusion reaction
stem: A patient develops suspected acute haemolytic transfusion reaction during a red-cell transfusion. What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.C: Give another unit of the same blood group
options.E: Wait for the laboratory cross-match report

why_correct: A suspected serious acute transfusion reaction requires the transfusion to be stopped while the patient is assessed and appropriate investigations and supportive management are initiated.

why_others_wrong.A: Increasing the rate would deliver more incompatible red cells and worsen haemolysis, renal injury and disseminated intravascular coagulation.
why_others_wrong.C: Giving another unit before the cause is identified risks further incompatible transfusion, particularly if a labelling or identification error has occurred.
why_others_wrong.D: Antihistamines treat minor allergic reactions only; continuing the transfusion in suspected haemolysis exposes the patient to more incompatible blood.
why_others_wrong.E: Waiting for laboratory results while the transfusion continues allows ongoing haemolysis; the blood must be stopped first and investigations sent.

exam_trap: Do not continue the transfusion while attempting to establish the exact diagnosis.
takeaway: Suspected serious transfusion reaction → stop transfusion first.
source: NICE NG24 Transfusion; acute transfusion reaction guidance; accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Suspected acute haemolytic reaction ↓ every further millilitre adds incompatible cells ↓ stop the source first ↓ then check identity, resuscitate and investigate ↓ Stop the transfusion
pearl: After stopping, keep venous access open with saline through a new giving set, recheck the patient identity against the unit, and return the unit with samples to the laboratory.

subject: Major trauma & fluids
title: Major trauma & fluids: abo blood groups
stem: Which antigen is present on the red-cell surface of a group A individual?
why_correct: Group A red cells express A antigen and the plasma contains naturally occurring anti-B antibodies.

why_others_wrong.A: B antigen alone is found on group B red cells, not group A.
why_others_wrong.C: Both A and B antigens are present on group AB red cells, which have no anti-A or anti-B in plasma.
why_others_wrong.D: Group O red cells lack both A and B antigens, whereas group A cells carry A antigen.
why_others_wrong.E: RhD status is a separate blood-group system and does not define the ABO group; a group A individual may be RhD positive or negative.

exam_trap: The ABO group describes red-cell antigens, whereas the naturally occurring antibodies are found in plasma.
takeaway: Group A = A antigen on red cells + anti-B in plasma.
source: Principles and Practice of Surgery, 7th ed.; RCS England recommended MRCS resource list, accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: ABO group is named by red-cell antigens ↓ group A cells carry A antigen ↓ plasma carries naturally occurring anti-B ↓ RhD is a separate system ↓ A antigen
pearl: Group O RhD-negative red cells are the emergency universal donor cells, whereas group AB plasma is the universal plasma because it contains neither anti-A nor anti-B.

subject: Major trauma & fluids
title: Major trauma & fluids: rhesus system
stem: Which blood-group antigen is most strongly associated with clinically important Rh haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn?
why_correct: The RhD antigen is the major clinically important Rh antigen in routine transfusion and pregnancy-related alloimmunisation.

why_others_wrong.A: Anti-C can cause haemolytic disease but is far less common and generally less severe than disease due to anti-D.
why_others_wrong.C: Anti-E is an uncommon cause of mild to moderate haemolytic disease and is much less important than anti-D.
why_others_wrong.D: Anti-Kell can cause severe fetal anaemia, but Kell belongs to a separate blood-group system and is not the major Rh antigen.
why_others_wrong.E: Lewis antibodies are mostly IgM and Lewis antigens are poorly developed on fetal red cells, so they do not cause haemolytic disease of the newborn.

exam_trap: ABO antibodies are usually naturally occurring, whereas clinically significant RhD antibodies generally arise following exposure.
takeaway: RhD is the key Rh antigen for routine transfusion and pregnancy compatibility.
source: Principles and Practice of Surgery, 7th ed.; RCS England recommended MRCS resource list, accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Rh haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn ↓ maternal IgG crosses the placenta after sensitisation ↓ RhD is the most immunogenic Rh antigen ↓ Kell and Lewis belong to other systems ↓ RhD
pearl: Anti-D immunoglobulin given to RhD-negative women antenatally and after sensitising events prevents maternal sensitisation and has made RhD haemolytic disease far less common.

subject: Major trauma & fluids
title: Transfusion: citrate
stem: A patient receives a very large-volume blood transfusion and subsequently develops perioral tingling and muscle twitching. Which electrolyte abnormality is most likely?
why_correct: Citrate used as an anticoagulant in stored blood products binds ionised calcium. During rapid or massive transfusion, citrate accumulation can produce clinically significant hypocalcaemia.

why_others_wrong.A: Hypermagnesaemia causes weakness, hyporeflexia and hypotension rather than perioral tingling and twitching; citrate also tends to lower magnesium.
why_others_wrong.C: Stored blood does not typically produce hyperphosphataemia, and the neuromuscular irritability described reflects citrate binding of ionised calcium.
why_others_wrong.D: Hyperkalaemia from stored red cells mainly causes arrhythmias and weakness, not perioral paraesthesia and muscle twitching.
why_others_wrong.E: Hypernatraemia causes thirst, confusion and reduced consciousness rather than the tetany-like features of citrate toxicity.

exam_trap: Hyperkalaemia is the transfusion complication candidates remember, but it causes arrhythmias and weakness; perioral tingling and twitching reflect citrate binding of ionised calcium.
takeaway: Massive transfusion + neuromuscular irritability → check ionised calcium.
source: Principles and Practice of Surgery, 7th ed.; RCS England recommended MRCS resource list, accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Very large-volume transfusion ↓ perioral tingling and muscle twitching = neuromuscular irritability ↓ citrate anticoagulant binds ionised calcium ↓ accumulates when infusion outpaces hepatic metabolism ↓ Hypocalcaemia
pearl: Citrate is metabolised by the liver, so hepatic impairment and hypothermia increase the risk of citrate toxicity; ionised calcium should be monitored and replaced during major transfusion.

subject: Genetics
title: Genetics: DNA repair
stem: A defect in mismatch repair genes predisposes to accumulation of replication errors in repetitive DNA sequences. Which molecular abnormality is characteristic?
why_correct: Mismatch repair corrects errors introduced during DNA replication. Failure of this system causes microsatellite instability and is associated with several malignancies, particularly colorectal and endometrial cancers.

why_others_wrong.B: Trisomy 21 results from chromosomal nondisjunction producing an extra chromosome 21, not from failure to correct replication errors in repetitive sequences.
why_others_wrong.C: Mitochondrial inheritance is maternal transmission of mitochondrial DNA variants, not the molecular signature of defective nuclear mismatch repair.
why_others_wrong.D: Telomere shortening relates to cell ageing and chromosome end replication, not to replication errors accumulating in microsatellite repeats.
why_others_wrong.E: Whole-genome triploidy is an extra complete chromosome set, usually from abnormal fertilisation, not a result of mismatch repair failure.

exam_trap: Microsatellite instability is a marker of defective mismatch repair, not defective nucleotide excision repair.
takeaway: Mismatch repair failure → microsatellite instability.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.; RCS England recommended MRCS preparation resources, accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Defective mismatch repair genes ↓ replication errors accumulate ↓ repetitive DNA sequences are most affected ↓ Microsatellite instability
pearl: Microsatellite-unstable, mismatch repair-deficient colorectal cancers often respond well to immune checkpoint inhibitors because of their high mutational burden.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Pathology: oncology & haematology: brca genes
stem: BRCA1 and BRCA2 are best classified as genes involved primarily in:
why_correct: BRCA1 and BRCA2 participate in homologous recombination repair of DNA double-strand breaks. Loss of their function increases genomic instability and cancer susceptibility.

why_others_wrong.B: Ribosomal protein synthesis relies on ribosomal genes and translation machinery, not on BRCA1 and BRCA2, which maintain genomic integrity.
why_others_wrong.C: Glycolysis is a cytoplasmic metabolic pathway unrelated to the DNA repair function of BRCA1 and BRCA2.
why_others_wrong.D: Complement activation is part of innate immunity and does not involve BRCA genes.
why_others_wrong.E: Collagen synthesis depends on collagen genes and vitamin C-dependent hydroxylation, not on BRCA1 or BRCA2.

exam_trap: BRCA genes are tumour-suppressor-related rather than oncogenes that are activated by mutation.
takeaway: BRCA1/2 → homologous recombination DNA repair.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.; RCS England recommended MRCS resource list, accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: BRCA1 and BRCA2 maintain genomic integrity ↓ they act in homologous recombination ↓ this repairs DNA double-strand breaks ↓ DNA double-strand break repair
pearl: BRCA-deficient tumours depend on alternative repair pathways, so PARP inhibitors such as olaparib cause synthetic lethality and are used in BRCA-mutated ovarian, breast and prostate cancers.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Pathology: oncology & haematology: tp53
stem: A cell experiences severe DNA damage that cannot be adequately repaired. Activation of functional p53 most directly promotes:

options.A: Uncontrolled progression through the cell cycle
options.B: Cell-cycle arrest and, if necessary, apoptosis

correct_answer: B. Cell-cycle arrest and, if necessary, apoptosis
why_correct: p53 acts as a critical cellular response to DNA damage. It can induce cell-cycle arrest, allowing repair, or promote apoptosis when damage is irreparable.

why_others_wrong.A: Functional p53 halts the cell cycle at the G1 checkpoint after DNA damage; uncontrolled progression is what follows loss of p53.
why_others_wrong.C: p53 tends to suppress angiogenesis, for example by inducing thrombospondin-1, rather than promoting it.
why_others_wrong.D: Increased telomerase activity supports replicative immortality in cancer cells and is not the direct response of p53 to DNA damage.
why_others_wrong.E: Complement activation against bacteria is an innate immune process unrelated to the p53 response to DNA damage.

exam_trap: Increased telomerase activity tempts because it is a hallmark of cancer, but it supports immortality; functional p53 eliminates damaged cells through arrest or apoptosis.
takeaway: DNA damage → p53 → arrest/repair or apoptosis.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.; RCS England recommended MRCS preparation resources, accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Severe DNA damage ↓ p53 is stabilised and activated ↓ it induces p21 to arrest the cycle for repair ↓ it triggers apoptosis if the damage is irreparable ↓ Cell-cycle arrest and, if necessary, apoptosis
pearl: TP53 is the most frequently mutated gene in human cancer, and a germline TP53 mutation causes a hereditary syndrome of early-onset sarcomas, breast cancer, brain tumours and other malignancies.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing: telomerase
stem: Which enzyme allows many malignant cells to maintain telomere length and continue dividing beyond the normal replicative limit?
why_correct: Telomerase adds telomeric DNA sequences to chromosome ends, helping cells maintain telomere length. Reactivation of telomerase is common in malignant cells and contributes to replicative immortality.

why_others_wrong.A: DNA ligase joins breaks in the DNA backbone during replication and repair but cannot extend telomeric repeats.
why_others_wrong.C: RNA polymerase II transcribes messenger RNA and has no role in maintaining telomere length.
why_others_wrong.D: Although telomerase is itself a reverse transcriptase, retroviral reverse transcriptase does not maintain telomeres in malignant cells.
why_others_wrong.E: Topoisomerase I relieves DNA supercoiling during replication and transcription but does not add telomeric sequences.

exam_trap: Telomerase is a reverse-transcriptase enzyme, but in this context the relevant answer is telomerase rather than generic reverse transcriptase.
takeaway: Cancer biology → telomerase → sustained replicative capacity.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.; RCS England recommended MRCS preparation resources, accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Normal somatic cells shorten their telomeres with each division ↓ a replicative limit is eventually reached ↓ malignant cells reactivate an enzyme that adds telomeric repeats ↓ Telomerase
pearl: Most normal somatic cells lack telomerase activity whereas germ cells and stem cells retain it; a minority of tumours maintain telomeres by a recombination-based alternative lengthening mechanism instead.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Anaesthesia: mac
stem: Minimum alveolar concentration (MAC) is most directly used to describe:

options.A: The concentration of intravenous anaesthetic required to produce amnesia
options.B: The potency of an inhalational anaesthetic
options.C: The rate of hepatic drug metabolism
options.E: The concentration required to reverse paralysis

correct_answer: B. The potency of an inhalational anaesthetic
why_correct: MAC is the alveolar concentration of an inhaled anaesthetic preventing movement in response to a standard surgical stimulus in 50% of subjects. A lower MAC indicates greater potency.

why_others_wrong.A: MAC applies to inhaled agents measured in alveolar gas, not to intravenous anaesthetics, and its endpoint is movement rather than amnesia.
why_others_wrong.C: MAC describes inhalational anaesthetic potency and says nothing about the rate of hepatic drug metabolism.
why_others_wrong.D: Neuromuscular blockade is assessed with train-of-four monitoring, not with minimum alveolar concentration.
why_others_wrong.E: Reversal of paralysis relates to drugs such as neostigmine or sugammadex, not to the alveolar concentration of a volatile agent.

exam_trap: MAC is not simply a measure of the depth of anaesthesia in an individual patient.
takeaway: Lower MAC = greater inhalational anaesthetic potency.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.; RCS England recommended MRCS preparation resource list, accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: MAC is an alveolar concentration ↓ it prevents movement to a surgical stimulus in 50% of subjects ↓ lower MAC means a more potent inhalational agent ↓ The potency of an inhalational anaesthetic
pearl: MAC is reduced by older age, hypothermia, pregnancy, opioids and acute alcohol intoxication, and increased in infants, hyperthermia and chronic alcohol use.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Perioperative medicine & nutrition: preoxygenation
stem: The principal physiological purpose of preoxygenation before induction of general anaesthesia is to:

options.B: Replace nitrogen in the functional residual capacity with oxygen

correct_answer: B. Replace nitrogen in the functional residual capacity with oxygen
why_correct: Preoxygenation increases the oxygen reservoir within the lungs, particularly the functional residual capacity, delaying arterial desaturation during the apnoeic period following induction.

why_others_wrong.A: Preoxygenation does not change haemoglobin concentration; it increases the oxygen stored in the lungs.
why_others_wrong.C: Preoxygenation has no aim of increasing carbon dioxide production, which reflects metabolic activity rather than inspired oxygen.
why_others_wrong.D: Preoxygenation does not work by raising pulmonary blood flow; it denitrogenates the functional residual capacity to build an oxygen reservoir.
why_others_wrong.E: Preoxygenation does not prevent airway obstruction; it extends the time before desaturation if ventilation is interrupted.

exam_trap: Preoxygenation does not prevent airway obstruction; it buys time before desaturation occurs if ventilation is temporarily interrupted.
takeaway: Preoxygenation = maximise the pulmonary oxygen reservoir before apnoea.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.; RCS England recommended MRCS preparation resource list, accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Apnoea follows induction of anaesthesia ↓ functional residual capacity is the lung oxygen store ↓ breathing 100% oxygen washes out nitrogen from the FRC ↓ Replace nitrogen in the functional residual capacity with oxygen
pearl: Adequate preoxygenation is often judged by an end-tidal oxygen fraction of about 0.9, and head-up positioning helps in obese patients by increasing functional residual capacity.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Perioperative medicine & nutrition: general anaesthesia and frc
stem: A patient with severe obesity undergoes induction of general anaesthesia. Which change contributes to increased risk of rapid oxygen desaturation?
why_correct: General anaesthesia reduces functional residual capacity. Obesity can further reduce FRC, decreasing the oxygen reservoir available during apnoea.

why_others_wrong.A: Obesity and anaesthesia reduce rather than increase functional residual capacity, and a larger FRC would slow desaturation.
why_others_wrong.C: Isolated increased residual volume is not the mechanism; the key change is a reduced FRC and hence a smaller oxygen reservoir.
why_others_wrong.D: Alveolar surface area is not increased in obesity, and a larger surface area would not explain faster desaturation during apnoea.
why_others_wrong.E: Obesity reduces total respiratory compliance through chest wall and abdominal loading rather than increasing it.

exam_trap: FRC is the key reservoir relevant to apnoeic oxygenation, not simply total lung capacity.
takeaway: Low FRC → smaller oxygen reservoir → faster desaturation during apnoea.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.; RCS England recommended MRCS preparation resource list, accessed 26 September 2026.
