thinking: Severe obesity ↓ abdominal and chest wall load push the diaphragm up ↓ general anaesthesia further reduces FRC ↓ smaller oxygen reservoir during apnoea ↓ Reduced functional residual capacity
pearl: Ramped head-up positioning, preoxygenation with positive pressure and high-flow nasal oxygen during apnoea are used to extend safe apnoea time in obese patients.

subject: Physiology
title: Renal Physiology: filtration fraction
stem: A patient has a GFR of 120 mL/min and an effective renal plasma flow of 600 mL/min. What is the approximate filtration fraction?
why_correct: Filtration fraction = GFR / renal plasma flow. 120 / 600 = 0.20 = 20%.

why_others_wrong.A: 5% would require a renal plasma flow far greater than 600 mL/min for a GFR of 120 mL/min; it does not match the calculation.
why_others_wrong.B: 10% would correspond to a GFR of about 60 mL/min at this plasma flow, not the 120 mL/min given.
why_others_wrong.D: 40% would require a GFR of about 240 mL/min at this plasma flow, double the value stated.
why_others_wrong.E: 50% would require a GFR of about 300 mL/min, far above the 120 mL/min given in the question.

exam_trap: Do not divide GFR by renal blood flow. The denominator is renal plasma flow.
takeaway: FF = GFR ÷ RPF.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.; RCS England recommended MRCS preparation resource list, accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Filtration fraction = GFR ÷ renal plasma flow ↓ GFR 120 mL/min, RPF 600 mL/min ↓ 120 ÷ 600 = 0.20 ↓ 20%
pearl: Angiotensin II–mediated efferent arteriolar constriction raises the filtration fraction, which helps preserve GFR when renal plasma flow falls in hypovolaemia or heart failure.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: renal acid excretion
stem: During prolonged metabolic acidosis, which renal process becomes particularly important for increasing net acid excretion?

options.C: Complete cessation of hydrogen ion secretion

why_correct: The kidney increases ammoniagenesis, particularly from glutamine, generating NH4+ for urinary excretion while contributing new bicarbonate to the circulation.

why_others_wrong.A: Bicarbonate is conserved and regenerated during acidosis, not excreted; excreting it would worsen rather than correct the acidosis.
why_others_wrong.C: Hydrogen ion secretion is maintained or increased, not stopped, in order to excrete the excess acid load.
why_others_wrong.D: Glutamine metabolism actually increases during acidosis, fuelling greater ammoniagenesis rather than being reduced.
why_others_wrong.E: Urinary buffering capacity (titratable acid and ammonium) increases, rather than decreases, to cope with the higher acid load.

exam_trap: Simply secreting free hydrogen ions is insufficient to account for the kidney's full capacity for acid excretion.
takeaway: Chronic acidosis → increased renal ammonium generation/excretion.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.; RCS England recommended MRCS preparation resource list, accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Prolonged metabolic acidosis ↓ proximal tubule increases glutamine metabolism ↓ ammonia buffers secreted hydrogen ions as ammonium ↓ each ammonium excreted returns new bicarbonate to the blood ↓ Ammonium excretion
pearl: Ammonium excretion can rise several-fold in chronic acidosis and becomes the main adaptive component of net acid excretion, because titratable acid is limited by the filtered phosphate load.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: GI physiology & metabolism: gastric physiology
stem: Which gastric cell is primarily responsible for secreting intrinsic factor?
why_correct: Parietal cells secrete hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor. Intrinsic factor is required for vitamin B12 absorption in the terminal ileum.

why_others_wrong.A: Chief cells secrete pepsinogen and gastric lipase, not intrinsic factor.
why_others_wrong.B: G cells in the antrum secrete gastrin, which stimulates acid secretion but not intrinsic factor.
why_others_wrong.D: D cells secrete somatostatin, which inhibits gastrin and acid release.
why_others_wrong.E: Enterochromaffin cells are neuroendocrine cells secreting serotonin, and do not produce intrinsic factor.

exam_trap: Chief cells (option A) are often picked because they also sit in the gastric glands, but they make pepsinogen; parietal cells make both HCl and intrinsic factor.
takeaway: Parietal cell = HCl + intrinsic factor.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.; RCS England recommended MRCS preparation resource list, accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Intrinsic factor is needed for B12 absorption ↓ it is secreted in the gastric body and fundus ↓ by the same cell that secretes HCl ↓ Parietal cell
pearl: Total gastrectomy removes all parietal cells, so lifelong B12 replacement is required; in pernicious anaemia, autoantibodies against parietal cells and intrinsic factor have the same effect.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: GI physiology & metabolism: pancreatic enzyme activation
stem: A pancreatic enzyme precursor is activated in the duodenum and subsequently activates other pancreatic protease precursors. Which enzyme initiates this process?
why_correct: Enteropeptidase on the duodenal brush border converts trypsinogen to trypsin. Trypsin then activates other pancreatic zymogens.

why_others_wrong.A: Pepsin is a gastric protease inactivated in the duodenum and does not activate pancreatic zymogens.
why_others_wrong.C: Trypsin activates other zymogens once formed, but it needs enteropeptidase to convert trypsinogen and start the cascade.
why_others_wrong.D: Lipase digests triglycerides and plays no part in activating protease precursors.
why_others_wrong.E: Amylase breaks down starch and does not activate pancreatic zymogens.

exam_trap: Trypsin is the major activator of other pancreatic protease zymogens, but it is not the enzyme that initiates activation in the intestinal lumen.
takeaway: Enteropeptidase → trypsinogen → trypsin → other pancreatic zymogens.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.; RCS England recommended MRCS preparation resource list, accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Precursor activated in the duodenum then activates other proteases ↓ that precursor is trypsinogen ↓ a brush-border enzyme converts it to trypsin ↓ Enteropeptidase
pearl: Congenital enteropeptidase deficiency causes severe protein malabsorption and failure to thrive, showing that trypsinogen activation depends on this brush-border enzyme.

subject: Anatomy
title: Hepatobiliary surgery: liver histology
stem: Within a classical hepatic lobule, blood flows from the portal triads towards the:
why_correct: Branches of the portal vein and hepatic artery at the portal triads supply blood into hepatic sinusoids, which flow towards the central vein. Bile flows in the opposite general direction through canaliculi towards the bile ducts.

why_others_wrong.A: Bile flows in the opposite direction to sinusoidal blood, passing from hepatocytes via canaliculi toward the bile ducts at the portal triads, not being the destination of blood flow.
why_others_wrong.C: The hepatic artery is one of the vessels supplying blood into the sinusoids at the portal triad, not the destination toward which sinusoidal flow travels.
why_others_wrong.D: The gallbladder stores bile and is not a destination of sinusoidal blood flow within the lobule.
why_others_wrong.E: Blood reaches the inferior vena cava only after first draining via the central vein into the hepatic veins, not directly from the sinusoids.

exam_trap: Bile duct may tempt because it lies in the portal triad, but bile flows towards the triads, opposite to blood; sinusoidal blood flows centrally to the central vein.
takeaway: Hepatic blood: portal triad → sinusoids → central vein. Bile: hepatocytes → canaliculi → bile ducts.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed.; RCS England recommended MRCS preparation resource list, accessed 26 September 2026. Liver microanatomy also described by TeachMeAnatomy.
thinking: Portal triads at the lobule periphery ↓ portal vein and hepatic artery blood enters sinusoids ↓ flows centrally ↓ drains to the central vein then hepatic veins ↓ Central vein
pearl: Zone 3 hepatocytes around the central vein receive the least oxygenated blood and are most susceptible to ischaemic and paracetamol injury (centrilobular necrosis).

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Hepatobiliary surgery: liver acinus
stem: Which zone of the hepatic acinus is most vulnerable to ischaemic injury?
why_correct: Zone 3 is furthest from the incoming blood supply and therefore receives the least oxygenated blood. It is consequently particularly vulnerable to hypoxic/ischaemic injury. Zone 3 is also the region where some metabolic toxic injury is prominent.

why_others_wrong.A: Zone 1 (periportal) is closest to the incoming portal and arterial blood supply and therefore receives the most oxygenated blood, making it the least, not most, vulnerable to ischaemic injury.
why_others_wrong.B: Zone 2 is intermediate in oxygen supply between zones 1 and 3 and is less vulnerable to ischaemic injury than the more hypoxic zone 3.
why_others_wrong.D: The portal tract is the site where the oxygenated blood supply enters the acinus, so it is not the zone most vulnerable to hypoxic injury.
why_others_wrong.E: Bile duct epithelium is a distinct structure from the hepatocyte zonation of the acinus and is not the classic site of greatest vulnerability to ischaemic injury within the acinus.

exam_trap: Zone 1 receives the most oxygenated blood; it is therefore not the first zone expected to suffer from reduced oxygen delivery.
takeaway: Hepatic acinus: Zone 1 = highest oxygen. Zone 3 = lowest oxygen → greatest ischaemic vulnerability.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.; RCS England recommended MRCS preparation resource list, accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Hepatic acinus ↓ zone 3 lies furthest from the portal inflow ↓ lowest oxygen tension ↓ Zone 3
pearl: Ischaemic hepatitis after cardiogenic shock produces centrilobular (zone 3) necrosis with very high transaminases that fall quickly once perfusion is restored.

subject: Immunology
title: Physiology: t-cell subsets
stem: A patient has impaired cell-mediated immunity following loss of a T-cell population. Which T-cell subset is primarily responsible for coordinating immune responses through cytokine secretion?
why_correct: CD4+ helper T cells coordinate adaptive immune responses through cytokine secretion and interaction with antigen-presenting cells and B cells. CD8+ T cells are primarily involved in killing infected or abnormal cells.

why_others_wrong.B: CD8+ cytotoxic T cells mainly kill infected or abnormal cells presenting peptide on MHC class I rather than coordinating the wider response.
why_others_wrong.C: Neutrophils are innate phagocytes, not a T-cell subset, and do not direct adaptive immunity through cytokine help.
why_others_wrong.D: Plasma cells are differentiated B cells that secrete antibody; they are not T cells and do not coordinate cell-mediated immunity.
why_others_wrong.E: Erythrocytes carry oxygen and have no role in coordinating immune responses.

exam_trap: Do not equate all T cells with cytotoxic activity. CD4+ and CD8+ cells have different principal functions.
takeaway: CD4 = immune coordination; CD8 = cytotoxic cell killing.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.; RCS England MRCS preparation resources, accessed 26 September 2026. RCS lists Robbins & Kumar 11th edition among its MRCS resources.
thinking: Loss of a T-cell population ↓ question asks which subset coordinates responses ↓ helper cells secrete cytokines that direct B cells, macrophages and CD8 cells ↓ CD4+ helper T cells
pearl: HIV infection depletes CD4+ helper T cells, and the CD4 count guides the risk of opportunistic infections such as Pneumocystis pneumonia.

subject: Immunology
title: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing: cytotoxic t cells
stem: A virus-infected cell displays viral peptides on its cell surface. Which lymphocyte is principally responsible for directly killing the infected cell?
why_correct: CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes recognise antigen presented on MHC class I molecules and can kill infected or malignant cells through cytotoxic mechanisms.

why_others_wrong.A: CD4+ helper T cells recognise MHC class II and mainly coordinate responses through cytokines rather than directly killing infected cells.
why_others_wrong.C: B lymphocytes recognise native antigen and give rise to antibody-secreting cells; they do not directly kill virus-infected cells.
why_others_wrong.D: Plasma cells secrete antibody and do not recognise viral peptides displayed on MHC class I or kill infected cells.
why_others_wrong.E: Neutrophils are innate phagocytes that act mainly against extracellular bacteria and fungi, not MHC class I-presented viral peptides.

exam_trap: MHC class II presentation is associated principally with CD4+ T cells, whereas MHC class I is associated with CD8+ T cells.
takeaway: MHC I → CD8 → target-cell killing.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.; RCS England MRCS preparation resources, accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Viral peptides displayed on an infected cell ↓ endogenous peptide is presented on MHC class I ↓ recognised by CD8+ T cells ↓ kill via perforin and granzymes ↓ CD8+ cytotoxic T cell
pearl: CD8+ cytotoxic T cells induce apoptosis of target cells through perforin-granzyme release and Fas-Fas ligand interaction.

subject: Immunology
title: Immunology: B-cell differentiation
stem: A B lymphocyte undergoes differentiation following antigen exposure and becomes a cell specialised in secreting large quantities of antibody. What is the resulting cell?
why_correct: Activated B lymphocytes can differentiate into plasma cells, which specialise in antibody production.

why_others_wrong.A: Macrophages arise from monocytes, not B lymphocytes, and are phagocytes and antigen-presenting cells rather than antibody factories.
why_others_wrong.C: Neutrophils are myeloid granulocytes derived from marrow precursors and do not secrete antibody.
why_others_wrong.D: Natural killer cells are innate lymphocytes that kill stressed or infected cells and do not develop from B cells or secrete antibody.
why_others_wrong.E: Mast cells are myeloid-derived tissue cells that bind IgE and release mediators but do not produce antibody.

exam_trap: Macrophage tempts because it is another antigen-presenting cell, but macrophages arise from monocytes; a B cell that differentiates to secrete large quantities of antibody becomes a plasma cell.
takeaway: Activated B cell → plasma cell → antibody secretion.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.; RCS England MRCS preparation resources, accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Activated B lymphocyte after antigen exposure ↓ terminal differentiation ↓ abundant rough endoplasmic reticulum for immunoglobulin synthesis ↓ Plasma cell
pearl: Plasma cells show an eccentric clock-face nucleus and perinuclear halo on histology, and a malignant plasma-cell clone causes multiple myeloma with a monoclonal paraprotein.

subject: Immunology
title: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing: immunoglobulin m
stem: Which immunoglobulin is generally the first major antibody produced during a primary immune response?
why_correct: IgM is typically the first immunoglobulin produced during a primary immune response. Subsequent class switching can produce other antibody classes such as IgG, IgA or IgE.

why_others_wrong.A: IgA predominates in mucosal secretions and appears after class switching, so it is not the first antibody of a primary response.
why_others_wrong.B: IgD is co-expressed with IgM as a receptor on naive B cells but is secreted in very small amounts and is not the main early antibody.
why_others_wrong.C: IgE is produced after class switching, typically in allergic and helminth responses, and is not the first antibody produced.
why_others_wrong.D: IgG is the predominant serum antibody and dominates secondary responses, but it follows IgM after class switching in a primary response.

exam_trap: IgG is the predominant immunoglobulin in serum but is not normally the first antibody produced in a primary response.
takeaway: Primary response → IgM first; class switching → other immunoglobulin classes.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.; RCS England MRCS preparation resources, accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Primary immune response ↓ naive B cells first secrete pentameric IgM ↓ class switching follows with T-cell help ↓ IgM
pearl: Detecting specific IgM indicates recent or acute infection, whereas IgG alone suggests past infection or immunity, which underpins serological diagnosis of hepatitis A and B.

subject: Immunology
title: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing: immunoglobulin g
stem: Which immunoglobulin is the principal antibody class capable of crossing the placenta?
why_correct: IgG can cross the placenta and provides passive humoral immunity to the fetus and newborn.

why_others_wrong.A: IgA is secreted into breast milk and mucosal secretions but is not transported across the placenta.
why_others_wrong.B: IgD is present in trace amounts in serum and is not actively transferred to the fetus.
why_others_wrong.C: IgE lacks the neonatal Fc receptor-mediated transport used by IgG and does not significantly cross the placenta.
why_others_wrong.E: IgM is a large pentamer and is not transported across the placenta, so raised fetal IgM suggests fetal infection.

exam_trap: IgM is a large pentamer and does not normally cross the placenta.
takeaway: Placental antibody transfer → IgG.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.; RCS England MRCS preparation resources, accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Antibody crossing the placenta ↓ actively transported by the neonatal Fc receptor ↓ only IgG uses this route ↓ IgG
pearl: Maternal anti-RhD IgG crossing the placenta causes haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn, which is why anti-D prophylaxis is given to RhD-negative mothers.

subject: Immunology
title: Pathology: oncology & haematology: natural killer cells
stem: A tumour cell has reduced expression of MHC class I molecules. Which immune cell can recognise the abnormal reduction in MHC I and contribute to killing the cell?
why_correct: Natural killer cells can recognise cells with reduced or altered MHC class I expression and contribute to elimination of infected or malignant cells.

why_others_wrong.B: Eosinophils mainly target helminths and contribute to allergic inflammation; they do not detect loss of MHC class I.
why_others_wrong.C: Plasma cells secrete antibody and have no receptors for sensing reduced MHC class I on target cells.
why_others_wrong.D: Basophils release histamine and other mediators in allergic reactions and do not kill cells lacking MHC class I.
why_others_wrong.E: Red blood cells carry oxygen and have no immune recognition or cytotoxic function.

exam_trap: Eosinophils and basophils tempt as cytotoxic granulocytes, but they cannot sense MHC class I; loss of class I removes the inhibitory signal to natural killer cells, which then kill the tumour cell.
takeaway: Reduced MHC I expression can trigger NK-cell-mediated killing.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.; RCS England MRCS preparation resources, accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Tumour cell with reduced MHC class I ↓ escapes CD8 T-cell recognition ↓ loss of inhibitory signal from MHC class I ↓ innate killer lymphocyte is released to kill ↓ Natural killer cell
pearl: NK cells and CD8 T cells are complementary: viruses and tumours that downregulate MHC class I to evade CD8 cells become targets for NK cells (the missing-self hypothesis).

subject: Immunology
title: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing: antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity
stem: An antibody coats a target cell. Which immune cell can recognise the Fc portion of the bound antibody and contribute to target-cell killing?
why_correct: Natural killer cells express Fc receptors that allow them to recognise antibody-coated target cells and mediate antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity.

why_others_wrong.B: Erythrocytes carry oxygen and have no cytotoxic effector machinery for killing antibody-coated targets.
why_others_wrong.C: Fibroblasts produce extracellular matrix in connective tissue and repair and are not effector cells of antibody-dependent cytotoxicity.
why_others_wrong.D: Platelets function mainly in haemostasis and are not the classic Fc receptor-bearing killer cells that mediate ADCC.
why_others_wrong.E: Osteoblasts build bone matrix and have no role in recognising antibody Fc regions or killing target cells.

exam_trap: Platelets tempt because they carry some Fc receptors, but they are not cytotoxic effector cells; natural killer cells bind the antibody Fc region through CD16 and kill the coated target by ADCC.
takeaway: Antibody-coated target + NK cell → ADCC.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.; RCS England MRCS preparation resources, accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Antibody coats a target cell ↓ Fc portion is exposed ↓ NK cells bind it through Fc gamma receptor CD16 ↓ antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity ↓ Natural killer cell
pearl: ADCC is one mechanism of therapeutic monoclonal antibodies such as rituximab and trastuzumab, where NK cells kill antibody-coated tumour cells.

subject: Immunology
title: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing: autoimmune tolerance
stem: A failure of central immune tolerance allows self-reactive lymphocytes to survive. Where does major T-cell central tolerance occur?
why_correct: Developing T cells undergo selection in the thymus. Central tolerance removes or functionally controls many strongly self-reactive T cells.

why_others_wrong.A: Bone marrow is the main site of B-cell central tolerance; T-cell precursors leave the marrow to undergo selection in the thymus.
why_others_wrong.C: The spleen is a secondary lymphoid organ where peripheral, not central, tolerance and immune responses to blood-borne antigens occur.
why_others_wrong.D: Lymph nodes are secondary lymphoid organs where mature T cells meet antigen; tolerance here is peripheral rather than central.
why_others_wrong.E: The liver has tolerogenic properties and fetal haemopoietic roles, but it is not the site of T-cell selection and central tolerance.

exam_trap: B-cell development occurs primarily in bone marrow, whereas T-cell maturation occurs in the thymus.
takeaway: T-cell central tolerance → thymus.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.; RCS England MRCS preparation resources, accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Central tolerance of T cells ↓ occurs where T cells develop ↓ positive and negative selection in the thymus ↓ AIRE drives expression of tissue antigens there ↓ Thymus
pearl: AIRE mutations impair thymic negative selection and cause autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 1 with hypoparathyroidism, adrenal failure and mucocutaneous candidiasis.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: renal glomerular filtration barrier
stem: Which layer of the glomerular filtration barrier is directly formed by specialised epithelial cells with interdigitating foot processes?
why_correct: Podocytes are specialised visceral epithelial cells surrounding glomerular capillaries. Their interdigitating foot processes form filtration slits that contribute to the glomerular filtration barrier.

why_others_wrong.A: The fenestrated endothelium is the innermost, pore-containing layer of the capillary wall; it is not formed by epithelial cells with interdigitating foot processes.
why_others_wrong.B: The glomerular basement membrane is an acellular extracellular matrix layer, not a cellular layer bearing foot processes.
why_others_wrong.D: "Mesangial capsule" is not a recognised component of the filtration barrier; mesangial cells provide structural support but do not form the barrier's cellular layers.
why_others_wrong.E: Proximal tubular epithelium lies downstream of the glomerulus and is involved in reabsorption, not in forming the filtration barrier.

exam_trap: Candidates may choose fenestrated endothelium (A) or basement membrane (B), but the endothelium is the inner layer and the GBM is acellular; foot processes belong to podocytes.
takeaway: Podocyte foot processes = final cellular component of the glomerular filtration barrier.
source: NCBI Bookshelf, Histology: Kidney and Glomerulus; accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Epithelial cells with interdigitating foot processes ↓ visceral layer of the glomerular capsule ↓ foot processes separated by slit diaphragms ↓ outermost layer of the filtration barrier ↓ Podocyte layer
pearl: Podocyte foot-process effacement on electron microscopy is the defining finding in minimal change disease, the commonest cause of nephrotic syndrome in children.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: mesangial cells
stem: Which function is most closely associated with glomerular mesangial cells?

options.B: Structural support and regulation of glomerular capillary surface area

correct_answer: B. Structural support and regulation of glomerular capillary surface area
why_correct: Mesangial cells provide structural support within the glomerulus and can contract, influencing the available filtration surface area. They also have phagocytic and matrix-producing functions.

why_others_wrong.A: Erythropoietin is produced by peritubular interstitial fibroblast-like cells in the renal cortex, not by mesangial cells.
why_others_wrong.C: Bile production is a hepatic function and has no connection to mesangial cells.
why_others_wrong.D: Insulin secretion is a pancreatic beta-cell function, unrelated to the glomerular mesangium.
why_others_wrong.E: Bladder urothelium derives from the urogenital sinus, whereas mesangial cells lie within the glomerular tuft and have no role in forming it.

exam_trap: Do not confuse mesangial cells with podocytes. Both are associated with the glomerulus but perform different roles.
takeaway: Mesangial cells = glomerular support + contractile regulation.
source: NCBI Bookshelf, Histology: Kidney and Glomerulus; accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Mesangial cells lie between glomerular capillary loops ↓ modified smooth-muscle-like cells ↓ contract to alter filtration surface area and provide support ↓ also phagocytose and produce matrix ↓ Structural support and regulation of glomerular capillary surface area
pearl: IgA nephropathy, the commonest primary glomerulonephritis worldwide, is defined by mesangial IgA deposition and often presents with visible haematuria shortly after an upper respiratory infection.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: proximal tubular glucose handling
stem: A patient develops marked hyperglycaemia exceeding the renal threshold for glucose reabsorption. Where does most filtered glucose normally undergo reabsorption?
why_correct: Under normal physiological conditions, essentially all filtered glucose is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule through sodium-glucose cotransport mechanisms.

why_others_wrong.B: The thin descending limb is a water-permeable segment and is not involved in glucose reabsorption.
why_others_wrong.C: The thick ascending limb reabsorbs NaCl via NKCC2 and has no role in glucose handling.
why_others_wrong.D: The distal convoluted tubule reabsorbs NaCl via NCC; glucose reabsorption here is minimal to absent under normal conditions.
why_others_wrong.E: The collecting duct fine-tunes water and electrolyte balance and is not a site of glucose reabsorption.

exam_trap: Candidates may choose the distal convoluted tubule (D) or collecting duct (E) because they fine-tune urine, but glucose reabsorption is essentially completed in the proximal tubule.
takeaway: Filtered glucose → proximal tubular reabsorption.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.; RCS England MRCS preparation resources, accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Filtered glucose ↓ reabsorbed by SGLT2 and SGLT1 sodium-glucose cotransporters ↓ these are located in the proximal tubule ↓ glycosuria appears once transport capacity is exceeded ↓ Proximal tubule
pearl: SGLT2 inhibitors block proximal glucose reabsorption and are usually withheld before major surgery because they can cause euglycaemic diabetic ketoacidosis.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: distal nephron acid-base control
stem: Which renal cell type is primarily responsible for hydrogen ion secretion in the collecting duct?
why_correct: Alpha-intercalated cells secrete hydrogen ions and contribute to acid-base regulation. Beta-intercalated cells have the opposite functional orientation, secreting bicarbonate.

why_others_wrong.A: Principal cells mediate sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion via ENaC and ROMK, not hydrogen ion secretion.
why_others_wrong.C: Beta-intercalated cells secrete bicarbonate via pendrin, the opposite functional orientation to hydrogen ion secretion.
why_others_wrong.D: Podocytes form part of the glomerular filtration barrier and play no role in tubular hydrogen ion secretion.
why_others_wrong.E: Macula densa cells sense distal tubular NaCl delivery for tubuloglomerular feedback; they do not secrete hydrogen ions.

exam_trap: Candidates choosing beta-intercalated cells (C) reverse the pair; alpha cells secrete acid, beta cells secrete bicarbonate, and principal cells handle sodium and potassium.
takeaway: Alpha-intercalated cell → H+ secretion.
source: NCBI Bookshelf, Histology: Nephron; accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Hydrogen ion secretion in the collecting duct ↓ alpha-intercalated cells use apical H+-ATPase and H+/K+-ATPase ↓ beta-intercalated cells secrete bicarbonate instead ↓ principal cells handle sodium and potassium ↓ Alpha-intercalated cell
pearl: Failure of distal acid secretion causes distal (type 1) renal tubular acidosis: a normal-anion-gap acidosis with inability to acidify the urine and a tendency to nephrocalcinosis and renal stones.

subject: Physiology
title: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care: renal potassium secretion
stem: Aldosterone increases potassium excretion primarily by acting on which nephron cell?
why_correct: Aldosterone promotes sodium reabsorption through ENaC in principal cells and increases potassium secretion into the tubular lumen.

why_others_wrong.A: Podocytes form the glomerular filtration barrier and have no aldosterone-responsive ion transport function.
why_others_wrong.C: The proximal tubule performs bulk reabsorption but is not the principal target of aldosterone-mediated potassium secretion.
why_others_wrong.D: The thin descending limb is predominantly water-permeable and has no aldosterone-responsive ENaC or ROMK channels.
why_others_wrong.E: Macula densa cells sense tubular sodium chloride for tubuloglomerular feedback and renin regulation, not for aldosterone-driven potassium secretion.

exam_trap: Aldosterone also acts on acid-base handling, but principal-cell potassium secretion is the key mechanism tested here.
takeaway: Aldosterone → ENaC-mediated Na+ retention + increased K+ secretion.
source: NCBI Bookshelf, Histology: Nephron; accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Aldosterone increases potassium excretion ↓ acts on mineralocorticoid receptors in principal cells ↓ more ENaC sodium uptake makes the lumen electronegative ↓ potassium is secreted through ROMK channels ↓ Principal cell
pearl: Hypokalaemia that fails to correct with replacement should prompt a magnesium check, because hypomagnesaemia increases distal potassium secretion.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: GI physiology & metabolism: gastrointestinal wall
stem: Which layer of the gastrointestinal tract contains the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus?
why_correct: The myenteric plexus lies between the inner circular and outer longitudinal layers of the muscularis externa and is strongly involved in regulation of gastrointestinal motility.

why_others_wrong.A: The mucosa contains the epithelium, lamina propria and muscularis mucosae but not the myenteric plexus.
why_others_wrong.B: The submucosa contains the submucosal (Meissner) plexus, which mainly regulates secretion and local blood flow.
why_others_wrong.D: The serosa is the outer connective tissue and mesothelial covering and does not contain an enteric plexus.
why_others_wrong.E: The lamina propria is loose connective tissue within the mucosa and does not house the myenteric plexus.

exam_trap: The submucosal (Meissner) plexus is located in the submucosa and has a greater role in secretion and local blood flow.
takeaway: Auerbach = muscularis externa; Meissner = submucosa.
source: NCBI Bookshelf, Gastrointestinal Physiology; accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: The myenteric plexus coordinates motility ↓ it lies between the muscle layers it controls ↓ inner circular and outer longitudinal muscle ↓ Muscularis externa
pearl: In achalasia, loss of inhibitory neurons in the oesophageal myenteric plexus prevents lower oesophageal sphincter relaxation; treatment includes pneumatic dilatation, laparoscopic myotomy or peroral endoscopic myotomy.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: GI physiology & metabolism: gastrointestinal pacemaker cells
stem: Which cells generate the slow-wave electrical activity underlying gastrointestinal smooth-muscle rhythmicity?
why_correct: Interstitial cells of Cajal act as pacemaker cells of the gastrointestinal tract and generate slow waves that coordinate smooth-muscle activity.

why_others_wrong.A: Paneth cells in the intestinal crypts secrete antimicrobial peptides such as defensins and lysozyme, not slow waves.
why_others_wrong.C: Goblet cells secrete mucus and have no pacemaker function.
why_others_wrong.D: Chief cells secrete pepsinogen in the gastric glands and do not generate electrical rhythm.
why_others_wrong.E: Kupffer cells are hepatic macrophages and play no role in gut motility.

exam_trap: The enteric nervous system modulates gastrointestinal activity but does not itself act as the primary pacemaker generating the basic slow-wave rhythm.
takeaway: GI pacemaker → interstitial cells of Cajal.
source: NCBI Bookshelf, Physiology of Peristalsis; accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Slow-wave rhythm of gut smooth muscle ↓ generated by specialised pacemaker cells rather than neurons ↓ KIT-expressing cells within the muscle layers ↓ Interstitial cells of Cajal
pearl: Gastrointestinal stromal tumours arise from interstitial cells of Cajal or their precursors and usually express KIT (CD117), which explains their response to imatinib.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: GI physiology & metabolism: gastric histology
stem: Which cell type produces pepsinogen in the stomach?
why_correct: Chief cells secrete pepsinogen, which is converted to active pepsin in the acidic gastric environment.

why_others_wrong.A: Parietal cells secrete hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor; the acid activates pepsinogen but they do not produce it.
why_others_wrong.C: G cells secrete gastrin, which stimulates acid secretion rather than producing pepsinogen.
why_others_wrong.D: D cells secrete somatostatin, which inhibits gastric secretion.
why_others_wrong.E: Enterochromaffin cells secrete serotonin and are not a source of pepsinogen.

exam_trap: Parietal cells produce hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor; chief cells produce pepsinogen.
takeaway: Chief cell → pepsinogen.
source: NCBI Bookshelf, Histology: Parietal Cells; accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Pepsinogen secretion ↓ a zymogen made in the gastric glands ↓ activated by acid to pepsin ↓ Chief cell
pearl: Chief cells sit deep in the glands of the gastric body and fundus; their loss with intestinal metaplasia on biopsy indicates chronic atrophic gastritis, a precursor of gastric adenocarcinoma.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: Physiology: intestinal absorption
stem: Which structural adaptation provides a major increase in small-intestinal absorptive surface area?
why_correct: The small intestine has folds, villi and microvilli that greatly increase surface area for digestion and absorption.

why_others_wrong.A: Haustrations are sacculations of the colon formed by taeniae coli and do not substantially increase absorptive surface area.
why_others_wrong.C: Taeniae coli are longitudinal muscle bands of the colon, not an absorptive adaptation of the small intestine.
why_others_wrong.D: Gastric rugae allow the stomach to distend and are not a small-intestinal absorptive feature.
why_others_wrong.E: Anal columns are mucosal folds of the anal canal with no role in nutrient absorption.

exam_trap: Haustra and taeniae coli are characteristic features of the colon rather than the principal adaptations of the small intestine.
takeaway: Small intestine → folds + villi + microvilli → large absorptive surface.
source: NCBI Bookshelf, Gastrointestinal Physiology; accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Absorptive surface of the small intestine ↓ circular folds, villi and microvilli ↓ villi and microvilli amplify the area most ↓ Villi and microvilli
pearl: Coeliac disease causes villous atrophy and crypt hyperplasia, reducing absorptive area and causing iron and folate deficiency; duodenal biopsy taken on a gluten-containing diet confirms it.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: GI physiology & metabolism: intestinal wall
stem: Which gastrointestinal layer contains the larger blood vessels and lymphatic channels supplying the mucosa?
why_correct: The submucosa contains connective tissue, larger blood and lymphatic vessels and the submucosal nerve plexus.

why_others_wrong.A: The epithelium is avascular and relies on underlying layers for its blood supply.
why_others_wrong.B: The lamina propria contains capillaries and lacteals, but the larger supplying vessels and lymphatics lie in the submucosa.
why_others_wrong.D: The muscularis externa is mainly smooth muscle and contains the myenteric plexus rather than the main vessels supplying the mucosa.
why_others_wrong.E: The serosa is the outer covering; vessels traverse it but it is not the layer containing the larger vessels supplying the mucosa.

exam_trap: The lamina propria also contains vessels, but the larger supporting vascular and lymphatic structures are classically associated with the submucosa.
takeaway: Submucosa = vessels + lymphatics + Meissner plexus.
source: NCBI Bookshelf, Gastrointestinal Physiology; accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Larger vessels and lymphatics supplying the mucosa ↓ the lamina propria contains only capillaries and lacteals ↓ the connective tissue layer beneath the mucosa carries the larger vessels and Meissner plexus ↓ Submucosa
pearl: The collagen-rich submucosa is the strongest layer of the bowel wall, so intestinal anastomotic sutures must include it to hold securely.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: GI physiology & metabolism: gi motility
stem: Which enteric plexus is most directly associated with coordination of gastrointestinal smooth-muscle motility?
why_correct: The myenteric plexus lies between the circular and longitudinal muscle layers and is particularly important in coordinating peristalsis and other motor activity.

why_others_wrong.B: The submucosal (Meissner) plexus mainly controls secretion, absorption and local blood flow rather than coordinating motility.
why_others_wrong.C: The choroid plexus lies in the cerebral ventricles and produces cerebrospinal fluid.
why_others_wrong.D: The cardiac plexus supplies autonomic fibres to the heart, not gastrointestinal smooth muscle.
why_others_wrong.E: The cervical sympathetic chain supplies the head, neck and upper limb and is not an enteric plexus.

exam_trap: The submucosal plexus is more strongly associated with secretion and local blood flow.
takeaway: Motility → myenteric/Auerbach plexus.
source: NCBI Bookshelf, Gastrointestinal Physiology; accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Coordination of smooth-muscle motility ↓ intrinsic enteric plexus lying between the muscle layers ↓ Auerbach plexus ↓ Myenteric plexus
pearl: Opioids act on enteric neurons to reduce propulsive motility, contributing to postoperative ileus and constipation, one reason enhanced recovery pathways favour opioid-sparing analgesia.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Cardiorespiratory physiology: oxygen delivery
stem: A patient has severe anaemia but a normal arterial oxygen saturation. Which factor has been most directly reduced?
why_correct: Most oxygen in arterial blood is carried bound to haemoglobin. Severe anaemia therefore reduces arterial oxygen content despite potentially normal oxygen saturation.

why_others_wrong.A: Dissolved plasma oxygen is a minor component of oxygen content and is essentially unaffected by haemoglobin concentration; it is not what is reduced in anaemia.
why_others_wrong.C: Pulmonary ventilation is a separate variable from haemoglobin concentration and is not reduced by anaemia itself.
why_others_wrong.D: Alveolar surface area relates to gas exchange capacity, not to the amount of haemoglobin available to carry oxygen once it has diffused into blood.
why_others_wrong.E: Pulmonary blood flow is not directly reduced by anaemia; the problem is the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood that does flow.

exam_trap: Oxygen saturation describes the percentage of available haemoglobin binding sites occupied by oxygen; it does not directly measure total oxygen content.
takeaway: Normal SpO2 does not exclude reduced oxygen content in severe anaemia.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.; RCS England MRCS preparation resources, accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Severe anaemia with normal saturation ↓ saturation is normal but there is less Hb to saturate ↓ total oxygen the blood can carry is reduced ↓ Blood oxygen-carrying capacity
pearl: Transfusion thresholds in stable surgical patients are commonly restrictive, but patients with active cardiac ischaemia may need a higher haemoglobin to protect myocardial oxygen delivery.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Oxygen Delivery: cardiac output
stem: A patient's haemoglobin concentration and oxygen saturation remain unchanged, but cardiac output falls substantially. What is the expected effect on systemic oxygen delivery?
why_correct: Systemic oxygen delivery depends substantially on arterial oxygen content and cardiac output. If oxygen content remains constant while cardiac output falls, oxygen delivery decreases.

why_others_wrong.A: Since oxygen delivery equals cardiac output multiplied by arterial oxygen content, a fall in cardiac output with unchanged content must lower, not raise, delivery.
why_others_wrong.C: Because delivery depends directly on cardiac output, a substantial fall in cardiac output cannot leave delivery unchanged when content is constant.
why_others_wrong.D: PaCO2 is not a determinant of the oxygen delivery equation (cardiac output × arterial oxygen content), so it cannot cause delivery to rise here.
why_others_wrong.E: Oxygen delivery is calculated as cardiac output multiplied by arterial oxygen content, so it is inherently dependent on, not independent of, cardiac output.

exam_trap: No change is chosen by candidates who focus only on saturation and haemoglobin; oxygen delivery falls in proportion to cardiac output when content is constant.
takeaway: DO2 depends on cardiac output × arterial oxygen content.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.; RCS England MRCS preparation resources, accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Hb and saturation unchanged ↓ arterial oxygen content therefore unchanged ↓ DO2 = cardiac output x CaO2 ↓ Decrease
pearl: Raising cardiac output with fluids or inotropes is often the quickest way to improve oxygen delivery in shock, because once saturation is normal, extra oxygen adds little to content unless haemoglobin is also raised.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: lactate
stem: A patient develops severe tissue hypoperfusion during shock. Which metabolic change is most likely to contribute to increased circulating lactate?
why_correct: When oxygen delivery is inadequate, cells increase anaerobic glycolysis and pyruvate is increasingly converted to lactate. Lactate may therefore rise during severe tissue hypoperfusion.

why_others_wrong.A: Hypoperfusion limits oxygen delivery, which impairs rather than increases aerobic oxidative phosphorylation, driving cells toward anaerobic pathways instead.
why_others_wrong.C: Glycolysis actually continues, and increases, in the absence of adequate oxygen, feeding pyruvate toward lactate rather than ceasing.
why_others_wrong.D: Hepatic urea synthesis relates to nitrogen handling and does not explain a rise in circulating lactate during hypoperfusion.
why_others_wrong.E: Increased fatty-acid storage is unrelated to hypoperfusion and does not account for the rise in lactate seen in shock.

exam_trap: Candidates choosing C wrongly think glycolysis stops without oxygen; it continues and accelerates, and impaired oxidative phosphorylation diverts pyruvate to lactate.
takeaway: Low effective oxygen delivery → anaerobic metabolism → lactate may rise.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.; RCS England MRCS preparation resources, accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Severe tissue hypoperfusion ↓ inadequate oxygen delivery limits oxidative phosphorylation ↓ glycolysis continues anaerobically ↓ pyruvate is converted to lactate to regenerate NAD+ ↓ Increased anaerobic glycolytic metabolism
pearl: Serial lactate measurements help guide resuscitation in shock, and a raised lactate with severe abdominal pain out of proportion to signs should raise suspicion of mesenteric ischaemia.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Anatomy: hypophosphataemia and oxygen delivery
stem: A patient with severe hypophosphataemia develops muscle weakness. Which cellular process is particularly affected by low phosphate availability?

options.A: ATP generation and cellular energy metabolism
options.D: Sodium filtration at the glomerulus only

correct_answer: A. ATP generation and cellular energy metabolism
why_correct: Phosphate is required for ATP and other high-energy phosphate compounds. Severe hypophosphataemia can therefore impair cellular energy metabolism and contribute to weakness and respiratory muscle dysfunction.

why_others_wrong.B: DNA base pairing depends on hydrogen bonding between bases and is not the process that explains weakness in hypophosphataemia.
why_others_wrong.C: Haemoglobin synthesis is not the key process affected; low phosphate impairs ATP generation and also 2,3-DPG production in red cells.
why_others_wrong.D: Glomerular sodium filtration is not the cellular process whose failure causes muscle weakness in severe hypophosphataemia.
why_others_wrong.E: Bile salt synthesis is a hepatic process unrelated to the energy failure in muscle that follows severe phosphate depletion.

exam_trap: Phosphate is not simply a bone mineral; it is essential for intracellular energy metabolism.
takeaway: Phosphate is central to ATP-dependent cellular function.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.; RCS England MRCS preparation resources, accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Severe hypophosphataemia ↓ phosphate is needed for ATP and creatine phosphate ↓ muscle cells cannot generate enough energy ↓ ATP generation and cellular energy metabolism
pearl: Severe hypophosphataemia can cause respiratory muscle failure that delays weaning from ventilation, and red cell 2,3-DPG depletion shifts the oxyhaemoglobin curve to the left, impairing oxygen delivery.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care: atherosclerosis
stem: Which cell type is a major component of the early fatty streak in atherosclerosis?
why_correct: Macrophages take up modified lipoproteins within the arterial intima and become lipid-laden foam cells, contributing to the fatty streak and subsequent atherosclerotic plaque development.

why_others_wrong.B: Osteoclasts are specialised bone-resorbing cells of monocyte lineage and play no role in the lipid-laden cell population of an early atherosclerotic lesion.
why_others_wrong.C: Neutrophils are not the characteristic cell of the early fatty streak, which is dominated by lipid-laden macrophages, and 'only' further overstates any isolated neutrophil role.
why_others_wrong.D: Erythrocytes are oxygen-carrying cells with no role in lipid uptake or foam-cell formation within the arterial intima.
why_others_wrong.E: Fibrocytes are not the characteristic cell of the fatty streak; the earliest lesion consists of lipid-laden foam macrophages, and the later fibrous cap comes mainly from intimal smooth muscle cells.

exam_trap: Candidates choose neutrophils (C) or fibrocytes (E), but the fatty streak consists of lipid-laden foam macrophages; smooth muscle cells form the later fibrous cap.
takeaway: Modified lipid uptake by macrophages → foam cells → fatty streak.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.; RCS England MRCS preparation resources, accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Early fatty streak ↓ oxidised LDL taken up by intimal macrophages ↓ lipid-laden foam cells ↓ Foam macrophage
pearl: Fatty streaks can be present in the aorta from childhood, and later fibrous caps derived from smooth muscle cells cover the lipid core of established plaques.

subject: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care
title: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care: aortic dissection
stem: An aortic dissection occurs when blood enters the wall of the aorta and separates its layers. Which layer is primarily involved in creating the false lumen?
why_correct: Aortic dissection typically begins with an intimal tear through which blood enters the medial layer, creating a blood-filled false lumen within the media.

why_others_wrong.A: The intima is where the entry tear begins, but blood tracks along a plane within the media rather than staying confined to the intima.
why_others_wrong.C: The adventitia forms the outer wall of the false lumen, but the dissection plane itself lies within the media; blood breaching the adventitia means rupture.
why_others_wrong.D: The pericardium surrounds the heart and ascending aorta; haemopericardium is a complication of type A dissection, not the site of the false lumen.
why_others_wrong.E: The endocardium lines the cardiac chambers and valves and is not a layer of the aortic wall.

exam_trap: The initiating tear may be in the intima, but the dissection plane is characteristically within the media.
takeaway: Intimal entry → blood tracks through media → false lumen.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.; RCS England MRCS preparation resources, accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Aortic dissection ↓ intimal tear allows entry of blood ↓ blood splits the wall within the media ↓ creating a false lumen ↓ Media
pearl: Cystic medial degeneration, as in inherited connective tissue disorders, predisposes to dissection, and hypertension is the most common risk factor.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Cardiorespiratory physiology: cardiac preload
stem: A patient receives a rapid intravenous fluid bolus and develops an increase in left ventricular end-diastolic volume. Which change would normally occur in a healthy heart?

options.A: Reduced myocardial fibre stretch and reduced stroke volume
options.B: Increased myocardial fibre stretch and increased stroke volume
options.C: Reduced venous return and increased stroke volume

correct_answer: B. Increased myocardial fibre stretch and increased stroke volume
why_correct: Within physiological limits, increased ventricular filling stretches myocardial fibres and increases the force of subsequent contraction through the Frank–Starling mechanism.

why_others_wrong.A: The stem describes increased end-diastolic volume from a fluid bolus, which stretches fibres further and, via the Frank–Starling mechanism, increases rather than reduces stroke volume.
why_others_wrong.C: A fluid bolus increases, rather than reduces, venous return, and the resulting rise in stroke volume comes with increased, not reduced, venous return.
why_others_wrong.D: A fluid bolus primarily raises preload through increased filling; it does not directly increase afterload or impair intrinsic contractility.
why_others_wrong.E: The stem explicitly describes an increase, not a reduction, in end-diastolic volume following the fluid bolus.

exam_trap: Option D is chosen by candidates who think extra volume increases afterload; a fluid bolus primarily raises preload and does not impair contractility.
takeaway: More filling → more fibre stretch → stronger contraction, within physiological limits.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.; RCS England MRCS preparation resources, accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Fluid bolus raises end-diastolic volume ↓ myocardial fibres are stretched further ↓ Frank-Starling increases force of contraction ↓ Increased myocardial fibre stretch and increased stroke volume
pearl: Fluid responsiveness is often tested with a passive leg raise or small bolus, looking for a rise in stroke volume that indicates the heart is on the steep part of the Starling curve.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Cardiorespiratory physiology: cardiac afterload
stem: A patient develops severe systemic hypertension. Which ventricular parameter is most directly increased?
why_correct: The left ventricle must generate greater pressure to eject blood against an increased systemic arterial pressure. This increases ventricular afterload.

why_others_wrong.B: Systemic hypertension raises the pressure the left ventricle ejects against; it does not directly determine right ventricular filling (preload), which depends on systemic venous return.
why_others_wrong.C: The immediate haemodynamic effect of systemic hypertension is increased afterload; any reduction in left ventricular compliance is a chronic secondary consequence (e.g. from hypertrophy), not the direct effect being asked about.
why_others_wrong.D: Right atrial pressure reflects right-sided filling and is not the parameter directly increased by elevated systemic arterial pressure, which affects the left ventricle.
why_others_wrong.E: Pulmonary venous pressure relates to the left atrium and pulmonary circulation, not to the direct consequence of increased systemic arterial pressure on the left ventricle.

exam_trap: Do not confuse systemic arterial pressure with preload. Preload relates primarily to ventricular filling.
takeaway: High systemic arterial pressure → increased LV afterload.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.; RCS England MRCS preparation resources, accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Severe systemic hypertension ↓ left ventricle ejects into a high-pressure aorta ↓ pressure opposing ejection is afterload ↓ Left ventricular afterload
pearl: Chronic pressure overload from hypertension drives concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, which in turn reduces compliance and causes diastolic dysfunction.

subject: Pharmacology
title: Pharmacology: baroreceptor location
stem: A sudden rise in arterial blood pressure activates high-pressure arterial baroreceptors. Where are the principal receptors located?
correct_answer: B. Carotid sinus and aortic arch
why_correct: Stretch-sensitive baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch detect changes in arterial pressure and contribute to rapid autonomic regulation of blood pressure.

why_others_wrong.A: Pulmonary veins and the left atrium contain low-pressure volume (stretch) receptors that respond to venous filling, not the high-pressure arterial baroreceptors responding to arterial pressure changes.
why_others_wrong.C: The renal arteries and portal vein are not the principal high-pressure baroreceptor sites; intrarenal pressure sensing at the afferent arteriole regulates renin release rather than the rapid baroreflex, and the portal vein is a low-pressure venous system.
why_others_wrong.D: The coronary sinus and vena cava are venous structures associated with low-pressure sensing, not the high-pressure arterial baroreceptor sites.
why_others_wrong.E: The cerebral ventricles contain no baroreceptors; they are involved in CSF circulation, not arterial pressure sensing.

exam_trap: Do not confuse arterial baroreceptors with low-pressure volume receptors in the atria and pulmonary circulation.
takeaway: Rapid BP sensing → carotid sinus + aortic arch.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.; RCS England MRCS preparation resources, accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Sudden rise in arterial pressure ↓ high-pressure stretch receptors in arterial walls ↓ located in the carotid sinus (glossopharyngeal afferents) and aortic arch (vagal afferents) ↓ Carotid sinus and aortic arch
pearl: Pressure on the carotid sinus, as in carotid sinus massage or during carotid endarterectomy, can trigger reflex bradycardia and hypotension; surgeons may infiltrate local anaesthetic around the sinus to blunt this.

subject: Pharmacology
title: Pharmacology: baroreceptor response
stem: A healthy patient suddenly loses a moderate volume of blood. Which immediate autonomic response is expected?

options.D: Increased vagal activity and reduced contractility

correct_answer: C. Increased sympathetic activity and tachycardia
why_correct: Reduced arterial pressure decreases baroreceptor firing, resulting in increased sympathetic and reduced parasympathetic activity. This produces tachycardia, increased myocardial contractility and peripheral vasoconstriction.

why_others_wrong.A: Increased parasympathetic activity and bradycardia would be the opposite compensatory response; falling arterial pressure reduces baroreceptor firing, which increases sympathetic and reduces parasympathetic tone.
why_others_wrong.B: Reduced sympathetic activity and vasodilatation would worsen hypotension after blood loss; the baroreceptor reflex instead increases sympathetic outflow and promotes vasoconstriction to defend pressure.
why_others_wrong.D: Increased vagal activity and reduced contractility would exacerbate a fall in cardiac output after haemorrhage, the opposite of the expected compensatory sympathetic response.
why_others_wrong.E: Catecholamine release is increased, not inhibited, as part of the sympathetic response to hypotension following blood loss.

exam_trap: The baroreceptor response is an immediate compensatory mechanism; it does not restore circulating volume.
takeaway: Acute blood loss → ↓ baroreceptor firing → ↑ sympathetic response.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.; RCS England MRCS preparation resources, accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Sudden moderate blood loss ↓ arterial pressure falls and baroreceptor firing decreases ↓ less inhibition of sympathetic outflow and reduced vagal tone ↓ tachycardia, increased contractility and vasoconstriction ↓ Increased sympathetic activity and tachycardia
pearl: Because the baroreflex and vasoconstriction maintain blood pressure early in haemorrhage, a fall in systolic pressure is a late sign; tachycardia and a narrowed pulse pressure appear first.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Cardiorespiratory physiology: Poiseuille's law
stem: A small artery undergoes a reduction in radius by 50%. Assuming other variables remain constant, what happens to resistance to laminar flow?
why_correct: For laminar flow, resistance is inversely proportional to the fourth power of radius (R ∝ 1/r⁴). Halving the radius therefore increases resistance by 1/(0.5⁴) = 16-fold.

why_others_wrong.A: Resistance rises rather than falls when radius decreases, since resistance is inversely related to the fourth power of radius.
why_others_wrong.B: A doubling would correspond to a linear (first-power) relationship between resistance and radius, not the fourth-power relationship that actually governs laminar flow.
why_others_wrong.C: A four-fold change would correspond to an inverse-square relationship, not the fourth-power relationship described by Poiseuille's law.
why_others_wrong.D: An eight-fold change would correspond to a third-power relationship, understating the true fourth-power dependence of resistance on radius.

exam_trap: Candidates choose a 4-fold rise (C) by applying an inverse-square law, but resistance depends on radius to the fourth power, so halving radius gives a 16-fold rise.
takeaway: Radius dominates resistance: halve radius → resistance ×16.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.; RCS England MRCS preparation resources, accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Laminar flow follows Poiseuille's law ↓ resistance is inversely proportional to radius to the fourth power ↓ halving radius gives 1/(0.5 x 0.5 x 0.5 x 0.5) ↓ 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 = 16 ↓ It increases approximately 16-fold
pearl: The same fourth-power rule explains why a short, wide-bore peripheral cannula delivers fluid faster than a longer, narrower central line, and why small changes in arteriolar calibre strongly control regional flow.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Physiology: venous compliance
stem: Which statement best describes the systemic venous circulation?

options.A: It is a low-capacitance system storing little blood
options.B: It contains a large proportion of the circulating blood volume
options.C: It generates most systemic vascular resistance
options.D: It has the highest blood pressure in the circulation
options.E: It is unaffected by sympathetic stimulation

correct_answer: B. It contains a large proportion of the circulating blood volume
why_correct: Veins are highly compliant and act as a major blood reservoir. Sympathetic venoconstriction can mobilise venous blood and increase venous return.

why_others_wrong.A: Veins are in fact a high-capacitance system that normally holds a large proportion (roughly two-thirds) of total circulating blood volume, not a low-capacitance one holding little blood.
why_others_wrong.C: Arterioles, not veins, are the principal generators of systemic vascular resistance due to their smooth-muscle tone.
why_others_wrong.D: Venous pressure is low compared with arterial pressure; the highest pressures in the circulation are found in the arterial system, particularly the aorta.
why_others_wrong.E: Veins are richly supplied with sympathetic innervation, and sympathetic venoconstriction meaningfully alters venous capacitance and return.

exam_trap: Option C is chosen by candidates who confuse capacitance with resistance; arterioles, not veins, generate most systemic vascular resistance.
takeaway: Veins = capacitance/reservoir vessels.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.; RCS England MRCS preparation resources, accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Veins are thin-walled and highly compliant ↓ they hold most of the circulating blood volume ↓ they act as capacitance vessels ↓ It contains a large proportion of the circulating blood volume
pearl: In haemorrhage, sympathetic venoconstriction mobilises blood from the venous reservoir, helping maintain venous return before blood pressure falls.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Physiology: ventricular compliance
stem: A patient has a stiff left ventricle due to concentric ventricular hypertrophy. Which change best describes ventricular compliance?
why_correct: Compliance describes the change in volume for a given change in pressure. A stiff ventricle has reduced compliance and requires a greater filling pressure to achieve a given ventricular volume.

why_others_wrong.A: Concentric hypertrophy stiffens the ventricular wall, which reduces compliance rather than increasing it.
why_others_wrong.C: The premise of a 'stiff' ventricle from hypertrophy implies an altered, reduced compliance, not an unchanged one.
why_others_wrong.D: Reduced compliance is a passive diastolic property distinct from contractility; a hypertrophied ventricle can still contract forcefully despite being stiff.
why_others_wrong.E: The question asks about ventricular, not venous, compliance; the scenario describes a change in the heart wall, not the venous system.

exam_trap: Reduced compliance is not synonymous with reduced contractility. A ventricle can contract strongly but still be abnormally stiff.
takeaway: Stiff ventricle → reduced compliance → higher filling pressure.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.; RCS England MRCS preparation resources, accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Concentric hypertrophy thickens the ventricular wall ↓ the ventricle becomes stiff ↓ less volume change per unit pressure ↓ Reduced compliance
pearl: A stiff hypertrophied ventricle depends heavily on atrial contraction for filling, so new atrial fibrillation can cause sudden decompensation.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Cardiorespiratory physiology: pulmonary vascular resistance
stem: Which change is expected when pulmonary alveolar oxygen tension becomes markedly reduced in a localised region of the lung?

options.D: Complete cessation of pulmonary blood flow

why_correct: Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction diverts blood away from poorly ventilated alveoli towards better-ventilated regions, helping improve ventilation-perfusion matching.

why_others_wrong.A: Localised alveolar hypoxia triggers pulmonary vasoconstriction, not vasodilatation, in that region, redirecting blood towards better-ventilated areas.
why_others_wrong.C: The hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction response is local to the pulmonary vasculature; systemic arterioles typically dilate, rather than constrict, in response to local tissue hypoxia.
why_others_wrong.D: Vasoconstriction reduces perfusion to the hypoxic region but does not abolish flow entirely.
why_others_wrong.E: Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction affects pulmonary vascular pressures (and potentially the right ventricle if widespread); it does not directly raise left ventricular afterload.

exam_trap: This response differs from the systemic circulation, where tissue hypoxia generally causes local vasodilatation.
takeaway: Pulmonary hypoxia → vasoconstriction; systemic tissue hypoxia → vasodilatation.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.; RCS England MRCS preparation resources, accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Localised alveolar hypoxia ↓ pulmonary arterioles constrict in response to low alveolar PO2 ↓ blood is diverted to better-ventilated lung ↓ Local pulmonary vasoconstriction
pearl: One-lung ventilation during thoracic surgery relies on hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction to limit shunt through the collapsed lung, and some vasodilators and volatile agents can blunt it.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Cardiorespiratory physiology: respiratory compliance
stem: A patient with pulmonary fibrosis has markedly reduced lung compliance. Which mechanical consequence is expected?

options.A: The lungs are easier to inflate
options.B: A greater pressure change is required to produce a given volume change
options.D: Airway resistance must always be increased
options.E: Functional residual capacity must always increase

correct_answer: B. A greater pressure change is required to produce a given volume change
why_correct: Compliance is the change in volume produced per unit change in pressure. Low compliance means the lungs are stiff and require greater pressure changes to achieve the same volume change.

why_others_wrong.A: Reduced compliance means the fibrotic lungs are stiffer and harder, not easier, to inflate.
why_others_wrong.C: Pulmonary fibrosis increases elastic recoil because of the added stiff, scarred tissue; it does not reduce recoil.
why_others_wrong.D: Fibrosis is primarily a parenchymal/compliance problem; airway resistance is not necessarily increased and is a separate mechanical property from lung compliance.
why_others_wrong.E: Restrictive fibrotic disease typically reduces lung volumes, including functional residual capacity, rather than increasing it.

exam_trap: Candidates pick reduced elastic recoil (C), confusing fibrosis with emphysema; fibrotic lungs are stiff, with increased recoil, and need more pressure to inflate.
takeaway: Fibrosis → stiff lung → ↓ compliance → ↑ elastic recoil.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.; RCS England MRCS preparation resources, accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Compliance = volume change per unit pressure change ↓ fibrosis stiffens the lung and lowers compliance ↓ a stiff lung needs a larger pressure swing for the same tidal volume ↓ A greater pressure change is required to produce a given volume change
pearl: Fibrotic lungs give a restrictive pattern with a reduced FVC, a normal or raised FEV1/FVC ratio and low gas transfer, and ventilated patients need higher airway pressures to deliver the same tidal volume.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Cardiorespiratory physiology: surfactant
stem: A premature infant has insufficient pulmonary surfactant. Which physical effect is most directly increased?
why_correct: Pulmonary surfactant reduces alveolar surface tension. Deficiency therefore increases surface tension, promotes alveolar collapse and reduces lung compliance.

why_others_wrong.B: Surfactant deficiency raises alveolar surface tension, which reduces alveolar compliance (making the lungs stiffer), not increases it.
why_others_wrong.C: Surfactant acts at the alveolar air-liquid interface; its deficiency does not directly alter pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure.
why_others_wrong.D: Oxygen-carrying capacity depends on haemoglobin, not on alveolar surfactant, so it is not the variable directly increased by surfactant deficiency.
why_others_wrong.E: Surfactant deficiency is an alveolar surface-tension problem, not a stimulus for increased pleural fluid production.

exam_trap: Alveolar compliance is chosen by candidates who link surfactant with compliance, but deficiency reduces compliance; it is surface tension that increases.
takeaway: Surfactant ↓ surface tension → prevents alveolar collapse.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.; RCS England MRCS preparation resources, accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Premature infant with surfactant deficiency ↓ surfactant normally lowers alveolar surface tension ↓ without it surface tension rises and alveoli collapse ↓ Alveolar surface tension
pearl: Exogenous surfactant given via the endotracheal tube is a standard treatment for neonatal respiratory distress syndrome.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Cardiorespiratory physiology: dead space
stem: A mechanically ventilated patient has a large pulmonary embolus. Which change is expected in the affected lung regions?

options.C: Complete alveolar collapse in every region
options.D: Increased shunt fraction in the affected alveoli
options.E: Increased pulmonary capillary recruitment in the embolised region

why_correct: A pulmonary embolus obstructs pulmonary blood flow. Ventilated alveoli that receive little or no perfusion contribute to physiological dead space.

why_others_wrong.A: Perfusion without ventilation describes shunt, the mismatch pattern opposite to that produced by a pulmonary embolus.
why_others_wrong.C: A pulmonary embolus obstructs blood flow but does not cause the airways or alveoli themselves to collapse; ventilation to the affected region is typically preserved.
why_others_wrong.D: Shunt refers to units that are perfused but poorly ventilated; a pulmonary embolus produces the opposite pattern of ventilated but poorly perfused alveoli.
why_others_wrong.E: An embolus obstructs pulmonary blood flow, reducing rather than increasing capillary recruitment/perfusion in the affected region.

exam_trap: Shunt describes perfusion without adequate ventilation; pulmonary embolism produces the opposite problem.
takeaway: PE → ventilated but poorly perfused alveoli → ↑ dead space.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.; RCS England MRCS preparation resources, accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Large pulmonary embolus ↓ pulmonary blood flow is obstructed ↓ affected alveoli remain ventilated ↓ Ventilation without effective perfusion
pearl: In massive pulmonary embolism, hypoxaemia also arises from redistribution of flow to other lung regions and low mixed venous oxygen, not from dead space alone.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Cardiorespiratory physiology: oxygen diffusion
stem: Which change would most directly impair diffusion of oxygen across the alveolar-capillary membrane?
why_correct: Gas diffusion across the alveolar-capillary membrane is impaired by increased diffusion distance, such as occurs with interstitial fibrosis or pulmonary oedema.

why_others_wrong.A: A reduced membrane thickness would shorten the diffusion distance and improve, not impair, gas diffusion, per Fick's law.
why_others_wrong.B: An increased surface area provides more area for gas exchange and improves diffusion rather than impairing it.
why_others_wrong.D: Increased pulmonary blood flow alone improves oxygen uptake by maintaining a favourable diffusion gradient; it does not impair diffusion across the membrane.
why_others_wrong.E: A higher haemoglobin concentration increases the blood's capacity to bind diffused oxygen and helps maintain the diffusion gradient; it does not impair membrane diffusion.

exam_trap: Reduced membrane thickness is chosen by misreading the direction of change; a thinner membrane shortens diffusion distance and improves gas transfer.
takeaway: Thicker alveolar-capillary membrane → poorer gas diffusion.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.; RCS England MRCS preparation resources, accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Diffusion across the alveolar-capillary membrane ↓ Fick law: rate falls as membrane thickness rises ↓ thickening occurs with fibrosis or interstitial oedema ↓ Increased membrane thickness
pearl: Diffusion impairment classically worsens on exercise, when faster capillary transit leaves less time for equilibration, so desaturation on exertion is typical of interstitial lung disease.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Cardiorespiratory physiology: ventilatory control
stem: Which arterial blood-gas change provides the strongest normal chemical stimulus for increased ventilation?

options.A: Mild reduction in arterial oxygen from 100 to 90 mmHg

correct_answer: B. Increase in arterial carbon dioxide
why_correct: Under normal conditions, changes in arterial CO2 and resulting CSF hydrogen-ion concentration are powerful regulators of ventilation.

why_others_wrong.A: A mild fall in PaO2 within this range produces little peripheral chemoreceptor stimulation compared with the powerful and continuous drive provided by arterial CO2.
why_others_wrong.C: A rise in arterial oxygen does not stimulate ventilation; if anything it can mildly reduce peripheral chemoreceptor drive, the opposite of the effect described.
why_others_wrong.D: Plasma sodium is not a recognised chemical stimulus sensed by the respiratory chemoreceptors that regulate ventilation.
why_others_wrong.E: Haemoglobin concentration affects oxygen-carrying capacity but is not itself a chemical signal that chemoreceptors use to drive ventilation.

exam_trap: Peripheral oxygen sensing becomes particularly important when arterial oxygen falls substantially; normal ventilation is more strongly influenced by CO2.
takeaway: Normal ventilatory drive → particularly sensitive to CO2.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.; RCS England MRCS preparation resources, accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Strongest normal chemical drive to breathe ↓ small rises in PaCO2 raise CSF H+ at central chemoreceptors ↓ hypoxic drive becomes strong only at a markedly low PaO2 ↓ Increase in arterial carbon dioxide
pearl: The hypoxic ventilatory response rises steeply only when PaO2 falls well below normal, matching the steep part of the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve.

subject: Physiology
title: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care: thyroid hormone synthesis
stem: Iodide is transported into thyroid follicular cells and subsequently incorporated into tyrosine residues on thyroglobulin. Which enzyme catalyses this organification step?
why_correct: Thyroid peroxidase catalyses oxidation and organification of iodide and contributes to coupling reactions involved in thyroid hormone synthesis.

why_others_wrong.B: Thyroglobulin is the protein scaffold onto which iodinated tyrosine residues are incorporated; it is the substrate, not the enzyme performing organification.
why_others_wrong.C: Deiodinase removes iodine from thyroid hormones peripherally (e.g., converting T4 to T3) and plays no role in the initial organification step.
why_others_wrong.D: The TSH receptor mediates the general stimulatory signal from TSH to the follicular cell but does not itself catalyse iodide organification.
why_others_wrong.E: Adenylate cyclase is a downstream signalling enzyme in the TSH-cAMP pathway, not the enzyme responsible for iodide organification.

exam_trap: Thyroglobulin is the protein scaffold containing tyrosine residues; it is not the enzyme catalysing iodide organification.
takeaway: Iodide organification → thyroid peroxidase.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.; RCS England MRCS preparation resources, accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Iodide trapped by the sodium-iodide symporter ↓ oxidised and attached to tyrosine residues on thyroglobulin ↓ organification and coupling catalysed by thyroid peroxidase ↓ Thyroid peroxidase
pearl: Carbimazole and propylthiouracil act by inhibiting thyroid peroxidase, and anti-TPO antibodies are the typical serological marker of autoimmune thyroiditis.

subject: Physiology
title: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care: thyroid hormone transport
stem: Most circulating thyroid hormone is transported in plasma bound to proteins. Which fraction is biologically active at tissues?

options.E: Thyroglobulin-bound hormone inside the thyroid only

why_correct: Most circulating thyroid hormone is protein-bound, providing a circulating reservoir. The free fraction is available to enter tissues and exert biological effects.

why_others_wrong.A: The protein-bound fraction acts as an inactive circulating reservoir and is not available to act at tissues.
why_others_wrong.C: Thyroid hormone is not stored within erythrocytes; this is not a recognised physiological transport compartment.
why_others_wrong.D: Thyroid hormone is not stored inside platelets; this is not a physiological reservoir for circulating hormone.
why_others_wrong.E: Thyroglobulin-bound hormone is the intrathyroidal storage form prior to secretion, not the circulating bioactive fraction that acts at peripheral tissues.

exam_trap: Total T4 can change because of altered binding proteins without producing the same proportional change in free hormone.
takeaway: Free thyroid hormone = biologically available fraction.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.; RCS England MRCS preparation resources, accessed 26 September 2026.
thinking: Most thyroid hormone is bound to TBG, transthyretin and albumin ↓ the bound fraction is a circulating reservoir ↓ only free hormone enters cells and binds receptors ↓ Free hormone fraction
pearl: Pregnancy and oestrogen therapy raise TBG and total T4, so thyroid status should be judged on free T4 and TSH rather than total hormone levels.

subject: Physiology
