why_correct: T-helper 1 cells produce interferon-gamma, which promotes macrophage activation and contributes to cell-mediated immune responses. Interferon-gamma is particularly important in responses against intracellular pathogens.

why_others_wrong.B: Neutrophils are short-lived phagocytes and are not a major source of interferon-gamma.
why_others_wrong.C: Erythrocytes are anucleate and lack the machinery to secrete cytokines.
why_others_wrong.D: Platelets release growth factors and mediators relevant to haemostasis and repair, not interferon-gamma.
why_others_wrong.E: Fibroblasts are matrix-producing repair cells, not a source of this T-cell-derived cytokine.

exam_trap: Candidates choose neutrophils (B) as the main inflammatory cell, but they are not a major interferon-gamma source; Th1 cells (and NK cells) produce it.
takeaway: Th1 → IFN-γ → macrophage activation.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed, 2017.
thinking: Macrophage activation by interferon-gamma ↓ cell-mediated immunity ↓ T helper 1 cells secrete IFN-gamma ↓ Th1 cells
pearl: Patients receiving anti-TNF therapy are screened for latent tuberculosis, because the Th1 and TNF pathway is needed to keep mycobacteria contained within granulomas.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing: (untitled)
stem: A patient develops a granulomatous inflammatory response to a persistent intracellular pathogen. Which cytokine is particularly important in maintaining macrophage activation within the granuloma?
why_correct: Interferon-gamma produced by T cells, particularly Th1 cells, promotes macrophage activation and is central to cell-mediated responses against persistent intracellular pathogens.

why_others_wrong.B: Insulin is a metabolic hormone regulating glucose uptake and has no role in macrophage activation within granulomas.
why_others_wrong.C: Erythropoietin stimulates erythropoiesis and is unrelated to cell-mediated immunity against intracellular pathogens.
why_others_wrong.D: Thyroxine regulates metabolic rate and is not involved in granuloma maintenance.
why_others_wrong.E: Aldosterone is a mineralocorticoid regulating sodium/potassium balance, unrelated to macrophage activation.

exam_trap: Candidates may be distracted by unrelated hormones (B-E), but granuloma maintenance depends on interferon-gamma from Th1 cells activating macrophages.
takeaway: Granulomatous immunity → Th1/IFN-γ/macrophage axis.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed, 2017.
thinking: Granuloma around an intracellular pathogen ↓ Th1 cells secrete interferon-gamma ↓ sustained macrophage activation ↓ Interferon-gamma
pearl: The interferon-gamma release assay used to detect latent tuberculosis measures interferon-gamma production by T cells exposed to mycobacterial antigens.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing: (untitled)
stem: A patient develops tissue destruction after prolonged chronic inflammation. Which cell is particularly important in producing enzymes and reactive species that contribute to chronic inflammatory tissue injury?
why_correct: Activated macrophages can release reactive oxygen species, proteases, cytokines and growth factors. Persistent activation can therefore contribute both to tissue damage and to repair/fibrosis.

why_others_wrong.B: Erythrocytes are oxygen carriers, not inflammatory effector cells; they do not secrete proteases or mount the oxidative burst that drives chronic inflammatory tissue injury.
why_others_wrong.C: Platelets contribute growth factors and mediators to haemostasis and repair, but are not the principal source of chronic tissue-damaging enzymes and reactive species.
why_others_wrong.D: Adipocytes are lipid-storage cells and are not characteristically responsible for chronic inflammatory tissue injury.
why_others_wrong.E: Chondrocytes are matrix-producing cartilage cells, not inflammatory effector cells.

exam_trap: Candidates choose platelets (C) because they release mediators, but platelets mainly serve haemostasis and early repair; activated macrophages drive chronic tissue injury.
takeaway: Macrophages can drive both chronic injury and repair.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed, 2017.
thinking: Chronic inflammatory tissue destruction ↓ persistently activated macrophages ↓ release proteases and reactive oxygen species ↓ Activated macrophage
pearl: Macrophage-derived TGF-beta and PDGF also drive fibrosis, so the same cell contributes both to tissue destruction and to scarring in chronic inflammation.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Physiology: (untitled)
stem: A surgical wound is healing by formation of new blood vessels. Which process describes formation of new vessels from pre-existing vessels?
why_correct: Angiogenesis is the formation of new blood vessels from existing vascular structures. It is important in wound healing, chronic inflammation and tumour growth. Vasculogenesis refers primarily to formation of vessels from endothelial precursor cells, particularly during development.

why_others_wrong.A: Vasculogenesis refers to de novo vessel formation from endothelial precursor cells, mainly during embryonic development, rather than sprouting from pre-existing vessels.
why_others_wrong.C: Fibrosis refers to excess deposition of collagenous connective tissue, not new vessel formation.
why_others_wrong.D: Metaplasia is reversible replacement of one differentiated cell type by another and is unrelated to vascular growth.
why_others_wrong.E: Calcification is deposition of calcium salts in tissue and is unrelated to new vessel formation.

exam_trap: Candidates choose vasculogenesis (A) because it also forms vessels, but vasculogenesis is de novo formation from precursors; sprouting from existing vessels is angiogenesis.
takeaway: Existing vessels → new vessels = angiogenesis.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed, 2017.
thinking: New blood vessels in a healing wound ↓ sprouting from pre-existing vessels ↓ angiogenesis ↓ Angiogenesis
pearl: Granulation tissue looks red and granular because of the numerous new capillary loops formed by angiogenesis, and it bleeds easily when touched.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Physiology: (untitled)
stem: Which growth factor is particularly important in stimulating endothelial proliferation and angiogenesis?
why_correct: Vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) stimulates endothelial cell proliferation, migration and new vessel formation. VEGF has major roles in wound healing and tumour-associated angiogenesis.

why_others_wrong.B: Erythropoietin stimulates erythroid precursor proliferation in the bone marrow, not endothelial proliferation.
why_others_wrong.C: Calcitonin regulates calcium homeostasis and has no angiogenic role.
why_others_wrong.D: Troponin is a cardiac contractile regulatory protein used as a marker of myocardial infarction, unrelated to angiogenesis.
why_others_wrong.E: Albumin is the major plasma oncotic protein and has no growth-factor activity on endothelium.

exam_trap: Candidates choose erythropoietin (B) because it is also hypoxia-driven, but it stimulates red cell production; VEGF drives endothelial proliferation.
takeaway: VEGF = major angiogenic growth factor.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed, 2017.
thinking: Endothelial proliferation and new vessels ↓ hypoxia induces HIF ↓ HIF drives VEGF expression ↓ VEGF
pearl: Anti-VEGF agents such as bevacizumab impair wound healing and increase the risk of anastomotic and wound complications, so they are usually stopped for several weeks around elective surgery.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing: (untitled)
stem: A patient has a wound containing abundant granulation tissue. Which combination best describes granulation tissue?

options.C: Mature dense collagen with no vessels

correct_answer: B. New capillaries and proliferating fibroblasts
why_correct: Granulation tissue consists of proliferating capillaries, fibroblasts and inflammatory cells within a loose extracellular matrix. It is characteristic of the proliferative phase of wound healing.

why_others_wrong.A: Necrotic tissue and bacteria describe an infected, non-viable wound bed, the opposite of the organised reparative tissue that granulation tissue represents.
why_others_wrong.C: Mature dense collagen with no vessels describes a remodelled scar, not the vascular, cellular tissue of the proliferative phase.
why_others_wrong.D: Cartilage and bone are irrelevant tissue types not formed during soft-tissue wound repair.
why_others_wrong.E: Adipocytes and skeletal muscle are normal tissue elements, not the reparative granulation response.

exam_trap: Candidates choose mature dense collagen (C), but that describes a remodelled scar; granulation tissue is vascular and cellular, composed of new capillaries and fibroblasts.
takeaway: Granulation tissue = new vessels + fibroblasts.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed, 2017.
thinking: Granulation tissue ↓ new capillary loops ↓ proliferating fibroblasts in loose matrix with inflammatory cells ↓ New capillaries and proliferating fibroblasts
pearl: Over-granulation (hypergranulation) above the level of the skin can delay epithelialisation and is commonly treated with pressure or topical steroid application.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Physiology: (untitled)
stem: Which process is primarily responsible for increasing the tensile strength of a healing wound during the later stages of repair?
why_correct: As wounds mature, collagen is reorganised and remodelled. Cross-linking and replacement of early collagen with stronger, better-organised collagen increase tensile strength. Wound strength increases progressively but does not normally return completely to the strength of uninjured tissue.

why_others_wrong.A: Neutrophil recruitment is an early inflammatory event that clears debris and contributes little to late tensile-strength gains.
why_others_wrong.C: Histamine release is an early mediator of vascular permeability with no role in late structural wound strengthening.
why_others_wrong.D: Platelet aggregation occurs immediately after injury during haemostasis, not during late remodelling.
why_others_wrong.E: Endothelial contraction is an acute mechanism of increased vascular permeability, unrelated to collagen cross-linking and scar strength.

exam_trap: Candidates choose platelet aggregation (D) or neutrophil recruitment (A), but these occur early; late tensile strength comes from collagen remodelling and cross-linking.
takeaway: Late wound healing = collagen remodelling → increased strength.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed, 2017.
thinking: Later stages of repair ↓ collagen reorganised and cross-linked ↓ type III replaced by type I ↓ Collagen remodelling and cross-linking
pearl: Lysyl oxidase, a copper-dependent enzyme, forms the covalent cross-links that give collagen fibres much of their tensile strength.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing: (untitled)
stem: A patient develops a wound complication because excessive matrix metalloproteinase activity is degrading extracellular matrix. Which molecule normally helps inhibit matrix metalloproteinases?
why_correct: Tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases (TIMPs) regulate matrix metalloproteinase activity and therefore help control extracellular matrix degradation during tissue remodelling. An imbalance between MMP activity and inhibition can contribute to excessive matrix degradation.

why_others_wrong.B: Histamine is a vasoactive amine affecting vessel permeability and has no inhibitory action on matrix metalloproteinases.
why_others_wrong.C: Thrombin is a coagulation protease that converts fibrinogen to fibrin; it does not restrain matrix metalloproteinase activity.
why_others_wrong.D: Albumin is a plasma protein with an oncotic function, not an MMP inhibitor.
why_others_wrong.E: Haemoglobin is an oxygen-carrying protein in erythrocytes and is unrelated to MMP regulation.

exam_trap: Candidates choose thrombin (C) because it is a well-known protease regulator in healing, but it is itself a coagulation protease; TIMPs are the endogenous MMP inhibitors.
takeaway: MMPs degrade matrix; TIMPs restrain MMP activity.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed, 2017.
thinking: Excessive MMP activity degrading matrix ↓ endogenous inhibitors ↓ tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases ↓ Tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases
pearl: Chronic wound fluid typically contains high MMP and low TIMP activity, which degrades growth factors and new matrix and contributes to non-healing ulcers.

subject: Plastic surgery
title: Plastic surgery: keloid versus hypertrophic scar
stem: A patient develops a hypertrophic scar following surgery. Which feature distinguishes a hypertrophic scar from a keloid?

options.A: It extends beyond the original wound boundaries
options.B: It remains confined to the original wound boundaries
options.D: It is caused by bacterial infection
options.E: It is always associated with malignancy

correct_answer: B. It remains confined to the original wound boundaries
why_correct: Hypertrophic scars remain within the boundaries of the original wound and may regress over time. Keloids extend beyond the original wound margins and may continue to enlarge.

why_others_wrong.A: Extending beyond the original wound boundaries is the defining feature of a keloid, not of a hypertrophic scar.
why_others_wrong.C: Hypertrophic scars contain an excess of collagen laid down in nodules, so an absence of collagen is incorrect.
why_others_wrong.D: Hypertrophic scarring results from excessive fibroblast activity during healing, often with tension or delayed healing, not from bacterial infection itself.
why_others_wrong.E: Hypertrophic scars are benign fibroproliferative lesions; malignant change in a scar, such as a Marjolin ulcer, is rare and not a distinguishing feature.

exam_trap: Option A is the keloid definition; candidates reverse the two, but extension beyond the original wound margins identifies a keloid, not a hypertrophic scar.
takeaway: Hypertrophic = within wound. Keloid = beyond wound.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed, 2017.
thinking: Hypertrophic scar versus keloid ↓ both are raised and contain excess collagen ↓ a hypertrophic scar stays within the wound and often regresses ↓ a keloid spreads beyond it ↓ It remains confined to the original wound boundaries
pearl: Tension across a wound, as over joints or the sternum, promotes hypertrophic scarring, which is why incisions placed along relaxed skin tension lines heal with finer scars.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: GI physiology & metabolism: (untitled)
stem: A patient develops acute pancreatitis with destruction of surrounding fat. Which type of necrosis is particularly characteristic of this process?
why_correct: Pancreatic lipases can digest adipose tissue, releasing fatty acids that combine with calcium to form soaps, producing enzymatic fat necrosis. This can produce chalky deposits around the pancreas.

why_others_wrong.A: Coagulative necrosis is typical of ischaemic infarction in solid organs such as the heart and kidney, not enzymatic fat destruction.
why_others_wrong.B: Liquefactive necrosis is typical of cerebral infarction and abscesses; it does not produce the calcium soaps seen in pancreatitis.
why_others_wrong.C: Caseous necrosis is the cheese-like necrosis of tuberculosis and some fungal infections.
why_others_wrong.E: Fibrinoid necrosis affects vessel walls in immune-mediated vasculitis and malignant hypertension, not peripancreatic fat.

exam_trap: Liquefactive necrosis (option B) tempts because enzymes are involved, but saponification of fat with calcium soaps is unique to enzymatic fat necrosis.
takeaway: Pancreatitis + peripancreatic fat destruction = enzymatic fat necrosis.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed, 2017.
thinking: Acute pancreatitis ↓ released pancreatic lipase digests peripancreatic fat ↓ fatty acids combine with calcium to form soaps ↓ Fat necrosis
pearl: Calcium sequestration in saponified fat contributes to hypocalcaemia in severe acute pancreatitis, and a low calcium is one of the markers used in severity scoring.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing: (untitled)
stem: A patient with severe hypertension develops fibrinoid necrosis within the wall of a small artery. Which process best describes fibrinoid necrosis?

options.A: Accumulation of lipid in the intima
options.B: Deposition of fibrin-like material within the damaged vessel wall

correct_answer: B. Deposition of fibrin-like material within the damaged vessel wall
why_correct: Fibrinoid necrosis occurs in certain vascular injuries, particularly immune-mediated vasculitis and severe hypertension. Plasma proteins, including fibrin, become deposited in the damaged vessel wall, producing a bright eosinophilic appearance microscopically.

why_others_wrong.A: Accumulation of lipid in the intima describes atherosclerotic change, not fibrinoid necrosis.
why_others_wrong.C: Complete liquefaction of tissue describes liquefactive necrosis, a different pattern from the fibrin deposition seen in fibrinoid necrosis.
why_others_wrong.D: Enzymatic digestion of adipose tissue describes fat necrosis, unrelated to vessel wall pathology.
why_others_wrong.E: Formation of a granuloma is a chronic inflammatory nodule of activated macrophages, not a necrotic vascular wall lesion.

exam_trap: Candidates choose accumulation of lipid in the intima (A) because hypertension is linked with atheroma, but fibrinoid necrosis is fibrin-like protein deposition in a damaged vessel wall.
takeaway: Fibrinoid necrosis = vascular wall injury + fibrin-like deposition.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed, 2017.
thinking: Severe hypertension ↓ small artery wall damage ↓ plasma proteins including fibrin deposited in the wall ↓ Deposition of fibrin-like material within the damaged vessel wall
pearl: Fibrinoid necrosis of arterioles is the hallmark lesion of malignant (accelerated) hypertension and is also seen in vasculitides such as polyarteritis nodosa.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Anatomy: (untitled)
stem: A patient has a thrombus forming in a deep vein. Which process describes extension of the thrombus along the direction of blood flow?
why_correct: Propagation refers to extension of a thrombus by further deposition of platelets and fibrin. A thrombus may subsequently undergo organisation, recanalisation, resolution or embolisation.

why_others_wrong.A: Organisation is ingrowth of granulation tissue, fibroblasts and capillaries into an established thrombus, which incorporates it into the vessel wall rather than extending it.
why_others_wrong.C: Recanalisation is formation of new channels through an organised thrombus that partly restore flow, not further growth of the thrombus.
why_others_wrong.D: Embolisation is detachment of thrombus fragments that travel downstream and lodge elsewhere, whereas the stem describes the thrombus itself enlarging.
why_others_wrong.E: Resolution is removal of a thrombus by fibrinolysis, the opposite of extension by further deposition of platelets and fibrin.

exam_trap: Embolisation tempts because thrombus travels downstream, but it means fragments detaching and lodging elsewhere; propagation is the thrombus itself extending along the flow.
takeaway: Thrombus gets bigger = propagation.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed, 2017.
thinking: Thrombus forming in a deep vein ↓ it extends in the direction of blood flow ↓ growth by further deposition of platelets and fibrin ↓ Propagation
pearl: Calf vein thrombi can propagate proximally into the popliteal and femoral veins, where the risk of pulmonary embolism is much higher, which is why proximal DVT is normally anticoagulated.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Physiology: (untitled)
stem: A venous thrombus becomes partially incorporated into the vessel wall and develops channels through which blood can flow. Which process has occurred?
why_correct: Older thrombi can become organised by ingrowth of endothelial cells, smooth muscle cells and fibroblasts. New vascular channels may then develop through the thrombus, a process known as recanalisation.

why_others_wrong.A: Propagation refers to extension/growth of the thrombus along the vessel, the opposite of incorporation with new channel formation.
why_others_wrong.C: Immediate lysis describes rapid fibrinolytic dissolution of the clot, not gradual fibrous incorporation with new vascular channels.
why_others_wrong.D: Arterial embolisation describes a fragment breaking off and lodging elsewhere, not local organisation of the thrombus in situ.
why_others_wrong.E: Vasospasm is a transient, smooth-muscle-mediated narrowing of the vessel, unrelated to structural change within an existing thrombus.

exam_trap: Candidates choose propagation (A) because the thrombus changes over time, but propagation is extension of clot; incorporation with new channels is organisation and recanalisation.
takeaway: Old thrombus → organisation → possible recanalisation.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed, 2017.
thinking: Venous thrombus ageing ↓ ingrowth of endothelial cells, smooth muscle and fibroblasts ↓ new channels re-establish flow ↓ Organisation and recanalisation
pearl: Post-thrombotic syndrome arises because organisation and recanalisation of a deep vein thrombus often damage the venous valves, causing chronic venous hypertension.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Pathology: oncology & haematology: (untitled)
stem: A patient develops a pulmonary embolus originating from a lower-limb deep vein. Which feature of venous blood flow is particularly important in the development of deep venous thrombosis?
why_correct: Virchow's triad consists of endothelial injury, abnormal blood flow such as stasis or turbulence, and hypercoagulability. Venous stasis is particularly important in the development of lower-limb DVT.

why_others_wrong.A: Endothelium is present in deep veins; endothelial injury is a separate limb of Virchow's triad, and the question asks about a feature of blood flow.
why_others_wrong.C: Pulsatility is a feature of arterial flow, whereas deep venous thrombosis is driven by slow, low-pressure flow and stasis in the veins.
why_others_wrong.D: Lymphatic drainage returns interstitial fluid and does not govern venous flow; increased drainage would not promote thrombus formation.
why_others_wrong.E: Pulmonary ventilation concerns gas exchange in the lungs and is not a feature of lower-limb venous blood flow contributing to DVT.

exam_trap: Absence of endothelial cells tempts as a nod to endothelial injury, but that is the separate vessel-wall limb of Virchow's triad, not a feature of venous flow.
takeaway: DVT risk = think Virchow triad, especially stasis.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed, 2017.
thinking: Lower-limb DVT leading to pulmonary embolism ↓ the question asks about a feature of venous blood flow ↓ the flow limb of Virchow's triad in low-pressure veins is stasis ↓ Venous stasis
pearl: Early mobilisation and intermittent pneumatic compression after surgery work by counteracting venous stasis in the calf, complementing pharmacological prophylaxis.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Pathology: oncology & haematology: (untitled)
stem: A patient with prolonged immobilisation develops a thrombus in the calf. Which change associated with venous stasis promotes thrombosis?

options.A: Increased clearance of activated clotting factors
options.B: Reduced contact between platelets and endothelium
options.C: Accumulation of activated clotting factors and reduced washout

correct_answer: C. Accumulation of activated clotting factors and reduced washout
why_correct: Stasis reduces normal blood-flow-mediated dilution and clearance of activated coagulation factors and can bring platelets and leukocytes into closer contact with the endothelium. This promotes thrombus formation.

why_others_wrong.A: Stasis reduces, rather than increases, the flow-mediated dilution and clearance of activated clotting factors, allowing them to accumulate locally.
why_others_wrong.B: Stasis brings platelets and leukocytes into closer contact with the endothelium by disrupting laminar flow, so reduced contact is the opposite of what occurs.
why_others_wrong.D: Stasis in calf veins tends to cause local hypoxia rather than increased arterial oxygenation, and arterial oxygen content does not explain venous thrombosis.
why_others_wrong.E: Immobilisation reduces the muscle-pump action that drives both venous and lymphatic flow, and increased lymphatic flow would not promote thrombosis.

exam_trap: Reduced contact between platelets and endothelium sounds logical with slow flow, but stasis disrupts laminar flow and brings platelets closer to the endothelium.
takeaway: Stasis = less washout + more coagulation-factor accumulation.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed, 2017.
thinking: Prolonged immobilisation ↓ venous stasis in the calf ↓ less washout and dilution of activated clotting factors ↓ platelets and leukocytes contact the endothelium ↓ Accumulation of activated clotting factors and reduced washout
pearl: The valve pockets of calf veins are the classic site of thrombus initiation, because flow there is slowest and local hypoxia activates the endothelium.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Pathology: oncology & haematology: (untitled)
stem: A patient has an inherited thrombophilia caused by a factor V mutation that makes factor V resistant to activated protein C. Which abnormality is present?
why_correct: Factor V Leiden is a factor V mutation that reduces its inactivation by activated protein C, producing a prothrombotic state. It is a common inherited thrombophilia.

why_others_wrong.B: Haemophilia A is an X-linked deficiency of factor VIII that causes bleeding, not a prothrombotic state from activated protein C resistance.
why_others_wrong.C: Von Willebrand disease impairs platelet adhesion and factor VIII stability, producing a bleeding tendency rather than thrombophilia.
why_others_wrong.D: Protein C deficiency is a thrombophilia caused by low levels of protein C itself, whereas here factor V is abnormal and protein C is normal.
why_others_wrong.E: Antithrombin deficiency reduces inhibition of thrombin and factor Xa and does not involve a factor V mutation resisting activated protein C.

exam_trap: Factor V Leiden is not a deficiency of factor V. It is resistance to activated protein C.
takeaway: Factor V Leiden = APC-resistant factor V.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed, 2017.
thinking: Inherited thrombophilia ↓ mutant factor V ↓ factor Va resists inactivation by activated protein C ↓ Factor V Leiden
pearl: Factor V Leiden is the commonest inherited thrombophilia in people of European ancestry, and oestrogen-containing contraception substantially increases venous thromboembolism risk in carriers.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care: (untitled)
stem: A patient with severe atherosclerosis has a plaque that suddenly ruptures. Which event most directly converts the disrupted plaque into an acute occlusive thrombus?
correct_answer: A. Exposure of thrombogenic subendothelial material
why_correct: Plaque disruption exposes thrombogenic material, including tissue factor and components of the extracellular matrix. Platelet adhesion, activation and aggregation then occur, with activation of the coagulation cascade. This can produce an acute arterial thrombus.

why_others_wrong.B: Increased lymphatic drainage is irrelevant to arterial plaque rupture and the formation of an occlusive clot.
why_others_wrong.C: Reduced platelet adhesion is the opposite of what happens; plaque rupture increases platelet adhesion to the exposed subendothelium.
why_others_wrong.D: Increased nitric oxide production is antithrombotic and vasodilatory; endothelial injury typically reduces, not increases, its bioavailability.
why_others_wrong.E: Decreased tissue factor exposure is the opposite of what occurs; rupture exposes tissue factor, which drives activation of the coagulation cascade.

exam_trap: Candidates choose decreased tissue factor exposure (E) or increased nitric oxide (D), but rupture exposes tissue factor and impairs nitric oxide, promoting thrombosis.
takeaway: Plaque rupture → thrombogenic surface exposed → platelet/coagulation activation.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed, 2017.
thinking: Plaque rupture ↓ exposed lipid core with tissue factor and collagen ↓ platelet adhesion and coagulation activation ↓ Exposure of thrombogenic subendothelial material
pearl: Vulnerable plaques have a thin fibrous cap and a large lipid core, which is why many acute coronary syndromes arise from plaques that were not severely stenotic beforehand.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Physiology: (untitled)
stem: A patient with a myocardial infarction develops a ventricular aneurysm several weeks later. Which process is primarily responsible for formation of the aneurysm?

options.B: Replacement of infarcted myocardium by scar tissue
options.D: New formation of functional cardiac muscle
options.E: Immediate coagulative necrosis of the pericardium

correct_answer: B. Replacement of infarcted myocardium by scar tissue
why_correct: Mature cardiomyocytes have very limited regenerative capacity. Following a large myocardial infarction, the damaged myocardium is progressively replaced by fibrous scar tissue. The scar can become thin and dyskinetic, producing a ventricular aneurysm.

why_others_wrong.A: Continued neutrophil infiltration without repair describes ongoing acute inflammation rather than the fibrous scarring process that actually thins and weakens the wall.
why_others_wrong.C: Regeneration of mature cardiomyocytes does not occur to any significant degree in adults, so this cannot explain aneurysm formation.
why_others_wrong.D: New formation of functional cardiac muscle does not happen; the infarcted area is replaced by non-contractile scar, not new functional myocardium.
why_others_wrong.E: Immediate coagulative necrosis of the pericardium is incorrect both in tissue (the process affects myocardium) and in timing (the aneurysm evolves over weeks via scarring, not an acute pericardial event).

exam_trap: The adult myocardium does not regenerate sufficiently to replace a large infarct with normal contractile tissue.
takeaway: MI → cardiomyocyte loss → scar → possible ventricular aneurysm.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed, 2017.
thinking: Large myocardial infarct ↓ cardiomyocytes cannot regenerate ↓ replaced by thin non-contractile scar ↓ dyskinetic bulging wall ↓ Replacement of infarcted myocardium by scar tissue
pearl: A left ventricular aneurysm should be suspected with persistent ST elevation weeks after infarction, and it predisposes to mural thrombus, arrhythmia and heart failure.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Pathology: oncology & haematology: (untitled)
stem: A tumour suppressor protein is activated following DNA damage and prevents progression through the cell cycle. Which protein is most directly responsible for this response?
why_correct: p53 is activated in response to cellular stress, particularly DNA damage. It can induce cell-cycle arrest, allowing DNA repair, or trigger apoptosis when the damage is too severe. Loss of p53 function therefore permits cells with damaged DNA to continue proliferating.

why_others_wrong.A: RAS is a proto-oncogene encoding a small GTPase that transmits growth signals; activating mutations drive proliferation rather than DNA-damage arrest.
why_others_wrong.B: MYC is a proto-oncogene transcription factor that promotes cell-cycle progression and growth, so it drives proliferation rather than halting it.
why_others_wrong.D: HER2 is a growth-factor receptor tyrosine kinase whose amplification promotes proliferation, notably in breast cancer, not a DNA-damage checkpoint protein.
why_others_wrong.E: Cyclin D partners with CDK4/6 to phosphorylate Rb and push cells from G1 into S phase, so it promotes rather than blocks progression.

exam_trap: p53 is a tumour suppressor, whereas RAS and MYC are associated with oncogenic signalling.
takeaway: DNA damage → p53 → arrest/repair or apoptosis.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed, 2017.
thinking: Tumour suppressor activated after DNA damage ↓ it halts the cell cycle to allow repair ↓ it triggers apoptosis if the damage is severe ↓ p53
pearl: p53 induces p21, a cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor that keeps Rb hypophosphorylated, linking the DNA-damage response to the G1/S checkpoint.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Pathology: oncology & haematology: (untitled)
stem: A carcinoma contains a mutation causing constitutive activation of a small GTP-binding signalling protein. Which oncogene is classically associated with this mechanism?
why_correct: RAS proteins are small GTPases involved in intracellular signalling downstream of growth-factor receptors. Mutations can impair GTP hydrolysis, resulting in persistent signalling through pathways promoting proliferation and survival.

why_others_wrong.B: RB is a tumour suppressor gene encoding a nuclear protein that restrains the G1/S transition, not a small GTP-binding signalling protein.
why_others_wrong.C: APC is a tumour suppressor that promotes degradation of beta-catenin in the Wnt pathway; it is inactivated, not constitutively activated, in colorectal tumours.
why_others_wrong.D: BRCA1 is a tumour suppressor involved in homologous recombination repair of DNA double-strand breaks, not a GTPase oncogene.
why_others_wrong.E: TP53 is a tumour suppressor encoding a transcription factor that responds to DNA damage, not a small GTP-binding signalling protein.

exam_trap: RAS is an oncogene; RB, APC and TP53 are tumour suppressor genes.
takeaway: RAS mutation → persistent growth signalling.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed, 2017.
thinking: Small GTP-binding signalling protein ↓ activating mutations impair GTP hydrolysis ↓ the protein stays switched on downstream of growth-factor receptors ↓ RAS
pearl: KRAS mutation in colorectal cancer predicts lack of benefit from anti-EGFR antibodies such as cetuximab, so RAS status is tested before these drugs are used.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Colorectal surgery: (untitled)
stem: A patient has a colorectal tumour caused by loss of function of a tumour suppressor involved in the Wnt signalling pathway. Which gene is most strongly associated with this mechanism?
why_correct: APC is a tumour suppressor involved in regulation of the Wnt/β-catenin pathway. Loss of APC function promotes accumulation of β-catenin and transcription of genes promoting cellular proliferation. APC mutation is a major early event in the conventional colorectal adenoma-carcinoma sequence.

why_others_wrong.B: RAS is an oncogene activated by gain-of-function mutation in growth-factor signalling, not a tumour suppressor regulating Wnt/beta-catenin.
why_others_wrong.C: MYC is an oncogene and a downstream transcriptional target of beta-catenin, so it is activated rather than lost in Wnt-driven tumours.
why_others_wrong.D: BRAF is an oncogene in the MAPK pathway, activated in serrated-pathway colorectal cancers, and is not a Wnt-pathway tumour suppressor.
why_others_wrong.E: HER2 is a receptor tyrosine kinase oncogene activated by amplification, mainly in breast and gastric cancer, not a Wnt tumour suppressor.

exam_trap: BRAF and RAS tempt because they appear in colorectal cancer pathways, but they are activated oncogenes; the Wnt tumour suppressor lost early in the sequence is APC.
takeaway: Colorectal adenoma sequence → think APC/Wnt/β-catenin.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed, 2017.
thinking: Colorectal tumour ↓ loss of a Wnt-pathway tumour suppressor ↓ beta-catenin accumulates and drives proliferation ↓ early event in the adenoma-carcinoma sequence ↓ APC
pearl: A germline APC mutation causes familial adenomatous polyposis with hundreds of colorectal adenomas, so prophylactic colectomy or proctocolectomy is offered, usually in early adulthood.

subject: Genetics
title: Genetics: APC and beta-catenin
stem: A patient has a mutation affecting a protein that normally restrains β-catenin-mediated transcription. What is the expected consequence of loss of APC function?

options.E: Increased apoptosis in all epithelial cells

why_correct: APC normally contributes to the destruction of cytoplasmic β-catenin. Loss of APC function allows β-catenin to accumulate and enter the nucleus, where it activates transcription of genes involved in proliferation.

why_others_wrong.A: Reduced signalling is the opposite of the expected effect, because APC normally promotes beta-catenin destruction, so its loss lets beta-catenin accumulate.
why_others_wrong.C: Loss of APC removes a brake on proliferation, driving growth through beta-catenin target genes rather than inhibiting cell division.
why_others_wrong.D: APC is a tumour suppressor in the Wnt pathway and has no role in increasing mismatch repair, which depends on genes such as MLH1 and MSH2.
why_others_wrong.E: APC loss favours cell survival and proliferation through beta-catenin signalling rather than causing widespread apoptosis in epithelial cells.

exam_trap: Reduced beta-catenin signalling is chosen by candidates who equate loss of a gene with loss of signalling; APC is a brake, so its loss increases signalling.
takeaway: APC loss → β-catenin accumulation → proliferation.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed, 2017.
thinking: APC normally promotes destruction of cytoplasmic beta-catenin ↓ loss of APC lets beta-catenin accumulate ↓ beta-catenin enters the nucleus ↓ proliferative target genes activated ↓ Increased beta-catenin signalling
pearl: APC loss is an early gatekeeper event in the adenoma-carcinoma sequence, followed by mutations such as KRAS and TP53 as adenomas progress to carcinoma.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Pathology: oncology & haematology: (untitled)
stem: A patient has a hereditary cancer syndrome caused by defective mismatch repair. Which molecular abnormality is particularly characteristic?
why_correct: Defective DNA mismatch repair causes accumulation of replication errors, particularly in repetitive DNA sequences known as microsatellites. This produces microsatellite instability. Lynch syndrome is associated with inherited defects in mismatch-repair genes.

why_others_wrong.B: Excess collagen synthesis is a feature of fibrosis and scarring and bears no relation to failed correction of DNA replication errors.
why_others_wrong.C: Mismatch repair acts on nuclear DNA replication errors, and its failure does not cause increased mitochondrial DNA replication.
why_others_wrong.D: Mismatch-repair deficiency does not abolish telomerase activity; many cancers instead reactivate telomerase to achieve replicative immortality.
why_others_wrong.E: Failure of haemoglobin synthesis underlies conditions such as thalassaemia, not the replication errors of defective mismatch repair.

exam_trap: Loss of all telomerase activity tempts as another genome-maintenance term, but mismatch-repair failure produces microsatellite instability, and most cancers actually reactivate telomerase.
takeaway: Mismatch-repair failure → microsatellite instability.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed, 2017.
thinking: Hereditary syndrome with defective mismatch repair ↓ replication errors go uncorrected ↓ errors accumulate in short repetitive sequences ↓ Microsatellite instability
pearl: In the UK newly diagnosed colorectal cancers are tested for mismatch-repair deficiency to identify Lynch syndrome, and mismatch-repair deficient tumours often respond well to immune checkpoint inhibitors.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Pathology: oncology & haematology: (untitled)
stem: A tumour continues to proliferate despite becoming distant from its original blood supply. Which adaptation particularly supports continued tumour growth under hypoxic conditions?
why_correct: Tumour hypoxia can promote expression of hypoxia-inducible pathways that increase VEGF production. VEGF stimulates angiogenesis, providing additional vascular supply to the growing tumour. Tumour-associated vessels are often structurally abnormal and inefficient.

why_others_wrong.B: Hypoxic tumour cells increase rather than reduce glycolysis, shifting to anaerobic metabolism to generate ATP when oxygen is scarce.
why_others_wrong.C: Tumour cells surviving hypoxia become less dependent on oxygen through glycolytic metabolism, so increased dependence would hinder growth.
why_others_wrong.D: Tumours commonly retain or overexpress growth-factor receptors to sustain proliferation, so losing them all would not support growth.
why_others_wrong.E: Endothelial migration is required for new vessel formation, so suppressing it would oppose the angiogenesis that sustains hypoxic tumours.

exam_trap: Reduced glycolysis tempts as an energy-saving response, but hypoxic tumour cells increase glycolysis; the adaptation that restores supply is VEGF-driven angiogenesis.
takeaway: Tumour hypoxia → angiogenic signalling → VEGF.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed, 2017.
thinking: Tumour outgrowing its blood supply ↓ hypoxia stabilises hypoxia-inducible factor ↓ HIF drives VEGF transcription ↓ VEGF-mediated angiogenesis
pearl: Bevacizumab is an anti-VEGF antibody used in metastatic colorectal cancer; because it impairs wound healing, it is withheld around elective surgery.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Pathology: oncology & haematology: (untitled)
stem: A carcinoma spreads from its primary site to regional lymph nodes. Which route of dissemination is being demonstrated?
why_correct: Carcinomas commonly spread initially through lymphatic channels to regional lymph nodes. Sarcomas more commonly demonstrate haematogenous dissemination, although both carcinomas and sarcomas can use multiple routes.

why_others_wrong.A: Haematogenous spread carries tumour cells through blood vessels to distant organs such as the liver and lungs, not to regional lymph nodes.
why_others_wrong.C: Transcoelomic spread seeds tumour across serosal surfaces of body cavities such as the peritoneum or pleura, not along lymphatic channels to nodes.
why_others_wrong.D: Perineural spread tracks along nerve sheaths, as in head and neck or pancreatic cancers, rather than reaching regional lymph nodes.
why_others_wrong.E: Direct endocrine spread is not a recognised route of tumour dissemination; endocrine refers to hormone secretion into the blood.

exam_trap: Haematogenous spread is chosen by candidates who equate any metastasis with blood-borne spread, but deposits in regional lymph nodes reflect lymphatic dissemination.
takeaway: Carcinoma → commonly lymphatic spread.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed, 2017.
thinking: Carcinoma spreading to regional lymph nodes ↓ carcinomas typically disseminate first via lymphatics ↓ sarcomas favour blood-borne spread ↓ Lymphatic spread
pearl: Sentinel lymph node biopsy exploits orderly lymphatic spread: if the first draining node is clear in breast cancer or melanoma, more extensive nodal dissection can usually be avoided.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Acute abdomen & GI surgery: (untitled)
stem: A patient has a large intra-abdominal tumour that deposits multiple tumour nodules across the peritoneal surfaces. Which route of spread is most likely?
why_correct: Tumours arising within or adjacent to serous cavities can disseminate across the cavity surfaces. This is termed transcoelomic spread. Peritoneal dissemination is an important route for several abdominal and pelvic malignancies.

why_others_wrong.B: Lymphatic dissemination carries tumour to regional lymph nodes, which does not explain multiple nodules implanted across the peritoneal surfaces.
why_others_wrong.C: Haematogenous spread typically produces deposits within organs such as the liver and lungs rather than implants scattered over serosal surfaces.
why_others_wrong.D: Perineural spread tracks along nerves locally and does not produce widespread nodules on the peritoneal surfaces.
why_others_wrong.E: Intracellular migration is not a route of tumour dissemination; tumour cells move between tissues, not within other cells.

exam_trap: Haematogenous dissemination tempts because it is common, but blood-borne deposits lie within organs; implants scattered over the peritoneal surface indicate transcoelomic spread.
takeaway: Peritoneal tumour deposits → think transcoelomic spread.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed, 2017.
thinking: Large intra-abdominal tumour ↓ multiple nodules across the peritoneal surfaces ↓ cells shed into the cavity and implant on serosa ↓ Transcoelomic dissemination
pearl: Ovarian and gastric cancers commonly spread transcoelomically, producing omental cake and malignant ascites; selected patients are treated with cytoreductive surgery in specialist centres.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Pathology: oncology & haematology: (untitled)
stem: A patient with a malignant tumour develops severe weight loss and muscle wasting despite apparently adequate food intake. Which term describes this syndrome?
why_correct: Cancer cachexia is a multifactorial syndrome involving weight loss, muscle wasting and metabolic abnormalities. Inflammatory cytokines and tumour-related metabolic changes contribute to the process. It is not simply equivalent to starvation.

why_others_wrong.B: Hypertrophy is an increase in cell size, usually in response to increased workload, which is the opposite of the muscle wasting described.
why_others_wrong.C: Metaplasia is replacement of one mature cell type by another, a local tissue adaptation that does not cause systemic weight loss.
why_others_wrong.D: Oedema is accumulation of interstitial fluid, which may mask weight loss but does not explain progressive muscle wasting.
why_others_wrong.E: Sarcoidosis is a granulomatous multisystem disease, not the syndrome of weight loss and muscle wasting driven by a malignant tumour.

exam_trap: Oedema tempts because fluid retention can mask weight change, but it does not explain muscle wasting; tumour-driven weight and muscle loss despite intake is cachexia.
takeaway: Cancer + involuntary weight/muscle loss = cachexia.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed, 2017.
thinking: Malignant tumour ↓ weight loss and muscle wasting despite adequate intake ↓ cytokine-driven catabolism rather than starvation ↓ Cachexia
pearl: Cachexia increases post-operative complications, so nutritional screening and pre-operative optimisation with dietetic input are part of enhanced recovery pathways for major cancer surgery.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: (untitled)
stem: A patient develops profound polyuria following a neurosurgical procedure. Which hormone deficiency is most directly responsible for inability to concentrate the urine?
why_correct: Antidiuretic hormone promotes water reabsorption in the collecting ducts by increasing insertion of aquaporin-2 channels into the apical membrane of principal cells. Deficiency causes central diabetes insipidus with excessive production of dilute urine.

why_others_wrong.A: Aldosterone regulates sodium and potassium balance rather than collecting duct water permeability; its deficiency would not directly cause this concentrating defect.
why_others_wrong.C: Cortisol has permissive metabolic and vascular effects but is not the primary regulator of collecting duct water permeability.
why_others_wrong.D: TSH belongs to the thyroid axis and has no role in renal water handling.
why_others_wrong.E: Insulin governs glucose metabolism and has no direct role in the kidney's ability to concentrate urine.

exam_trap: Candidates choosing aldosterone (A) link polyuria with salt loss, but aldosterone controls sodium and potassium; failure to concentrate urine after neurosurgery reflects ADH deficiency.
takeaway: ADH → aquaporin-2 → collecting-duct water reabsorption.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed, 2021.
thinking: Profound polyuria after neurosurgery ↓ damage to the hypothalamus or posterior pituitary ↓ ADH deficiency prevents aquaporin-2 insertion ↓ collecting duct stays water-impermeable, giving large volumes of dilute urine ↓ ADH
pearl: Central diabetes insipidus is suggested by dilute urine with rising serum sodium and responds to desmopressin, unlike nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: (untitled)
stem: A patient has severe dehydration and increased plasma osmolality. Which change normally stimulates ADH secretion?
why_correct: Hypothalamic osmoreceptors detect changes in plasma osmolality. Increased osmolality stimulates ADH release, promoting renal water retention. Significant reduction in circulating volume also stimulates ADH release through haemodynamic mechanisms.

why_others_wrong.A: Reduced plasma osmolality would suppress, not stimulate, ADH release, the opposite of the scenario described.
why_others_wrong.C: Increased atrial stretch signals volume expansion, which suppresses ADH release rather than stimulating it.
why_others_wrong.D: Reduced osmoreceptor activity would decrease, not increase, ADH secretion.
why_others_wrong.E: Increased urine volume is a consequence of low ADH activity, not a stimulus that triggers ADH release.

exam_trap: Candidates choosing atrial stretch (C) reverse the volume signal; increased atrial stretch indicates expansion and suppresses ADH, whereas raised osmolality and hypovolaemia stimulate it.
takeaway: ↑ plasma osmolality → ↑ ADH.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed, 2021.
thinking: Dehydration raises plasma osmolality ↓ hypothalamic osmoreceptors are stimulated ↓ ADH released from the posterior pituitary ↓ collecting-duct water reabsorption increases ↓ Increased plasma osmolality
pearl: Osmoreceptors respond to small changes in osmolality, whereas haemodynamic stimuli need a larger fall in volume but then override osmotic control, which is why hypovolaemic patients retain water despite hyponatraemia.

subject: Pharmacology
title: Pharmacology: (untitled)
stem: ADH acts on the collecting duct through a receptor that increases intracellular cyclic AMP. Which receptor is involved?
why_correct: ADH binds V2 receptors on renal collecting-duct principal cells. This activates adenylate cyclase, increases cyclic AMP and promotes aquaporin-2 insertion. V1 receptors mediate vascular smooth-muscle effects.

why_others_wrong.A: V1 receptors mediate ADH's vasoconstrictor effect on vascular smooth muscle via a different (phospholipase C/calcium) signalling pathway, not the cAMP-mediated collecting duct water reabsorption described.
why_others_wrong.C: Alpha-1 receptors act via Gq/phospholipase C signalling on vascular and other smooth muscle, not via cAMP-mediated water reabsorption in the collecting duct.
why_others_wrong.D: Beta-1 receptors act via Gs/cAMP but are located mainly in the heart, mediating chronotropic and inotropic effects, not renal water reabsorption.
why_others_wrong.E: M3 muscarinic receptors act via Gq/phospholipase C signalling on smooth muscle and glands, not via the Gs/cAMP pathway described for ADH's renal action.

exam_trap: V1 receptor is chosen by candidates who remember only that vasopressin has a numbered receptor, but V1 mediates vasoconstriction via phospholipase C; renal water reabsorption via cAMP is V2.
takeaway: ADH kidney = V2 → cAMP → aquaporin-2.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed, 2021.
thinking: ADH acting on the collecting duct ↓ receptor raises intracellular cAMP, so it is Gs-coupled ↓ the renal vasopressin receptor is V2 ↓ aquaporin-2 channels are inserted into the apical membrane ↓ V2 receptor
pearl: Desmopressin is a selective V2 agonist used for cranial diabetes insipidus and to raise factor VIII and von Willebrand factor in mild haemophilia A and von Willebrand disease before surgery.

subject: Physiology
title: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care: (untitled)
stem: A patient has primary hyperparathyroidism. Which renal effect of parathyroid hormone contributes directly to increased serum calcium?
why_correct: PTH increases renal calcium reabsorption while reducing phosphate reabsorption. It also stimulates renal formation of calcitriol, increasing intestinal calcium absorption.

why_others_wrong.B: PTH promotes renal calcium reabsorption, thereby reducing rather than increasing urinary calcium excretion.
why_others_wrong.C: PTH stimulates, rather than inhibits, renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase, increasing calcitriol formation.
why_others_wrong.D: PTH reduces proximal tubular phosphate reabsorption, promoting phosphate excretion rather than increasing its reabsorption.
why_others_wrong.E: PTH enhances, rather than reduces, distal tubular calcium reabsorption.

exam_trap: Candidates choosing B recall the hypercalciuria and stones of hyperparathyroidism, but that reflects a higher filtered load; PTH itself increases tubular calcium reabsorption.
takeaway: PTH → retain calcium, excrete phosphate.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed, 2021.
thinking: Primary hyperparathyroidism with raised calcium ↓ PTH acts on the distal nephron ↓ increases tubular calcium reabsorption ↓ also stimulates calcitriol formation ↓ Increased calcium reabsorption
pearl: Despite increased tubular reabsorption, patients with primary hyperparathyroidism often have hypercalciuria because the filtered calcium load is high, which explains their risk of renal stones.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: GI physiology & metabolism: (untitled)
stem: A patient develops hyperglycaemia after pancreatic beta-cell destruction. Which intracellular signalling mechanism normally mediates many of insulin's metabolic effects?

options.C: Direct opening of voltage-gated sodium channels

why_correct: The insulin receptor is a receptor tyrosine kinase. Binding of insulin causes receptor autophosphorylation and activation of intracellular signalling pathways, including pathways promoting glucose uptake and metabolic storage.

why_others_wrong.B: Nuclear steroid receptors mediate lipid-soluble hormones such as cortisol; insulin is a peptide acting on a cell-surface receptor.
why_others_wrong.C: Insulin does not directly open voltage-gated sodium channels; its effects follow receptor tyrosine kinase signalling.
why_others_wrong.D: V2 receptors are G protein-coupled receptors for ADH in the renal collecting duct, not insulin receptors.
why_others_wrong.E: Nicotinic acetylcholine receptors are ligand-gated ion channels for acetylcholine and do not mediate insulin action.

exam_trap: Insulin is not a steroid hormone. Its receptor is located on the cell membrane.
takeaway: Insulin receptor = receptor tyrosine kinase.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed, 2021.
thinking: Insulin is a peptide hormone ↓ it binds a cell-surface receptor ↓ the receptor autophosphorylates on tyrosine residues ↓ downstream signalling drives glucose uptake ↓ Receptor tyrosine kinase activation
pearl: Insulin also drives potassium into cells by stimulating the Na+/K+ ATPase, which is why insulin with glucose is used in the emergency treatment of hyperkalaemia.

subject: Pharmacology
title: Pharmacology: (untitled)
stem: Which intracellular messenger is classically increased by glucagon binding to its receptor on hepatocytes?
why_correct: Glucagon binds a G-protein-coupled receptor coupled predominantly to Gs. This activates adenylate cyclase, increasing intracellular cAMP and activating protein kinase A. This promotes hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.

why_others_wrong.B: cGMP is generated via guanylate cyclase, typically activated by nitric oxide or natriuretic peptides, not by hepatic glucagon receptor signalling.
why_others_wrong.C: IP3 generation requires Gq-coupled phospholipase C activation; the glucagon receptor couples predominantly to Gs, not Gq, so IP3 is not the classical second messenger here.
why_others_wrong.D: Nitric oxide is produced via endothelial NOS activation, not by hepatic glucagon receptor signalling, which classically works through Gs and cAMP.
why_others_wrong.E: Glucagon receptor signalling does not act through chloride channel flux; its classical second messenger is cAMP via adenylate cyclase.

exam_trap: IP3 is chosen by candidates who recall that hormones use second messengers but not which pathway, yet glucagon signals mainly via Gs and cAMP, not Gq and IP3.
takeaway: Glucagon → Gs → adenylate cyclase → cAMP.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed, 2021.
thinking: Glucagon binds a hepatocyte G-protein-coupled receptor ↓ couples predominantly to Gs ↓ adenylate cyclase is activated ↓ cAMP activates protein kinase A, driving glycogenolysis ↓ cAMP
pearl: Because glucagon raises cAMP independently of beta-receptors, it is used in beta-blocker overdose to increase heart rate and contractility; intramuscular glucagon also treats severe hypoglycaemia when IV access is unavailable.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Pathology: oncology & haematology: (untitled)
stem: A patient develops excessive bleeding after receiving a drug that inhibits platelet aggregation. Which change in platelet second messengers normally follows activation of the P2Y12 pathway?
why_correct: The platelet P2Y12 receptor is coupled to Gi. Activation inhibits adenylate cyclase and reduces intracellular cAMP, promoting platelet activation and aggregation. P2Y12 inhibitors such as clopidogrel therefore impair platelet activation.

why_others_wrong.A: P2Y12 is coupled to Gi, which inhibits adenylate cyclase, so cAMP falls rather than rises; raised platelet cAMP inhibits activation.
why_others_wrong.C: cGMP is raised in platelets by nitric oxide and is inhibitory, whereas P2Y12 signalling works through Gi to lower cAMP.
why_others_wrong.D: Nitric oxide is released by endothelium and inhibits platelets via cGMP; it is not a second messenger generated by P2Y12 activation.
why_others_wrong.E: ATP depletion is not the signalling mechanism of P2Y12; the receptor lowers cAMP through Gi-mediated inhibition of adenylate cyclase.

exam_trap: Increased cAMP is the common slip, but raised platelet cAMP, as produced by prostacyclin, inhibits activation; P2Y12 acts through Gi to lower cAMP.
takeaway: P2Y12 → Gi → ↓ cAMP → platelet activation.
source: British National Formulary, antiplatelet medicines, accessed 2026; pharmacology standard texts.
thinking: P2Y12 is a platelet ADP receptor ↓ it is coupled to the inhibitory G protein Gi ↓ Gi inhibits adenylate cyclase ↓ falling cAMP promotes platelet activation ↓ Reduced cAMP
pearl: Clopidogrel irreversibly blocks P2Y12 and is usually stopped several days before elective major surgery, but never without cardiology input when a recent coronary stent is present because of the risk of stent thrombosis.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: (untitled)
stem: A patient has severe diarrhoea causing loss of bicarbonate. Which acid-base abnormality is most likely?
why_correct: Loss of bicarbonate-rich intestinal fluid causes a metabolic acidosis. Chloride rises to maintain electrical neutrality, so the anion gap is generally normal. This is also called hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis.

why_others_wrong.A: In diarrhoea, bicarbonate lost is replaced by a rise in plasma chloride to maintain electroneutrality, so the anion gap stays normal.
why_others_wrong.C: Loss of bicarbonate-rich fluid causes acidosis, not alkalosis, so this is the opposite acid-base disturbance.
why_others_wrong.D: This is a primary metabolic process from gastrointestinal bicarbonate loss, not a primary respiratory disturbance driven by CO2 retention.
why_others_wrong.E: Diarrhoea produces a primary metabolic acid-base disturbance, not a primary respiratory alkalosis.

exam_trap: Diarrhoea causes bicarbonate loss and therefore metabolic acidosis; vomiting has the opposite typical acid-base effect.
takeaway: Diarrhoea → HCO3− loss → normal-gap metabolic acidosis.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed, 2021.
thinking: Severe diarrhoea ↓ bicarbonate-rich intestinal fluid lost ↓ metabolic acidosis ↓ chloride rises to maintain electroneutrality ↓ Normal-anion-gap metabolic acidosis
pearl: High-output stomas and small-bowel fistulae cause bicarbonate and sodium loss, and the resulting hyperchloraemic acidosis can be worsened by large volumes of 0.9% sodium chloride.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: (untitled)
stem: A patient with severe vomiting develops metabolic alkalosis. Which renal response helps compensate for the alkalosis when effective circulating volume is restored?
why_correct: When volume and renal perfusion are adequate, the kidneys can increase bicarbonate excretion to help correct metabolic alkalosis. However, in chloride-depletion and volume-depleted states, renal bicarbonate retention can persist, helping maintain the alkalosis.

why_others_wrong.B: With adequate volume and renal perfusion the kidney excretes surplus bicarbonate to correct alkalosis; it does not retain more bicarbonate.
why_others_wrong.C: Hydrogen-ion secretion is modulated rather than completely abolished, and this description does not represent the corrective mechanism for alkalosis.
why_others_wrong.D: Increased ammonium production is the kidney's response to acidosis, not the mechanism by which it corrects alkalosis.
why_others_wrong.E: Correction of alkalosis by the kidney is chloride-dependent (chloride repletion permits bicarbonate excretion), not an independent process of new bicarbonate generation.

exam_trap: Candidates choosing B describe the maintenance phase of volume and chloride depletion; once circulating volume is restored, the kidney excretes the surplus bicarbonate instead.
takeaway: Metabolic alkalosis + adequate renal function → renal HCO3− excretion helps correct it.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed, 2021.
thinking: Vomiting loses hydrochloric acid, raising bicarbonate ↓ volume and chloride depletion make the kidney retain bicarbonate ↓ once volume and chloride are restored ↓ the kidney excretes the surplus bicarbonate ↓ Increased bicarbonate excretion
pearl: Vomiting-induced alkalosis is therefore treated with intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride and potassium replacement; without chloride the kidney cannot excrete bicarbonate and the alkalosis persists.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: (untitled)
stem: A patient develops acute kidney injury with reduced glomerular filtration. Which change most directly reduces the amount of filtered plasma?
correct_answer: B. Reduced glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure
why_correct: Glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure is a major force driving filtration. A reduction in this pressure reduces net filtration pressure and therefore GFR. This can occur with reduced renal perfusion.

why_others_wrong.A: An increase in glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure would raise, not reduce, net filtration pressure and GFR.
why_others_wrong.C: A higher filtration coefficient would increase, not decrease, the amount of plasma filtered.
why_others_wrong.D: Reduced Bowman's space pressure lowers the opposing force to filtration, which would favour a higher, not lower, filtration rate.
why_others_wrong.E: A reduction in plasma oncotic pressure removes an opposing force to filtration and would tend to increase, not decrease, the filtered volume.

exam_trap: Reduced Bowman's space pressure (D) and reduced plasma oncotic pressure (E) are chosen by confusing the opposing forces; lowering them favours, rather than reduces, filtration.
takeaway: ↓ glomerular hydrostatic pressure → ↓ filtration.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed, 2021.
thinking: AKI with reduced glomerular filtration ↓ GFR depends on net filtration pressure across the glomerular capillary ↓ glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure is the main force driving filtration ↓ a fall in this pressure, as with reduced renal perfusion, lowers filtration ↓ Reduced glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure
pearl: In hypovolaemia angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole to maintain glomerular pressure, so ACE inhibitors and ARBs can precipitate AKI in dehydrated patients, and NSAIDs add to this by blocking afferent prostaglandin-mediated vasodilatation.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: (untitled)
stem: A patient develops urinary obstruction causing increased pressure within Bowman's space. What is the expected effect on GFR?

options.D: Complete cessation of renal blood flow
options.E: Increase only in the contralateral kidney

why_correct: Increased pressure within Bowman's space opposes the hydrostatic pressure driving filtration across the glomerular capillary. Therefore net filtration pressure and GFR fall. This mechanism is relevant to obstructive uropathy.

why_others_wrong.A: Increased Bowman's space pressure opposes filtration, so the correct direction is a decrease, not an increase, in GFR.
why_others_wrong.C: Net filtration pressure is altered by the rise in opposing Bowman's space pressure, so "no change" is incorrect.
why_others_wrong.D: Obstruction raises Bowman's space pressure and reduces GFR, but this does not necessarily cause complete cessation of renal blood flow, which is an overstatement.
why_others_wrong.E: The Starling-force change reduces GFR in the obstructed kidney; any later rise in the other kidney is adaptive and does not describe this effect.

exam_trap: Candidates choosing D overstate the effect; obstruction reduces GFR through raised Bowman's space pressure, but it does not simply stop renal blood flow.
takeaway: Urinary obstruction → ↑ Bowman's pressure → ↓ GFR.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed, 2021.
thinking: Urinary obstruction ↓ back-pressure raises Bowman's space hydrostatic pressure ↓ this opposes glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure ↓ net filtration pressure falls ↓ Decrease
pearl: An obstructed, infected kidney is a urological emergency needing urgent decompression by nephrostomy or ureteric stent, because antibiotics alone cannot clear infection behind an obstruction.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: (untitled)
stem: A patient develops severe hypoalbuminaemia. Which change occurs within glomerular capillaries as a direct consequence of reduced plasma protein concentration?
why_correct: Plasma proteins generate oncotic pressure within glomerular capillaries, opposing filtration. Hypoalbuminaemia reduces this opposing force and can therefore increase filtration pressure, although the overall effect on GFR depends on the wider physiological context.

why_others_wrong.A: Hypoalbuminaemia reduces, rather than increases, plasma oncotic pressure.
why_others_wrong.C: Reduced plasma protein does not directly raise Bowman's space pressure; that pressure is governed by tubular flow and outlet resistance, not plasma protein concentration.
why_others_wrong.D: Glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure is governed mainly by arteriolar tone, not directly by plasma protein concentration.
why_others_wrong.E: Increased tubular pressure is not a direct Starling-force consequence of reduced plasma protein concentration at the glomerulus.

exam_trap: Candidates choosing A reverse the relationship; fewer plasma proteins mean lower plasma oncotic pressure, reducing the force that opposes glomerular filtration.
takeaway: Low plasma protein → ↓ glomerular oncotic opposition to filtration.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed, 2021.
thinking: Severe hypoalbuminaemia ↓ albumin generates most plasma oncotic pressure ↓ glomerular capillary oncotic pressure falls ↓ less opposition to filtration ↓ Reduced plasma oncotic pressure
pearl: In nephrotic syndrome, heavy proteinuria lowers plasma oncotic pressure and contributes to oedema, and the accompanying hypercoagulable state increases the risk of renal vein thrombosis.

subject: Physiology
title: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care: (untitled)
stem: A patient has reduced renal perfusion. Which renal cells release renin in response to reduced afferent arteriolar pressure?
why_correct: Juxtaglomerular cells are modified smooth-muscle cells in the wall of the afferent arteriole. They release renin in response to reduced renal perfusion pressure and other signals.

why_others_wrong.A: Podocytes form the glomerular filtration barrier and do not secrete renin.
why_others_wrong.C: Principal cells are located in the collecting duct and handle sodium, potassium and water transport, not renin secretion.
why_others_wrong.D: Mesangial macrophages are not the classic renin-secreting cell type; renin comes from modified smooth muscle cells in the afferent arteriolar wall.
why_others_wrong.E: Proximal tubular epithelial cells perform bulk reabsorption and have no renin-secreting function.

exam_trap: Candidates choosing mesangial macrophages (D) confuse components of the juxtaglomerular apparatus; renin comes from granular modified smooth-muscle cells in the afferent arteriole wall.
takeaway: Afferent arteriole pressure falls → JG cells release renin.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed, 2021.
thinking: Reduced renal perfusion ↓ afferent arteriolar stretch falls ↓ granular juxtaglomerular cells release renin ↓ renin starts the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone cascade ↓ Juxtaglomerular cells
pearl: Renin release is also stimulated by sympathetic beta-1 activity and by reduced NaCl delivery to the macula densa, which is one reason beta-blockers lower renin levels.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: (untitled)
stem: Which structure provides the principal site for sensing tubular sodium chloride concentration as part of tubuloglomerular feedback?
why_correct: Macula densa cells in the distal nephron sense tubular sodium chloride delivery and communicate with the juxtaglomerular apparatus to regulate renin release and glomerular filtration.

why_others_wrong.B: Podocytes form part of the filtration barrier and are not tubular chemosensors for sodium chloride.
why_others_wrong.C: Collecting-duct principal cells handle sodium, potassium and water transport and play no role in tubuloglomerular feedback sensing.
why_others_wrong.D: Juxtaglomerular cells are the effector cells that release renin in response to signals from the macula densa; they are not themselves the sodium chloride sensor.
why_others_wrong.E: The renal capsule is connective tissue covering the kidney and has no sensory function.

exam_trap: Candidates choosing juxtaglomerular cells (D) confuse sensor with effector; the macula densa senses tubular NaCl and signals the JG cells to alter renin release.
takeaway: Macula densa = distal-tubule NaCl sensor.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed, 2021.
thinking: Tubuloglomerular feedback ↓ macula densa cells in the distal tubule wall at the vascular pole ↓ sense NaCl delivery through NKCC2 ↓ signal the afferent arteriole and juxtaglomerular cells ↓ Macula densa
pearl: Loop diuretics block macula densa NKCC2, so the cells sense low NaCl and stimulate renin release, contributing to activation of the renin-angiotensin system during diuretic therapy.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: (untitled)
stem: A patient has an inherited disorder affecting the proximal renal tubule. Which substance is normally almost completely reabsorbed from the glomerular filtrate under normal conditions?
why_correct: Filtered glucose is normally almost completely reabsorbed in the proximal tubule, primarily through sodium-glucose cotransport mechanisms. Glucose begins to appear in urine when the filtered load exceeds tubular reabsorptive capacity.

why_others_wrong.B: Creatinine is filtered and not significantly reabsorbed (with slight secretion), which is precisely why it is used as a marker of GFR rather than being described as almost completely reabsorbed.
why_others_wrong.C: Inulin is filtered and undergoes essentially no reabsorption or secretion, making it the classic exogenous GFR marker rather than a reabsorbed substance.
why_others_wrong.D: Urea is only partially reabsorbed, with a substantial fraction excreted, unlike glucose which is almost completely reabsorbed under normal conditions.
why_others_wrong.E: Para-aminohippurate is filtered and actively secreted, so the amount excreted exceeds the filtered load; it is not reabsorbed.

exam_trap: Candidates choosing urea (D) recall that it is reabsorbed, but only partially; glucose is the substance normally almost completely reclaimed in the proximal tubule.
takeaway: Normal filtered glucose → essentially complete proximal reabsorption.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed, 2021.
thinking: Almost completely reabsorbed solute ↓ glucose reclaimed by SGLT cotransporters in the proximal tubule ↓ creatinine and inulin are filtration markers ↓ PAH is secreted and urea only partly reabsorbed ↓ Glucose
pearl: Generalised proximal tubular dysfunction causes glycosuria with normal blood glucose together with aminoaciduria, phosphaturia and a proximal renal tubular acidosis.

subject: Physiology
title: Renal physiology: NKCC2 thick ascending limb
stem: A patient has a mutation affecting the protein responsible for moving sodium and chloride across the apical membrane of cells in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle. Which transporter is affected?
why_correct: The Na+-K+-2Cl− cotransporter (NKCC2) is located in the apical membrane of cells in the thick ascending limb. This segment actively reabsorbs sodium, potassium and chloride and is important in generating the renal medullary osmotic gradient.

why_others_wrong.A: ENaC is the epithelial sodium channel of collecting duct principal cells, carrying sodium alone rather than sodium with chloride in the thick ascending limb.
why_others_wrong.C: SGLT2 is the sodium-glucose cotransporter of the proximal convoluted tubule, reabsorbing glucose with sodium rather than chloride in the thick ascending limb.
why_others_wrong.D: NCC is the thiazide-sensitive sodium-chloride cotransporter of the distal convoluted tubule, not the transporter of the thick ascending limb.
why_others_wrong.E: The sodium-hydrogen exchanger works mainly in the proximal tubule, exchanging sodium for hydrogen ions rather than cotransporting sodium and chloride.

exam_trap: NKCC2 = thick ascending limb. NCC = distal convoluted tubule. ENaC = collecting duct principal cells.
takeaway: Thick ascending limb = NKCC2.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed, 2021.
thinking: Apical sodium-chloride transport ↓ thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle ↓ Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in that segment ↓ NKCC2
pearl: NKCC2 is the target of loop diuretics such as furosemide, and loss-of-function variants cause Bartter syndrome with hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: (untitled)
stem: A patient has a defect in the distal convoluted tubule sodium-chloride cotransporter. Which transporter is affected?
why_correct: The sodium-chloride cotransporter (NCC) is located in the apical membrane of the distal convoluted tubule. This distinguishes it from NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb and ENaC in the collecting duct.

why_others_wrong.A: NKCC2 is located in the thick ascending limb, the target of loop diuretics, not the distal convoluted tubule.
why_others_wrong.B: ENaC is an aldosterone-regulated sodium channel of the late distal nephron and collecting duct, not the thiazide-sensitive sodium-chloride cotransporter of the distal convoluted tubule.
why_others_wrong.D: SGLT2 is located in the proximal tubule and mediates sodium-glucose cotransport, unrelated to distal tubular sodium-chloride transport.
why_others_wrong.E: Na+/K+ ATPase is a basolateral pump present throughout the nephron that sets up the driving gradient for transport, rather than being the apical sodium-chloride cotransporter itself.

exam_trap: Candidates choosing NKCC2 (A) recall the loop-diuretic cotransporter, but NKCC2 lies in the thick ascending limb; the distal convoluted tubule uses the thiazide-sensitive NCC.
takeaway: DCT = NCC. TAL = NKCC2. Collecting duct = ENaC.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed, 2021.
thinking: Distal convoluted tubule sodium-chloride cotransport ↓ apical NCC transporter ↓ the thiazide-sensitive transporter ↓ NKCC2 is in the thick ascending limb and ENaC in the collecting duct ↓ NCC
pearl: Thiazides inhibit NCC and reduce urinary calcium excretion, which is why they help prevent recurrent calcium stones, but they can cause hyponatraemia and hypokalaemia.

subject: Genetics
title: Genetics: penetrance
stem: A child inherits a pathogenic variant in one copy of a gene and is currently unaffected. The associated disease has a penetrance of 70%. Which statement best describes the meaning of this penetrance?

options.A: The mutation is present in 70% of the child's cells
options.B: The child has a 70% probability of expressing the phenotype associated with the variant
options.C: The mutation has altered 70% of the gene sequence
options.D: The disease is transmitted in 70% of pregnancies
options.E: The child has 70 copies of the abnormal gene

correct_answer: B. The child has a 70% probability of expressing the phenotype associated with the variant
why_correct: Penetrance describes the proportion of individuals carrying a particular genotype who express the associated phenotype. Incomplete penetrance means that not all individuals with the pathogenic variant develop the clinical phenotype.

why_others_wrong.A: The proportion of cells carrying a mutation relates to mosaicism, whereas penetrance is the proportion of carriers who express the phenotype.
why_others_wrong.C: Penetrance does not measure how much of the gene sequence is altered; it describes how often carriers of the genotype develop the phenotype.
why_others_wrong.D: The chance of transmitting the variant to offspring depends on the inheritance pattern, such as 50% for a heterozygous dominant parent, not on penetrance.
why_others_wrong.E: The child inherited a variant in one copy of the gene, and penetrance says nothing about gene copy number; it describes phenotype expression among carriers.

exam_trap: Option D is chosen by candidates who confuse penetrance with transmission risk; the chance of passing on a variant depends on the inheritance pattern, not penetrance.
takeaway: Penetrance = proportion of carriers who express the phenotype.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed, 2017.
thinking: Penetrance of 70% ↓ proportion of carriers who express the phenotype ↓ applied to one unaffected carrier child ↓ Child has a 70% probability of expressing the phenotype
pearl: A carrier who is currently unaffected may still develop the condition later, because penetrance for many adult-onset disorders increases with age.

subject: Genetics
title: Genetics: anticipation
