why_others_wrong.B: C5 deficiency impairs membrane attack complex formation and predisposes mainly to Neisseria infection, with normal B-cell numbers and immunoglobulin levels.
why_others_wrong.C: Thymic aplasia, as in DiGeorge syndrome, causes a T-cell deficiency, whereas here T cells are preserved and mature B cells are absent.
why_others_wrong.D: NADPH oxidase deficiency causes chronic granulomatous disease, a phagocyte killing defect with catalase-positive infections and normal B cells and antibody levels.
why_others_wrong.E: IL-2 receptor defects mainly disrupt T-cell development or regulation, with gamma-chain loss causing X-linked SCID and normal B-cell numbers, not isolated B-cell absence.

exam_trap: Bruton's = failure of B-cell maturation; DiGeorge = T-cell deficiency from thymic abnormalities.
takeaway: BTK deficiency → no mature B cells → very low immunoglobulins.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed., Elsevier, 2022.
thinking: Recurrent encapsulated bacterial infections ↓ mature B cells absent and immunoglobulins very low ↓ T cells preserved ↓ B-cell maturation block (X-linked agammaglobulinaemia) ↓ Bruton's tyrosine kinase deficiency
pearl: X-linked agammaglobulinaemia typically presents after about six months of age, once transplacental maternal IgG has waned, and is treated with lifelong immunoglobulin replacement.

subject: Anatomy
title: Physiology: (untitled)
stem: A neonate has characteristic facial features, hypocalcaemia and recurrent viral/fungal infections. Imaging suggests absence or severe hypoplasia of the thymus. Which embryological structure is most directly implicated?
why_correct: The thymus develops from the third pharyngeal pouch. Failure of normal thymic development causes T-cell deficiency and is characteristic of DiGeorge syndrome. The inferior parathyroids also arise from the third pouch, explaining the association with hypocalcaemia.

why_others_wrong.A: The first pharyngeal pouch gives rise to the middle ear cavity and auditory tube, not the thymus.
why_others_wrong.B: The second pharyngeal pouch contributes to the palatine tonsil, not the thymus.
why_others_wrong.D: The fourth pharyngeal pouch gives rise to the superior parathyroid glands (and contributes to the ultimobranchial body), not the thymus.
why_others_wrong.E: The first pharyngeal cleft is an ectodermal structure that forms the external auditory meatus, unrelated to thymic development.

exam_trap: Fourth pharyngeal pouch is chosen because it also forms parathyroid tissue, but it gives the superior parathyroids, not the thymus or inferior parathyroids.
takeaway: 3rd pouch → thymus + inferior parathyroids.
source: Gray's Anatomy, 42nd ed., Elsevier, 2020.
thinking: Hypocalcaemia, recurrent infections and absent thymus ↓ DiGeorge pattern of pharyngeal pouch failure ↓ the thymus and inferior parathyroids share one pouch of origin ↓ Third pharyngeal pouch
pearl: Because the inferior parathyroids migrate with the thymus from the third pouch, they are more variable in position than the superior glands and may lie in the thymus or anterior mediastinum during parathyroid surgery.

subject: Microbiology & surgical infection
title: Microbiology & surgical infection: (untitled)
stem: A methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus isolate remains resistant to β-lactam antibiotics despite inhibition of its usual penicillin-binding proteins. Which mechanism best explains this?

options.A: Acquisition of an altered penicillin-binding protein
options.B: Increased renal excretion of the antibiotic
options.E: Inhibition of bacterial ribosomal RNA synthesis

correct_answer: A. Acquisition of an altered penicillin-binding protein
why_correct: MRSA characteristically acquires resistance through an altered penicillin-binding protein with reduced affinity for β-lactam antibiotics.

why_others_wrong.B: Renal excretion of an antibiotic is a host pharmacokinetic factor and cannot make the bacterial isolate itself resistant.
why_others_wrong.C: Reduced ATP production is not the mechanism of methicillin resistance, which depends on a low-affinity penicillin-binding protein.
why_others_wrong.D: Host antibody production would aid clearance of the organism and has nothing to do with bacterial resistance to beta-lactams.
why_others_wrong.E: Inhibition of bacterial rRNA synthesis would impair bacterial growth and is not a mechanism by which MRSA resists beta-lactams.

exam_trap: Candidates expecting beta-lactamase look for drug destruction, but MRSA resistance is target modification; low-affinity PBP2a keeps building the cell wall despite the antibiotic.
takeaway: MRSA → altered PBP → reduced β-lactam binding.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed., Elsevier, 2022.
thinking: MRSA resistant despite its usual PBPs being inhibited ↓ an additional PBP takes over cell-wall cross-linking ↓ mecA encodes PBP2a with low beta-lactam affinity ↓ Acquisition of an altered penicillin-binding protein
pearl: Because PBP2a confers resistance to nearly all beta-lactams, serious MRSA infection is usually treated with agents such as vancomycin, teicoplanin, linezolid or daptomycin according to local policy.

subject: Microbiology & surgical infection
title: Microbiology & surgical infection: (untitled)
stem: A patient is given a glycopeptide antibiotic for a serious Gram-positive infection. Which bacterial process is directly inhibited by this class of drug?
why_correct: Glycopeptides such as vancomycin inhibit bacterial cell-wall synthesis by binding the D-Ala-D-Ala terminus of peptidoglycan precursors.

why_others_wrong.A: DNA gyrase is inhibited by fluoroquinolones such as ciprofloxacin, not by glycopeptides.
why_others_wrong.B: Folate synthesis is inhibited by sulfonamides and trimethoprim, not by glycopeptides such as vancomycin.
why_others_wrong.D: The 30S ribosomal subunit is the target of aminoglycosides and tetracyclines rather than glycopeptides.
why_others_wrong.E: RNA polymerase is inhibited by rifampicin, whereas glycopeptides act on cell-wall precursors.

exam_trap: Candidates who link vancomycin to protein synthesis choose 30S translation, but glycopeptides bind D-Ala-D-Ala precursors, blocking cell-wall synthesis at a different step from beta-lactams.
takeaway: β-lactams → PBPs; glycopeptides → D-Ala-D-Ala-containing precursors.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed., Elsevier, 2022.
thinking: Glycopeptide such as vancomycin ↓ binds the D-Ala-D-Ala end of peptidoglycan precursors ↓ blocks their incorporation and cross-linking into the wall ↓ Cell-wall peptidoglycan synthesis
pearl: Vancomycin-resistant enterococci replace D-Ala-D-Ala with D-Ala-D-Lac, which vancomycin binds poorly, a classic example of resistance by target modification.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: Physiology: (untitled)
stem: A patient stops eating but continues to drink water. During the early phase of fasting, which fuel is preferentially mobilised to maintain blood glucose?

options.B: Muscle glycogen directly released into blood
options.C: Ketone bodies as the sole glucose source

why_correct: During the early fasting period, hepatic glycogenolysis is an important mechanism for maintaining blood glucose. As fasting continues and hepatic glycogen stores become depleted, gluconeogenesis becomes increasingly important and ketone production rises.

why_others_wrong.B: Muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase, so its glycogen is used locally and cannot be released directly into the blood as glucose.
why_others_wrong.C: Ketone bodies are an alternative fuel produced later in fasting; they are not converted into glucose and cannot be a glucose source.
why_others_wrong.D: Muscle protein supplies amino acids for gluconeogenesis as fasting progresses, but it is not the main early glucose source and the body tries to spare it.
why_others_wrong.E: Dietary triglyceride is not available in fasting, and fatty acids cannot be converted into net glucose.

exam_trap: Liver glycogen can support blood glucose; muscle glycogen is primarily used locally.
takeaway: Early fasting → hepatic glycogenolysis; later → gluconeogenesis + ketogenesis.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Elsevier, 2020/2021 publication cycle.
thinking: Early fasting: insulin falls and glucagon rises ↓ liver glycogen is broken down and released as glucose ↓ muscle glycogen cannot leave the cell (no glucose-6-phosphatase) ↓ gluconeogenesis and ketogenesis take over later ↓ Hepatic glycogen
pearl: Liver glycogen is largely depleted within about 24 hours of fasting, after which gluconeogenesis from amino acids, lactate and glycerol maintains glucose, which is why prolonged preoperative starvation promotes muscle catabolism.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: Physiology: (untitled)
stem: During prolonged starvation, which metabolic adaptation allows the brain to reduce its dependence on glucose?

options.C: Complete cessation of hepatic fatty-acid oxidation

correct_answer: A. Increased use of ketone bodies
why_correct: During prolonged starvation, hepatic fatty-acid oxidation generates ketone bodies. The brain progressively increases its use of ketone bodies, reducing its glucose requirement and therefore reducing the need for amino-acid-derived gluconeogenesis.

why_others_wrong.B: There is no dietary glucose intake during starvation, so increased use of it cannot be the adaptation that spares brain glucose.
why_others_wrong.C: Hepatic fatty-acid oxidation increases in starvation, and it is this that supplies the ketone bodies the brain uses.
why_others_wrong.D: Insulin secretion falls during starvation; low insulin permits lipolysis and ketogenesis rather than reducing brain glucose dependence.
why_others_wrong.E: Glycogen synthesis is suppressed in starvation because stores are being mobilised, and it does not provide the brain with an alternative fuel.

exam_trap: The brain cannot directly use circulating long-chain fatty acids as its principal alternative fuel, but it can use ketone bodies.
takeaway: Prolonged starvation → ↑ hepatic ketogenesis → brain ↑ ketone utilisation → protein sparing.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Elsevier, 2020/2021 publication cycle.
thinking: Prolonged starvation ↓ low insulin drives lipolysis and hepatic fatty-acid oxidation ↓ the liver produces ketone bodies ↓ the brain increasingly oxidises them, sparing protein ↓ Increased use of ketone bodies
pearl: The liver makes ketone bodies but cannot use them because it lacks the enzyme succinyl-CoA:3-ketoacid CoA transferase, so they are exported for use by brain, heart and muscle.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: (untitled)
stem: A patient undergoes major surgery and develops hyperglycaemia despite no previous diagnosis of diabetes. Which physiological change is most responsible for this response?

options.C: Increased insulin resistance driven by the surgical stress response

correct_answer: C. Increased insulin resistance driven by the surgical stress response
why_correct: Major surgery activates the neuroendocrine stress response, including catecholamines, cortisol, glucagon and growth hormone. These changes promote hepatic glucose production and reduce peripheral insulin sensitivity, producing stress hyperglycaemia.

why_others_wrong.A: Surgical stress causes insulin resistance, not increased sensitivity; tissues become less responsive to insulin, contributing to hyperglycaemia.
why_others_wrong.B: Catecholamine secretion rises sharply as part of the neuroendocrine stress response, rather than being reduced.
why_others_wrong.D: Glucagon secretion increases rather than being suppressed, contributing to increased hepatic glucose output during the stress response.
why_others_wrong.E: Peripheral glucose uptake is reduced, not increased, due to stress-induced insulin resistance, which is part of why plasma glucose rises.

exam_trap: Candidates choosing B misremember the stress response; catecholamines rise rather than fall after surgery and, with cortisol and glucagon, drive insulin resistance and hepatic glucose output.
takeaway: Surgical stress → catecholamines/cortisol/glucagon/GH ↑ → insulin resistance + hepatic glucose output ↑ → stress hyperglycaemia.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Elsevier, 2020/2021 publication cycle.
thinking: Major surgery triggers the neuroendocrine stress response ↓ catecholamines, cortisol, glucagon and GH rise ↓ hepatic glucose output increases and peripheral insulin sensitivity falls ↓ Increased insulin resistance driven by the surgical stress response
pearl: Enhanced recovery measures such as preoperative carbohydrate loading, minimally invasive surgery and effective regional analgesia help reduce postoperative insulin resistance.

subject: Major trauma & fluids
title: Major trauma & fluids: (untitled)
stem: A patient with severe haemorrhage develops a fall in cardiac output. Which change occurs as part of the immediate baroreceptor response?
why_correct: Acute blood loss reduces arterial pressure and therefore reduces firing from arterial baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch. This increases sympathetic and reduces parasympathetic activity, producing tachycardia, increased contractility and peripheral vasoconstriction.

why_others_wrong.A: Reduced baroreceptor firing lowers vagal outflow to the heart; increased vagal activity would slow the heart and worsen hypotension.
why_others_wrong.B: Baroreceptor unloading increases sympathetic outflow to the heart and vessels rather than reducing it.
why_others_wrong.D: The response to haemorrhage conserves sodium through sympathetic and renin-angiotensin-aldosterone effects, so sodium excretion falls.
why_others_wrong.E: Sympathetic vasoconstriction increases systemic vascular resistance to support arterial pressure after blood loss.

exam_trap: The baroreceptor reflex responds rapidly to changes in arterial pressure; it is not the same as the slower renin-angiotensin-aldosterone response.
takeaway: Acute blood loss → ↓ baroreceptor firing → ↑ sympathetic tone → tachycardia + vasoconstriction.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Elsevier, 2020.
thinking: Severe haemorrhage lowers cardiac output and arterial pressure ↓ carotid sinus and aortic arch baroreceptors fire less ↓ sympathetic outflow rises and vagal outflow falls ↓ tachycardia within seconds ↓ Increased heart rate
pearl: Carotid sinus afferents run in the glossopharyngeal nerve and aortic arch afferents in the vagus, both relaying to the nucleus tractus solitarius in the medulla.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Cardiorespiratory physiology: pressure overload hypertrophy
stem: A patient has severe aortic stenosis. Which change in left ventricular physiology is most likely to develop chronically?

options.C: Eccentric hypertrophy caused primarily by volume overload

why_correct: Aortic stenosis creates chronic pressure overload on the left ventricle. The ventricle adapts by developing concentric hypertrophy, increasing wall thickness and helping to normalise wall stress.

why_others_wrong.A: Aortic stenosis increases, not reduces, the afterload faced by the left ventricle because of the fixed outflow obstruction.
why_others_wrong.C: Eccentric hypertrophy driven by volume overload characterises regurgitant lesions such as mitral or aortic regurgitation, not the pressure-overload state of aortic stenosis.
why_others_wrong.D: Wall stress is initially raised by the chronic pressure load; the ventricle responds by hypertrophying (thickening) to normalise stress, rather than showing no hypertrophy.
why_others_wrong.E: Aortic stenosis places a pressure load on the left ventricle, not the right ventricle, so isolated right ventricular hypertrophy would not be the expected chronic change.

exam_trap: Eccentric hypertrophy is chosen by mixing up the overload patterns; eccentric dilatation follows volume overload in regurgitation, not pressure overload in stenosis.
takeaway: Pressure overload = thick wall; volume overload = dilated chamber.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Elsevier, 2020.
thinking: Severe aortic stenosis ↓ fixed outflow obstruction causes chronic pressure overload ↓ sarcomeres added in parallel thicken the wall ↓ Concentric ventricular hypertrophy
pearl: In severe aortic stenosis the hypertrophied ventricle has increased oxygen demand and reduced coronary reserve, so angina can occur even with normal coronary arteries.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Cardiorespiratory physiology: volume overload
stem: A patient with chronic severe mitral regurgitation develops left ventricular dilatation. Which haemodynamic load is primarily responsible?
why_correct: During systole in mitral regurgitation, blood is ejected both into the aorta and back into the left atrium. The increased volume returning to the left ventricle during diastole produces chronic volume overload and chamber dilatation.

why_others_wrong.A: Chronic pressure overload characterises stenotic lesions such as aortic stenosis, not a regurgitant lesion like mitral regurgitation, which loads the ventricle with extra volume rather than pressure.
why_others_wrong.C: Mitral regurgitation increases the effective volume returning to the left ventricle each diastole; it does not reduce venous return.
why_others_wrong.D: Increased pulmonary vascular resistance may occur later as a consequence of chronic mitral regurgitation, but it is not the primary haemodynamic load driving left ventricular dilatation.
why_others_wrong.E: Mitral regurgitation raises, rather than reduces, effective preload on the left ventricle because of the regurgitant volume returning during diastole.

exam_trap: Do not confuse the pressure load of aortic stenosis with the volume load of mitral regurgitation.
takeaway: Aortic stenosis → pressure overload → concentric hypertrophy. Mitral regurgitation → volume overload → dilatation/eccentric hypertrophy.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Elsevier, 2020.
thinking: Chronic severe mitral regurgitation ↓ regurgitant blood returns to the ventricle each diastole ↓ increased end-diastolic volume causes volume overload ↓ Chronic volume overload
pearl: Surgery for chronic severe mitral regurgitation is generally recommended before the ventricle dilates and fails irreversibly, as afterload reduction can mask poor function.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Cardiorespiratory physiology: heart rate and diastole
stem: A patient develops a large increase in heart rate. Which part of the cardiac cycle is shortened disproportionately?
why_correct: As heart rate increases, both systole and diastole shorten, but diastole shortens disproportionately. This is important because coronary perfusion of the left ventricular myocardium occurs predominantly during diastole.

why_others_wrong.B: Isovolumetric contraction is a very brief phase and does not shorten disproportionately with tachycardia compared to the filling period.
why_others_wrong.C: Ventricular ejection does shorten somewhat with tachycardia, but not to the disproportionate degree that diastole (filling time) does.
why_others_wrong.D: Isovolumetric relaxation is a brief phase and is not the component of the cycle that shortens disproportionately with a rising heart rate.
why_others_wrong.E: Atrial systole is only a brief part of diastole itself and is not the broader phase (diastole as a whole) that is disproportionately shortened.

exam_trap: Ventricular ejection only is chosen because it shortens with tachycardia, but systole shortens far less than diastole, which bears most of the reduction.
takeaway: Tachycardia → disproportionately shorter diastole → less filling + less coronary perfusion time.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Elsevier, 2020.
thinking: Large rise in heart rate ↓ systole shortens modestly ↓ diastole shortens much more ↓ Diastole
pearl: Because left coronary flow is mainly diastolic, tachycardia increases myocardial oxygen demand while reducing supply time, which is why rate control matters in ischaemic heart disease.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Cardiorespiratory physiology: ventricular compliance
stem: A patient has reduced left ventricular compliance. Which pressure-volume relationship is most likely?

options.A: A smaller increase in pressure for a given increase in volume
options.B: A larger increase in pressure for a given increase in volume

correct_answer: B. A larger increase in pressure for a given increase in volume
why_correct: Compliance describes the change in volume for a given change in pressure. A stiff ventricle has reduced compliance, so a relatively small increase in volume produces a larger increase in ventricular filling pressure.

why_others_wrong.A: A smaller pressure rise for a given volume increase would indicate increased, not reduced, compliance, the opposite of the scenario described.
why_others_wrong.C: Reduced compliance means filling pressure changes markedly with volume; stating there is no change in filling pressure contradicts the definition of reduced compliance.
why_others_wrong.D: Fibrosis stiffens the myocardium and reduces compliance; it does not increase compliance as this option claims.
why_others_wrong.E: Reduced compliance causes filling pressure to rise, not fall, as ventricular volume increases.

exam_trap: Option A is chosen by candidates who invert the definition; a smaller pressure rise for a given volume would mean increased, not reduced, compliance.
takeaway: ↓ compliance → ↑ pressure for the same filling volume.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Elsevier, 2020.
thinking: Reduced LV compliance ↓ compliance = volume change per unit pressure change ↓ stiff ventricle shows a larger pressure rise for each volume added ↓ A larger increase in pressure for a given increase in volume
pearl: In a stiff ventricle small volume loads cause large rises in left atrial pressure, so such patients are prone to pulmonary oedema with fluid overload.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Cardiorespiratory physiology: venous capacitance
stem: A patient has a severe fall in circulating blood volume. Which vascular compartment contains the greatest proportion of the body's blood volume under normal conditions?
why_correct: The systemic venous circulation is the major blood reservoir because veins and venules are highly compliant. Changes in venous tone can therefore redistribute substantial blood volumes.

why_others_wrong.A: Arteries are a high-pressure, relatively low-volume compartment and hold a much smaller share of total blood volume than the venous system.
why_others_wrong.B: Arterioles are primarily resistance vessels with a very small lumen volume and contain only a minor fraction of total blood volume.
why_others_wrong.C: Capillaries, despite their large collective surface area, hold only a small proportion of total circulating blood volume at any moment.
why_others_wrong.E: Pulmonary capillaries form a small, specialised compartment and contain far less blood than the highly compliant systemic venous system.

exam_trap: Arteries are high-pressure vessels, but veins contain the largest proportion of circulating blood volume.
takeaway: Veins = capacitance vessels and major blood reservoir.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Elsevier, 2020.
thinking: Distribution of blood volume ↓ veins and venules are thin-walled and highly compliant ↓ they hold most of the circulating blood ↓ Veins and venules
pearl: Splanchnic and cutaneous venoconstriction in early haemorrhage can return a substantial volume to the central circulation, partly masking blood loss.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Cardiorespiratory physiology: hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction
stem: A patient has severe hypoxaemia caused by an alveolar process. Which local pulmonary response helps divert blood away from poorly ventilated alveoli?
why_correct: Low alveolar oxygen causes local pulmonary arteriolar vasoconstriction. This diverts blood toward better-ventilated regions and helps reduce ventilation-perfusion mismatch.

why_others_wrong.A: Pulmonary vasodilatation would increase blood flow to the poorly ventilated alveoli, worsening rather than correcting the ventilation-perfusion mismatch.
why_others_wrong.C: Systemic arteriolar vasoconstriction affects the peripheral systemic circulation and does not redirect blood flow within the pulmonary vasculature toward better-ventilated regions.
why_others_wrong.D: The bronchial arteries are part of the separate systemic circulation supplying airway tissue; constricting them does not redirect pulmonary alveolar blood flow.
why_others_wrong.E: Increased pulmonary capillary permeability would promote fluid leakage and oedema, not divert blood flow away from the hypoxic alveoli.

exam_trap: Hypoxia causes vasoconstriction in the pulmonary circulation but generally vasodilatation in systemic tissues.
takeaway: Pulmonary hypoxia → vasoconstriction → blood redirected toward better-ventilated alveoli.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Elsevier, 2020.
thinking: Alveolar hypoxia from an alveolar process ↓ local pulmonary arterioles constrict ↓ blood is diverted to better-ventilated alveoli ↓ Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction
pearl: Pulmonary vasodilators and some anaesthetic agents can blunt hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction and worsen oxygenation by increasing perfusion of poorly ventilated lung.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Cardiorespiratory physiology: dynamic airway compression
stem: A patient with obstructive lung disease has air trapping. Which change most directly contributes to dynamic airway compression during forced expiration?

options.A: Increased intrapleural pressure compressing intrathoracic airways
options.D: Increased airway cartilage throughout the bronchioles

correct_answer: A. Increased intrapleural pressure compressing intrathoracic airways
why_correct: During forced expiration, intrapleural pressure rises. Beyond the equal pressure point, airway pressure may fall below surrounding pleural pressure, producing dynamic airway compression. Loss of elastic recoil in emphysema worsens this effect.

why_others_wrong.B: Increased surfactant production would reduce surface tension and support alveolar/airway stability, and is not what drives dynamic compression during forced expiration.
why_others_wrong.C: Alveolar pressure is not reduced during forced expiration; it becomes positive due to the combination of elastic recoil and raised pleural pressure, which is what drives the compressive phenomenon.
why_others_wrong.D: Small bronchioles normally lack cartilage, which is precisely why they are prone to dynamic collapse; stating that cartilage increases throughout the bronchioles is anatomically incorrect and reverses the mechanism.
why_others_wrong.E: Increased pulmonary capillary pressure relates to fluid filtration and oedema, not to the mechanical airway compression seen with forced expiration.

exam_trap: Reduced alveolar pressure is chosen by candidates who assume compression needs low pressure inside; alveolar pressure is actually raised during forced expiration.
takeaway: Forced expiration + reduced elastic recoil → dynamic small-airway compression → air trapping.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Elsevier, 2020.
thinking: Obstructive disease with air trapping ↓ forced expiration raises intrapleural pressure ↓ beyond the equal pressure point this compresses intrathoracic airways ↓ Increased intrapleural pressure compressing intrathoracic airways
pearl: Airways outside the thorax behave oppositely, collapsing on inspiration, which is why extrathoracic obstruction causes inspiratory stridor and intrathoracic obstruction causes expiratory wheeze.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: Hepatobiliary surgery: (untitled)
stem: A patient with chronic liver disease develops jaundice and pale stools. Which substances normally give bile its yellow-green colour and, after intestinal metabolism, give stool its brown colour?
why_correct: Haem breakdown produces bilirubin, which is processed by the liver and excreted into bile. Intestinal metabolism produces pigments including urobilinogen and stercobilin, contributing to stool and urine colour. Pale stools can occur when reduced bile delivery to the intestine limits formation of normal stool pigments.

why_others_wrong.A: Albumin is a colourless plasma protein that carries unconjugated bilirubin in the blood but is not a bile pigment.
why_others_wrong.C: Cholesterol is a colourless lipid component of bile and does not give bile or stool its colour.
why_others_wrong.D: Bile acids are essential for fat emulsification and micelle formation but are not the pigments responsible for colour.
why_others_wrong.E: Phospholipids such as lecithin help solubilise cholesterol in bile micelles but are not pigmented.

exam_trap: Bile acids are essential for fat digestion but are not responsible for the characteristic pigment colour.
takeaway: Haem → bilirubin → hepatic conjugation → bile → intestinal pigments.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed., Elsevier, 2022.
thinking: Jaundice with pale stools ↓ bile is not reaching the gut ↓ bile colour comes from bilirubin, which gut bacteria convert to stercobilin ↓ Bilirubin derivatives
pearl: Pale stools with dark urine indicate a cholestatic pattern, because conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble and appears in urine while stercobilin production in the gut falls.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: Hepatobiliary surgery: (untitled)
stem: A patient develops extrahepatic biliary obstruction. Which bilirubin pattern is most likely?

options.D: Reduced conjugated bilirubin with increased faecal bilirubin

why_correct: In extrahepatic obstruction, hepatocytes can conjugate bilirubin but excretion into the intestine is impaired. Conjugated bilirubin therefore accumulates and can reflux into the bloodstream.

why_others_wrong.A: Predominantly unconjugated bilirubin suggests haemolysis or impaired conjugation, whereas in obstruction conjugation is intact and excretion is blocked.
why_others_wrong.C: Obstruction raises plasma bilirubin as conjugated bilirubin refluxes into the blood, the opposite of having none in plasma.
why_others_wrong.D: Obstruction stops bilirubin reaching the gut, so faecal pigment falls and stools become pale while conjugated bilirubin rises.
why_others_wrong.E: Haemoglobinuria reflects intravascular haemolysis with free haemoglobin in urine, not a bilirubin pattern of biliary obstruction.

exam_trap: Failure to conjugate bilirubin produces predominantly unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia; obstruction after conjugation produces predominantly conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia.
takeaway: Before conjugation problem → unconjugated. After conjugation but blocked excretion → conjugated.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed., Elsevier, 2022.
thinking: Extrahepatic biliary obstruction ↓ hepatocytes still conjugate bilirubin ↓ excretion into the duodenum is blocked ↓ conjugated bilirubin refluxes into the blood ↓ Predominantly conjugated bilirubin
pearl: Painless obstructive jaundice with a palpable gallbladder suggests malignant obstruction, such as pancreatic head cancer, rather than gallstones.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: Hepatobiliary surgery: (untitled)
stem: A liver biopsy demonstrates hepatocytes surrounding a central vein with relatively low oxygen availability compared with regions near the portal triad. Which acinar zone is being described?
why_correct: Zone 3 is closest to the central vein and receives blood with the lowest oxygen concentration within the hepatic acinus. It is therefore particularly susceptible to hypoxic injury. Zone 1 is closest to the portal triad and receives the most oxygenated blood.

why_others_wrong.A: Zone 1 is the periportal zone next to the portal triad, which receives the best-oxygenated blood.
why_others_wrong.B: Zone 2 is the intermediate midzonal region between portal triad and central vein, not the region immediately around the central vein.
why_others_wrong.D: The portal tract contains the hepatic artery, portal vein and bile duct branches and carries the most oxygenated inflow, not the lowest.
why_others_wrong.E: Bile duct zone is not a recognised acinar zone; bile ductules lie within the portal tract, not around the central vein.

exam_trap: Zone 1 (option A) is chosen by candidates who reverse the numbering, but zone 1 is periportal and best oxygenated; zone 3 surrounds the central vein.
takeaway: Portal triad → zone 1 → zone 2 → central vein → zone 3.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed., Elsevier, 2022.
thinking: Hepatocytes around the central vein ↓ blood flows from the portal triad toward the central vein ↓ oxygen falls along the sinusoid ↓ the pericentral region receives the least oxygen ↓ Zone 3
pearl: Zone 3 is also rich in cytochrome P450 enzymes, so it is the site of centrilobular necrosis in paracetamol overdose as well as in ischaemic hepatitis.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Hepatobiliary surgery: (untitled)
stem: A patient takes an overdose of a drug that undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism. The liver develops a centrilobular pattern of necrosis. Which region is most likely affected?
why_correct: The centrilobular region is relatively hypoxic and contains high concentrations of some cytochrome P450 enzymes capable of generating toxic metabolites. It is therefore particularly vulnerable to certain drug-induced injuries.

why_others_wrong.A: Zone 1 is the periportal region, closest to the oxygen- and nutrient-rich portal blood supply, and is therefore relatively protected rather than the site of centrilobular necrosis.
why_others_wrong.B: Zone 2 is the mid-zonal region, intermediate in oxygenation and less characteristically affected than the centrilobular zone.
why_others_wrong.D: The portal vein is a vascular structure, not a hepatocyte zone, and is not the site of centrilobular necrosis.
why_others_wrong.E: Bile duct epithelium is affected in cholestatic/biliary injury patterns, not in centrilobular hepatocyte necrosis from toxic metabolites.

exam_trap: Candidates choose zone 1 (A) because portal blood carries absorbed drug, but zone 1 is periportal; centrilobular means around the central vein, which is zone 3.
takeaway: Zone 3 is vulnerable because of both relatively low oxygenation and metabolic activation of some toxins.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed., Elsevier, 2022.
thinking: Drug overdose with hepatic metabolism ↓ centrilobular necrosis ↓ zone 3 has most cytochrome P450 and least oxygen ↓ Zone 3
pearl: In paracetamol overdose, CYP2E1 in zone 3 generates the toxic metabolite NAPQI, and acetylcysteine works by replenishing glutathione to detoxify it.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: Hepatobiliary surgery: (untitled)
stem: A patient has chronic cholestatic liver disease. Which structure is primarily responsible for modifying bile composition by secreting bicarbonate-rich fluid into bile ducts?
why_correct: Cholangiocytes line the intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts and contribute to bile modification, including bicarbonate-rich secretion.

why_others_wrong.A: Hepatocytes produce primary canalicular bile, but the bicarbonate-rich ductal modification of bile is performed by cholangiocytes.
why_others_wrong.C: Kupffer cells are resident hepatic macrophages in the sinusoids and do not secrete fluid into the bile ducts.
why_others_wrong.D: Hepatic stellate cells store vitamin A and drive fibrosis when activated, but they do not modify bile.
why_others_wrong.E: Sinusoidal endothelial cells form the fenestrated lining of the sinusoids and have no role in secreting fluid into bile ducts.

exam_trap: Hepatocytes (option A) tempt because they make bile, but they produce primary canalicular bile; cholangiocytes lining the ducts add the bicarbonate-rich fluid.
takeaway: Hepatocytes make bile; cholangiocytes modify it.
source: Gray's Anatomy, 42nd ed., Elsevier, 2020; Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed., Elsevier, 2022.
thinking: Bicarbonate-rich fluid added to bile ↓ this happens after canalicular bile leaves hepatocytes ↓ the epithelium lining the bile ducts secretes it, partly under secretin ↓ Cholangiocytes
pearl: Cholangiocytes are the target of injury in primary sclerosing cholangitis and primary biliary cholangitis, and they are the cell of origin of cholangiocarcinoma.

subject: Anatomy
title: Hepatobiliary surgery: (untitled)
stem: A liver specimen contains macrophages located within the hepatic sinusoids. Which cells are these?
why_correct: Kupffer cells are resident macrophages located within hepatic sinusoids. They participate in phagocytosis and innate immune surveillance. Hepatic stellate cells, historically called Ito cells, are different cells located in the perisinusoidal space.

why_others_wrong.B: Ito (hepatic stellate) cells reside in the perisinusoidal space of Disse, not within the sinusoidal lumen, and function in vitamin A storage and fibrosis rather than phagocytosis.
why_others_wrong.C: Cholangiocytes are the epithelial cells lining bile ductules, unrelated to sinusoidal macrophage function.
why_others_wrong.D: Hepatocytes are the main parenchymal cells of the liver, not resident macrophages.
why_others_wrong.E: Paneth cells are found in intestinal crypts, not in the liver.

exam_trap: Kupffer = macrophage; stellate/Ito = perisinusoidal cell involved in vitamin A storage and fibrosis.
takeaway: Kupffer cells = liver macrophages.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed., Elsevier, 2022.
thinking: Macrophages ↓ resident within the hepatic sinusoids ↓ stellate cells lie outside the sinusoid in the space of Disse ↓ Kupffer cells
pearl: Hepatic stellate cells, not Kupffer cells, are the main producers of collagen in liver fibrosis; when activated they lose their vitamin A stores and become myofibroblast-like.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Hepatobiliary surgery: (untitled)
stem: A patient develops progressive hepatic fibrosis after chronic liver injury. Which cell is primarily responsible for producing excess extracellular matrix in hepatic fibrosis?
why_correct: Chronic liver injury activates hepatic stellate cells, which acquire a myofibroblast-like phenotype and produce excess extracellular matrix, including collagen.

why_others_wrong.A: Kupffer cells are the liver's resident macrophages and can trigger and perpetuate injury/inflammation, but they are not the principal matrix-producing cell.
why_others_wrong.C: Cholangiocytes are bile duct epithelial cells, not fibrogenic matrix-producing cells.
why_others_wrong.D: Sinusoidal endothelial cells line the hepatic sinusoids and undergo capillarisation in fibrosis, but are not the main source of excess matrix.
why_others_wrong.E: Neutrophils are acute inflammatory cells, not a source of chronic fibrogenic matrix deposition.

exam_trap: Candidates choose Kupffer cells (A) because they drive hepatic inflammation, but these resident macrophages signal fibrosis; stellate cells produce the excess matrix.
takeaway: Chronic liver injury → stellate-cell activation → collagen deposition → fibrosis.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed., Elsevier, 2022.
thinking: Chronic liver injury ↓ hepatic stellate cells activated ↓ transform into myofibroblast-like cells ↓ deposit collagen ↓ Hepatic stellate cell
pearl: Stellate cells store vitamin A in the space of Disse when quiescent, and their activation is driven largely by TGF-beta released by Kupffer cells and damaged hepatocytes.

subject: Physiology
title: GI physiology & metabolism: (untitled)
stem: A patient has a pituitary tumour secreting excess prolactin. Which hypothalamic hormone normally exerts tonic inhibition of prolactin secretion?
why_correct: Dopamine released from the hypothalamus reaches the anterior pituitary through the hypophyseal portal circulation and tonically inhibits prolactin secretion.

why_others_wrong.A: TRH is primarily a stimulatory releasing hormone for TSH (and can mildly raise prolactin), but it is not the principal tonic inhibitor of prolactin secretion.
why_others_wrong.B: GnRH regulates gonadotrophin (LH/FSH) release from the anterior pituitary and has no inhibitory role over prolactin.
why_others_wrong.D: CRH stimulates ACTH secretion from corticotrophs and has no direct inhibitory action on lactotroph prolactin release.
why_others_wrong.E: GHRH stimulates growth hormone secretion from somatotrophs and plays no role in the tonic control of prolactin.

exam_trap: Prolactin is unusual among anterior pituitary hormones because its principal hypothalamic control is inhibitory.
takeaway: Dopamine = tonic brake on prolactin.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Elsevier, 2020.
thinking: Prolactin-secreting pituitary tumour ↓ prolactin is normally under tonic hypothalamic inhibition ↓ dopamine reaches lactotrophs via the portal circulation ↓ acts on D2 receptors ↓ Dopamine
pearl: Prolactinomas are usually treated first with dopamine agonists such as cabergoline rather than surgery, even when large, because these often shrink the tumour.

subject: Anatomy
title: Physiology: (untitled)
stem: A patient has a pituitary adenoma compressing the optic chiasm. Which visual field defect is classically produced?
why_correct: The optic chiasm contains crossing nasal retinal fibres. Compression from a midline sellar mass therefore preferentially affects fibres carrying temporal visual fields from both eyes, producing bitemporal hemianopia.

why_others_wrong.A: A right homonymous hemianopia results from a lesion posterior to the chiasm (e.g., left optic tract, radiation, or occipital cortex), not from chiasmal compression itself.
why_others_wrong.B: A left homonymous hemianopia results from a lesion posterior to the chiasm on the right side, not from a midline chiasmal lesion.
why_others_wrong.D: An isolated central scotoma suggests a lesion of the macular fibres or optic nerve itself, not compression of the crossing chiasmal fibres.
why_others_wrong.E: Monocular blindness implies a lesion anterior to the chiasm affecting one optic nerve alone, not the bilaterally crossing nasal fibres compressed here.

exam_trap: Chiasmal lesions produce a binocular field defect; optic tract lesions produce homonymous hemianopia.
takeaway: Optic chiasm compression → nasal retinal fibres → bitemporal hemianopia.
source: Gray's Anatomy, 42nd ed., Elsevier, 2020.
thinking: Pituitary adenoma pressing on the optic chiasm ↓ the crossing fibres come from the nasal retina of each eye ↓ nasal retina sees the temporal visual field ↓ Bitemporal hemianopia
pearl: Pituitary adenomas compress the chiasm from below, so the superior temporal quadrants are usually lost first, whereas craniopharyngiomas pressing from above often affect the inferior quadrants first.

subject: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care
title: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care: (untitled)
stem: A patient has primary hyperparathyroidism caused by a parathyroid adenoma. Which biochemical pattern is most likely?

options.A: Low calcium, high phosphate, high PTH
options.B: High calcium, low phosphate, high PTH
options.C: High calcium, high phosphate, low PTH
options.D: Low calcium, low phosphate, low PTH
options.E: Normal calcium, high phosphate, suppressed PTH

correct_answer: B. High calcium, low phosphate, high PTH
why_correct: Primary hyperparathyroidism causes autonomous PTH secretion. PTH increases renal calcium reabsorption, promotes vitamin D activation and increases bone resorption. It also decreases proximal tubular phosphate reabsorption, producing phosphate loss.

why_others_wrong.A: Low calcium with high phosphate and high PTH describes secondary hyperparathyroidism, for example in chronic kidney disease, not a parathyroid adenoma.
why_others_wrong.C: High calcium with low PTH indicates PTH-independent hypercalcaemia, such as malignancy or vitamin D excess, rather than an adenoma secreting PTH.
why_others_wrong.D: Low calcium with low PTH indicates PTH deficiency or suppression, the opposite of an adenoma autonomously secreting PTH, which raises calcium.
why_others_wrong.E: Suppressed PTH with high phosphate is incompatible with an adenoma autonomously secreting PTH, which raises calcium and causes phosphate loss.

exam_trap: PTH does not simply increase both calcium and phosphate. Its renal effects tend to increase calcium while lowering phosphate.
takeaway: Primary hyperparathyroidism → ↑ PTH → ↑ calcium + ↓ phosphate.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Elsevier, 2020.
thinking: Parathyroid adenoma ↓ autonomous PTH secretion ↓ raises calcium by bone, renal and gut effects ↓ reduces proximal tubular phosphate reabsorption ↓ High calcium, low phosphate, high PTH
pearl: Indications for parathyroidectomy in primary hyperparathyroidism include symptomatic disease, renal stones, osteoporosis and markedly raised calcium.

subject: Physiology
title: GI physiology & metabolism: (untitled)
stem: A patient has a catecholamine-secreting adrenal medullary tumour. Which biochemical substance is derived from the same precursor pathway as adrenaline and noradrenaline?
why_correct: Catecholamines are synthesised from tyrosine: Tyrosine → L-DOPA → dopamine → noradrenaline → adrenaline. Dopamine is therefore an intermediate in catecholamine synthesis.

why_others_wrong.A: Cortisol is a corticosteroid synthesised from cholesterol via a distinct adrenal cortical pathway, unrelated to catecholamine synthesis from tyrosine.
why_others_wrong.B: Aldosterone is a mineralocorticoid derived from cholesterol in the zona glomerulosa, not part of the tyrosine-derived catecholamine pathway.
why_others_wrong.D: Progesterone is a steroid hormone synthesised from cholesterol, structurally and biosynthetically unrelated to the catecholamine pathway.
why_others_wrong.E: Testosterone is a steroid derived from cholesterol via gonadal/adrenal steroidogenesis, not from the tyrosine pathway that produces catecholamines.

exam_trap: Adrenal cortical steroids are derived from cholesterol, whereas catecholamines are derived from tyrosine.
takeaway: Tyrosine → L-DOPA → dopamine → noradrenaline → adrenaline.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Elsevier, 2020.
thinking: Catecholamine-secreting medullary tumour ↓ catecholamines derive from tyrosine ↓ tyrosine, L-DOPA, dopamine, noradrenaline, adrenaline ↓ dopamine is an intermediate of the pathway ↓ Dopamine
pearl: Phaeochromocytoma is diagnosed with plasma or urinary metanephrines, and preoperative alpha-blockade followed by beta-blockade prevents hypertensive crises during tumour handling.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Pathology: oncology & haematology: (untitled)
stem: A patient has a germline mutation in a tumour suppressor gene. Which genetic principle best explains why loss of the remaining normal allele may permit tumour development?
why_correct: Tumour suppressor genes commonly require loss or inactivation of both functional alleles for loss of tumour-suppressive activity. In hereditary cancer syndromes, a germline mutation provides the first hit and somatic loss of the remaining normal allele can provide the second.

why_others_wrong.A: A single hit is typically sufficient for oncogene activation, whereas a tumour suppressor usually needs loss of both alleles before function is lost.
why_others_wrong.C: Anticipation is earlier onset or greater severity in successive generations, typically from expanding trinucleotide repeats, not loss of a second allele.
why_others_wrong.D: Genomic imprinting is parent-of-origin-specific gene expression and does not explain somatic loss of the remaining normal tumour suppressor allele.
why_others_wrong.E: Mitochondrial inheritance is maternal transmission of mitochondrial DNA and has no bearing on inactivation of a nuclear tumour suppressor gene.

exam_trap: This contrasts with many oncogenes, where activation of a single allele can be sufficient for a gain-of-function effect.
takeaway: Tumour suppressor loss commonly follows the two-hit model.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed., Elsevier, 2022.
thinking: Germline mutation in a tumour suppressor gene ↓ one allele is already inactive in every cell ↓ somatic loss of the remaining normal allele abolishes function ↓ Two-hit hypothesis
pearl: The two-hit model explains why hereditary cancers present earlier and are often bilateral or multifocal: every cell already carries the first hit.

subject: Genetics
title: Genetics: FAP inheritance
stem: A patient with familial adenomatous polyposis develops numerous colorectal adenomas. Which inheritance pattern is characteristic of this syndrome?
why_correct: Familial adenomatous polyposis is caused by germline pathogenic variants in the APC tumour suppressor gene and is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner.

why_others_wrong.A: Autosomal recessive inheritance fits MUTYH-associated polyposis, not classic familial adenomatous polyposis, which is dominant from a single germline APC variant.
why_others_wrong.B: APC lies on chromosome 5, so familial adenomatous polyposis affects both sexes equally and does not follow an X-linked pattern.
why_others_wrong.D: Mitochondrial inheritance passes through the maternal line via mtDNA, whereas familial adenomatous polyposis is caused by a nuclear APC gene variant.
why_others_wrong.E: Y-linked inheritance would affect only males through the paternal line, but familial adenomatous polyposis is autosomal and affects both sexes.

exam_trap: Autosomal recessive is chosen by candidates who recall MUTYH-associated polyposis, which is recessive; classic FAP from a germline APC variant is autosomal dominant.
takeaway: FAP → APC mutation → autosomal dominant inheritance → numerous colorectal adenomas.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed., Elsevier, 2022.
thinking: Familial adenomatous polyposis ↓ germline APC tumour suppressor variant ↓ one inherited variant is enough to cause polyposis ↓ Autosomal dominant
pearl: Up to about a quarter of FAP cases arise from new APC mutations, so a patient may have no family history, but their children still have a 50% risk.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Pathology: oncology & haematology: (untitled)
stem: A patient with hereditary retinoblastoma develops a second malignancy later in life. Which protein directly binds and restrains E2F transcription factors, preventing progression from G1 into S phase?
why_correct: The retinoblastoma protein (Rb) regulates the G1/S transition by restraining E2F-dependent transcription. Loss of Rb function permits inappropriate progression into S phase.

why_others_wrong.A: p53 also contributes to G1 arrest after DNA damage, but indirectly: it induces p21, which inhibits cyclin-CDK complexes and so keeps Rb hypophosphorylated. p53 does not itself bind E2F.
why_others_wrong.C: BRCA1 functions in homologous recombination repair of DNA double-strand breaks and is linked to breast and ovarian cancer, not retinoblastoma.
why_others_wrong.D: APC regulates beta-catenin in the Wnt pathway and is linked to familial adenomatous polyposis, not to G1/S control in retinoblastoma.
why_others_wrong.E: BCL-2 is an anti-apoptotic mitochondrial protein that promotes cell survival and does not regulate the G1/S checkpoint.

exam_trap: p53 also causes G1 arrest, but indirectly through p21; the protein that directly binds and restrains E2F at the G1/S transition is Rb.
takeaway: Rb = G1/S checkpoint brake.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed., Elsevier, 2022.
thinking: Hereditary retinoblastoma with a later second malignancy ↓ germline RB1 loss ↓ Rb protein normally binds and restrains E2F ↓ this blocks progression from G1 into S phase ↓ Rb
pearl: Survivors of hereditary retinoblastoma are particularly prone to osteosarcoma, illustrating the two-hit model: one inherited and one acquired mutation of the same gene.

subject: Immunology
title: Immunology: cellular transplant rejection
stem: A patient receives an organ transplant. Which immune cells are primarily responsible for recognising donor MHC molecules and initiating cellular rejection?
why_correct: T lymphocytes recognise donor-derived major histocompatibility complex molecules and play a central role in cellular transplant rejection. Both CD4 and CD8 T cells can contribute, through cytokine-mediated inflammation and direct cytotoxic mechanisms.

why_others_wrong.A: Neutrophils may infiltrate an injured graft but do not recognise donor MHC molecules through antigen-specific receptors or initiate cellular rejection.
why_others_wrong.C: Erythrocytes carry oxygen and have no antigen receptors, so they cannot recognise donor MHC or drive graft rejection.
why_others_wrong.D: Platelets contribute to thrombosis in antibody-mediated graft injury, but they do not recognise donor MHC or initiate cellular rejection.
why_others_wrong.E: Eosinophils are mainly involved in allergic and antiparasitic responses and lack the antigen-specific recognition of donor MHC that T cells provide.

exam_trap: Neutrophils tempt because they infiltrate an injured graft, but they lack antigen-specific receptors; recognising donor MHC and initiating cellular rejection is the role of recipient T lymphocytes.
takeaway: Acute cellular rejection → T-cell-mediated immune response against the graft.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed., Elsevier, 2022.
thinking: Organ transplant recognised as foreign ↓ donor MHC is the main alloantigen ↓ recognised by recipient T-cell receptors ↓ CD4 and CD8 cells drive cellular rejection ↓ T lymphocytes
pearl: Acute cellular rejection usually responds to pulsed high-dose corticosteroids, with T-cell-depleting antibody reserved for steroid-resistant episodes.

subject: Immunology
title: Immunology: graft-versus-host disease
stem: A patient develops graft-versus-host disease after an allogeneic haematopoietic stem-cell transplant. Which cells are primarily responsible for attacking the recipient's tissues?
why_correct: Graft-versus-host disease occurs when immunocompetent donor T cells recognise recipient tissues as foreign and mount an immune response against them. This differs conceptually from conventional solid-organ rejection, in which the recipient immune system attacks the graft.

why_others_wrong.A: Recipient neutrophils are part of the host's own innate defence; in graft-versus-host disease the attacking cells come from the donor graft.
why_others_wrong.C: Recipient erythrocytes carry oxygen and have no immune effector function, so they cannot attack host tissues.
why_others_wrong.D: Donor platelets are involved in haemostasis and lack antigen-specific receptors, so they do not recognise and attack recipient tissues.
why_others_wrong.E: Recipient B cells belong to the host, and graft-versus-host disease is driven by donor T cells rather than host antibody production.

exam_trap: Candidates who think of ordinary rejection pick recipient cells, but in graft-versus-host disease the donor T cells in the graft attack the immunosuppressed recipient tissues.
takeaway: GVHD → donor T cells attack recipient tissues.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed., Elsevier, 2022.
thinking: Allogeneic haematopoietic stem-cell transplant ↓ graft contains immunocompetent donor lymphocytes ↓ they recognise recipient tissue as foreign ↓ Donor immunocompetent T lymphocytes
pearl: Transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease is prevented by irradiating cellular blood components for at-risk recipients, which inactivates donor lymphocytes.

subject: Burns & paediatric fluids
title: Burns & paediatric fluids: (untitled)
stem: A patient with severe burns develops a prolonged hypermetabolic state. Which hormonal pattern contributes to increased catabolism?

options.A: Reduced catecholamines and increased insulin sensitivity
options.D: Increased insulin with suppressed counter-regulatory hormones
options.E: Complete suppression of hepatic glucose production

correct_answer: B. Increased catecholamines, cortisol and glucagon
why_correct: Major trauma and burns produce a pronounced stress response. Catecholamines, cortisol and glucagon increase, promoting hepatic glucose production, lipolysis and protein catabolism, together with insulin resistance.

why_others_wrong.A: After major burns catecholamines rise sharply and insulin resistance develops, so reduced catecholamines with better insulin sensitivity is the reverse of the stress response.
why_others_wrong.C: Cortisol and glucagon are raised, not reduced, after severe burns, driving gluconeogenesis, lipolysis and protein breakdown.
why_others_wrong.D: Counter-regulatory hormones are increased after major burns and insulin action is blunted by insulin resistance, so this describes an anabolic rather than catabolic state.
why_others_wrong.E: Hepatic glucose production increases after major burns through gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis, producing stress hyperglycaemia rather than suppression.

exam_trap: Option D tempts because stress hyperglycaemia suggests raised insulin, but counter-regulatory hormones rise and insulin resistance develops, producing catabolism rather than an anabolic state.
takeaway: Major injury → stress hormones ↑ → hypermetabolism + insulin resistance + catabolism.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Elsevier, 2020.
thinking: Severe burn causes a prolonged hypermetabolic stress response ↓ catecholamines, cortisol and glucagon rise ↓ hepatic glucose output, lipolysis and protein breakdown increase ↓ insulin resistance develops ↓ Increased catecholamines, cortisol and glucagon
pearl: Burn hypermetabolism can persist for months, so early enteral feeding, early excision and grafting of the wound and a warm environment are used to limit muscle wasting.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: (untitled)
stem: During prolonged fasting, adipose tissue releases free fatty acids into the circulation. Which of these hormones forms part of the fasting counter-regulatory response that favours lipolysis?
why_correct: During fasting, the fall in insulin and the rise in counter-regulatory hormones promote hormone-sensitive lipase activity and mobilisation of stored triglyceride. Glucagon is part of this fasting hormonal profile, although in humans the fall in insulin and increased catecholamine activity are the dominant drivers of lipolysis.

why_others_wrong.A: Insulin suppresses lipolysis and promotes fat storage; it acts in the opposite direction to what occurs during fasting.
why_others_wrong.C: Calcitonin regulates calcium homeostasis by inhibiting osteoclast activity and has no established role in promoting lipolysis during fasting.
why_others_wrong.D: Aldosterone regulates renal sodium and potassium handling and has no direct role in adipose tissue lipolysis.
why_others_wrong.E: Growth hormone-binding protein is a carrier protein for growth hormone in the circulation, not itself a hormone that drives lipolysis.

exam_trap: Insulin (A) is chosen as the best-known metabolic hormone, but it suppresses hormone-sensitive lipase; fasting lipolysis follows falling insulin and rising counter-regulatory hormones.
takeaway: Fasting → insulin ↓ + counter-regulatory hormones ↑ → lipolysis ↑.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Elsevier, 2020.
thinking: Prolonged fasting ↓ insulin falls and counter-regulatory hormones, including glucagon and catecholamines, rise ↓ hormone-sensitive lipase is activated in adipose tissue ↓ stored triglyceride is mobilised as free fatty acids ↓ Glucagon
pearl: In prolonged starvation the liver converts fatty acids to ketone bodies, which the brain increasingly uses for fuel, sparing muscle protein that would otherwise be broken down for gluconeogenesis.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Perioperative medicine & nutrition: (untitled)
stem: A patient is given prolonged parenteral nutrition with no enteral intake. Which consequence is most directly related to prolonged absence of enteral stimulation of the gastrointestinal tract?

options.C: Increased villous height in all circumstances

why_correct: Prolonged absence of enteral nutrient delivery can reduce gastrointestinal trophic stimulation and contribute to mucosal atrophy and altered gut function. Enteral nutrition, when feasible, helps maintain gastrointestinal structure and function.

why_others_wrong.A: Absence of luminal nutrients reduces, rather than increases, the trophic stimulation that maintains the intestinal mucosa.
why_others_wrong.C: Villous height tends to fall without enteral nutrients, reflecting atrophy rather than growth.
why_others_wrong.D: Mucosal atrophy may impair barrier function, so prolonged parenteral nutrition does not prevent bacterial translocation.
why_others_wrong.E: Lack of enteral stimulation tends to impair normal gut motility and function rather than increase it.

exam_trap: “Parenteral nutrition provides calories” does not mean it provides the same gastrointestinal trophic effects as enteral feeding.
takeaway: Gut needs nutrients through the gut for normal trophic stimulation.
source: Principles and Practice of Surgery, 7th ed., Elsevier; current RCS MRCS preparation resource list.
thinking: Prolonged parenteral nutrition with no enteral intake ↓ luminal nutrients normally provide trophic stimulation to the gut mucosa ↓ without them the mucosa is not maintained ↓ villi shorten and barrier function weakens ↓ Intestinal mucosal atrophy
pearl: Where the gut works, enteral feeding (including nasojejunal or feeding jejunostomy routes after major upper GI surgery) is preferred to parenteral nutrition, which also carries line sepsis and metabolic risks.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: (untitled)
stem: During abdominal surgery, a surgeon identifies a vessel running along the lesser curvature of the stomach. Which arteries anastomose to form this lesser curvature arcade?

options.E: Middle colic and right colic arteries

correct_answer: A. Right and left gastric arteries
why_correct: The right and left gastric arteries run along the lesser curvature and form an arterial anastomotic arcade. The right and left gastro-omental arteries form an arcade along the greater curvature.

why_others_wrong.B: The right and left gastro-omental arteries form the arcade along the greater curvature, not the lesser curvature.
why_others_wrong.C: The pancreaticoduodenal arteries form arcades around the pancreatic head and duodenum, linking coeliac and superior mesenteric territories.
why_others_wrong.D: Short gastric arteries arise from the splenic artery and supply the fundus near the greater curvature; they form no lesser curvature arcade.
why_others_wrong.E: The middle and right colic arteries are superior mesenteric branches supplying the colon, well away from the stomach.

exam_trap: Right and left gastro-omental arteries are chosen because they also form a gastric arcade, but theirs runs along the greater curvature, not the lesser curvature.
takeaway: Lesser curvature → right + left gastric arteries. Greater curvature → right + left gastro-omental arteries.
source: Gray's Anatomy, 42nd ed., Elsevier, 2020.
thinking: Vessel along the lesser curvature ↓ the left gastric artery from the coeliac trunk runs down from the cardia ↓ the right gastric artery, usually from the hepatic artery, runs up from the pylorus ↓ they anastomose within the lesser omentum ↓ Right and left gastric arteries
pearl: Bleeding from a lesser curve gastric ulcer is typically from the left gastric artery, whereas a posterior duodenal ulcer erodes the gastroduodenal artery.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: (untitled)
stem: During surgery for a distal oesophageal lesion, the surgeon considers the lymphatic drainage of the lower oesophagus. Which feature is particularly important clinically?

options.A: Lymphatic drainage is restricted entirely to the immediate para-oesophageal nodes
options.B: Oesophageal lymphatics can permit longitudinal spread along the oesophagus
options.C: The lower oesophagus drains exclusively to cervical lymph nodes
options.D: Lymphatic drainage is absent in the submucosa
options.E: Oesophageal lymphatics drain directly into the thoracic duct without nodal stations

correct_answer: B. Oesophageal lymphatics can permit longitudinal spread along the oesophagus
why_correct: The oesophagus has a rich submucosal lymphatic network with longitudinal connections. This can permit tumour spread beyond the immediately adjacent segment and is one reason oesophageal malignancy may involve lymph nodes at more distant levels than expected from the primary lesion alone.

why_others_wrong.A: Drainage is not confined to adjacent para-oesophageal nodes; the submucosal plexus allows spread to distant cervical, mediastinal and coeliac nodes.
why_others_wrong.C: The lower oesophagus drains mainly to posterior mediastinal and left gastric/coeliac nodes; cervical nodes drain the upper third.
why_others_wrong.D: The submucosa contains a rich longitudinal lymphatic plexus, which is exactly why oesophageal cancer spreads widely.
why_others_wrong.E: Oesophageal lymph normally passes through regional nodal stations; bypassing all nodes is not the usual pattern even if some direct duct channels exist.

exam_trap: Option A appeals because lymph drainage is often taught segment by segment, but the longitudinal submucosal plexus allows skip spread well beyond the adjacent para-oesophageal nodes.
takeaway: Oesophagus = rich longitudinal submucosal lymphatics → potentially extensive nodal spread.
source: Gray's Anatomy, 42nd ed., Elsevier, 2020; Principles and Practice of Surgery, 7th ed., Elsevier.
thinking: Distal oesophageal lesion ↓ dense submucosal lymphatic plexus ↓ the plexus runs longitudinally over long distances ↓ nodes far from the primary may be involved ↓ Oesophageal lymphatics can permit longitudinal spread along the oesophagus
pearl: Lower oesophageal cancers commonly spread to left gastric and coeliac nodes, so oesophagectomy includes an abdominal as well as a mediastinal lymphadenectomy.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: lung root relations
stem: During a thoracic operation, a surgeon traces a nerve descending on the lateral surface of the fibrous pericardium. Which nerve passes anterior to the root of the lung?
why_correct: The phrenic nerve descends anterior to the root of the lung, whereas the vagus nerve passes posterior to the root.

why_others_wrong.A: The vagus nerve passes posterior to the lung root, where it contributes to the posterior pulmonary plexus.
why_others_wrong.B: The recurrent laryngeal nerves hook under the aortic arch or right subclavian artery and ascend to the larynx; they do not reach the lung root.
why_others_wrong.D: The greater splanchnic nerve arises from the T5-T9 sympathetic ganglia on the posterior thoracic wall, well behind the lung root.
why_others_wrong.E: The sympathetic trunk lies on the heads of the ribs on the posterior chest wall, posterior to the lung root.

exam_trap: Vagus nerve is chosen because it also descends near the lung root, but it passes posterior to the root; only the phrenic nerve runs anterior to it.
takeaway: Phrenic = anterior to lung root. Vagus = posterior to lung root.
source: Gray's Anatomy, 42nd ed., Elsevier, 2020.
thinking: Nerve on the lateral surface of the fibrous pericardium ↓ descends anterior to the lung root ↓ the vagus passes behind the root instead ↓ Phrenic nerve
pearl: The phrenic nerve travels with the pericardiacophrenic vessels and must be identified and protected during pericardial and lung root dissection, as injury paralyses the ipsilateral hemidiaphragm.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: (untitled)
stem: A patient undergoes surgery near the left pulmonary hilum. Injury to the vagus nerve at the lung root would most directly affect which function?

options.A: Somatic motor supply to the diaphragm
options.D: Sensory supply from the skin of the chest
options.E: Sympathetic supply to the upper limb

correct_answer: B. Parasympathetic supply to thoracic viscera
why_correct: The vagus nerve provides major parasympathetic innervation to the thoracic viscera, including the heart and lungs, and contributes to the pulmonary and oesophageal plexuses. The phrenic nerve supplies motor innervation to the diaphragm.

why_others_wrong.A: Somatic motor supply to the diaphragm comes from the phrenic nerve (C3-C5), which passes anterior, not posterior, to the lung root.
why_others_wrong.C: The intercostal muscles are supplied by the intercostal nerves (anterior rami of T1-T11), not the vagus.
why_others_wrong.D: Chest wall skin is supplied by cutaneous branches of intercostal nerves; the vagus carries no cutaneous thoracic sensation.
why_others_wrong.E: Sympathetic supply to the upper limb comes from the cervicothoracic sympathetic chain via grey rami to the brachial plexus, not the vagus.

exam_trap: Do not confuse vagal visceral innervation with phrenic motor supply to the diaphragm.
takeaway: Vagus = thoracic parasympathetic. Phrenic = diaphragm motor.
source: Gray's Anatomy, 42nd ed., Elsevier, 2020.
thinking: Vagus nerve at the lung root ↓ passes posterior to the root to form the pulmonary plexus ↓ carries preganglionic parasympathetic fibres ↓ supplies the heart, lungs and oesophagus ↓ Parasympathetic supply to thoracic viscera
pearl: On the left the vagus gives off the recurrent laryngeal nerve around the aortic arch, so mediastinal disease near the aortopulmonary window can present with hoarseness.

subject: Anatomy
title: Physiology: (untitled)
stem: A patient develops a left-sided pleural effusion. Which structure forms the lowest part of the pleural cavity in the upright patient?
why_correct: The costodiaphragmatic recess is the potential space between costal and diaphragmatic pleura. In an upright patient, pleural fluid tends to collect in the dependent costodiaphragmatic region.

why_others_wrong.A: The costomediastinal recess lies anteriorly between costal and mediastinal pleura and is not the dependent space affected by gravity in an upright patient.
why_others_wrong.C: The pulmonary ligament is a fold of mediastinal pleura below the hilum, not a pleural recess where fluid collects.
why_others_wrong.D: The oblique fissure separates lung lobes and is not a pleural space at all.
why_others_wrong.E: The hilum is where structures enter and leave the lung; it is not a pleural recess and does not collect fluid.

exam_trap: The costomediastinal recess is anterior and is not the principal dependent pleural space.
takeaway: Pleural fluid gravitates to the costodiaphragmatic recess.
source: Gray's Anatomy, 42nd ed., Elsevier, 2020.
thinking: Upright patient with a pleural effusion ↓ fluid gravitates to the most dependent pleural space ↓ costal and diaphragmatic pleura meet in a deep recess ↓ Costodiaphragmatic recess
pearl: Blunting of the costophrenic angle on an erect chest X-ray is an early sign of effusion, and because the recess extends below the lung, ultrasound guidance is recommended for pleural aspiration to avoid the liver or spleen.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: (untitled)
stem: A surgeon is operating near the posterior mediastinum. Which structure passes through the diaphragm with the oesophagus?
correct_answer: C. Anterior and posterior vagal trunks
why_correct: The oesophagus passes through the diaphragm at approximately T10, accompanied by the anterior and posterior vagal trunks. The inferior vena cava passes through the central tendon at approximately T8, while the aorta passes posteriorly through the aortic hiatus at approximately T12.

why_others_wrong.A: The inferior vena cava passes through the central tendon at T8, separately from the oesophagus.
why_others_wrong.B: The aorta passes behind the median arcuate ligament at T12, posterior to the diaphragm rather than through the oesophageal hiatus.
why_others_wrong.D: The thoracic duct passes through the aortic hiatus at T12 with the aorta and azygos vein, not with the oesophagus.
why_others_wrong.E: The sympathetic trunks pass behind the medial arcuate ligaments, not through the oesophageal hiatus.

exam_trap: Thoracic duct only is chosen because the duct lies close to the oesophagus in the posterior mediastinum, but it passes through the aortic hiatus at T12 with the aorta and azygos vein.
takeaway: IVC 8, oesophagus 10, aorta 12.
source: Gray's Anatomy, 42nd ed., Elsevier, 2020.
thinking: Structures traversing the oesophageal hiatus ↓ the oesophagus passes through at about T10 ↓ the anterior and posterior vagal trunks accompany it ↓ Anterior and posterior vagal trunks
pearl: The vagal trunks are identified and preserved at the hiatus during fundoplication and hiatus hernia repair; injury can cause delayed gastric emptying, and the posterior trunk lies behind the oesophagus close to the right crus.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: (untitled)
stem: A patient has an injury to the thoracic duct just before it enters the venous circulation. Which region would normally drain through this duct?

options.B: Right side of the head and neck only
options.E: Right upper limb and right thorax

why_correct: The thoracic duct drains lymph from both lower limbs, the abdomen, the left thorax, left upper limb and left side of the head and neck. The right lymphatic duct drains the right upper quadrant.

why_others_wrong.A: The right upper limb drains to the right lymphatic duct, so it would be unaffected by thoracic duct injury.
why_others_wrong.B: The right side of the head and neck drains via the right jugular trunk to the right lymphatic duct.
why_others_wrong.D: The right thorax drains through the right bronchomediastinal trunk into the right lymphatic duct.
why_others_wrong.E: The right upper limb and right thorax together form the right lymphatic duct territory, not the thoracic duct territory.

exam_trap: Right-sided options are chosen by those unsure of laterality, but the right upper limb, right thorax and right head and neck all drain to the right lymphatic duct.
takeaway: Thoracic duct = everything except the right upper quadrant.
source: Gray's Anatomy, 42nd ed., Elsevier, 2020.
thinking: Thoracic duct injury near its termination ↓ the duct carries lymph from below the diaphragm and the left upper body ↓ every other option is right lymphatic duct territory ↓ Both lower limbs
pearl: Persistent chylothorax after thoracic duct injury is first managed with drainage and a low-fat diet using medium-chain triglycerides, with duct ligation or embolisation if output stays high.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: (untitled)
stem: A patient has a penetrating wound to the anterior thorax. Which artery is the principal source of blood supply to the anterior intercostal spaces?
why_correct: The internal thoracic artery gives rise to anterior intercostal branches supplying the anterior intercostal spaces. Posterior intercostal arteries arise mainly from the thoracic aorta.

why_others_wrong.A: Posterior intercostal arteries from the aorta supply the spaces posteriorly and laterally, but anteriorly the internal thoracic branches predominate.
why_others_wrong.C: The thoracoacromial artery from the axillary artery supplies pectoral muscles, deltoid and the acromial region, not the intercostal spaces.
why_others_wrong.D: The superior mesenteric artery is an abdominal midgut vessel with no thoracic wall branches.
why_others_wrong.E: The subscapular artery supplies the scapular muscles and latissimus dorsi region, not the anterior intercostal spaces.

exam_trap: Posterior intercostal arteries only is chosen because they supply most of each space, but anteriorly the intercostal spaces are supplied by internal thoracic branches.
takeaway: Internal thoracic → anterior intercostals.
source: Gray's Anatomy, 42nd ed., Elsevier, 2020.
thinking: Anterior intercostal spaces ↓ supplied by anterior intercostal arteries ↓ these arise from the internal thoracic artery and its musculophrenic branch ↓ Internal thoracic artery
pearl: The internal thoracic artery runs just lateral to the sternal edge, so parasternal stab wounds can cause a massive haemothorax; the left internal thoracic artery is also the preferred conduit to the left anterior descending artery in coronary bypass.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care: (untitled)
stem: A patient has an arterial aneurysm associated with chronic inflammation and degradation of the extracellular matrix of the vessel wall. Which enzyme family contributes to breakdown of extracellular matrix proteins?
why_correct: Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) degrade extracellular matrix components including collagen and elastin. Their activity contributes to vascular wall remodelling and can contribute to aneurysm formation. Tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases (TIMPs) provide endogenous inhibition.

why_others_wrong.A: DNA polymerases are enzymes involved in DNA replication, unrelated to extracellular matrix turnover.
why_others_wrong.C: Cyclo-oxygenases generate prostaglandins from arachidonic acid, mediating inflammation and pain, but they do not degrade matrix proteins.
why_others_wrong.D: Lipoprotein lipases hydrolyse triglycerides within lipoproteins, a lipid-metabolism function unrelated to matrix degradation.
why_others_wrong.E: Aminotransferases are enzymes involved in amino acid metabolism (e.g., ALT/AST), unrelated to extracellular matrix breakdown.

exam_trap: Candidates choose cyclo-oxygenases (C) because the wall is inflamed, but COX enzymes produce prostaglandins; matrix metalloproteinases degrade collagen and elastin.
takeaway: MMP ↑ → ECM degradation → weakened vascular wall.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed., Elsevier, 2022.
thinking: Inflamed aneurysmal wall ↓ extracellular matrix breakdown ↓ collagen and elastin degraded by MMPs ↓ Matrix metalloproteinases
pearl: An inflammatory abdominal aortic aneurysm has a thick peri-aortic fibrotic rind that can involve the ureters and duodenum, making open repair technically more difficult.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: Physiology: (untitled)
stem: A patient develops an atherosclerotic plaque. Which lipoprotein is most strongly associated with cholesterol delivery to peripheral tissues and atherogenesis?
why_correct: LDL transports cholesterol from the liver toward peripheral tissues. Retention and modification of LDL within the arterial wall contribute to atherosclerotic plaque development. HDL participates in reverse cholesterol transport.

why_others_wrong.A: HDL mediates reverse cholesterol transport from peripheral tissues back to the liver and is associated with reduced atherosclerotic risk.
why_others_wrong.C: Chylomicrons carry dietary triglyceride from the gut and are largely too big to enter the arterial wall, so they are not the main atherogenic particle.
why_others_wrong.D: Albumin is a plasma protein that carries free fatty acids and drugs, not a lipoprotein that delivers cholesterol to tissues.
why_others_wrong.E: Lipoprotein(a) is atherogenic, but it is not the main cholesterol-delivering particle, and the word only wrongly excludes LDL.

exam_trap: HDL (option A) is chosen because it also carries cholesterol, but it mediates reverse transport back to the liver and is inversely associated with atherosclerotic risk.
