takeaway: LDL → arterial cholesterol delivery/retention → atherogenesis.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed., Elsevier, 2022.
thinking: Atherosclerotic plaque ↓ cholesterol delivered from the liver to peripheral tissues ↓ the particle is retained and oxidised in the arterial intima ↓ LDL
pearl: Oxidised LDL is taken up by macrophage scavenger receptors to form foam cells and the fatty streak, which is why lowering LDL with statins reduces cardiovascular events.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Pathology: oncology & haematology: (untitled)
stem: A patient develops a thrombus over a ruptured atherosclerotic plaque. Which event most directly initiates platelet adhesion at the site of endothelial disruption?

options.A: Exposure of subendothelial collagen with vWF-mediated platelet adhesion

correct_answer: A. Exposure of subendothelial collagen with vWF-mediated platelet adhesion
why_correct: Endothelial disruption exposes thrombogenic subendothelial structures. von Willebrand factor helps mediate platelet adhesion through platelet glycoprotein Ib. Platelet activation then promotes further aggregation and thrombus formation.

why_others_wrong.B: Suppression of thrombin generation would oppose thrombosis, and thrombin acts later to activate platelets and form fibrin rather than initiate adhesion.
why_others_wrong.C: Prostacyclin is released by intact endothelium to inhibit platelet activation, so increased release would oppose platelet adhesion.
why_others_wrong.D: Reduced platelet activation would limit thrombus formation, whereas plaque rupture triggers adhesion followed by increased activation.
why_others_wrong.E: Nitric oxide from healthy endothelium causes vasodilatation and inhibits platelets, so increased production would oppose adhesion.

exam_trap: vWF-mediated adhesion is distinct from platelet aggregation mediated through activated GPIIb/IIIa.
takeaway: Adhesion = vWF–GPIb. Aggregation = fibrinogen–GPIIb/IIIa.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed., Elsevier, 2022.
thinking: Ruptured atherosclerotic plaque ↓ subendothelial collagen is exposed ↓ von Willebrand factor binds collagen and platelet GPIb ↓ Exposure of subendothelial collagen with vWF-mediated platelet adhesion
pearl: Arterial thrombi are platelet-rich, so antiplatelet drugs are the mainstay after acute coronary syndromes, whereas venous thrombi are fibrin- and red-cell-rich and are treated with anticoagulants.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Pathology: oncology & haematology: (untitled)
stem: A patient develops an unprovoked deep vein thrombosis despite a normal platelet count. Which inherited abnormality increases thrombosis risk by reducing inactivation of activated factor V?

options.A: Activated protein C resistance due to factor V Leiden

correct_answer: A. Activated protein C resistance due to factor V Leiden
why_correct: Factor V Leiden is a factor V variant that is relatively resistant to activated protein C. This prolongs procoagulant activity and increases venous thrombotic risk.

why_others_wrong.B: Factor VIII deficiency is haemophilia A, an X-linked bleeding disorder, and does not increase thrombotic risk.
why_others_wrong.C: Von Willebrand disease impairs platelet adhesion and lowers factor VIII, producing mucocutaneous bleeding rather than thrombosis.
why_others_wrong.D: Factor XIII deficiency prevents fibrin cross-linking and causes delayed bleeding, not a thrombotic tendency.
why_others_wrong.E: Protein S is a cofactor for activated protein C, so excess would enhance anticoagulation; it is protein S deficiency that is thrombophilic.

exam_trap: Factor V Leiden causes thrombosis; haemophilia A and von Willebrand disease cause bleeding.
takeaway: Factor V Leiden = APC resistance = thrombophilia.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed., Elsevier, 2022.
thinking: Unprovoked DVT with a normal platelet count ↓ inherited thrombophilia ↓ activated factor V resists inactivation by activated protein C ↓ factor V Leiden variant ↓ Activated protein C resistance due to factor V Leiden
pearl: Factor V Leiden is the commonest inherited thrombophilia in people of European ancestry, and its venous thrombosis risk is multiplied by oestrogen-containing contraception or pregnancy.

subject: Paediatric surgery
title: Paediatric surgery: malrotation
stem: An infant develops bilious vomiting shortly after birth. An upper gastrointestinal contrast study shows the duodenojejunal flexure lying to the right of the midline with a corkscrew course of the proximal jejunum. Which embryological abnormality is most likely?
why_correct: The embryological midgut normally undergoes approximately 270° counterclockwise rotation around the superior mesenteric artery. Abnormal rotation can produce malrotation and predispose to volvulus, causing intestinal obstruction and ischaemia.

why_others_wrong.A: A Meckel diverticulum is a persistent vitellointestinal duct remnant that may bleed or cause intussusception, but it is not a failure of midgut rotation around the superior mesenteric artery.
why_others_wrong.C: Hirschsprung disease results from failed neural crest migration leaving aganglionic distal bowel, not from abnormal rotation of the midgut.
why_others_wrong.D: Pyloric stenosis is an acquired muscular hypertrophy causing non-bilious vomiting at a few weeks old, not an embryological rotation defect.
why_others_wrong.E: Oesophageal atresia is a foregut separation defect causing drooling and choking with feeds, with regurgitated milk from the blind pouch rather than bilious vomiting.

exam_trap: Pyloric stenosis and oesophageal atresia tempt as causes of infant vomiting, but both give non-bilious vomiting; bilious vomiting with a right-sided duodenojejunal flexure means malrotation with volvulus.
takeaway: Abnormal midgut rotation → narrow mesenteric base → volvulus risk.
source: Gray's Anatomy, 42nd ed., Elsevier, 2020.
thinking: Bilious vomiting shortly after birth ↓ obstruction distal to the ampulla ↓ duodenojejunal flexure right of the midline ↓ corkscrew proximal jejunum indicates twisting ↓ Midgut malrotation with volvulus
pearl: Suspected midgut volvulus is a surgical emergency treated by urgent laparotomy to derotate the bowel, divide abnormal peritoneal bands and widen the mesenteric base, usually with appendicectomy.

subject: Anatomy
title: Acute abdomen & GI surgery: (untitled)
stem: A patient undergoes surgery for a Meckel diverticulum. From which embryological structure does it arise?
why_correct: Meckel diverticulum results from persistence of the vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct. It is a true diverticulum because it contains all layers of the intestinal wall.

why_others_wrong.B: The urachus is the allantoic remnant connecting the bladder to the umbilicus; its persistence causes urachal anomalies, not a Meckel diverticulum.
why_others_wrong.C: The allantois is related to bladder and urachal development, not to formation of the ileal diverticulum.
why_others_wrong.D: It is the vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct itself, not merely its accompanying artery, whose persistence forms the diverticulum.
why_others_wrong.E: The dorsal pancreatic bud contributes to pancreatic development and has no relationship to Meckel diverticulum.

exam_trap: Urachus is chosen because it is another umbilical remnant, but it derives from the allantois and connects to the bladder, not to the ileum.
takeaway: Meckel diverticulum = persistent vitelline duct remnant.
source: Gray's Anatomy, 42nd ed., Elsevier, 2020.
thinking: Meckel diverticulum ↓ true diverticulum on the antimesenteric border of the ileum ↓ remnant of the embryonic connection between midgut and yolk sac ↓ Vitelline duct
pearl: A Meckel diverticulum may contain ectopic gastric mucosa, which explains painless rectal bleeding in children and is detected by a technetium-99m pertechnetate scan.

subject: Paediatric surgery
title: Paediatric surgery: gastroschisis
stem: A neonate has a congenital abdominal wall defect immediately adjacent to the umbilicus. The bowel is not covered by a membrane. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Gastroschisis is usually a paraumbilical abdominal wall defect with exposed bowel lacking a covering membrane. Omphalocele is a midline defect in which herniated abdominal contents are covered by a membrane.

why_others_wrong.A: An omphalocele lies centrally at the umbilicus with contents covered by a membrane, so uncovered bowel beside the umbilicus does not fit.
why_others_wrong.C: An umbilical hernia is covered by skin and usually closes spontaneously in early childhood; it does not leave bowel exposed.
why_others_wrong.D: A patent urachus presents with urine discharging from the umbilicus rather than bowel protruding through an abdominal wall defect.
why_others_wrong.E: A Meckel diverticulum is an ileal remnant of the vitellointestinal duct inside the abdomen and does not produce an uncovered wall defect.

exam_trap: Omphalocele tempts as the other abdominal wall defect, but its viscera sit in a membrane at the umbilicus; uncovered bowel beside the cord means gastroschisis.
takeaway: Paraumbilical + uncovered bowel = gastroschisis.
source: Gray's Anatomy, 42nd ed., Elsevier, 2020.
thinking: Congenital abdominal wall defect ↓ immediately adjacent to the umbilicus ↓ bowel not covered by a membrane ↓ uncovered paraumbilical defect ↓ Gastroschisis
pearl: Gastroschisis is associated with young maternal age, and the exposed bowel is often thickened and matted from contact with amniotic fluid.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: Physiology: (untitled)
stem: A patient has congenital absence of enteric ganglion cells in the distal colon. Which part of the enteric nervous system is absent in the affected segment?

options.C: Both myenteric and submucosal ganglion cells
options.E: Only parasympathetic ganglia in the spinal cord

correct_answer: C. Both myenteric and submucosal ganglion cells
why_correct: Hirschsprung disease results from failure of neural crest-derived enteric ganglion cells to migrate into the affected distal bowel. Both the myenteric (Auerbach) and submucosal (Meissner) plexuses are absent. The aganglionic segment cannot relax normally, producing functional obstruction.

why_others_wrong.A: Hirschsprung disease is not confined to the submucosal plexus; ganglion cells are missing from the myenteric plexus as well.
why_others_wrong.B: The myenteric plexus is affected, but the submucosal plexus also lacks ganglion cells in the aganglionic segment.
why_others_wrong.D: Sympathetic ganglia lie outside the bowel wall and are not part of the enteric plexuses missing in Hirschsprung disease.
why_others_wrong.E: Parasympathetic preganglionic neurons lie in the brainstem and sacral cord and are not the enteric ganglion cells absent in the distal colon.

exam_trap: Only the myenteric plexus (option B) tempts because motility fails, but both myenteric and submucosal ganglion cells are absent, which is why a submucosal suction biopsy is diagnostic.
takeaway: Hirschsprung = failed neural crest migration → absent enteric ganglia.
source: Gray's Anatomy, 42nd ed., Elsevier, 2020.
thinking: Congenital absence of enteric ganglion cells in the distal colon ↓ Hirschsprung disease ↓ failed neural crest migration affects the whole enteric nervous system ↓ Both myenteric and submucosal ganglion cells
pearl: Diagnosis is by rectal suction biopsy showing absent submucosal ganglion cells with hypertrophied nerve trunks and increased acetylcholinesterase staining.

subject: Anatomy
title: Physiology: (untitled)
stem: A patient has a congenital diaphragmatic hernia caused by failure of closure of the posterolateral diaphragm. Which type is most likely?
why_correct: A Bochdalek hernia is a posterolateral congenital diaphragmatic defect, usually on the left side. Herniation of abdominal contents can impair fetal lung development. A Morgagni hernia is an anterior parasternal diaphragmatic defect.

why_others_wrong.A: A Morgagni hernia is an anterior, parasternal diaphragmatic defect, not a posterolateral one.
why_others_wrong.C: A hiatus hernia involves the oesophageal hiatus and is typically an acquired adult condition, not a congenital posterolateral defect.
why_others_wrong.D: A paraumbilical hernia is an anterior abdominal wall defect near the umbilicus and has nothing to do with the diaphragm.
why_others_wrong.E: A Spigelian hernia occurs through the linea semilunaris of the anterior abdominal wall, not through the diaphragm.

exam_trap: Morgagni hernia is chosen as the other named congenital diaphragmatic defect, but it is an anterior parasternal defect, not a posterolateral one.
takeaway: Posterolateral congenital diaphragmatic hernia = Bochdalek.
source: Gray's Anatomy, 42nd ed., Elsevier, 2020.
thinking: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia ↓ failure of closure of the posterolateral pleuroperitoneal canal ↓ usually left-sided ↓ Bochdalek hernia
pearl: The main threat in congenital diaphragmatic hernia is pulmonary hypoplasia with pulmonary hypertension, so the neonate is stabilised and ventilated first and the defect repaired once stable rather than as an immediate emergency.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: GI physiology & metabolism: (untitled)
stem: A patient with chronic gastric inflammation develops replacement of normal gastric epithelium by intestinal-type epithelium. Which pathological process is occurring?
why_correct: Metaplasia is a reversible adaptive change in which one differentiated cell type is replaced by another differentiated cell type better able to tolerate the altered environment. Chronic irritation can therefore produce intestinal metaplasia in the stomach.

why_others_wrong.A: Dysplasia is disordered growth with cytological atypia and loss of maturation, not replacement by another normal mature epithelium.
why_others_wrong.C: Hypertrophy is an increase in cell size without any change in cell type.
why_others_wrong.D: Apoptosis is programmed death of individual cells and does not replace one epithelial type with another.
why_others_wrong.E: Anaplasia is loss of differentiation seen in malignant cells, the opposite of replacement by another well-differentiated epithelium.

exam_trap: Metaplasia is not synonymous with dysplasia or invasive cancer, although some metaplastic changes can increase subsequent malignant risk.
takeaway: Metaplasia = adaptive replacement of one mature cell type by another.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed., Elsevier, 2022.
thinking: Chronic gastric inflammation ↓ normal gastric epithelium replaced by intestinal-type epithelium ↓ one mature cell type substituted by another ↓ Metaplasia
pearl: Gastric intestinal metaplasia, usually after chronic H. pylori gastritis, is a step towards intestinal-type gastric adenocarcinoma, and extensive disease may warrant endoscopic surveillance.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Colorectal surgery: (untitled)
stem: A patient with long-standing inflammatory bowel disease develops colorectal dysplasia. Which pathological change best describes dysplasia?

options.A: Increased cell size without architectural abnormality
options.B: Disordered epithelial maturation with cytological atypia
options.C: Replacement of one mature cell type by another
options.D: Complete loss of cellular differentiation in all benign tissues

correct_answer: B. Disordered epithelial maturation with cytological atypia
why_correct: Dysplasia is characterised by disordered epithelial growth and maturation, with cytological atypia and architectural abnormalities. It is a premalignant lesion rather than synonymous with invasive malignancy.

why_others_wrong.A: Increased cell size without architectural abnormality describes hypertrophy, which lacks the atypia and disordered maturation of dysplasia.
why_others_wrong.C: Replacement of one mature cell type by another is metaplasia, which may precede dysplasia but is a distinct process without atypia.
why_others_wrong.D: Complete loss of differentiation is anaplasia, a feature of poorly differentiated malignant tumours, not of dysplasia in benign tissues.
why_others_wrong.E: Increased extracellular fluid is oedema, an inflammatory or haemodynamic change unrelated to disordered epithelial growth.

exam_trap: Replacement of one mature cell type by another tempts as a precancerous change, but that is metaplasia without atypia; dysplasia shows atypia and disordered maturation.
takeaway: Dysplasia = atypia + disordered maturation/architecture.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed., Elsevier, 2022.
thinking: Long-standing inflammatory bowel disease ↓ chronic inflammation drives epithelial neoplasia ↓ dysplasia = cytological atypia with disordered maturation ↓ Disordered epithelial maturation with cytological atypia
pearl: Long-standing extensive colitis warrants colonoscopic surveillance, and dysplasia that cannot be completely resected endoscopically, or is multifocal, is an indication to consider colectomy.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Colorectal surgery: (untitled)
stem: A patient with colorectal cancer develops tumour deposits on the peritoneal surface. Which route of metastatic spread does this represent?
why_correct: Tumour cells can disseminate across serosal surfaces and implant on the peritoneum. This is termed transcoelomic spread. This mechanism is particularly relevant to abdominal and pelvic malignancies.

why_others_wrong.A: Haematogenous spread from colorectal cancer typically seeds the liver via the portal vein rather than implanting on the peritoneal surface.
why_others_wrong.C: Perineural spread tracks along nerve sheaths locally and does not account for deposits scattered over the peritoneal surface.
why_others_wrong.D: Intraductal spread describes tumour extending within ducts, as in breast or pancreatic ductal systems, not implantation across the peritoneum.
why_others_wrong.E: Lymphatic spread carries colorectal cancer to mesenteric and regional nodes rather than seeding the serosal surfaces of the peritoneal cavity.

exam_trap: Haematogenous spread tempts because colorectal metastases often reach the liver, but portal spread seeds organ parenchyma; serosal implants indicate transcoelomic spread.
takeaway: Serosal/peritoneal implantation = transcoelomic spread.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed., Elsevier, 2022.
thinking: Colorectal cancer ↓ deposits on the peritoneal surface ↓ cells shed into the peritoneal cavity and implant on serosa ↓ Transcoelomic spread
pearl: Small peritoneal metastases are easily missed on CT, and selected patients with limited colorectal peritoneal disease may be considered for cytoreductive surgery at specialist centres.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing: (untitled)
stem: A patient has severe ulcerative colitis. Which histological feature is most characteristic of ulcerative colitis compared with Crohn disease?

options.C: Skip lesions throughout the gastrointestinal tract
options.D: Fistula formation as the defining feature

why_correct: Ulcerative colitis classically causes continuous inflammation beginning in the rectum and extending proximally to varying degrees. The principal inflammatory process is mucosal, although severe disease can produce deeper complications. Crohn disease more characteristically produces transmural inflammation and skip lesions.

why_others_wrong.A: Transmural granulomatous inflammation is characteristic of Crohn disease, not ulcerative colitis.
why_others_wrong.C: Skip lesions throughout the gastrointestinal tract are a hallmark of Crohn disease; ulcerative colitis is continuous, not skipped.
why_others_wrong.D: Fistula formation arises from transmural inflammation and is typical of Crohn disease, not ulcerative colitis.
why_others_wrong.E: Full-thickness bowel-wall inflammation describes Crohn disease; ulcerative colitis is predominantly a mucosal process.

exam_trap: Transmural granulomatous and full-thickness inflammation describe Crohn disease; ulcerative colitis is characteristically continuous and mainly mucosal, starting at the rectum.
takeaway: UC = continuous + rectum + mucosa. Crohn = skip + transmural.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed., Elsevier, 2022.
thinking: Severe ulcerative colitis ↓ need the feature favouring UC over Crohn disease ↓ transmural granulomas, skip lesions and fistulae belong to Crohn disease ↓ UC is continuous from the rectum and mainly mucosal ↓ Continuous mucosal inflammation
pearl: Because ulcerative colitis is confined to the colon and rectum, proctocolectomy is potentially curative, whereas surgery does not cure Crohn disease.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: (untitled)
stem: A patient with severe chronic diarrhoea develops metabolic acidosis. Which mechanism best explains the acid-base disturbance?

options.D: Increased chloride loss exceeding sodium loss
options.E: Increased lactate production as the sole mechanism

correct_answer: B. Loss of bicarbonate-rich intestinal fluid
why_correct: Diarrhoea can cause loss of bicarbonate-rich gastrointestinal fluid, producing a normal-anion-gap (hyperchloraemic) metabolic acidosis. The kidneys retain chloride relative to bicarbonate to maintain electroneutrality.

why_others_wrong.A: Increased gastric HCl loss describes the mechanism behind vomiting-induced metabolic alkalosis, not the bicarbonate loss seen with diarrhoea.
why_others_wrong.C: Renal bicarbonate production would be a compensatory response to acidosis, not the cause of the acid-base disturbance itself.
why_others_wrong.D: A relatively greater chloride loss than sodium loss would tend to promote alkalosis, not acidosis; diarrhoeal acidosis instead reflects bicarbonate-rich fluid loss with relative chloride retention.
why_others_wrong.E: Increased lactate can contribute in some settings, but describing it as the sole mechanism overstates its role and ignores the primary cause, which is intestinal bicarbonate loss.

exam_trap: Candidates choosing A transfer the vomiting mechanism; gastric HCl loss produces metabolic alkalosis, whereas lower-gut bicarbonate loss causes a normal-anion-gap metabolic acidosis.
takeaway: Diarrhoea → HCO3− loss → normal-anion-gap metabolic acidosis.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Elsevier, 2020.
thinking: Severe chronic diarrhoea ↓ intestinal secretions below the stomach are bicarbonate-rich ↓ bicarbonate loss lowers plasma bicarbonate ↓ chloride rises, so the anion gap stays normal ↓ Loss of bicarbonate-rich intestinal fluid
pearl: Urinary diversions using bowel, such as ureterosigmoidostomy, cause a similar hyperchloraemic acidosis because the bowel absorbs urinary chloride in exchange for bicarbonate.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: GI physiology & metabolism: (untitled)
stem: A patient has severe persistent vomiting from gastric outlet obstruction. Which acid-base abnormality is most likely?
why_correct: Persistent vomiting causes loss of gastric hydrochloric acid and chloride, producing metabolic alkalosis. Volume depletion can further maintain alkalosis through renal mechanisms.

why_others_wrong.A: Normal-anion-gap acidosis follows bicarbonate loss, for example from diarrhoea or a fistula, whereas vomiting loses acid.
why_others_wrong.B: High-anion-gap acidosis comes from added acids such as lactate or ketones and is not the primary result of losing gastric HCl.
why_others_wrong.D: Respiratory acidosis reflects hypoventilation with a raised PaCO2 as the primary problem; any rise in CO2 here is only compensation.
why_others_wrong.E: Respiratory alkalosis results from hyperventilation with a low PaCO2, whereas gastric outlet obstruction causes a primary metabolic alkalosis.

exam_trap: Do not simply associate all gastrointestinal losses with acidosis; the composition of the lost fluid matters.
takeaway: Vomiting gastric HCl → metabolic alkalosis.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Elsevier, 2020.
thinking: Persistent vomiting from gastric outlet obstruction ↓ loss of gastric hydrochloric acid ↓ chloride and volume depletion sustain renal bicarbonate retention ↓ Metabolic alkalosis
pearl: The classic picture is hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, sometimes with paradoxical aciduria, corrected with intravenous sodium chloride and potassium before surgery.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: (untitled)
stem: A patient has severe hypoalbuminaemia. Which effect on plasma oncotic pressure is expected?

options.D: Increased hydrostatic pressure caused directly by albumin

why_correct: Albumin is the major contributor to plasma colloid oncotic pressure. Reduced albumin lowers the force retaining water within the intravascular compartment and can contribute to oedema.

why_others_wrong.A: This is the opposite of what occurs; loss of the major plasma protein lowers, rather than raises, oncotic pressure.
why_others_wrong.C: Albumin normally provides the majority of plasma colloid oncotic pressure, so a marked fall in albumin cannot leave oncotic pressure unchanged.
why_others_wrong.D: Albumin concentration influences oncotic (colloid osmotic) pressure, not hydrostatic pressure, which is determined by vascular and haemodynamic factors.
why_others_wrong.E: Reduced oncotic pressure favours fluid movement into the interstitium and predisposes to oedema, rather than preventing it.

exam_trap: Albumin affects oncotic pressure, whereas hydrostatic pressure is primarily determined by vascular pressures and haemodynamics.
takeaway: Low albumin → low oncotic pressure → tendency to oedema.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Elsevier, 2020.
thinking: Severe hypoalbuminaemia ↓ albumin provides most plasma oncotic pressure ↓ plasma oncotic pressure falls ↓ fluid moves into the interstitium ↓ Reduced plasma oncotic pressure
pearl: Hypoalbuminaemia also lowers total serum calcium without changing ionised calcium, so calcium should be adjusted for albumin or measured as ionised calcium.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Physiology: (untitled)
stem: A patient undergoes major surgery and develops an acute-phase response. Which hepatic protein is expected to increase?
why_correct: C-reactive protein is a positive acute-phase protein produced by the liver, with hepatic production stimulated particularly by inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6. Albumin and several other proteins behave as negative acute-phase reactants.

why_others_wrong.A: Albumin behaves as a negative acute-phase reactant, typically falling rather than rising during the acute-phase response.
why_others_wrong.C: Transferrin also behaves as a negative acute-phase reactant, decreasing during systemic inflammation.
why_others_wrong.D: Prealbumin (transthyretin) is a negative acute-phase reactant that falls during systemic inflammation, which is why it is unreliable as a nutritional marker in acute illness.
why_others_wrong.E: Thyroxine-binding globulin is not characteristically raised as part of the hepatic acute-phase response and is not a recognised positive acute-phase protein.

exam_trap: A falling albumin during acute illness does not necessarily indicate acute nutritional deterioration.
takeaway: Acute inflammation → CRP ↑; albumin may fall as a negative acute-phase reactant.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed., Elsevier, 2022.
thinking: Acute-phase response after surgery ↓ IL-6 drives hepatic protein synthesis ↓ CRP rises while albumin and transferrin fall ↓ C-reactive protein
pearl: CRP normally peaks around 48 hours after major surgery; a CRP that continues rising after the third post-operative day suggests an infective complication such as anastomotic leak.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing: (untitled)
stem: A patient has severe protein deficiency and poor wound healing. Which process is most directly impaired by inadequate availability of amino acids?
why_correct: Protein is required for synthesis of collagen and other extracellular matrix proteins. Severe protein deficiency can therefore impair wound healing, immune function and tissue repair.

why_others_wrong.B: Oxygen diffusion through alveoli is a respiratory physiological process unrelated to amino-acid availability.
why_others_wrong.C: Platelet adhesion occurs in initial haemostasis and is not the process limiting repair in protein deficiency, where reduced collagen and matrix synthesis is the key defect.
why_others_wrong.D: Bile secretion is a hepatobiliary function unrelated to protein/amino-acid substrate for wound repair.
why_others_wrong.E: Glomerular filtration is a renal physiological process unrelated to amino-acid-dependent collagen synthesis.

exam_trap: Candidates choose platelet adhesion (C) because bleeding affects wounds, but protein deficiency most directly limits the amino acid substrate for collagen synthesis.
takeaway: Protein deficiency → impaired collagen/ECM synthesis → impaired wound healing.
source: Principles and Practice of Surgery, 7th ed., Elsevier.
thinking: Severe protein deficiency ↓ insufficient amino acids ↓ collagen and matrix synthesis impaired ↓ Collagen synthesis
pearl: Malnourished surgical patients should be identified with a screening tool such as MUST, and pre-operative nutritional support reduces complications in those severely malnourished.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing: (untitled)
stem: A patient has poor wound healing because of severe local tissue hypoxia. Which cellular process is particularly impaired?
why_correct: Adequate oxygenation is required for collagen hydroxylation, which is important for stable collagen formation. Tissue hypoxia therefore impairs wound repair and increases susceptibility to wound complications. Vitamin C is also required for collagen hydroxylation.

why_others_wrong.B: DNA transcription itself is not the specific oxygen-dependent step; the process impaired in hypoxic wounds is the post-translational hydroxylation of collagen.
why_others_wrong.C: Bile acid synthesis is a hepatic metabolic process unrelated to local wound tissue oxygenation.
why_others_wrong.D: Red-cell glycolysis is anaerobic and is not the process impaired by local tissue hypoxia at a wound site.
why_others_wrong.E: Platelet production occurs in bone marrow via thrombopoiesis and is unrelated to local wound-site oxygen tension.

exam_trap: Candidates choose red-cell glycolysis (D) because hypoxia shifts metabolism to glycolysis, but red cells are already anaerobic; oxygen-dependent collagen hydroxylation fails.
takeaway: Good wound healing needs oxygen + vitamin C + amino-acid substrate.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed., Elsevier, 2022.
thinking: Severe local tissue hypoxia ↓ prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases need molecular oxygen ↓ unstable collagen with poor cross-linking ↓ Collagen hydroxylation and cross-linking
pearl: Neutrophil oxidative killing also depends on oxygen, so hypoxic wounds are prone both to weak collagen and to infection; smoking cessation before surgery improves wound outcomes.

subject: Microbiology & surgical infection
title: Microbiology & surgical infection: (untitled)
stem: A bacterial strain becomes resistant to an antibiotic because a mutation reduces expression of the bacterial membrane protein through which the drug normally enters. Which resistance mechanism is this?
why_correct: Reduced bacterial uptake can result from altered or reduced membrane channels or other permeability changes, decreasing intracellular antibiotic concentration. This is distinct from enzymatic drug destruction and target modification.

why_others_wrong.A: An altered target, such as a modified penicillin-binding protein, changes the drug's binding site rather than reducing drug entry through membrane channels.
why_others_wrong.C: Drug inactivation involves enzymes such as beta-lactamases that destroy or modify the antibiotic, not reduced membrane porin expression.
why_others_wrong.D: Increased target expression can raise drug requirement but does not describe loss of the membrane channel used for drug entry.
why_others_wrong.E: Host immunosuppression affects the patient's ability to clear infection and is not a bacterial resistance mechanism.

exam_trap: Altered target tempts because the resistance follows a mutation, but here the drug's binding site is unchanged; loss of the entry channel reduces permeability.
takeaway: Less entry = reduced intracellular drug concentration = resistance.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed., Elsevier, 2022.
thinking: Mutation reduces a membrane protein used for drug entry ↓ loss of the porin channel lowers drug uptake ↓ intracellular drug concentration falls ↓ target and drug are unchanged ↓ Reduced permeability
pearl: Loss of outer-membrane porins in Gram-negative organisms such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a recognised cause of carbapenem resistance, often combined with efflux pumps or beta-lactamases.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: internal capsule
stem: A 67-year-old man develops sudden weakness of the right face, arm and leg. He has no visual field defect, sensory level or aphasia. MRI demonstrates a small infarct involving the left internal capsule. Which structure is most likely to be affected?

options.D: Spinothalamic tract in the spinal cord

why_correct: The posterior limb of the internal capsule carries corticospinal fibres to the arm and leg, and the adjacent genu carries corticobulbar fibres to the face. Because these fibres are densely packed, a small capsular infarct causes contralateral weakness of the face, arm and leg.

why_others_wrong.A: The optic radiation lies in the retrolenticular and sublenticular parts of the capsule; damage would cause a homonymous field defect, which is absent.
why_others_wrong.C: The medial longitudinal fasciculus lies in the brainstem and causes internuclear ophthalmoplegia, not hemiparesis.
why_others_wrong.D: The spinal spinothalamic tract carries pain and temperature, and a cord lesion would not produce facial weakness.
why_others_wrong.E: The medial lemniscus carries dorsal column sensation, and a medullary lesion does not match an infarct in the internal capsule.

exam_trap: Do not assume that a small cortical stroke is required to produce dense hemiparesis. The internal capsule contains densely packed motor fibres.
takeaway: Internal capsule lesion → contralateral face, arm and leg weakness (corticobulbar fibres in the genu, corticospinal fibres in the posterior limb).
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed.; RCS England MRCS preparation resources, accessed September 2026.
thinking: Pure right face, arm and leg weakness ↓ no field defect, sensory loss or aphasia ↓ small left internal capsule infarct ↓ densely packed descending motor fibres in the genu and posterior limb ↓ Corticospinal fibres
pearl: Pure motor hemiparesis without cortical signs is a classic lacunar syndrome, typically due to small vessel disease associated with hypertension, diabetes and smoking.

subject: Anatomy
title: Physiology: medial longitudinal fasciculus
stem: A patient with a brainstem lesion is asked to look to the left. The left eye abducts normally, but the right eye fails to adduct. Convergence is preserved. Which structure is most likely damaged?
why_correct: The medial longitudinal fasciculus connects the abducens nucleus of one side with the contralateral oculomotor nucleus. A right MLF lesion prevents the right eye from adducting during left gaze while the left eye abducts. This produces internuclear ophthalmoplegia.

why_others_wrong.A: A right optic nerve lesion would cause a visual/afferent deficit in the right eye, not the isolated adduction failure with preserved abduction elsewhere seen here.
why_others_wrong.B: A left abducens nerve lesion would impair abduction of the left eye, but in this case the left eye abducts normally.
why_others_wrong.D: A left oculomotor nerve lesion would impair movements (including adduction) of the left eye, but the deficit described is failure of the right eye to adduct.
why_others_wrong.E: The right trochlear nerve controls the superior oblique, responsible for depression and intorsion in adduction, not horizontal adduction, so its lesion would not produce this pattern.

exam_trap: The side of the MLF lesion is the side of the eye that fails to adduct.
takeaway: INO = ipsilateral failure of adduction with preserved abduction of the opposite eye → MLF lesion.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed.; RCS Applied Anatomy for MRCS Preparation, current course content accessed September 2026.
thinking: On left gaze the right eye fails to adduct ↓ the left eye abducts and convergence is preserved ↓ medial rectus and the oculomotor nerve are therefore intact ↓ the link from left abducens nucleus to right oculomotor nucleus is broken ↓ Right medial longitudinal fasciculus
pearl: Bilateral internuclear ophthalmoplegia in a young adult strongly suggests multiple sclerosis, whereas a unilateral one in an older patient is more often vascular.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: cavernous sinus
stem: A patient with a cavernous sinus thrombosis develops ophthalmoplegia, facial sensory loss and reduced corneal sensation. Which cranial nerve travels within the cavernous sinus alongside the internal carotid artery?
why_correct: The abducens nerve runs within the cavernous sinus alongside the internal carotid artery. The oculomotor, trochlear and V1/V2 divisions of trigeminal nerve travel in the lateral wall.

why_others_wrong.A: The optic nerve runs through the optic canal above and medial to the cavernous sinus, not within it.
why_others_wrong.B: The oculomotor nerve lies in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus, not free within it beside the internal carotid artery.
why_others_wrong.C: The mandibular division leaves the trigeminal ganglion through the foramen ovale and does not traverse the cavernous sinus.
why_others_wrong.E: The facial nerve enters the internal acoustic meatus in the posterior cranial fossa, well away from the cavernous sinus.

exam_trap: CN VI is the cranial nerve actually within the venous sinus proper; III, IV, V1 and V2 are associated with its lateral wall.
takeaway: Cavernous sinus contents: ICA + VI centrally; III, IV, V1 and V2 in the lateral wall.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed.; RCS Applied Anatomy for MRCS Preparation, accessed September 2026.
thinking: Ophthalmoplegia + facial sensory loss + reduced corneal sensation ↓ cavernous sinus pathology ↓ III, IV, V1 and V2 lie in the lateral wall ↓ only one nerve runs free in the sinus beside the ICA ↓ Abducens nerve
pearl: Because the abducens nerve lies free within the sinus next to the internal carotid artery, a lateral rectus palsy is often the earliest ocular sign of cavernous sinus thrombosis or an intracavernous carotid aneurysm.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: brainstem motor tracts
stem: A patient develops ipsilateral cranial nerve dysfunction with contralateral weakness following a brainstem infarction. What anatomical principle best explains this pattern?

options.A: All cranial nerve fibres cross in the spinal cord
options.B: Long motor pathways may cross separately from cranial nerve pathways
options.C: The cerebellum always produces contralateral signs
options.E: The corticospinal tract crosses at the midbrain

correct_answer: B. Long motor pathways may cross separately from cranial nerve pathways
why_correct: Brainstem lesions can produce “crossed” neurological signs: ipsilateral cranial nerve deficits with contralateral limb weakness. The corticospinal tract crosses predominantly at the pyramidal decussation in the caudal medulla.

why_others_wrong.A: Cranial nerve fibres emerge from the brainstem and do not cross in the spinal cord; their deficits are ipsilateral.
why_others_wrong.C: Cerebellar lesions typically produce ipsilateral, not contralateral, signs because of the double crossing of cerebellar pathways.
why_others_wrong.D: Both major sensory pathways cross: the dorsal column pathway in the medulla and the spinothalamic tract in the spinal cord.
why_others_wrong.E: Corticospinal fibres cross at the pyramidal decussation in the caudal medulla, not in the midbrain.

exam_trap: Option E is tempting because the midbrain is a classic crossed-syndrome site, but corticospinal fibres decussate in the caudal medulla, not in the midbrain.
takeaway: Ipsilateral cranial nerve deficit + contralateral limb weakness = localise to brainstem until proven otherwise.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed.; RCS Applied Anatomy for MRCS Preparation, accessed September 2026.
thinking: Ipsilateral cranial nerve deficit with contralateral weakness ↓ cranial nerve nuclei and roots are hit on the side of the lesion ↓ corticospinal fibres have not yet crossed, decussating in the caudal medulla ↓ Long motor pathways may cross separately from cranial nerve pathways
pearl: The cranial nerve involved localises the level: an oculomotor palsy with contralateral hemiparesis points to the midbrain, while abducens or facial involvement points to the pons.

subject: Major trauma & fluids
title: Major trauma & fluids: spinal cord syndrome
stem: A patient sustains a penetrating injury to the right side of the spinal cord. Examination demonstrates loss of vibration and proprioception on the right below the lesion, with loss of pain and temperature on the left beginning a few segments below. Which syndrome is described?
why_correct: Hemisection of the spinal cord produces ipsilateral corticospinal weakness and ipsilateral loss of vibration and proprioception below the lesion, with contralateral loss of pain and temperature beginning one or two segments below because spinothalamic fibres cross within the cord.

why_others_wrong.A: Anterior cord syndrome causes bilateral motor loss and bilateral loss of pain and temperature with preserved dorsal-column sensation.
why_others_wrong.C: Central cord syndrome causes weakness affecting the arms more than the legs, typically after hyperextension, rather than a unilateral sensory split.
why_others_wrong.D: Cauda equina syndrome affects lumbosacral nerve roots below the cord, causing saddle anaesthesia and sphincter disturbance rather than crossed sensory loss.
why_others_wrong.E: Conus medullaris syndrome produces early sphincter dysfunction and symmetrical perianal sensory loss, not ipsilateral dorsal-column with contralateral spinothalamic loss.

exam_trap: Pain and temperature loss is contralateral and begins one or two segments below the lesion because spinothalamic fibres ascend in Lissauer's tract before crossing.
takeaway: Brown-Séquard = ipsilateral motor/proprioception loss + contralateral pain/temperature loss.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed.; RCS Applied Anatomy resources, accessed September 2026.
thinking: Penetrating injury to the right side of the cord ↓ ipsilateral loss of vibration and proprioception (dorsal columns uncrossed) ↓ contralateral pain and temperature loss a few segments lower (spinothalamic fibres crossed) ↓ cord hemisection ↓ Brown-Séquard syndrome
pearl: Brown-Séquard syndrome carries the best prognosis for functional recovery among the incomplete cord syndromes, whereas anterior cord syndrome carries the worst.

subject: Urology
title: Urology: autonomic fibre location
stem: During pelvic surgery, a nerve plexus is damaged and the patient subsequently develops bladder and sexual dysfunction. Which structure is most directly associated with parasympathetic outflow to the pelvic viscera?
why_correct: Pelvic splanchnic nerves arise from S2–S4 and carry parasympathetic fibres to pelvic viscera, including the bladder and distal bowel. They also contribute to autonomic pathways involved in erection.

why_others_wrong.A: The greater splanchnic nerves carry preganglionic sympathetic fibres from T5-T9 to the coeliac ganglia, supplying foregut viscera rather than parasympathetic outflow to the pelvis.
why_others_wrong.B: The lesser splanchnic nerves are sympathetic (T10-T11) and pass to the aorticorenal and superior mesenteric ganglia, so they do not provide pelvic parasympathetic outflow.
why_others_wrong.D: The lumbar sympathetic trunks give sympathetic fibres to the hypogastric plexuses; injury tends to affect ejaculation rather than removing parasympathetic supply to bladder and erection.
why_others_wrong.E: The phrenic nerves arise from C3-C5 and supply the diaphragm, so they have no role in pelvic visceral innervation or bladder and sexual function.

exam_trap: “Sacral splanchnic” and “pelvic splanchnic” are not interchangeable. Pelvic splanchnic nerves are parasympathetic.
takeaway: Pelvic parasympathetic outflow = S2–S4 pelvic splanchnic nerves.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed.; RCS Applied Anatomy, accessed September 2026.
thinking: Pelvic surgery followed by bladder and sexual dysfunction ↓ pelvic parasympathetic outflow is sacral ↓ S2 to S4 roots form the pelvic splanchnic nerves ↓ they drive detrusor contraction and erection ↓ Pelvic splanchnic nerves
pearl: Total mesorectal excision is performed in the correct plane partly to preserve the hypogastric nerves and pelvic splanchnic nerves, reducing postoperative urinary and sexual dysfunction.

subject: Pharmacology
title: Pharmacology: free water clearance
stem: A patient drinks a large volume of water. Plasma osmolality falls and ADH secretion is suppressed. Which renal response is expected?
why_correct: Reduced plasma osmolality suppresses ADH. Collecting ducts become less permeable to water because aquaporin-2 insertion falls, allowing relatively dilute urine and positive free-water clearance.

why_others_wrong.A: With ADH suppressed, aquaporin-2 insertion falls and collecting-duct water permeability decreases rather than increases.
why_others_wrong.B: Low ADH reduces, rather than increases, aquaporin-2 trafficking to the apical membrane.
why_others_wrong.D: Medullary urea recycling is promoted by ADH; with ADH suppressed this concentrating mechanism is reduced, not increased.
why_others_wrong.E: Suppressed ADH reduces distal/collecting-duct water reabsorption, producing dilute urine and free-water excretion, the opposite of increased reabsorption.

exam_trap: Water loading does not simply increase urine volume; it increases excretion of water in excess of solute.
takeaway: Low plasma osmolality → low ADH → dilute urine → positive free-water clearance.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.; RCS MRCS preparation resources, accessed September 2026.
thinking: Large water intake ↓ plasma osmolality falls and ADH is suppressed ↓ fewer aquaporin-2 channels in the collecting duct ↓ dilute urine with water excreted in excess of solute ↓ Increased free-water excretion
pearl: Primary polydipsia and cranial diabetes insipidus both produce dilute polyuria; in a water deprivation test, urine concentrates normally in primary polydipsia but not in diabetes insipidus.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: fgf23
stem: A patient with chronic kidney disease develops phosphate retention and abnormal mineral metabolism. Which hormone normally promotes renal phosphate excretion?
why_correct: Fibroblast growth factor 23 is produced predominantly by bone and promotes renal phosphate excretion by reducing proximal tubular phosphate reabsorption. It also suppresses renal calcitriol production.

why_others_wrong.A: Aldosterone regulates renal sodium and potassium handling in the distal nephron and is not a principal regulator of phosphate excretion.
why_others_wrong.C: Calcitriol increases intestinal phosphate absorption and is itself suppressed by FGF23, so it acts in the opposite direction to promoting renal phosphate loss.
why_others_wrong.D: ADH governs collecting-duct water permeability and has no established role in phosphate excretion.
why_others_wrong.E: Erythropoietin stimulates red cell production in bone marrow and has no role in phosphate handling.

exam_trap: PTH and FGF23 both promote phosphate excretion, but FGF23 also suppresses calcitriol synthesis.
takeaway: FGF23 → phosphaturia + reduced calcitriol.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.; Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Chronic kidney disease with phosphate retention ↓ osteocytes increase FGF23 secretion ↓ FGF23 reduces proximal phosphate reabsorption ↓ and suppresses calcitriol synthesis ↓ FGF23
pearl: FGF23 rises early in chronic kidney disease, before serum phosphate increases, and FGF23 secreted by certain mesenchymal tumours causes tumour-induced osteomalacia with hypophosphataemia.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: phosphate–calcium integration
stem: A patient has markedly reduced renal phosphate excretion. Which immediate change would tend to occur if the other major regulatory systems remain unchanged?

options.D: Increased faecal calcium loss as the primary response

why_correct: Reduced renal phosphate excretion causes phosphate retention and therefore tends to increase serum phosphate concentration. Phosphate is closely linked to calcium and vitamin D metabolism, but the direct consequence of impaired phosphate excretion is phosphate retention.

why_others_wrong.A: This is the opposite effect; retaining phosphate due to reduced excretion raises, rather than lowers, serum phosphate.
why_others_wrong.C: Urinary phosphate excretion is reduced, not increased, given the impaired ability to excrete phosphate described in the stem.
why_others_wrong.D: Increased faecal calcium loss is not a direct or immediate consequence of reduced renal phosphate excretion.
why_others_wrong.E: Reduced bone mineral content is a longer-term secondary consequence of disturbed mineral metabolism, not an immediate effect of impaired phosphate excretion.

exam_trap: Candidates choosing A confuse reduced phosphate excretion with reduced serum phosphate; impaired renal excretion causes phosphate retention and a rising serum level.
takeaway: Reduced phosphate clearance → phosphate retention → hyperphosphataemia.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Markedly reduced renal phosphate excretion ↓ dietary phosphate intake continues ↓ phosphate is retained in extracellular fluid ↓ serum phosphate rises ↓ Increased serum phosphate
pearl: Hyperphosphataemia binds calcium and promotes hypocalcaemia and vascular and soft-tissue calcification, which is why patients with chronic kidney disease take phosphate binders with meals.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: titratable acid
stem: A patient with metabolic acidosis increases urinary acid excretion through phosphate buffering. Which urinary component represents titratable acid?
why_correct: Titratable acid is predominantly hydrogen ions buffered by urinary buffers such as phosphate. It represents acid excretion that can be quantified by titration of urine back to plasma pH. Ammonium excretion is a separate major mechanism of net acid excretion.

why_others_wrong.A: Glucose is not involved in urinary hydrogen ion buffering and has no role in titratable acid.
why_others_wrong.B: Bicarbonate is largely reabsorbed rather than remaining in urine to buffer secreted acid, so it does not represent titratable acid.
why_others_wrong.D: Ammonium excretion is a distinct, separate mechanism of net acid excretion and is not counted within the traditional titratable acid measurement.
why_others_wrong.E: Sodium chloride is an electrolyte with no buffering capacity for hydrogen ions and does not constitute titratable acid.

exam_trap: Titratable acid ≠ total urinary acid. Ammonium is not included in the traditional titratable-acid measurement.
takeaway: Titratable acid = mainly H+ buffered by phosphate.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Titratable acid ↓ secreted hydrogen ions bound to filtered buffers ↓ mainly phosphate ↓ measured by titrating urine back to plasma pH ↓ Phosphate-bound hydrogen ions
pearl: Ammonium is excluded from titratable acid because its pKa of about 9.2 means it does not release hydrogen ions when urine is titrated back to plasma pH.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: foregut vascular territory
stem: A surgeon ligates the artery supplying the foregut during an operation. Which territory is most directly threatened?
why_correct: The foregut is supplied by the coeliac trunk. Its derivatives include the abdominal oesophagus, stomach, proximal duodenum, liver, gallbladder, biliary tree, pancreas and spleen.

why_others_wrong.A: The distal ileum is midgut, supplied by ileal branches of the superior mesenteric artery.
why_others_wrong.B: The ascending colon is midgut, supplied by the ileocolic and right colic branches of the superior mesenteric artery.
why_others_wrong.D: The proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon is midgut, supplied mainly by the middle colic artery.
why_others_wrong.E: The distal third of the transverse colon is hindgut, supplied by the left colic branch of the inferior mesenteric artery.

exam_trap: Distal one-third of transverse colon is chosen by misplacing the gut boundaries; it is hindgut supplied by the IMA, whereas the stomach is coeliac foregut.
takeaway: Coeliac trunk = foregut; SMA = midgut; IMA = hindgut.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed.; RCS Applied Anatomy for MRCS Preparation, accessed September 2026.
thinking: Artery of the foregut ↓ coeliac trunk ↓ foregut derivatives include stomach, liver, pancreas and proximal duodenum ↓ Stomach
pearl: The stomach rarely becomes ischaemic after a single vessel ligation because arcades along both curvatures and the short gastric vessels provide extensive collateral flow.

subject: Anatomy
title: Acute abdomen & GI surgery: mesenteric ischaemia
stem: A patient develops acute abdominal pain out of proportion to abdominal examination findings. CT angiography demonstrates superior mesenteric artery occlusion. Which region is most directly supplied by this artery?

options.E: Anal canal below the pectinate line

why_correct: The superior mesenteric artery supplies the midgut, including the distal duodenum, jejunum, ileum, caecum, appendix, ascending colon and proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon.

why_others_wrong.A: The distal transverse colon and rectum are supplied mainly by the inferior mesenteric artery (hindgut territory), not the SMA.
why_others_wrong.B: The stomach and spleen are supplied by the coeliac trunk (via the splenic artery), foregut territory, not the SMA.
why_others_wrong.D: The oesophagus receives its supply from branches of the thoracic aorta, inferior phrenic and left gastric arteries, not the SMA.
why_others_wrong.E: The anal canal below the pectinate line is supplied by the inferior rectal artery from the internal pudendal artery, not the SMA.

exam_trap: Distal transverse colon and rectum is chosen because the colon is ischaemia-prone, but that is hindgut territory of the IMA rather than SMA midgut.
takeaway: SMA = distal duodenum → jejunum → ileum → caecum → appendix → ascending colon → proximal 2/3 transverse colon.
source: Principles and Practice of Surgery, 7th ed.; Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed.
thinking: Pain out of proportion to examination ↓ acute mesenteric ischaemia ↓ the superior mesenteric artery supplies the midgut ↓ jejunum and ileum are midgut ↓ Jejunum and ileum
pearl: An SMA embolus typically lodges a short distance beyond the origin, often sparing the proximal jejunum, whereas thrombosis at the origin usually causes more extensive ischaemia.

subject: Colorectal surgery
title: Colorectal surgery: watershed colon
stem: An elderly patient develops colonic ischaemia at a watershed region between major arterial territories. Which location is classically vulnerable?
why_correct: The splenic flexure is a classic watershed region between SMA and IMA territories and may be vulnerable to hypoperfusion.

why_others_wrong.A: The caecum lies within the superior mesenteric territory supplied by the ileocolic artery, so it is not the classic watershed between SMA and IMA supply.
why_others_wrong.C: The appendix is supplied by the appendicular branch of the ileocolic artery and does not sit at a watershed between major colonic arterial territories.
why_others_wrong.D: The rectum has a rich dual supply from superior, middle and inferior rectal arteries, so it is relatively protected from ischaemia; the rectosigmoid junction is the lower watershed.
why_others_wrong.E: The ascending colon is supplied by the right colic and ileocolic branches of the SMA, well within one territory rather than at the SMA-IMA junction.

exam_trap: The splenic flexure is associated with Griffith’s point; the rectosigmoid junction is another watershed region.
takeaway: Watershed colon → splenic flexure and rectosigmoid region.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed.; Principles and Practice of Surgery, 7th ed.
thinking: Elderly patient with colonic ischaemia ↓ watershed zones lie where two arterial territories meet ↓ SMA (middle colic) and IMA (left colic) territories meet at the splenic flexure ↓ the marginal artery may be weak or discontinuous there ↓ Splenic flexure
pearl: Ischaemic colitis usually follows a low-flow state and often settles with supportive care, but peritonitis or full-thickness necrosis needs resection; sigmoid ischaemia is a recognised complication of aortic surgery with IMA ligation.

subject: Anatomy
title: Hepatobiliary surgery: portal-systemic anastomosis
stem: A patient with portal hypertension develops dilated veins in the lower oesophagus. Which two venous systems communicate at this site?

options.C: Superior mesenteric and inferior vena cava

why_correct: The lower oesophageal veins provide a portal-systemic communication between tributaries of the left gastric vein and systemic oesophageal veins draining toward the azygos system. Portal hypertension can therefore produce oesophageal varices.

why_others_wrong.A: Splenic and renal venous communication is used surgically (e.g., in shunting) but is not the natural site of oesophageal portosystemic anastomosis.
why_others_wrong.C: There is no direct anastomotic communication between the superior mesenteric vein and the inferior vena cava.
why_others_wrong.D: The inferior mesenteric and renal veins relate to retroperitoneal collateral pathways elsewhere, not to the oesophagus.
why_others_wrong.E: The portal vein and pulmonary vein do not anastomose with one another.

exam_trap: Splenic and renal is chosen because a splenorenal connection can decompress portal hypertension, but that is a surgical or spontaneous shunt, not the oesophageal anastomosis.
takeaway: Oesophageal varices = portal-systemic anastomosis involving left gastric and azygos territories.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed.; Principles and Practice of Surgery, 7th ed.
thinking: Dilated lower oesophageal veins in portal hypertension ↓ the portal side drains via the left gastric vein ↓ the systemic side drains via oesophageal veins to the azygos ↓ Left gastric and azygos
pearl: Other portosystemic sites include the anorectal junction, the umbilicus via paraumbilical veins producing caput medusae, and retroperitoneal veins draining the bare areas of gut.

subject: Anatomy
title: Hepatobiliary surgery: portal venous flow
stem: A thrombus completely obstructs the portal vein proximal to its intrahepatic branches. Which venous blood supply to the liver is most directly reduced?
why_correct: The portal vein carries nutrient-rich venous blood from the gastrointestinal tract and spleen to the liver. Obstruction reduces portal venous inflow while hepatic arterial inflow remains anatomically distinct.

why_others_wrong.A: The hepatic artery is an anatomically separate inflow to the liver and is not directly reduced by portal vein thrombosis.
why_others_wrong.C: Hepatic venous outflow drains via the hepatic veins into the IVC and is not the inflow-side pathway obstructed by portal vein thrombosis.
why_others_wrong.D: Inferior vena cava flow represents systemic venous return and is not the vessel occluded in this scenario.
why_others_wrong.E: Splenic arterial flow supplies the spleen and is anatomically distinct from portal venous drainage to the liver.

exam_trap: Hepatic venous outflow is chosen by confusing portal vein thrombosis with hepatic vein obstruction, which is a different syndrome of outflow failure.
takeaway: Liver has dual inflow: portal vein + hepatic artery; hepatic veins provide outflow.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed.; RCS Applied Anatomy for MRCS Preparation, accessed September 2026.
thinking: Portal vein thrombosis before its intrahepatic branches ↓ the portal vein is a liver inflow vessel ↓ the hepatic artery is a separate inflow and is spared ↓ Portal venous inflow
pearl: Because the hepatic artery compensates, portal vein thrombosis rarely causes hepatic infarction and more often presents with portal hypertension, varices and splenomegaly.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Pathology: oncology & haematology: apoptosis
stem: A tumour cell acquires a mutation that prevents activation of programmed cell death following severe DNA damage. Which process has been impaired?
why_correct: Apoptosis is regulated programmed cell death. It is an important mechanism for removing cells with severe DNA damage and is frequently disrupted during carcinogenesis.

why_others_wrong.A: Necrosis is uncontrolled cell death from injury such as ischaemia, with inflammation, rather than the regulated programme triggered by DNA damage.
why_others_wrong.C: Autophagy is lysosomal self-digestion that mainly supports survival under stress and is not the principal programmed death response to DNA damage.
why_others_wrong.D: Metaplasia is an adaptive change from one mature cell type to another and is not a form of cell death.
why_others_wrong.E: Hypertrophy is an increase in cell size in response to workload and has no role in eliminating cells with DNA damage.

exam_trap: Loss of apoptosis is not simply “more cell growth”; it allows damaged cells to survive.
takeaway: Cancer biology often involves both increased proliferation and failure of programmed cell death.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.; RCS MRCS preparation resources, accessed September 2026.
thinking: Severe DNA damage normally triggers programmed cell death ↓ the mutation blocks this response ↓ regulated, non-inflammatory cell death = apoptosis ↓ Apoptosis
pearl: Many chemotherapy agents and radiotherapy kill tumour cells largely by triggering apoptosis, so defects in apoptotic pathways contribute to treatment resistance.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Physiology: bcl-2
stem: A lymphoma is found to overexpress BCL-2. What is the principal effect of BCL-2 in this context?
why_correct: BCL-2 is an anti-apoptotic protein that helps prevent mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilisation and cytochrome c release. Overexpression can therefore allow abnormal lymphoid cells to survive.

why_others_wrong.A: BCL-2 blocks mitochondrial apoptosis by preventing outer membrane permeabilisation, so it does not promote this pathway.
why_others_wrong.C: BCL-2 prevents cytochrome c release and so indirectly prevents caspase-9 activation in the apoptosome rather than activating it.
why_others_wrong.D: DNA mismatch repair is carried out by proteins such as MLH1 and MSH2, not by BCL-2, which regulates apoptosis.
why_others_wrong.E: Neutrophil chemotaxis is driven by mediators such as IL-8 and C5a, not by BCL-2 overexpression in lymphoma cells.

exam_trap: Promotes mitochondrial apoptosis tempts because BCL-2 acts at mitochondria, but it is anti-apoptotic; pro-apoptotic family members such as BAX and BAK drive membrane permeabilisation.
takeaway: BCL-2 = anti-apoptotic survival signal.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Lymphoma overexpressing BCL-2 ↓ BCL-2 stabilises the mitochondrial outer membrane ↓ it blocks cytochrome c release and caspase activation ↓ Inhibits apoptosis
pearl: Follicular lymphoma typically carries t(14;18), which places BCL-2 next to the immunoglobulin heavy chain locus; venetoclax, a BCL-2 inhibitor, is used in chronic lymphocytic leukaemia.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Pathology: oncology & haematology: homologous recombination
stem: A patient carries a pathogenic BRCA1 mutation. Which cellular process is most directly impaired?
why_correct: BRCA1 and BRCA2 are important in homologous recombination-mediated repair of DNA double-strand breaks.

why_others_wrong.B: Mismatch repair is performed by genes such as MLH1, MSH2, MSH6 and PMS2, whose defects cause Lynch syndrome rather than BRCA-related cancer.
why_others_wrong.C: Pyrimidine synthesis is a nucleotide metabolic pathway, targeted by drugs such as 5-fluorouracil, and is not a BRCA1 function.
why_others_wrong.D: RNA splicing is carried out by the spliceosome to process pre-mRNA and is not the process impaired by BRCA1 mutation.
why_others_wrong.E: Ribosomal assembly takes place in the nucleolus for protein synthesis and is not the DNA repair role of BRCA1.

exam_trap: Mismatch repair tempts as another DNA repair pathway, but its genes (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2) underlie Lynch syndrome; BRCA1 acts in homologous recombination.
takeaway: BRCA1/2 → homologous recombination repair of double-strand DNA damage.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Pathogenic BRCA1 mutation ↓ BRCA1 repairs DNA double-strand breaks ↓ it does so by error-free repair using the sister chromatid ↓ Homologous recombination DNA repair
pearl: Carriers are offered enhanced breast surveillance and discussion of risk-reducing mastectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, as there is no effective screening test for ovarian cancer.

subject: Immunology
title: Physiology: t-cell co-stimulation
stem: A naïve T lymphocyte recognises antigen presented by an antigen-presenting cell but receives no co-stimulatory signal. What is the likely outcome?
why_correct: T-cell activation requires antigen recognition plus appropriate co-stimulation. Recognition without adequate co-stimulation can induce functional unresponsiveness, or anergy. The classic co-stimulatory interaction is CD28 on the T cell with B7 molecules on the antigen-presenting cell.

why_others_wrong.A: T cells do not secrete antibody; antibody is produced by plasma cells, and an unstimulated naive T cell would not trigger immediate secretion.
why_others_wrong.C: Complement activation is triggered by antibody, lectins or microbial surfaces, not by a T cell recognising antigen without co-stimulation.
why_others_wrong.D: Neutrophil degranulation is an innate effector response and is not the outcome of antigen recognition by a naive T cell lacking co-stimulation.
why_others_wrong.E: Class switching occurs in B cells and needs help from fully activated T cells, which is exactly what is missing without co-stimulation.

exam_trap: Class switching tempts candidates who link T-cell help with antibody, but it needs fully activated T cells; antigen recognition without co-stimulation produces anergy.
takeaway: T-cell activation requires antigen recognition + co-stimulation.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Naive T cell recognises antigen ↓ no co-stimulatory signal (no CD28-B7) ↓ signal 1 without signal 2 ↓ cell becomes functionally unresponsive ↓ T-cell anergy
pearl: Anergy is a mechanism of peripheral tolerance, because antigen presented by resting cells without co-stimulation switches off self-reactive T cells.

subject: Immunology
title: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing: transplant immunology
stem: A transplanted organ is recognised as foreign and is attacked predominantly by recipient T lymphocytes. Which mechanism is most characteristic?
why_correct: Acute cellular rejection is predominantly T-cell mediated and can occur after transplantation as recipient immune cells recognise donor antigens.

why_others_wrong.B: Hyperacute rejection is driven by preformed recipient antibodies and occurs within minutes to hours, rather than being predominantly T-cell mediated.
why_others_wrong.C: Graft-versus-host disease occurs when donor immune cells attack the recipient, the reverse direction of recipient T cells attacking the graft.
why_others_wrong.D: Type I hypersensitivity is an IgE-mediated mast-cell reaction to allergens and does not describe T-cell recognition of a transplanted organ.
why_others_wrong.E: Immune tolerance is the absence of a damaging response to antigen, which contradicts a graft being recognised and attacked.

exam_trap: Recipient attacks graft = rejection; donor immune cells attack recipient = GVHD.
takeaway: Recipient T cells attacking graft → acute cellular rejection.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Transplanted organ attacked by recipient T lymphocytes ↓ not preformed antibody ↓ not donor cells attacking host ↓ Acute cellular rejection
pearl: Acute rejection is diagnosed on graft biopsy; in kidneys the Banff classification grades tubulitis and arteritis to guide treatment.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Perioperative medicine & nutrition: perioperative hypothermia
stem: A patient undergoing prolonged surgery develops significant perioperative hypothermia. Which physiological consequence is most likely?

options.B: Increased oxygen consumption from shivering only

why_correct: Hypothermia can impair platelet function and coagulation enzyme activity, contributing to perioperative bleeding. It may also affect immune function and wound healing.

why_others_wrong.A: Hypothermia impairs platelet function rather than enhancing it, which contributes to perioperative bleeding.
why_others_wrong.B: Shivering does raise oxygen consumption, but the most important consequence here is coagulopathy, and shivering is not the sole effect.
why_others_wrong.D: Hypothermia is associated with an increased, not reduced, risk of surgical wound infection through vasoconstriction and impaired immunity.
why_others_wrong.E: Hypothermia generally lowers metabolic rate and drug metabolism, and any rise from shivering is limited and costly.

exam_trap: Option B tempts because shivering does raise oxygen consumption, but the word only makes it wrong, and impaired coagulation is the more important consequence of significant hypothermia.
takeaway: Perioperative hypothermia → coagulopathy + impaired host defence + other complications.
source: Principles and Practice of Surgery, 7th ed.; current RCS surgical preparation resources, accessed September 2026.
thinking: Prolonged surgery with significant hypothermia ↓ coagulation enzymes are temperature dependent ↓ platelet function is impaired by cold ↓ Impaired coagulation
pearl: Standard coagulation tests are run at 37 degrees Celsius, so they can look normal despite clinically significant hypothermic coagulopathy; active warming is part of the treatment of bleeding.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Cardiorespiratory physiology: oxygen delivery
stem: A patient has severe anaemia but a normal arterial oxygen saturation. Which change most directly explains reduced oxygen delivery to tissues?
why_correct: Arterial oxygen content depends predominantly on haemoglobin-bound oxygen. Therefore, severe anaemia reduces arterial oxygen content and oxygen delivery despite normal oxygen saturation. Oxygen delivery is approximately: DO2 = cardiac output × arterial oxygen content.

why_others_wrong.B: The stem specifies normal arterial oxygen saturation, so a reduced inspired oxygen concentration (which would lower saturation) is not the operative mechanism here.
why_others_wrong.C: Oxygen saturation is stated to be normal in this patient; the reduced delivery is explained by low haemoglobin concentration, not by a fall in saturation.
why_others_wrong.D: Increased alveolar oxygen tension would tend to raise, not reduce, arterial oxygen content and delivery.
why_others_wrong.E: Changes in arterial pH shift the position of the oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve but are not the primary explanation for reduced oxygen delivery in this anaemic patient with normal saturation.

exam_trap: Reduced oxygen saturation is chosen by candidates who equate saturation with oxygen supply, but the stem states saturation is normal; low haemoglobin explains the deficit.
takeaway: Anaemia can markedly reduce oxygen delivery despite normal PaO2 and SpO2.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Severe anaemia with normal saturation ↓ arterial content depends mainly on Hb x saturation ↓ saturation is normal so Hb is the deficit ↓ Reduced haemoglobin concentration
pearl: Pulse oximetry can read normally in severe anaemia and may become unreliable in very low haemoglobin, so laboratory haemoglobin is needed to assess oxygen-carrying capacity.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Perioperative medicine & nutrition: perioperative fluid shift
stem: A patient undergoes major abdominal surgery and receives large volumes of intravenous crystalloid. Several hours later, peripheral and interstitial oedema develops despite no evidence of heart failure. Which physiological mechanism best explains this?

options.B: Crystalloid distributes across the extracellular fluid compartment
options.D: Plasma proteins are completely retained intravascularly
options.E: Crystalloid remains within the lymphatic system

correct_answer: B. Crystalloid distributes across the extracellular fluid compartment
why_correct: Isotonic crystalloid initially expands the extracellular fluid compartment. Only a proportion remains intravascular; the remainder distributes into the interstitial space. Inflammation and endothelial permeability changes during major surgery can further promote interstitial fluid accumulation.

why_others_wrong.A: Most infused isotonic crystalloid redistributes into the interstitial space, so it does not all remain intravascular.
why_others_wrong.C: Isotonic crystalloid stays largely extracellular because its sodium content matches plasma, so it does not move exclusively into cells.
why_others_wrong.D: Surgical inflammation increases endothelial permeability, so plasma proteins can leak into the interstitium rather than being fully retained.
why_others_wrong.E: Lymphatics return interstitial fluid to the circulation; crystalloid is not held within the lymphatic system.

exam_trap: Option A tempts candidates who think IV fluid stays in the vessels, but isotonic crystalloid distributes across the extracellular space, so most leaves the circulation.
takeaway: Crystalloid → extracellular distribution; only a fraction remains intravascular.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.; Principles and Practice of Surgery, 7th ed.
thinking: Large-volume isotonic crystalloid ↓ it distributes across the whole extracellular compartment ↓ most moves from plasma into the interstitium ↓ surgical inflammation increases capillary leak ↓ Crystalloid distributes across the extracellular fluid compartment
pearl: Interstitial oedema of the bowel wall after excessive crystalloid is associated with prolonged ileus and anastomotic complications, one reason enhanced recovery pathways avoid large positive fluid balances.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: aortic arch derivatives
stem: A newborn is diagnosed with an abnormality involving the third aortic arch. Which major vessel is derived from the third aortic arch?
why_correct: The third aortic arches contribute to the common carotid arteries and the proximal portions of the internal carotid arteries.

why_others_wrong.A: The pulmonary arteries derive from the sixth aortic arches, not the third.
why_others_wrong.C: The ductus arteriosus derives from the distal part of the left sixth arch.
why_others_wrong.D: The maxillary arteries are remnants of the first aortic arches.
why_others_wrong.E: The left subclavian comes from the seventh intersegmental artery and the proximal right subclavian from the right fourth arch, not the third.

exam_trap: Do not confuse the third arch with the fourth arch. Third → carotids; fourth → parts of the aortic arch/right subclavian artery.
takeaway: Third aortic arch → common carotids + proximal internal carotids.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed.
thinking: Third aortic arch ↓ forms the common carotid arteries ↓ also forms the proximal internal carotid arteries ↓ Common carotid arteries
pearl: Each pharyngeal arch has its own nerve: the third arch is supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve, the fourth by the superior laryngeal branch of the vagus and the sixth by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: fourth aortic arch
stem: During embryological development, the left fourth aortic arch contributes to which structure?
correct_answer: C. Part of the aortic arch
why_correct: The left fourth aortic arch contributes to part of the definitive aortic arch between the left common carotid and left subclavian arteries. The right fourth arch contributes to part of the right subclavian artery.

why_others_wrong.A: The ductus arteriosus arises from the left sixth arch, not the fourth.
why_others_wrong.B: The left pulmonary artery derives from the proximal part of the left sixth arch.
why_others_wrong.D: The common carotid arteries derive from the third aortic arches.
why_others_wrong.E: There is no descending pulmonary artery; the pulmonary arteries derive from the sixth arches.

exam_trap: Ductus arteriosus is chosen by confusing the fourth and sixth arches; the ductus comes from the left sixth arch, not from the fourth.
takeaway: Fourth arch: left → aortic arch; right → proximal right subclavian contribution.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed.
thinking: Left fourth aortic arch ↓ persists as a segment of the definitive aortic arch ↓ between the left common carotid and left subclavian arteries ↓ Part of the aortic arch
pearl: Abnormal regression of the fourth arches can leave a double aortic arch or right-sided arch forming a vascular ring, which presents in infancy with stridor and dysphagia.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: sixth aortic arch
stem: A congenital cardiovascular anomaly involves persistence of a fetal vascular connection between the pulmonary artery and aorta. Which embryological structure has failed to close?
why_correct: The ductus arteriosus connects the pulmonary trunk to the descending aorta in fetal life and normally closes after birth. It is derived from the left sixth aortic arch.

why_others_wrong.A: The foramen ovale is an interatrial opening, not a vessel connecting the pulmonary artery and aorta.
why_others_wrong.B: The ductus venosus shunts umbilical venous blood past the liver to the inferior vena cava, not between pulmonary artery and aorta.
why_others_wrong.D: The umbilical vein carries oxygenated blood from the placenta and becomes the ligamentum teres, unrelated to the aorta.
why_others_wrong.E: Vitelline arteries supply the yolk sac and form the coeliac, superior and inferior mesenteric arteries.

exam_trap: Foramen ovale or ductus venosus are chosen as other fetal shunts, but they link the atria and bypass the liver respectively, not the pulmonary artery and aorta.
takeaway: Left sixth arch → ductus arteriosus.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed.
thinking: Persistent fetal channel between pulmonary artery and aorta ↓ a fetal shunt diverting blood away from the lungs ↓ derived from the left sixth arch ↓ Ductus arteriosus
