pearl: A patent ductus arteriosus classically gives a continuous machinery murmur; in preterm infants closure can be encouraged with NSAIDs or paracetamol, while prostaglandin keeps it open in duct-dependent lesions.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: interatrial septation
stem: During fetal cardiac development, the septum secundum forms an incomplete partition between the atria. What structure remains functionally open before birth?
why_correct: The foramen ovale allows blood to pass from the right atrium to the left atrium during fetal life, bypassing the non-functioning fetal lungs. After birth, increased left atrial pressure normally apposes the septum primum against the septum secundum.

why_others_wrong.A: The ductus arteriosus is a great-vessel shunt from pulmonary trunk to aorta, not an interatrial opening related to septum secundum.
why_others_wrong.C: The ductus venosus shunts umbilical venous blood past the liver and is not part of the atrial septum.
why_others_wrong.D: The coronary sinus drains cardiac veins into the right atrium and is not an interatrial communication.
why_others_wrong.E: The sinus venosus is the embryonic venous inflow chamber incorporated into the right atrium, not a patent interatrial opening.

exam_trap: Ductus arteriosus is chosen as the best-known fetal shunt, but it connects pulmonary trunk to aorta; only the foramen ovale relates to the atrial septum.
takeaway: Foramen ovale → fetal RA-to-LA shunt; closes functionally when LA pressure rises after birth.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed.
thinking: Septum secundum forms an incomplete partition ↓ the gap is covered on the left by the septum primum flap ↓ fetal blood passes right to left between the atria ↓ Foramen ovale
pearl: Incomplete fusion leaves a patent foramen ovale in a substantial minority of adults, which can allow paradoxical embolism of venous thrombus into the systemic circulation and cause stroke.

subject: Anatomy
title: ENT: head & neck: recurrent laryngeal nerve embryology
stem: A congenital vascular anomaly alters the usual course of the right recurrent laryngeal nerve. Which arterial developmental change can produce a non-recurrent right laryngeal nerve?
why_correct: The right recurrent laryngeal nerve normally hooks around the right subclavian artery. An aberrant right subclavian artery can arise distal to the left subclavian artery and pass posteriorly toward the right arm. In this setting, the nerve may fail to descend and instead become non-recurrent.

why_others_wrong.A: A persistent right sixth arch would hold the right nerve lower, keeping it recurrent; a non-recurrent nerve arises when no right subclavian loop exists to hook around.
why_others_wrong.C: A persistent ductus arteriosus is a left-sided structure tied to the normal course of the left recurrent laryngeal nerve, not a cause of a non-recurrent right nerve.
why_others_wrong.D: Left pulmonary artery stenosis is unrelated to the embryological basis of a non-recurrent right laryngeal nerve.
why_others_wrong.E: A persistent umbilical artery is a lower abdominal/pelvic vascular remnant with no bearing on laryngeal nerve embryology.

exam_trap: Persistent ductus arteriosus is chosen because it shapes the left recurrent laryngeal nerve, but it plays no part in producing a non-recurrent right nerve.
takeaway: Aberrant right subclavian artery → possible non-recurrent right recurrent laryngeal nerve.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed.
thinking: Non-recurrent right laryngeal nerve ↓ the right nerve normally hooks under the right subclavian artery ↓ an aberrant right subclavian from the distal arch leaves no loop to hook around ↓ the nerve passes directly from the vagus to the larynx ↓ Aberrant right subclavian artery
pearl: An aberrant right subclavian artery passes behind the oesophagus and can cause dysphagia; in thyroid surgery a non-recurrent nerve runs transversely from the vagus and can be mistaken for the inferior thyroid artery.

subject: Anatomy
title: Acute abdomen & GI surgery: retroperitoneal structures
stem: A CT scan is reviewed before pancreatic surgery. Which structure is secondarily retroperitoneal in the adult?
correct_answer: D. Duodenum, except its first part
why_correct: Most of the duodenum becomes secondarily retroperitoneal during development. The first part is relatively mobile, whereas the remainder is largely fixed retroperitoneally.

why_others_wrong.A: The stomach is fully intraperitoneal, suspended by the lesser and greater omenta.
why_others_wrong.B: The jejunum is intraperitoneal, freely mobile on its mesentery.
why_others_wrong.C: The transverse colon is intraperitoneal, suspended by the transverse mesocolon.
why_others_wrong.E: The spleen is intraperitoneal, supported by peritoneal ligaments rather than being secondarily retroperitoneal.

exam_trap: “Duodenum” is not uniformly retroperitoneal. The first part has a different relationship.
takeaway: Secondarily retroperitoneal: most of duodenum, pancreas except tail, ascending and descending colon.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed.
thinking: Secondarily retroperitoneal = once had a mesentery that fused to the posterior wall ↓ stomach, jejunum, transverse colon and spleen keep mesenteries or ligaments ↓ the duodenum fuses except for its mobile first part ↓ Duodenum, except its first part
pearl: Retroperitoneal duodenal injuries after blunt trauma can be clinically silent early, so retroperitoneal gas or fluid around the duodenum on CT should prompt suspicion of perforation.

subject: Anatomy
title: Acute abdomen & GI surgery: pancreatic tail
stem: A surgeon performs a distal pancreatectomy and must identify the part of the pancreas that remains within the peritoneal cavity between the splenic ligaments. Which part of the pancreas is relatively intraperitoneal?
why_correct: The pancreas is predominantly retroperitoneal, but its tail extends within the splenorenal ligament toward the splenic hilum and has a more intraperitoneal relationship.

why_others_wrong.A: The head of the pancreas is firmly retroperitoneal, nestled within the duodenal C-loop.
why_others_wrong.B: The uncinate process is a retroperitoneal extension of the head, lying posterior to the superior mesenteric vessels.
why_others_wrong.C: The neck of the pancreas is retroperitoneal, lying anterior to the site of portal vein formation.
why_others_wrong.D: The body of the pancreas is retroperitoneal, crossing anterior to the aorta and left renal vessels.

exam_trap: Body is chosen because it lies next to the tail, but the body is retroperitoneal across the aorta; only the tail runs within the splenorenal ligament.
takeaway: Pancreas is mostly retroperitoneal; the tail extends into the splenorenal ligament.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed.
thinking: Distal pancreatectomy near the splenic hilum ↓ head, neck, body and uncinate process are retroperitoneal ↓ only one part extends into the splenorenal ligament ↓ Tail
pearl: The pancreatic tail lies close to the splenic hilum, so it can be injured during splenectomy and cause a pancreatic leak or fistula; conversely, distal pancreatectomy is often combined with splenectomy.

subject: Urology
title: Urology: renal fascia
stem: A renal infection spreads into the surrounding retroperitoneal tissues but remains contained within the fascial compartment surrounding the kidney. Which fascia is most relevant?
why_correct: The kidneys and surrounding perirenal fat are enclosed by renal fascia, which forms an important anatomical boundary within the retroperitoneum.

why_others_wrong.A: Camper fascia is the fatty superficial layer of the anterior abdominal wall subcutaneous tissue and plays no part in enclosing the kidney within the retroperitoneum.
why_others_wrong.B: Scarpa fascia is the membranous layer of the anterior abdominal wall subcutaneous tissue, so it cannot contain spread of infection around the kidney.
why_others_wrong.D: Colles fascia is the membranous layer of the superficial perineum, which directs extravasated urine from urethral injury rather than bounding the perirenal space.
why_others_wrong.E: Buck fascia is the deep fascia of the penis enclosing the erectile bodies, so it is unrelated to the retroperitoneal compartment around the kidney.

exam_trap: Candidates choose Scarpa or Camper fascia as familiar abdominal fascial names, but these are anterior abdominal wall layers; the perirenal space is bounded by renal fascia.
takeaway: Renal fascia encloses the perirenal compartment and helps constrain spread of retroperitoneal pathology.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed.
thinking: Renal infection spreading into retroperitoneal tissues ↓ contained around the kidney ↓ perirenal fat is enclosed by renal fascia ↓ the fascia forms the perirenal compartment boundary ↓ Renal fascia
pearl: Renal fascia is closed superiorly and laterally but relatively open inferiorly along the ureter, so perinephric collections can track down towards the pelvis.

subject: Urology
title: Urology: ureteric crossing
stem: A patient has a pelvic mass compressing the ureter near the pelvic brim. Which structure does the ureter cross near this location?
why_correct: The ureter crosses the pelvic brim in relation to the common iliac vessels or their bifurcation. This is an important anatomical site for ureteric obstruction.

why_others_wrong.A: The right ureter often crosses the origin of the external iliac artery, but the usual landmark on both sides is the common iliac bifurcation.
why_others_wrong.C: The inferior epigastric artery runs up the anterior abdominal wall from the external iliac artery near the deep inguinal ring, well away from the ureter at the brim.
why_others_wrong.D: The femoral artery lies below the inguinal ligament in the thigh, so it has no relationship to the ureter at the pelvic brim.
why_others_wrong.E: The superior mesenteric artery arises from the aorta at about L1 and supplies midgut, lying far above where the ureter enters the pelvis.

exam_trap: Candidates choose the external iliac artery because the right ureter often crosses its origin, but the standard landmark on both sides is the common iliac bifurcation.
takeaway: Ureter crosses the pelvic brim near the common iliac vessels.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed.
thinking: Pelvic mass compressing the ureter at the pelvic brim ↓ ureter enters the pelvis here ↓ it crosses the iliac vessels near the common iliac bifurcation ↓ a recognised point of narrowing ↓ Common iliac bifurcation/iliac vessels
pearl: The pelvic brim is one of three classic sites of ureteric narrowing where stones lodge, alongside the pelviureteric junction and the vesicoureteric junction.

subject: Pharmacology
title: Pharmacology: renal blood flow
stem: A drug causes marked constriction of the renal afferent arteriole. What is the immediate effect on glomerular filtration?

options.D: Increased filtration fraction with increased GFR
options.E: Complete cessation of renal venous flow

why_correct: Afferent arteriolar constriction reduces blood flow and hydrostatic pressure within the glomerular capillaries, thereby reducing GFR.

why_others_wrong.A: Afferent constriction reduces glomerular blood flow and hydrostatic pressure, lowering rather than raising GFR.
why_others_wrong.C: Reduced glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure from afferent constriction directly lowers GFR, so it does not remain unchanged.
why_others_wrong.D: Afferent constriction reduces both renal plasma flow and GFR together; it does not raise GFR or filtration fraction in this way.
why_others_wrong.E: Afferent constriction reduces flow into the glomerulus but does not cause complete cessation of renal venous outflow.

exam_trap: No change in GFR may tempt candidates relying on autoregulation, but marked afferent constriction overrides it, reducing glomerular blood flow, capillary pressure and therefore GFR.
takeaway: Afferent constriction → ↓ renal blood flow + ↓ glomerular pressure → ↓ GFR.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Marked afferent arteriolar constriction ↓ less blood enters the glomerulus ↓ glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure falls ↓ net filtration pressure falls ↓ Decreased GFR
pearl: NSAIDs reduce prostaglandin-mediated afferent dilatation, which is why they can cause acute kidney injury in hypovolaemic or perioperative patients whose GFR depends on that dilatation.

subject: Pharmacology
title: Pharmacology: efferent arteriole
stem: A patient receives a drug that selectively constricts the efferent arteriole moderately. What is the immediate effect on glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure?
why_correct: Moderate efferent arteriolar constriction increases resistance to blood leaving the glomerulus, increasing glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure and tending to support GFR. With severe efferent constriction, however, renal blood flow can fall substantially and filtration may eventually decrease.

why_others_wrong.A: Efferent constriction increases resistance to outflow from the glomerulus, which raises, rather than lowers, glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure at moderate degrees of constriction.
why_others_wrong.C: Moderate efferent constriction raises glomerular pressure; it does not reduce it to zero.
why_others_wrong.D: Changing resistance at the efferent arteriole directly alters the pressure gradient across the glomerulus, so pressure is affected, not unaffected.
why_others_wrong.E: Glomerular capillary pressure does not "reverse" into venous pressure with efferent constriction; it rises because of increased outflow resistance.

exam_trap: Do not apply the simplistic rule “efferent constriction always increases GFR.” The effect depends on the degree of constriction.
takeaway: Moderate efferent constriction → ↑ glomerular capillary pressure; severe constriction can ultimately reduce GFR.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Moderate efferent arteriolar constriction ↓ resistance to blood leaving the glomerulus rises ↓ blood dams back in the glomerular capillaries ↓ It increases
pearl: Angiotensin II maintains GFR in low-perfusion states by constricting the efferent arteriole; removing this effect with ACE inhibitors or ARBs explains acute falls in GFR in hypovolaemia or renal artery stenosis.

subject: Physiology
title: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care: adrenal cortex feedback
stem: A patient has autonomous cortisol production from an adrenal cortical tumour. Which change is expected?

options.E: Increased ACTH with no change in CRH

correct_answer: C. Reduced CRH and reduced ACTH
why_correct: Cortisol exerts negative feedback at both the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary. Autonomous adrenal cortisol production therefore suppresses CRH and ACTH secretion.

why_others_wrong.A: Autonomous adrenal cortisol production suppresses, rather than increases, both CRH and ACTH through negative feedback.
why_others_wrong.B: Cortisol feeds back on the hypothalamus as well as the pituitary, so CRH is suppressed rather than increased by autonomous cortisol excess.
why_others_wrong.D: A reduced CRH with increased ACTH would suggest an autonomous pituitary ACTH source, not an adrenal tumour producing cortisol independently of pituitary drive.
why_others_wrong.E: Autonomous cortisol excess suppresses ACTH via negative feedback; ACTH does not remain unaffected while cortisol rises.

exam_trap: Candidates choosing B remember pituitary feedback but forget the hypothalamus; cortisol suppresses CRH as well as ACTH, so both are reduced.
takeaway: High cortisol → ↓ CRH + ↓ ACTH through negative feedback.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Autonomous adrenal cortisol production ↓ cortisol feeds back on hypothalamus and pituitary ↓ CRH and ACTH both fall ↓ Reduced CRH and reduced ACTH
pearl: In ACTH-independent cortisol excess, the suppressed ACTH causes atrophy of the contralateral adrenal, so glucocorticoid replacement is needed after unilateral adrenalectomy.

subject: Physiology
title: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care: primary hypothyroidism feedback
stem: A patient has primary thyroid gland failure. Which hormonal pattern is most likely?
why_correct: Primary thyroid failure causes reduced thyroid hormone production. Loss of negative feedback increases hypothalamic TRH and pituitary TSH secretion.

why_others_wrong.A: Low T4 with low TSH describes secondary (central) hypothyroidism from pituitary or hypothalamic failure, not primary thyroid gland failure.
why_others_wrong.C: High T4 with high TSH would suggest a TSH-secreting tumour or thyroid hormone resistance, not primary gland failure, which lowers T4.
why_others_wrong.D: High T4 with low TSH is the pattern of primary hyperthyroidism, the opposite condition to thyroid gland failure.
why_others_wrong.E: An absent TSH is inconsistent with a failing thyroid gland, where loss of negative feedback should raise, not eliminate, TSH.

exam_trap: “Primary” means the endocrine gland itself is failing; expect the trophic hormone to rise when negative feedback is lost.
takeaway: Primary gland failure → low target hormone + high trophic hormone.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Primary thyroid failure ↓ T4 production falls ↓ loss of negative feedback ↓ TRH and TSH rise ↓ Low T4, high TSH
pearl: Subclinical hypothyroidism shows a raised TSH with a normal free T4, reflecting how sensitively the pituitary responds to small falls in thyroid hormone.

subject: Physiology
title: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care: primary adrenal failure
stem: A patient has autoimmune destruction of the adrenal cortex. Which hormonal pattern is expected?
why_correct: Primary adrenal cortical failure reduces cortisol production. Loss of negative feedback increases ACTH secretion. ACTH is therefore high in primary adrenal insufficiency.

why_others_wrong.A: High cortisol with low ACTH describes autonomous adrenal cortisol excess, the opposite of gland destruction and failure.
why_others_wrong.C: Low ACTH would indicate a central (secondary) cause of adrenal insufficiency, not primary destruction of the adrenal cortex itself.
why_others_wrong.D: High cortisol is inconsistent with a destroyed adrenal cortex, which cannot produce adequate cortisol regardless of ACTH drive.
why_others_wrong.E: Cortisol is low, not normal, in overt primary adrenal failure, since the gland itself cannot respond adequately even to a high ACTH drive.

exam_trap: Candidates choosing C describe central adrenal insufficiency; with autoimmune destruction of the cortex, loss of cortisol feedback makes ACTH high, not low.
takeaway: Primary adrenal failure → ↓ cortisol + ↑ ACTH.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Autoimmune adrenalitis is primary adrenal failure ↓ cortisol production falls ↓ loss of feedback raises CRH and ACTH ↓ Low cortisol, high ACTH
pearl: Because the whole cortex is destroyed, aldosterone is also deficient, producing hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and a raised renin that are absent in pituitary causes.

subject: Physiology
title: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care: growth hormone axis
stem: A child has excessive growth hormone secretion from a pituitary adenoma. Which mediator is responsible for many of the growth-promoting effects of GH?
why_correct: Growth hormone stimulates production of insulin-like growth factor 1, particularly from the liver. IGF-1 mediates many of the anabolic and growth-promoting effects of GH.

why_others_wrong.A: ACTH regulates adrenal cortisol production and has no role in mediating GH's growth-promoting effects.
why_others_wrong.C: TSH regulates thyroid hormone secretion and is unrelated to the growth-mediating actions of GH.
why_others_wrong.D: Aldosterone regulates sodium and potassium balance and plays no part in mediating growth effects of GH.
why_others_wrong.E: Calcitonin regulates calcium homeostasis by inhibiting osteoclasts and is unrelated to GH-mediated growth promotion.

exam_trap: Candidates may pick ACTH (A) or TSH (C) as other pituitary hormones, but these act on the adrenal and thyroid; IGF-1 mediates growth hormone's growth-promoting effects.
takeaway: GH → IGF-1 → major growth-promoting effects.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Childhood growth hormone excess ↓ GH stimulates hepatic IGF-1 production ↓ IGF-1 acts on growth plates ↓ excess before epiphyseal fusion causes gigantism ↓ IGF-1
pearl: GH excess before epiphyseal fusion causes gigantism, whereas after fusion it causes acromegaly with acral and soft-tissue overgrowth rather than increased height.

subject: Physiology
title: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care: prolactin regulation
stem: A woman develops a pituitary stalk lesion. Which anterior pituitary hormone is most likely to increase because its normal hypothalamic inhibition has been interrupted?
why_correct: Dopamine from the hypothalamus normally inhibits prolactin secretion. Interruption of the hypothalamic-pituitary connection reduces dopamine delivery to lactotrophs and can therefore increase prolactin.

why_others_wrong.A: ACTH secretion depends on stimulatory CRH input from the hypothalamus, so a stalk lesion interrupting this connection would reduce, not increase, ACTH.
why_others_wrong.B: TSH is driven by stimulatory TRH via the hypophyseal portal system; interrupting the stalk removes this stimulus and would lower, not raise, TSH.
why_others_wrong.D: GH secretion depends on stimulatory GHRH from the hypothalamus, so stalk interruption would reduce, not increase, GH output.
why_others_wrong.E: FSH release depends on stimulatory GnRH; loss of hypothalamic-pituitary connectivity would reduce, not increase, gonadotrophin secretion.

exam_trap: Most pituitary hormones are stimulated by hypothalamic releasing hormones; prolactin is unusual because its dominant hypothalamic control is inhibitory.
takeaway: Pituitary stalk interruption → loss of dopamine inhibition → ↑ prolactin.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Pituitary stalk lesion ↓ portal delivery of hypothalamic hormones is interrupted ↓ hormones under stimulatory control fall ↓ prolactin loses tonic dopamine inhibition and rises ↓ Prolactin
pearl: Hyperprolactinaemia from stalk compression is usually modest, so a markedly raised prolactin with a large pituitary mass suggests a prolactinoma instead.

subject: Physiology
title: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care: calcium-sensing receptor
stem: A patient has a mutation causing reduced sensitivity of the calcium-sensing receptor in the parathyroid glands. What would this tend to cause?

options.A: Reduced PTH secretion at any given calcium concentration
options.B: Increased PTH secretion at a given calcium concentration

correct_answer: B. Increased PTH secretion at a given calcium concentration
why_correct: The calcium-sensing receptor helps parathyroid cells detect extracellular calcium. Reduced receptor sensitivity means a higher calcium concentration is required to suppress PTH secretion.

why_others_wrong.A: Reduced receptor sensitivity means higher, not lower, calcium levels are needed to suppress PTH, so secretion at any given calcium concentration tends to increase rather than decrease.
why_others_wrong.C: The defect shifts the calcium set point for PTH suppression rather than abolishing PTH secretion entirely.
why_others_wrong.D: The mutation acts through altered parathyroid calcium sensing and PTH release, not through an isolated effect confined only to renal calcium reabsorption.
why_others_wrong.E: This option is too narrow; the primary consequence is altered PTH secretion in response to calcium, not an isolated reduction in intestinal calcium absorption.

exam_trap: A defect in calcium sensing shifts the calcium-PTH relationship rather than simply eliminating PTH.
takeaway: Reduced CaSR sensitivity → higher “set point” for calcium suppression of PTH.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: CaSR detects extracellular calcium ↓ receptor sensitivity is reduced ↓ a higher calcium is needed to suppress PTH ↓ more PTH is secreted at any given calcium ↓ Increased PTH secretion at a given calcium concentration
pearl: Inactivating CaSR mutations cause familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia, recognised by a low urinary calcium excretion, and parathyroidectomy does not help these patients.

subject: Genetics
title: Genetics: autosomal dominant negative effect
stem: A patient has a mutation in a structural protein. The abnormal protein interferes with the function of protein produced from the normal allele. What mechanism is this?
why_correct: A dominant-negative mutation produces an abnormal protein that interferes with the function of the normal protein. This is particularly relevant to proteins that function as multimers or complexes.

why_others_wrong.A: Haploinsufficiency is disease from too little product when one allele is lost, whereas here the abnormal protein actively interferes with the normal one.
why_others_wrong.C: Mitochondrial inheritance describes maternal transmission of mtDNA variants, not a mechanism by which one abnormal protein disrupts its normal counterpart.
why_others_wrong.D: Anticipation is earlier onset or greater severity across generations and does not describe how a mutant protein affects normal protein function.
why_others_wrong.E: Genomic imprinting is parent-of-origin-specific gene expression, not interference of a mutant structural protein with the normal allele's product.

exam_trap: Haploinsufficiency is the trap; it describes too little normal protein after loss of one allele, whereas here the abnormal protein actively disrupts the normal one.
takeaway: Dominant-negative mutations can cause disease despite one normal allele remaining.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Mutant structural protein ↓ interferes with protein from the normal allele ↓ multimeric proteins especially affected ↓ Dominant-negative effect
pearl: Osteogenesis imperfecta can be caused by dominant-negative collagen type I mutations, because abnormal chains incorporated into the triple helix disrupt the whole molecule.

subject: Genetics
title: Genetics: haploinsufficiency
stem: A patient has a heterozygous deletion of a gene. The remaining normal allele cannot produce enough protein to maintain normal function. What genetic mechanism best explains the phenotype?
why_correct: Haploinsufficiency occurs when one functional allele does not produce enough gene product to maintain the normal phenotype.

why_others_wrong.B: Anticipation is earlier onset or worsening across generations, usually from repeat expansion, not insufficient protein from a single remaining allele.
why_others_wrong.C: Uniparental disomy is inheritance of both homologues from one parent, not a heterozygous deletion leaving too little gene product.
why_others_wrong.D: Mitochondrial inheritance involves maternally transmitted mtDNA variants, whereas this is a nuclear gene deletion reducing protein dosage.
why_others_wrong.E: Somatic mosaicism means a variant is present in only some cells, which does not describe a heterozygous deletion causing reduced dosage.

exam_trap: A dominant phenotype does not necessarily require the abnormal allele to produce an abnormal protein; insufficient normal product can be enough.
takeaway: One normal allele + insufficient gene product → haploinsufficiency.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Heterozygous gene deletion ↓ one normal allele remains ↓ its output is insufficient for normal function ↓ Haploinsufficiency
pearl: Haploinsufficiency explains why whole-gene deletions can cause dominant disease, for example deletions of one copy of a tumour suppressor or developmental gene.

subject: Genetics
title: Genetics: uniparental disomy
stem: A child inherits both copies of a chromosome from the same parent. What is this phenomenon called?
why_correct: Uniparental disomy means both homologous chromosomes, or both copies of a particular chromosomal region, are inherited from one parent. It can have clinical consequences when genomic imprinting is involved.

why_others_wrong.A: Anticipation is earlier onset or increased severity across generations and says nothing about which parent supplied a chromosome pair.
why_others_wrong.C: Mosaicism means genetically different cell lines within one person, not both copies of a chromosome coming from the same parent.
why_others_wrong.D: Nondisjunction is a segregation error that can lead to uniparental disomy via trisomy rescue, but it names the mechanism rather than the outcome.
why_others_wrong.E: Variable expressivity describes differing severity among people with the same genotype, not the parental origin of a chromosome pair.

exam_trap: Nondisjunction can contribute to the mechanisms producing uniparental disomy, but the two terms are not synonymous.
takeaway: Both homologues from one parent = uniparental disomy.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Both copies of a chromosome inherited ↓ all from one parent ↓ outcome rather than mechanism ↓ Uniparental disomy
pearl: Uniparental disomy matters clinically when it involves an imprinted region, for example maternal disomy of chromosome 15 causing Prader-Willi syndrome.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Pathology: oncology & haematology: loss of heterozygosity
stem: A tumour suppressor gene is inherited in a heterozygous state. A tumour cell subsequently loses the remaining normal allele. What is this event called?
why_correct: Loss of heterozygosity occurs when a cell that initially contains one normal and one altered allele loses the remaining normal allele or otherwise loses its functional contribution. This is an important mechanism in tumour suppressor inactivation.

why_others_wrong.B: Anticipation is earlier or more severe disease in successive generations, usually from expanding repeats, not loss of a normal allele in a tumour cell.
why_others_wrong.C: Gene amplification is an increase in copy number of a gene, typically activating an oncogene, rather than loss of a tumour suppressor allele.
why_others_wrong.D: A translocation exchanges segments between chromosomes, often creating fusion genes such as BCR-ABL, and does not by itself mean loss of the normal allele.
why_others_wrong.E: Alternative splicing produces different mRNA isoforms from one gene and does not describe loss of the remaining functional allele.

exam_trap: Loss of heterozygosity does not necessarily mean the DNA sequence was directly deleted; several mechanisms can produce functional loss of the normal allele.
takeaway: Inherited tumour suppressor defect + loss of normal allele → loss of heterozygosity.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Tumour suppressor inherited in a heterozygous state ↓ the tumour cell loses the remaining normal allele ↓ the cell is no longer heterozygous at that locus ↓ Loss of heterozygosity
pearl: Loss of heterozygosity is detected by comparing tumour and normal DNA at polymorphic markers, and recurrent regions of loss helped locate tumour suppressor genes such as RB1.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Pathology: oncology & haematology: gene amplification
stem: A carcinoma demonstrates many additional copies of a gene encoding a growth-promoting receptor. Which molecular abnormality is present?
why_correct: Gene amplification is an increase in the copy number of a particular gene. Amplification of oncogenes can increase production of growth-promoting proteins.

why_others_wrong.B: Loss of heterozygosity is loss of the remaining normal allele, typically inactivating a tumour suppressor, not an increase in gene copies.
why_others_wrong.C: A frameshift deletion alters the reading frame of a gene and usually causes loss of function, not multiple extra copies of a gene.
why_others_wrong.D: Nondisjunction is failure of chromosome separation causing whole-chromosome aneuploidy, not selective multiple copies of a single gene.
why_others_wrong.E: Mitochondrial inheritance is maternal transmission of mitochondrial DNA and does not describe extra copies of a nuclear receptor gene.

exam_trap: Amplification is a copy-number abnormality, not simply increased transcription from a single gene.
takeaway: More copies of an oncogene → gene amplification → potentially increased oncogenic signalling.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Many extra copies of a growth-receptor gene ↓ copy-number increase of one gene ↓ overexpression of the oncogene product ↓ Gene amplification
pearl: HER2 amplification is tested by immunohistochemistry and in situ hybridisation in breast and gastric cancers because it predicts benefit from trastuzumab.

subject: Genetics
title: Genetics: frameshift mutation
stem: A deletion of two nucleotides occurs within a protein-coding gene. What is the most likely consequence?

options.A: No change because two is an even number
options.B: Frameshift altering the downstream reading frame

correct_answer: B. Frameshift altering the downstream reading frame
why_correct: Insertions or deletions that are not multiples of three alter the reading frame of the coding sequence. A two-nucleotide deletion therefore produces a frameshift and may generate a premature stop codon.

why_others_wrong.A: Reading-frame preservation depends on multiples of three, not even numbers, so losing two nucleotides shifts every downstream codon.
why_others_wrong.C: A single amino-acid substitution follows a missense point change; a two-nucleotide deletion shifts the frame and alters all downstream codons.
why_others_wrong.D: Gene amplification is an increase in copies of a gene or region, not the result of deleting two nucleotides within a coding sequence.
why_others_wrong.E: Chromosomal nondisjunction is failed chromosome separation causing aneuploidy, unrelated to a small deletion within one gene.

exam_trap: Option A is chosen by candidates who think even numbers keep the frame; only deletions in multiples of three preserve the downstream reading frame.
takeaway: 1–2–4–5 nucleotide insertion/deletion → frameshift; multiples of 3 preserve the reading frame.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Deletion of two nucleotides in a coding sequence ↓ not a multiple of three ↓ downstream reading frame shifted ↓ Frameshift altering the downstream reading frame
pearl: Frameshift mutations often create a premature stop codon, leading to nonsense-mediated mRNA decay and loss of protein; many APC and BRCA mutations are of this type.

subject: Genetics
title: Genetics: nonsense mutation
stem: A point mutation converts a codon encoding an amino acid into a premature stop codon. What type of mutation is this?
why_correct: A nonsense mutation introduces a premature termination codon, potentially producing a truncated and non-functional protein.

why_others_wrong.A: A missense mutation changes a codon to one encoding a different amino acid, rather than creating a premature stop codon.
why_others_wrong.C: A silent mutation changes a codon without altering the encoded amino acid, so it produces neither a stop codon nor a truncated protein.
why_others_wrong.D: A frameshift arises from insertion or deletion of bases not in multiples of three, whereas this is a single substitution creating a stop codon.
why_others_wrong.E: A splice-site mutation disrupts intron-exon boundary recognition during pre-mRNA processing, not direct conversion of a codon to a stop codon.

exam_trap: Missense is the usual wrong choice; it changes one amino acid for another, whereas a codon converted to a stop signal is a nonsense mutation.
takeaway: Nonsense = premature stop codon → truncated protein.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Point mutation ↓ amino-acid codon converted to a stop codon ↓ premature termination of translation ↓ Nonsense
pearl: Most nonsense and frameshift mutations in APC lead to a truncated protein, which is why protein truncation was historically used as a screening test in FAP.

subject: Genetics
title: Genetics: splice-site mutation
stem: A mutation occurs at an intron-exon boundary and causes abnormal removal of an intron. Which process has been directly disrupted?
why_correct: Splice-site mutations can interfere with recognition of intron-exon boundaries during pre-mRNA processing, resulting in abnormal mature mRNA.

why_others_wrong.A: DNA replication copies the whole genome before division and does not involve intron removal, which occurs during pre-mRNA processing.
why_others_wrong.C: Protein phosphorylation is a post-translational modification by kinases and cannot explain abnormal removal of an intron from pre-mRNA.
why_others_wrong.D: Translation initiation begins protein synthesis at the start codon on mature mRNA, after introns have already been removed by splicing.
why_others_wrong.E: DNA methylation is an epigenetic mark controlling transcription and does not directly govern intron removal at intron-exon boundaries.

exam_trap: Translation initiation is chosen by candidates who equate all protein defects with translation, but introns are removed during splicing before translation begins.
takeaway: Intron-exon boundary mutation → abnormal pre-mRNA splicing.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Mutation at an intron-exon boundary ↓ boundary recognised during pre-mRNA processing ↓ abnormal intron removal ↓ RNA splicing
pearl: Splice-site mutations can cause exon skipping or intron retention, and some beta-thalassaemias result from such mutations in the beta-globin gene.

subject: Immunology
title: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing: type ii hypersensitivity
stem: A patient develops autoimmune haemolytic anaemia due to antibodies directed against antigens on the patient's red blood cells. Which hypersensitivity mechanism is involved?
why_correct: Type II hypersensitivity involves antibodies directed against fixed cell-surface or extracellular-matrix antigens. In autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, antibodies bind red-cell antigens and promote destruction through mechanisms including complement and Fc-receptor-mediated phagocytosis.

why_others_wrong.A: Type I hypersensitivity is an immediate IgE-mediated mast-cell reaction to allergens, not antibody destruction of red cells.
why_others_wrong.C: Type III hypersensitivity is caused by circulating immune complexes depositing in tissues, whereas here antibody binds antigen fixed on red cells.
why_others_wrong.D: Type IV hypersensitivity is a delayed T-cell-mediated reaction and does not involve antibodies binding red-cell antigens.
why_others_wrong.E: Stimulatory anti-receptor antibody reactions, sometimes called type V, are usually grouped within type II, and haemolysis from red-cell antibodies is the classic type II example.

exam_trap: Type III is the common slip because antibody is involved, but immune complexes circulate and deposit; antibody binding antigen fixed on red cells is type II.
takeaway: Type II = antibody against a fixed target.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia ↓ antibody binds antigens fixed on red cells ↓ complement and Fc-receptor phagocytosis destroy them ↓ Type II
pearl: A positive direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test confirms antibody or complement bound to red cells, supporting an immune haemolytic process.

subject: Immunology
title: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing: type iii hypersensitivity
stem: A patient develops tissue injury because circulating antigen-antibody complexes deposit in small vessels and activate complement. Which hypersensitivity mechanism is responsible?
why_correct: Type III hypersensitivity results from deposition of circulating immune complexes, followed by complement activation and inflammatory injury.

why_others_wrong.A: Type I hypersensitivity is an immediate IgE-mediated mast-cell reaction, not injury from immune complexes depositing in vessels.
why_others_wrong.B: Type II hypersensitivity involves antibody binding antigen fixed on cells or matrix, rather than circulating complexes that lodge in small vessels.
why_others_wrong.D: Type IV hypersensitivity is a delayed reaction mediated by T cells and does not depend on antigen-antibody complexes or complement.
why_others_wrong.E: An immediate IgE-mediated reaction is type I hypersensitivity, driven by mast-cell degranulation rather than immune-complex deposition.

exam_trap: Type II is the closest distractor, but it involves antibody binding fixed cell or matrix antigen; complexes forming in the circulation and lodging in vessels define type III.
takeaway: Type III = immune-complex deposition → complement activation → inflammation.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Circulating antigen-antibody complexes ↓ deposit in small vessels ↓ activate complement and recruit neutrophils ↓ Type III
pearl: Low serum C3 and C4 in a patient with vasculitis or nephritis suggest complement consumption by immune complexes, as in active lupus.

subject: Immunology
title: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing: type iv hypersensitivity
stem: A patient develops an eczematous rash 48 hours after contact with a sensitising chemical. Which mechanism is most likely?
why_correct: Contact dermatitis is a classic delayed type IV hypersensitivity reaction. Sensitised T lymphocytes recognise antigen and release cytokines and/or directly damage target cells.

why_others_wrong.A: IgE-mediated mast-cell activation causes immediate urticaria or anaphylaxis within minutes, not an eczematous rash appearing after 48 hours.
why_others_wrong.B: Immune-complex deposition is type III hypersensitivity, typically producing vasculitis or serum sickness rather than delayed contact eczema.
why_others_wrong.D: Antibody-mediated complement lysis is a type II mechanism targeting cells such as red cells, not a delayed reaction to a skin sensitiser.
why_others_wrong.E: Neutrophil deficiency predisposes to bacterial and fungal infection and does not cause an eczematous reaction to a sensitising chemical.

exam_trap: IgE-mediated mast-cell activation is chosen by candidates who equate all allergy with IgE, but IgE reactions occur within minutes; delayed eczema is T-cell mediated.
takeaway: Delayed contact reaction → type IV → T-cell mediated.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Eczematous rash 48 hours after contact ↓ sensitising chemical (hapten) ↓ delayed-type, contact dermatitis ↓ sensitised T cells release cytokines ↓ T-cell-mediated inflammation
pearl: Allergic contact dermatitis to dressings, adhesives or nickel is confirmed by patch testing read at about 48 and 96 hours.

subject: Immunology
title: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing: immunodeficiency and opportunistic infection
stem: A patient with profound T-cell deficiency develops recurrent opportunistic infections, including viral and fungal infections. Which immune function is most directly compromised?
why_correct: T lymphocytes are central to cell-mediated immunity. Severe T-cell deficiency impairs immune responses against intracellular pathogens and also affects coordination of other immune cells.

why_others_wrong.A: Platelet activation is part of haemostasis and is not the immune function lost in T-cell deficiency with opportunistic infection.
why_others_wrong.C: Red-cell oxygen carriage depends on haemoglobin and is unrelated to T-cell function or susceptibility to viral and fungal infection.
why_others_wrong.D: Coagulation is a haemostatic process, and a T-cell deficiency does not directly compromise it or explain opportunistic infections.
why_others_wrong.E: Neutrophil production occurs in the bone marrow largely independently of T cells, and neutropenia gives a different infection pattern from T-cell deficiency.

exam_trap: Neutrophil production only tempts because neutropenia also causes infection, but it gives bacterial and fungal sepsis; recurrent viral and opportunistic infections with T-cell loss reflect failed cell-mediated immunity.
takeaway: Severe T-cell deficiency → profound impairment of cell-mediated immunity and susceptibility to opportunistic infection.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Profound T-cell deficiency ↓ recurrent viral and fungal opportunistic infections ↓ intracellular pathogens are controlled by T cells ↓ Cell-mediated immunity
pearl: Transplant recipients and patients with advanced HIV need prophylaxis against opportunistic infections such as Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, usually with co-trimoxazole.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing: systemic inflammatory response
stem: A patient develops severe systemic inflammation with widespread vasodilatation and increased vascular permeability. Which mediator is particularly important in producing endothelial activation and systemic inflammatory effects?
why_correct: Tumour necrosis factor (TNF) is a major pro-inflammatory cytokine. In severe systemic inflammation, TNF contributes to endothelial activation, fever, increased vascular permeability and systemic haemodynamic effects.

why_others_wrong.B: Albumin is a plasma protein whose levels fall during inflammation; it is not a mediator that activates endothelium.
why_others_wrong.C: Erythropoietin stimulates erythropoiesis and is unrelated to systemic inflammatory endothelial activation.
why_others_wrong.D: Insulin is a metabolic hormone regulating glucose uptake, not a pro-inflammatory cytokine.
why_others_wrong.E: Calcitonin regulates calcium homeostasis and is unrelated to systemic inflammatory signalling.

exam_trap: Candidates may be distracted by albumin (B), which falls in sepsis and leaks from vessels, but the mediator activating endothelium is the cytokine TNF.
takeaway: TNF = major systemic pro-inflammatory cytokine → endothelial activation + fever + inflammatory haemodynamic effects.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Severe systemic inflammation ↓ macrophage-derived cytokines ↓ TNF activates endothelium, causes fever and vasodilatation ↓ TNF
pearl: TNF, IL-1 and IL-6 are the main mediators of the systemic inflammatory response, and IL-6 drives hepatic production of acute-phase proteins such as CRP.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: coronary artery embryology
stem: The primitive coronary vascular plexus normally establishes connections with the aortic sinuses during development. Which vessels provide the main arterial supply to the adult myocardium?
why_correct: The definitive coronary arteries develop from vascular structures associated with the developing heart and establish connections with the aortic sinuses. They provide the principal arterial supply to the adult myocardium.

why_others_wrong.A: The pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood to the lungs and do not supply the myocardium.
why_others_wrong.C: Internal thoracic arteries supply the anterior chest wall and are used as bypass grafts, but are not the native myocardial supply.
why_others_wrong.D: Bronchial arteries supply lung and bronchial tissue, not heart muscle.
why_others_wrong.E: The superior vena cava is a vein returning blood to the right atrium and supplies no arterial blood.

exam_trap: Do not confuse coronary arterial supply with the collateral contribution that may arise from extracardiac arteries.
takeaway: Adult myocardium receives its principal arterial supply from the coronary arteries arising from the aortic root.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: coronary dominance
stem: During coronary angiography, the posterior descending artery is found to arise from the right coronary artery. How is this circulation classified?
why_correct: Coronary dominance is defined by the artery giving rise to the posterior descending artery. In most people this is the right coronary artery, making the circulation right dominant.

why_others_wrong.A: Left dominance means the posterior descending artery arises from the circumflex branch of the left coronary artery.
why_others_wrong.C: Codominance means the posterior inferior septum is supplied by both the right coronary and the circumflex, not by the right alone.
why_others_wrong.D: Non-dominant is not a recognised category; every heart is classed as right dominant, left dominant or codominant.
why_others_wrong.E: Pulmonary dominant is not a coronary classification; the pulmonary arteries do not supply the myocardium.

exam_trap: Dominance is defined by the origin of the posterior descending artery, not simply by which coronary artery is larger.
takeaway: PDA from RCA → right-dominant circulation.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed.
thinking: Posterior descending artery origin defines dominance ↓ here the PDA comes from the right coronary artery ↓ this is the most common pattern ↓ Right dominant
pearl: In right-dominant hearts the RCA usually also supplies the AV node, which is why inferior myocardial infarction is often accompanied by bradycardia and heart block.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Cardiorespiratory physiology: cardiac conduction
stem: A patient develops complete atrioventricular block. Which structure normally provides the only major electrical connection between the atria and ventricles?
why_correct: The fibrous skeleton electrically separates atrial from ventricular myocardium. The normal conducting pathway through the AV node and His bundle provides the principal electrical connection between the two chambers.

why_others_wrong.A: The sinoatrial node generates the cardiac impulse as the pacemaker but is not the structure that electrically connects the atria to the ventricles.
why_others_wrong.C: Purkinje fibres form the terminal ventricular conduction network and depend on prior conduction through the AV node and His bundle; they do not by themselves span the atrioventricular junction.
why_others_wrong.D: The bundle branches lie distal to the His bundle within the ventricular septum and are not the structure providing the atrioventricular electrical connection itself.
why_others_wrong.E: The coronary sinus is a venous structure that drains cardiac veins into the right atrium and plays no role in atrioventricular electrical conduction.

exam_trap: The AV node delays conduction, but the electrically continuous pathway continues through the His bundle into the bundle branches.
takeaway: Atrial-to-ventricular electrical continuity normally occurs through the AV node–His pathway.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Complete heart block = atrial impulses fail to reach the ventricles ↓ the fibrous skeleton electrically insulates atrial from ventricular myocardium ↓ the only normal conducting route through it is the AV node and penetrating His bundle ↓ Atrioventricular node/His bundle pathway
pearl: The His bundle runs close to the membranous septum and the aortic and tricuspid valve annuli, so heart block is a recognised complication of aortic valve replacement (including TAVI) and VSD repair, sometimes requiring permanent pacing.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Cardiorespiratory physiology: pericardial sinuses
stem: During cardiac surgery, the surgeon passes a finger posterior to the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk. Which pericardial space is being entered?
why_correct: The transverse pericardial sinus lies posterior to the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk, anterior to the superior vena cava and superior to the atria. It is clinically relevant during cardiac surgery because a clamp or ligature can be passed through it around the arterial outflow vessels.

why_others_wrong.A: The costodiaphragmatic recess is a pleural space between costal and diaphragmatic pleura, not a pericardial space, and is unrelated to the great vessels.
why_others_wrong.C: The oblique pericardial sinus lies behind the left atrium, bounded by the pulmonary veins and inferior vena cava, not behind the aorta and pulmonary trunk.
why_others_wrong.D: The pleural cavity is a separate serous cavity surrounding each lung and has no direct relationship to the pericardial space behind the great arteries.
why_others_wrong.E: The coronary sinus is a venous channel running in the atrioventricular groove and is unrelated to this pericardial recess around the arterial outflow tracts.

exam_trap: Candidates pick the oblique sinus because both are pericardial recesses, but the oblique sinus lies behind the left atrium among the pulmonary veins, not behind the great arteries.
takeaway: Transverse pericardial sinus → posterior to ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed.
thinking: Finger passed behind the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk ↓ space within the serous pericardium between the arterial and venous reflections ↓ lies anterior to the SVC and superior to the atria ↓ Transverse pericardial sinus
pearl: In cardiac surgery a ligature or clamp is passed through the transverse sinus to encircle the aorta and pulmonary trunk together, for example when establishing cardiopulmonary bypass.

subject: Anatomy
title: Physiology: oblique pericardial sinus
stem: A surgeon explores the pericardial space posterior to the left atrium. Which structure is most closely associated with this recess?
why_correct: The oblique pericardial sinus is a blind recess posterior to the left atrium, formed by reflections of serous pericardium around the pulmonary veins and inferior vena cava.

why_others_wrong.B: The transverse pericardial sinus lies behind the aorta and pulmonary trunk and in front of the superior vena cava and atria, superior to the oblique sinus.
why_others_wrong.C: The costophrenic recess is a pleural, not pericardial, space and is unrelated to this location.
why_others_wrong.D: The lesser sac is a peritoneal space in the abdomen, structurally and anatomically distinct from the pericardium.
why_others_wrong.E: The greater omentum is an abdominal peritoneal fold and has no relationship to pericardial anatomy.

exam_trap: Transverse pericardial sinus is chosen because it is the more familiar surgical sinus, but it lies behind the great arteries, superior to the oblique sinus.
takeaway: Oblique sinus = blind pericardial recess behind the left atrium.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed.
thinking: Pericardial recess behind the left atrium ↓ bounded by serous pericardial reflections around the pulmonary veins and IVC ↓ forms a blind-ended pocket ↓ Oblique pericardial sinus
pearl: The transverse sinus, not the oblique sinus, is used in cardiac surgery to pass a clamp or ligature behind the aorta and pulmonary trunk.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: mediastinal relationship
stem: A mediastinal mass is found immediately posterior to the heart and anterior to the vertebral column. Which compartment is involved?
why_correct: The posterior mediastinum lies posterior to the pericardium and anterior to the vertebral bodies. Important structures include the descending thoracic aorta, oesophagus, thoracic duct and azygos system.

why_others_wrong.A: The anterior mediastinum lies between the sternum and the pericardium, anterior to the heart.
why_others_wrong.B: The middle mediastinum contains the heart and pericardium themselves rather than the space behind them.
why_others_wrong.D: The pleural cavities lie lateral to the mediastinum around the lungs, not between heart and vertebrae.
why_others_wrong.E: The pericardial cavity is the potential space around the heart within the middle mediastinum, not behind it.

exam_trap: Middle mediastinum is chosen because the mass abuts the heart, but the middle compartment contains the heart and pericardium themselves, not the space behind them.
takeaway: Posterior mediastinum → oesophagus + descending thoracic aorta + thoracic duct + azygos system.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed.
thinking: Mass behind the heart ↓ anterior to the vertebral bodies ↓ below the plane of the sternal angle ↓ Posterior mediastinum
pearl: Posterior mediastinal masses are most often neurogenic tumours arising from the sympathetic chain or nerve roots, so MRI is used to look for extension into the spinal canal.

subject: Anatomy
title: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care: thoracic aorta
stem: A thoracic aortic aneurysm is located posterior to the left main bronchus and oesophagus. Which major vessel is involved?
why_correct: The descending thoracic aorta lies in the posterior mediastinum, initially to the left of the vertebral bodies, and has important relationships with the oesophagus and thoracic duct.

why_others_wrong.A: The ascending aorta lies anteriorly within the pericardial sac, not posterior to the left main bronchus and oesophagus.
why_others_wrong.B: The aortic arch lies superiorly, arching over the left main bronchus, rather than sitting posterior to it.
why_others_wrong.D: The pulmonary trunk lies anterior to the aorta in the middle mediastinum, not posterior to the bronchus and oesophagus.
why_others_wrong.E: The superior vena cava lies in the right side of the superior mediastinum and has no relationship to this posterior location.

exam_trap: Aortic arch only is chosen because the arch is closely related to the left main bronchus, but it arches over the bronchus rather than lying behind it.
takeaway: Descending thoracic aorta = posterior mediastinum.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed.
thinking: Aneurysm behind the left main bronchus and oesophagus ↓ lies in the posterior mediastinum ↓ the arch passes over the left main bronchus and continues downward ↓ Descending thoracic aorta
pearl: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the arch beside the ligamentum arteriosum, so aneurysms of the distal arch can present with hoarseness.

subject: Anatomy
title: Physiology: oesophageal blood supply
stem: A patient undergoes oesophagectomy. Which statement best describes the arterial supply of the thoracic oesophagus?

options.A: It is supplied exclusively by the coeliac trunk
options.B: It receives segmental branches from thoracic vessels
options.C: It is supplied exclusively by the inferior mesenteric artery
options.E: It is supplied exclusively by the superior mesenteric artery

correct_answer: B. It receives segmental branches from thoracic vessels
why_correct: The oesophagus has a segmental arterial supply. Thoracic portions receive branches including oesophageal branches of the thoracic aorta and bronchial arteries, while abdominal portions receive branches associated with the left gastric and inferior phrenic arteries.

why_others_wrong.A: The coeliac trunk supplies only the abdominal (not thoracic) oesophagus, so exclusive coeliac supply is incorrect.
why_others_wrong.C: The inferior mesenteric artery supplies hindgut structures far removed from the oesophagus and plays no role in its supply.
why_others_wrong.D: The oesophagus has a well-recognised segmental anastomotic arterial supply, contradicting the claim of no anastomoses.
why_others_wrong.E: The superior mesenteric artery supplies midgut structures and has no direct branches to the oesophagus.

exam_trap: Option A is chosen because the abdominal oesophagus gets left gastric branches from the coeliac trunk, but the thoracic segment depends on aortic and bronchial branches.
takeaway: Oesophageal arterial supply is segmental and anastomotic.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed.
thinking: Thoracic oesophagus ↓ supplied segmentally by nearby vessels ↓ oesophageal branches of the thoracic aorta and bronchial arteries ↓ the abdominal part receives left gastric and inferior phrenic branches ↓ It receives segmental branches from thoracic vessels
pearl: After oesophagectomy the gastric conduit relies on the right gastro-omental arcade, so its tip near the anastomosis is the least well perfused part and the usual site of leak or necrosis.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Pathology: oncology & haematology: lymphatic drainage of oesophagus
stem: A carcinoma is located in the lower thoracic oesophagus. Which lymphatic feature helps explain why oesophageal malignancy may spread over a considerable vertical distance?

options.D: Lymphatic drainage exclusively to axillary nodes
options.E: Direct drainage only to the liver

why_correct: The oesophagus contains longitudinal lymphatic channels in the submucosa. These can permit longitudinal tumour spread and contribute to the phenomenon of skip metastases.

why_others_wrong.A: The oesophagus has a rich submucosal lymphatic network, and it is this network that allows cancer to spread widely.
why_others_wrong.C: Oesophageal lymphatics lie mainly in the submucosa rather than being confined to the muscularis, and it is submucosal channels that permit longitudinal spread.
why_others_wrong.D: Oesophageal lymph drains to cervical, mediastinal and coeliac nodes, not to axillary nodes, which drain the upper limb and breast.
why_others_wrong.E: Lower oesophageal lymph drains to left gastric and coeliac nodes; the liver is a site of haematogenous rather than direct lymphatic spread.

exam_trap: Lymphatics confined to the muscularis tempts candidates reasoning from wall layers, but the key longitudinal channels lie in the submucosa and allow skip metastases.
takeaway: Longitudinal submucosal lymphatics → potentially extensive vertical spread of oesophageal cancer.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed.; Principles and Practice of Surgery, 7th ed.
thinking: Lower thoracic oesophageal carcinoma ↓ spread over a long vertical distance ↓ submucosal lymphatics run longitudinally ↓ allows skip lesions and distant nodal spread ↓ Longitudinal submucosal lymphatic channels
pearl: The oesophagus also lacks a serosa, permitting early spread into adjacent structures; together these features explain why oesophagectomy needs generous longitudinal margins and why nodal disease is common at presentation.

subject: Anatomy
title: Acute abdomen & GI surgery: retroperitoneal vessels
stem: During surgery, the surgeon identifies the left renal vein passing anterior to the abdominal aorta. Which additional structure does the left renal vein normally pass posterior to?
why_correct: The left renal vein crosses anterior to the aorta and posterior to the superior mesenteric artery. Compression between these structures can contribute to nutcracker syndrome.

why_others_wrong.B: The inferior mesenteric artery arises at about L3, below the left renal vein, so it does not cross anterior to the vein as it passes over the aorta.
why_others_wrong.C: The coeliac trunk arises above the level of the left renal vein and is not the vessel compressing it in this relationship.
why_others_wrong.D: The common hepatic artery is a branch of the coeliac trunk and is not the structure the left renal vein passes posterior to.
why_others_wrong.E: The splenic artery runs along the superior border of the pancreas toward the spleen, not across the aorta posterior to the left renal vein.

exam_trap: Inferior mesenteric artery is chosen because it is also an anterior aortic branch, but it arises lower, at about L3, below where the left renal vein crosses.
takeaway: SMA → anterior; aorta → posterior; left renal vein passes between them.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed.
thinking: Left renal vein crosses anterior to the aorta ↓ it runs in the angle just below the SMA origin ↓ so it lies posterior to the SMA ↓ Superior mesenteric artery
pearl: Because the left renal vein receives the left gonadal and adrenal veins, nutcracker compression can present with haematuria, flank pain and a left varicocele.

subject: Anatomy
title: Physiology: renal segmental arteries
stem: A surgeon plans a partial nephrectomy. Why can renal segments often be surgically separated according to their arterial supply?

options.B: Segmental renal arteries are functionally end arteries
options.C: Each kidney receives only one venous segment
options.D: Intrarenal veins have no anastomoses between segments
options.E: The renal artery supplies only the renal capsule

correct_answer: B. Segmental renal arteries are functionally end arteries
why_correct: Renal arterial branches divide into segmental arteries that are essentially end arteries, producing relatively discrete vascular territories. This anatomical arrangement supports renal-sparing segmental surgery.

why_others_wrong.A: Renal arteries do branch, dividing into anterior and posterior divisions and then segmental arteries; they are not without branches.
why_others_wrong.C: Having a single venous segment is not the anatomical basis for segmental surgical separation, which depends on end-arterial territories rather than venous drainage.
why_others_wrong.D: Intrarenal veins anastomose freely between segments; segmental surgery relies on the arterial, not the venous, arrangement.
why_others_wrong.E: The renal artery supplies the entire renal parenchyma via its segmental branches, not merely the capsule.

exam_trap: Option D is chosen by assuming the veins define segments too, but intrarenal veins anastomose freely; segmental separation depends on the end-arterial pattern of supply.
takeaway: Renal segmental arteries behave as end arteries → useful basis for partial nephrectomy.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed.
thinking: Partial nephrectomy along segmental territories ↓ the renal artery divides into anterior and posterior divisions and then segmental arteries ↓ segmental arteries do not anastomose, so each supplies a discrete territory ↓ intrarenal veins anastomose freely and do not define segments ↓ Segmental renal arteries are functionally end arteries
pearl: Because segmental arteries are end arteries, dividing an accessory or segmental artery causes infarction of its territory, whereas a segmental vein can usually be divided safely because intrarenal veins anastomose.

subject: Anatomy
title: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care: adrenal blood supply
stem: A patient undergoes adrenal surgery. Which statement best describes the arterial supply of the adrenal gland?

options.A: Single artery from the renal artery
options.B: Superior, middle and inferior adrenal arteries
options.C: Exclusively from the inferior mesenteric artery
options.E: Supplied only by the abdominal aorta

correct_answer: B. Superior, middle and inferior adrenal arteries
why_correct: The adrenal glands have a rich arterial supply from superior adrenal arteries, middle adrenal arteries and inferior adrenal arteries. The middle adrenal arteries arise from the abdominal aorta, while superior and inferior branches arise from other nearby arterial sources.

why_others_wrong.A: A single renal-artery branch understates the adrenal supply, which is characteristically rich and derives from several separate sources, not one renal branch alone.
why_others_wrong.C: The inferior mesenteric artery supplies hindgut structures and has no branch supplying the adrenal gland.
why_others_wrong.D: The coeliac trunk is not the sole source; adrenal supply instead comes from superior, middle and inferior adrenal arteries via different parent vessels.
why_others_wrong.E: Only the middle adrenal artery arises directly from the aorta; the superior and inferior adrenal arteries arise from the inferior phrenic and renal arteries respectively, so supply is not from the aorta alone.

exam_trap: The adrenal gland is highly vascular; do not reduce its arterial supply to the renal artery alone.
takeaway: Adrenal arterial supply = superior + middle + inferior adrenal arteries.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed.
thinking: Adrenal arterial supply ↓ superior adrenal arteries from the inferior phrenic artery ↓ middle adrenal artery directly from the aorta ↓ inferior adrenal artery from the renal artery ↓ Superior, middle and inferior adrenal arteries
pearl: In adrenalectomy the many small arteries are easily sealed, whereas the single adrenal vein is the key structure to control early, especially on the right where it is short and enters the IVC.

subject: Anatomy
title: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care: adrenal venous drainage
stem: During right adrenalectomy, the surgeon must identify the short adrenal vein. Where does the right adrenal vein usually drain?
why_correct: The right adrenal vein is short and usually drains directly into the inferior vena cava. The left adrenal vein usually drains into the left renal vein, often after joining the inferior phrenic vein.

why_others_wrong.A: Drainage into the left renal vein describes the LEFT adrenal vein, not the right.
why_others_wrong.C: The portal vein has no role in adrenal venous drainage.
why_others_wrong.D: The splenic vein drains the spleen and pancreatic region and is unrelated to adrenal venous drainage.
why_others_wrong.E: The superior mesenteric vein drains gut structures and is unrelated to the adrenal gland.

exam_trap: Right adrenal vein → IVC directly; left adrenal vein → usually left renal vein.
takeaway: Right adrenal vein is short and drains directly to the IVC.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed.
thinking: Right adrenalectomy with a short adrenal vein ↓ the right adrenal lies directly against the IVC ↓ its vein drains straight into the IVC ↓ Inferior vena cava
pearl: The short right adrenal vein can be torn from the IVC during dissection, causing troublesome haemorrhage, so it is identified and secured early in right adrenalectomy.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: pituitary portal system
stem: A hormone released from the hypothalamus must reach the anterior pituitary without first undergoing systemic dilution. Which vascular arrangement enables this?
why_correct: The hypothalamic-hypophyseal portal system carries hypothalamic releasing and inhibiting hormones directly to the anterior pituitary through a portal vascular network.

why_others_wrong.A: The coronary circulation supplies the myocardium and has no connection to the pituitary.
why_others_wrong.C: The hepatic portal system carries gut blood to the liver, not hypothalamic hormones to the pituitary.
why_others_wrong.D: The pulmonary circulation carries blood through the lungs and would expose hormones to systemic dilution.
why_others_wrong.E: The azygos system drains the posterior thoracic wall into the superior vena cava and has no role in pituitary signalling.

exam_trap: Hepatic portal system is chosen because it is the best-known portal system, but it links gut and liver capillary beds, not the hypothalamus and pituitary.
takeaway: Hypothalamic releasing hormones → hypophyseal portal vessels → anterior pituitary.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Hypothalamic hormone must reach the anterior pituitary undiluted ↓ capillaries in the median eminence collect releasing hormones ↓ portal veins carry them to a second capillary bed in the anterior pituitary ↓ Hypophyseal portal system
pearl: Pituitary stalk compression interrupts dopamine delivery through the portal vessels, so prolactin rises modestly while other anterior pituitary hormones tend to fall.

subject: Pharmacology
title: Pharmacology: adh receptor
stem: A patient with central diabetes insipidus receives desmopressin. Which renal receptor is primarily targeted by its antidiuretic effect?

options.A: V1 receptor on vascular smooth muscle
options.B: V2 receptor on collecting-duct principal cells

correct_answer: B. V2 receptor on collecting-duct principal cells
why_correct: ADH acts on V2 receptors on renal collecting-duct principal cells. V2 activation increases cAMP and promotes aquaporin-2 insertion into the apical membrane, increasing water reabsorption.

why_others_wrong.A: V1 receptors mediate vasoconstriction on vascular smooth muscle, not the renal antidiuretic effect that desmopressin is given for.
why_others_wrong.C: M2 is a cardiac muscarinic receptor and is unrelated to ADH/desmopressin action on the kidney.
why_others_wrong.D: α1 mediates vascular smooth muscle contraction via Gq, not the renal water-reabsorption effect of desmopressin.
why_others_wrong.E: β1 mediates cardiac chronotropy and inotropy via Gs, and is unrelated to desmopressin's renal action.

exam_trap: V1 receptor on vascular smooth muscle tempts candidates who know vasopressin has two receptors, but V1 mediates vasoconstriction; desmopressin's antidiuretic effect is via renal V2 receptors.
takeaway: ADH → V2 → cAMP → aquaporin-2 → water reabsorption.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Central diabetes insipidus means ADH deficiency ↓ desmopressin is a synthetic ADH analogue with selective antidiuretic action ↓ the antidiuretic receptor is on collecting-duct principal cells ↓ V2 receptor on collecting-duct principal cells
pearl: Desmopressin has little V1 vasoconstrictor activity, unlike vasopressin; overtreatment can cause water retention and hyponatraemia, so sodium is monitored after pituitary surgery.

subject: Physiology
title: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care: pth receptor location
stem: On which renal tubular cells does parathyroid hormone act directly to increase calcium reabsorption?
why_correct: PTH increases calcium reabsorption in the distal nephron while reducing phosphate reabsorption predominantly in the proximal tubule. This distinction is important: PTH's renal actions occur at different nephron sites.

why_others_wrong.A: The proximal tubule is where PTH reduces phosphate reabsorption; its calcium-reabsorptive action is in the distal convoluted and connecting tubules.
why_others_wrong.C: Collecting-duct intercalated cells are primarily involved in acid-base handling, not the principal site of PTH-stimulated calcium reabsorption.
why_others_wrong.D: Podocytes are structural filtration barrier cells in the glomerulus with no role in tubular calcium reabsorption or PTH responsiveness.
why_others_wrong.E: Macula densa cells sense tubular NaCl for tubuloglomerular feedback and renin regulation; they are not the site of PTH-mediated calcium reabsorption.

exam_trap: PTH causes phosphate wasting through the proximal tubule but increases calcium reabsorption in the distal nephron.
takeaway: PTH → proximal tubule: ↓ phosphate reabsorption; distal nephron: ↑ calcium reabsorption.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: PTH increases renal calcium reabsorption ↓ acts on distal convoluted and connecting tubule cells ↓ the proximal tubule is where it reduces phosphate reabsorption ↓ Distal nephron tubular cells
pearl: Thiazide diuretics also increase distal calcium reabsorption, which is why they can unmask or worsen hypercalcaemia in primary hyperparathyroidism.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: vitamin d activation
stem: A patient has severe chronic kidney disease and develops impaired activation of vitamin D. Which renal enzyme normally performs the final activation step?
why_correct: The kidney converts 25-hydroxyvitamin D to active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol) through 1α-hydroxylase.

why_others_wrong.A: 11β-hydroxylase is involved in adrenal cortical steroidogenesis (cortisol and aldosterone pathways), not vitamin D activation.
why_others_wrong.C: Thyroid peroxidase catalyses iodination steps in thyroid hormone synthesis and has no role in vitamin D metabolism.
why_others_wrong.D: Aromatase converts androgens to oestrogens in gonadal and peripheral tissue, unrelated to vitamin D activation.
why_others_wrong.E: Carbonic anhydrase catalyses CO2/bicarbonate interconversion for acid-base handling and has no role in vitamin D activation.

exam_trap: The liver performs the 25-hydroxylation step; the kidney performs the important 1α-hydroxylation step.
takeaway: Liver → 25-OH vitamin D; kidney → 1,25-(OH)₂ vitamin D.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Vitamin D is activated in two steps ↓ liver performs 25-hydroxylation ↓ kidney performs 1-alpha-hydroxylation to calcitriol ↓ chronic kidney disease loses the renal step ↓ 1α-hydroxylase
pearl: Activated vitamin D analogues such as alfacalcidol bypass the failed renal step, which is why they are used to treat hypocalcaemia and secondary hyperparathyroidism in chronic kidney disease.

subject: Physiology
title: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care: calcitriol feedback
stem: A rise in circulating calcitriol produces which effect on parathyroid hormone secretion?
why_correct: Calcitriol contributes to negative regulation of PTH synthesis. This forms part of the calcium-phosphate-vitamin D feedback system.

why_others_wrong.A: This is the opposite effect; rising calcitriol suppresses, rather than stimulates, PTH synthesis and secretion.
why_others_wrong.C: Calcitriol has a well-established inhibitory endocrine effect on the parathyroid glands, so it is incorrect to say it has no effect.
why_others_wrong.D: Calcitriol's principal endocrine feedback role concerns PTH regulation, not direct stimulation of aldosterone secretion.
why_others_wrong.E: Calcitriol does not act on the renin-angiotensin system in this way; its established feedback role is suppression of PTH, not stimulation of renin.

exam_trap: Vitamin D is not simply a calcium-raising hormone; it also participates in feedback control of PTH.
takeaway: Calcitriol ↑ → PTH synthesis suppressed.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Calcitriol acts on parathyroid vitamin D receptors ↓ suppresses PTH gene transcription ↓ completes the calcium-vitamin D-PTH feedback loop ↓ Suppresses PTH synthesis/secretion
pearl: This feedback is exploited in chronic kidney disease, where activated vitamin D analogues help suppress secondary hyperparathyroidism, with monitoring for hypercalcaemia.

subject: Physiology
title: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care: renin-angiotensin system
stem: A fall in renal perfusion activates renin release. Which substrate does renin act upon?
why_correct: Renin cleaves circulating angiotensinogen, produced by the liver, to form angiotensin I. ACE then converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II.

why_others_wrong.A: Angiotensin I is the product generated when renin cleaves angiotensinogen, not the substrate renin acts upon.
why_others_wrong.C: Angiotensin II is formed from angiotensin I by ACE, two steps downstream of renin's direct substrate.
why_others_wrong.D: Aldosterone is a downstream effector hormone released in response to angiotensin II, not a substrate for renin.
why_others_wrong.E: Renal kallikrein belongs to a separate enzymatic system and is not the substrate cleaved by renin.

exam_trap: Candidates choosing angiotensin I (A) confuse renin's product with its substrate; renin cleaves angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, which ACE then converts to angiotensin II.
takeaway: Renin: angiotensinogen → angiotensin I → ACE → angiotensin II.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Reduced renal perfusion releases renin ↓ renin is a protease ↓ it cleaves liver-derived angiotensinogen ↓ angiotensin I is produced ↓ Angiotensinogen
pearl: Direct renin inhibitors such as aliskiren block this first step, whereas ACE inhibitors act at the next step and also reduce bradykinin breakdown, causing cough and angioedema.

subject: Physiology
title: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care: angiotensin ii
stem: Which effect is directly associated with angiotensin II?
why_correct: Angiotensin II promotes vasoconstriction, stimulates aldosterone secretion, increases thirst and enhances sympathetic activity.

why_others_wrong.A: Angiotensin II is a potent vasoconstrictor, so it causes vasoconstriction, not systemic vasodilatation.
