why_others_wrong.B: This is the opposite effect; angiotensin II stimulates, rather than reduces, aldosterone secretion from the adrenal cortex.
why_others_wrong.D: Angiotensin II increases thirst by acting on hypothalamic centres, rather than reducing it.
why_others_wrong.E: Angiotensin II enhances, rather than reduces, sympathetic nervous system activity.

exam_trap: Candidates may choose systemic vasodilatation (A) or reduced aldosterone (B), but angiotensin II acts on AT1 receptors to constrict vessels and to stimulate aldosterone secretion from the zona glomerulosa.
takeaway: Angiotensin II → vasoconstriction + aldosterone + thirst + sympathetic facilitation.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Angiotensin II acts on AT1 receptors ↓ causes vasoconstriction ↓ stimulates zona glomerulosa aldosterone secretion ↓ also increases thirst and sympathetic activity ↓ Increased aldosterone secretion
pearl: Patients taking ACE inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers may develop marked hypotension after induction of anaesthesia because angiotensin II–mediated vasoconstriction is blunted.

subject: Physiology
title: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care: aldosterone escape
stem: A patient has persistently elevated aldosterone. Which mechanism helps prevent unlimited expansion of extracellular fluid volume despite continued mineralocorticoid activity?

options.B: Pressure natriuresis and increased renal sodium excretion

correct_answer: B. Pressure natriuresis and increased renal sodium excretion
why_correct: With sustained aldosterone excess, extracellular volume initially expands. Increased arterial pressure promotes renal sodium and water excretion, limiting further volume expansion. This phenomenon is part of aldosterone escape.

why_others_wrong.A: Sodium reabsorption does not stop completely; aldosterone escape reflects a balance where reabsorption continues but is matched by increased excretion, limiting further volume gain.
why_others_wrong.C: GFR is not permanently suppressed; escape occurs because raised renal perfusion pressure reduces tubular sodium reabsorption, increasing sodium excretion.
why_others_wrong.D: ADH mainly governs water handling rather than being the principal mechanism limiting sodium/volume expansion in aldosterone escape.
why_others_wrong.E: Potassium wasting characteristically continues despite aldosterone escape; only the sodium/volume retention effect is limited, not potassium excretion.

exam_trap: Aldosterone escape prevents indefinite sodium and water retention, but potassium wasting may continue.
takeaway: Persistent aldosterone → initial volume expansion → pressure natriuresis limits further volume gain.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Persistent aldosterone excess ↓ sodium retention expands extracellular volume ↓ arterial pressure and natriuretic peptides rise ↓ pressure natriuresis increases sodium excretion ↓ Pressure natriuresis and increased renal sodium excretion
pearl: Aldosterone escape explains why primary hyperaldosteronism usually presents with hypertension and hypokalaemia but without marked peripheral oedema.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Acid-Base: Winter'S Formula
stem: A patient has a metabolic acidosis with a bicarbonate concentration of 12 mmol/L. The measured PaCO₂ is 24 mmHg. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
why_correct: Expected PaCO₂ in metabolic acidosis can be estimated using Winter's formula: expected PaCO₂ ≈ 1.5 × HCO₃⁻ + 8 ± 2. For HCO₃⁻ 12: 1.5 × 12 + 8 = 26 mmHg, with an expected range of approximately 24–28 mmHg. The measured PaCO₂ of 24 mmHg is therefore appropriate compensation.

why_others_wrong.B: A concurrent respiratory acidosis would mean the measured PaCO2 exceeds the Winter's-predicted range; here 24 mmHg falls within the expected 24-28 mmHg range, so this is not present.
why_others_wrong.C: A concurrent respiratory alkalosis would mean the PaCO2 is lower than predicted by Winter's formula; 24 mmHg sits at the lower edge of, not below, the expected range.
why_others_wrong.D: A primary respiratory acidosis would present with an elevated PaCO2 driving the acid-base disturbance, which is inconsistent with the low bicarbonate and appropriately low PaCO2 seen here.
why_others_wrong.E: An acid-base disorder is clearly present, since the bicarbonate of 12 mmol/L reflects an underlying metabolic acidosis.

exam_trap: Do not simply say “the PaCO₂ is low, therefore respiratory alkalosis.” In metabolic acidosis, a low PaCO₂ is expected compensation.
takeaway: Winter's formula = 1.5 × HCO₃⁻ + 8 ± 2.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Low HCO3- of 12 mmol/L = metabolic acidosis ↓ Winter's formula: 1.5 × 12 + 8 = 26 ± 2 mmHg ↓ measured PaCO2 of 24 mmHg lies within the expected 24-28 mmHg ↓ Appropriate respiratory compensation
pearl: Winter's formula works in mmHg; when the gas is reported in kPa, convert by multiplying by 7.5 first, otherwise appropriate compensation can be misread as a mixed disorder.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Acid-Base: Mixed Disorder
stem: A patient has metabolic acidosis with HCO₃⁻ 10 mmol/L. Winter's expected PaCO₂ is approximately 23 ± 2 mmHg, but the measured PaCO₂ is 35 mmHg. What is the most likely interpretation?
why_correct: The measured PaCO₂ is substantially higher than expected for the degree of metabolic acidosis. This indicates inadequate ventilatory compensation and therefore an additional respiratory acidosis.

why_others_wrong.A: Appropriate compensation would require the measured PaCO2 to fall within the Winter's-predicted range of roughly 21-25 mmHg; the measured value of 35 mmHg is well above this, so compensation is inadequate, not appropriate.
why_others_wrong.C: An additional respiratory alkalosis would push PaCO2 below, not above, the expected compensatory range, which is the opposite of what is observed.
why_others_wrong.D: An isolated respiratory alkalosis would not coexist with a primary metabolic acidosis and does not explain why PaCO2 is higher than the compensated range predicts.
why_others_wrong.E: Metabolic alkalosis would be associated with a raised bicarbonate, not the low bicarbonate of 10 mmol/L given in the stem.

exam_trap: In metabolic acidosis, compare measured PaCO₂ with the expected compensatory value rather than interpreting it in isolation.
takeaway: PaCO₂ above Winter's expected range → additional respiratory acidosis.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: HCO3- of 10 mmol/L = metabolic acidosis ↓ expected PaCO2 by Winter's formula is about 21-25 mmHg ↓ measured PaCO2 of 35 mmHg is well above that range ↓ ventilation is failing to compensate ↓ Additional respiratory acidosis
pearl: A PaCO2 that fails to fall appropriately in severe metabolic acidosis, for example in sepsis or diabetic ketoacidosis, suggests respiratory fatigue or depressed drive and warns that ventilatory support may be needed.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Cardiorespiratory physiology: oxygen delivery
stem: A shocked patient has a cardiac output of 4 L/min and arterial oxygen content of 100 mL/L. What is the approximate oxygen delivery?
why_correct: Oxygen delivery: DO₂ = cardiac output × arterial oxygen content = 4 L/min × 100 mL/L = 400 mL/min.

why_others_wrong.A: 40 mL/min results from using oxygen content per decilitre (10 mL/dL) with cardiac output in litres, a tenfold units error.
why_others_wrong.B: 100 mL/min corresponds only to the oxygen content value itself and ignores the cardiac output multiplier required by the DO2 formula.
why_others_wrong.C: 200 mL/min would require a cardiac output of only 2 L/min; 4 L/min multiplied by 100 mL/L gives 400 mL/min.
why_others_wrong.E: 1000 mL/min is roughly normal resting oxygen delivery and would need a cardiac output of 10 L/min at this oxygen content.

exam_trap: Check the units: oxygen content is expressed per litre of blood, so multiply directly by cardiac output in L/min.
takeaway: DO₂ = CO × CaO₂.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: DO2 = cardiac output × arterial oxygen content ↓ content is already in mL/L and cardiac output in L/min ↓ 4 × 100 = 400 ↓ 400 mL/min
pearl: Normal resting oxygen delivery is roughly 1,000 mL/min, so 400 mL/min represents severely reduced delivery at which oxygen consumption is likely to become supply-dependent with a rising lactate.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Pathology: oncology & haematology: oxygen content
stem: A patient's haemoglobin is 70 g/L, arterial oxygen saturation is 100%, and PaO₂ is normal. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Arterial oxygen content is necessarily normal
options.B: Oxygen content is reduced because haemoglobin concentration is reduced

correct_answer: B. Oxygen content is reduced because haemoglobin concentration is reduced
why_correct: Most arterial oxygen is carried bound to haemoglobin. A low haemoglobin concentration therefore reduces arterial oxygen content even when oxygen saturation and PaO2 are normal. Approximate formula: CaO2 (mL/dL) = 1.34 x Hb (g/dL) x SaO2 + 0.0225 x PaO2 (kPa).

why_others_wrong.A: Arterial oxygen content is not necessarily normal here, since content depends heavily on haemoglobin concentration, which is markedly reduced in this patient.
why_others_wrong.C: The stem states PaO2 is normal; a low haemoglobin concentration does not drive PaO2 to zero, since PaO2 reflects dissolved oxygen tension, not haemoglobin-bound oxygen.
why_others_wrong.D: Oxygen saturation can still be measured normally by pulse oximetry regardless of haemoglobin concentration; anaemia does not prevent its measurement.
why_others_wrong.E: Oxygen delivery depends on both oxygen content and cardiac output; because reduced haemoglobin lowers content, delivery is not necessarily normal despite normal saturation.

exam_trap: Candidates choose 'arterial oxygen content is necessarily normal' because saturation and PaO2 are normal, but content depends mainly on haemoglobin concentration multiplied by saturation.
takeaway: Normal PaO₂/SpO₂ ≠ normal oxygen content when Hb is low.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Hb 70 g/L with SaO2 100% and normal PaO2 ↓ almost all arterial oxygen is carried bound to haemoglobin ↓ less haemoglobin means less bound oxygen per litre despite full saturation ↓ Oxygen content is reduced because haemoglobin concentration is reduced
pearl: Pulse oximetry reports saturation, not content, so a severely anaemic patient can read 100% while oxygen delivery is markedly reduced; raising haemoglobin increases content far more than extra inspired oxygen.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Cardiorespiratory physiology: starling forces
stem: A patient develops severe hypoalbuminaemia. Which change promotes movement of fluid from the intravascular compartment into the interstitial space?

options.E: Increased interstitial oncotic pressure with no other change

why_correct: Albumin is the major contributor to plasma colloid oncotic pressure. Severe hypoalbuminaemia reduces plasma oncotic pressure and favours movement of fluid into the interstitial compartment, contributing to oedema.

why_others_wrong.A: An increase in plasma oncotic pressure would draw fluid into, not out of, the vasculature, which is the opposite effect to what hypoalbuminaemia produces.
why_others_wrong.C: A reduction in capillary hydrostatic pressure would favour fluid reabsorption into the capillary, not filtration out of it, and is not the mechanism at play with low albumin.
why_others_wrong.D: Increased lymphatic drainage would help clear interstitial fluid and oppose, rather than promote, oedema formation.
why_others_wrong.E: An isolated rise in interstitial oncotic pressure with no other change is not the mechanism described; hypoalbuminaemia specifically lowers plasma (not interstitial) oncotic pressure.

exam_trap: Think of Starling forces as competing hydrostatic and oncotic pressures rather than simply “albumin holds water in.”
takeaway: ↓ plasma albumin → ↓ plasma oncotic pressure → ↑ tendency to interstitial oedema.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Severe hypoalbuminaemia ↓ albumin is the main contributor to plasma oncotic pressure ↓ the inward oncotic force at the capillary falls ↓ net filtration into the interstitium increases ↓ Reduced plasma oncotic pressure
pearl: Hypoalbuminaemic oedema occurs in nephrotic syndrome, cirrhosis and protein-losing states, and albumin infusion alone tends to give only transient benefit unless the cause of protein loss or poor synthesis is addressed.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: lymphatic return
stem: A patient develops lymphatic obstruction after extensive pelvic lymph-node dissection. Which substance is particularly likely to accumulate in the interstitial fluid?
why_correct: Lymphatics return excess interstitial fluid and proteins to the circulation. Lymphatic obstruction therefore causes accumulation of protein-rich interstitial fluid and chronic lymphoedema.

why_others_wrong.B: Oxygen diffuses freely through capillary walls and is consumed by tissues, so it does not rely on lymphatic removal.
why_others_wrong.C: Carbon dioxide is highly diffusible and is removed by capillary blood, not lymph.
why_others_wrong.D: Glucose is small and readily reabsorbed or used by cells; its clearance does not depend on lymphatics.
why_others_wrong.E: Sodium equilibrates freely across capillaries, so lymphatic obstruction does not cause selective sodium accumulation.

exam_trap: Sodium only is chosen because oedema is linked to salt retention, but sodium crosses capillaries freely; the lymph-dependent component that accumulates is protein.
takeaway: Lymphatic obstruction → protein-rich interstitial oedema.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Lymphatic obstruction after pelvic node dissection ↓ lymph returns filtered fluid and protein to the circulation ↓ gases and small solutes diffuse back into capillaries ↓ protein cannot, so it accumulates ↓ Protein
pearl: Protein-rich interstitial fluid promotes fibrosis and fat deposition, which is why chronic lymphoedema becomes non-pitting; management centres on compression and skin care to prevent cellulitis.

subject: Microbiology & surgical infection
title: Microbiology & surgical infection: fever
stem: A patient with bacterial infection develops a fever. Which mechanism best explains the raised body temperature?

options.A: Destruction of the hypothalamic temperature set point
options.B: Pyrogen-mediated upward resetting of the hypothalamic set point
options.D: Direct warming of the blood by bacteria

correct_answer: B. Pyrogen-mediated upward resetting of the hypothalamic set point
why_correct: Endogenous cytokines such as IL-1 and TNF can induce prostaglandin E₂ production in the hypothalamic thermoregulatory pathway, raising the set point. The body then responds with vasoconstriction and shivering until the new set point is reached.

why_others_wrong.A: In fever the hypothalamic set point is raised and actively regulated, not destroyed; loss of thermoregulation is not the mechanism.
why_others_wrong.C: Sweating is not permanently lost in fever; it is reduced while temperature rises and returns as the set point falls during defervescence.
why_others_wrong.D: Bacteria do not warm the blood directly; the rise in temperature results from host responses to pyrogenic cytokines.
why_others_wrong.E: Fever is driven by increased prostaglandin E2 synthesis, which is why NSAIDs that reduce prostaglandin production are antipyretic.

exam_trap: Reduced prostaglandin synthesis is the reversed distractor; fever needs increased PGE2, and reducing prostaglandin production is how antipyretics such as NSAIDs work.
takeaway: Fever = raised hypothalamic set point, commonly mediated through PGE₂.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.; Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Infection triggers IL-1, IL-6 and TNF release ↓ PGE2 is produced in the hypothalamus ↓ the thermoregulatory set point is raised ↓ vasoconstriction and shivering raise temperature to the new set point ↓ Pyrogen-mediated upward resetting of the hypothalamic set point
pearl: Paracetamol and NSAIDs lower fever by reducing prostaglandin synthesis, so regular antipyretics can mask fever as an early sign of postoperative complications such as anastomotic leak.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Perioperative medicine & nutrition: shivering
stem: A patient with postoperative hypothermia begins to shiver. What is the principal physiological purpose of shivering?

options.B: Increase heat production through involuntary muscle activity

correct_answer: B. Increase heat production through involuntary muscle activity
why_correct: Shivering consists of rapid involuntary skeletal-muscle contractions that increase metabolic heat production.

why_others_wrong.A: Shivering aims to conserve body temperature by generating heat, not to increase heat loss.
why_others_wrong.C: Shivering increases metabolic activity in skeletal muscle rather than reducing it.
why_others_wrong.D: Evaporative cooling through sweating is a response to heat, the opposite of the goal in a hypothermic patient.
why_others_wrong.E: Cold exposure and shivering are accompanied by increased, not reduced, sympathetic activity.

exam_trap: Option D tempts those who mix up thermoregulatory responses, but evaporative cooling is a heat-loss mechanism; shivering generates heat through muscle activity.
takeaway: Shivering = involuntary muscle activity → increased heat production.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Postoperative hypothermia ↓ hypothalamus triggers thermoregulatory responses ↓ involuntary rhythmic skeletal muscle contraction ↓ Increase heat production through involuntary muscle activity
pearl: Anaesthesia lowers the shivering and vasoconstriction thresholds, so patients cool during surgery and often shiver on emergence as thermoregulation resets.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Perioperative medicine & nutrition: surgical stress and metabolism
stem: Following major surgery, a patient develops hyperglycaemia despite no previous diabetes. Which physiological change contributes most directly?

options.D: Complete suppression of hepatic glucose production

why_correct: Major surgery activates the neuroendocrine stress response, increasing catecholamines, cortisol, glucagon and other mediators. This promotes hepatic glucose production and peripheral insulin resistance, contributing to postoperative hyperglycaemia.

why_others_wrong.A: Surgical stress reduces insulin sensitivity, so increased sensitivity would lower rather than raise blood glucose.
why_others_wrong.B: Counter-regulatory hormones such as cortisol, glucagon and catecholamines increase after surgery and drive hyperglycaemia.
why_others_wrong.D: Hepatic glucose production rises after major surgery, contributing to hyperglycaemia rather than being suppressed.
why_others_wrong.E: Peripheral glucose uptake is reduced by stress-mediated insulin resistance, which is why blood glucose rises.

exam_trap: Option B tempts candidates who expect hormonal shutdown after surgery, but counter-regulatory hormones increase and drive both insulin resistance and hepatic glucose output.
takeaway: Surgery → stress hormones ↑ → insulin resistance + hepatic glucose output ↑ → hyperglycaemia.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.; Principles and Practice of Surgery, 7th ed.
thinking: Postoperative hyperglycaemia without diabetes ↓ stress hormones rise after major surgery ↓ peripheral tissues become resistant to insulin ↓ Stress-mediated insulin resistance
pearl: Preoperative carbohydrate loading, minimally invasive surgery and good analgesia are used in enhanced recovery pathways to reduce postoperative insulin resistance.

subject: Anatomy
title: Physiology: medial lemniscus
stem: A patient has a lesion affecting the right medial lemniscus in the pons. Which deficit is most likely?

options.A: Loss of right-sided pain and temperature from the face
options.B: Loss of right-sided vibration and proprioception from the body
options.C: Loss of left-sided vibration and proprioception from the body
options.D: Loss of bilateral pain and temperature from the body
options.E: Ipsilateral lower motor neuron facial weakness

correct_answer: C. Loss of left-sided vibration and proprioception from the body
why_correct: The medial lemniscus carries fine touch, vibration and proprioception from the contralateral body after fibres have crossed in the medulla as internal arcuate fibres. Therefore, a right pontine medial lemniscus lesion produces loss of these modalities on the left side of the body.

why_others_wrong.A: Facial pain and temperature travel in the spinal trigeminal tract and crossed trigeminothalamic fibres, not the medial lemniscus, and a right-sided loss would not follow.
why_others_wrong.B: Dorsal column fibres have already decussated as internal arcuate fibres before entering the medial lemniscus, so a right-sided lemniscal lesion affects the left, not the right, side of the body.
why_others_wrong.D: The medial lemniscus carries vibration and proprioception, not pain and temperature (carried by the spinothalamic tract), and the lesion described is unilateral, not bilateral.
why_others_wrong.E: Ipsilateral lower motor neuron facial weakness implies a facial nerve or nucleus lesion, unrelated to the sensory medial lemniscus.

exam_trap: Do not confuse the dorsal columns themselves with the medial lemniscus. Dorsal-column fibres cross in the medulla; the medial lemniscus therefore carries contralateral body sensation.
takeaway: Dorsal columns → medulla crossing → medial lemniscus → contralateral fine touch/vibration/proprioception.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020); RCS England MRCS Part A framework, current 2026.
thinking: Right medial lemniscus lesion in the pons ↓ carries vibration, proprioception and fine touch ↓ dorsal column fibres already crossed as internal arcuate fibres in the medulla ↓ deficit is on the opposite side of the body ↓ Loss of left-sided vibration and proprioception from the body
pearl: Above the medulla the medial lemniscus and spinothalamic pathways run close together, so an upper brainstem lesion tends to cause contralateral loss of all body sensory modalities together.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: spinothalamic tract
stem: A lesion of the left anterolateral spinal cord at T8 damages the spinothalamic tract. Which finding is expected?

options.A: Loss of vibration on the left below T8
options.B: Loss of pain and temperature on the right below the lesion
options.C: Loss of proprioception on the right below the lesion
options.D: Bilateral loss of motor function below T8

correct_answer: B. Loss of pain and temperature on the right below the lesion
why_correct: Pain and temperature fibres enter the spinal cord, synapse and cross through the anterior white commissure before ascending in the contralateral spinothalamic tract. A left-sided lesion therefore affects pain and temperature from the right side of the body, usually beginning slightly below the anatomical lesion because of ascending/descending fibres near entry.

why_others_wrong.A: Vibration travels in the dorsal columns, which are posterior and not in the anterolateral cord.
why_others_wrong.C: Proprioception travels in the dorsal columns, which an anterolateral lesion spares, and dorsal column damage would give left-sided, not right-sided, loss.
why_others_wrong.D: A unilateral anterolateral lesion does not cause bilateral paralysis; that would need bilateral corticospinal involvement.
why_others_wrong.E: Facial sensation is carried by the trigeminal system, which is not affected by a thoracic cord lesion.

exam_trap: Option A is chosen by assuming all sensory loss is ipsilateral, but vibration travels in the dorsal columns, which an anterolateral lesion spares.
takeaway: The key anatomical event is spinal crossing of pain-temperature fibres.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020); Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed (2023).
thinking: Left anterolateral cord lesion at T8 ↓ the spinothalamic tract carries pain and temperature ↓ its fibres crossed in the anterior white commissure near their entry level ↓ loss is contralateral, starting slightly below the lesion ↓ Loss of pain and temperature on the right below the lesion
pearl: Anterolateral cordotomy exploits this anatomy, dividing the spinothalamic tract to relieve intractable unilateral cancer pain on the opposite side of the body.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: internal capsule
stem: A small infarct affects the posterior limb of the right internal capsule. Which combination is most likely?
correct_answer: B. Left facial and limb weakness
why_correct: The posterior limb of the internal capsule contains densely packed corticospinal and major sensory fibres. A lesion produces contralateral motor and often sensory deficits. A right-sided lesion therefore causes left-sided weakness, often affecting the face, arm and leg.

why_others_wrong.A: Right-sided weakness would follow a left capsular lesion, because corticospinal and corticobulbar fibres serve the opposite side.
why_others_wrong.C: Pure sensory stroke is typically thalamic; a posterior limb lesion characteristically involves the densely packed corticospinal fibres.
why_others_wrong.D: A unilateral capsular lesion affects the contralateral side only, not both lower limbs.
why_others_wrong.E: Capsular lesions produce contralateral deficits; ipsilateral cerebellar ataxia points to a lesion of the cerebellar hemisphere or its peduncles.

exam_trap: Right facial and limb weakness is chosen by forgetting that corticospinal and corticobulbar fibres cross below the internal capsule, so the deficit is contralateral.
takeaway: Internal capsule lesion = dense contralateral deficit.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020); Principles and Practice of Surgery, 7th ed (2023).
thinking: Right posterior limb of the internal capsule ↓ densely packed corticospinal fibres with corticobulbar fibres nearby ↓ these fibres cross below this level ↓ deficit affects the contralateral face, arm and leg ↓ Left facial and limb weakness
pearl: Capsular strokes cause an upper motor neurone facial weakness that spares the forehead, because the upper face receives bilateral cortical input.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: corticospinal decussation
stem: A patient develops weakness of the left hand following a lesion affecting the left lateral corticospinal tract in the cervical spinal cord. What explains the side of the weakness?

options.A: Corticospinal fibres cross at the optic chiasm
options.B: Corticospinal fibres cross in the midbrain
options.C: Most corticospinal fibres cross at the pyramidal decussation in the caudal medulla
options.D: Corticospinal fibres cross at the level of the spinal nerve root

correct_answer: C. Most corticospinal fibres cross at the pyramidal decussation in the caudal medulla
why_correct: Approximately 85–90% of corticospinal fibres decussate at the pyramidal decussation in the caudal medulla and then descend as the lateral corticospinal tract. Therefore, a left lateral corticospinal tract lesion in the spinal cord causes ipsilateral weakness below the lesion.

why_others_wrong.A: The optic chiasm is where nasal retinal fibres cross; it carries visual, not motor, fibres.
why_others_wrong.B: Corticospinal fibres pass through the cerebral peduncles of the midbrain without crossing; they decussate lower, in the caudal medulla.
why_others_wrong.D: Only the small anterior corticospinal tract crosses at segmental levels, within the anterior white commissure of the cord, not at the nerve roots; the lateral tract crossed in the medulla.
why_others_wrong.E: Most corticospinal fibres (about 85-90%) do cross, at the pyramidal decussation; only the small anterior corticospinal tract stays uncrossed until cord level.

exam_trap: Above the pyramidal decussation → corticospinal weakness is contralateral. Below it → weakness is ipsilateral.
takeaway: Find the lesion relative to the pyramidal decussation before deciding the side of weakness.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: Left lateral corticospinal tract lesion in the cervical cord ↓ fibres in the lateral tract have already crossed ↓ crossing occurred at the pyramidal decussation in the caudal medulla ↓ so the weakness is on the same side as the cord lesion ↓ Most corticospinal fibres cross at the pyramidal decussation in the caudal medulla
pearl: Upper motor neurone weakness below a cord lesion is ipsilateral, which is why a cord hemisection gives same-side weakness with opposite-side pain and temperature loss.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: cavernous sinus
stem: A patient with a cavernous sinus lesion develops diplopia and inability to abduct the right eye. Which cranial nerve is most directly responsible for this deficit?
why_correct: The abducens nerve supplies lateral rectus and is particularly vulnerable within the cavernous sinus. Damage causes failure of abduction and therefore horizontal diplopia.

why_others_wrong.A: The oculomotor nerve supplies medial rectus, so its palsy impairs adduction and gives a down-and-out eye, not failed abduction.
why_others_wrong.B: The trochlear nerve supplies superior oblique, causing vertical diplopia worse on looking down and in, not abduction failure.
why_others_wrong.C: The ophthalmic division is sensory to the forehead and cornea and has no motor role in eye movement.
why_others_wrong.E: The facial nerve supplies orbicularis oculi for eye closure, not the extraocular muscles.

exam_trap: CN VI runs within the cavernous sinus alongside the internal carotid artery, while cranial nerves III, IV, V1 and V2 are embedded in the lateral wall.
takeaway: Cavernous sinus + failure of abduction = think CN VI.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: Cavernous sinus lesion ↓ failure of abduction of the right eye ↓ lateral rectus is supplied by the abducens nerve, which runs free in the sinus ↓ VI
pearl: Because the abducens nerve has a long intracranial course, a sixth nerve palsy can be a false localising sign of raised intracranial pressure rather than a focal lesion.

subject: Anatomy
title: ENT: head & neck: horner syndrome
stem: A patient develops partial ptosis and miosis after a lesion affecting the cervical sympathetic pathway. Which additional finding is most likely?
why_correct: Horner syndrome results from interruption of sympathetic innervation to the eye and face. The classic features are miosis, mild ptosis and ipsilateral facial anhidrosis. Apparent enophthalmos may also occur.

why_others_wrong.A: Horner syndrome classically produces apparent enophthalmos (sunken appearance) rather than proptosis.
why_others_wrong.B: Loss of corneal sensation reflects an ophthalmic-division trigeminal deficit, not interruption of the sympathetic pathway.
why_others_wrong.D: Facial paralysis implies a facial (motor) nerve lesion, which is unrelated to sympathetic chain interruption.
why_others_wrong.E: Complete ophthalmoplegia would suggest oculomotor or other cranial nerve involvement, well beyond the isolated features of Horner syndrome.

exam_trap: Proptosis is chosen because the eye looks abnormal, but Horner syndrome causes apparent enophthalmos from a narrowed palpebral fissure, not proptosis.
takeaway: Miosis + mild ptosis + anhidrosis = sympathetic pathway lesion.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020); Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed (2021).
thinking: Partial ptosis and miosis ↓ interruption of sympathetic supply to the eye and face ↓ sympathetic fibres also drive facial sweating ↓ Anhidrosis
pearl: An acute painful Horner syndrome should raise suspicion of carotid artery dissection, while Horner syndrome with arm pain or hand wasting suggests an apical lung tumour.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: autonomic denervation
stem: A patient undergoes interruption of a sympathetic nerve pathway to a limb. Which vascular effect is expected?

options.B: Loss of resting sympathetic vasoconstrictor tone
options.C: Increased parasympathetic innervation of skeletal muscle vessels
options.D: Complete abolition of local metabolic vasodilatation

correct_answer: B. Loss of resting sympathetic vasoconstrictor tone
why_correct: Many systemic blood vessels are maintained partly by tonic sympathetic vasoconstrictor activity. Removing sympathetic input reduces this vasoconstrictor tone and can produce vasodilatation.

why_others_wrong.A: Removing sympathetic input removes vasoconstrictor drive, so vessels dilate rather than constrict maximally.
why_others_wrong.C: Skeletal muscle vessels have no significant parasympathetic innervation, and sympathectomy does not create one.
why_others_wrong.D: Local metabolic vasodilatation is intrinsic to the tissue and persists after sympathetic denervation.
why_others_wrong.E: Sympathectomy increases limb blood flow and does not cause arterial thrombosis.

exam_trap: Complete abolition of local metabolic vasodilatation is chosen by overestimating neural control, but metabolic autoregulation is intrinsic to the tissue and persists after sympathectomy.
takeaway: Sympathetic nerves provide important resting vascular tone.
source: Guyton & Hall, 14th ed (2021).
thinking: Sympathetic pathway to a limb interrupted ↓ vessels normally receive tonic sympathetic vasoconstrictor drive ↓ removing it allows vasodilatation ↓ local metabolic control persists ↓ Loss of resting sympathetic vasoconstrictor tone
pearl: Thoracoscopic sympathectomy is used for severe palmar hyperhidrosis, and compensatory sweating elsewhere on the trunk is a common troublesome side effect to counsel patients about.

subject: Pharmacology
title: Pharmacology: free water clearance
stem: A patient has a urine flow rate of 3 L/day with a urine osmolality of 100 mOsm/kg. Plasma osmolality is 300 mOsm/kg. What is the most likely interpretation?

options.A: The kidneys are retaining free water
options.B: The kidneys are excreting free water
options.E: The patient has zero osmolar clearance

correct_answer: B. The kidneys are excreting free water
why_correct: When urine osmolality is below plasma osmolality, the kidneys are excreting water in excess of solute: positive free water clearance. This occurs with low ADH activity, assuming appropriate renal function.

why_others_wrong.A: A urine osmolality (100) well below plasma osmolality (300) indicates dilute urine is being excreted, i.e. free water is being lost, not retained.
why_others_wrong.C: Maximal ADH activity would produce maximally concentrated urine (high osmolality), not dilute urine well below plasma osmolality.
why_others_wrong.D: Urine osmolality here is far lower than plasma osmolality, the opposite of maximal concentration.
why_others_wrong.E: Osmolar clearance is not zero in this scenario; solute is still being excreted alongside a larger volume of water, giving a positive free-water clearance rather than zero clearance.

exam_trap: Dilute urine does not simply mean “high urine output”; it specifically indicates excretion of relatively solute-free water.
takeaway: Urine osmolality < plasma osmolality → positive free-water clearance.
source: Guyton & Hall, 14th ed (2021).
thinking: Urine osmolality 100 mOsm/kg with plasma 300 mOsm/kg ↓ urine is more dilute than plasma ↓ water is excreted in excess of solute ↓ positive free-water clearance with low ADH effect ↓ The kidneys are excreting free water
pearl: Free-water clearance equals urine flow minus osmolar clearance; here osmolar clearance is about 1 L/day (3 x 100 / 300), so about 2 L/day of solute-free water is excreted.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: fgf23
stem: A patient with increased fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23) develops hypophosphataemia. Which renal effect is primarily responsible?

options.D: Increased PTH secretion as the direct primary action

correct_answer: B. Reduced proximal tubular phosphate reabsorption
why_correct: FGF23 reduces proximal tubular phosphate reabsorption, increasing urinary phosphate excretion. It also suppresses renal 1α-hydroxylase activity, reducing calcitriol production.

why_others_wrong.A: This is the opposite effect; FGF23 reduces, rather than increases, proximal tubular phosphate reabsorption.
why_others_wrong.C: FGF23 suppresses calcitriol production, which would tend to reduce, not increase, intestinal phosphate absorption.
why_others_wrong.D: FGF23 directly suppresses PTH secretion via FGFR1 and Klotho in the parathyroid; its primary renal action is phosphaturia.
why_others_wrong.E: FGF23 suppresses, rather than increases, calcitriol synthesis by inhibiting renal 1α-hydroxylase.

exam_trap: FGF23 is a major phosphaturic hormone. Do not confuse it with PTH, although both promote renal phosphate excretion.
takeaway: FGF23 → ↓ proximal phosphate reabsorption + ↓ calcitriol.
source: Guyton & Hall, 14th ed (2021); Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed (2023).
thinking: Raised FGF23 ↓ acts with Klotho on the proximal tubule ↓ sodium-phosphate cotransporters are reduced ↓ phosphaturia causes hypophosphataemia ↓ Reduced proximal tubular phosphate reabsorption
pearl: X-linked hypophosphataemia and tumour-induced osteomalacia are FGF23-excess states, and removal of the culprit mesenchymal tumour cures the latter.

subject: Physiology
title: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care: vitamin d activation
stem: A patient with severe chronic kidney disease develops hypocalcaemia and secondary hyperparathyroidism. Which renal process is impaired?

options.C: Conversion of vitamin D to 25-hydroxyvitamin D in skin
options.D: Binding of vitamin D to albumin
options.E: Intestinal calcium transport directly by PTH

why_correct: The kidney converts 25-hydroxyvitamin D to active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol) through 1α-hydroxylase. Chronic kidney disease reduces this activation, contributing to hypocalcaemia and secondary hyperparathyroidism.

why_others_wrong.A: 25-hydroxylation of vitamin D occurs in the liver and is not the renal process impaired in chronic kidney disease.
why_others_wrong.C: 25-hydroxylation does not occur in the skin; the skin makes cholecalciferol under UV light, and 25-hydroxylation is a hepatic, not renal, step.
why_others_wrong.D: Protein binding of vitamin D to its carrier is a transport phenomenon, not an enzymatic renal activation step affected by CKD.
why_others_wrong.E: PTH does not directly transport calcium in the intestine; intestinal calcium absorption is mediated by calcitriol, and this is not the impaired renal process described.

exam_trap: Candidates choosing A pick the hepatic step; 25-hydroxylation occurs in the liver, whereas the kidney's 1-alpha-hydroxylation is the step lost in chronic kidney disease.
takeaway: Liver → 25-OH vitamin D. Kidney → 1,25-(OH)₂ vitamin D.
source: Guyton & Hall, 14th ed (2021).
thinking: Severe chronic kidney disease with hypocalcaemia ↓ renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity falls ↓ less calcitriol means less gut calcium absorption ↓ hypocalcaemia stimulates PTH ↓ 1α-hydroxylation of 25-hydroxyvitamin D
pearl: Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D reflects vitamin D stores, so in chronic kidney disease active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D can be low even when 25-hydroxyvitamin D is adequate.

subject: Physiology
title: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care: pth and calcitriol integration
stem: Which combination is produced by PTH in the kidney?

options.A: Increased phosphate reabsorption and reduced calcium reabsorption
options.B: Reduced phosphate reabsorption and increased calcium reabsorption
options.C: Reduced calcium reabsorption and reduced calcitriol formation

correct_answer: B. Reduced phosphate reabsorption and increased calcium reabsorption
why_correct: PTH increases calcium reabsorption, particularly in the distal nephron, while reducing proximal phosphate reabsorption. PTH also stimulates renal 1α-hydroxylase, increasing calcitriol formation.

why_others_wrong.A: This reverses PTH's actual effects; PTH decreases phosphate reabsorption and increases calcium reabsorption, not the opposite.
why_others_wrong.C: PTH increases, rather than decreases, calcium reabsorption and stimulates, rather than reduces, calcitriol formation via 1α-hydroxylase.
why_others_wrong.D: PTH increases calcium reabsorption, thereby reducing urinary calcium excretion, rather than increasing excretion of both ions.
why_others_wrong.E: PTH stimulates calcitriol synthesis by activating renal 1α-hydroxylase; it does not increase its breakdown.

exam_trap: Candidates choosing A reverse PTH's renal actions; it increases calcium reabsorption but decreases phosphate reabsorption, producing phosphaturia.
takeaway: PTH = retain Ca, excrete phosphate, activate vitamin D.
source: Guyton & Hall, 14th ed (2021).
thinking: PTH in the kidney ↓ proximal tubule: phosphate reabsorption falls ↓ distal nephron: calcium reabsorption rises ↓ also stimulates 1-alpha-hydroxylase ↓ Reduced phosphate reabsorption and increased calcium reabsorption
pearl: This calcium-raising, phosphate-lowering pattern explains why primary hyperparathyroidism shows high calcium with low phosphate, whereas hypoparathyroidism shows the reverse.

subject: Physiology
title: GI physiology & metabolism: thyroid feedback
stem: A patient has a pituitary macroadenoma secreting biologically active TSH. Which biochemical pattern is most likely?

options.A: Low free T4 and low TSH
options.B: High free T4 and low TSH
options.C: High free T4 and inappropriately normal/high TSH
options.D: Low free T4 and high TSH
options.E: Normal free T4 and absent TSH

correct_answer: C. High free T4 and inappropriately normal/high TSH
why_correct: A TSH-secreting pituitary tumour causes inappropriate TSH secretion despite elevated circulating thyroid hormone. Therefore free T4 is elevated while TSH is not appropriately suppressed.

why_others_wrong.A: Low free T4 with low TSH describes secondary hypothyroidism, the opposite biochemical pattern to a TSH-secreting tumour with elevated thyroid hormone.
why_others_wrong.B: High free T4 with appropriately low TSH describes primary hyperthyroidism, where the pituitary correctly suppresses TSH, not the inappropriate TSH secretion seen with a TSH-secreting tumour.
why_others_wrong.D: Low free T4 with high TSH describes primary hypothyroidism, the opposite pattern to elevated thyroid hormone from a TSH-secreting tumour.
why_others_wrong.E: An absent TSH with normal T4 does not fit an actively TSH-secreting tumour, which produces biologically active TSH driving elevated thyroid hormone.

exam_trap: In thyrotoxicosis, TSH should normally be suppressed. A non-suppressed TSH is the key clue to central hyperthyroidism or thyroid hormone resistance.
takeaway: High T4 + non-suppressed TSH = think central hyperthyroidism or thyroid hormone resistance.
source: Guyton & Hall, 14th ed (2021).
thinking: TSH-secreting pituitary macroadenoma ↓ TSH drives thyroid hormone production ↓ free T4 rises ↓ the tumour ignores feedback, so TSH is not suppressed ↓ High free T4 and inappropriately normal/high TSH
pearl: First-line treatment of a TSH-secreting adenoma is trans-sphenoidal surgery, with somatostatin analogues used when surgery fails or is unsuitable.

subject: Physiology
title: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care: adrenal androgens
stem: Which adrenal cortical zone is the principal source of adrenal androgens such as DHEA?
why_correct: The zona reticularis produces adrenal androgens, particularly dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) and related steroids.

why_others_wrong.A: The zona glomerulosa produces mineralocorticoids such as aldosterone, not adrenal androgens like DHEA.
why_others_wrong.B: The zona fasciculata produces glucocorticoids, principally cortisol, rather than adrenal androgens.
why_others_wrong.D: The adrenal medulla produces catecholamines (adrenaline and noradrenaline) via chromaffin cells, not steroid androgens.
why_others_wrong.E: The adrenal capsule is a connective tissue covering with no hormone-secreting function.

exam_trap: Use the sequence GFR: Glomerulosa = salt, Fasciculata = sugar, Reticularis = sex.
takeaway: GFR = aldosterone, cortisol, androgens.
source: Guyton & Hall, 14th ed (2021).
thinking: Adrenal androgens such as DHEA ↓ innermost cortical zone ↓ salt, sugar, sex from outside in ↓ Zona reticularis
pearl: An adrenal mass with rapidly progressive virilisation or a very high DHEA sulphate should raise suspicion of adrenocortical carcinoma.

subject: Genetics
title: Genetics: DNA repair
stem: A patient has a defect in nucleotide excision repair. Which type of DNA damage is particularly associated with this pathway?

options.A: Double-strand breaks caused by ionising radiation
options.B: Bulky DNA lesions caused by ultraviolet radiation

correct_answer: B. Bulky DNA lesions caused by ultraviolet radiation
why_correct: Nucleotide excision repair removes bulky, helix-distorting DNA lesions, including pyrimidine dimers produced by ultraviolet radiation.

why_others_wrong.A: Double-strand breaks from ionising radiation are repaired mainly by homologous recombination or non-homologous end joining, not nucleotide excision repair.
why_others_wrong.C: Nucleotide excision repair acts on damaged DNA, not on errors in RNA transcripts, which are short-lived and not repaired by this pathway.
why_others_wrong.D: Failure of chromosome segregation is a mitotic or meiotic error causing aneuploidy, not a DNA lesion that excision repair can remove.
why_others_wrong.E: Telomere shortening results from incomplete end replication with each division and is countered by telomerase, not nucleotide excision repair.

exam_trap: Option A is chosen because radiation damage sounds similar, but ionising-radiation double-strand breaks are repaired by recombination or end joining, not excision repair.
takeaway: Bulky DNA distortion → nucleotide excision repair.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed (2023).
thinking: Nucleotide excision repair defect ↓ pathway removes helix-distorting lesions ↓ typical cause is ultraviolet light ↓ Bulky DNA lesions caused by ultraviolet radiation
pearl: Xeroderma pigmentosum is the classic nucleotide excision repair disorder, with skin cancers developing at a young age, whereas defective double-strand break signalling in ataxia telangiectasia causes marked sensitivity to ionising radiation.

subject: Genetics
title: Genetics: homologous recombination
stem: Which DNA repair mechanism uses a homologous DNA template to accurately repair a double-strand break?
why_correct: Homologous recombination repairs double-strand breaks using a homologous DNA template, allowing high-fidelity repair, particularly during S and G2 phases when a sister chromatid is available.

why_others_wrong.A: Non-homologous end joining ligates broken ends directly without a template, so it is faster but more error-prone than template-guided repair.
why_others_wrong.C: Nucleotide excision repair removes bulky helix-distorting lesions such as ultraviolet pyrimidine dimers, not double-strand breaks.
why_others_wrong.D: Base excision repair removes small damaged or inappropriate bases from a single strand, not double-strand breaks needing a homologous template.
why_others_wrong.E: Mismatch repair corrects mispaired bases left after replication and does not repair double-strand breaks using a homologous template.

exam_trap: Non-homologous end joining is the tempting option because it also repairs double-strand breaks, but it ligates ends directly without a template and is error-prone.
takeaway: Double-strand break + accurate template repair = homologous recombination.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed (2023).
thinking: Double-strand break ↓ accurate repair needs a homologous template ↓ sister chromatid available in S and G2 phases ↓ Homologous recombination
pearl: BRCA1 and BRCA2 are essential for homologous recombination, and tumours lacking them are sensitive to PARP inhibitors through synthetic lethality.

subject: Genetics
title: Genetics: non-homologous end joining
stem: Which statement best describes non-homologous end joining?

options.A: It requires an identical sister chromatid
options.B: It repairs only UV-induced pyrimidine dimers
options.C: It directly rejoins broken DNA ends without a homologous template
options.E: It requires mismatch recognition during DNA replication

correct_answer: C. It directly rejoins broken DNA ends without a homologous template
why_correct: Non-homologous end joining repairs double-strand DNA breaks by processing and joining the broken ends without requiring a homologous template. Because end processing may occur, small insertions or deletions can result.

why_others_wrong.A: Needing an identical sister chromatid describes homologous recombination; non-homologous end joining works without any homologous template.
why_others_wrong.B: Ultraviolet-induced pyrimidine dimers are removed by nucleotide excision repair; non-homologous end joining repairs double-strand breaks.
why_others_wrong.D: Non-homologous end joining repairs double-strand breaks; single-base damage is handled by base excision or mismatch repair.
why_others_wrong.E: Mismatch recognition during replication is the basis of mismatch repair, not of non-homologous end joining of broken DNA ends.

exam_trap: Option A is chosen by candidates who mix up the two double-strand break pathways; needing a sister chromatid template defines homologous recombination, not end joining.
takeaway: NHEJ = broken ends joined directly; no homologous template required.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed (2023).
thinking: Non-homologous end joining ↓ repairs double-strand breaks ↓ broken ends processed and ligated directly ↓ no homologous template needed ↓ Directly rejoins broken DNA ends without a homologous template
pearl: Non-homologous end joining is also used deliberately in V(D)J recombination of lymphocytes, and defects in it cause forms of severe combined immunodeficiency with radiosensitivity.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing: apoptosis
stem: Which feature most strongly distinguishes apoptosis from necrosis?

options.C: Cell shrinkage with formation of apoptotic bodies
options.E: Random enzymatic digestion of adjacent tissue

correct_answer: C. Cell shrinkage with formation of apoptotic bodies
why_correct: Apoptosis is programmed cell death characterised by cell shrinkage, chromatin condensation, nuclear fragmentation and formation of membrane-bound apoptotic bodies, generally without the marked inflammatory response typical of necrosis.

why_others_wrong.A: Cell swelling (oncosis) is characteristic of necrosis, the opposite of the shrinkage seen in apoptosis.
why_others_wrong.B: Early plasma membrane rupture is typical of necrosis, causing leakage of cell contents; apoptotic cells maintain membrane integrity until late, packaging contents into apoptotic bodies.
why_others_wrong.D: Marked surrounding neutrophilic inflammation is characteristic of necrosis, which releases cellular contents that trigger inflammation, unlike the typically non-inflammatory clearance of apoptotic bodies.
why_others_wrong.E: Random enzymatic digestion of adjacent tissue describes necrosis, in contrast to the regulated, contained process of apoptosis.

exam_trap: Candidates choose cell swelling (A) or early membrane rupture (B), but these define necrosis; apoptosis shows shrinkage and membrane-bound apoptotic bodies.
takeaway: Apoptosis = cell shrinkage + fragmentation + minimal inflammation.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed (2023).
thinking: Apoptosis versus necrosis ↓ cell shrinks rather than swells ↓ apoptotic bodies, membranes intact ↓ Cell shrinkage with formation of apoptotic bodies
pearl: Nuclear fragmentation in apoptosis produces a characteristic DNA ladder pattern on gel electrophoresis, due to cleavage between nucleosomes.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing: caspases
stem: The execution phase of apoptosis is principally mediated by which enzymes?
why_correct: Caspases are cysteine proteases that execute apoptosis by cleaving multiple cellular substrates. Initiator caspases activate downstream executioner caspases.

why_others_wrong.A: Cyclooxygenases generate prostaglandins in the inflammatory pathway, unrelated to the apoptotic execution machinery.
why_others_wrong.C: Matrix metalloproteinases degrade extracellular matrix proteins, not the intracellular substrates cleaved in apoptosis.
why_others_wrong.D: DNA polymerases synthesise DNA during replication, the opposite function to the degradative caspase cascade of apoptosis.
why_others_wrong.E: Telomerases maintain telomere length during cell division and are unrelated to programmed cell death execution.

exam_trap: Candidates choose matrix metalloproteinases (C) because they are also proteases, but MMPs degrade extracellular matrix; caspases execute apoptosis inside the cell.
takeaway: Apoptosis execution = caspase cascade.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed (2023).
thinking: Execution phase of apoptosis ↓ cysteine proteases cleave cellular substrates ↓ caspases ↓ Caspases
pearl: Initiator caspase-9 (intrinsic) and caspase-8 (extrinsic) converge on executioner caspase-3, which dismantles the cytoskeleton and activates DNA-cleaving enzymes.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Physiology: bcl-2 family
stem: Which protein is classically anti-apoptotic?
why_correct: BCL-2 is an anti-apoptotic member of the BCL-2 family. Pro-apoptotic proteins such as BAX and BAK promote mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilisation, facilitating cytochrome c release and caspase activation.

why_others_wrong.A: BAX is a pro-apoptotic protein that promotes mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilisation, the opposite function to the anti-apoptotic role described.
why_others_wrong.B: BAK is also pro-apoptotic, facilitating cytochrome c release, the opposite of an anti-apoptotic protein.
why_others_wrong.D: Cytochrome c is released from mitochondria to trigger apoptosome formation and caspase activation; it promotes apoptosis rather than inhibiting it.
why_others_wrong.E: Caspase-3 is an executioner caspase that carries out apoptosis, not a protein that protects against it.

exam_trap: Remember the functional split: BCL-2 protects against apoptosis; BAX/BAK promote mitochondrial apoptosis.
takeaway: BCL-2 = anti-apoptotic; BAX/BAK = pro-apoptotic.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed (2023).
thinking: Anti-apoptotic protein ↓ BCL-2 family members guard mitochondrial membrane integrity ↓ BAX and BAK are pro-apoptotic ↓ BCL-2
pearl: The BCL-2 inhibitor venetoclax restores apoptosis and is used in chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, showing the therapeutic relevance of this family.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Pathology: oncology & haematology: ras signal transduction
stem: A tumour contains a constitutively active RAS protein. Which effect is most likely?

options.E: Loss of all receptor tyrosine kinase signalling

why_correct: RAS is a small GTP-binding protein involved in intracellular growth signalling downstream of many receptor tyrosine kinases. Activating mutations can maintain downstream proliferative signalling even in the absence of appropriate external stimulation.

why_others_wrong.B: Activated RAS drives proliferation rather than inhibiting it; permanent growth arrest would be expected from tumour-suppressor activity, not an activated oncogene.
why_others_wrong.C: Mismatch repair is carried out by MMR proteins such as MLH1 and MSH2, and RAS activation does not increase this repair activity.
why_others_wrong.D: Constitutive RAS signalling through pathways such as PI3K-AKT tends to promote cell survival, not caspase-mediated apoptosis.
why_others_wrong.E: RAS lies downstream of receptor tyrosine kinases, so its activation keeps their signalling pathway switched on rather than abolishing it.

exam_trap: Loss of all receptor tyrosine kinase signalling tempts because RAS sits downstream of these receptors, but its activation keeps the pathway switched on regardless of receptor input.
takeaway: Oncogene activation usually behaves like a stuck accelerator.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed (2023).
thinking: Constitutively active RAS ↓ RAS normally relays receptor tyrosine kinase signals ↓ it is locked in the GTP-bound state ↓ persistent MAPK and PI3K signalling ↓ Persistent growth-signalling pathway activation
pearl: Because mutant RAS signals downstream of the receptor, blocking the receptor upstream, as with anti-EGFR antibodies, is ineffective in RAS-mutant colorectal cancer.

subject: Immunology
title: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing: transplant rejection
stem: A transplanted kidney develops graft dysfunction three weeks after transplantation, and biopsy shows tubulitis with a dense lymphocytic interstitial infiltrate. Which immune mechanism is central?

options.B: T-cell recognition of alloantigens with cellular immune activation

correct_answer: B. T-cell recognition of alloantigens with cellular immune activation
why_correct: Acute cellular rejection is mediated predominantly by recipient T lymphocytes recognising donor alloantigens, producing inflammatory injury and direct cellular cytotoxicity.

why_others_wrong.A: IgE-mediated mast-cell degranulation underlies type I hypersensitivity and allergy, not T-cell-driven rejection of a kidney graft.
why_others_wrong.C: Complement deficiency increases infection risk and is not the mechanism by which recipient T cells damage a transplanted kidney.
why_others_wrong.D: Neutrophil depletion would reduce innate inflammation and does not describe the T-cell recognition of donor alloantigens in cellular rejection.
why_others_wrong.E: Acute cellular rejection is driven by recipient T cells recognising alloantigens, not by an isolated loss of B-cell tolerance.

exam_trap: Do not equate all transplant rejection with antibodies. Cellular rejection is T-cell driven.
takeaway: Acute cellular rejection → recipient T cells attacking the graft.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed (2023).
thinking: Graft dysfunction three weeks after transplantation ↓ biopsy shows tubulitis with a lymphocytic interstitial infiltrate ↓ recipient T cells recognise donor HLA alloantigens ↓ cellular cytotoxic and inflammatory injury follows ↓ T-cell recognition of alloantigens with cellular immune activation
pearl: Acute cellular rejection usually responds to pulsed high-dose corticosteroids, with T-cell-depleting antibodies reserved for steroid-resistant rejection.

subject: Immunology
title: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing: hyperacute transplant rejection
stem: A transplanted kidney becomes cyanotic and fails almost immediately after reperfusion. What is the most likely mechanism?

options.A: Recipient T-cell activation developing over several weeks
options.B: Pre-existing recipient antibodies against donor antigens
options.C: Chronic fibrosis from long-term immune injury

correct_answer: B. Pre-existing recipient antibodies against donor antigens
why_correct: Hyperacute rejection occurs rapidly after transplantation because the recipient already has circulating antibodies against donor antigens, commonly ABO or HLA antigens. These activate endothelial injury, thrombosis and graft ischaemia.

why_others_wrong.A: Recipient T-cell activation over weeks describes acute cellular rejection, which is too slow to explain graft failure immediately after reperfusion.
why_others_wrong.C: Chronic fibrosis from long-term immune injury develops over months to years and causes gradual decline, not failure at reperfusion.
why_others_wrong.D: Delayed-type hypersensitivity is a slow T-cell-mediated response and cannot produce a cyanotic graft within minutes of reperfusion.
why_others_wrong.E: Isolated neutrophil deficiency predisposes to infection and does not cause immediate thrombosis and failure of a transplanted kidney.

exam_trap: Recipient T-cell activation is the tempting answer for any rejection, but T-cell responses take days; failure at reperfusion means preformed recipient antibodies against donor antigens.
takeaway: Hyperacute rejection = preformed antibodies + endothelial injury + thrombosis.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed (2023).
thinking: Kidney cyanotic and failing at reperfusion ↓ minutes after anastomosis ↓ too fast for T-cell activation ↓ preformed ABO or HLA antibodies fix complement on endothelium ↓ Pre-existing recipient antibodies against donor antigens
pearl: Hyperacute rejection is seen on table as a mottled, cyanotic, flaccid graft soon after clamp release, and a positive pre-transplant crossmatch is the key warning.

subject: Immunology
title: Immunology: chronic transplant rejection
stem: A renal transplant recipient develops gradual deterioration in graft function over several years with vascular intimal thickening and interstitial fibrosis. Which process is most likely?

options.B: Acute cellular rejection occurring minutes after transplantation

why_correct: Chronic rejection is characterised by progressive vascular changes, interstitial fibrosis and parenchymal atrophy, resulting in gradual loss of graft function.

why_others_wrong.A: Hyperacute rejection occurs within minutes to hours of reperfusion due to preformed antibodies, not as gradual decline over several years.
why_others_wrong.B: Acute cellular rejection typically develops over days to months, not minutes, and does not explain slowly progressive fibrosis over years.
why_others_wrong.D: Complement deficiency is not a cause of graft rejection and would not produce vascular intimal thickening and interstitial fibrosis.
why_others_wrong.E: Surgical ischaemia causes early graft injury around the time of transplantation, rather than progressive vascular and fibrotic changes years later.

exam_trap: Chronic rejection is a pathological pattern of progressive vascular narrowing and fibrosis rather than an immediate graft event.
takeaway: Years + vascular intimal thickening + fibrosis = chronic rejection.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed (2023).
thinking: Gradual graft decline over several years ↓ vascular intimal thickening and interstitial fibrosis ↓ not hyperacute (minutes) or acute (days to months) ↓ chronic immune and non-immune injury ↓ Chronic rejection
pearl: Chronic allograft injury responds poorly to increased immunosuppression and is a leading cause of late graft loss; calcineurin inhibitor nephrotoxicity can produce similar fibrosis.

subject: Immunology
title: Immunology: graft-versus-host disease
stem: A patient develops fever, widespread skin rash, diarrhoea and liver dysfunction following an allogeneic haematopoietic stem-cell transplant. Which mechanism best explains the syndrome?

options.A: Recipient T cells attacking donor tissue
options.B: Donor immunocompetent T cells attacking recipient tissues
options.C: Preformed recipient antibodies attacking donor kidney

correct_answer: B. Donor immunocompetent T cells attacking recipient tissues
why_correct: Graft-versus-host disease occurs when immunocompetent donor T cells recognise recipient tissues as foreign and mount an immune response. Skin, gastrointestinal tract and liver are major target organs.

why_others_wrong.A: Recipient T cells attacking donor tissue describes graft rejection, the opposite direction to graft-versus-host disease after stem-cell transplant.
why_others_wrong.C: Preformed recipient antibodies against a donor kidney cause hyperacute renal rejection, which does not fit rash, diarrhoea and liver dysfunction after stem-cell transplant.
why_others_wrong.D: IgE-mediated hypersensitivity causes immediate allergic reactions and does not explain a multi-organ syndrome following allogeneic stem-cell transplant.
why_others_wrong.E: Complement deficiency predisposes to infection and does not explain donor-derived immune attack on the recipient's skin, gut and liver.

exam_trap: Recipient T cells attacking donor tissue is the reversed direction and describes rejection; after stem-cell transplant the skin, gut and liver injury comes from donor T cells.
takeaway: Graft-versus-host = donor immune cells → recipient tissues.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed (2023).
thinking: Rash, diarrhoea and liver dysfunction ↓ after allogeneic stem-cell transplant ↓ skin, gut and liver are GVHD targets ↓ donor T cells attack the host ↓ Donor immunocompetent T cells attacking recipient tissues
pearl: Graft-versus-host disease also has a beneficial counterpart, the graft-versus-leukaemia effect, in which donor T cells attack residual malignant cells.

subject: Immunology
title: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing: complement terminal pathway
stem: A patient with recurrent Neisseria meningitidis infection is found to have deficiency of the terminal complement components. Which complex is directly impaired?
why_correct: The terminal complement pathway forms the membrane attack complex (MAC), consisting of C5b–C9. Deficiency predisposes particularly to recurrent Neisseria infections.

why_others_wrong.A: C1 inhibitor regulates early classical pathway activation, and its deficiency causes hereditary angioedema rather than recurrent Neisseria infection.
why_others_wrong.B: C3 convertase acts early in complement activation and generates C3b, so it is upstream of the terminal components C5 to C9.
why_others_wrong.D: The IgE receptor on mast cells and basophils mediates allergic reactions and is not a component of the terminal complement pathway.
why_others_wrong.E: The B-cell receptor is membrane-bound immunoglobulin used for antigen recognition and is not part of the complement system.

exam_trap: C3 convertase tempts because C3 is central to complement, but it acts upstream; terminal C5b-C9 deficiency removes the membrane attack complex, which is the key defence against Neisseria.
takeaway: C5–C9 deficiency → impaired MAC → recurrent Neisseria.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed (2023).
thinking: Recurrent Neisseria meningitidis ↓ terminal complement deficiency ↓ C5b-C9 assemble the lytic pore ↓ Membrane attack complex
pearl: Eculizumab blocks C5 and so produces the same susceptibility; patients receive meningococcal vaccination before starting it.

subject: Microbiology & surgical infection
title: Microbiology & surgical infection: splenic function and encapsulated bacteria
stem: A patient undergoes splenectomy. Which infection risk is particularly increased because of loss of splenic clearance of opsonised organisms?

options.B: Encapsulated bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae

correct_answer: B. Encapsulated bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae
why_correct: The spleen plays an important role in filtering blood and clearing opsonised organisms, particularly encapsulated bacteria. Asplenic patients are therefore at increased risk of overwhelming infection with organisms such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis and Haemophilus influenzae.

why_others_wrong.A: Neisseria gonorrhoeae is not a typical post-splenectomy threat; the related Neisseria meningitidis is, along with other encapsulated organisms.
why_others_wrong.C: Candida albicans infection is linked to neutropenia, broad-spectrum antibiotics and indwelling lines rather than loss of splenic clearance.
why_others_wrong.D: Dermatophytes cause superficial skin, hair and nail infections and are not associated with asplenia.
why_others_wrong.E: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is controlled mainly by cell-mediated immunity, so its risk is not particularly raised by splenectomy.

exam_trap: Neisseria gonorrhoeae only may tempt because Neisseria is linked to asplenia, but the relevant species is N. meningitidis, alongside pneumococcus and Haemophilus influenzae type b.
takeaway: Asplenia = impaired blood filtration + impaired clearance of encapsulated organisms.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed (2023); Principles and Practice of Surgery, 7th ed (2023).
thinking: Splenectomy ↓ loss of blood filtration and splenic antibody production ↓ encapsulated organisms evade other defences ↓ Encapsulated bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae
pearl: Overwhelming post-splenectomy infection can progress to septic shock within hours, so asplenic patients with fever need urgent antibiotics; the risk is greatest in the early years but lifelong.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: GI physiology & metabolism: gastric emptying
stem: A patient eats a meal containing a large amount of fat. Which physiological response is most likely to delay gastric emptying?

options.D: Increased vagal stimulation of the stomach

why_correct: Fat entering the duodenum stimulates cholecystokinin (CCK) release. CCK contributes to slowing gastric emptying, allowing more time for intestinal digestion and absorption.

why_others_wrong.A: Gastrin increases acid secretion and antral motility and does not account for the slowed emptying seen after a fatty meal.
why_others_wrong.C: Increased gastric motility would speed emptying, the opposite of the delay that duodenal fat produces.
why_others_wrong.D: Vagal stimulation generally increases gastric motility and would tend to speed emptying rather than delay it.
why_others_wrong.E: Duodenal feedback is increased, not reduced, by fat; the enterogastric reflex and hormones such as CCK slow emptying.

exam_trap: A fatty meal does not simply stimulate more gastric activity; intestinal feedback mechanisms slow gastric delivery.
takeaway: Duodenal fat → CCK → slower gastric emptying.
source: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed (2021).
thinking: Fat enters the duodenum ↓ I cells release cholecystokinin ↓ CCK reduces antral motility and increases pyloric tone ↓ gastric emptying slows ↓ Increased cholecystokinin release
pearl: CCK also contracts the gallbladder and relaxes the hepatopancreatic sphincter, which is why fatty meals provoke biliary colic.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: GI physiology & metabolism: pancreatic bicarbonate
stem: Which pancreatic cell population is primarily responsible for secretion of bicarbonate-rich fluid?
why_correct: Pancreatic ductal cells secrete a bicarbonate-rich aqueous fluid, particularly under the influence of secretin. This helps neutralise gastric acid entering the duodenum.

why_others_wrong.A: Acinar cells secrete digestive enzymes and a small-volume chloride-rich fluid; bicarbonate-rich fluid comes from the ducts.
why_others_wrong.C: Islet alpha cells are endocrine cells secreting glucagon into the blood, not exocrine bicarbonate.
why_others_wrong.D: Islet beta cells are endocrine cells secreting insulin and do not produce bicarbonate-rich pancreatic juice.
why_others_wrong.E: Pancreatic stellate cells drive fibrosis in chronic pancreatitis and have no secretory role in bicarbonate production.

exam_trap: Acinar cells (option A) are chosen as the main exocrine cells, but they secrete enzymes with a small chloride-rich fluid; ductal cells produce the bicarbonate-rich fluid.
takeaway: Pancreatic acini digest; pancreatic ducts neutralise.
source: Guyton & Hall, 14th ed (2021).
thinking: Bicarbonate-rich pancreatic fluid ↓ acinar cells secrete enzymes ↓ duct cells secrete bicarbonate via CFTR-dependent anion exchange under secretin ↓ Ductal cells
pearl: In cystic fibrosis, defective CFTR in pancreatic duct cells reduces bicarbonate and fluid secretion, so thick secretions block the ducts and cause exocrine pancreatic insufficiency.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: GI physiology & metabolism: enterohepatic circulation
stem: A patient has extensive terminal ileal resection. Which process is most directly impaired?
correct_answer: B. Enterohepatic recycling of bile salts
why_correct: Most bile salts are reabsorbed in the terminal ileum and returned to the liver through the portal circulation. Extensive terminal ileal resection therefore disrupts enterohepatic circulation and increases faecal bile salt loss.

why_others_wrong.A: Gastric acid secretion depends on parietal cells in the stomach, which are not removed by ileal resection.
why_others_wrong.C: Insulin comes from pancreatic beta cells, which are unaffected by terminal ileal resection.
why_others_wrong.D: Colonic fermentation may change as more bile salts reach the colon, but the most direct loss is bile salt reabsorption, and the colon is not resected.
why_others_wrong.E: Salivary amylase is secreted in the mouth and is unaffected by removal of the terminal ileum.

exam_trap: Terminal ileum is not just about vitamin B12; it is also the principal site of bile salt reabsorption.
takeaway: Terminal ileum → bile salt recovery + vitamin B12 absorption.
source: Guyton & Hall, 14th ed (2021).
thinking: Extensive terminal ileal resection ↓ the terminal ileum actively reabsorbs most bile salts ↓ more bile salts are lost in faeces ↓ Enterohepatic recycling of bile salts
pearl: Bile salt loss after ileal resection causes fat malabsorption, and patients with an intact colon are prone to oxalate renal stones as well as cholesterol gallstones.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: GI physiology & metabolism: vitamin b12 absorption
stem: Which combination is required for normal absorption of vitamin B12?
correct_answer: B. Intrinsic factor and terminal ileum
why_correct: Vitamin B12 binds intrinsic factor and is absorbed in the terminal ileum. Loss of either intrinsic factor or the appropriate ileal absorptive surface can therefore cause B12 deficiency.

why_others_wrong.A: Gastrin stimulates acid secretion and the duodenum is the site of iron absorption; neither is the specific requirement for B12 absorption.
why_others_wrong.C: Secretin drives pancreatic bicarbonate secretion and the jejunal brush border does not absorb the B12-intrinsic factor complex.
why_others_wrong.D: Parietal cells produce intrinsic factor, but CCK has no role in B12 uptake and the absorptive site, the terminal ileum, is missing.
why_others_wrong.E: Bile salts aid fat absorption and the colon has no mechanism for absorbing B12-intrinsic factor complexes.

exam_trap: Option D tempts because parietal cells do make intrinsic factor, but CCK has no role in B12 uptake and the essential absorptive site, the terminal ileum, is missing.
takeaway: B12 → intrinsic factor → terminal ileum.
source: Guyton & Hall, 14th ed (2021).
thinking: B12 absorption needs a binding factor and an absorptive site ↓ intrinsic factor comes from parietal cells ↓ the intrinsic factor-B12 complex is absorbed in the terminal ileum ↓ Intrinsic factor and terminal ileum
pearl: In pernicious anaemia, intramuscular hydroxocobalamin is standard UK treatment, particularly when there is neurological involvement.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: GI physiology & metabolism: iron absorption
stem: Which part of the gastrointestinal tract is the principal site of dietary iron absorption?
why_correct: Dietary iron is absorbed predominantly in the duodenum and proximal jejunum. Regulation includes hepcidin-mediated control of ferroportin.

why_others_wrong.A: Gastric acid helps convert ferric iron to the absorbable ferrous form, but the stomach itself absorbs little iron.
why_others_wrong.C: The terminal ileum is the site of vitamin B12 and bile salt absorption, not the main site of iron uptake.
why_others_wrong.D: The caecum mainly absorbs water and electrolytes and plays no significant role in dietary iron absorption.
why_others_wrong.E: The rectum stores faeces and absorbs minimal nutrients, so it is not a site of iron absorption.

exam_trap: Terminal ileum (option C) is a reflex answer for absorption questions, but it handles vitamin B12 and bile salts; iron is absorbed in the duodenum and proximal jejunum.
takeaway: Duodenum → iron. Terminal ileum → B12/bile salts.
source: Guyton & Hall, 14th ed (2021).
thinking: Dietary iron ↓ reduced to the ferrous form at the brush border ↓ taken up by DMT1 in the proximal small bowel ↓ Duodenum and proximal jejunum
pearl: Oral iron is better absorbed with vitamin C and on an empty stomach, while tea, calcium and proton pump inhibitors reduce absorption.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: GI physiology & metabolism: hepcidin
stem: A patient with chronic inflammation develops anaemia despite adequate body iron stores. Which hepatic hormone contributes to this process by reducing intestinal iron absorption and iron release from macrophages?
why_correct: Hepcidin is produced by the liver and reduces iron availability by promoting degradation of ferroportin. This decreases intestinal iron export into plasma and iron release from macrophage stores.

why_others_wrong.A: Erythropoietin is produced mainly by the kidney and stimulates red-cell production; it does not block iron absorption or release.
why_others_wrong.C: Renin is a renal enzyme in the renin-angiotensin system controlling blood pressure and has no role in iron handling.
why_others_wrong.D: Gastrin stimulates gastric acid, which may slightly aid iron absorption, and does not trap iron in macrophages.
why_others_wrong.E: Calcitonin is a thyroid C-cell hormone that lowers calcium and does not regulate iron availability.

exam_trap: Erythropoietin (option A) tempts because it relates to anaemia, but it stimulates red-cell production; hepcidin from the liver blocks ferroportin and traps iron in stores.
takeaway: Hepcidin high → ferroportin down → iron trapped in stores.
source: Guyton & Hall, 14th ed (2021); Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed (2023).
thinking: Anaemia of chronic inflammation with adequate iron stores ↓ inflammatory cytokines increase a hepatic iron-regulating hormone ↓ it degrades ferroportin ↓ gut iron export and macrophage iron release fall ↓ Hepcidin
pearl: In anaemia of chronic disease, ferritin is normal or raised as an acute-phase reactant with low serum iron, whereas a low ferritin indicates true iron deficiency.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Pathology: oncology & haematology: erythropoietin
stem: Which renal cell population is the major source of erythropoietin in adults?
why_correct: In adults, erythropoietin is produced predominantly by specialised interstitial cells in the renal cortex and outer medulla in response to reduced tissue oxygenation.

why_others_wrong.A: Glomerular podocytes form the filtration barrier with their foot processes and slit diaphragms; they are not the main source of erythropoietin.
why_others_wrong.C: Proximal tubular cells reabsorb filtered solutes and water; adult erythropoietin comes mainly from peritubular interstitial fibroblast-like cells.
why_others_wrong.D: Juxtaglomerular cells in the afferent arteriole secrete renin, the classic confusion with the interstitial cells that produce erythropoietin.
why_others_wrong.E: Macula densa cells sense distal tubular sodium chloride delivery to regulate renin release and glomerular filtration, not erythropoietin production.

exam_trap: Do not confuse the renal cells producing erythropoietin with those producing renin.
takeaway: Kidney oxygen sensing → erythropoietin → marrow erythropoiesis.
source: Guyton & Hall, 14th ed (2021).
