why_others_wrong.D: Loss to follow-up occurs after enrolment and is not prevented by concealing the upcoming allocation.
why_others_wrong.E: Publication bias concerns which trials get published, not how treatment assignment is protected at recruitment.

exam_trap: Allocation concealment occurs before/at enrolment; blinding concerns knowledge of treatment after allocation.
takeaway: Conceal allocation → protect randomisation from selection bias.
source: Standard randomised-trial methodology; Principles and Practice of Surgery, 7th ed (2023).
thinking: Allocation concealment acts before enrolment ↓ recruiter cannot predict the next assignment ↓ prevents selective enrolment ↓ Prevents investigators predicting the upcoming allocation before enrolment
pearl: Trials with inadequate allocation concealment tend to exaggerate treatment effects; predictable schemes such as alternate days or hospital number parity should not be used.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing: lung compliance
stem: A patient with pulmonary fibrosis undergoes respiratory function testing. Which change is most characteristic of pulmonary fibrosis?

options.C: Increased residual volume due to loss of elastic recoil

why_correct: Pulmonary fibrosis produces stiff lungs with increased elastic recoil and reduced compliance. Greater pressure is therefore required to generate a given change in lung volume.

why_others_wrong.A: Increased compliance describes emphysema, where elastic tissue is destroyed; fibrosis instead stiffens the lung and reduces compliance.
why_others_wrong.C: Fibrotic lungs have increased, not reduced, elastic recoil, and restrictive disease typically reduces rather than increases residual volume.
why_others_wrong.D: Fibrosis produces a restrictive pattern with reduced, not increased, total lung capacity.
why_others_wrong.E: Fibrosis increases elastic recoil (the lungs recoil more strongly, not less), the opposite of this option.

exam_trap: Emphysema and fibrosis are physiological opposites: emphysema has increased compliance and reduced recoil, whereas fibrosis has reduced compliance and increased recoil.
takeaway: Fibrosis = stiff lung = low compliance.
source: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed (2021).
thinking: Pulmonary fibrosis = interstitial scarring ↓ lungs become stiff with increased elastic recoil ↓ more pressure is needed for each change in volume ↓ Reduced lung compliance
pearl: Fibrosis produces a restrictive pattern with reduced lung volumes, a normal or raised FEV1/FVC ratio and a reduced transfer factor, unlike the obstructive pattern of emphysema.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Cardiorespiratory physiology: emphysema and elastic recoil
stem: Which physiological change is characteristic of pulmonary emphysema?

options.E: Increased alveolar-capillary membrane thickness as the primary abnormality

why_correct: Destruction of alveolar walls in emphysema reduces elastic recoil and increases lung compliance. This contributes to expiratory airway collapse and air trapping.

why_others_wrong.A: Destruction of alveolar elastic tissue in emphysema reduces, not increases, elastic recoil.
why_others_wrong.B: Loss of elastic tissue in emphysema increases lung compliance rather than reducing it.
why_others_wrong.D: Emphysema causes hyperinflation and air trapping, increasing rather than reducing total lung capacity.
why_others_wrong.E: The primary abnormality in emphysema is destruction of alveolar walls/parenchyma, not thickening of the alveolar-capillary membrane, which is characteristic of interstitial lung disease instead.

exam_trap: High compliance does not mean good lung function. In emphysema, excessive compliance accompanies poor elastic recoil.
takeaway: Emphysema = ↑ compliance + ↓ elastic recoil + air trapping.
source: Guyton & Hall, 14th ed (2021).
thinking: Emphysema destroys alveolar walls and elastic fibres ↓ elastic recoil falls ↓ the lung becomes more compliant and small airways lose radial traction ↓ airways collapse on expiration, causing air trapping ↓ Reduced elastic recoil
pearl: Loss of radial traction explains expiratory small-airway collapse, which is why patients with emphysema often breathe out through pursed lips to keep airway pressure up.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Cardiorespiratory physiology: frc and closing capacity
stem: In an elderly patient, closing capacity rises above functional residual capacity. What is the likely consequence during normal tidal breathing?

options.A: Increased alveolar ventilation in dependent lung regions

why_correct: When closing capacity exceeds FRC, dependent small airways can close during normal expiration. This produces ventilation-perfusion mismatch and may impair oxygenation.

why_others_wrong.A: Closure of dependent small airways reduces, not increases, alveolar ventilation to those regions, producing V/Q mismatch.
why_others_wrong.C: This is a mechanical airway-closure phenomenon unrelated to surfactant production, which is not altered by closing capacity exceeding FRC.
why_others_wrong.D: Airway closure creates perfused but poorly ventilated units (shunt-like effect), which does not reduce physiological dead space.
why_others_wrong.E: Airway closure impairs gas exchange to affected units, worsening rather than improving effective diffusion capacity.

exam_trap: Closing capacity increases with age and can exceed FRC, especially under anaesthesia or supine conditions.
takeaway: Closing capacity > FRC → airway closure during tidal breathing.
source: Guyton & Hall, 14th ed (2021).
thinking: Closing capacity rises with age ↓ when it exceeds FRC, small airways close within the tidal range ↓ dependent units become underventilated but remain perfused ↓ Small-airway closure during expiration
pearl: Supine posture, obesity and general anaesthesia all reduce FRC, so elderly surgical patients are especially prone to airway closure, atelectasis and postoperative hypoxaemia; upright positioning and PEEP help.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Cardiorespiratory physiology: surfactant
stem: Which cell produces pulmonary surfactant?
why_correct: Type II pneumocytes synthesise and secrete pulmonary surfactant. Surfactant reduces alveolar surface tension and helps prevent alveolar collapse.

why_others_wrong.A: Type I pneumocytes are thin squamous cells specialised for gas diffusion, not surfactant secretion.
why_others_wrong.C: Alveolar macrophages are phagocytic immune cells that clear debris and pathogens; they do not synthesise surfactant.
why_others_wrong.D: Ciliated epithelial cells line the conducting airways and clear mucus via ciliary beating; they are not present at the alveolar surface producing surfactant.
why_others_wrong.E: Pulmonary endothelial cells form the capillary wall involved in gas exchange and are not the source of surfactant.

exam_trap: Candidates choose type I pneumocytes because they cover most of the alveolar surface, but these thin cells are for gas exchange; surfactant comes from the cuboidal type II cells.
takeaway: Type II pneumocyte → surfactant.
source: Guyton & Hall, 14th ed (2021).
thinking: Surfactant is a phospholipid-rich film at the alveolar surface ↓ it is stored in lamellar bodies of cuboidal alveolar cells ↓ these cells also act as progenitors for type I cells ↓ Type II pneumocyte
pearl: Antenatal corticosteroids given before anticipated preterm delivery accelerate surfactant production by type II pneumocytes and reduce neonatal respiratory distress syndrome.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Cardiorespiratory physiology: law of laplace in alveoli
stem: Why are small alveoli particularly vulnerable to collapse if surfactant is deficient?

options.A: They have lower surface tension than larger alveoli
options.B: They have higher collapsing pressure for a given surface tension
options.D: They receive no pulmonary blood flow
options.E: They have a higher atmospheric pressure inside them

correct_answer: B. They have higher collapsing pressure for a given surface tension
why_correct: For a roughly spherical alveolus, collapsing pressure is related to surface tension and inversely related to radius. Smaller alveoli therefore have greater collapsing pressure when surface tension is not adequately reduced by surfactant.

why_others_wrong.A: Without adequate surfactant, small alveoli do not have lower surface tension than large ones; surfactant is what normally lowers tension preferentially in small alveoli, and its absence removes this protection.
why_others_wrong.C: Alveoli do contain elastic tissue; the vulnerability to collapse relates to the surface-tension/radius relationship (Laplace's law), not absence of elastic fibres.
why_others_wrong.D: Alveolar perfusion is unrelated to the physical collapsing-pressure relationship that determines vulnerability to collapse.
why_others_wrong.E: Atmospheric pressure does not differ between alveoli of different sizes; the issue is the collapsing pressure generated by surface tension acting on a smaller radius, per Laplace's law.

exam_trap: Candidates choose 'lower surface tension in small alveoli', which applies only when surfactant is working; with deficiency the problem is higher collapsing pressure from the smaller radius.
takeaway: Small radius + high surface tension → high collapsing pressure.
source: Guyton & Hall, 14th ed (2021).
thinking: Laplace relationship: collapsing pressure = 2 × surface tension / radius ↓ a smaller radius gives a higher pressure for the same surface tension ↓ without surfactant, small alveoli tend to empty into larger ones ↓ They have higher collapsing pressure for a given surface tension
pearl: Surfactant lowers surface tension more as alveoli shrink, stabilising alveoli of different sizes; surfactant dysfunction in ARDS and after cardiopulmonary bypass contributes to atelectasis.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Pathology: oncology & haematology: bohr effect
stem: A rise in tissue CO2 concentration facilitates oxygen unloading from haemoglobin. What is this phenomenon called?
why_correct: The Bohr effect describes reduced haemoglobin affinity for oxygen in the presence of increased CO2 and hydrogen ions, facilitating oxygen unloading in metabolically active tissues.

why_others_wrong.A: The Haldane effect describes how oxygenation of haemoglobin affects CO2 carriage, the reverse relationship to the CO2-driven O2 unloading described here.
why_others_wrong.C: "Fick effect" is not a recognised term for this interaction; the Fick principle relates to diffusion/flow calculations, not CO2-mediated O2 unloading.
why_others_wrong.D: The Starling effect refers to fluid movement across capillary walls (or the cardiac Frank-Starling mechanism), unrelated to haemoglobin-oxygen affinity.
why_others_wrong.E: The Venturi effect is a fluid-dynamics phenomenon concerning pressure and flow velocity, unrelated to haemoglobin's oxygen affinity.

exam_trap: Candidates choose the Haldane effect, which describes oxygenation altering CO2 carriage; CO2 and H+ reducing haemoglobin's oxygen affinity is the Bohr effect.
takeaway: More metabolically active tissue → more CO2/H+ → right shift → O2 unloading.
source: Guyton & Hall, 14th ed (2021).
thinking: Raised tissue CO2 and H+ ↓ haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen falls ↓ the dissociation curve shifts to the right ↓ more oxygen is released to active tissue ↓ Bohr effect
pearl: The curve is shifted right by raised CO2, H+, temperature and 2,3-BPG, while hypothermia, alkalosis and stored blood low in 2,3-BPG shift it left and impair tissue oxygen unloading.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Cardiorespiratory physiology: haldane effect
stem: Which statement best describes the Haldane effect?

options.B: Oxygenation of haemoglobin in the lungs facilitates release of CO2
options.C: CO2 directly increases haemoglobin affinity for oxygen
options.D: Increased temperature shifts the curve left

correct_answer: B. Oxygenation of haemoglobin in the lungs facilitates release of CO2
why_correct: Oxygenation of haemoglobin in the pulmonary circulation reduces its capacity to carry CO2 and H+, promoting CO2 unloading in the lungs.

why_others_wrong.A: This is the opposite of the truth: deoxygenated haemoglobin actually carries more CO2 (as carbaminohaemoglobin and via enhanced buffering), which is the basis of the Haldane effect, not less.
why_others_wrong.C: This misstates the Bohr effect: CO2 and H+ decrease, not increase, haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen.
why_others_wrong.D: Increased temperature shifts the oxygen dissociation curve to the right, not left, and this is unrelated to the CO2-carriage mechanism of the Haldane effect.
why_others_wrong.E: Oxygenation alters haemoglobin's CO2-carrying capacity and promotes CO2 release, but bicarbonate formation continues via carbonic anhydrase and is not prevented by oxygen binding.

exam_trap: Candidates choose 'deoxygenated haemoglobin carries less CO2', reversing the effect; deoxygenated haemoglobin carries more CO2, which is why oxygenation in the lungs releases it.
takeaway: Haldane effect: oxygenation in lungs → CO2 unloading.
source: Guyton & Hall, 14th ed (2021).
thinking: Haldane effect concerns how oxygenation alters CO2 carriage ↓ deoxygenated haemoglobin binds more CO2 and H+ ↓ oxygenation in the lungs reduces this capacity ↓ CO2 is released for exhalation ↓ Oxygenation of haemoglobin in the lungs facilitates release of CO2
pearl: The Haldane effect contributes, alongside worsened V/Q matching, to the rise in PaCO2 when some patients with chronic hypercapnic COPD are given uncontrolled high-concentration oxygen.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Physiology: carbon dioxide transport
stem: Most carbon dioxide in venous blood is transported in which form?
why_correct: Most CO2 is transported as bicarbonate following conversion within red blood cells through carbonic anhydrase-mediated reactions.

why_others_wrong.A: Dissolved CO2 accounts for only a small fraction of total CO2 transport (roughly 7%); it is far less than the bicarbonate fraction, which dominates.
why_others_wrong.B: Carbaminohaemoglobin carries a moderate proportion of CO2 (around a quarter) but this is less than the bicarbonate fraction, which is the largest component.
why_others_wrong.D: Carbonic acid is a short-lived intermediate that rapidly dissociates into bicarbonate and H+; it is not itself a major stable transport form.
why_others_wrong.E: Carbon monoxide is a distinct, toxic gas unrelated to normal physiological CO2 transport.

exam_trap: Carbon dioxide carriage in order of size: bicarbonate is largest, then carbamino compounds, then dissolved carbon dioxide.
takeaway: Most CO2 travels as HCO3−.
source: Guyton & Hall, 14th ed (2021).
thinking: CO2 diffuses into red cells ↓ carbonic anhydrase converts it to carbonic acid, which dissociates ↓ bicarbonate leaves the cell and is carried in plasma ↓ Bicarbonate
pearl: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors such as acetazolamide reduce renal bicarbonate reabsorption and can cause a hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Physiology: chloride shift
stem: In systemic capillaries, bicarbonate leaves the red cell in exchange for chloride. What is this process called?
why_correct: The chloride shift maintains electroneutrality as bicarbonate exits red cells during systemic CO2 transport. Chloride enters the red cell in exchange.

why_others_wrong.A: The Bohr effect describes how CO2/H+ affect haemoglobin's oxygen affinity, a different phenomenon from the bicarbonate-chloride exchange described here.
why_others_wrong.C: The Haldane effect describes how oxygenation state affects CO2-carrying capacity, not the ionic exchange across the red cell membrane.
why_others_wrong.D: The anion gap is a calculated value used to classify metabolic acidosis, not the process of bicarbonate-chloride exchange across the red cell membrane.
why_others_wrong.E: Countercurrent exchange is passive exchange between adjacent vessels with opposing flow, such as the vasa recta, and is unrelated to red cell anion exchange.

exam_trap: Candidates pick the Haldane effect (C) because it also concerns CO2 transport, but it describes oxygenation altering CO2 carriage, not bicarbonate-chloride exchange.
takeaway: Chloride shift maintains RBC electroneutrality during CO2 transport.
source: Guyton & Hall, 14th ed (2021).
thinking: CO2 enters red cells in systemic capillaries ↓ carbonic anhydrase forms H+ and HCO3− ↓ HCO3− leaves through the band 3 anion exchanger ↓ Cl− enters to preserve electroneutrality ↓ Chloride shift
pearl: Because chloride and water move into red cells as CO2 is loaded, venous red cells are slightly larger than arterial ones, and the shift reverses in the pulmonary capillaries.

subject: Anatomy
title: Hepatobiliary surgery: hepatic portal vein formation
stem: The portal vein is formed posterior to the neck of the pancreas by the union of which two vessels?

options.A: Splenic vein and superior mesenteric vein
options.B: Inferior mesenteric vein and inferior vena cava
options.C: Superior mesenteric artery and splenic artery
options.D: Left gastric vein and hepatic vein
options.E: Right gastric vein and superior mesenteric artery

correct_answer: A. Splenic vein and superior mesenteric vein
why_correct: The portal vein is formed by union of the splenic vein and superior mesenteric vein, usually posterior to the neck of the pancreas.

why_others_wrong.B: The inferior mesenteric vein most commonly drains into the splenic vein (or occasionally the SMV) rather than the IVC, and the IVC plays no role in forming the portal vein.
why_others_wrong.C: The superior mesenteric and splenic arteries are arterial vessels, not the veins that unite to form the portal vein.
why_others_wrong.D: Neither the left gastric vein nor the hepatic vein is involved in the union that forms the portal vein behind the pancreatic neck.
why_others_wrong.E: The right gastric vein is a small tributary that joins the portal vein later, and an artery (superior mesenteric artery) cannot unite with a vein to form the portal vein.

exam_trap: Inferior mesenteric vein and IVC is chosen because the IMV is a portal tributary, but it usually drains into the splenic vein, and the IVC is a systemic vein.
takeaway: Portal vein forms behind pancreatic neck.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: Portal vein formation ↓ occurs behind the neck of the pancreas ↓ union of two large veins ↓ the splenic vein (often with the IMV) joins the superior mesenteric vein ↓ Splenic vein and superior mesenteric vein
pearl: The SMV and portal vein run directly behind the pancreatic neck, so tumour contact with them is central to judging resectability before pancreaticoduodenectomy.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: hepatic veins
stem: Where do the major hepatic veins ultimately drain?
why_correct: The right, middle and left hepatic veins drain deoxygenated blood from the liver directly into the inferior vena cava.

why_others_wrong.A: The portal vein brings blood into the liver; hepatic veins carry blood out of it.
why_others_wrong.B: The splenic vein drains the spleen and joins the superior mesenteric vein to form the portal vein, which is inflow, not outflow.
why_others_wrong.D: The superior mesenteric vein drains the midgut into the portal vein and receives no hepatic venous blood.
why_others_wrong.E: The hepatic veins join the inferior vena cava just below the diaphragm; they do not reach the superior vena cava.

exam_trap: Portal vein is chosen by confusing liver inflow with outflow; the portal vein brings blood into the liver, while the hepatic veins drain it to the IVC.
takeaway: Hepatic veins → IVC.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: Hepatic veins drain blood out of the liver ↓ the portal vein and hepatic artery are the inflow ↓ hepatic veins leave the posterior liver ↓ they enter just below the diaphragm ↓ Inferior vena cava
pearl: The three hepatic veins mark the planes between liver segments, and their junction with the IVC is a hazardous area for bleeding in liver resection and trauma.

subject: Anatomy
title: Hepatobiliary surgery: cystic artery
stem: The cystic artery most commonly arises from which vessel?
why_correct: The cystic artery most commonly arises from the right hepatic artery, although anatomical variation is common.

why_others_wrong.A: The cystic artery typically arises from the right hepatic artery rather than the left, given the gallbladder's right-sided anatomical position.
why_others_wrong.C: The gastroduodenal artery supplies the pylorus, duodenum and pancreas via other branches and is not the typical origin of the cystic artery.
why_others_wrong.D: The splenic artery supplies the spleen and pancreas, anatomically distant from the gallbladder.
why_others_wrong.E: The superior mesenteric artery supplies midgut structures and has no direct relationship to gallbladder blood supply.

exam_trap: Gastroduodenal artery is chosen because some cystic arteries arise from it as a variant, but the commonest origin by far is the right hepatic artery.
takeaway: Cystic artery usually comes from right hepatic artery.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: Gallbladder lies under the right lobe ↓ the cystic artery usually arises within the hepatocystic triangle ↓ its commonest parent vessel is the right hepatic artery ↓ Right hepatic artery
pearl: Achieving the critical view of safety before clipping is essential at cholecystectomy, because the right hepatic artery can loop close to the gallbladder and be mistaken for the cystic artery.

subject: Anatomy
title: Acute abdomen & GI surgery: coeliac trunk
stem: Which structure is primarily supplied by the coeliac trunk?
why_correct: The coeliac trunk supplies the embryological foregut, including the stomach, proximal duodenum, liver, gallbladder, pancreas and spleen.

why_others_wrong.A: The jejunum is a midgut structure supplied by the superior mesenteric artery, not the coeliac trunk.
why_others_wrong.B: The ileum is also midgut, supplied by the superior mesenteric artery, not the coeliac trunk.
why_others_wrong.D: The ascending colon is a midgut derivative supplied by the SMA (via the ileocolic/right colic arteries), not the coeliac trunk.
why_others_wrong.E: The proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon is midgut territory supplied by the SMA (middle colic artery), not the coeliac trunk.

exam_trap: Proximal two-thirds of transverse colon is chosen because it lies near the stomach, but it is midgut supplied by the middle colic branch of the SMA.
takeaway: Stomach = coeliac territory.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: Coeliac trunk ↓ artery of the foregut ↓ the stomach is a foregut derivative ↓ every other option is midgut supplied by the SMA ↓ Stomach
pearl: The coeliac trunk arises at about T12 and divides into the left gastric, splenic and common hepatic arteries; compression by the median arcuate ligament can cause postprandial pain.

subject: Anatomy
title: Acute abdomen & GI surgery: inferior mesenteric artery
stem: Which structure is supplied by the inferior mesenteric artery?
why_correct: The inferior mesenteric artery supplies the embryological hindgut, including the distal one-third of the transverse colon, descending colon, sigmoid colon and upper rectum.

why_others_wrong.A: The jejunum is a midgut structure supplied by the superior mesenteric artery, not the IMA.
why_others_wrong.B: The caecum is a midgut structure supplied by the ileocolic branch of the SMA, not the IMA.
why_others_wrong.C: The appendix is supplied by the appendicular artery, part of the SMA system, not the IMA.
why_others_wrong.E: The proximal transverse colon is supplied by the middle colic artery from the SMA, not the IMA.

exam_trap: Proximal transverse colon is chosen because the transverse colon spans both territories, but its proximal two-thirds is midgut supplied by the middle colic artery from the SMA.
takeaway: IMA = distal transverse colon → descending → sigmoid → upper rectum.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: Inferior mesenteric artery ↓ artery of the hindgut ↓ territory runs from distal third of transverse colon to upper rectum ↓ the descending colon lies within it ↓ Descending colon
pearl: The IMA is ligated at or near its origin in left colon and rectal cancer surgery to remove the draining lymph nodes, leaving colonic perfusion dependent on the marginal artery.

subject: Anatomy
title: Physiology: portal versus systemic circulation
stem: Which statement about the hepatic portal circulation is correct?

options.A: It carries blood directly from the liver to the heart
options.B: It connects two capillary beds in series
options.C: It is formed entirely by arteries
options.D: It drains directly into the superior vena cava

correct_answer: B. It connects two capillary beds in series
why_correct: The portal system carries venous blood from gastrointestinal and splenic capillary beds through the portal vein to hepatic sinusoids, creating two capillary beds in series before systemic venous drainage.

why_others_wrong.A: This describes hepatic venous drainage carrying blood away from the liver toward the heart, not the portal system, which delivers blood to the liver from the gut.
why_others_wrong.C: The portal system is venous, formed by veins draining the gut and spleen, not formed by arteries.
why_others_wrong.D: Portal blood passes through hepatic sinusoids and hepatic veins into the inferior vena cava, not directly into the superior vena cava.
why_others_wrong.E: The defining feature of the hepatic portal system is that it specifically delivers gut/splenic venous blood to the liver, rather than bypassing it.

exam_trap: Option A is chosen by confusing portal inflow with hepatic venous outflow; the portal vein brings gut blood to the liver rather than from the liver to the heart.
takeaway: Portal system links GI/splenic capillaries to hepatic sinusoids.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: Hepatic portal circulation ↓ blood leaves gut and splenic capillary beds ↓ it is collected by the portal vein ↓ and delivered to a second bed in the hepatic sinusoids ↓ It connects two capillary beds in series
pearl: Portal blood passes through the liver before reaching the systemic circulation, which explains first-pass metabolism of oral drugs and why the liver is a common site of gut-derived metastases.

subject: Pharmacology
title: Pharmacology: renal clearance
stem: A substance is freely filtered at the glomerulus and is neither reabsorbed nor secreted by the renal tubules. Its renal clearance most closely approximates which physiological measurement?
why_correct: For a substance that is freely filtered and neither reabsorbed nor secreted, its clearance equals the GFR. Inulin is the classic example.

why_others_wrong.A: Renal plasma flow is estimated using a substance that is both filtered and secreted (e.g. PAH), not one handled by filtration alone.
why_others_wrong.C: Renal blood flow requires correcting renal plasma flow for haematocrit; it is not directly given by the clearance of a filtration-only marker.
why_others_wrong.D: Filtration fraction is the ratio of GFR to renal plasma flow, a derived ratio, not the clearance value itself.
why_others_wrong.E: Urine flow rate is a separate measured parameter used within the clearance calculation, not the physiological quantity the clearance value represents.

exam_trap: Renal plasma flow is chosen by candidates who confuse inulin with PAH, but PAH, which is filtered and secreted, estimates renal plasma flow; filtration-only markers measure GFR.
takeaway: Filtered only → clearance = GFR.
source: Guyton & Hall, 14th ed (2021).
thinking: Substance freely filtered ↓ neither reabsorbed nor secreted ↓ the amount excreted equals the amount filtered ↓ clearance therefore equals the filtration rate ↓ Glomerular filtration rate
pearl: Inulin clearance is the gold-standard GFR measure, but in practice creatinine is used; because creatinine is slightly secreted by the tubules, creatinine clearance modestly overestimates GFR.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: renal autoregulation
stem: A sudden moderate rise in systemic arterial pressure occurs in a healthy person. Which mechanism helps prevent a large increase in renal blood flow?

options.C: Increased renin secretion as the sole mechanism

why_correct: The renal myogenic mechanism causes afferent arteriolar constriction in response to increased vascular stretch, helping stabilise renal blood flow and GFR.

why_others_wrong.B: Complete efferent arteriolar paralysis is not a recognised autoregulatory response and would not explain the stabilisation of renal blood flow with rising pressure.
why_others_wrong.C: Renin-mediated changes act over a longer timescale via the renin-angiotensin system and are not the immediate mechanism, nor is renin release the sole contributor to autoregulation.
why_others_wrong.D: ADH regulates water reabsorption in the collecting duct and is not part of the rapid myogenic autoregulatory response to a pressure rise.
why_others_wrong.E: Glucose is reabsorbed, not secreted, by the proximal tubule, and glucose handling plays no role in renal blood flow autoregulation.

exam_trap: Candidates choosing renin (C) pick a slower hormonal system; the immediate intrinsic response to stretch is afferent arteriolar myogenic constriction, supported by tubuloglomerular feedback.
takeaway: Renal pressure rises → afferent arteriole constricts → protects GFR.
source: Guyton & Hall, 14th ed (2021).
thinking: Sudden rise in arterial pressure ↓ afferent arteriolar wall is stretched ↓ smooth muscle contracts within seconds ↓ renal blood flow and GFR stay stable ↓ Afferent arteriolar myogenic constriction
pearl: Chronic hypertension shifts the autoregulatory range upwards, so rapid lowering of blood pressure in such patients can reduce renal perfusion and GFR.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: macula densa
stem: The macula densa primarily senses which variable?
why_correct: Macula densa cells in the distal nephron sense tubular NaCl delivery and participate in tubuloglomerular feedback and renin regulation.

why_others_wrong.A: Plasma glucose is not the variable sensed by the macula densa; its role concerns tubular fluid composition, not systemic glucose.
why_others_wrong.C: Plasma calcium is regulated by other systems (PTH, calcitriol); it is not what the macula densa detects.
why_others_wrong.D: Urine protein concentration is unrelated to macula densa function, which centres on distal tubular NaCl delivery.
why_others_wrong.E: Renal venous oxygen saturation is not the signal sensed by the macula densa in tubuloglomerular feedback.

exam_trap: Candidates may choose plasma glucose (A) or calcium (C) as systemic variables, but the macula densa senses distal tubular NaCl delivery, not plasma composition.
takeaway: NaCl delivery at macula densa helps regulate GFR and renin.
source: Guyton & Hall, 14th ed (2021).
thinking: Macula densa cells in the distal tubule wall ↓ apical NKCC2 senses luminal NaCl ↓ signals afferent arteriolar tone and renin release ↓ Tubular sodium chloride concentration
pearl: SGLT2 inhibitors increase NaCl delivery to the macula densa, triggering afferent vasoconstriction that lowers intraglomerular pressure, part of their renoprotective effect.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: tubuloglomerular feedback
stem: Increased NaCl delivery to the macula densa normally produces which renal response?

options.A: Afferent arteriolar dilatation and increased renin release
options.B: Afferent arteriolar constriction and reduced renin release
options.D: Increased ADH secretion from the posterior pituitary

correct_answer: B. Afferent arteriolar constriction and reduced renin release
why_correct: High distal tubular NaCl delivery signals that filtration may be excessive. Tubuloglomerular feedback promotes afferent arteriolar constriction and suppresses renin release.

why_others_wrong.A: This is the opposite response; high distal NaCl delivery causes afferent arteriolar constriction and reduced renin release, not dilatation and increased renin.
why_others_wrong.C: The tubuloglomerular feedback mechanism acts through afferent arteriolar constriction, not through obstruction of the efferent arteriole.
why_others_wrong.D: ADH secretion from the posterior pituitary is regulated by osmolality and volume status, not directly by macula densa NaCl sensing in this feedback loop.
why_others_wrong.E: Erythropoietin release is triggered by tissue hypoxia via a separate pathway and is not part of the tubuloglomerular feedback response to NaCl delivery.

exam_trap: Candidates choosing A reverse the response; high NaCl at the macula densa signals excess filtration, so the afferent arteriole constricts and renin release falls.
takeaway: Macula densa high NaCl → afferent constriction + ↓ renin.
source: Guyton & Hall, 14th ed (2021).
thinking: High distal NaCl delivery signals excess filtration ↓ macula densa releases local mediators such as adenosine ↓ afferent arteriole constricts, lowering GFR ↓ renin release is suppressed ↓ Afferent arteriolar constriction and reduced renin release
pearl: Adenosine is a key mediator of this afferent constriction, making the kidney one of the few vascular beds where adenosine causes vasoconstriction rather than vasodilatation.

subject: Physiology
title: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care: fgf23
stem: Which hormone primarily promotes renal phosphate excretion and suppresses renal calcitriol production?
why_correct: Fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23), produced predominantly by osteocytes and osteoblast-lineage cells, reduces renal phosphate reabsorption and suppresses 1α-hydroxylase activity, thereby reducing calcitriol production.

why_others_wrong.A: Aldosterone regulates distal nephron sodium and potassium handling and does not primarily control phosphate excretion or calcitriol production.
why_others_wrong.C: Calcitonin acts mainly to inhibit osteoclast activity and lower plasma calcium; it is not the principal regulator of renal phosphate excretion or calcitriol suppression.
why_others_wrong.D: ADH regulates collecting-duct water permeability and has no established role in phosphate handling or calcitriol suppression.
why_others_wrong.E: Growth hormone has broader metabolic and growth-promoting effects but is not the primary hormone responsible for renal phosphate excretion and calcitriol suppression.

exam_trap: PTH and FGF23 both promote phosphate excretion, but FGF23 also suppresses calcitriol.
takeaway: FGF23 → phosphate excretion ↑ + calcitriol ↓.
source: Guyton & Hall, 14th ed (2021).
thinking: Increases phosphate excretion and suppresses calcitriol ↓ PTH raises calcitriol, so it does not fit ↓ FGF23 from osteocytes does both ↓ FGF23
pearl: Raised FGF23 in chronic kidney disease is associated with left ventricular hypertrophy and mortality, making it a marker of the severity of mineral and bone disorder.

subject: Pharmacology
title: Pharmacology: calcium-sensing receptor
stem: A rise in extracellular calcium is detected by which receptor?
why_correct: The calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR) detects extracellular calcium concentrations, particularly in the parathyroid glands and kidneys.

why_others_wrong.A: The mineralocorticoid receptor binds aldosterone and regulates sodium/potassium handling; it is not the sensor for extracellular calcium.
why_others_wrong.C: V2 receptors respond to ADH to regulate renal water reabsorption, unrelated to calcium sensing.
why_others_wrong.D: AT1 receptors mediate angiotensin II effects such as vasoconstriction and aldosterone release, not calcium detection.
why_others_wrong.E: The insulin receptor is a tyrosine kinase receptor involved in glucose regulation, unrelated to extracellular calcium sensing.

exam_trap: Mineralocorticoid receptor may be chosen by candidates who link electrolyte sensing with hormone receptors, but it binds aldosterone; extracellular calcium is detected by the calcium-sensing receptor.
takeaway: High extracellular Ca2+ sensed by CaSR → PTH suppression.
source: Guyton & Hall, 14th ed (2021).
thinking: Rise in extracellular calcium ↓ detected by a G-protein-coupled sensor on parathyroid chief cells and in the kidney ↓ activation suppresses PTH release ↓ Calcium-sensing receptor
pearl: Inactivating CaSR mutations cause familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia, which mimics primary hyperparathyroidism but has low urinary calcium and is not treated by parathyroidectomy; cinacalcet is a CaSR agonist.

subject: Physiology
title: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care: pth and phosphate
stem: A patient develops increased PTH secretion. Which renal change is expected?

options.B: Reduced phosphate reabsorption in the proximal tubule
options.E: Increased urinary calcium excretion as the principal direct effect

correct_answer: B. Reduced phosphate reabsorption in the proximal tubule
why_correct: PTH decreases proximal tubular phosphate reabsorption, increasing urinary phosphate excretion. It simultaneously promotes renal calcium reabsorption and stimulates calcitriol production.

why_others_wrong.A: This is the opposite of PTH's action; PTH decreases, rather than increases, proximal tubular phosphate reabsorption.
why_others_wrong.C: PTH promotes, rather than inhibits, renal calcium reabsorption; complete inhibition is the opposite of its physiological effect.
why_others_wrong.D: PTH stimulates renal 1α-hydroxylase, increasing calcitriol production, rather than reducing it.
why_others_wrong.E: PTH's principal direct renal calcium effect is to increase reabsorption (reducing excretion), not to increase urinary calcium loss as its main action.

exam_trap: Candidates choosing E recall the hypercalciuria of hyperparathyroidism, but PTH's direct renal effect increases calcium reabsorption; urinary calcium rises only from the higher filtered load.
takeaway: PTH = Ca retention + phosphate wasting + calcitriol activation.
source: Guyton & Hall, 14th ed (2021).
thinking: Increased PTH ↓ acts on the proximal tubule ↓ sodium-phosphate cotransporters removed from the membrane ↓ phosphate reabsorption falls ↓ Reduced phosphate reabsorption in the proximal tubule
pearl: Despite its direct calcium-sparing action, high PTH often causes hypercalciuria because the filtered calcium load rises, explaining the renal stones of hyperparathyroidism.

subject: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care
title: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care: adrenal cortex
stem: Which adrenal cortical zone produces aldosterone?
why_correct: The adrenal cortex follows the mnemonic GFR: glomerulosa → mineralocorticoids; fasciculata → glucocorticoids; reticularis → androgens.

why_others_wrong.B: The zona fasciculata produces glucocorticoids, mainly cortisol, under ACTH control rather than aldosterone.
why_others_wrong.C: The zona reticularis produces adrenal androgens such as DHEA, not the mineralocorticoid aldosterone.
why_others_wrong.D: The adrenal medulla is neural crest tissue that secretes catecholamines, not steroid hormones such as aldosterone.
why_others_wrong.E: The capsule is a connective tissue covering of the gland and does not synthesise hormones.

exam_trap: Candidates choose zona fasciculata because it is the largest cortical zone, but it produces cortisol; aldosterone comes from the outermost zona glomerulosa.
takeaway: Glomerulosa = aldosterone.
source: Guyton & Hall, 14th ed (2021).
thinking: Adrenal cortex zones from outside in ↓ glomerulosa, fasciculata, reticularis ↓ glomerulosa makes mineralocorticoids ↓ aldosterone is the mineralocorticoid ↓ Zona glomerulosa
pearl: Aldosterone secretion is driven mainly by angiotensin II and potassium rather than ACTH, so mineralocorticoid function is preserved in secondary adrenal insufficiency.

subject: Physiology
title: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care: cortisol and glucose
stem: Which metabolic effect is associated with cortisol?

options.A: Increased peripheral glucose uptake as its dominant effect
options.C: Complete inhibition of hepatic glucose production
options.E: Immediate stimulation of insulin secretion as its main action

why_correct: Cortisol promotes gluconeogenesis and contributes to the metabolic response to stress. It also has permissive effects on catecholamine-mediated vascular responses and contributes to insulin resistance.

why_others_wrong.A: Cortisol tends to reduce, not increase, peripheral glucose uptake, contributing to insulin resistance rather than enhanced glucose disposal.
why_others_wrong.C: Cortisol promotes hepatic glucose output through gluconeogenesis rather than inhibiting it.
why_others_wrong.D: Cortisol has a permissive effect that enhances, rather than reduces, tissue responsiveness to catecholamines.
why_others_wrong.E: Cortisol's dominant metabolic role is to antagonise insulin action and raise glucose, not to directly stimulate insulin secretion as its main effect.

exam_trap: Candidates choosing D miss cortisol's permissive role; it enhances vascular responsiveness to catecholamines rather than reducing it, and it raises glucose via gluconeogenesis.
takeaway: Cortisol → gluconeogenesis + insulin resistance + permissive catecholamine effects.
source: Guyton & Hall, 14th ed (2021).
thinking: Cortisol is a counter-regulatory hormone ↓ promotes hepatic gluconeogenesis ↓ reduces peripheral glucose uptake ↓ raises blood glucose ↓ Increased gluconeogenesis
pearl: Hyperglycaemia from a single morning dose of prednisolone typically peaks in the afternoon and evening, so glucose monitoring should be timed accordingly.

subject: Physiology
title: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care: thyroid hormone receptor
stem: How do thyroid hormones principally exert their effects at target cells?

options.A: Through a cell-surface G-protein receptor only
options.B: Through intracellular/nuclear receptors regulating gene transcription
options.C: Through direct activation of voltage-gated sodium channels

correct_answer: B. Through intracellular/nuclear receptors regulating gene transcription
why_correct: Thyroid hormones enter cells and interact with nuclear thyroid hormone receptors that regulate transcription of target genes. Their physiological effects therefore develop over a relatively longer timescale than many membrane-receptor-mediated responses.

why_others_wrong.A: Thyroid hormones act via intracellular/nuclear receptors that regulate gene transcription, not through cell-surface G-protein-coupled receptors.
why_others_wrong.C: Thyroid hormones do not act by directly gating voltage-sensitive ion channels; their principal mechanism is nuclear receptor-mediated transcriptional regulation.
why_others_wrong.D: Thyroid hormone signalling occurs through its own distinct nuclear receptor family, unrelated to the insulin receptor pathway.
why_others_wrong.E: The V2 receptor mediates vasopressin (ADH) action in the renal collecting duct and is unrelated to thyroid hormone signalling.

exam_trap: Candidates choosing A apply peptide-hormone signalling; thyroid hormones are transported into cells and act through nuclear receptors rather than via cell-surface G-protein receptors.
takeaway: Thyroid hormone → intracellular/nuclear receptor → altered gene transcription.
source: Guyton & Hall, 14th ed (2021).
thinking: Thyroid hormones enter cells via membrane transporters ↓ T4 is converted to T3 ↓ T3 binds nuclear receptors on DNA ↓ gene transcription is altered ↓ Through intracellular/nuclear receptors regulating gene transcription
pearl: Because effects depend on gene transcription, the full response to a levothyroxine dose change takes several weeks, so TSH is rechecked after about six to eight weeks.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: corticospinal tract
stem: A patient develops weakness of the right arm and leg following a small lesion in the left posterior limb of the internal capsule. Which tract is primarily affected?
why_correct: The posterior limb of the internal capsule contains major descending corticospinal fibres. A lesion above the pyramidal decussation produces contralateral upper motor neuron weakness.

why_others_wrong.A: The spinothalamic tract carries pain and temperature and does not cause limb weakness when damaged.
why_others_wrong.C: The dorsal columns carry proprioception, vibration and fine touch, so their loss causes sensory ataxia rather than weakness.
why_others_wrong.D: The medial longitudinal fasciculus is a brainstem pathway coordinating eye movements, not limb power.
why_others_wrong.E: Spinocerebellar tracts carry unconscious proprioception to the cerebellum and do not pass through the internal capsule.

exam_trap: Internal capsule lesions can produce dense contralateral weakness because motor fibres are tightly packed.
takeaway: Internal capsule corticospinal lesion → contralateral UMN weakness.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: Right arm and leg weakness ↓ lesion in left posterior limb of internal capsule ↓ descending motor fibres packed there, above the pyramidal decussation ↓ contralateral upper motor neuron weakness ↓ Corticospinal tract
pearl: Small deep (lacunar) infarcts of the internal capsule can produce a pure motor hemiparesis of face, arm and leg without cortical signs such as dysphasia or visual field loss.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: pyramidal decussation
stem: Where do most corticospinal fibres cross from one side of the nervous system to the other?
why_correct: Most corticospinal fibres cross at the pyramidal decussation in the caudal medulla before descending in the lateral corticospinal tract.

why_others_wrong.A: Corticospinal fibres pass uncrossed through the cerebral peduncles of the midbrain.
why_others_wrong.B: In the pons corticospinal fibres are broken into bundles by pontine nuclei but remain uncrossed.
why_others_wrong.D: The thalamus is a sensory relay; corticospinal fibres pass lateral to it in the internal capsule without crossing.
why_others_wrong.E: The internal capsule carries corticospinal fibres on the same side as their cortex of origin; no crossing occurs there.

exam_trap: Midbrain is chosen because crossed brainstem syndromes occur there, but corticospinal fibres pass through the cerebral peduncles uncrossed and decussate in the caudal medulla.
takeaway: Corticospinal crossing = caudal medulla.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: Corticospinal fibres descend uncrossed through internal capsule, peduncles and pons ↓ they form the pyramids on the front of the medulla ↓ most cross at the caudal end of the medulla ↓ Medullary pyramids
pearl: Lesions above the pyramidal decussation cause contralateral upper motor neurone weakness, whereas spinal cord lesions below it cause ipsilateral weakness.

subject: Anatomy
title: Physiology: brown-séquard syndrome
stem: A patient sustains a hemisection of the right side of the spinal cord at T10. Which combination is most likely below the lesion?

options.A: Left-sided loss of vibration and right-sided loss of pain
options.B: Right-sided loss of vibration and proprioception with left-sided loss of pain and temperature
options.D: Right-sided loss of pain with bilateral motor paralysis
options.E: Left-sided motor paralysis with right-sided proprioceptive loss

correct_answer: B. Right-sided loss of vibration and proprioception with left-sided loss of pain and temperature
why_correct: A right hemisection causes right-sided weakness and loss of vibration and proprioception below the lesion, with left-sided loss of pain and temperature.

why_others_wrong.A: This reverses the true pattern: dorsal column loss (vibration) should be ipsilateral to the lesion (right), while pain loss should be contralateral (left), not as stated here.
why_others_wrong.C: A hemisection produces unilateral, ipsilateral dorsal column loss, not bilateral proprioceptive loss, and motor and pain pathways are also affected, not spared.
why_others_wrong.D: Pain/temperature loss from a right hemisection should be contralateral (left), not right-sided, and motor paralysis is ipsilateral only, not bilateral.
why_others_wrong.E: Motor paralysis from a right-sided hemisection is ipsilateral (right-sided), not left-sided, so this option reverses the correct laterality.

exam_trap: Option A is chosen by reversing the laterality; dorsal column loss is ipsilateral to the hemisection, whereas pain and temperature loss is contralateral.
takeaway: Cord hemisection → same-side motor/proprioception, opposite-side pain/temp.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: Right hemisection at T10 ↓ corticospinal and dorsal column fibres are ipsilateral within the cord ↓ spinothalamic fibres have already crossed near their entry level ↓ right weakness and dorsal column loss, left pain and temperature loss ↓ Right-sided loss of vibration and proprioception with left-sided loss of pain and temperature
pearl: A pure cord hemisection is rare; penetrating trauma and asymmetric compression more often produce partial Brown-Séquard patterns, which carry a relatively good prognosis among incomplete cord syndromes.

subject: Anatomy
title: Major trauma & fluids: anterior cord syndrome
stem: A patient develops paraplegia and bilateral loss of pain and temperature after spinal cord infarction. Which pathway is most likely spared?
why_correct: Anterior cord syndrome affects the anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord, including corticospinal and spinothalamic pathways, while the posterior columns are relatively spared.

why_others_wrong.A: The corticospinal tract lies within the anterior two-thirds of the cord and is affected in anterior cord syndrome (causing paraplegia), not spared.
why_others_wrong.B: The spinothalamic tract also lies in the anterior two-thirds of the cord and is affected (causing bilateral pain/temperature loss), not spared.
why_others_wrong.C: Anterior horn cells lie within the anterior spinal artery's territory and are affected by the infarction, not spared.
why_others_wrong.E: The anterior spinal artery territory is precisely the region that is infarcted in this syndrome, not the spared structure.

exam_trap: Anterior spinal artery territory is chosen because it sounds anatomical, but that is the infarcted region; the dorsal columns are spared because the posterior spinal arteries supply them.
takeaway: Anterior cord → motor + pain/temp lost; dorsal columns relatively spared.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: Spinal cord infarction with paraplegia ↓ bilateral loss of pain and temperature ↓ the anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior two-thirds of the cord ↓ posterior spinal arteries supply the dorsal columns ↓ Dorsal columns
pearl: Anterior cord infarction is a recognised complication of thoracoabdominal aortic aneurysm repair, partly because the main segmental feeder to the anterior spinal artery can be interrupted.

subject: Anatomy
title: Physiology: posterior columns
stem: Which modality is primarily transmitted in the dorsal columns of the spinal cord?
why_correct: The dorsal columns carry vibration, conscious proprioception and discriminative/fine touch.

why_others_wrong.A: Pain is carried by the spinothalamic tract, not the dorsal columns.
why_others_wrong.B: Temperature is also carried by the spinothalamic tract, not the dorsal columns.
why_others_wrong.D: Motor output is carried by descending tracts such as the corticospinal tract, whereas the dorsal columns are an ascending sensory pathway.
why_others_wrong.E: Autonomic sympathetic activity travels via distinct pathways such as the intermediolateral cell column outflow, not the dorsal columns.

exam_trap: Dorsal column fibres ascend ipsilaterally and cross in the medulla, whereas spinothalamic fibres cross within a segment or two of entering the cord.
takeaway: Dorsal column = vibration + proprioception + fine touch.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: Dorsal columns ↓ ascending sensory pathway in the posterior cord ↓ carry vibration, conscious proprioception and fine touch ↓ Vibration
pearl: Vitamin B12 deficiency (subacute combined degeneration) and tabes dorsalis selectively damage the dorsal columns, causing sensory ataxia that worsens when the eyes are closed.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: spinothalamic decussation
stem: A patient has a small lesion affecting the left anterolateral spinal cord. Which sensory deficit would be expected below the lesion?

options.C: Right-sided loss of pain and temperature

correct_answer: C. Right-sided loss of pain and temperature
why_correct: Spinothalamic fibres carrying pain and temperature cross within the spinal cord, usually through the anterior white commissure, and then ascend contralaterally.

why_others_wrong.A: Vibration travels in the dorsal columns, which lie posteriorly and are spared by an anterolateral lesion.
why_others_wrong.B: Proprioception is carried in the dorsal columns, not the anterolateral cord.
why_others_wrong.D: A small unilateral lesion cannot cause bilateral dorsal column loss, and the dorsal columns are posterior in any case.
why_others_wrong.E: Corticospinal fibres in the cord are already crossed, so any motor loss would be left-sided, and the question asks about sensation.

exam_trap: Spinothalamic crossing occurs near the level of entry in the spinal cord; dorsal-column crossing occurs in the medulla.
takeaway: Pain/temp cross in spinal cord; vibration/proprioception cross in medulla.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: Left anterolateral cord lesion ↓ the spinothalamic tract lies anterolaterally ↓ its fibres crossed in the anterior white commissure near their entry level ↓ the deficit appears on the opposite side ↓ Right-sided loss of pain and temperature
pearl: A central cord lesion such as syringomyelia first damages the crossing fibres in the anterior white commissure, producing bilateral cape-like loss of pain and temperature with preserved touch.

subject: Anatomy
title: Physiology: medial lemniscus
stem: The medial lemniscus carries which information after decussation in the medulla?
why_correct: Dorsal-column fibres synapse in the gracile and cuneate nuclei, cross as internal arcuate fibres in the medulla and then ascend as the medial lemniscus carrying contralateral discriminative sensation.

why_others_wrong.A: Pain and temperature are carried by the spinothalamic tract, which decussates at spinal cord level, not by the medial lemniscus.
why_others_wrong.B: The medial lemniscus is an ascending sensory pathway, not a motor one, so it does not carry motor information.
why_others_wrong.D: Auditory information ascends via the lateral lemniscus and auditory pathways, not the medial lemniscus.
why_others_wrong.E: Autonomic output travels via separate descending and peripheral pathways, not the medial lemniscus.

exam_trap: Once dorsal-column fibres cross in the medulla, they become the medial lemniscus.
takeaway: Medial lemniscus = contralateral vibration/proprioception/fine touch.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: Dorsal columns ascend ipsilaterally ↓ synapse in gracile and cuneate nuclei ↓ cross as internal arcuate fibres in the medulla ↓ ascend as the medial lemniscus ↓ Contralateral vibration and proprioception
pearl: A cord lesion gives loss of vibration and proprioception on the same side below it, whereas a lesion above the medullary decussation gives contralateral loss, which helps localise the level.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: thalamic sensory relay
stem: Which thalamic nucleus is the major relay for somatosensory information from the body to the cerebral cortex?
why_correct: The ventral posterolateral (VPL) nucleus relays somatosensory information from the body. The VPM principally receives facial somatosensory information and taste.

why_others_wrong.B: The ventral posteromedial nucleus relays trigeminal sensation from the face and taste, not from the body.
why_others_wrong.C: The lateral geniculate nucleus relays visual information from the optic tract to the visual cortex.
why_others_wrong.D: The medial geniculate nucleus relays auditory information to the auditory cortex.
why_others_wrong.E: The anterior nucleus is part of the limbic (Papez) circuit, linking the mammillary bodies to the cingulate gyrus.

exam_trap: Ventral posteromedial nucleus is chosen because it is the neighbouring sensory relay, but it serves trigeminal sensation from the face and taste, not the body.
takeaway: Body sensation → VPL; face sensation → VPM.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: Somatosensation from the body ↓ dorsal column and spinothalamic pathways ascend to the thalamus ↓ body sensation relays laterally in the ventral posterior complex; the face medially ↓ Ventral posterolateral nucleus
pearl: A small thalamic lacunar infarct can cause a pure sensory stroke of the contralateral face, arm and leg and may later be followed by central post-stroke pain.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: trigeminal sensory relay
stem: Which thalamic nucleus principally relays somatosensory information from the face?
why_correct: The ventral posteromedial nucleus receives major sensory input from the face through trigeminal pathways.

why_others_wrong.A: The ventral posterolateral nucleus relays somatosensation from the body and limbs, not the face.
why_others_wrong.C: The lateral geniculate nucleus is the visual relay nucleus of the thalamus.
why_others_wrong.D: The medial geniculate nucleus is the auditory relay nucleus of the thalamus.
why_others_wrong.E: The pulvinar is involved in visual attention and association, not primary facial sensory relay.

exam_trap: The “M” in VPM can help recall “mouth/face”; the “L” in VPL can help recall the limb/body.
takeaway: Trigeminal sensory information → VPM.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: Somatosensory relay from the face ↓ trigeminal pathways ascend to the ventral posterior thalamus ↓ VPL serves the body and limbs, VPM serves the face ↓ VPM
pearl: VPM also relays taste from the nucleus of the solitary tract, and a small infarct in the ventral posterior thalamus produces a pure contralateral hemisensory loss of face, arm and leg.

subject: Anatomy
title: Physiology: corticobulbar tract
stem: A lesion affecting corticobulbar fibres above the facial nucleus typically causes which pattern of facial weakness?

options.B: Complete contralateral facial paralysis including forehead
options.C: Contralateral lower facial weakness with relative forehead sparing
options.D: Bilateral upper and lower facial paralysis

correct_answer: C. Contralateral lower facial weakness with relative forehead sparing
why_correct: The upper facial nucleus receives bilateral cortical input, whereas the lower facial nucleus receives predominantly contralateral cortical input. A unilateral supranuclear lesion therefore causes contralateral lower facial weakness with relative forehead sparing.

why_others_wrong.A: Complete ipsilateral facial paralysis describes a lower motor neuron lesion of the facial nerve or nucleus, not an upper motor neuron corticobulbar lesion.
why_others_wrong.B: The forehead is spared in a supranuclear lesion because the upper facial muscles receive bilateral cortical input; complete contralateral paralysis including the forehead does not occur.
why_others_wrong.D: Bilateral upper and lower facial paralysis would suggest bilateral corticobulbar or bilateral lower motor neuron lesions, not a single unilateral supranuclear lesion.
why_others_wrong.E: The forehead is spared rather than selectively paralysed, and any weakness from a supranuclear lesion is contralateral, not ipsilateral.

exam_trap: UMN facial weakness = contralateral lower face with forehead sparing. LMN facial weakness = whole ipsilateral face.
takeaway: Forehead sparing → think supranuclear corticobulbar lesion.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: Lesion of corticobulbar fibres above the facial nucleus ↓ upper motor neuron lesion ↓ upper facial nucleus has bilateral cortical input; lower facial nucleus mainly contralateral ↓ Contralateral lower facial weakness with relative forehead sparing
pearl: Forehead sparing is the key bedside sign separating a cortical or internal capsule stroke from a lower motor neuron facial palsy, which involves the whole hemiface and can prevent eye closure.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: facial nerve nucleus
stem: A lesion of the left facial nerve nucleus in the pons would most likely cause:
why_correct: A lesion involving the facial nucleus or facial nerve after its nuclear origin produces a lower motor neuron pattern affecting the entire ipsilateral side of the face.

why_others_wrong.A: Lower facial weakness with forehead sparing indicates an upper motor neuron lesion, whereas nuclear damage affects the whole ipsilateral face.
why_others_wrong.B: The facial nucleus supplies the same side, so a left nuclear lesion does not cause right facial weakness.
why_others_wrong.D: A unilateral nuclear lesion does not cause bilateral weakness, and it involves more than the forehead.
why_others_wrong.E: Facial sensation is trigeminal; a facial motor nucleus lesion causes weakness, not sensory loss.

exam_trap: Candidates pick A by recalling forehead sparing, but that is the upper motor neuron pattern; a nuclear lesion is lower motor neuron and paralyses the whole ipsilateral face.
takeaway: Facial nucleus lesion → ipsilateral LMN facial palsy.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: Lesion of the left facial nucleus in the pons ↓ the nucleus is the lower motor neuron ↓ every ipsilateral muscle of facial expression loses its supply, forehead included ↓ Left whole-face weakness
pearl: Facial nerve fibres loop around the abducens nucleus at the facial colliculus, so a dorsal pontine lesion often combines an ipsilateral lower motor neuron facial palsy with lateral rectus or horizontal gaze weakness.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: oculomotor nerve
stem: A patient has a complete right oculomotor nerve palsy. Which eye position is most characteristic?
why_correct: CN III supplies medial rectus, superior rectus, inferior rectus and inferior oblique, as well as levator palpebrae. With CN III paralysis, the intact lateral rectus and superior oblique pull the eye laterally and downward.

why_others_wrong.B: Adduction and elevation depend on medial rectus, superior rectus and inferior oblique, all of which are paralysed in third nerve palsy.
why_others_wrong.C: Elevation requires superior rectus and inferior oblique, both lost in oculomotor palsy, so the eye cannot sit elevated.
why_others_wrong.D: The unopposed lateral rectus and superior oblique pull the eye out of neutral into a down-and-out position.
why_others_wrong.E: Adduction needs the medial rectus, which is paralysed, so the eye is abducted rather than adducted.

exam_trap: Candidates choose E because they remember the eye is down, but medial rectus is paralysed and unopposed lateral rectus abducts it: down and out, not down and in.
takeaway: CN III palsy → down-and-out eye ± ptosis/pupil involvement.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: Complete CN III palsy ↓ medial, superior and inferior rectus, inferior oblique and levator paralysed ↓ only lateral rectus (VI) and superior oblique (IV) still act ↓ Abducted and depressed
pearl: A third nerve palsy with a dilated pupil suggests compression, classically a posterior communicating artery aneurysm, and needs urgent vascular imaging; pupil-sparing palsies are more often microvascular, for example in diabetes.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: trochlear nerve
stem: Which extraocular muscle is supplied by the trochlear nerve?
why_correct: The trochlear nerve (CN IV) supplies the superior oblique muscle.

why_others_wrong.A: Lateral rectus is supplied by the abducens nerve (CN VI).
why_others_wrong.C: Medial rectus is supplied by the inferior division of the oculomotor nerve.
why_others_wrong.D: Inferior oblique is supplied by the inferior division of the oculomotor nerve.
why_others_wrong.E: Superior rectus is supplied by the superior division of the oculomotor nerve.

exam_trap: Candidates reverse the two obliques and pick D; inferior oblique is supplied by the oculomotor nerve, whereas CN IV supplies only superior oblique.
takeaway: CN IV → superior oblique.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: Trochlear nerve = CN IV ↓ LR6 SO4, all the rest III ↓ the trochlea is the pulley of superior oblique ↓ Superior oblique
pearl: Trochlear palsy causes vertical diplopia worst on looking down and in, such as reading or descending stairs, and patients often tilt the head away from the affected side to compensate.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: abducens nerve
stem: A lesion of the left abducens nerve produces which deficit?

options.E: Bilateral inability to elevate the eyes

correct_answer: A. Failure of left eye abduction
why_correct: CN VI supplies the lateral rectus, which abducts the eye. A left abducens palsy therefore causes impaired abduction of the left eye and horizontal diplopia.

why_others_wrong.B: Adduction depends on medial rectus, supplied by the oculomotor nerve, so it is preserved in abducens palsy.
why_others_wrong.C: Ptosis follows oculomotor or sympathetic lesions, and a left nerve lesion would not affect the right eyelid.
why_others_wrong.D: Pupillary constriction is parasympathetic via the oculomotor nerve; the abducens carries no pupillary fibres.
why_others_wrong.E: Elevation is by superior rectus and inferior oblique (CN III), and a single abducens lesion is unilateral.

exam_trap: Candidates drawn to ptosis or pupil options (C, D) forget that the abducens carries no eyelid or pupillary fibres; its lesion causes ipsilateral failure of abduction only.
takeaway: CN VI palsy → ipsilateral failure of abduction.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: Left CN VI lesion ↓ CN VI supplies only lateral rectus ↓ lateral rectus abducts the eye ↓ Failure of left eye abduction
pearl: The abducens has a long intracranial course and bends over the petrous apex, so a sixth nerve palsy can be a false localising sign of raised intracranial pressure.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: cavernous sinus
stem: Which cranial nerve lies within the cavernous sinus alongside the internal carotid artery?
why_correct: CN VI travels within the cavernous sinus alongside the internal carotid artery. Cranial nerves III, IV, V1 and V2 are located in the lateral wall.

why_others_wrong.A: The optic nerve passes through the optic canal, superomedial to the cavernous sinus.
why_others_wrong.B: The olfactory nerve passes through the cribriform plate in the anterior cranial fossa.
why_others_wrong.D: The facial nerve enters the internal acoustic meatus in the posterior cranial fossa.
why_others_wrong.E: The hypoglossal nerve leaves through the hypoglossal canal near the foramen magnum.

exam_trap: Within cavernous sinus proper: ICA + VI. Lateral wall: III, IV, V1, V2.
takeaway: CN VI is the cranial nerve running beside the ICA inside the cavernous sinus.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: Nerve lying inside the cavernous sinus beside the ICA ↓ III, IV, V1 and V2 sit in the lateral wall ↓ only one cranial nerve runs free within the sinus ↓ Abducens nerve
pearl: An intracavernous carotid aneurysm or carotid-cavernous fistula often affects CN VI first; a fistula also causes pulsatile proptosis, chemosis and an orbital bruit.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: cavernous sinus lesion
stem: A patient with a cavernous sinus lesion develops ophthalmoplegia, loss of corneal sensation and impaired abduction. Which combination of cranial nerves is involved?

options.B: III, IV, V1, V2 and VI

correct_answer: B. III, IV, V1, V2 and VI
why_correct: The cavernous sinus contains CN III, IV, V1 and V2 in its lateral wall and CN VI with the internal carotid artery within the sinus.

why_others_wrong.A: The optic nerve lies outside the sinus, and VII and VIII enter the internal acoustic meatus, not the cavernous sinus.
why_others_wrong.C: V3 leaves via the foramen ovale, and VII, IX and X are posterior fossa nerves unrelated to the cavernous sinus.
why_others_wrong.D: IX to XII are lower cranial nerves of the jugular foramen and hypoglossal canal, not the cavernous sinus.
why_others_wrong.E: The olfactory and optic nerves do not traverse the cavernous sinus, and this set omits the nerves causing abduction and corneal loss.

exam_trap: Candidates pick C by misplacing the trigeminal divisions, but V3 leaves through the foramen ovale and never enters the sinus; V1 explains the corneal loss and VI the abduction failure.
takeaway: Cavernous sinus syndrome = III, IV, V1, V2, VI.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: Ophthalmoplegia + corneal anaesthesia + impaired abduction ↓ eye-movement nerves III, IV and VI plus V1 for the cornea ↓ all lie in or on the cavernous sinus with V2 ↓ III, IV, V1, V2 and VI
pearl: Cavernous sinus thrombosis usually spreads from infection of the central face or sphenoid sinus via the valveless facial and ophthalmic veins, presenting with proptosis, chemosis and painful ophthalmoplegia that can become bilateral.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: foramen ovale
stem: Which cranial nerve division passes through the foramen ovale?
why_correct: The mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (V3) passes through the foramen ovale.

why_others_wrong.A: The ophthalmic division passes through the superior orbital fissure.
why_others_wrong.B: The maxillary division passes through the foramen rotundum into the pterygopalatine fossa.
why_others_wrong.D: The facial nerve enters the internal acoustic meatus and leaves the skull via the stylomastoid foramen.
why_others_wrong.E: The glossopharyngeal nerve leaves through the jugular foramen.

exam_trap: Candidates swap the two foramina and choose B; V2 passes through the foramen rotundum, whereas V3 uses the foramen ovale to reach the infratemporal fossa.
takeaway: Foramen ovale → V3.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: Foramen ovale in the greater wing of sphenoid ↓ opens into the infratemporal fossa ↓ carries the mandibular division with the lesser petrosal nerve ↓ V3
pearl: The foramen ovale is the route used for percutaneous needle procedures on the trigeminal ganglion to treat trigeminal neuralgia.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: foramen rotundum
stem: Which structure passes through the foramen rotundum?
why_correct: The maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve (V2) passes through the foramen rotundum to reach the pterygopalatine fossa.

why_others_wrong.A: The ophthalmic division enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure.
why_others_wrong.C: The mandibular division passes through the foramen ovale into the infratemporal fossa.
why_others_wrong.D: The middle meningeal artery enters the skull through the foramen spinosum.
why_others_wrong.E: The facial nerve uses the internal acoustic meatus and stylomastoid foramen, not the foramen rotundum.

exam_trap: Candidates confuse neighbouring sphenoid foramina and pick C or D; V3 uses the foramen ovale and the middle meningeal artery the foramen spinosum, leaving V2 in the rotundum.
takeaway: Foramen rotundum → V2.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: Foramen rotundum ↓ opens forward into the pterygopalatine fossa ↓ carries the maxillary division of trigeminal ↓ V2
pearl: The middle meningeal artery, entering through the neighbouring foramen spinosum, runs deep to the pterion, where a temporal bone fracture can tear it and cause an extradural haematoma.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: superior orbital fissure
stem: Which cranial nerve does NOT normally pass through the superior orbital fissure?
why_correct: CN III, IV, V1 and VI pass through the superior orbital fissure. V3 passes through the foramen ovale.

why_others_wrong.A: The oculomotor nerve does pass through the superior orbital fissure, within the common tendinous ring.
why_others_wrong.B: The trochlear nerve does pass through the superior orbital fissure, above and outside the tendinous ring.
why_others_wrong.C: The ophthalmic division does pass through the fissure as its lacrimal, frontal and nasociliary branches.
why_others_wrong.D: The abducens nerve does pass through the superior orbital fissure, inside the tendinous ring, to reach lateral rectus.

exam_trap: Candidates miss the NOT and pick a nerve that does pass through the fissure; III, IV, V1 and VI all enter the orbit there, whereas V3 exits via the foramen ovale.
takeaway: V3 is the odd trigeminal division — it uses foramen ovale.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: Which nerve does NOT use the superior orbital fissure ↓ the fissure transmits III, IV, V1 and VI into the orbit ↓ V3 descends through the foramen ovale instead ↓ V3
pearl: A superior orbital fissure lesion causes ophthalmoplegia, ptosis and forehead and corneal anaesthesia; added visual loss from optic nerve involvement indicates an orbital apex syndrome.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: internal acoustic meatus
stem: Which cranial nerves enter the internal acoustic meatus?
why_correct: The facial and vestibulocochlear nerves enter the internal acoustic meatus. They subsequently follow different courses within the temporal bone.

why_others_wrong.A: The trigeminal divisions leave via the superior orbital fissure, foramen rotundum and foramen ovale, not the internal acoustic meatus.
why_others_wrong.C: The glossopharyngeal nerve exits through the jugular foramen; only VIII of this pair uses the internal acoustic meatus.
why_others_wrong.D: The abducens nerve runs through Dorello canal and the cavernous sinus to the superior orbital fissure.
why_others_wrong.E: The glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves both exit through the jugular foramen.

exam_trap: Candidates pick C or E by mixing up posterior fossa exits; IX and X leave through the jugular foramen, while only VII and VIII enter the internal acoustic meatus.
takeaway: IAM → facial + vestibulocochlear nerves.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: Internal acoustic meatus in the petrous temporal bone ↓ transmits the facial and vestibulocochlear nerves with the labyrinthine artery ↓ VII and VIII
pearl: A vestibular schwannoma in the internal acoustic meatus typically presents with unilateral sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus, with facial weakness a late feature; asymmetrical hearing loss warrants MRI of the internal acoustic meati.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: jugular foramen
stem: Which cranial nerves pass through the jugular foramen?
why_correct: Cranial nerves IX, X and XI pass through the jugular foramen alongside major venous structures.

why_others_wrong.A: The facial and vestibulocochlear nerves enter the internal acoustic meatus.
why_others_wrong.C: III, IV and VI pass through the cavernous sinus region and superior orbital fissure to the orbit.
why_others_wrong.D: V1 uses the superior orbital fissure and V2 the foramen rotundum.
why_others_wrong.E: The hypoglossal nerve exits via the hypoglossal canal, and this pair omits IX and X.

exam_trap: Candidates choose E by adding XII to the jugular foramen; the hypoglossal nerve has its own canal, and the jugular foramen carries IX, X and XI with the internal jugular vein.
takeaway: Jugular foramen → IX, X, XI.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: Jugular foramen between petrous temporal and occipital bones ↓ transmits the internal jugular vein and inferior petrosal sinus ↓ plus glossopharyngeal, vagus and accessory nerves ↓ IX, X and XI
pearl: A jugular foramen lesion such as a glomus tumour causes loss of gag, dysphagia, hoarseness and trapezius and sternocleidomastoid weakness; an added tongue palsy suggests spread to the hypoglossal canal.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: hypoglossal canal
stem: The hypoglossal nerve exits the skull through which opening?
why_correct: CN XII exits the posterior cranial fossa through the hypoglossal canal.

why_others_wrong.A: The jugular foramen transmits IX, X and XI and the internal jugular vein, not the hypoglossal nerve.
why_others_wrong.B: The foramen ovale transmits V3, the lesser petrosal nerve and the accessory meningeal artery.
why_others_wrong.D: The internal acoustic meatus transmits VII, VIII and the labyrinthine artery.
why_others_wrong.E: The foramen spinosum transmits the middle meningeal artery and the meningeal branch of V3.

exam_trap: Candidates pick A, assuming XII travels with IX, X and XI through the jugular foramen; it leaves separately through the hypoglossal canal above the occipital condyle.
takeaway: Hypoglossal nerve → hypoglossal canal.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: Hypoglossal nerve = CN XII ↓ emerges from the medulla between pyramid and olive ↓ leaves the posterior cranial fossa through its own canal above the occipital condyle ↓ Hypoglossal canal
pearl: A hypoglossal nerve lesion makes the protruded tongue deviate towards the side of the lesion; the nerve is at risk in carotid endarterectomy where it crosses the internal and external carotid arteries.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: hyperglycaemia and osmolality
stem: A patient develops marked hyperglycaemia. Which change is expected initially as extracellular osmolality rises?

options.A: Movement of water from extracellular to intracellular fluid
options.B: Movement of water from intracellular to extracellular fluid
options.D: Increased intracellular sodium concentration as the primary response

correct_answer: B. Movement of water from intracellular to extracellular fluid
why_correct: Marked hyperglycaemia increases extracellular effective osmolality. Water therefore shifts from intracellular to extracellular fluid, producing cellular dehydration.

why_others_wrong.A: This is the opposite direction; a hyperosmolar extracellular fluid draws water out of cells rather than pulling water into them.
why_others_wrong.C: Glucose accumulation raises, not reduces, extracellular osmolality; this option contradicts the stem's own premise.
why_others_wrong.D: The primary early effect is an osmotic water shift out of cells, not a change in intracellular sodium concentration.
why_others_wrong.E: Rising effective osmolality stimulates thirst via osmoreceptors; it does not suppress it.

exam_trap: Candidates choosing A reverse the osmotic gradient; water moves towards the higher effective osmolality, so hyperglycaemia draws water out of cells and dehydrates them.
takeaway: Hyperosmolar ECF → water leaves cells.
source: Guyton & Hall, 14th ed (2021).
thinking: Marked hyperglycaemia ↓ glucose acts as an effective osmole in the extracellular fluid ↓ extracellular osmolality rises ↓ water moves out of cells ↓ Movement of water from intracellular to extracellular fluid
pearl: This water shift dilutes plasma sodium, so measured sodium is low in severe hyperglycaemia and should be corrected for glucose before judging water balance.

subject: Pharmacology
title: Pharmacology: adh and collecting duct
stem: Which renal change is directly produced by ADH acting at V2 receptors?

options.D: Increased sodium loss from the proximal tubule

why_correct: ADH binds V2 receptors on collecting-duct principal cells, activating cAMP-dependent pathways that promote aquaporin-2 insertion into the apical membrane.

why_others_wrong.A: ADH acting via V2 receptors increases, not reduces, aquaporin-2 insertion into the apical membrane.
