why_others_wrong.C: ADH increases collecting-duct water permeability; it does not directly reduce the medullary interstitial osmotic gradient, which it in fact helps to exploit via urea recycling.
why_others_wrong.D: ADH's classic direct action at V2 receptors is on collecting-duct water permeability, not on proximal tubular sodium handling.
why_others_wrong.E: ADH promotes, rather than inhibits, water reabsorption at the collecting duct.

exam_trap: Reduced medullary osmotic gradient may tempt candidates who know ADH affects the medulla, but ADH helps maintain the gradient; its direct V2 effect is increased collecting-duct water permeability.
takeaway: ADH → V2 → aquaporin-2 → water reabsorption.
source: Guyton & Hall, 14th ed (2021).
thinking: ADH binds V2 receptors on collecting-duct principal cells ↓ cAMP rises and protein kinase A is activated ↓ aquaporin-2 channels are inserted into the apical membrane ↓ Increased collecting-duct water permeability
pearl: SIADH after surgery, head injury or with some drugs causes concentrated urine despite low plasma osmolality; fluid restriction is first-line, and hypertonic saline is reserved for severe symptomatic hyponatraemia.

subject: Anatomy
title: Physiology: sympathetic preganglionic neurons
stem: Where are the cell bodies of sympathetic preganglionic neurons located?
why_correct: Sympathetic preganglionic neurons arise from the intermediolateral cell columns of the thoracolumbar spinal cord, classically T1–L2.

why_others_wrong.A: Brainstem nuclei give rise to parasympathetic (craniosacral) preganglionic neurons, not sympathetic ones.
why_others_wrong.B: The sacral spinal cord is the source of sacral parasympathetic outflow, not sympathetic preganglionic neurons.
why_others_wrong.D: Dorsal root ganglia contain sensory neuron cell bodies, not autonomic preganglionic neurons.
why_others_wrong.E: The adrenal medulla contains modified postganglionic sympathetic (chromaffin) cells, not the preganglionic neuron cell bodies themselves.

exam_trap: Candidates choose E because the adrenal medulla is sympathetic, but its chromaffin cells are equivalent to postganglionic neurons; preganglionic cell bodies lie in the T1–L2 lateral horn.
takeaway: Sympathetic outflow = T1–L2.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: Sympathetic preganglionic cell bodies ↓ thoracolumbar outflow ↓ intermediolateral cell column of T1–L2 ↓ Thoracolumbar spinal cord
pearl: Sympathetic outflow to the head leaves at T1, so an apical lung tumour or lower brachial plexus injury involving T1 can cause ipsilateral ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: parasympathetic sacral outflow
stem: Which spinal cord levels contain parasympathetic preganglionic neurons supplying pelvic viscera?
why_correct: Sacral parasympathetic preganglionic neurons arise from S2–S4 and contribute to pelvic splanchnic nerves.

why_others_wrong.A: T1–T4 is part of the sympathetic thoracolumbar outflow, not the parasympathetic sacral outflow.
why_others_wrong.B: T5–T9 lies within the sympathetic outflow, well rostral to the sacral parasympathetic levels.
why_others_wrong.C: T10–L2 is the lower extent of sympathetic outflow (splanchnic nerves to abdominal viscera), not parasympathetic outflow.
why_others_wrong.E: L4–S1 is too rostral; sacral parasympathetic preganglionic neurons begin at S2, not L4.

exam_trap: Candidates choosing T10–L2 (C) pick the sympathetic supply to pelvic organs; parasympathetic preganglionic neurons for the pelvis arise from S2–S4 and travel in the pelvic splanchnic nerves.
takeaway: S2–S4 → pelvic parasympathetic outflow.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: Parasympathetic outflow is craniosacral ↓ the sacral component supplies pelvic viscera ↓ preganglionic cell bodies lie at S2–S4 ↓ they travel in the pelvic splanchnic nerves ↓ S2–S4
pearl: Pelvic autonomic nerves can be injured during rectal cancer surgery, causing bladder and sexual dysfunction, which is why total mesorectal excision aims to preserve them.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: pelvic splanchnic nerves
stem: Which function is primarily mediated by pelvic splanchnic nerves?

options.A: Sympathetic vasoconstriction of the lower limb
options.D: Sensory supply to the anterior thigh
options.E: Sympathetic supply to the adrenal medulla

correct_answer: B. Parasympathetic supply to pelvic viscera
why_correct: Pelvic splanchnic nerves arise from S2–S4 and carry parasympathetic fibres to pelvic viscera, including the distal bowel and bladder.

why_others_wrong.A: Lower limb vasoconstriction is sympathetic, via grey rami from the lumbar and sacral sympathetic trunk.
why_others_wrong.C: Quadriceps is supplied by the femoral nerve (L2-L4), a somatic motor nerve.
why_others_wrong.D: Anterior thigh skin is supplied by femoral and lateral femoral cutaneous nerves, which are somatic not autonomic.
why_others_wrong.E: The adrenal medulla receives preganglionic sympathetic fibres mainly from the thoracic splanchnic nerves.

exam_trap: Pelvic splanchnic = parasympathetic. Thoracic/lumbar splanchnic nerves are predominantly sympathetic.
takeaway: Pelvic splanchnic nerves = S2–S4 parasympathetic.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: Pelvic splanchnic nerves ↓ arise from S2–S4 anterior rami ↓ sacral part of craniosacral parasympathetic outflow ↓ Parasympathetic supply to pelvic viscera
pearl: Pelvic splanchnic nerves mediate erection, detrusor contraction and distal colonic motility, so pelvic dissection in rectal or prostate surgery can cause erectile and bladder dysfunction if they are damaged.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: horner syndrome
stem: A lesion interrupts the sympathetic pathway to the eye. Which combination is most characteristic?
why_correct: Horner syndrome results from interruption of sympathetic innervation to the head and eye. Typical features include mild ptosis, miosis and ipsilateral facial anhidrosis.

why_others_wrong.B: Mydriasis is wrong; loss of sympathetic tone leaves the pupil constrictor unopposed, producing miosis rather than pupil dilation.
why_others_wrong.C: This combination describes sympathetic overactivity features rather than sympathetic loss, and Horner's causes anhidrosis, not hyperhidrosis.
why_others_wrong.D: Horner syndrome is characteristically unilateral, and this option omits anhidrosis, so it is less characteristic than the full ipsilateral triad.
why_others_wrong.E: Corneal sensation is carried by the trigeminal nerve (V1), not sympathetic fibres, so it is unrelated to Horner syndrome.

exam_trap: Candidates choosing B confuse sympathetic loss with oculomotor palsy; third nerve palsy causes ptosis with mydriasis, whereas sympathetic loss causes mild ptosis with miosis.
takeaway: Sympathetic interruption → miosis + ptosis + anhidrosis.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: Interrupted sympathetic supply to the eye ↓ loss of superior tarsal muscle tone causes mild ptosis ↓ unopposed pupillary constriction causes miosis ↓ loss of sudomotor fibres causes anhidrosis ↓ Ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis
pearl: A new painful Horner syndrome with neck pain should prompt urgent imaging for carotid artery dissection, and an apical lung tumour is another classic cause.

subject: Pharmacology
title: Pharmacology: autonomic receptors
stem: Which receptor mediates sympathetic stimulation of the sinoatrial node to increase heart rate?
why_correct: Sympathetic stimulation of cardiac β1 receptors increases heart rate and contractility through Gs-mediated increases in intracellular cAMP.

why_others_wrong.A: α1 mediates vascular smooth muscle contraction via Gq, not sinoatrial node chronotropy.
why_others_wrong.B: α2 is largely presynaptic and Gi-coupled, reducing noradrenaline release, rather than being the receptor mediating direct sinoatrial chronotropic effects.
why_others_wrong.D: β2 mediates smooth muscle relaxation, such as bronchodilation and vasodilation, and plays a lesser cardiac role than β1, which is the principal receptor for sympathetic chronotropy.
why_others_wrong.E: M3 receptors are Gq-coupled and act mainly on smooth muscle and glands; vagal slowing of the sinoatrial node is mediated by M2 receptors, and neither is the sympathetic receptor.

exam_trap: β2 is chosen by candidates who recall that some cardiac beta-2 receptors exist, but beta-1 is the principal receptor for sympathetic chronotropy; beta-2 mainly mediates smooth muscle relaxation.
takeaway: Sympathetic cardiac chronotropy = β1.
source: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed (2021).
thinking: Sympathetic stimulation of the sinoatrial node ↓ noradrenaline acts on cardiac beta-1 receptors ↓ Gs raises cAMP, steepening pacemaker depolarisation ↓ heart rate increases ↓ β1
pearl: Beta-1-selective blockers such as bisoprolol slow the heart rate and are used for rate control in atrial fibrillation; in elderly surgical patients, beta blockade can mask the tachycardia of haemorrhage or sepsis.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Physiology: intrinsic apoptotic pathway
stem: Which organelle is central to activation of the intrinsic apoptotic pathway?
why_correct: The intrinsic pathway is regulated at the mitochondrion. Increased mitochondrial outer-membrane permeability permits release of cytochrome c, which contributes to apoptosome formation and activation of initiator caspase-9.

why_others_wrong.A: Lysosomes mediate autophagy and enzymatic digestion but are not the source of cytochrome c release that drives the intrinsic pathway.
why_others_wrong.C: The Golgi apparatus processes and packages secretory proteins and has no central regulatory role in apoptosome formation.
why_others_wrong.D: Peroxisomes handle fatty-acid oxidation and detoxification but are not the site of cytochrome c release central to intrinsic apoptosis.
why_others_wrong.E: The nucleolus is involved in ribosome biogenesis, not mitochondrial outer-membrane permeabilisation.

exam_trap: Candidates choose lysosome (A) because lysosomal enzymes digest dead cells, but the intrinsic pathway centres on mitochondrial cytochrome c release.
takeaway: Mitochondrial cytochrome c release → caspase cascade.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed (2023).
thinking: Intrinsic apoptotic pathway ↓ mitochondrial outer-membrane permeabilisation ↓ cytochrome c forms the apoptosome with caspase-9 ↓ Mitochondrion
pearl: The intrinsic pathway is triggered by DNA damage via p53, growth factor withdrawal and cellular stress, which is why many chemotherapy agents depend on functional p53 and mitochondrial apoptosis.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Pharmacology: death-receptor pathway
stem: The extrinsic apoptotic pathway is initiated principally by activation of which type of receptor?
why_correct: Extrinsic apoptosis is initiated by cell-surface death receptors such as Fas (CD95) and TNF receptor family members. Receptor activation promotes formation of signalling complexes that activate initiator caspases, particularly caspase-8.

why_others_wrong.A: Intracellular steroid receptors act as ligand-activated transcription factors and do not trigger caspase-8 activation at the cell surface.
why_others_wrong.B: Receptor tyrosine kinases transduce growth-factor signalling that generally promotes survival/proliferation, not extrinsic apoptosis.
why_others_wrong.D: Voltage-gated ion channels regulate membrane electrical activity and are unrelated to death-receptor signalling.
why_others_wrong.E: Nuclear thyroid receptors regulate gene transcription in response to thyroid hormone and have no role in extrinsic apoptosis initiation.

exam_trap: Candidates choose receptor tyrosine kinase (B) because it is a cell-surface receptor, but these mainly promote survival; extrinsic apoptosis starts at death receptors.
takeaway: Extrinsic apoptosis begins at a cell-surface death receptor.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed (2023).
thinking: Extrinsic apoptotic pathway ↓ cell-surface death receptors such as Fas and TNF receptor ↓ death-inducing signalling complex activates caspase-8 ↓ Death receptor
pearl: Cytotoxic T cells kill target cells partly through Fas ligand binding to Fas, and defects in this pathway cause autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Pathology: oncology & haematology: oncogenes
stem: Which statement best describes an oncogene?

options.A: A gene whose loss always causes apoptosis
options.B: A mutated or dysregulated gene that promotes inappropriate cellular proliferation or survival
options.C: A gene responsible only for DNA mismatch repair
options.D: A gene expressed exclusively in embryonic tissue
options.E: A gene that always acts recessively at the cellular level

correct_answer: B. A mutated or dysregulated gene that promotes inappropriate cellular proliferation or survival
why_correct: Oncogenes are activated or overexpressed forms of normal proto-oncogenes that promote proliferation, survival or other malignant behaviours.

why_others_wrong.A: Loss of an oncogene does not reliably cause apoptosis, and oncogenes act by gain of function rather than being defined by the effect of their loss.
why_others_wrong.C: DNA mismatch repair genes such as MLH1 and MSH2 behave as tumour suppressors, since their loss rather than activation promotes cancer.
why_others_wrong.D: Oncogenes derive from normal proto-oncogenes expressed in many adult tissues; oncofetal antigens such as CEA are a different concept.
why_others_wrong.E: Oncogenes typically act dominantly, so one activated allele is enough; recessive loss of both copies describes tumour suppressor genes.

exam_trap: 'Always acts recessively' tempts candidates who mix up gene classes; oncogenes act dominantly with one activated allele, while recessive loss of both copies defines tumour suppressors.
takeaway: Oncogene activation pushes the cell toward growth/survival.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed (2023).
thinking: Oncogene = activated or overexpressed proto-oncogene ↓ gain of function, dominant at the cellular level ↓ promotes proliferation or survival ↓ A mutated or dysregulated gene that promotes inappropriate cellular proliferation or survival
pearl: Translocation can activate an oncogene by placing it beside a highly active promoter, as when MYC is moved next to the immunoglobulin heavy chain locus in some aggressive B-cell lymphomas.

subject: Immunology
title: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing: ctla-4
stem: Which molecule provides an inhibitory signal to T cells by competing with CD28 for B7 binding?
why_correct: CTLA-4 binds B7 molecules with higher affinity than CD28 and provides an inhibitory signal that helps regulate T-cell activation.

why_others_wrong.A: CD3 is the signalling complex associated with the T-cell receptor and transmits the activating antigen signal rather than competing for B7.
why_others_wrong.C: CD8 is a co-receptor that binds MHC class I on target cells and does not compete with CD28 for B7 binding.
why_others_wrong.D: MHC class I presents intracellular peptides to CD8 T cells and is not an inhibitory receptor that binds B7.
why_others_wrong.E: The B-cell receptor is membrane immunoglobulin on B cells used for antigen recognition and plays no role in B7 competition on T cells.

exam_trap: CD3 tempts because it sits on T cells beside the receptor, but it transmits the activating signal; the inhibitory competitor for B7 is CTLA-4.
takeaway: CTLA-4 restrains T-cell activation.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed (2023).
thinking: Molecule competing with CD28 for B7 ↓ binds B7 with higher affinity ↓ delivers an inhibitory checkpoint signal ↓ CTLA-4
pearl: Checkpoint inhibitors such as ipilimumab (anti-CTLA-4) enhance anti-tumour immunity but can cause immune-related colitis, hepatitis and endocrinopathies.

subject: Immunology
title: Immunology: acute cellular rejection
stem: A renal transplant develops graft dysfunction several weeks after transplantation. Biopsy shows lymphocytic infiltration and vascular injury. Which mechanism is most likely?

options.B: Acute cellular rejection mediated by recipient T cells

correct_answer: B. Acute cellular rejection mediated by recipient T cells
why_correct: Acute cellular rejection commonly occurs days to months after transplantation and involves recipient T-cell responses against donor antigens, producing lymphocytic inflammation and tissue injury.

why_others_wrong.A: Hyperacute rejection from preformed antibodies occurs within minutes to hours of reperfusion, not several weeks after transplantation.
why_others_wrong.C: Passive transfer of donor antibodies is not a recognised cause of graft rejection and does not explain lymphocytic infiltration of the graft.
why_others_wrong.D: IgE-mediated reactions cause immediate allergic responses and are not a mechanism of renal graft rejection.
why_others_wrong.E: Complement deficiency predisposes to infection and does not produce a lymphocytic infiltrate with graft dysfunction.

exam_trap: Candidates choose hyperacute rejection (A) because of the vascular injury, but it occurs within minutes to hours; lymphocytic injury weeks later means acute cellular rejection.
takeaway: T-cell-mediated graft injury → acute cellular rejection.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed (2023).
thinking: Graft dysfunction several weeks after transplantation ↓ lymphocytic infiltration with vascular injury ↓ timing excludes hyperacute rejection ↓ recipient T cells attack donor antigens ↓ Acute cellular rejection mediated by recipient T cells
pearl: Hyperacute rejection is now rare because pre-transplant crossmatching detects preformed donor-specific antibodies, for example from previous transplants, pregnancy or transfusion.

subject: Immunology
title: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing: type iv hypersensitivity
stem: Which immune mechanism underlies type IV hypersensitivity?
why_correct: Type IV hypersensitivity is cell-mediated and involves T lymphocytes. It is therefore also called delayed-type hypersensitivity.

why_others_wrong.A: IgE mediates type I immediate hypersensitivity through mast-cell activation, whereas type IV reactions are driven by T cells.
why_others_wrong.B: IgM participates in type II and type III reactions through antibody and complement, not in T-cell-mediated delayed hypersensitivity.
why_others_wrong.D: Immune-complex deposition is the mechanism of type III hypersensitivity, whereas type IV does not rely on antibody.
why_others_wrong.E: Mast-cell degranulation is the effector mechanism of type I immediate hypersensitivity, not the delayed T-cell response of type IV.

exam_trap: Immune-complex deposition tempts because type III reactions also develop over hours to days, but they are antibody-driven; type IV hypersensitivity is mediated by T lymphocytes.
takeaway: Type IV = T cells = delayed hypersensitivity.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed (2023).
thinking: Type IV hypersensitivity ↓ delayed-type, cell-mediated ↓ no antibody involved ↓ T lymphocytes
pearl: Granulomatous inflammation in tuberculosis and sarcoidosis is a type IV response, with Th1 cells activating macrophages via IFN-gamma.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Cardiorespiratory physiology: oxygen delivery
stem: A patient has a cardiac output of 5 L/min and an arterial oxygen content of 200 mL/L. What is the approximate systemic oxygen delivery?
why_correct: Oxygen delivery: DO2 = cardiac output × arterial oxygen content = 5 L/min × 200 mL/L = 1,000 mL/min.

why_others_wrong.A: 100 mL/min substantially underestimates the correct product of 5 L/min × 200 mL/L, which equals 1,000 mL/min.
why_others_wrong.B: 500 mL/min is roughly half the correct value, as if the cardiac output or oxygen content used were halved.
why_others_wrong.D: 2,000 mL/min doubles the correct answer, as would occur if cardiac output were mistakenly taken as 10 L/min.
why_others_wrong.E: 10,000 mL/min greatly overestimates delivery, as would occur if oxygen content were mistakenly taken as 2,000 mL/L rather than 200 mL/L.

exam_trap: Candidates who mix mL/dL with mL/L produce tenfold errors such as 100 or 10,000 mL/min; keep content in mL/L when cardiac output is in L/min.
takeaway: DO2 = CO × CaO2.
source: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed (2021).
thinking: DO2 = cardiac output × arterial oxygen content ↓ content is given in mL/L and cardiac output in L/min ↓ 5 × 200 = 1,000 ↓ 1,000 mL/min
pearl: At rest oxygen delivery is roughly four times oxygen consumption, giving a large reserve before consumption becomes supply-dependent.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Cardiorespiratory physiology: oxygen consumption
stem: A patient's oxygen delivery is 1,000 mL/min and oxygen consumption is 250 mL/min. What is the approximate oxygen extraction ratio?
why_correct: Oxygen extraction ratio: VO2 / DO2 = 250 / 1,000 = 0.25 = 25%.

why_others_wrong.A: 5% is far too low; 250/1,000 does not equal 0.05, considerably underestimating the true extraction ratio.
why_others_wrong.B: 10% still underestimates the true ratio of 250/1,000, which equals 0.25 (25%).
why_others_wrong.D: 50% overestimates the ratio; this would require consumption of roughly 500 mL/min against the stated delivery of 1,000 mL/min.
why_others_wrong.E: 75% substantially overestimates extraction, which would only occur if delivery and consumption were much closer together than stated.

exam_trap: Candidates invert the ratio or confuse it with venous saturation; extraction is consumption divided by delivery, so 250/1,000 gives 25%, leaving about 75% unused.
takeaway: O2 extraction ratio = VO2 / DO2.
source: Guyton & Hall, 14th ed (2021).
thinking: Extraction ratio = VO2 / DO2 ↓ 250 / 1,000 = 0.25 ↓ one quarter of delivered oxygen is used ↓ 25%
pearl: A normal resting extraction ratio of about 25% corresponds to a mixed venous saturation of roughly 75%, so a falling SvO2 indicates rising extraction from inadequate delivery.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Cardiorespiratory physiology: shock and oxygen extraction
stem: During progressive haemorrhagic shock, oxygen delivery falls. Which compensatory response initially helps maintain tissue oxygen consumption?

options.D: Increased arterial oxygen saturation to 100% in every case

why_correct: When oxygen delivery falls, tissues can initially compensate by extracting a greater proportion of delivered oxygen. Once compensatory reserve is exhausted, oxygen consumption becomes supply-dependent and anaerobic metabolism increases.

why_others_wrong.A: This is the opposite of the compensatory response; tissues increase, not reduce, the fraction of delivered oxygen they extract as delivery falls.
why_others_wrong.C: Mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation continues while some oxygen is supplied; as supply fails, cytosolic anaerobic glycolysis and lactate production increase instead.
why_others_wrong.D: Arterial saturation is not guaranteed to reach 100% in shock and is not itself the compensatory mechanism for falling delivery; the key early response is peripheral extraction.
why_others_wrong.E: Anaerobic metabolism actually increases, not disappears, once compensatory extraction is exhausted and delivery remains inadequate.

exam_trap: Candidates choose a rise in saturation to 100% as compensation, but saturation is not reliably raised in shock; the body compensates by increasing peripheral oxygen extraction.
takeaway: Falling DO2 → extraction rises first, then oxygen consumption fails.
source: Guyton & Hall, 14th ed (2021).
thinking: Haemorrhage reduces cardiac output and oxygen delivery ↓ tissues first extract more of the delivered oxygen ↓ VO2 is maintained until a critical delivery is reached ↓ beyond that, consumption becomes supply-dependent with rising lactate ↓ Increased oxygen extraction
pearl: A rising serum lactate in a bleeding patient signals that extraction reserve is exhausted and consumption has become supply-dependent, and falling lactate is used to track resuscitation.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Acid-Base: Compensation
stem: A patient has a primary metabolic acidosis. Which respiratory response is expected?

options.D: Reduced respiratory drive from low bicarbonate

why_correct: Metabolic acidosis stimulates ventilation, reducing PaCO2 and partially compensating for the fall in bicarbonate.

why_others_wrong.A: Hypoventilation would raise PaCO2 and worsen the acidosis; the appropriate response to metabolic acidosis is hyperventilation to lower PaCO2.
why_others_wrong.C: Apnoea would prevent any compensatory fall in PaCO2 and is not a physiological response to acidosis.
why_others_wrong.D: The resulting acidaemia from low bicarbonate stimulates, rather than reduces, respiratory drive via chemoreceptor activation.
why_others_wrong.E: Respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis is a well-recognised, rapid physiological response, not an absent one.

exam_trap: Candidates choose 'reduced drive from low bicarbonate', but the acidaemia stimulates chemoreceptors and increases ventilation; low bicarbonate does not suppress respiratory drive.
takeaway: Metabolic acidosis → hyperventilate → PaCO2 falls.
source: Guyton & Hall, 14th ed (2021).
thinking: Primary metabolic acidosis ↓ H+ stimulates peripheral and central chemoreceptors ↓ ventilation increases to blow off CO2 ↓ PaCO2 falls and pH moves towards normal ↓ Hyperventilation
pearl: Deep, sighing respiration in diabetic ketoacidosis is the bedside sign of this compensation, and its loss in severe acidosis can indicate respiratory exhaustion.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: lactate
stem: A patient with severe tissue hypoperfusion develops a rising lactate concentration. Which process most directly contributes to lactate production?

options.B: Conversion of pyruvate to lactate during anaerobic glycolysis

correct_answer: B. Conversion of pyruvate to lactate during anaerobic glycolysis
why_correct: When oxygen availability is insufficient for adequate oxidative phosphorylation, pyruvate is converted to lactate, allowing regeneration of NAD+ and continuation of glycolysis.

why_others_wrong.A: Hypoperfusion impairs oxidative phosphorylation because of inadequate oxygen delivery; it does not increase it.
why_others_wrong.C: Beta-oxidation still requires oxygen and does not itself generate lactate, so it does not explain the rising lactate.
why_others_wrong.D: Glycolysis continues (or increases) to generate ATP anaerobically; lactate results from ongoing glycolysis feeding pyruvate reduction, not from reduced glycolysis.
why_others_wrong.E: The urea cycle handles nitrogen waste and is not linked to anaerobic lactate generation.

exam_trap: Candidates choosing D think lactate reflects failing glycolysis, but glycolysis continues and accelerates; lack of oxygen diverts its pyruvate to lactate.
takeaway: Pyruvate → lactate when glycolytic NAD+ regeneration is needed.
source: Guyton & Hall, 14th ed (2021).
thinking: Severe tissue hypoperfusion ↓ oxygen delivery is insufficient for oxidative phosphorylation ↓ glycolysis continues ↓ pyruvate is reduced to lactate to regenerate NAD+ ↓ Conversion of pyruvate to lactate during anaerobic glycolysis
pearl: Lactate can also rise without hypoperfusion, for example with adrenaline infusion, liver failure or metformin, so it should be interpreted with the clinical picture.

subject: Statistics & evidence-based medicine
title: Statistics & evidence-based medicine: number needed to treat
stem: A randomised trial reports an absolute risk reduction of 5%. What is the approximate number needed to treat?

why_others_wrong.A: An NNT of 2 results from a decimal error, treating 5% as 0.5 instead of 0.05 before taking the reciprocal.
why_others_wrong.B: Five is the percentage absolute risk reduction itself quoted as the NNT, without converting it to 0.05 and taking the reciprocal to give 20.
why_others_wrong.C: An NNT of 10 corresponds to an absolute risk reduction of 10%, double the 5% reported in this trial.
why_others_wrong.E: An NNT of 50 corresponds to an absolute risk reduction of 2%, not the 5% given, so the reciprocal has been taken of the wrong value.

exam_trap: Choosing 5 quotes the ARR itself, and 2 treats 5% as 0.5; converting 5% to 0.05 and taking the reciprocal gives an NNT of 20.
takeaway: ARR 5% → NNT 20.
source: Rothman, Greenland & Lash, Modern Epidemiology, 4th ed (2021).
thinking: ARR 5% ↓ convert to 0.05 ↓ NNT = 1 / ARR ↓ 20
pearl: An NNT from a trial applies to patients similar to those studied over the trial's follow-up period; in higher-risk patients the absolute benefit is larger and the NNT smaller.

subject: Statistics & evidence-based medicine
topic: confidence interval for an absolute risk difference
title: Statistics & evidence-based medicine: confidence interval for an absolute risk difference
stem: A trial reports an absolute risk difference of −4% with a 95% confidence interval of −8% to +1%. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.C: The confidence interval includes no difference
options.E: The confidence interval demonstrates statistical significance at the 5% level

correct_answer: C. The confidence interval includes no difference
why_correct: For an absolute risk difference, the null value is 0. Because the 95% confidence interval extends from −8% to +1%, it includes 0 and therefore does not exclude no difference at the conventional 5% significance threshold.

why_others_wrong.A: The interval extends to +1%, so it includes zero and a real reduction in risk cannot be stated with confidence at the 5% level.
why_others_wrong.B: The point estimate of minus 4% and most of the interval lie on the side of risk reduction, so there is no evidence that treatment definitely increases risk.
why_others_wrong.D: Failure to exclude no difference is not proof of equivalence, which requires the whole interval to lie within prespecified equivalence margins.
why_others_wrong.E: Statistical significance at the 5% level for a risk difference requires the 95% interval to exclude zero, but this interval crosses zero.

exam_trap: Candidates who focus on the minus 4% point estimate choose a definite reduction, but the interval reaches plus 1% and so includes zero, the null for a difference.
takeaway: CI for risk difference crossing 0 → no statistically significant difference demonstrated.
source: Rothman, Greenland & Lash, Modern Epidemiology, 4th ed (2021).
thinking: Absolute risk difference, null value 0 ↓ 95% CI −8% to +1% includes 0 ↓ not significant at the 5% level ↓ The confidence interval includes no difference
pearl: A non-significant interval that is mostly on the side of benefit may still justify a larger trial; it should not be reported as showing the treatment is ineffective.

subject: Anatomy
title: Physiology: thoracic sympathetic chain
stem: A patient undergoes surgery near the heads of the ribs and subsequently develops ipsilateral Horner syndrome. Which structure is most likely to have been injured?
why_correct: The sympathetic pathway to the head and neck originates from thoracic sympathetic outflow and ascends through the sympathetic chain. Injury to the cervical/upper thoracic sympathetic pathway can produce Horner syndrome.

why_others_wrong.A: The phrenic nerve supplies the diaphragm with some sensory fibres, and has no role in pupillary or facial sympathetic function.
why_others_wrong.C: The vagus nerve provides parasympathetic supply to thoracic and abdominal viscera, unrelated to the sympathetic deficit of Horner syndrome.
why_others_wrong.D: The thoracic duct is a lymphatic structure and plays no part in sympathetic innervation.
why_others_wrong.E: The greater splanchnic nerve carries sympathetic fibres to abdominal viscera via the coeliac ganglion, not to the head and eye, so its injury would not produce Horner syndrome.

exam_trap: Horner syndrome indicates interruption of the sympathetic pathway to the eye, not a primary cranial nerve lesion.
takeaway: Sympathetic chain injury → ipsilateral Horner syndrome.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: Surgery near the heads of the ribs ↓ the sympathetic trunk lies on the rib heads in the posterior thorax ↓ Horner syndrome = interrupted sympathetic supply to the eye ↓ Thoracic sympathetic trunk
pearl: In thoracoscopic sympathectomy for hyperhidrosis the chain is divided below the stellate ganglion to avoid Horner syndrome, and compensatory sweating elsewhere is a common side effect.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: phrenic nerve roots
stem: Which spinal nerve roots contribute most importantly to the phrenic nerve?
why_correct: The phrenic nerve arises principally from C3–C5, with C4 contributing most prominently. It provides the motor supply to the diaphragm.

why_others_wrong.A: C1-C2 fibres travel with the hypoglossal nerve and ansa cervicalis, not the phrenic nerve.
why_others_wrong.B: C2-C3 supply the ansa cervicalis and cervical plexus skin branches; the phrenic nerve's main root is C4.
why_others_wrong.D: C5-C7 form the upper brachial plexus; only C5 contributes to the phrenic nerve, and C6-C7 do not.
why_others_wrong.E: T1-T3 are thoracic roots supplying intercostal structures, too low for the diaphragm's cervical origin.

exam_trap: “C3, 4, 5 keep the diaphragm alive” is useful, but do not confuse C5 with the brachial plexus.
takeaway: Phrenic nerve = C3–C5.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: Phrenic nerve ↓ arises from the cervical plexus ↓ C3, 4 and 5 with C4 dominant ↓ C3–C5
pearl: Diaphragmatic irritation, for example from a subphrenic abscess or blood after splenic injury, refers pain to the shoulder tip through the shared C4 dermatome.

subject: Anatomy
title: ENT: head & neck: recurrent laryngeal nerve
stem: During thyroid surgery, a nerve is identified running close to the inferior thyroid artery. Which nerve is at risk?
why_correct: The recurrent laryngeal nerve has an important relationship with the inferior thyroid artery and is vulnerable during thyroid surgery. It supplies the intrinsic laryngeal muscles responsible for most movements of the vocal cords.

why_others_wrong.A: The external laryngeal nerve runs with the superior thyroid artery near the upper pole, not the inferior thyroid artery, and supplies cricothyroid rather than the vocal cord abductors/adductors at risk here.
why_others_wrong.C: The hypoglossal nerve supplies the tongue musculature and runs much higher in the neck, near the hyoid bone and submandibular triangle, not alongside the inferior thyroid artery.
why_others_wrong.D: The glossopharyngeal nerve is a nasopharyngeal/oropharyngeal and carotid-body nerve that passes well above the thyroid gland and has no close relationship to the inferior thyroid artery.
why_others_wrong.E: The phrenic nerve runs on the surface of anterior scalene, lateral and posterior to the carotid sheath, and is not intimately related to the inferior thyroid artery at the gland itself.

exam_trap: Inferior thyroid vessels → think recurrent laryngeal nerve. Superior thyroid vessels → think external laryngeal nerve.
takeaway: Thyroid surgery: protect the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: Thyroid surgery ↓ nerve closely related to the inferior thyroid artery ↓ it ascends in the tracheo-oesophageal groove to the larynx ↓ Recurrent laryngeal nerve
pearl: Unilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury causes hoarseness, whereas bilateral injury can leave both cords near the midline with stridor, so vocal cord function is checked before and after thyroidectomy.

subject: Anatomy
title: ENT: head & neck: external laryngeal nerve
stem: Which muscle is paralysed following injury to the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve?
why_correct: The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve supplies the cricothyroid muscle, which increases vocal-cord tension and contributes to production of high-pitched sounds.

why_others_wrong.A: Posterior cricoarytenoid is supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve, not the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, and its paralysis affects vocal cord abduction rather than pitch.
why_others_wrong.B: Lateral cricoarytenoid is an intrinsic adductor supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve, not the external laryngeal nerve.
why_others_wrong.D: Thyroarytenoid is supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve and functions in cord relaxation/adduction, not by the external laryngeal nerve.
why_others_wrong.E: Vocalis, part of thyroarytenoid, is likewise innervated by the recurrent laryngeal nerve, not the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve.

exam_trap: Candidates pick A or D by assuming any laryngeal nerve injury affects cord abduction or adduction; every intrinsic muscle except cricothyroid is supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
takeaway: External laryngeal nerve injury → difficulty producing high-pitched sounds.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve ↓ descends with the superior thyroid artery ↓ supplies the only intrinsic laryngeal muscle outside recurrent laryngeal supply ↓ Cricothyroid
pearl: The nerve is at risk when the superior thyroid pedicle is ligated; tying branches close to the gland capsule protects it, and injury causes voice fatigue and loss of high pitch, which matters greatly to singers.

subject: Anatomy
title: ENT: head & neck: thyroid blood supply
stem: The superior thyroid artery usually arises directly from which artery?
why_correct: The superior thyroid artery usually arises from the external carotid artery near its origin.

why_others_wrong.A: The common carotid artery usually has no cervical branches before its bifurcation; the superior thyroid artery only occasionally arises from it as a variant.
why_others_wrong.C: The internal carotid artery has no branches in the neck; it supplies the cranial cavity and orbit, not the thyroid gland.
why_others_wrong.D: The subclavian artery gives rise to the thyrocervical trunk, which in turn gives the inferior (not superior) thyroid artery.
why_others_wrong.E: The inferior thyroid artery is a separate vessel arising from the thyrocervical trunk off the subclavian artery, not the parent of the superior thyroid artery.

exam_trap: Candidates pick A because the artery arises close to the carotid bifurcation, or D by confusing it with the inferior thyroid; it is usually the first anterior branch of the external carotid.
takeaway: Superior thyroid artery = ECA branch.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: Superior thyroid artery ↓ first anterior branch of the external carotid just above the bifurcation ↓ the inferior thyroid comes from the thyrocervical trunk instead ↓ External carotid artery
pearl: At carotid surgery the external carotid is recognised by its cervical branches, the superior thyroid usually being the first, whereas the internal carotid has no branches in the neck.

subject: Anatomy
title: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care: parathyroid embryology
stem: A surgeon accidentally removes an inferior parathyroid gland during a thyroid operation. Which embryological structure normally accompanies the inferior parathyroids during their descent?
why_correct: The inferior parathyroids arise from the third pharyngeal pouch and descend with the thymus. Their migration is therefore more variable than that of the superior parathyroids.

why_others_wrong.A: The thyroglossal duct relates to thyroid gland descent from the tongue base, not to parathyroid descent, and has no association with the inferior parathyroids.
why_others_wrong.C: The first pharyngeal pouch gives rise to the auditory (Eustachian) tube and middle ear cavity, not the parathyroid glands or thymus.
why_others_wrong.D: The palatine tonsil develops from the second pharyngeal pouch and has no embryological link to parathyroid descent.
why_others_wrong.E: The ultimobranchial body derives from the fourth/fifth pharyngeal pouch complex and contributes parafollicular (C) cells to the thyroid, not the inferior parathyroids.

exam_trap: Candidates choose E or A by assuming the inferior parathyroids follow the thyroid; they arise from the third pouch with the thymus and may descend as far as the anterior mediastinum.
takeaway: Inferior parathyroid travels with thymus.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: Inferior parathyroid ↓ arises from the third pharyngeal pouch together with the thymus ↓ descends with the thymus past the fourth-pouch glands ↓ Thymus
pearl: Because of this shared descent, an inferior parathyroid adenoma not found in the neck is often located in the thymus or anterior mediastinum, and a cervical thymectomy may be used to retrieve it.

subject: Anatomy
title: ENT: head & neck: superior parathyroids
stem: The superior parathyroid glands are derived embryologically from which pharyngeal pouch?
why_correct: The superior parathyroids derive from the fourth pharyngeal pouch, whereas the inferior parathyroids derive from the third pouch.

why_others_wrong.A: The first pharyngeal pouch forms the middle ear and auditory tube, not any parathyroid tissue.
why_others_wrong.B: The second pharyngeal pouch contributes to the palatine tonsil, not the parathyroid glands.
why_others_wrong.C: The third pharyngeal pouch gives rise to the thymus and, paradoxically, the inferior (not superior) parathyroid glands.
why_others_wrong.E: The sixth pharyngeal arch/pouch complex is associated with laryngeal cartilages and intrinsic laryngeal muscles, not the parathyroid glands.

exam_trap: The names “superior” and “inferior” do not correspond to their embryological pouch order.
takeaway: 4th pouch = superior parathyroids. 3rd pouch = inferior parathyroids + thymus.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: Superior parathyroid ↓ fourth pharyngeal pouch ↓ third-pouch glands descend further with the thymus and end up inferior ↓ Fourth
pearl: Superior parathyroids are more constant in position, usually on the posterior upper thyroid near the cricothyroid junction close to the recurrent laryngeal nerve, whereas inferior glands vary more.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: lingual nerve
stem: A patient develops loss of general sensation from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue after mandibular third-molar surgery. Which nerve has most likely been injured?
why_correct: The lingual nerve, a branch of V3, provides general somatic sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. It is vulnerable during lower third-molar surgery.

why_others_wrong.A: The hypoglossal nerve is motor to the tongue muscles and carries no general sensation.
why_others_wrong.C: The glossopharyngeal nerve provides general sensation and taste to the posterior third, not the anterior two-thirds.
why_others_wrong.D: The chorda tympani carries taste and secretomotor fibres, not general sensation, though it travels with the lingual nerve.
why_others_wrong.E: The greater petrosal nerve carries taste from the palate and secretomotor fibres to the lacrimal gland, not tongue sensation.

exam_trap: Candidates pick D because the chorda tympani travels with the lingual nerve, but it carries taste and secretomotor fibres; loss of general sensation points to the lingual nerve itself.
takeaway: Lower wisdom-tooth surgery can injure the lingual nerve.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: Loss of general sensation, anterior two-thirds of tongue ↓ after lower third-molar surgery ↓ lingual nerve (V3) lies against the lingual plate beside the third molar ↓ Lingual nerve
pearl: Lingual nerve injury often also causes ipsilateral loss of anterior tongue taste, because chorda tympani fibres travel within the lingual nerve beyond their junction in the infratemporal fossa.

subject: Anatomy
title: Physiology: chorda tympani
stem: Which combination of functions is carried by the chorda tympani?

options.A: General tongue sensation and motor supply
options.B: Taste from anterior two-thirds of tongue and parasympathetic fibres to submandibular/sublingual glands
options.C: Taste from posterior third of tongue
options.D: Motor supply to muscles of mastication

correct_answer: B. Taste from anterior two-thirds of tongue and parasympathetic fibres to submandibular/sublingual glands
why_correct: Chorda tympani, a branch of the facial nerve, carries taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and preganglionic parasympathetic fibres that ultimately supply the submandibular and sublingual glands.

why_others_wrong.A: General somatic sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is carried by the lingual nerve (a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve), and the chorda tympani carries no motor fibres to the tongue.
why_others_wrong.C: Taste from the posterior third of the tongue is carried by the glossopharyngeal nerve, not the chorda tympani, which supplies only the anterior two-thirds.
why_others_wrong.D: Motor supply to the muscles of mastication comes from the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve, not the facial nerve's chorda tympani branch.
why_others_wrong.E: Sensory supply to the larynx is provided by branches of the vagus nerve (internal laryngeal and recurrent laryngeal nerves), unrelated to the chorda tympani.

exam_trap: Candidates choose A, giving general tongue sensation to the chorda tympani; that is the lingual nerve, whereas the chorda carries anterior taste and salivary secretomotor fibres.
takeaway: Chorda tympani = anterior tongue taste + salivary parasympathetic fibres.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: Chorda tympani = facial nerve branch ↓ joins the lingual nerve in the infratemporal fossa ↓ carries anterior two-thirds taste and preganglionic fibres to the submandibular ganglion ↓ Taste anterior two-thirds plus submandibular/sublingual parasympathetic fibres
pearl: The chorda tympani crosses the medial surface of the tympanic membrane, so it can be damaged in middle ear surgery, causing altered taste on that side of the tongue.

subject: Anatomy
title: ENT: head & neck: parotid gland
stem: Which cranial nerve traverses the parotid gland and divides into its major terminal branches within it?
why_correct: The facial nerve enters the parotid gland and divides into its major terminal branches within the gland. It does not provide the gland's secretomotor supply.

why_others_wrong.A: The trigeminal nerve provides sensory innervation to the face and motor supply to mastication muscles, but it does not pass through or branch within the parotid gland.
why_others_wrong.C: The glossopharyngeal nerve provides the parasympathetic secretomotor pathway to the parotid via the otic ganglion, but it does not itself traverse the gland substance or form its terminal branches.
why_others_wrong.D: The vagus nerve passes within the carotid sheath posterior to the parotid region and does not run through or divide within the gland.
why_others_wrong.E: The hypoglossal nerve lies deep and inferior to the parotid, supplying tongue musculature, and does not traverse or branch within the gland.

exam_trap: Facial nerve passes through the parotid but does NOT provide its secretomotor innervation.
takeaway: Parotid: facial nerve traverses; glossopharyngeal provides secretomotor pathway.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: Nerve traversing the parotid ↓ facial nerve leaves the stylomastoid foramen and enters the gland ↓ divides into temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular and cervical branches ↓ Facial nerve
pearl: A parotid mass with facial nerve weakness strongly suggests malignancy, because benign tumours such as pleomorphic adenoma rarely cause palsy; parotidectomy begins by identifying the main nerve trunk.

subject: Anatomy
title: Acute abdomen & GI surgery: femoral sheath
stem: Which structure lies within the femoral sheath?
why_correct: The femoral sheath contains the femoral artery, femoral vein and femoral canal. The femoral nerve lies outside the sheath.

why_others_wrong.A: The femoral nerve lies lateral to the femoral sheath, outside it, separated from the artery by the fascia iliaca/psoas fascia, so it is not a sheath content.
why_others_wrong.C: Sartorius forms the lateral border of the femoral triangle and lies outside the femoral sheath, which encloses only the femoral artery, vein and canal.
why_others_wrong.D: The saphenous nerve is a cutaneous branch of the femoral nerve; like its parent nerve it lies outside the femoral sheath, later accompanying the femoral vessels in the adductor canal.
why_others_wrong.E: The obturator nerve passes through the obturator canal into the medial thigh, entirely separate from the femoral sheath and its contents.

exam_trap: Femoral NAV: nerve — artery — vein — canal. Only artery, vein and canal are within the sheath.
takeaway: Femoral nerve is outside the femoral sheath.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: Femoral sheath has three compartments ↓ lateral holds the femoral artery, intermediate the femoral vein and medial the femoral canal ↓ the femoral nerve lies lateral to and outside the sheath ↓ Femoral artery
pearl: The femoral canal is the medial compartment of the sheath and the route of a femoral hernia; its narrow, rigid neck explains why femoral hernias carry a high risk of strangulation.

subject: Anatomy
title: Acute abdomen & GI surgery: femoral canal
stem: What is the principal anatomical significance of the femoral canal?

options.B: It contains lymphatics and allows expansion of the femoral vein
options.E: It contains the great saphenous vein

correct_answer: B. It contains lymphatics and allows expansion of the femoral vein
why_correct: The femoral canal is the medial compartment of the femoral sheath. It contains lymphatic vessels, lymph nodes and connective tissue and permits expansion of the femoral vein.

why_others_wrong.A: The femoral nerve lies lateral to the femoral sheath altogether and is not related to the femoral canal, its medial compartment.
why_others_wrong.C: The femoral artery occupies the lateral compartment of the femoral sheath, not the medial femoral canal.
why_others_wrong.D: The obturator nerve travels through the separate obturator canal in the pelvis, not through the femoral canal.
why_others_wrong.E: The great saphenous vein drains into the femoral vein at the saphenofemoral junction but is a superficial vein outside the femoral sheath, not a canal content.

exam_trap: Candidates pick C or E by naming a femoral vessel; the femoral canal is the medial compartment holding lymphatics and a lymph node, which leaves room for femoral vein distension.
takeaway: Femoral canal = lymphatics + potential space for femoral-vein expansion.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: Femoral canal ↓ medial compartment of the femoral sheath ↓ contains lymphatics, a lymph node and fat ↓ this dead space lets the femoral vein distend ↓ Lymphatics and room for femoral vein expansion
pearl: The femoral ring is bounded by the inguinal ligament, lacunar ligament, pectineal ligament and femoral vein, and its rigid, narrow margins explain why femoral hernias strangulate readily.

subject: Anatomy
title: Acute abdomen & GI surgery: femoral hernia relationship
stem: A femoral hernia emerges through the femoral canal. Relative to the pubic tubercle, where is it classically located?
why_correct: A femoral hernia lies below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, passing through the femoral canal.

why_others_wrong.A: Above and medial to the pubic tubercle describes the superficial inguinal ring/inguinal hernia exit point, not the femoral hernia position.
why_others_wrong.B: Above and lateral does not correspond to either classic hernia site; inguinal hernias emerge above the tubercle medially, not laterally.
why_others_wrong.D: Below and medial is not the femoral canal's position relative to the tubercle; the canal lies lateral to the pubic tubercle, not medial to it.
why_others_wrong.E: A femoral hernia is not classically located directly posterior to the pubic tubercle; its defining relationship is inferolateral to it.

exam_trap: Candidates choose A, the inguinal hernia position; a femoral hernia lies below the inguinal ligament and lateral to the pubic tubercle, whereas an inguinal hernia emerges above and medial.
takeaway: Femoral hernia → below and lateral to pubic tubercle.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: Femoral hernia passes through the femoral canal ↓ canal lies below the inguinal ligament ↓ and lateral to the pubic tubercle ↓ Below and lateral
pearl: Femoral hernias are more common in women and often present as a small irreducible groin lump in older patients; their high strangulation risk means they are usually repaired even when asymptomatic.

subject: Anatomy
title: Acute abdomen & GI surgery: direct inguinal hernia
stem: A direct inguinal hernia protrudes through which region?
why_correct: Direct inguinal hernias protrude through Hesselbach's triangle, medial to the inferior epigastric vessels, due to weakness in the posterior wall of the inguinal canal.

why_others_wrong.A: The deep inguinal ring is the site of entry for an indirect, not direct, inguinal hernia, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels.
why_others_wrong.B: The femoral canal is the route for a femoral hernia, a distinct entity from a direct inguinal hernia and located below the inguinal ligament.
why_others_wrong.D: The obturator canal is the exit point for an obturator hernia, an uncommon pelvic floor hernia unrelated to the inguinal canal's posterior wall.
why_others_wrong.E: A defect at the linea semilunaris, the lateral border of rectus, produces a Spigelian (lateral ventral) hernia above the inguinal region, not a direct inguinal hernia through the posterior wall of the canal.

exam_trap: Deep inguinal ring is chosen because it is the classic hernia entry point, but it lies lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels and is the route of an indirect hernia.
takeaway: Direct inguinal hernia → Hesselbach triangle.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: Direct inguinal hernia ↓ protrudes through a weak posterior wall of the inguinal canal ↓ medial to the inferior epigastric vessels ↓ area bounded by the inferior epigastric vessels, lateral border of rectus and inguinal ligament ↓ Hesselbach triangle
pearl: Direct hernias are acquired, occur mainly in older men and rarely strangulate because of their wide neck, whereas indirect hernias are the commonest groin hernia in both sexes.

subject: Anatomy
title: Acute abdomen & GI surgery: inferior epigastric vessels
stem: An indirect inguinal hernia lies in which relationship to the inferior epigastric vessels?
why_correct: Indirect inguinal hernias pass through the deep inguinal ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels.

why_others_wrong.A: A medial relationship to the inferior epigastric vessels describes a direct inguinal hernia, which protrudes through Hesselbach's triangle, not the indirect variety.
why_others_wrong.C: The relationship of an indirect hernia to the vessels is a coronal-plane (medial/lateral) one at the deep ring, not simply anterior.
why_others_wrong.D: The indirect hernia's defining relationship is lateral to the vessels, not posterior; posterior describes neither hernia type.
why_others_wrong.E: Hernia classification relative to the inferior epigastric vessels is described in the medial/lateral plane, not inferior, which is not the relevant descriptor here.

exam_trap: Candidates choose A by mixing up hernia types; medial to the inferior epigastric vessels describes a direct hernia, whereas an indirect hernia enters the deep ring lateral to them.
takeaway: Indirect = lateral to inferior epigastric vessels. Direct = medial.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: Indirect inguinal hernia ↓ enters the deep inguinal ring ↓ deep ring lies lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels ↓ Lateral
pearl: Indirect hernias follow a patent processus vaginalis, so they are the usual type in children and young men and can extend into the scrotum.

subject: Anatomy
title: Acute abdomen & GI surgery: obturator hernia
stem: An obturator hernia is most likely to compress which nerve?
why_correct: An obturator hernia passes through the obturator canal and may compress the obturator nerve, producing pain radiating along the medial thigh.

why_others_wrong.A: The femoral nerve enters the thigh lateral to the femoral sheath beneath the inguinal ligament, well away from the obturator canal.
why_others_wrong.C: The sciatic nerve exits through the greater sciatic foramen posteriorly and is unrelated to the obturator canal or obturator hernias.
why_others_wrong.D: The pudendal nerve travels through the lesser sciatic foramen to the perineum and is not compressed by herniation through the obturator canal.
why_others_wrong.E: The common fibular nerve is a branch of the sciatic nerve found in the posterior thigh/popliteal region, anatomically remote from the obturator canal.

exam_trap: Candidates pick A because the femoral nerve is the familiar groin nerve; an obturator hernia compresses the obturator nerve in its canal, giving pain along the medial thigh.
takeaway: Obturator canal hernia → obturator nerve compression.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: Obturator hernia ↓ passes through the obturator canal ↓ canal also transmits the obturator nerve and vessels ↓ Obturator nerve
pearl: Obturator hernias classically affect thin elderly women and often present as small bowel obstruction with pain down the medial thigh to the knee; the diagnosis is usually made on CT.

subject: Anatomy
title: Hand trauma: axillary artery
stem: Which artery is a continuation of the subclavian artery after it crosses the lateral border of the first rib?
why_correct: The subclavian artery becomes the axillary artery at the lateral border of the first rib. It becomes the brachial artery at the inferior border of teres major.

why_others_wrong.A: The brachial artery begins at the inferior border of teres major, not at the first rib.
why_others_wrong.C: The radial artery is a terminal branch of the brachial artery in the cubital fossa.
why_others_wrong.D: The ulnar artery is the other terminal branch of the brachial artery in the cubital fossa.
why_others_wrong.E: The internal thoracic artery is a branch of the first part of the subclavian artery, not its continuation.

exam_trap: Subclavian → axillary at first rib. Axillary → brachial at teres major.
takeaway: Lateral border first rib = axillary artery begins.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: Subclavian artery crosses the lateral border of the first rib ↓ becomes the axillary artery ↓ axillary becomes brachial at the lower border of teres major ↓ Axillary artery
pearl: The scapular anastomosis between subclavian branches and the subscapular artery can maintain limb perfusion if the axillary artery is ligated proximal to the subscapular origin.

subject: Anatomy
title: Hand trauma: axillary artery second part
stem: Which muscle is used to divide the axillary artery into three parts?
why_correct: The pectoralis minor crosses anterior to the second part of the axillary artery. The three parts of the axillary artery are defined by their relationship to pectoralis minor.

why_others_wrong.A: Pectoralis major covers the whole axillary artery anteriorly but is not the landmark defining its parts.
why_others_wrong.C: Subclavius lies under the clavicle above the axillary artery and does not cross its second part.
why_others_wrong.D: Serratus anterior forms the medial wall of the axilla and lies medial to the artery.
why_others_wrong.E: Latissimus dorsi forms part of the posterior axillary wall near the third part and plays no role in dividing the artery.

exam_trap: Axillary artery parts are named relative to pectoralis minor, not pectoralis major.
takeaway: Pectoralis minor divides axillary artery into three parts.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: Axillary artery divided into three parts ↓ by the muscle crossing in front of it ↓ first part above, second behind, third below pectoralis minor ↓ Pectoralis minor
pearl: The three parts give one, two and three branches: superior thoracic; thoracoacromial and lateral thoracic; then subscapular with the anterior and posterior circumflex humeral arteries.

subject: Anatomy
title: Hand trauma: radial nerve
stem: A fracture through the midshaft of the humerus is followed by wrist drop. Which nerve is most likely injured?
why_correct: The radial nerve runs in the radial groove on the posterior aspect of the humerus and is vulnerable to midshaft humeral fractures. Injury can cause weakness of wrist and finger extension.

why_others_wrong.A: Median nerve injury weakens wrist and finger flexion, pronation and thenar function rather than causing wrist drop, and is classically linked to supracondylar fractures.
why_others_wrong.B: Ulnar nerve injury causes intrinsic hand weakness and clawing and is associated with the medial epicondyle, not the humeral midshaft.
why_others_wrong.D: The musculocutaneous nerve pierces coracobrachialis and runs between biceps and brachialis; injury weakens elbow flexion rather than causing wrist drop.
why_others_wrong.E: The axillary nerve is at risk with surgical neck fractures and shoulder dislocation, causing deltoid weakness rather than wrist drop.

exam_trap: Axillary nerve is chosen because it is the other classic humeral nerve injury, but it is damaged at the surgical neck and causes deltoid weakness, not wrist drop.
takeaway: Radial groove injury → wrist drop.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: Midshaft humeral fracture ↓ the radial nerve runs in the radial groove on the posterior humerus ↓ injury causes loss of wrist and finger extension ↓ wrist drop ↓ Radial
pearl: Most radial nerve palsies with closed humeral shaft fractures are neurapraxias that recover spontaneously, so initial management is usually expectant with a wrist extension splint.

subject: Anatomy
title: Hand trauma: axillary nerve
stem: A fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus produces difficulty abducting the arm beyond the initial range. Which nerve is most likely injured?
why_correct: The axillary nerve winds around the surgical neck of the humerus and supplies the deltoid. Injury causes impaired shoulder abduction after the initial movement and sensory loss over the regimental-badge area.

why_others_wrong.A: The radial nerve is at risk in midshaft humeral fractures and causes wrist drop, not selective loss of abduction.
why_others_wrong.C: The median nerve supplies forearm flexors and thenar muscles and plays no part in shoulder abduction.
why_others_wrong.D: The ulnar nerve is related to the medial epicondyle and supplies hand intrinsics, not the shoulder abductors.
why_others_wrong.E: The musculocutaneous nerve supplies the anterior arm flexors and would cause weak elbow flexion rather than impaired abduction.

exam_trap: Radial nerve is chosen by candidates who link all humeral fractures with it, but it is at risk in shaft fractures; surgical neck fractures endanger the axillary nerve.
takeaway: Surgical neck → axillary nerve.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: Surgical neck fracture of the humerus ↓ abduction lost after the initial range ↓ deltoid paralysed, supraspinatus intact ↓ axillary nerve winds round the surgical neck ↓ Axillary
pearl: Axillary nerve function should be documented before and after reduction of a shoulder dislocation, by testing sensation over the regimental badge area and deltoid contraction.

subject: Hand trauma
title: Hand trauma: median nerve in the forearm
stem: Which muscle is supplied by the anterior interosseous nerve, a branch of the median nerve?

options.B: Flexor digitorum profundus to the index finger

correct_answer: B. Flexor digitorum profundus to the index finger
why_correct: The anterior interosseous nerve supplies flexor pollicis longus, pronator quadratus and the lateral part of flexor digitorum profundus, including the index finger component.

why_others_wrong.A: Flexor carpi ulnaris is supplied by the ulnar nerve, not the anterior interosseous nerve.
why_others_wrong.C: Palmaris longus is supplied by the main trunk of the median nerve before the anterior interosseous branch arises.
why_others_wrong.D: Flexor carpi radialis is supplied by the main trunk of the median nerve, not by its anterior interosseous branch.
why_others_wrong.E: Pronator teres is supplied by the main median nerve trunk in the cubital fossa; the anterior interosseous nerve supplies pronator quadratus instead.

exam_trap: Pronator teres is chosen because it is median-supplied, but its branch arises from the main median trunk; the anterior interosseous nerve supplies pronator quadratus.
takeaway: AIN lesion → impaired pinch/“OK sign”.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: Anterior interosseous branch of the median nerve ↓ supplies FPL, pronator quadratus and lateral FDP ↓ index finger FDP is in that lateral part ↓ Flexor digitorum profundus to the index finger
pearl: FDP to the index and middle fingers is median-supplied via the anterior interosseous nerve, whereas FDP to the ring and little fingers is ulnar-supplied.

subject: Hand trauma
title: Hand trauma: ulnar nerve at the elbow
stem: A patient develops numbness in the little finger and medial half of the ring finger after trauma around the medial epicondyle. Which nerve is affected?
why_correct: The ulnar nerve passes posterior to the medial epicondyle and supplies sensation to the little finger and adjacent half of the ring finger.

why_others_wrong.A: The median nerve supplies the thumb, index, middle and radial half of the ring finger and lies anterior to the elbow, not behind the medial epicondyle.
why_others_wrong.B: The radial nerve passes anterior to the lateral epicondyle and supplies dorsal radial hand skin, not the little finger.
why_others_wrong.D: The musculocutaneous nerve gives sensation to the lateral forearm and does not supply any of the fingers.
why_others_wrong.E: The axillary nerve supplies skin over the lateral shoulder and is unrelated to the medial epicondyle or the fingers.

exam_trap: Median nerve tempts candidates because it also crosses the elbow, but it lies anterior and supplies the radial digits, not the little and ring fingers.
takeaway: Medial epicondyle → ulnar nerve.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed (2020).
thinking: Trauma at the medial epicondyle ↓ numb little finger and medial half of the ring finger ↓ ulnar nerve runs behind the medial epicondyle ↓ Ulnar
pearl: Ulnar nerve compression at the elbow (cubital tunnel syndrome) is the second commonest upper limb entrapment neuropathy after carpal tunnel syndrome.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Pathology: oncology & haematology: heparin mechanism
stem: Unfractionated heparin produces anticoagulation primarily by enhancing the activity of which endogenous anticoagulant?
why_correct: Heparin binds antithrombin and accelerates inhibition of thrombin and factor Xa, among other activated clotting factors.

why_others_wrong.A: Protein C is activated by thrombin-thrombomodulin and inactivates factors Va and VIIIa; heparin does not act by enhancing it.
why_others_wrong.C: Plasmin is the fibrinolytic enzyme that breaks down fibrin, and heparin does not work by increasing its activity.
why_others_wrong.D: Protein S is the cofactor for activated protein C and is not the anticoagulant potentiated by heparin binding.
why_others_wrong.E: Tissue factor initiates the extrinsic coagulation pathway with factor VIIa, so it is procoagulant rather than an endogenous anticoagulant.

exam_trap: Protein C tempts as a familiar natural anticoagulant, but it is activated by thrombin bound to thrombomodulin; heparin works by accelerating antithrombin's inhibition of thrombin and factor Xa.
takeaway: Unfractionated heparin potentiates antithrombin.
source: Principles and Practice of Surgery, 7th ed (2023).
thinking: Unfractionated heparin ↓ binds antithrombin through a specific pentasaccharide ↓ accelerates inactivation of thrombin and factor Xa ↓ Antithrombin
pearl: Unfractionated heparin is monitored with the APTT and fully reversed by protamine, which suits perioperative use when rapid reversal may be needed; heparin-induced thrombocytopenia is a prothrombotic complication to watch for.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Pathology: oncology & haematology: warfarin
stem: Warfarin reduces synthesis of which group of coagulation factors?
why_correct: Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase and reduces synthesis of vitamin K-dependent factors II, VII, IX and X, as well as proteins C and S.

why_others_wrong.A: Fibrinogen, factors V and VIII and factor XIII are not vitamin K-dependent, so warfarin does not reduce their synthesis.
why_others_wrong.C: Factors VIII, XI and XII are not vitamin K-dependent; only factor IX in this group is affected by warfarin.
why_others_wrong.D: Only prothrombin (factor II) in this group is vitamin K-dependent; fibrinogen and factors V and VIII are unaffected by warfarin.
why_others_wrong.E: Factor VII is vitamin K-dependent, but factors V, XI and XIII are not, so this group does not match warfarin's action.

exam_trap: The VIII, IX, XI, XII set tempts because it includes factor IX, but factors VIII, XI and XII are not vitamin K dependent; warfarin lowers II, VII, IX and X.
takeaway: Warfarin reduces II, VII, IX, X + proteins C/S.
source: Principles and Practice of Surgery, 7th ed (2023).
thinking: Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase ↓ gamma-carboxylation of vitamin K-dependent factors fails ↓ factors II, VII, IX and X fall ↓ II, VII, IX, X
pearl: Warfarin also lowers proteins C and S, and protein C falls quickly, so early therapy can be transiently prothrombotic; this is why heparin cover is given when starting warfarin for acute thrombosis.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Pathology: oncology & haematology: protein c
stem: Protein C becomes an anticoagulant after activation by thrombin bound to which endothelial receptor?
why_correct: Thrombin bound to thrombomodulin activates protein C. Activated protein C, with protein S as a cofactor, inactivates factors Va and VIIIa.

why_others_wrong.A: Tissue factor binds factor VIIa to initiate coagulation and does not bind thrombin to activate protein C.
why_others_wrong.C: Glycoprotein Ib is a platelet receptor for von Willebrand factor mediating adhesion, not an endothelial thrombin receptor.
why_others_wrong.D: P2Y12 is a platelet ADP receptor targeted by clopidogrel and has no role in protein C activation.
why_others_wrong.E: PAR-1 is a thrombin receptor on platelets and endothelium that mediates procoagulant and cellular signalling, not protein C activation.

exam_trap: PAR-1 tempts because it is a thrombin receptor on endothelium, but it mediates cell signalling and platelet activation; thrombin activates protein C only when bound to thrombomodulin.
takeaway: Thrombomodulin converts thrombin from procoagulant to protein-C activating pathway.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed (2023).
thinking: Protein C needs activation to act as an anticoagulant ↓ thrombin binds an endothelial receptor ↓ the complex switches thrombin from procoagulant to anticoagulant ↓ Thrombomodulin
pearl: Activated protein C with protein S inactivates factors Va and VIIIa; inherited protein C or S deficiency causes thrombophilia and predisposes to warfarin-induced skin necrosis.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Pathology: oncology & haematology: von willebrand factor
stem: Which platelet receptor binds von Willebrand factor during initial platelet adhesion?
why_correct: GPIb on platelets binds von Willebrand factor attached to exposed subendothelial structures, mediating platelet adhesion under conditions of high shear.

why_others_wrong.A: GPIIb/IIIa binds fibrinogen to mediate platelet aggregation, which follows the initial GPIb-dependent adhesion to von Willebrand factor.
why_others_wrong.C: P2Y12 is an ADP receptor that amplifies platelet activation and is the target of clopidogrel, not the von Willebrand factor receptor.
why_others_wrong.D: PAR-1 is a thrombin receptor that triggers platelet activation rather than binding von Willebrand factor for adhesion.
why_others_wrong.E: GPVI binds exposed collagen directly and contributes to activation, whereas initial high-shear adhesion via von Willebrand factor uses GPIb.

exam_trap: GPIIb/IIIa is the commonest wrong choice, but it binds fibrinogen for aggregation; adhesion to von Willebrand factor under high shear uses GPIb.
takeaway: vWF ↔ GPIb = platelet adhesion.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed (2023).
thinking: Initial platelet adhesion ↓ von Willebrand factor is attached to exposed subendothelium ↓ the platelet receptor that captures it under high shear is GPIb ↓ GPIb
pearl: Inherited GPIb deficiency causes a rare bleeding disorder with giant platelets and thrombocytopenia, whereas GPIIb/IIIa deficiency gives a normal platelet count with absent aggregation.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Pathology: oncology & haematology: platelet aggregation
stem: Which platelet receptor is essential for fibrinogen-mediated platelet aggregation?
why_correct: Activated GPIIb/IIIa receptors bind fibrinogen, allowing fibrinogen to bridge adjacent platelets and produce aggregation.

why_others_wrong.A: GPIb binds von Willebrand factor to mediate platelet adhesion, not fibrinogen bridging between platelets.
why_others_wrong.C: P2Y1 is an ADP receptor that contributes to platelet shape change and activation but does not itself bind fibrinogen.
why_others_wrong.D: Human platelets respond to thrombin through PAR-1 and PAR-4, not PAR-2, and no PAR receptor binds fibrinogen to bridge platelets during aggregation.
why_others_wrong.E: GPVI is a collagen receptor that triggers activation; fibrinogen-mediated aggregation depends on activated GPIIb/IIIa.

exam_trap: GPIb tempts because it is the best-known platelet receptor, but it binds von Willebrand factor for adhesion; fibrinogen bridging during aggregation requires activated GPIIb/IIIa.
takeaway: Platelet aggregation requires activated GPIIb/IIIa.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed (2023).
thinking: Fibrinogen-mediated aggregation ↓ fibrinogen bridges adjacent activated platelets ↓ the receptor it binds is activated GPIIb/IIIa ↓ GPIIb/IIIa
pearl: GPIIb/IIIa is the final common pathway of platelet aggregation, so intravenous GPIIb/IIIa inhibitors such as tirofiban are potent antiplatelet agents used in selected high-risk coronary interventions.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Pathology: oncology & haematology: fibrin cross-linking
stem: Which coagulation factor stabilises the fibrin clot by cross-linking fibrin strands?
why_correct: Factor XIII is activated by thrombin and calcium and cross-links fibrin, strengthening and stabilising the clot.

why_others_wrong.A: Factor II (prothrombin) is converted to thrombin, which cleaves fibrinogen and activates factor XIII but does not itself cross-link fibrin.
why_others_wrong.B: Factor V is a cofactor in the prothrombinase complex that accelerates thrombin generation, not a fibrin cross-linking enzyme.
why_others_wrong.C: Factor VII combines with tissue factor to initiate coagulation and has no role in stabilising fibrin strands.
why_others_wrong.E: Factor XII initiates contact activation in vitro and is not needed for haemostasis; it does not cross-link fibrin.

exam_trap: Factor XII tempts because of its similar numbering, but it initiates contact activation in vitro; factor XIII, a transglutaminase, cross-links fibrin strands.
takeaway: Factor XIII = fibrin cross-linking.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed (2023).
thinking: Stabilisation of the fibrin clot ↓ fibrin strands must be covalently cross-linked ↓ this transglutaminase is activated by thrombin and calcium ↓ Factor XIII
pearl: Because factor XIII acts after fibrin forms, its deficiency leaves the PT and APTT normal, so unexplained delayed surgical bleeding needs a specific factor XIII assay.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Pathology: oncology & haematology: desmopressin
stem: A patient with mild haemophilia A requires a minor surgical procedure. Which drug may increase endogenous factor VIII and von Willebrand factor?
why_correct: Desmopressin (DDAVP), a vasopressin analogue, can increase endothelial release of von Willebrand factor and factor VIII and is useful in selected patients with mild haemophilia A and some forms of von Willebrand disease.

why_others_wrong.A: Protamine neutralises heparin by forming a stable complex and does not increase factor VIII or von Willebrand factor release.
why_others_wrong.C: Vitamin K supports synthesis of factors II, VII, IX and X and does not raise factor VIII, which is deficient in haemophilia A.
why_others_wrong.D: Tranexamic acid is a useful antifibrinolytic adjunct but does not raise endogenous factor VIII or von Willebrand factor levels.
why_others_wrong.E: Warfarin is an anticoagulant that reduces vitamin K-dependent factors and would worsen bleeding in haemophilia.

exam_trap: DDAVP is useful in selected mild haemophilia A patients, not severe haemophilia A where factor replacement is required.
takeaway: Desmopressin → ↑ vWF + factor VIII release.
source: BNF, current edition (accessed 2026).
thinking: Mild haemophilia A needing minor surgery ↓ aim is to raise the patient's own factor VIII ↓ a vasopressin analogue releases stored vWF and factor VIII from endothelium ↓ Desmopressin
pearl: A trial dose response should be confirmed before relying on desmopressin, and repeated doses cause tachyphylaxis as endothelial stores deplete; its antidiuretic effect can cause hyponatraemia, so fluids are restricted.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Pathology: oncology & haematology: tranexamic acid
stem: What is the principal mechanism of tranexamic acid?

options.C: Inhibition of plasminogen binding/activation and therefore fibrinolysis

correct_answer: C. Inhibition of plasminogen binding/activation and therefore fibrinolysis
why_correct: Tranexamic acid is an antifibrinolytic. It binds lysine-binding sites on plasminogen/plasmin and reduces plasminogen activation and interaction with fibrin, thereby reducing fibrin breakdown.

why_others_wrong.A: Direct thrombin inhibition describes drugs such as dabigatran and argatroban; tranexamic acid acts on the fibrinolytic system instead.
why_others_wrong.B: Activating plasminogen is the action of thrombolytics such as alteplase, the opposite of tranexamic acid's antifibrinolytic effect.
why_others_wrong.D: Irreversible platelet COX-1 inhibition is the mechanism of aspirin, which reduces thromboxane A2 rather than fibrinolysis.
why_others_wrong.E: Vitamin K antagonism is the mechanism of warfarin, which reduces synthesis of clotting factors rather than blocking fibrinolysis.

exam_trap: Option B, activation of plasminogen, is the opposite effect: it describes thrombolytics such as alteplase, whereas tranexamic acid blocks plasminogen binding and activation.
takeaway: TXA = antifibrinolytic → preserves formed fibrin clot.
source: BNF, current edition (accessed 2026).
thinking: Tranexamic acid is a lysine analogue ↓ binds lysine-binding sites on plasminogen ↓ plasminogen cannot bind fibrin and be activated to plasmin ↓ Inhibition of plasminogen binding/activation and therefore fibrinolysis
