source: Standard clinical trial methodology; MRCS Part A applied evidence-based medicine principles.
thinking: Non-inferiority trial ↓ maximum acceptable loss of efficacy ↓ fixed before recruitment ↓ Non-inferiority margin
pearl: The margin is usually set as a fraction of the known benefit of the standard treatment over placebo, so that a non-inferior new treatment still retains a clinically meaningful benefit.

subject: Research methods & screening
title: Statistics & evidence-based medicine: cluster randomisation
stem: A hospital study randomises entire hospitals rather than individual patients. What type of randomised trial is this?
why_correct: In a cluster randomised trial, groups or clusters—such as hospitals, practices, wards or schools—are randomised rather than individual participants.

why_others_wrong.A: A crossover trial gives each participant both treatments in sequence, rather than randomising whole hospitals to one arm.
why_others_wrong.C: A case-control study is observational and involves no randomisation, so it cannot describe randomising hospitals.
why_others_wrong.D: An ecological study analyses group-level data but is observational, whereas here the hospitals are randomly allocated.
why_others_wrong.E: A diagnostic cohort study evaluates a test's accuracy in a group of patients and does not involve randomising hospitals.

exam_trap: Ecological study is tempting because hospitals are groups, but ecological studies are observational; randomly allocating whole hospitals to an intervention defines a cluster randomised trial.
takeaway: Who gets randomised? Individual = individual RCT; group = cluster RCT.
source: Standard clinical epidemiology principles; MRCS Part A scope.
thinking: Entire hospitals randomised ↓ unit of randomisation is a group, not the patient ↓ Cluster randomised trial
pearl: Stepped-wedge designs are a variant of cluster randomisation in which every cluster eventually receives the intervention, with the timing of crossover randomised.

subject: Research methods & screening
title: Statistics & evidence-based medicine: cluster trial analysis
stem: A cluster-randomised trial includes patients treated within the same hospitals. Why can treating all patients as completely independent observations produce misleadingly precise estimates?

options.A: Patients within a cluster may be correlated
options.E: Cluster trials have no control group

correct_answer: A. Patients within a cluster may be correlated
why_correct: Patients within the same cluster can share clinicians, policies, environment and other characteristics. Their outcomes may therefore be correlated, violating the assumption of independence.

why_others_wrong.B: Randomisation is possible in cluster trials; it is simply applied to clusters such as hospitals rather than individuals.
why_others_wrong.C: Clusters are not identical; the issue is that patients within the same cluster tend to resemble one another.
why_others_wrong.D: Outcomes can be measured in cluster trials; the problem is that correlated outcomes reduce the effective sample size.
why_others_wrong.E: Cluster trials do have control clusters, so a missing control group is not why estimates appear too precise.

exam_trap: Candidates may think randomisation is impossible in cluster trials, but clusters are randomised; the problem is correlated outcomes within a cluster, which shrink the effective sample size.
takeaway: A cluster RCT is not simply an ordinary RCT with bigger groups.
source: Standard clinical epidemiology principles.
thinking: Patients within one hospital share clinicians and policies ↓ outcomes within a cluster are correlated ↓ observations not independent ↓ effective sample size smaller ↓ Patients within a cluster may be correlated
pearl: The design effect, calculated from the cluster size and the intracluster correlation coefficient, quantifies how much a cluster trial's sample size must be inflated compared with individual randomisation.

subject: Research methods & screening
title: Statistics & evidence-based medicine: crossover trial
stem: A stable chronic condition is studied using a trial in which each participant receives treatment A and treatment B in separate periods. Which design is being used?
why_correct: In a crossover trial, participants receive more than one intervention sequentially, usually in a randomised order.

why_others_wrong.A: In a parallel-group trial each participant receives only one treatment, whereas here each receives both in separate periods.
why_others_wrong.C: A cluster trial randomises groups such as wards or hospitals, not the sequence of treatments within one participant.
why_others_wrong.D: A case-control study is observational and retrospective, with no treatments given to participants by the investigators.
why_others_wrong.E: An ecological study compares populations using aggregate data and does not give individual participants sequential treatments.

exam_trap: Parallel-group trial is the main distractor, but in a parallel design each participant gets one treatment only; receiving both in separate periods defines a crossover trial.
takeaway: Same patient + A then B = crossover design.
source: Standard clinical trial methodology.
thinking: Stable chronic condition ↓ each participant receives A and B in separate periods ↓ within-person comparison ↓ Crossover trial
pearl: Analysis of a crossover trial should test for period and sequence effects, since outcomes may differ simply because one treatment is given first.

subject: Research methods & screening
title: Statistics & evidence-based medicine: carryover effect
stem: A crossover trial compares two treatments for a chronic disease. The effect of the first treatment persists into the second treatment period. What is this called?
why_correct: A carryover effect occurs when the effect of an intervention persists into the subsequent treatment period, potentially contaminating comparison between periods.

why_others_wrong.A: Selection bias concerns how participants enter or are allocated in a study, not a treatment effect persisting into the next period.
why_others_wrong.C: Recall bias arises from inaccurate recollection of past exposures, not from lingering pharmacological effects between periods.
why_others_wrong.D: Verification bias occurs when the reference standard is applied selectively in diagnostic studies, not in crossover treatment periods.
why_others_wrong.E: Spectrum bias relates to an unrepresentative patient mix in diagnostic studies and does not describe persisting treatment effects.

exam_trap: Crossover trials need sufficient washout when pharmacological or clinical effects may persist.
takeaway: First treatment still acting in period 2 = carryover.
source: Standard clinical trial methodology.
thinking: Crossover trial ↓ first treatment's effect persists into period 2 ↓ contaminates comparison ↓ Carryover effect
pearl: A washout period longer than several half-lives of the first drug is the main protection against carryover; if carryover is likely, a parallel-group design should be used instead.

subject: Research methods & screening
title: Statistics & evidence-based medicine: funnel plot
stem: A meta-analysis contains studies of different sizes. Investigators plot treatment effect against study precision and note marked asymmetry. What problem can funnel-plot asymmetry suggest?
why_correct: Funnel-plot asymmetry can suggest publication bias, particularly if smaller studies with certain results appear to be missing. However, asymmetry can have other explanations and does not prove publication bias.

why_others_wrong.B: Randomisation operates within individual trials and funnel-plot asymmetry says nothing to suggest it was perfect.
why_others_wrong.C: Asymmetry suggests small-study effects or missing studies, and it may coexist with heterogeneity rather than indicating its absence.
why_others_wrong.D: Sensitivity is a diagnostic test property and is not what a funnel plot of treatment effect against precision assesses.
why_others_wrong.E: Specificity is a diagnostic test property and is unrelated to asymmetry in a funnel plot of trial results.

exam_trap: Absence of heterogeneity is a tempting pick, but asymmetry indicates small-study effects such as publication bias, which may coexist with heterogeneity; it suggests rather than proves bias.
takeaway: Funnel asymmetry is a warning signal, not automatic proof of publication bias.
source: Standard systematic-review methodology.
thinking: Effect plotted against study precision ↓ small studies should scatter symmetrically ↓ asymmetry suggests small negative studies missing ↓ Publication bias
pearl: Funnel-plot asymmetry can also arise from genuine heterogeneity or poorer methodological quality in small studies, and the plot is unreliable with fewer than about ten studies.

subject: Statistics & evidence-based medicine
title: Research methods & screening: calibration
stem: A clinical risk model predicts that a group of patients has an average 10% risk of postoperative complication. In that group, approximately 10% actually develop the complication. Which property of the model is being demonstrated?
why_correct: Calibration describes agreement between predicted probabilities and observed event frequencies.

why_others_wrong.A: Sensitivity is the proportion of people with the complication correctly identified at a threshold, not agreement between a predicted 10% and an observed 10%.
why_others_wrong.C: Specificity is the proportion of people without the complication correctly identified as negative, which says nothing about predicted versus observed risk.
why_others_wrong.D: Positive predictive value is the proportion of test-positive people who have the outcome; the stem compares predicted with observed average risk instead.
why_others_wrong.E: Discrimination is the ability to rank patients who do and do not develop the complication, and a well-calibrated model need not discriminate well.

exam_trap: Candidates may pick high discrimination, but discrimination is the ability to separate patients with and without the outcome; agreement between a predicted 10% and an observed 10% is calibration.
takeaway: Predicted 10% and observed about 10% → calibration.
source: Standard clinical prediction-model methodology.
thinking: Model predicts an average 10% risk ↓ about 10% actually develop the complication ↓ predicted and observed risks agree ↓ Good calibration
pearl: Calibration is often displayed with a calibration plot of predicted against observed risk; points lying on the 45-degree line indicate good calibration.

subject: Statistics & evidence-based medicine
title: Research methods & screening: discrimination
stem: Two patients are assessed using a postoperative risk model. One develops the complication and the other does not. The model consistently assigns higher predicted risk to patients who develop the complication. Which property is primarily being assessed?
why_correct: Discrimination describes how well a model separates individuals who experience an outcome from those who do not. The area under the ROC curve is commonly used to quantify discrimination.

why_others_wrong.A: Calibration compares predicted with observed risk levels; consistently ranking those who develop the complication higher describes separation, which is discrimination.
why_others_wrong.C: External validity concerns whether a model performs in a new population, not its ability to separate patients who do and do not develop the outcome.
why_others_wrong.D: Allocation concealment protects the randomisation sequence in trials and has no bearing on how a prediction model ranks patients.
why_others_wrong.E: Publication bias arises when studies are selectively published according to their results, not from the performance of a single risk model.

exam_trap: Calibration is the usual wrong pick; it compares predicted with observed risk levels, whereas consistently ranking affected patients higher is discrimination.
takeaway: Discrimination asks whether the model separates high-risk from low-risk patients.
source: Standard clinical prediction-model methodology. ==================================================
thinking: One patient develops the complication, the other does not ↓ model ranks the affected patient higher ↓ ability to separate those with and without the outcome ↓ Discrimination
pearl: The concordance (C) statistic, equivalent to the ROC AUC for binary outcomes, quantifies discrimination; 0.5 is chance and 1.0 perfect separation.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Perioperative medicine & nutrition: iv fluid maintenance in adults
stem: A 68-year-old man weighing 70 kg is unable to take oral fluids after surgery. He has no significant cardiac or renal impairment and requires IV fluids for routine maintenance only. Which initial daily volume is most consistent with NICE guidance?
why_correct: For routine maintenance in adults, NICE recommends an initial prescription of approximately 25–30 ml/kg/day of water in appropriate patients. For 70 kg this is 70 × 25 = 1750 ml/day to 70 × 30 = 2100 ml/day.

why_others_wrong.A: 500 to 750 ml is well below 25 to 30 ml/kg/day for a 70 kg man and would leave him progressively dehydrated.
why_others_wrong.B: 1000 to 1200 ml equates to roughly 15 ml/kg/day, below even the reduced 20 to 25 ml/kg/day NICE suggests for frail or cardiac patients.
why_others_wrong.D: 2500 to 3000 ml exceeds 30 ml/kg/day for 70 kg and risks fluid overload in a patient needing routine maintenance only.
why_others_wrong.E: 3500 to 4000 ml is around 50 to 57 ml/kg/day, nearly double routine maintenance needs, and risks fluid overload.

exam_trap: Option D tempts because 2.5-3 litres is often prescribed by habit, but that exceeds 30 ml/kg/day for a 70 kg man and risks overload when only maintenance is needed.
takeaway: Maintenance ≈ 25–30 ml/kg/day in the appropriate adult.
source: NICE CG174, Intravenous fluid therapy in adults in hospital; current NICE recommendations accessed September 2026.
thinking: Routine maintenance only, no cardiac or renal impairment ↓ NICE starting volume is 25-30 ml/kg/day ↓ 70 kg x 25-30 ml ↓ 1750–2100 ml
pearl: A practical day-one regimen within NICE guidance is sodium chloride 0.18% in 4% glucose with potassium, prescribed by weight and rounded to the nearest available bag size, then adjusted to oral intake and electrolytes.

subject: Major trauma & fluids
title: Major trauma & fluids: iv fluid resuscitation
stem: A 75 kg adult presents with hypovolaemia and requires IV fluid resuscitation. According to current NICE guidance, which initial crystalloid strategy is appropriate?
correct_answer: C. 500 ml over less than 15 minutes
why_correct: NICE recommends a crystalloid containing sodium in the range 130–154 mmol/L, given as a 500 ml bolus over less than 15 minutes when adult IV fluid resuscitation is required.

why_others_wrong.A: 100 ml over an hour is too little and too slow to act as a resuscitation bolus in a hypovolaemic adult.
why_others_wrong.B: 250 ml over 2 hours is too slow for resuscitation; NICE CG174 specifies a 500 ml bolus given over less than 15 minutes.
why_others_wrong.D: A routine 1 litre bolus exceeds the NICE CG174 500 ml bolus and removes the chance to reassess before more fluid is given.
why_others_wrong.E: A routine 2 litre infusion risks fluid overload and ignores the NICE principle of a 500 ml bolus followed by reassessment.

exam_trap: Do not use the 25–30 ml/kg/day maintenance rule for acute resuscitation.
takeaway: General adult IV resuscitation (NICE CG174): 500 ml crystalloid bolus over less than 15 minutes, then reassess; sepsis now starts with 250 ml, and active bleeding needs blood products.
source: NICE CG174; current recommendations accessed September 2026.
thinking: Hypovolaemic adult needing IV resuscitation ↓ general NICE adult IV-fluid guidance, not sepsis-specific ↓ crystalloid with sodium 130–154 mmol/L ↓ 500 ml bolus over less than 15 minutes, then reassess ↓ 500 ml over less than 15 minutes
pearl: NICE adult IV-fluid guidance advises seeking expert help if a patient still needs fluid resuscitation after about 2,000 ml of boluses.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Perioperative medicine & nutrition: iv potassium safety
stem: A junior doctor plans to add potassium chloride manually to an IV fluid bag because the patient's maintenance prescription requires potassium. Which principle is most appropriate?

options.A: Add any required dose directly to the bag
options.B: Potassium should routinely be added to all crystalloid bags
options.C: Use appropriate pre-prepared potassium-containing fluids and prescribed formulations
options.D: Give potassium as a rapid IV bolus
options.E: Potassium can be added without considering renal function

correct_answer: C. Use appropriate pre-prepared potassium-containing fluids and prescribed formulations
why_correct: NICE specifically warns that potassium should not be added manually to IV fluid bags because this is dangerous. Appropriate available preparations should be prescribed and used according to local policy and the patient's clinical circumstances.

why_others_wrong.A: Manually adding potassium chloride to a bag is the practice NICE warns against because errors in concentration and mixing can be fatal.
why_others_wrong.B: Potassium need depends on the patient's serum level, renal function and losses, so it should not be added routinely to every crystalloid bag.
why_others_wrong.D: Rapid IV bolus potassium can cause cardiac arrest and is not an acceptable way to give maintenance potassium.
why_others_wrong.E: Renal impairment reduces potassium excretion, so ignoring renal function risks life-threatening hyperkalaemia.

exam_trap: Option A tempts as a quick way to meet the prescription, but manual addition of potassium chloride to bags is the practice NICE warns against because errors can be fatal.
takeaway: Never improvise IV potassium by manually adding it to a bag.
source: NICE CG174; current recommendations accessed September 2026.
thinking: Maintenance prescription needs potassium ↓ manual addition of potassium chloride to bags risks concentration and mixing errors ↓ such errors can cause fatal arrhythmias ↓ Use appropriate pre-prepared potassium-containing fluids and prescribed formulations
pearl: Concentrated potassium chloride ampoules are a controlled, high-risk medicine in UK hospitals, and intravenous potassium is normally infused no faster than about 10 mmol per hour on a general ward.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Perioperative medicine & nutrition: maintenance fluids in frailty
stem: An 82-year-old frail woman with chronic heart failure requires IV fluids for maintenance because she temporarily cannot drink. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.B: Use the lower end of the maintenance range and reassess frequently
options.D: Give no fluid because heart failure is present

correct_answer: B. Use the lower end of the maintenance range and reassess frequently
why_correct: NICE advises considering less fluid, such as 20–25 ml/kg/day, in people who are older or frail, have renal impairment or cardiac failure, or are at risk of refeeding syndrome.

why_others_wrong.A: 35 to 40 ml/kg/day is above the standard adult range, and this frail woman with heart failure warrants less fluid, not more.
why_others_wrong.C: A fixed 4 litres daily ignores her weight and cardiac failure and would very likely cause pulmonary oedema and fluid overload.
why_others_wrong.D: Heart failure is a reason for caution, not for withholding fluid entirely from a patient who cannot drink and needs maintenance.
why_others_wrong.E: Hypertonic saline is not a maintenance fluid and its sodium load would be hazardous in a patient with chronic heart failure.

exam_trap: Option D tempts because heart failure makes fluid seem dangerous, but withholding all fluid from a patient who cannot drink causes dehydration; the volume is reduced, not abolished.
takeaway: Frail, elderly or cardiac failure → consider lower maintenance volume + close reassessment.
source: NICE CG174; current recommendations accessed September 2026.
thinking: Frail 82-year-old with chronic heart failure ↓ temporarily unable to drink ↓ NICE advises considering lower volumes such as 20-25 ml/kg/day ↓ reassess frequently for overload ↓ Use the lower end of the maintenance range and reassess frequently
pearl: Signs of overload to watch for in such patients include rising weight, peripheral oedema, a raised jugular venous pressure, basal crackles and falling oxygen saturations.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Perioperative medicine & nutrition: obesity and iv maintenance
stem: A 45-year-old man with BMI 43 kg/m² requires IV maintenance fluid. Which principle is most consistent with NICE guidance?

options.A: Use actual body weight without modification
options.B: Use ideal body weight and the lower range of fluid requirements
options.D: Use body weight multiplied by 100 ml/day

correct_answer: B. Use ideal body weight and the lower range of fluid requirements
why_correct: NICE recommends adjusting IV fluid prescriptions in people who are obese using ideal body weight, with lower-range volumes per kg, and advises expert help in severe obesity.

why_others_wrong.A: Multiplying a markedly raised actual body weight by standard ml/kg rates overestimates water needs and risks fluid overload in obesity.
why_others_wrong.C: 50 ml/kg/day is well above the adult maintenance range of 25 to 30 ml/kg/day and would be excessive, especially using actual weight.
why_others_wrong.D: 100 ml/kg/day is a paediatric-style figure for the first 10 kg of a child's weight, not an adult maintenance calculation.
why_others_wrong.E: Obesity changes how the volume is calculated but does not remove the need for maintenance fluid in a patient who cannot drink.

exam_trap: Option A tempts because weight-based prescribing seems precise, but multiplying a markedly raised actual body weight by 25-30 ml/kg overestimates water needs and risks overload.
takeaway: Obesity → consider ideal body weight for the maintenance calculation.
source: NICE CG174; current recommendations accessed September 2026.
thinking: BMI 43 kg/m2 needing maintenance fluid ↓ actual body weight overestimates water needs ↓ NICE advises ideal body weight with lower-range volumes per kg ↓ seek expert help when BMI exceeds 40 ↓ Use ideal body weight and the lower range of fluid requirements
pearl: NICE notes that patients rarely need more than about 3 litres of maintenance fluid a day, and recommends expert advice for prescribing in people with a BMI over 40 kg/m2.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
topic: mechanical vte prophylaxis in peripheral arterial disease
title: Perioperative medicine & nutrition: mechanical vte prophylaxis in peripheral arterial disease
stem: A patient with severe peripheral arterial disease is admitted after surgery. Which mechanical VTE prophylaxis intervention should generally be avoided?
why_correct: NICE advises against anti-embolism stockings in people with suspected or proven peripheral arterial disease because they may cause harm.

why_others_wrong.A: Intermittent pneumatic compression is a mechanical option that NICE does not single out as contraindicated in peripheral arterial disease in the way it does stockings.
why_others_wrong.B: Early mobilisation is encouraged for all surgical patients to reduce VTE risk and poses no particular hazard in peripheral arterial disease.
why_others_wrong.D: Adequate hydration is a general VTE-reducing measure and is not harmful in peripheral arterial disease.
why_others_wrong.E: Regular reassessment of VTE and bleeding risk is good practice for every inpatient and is not something to avoid.

exam_trap: Option A tempts candidates who treat all mechanical methods as equivalent, but NICE singles out anti-embolism stockings as contraindicated in peripheral arterial disease.
takeaway: PAD → do not automatically use anti-embolism stockings.
source: NICE NG89; current recommendations accessed September 2026.
thinking: Severe peripheral arterial disease ↓ graduated compression stockings reduce skin perfusion ↓ risk of skin necrosis and limb ischaemia ↓ NICE advises against stockings in PAD ↓ Anti-embolism stockings
pearl: Other contraindications to anti-embolism stockings include peripheral neuropathy, severe leg oedema, fragile skin or dermatitis, and leg deformity preventing correct fitting.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Perioperative medicine & nutrition: abdominal surgery vte prophylaxis
stem: A patient undergoes major abdominal surgery and has increased VTE risk without a major bleeding contraindication. Which prophylactic approach is recommended by NICE?

options.B: Mechanical prophylaxis only for one hour
options.C: Mechanical prophylaxis plus pharmacological prophylaxis when VTE risk outweighs bleeding risk

correct_answer: C. Mechanical prophylaxis plus pharmacological prophylaxis when VTE risk outweighs bleeding risk
why_correct: For abdominal surgery, NICE recommends mechanical prophylaxis on admission in patients at increased VTE risk and adding pharmacological prophylaxis for at least 7 days when VTE risk outweighs bleeding risk.

why_others_wrong.A: Offering no prophylaxis to a major abdominal surgery patient at increased VTE risk without bleeding contraindication falls short of NICE guidance.
why_others_wrong.B: Mechanical prophylaxis for one hour is far too brief; it should continue until mobility is no longer significantly reduced, with pharmacological cover added.
why_others_wrong.D: Therapeutic-dose anticoagulation treats established VTE and carries unnecessary bleeding risk when only prophylactic dosing is required.
why_others_wrong.E: Aspirin alone is not the NICE-recommended pharmacological prophylaxis after abdominal surgery, where LMWH or fondaparinux is used.

exam_trap: Option D tempts those who think high risk requires full anticoagulation, but prophylactic dosing is used; therapeutic anticoagulation treats established VTE and adds bleeding risk.
takeaway: Abdominal surgery + increased VTE risk → mechanical prophylaxis on admission + add LMWH or fondaparinux for at least 7 days if VTE risk outweighs bleeding risk.
source: NICE NG89; current recommendations accessed September 2026.
thinking: Major abdominal surgery ↓ increased VTE risk without major bleeding contraindication ↓ mechanical prophylaxis from admission ↓ add pharmacological prophylaxis for at least 7 days ↓ Mechanical prophylaxis plus pharmacological prophylaxis when VTE risk outweighs bleeding risk
pearl: Low molecular weight heparin dosing is reduced in severe renal impairment, so renal function should be checked when prescribing pharmacological prophylaxis.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Physiology: lmwh after elective spinal surgery
stem: A patient has undergone elective spinal surgery. VTE risk outweighs bleeding risk. When does NICE suggest starting LMWH when pharmacological prophylaxis is used?

options.A: Immediately before induction in all patients
options.B: 24–48 hours postoperatively according to clinical judgement

correct_answer: B. 24–48 hours postoperatively according to clinical judgement
why_correct: For elective spinal surgery, NICE recommends considering LMWH when VTE risk outweighs bleeding risk and, when used, starting it 24–48 hours postoperatively according to clinical judgement and patient/procedure factors.

why_others_wrong.A: Giving LMWH before induction in all spinal patients raises the risk of epidural haematoma and cord compression, which is why NICE advises postoperative timing.
why_others_wrong.C: Waiting seven days leaves the early postoperative period unprotected when VTE risk is judged to outweigh bleeding risk.
why_others_wrong.D: Starting only after discharge leaves the patient without prophylaxis throughout the inpatient period of reduced mobility.
why_others_wrong.E: Six weeks postoperatively is far too late to prevent VTE in the high-risk early postoperative period.

exam_trap: Option A tempts because preoperative heparin is used in some settings, but pre-induction LMWH in spinal surgery increases the risk of epidural haematoma and cord compression.
takeaway: Spinal surgery + LMWH → typically 24–48 h post-op, individualised.
source: NICE NG89; current recommendations accessed September 2026.
thinking: Elective spinal surgery ↓ epidural haematoma could cause cord compression ↓ pharmacological prophylaxis delayed until early haemostasis is secure ↓ NICE suggests starting LMWH 24-48 hours postoperatively ↓ 24–48 hours postoperatively according to clinical judgement
pearl: Mechanical prophylaxis is started on admission for elective spinal surgery, and any new leg weakness or sphincter disturbance after starting anticoagulation needs urgent MRI to exclude a spinal haematoma.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Perioperative medicine & nutrition: vte prophylaxis after lower-limb immobilisation
stem: A patient is discharged with a below-knee immobilisation following a lower-limb injury. His VTE risk is judged to outweigh bleeding risk. Which drug is specifically recommended by NICE as an option?
why_correct: NICE recommends considering pharmacological VTE prophylaxis with LMWH or fondaparinux for lower-limb immobilisation when VTE risk outweighs bleeding risk.

why_others_wrong.B: Warfarin needs INR monitoring and has a slow, unpredictable onset, so it is not the NICE-recommended option for lower-limb immobilisation prophylaxis.
why_others_wrong.C: Aspirin is not one of the agents NICE recommends for VTE prophylaxis in lower-limb immobilisation, where LMWH or fondaparinux is advised.
why_others_wrong.D: Dabigatran is not among the options NICE specifies for lower-limb immobilisation, and giving it to all patients ignores individual risk assessment.
why_others_wrong.E: Alteplase is a thrombolytic used to dissolve established clot, not a prophylactic agent, and would carry major bleeding risk.

exam_trap: Aspirin tempts as a convenient oral agent used in some orthopaedic settings, but NICE recommends LMWH or fondaparinux for lower-limb immobilisation, not routine aspirin.
takeaway: Lower-limb immobilisation + VTE risk > bleeding risk → consider LMWH or fondaparinux.
source: NICE NG89; current recommendations accessed September 2026.
thinking: Lower-limb immobilisation in a cast or boot ↓ VTE risk outweighs bleeding risk ↓ NICE options are LMWH or fondaparinux ↓ LMWH
pearl: Prophylaxis for lower-limb immobilisation is usually continued for as long as the leg remains immobilised, and the decision should be reassessed when the cast or boot is removed.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Surgical-Site Infection: Hair Removal
stem: A patient requires an elective abdominal operation and has abdominal hair over the planned incision. What is the recommended approach?

options.A: Routinely shave the area the night before
options.D: Apply depilatory cream to every patient
options.E: Remove hair with a razor on the morning of surgery

correct_answer: C. Do not remove hair routinely
why_correct: NICE recommends not using hair removal routinely to reduce surgical-site infection risk. If hair must be removed, electric clippers with a single-use head should be used on the day of surgery.

why_others_wrong.A: Shaving the night before causes skin microabrasions that become colonised overnight, increasing surgical-site infection risk.
why_others_wrong.B: Shaving with a razor, even immediately before surgery, causes skin trauma and raises SSI risk; clippers are used only if removal is necessary.
why_others_wrong.D: Depilatory cream for every patient implies routine hair removal, which NICE advises against, and creams can cause skin reactions.
why_others_wrong.E: Razors cause microscopic skin cuts that increase SSI risk; if hair must go, electric clippers with a single-use head are recommended.

exam_trap: Option B tempts because shaving just before surgery seems to avoid overnight colonisation, but razors still cause skin trauma; if hair must be removed, clippers are used.
takeaway: No routine hair removal; if necessary → electric clippers on the day.
source: NICE NG125, Surgical site infections; current recommendations accessed September 2026.
thinking: Hair over the planned incision ↓ shaving causes skin microabrasions that become colonised ↓ NICE advises against routine hair removal ↓ if needed, use electric clippers on the day ↓ Do not remove hair routinely
pearl: Other NICE measures to reduce surgical site infection include preoperative showering with soap, alcohol-based chlorhexidine skin preparation, appropriate prophylactic antibiotics and maintaining normothermia.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Cardiorespiratory physiology: surgical-site infection and oxygenation
stem: During major surgery, a patient's oxygen saturation falls substantially. Why is maintaining adequate oxygenation relevant to surgical-site infection prevention?

options.A: Tissue oxygenation supports host defence and healing

correct_answer: A. Tissue oxygenation supports host defence and healing
why_correct: Adequate tissue oxygenation supports immune-cell function and wound healing. NICE recommends maintaining optimal oxygenation during surgery and recovery.

why_others_wrong.B: Oxygen supports immune cell (oxidative) killing mechanisms and collagen synthesis but does not act as a direct sterilising agent on the wound itself.
why_others_wrong.C: Adequate oxygenation is an adjunct to, not a replacement for, antimicrobial therapy.
why_others_wrong.D: High-concentration oxygen does not eliminate bacteria; evidence for routine hyperoxia is mixed, and infection prevention depends on many measures beyond oxygenation.
why_others_wrong.E: Oxygenation reduces infection risk but does not guarantee prevention of every postoperative infection, which depends on many other factors.

exam_trap: Candidates may choose absolute options such as hyperoxia eliminating all bacteria; oxygen helps by supporting host defence and healing, not by sterilising wounds or replacing antibiotics.
takeaway: Good oxygenation → better wound defence and healing.
source: NICE NG125; current recommendations accessed September 2026.
thinking: Surgical-site infection depends on host defence in the wound ↓ neutrophil oxidative killing requires molecular oxygen ↓ collagen deposition and healing also need oxygen ↓ Tissue oxygenation supports host defence and healing
pearl: Other perioperative measures that protect wound oxygenation and reduce infection include maintaining normothermia and adequate perfusion, and stopping smoking before surgery.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Physiology: surgical wound irrigation
stem: A surgeon routinely irrigates an uncomplicated surgical wound before closure solely to reduce SSI risk. Which statement best reflects NICE guidance?

options.B: Routine wound irrigation is not recommended solely to reduce SSI risk
options.C: Irrigation with antibiotic solution is mandatory

correct_answer: B. Routine wound irrigation is not recommended solely to reduce SSI risk
why_correct: NICE recommends against using wound irrigation to reduce the risk of SSI and also recommends against intracavity lavage for this purpose.

why_others_wrong.A: NICE recommends against wound irrigation for the purpose of reducing SSI, so routine irrigation is not recommended.
why_others_wrong.C: Antibiotic irrigation is not mandatory; NICE does not support wound irrigation, including with antibiotics, to reduce SSI.
why_others_wrong.D: NICE advises against intracavity lavage to reduce SSI, so it is not required in every case.
why_others_wrong.E: Irrigation does not substitute for skin antisepsis, which remains an evidence-based part of SSI prevention.

exam_trap: Option C tempts because antibiotic washout sounds protective, but NICE does not support wound irrigation, including with antibiotic solutions, to reduce surgical site infection.
takeaway: Do not add routine wound irrigation just to prevent SSI.
source: NICE NG125; current recommendations accessed September 2026.
thinking: Routine wound irrigation before closure ↓ aim is solely to reduce surgical site infection ↓ NICE does not recommend wound irrigation or intracavity lavage for this purpose ↓ Routine wound irrigation is not recommended solely to reduce SSI risk
pearl: Evidence-based measures for reducing surgical site infection include appropriate timing of prophylactic antibiotics, alcohol-based chlorhexidine skin preparation, avoiding routine hair removal and maintaining normothermia.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Perioperative medicine & nutrition: perioperative carbohydrate drinks
stem: A patient is undergoing major abdominal surgery. What is one reason NICE recommends considering preoperative carbohydrate drinks in appropriate patients?

options.E: To eliminate the need for postoperative nutrition

correct_answer: B. To improve postoperative recovery-related outcomes
why_correct: NICE recommends considering carbohydrate drinks before surgery for people undergoing abdominal major or complex surgery. Taking a carbohydrate drink up to 2 hours before surgery shortens the fasted state, reduces postoperative insulin resistance and catabolism, and improves patient comfort, which supports recovery.

why_others_wrong.A: Carbohydrate loading aims to reduce the fasted catabolic state and insulin resistance, the opposite of inducing ketosis.
why_others_wrong.C: Carbohydrate drinks have no antimicrobial effect and do not replace antibiotic prophylaxis for surgical-site infection.
why_others_wrong.D: Preoperative carbohydrate drinks are clear fluids that help prevent, rather than cause, dehydration from prolonged fasting.
why_others_wrong.E: A single preoperative drink does not meet postoperative nutritional requirements, which still need planning after major surgery.

exam_trap: Option A tempts candidates who link carbohydrate loading with metabolic manipulation, but the aim is to prevent the fasted catabolic, ketotic state, not to induce ketosis.
takeaway: Major or complex abdominal surgery → consider preop carbohydrate drinks.
source: NICE NG180; current recommendations accessed September 2026.
thinking: Major abdominal surgery ↓ prolonged fasting worsens insulin resistance and catabolism ↓ preoperative carbohydrate drinks reduce this fasted state ↓ To improve postoperative recovery-related outcomes
pearl: Carbohydrate loading is a standard element of enhanced recovery pathways, but it is used with caution in patients with diabetes or delayed gastric emptying.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Cardiorespiratory physiology: mixed acid-base disorder
stem: A postoperative patient has an arterial blood gas showing pH 7.29, PaCO₂ 4.2 kPa and HCO₃⁻ 15 mmol/L. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
correct_answer: C. Metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation
why_correct: The low pH indicates acidaemia. Bicarbonate is low, identifying metabolic acidosis. The low PaCO₂ indicates hyperventilatory compensation.

why_others_wrong.A: A primary respiratory acidosis would show a raised, not reduced, PaCO2; here PaCO2 is low, consistent with compensation rather than a primary respiratory problem.
why_others_wrong.B: The pH is acidaemic (7.29) and bicarbonate is low, not high, which is inconsistent with metabolic alkalosis.
why_others_wrong.D: The low pH indicates acidaemia, not alkalaemia, so a primary respiratory alkalosis (which raises pH) does not fit; the low PaCO2 here represents compensation for a primary metabolic acidosis.
why_others_wrong.E: Respiratory alkalosis alone would raise pH above normal, not produce the acidaemia seen here, and does not explain the low bicarbonate.

exam_trap: Candidates see a low PaCO2 and pick respiratory alkalosis with metabolic compensation (D), but the pH is acidaemic, so the low PaCO2 must be compensatory.
takeaway: Low pH + low HCO₃⁻ = metabolic acidosis.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.; standard acid-base physiology.
thinking: pH 7.29 = acidaemia ↓ HCO3− 15 mmol/L is low, so the primary process is metabolic acidosis ↓ PaCO2 4.2 kPa is low, reflecting hyperventilation ↓ the low PaCO2 is compensatory, not primary ↓ Metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation
pearl: In a postoperative metabolic acidosis, calculate the anion gap: a raised gap points to lactate from hypoperfusion or ischaemic bowel, or ketones, whereas a normal gap suggests chloride loading from large volumes of 0.9% saline or bicarbonate loss.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: anion gap
stem: A patient has: Na⁺ = 140 mmol/L Cl⁻ = 104 mmol/L HCO₃⁻ = 18 mmol/L. What is the anion gap?
why_correct: Anion gap = Na − (Cl + HCO₃) = 140 − (104 + 18) = 140 − 122 = 18 mmol/L.

why_others_wrong.A: This underestimates the gap; 140 − (104 + 18) correctly works out to 18, not 8.
why_others_wrong.B: 12 is roughly a normal reference anion gap, not the value calculated from these results, which is 18 mmol/L.
why_others_wrong.D: A gap of 22 would require chloride plus bicarbonate to total 118 mmol/L, whereas the given values total 122 mmol/L, giving a gap of 18 mmol/L.
why_others_wrong.E: 36 is obtained by subtracting only chloride from sodium and forgetting to subtract bicarbonate.

exam_trap: Candidates choosing B (12 mmol/L) recall a typical normal anion gap instead of calculating; the values given yield 140 minus 122, which is 18 mmol/L.
takeaway: AG = Na − (Cl + HCO₃).
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
pearl: Some laboratories include potassium in the anion gap, which raises the result by a few mmol/L, so the reference range used must match the formula chosen.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Cardiorespiratory physiology: compensation in metabolic acidosis
stem: A patient with metabolic acidosis develops a marked increase in minute ventilation. What is the principal purpose of this response?

options.C: Reduce PaCO₂ and partially raise pH

correct_answer: C. Reduce PaCO₂ and partially raise pH
why_correct: Hyperventilation removes CO₂, shifting the bicarbonate buffer equilibrium and helping to compensate for metabolic acidosis.

why_others_wrong.A: Hyperventilation lowers, not raises, PaCO2; increasing PaCO2 would worsen rather than compensate for the acidosis.
why_others_wrong.B: Bicarbonate retention is a renal compensatory mechanism operating over a much slower timescale than the acute hyperventilatory response described.
why_others_wrong.D: Hyperventilation is a compensatory response that helps correct acidosis; it does not increase acid production, which would worsen the disorder.
why_others_wrong.E: The goal of the increased ventilation is CO2 clearance to raise pH, not reduction of oxygen uptake, which is not a recognised physiological aim here.

exam_trap: Candidates choose bicarbonate retention, which is the slow renal compensation for respiratory disorders; the rapid response to metabolic acidosis is ventilatory CO2 removal.
takeaway: Metabolic acidosis → hyperventilation → ↓ PaCO₂.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Metabolic acidosis lowers pH ↓ chemoreceptors drive an increase in minute ventilation ↓ CO2 removal shifts the bicarbonate buffer equilibrium ↓ pH is partly restored ↓ Reduce PaCO₂ and partially raise pH
pearl: When intubating a patient with severe metabolic acidosis, the ventilator must match their previous high minute ventilation, otherwise PaCO2 rises and pH can fall dangerously.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Cardiorespiratory physiology: renal compensation for respiratory acidosis
stem: A patient has chronic hypercapnia from longstanding respiratory disease. Which renal adaptation helps compensate?

options.B: Increased bicarbonate retention and increased hydrogen-ion excretion

correct_answer: B. Increased bicarbonate retention and increased hydrogen-ion excretion
why_correct: Chronic respiratory acidosis stimulates renal hydrogen-ion excretion and increased bicarbonate generation/reabsorption, helping to restore pH toward normal.

why_others_wrong.A: This is the opposite of the compensatory response; chronic respiratory acidosis triggers increased, not reduced, renal bicarbonate reabsorption/generation.
why_others_wrong.C: Reduced H+ excretion would worsen, not compensate for, the acidosis; the kidney instead increases H+ excretion.
why_others_wrong.D: Ammonium excretion (a vehicle for H+ excretion) increases, not decreases, as part of the renal compensatory response.
why_others_wrong.E: This would exacerbate acidosis by losing buffer; the kidney instead retains bicarbonate to compensate for chronic respiratory acidosis.

exam_trap: Candidates pick increased bicarbonate loss or reduced ammonium excretion; in chronic respiratory acidosis the kidney retains bicarbonate and increases acid excretion, largely as ammonium.
takeaway: Chronic CO₂ retention → renal H⁺ excretion + HCO₃⁻ retention.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Chronic hypercapnia = chronic respiratory acidosis ↓ the kidneys compensate over days ↓ more H+ is excreted (largely as ammonium) and more bicarbonate is generated and reabsorbed ↓ plasma bicarbonate rises ↓ Increased bicarbonate retention and increased hydrogen-ion excretion
pearl: A raised bicarbonate in a patient with COPD suggests chronic CO2 retention, and if ventilation is corrected rapidly the retained bicarbonate can leave a post-hypercapnic metabolic alkalosis.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Cardiorespiratory physiology: oxygen delivery
stem: A patient develops severe anaemia but has a normal arterial oxygen saturation. Which variable is most directly reduced?
why_correct: Most arterial oxygen is carried bound to haemoglobin. Severe anaemia therefore reduces arterial oxygen content even when PaO₂ and oxygen saturation remain normal.

why_others_wrong.B: FiO2 is an inspired-gas/ventilatory parameter unaffected by red cell mass; it is not reduced by anaemia.
why_others_wrong.C: PaO2 reflects dissolved oxygen tension and depends on gas exchange, not haemoglobin concentration, so it remains normal in isolated anaemia.
why_others_wrong.D: Alveolar ventilation is a respiratory mechanical parameter unrelated to haemoglobin concentration and is not directly reduced by anaemia.
why_others_wrong.E: Atmospheric oxygen concentration is an environmental constant unaffected by a patient's haemoglobin level.

exam_trap: Candidates choose a reduced PaO2, but PaO2 reflects dissolved oxygen tension set by gas exchange; anaemia lowers the haemoglobin-bound content, not PaO2 or saturation.
takeaway: Anaemia → ↓ Hb → ↓ O₂ content → risk of ↓ O₂ delivery.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Severe anaemia with normal SaO2 ↓ saturation is the percentage of available haemoglobin carrying oxygen ↓ less haemoglobin means less bound oxygen per litre ↓ PaO2 and ventilation are unaffected ↓ Haemoglobin-bound oxygen content
pearl: Anaemic patients compensate mainly by raising cardiac output and extraction, so those with limited cardiac reserve tolerate anaemia poorly, which is why ischaemic heart disease influences transfusion decisions.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Cardiorespiratory physiology: shock and oxygen extraction
stem: A patient develops a substantial fall in cardiac output. Which physiological response can initially help maintain tissue oxygen consumption?

options.C: Reduced haemoglobin affinity for oxygen only
options.E: Reduced tissue blood flow with no compensatory response

why_correct: When oxygen delivery falls, tissues can initially compensate by extracting a greater proportion of the oxygen delivered in arterial blood. If oxygen delivery falls sufficiently, this compensation becomes inadequate and anaerobic metabolism may develop.

why_others_wrong.A: This is the opposite response; tissues increase extraction as an early compensation for falling delivery, not reduce it.
why_others_wrong.C: While a rightward shift in the oxygen dissociation curve can assist unloading, this option incorrectly limits the compensatory response to affinity change alone rather than the broader extraction response.
why_others_wrong.D: Anaerobic metabolism increases, not ceases, once oxygen delivery falls below the level needed to sustain fully aerobic consumption.
why_others_wrong.E: This denies any compensatory mechanism, whereas increased oxygen extraction is precisely the compensatory response that initially maintains consumption.

exam_trap: Candidates choose reduced haemoglobin affinity alone; a right shift can aid unloading, but it is only one contributor to the broader rise in extraction that preserves consumption.
takeaway: ↓ DO₂ → early compensation = ↑ O₂ extraction.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Substantial fall in cardiac output reduces oxygen delivery ↓ tissues extract more oxygen from each litre of blood ↓ the arteriovenous difference widens ↓ VO2 is preserved until delivery becomes critical ↓ Increased oxygen extraction
pearl: A low central venous saturation with poor cardiac output reflects high extraction, whereas an inappropriately high value in septic shock can reflect impaired tissue oxygen utilisation.

subject: Immunology
title: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing: lectin complement pathway
stem: Which molecule initiates the lectin pathway of complement activation by recognising microbial carbohydrate patterns?
why_correct: Mannose-binding lectin recognises carbohydrate structures on microbial surfaces and activates associated serine proteases, initiating the lectin complement pathway.

why_others_wrong.B: IgE binds Fc receptors on mast cells and basophils to mediate allergy and does not initiate the lectin complement pathway.
why_others_wrong.C: Factor VIII is a cofactor in the intrinsic coagulation pathway and plays no part in recognising microbial carbohydrates for complement.
why_others_wrong.D: Plasminogen is the precursor of plasmin in fibrinolysis and does not initiate complement activation.
why_others_wrong.E: C-reactive protein is an acute-phase protein that binds phosphocholine and can activate the classical pathway via C1q, rather than initiating the lectin pathway.

exam_trap: C-reactive protein tempts as an acute-phase pattern-recognition protein, but it activates the classical pathway via C1q; the lectin pathway starts with mannose-binding lectin.
takeaway: Lectin pathway → microbial carbohydrates → MBL.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Lectin pathway ↓ recognises microbial carbohydrate such as mannose ↓ binds MBL-associated serine proteases ↓ Mannose-binding lectin
pearl: MBL and C-reactive protein are both hepatic acute-phase proteins, but CRP activates complement through C1q of the classical pathway.

subject: Research methods & screening
title: Statistics & evidence-based medicine: crossover trial limitation
stem: A clinical trial compares two treatments for chronic postoperative pain. Every participant receives both treatments in random order. Which characteristic is essential to consider when interpreting this design?

options.A: Each participant can act as their own control
options.D: The design is always inappropriate for chronic conditions

correct_answer: A. Each participant can act as their own control
why_correct: A crossover trial allows each participant to receive both interventions, reducing the influence of between-participant variability. However, adequate washout and absence of important carryover are important assumptions.

why_others_wrong.B: Carryover is the main hazard of a crossover design, because the first treatment's effect can persist into the second period unless washout is adequate.
why_others_wrong.C: Randomising the order of treatments is still needed, so that period and sequence effects do not bias the within-patient comparison.
why_others_wrong.D: Crossover designs suit stable chronic conditions such as chronic pain well; they are unsuitable mainly for curable or rapidly changing conditions.
why_others_wrong.E: Using each patient as their own control reduces between-participant variability, but it does not remove it entirely or eliminate within-patient variation.

exam_trap: Candidates may choose that between-participant variability is eliminated completely, but crossover only reduces it; carryover remains the key threat, so washout must be adequate.
takeaway: Crossover = each patient as their own control, provided carryover is manageable.
source: Standard clinical trial methodology; MRCS Part A applied evidence-based medicine principles. ==================================================
thinking: Every participant receives both treatments in random order ↓ chronic stable postoperative pain ↓ within-patient comparison ↓ Each participant can act as their own control
pearl: Crossover designs are efficient for symptomatic treatments in stable chronic conditions such as chronic pain, provided there is an adequate washout between treatment periods.

subject: Research methods & screening
title: Perioperative medicine & nutrition: non-inferiority trials
stem: A new perioperative antibiotic is being compared with the standard antibiotic in a randomised trial. The investigators aim to demonstrate that the new drug is not unacceptably worse than the standard treatment, using a predefined non-inferiority margin. Which analysis is particularly important if the trial is intended to establish non-inferiority?
why_correct: In a non-inferiority trial, protocol deviations and treatment crossover can make two treatments appear more similar and therefore falsely support non-inferiority. A per-protocol analysis is therefore particularly important, alongside intention-to-treat analysis, when assessing whether non-inferiority has genuinely been demonstrated.

why_others_wrong.A: Relying on intention-to-treat alone is risky here, because non-adherence and crossover dilute differences and can make the new antibiotic falsely look non-inferior.
why_others_wrong.C: A case-control analysis compares people with and without an outcome by past exposure; it is an observational design, not an analysis within a randomised trial.
why_others_wrong.D: A cross-sectional analysis measures exposure and outcome at a single time point, so it cannot test non-inferiority between randomised treatment arms.
why_others_wrong.E: An ecological analysis uses group-level data such as population rates, not individual randomised participants, so it cannot assess non-inferiority in this trial.

exam_trap: In superiority trials, ITT is generally preferred because it preserves the benefits of randomisation. In non-inferiority trials, both ITT and per-protocol analyses are important because ITT alone can bias towards apparent similarity.
takeaway: Non-inferiority → check both ITT and per-protocol.
source: Standard clinical epidemiology and trial methodology; consistent with MRCS Applied Basic Sciences scope. RCS England current MRCS Part A framework, accessed September 2026.
thinking: Non-inferiority design ↓ non-adherence and crossover make arms look alike ↓ ITT alone can falsely suggest non-inferiority ↓ Per-protocol analysis
pearl: Non-inferiority is most convincing when both intention-to-treat and per-protocol analyses show the confidence interval lying within the prespecified margin.

subject: Research methods & screening
title: Statistics & evidence-based medicine: intention-to-treat principle
stem: A randomised surgical trial compares two postoperative rehabilitation programmes. Some participants assigned to programme A do not complete it and instead receive elements of programme B. Which analysis preserves the original randomisation and should generally be used as the primary analysis in a superiority randomised controlled trial?
why_correct: Intention-to-treat analysis analyses participants according to the treatment group to which they were originally randomised, regardless of subsequent adherence or crossover. This preserves the prognostic balance generated by randomisation.

why_others_wrong.A: Per-protocol analysis includes only participants who adhered to programme A or B, so it breaks the prognostic balance created by randomisation.
why_others_wrong.B: As-treated analysis groups participants by the rehabilitation they actually received, so those who switched to elements of programme B are moved and randomisation is lost.
why_others_wrong.D: Subgroup analysis examines effects within particular categories of participants; it is secondary and exploratory rather than the primary randomised comparison.
why_others_wrong.E: Complete-case analysis drops participants with missing outcome data, which can introduce bias and does not keep everyone in their randomised group.

exam_trap: Do not confuse ITT with “everyone completed treatment”. ITT is about analysing participants according to their original allocation.
takeaway: Randomised → analyse by original allocation.
source: Standard RCT methodology; RCS England MRCS Part A current framework, accessed September 2026.
thinking: Superiority trial with partial crossover between programmes ↓ primary analysis must keep randomised groups intact ↓ analyse by original allocation ↓ Intention-to-treat analysis
pearl: Intention-to-treat estimates the effect of offering a treatment in real practice, including the impact of non-adherence, which makes it the pragmatic and conservative primary analysis.

subject: Research methods & screening
title: Statistics & evidence-based medicine: cluster randomised trial
stem: A study evaluates whether introducing a new surgical safety protocol reduces postoperative complications. Entire hospitals, rather than individual patients, are randomised to either the new protocol or usual practice. What type of trial is this?
why_correct: When groups such as hospitals, practices, wards or schools are randomised as units, the study is a cluster randomised controlled trial.

why_others_wrong.A: In a crossover trial each participant receives both interventions in sequence, whereas here hospitals are randomised to only one of the two arms.
why_others_wrong.C: A case-control study selects people by outcome status and looks back at exposures; it involves no randomisation of hospitals to an intervention.
why_others_wrong.D: A cohort study follows people with different exposures over time without the investigator allocating them, whereas here hospitals are randomly allocated.
why_others_wrong.E: A factorial trial tests two or more interventions simultaneously in combinations, which does not describe randomising hospitals to one protocol versus usual practice.

exam_trap: The unit of randomisation is the key clue. If the hospital is randomised, it is a cluster trial even though outcomes are measured in individual patients.
takeaway: Randomisation of groups → cluster RCT.
source: Standard epidemiological trial methodology; MRCS Applied Basic Sciences level.
thinking: Safety protocol introduced at hospital level ↓ entire hospitals randomised ↓ outcomes measured in individual patients ↓ Cluster randomised controlled trial
pearl: Hospital-level interventions such as safety checklists suit cluster randomisation because randomising individual patients within one hospital would lead to contamination between arms.

subject: Research methods & screening
title: Statistics & evidence-based medicine: cluster trials and statistical independence
stem: In a cluster randomised trial, patients treated in the same hospital tend to have more similar outcomes than patients treated in different hospitals. What statistical problem does this create?
correct_answer: B. Lack of independence between observations
why_correct: Patients within the same cluster may share clinicians, protocols, facilities and patient characteristics. Their outcomes are therefore correlated rather than statistically independent. Analyses must account for clustering.

why_others_wrong.A: Lead-time bias is a screening problem in which earlier diagnosis lengthens apparent survival without delaying death, unrelated to correlated outcomes within hospitals.
why_others_wrong.C: Recall bias arises when participants remember past exposures inaccurately, typically in case-control studies, not from similarity of outcomes within a cluster.
why_others_wrong.D: Verification bias occurs in diagnostic accuracy studies when only some test results are checked against the reference standard, not in clustered trial outcomes.
why_others_wrong.E: Spectrum bias concerns diagnostic test performance varying with the mix of disease severity studied, not correlation between patients in the same hospital.

exam_trap: A cluster trial does not provide as much independent information as the same number of completely independent participants.
takeaway: Same cluster → correlated outcomes → adjust the analysis.
source: Standard cluster-RCT methodology; MRCS Applied Basic Sciences level.
thinking: Patients in the same hospital share clinicians and protocols ↓ their outcomes resemble each other ↓ observations are correlated ↓ Lack of independence between observations
pearl: Analyses of cluster trials use methods such as mixed-effects (multilevel) models or generalised estimating equations; ignoring clustering gives falsely narrow confidence intervals and spuriously small p-values.

subject: Research methods & screening
title: Statistics & evidence-based medicine: funnel plots
stem: A meta-analysis contains several studies evaluating the same surgical intervention. The investigators use a funnel plot to explore whether smaller studies with certain results may be missing from the published literature. What problem are they primarily investigating?
why_correct: A funnel plot can be used to investigate possible small-study effects and publication bias. In the absence of important small-study effects, study estimates may form an approximately symmetrical funnel around the pooled estimate.

why_others_wrong.B: Recall bias concerns inaccurate recollection of exposures by individual participants, which a funnel plot of study effect sizes cannot detect.
why_others_wrong.C: Selection bias in individual patients operates within a single study, whereas a funnel plot examines whether whole studies are missing from the literature.
why_others_wrong.D: Lead-time bias is an artefact of earlier diagnosis in screening studies and is not what a funnel plot of published studies is designed to explore.
why_others_wrong.E: Confounding is distortion by a third variable linked to exposure and outcome within studies; a funnel plot does not assess it.

exam_trap: Funnel-plot asymmetry does not prove publication bias. Small-study effects, heterogeneity and methodological differences can also contribute.
takeaway: Funnel plot → look for publication bias or small-study effects.
source: Standard systematic-review and meta-analysis methodology; MRCS Applied Basic Sciences level.
thinking: Meta-analysis of the same intervention ↓ funnel plot of effect against precision ↓ looking for missing small studies with certain results ↓ Publication bias
pearl: In a symmetrical funnel plot, large precise studies cluster near the pooled estimate at the top while small studies scatter widely and evenly on both sides at the bottom.

subject: Research methods & screening
title: Statistics & evidence-based medicine: publication bias
stem: A meta-analysis of a new surgical technique identifies predominantly small studies showing substantial benefit. The investigators discover that several completed studies with neutral results were never published. What type of bias is most directly demonstrated?
why_correct: Publication bias occurs when the probability of publication depends on the study's findings. Studies with statistically significant or apparently positive results may be more likely to be published than neutral or negative studies.

why_others_wrong.A: Recall bias is inaccurate recollection of past exposures by participants, not the non-publication of completed studies with neutral results.
why_others_wrong.C: Attrition bias is systematic loss of participants during follow-up within one study, whereas here entire completed studies are missing from the literature.
why_others_wrong.D: Measurement bias results from inaccurate or inconsistent measurement of exposures or outcomes within studies, not from which studies reach publication.
why_others_wrong.E: Confounding is distortion of an association by a third factor within a study, and does not explain neutral studies going unpublished.

exam_trap: Publication bias affects the evidence base as a whole; it is not simply loss of participants from an individual study.
takeaway: Positive studies published, negative studies missing → publication bias.
source: Standard evidence-based medicine methodology; MRCS Applied Basic Sciences level.
thinking: Mostly small positive studies identified ↓ completed neutral studies never published ↓ publication depended on results ↓ Publication bias
pearl: Prospective registration of trials before recruitment, now required by major journals, allows reviewers to identify completed trials that were never published.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Pathology: oncology & haematology: calibration
stem: A clinical prediction model estimates that a group of postoperative patients has a 20% risk of venous thromboembolism. The investigators compare these predicted risks with the actual proportion of patients who subsequently develop VTE. Which characteristic of the prediction model are they primarily assessing?
why_correct: Calibration assesses agreement between predicted probabilities and observed outcomes. A well-calibrated model predicting a 20% risk should identify approximately 20 events among 100 similar patients, when assessed appropriately.

why_others_wrong.A: Sensitivity is the proportion of patients who develop VTE correctly classed as positive at a threshold, not agreement of predicted and observed risk.
why_others_wrong.B: Specificity is the proportion of patients without VTE correctly classed as negative, which does not test whether predicted probabilities are accurate.
why_others_wrong.D: Discrimination, often measured by the C-statistic, asks whether the model ranks higher-risk above lower-risk patients, not whether absolute risks match.
why_others_wrong.E: Positive predictive value is the proportion of test-positive patients who have the outcome at a threshold, not the fit of predicted to observed risk.

exam_trap: Calibration asks “Are the predicted probabilities accurate?” Discrimination asks “Can the model separate higher-risk from lower-risk patients?”
takeaway: Calibration → predicted risk vs observed risk.
source: Standard clinical prediction-model methodology; MRCS Applied Basic Sciences level.
thinking: Model predicts a 20% VTE risk ↓ investigators compare predicted risk with the observed proportion ↓ this tests agreement of absolute probabilities, not ranking of patients ↓ Calibration
pearl: A model can discriminate well, with a high C-statistic, yet be poorly calibrated when applied to a population with a different baseline risk, so external validation should report both properties.

subject: Statistics & evidence-based medicine
title: Research methods & screening: discrimination
stem: A postoperative risk model assigns higher predicted risk scores to patients who subsequently develop complications than to those who remain complication-free. Which property of the model is being assessed?
why_correct: Discrimination refers to the ability of a prediction model to distinguish between patients who experience an outcome and those who do not. The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve is commonly used to assess discrimination.

why_others_wrong.A: Calibration concerns whether predicted probabilities match observed event rates, whereas assigning higher scores to those who develop complications describes discrimination.
why_others_wrong.C: External validity asks whether the model performs in a different population or setting, not whether it separates patients with and without complications.
why_others_wrong.D: Reliability concerns the consistency of repeated measurements, not a model's ability to rank patients by their eventual outcome.
why_others_wrong.E: Sensitivity is a single-threshold measure of detecting those with the outcome, whereas ranking across all scores is discrimination, usually summarised by the ROC area.

exam_trap: A model can discriminate well but be poorly calibrated. These are related but different properties.
takeaway: Discrimination → separates high-risk from low-risk patients.
source: Standard prediction-model methodology; MRCS Applied Basic Sciences level.
thinking: Higher scores given to patients who later develop complications ↓ model separates outcome groups ↓ summarised by ROC area ↓ Discrimination
pearl: Surgical risk tools such as P-POSSUM and NELA scores are judged on both discrimination and calibration, and may overpredict mortality in modern cohorts if not recalibrated.

subject: Research methods & screening
title: Research methods & screening: number needed to screen
stem: A screening programme detects a clinically important disease in 1 out of every 100 people screened. Approximately how many people need to undergo screening to detect one case?
why_correct: The number needed to screen is the reciprocal of the absolute probability of detecting the desired outcome. Detection probability = 1/100 = 0.01. NNS = 1 / 0.01 = 100. Therefore, approximately 100 people need to be screened to detect one case.

why_others_wrong.A: Screening one person would detect a case only if every person screened had the disease, but the detection rate here is 1 in 100.
why_others_wrong.B: Ten would correspond to a detection rate of 1 in 10 (10%), ten times higher than the 1% stated in the stem.
why_others_wrong.C: Fifty would correspond to a detection rate of 2%, double the 1 in 100 rate given in the stem.
why_others_wrong.E: One thousand would correspond to a detection rate of 0.1%, whereas 1 in 100 gives 1 divided by 0.01, which is 100.

exam_trap: Do not confuse NNS with NNT. NNT concerns the number needed to treat to produce one additional beneficial outcome.
takeaway: NNS = 1 / absolute detection probability.
source: Standard epidemiological calculation; MRCS Applied Basic Sciences level.
thinking: Detection rate 1 case per 100 screened ↓ absolute probability of detection = 0.01 ↓ NNS = 1 / 0.01 ↓ 100
pearl: Like NNT, the number needed to screen depends on baseline risk, so targeting a higher-prevalence group, such as a defined age band, reduces the number needed to screen.

subject: Statistics & evidence-based medicine
title: Colorectal surgery: competing risks
stem: A study investigates time to death from colorectal cancer. Some participants die from unrelated cardiovascular disease before they develop the cancer outcome. What statistical issue does this create?
why_correct: Death from another cause prevents the participant from subsequently experiencing death from colorectal cancer during the observation period. This is a competing risk.

why_others_wrong.B: Recall bias arises when participants remember past exposures inaccurately, typically in case-control studies, not when another cause of death intervenes.
why_others_wrong.C: Lead-time bias is an apparent survival gain from earlier diagnosis by screening, not the removal of participants by an unrelated fatal event.
why_others_wrong.D: Publication bias concerns selective publication of studies, not events within a single cohort that prevent the outcome of interest.
why_others_wrong.E: Verification bias arises in diagnostic studies when only some patients receive the reference standard, which is not the situation described.

exam_trap: A competing event is not simply “missing data”. It changes the probability of observing the event of interest.
takeaway: One event that prevents another from occurring or being observed → competing risk.
source: Standard time-to-event methodology; MRCS Applied Basic Sciences level.
thinking: Outcome is death from colorectal cancer ↓ some die of cardiovascular disease first ↓ the other death prevents the event of interest ↓ Competing risk
pearl: Standard survival-curve analysis that censors competing deaths overestimates the cumulative incidence of the event of interest; cumulative incidence functions are used instead.

subject: Pharmacology
title: Pharmacology: active drug metabolites
stem: A patient is prescribed a drug that is metabolised to an active metabolite. Renal function subsequently deteriorates. Which pharmacological consequence is particularly important?

options.B: Possible accumulation of the active metabolite
options.E: Elimination becomes independent of renal function

correct_answer: B. Possible accumulation of the active metabolite
why_correct: If an active metabolite depends substantially on renal elimination, reduced renal function may cause its accumulation and prolong or increase pharmacological effects.

why_others_wrong.A: Accumulation of an active metabolite would tend to prolong or increase, not guarantee a reduction in, the overall drug effect.
why_others_wrong.C: Renal impairment affects elimination of the metabolite, not gastrointestinal absorption or oral bioavailability of the parent drug.
why_others_wrong.D: Reduced renal function does not prevent hepatic metabolism, which generates the active metabolite in the first place.
why_others_wrong.E: This is the opposite of the concern raised — the issue is precisely that the metabolite's elimination remains dependent on renal function, risking accumulation.

exam_trap: Guaranteed reduction in drug effect is chosen by candidates who focus only on the parent drug, but an accumulating active metabolite prolongs or increases the drug's effect.
takeaway: Renal impairment → think parent drug + active metabolites.
source: Standard pharmacology; consistent with Guyton and Hall and MRCS pharmacology principles.
thinking: Drug metabolised to an active metabolite ↓ renal function deteriorates ↓ a renally excreted active metabolite is no longer cleared ↓ prolonged or increased drug effect ↓ Possible accumulation of the active metabolite
pearl: Morphine (morphine-6-glucuronide) and pethidine (norpethidine, which can cause seizures) are surgical examples where accumulation of an active metabolite in renal failure causes toxicity.

subject: Pharmacology
title: Pharmacology: enzyme inhibition
stem: A patient taking a drug metabolised by hepatic CYP enzymes is started on a potent inhibitor of the relevant enzyme. What is the most likely immediate pharmacokinetic effect?

options.C: Reduced drug metabolism and potentially increased drug concentration
options.E: Reduced absorption from the gastrointestinal tract

correct_answer: C. Reduced drug metabolism and potentially increased drug concentration
why_correct: Enzyme inhibition reduces metabolic clearance of susceptible drugs. Plasma concentrations may therefore increase, potentially increasing adverse effects.

why_others_wrong.A: This is the opposite effect — enzyme inhibition reduces, rather than increases, the metabolic clearance of the affected drug.
why_others_wrong.B: Inhibited metabolism raises, rather than reduces, plasma drug concentration, which is what predisposes to toxicity.
why_others_wrong.D: CYP enzyme inhibition affects hepatic metabolism and has no direct effect on glomerular filtration or renal clearance.
why_others_wrong.E: Enzyme inhibition acts on post-absorptive hepatic metabolism, not on gastrointestinal absorption.

exam_trap: Reduced plasma drug concentration is chosen by candidates who confuse inhibition with induction; enzyme inhibition reduces metabolism and raises, rather than lowers, plasma concentration.
takeaway: CYP inhibition → ↓ metabolism → ↑ drug exposure.
source: Standard pharmacology; MRCS Applied Basic Sciences level.
thinking: Drug metabolised by hepatic CYP enzymes ↓ potent inhibitor of the relevant enzyme started ↓ metabolic clearance falls quickly ↓ plasma concentration may rise ↓ Reduced drug metabolism and potentially increased drug concentration
pearl: Amiodarone inhibits warfarin metabolism and can markedly raise the INR, so warfarin doses are usually reduced and the INR monitored closely when amiodarone is started.

subject: Pharmacology
title: Pharmacology: enzyme induction
stem: A patient has been taking a drug metabolised by a hepatic enzyme for several weeks. Another medicine is introduced that induces expression of this enzyme. What is the likely effect on a substrate drug?

options.D: Reduced hepatic blood flow in every case

why_correct: Enzyme induction increases the amount or activity of relevant metabolic enzymes. For a substrate drug, this can increase metabolism and clearance, potentially reducing its concentration and effect.

why_others_wrong.A: This is the opposite effect — enzyme induction increases, rather than reduces, metabolic clearance of the substrate drug.
why_others_wrong.C: Enzyme induction is a metabolic (biotransformation) effect; it does not act through direct receptor blockade.
why_others_wrong.D: Induction increases hepatic enzyme activity/synthesis; it does not necessarily reduce hepatic blood flow, which is a separate determinant of clearance.
why_others_wrong.E: Enzyme induction concerns hepatic metabolic pathways, not renal excretion, and does not cause complete inhibition of renal elimination.

exam_trap: Induction generally develops more slowly than enzyme inhibition because synthesis of additional enzyme is involved.
takeaway: Induction → more enzyme → ↑ metabolism → often ↓ drug exposure.
source: Standard pharmacology; MRCS Applied Basic Sciences level.
thinking: Substrate drug metabolised by a hepatic enzyme ↓ new medicine induces expression of that enzyme ↓ more enzyme protein is available ↓ substrate is metabolised and cleared faster ↓ Increased metabolic clearance
pearl: Prednisolone, ciclosporin and tacrolimus levels can fall when inducers such as rifampicin are started, risking graft rejection in transplant patients.

subject: Pharmacology
title: Pharmacology: loading dose
stem: A drug has a volume of distribution of 40 L. The target plasma concentration is 5 mg/L. Assuming complete systemic availability, what loading dose is required?
why_correct: Loading dose ≈ target concentration × volume of distribution. 5 mg/L × 40 L = 200 mg. Therefore, the loading dose is 200 mg.

why_others_wrong.A: 8 mg comes from dividing the volume of distribution by the target concentration (40 ÷ 5) instead of multiplying them to give 200 mg.
why_others_wrong.B: 20 mg underestimates the correct dose roughly ten-fold and does not match the 5 mg/L × 40 L calculation.
why_others_wrong.C: 45 mg comes from adding the target concentration and volume of distribution (5 + 40) instead of multiplying them to give 200 mg.
why_others_wrong.E: 400 mg is double the correct loading dose of 200 mg (5 mg/L × 40 L) and would overshoot the target concentration.

exam_trap: 8 mg is chosen by candidates who divide volume of distribution by the target concentration; the loading dose is their product, 5 mg/L x 40 L = 200 mg.
takeaway: Loading dose ≈ target concentration × Vd / bioavailability.
source: Standard pharmacokinetic principle; MRCS Applied Basic Sciences level.
thinking: Loading dose = target concentration x Vd / bioavailability ↓ systemic availability is complete ↓ 5 mg/L x 40 L ↓ 200 mg
