thinking: Dominant inferior frontal gyrus ↓ Broca area for speech production ↓ lesion gives effortful, non-fluent speech ↓ comprehension is relatively spared ↓ Non-fluent speech with relatively preserved comprehension
pearl: Broca area lies in MCA territory beside the motor cortex, so expressive aphasia is often accompanied by contralateral face and arm weakness.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: basal ganglia
stem: A 45-year-old man develops progressive involuntary jerky movements, irritability and cognitive decline. His father had a similar illness. Which pathological process is characteristic of this condition?

options.A: Loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra only
options.E: Loss of cerebellar Purkinje cells exclusively

why_correct: Huntington disease is associated with degeneration of neurons within the striatum, particularly the caudate and putamen, producing chorea and behavioural/cognitive changes.

why_others_wrong.A: Loss of nigral dopaminergic neurons is the hallmark of Parkinson disease, causing bradykinesia and rigidity rather than chorea.
why_others_wrong.C: Anterior horn cell loss causes lower motor neuron weakness, as in motor neuron disease or poliomyelitis.
why_others_wrong.D: Peripheral demyelination causes neuropathy, as in Guillain-Barre syndrome, not chorea or behavioural change.
why_others_wrong.E: Purkinje cell loss produces cerebellar ataxia, not the chorea and caudate atrophy of Huntington disease.

exam_trap: Loss of nigral dopaminergic neurons is chosen because both are basal ganglia disorders, but that defines Parkinson disease with bradykinesia and rigidity; chorea reflects striatal degeneration.
takeaway: Huntington disease = striatal degeneration.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed.; Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Progressive chorea with behavioural and cognitive decline ↓ affected father suggests autosomal dominant Huntington disease ↓ the striatum (caudate and putamen), especially its GABAergic projection neurons, degenerates ↓ Degeneration of striatal neurons
pearl: Huntington disease is caused by a CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion that shows anticipation, so it can present earlier in successive generations, particularly when inherited from the father.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: cerebellar physiology
stem: A patient has a cerebellar hemisphere lesion. Which neurological finding is most likely?
why_correct: Cerebellar hemisphere lesions characteristically produce ipsilateral limb coordination deficits, including dysmetria and ataxia.

why_others_wrong.A: Contralateral spastic hemiparesis indicates an upper motor neuron lesion above the pyramidal decussation.
why_others_wrong.C: The cerebellum does not process conscious sensation, so hemisphere lesions do not cause sensory loss.
why_others_wrong.D: Expressive aphasia results from damage to Broca area in the dominant inferior frontal gyrus.
why_others_wrong.E: Bitemporal hemianopia results from compression of the optic chiasm, typically by a pituitary tumour.

exam_trap: Contralateral spastic hemiparesis (A) fits a cerebral lesion; candidates assume all brain lesions give contralateral signs, but cerebellar signs are ipsilateral.
takeaway: Cerebellar hemisphere lesion → ipsilateral ataxia.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed.
thinking: Cerebellar hemisphere controls the ipsilateral limbs ↓ its output pathways cross twice ↓ lesion gives ipsilateral dysmetria, intention tremor and dysdiadochokinesia ↓ Ipsilateral limb ataxia
pearl: Vermis lesions cause truncal and gait ataxia, while hemisphere lesions cause limb ataxia; a cerebellar haematoma or infarct can cause hydrocephalus and brainstem compression needing neurosurgical decompression.

subject: Physiology
title: GI physiology & metabolism: endocrine feedback
stem: A patient has a pituitary adenoma secreting excess ACTH. Which hormonal pattern is most likely?
correct_answer: B. High ACTH and high cortisol
why_correct: An ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma causes increased ACTH secretion, stimulating the adrenal cortex and increasing cortisol production.

why_others_wrong.A: This describes a state of combined deficiency, which does not fit an adenoma that is actively oversecreting ACTH and thereby stimulating cortisol.
why_others_wrong.C: An ACTH-secreting adenoma would be expected to stimulate the adrenal cortex, raising cortisol rather than leaving it low despite high ACTH.
why_others_wrong.D: Low ACTH with high cortisol describes a primary adrenal problem (autonomous cortisol excess suppressing ACTH), not a pituitary ACTH-secreting adenoma.
why_others_wrong.E: TSH belongs to a separate axis; an ACTH-secreting adenoma would not characteristically raise TSH while lowering cortisol.

exam_trap: Option D (low ACTH, high cortisol) tempts those focused on cortisol excess, but that pattern indicates an adrenal or exogenous source, not a pituitary ACTH tumour.
takeaway: ACTH-secreting pituitary lesion → ↑ ACTH + ↑ cortisol.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Pituitary adenoma secreting ACTH ↓ ACTH is high at its source ↓ adrenal cortex is driven continuously ↓ cortisol rises and cannot suppress the autonomous tumour ↓ High ACTH and high cortisol
pearl: ACTH-dependent hypercortisolism from a pituitary adenoma is treated first-line by transsphenoidal surgery, whereas suppressed ACTH with high cortisol points to an adrenal tumour or exogenous steroids.

subject: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care
title: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care: adrenal physiology
stem: A patient has a primary adrenal cortical disorder causing excess aldosterone production. Which combination is most likely?

options.E: Normal blood pressure, hyperkalaemia and alkalosis

why_correct: Excess aldosterone increases sodium reabsorption and promotes potassium and hydrogen ion secretion in the distal nephron. This can cause hypertension, hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis.

why_others_wrong.A: Hypotension, hyperkalaemia and acidosis reflect aldosterone deficiency, as in Addison disease, the opposite of aldosterone excess.
why_others_wrong.C: Aldosterone excess retains sodium and raises blood pressure and drives hydrogen ion loss causing alkalosis, so hypotension with acidosis does not fit.
why_others_wrong.D: Hypertension fits, but aldosterone promotes potassium and hydrogen ion excretion, so hyperkalaemia and acidosis are not expected.
why_others_wrong.E: Excess aldosterone typically raises blood pressure and lowers potassium, so normal blood pressure with hyperkalaemia is inconsistent.

exam_trap: Candidates choose option D, matching hypertension but with hyperkalaemia and acidosis; aldosterone excess causes potassium and hydrogen ion loss, giving hypokalaemia and alkalosis.
takeaway: Primary hyperaldosteronism → hypertension, low potassium and metabolic alkalosis.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Primary aldosterone excess ↓ sodium retention raises blood pressure ↓ potassium secretion in distal nephron ↓ hydrogen ion secretion produces alkalosis ↓ Hypertension, hypokalaemia, metabolic alkalosis
pearl: Primary hyperaldosteronism is screened with the aldosterone-to-renin ratio, and a unilateral aldosterone-producing adenoma can be treated by laparoscopic adrenalectomy.

subject: Physiology
title: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care: thyroid physiology
stem: A patient has severe primary hypothyroidism. Which hormonal pattern is expected?

options.A: High free T4 and low TSH
options.B: Low free T4 and high TSH
options.C: High free T4 and high TSH
options.D: Normal free T4 and absent TSH
options.E: Low free T4 and low TSH in all cases

correct_answer: B. Low free T4 and high TSH
why_correct: In primary hypothyroidism, the thyroid gland fails to produce sufficient thyroid hormone. Reduced negative feedback causes increased hypothalamic-pituitary stimulation and therefore increased TSH.

why_others_wrong.A: High free T4 with low TSH describes a hyperthyroid or thyroid-hormone-excess state, the opposite of primary hypothyroidism.
why_others_wrong.C: High free T4 with a non-suppressed TSH points to a TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma or thyroid hormone resistance, not primary gland failure, where T4 is low.
why_others_wrong.D: Primary gland failure produces a clearly abnormal, not normal, free T4, together with an elevated rather than absent TSH.
why_others_wrong.E: Low T4 with low TSH describes central (secondary) hypothyroidism from pituitary or hypothalamic failure, not primary thyroid gland failure.

exam_trap: Option E (low T4, low TSH) tempts those who expect everything to be low in hypothyroidism, but that pattern is central disease; primary gland failure raises TSH.
takeaway: Primary hypothyroidism = low T4 + high TSH.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Primary hypothyroidism means thyroid gland failure ↓ free T4 falls ↓ reduced negative feedback on the pituitary ↓ TSH rises ↓ Low free T4 and high TSH
pearl: After total thyroidectomy patients need lifelong levothyroxine titrated against TSH, whereas in central hypothyroidism TSH is unreliable and free T4 is used to guide replacement.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: calcium physiology
stem: A patient has a fall in serum ionised calcium. Which immediate hormonal response is expected?

options.D: Complete suppression of vitamin D metabolism
options.E: Increased FGF23 secretion as the sole response

why_correct: Parathyroid chief cells sense extracellular calcium through the calcium-sensing receptor. A fall in ionised calcium stimulates PTH secretion. PTH increases renal calcium reabsorption, promotes phosphate excretion and stimulates renal activation of vitamin D.

why_others_wrong.A: This is the opposite of the expected response; a fall in ionised calcium stimulates, rather than reduces, PTH secretion.
why_others_wrong.C: Calcitonin lowers plasma calcium and is not the immediate parathyroid response to hypocalcaemia.
why_others_wrong.D: PTH stimulates, rather than suppresses, renal activation of vitamin D in response to falling calcium.
why_others_wrong.E: FGF23 is not the immediate calcium-sensing hormonal response to hypocalcaemia; PTH secretion is the primary and immediate change.

exam_trap: Calcitonin (C) tempts as a calcium-regulating hormone, but it is released by high calcium; the immediate response to hypocalcaemia is increased PTH secretion.
takeaway: Low Ca2+ → ↑ PTH.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Fall in serum ionised calcium ↓ detected by the parathyroid calcium-sensing receptor ↓ PTH secretion rises within minutes ↓ Increased PTH secretion
pearl: Ionised calcium is the physiologically active fraction; in hypoalbuminaemia total calcium underestimates it, so use adjusted calcium or measure ionised calcium on a blood gas analyser.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: GI physiology & metabolism: insulin physiology
stem: A patient has an insulin-secreting pancreatic β-cell tumour. Which metabolic effect would be expected?

options.B: Increased cellular glucose uptake in insulin-sensitive tissues

correct_answer: B. Increased cellular glucose uptake in insulin-sensitive tissues
why_correct: Insulin promotes glucose uptake into skeletal muscle and adipose tissue through increased GLUT4 translocation to the cell surface. It also promotes glycogen synthesis and suppresses lipolysis and ketogenesis.

why_others_wrong.A: Insulin inhibits hepatic glycogenolysis and promotes glycogen synthesis, so an insulinoma reduces rather than increases glycogen breakdown.
why_others_wrong.C: Insulin suppresses ketogenesis by inhibiting lipolysis and fatty-acid entry into mitochondria, so ketone production falls with excess insulin.
why_others_wrong.D: Insulin inhibits hormone-sensitive lipase in adipose tissue, so lipolysis is reduced rather than increased.
why_others_wrong.E: Insulin suppresses hepatic gluconeogenesis, which contributes to the fasting hypoglycaemia seen with an insulinoma.

exam_trap: Option E attracts candidates who link hypoglycaemia with counter-regulation, but excess insulin suppresses hepatic gluconeogenesis, which contributes to the fasting hypoglycaemia of insulinoma.
takeaway: Insulin = store glucose + suppress fuel mobilisation.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Insulin-secreting beta-cell tumour means excess insulin ↓ insulin translocates GLUT4 to muscle and adipocyte membranes ↓ glucose uptake rises while glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis, lipolysis and ketogenesis are suppressed ↓ Increased cellular glucose uptake in insulin-sensitive tissues
pearl: Insulinoma is confirmed during a supervised prolonged fast showing hypoglycaemia with inappropriately raised insulin and C-peptide; a low C-peptide instead points to exogenous insulin.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Physiology: dna repair
stem: A patient has a hereditary defect in a pathway responsible for repairing bulky DNA lesions caused by ultraviolet radiation. Which repair mechanism is affected?
why_correct: Nucleotide excision repair removes bulky DNA lesions, including UV-induced pyrimidine dimers.

why_others_wrong.B: Mismatch repair corrects base mispairs and small insertion or deletion loops from replication errors, as in Lynch syndrome, not UV-induced bulky lesions.
why_others_wrong.C: Homologous recombination repairs double-strand breaks, as with BRCA1 and BRCA2, rather than UV-induced pyrimidine dimers.
why_others_wrong.D: Base excision repair removes small non-bulky damaged bases, such as oxidised or deaminated bases, not bulky UV lesions.
why_others_wrong.E: RNA splicing processes pre-mRNA transcripts and is not a DNA repair pathway.

exam_trap: Mismatch repair (B) tempts as the best-known inherited repair defect, but it corrects replication mispairs as in Lynch syndrome, not UV-induced bulky lesions.
takeaway: UV damage = nucleotide excision repair.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Hereditary DNA repair defect ↓ bulky lesions from ultraviolet light, such as pyrimidine dimers ↓ helix-distorting damage is removed by excising an oligonucleotide stretch ↓ Nucleotide excision repair
pearl: Inherited nucleotide excision repair defects cause xeroderma pigmentosum, with extreme sun sensitivity and multiple skin cancers, including melanoma, from childhood.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Pathology: oncology & haematology: cell-cycle control
stem: A tumour cell loses functional p53. Which consequence is most directly associated with this defect?

options.B: Reduced ability to arrest the cell cycle after DNA damage
options.E: Increased apoptosis after every DNA insult

correct_answer: B. Reduced ability to arrest the cell cycle after DNA damage
why_correct: p53 is a major tumour suppressor that responds to cellular stress and DNA damage. It can induce cell-cycle arrest and, when damage is severe, promote apoptosis. Loss of p53 therefore permits damaged cells to continue proliferating.

why_others_wrong.A: Loss of p53 weakens DNA damage surveillance, allowing damaged cells to continue dividing, rather than improving it.
why_others_wrong.C: p53 loss does not promote normal differentiation; it favours proliferation of genetically unstable cells.
why_others_wrong.D: Loss of a tumour suppressor removes a brake on proliferation, so it permits rather than permanently inhibits cell division.
why_others_wrong.E: Functional p53 promotes apoptosis after severe DNA damage, so its loss reduces rather than increases apoptosis.

exam_trap: p53 is not simply an “apoptosis protein”; it can also produce cell-cycle arrest and facilitate DNA repair.
takeaway: p53 = DNA damage checkpoint + repair/arrest/apoptosis.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Tumour cell loses functional p53 ↓ p53 normally induces p21 to halt the cycle after DNA damage ↓ without it damaged cells keep dividing ↓ Reduced ability to arrest the cell cycle after DNA damage
pearl: Loss of p53 also blunts apoptosis after chemotherapy or radiotherapy-induced DNA damage, so TP53-mutant tumours are often more treatment-resistant.

subject: Major trauma & fluids
title: Major trauma & fluids: transfusion medicine
stem: A patient develops fever, back pain and dark urine shortly after a blood transfusion. What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.C: Give another unit of the same blood immediately
options.E: Wait for the haemoglobin result before acting

why_correct: An acute haemolytic transfusion reaction is potentially life-threatening. The transfusion should be stopped immediately and the patient assessed and managed according to the local transfusion-reaction protocol.

why_others_wrong.A: Continuing the transfusion, even slowly, delivers more incompatible blood and worsens haemolysis in a suspected acute haemolytic reaction.
why_others_wrong.C: Giving another unit before the cause is identified risks further incompatible transfusion, especially if an identification error has occurred.
why_others_wrong.D: Increasing the rate would accelerate haemolysis and raise the risk of shock, acute kidney injury and disseminated intravascular coagulation.
why_others_wrong.E: Fever, back pain and dark urine suggest haemolysis; the transfusion must be stopped before any results are awaited.

exam_trap: Continuing the transfusion slowly or waiting for the haemoglobin result both let more incompatible blood enter; suspected haemolysis requires the transfusion to be stopped immediately.
takeaway: Stop the blood before chasing the diagnosis.
source: Principles and Practice of Surgery, 7th ed.; current UK transfusion practice principles.
thinking: Fever, back pain and dark urine ↓ shortly after a transfusion ↓ dark urine = haemoglobinuria from intravascular haemolysis ↓ remove the source first ↓ Stop the transfusion
pearl: Acute haemolytic reactions can cause disseminated intravascular coagulation and acute kidney injury, so a coagulation screen, renal function and close urine output monitoring are part of the immediate work-up.

subject: Major trauma & fluids
title: Major trauma & fluids: transfusion physiology
stem: A patient receives a large-volume blood transfusion and develops perioral tingling, hypotension and a prolonged QT interval. Which abnormality is most likely?
why_correct: Citrate used as an anticoagulant in blood components binds ionised calcium. During rapid or massive transfusion, citrate accumulation can produce clinically significant ionised hypocalcaemia.

why_others_wrong.A: Hypermagnesaemia causes weakness and hypotension but not perioral tingling, and citrate tends to lower magnesium rather than raise it.
why_others_wrong.C: Hyperphosphataemia is not a recognised consequence of massive transfusion and does not explain the neuromuscular and QT changes.
why_others_wrong.D: Severe hypernatraemia causes confusion and reduced consciousness and is not a typical complication of citrated blood transfusion.
why_others_wrong.E: Hyperkalaemia from stored blood causes peaked T waves and arrhythmias, not perioral tingling and QT prolongation, so it cannot explain this picture alone.

exam_trap: Hyperkalaemia as the sole explanation is tempting, but stored-blood hyperkalaemia causes peaked T waves, not perioral tingling with QT prolongation, which indicate ionised hypocalcaemia.
takeaway: Citrate binds Ca2+ → hypocalcaemia.
source: Principles and Practice of Surgery, 7th ed.
thinking: Large-volume transfusion ↓ perioral tingling, hypotension and QT prolongation ↓ citrate anticoagulant chelates ionised calcium ↓ the ionised fraction falls even when total calcium looks less abnormal ↓ Ionised hypocalcaemia
pearl: Blood gas analysers give a rapid ionised calcium result, which is more useful than a laboratory total calcium during major transfusion.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Pathology: oncology & haematology: coagulation
stem: A patient has a deficiency of factor XIII. Which finding is most characteristic?

options.B: Normal PT and APTT with impaired fibrin stabilisation

correct_answer: B. Normal PT and APTT with impaired fibrin stabilisation
why_correct: Factor XIII cross-links fibrin after fibrin formation. Because PT and APTT assess earlier parts of coagulation, factor XIII deficiency can occur with normal PT and APTT despite defective clot stabilisation.

why_others_wrong.A: Prolonged PT and APTT suggest a common-pathway or multiple-factor deficiency, such as factor X, V or II deficiency, liver disease or vitamin K deficiency, whereas factor XIII deficiency leaves both normal.
why_others_wrong.C: An isolated prolonged PT points to factor VII deficiency or early warfarin effect, not factor XIII, which leaves both tests normal.
why_others_wrong.D: An isolated prolonged APTT suggests deficiency of factors VIII, IX, XI or XII, not factor XIII.
why_others_wrong.E: Factor XIII is a coagulation factor for fibrin cross-linking and its deficiency does not reduce the platelet count.

exam_trap: Prolonged PT and APTT (A) or isolated prolonged APTT (D) tempt candidates who assume every factor deficiency prolongs screening tests, but factor XIII acts after their fibrin end-point.
takeaway: Factor XIII = fibrin cross-linking after the standard clotting tests.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Factor XIII deficiency ↓ factor XIIIa cross-links fibrin after it has formed ↓ PT and APTT end-points are the first appearance of fibrin ↓ so both tests are normal despite an unstable clot ↓ Normal PT and APTT with impaired fibrin stabilisation
pearl: Factor XIII deficiency classically presents with delayed bleeding, such as umbilical stump bleeding in neonates, and poor wound healing; diagnosis needs a specific factor XIII assay.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Pathology: oncology & haematology: coagulation physiology
stem: Thrombin is generated during activation of the coagulation cascade. Which reaction is catalysed directly by thrombin?

options.D: Conversion of factor XIII to collagen

correct_answer: A. Conversion of fibrinogen to fibrin
why_correct: Thrombin cleaves fibrinogen to form fibrin, which then polymerises. Thrombin also activates several coagulation factors and platelets.

why_others_wrong.B: Plasminogen is converted to plasmin by plasminogen activators, and the reverse conversion does not occur, nor is it catalysed by thrombin.
why_others_wrong.C: Collagen is a structural extracellular matrix protein and cannot be converted into fibrinogen, which is synthesised by the liver.
why_others_wrong.D: Thrombin activates factor XIII to factor XIIIa, a transglutaminase that cross-links fibrin; it does not turn it into collagen.
why_others_wrong.E: Thrombin activates platelets through PAR receptors, promoting aggregation, rather than destroying them.

exam_trap: Conversion of plasmin to plasminogen (B) reverses the real reaction: plasminogen activators convert plasminogen to plasmin, and thrombin plays no part.
takeaway: Thrombin → fibrinogen → fibrin.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Thrombin generated by the cascade ↓ its key substrate is soluble fibrinogen ↓ it cleaves fibrinopeptides to release fibrin monomers that polymerise ↓ Conversion of fibrinogen to fibrin
pearl: Thrombin also activates factors V, VIII, XI and XIII and platelets, amplifying its own generation, yet when bound to thrombomodulin it switches to activating protein C.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Perioperative medicine & nutrition: postoperative catabolism
stem: Following major surgery, a patient develops negative nitrogen balance. Which process contributes most directly?
why_correct: Major surgery produces a catabolic stress response with increased protein breakdown and mobilisation of amino acids for gluconeogenesis and acute-phase protein synthesis. This can produce negative nitrogen balance.

why_others_wrong.A: Protein synthesis exceeding breakdown produces positive nitrogen balance, the opposite of the catabolic state after major surgery.
why_others_wrong.C: Gluconeogenesis is increased after surgery, using amino acids from muscle breakdown, rather than being inhibited.
why_others_wrong.D: Collagen storage does not explain nitrogen loss; negative balance reflects net protein breakdown exceeding synthesis.
why_others_wrong.E: Amino-acid mobilisation from muscle is increased, not reduced, as part of the postoperative catabolic response.

exam_trap: The postoperative catabolic response is not simply “lack of food”; endocrine stress responses actively drive protein breakdown.
takeaway: Major surgery → catabolism → muscle proteolysis → negative nitrogen balance.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Negative nitrogen balance after major surgery ↓ cortisol and inflammatory cytokines drive muscle catabolism ↓ amino acids are released for gluconeogenesis and acute phase proteins ↓ Increased skeletal-muscle protein breakdown
pearl: Prolonged postoperative catabolism causes loss of respiratory and limb muscle strength, so early nutrition and mobilisation are used to limit deconditioning, particularly in older patients.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Perioperative medicine & nutrition: refeeding physiology
stem: A severely malnourished patient begins nutritional rehabilitation. Shortly afterwards, the serum phosphate concentration falls markedly. Which hormonal change is most responsible?

options.E: Complete suppression of cellular glucose uptake

why_correct: Refeeding, particularly with carbohydrate, increases insulin secretion. Insulin drives glucose and phosphate into cells and increases anabolic processes, which can produce significant hypophosphataemia in a severely malnourished patient.

why_others_wrong.A: Refeeding, especially with carbohydrate, raises insulin secretion; reduced insulin would not drive phosphate into cells.
why_others_wrong.C: Glucagon is a catabolic hormone that falls with feeding and does not cause the intracellular phosphate shift of refeeding.
why_others_wrong.D: Cortisol is not the driver of refeeding hypophosphataemia; the key change is the insulin surge with carbohydrate intake.
why_others_wrong.E: Refeeding increases cellular glucose uptake under insulin, and this uptake carries phosphate into cells rather than being suppressed.

exam_trap: The phosphate was already depleted intracellularly and in total body stores; serum phosphate can fall dramatically when anabolic metabolism resumes.
takeaway: Refeeding → insulin surge → intracellular phosphate shift.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.; Principles and Practice of Surgery, 7th ed.
thinking: Severe malnutrition then refeeding ↓ carbohydrate intake triggers an insulin surge ↓ insulin drives glucose and phosphate into cells ↓ serum phosphate falls ↓ Increased insulin secretion
pearl: Phosphate is consumed in phosphorylating glucose and generating ATP once anabolism resumes, which is why the fall in phosphate is greatest when carbohydrate is reintroduced rapidly.

subject: Statistics & evidence-based medicine
title: Research methods & screening: diagnostic testing
stem: A diagnostic test is highly sensitive for a serious disease. A patient with a negative test result is being assessed. Which property makes the negative result particularly useful for excluding disease?
why_correct: A low negative likelihood ratio means that a negative result substantially reduces the odds of disease.

why_others_wrong.A: A high positive likelihood ratio helps a positive result rule disease in; it does not determine how well a negative result excludes it.
why_others_wrong.C: Low specificity means more false positives and does not make a negative result more reassuring; rule-out value depends on high sensitivity.
why_others_wrong.D: High prevalence raises the pre-test probability, so a negative result leaves more residual risk, reducing its usefulness for excluding disease.
why_others_wrong.E: Positive predictive value describes how often a positive result is correct and says nothing about the value of a negative result.

exam_trap: SNOUT: Sensitive test + Negative = useful for ruling OUT, particularly when LR− is low.
takeaway: Negative test with a low LR− → stronger rule-out value.
source: Standard diagnostic-test methodology.
thinking: Highly sensitive test ↓ few false negatives ↓ LR− = (1 − sensitivity) / specificity is low ↓ negative result sharply lowers odds ↓ Low negative likelihood ratio
pearl: D-dimer in low-probability suspected venous thromboembolism is a classic surgical example of a sensitive test whose negative result safely rules out disease.

subject: Statistics & evidence-based medicine
title: Research methods & screening: bayesian diagnostics
stem: A diagnostic test has a fixed likelihood ratio, but it is applied to two different populations. Disease prevalence is much higher in the second population. What happens to the pre-test probability in the second population?

options.E: It is determined solely by specificity

why_correct: Pre-test probability reflects the probability of disease before the test result and is influenced by disease prevalence and the clinical context. A higher-prevalence population begins with a higher pre-test probability, so the same test result may produce a different post-test probability.

why_others_wrong.A: Pre-test probability tracks prevalence, so moving to a population with much higher prevalence raises rather than lowers the starting probability of disease.
why_others_wrong.C: A pre-test probability of zero would mean disease is impossible, which cannot apply to a population where the disease is common.
why_others_wrong.D: Pre-test probability is largely set by prevalence and clinical context, so it is directly dependent on prevalence rather than independent of it.
why_others_wrong.E: Specificity is a property of the test, whereas pre-test probability is the chance of disease before any test is applied and reflects prevalence.

exam_trap: Option E tempts candidates who link pre-test probability to test properties, but it reflects prevalence and clinical context, not specificity.
takeaway: Consider pre-test probability before you interpret the test.
source: Standard Bayesian diagnostic methodology.
thinking: Same test, same likelihood ratio ↓ second population has much higher prevalence ↓ pre-test probability reflects prevalence and context ↓ It increases
pearl: Because the starting point differs, the same positive result yields a higher post-test probability in a high-prevalence population than in a low-prevalence one.

subject: Statistics & evidence-based medicine
title: Research methods & screening: number needed to screen
stem: A screening programme reduces disease-specific mortality from 4% to 3% in a defined screened population over the study period. Approximately how many people need to be screened to prevent one disease-specific death?
why_correct: Absolute risk reduction: 4% − 3% = 1% = 0.01. Number needed to screen: 1 / 0.01 = 100. Therefore, approximately 100 people need to be screened to prevent one disease-specific death over the specified period, assuming the reported risks apply directly to the screened population.

why_others_wrong.A: Ten would need an absolute risk reduction of 10%, a decimal slip that treats the 1% difference as 0.1 instead of 0.01.
why_others_wrong.B: Twenty-five comes from dividing 1 by the 4% baseline risk rather than by the 1% absolute risk reduction between screened and unscreened groups.
why_others_wrong.C: Fifty would correspond to an absolute risk reduction of 2%, double the 4% minus 3% difference actually reported here.
why_others_wrong.E: Two hundred and fifty would require an absolute risk reduction of 0.4%, overstating the number screened for a 1% difference by a factor of 2.5.

exam_trap: Choosing 25 divides 1 by the 4% baseline risk; the number needed to screen uses the 1-point absolute reduction, giving 100.
takeaway: NNS = 1 / absolute risk reduction.
source: Standard epidemiological methodology.
thinking: Mortality falls from 4% to 3% ↓ ARR = 0.01 ↓ NNS = 1 / 0.01 ↓ 100
pearl: The NNS applies only over the stated follow-up period; longer follow-up of screening trials often lowers the NNS as more deaths are prevented.

subject: Research methods & screening
title: Pathology: oncology & haematology: screening outcomes
stem: A new screening programme detects a cancer several years earlier than usual. However, population mortality from the cancer does not change. Which phenomenon could make survival after diagnosis appear longer without improving mortality?
why_correct: Lead-time bias occurs when earlier diagnosis increases the measured time from diagnosis to death even though the actual time of death has not changed. Example: Without screening: Diagnosis at year 5 → death at year 8 = 3-year survival. With screening: Diagnosis at year 2 → death at year 8 = 6-year survival. Measured survival improves, but mortality is unchanged.

why_others_wrong.B: Recall bias concerns inaccurate participant memory of past exposures, not an apparent survival gain from diagnosing cancer earlier.
why_others_wrong.C: Allocation concealment is a safeguard in randomised trials against foreknowledge of assignment, not a cause of inflated post-diagnosis survival.
why_others_wrong.D: Effect modification means an effect differs across levels of another variable, which does not explain longer survival without lower mortality.
why_others_wrong.E: Confounding by indication arises when treatment choice reflects prognosis, whereas this apparent gain comes from moving the date of diagnosis earlier.

exam_trap: Confounding by indication may be chosen as a general bias term, but the apparent gain here comes solely from moving the diagnosis date earlier, which is lead-time bias.
takeaway: Earlier diagnosis does not mean longer life.
source: Standard screening and epidemiological methodology.
thinking: Cancer detected years earlier ↓ population mortality unchanged ↓ survival from diagnosis lengthens without longer life ↓ Lead-time bias
pearl: Survival rates from diagnosis are misleading when comparing screened and unscreened groups; mortality rates per head of population are unaffected by lead time.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: GI physiology & metabolism: starling forces
stem: A patient develops marked hypoalbuminaemia following extensive gastrointestinal disease. He develops bilateral peripheral oedema despite having no evidence of heart failure. Which change most directly contributes to the oedema?
why_correct: Albumin is the major contributor to plasma colloid oncotic pressure. Reduced plasma albumin lowers the force retaining fluid within the intravascular compartment, favouring movement of fluid into the interstitium.

why_others_wrong.A: A rise in plasma oncotic pressure would draw fluid into capillaries and oppose oedema; hypoalbuminaemia lowers it.
why_others_wrong.C: Reduced capillary hydrostatic pressure would lessen fluid filtration and so protect against, rather than cause, oedema.
why_others_wrong.D: Increased lymphatic drainage removes interstitial fluid and acts as a safety factor against oedema rather than causing it.
why_others_wrong.E: Lower interstitial oncotic pressure reduces the pull of fluid out of capillaries and would oppose oedema formation.

exam_trap: Option A is chosen by mixing up the direction: high plasma oncotic pressure holds fluid in vessels, whereas hypoalbuminaemia lowers it and favours oedema.
takeaway: Low albumin → ↓ plasma oncotic pressure → oedema.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Marked hypoalbuminaemia with oedema but no heart failure ↓ albumin generates most of the plasma oncotic pressure ↓ lower oncotic pressure lets capillary filtration exceed reabsorption ↓ Reduced plasma oncotic pressure
pearl: Low albumin in surgical patients mostly reflects inflammation, capillary leak and dilution rather than nutrition, so it is a marker of illness severity rather than a reliable nutritional index.

subject: Physiology
title: Anatomy: lymphatic physiology
stem: A patient undergoes extensive axillary lymph-node surgery and subsequently develops chronic swelling of the ipsilateral upper limb. Which substance is particularly important in the lymphatic return from the interstitium?
why_correct: The lymphatic system is particularly important for returning escaped interstitial proteins to the circulation, as well as excess interstitial fluid. When lymphatic drainage is disrupted, protein-rich fluid accumulates in the interstitium and contributes to chronic lymphoedema.

why_others_wrong.B: Red blood cells are not the key lymphatic component whose failed return underlies chronic lymphoedema.
why_others_wrong.C: Bile salts relate to hepatobiliary physiology and are not relevant to peripheral limb lymphatic drainage.
why_others_wrong.D: Haemoglobin is intracellular to red blood cells and is not the interstitial substance whose accumulation drives lymphoedema.
why_others_wrong.E: Platelets are not a significant component of interstitial fluid returned by the lymphatics in this context.

exam_trap: Candidates may think of lymph only as excess water or pick a cellular component such as red cells (B) or platelets (E), but protein return is the key lymphatic function.
takeaway: Lymphatics return interstitial fluid + protein.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Axillary surgery then chronic arm swelling ↓ lymphatics return filtered fluid and escaped protein ↓ protein has no other route back into the circulation ↓ Plasma proteins
pearl: Established lymphoedema becomes non-pitting with skin thickening; diagnosis is mainly clinical, supported by limb volume measurement or lymphoscintigraphy when doubt remains.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: GI physiology & metabolism: acid–base physiology
stem: A postoperative patient has persistent vomiting from gastric outlet obstruction. Which acid–base abnormality is most likely?
why_correct: Persistent vomiting causes loss of gastric hydrochloric acid. Loss of hydrogen ions produces metabolic alkalosis. Volume depletion and chloride depletion can help maintain the alkalosis.

why_others_wrong.A: A high-anion-gap acidosis arises from added acids such as lactate or ketones, whereas vomiting removes acid from the body.
why_others_wrong.B: Normal-anion-gap acidosis typically follows lower gastrointestinal bicarbonate loss such as diarrhoea, the opposite of losing gastric acid.
why_others_wrong.D: Respiratory acidosis reflects carbon dioxide retention from hypoventilation; any hypoventilation with vomiting is compensation for a primary metabolic alkalosis.
why_others_wrong.E: Respiratory alkalosis results from hyperventilation lowering PaCO2, which is not the primary disturbance produced by loss of gastric hydrochloric acid.

exam_trap: Normal-anion-gap acidosis (option B) is chosen by confusing upper and lower GI losses; diarrhoea loses bicarbonate, whereas vomiting loses acid and causes alkalosis.
takeaway: Vomiting → H+ loss → metabolic alkalosis.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Persistent vomiting from gastric outlet obstruction ↓ loss of gastric hydrochloric acid ↓ bicarbonate is retained, and volume and chloride depletion sustain it ↓ Metabolic alkalosis
pearl: The classic picture is a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria, corrected with intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride and potassium before surgery for the obstruction.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Cardiorespiratory physiology: renal compensation
stem: A patient has chronic respiratory alkalosis caused by persistent hyperventilation. Which renal adaptation helps compensate?

options.E: Increased ammonium generation as the sole response

why_correct: In chronic respiratory alkalosis, the kidneys compensate by reducing hydrogen-ion secretion and bicarbonate reabsorption, resulting in increased bicarbonate excretion. This lowers plasma bicarbonate and helps move pH toward normal.

why_others_wrong.A: Increased bicarbonate reabsorption would raise plasma bicarbonate further, worsening rather than compensating for the alkalosis.
why_others_wrong.B: Reduced bicarbonate excretion would retain bicarbonate and worsen, not correct, the respiratory alkalosis.
why_others_wrong.D: Hydrogen-ion secretion is reduced, not completely stopped, as part of renal compensation.
why_others_wrong.E: Ammonium generation relates to net acid excretion relevant to acidosis; it is not the compensatory mechanism for alkalosis, and framing it as the sole response is inaccurate.

exam_trap: Candidates reflexly choose increased bicarbonate reabsorption, but that is the compensation for respiratory acidosis; in respiratory alkalosis the kidneys excrete bicarbonate.
takeaway: Chronic respiratory alkalosis → renal HCO₃⁻ loss.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Chronic hyperventilation lowers PaCO2 ↓ the kidneys compensate over days ↓ H+ secretion and bicarbonate reabsorption are reduced ↓ bicarbonate is excreted and plasma HCO3- falls ↓ Increased bicarbonate excretion
pearl: Chronic respiratory alkalosis, as in pregnancy or at altitude, is the primary disorder in which renal compensation most often brings pH close to normal.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Cardiorespiratory physiology: acid–base interpretation
stem: An arterial blood gas shows pH 7.48, PaCO2 3.0 kPa and HCO3− 17 mmol/L. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.E: Mixed respiratory acidosis and metabolic alkalosis

correct_answer: C. Respiratory alkalosis with metabolic compensation
why_correct: The pH is alkalotic and PaCO2 is reduced, identifying respiratory alkalosis as the primary disturbance. The reduced bicarbonate indicates renal metabolic compensation, particularly if the respiratory alkalosis is chronic.

why_others_wrong.A: A pure metabolic alkalosis would not explain the markedly reduced PaCO2, which points to a primary respiratory disturbance.
why_others_wrong.B: A "pure" respiratory alkalosis would not account for the reduced bicarbonate, which reflects renal metabolic compensation.
why_others_wrong.D: The pH is alkalotic, not acidotic, so a diagnosis of metabolic acidosis is inconsistent with the given values.
why_others_wrong.E: PaCO2 is low, not high as would be seen in respiratory acidosis, so this mixed picture does not match the values given.

exam_trap: Candidates see the low bicarbonate and choose metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation (D), but the pH is alkalaemic, so the low PaCO2 is the primary change.
takeaway: Alkalotic pH + low CO2 = primary respiratory alkalosis.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: pH 7.48 = alkalaemia ↓ PaCO2 3.0 kPa is low, which explains the alkalaemia ↓ so the primary disturbance is respiratory alkalosis ↓ HCO3− 17 mmol/L is low, reflecting renal compensation ↓ Respiratory alkalosis with metabolic compensation
pearl: A clear fall in bicarbonate implies the hyperventilation has lasted long enough for renal compensation; in surgical patients causes include pain, anxiety, sepsis, pulmonary embolism and liver failure.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: Hepatobiliary surgery: liver physiology
stem: A patient with severe liver failure develops a rising plasma ammonia concentration. Which metabolic process is primarily impaired?
why_correct: The liver is the principal organ responsible for converting toxic ammonia into urea through the urea cycle. Severe hepatic dysfunction can therefore result in hyperammonaemia.

why_others_wrong.B: Glycogen synthesis may be impaired in liver failure but does not dispose of nitrogen, so its loss does not explain rising ammonia.
why_others_wrong.C: Fatty-acid beta oxidation provides energy and acetyl-CoA; it is not the pathway that detoxifies ammonia.
why_others_wrong.D: Lactate production occurs through anaerobic glycolysis and is unrelated to ammonia clearance.
why_others_wrong.E: Ketone use by skeletal muscle concerns fuel supply during fasting and does not remove ammonia from the blood.

exam_trap: Glycogen synthesis (option B) is also lost in liver failure and explains hypoglycaemia, but it disposes of no nitrogen; rising ammonia reflects failed urea synthesis.
takeaway: Liver failure → ↓ urea cycle → ↑ ammonia.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Severe liver failure with rising plasma ammonia ↓ ammonia is normally detoxified by hepatocytes ↓ the urea cycle converts ammonia into urea for renal excretion ↓ Urea synthesis
pearl: Lactulose lowers ammonia in hepatic encephalopathy by acidifying colonic contents and reducing ammonia absorption, and rifaximin is added to prevent recurrent episodes.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: GI physiology & metabolism: urea cycle
stem: A patient has severe hepatic dysfunction. Which nitrogen-containing substance is normally produced by the urea cycle for renal excretion?
why_correct: The urea cycle converts toxic nitrogen derived from amino-acid metabolism into urea, which is transported in blood and excreted by the kidneys.

why_others_wrong.A: Ammonia is the toxic nitrogen substrate that enters the urea cycle; the cycle converts it into urea rather than producing it.
why_others_wrong.C: Creatinine comes from non-enzymatic breakdown of muscle creatine phosphate, not from the urea cycle.
why_others_wrong.D: Uric acid is the end product of purine breakdown via xanthine oxidase, not of the urea cycle.
why_others_wrong.E: Bilirubin is a tetrapyrrole formed from haem breakdown in macrophages and excreted mainly in bile, not a product of the hepatic urea cycle.

exam_trap: Ammonia (option A) is chosen because the cycle handles it, but ammonia is the substrate entering the cycle; urea is the product sent to the kidneys.
takeaway: Urea = safe nitrogen transport product.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Question asks for the end product of the urea cycle ↓ toxic ammonia from amino-acid breakdown enters the cycle ↓ the cycle produces a water-soluble, non-toxic compound excreted by the kidneys ↓ Urea
pearl: Because urea is made in the liver, serum urea is often low in severe liver disease, whereas a urea raised out of proportion to creatinine suggests upper GI bleeding or dehydration.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: Hepatobiliary surgery: hepatic blood flow
stem: A patient undergoes an operation involving temporary clamping of the portal vein. Which mechanism partially compensates by increasing hepatic arterial flow?
why_correct: The liver receives blood from both the portal vein and the hepatic artery. When portal venous flow falls, adenosine is washed out less from around the hepatic arterioles, so it accumulates, dilates them and increases hepatic arterial flow: the hepatic arterial buffer response. The reverse does not occur, because the portal vein cannot increase its flow to make up for reduced arterial inflow.

why_others_wrong.B: Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction diverts pulmonary blood away from poorly ventilated alveoli and has no role in hepatic perfusion.
why_others_wrong.C: Tubuloglomerular feedback adjusts afferent arteriolar tone via the macula densa to stabilise renal filtration, not hepatic blood flow.
why_others_wrong.D: Coronary steal is the diversion of flow away from stenosed coronary territories during vasodilation, not a hepatic compensatory mechanism.
why_others_wrong.E: Cerebral autoregulation maintains brain blood flow across a range of perfusion pressures and does not act on the liver.

exam_trap: Cerebral autoregulation is chosen as the best-known flow-preserving mechanism, but it acts only in the brain; the liver’s own adenosine-mediated response is the hepatic arterial buffer response.
takeaway: Liver = dual blood supply; ↓ portal flow → ↑ hepatic arterial flow (hepatic arterial buffer response).
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Temporary portal vein clamping reduces portal inflow ↓ adenosine accumulates around hepatic arterioles as its washout falls ↓ hepatic arteriolar dilatation increases arterial inflow ↓ Hepatic arterial buffer response
pearl: Portal vein embolisation before major hepatectomy diverts portal flow to the future liver remnant to induce its hypertrophy, while arterial inflow to the embolised side is preserved.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: Physiology: hepatic metabolism
stem: A patient undergoes prolonged fasting. Which organ is principally responsible for maintaining circulating glucose during the later stages of fasting through gluconeogenesis?
why_correct: The liver is a major site of gluconeogenesis and maintains blood glucose during fasting using substrates including lactate, glycerol and amino acids. The kidneys can also contribute, particularly during prolonged fasting, but the liver remains a major site.

why_others_wrong.B: The spleen filters blood and has immune functions but does not perform gluconeogenesis to maintain fasting glucose.
why_others_wrong.C: Thyroid hormones influence metabolic rate, but the thyroid itself does not produce glucose during fasting.
why_others_wrong.D: The pancreas regulates glucose through glucagon and insulin but does not itself synthesise glucose for the circulation.
why_others_wrong.E: The gallbladder stores and concentrates bile and has no role in producing glucose.

exam_trap: Do not confuse glucose regulation by the pancreas with glucose production by the liver.
takeaway: Pancreas regulates glucose; liver produces/stores glucose.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Prolonged fasting depletes hepatic glycogen ↓ blood glucose then depends on gluconeogenesis from lactate, glycerol and amino acids ↓ the liver is the main gluconeogenic organ, with the kidney contributing later ↓ Liver
pearl: Muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase, so its glycogen cannot release free glucose into the blood; only the liver and kidney can export glucose to the circulation.

subject: Trauma & orthopaedics
title: Trauma & orthopaedics: bone physiology
stem: A patient undergoes prolonged immobilisation after major trauma. Which cellular process contributes to loss of bone mass?
why_correct: Reduced mechanical loading promotes bone loss. Increased resorption relative to formation contributes to disuse osteopenia.

why_others_wrong.A: Osteoblast activity falls rather than rises with unloading, and increased bone formation would add bone rather than cause its loss.
why_others_wrong.C: Bone turnover continues during immobilisation but becomes unbalanced, with resorption exceeding formation, rather than stopping altogether.
why_others_wrong.D: Increased cartilage formation is not a feature of disuse and would not account for the loss of bone mass after immobilisation.
why_others_wrong.E: Increased osteoid mineralisation would raise bone mineral content, the reverse of the disuse osteopenia seen after prolonged immobilisation.

exam_trap: Candidates choose complete inhibition of bone turnover, but turnover continues during disuse and becomes unbalanced, with resorption exceeding formation.
takeaway: Immobilisation → reduced loading → bone loss through increased resorption.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Prolonged immobilisation after trauma ↓ loss of mechanical loading ↓ osteocytes signal increased resorption and reduced formation ↓ resorption outpaces formation ↓ Increased osteoclast-mediated bone resorption
pearl: Immobilisation-related resorption can cause hypercalciuria and, in some patients such as adolescents or those with spinal cord injury, hypercalcaemia; early mobilisation limits disuse bone loss.

subject: Trauma & orthopaedics
title: Trauma & orthopaedics: bone remodelling
stem: A patient has increased bone turnover with raised markers of resorption. Which cell is responsible for the direct resorption of mineralised bone?
why_correct: Osteoclasts are multinucleated cells specialised for bone resorption. They create a local acidic and enzyme-rich environment that breaks down mineral and organic bone matrix.

why_others_wrong.A: Osteoblasts synthesise osteoid and signal to osteoclasts via RANKL, but they build bone rather than directly resorbing it.
why_others_wrong.C: Osteocytes act as mechanosensors within lacunae and regulate remodelling, but direct resorption of mineralised bone is performed by osteoclasts.
why_others_wrong.D: Chondrocytes maintain cartilage matrix and have no direct role in resorbing mineralised bone.
why_others_wrong.E: Fibroblasts produce collagen in soft connective tissues and lack the ruffled border and acid secretion needed to resorb mineralised bone.

exam_trap: Osteocyte (C) is chosen because it regulates remodelling as a mechanosensor, but direct resorption of mineralised bone is performed by osteoclasts.
takeaway: Osteoclast = bone resorption.
source: Gray’s Basic Anatomy, 3rd ed.; Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Raised bone resorption markers ↓ mineralised bone is resorbed by multinucleated cells with a ruffled border ↓ they secrete acid and proteolytic enzymes onto the bone surface ↓ Osteoclast
pearl: Bisphosphonates inhibit osteoclasts and denosumab blocks RANKL-driven osteoclast formation; both are linked to rare atypical femoral fractures and osteonecrosis of the jaw.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Perioperative medicine & nutrition: muscle physiology
stem: A patient undergoes neuromuscular blockade during general anaesthesia. Which event normally initiates skeletal-muscle contraction following motor-neuron activation?

options.A: Acetylcholine release followed by nicotinic receptor activation
options.B: Dopamine release followed by muscarinic receptor activation
options.C: Noradrenaline release followed by β1 activation
options.D: GABA release followed by chloride influx

correct_answer: A. Acetylcholine release followed by nicotinic receptor activation
why_correct: At the neuromuscular junction, a motor neuron releases acetylcholine. Acetylcholine activates nicotinic Nm receptors on the skeletal-muscle end plate, producing depolarisation that initiates the muscle action potential.

why_others_wrong.B: Dopamine and muscarinic receptors are not involved at the skeletal neuromuscular junction, which uses acetylcholine acting on nicotinic receptors.
why_others_wrong.C: Noradrenaline and beta-1 receptors mediate sympathetic effects on the heart, not skeletal-muscle excitation.
why_others_wrong.D: GABA with chloride influx is an inhibitory central mechanism that hyperpolarises neurones rather than triggering muscle contraction.
why_others_wrong.E: Serotonin and 5-HT3 receptors act in the gut and central nervous system, including emesis, not at the neuromuscular junction.

exam_trap: Option B tempts candidates who recall that acetylcholine acts on muscarinic receptors elsewhere, but skeletal muscle end-plates use nicotinic receptors; dopamine plays no role.
takeaway: Motor nerve → ACh → Nm receptor → muscle depolarisation.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Motor neuron action potential reaches the terminal ↓ calcium entry triggers acetylcholine release ↓ acetylcholine activates nicotinic Nm receptors on the end-plate ↓ Acetylcholine release followed by nicotinic receptor activation
pearl: Botulinum toxin prevents acetylcholine release and myasthenia gravis reduces functional nicotinic receptors, so both produce weakness by interrupting the same junctional sequence at different points.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: skeletal muscle
stem: A patient develops profound hypocalcaemia with perioral tingling and carpopedal spasm. Which mechanism best explains these features?

options.E: Increased potassium permeability as the sole mechanism

why_correct: Reduced extracellular calcium lowers the threshold for activation of excitable membranes, increasing neuromuscular excitability and potentially producing paraesthesia, carpopedal spasm and tetany.

why_others_wrong.A: Hypocalcaemia increases, not reduces, membrane excitability; reduced excitability is seen with hypercalcaemia.
why_others_wrong.C: Blockade of acetylcholine release causes flaccid weakness, as in botulism, rather than spasm and tetany.
why_others_wrong.D: Hypocalcaemia causes tetany and spasm; permanent paralysis is not the mechanism.
why_others_wrong.E: The mechanism is lowering of the sodium channel activation threshold, not increased potassium permeability, which would hyperpolarise.

exam_trap: Reduced neuronal excitability is chosen by assuming less calcium means less activity, but low extracellular calcium lowers the activation threshold, making membranes hyperexcitable.
takeaway: Hypocalcaemia → increased neuromuscular excitability.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Hypocalcaemia with perioral tingling and carpopedal spasm ↓ low extracellular calcium lowers the threshold for sodium channel activation ↓ nerves fire spontaneously ↓ paraesthesia and tetany follow ↓ Increased neuronal membrane excitability
pearl: Hypocalcaemia is a recognised complication of total thyroidectomy and parathyroidectomy; postoperative corrected calcium should be checked, and latent tetany can be elicited by tapping over the facial nerve or inflating a blood pressure cuff.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: autonomic physiology
stem: A patient develops a lesion affecting sympathetic fibres supplying the eye. Which combination is most characteristic of Horner syndrome?

options.B: Miosis, ptosis and reduced facial sweating

correct_answer: B. Miosis, ptosis and reduced facial sweating
why_correct: Horner syndrome results from interruption of the sympathetic pathway to the eye and face. Typical features include miosis, partial ptosis and ipsilateral anhidrosis.

why_others_wrong.A: Mydriasis and increased sweating are the opposite of the sympathetic loss seen in Horner syndrome, which causes miosis and reduced sweating.
why_others_wrong.C: Mydriasis, exophthalmos and increased sweating describe features of sympathetic overactivity or thyroid eye disease, not the sympathetic underactivity of Horner syndrome.
why_others_wrong.D: Horner syndrome does not cause blindness, and the sympathetic lesion producing it is typically unilateral, not bilateral.
why_others_wrong.E: Facial paralysis with deafness describes a lesion of the facial and vestibulocochlear nerves, an unrelated cranial nerve problem, not interruption of the sympathetic pathway.

exam_trap: Option A tempts those who remember ptosis but forget that the pupil is small; sympathetic loss causes miosis and anhidrosis, never mydriasis or increased sweating.
takeaway: Horner = ipsilateral miosis + ptosis + anhidrosis.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed.
thinking: Lesion of sympathetic fibres to the eye ↓ loss of dilator pupillae gives miosis ↓ loss of the superior tarsal muscle gives partial ptosis ↓ loss of sudomotor fibres gives reduced sweating ↓ Miosis, ptosis and reduced facial sweating
pearl: A new painful Horner syndrome after neck trauma or manipulation should prompt imaging for carotid artery dissection, and an apical lung tumour must be excluded in smokers with Horner syndrome and arm pain.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: parasympathetic anatomy
stem: A patient has damage to the pelvic splanchnic nerves. Which function is most likely to be impaired?

options.B: Sympathetic supply to the lower limb
options.D: Sensory supply of the upper limb

correct_answer: A. Parasympathetic control of pelvic viscera
why_correct: Pelvic splanchnic nerves arise from S2–S4 and carry parasympathetic fibres to pelvic viscera. They contribute to bladder emptying, distal bowel function and erectile physiology.

why_others_wrong.B: Sympathetic supply to the lower limb comes from T10-L2 via the lumbar sympathetic chain, not pelvic splanchnic nerves.
why_others_wrong.C: Quadriceps is supplied by the femoral nerve (L2-L4), a somatic nerve.
why_others_wrong.D: Upper limb sensation comes from the brachial plexus (C5-T1).
why_others_wrong.E: Cardiac sympathetic supply arises from T1-T4 and the cervical ganglia via cardiac nerves.

exam_trap: Sympathetic supply to the lower limb (B) attracts those who assume 'splanchnic' means sympathetic; pelvic splanchnic nerves are the parasympathetic exception.
takeaway: Pelvic splanchnic = S2–S4 parasympathetic.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed.
thinking: Pelvic splanchnic nerves ↓ arise from the S2–S4 anterior rami ↓ the only splanchnic nerves carrying parasympathetic fibres ↓ supply bladder, distal colon and rectum and erectile tissue ↓ Parasympathetic control of pelvic viscera
pearl: Injury during low anterior resection or radical hysterectomy can cause an atonic bladder with urinary retention and erectile dysfunction.

subject: Anatomy
title: Acute abdomen & GI surgery: embryology
stem: A newborn has a large defect of the anterior abdominal wall through which loops of bowel protrude. Failure of which embryonic process is most directly responsible?
why_correct: Normal embryonic folding brings the lateral body walls together and contributes to formation of the anterior abdominal wall. Failure of this process can produce major ventral body-wall defects.

why_others_wrong.B: Failure of neural-tube closure produces neural tube defects such as spina bifida or anencephaly, not a ventral abdominal wall defect.
why_others_wrong.C: Abnormal midgut rotation alone produces malrotation or volvulus; it does not by itself cause a large ventral wall defect through which bowel herniates.
why_others_wrong.D: Urogenital sinus development concerns formation of the bladder and lower genital tract, not closure of the ventral body wall.
why_others_wrong.E: Pharyngeal pouch development contributes to head and neck structures (e.g. parathyroids, thymus) and has no role in anterior abdominal wall closure.

exam_trap: Midgut rotation alone is chosen because bowel lies outside the abdomen, but abnormal rotation produces malrotation; a ventral wall defect reflects failed lateral body-fold fusion.
takeaway: Lateral folding + fusion → anterior body wall.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed.
thinking: Newborn with bowel protruding through an anterior wall defect ↓ the ventral body wall forms when the lateral body folds meet in the midline ↓ failure of fusion leaves a ventral wall defect ↓ Lateral body-fold fusion
pearl: Gastroschisis usually lies to the right of the umbilicus with no covering sac, whereas exomphalos is a midline, sac-covered defect at the umbilicus more often associated with chromosomal and cardiac anomalies.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: embryology
stem: A newborn develops bile-stained vomiting and intestinal obstruction due to abnormal positioning of the small bowel and caecum. Which developmental abnormality is most likely?
why_correct: Normal midgut development involves substantial rotation around the superior mesenteric artery. Abnormal rotation can produce malposition and predispose to volvulus and obstruction.

why_others_wrong.B: Neural tube defects produce spina bifida or anencephaly, not malposition of the bowel.
why_others_wrong.C: Failure of renal ascent gives a pelvic kidney, which does not cause bilious vomiting in the newborn.
why_others_wrong.D: A persistent urachus leaks urine from the umbilicus and does not cause small-bowel malposition.
why_others_wrong.E: Undescended testis causes an empty scrotum, not intestinal obstruction.

exam_trap: Neonatal bilious vomiting is obstruction distal to the ampulla until proven otherwise.
takeaway: Neonatal bilious vomiting + obstruction → think midgut malrotation/volvulus.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed.; Principles and Practice of Surgery, 7th ed.
thinking: Neonatal bilious vomiting ↓ obstruction distal to the ampulla ↓ small bowel and caecum abnormally positioned ↓ incomplete midgut rotation around the SMA, risking volvulus ↓ Malrotation of the midgut
pearl: Suspected malrotation with volvulus is a surgical emergency; an upper GI contrast study shows an abnormally placed duodenojejunal flexure, and delay risks loss of the entire midgut.

subject: Immunology
title: Immunology: B-cell deficiency
stem: A patient has selective loss of B lymphocytes. Which immune function is most directly impaired?
why_correct: B lymphocytes differentiate into plasma cells, which produce antibodies. Loss or severe dysfunction of B cells therefore impairs humoral immunity.

why_others_wrong.B: Neutrophil chemotaxis depends on innate signals such as C5a and IL-8 and is not primarily a B-cell function.
why_others_wrong.C: Complement proteins are synthesised mainly by hepatocytes, so B-cell loss does not impair their production.
why_others_wrong.D: Natural killer-cell cytotoxicity is an innate function that does not rely on B lymphocytes.
why_others_wrong.E: Platelet aggregation is a haemostatic process involving receptors such as GPIIb/IIIa and is unrelated to B lymphocytes.

exam_trap: Complement synthesis tempts because complement works with antibody, but it is made by hepatocytes; selective B-cell loss directly impairs antibody production.
takeaway: B-cell failure = humoral immunodeficiency.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Selective loss of B lymphocytes ↓ B cells become plasma cells ↓ plasma cells secrete antibody ↓ Antibody production
pearl: Rituximab (anti-CD20) depletes B cells and can cause hypogammaglobulinaemia and impaired vaccine responses, so immunoglobulin levels are monitored during prolonged treatment.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Microbiology & surgical infection: inflammation
stem: A patient with acute bacterial infection has neutrophils migrating from the bloodstream into infected tissue. Which process describes passage of neutrophils through the endothelial layer?
why_correct: Diapedesis is the movement of leukocytes across the endothelial barrier into tissues. Chemotaxis is directed movement towards a chemical gradient and occurs after leukocytes have entered the tissue.

why_others_wrong.A: Opsonisation is coating of a pathogen with molecules such as antibody or complement to enhance phagocytic recognition, not the physical passage of neutrophils across the endothelium.
why_others_wrong.C: Chemotaxis is directed movement of leukocytes towards a chemical gradient once they are within the tissue, distinct from the act of crossing the endothelial barrier itself.
why_others_wrong.D: Phagocytosis is engulfment of a target particle by a leukocyte, which occurs after the neutrophil has already migrated into the tissue, not the process of crossing the vessel wall.
why_others_wrong.E: Degranulation is release of granule contents by an activated leukocyte, an effector function distinct from the physical transendothelial migration described.

exam_trap: Candidates choose chemotaxis (C) because neutrophils are moving towards infection, but chemotaxis is directed migration along a gradient; physically crossing the endothelium is diapedesis.
takeaway: Leukocyte exit from a vessel = diapedesis.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Neutrophils leave the bloodstream for infected tissue ↓ question asks about crossing the endothelial layer itself ↓ margination, rolling and adhesion come first ↓ transmigration through the vessel wall ↓ Diapedesis
pearl: Neutrophil transmigration occurs mainly in post-capillary venules, where adhesion molecules are concentrated, and the cells then cross the basement membrane using secreted enzymes.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Microbiology & surgical infection: acute inflammation
stem: A patient has an acute bacterial wound infection. Which leukocyte is usually predominant during the early phase of acute inflammation?
why_correct: Neutrophils are the predominant early leukocytes in most acute bacterial inflammatory responses. They migrate rapidly into tissues and contribute to microbial killing.

why_others_wrong.B: Plasma cells are terminally differentiated antibody-producing B cells that appear later, in chronic inflammatory and immune responses, not during the early phase of acute bacterial infection.
why_others_wrong.C: Eosinophils are predominant in parasitic infections and allergic or hypersensitivity reactions, not the typical early cellular response to acute bacterial infection.
why_others_wrong.D: B lymphocytes participate in adaptive humoral immunity and are recruited later, not as the predominant early responders in acute inflammation.
why_others_wrong.E: Fibroblasts are mesenchymal cells involved in the proliferative and repair phase of wound healing, appearing after the acute inflammatory infiltrate, not as the predominant early cell type.

exam_trap: Candidates pick plasma cells (B) or B lymphocytes (D) by thinking of fighting infection, but these belong to later adaptive and chronic responses; neutrophils dominate early acute inflammation.
takeaway: Early acute bacterial inflammation = neutrophils.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Acute bacterial wound infection ↓ early phase of acute inflammation ↓ first leukocytes recruited within hours ↓ Neutrophil
pearl: Pus is largely composed of dead neutrophils and debris, and antibiotics penetrate an established abscess poorly, so drainage remains the key treatment.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing: wound healing
stem: A surgical wound develops a healthy red, granular base several days after injury. Which tissue is characteristic of this stage of healing?
why_correct: Granulation tissue contains newly formed capillaries, proliferating fibroblasts and inflammatory cells. It is characteristic of the proliferative phase of wound healing.

why_others_wrong.B: Caseous necrosis is a cheese-like, granular necrotic pattern typically seen in tuberculosis, not the vascularised, red granular tissue of active wound repair.
why_others_wrong.C: Dense mature scar forms later, after remodelling and cross-linking of collagen has reduced vascularity, giving a pale rather than red, granular appearance.
why_others_wrong.D: Coagulative necrosis describes ischaemic cell death with preserved but non-viable architecture, the opposite of the actively repairing, vascularised tissue described.
why_others_wrong.E: Cartilage is a specialised avascular connective tissue and is not the tissue type formed during the proliferative phase of cutaneous wound healing.

exam_trap: Candidates misread 'granular' and choose caseous necrosis (B), which is the cheesy necrotic pattern of tuberculosis, not the red, vascular tissue of active repair.
takeaway: Granulation tissue = capillaries + fibroblasts + repair.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Surgical wound several days after injury ↓ healthy red, granular base ↓ new capillary loops give the red granular look ↓ proliferative phase tissue ↓ Granulation tissue
pearl: Healthy granulation tissue is red and bleeds easily; pale or grey granulations suggest poor perfusion or infection, and exuberant overgranulation above skin level delays epithelialisation.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: GI physiology & metabolism: surgical nutrition
stem: A patient has a functioning gastrointestinal tract but cannot meet nutritional requirements orally because of severe dysphagia. Which route is generally preferred if nutritional support is required and the gastrointestinal tract is usable?

options.B: Total parenteral nutrition as first choice

why_correct: When the gastrointestinal tract is functional but oral intake is inadequate or unsafe, enteral nutrition is generally preferred. It maintains gastrointestinal use and avoids many complications associated with intravenous nutrition.

why_others_wrong.B: Parenteral nutrition is reserved for a non-functioning, inaccessible or inadequate gut and carries line and metabolic risks, so it is not first choice here.
why_others_wrong.C: Intramuscular glucose is not a recognised feeding route and could not deliver meaningful calories or protein.
why_others_wrong.D: Subcutaneous amino acids are not a recognised route for nutritional support and could not meet nutritional requirements.
why_others_wrong.E: Withholding support in a patient unable to meet requirements risks malnutrition and poorer outcomes when a usable enteral route exists.

exam_trap: Total parenteral nutrition is chosen because it seems more complete, but with a usable gut it adds line sepsis and metabolic risk without benefit; enteral feeding comes first.
takeaway: If the gut works and oral intake is inadequate → enteral first.
source: Principles and Practice of Surgery, 7th ed.
thinking: Functioning gastrointestinal tract ↓ oral intake inadequate because of severe dysphagia ↓ feed beyond the swallowing problem by nasogastric or gastrostomy tube ↓ Enteral nutrition
pearl: When dysphagia is expected to be prolonged, a gastrostomy (endoscopic or radiological) is usually preferred to a long-term nasogastric tube for comfort and tube security.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: GI physiology & metabolism: surgical nutrition
stem: A patient receives prolonged total parenteral nutrition without meaningful enteral stimulation. Which gastrointestinal change may occur?

options.C: Complete prevention of bacterial translocation in every patient
options.E: Immediate restoration of normal gut physiology

why_correct: Lack of enteral nutrient stimulation can reduce gastrointestinal trophic signalling and contribute to mucosal atrophy and altered gut function. This is one reason enteral nutrition is preferred when the gastrointestinal tract is functional and can safely be used.

why_others_wrong.A: Parenteral feeding removes luminal nutrients, so trophic stimulation of the intestinal mucosa decreases rather than increases.
why_others_wrong.C: Lack of enteral stimulation may weaken barrier function, and no nutritional route prevents bacterial translocation in every patient.
why_others_wrong.D: Without luminal nutrients, motility and gut hormone release tend to diminish rather than produce increased normal peristalsis.
why_others_wrong.E: Prolonged parenteral nutrition is associated with mucosal atrophy, and gut function recovers gradually after enteral feeding resumes rather than immediately.

exam_trap: Option C appeals because parenteral feeding bypasses the gut, but mucosal atrophy may weaken barrier function, and no route prevents bacterial translocation in every patient.
takeaway: Use the gut when possible — enteral nutrition supports gut structure and function.
source: Principles and Practice of Surgery, 7th ed.
thinking: Prolonged parenteral nutrition with no luminal nutrients ↓ loss of enteral trophic and gut hormone stimulation ↓ villous height and mucosal mass decline ↓ Intestinal mucosal atrophy
pearl: Long-term parenteral nutrition is also associated with cholestasis and gallbladder sludge, partly from lack of enteral CCK stimulation, alongside catheter-related bloodstream infection.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: perineal anatomy
stem: A man sustains a penetrating injury to the perineum. The injury is confined to the superficial perineal compartment. Which structure would normally be found within this compartment?
why_correct: The superficial perineal pouch contains the erectile tissues and associated muscles, including bulbospongiosus, ischiocavernosus and superficial transverse perineal muscles.

why_others_wrong.A: The prostate lies above the perineal membrane and deep pouch, within the pelvis.
why_others_wrong.B: Ischiorectal fat fills the ischioanal fossa in the anal triangle, outside the superficial perineal compartment.
why_others_wrong.D: Levator ani forms the pelvic diaphragm above the perineum.
why_others_wrong.E: Obturator internus lies on the lateral pelvic wall and ischioanal fossa, not in the superficial pouch.

exam_trap: Do not confuse the superficial perineal pouch with the ischioanal fossa.
takeaway: Superficial perineal pouch = erectile tissues + superficial perineal muscles.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed.
thinking: Superficial perineal compartment ↓ below the perineal membrane and deep to Colles fascia ↓ contains bulbospongiosus, ischiocavernosus, superficial transverse perineal muscles and erectile tissue ↓ Bulbospongiosus muscle
pearl: Bulbospongiosus contraction produces rhythmic expulsion of semen and final emptying of the bulbar urethra; it is supplied by the perineal branch of the pudendal nerve.

subject: Anatomy
title: Acute abdomen & GI surgery: perineal fascia
stem: A patient develops an extensive perineal soft-tissue infection after a urethral injury. The swelling extends onto the lower anterior abdominal wall but not into the thighs. Which membranous layer of the abdominal wall, by fusing with the fascia lata just below the inguinal ligament, explains this pattern?
why_correct: Urine or infection entering the superficial perineal tissues can spread through the continuity of Colles fascia with Scarpa fascia of the anterior abdominal wall. The attachment of Scarpa fascia to the fascia lata limits spread into the thighs.

why_others_wrong.A: Colles' fascia is the perineal part of the membranous layer; it attaches to the ischiopubic rami and perineal membrane, not to the fascia lata below the inguinal ligament.
why_others_wrong.B: The fascia lata is the deep fascia of the thigh to which Scarpa's fascia fuses; it is not itself a layer of the abdominal wall.
why_others_wrong.D: Transversalis fascia is a deep abdominal wall layer internal to the musculature and has no continuity with the superficial perineal fascial plane.
why_others_wrong.E: Endopelvic fascia is a deep pelvic visceral fascia unrelated to the superficial Colles–Scarpa fascial continuity responsible for this tracking pattern.

exam_trap: Fluid tracks from the perineum onto the abdominal wall through the Colles-Scarpa continuity, but it is Scarpa's fusion with the fascia lata that keeps it out of the thighs.
takeaway: Perineal fluid tracking = Colles fascia → Scarpa fascia.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed.
thinking: Infection spreads onto the lower abdominal wall but not into the thighs ↓ perineal Colles fascia is continuous with Scarpa fascia ↓ Scarpa fuses with the fascia lata just below the inguinal ligament ↓ that fusion blocks spread into the thighs ↓ Scarpa fascia
pearl: Necrotising fasciitis of the perineum, scrotum and abdominal wall spreads along these fascial planes and is a surgical emergency needing resuscitation, broad-spectrum antibiotics and early radical debridement.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: ischioanal fossa
stem: A deep perineal abscess is found lateral to the anal canal. Which structure forms the lateral wall of the ischioanal fossa?
why_correct: The ischioanal fossa is a fat-filled space lateral to the anal canal. Its lateral wall is formed principally by obturator internus and its fascia.

why_others_wrong.A: Levator ani forms the superomedial wall (roof) of the ischioanal fossa, sloping down to the anal canal.
why_others_wrong.C: The external anal sphincter lies medially, surrounding the anal canal.
why_others_wrong.D: Bulbospongiosus lies in the superficial perineal pouch of the urogenital triangle, anterior to the fossa.
