why_others_wrong.B: C3 is activated downstream of C1, C4 and C2 in the classical pathway, so it is not the earliest component and the pathway involves more than C3 alone.
why_others_wrong.C: C5 is cleaved late in the cascade by C5 convertase and begins membrane attack complex assembly, well after the initial C1 activation.
why_others_wrong.D: C9 is the terminal component that polymerises to form the membrane attack complex pore, the final step rather than an early one.
why_others_wrong.E: Factor B belongs to the alternative pathway, which is activated on microbial surfaces without antibody, not the antibody-initiated classical pathway.

exam_trap: Factor B tempts because it also acts early, but it belongs to the alternative pathway; the classical pathway starts with C1 binding antigen-bound antibody.
takeaway: Classical complement starts with C1.
source: Janeway's Immunobiology, 10th ed. Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Antibody bound to antigen ↓ classical pathway ↓ C1 complex (C1q, C1r, C1s) binds the Fc region first ↓ C1
pearl: C1 esterase inhibitor regulates activated C1r and C1s, and its deficiency causes hereditary angioedema with low C4 between and during attacks.

subject: Immunology
title: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing: complement regulation
stem: A healthy host cell avoids complement-mediated damage despite being exposed to circulating complement proteins. Which mechanism helps protect host tissues?

options.C: Permanent formation of membrane attack complexes

correct_answer: A. Expression of complement regulatory proteins
why_correct: Host cells express complement regulatory proteins that limit inappropriate complement activation and protect self-tissues from complement-mediated injury. This is essential because complement components can otherwise cause substantial cellular damage.

why_others_wrong.B: Continuous activation of C3 on host cells would deposit C3b and drive complement damage, the opposite of the protection described.
why_others_wrong.C: Membrane attack complexes form pores that lyse cells, so their formation on host cells would cause injury rather than prevent it.
why_others_wrong.D: C5a is a potent anaphylatoxin and chemoattractant that amplifies inflammation, so increased production would promote rather than limit tissue damage.
why_others_wrong.E: Loss of membrane regulatory proteins, as in paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria, leaves cells vulnerable to complement lysis rather than protecting them.

exam_trap: Loss of membrane proteins tempts but describes paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria, where missing CD55 and CD59 cause lysis; host protection comes from expressing regulatory proteins.
takeaway: Complement needs regulation to avoid self-injury.
source: Janeway's Immunobiology, 10th ed. Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Healthy host cell exposed to complement ↓ avoids damage ↓ membrane regulators inactivate convertases and block MAC ↓ Expression of complement regulatory proteins
pearl: Factor H mutations remove protection of glomerular endothelium from alternative pathway activation and cause atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome.

subject: Immunology
title: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing: peripheral tolerance
stem: A self-reactive lymphocyte escapes deletion during development but is prevented from mounting an effective immune response in peripheral tissues. Which concept best describes this?
why_correct: Central tolerance occurs during lymphocyte development in primary lymphoid organs. Peripheral tolerance controls self-reactive lymphocytes that remain outside those organs, through mechanisms including anergy, suppression by regulatory T cells and deletion.

why_others_wrong.A: Central tolerance acts during development in primary lymphoid organs, whereas this cell has already escaped deletion and is controlled in peripheral tissues.
why_others_wrong.C: Clonal expansion is proliferation of antigen-activated lymphocytes, which would enlarge rather than restrain a self-reactive response.
why_others_wrong.D: Somatic hypermutation alters antibody variable-region genes in germinal-centre B cells to improve affinity and is not a mechanism of self-tolerance.
why_others_wrong.E: Class switching changes the antibody heavy-chain constant region, altering isotype rather than preventing a self-reactive lymphocyte from responding.

exam_trap: Central tolerance tempts because deletion is mentioned, but the cell has already escaped development; control of mature self-reactive cells in tissues is peripheral tolerance.
takeaway: Escaped self-reactive cell in periphery → peripheral tolerance.
source: Janeway's Immunobiology, 10th ed.
thinking: Self-reactive lymphocyte escapes developmental deletion ↓ now a mature cell in peripheral tissues ↓ restrained by anergy, Tregs or deletion ↓ Peripheral tolerance
pearl: Peripheral tolerance failure is relevant to checkpoint inhibitor therapy, which can unleash autoimmune colitis, thyroiditis and hepatitis.

subject: Immunology
title: Pharmacology: pd-1 immune checkpoint
stem: A T lymphocyte expresses an inhibitory receptor that limits T-cell activity after binding its ligands on other cells. Which receptor is this?
why_correct: Programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) is an inhibitory immune checkpoint receptor expressed on activated T cells. Engagement by PD-L1 or PD-L2 can reduce T-cell activation and effector function.

why_others_wrong.A: CD28 is a co-stimulatory receptor that binds CD80 and CD86 to enhance T-cell activation, rather than an inhibitory receptor.
why_others_wrong.C: CD8 is the co-receptor on cytotoxic T cells that binds MHC class I and supports activation; it is not an inhibitory checkpoint.
why_others_wrong.D: CD4 is the helper T-cell co-receptor that binds MHC class II and assists activation rather than limiting T-cell activity.
why_others_wrong.E: CD19 is a B-cell surface marker and co-receptor component, not a receptor expressed on T lymphocytes to inhibit their activity.

exam_trap: CD28 is the trap because it also binds ligands on antigen-presenting cells, but it is stimulatory; the inhibitory checkpoint receptor engaged by PD-L1 is PD-1.
takeaway: PD-1 = T-cell inhibitory checkpoint.
source: Janeway's Immunobiology, 10th ed. Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Inhibitory receptor on activated T cells ↓ engaged by PD-L1 or PD-L2 ↓ dampens T-cell effector function ↓ PD-1
pearl: Anti-PD-1 drugs such as pembrolizumab and nivolumab release this brake to treat cancers but can cause immune-related colitis, pneumonitis and endocrinopathies.

subject: Immunology
title: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing: b-cell antigen receptor
stem: A mature B lymphocyte recognises antigen through its surface immunoglobulin. What is this receptor called?
why_correct: The B-cell receptor is membrane-bound immunoglobulin associated with signalling proteins. Recognition of antigen through the B-cell receptor can initiate B-cell activation, followed by differentiation and antibody production when appropriate signals are present.

why_others_wrong.A: The T-cell receptor is found on T lymphocytes and recognises peptide presented by MHC, not native antigen via surface immunoglobulin on B cells.
why_others_wrong.C: MHC class I presents intracellular peptides to CD8 T cells; it is not the membrane immunoglobulin a B cell uses to recognise antigen.
why_others_wrong.D: MHC class II on B cells presents processed peptide to CD4 helper T cells, whereas antigen recognition itself occurs through surface immunoglobulin.
why_others_wrong.E: Fc receptors bind the constant region of antibodies already made, rather than recognising antigen through a variable antigen-binding site.

exam_trap: T-cell receptor tempts because it is the other antigen receptor, but it sits on T cells and sees MHC-bound peptide; surface immunoglobulin on B cells is the B-cell receptor.
takeaway: B-cell recognition = B-cell receptor.
source: Janeway's Immunobiology, 10th ed.
thinking: Mature B cell ↓ recognises native antigen ↓ via membrane-bound immunoglobulin with Ig-alpha/Ig-beta signalling ↓ B-cell receptor
pearl: Unlike T cells, B cells can recognise intact, unprocessed antigen in its native shape, including polysaccharides and lipids.

subject: Immunology
title: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing: somatic hypermutation
stem: After activation in a germinal centre, B cells undergo mutations in their immunoglobulin variable-region genes. What is this process called?
why_correct: Somatic hypermutation introduces mutations into immunoglobulin variable-region genes after B-cell activation. Selection of B cells with improved antigen binding contributes to affinity maturation.

why_others_wrong.A: Class switching changes the heavy-chain constant region and antibody isotype, rather than introducing point mutations into variable-region genes.
why_others_wrong.C: V(D)J recombination rearranges gene segments during early B-cell development in the bone marrow, before antigen encounter rather than after germinal-centre activation.
why_others_wrong.D: Central deletion removes strongly self-reactive immature lymphocytes in primary lymphoid organs and does not mutate variable-region genes of activated B cells.
why_others_wrong.E: Clonal deletion is removal of self-reactive lymphocytes by apoptosis, a tolerance mechanism rather than mutation of immunoglobulin variable-region genes.

exam_trap: Class switching tempts because it also occurs in germinal centres, but it changes the constant region; mutations in variable-region genes are somatic hypermutation.
takeaway: Germinal centre → somatic hypermutation → affinity maturation.
source: Janeway's Immunobiology, 10th ed. Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Activated B cells in a germinal centre ↓ point mutations in variable-region genes ↓ selection of higher-affinity clones ↓ Somatic hypermutation
pearl: Somatic hypermutation needs activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID), the same enzyme required for class-switch recombination.

subject: Genetics
title: Genetics: robertsonian translocation
stem: A chromosomal rearrangement involves fusion of the long arms of two acrocentric chromosomes. Which term best describes this abnormality?
why_correct: Robertsonian translocations result from fusion involving the long arms of two acrocentric chromosomes. Carriers can have an apparently balanced chromosome complement but may have reproductive risks because of unbalanced gametes.

why_others_wrong.B: An inversion is a segment of one chromosome reversed end to end, not a fusion of the long arms of two acrocentric chromosomes.
why_others_wrong.C: A deletion is loss of a chromosome segment, whereas the stem describes two acrocentric chromosomes joining at their long arms.
why_others_wrong.D: A duplication is an extra copy of a chromosome segment, not fusion of two acrocentric chromosomes.
why_others_wrong.E: A ring chromosome forms when both ends of one chromosome are lost and the broken ends join, not from fusion of two acrocentric chromosomes.

exam_trap: Ring chromosome is the tempting option because it also involves chromosome ends joining, but it arises from one chromosome, not fusion of two acrocentrics.
takeaway: Acrocentric long-arm fusion = Robertsonian translocation.
source: Thompson & Thompson Genetics in Medicine, 10th ed.
thinking: Fusion of two chromosomes ↓ both are acrocentric ↓ long arms joined, short arms lost ↓ Robertsonian translocation
pearl: The acrocentric chromosomes are 13, 14, 15, 21 and 22; a Robertsonian translocation involving chromosome 21 causes familial translocation Down syndrome.

subject: Genetics
title: Genetics: fragile x syndrome
stem: A genetic disorder is caused by expansion of a CGG trinucleotide repeat in the FMR1 gene, with increased methylation and reduced gene expression. Which disorder is this?
why_correct: Fragile X syndrome results from CGG repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene. Large expansions can result in methylation and silencing of the gene.

why_others_wrong.A: Huntington disease is caused by a CAG repeat expansion in the HTT gene, not a CGG expansion in FMR1.
why_others_wrong.C: Marfan syndrome results from pathogenic variants in FBN1 encoding fibrillin-1, not from a trinucleotide repeat expansion.
why_others_wrong.D: Neurofibromatosis type 1 is caused by loss-of-function variants in the NF1 tumour suppressor gene, not by FMR1 repeat expansion.
why_others_wrong.E: Duchenne muscular dystrophy usually results from deletions in the DMD gene encoding dystrophin, not from a CGG repeat expansion.

exam_trap: Huntington disease is chosen because it is the best-known repeat disorder, but it results from a CAG expansion in HTT rather than a CGG expansion in FMR1.
takeaway: FMR1 + CGG expansion + methylation = fragile X.
source: Thompson & Thompson Genetics in Medicine, 10th ed.
thinking: CGG repeat expansion ↓ FMR1 gene ↓ hypermethylation silences the gene ↓ Fragile X syndrome
pearl: Fragile X is the commonest inherited cause of learning disability, and premutation carriers can develop fragile X-associated tremor-ataxia or premature ovarian insufficiency.

subject: Pharmacology
title: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing: drug tolerance
stem: A patient has been taking an opioid regularly for several months. A progressively larger dose is required to produce the same analgesic effect. Which term best describes this phenomenon?
why_correct: Tolerance is a gradual reduction in response to a drug following repeated or prolonged exposure, resulting in a need for a higher dose to produce the same effect. Mechanisms include receptor adaptation and changes in downstream signalling.

why_others_wrong.A: Tachyphylaxis describes a rapid decline in response occurring over a short period, not the gradual dose escalation needed over several months described here.
why_others_wrong.C: Idiosyncrasy describes an unpredictable, abnormal reaction, not a gradual reduction in response requiring escalating doses.
why_others_wrong.D: Potentiation describes enhancement of drug effect, which is the opposite of the reduced effect requiring dose escalation described.
why_others_wrong.E: Hypersensitivity is an immune-mediated reaction, unrelated to the gradual need for higher doses to achieve the same analgesic effect.

exam_trap: Tolerance is usually considered a more gradual phenomenon than tachyphylaxis.
takeaway: Prolonged exposure → less effect at the same dose = tolerance.
source: Rang & Dale's Pharmacology, 10th ed. Goodman & Gilman's The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics, 14th ed.
thinking: Regular opioid use over several months ↓ progressively larger dose needed for the same analgesia ↓ gradual onset rather than rapid ↓ Tolerance
pearl: Tolerance to opioid analgesia, sedation and respiratory depression develops, but little tolerance develops to constipation or miosis, so regular laxatives should accompany long-term opioids.

subject: Pharmacology
title: Pharmacology: drug potency
stem: Two agonist drugs produce the same maximum response in an experimental tissue. Drug A produces this response at a lower concentration than drug B. Which statement is correct?

options.D: Drug B has greater intrinsic activity
options.E: The drugs have different maximum responses

correct_answer: B. Drug A has greater potency
why_correct: Potency describes the concentration or dose required to produce a specified effect. If Drug A produces the same response at a lower concentration, it is more potent. Efficacy refers to the maximum response that can be produced.

why_others_wrong.A: Efficacy relates to the maximal response (Emax), which is stated to be equal between the two drugs; the difference described here is in the concentration required, i.e. potency.
why_others_wrong.C: This is the opposite of what is shown; Drug B requires a higher concentration to produce the same effect and is therefore less, not more, potent.
why_others_wrong.D: Intrinsic activity/efficacy is equal since both drugs achieve the same maximum response; the scenario does not demonstrate a difference in intrinsic activity.
why_others_wrong.E: This contradicts the stem, which states both drugs produce the same maximum response; only the concentration required to reach it differs.

exam_trap: Candidates confuse potency with efficacy and choose greater efficacy, but equal maximum responses mean equal efficacy; the lower concentration needed for that response shows greater potency.
takeaway: Lower concentration for the same effect = greater potency.
source: Rang & Dale's Pharmacology, 10th ed.
thinking: Both drugs reach the same maximum response ↓ so efficacy is equal ↓ drug A reaches it at a lower concentration ↓ potency describes the concentration needed for an effect ↓ Drug A has greater potency
pearl: Potency alone does not make a drug clinically better: fentanyl is far more potent than morphine, yet both are full agonists with similar maximal analgesic effect when dosed appropriately.

subject: Pharmacology
title: Pharmacology: drug efficacy
stem: Drug A and Drug B act on the same receptor. Drug A produces a greater maximum response than Drug B, even when the concentration of each drug is increased sufficiently. Which property is greater for Drug A?
why_correct: Efficacy describes the maximum response a drug can produce through its receptor system. Drug A has a greater maximum effect and therefore greater efficacy.

why_others_wrong.A: Bioavailability describes the fraction of dose reaching systemic circulation and is unrelated to comparing the maximal receptor-mediated response of two agonists.
why_others_wrong.B: Potency concerns the concentration required to produce a given effect, not the maximal response achievable, which is what differs between Drug A and Drug B here.
why_others_wrong.D: Clearance is a pharmacokinetic elimination parameter, unrelated to comparing the maximal pharmacodynamic response of two agonists at the same receptor.
why_others_wrong.E: Half-life is a pharmacokinetic parameter describing elimination, unrelated to comparing the maximum effect two agonists can produce.

exam_trap: Compare Emax for efficacy; compare concentration required for a specified effect for potency.
takeaway: Higher Emax = greater efficacy.
source: Rang & Dale's Pharmacology, 10th ed. Goodman & Gilman's The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics, 14th ed.
thinking: Two drugs act on the same receptor ↓ drug A gives a greater maximum response even at high concentrations ↓ the ceiling of response defines efficacy ↓ Efficacy
pearl: Buprenorphine, a partial mu-opioid agonist, has a ceiling to its respiratory depressant effect and can displace full agonists, precipitating withdrawal in patients dependent on them.

subject: Pharmacology
title: Pharmacology: spare receptors
stem: An experimental tissue reaches its maximum response when only a fraction of its total receptors are occupied by an agonist. What does this demonstrate?
why_correct: Receptor reserve, or spare receptors, means that maximal tissue response can occur without occupation of all available receptors. This reflects amplification within the receptor-effector signalling system.

why_others_wrong.A: This contradicts the scenario, in which the tissue does reach a maximal response, indicating that receptor signalling is actively occurring.
why_others_wrong.C: Competitive antagonism describes inhibition of agonist binding by another ligand competing for the receptor, not a maximal response occurring below full receptor occupancy.
why_others_wrong.D: This contradicts the scenario, which describes the tissue still achieving its maximum response despite only partial receptor occupancy.
why_others_wrong.E: Irreversible receptor blockade describes an antagonist permanently reducing available receptors, not the phenomenon of an agonist producing a maximal effect without occupying all receptors.

exam_trap: Reduced efficacy may be chosen because not all receptors are used, but the tissue still reaches its full maximum; maximal response at partial occupancy indicates spare receptors.
takeaway: Maximum response without full receptor occupancy = spare receptors.
source: Rang & Dale's Pharmacology, 10th ed.
thinking: Maximal tissue response is reached at partial receptor occupancy ↓ signal amplification downstream of the receptor ↓ remaining receptors are not needed for maximal effect ↓ Receptor reserve
pearl: The neuromuscular junction has a large receptor reserve: most acetylcholine receptors must be occupied by a non-depolarising blocker before twitch height falls, so a normal single twitch does not exclude residual blockade.

subject: Pharmacology
title: Pharmacology: irreversible antagonism
stem: An antagonist binds irreversibly to a proportion of receptors. Even at high concentrations, the agonist cannot restore the original maximum response. Which change is expected on the agonist concentration-response curve?
why_correct: An irreversible antagonist reduces the number of available functional receptors. If sufficient receptor reserve is absent, the maximum achievable response falls.

why_others_wrong.A: This is the opposite of what is expected; irreversible antagonism reduces available functional receptors and can reduce Emax, it does not shift the curve left or increase Emax.
why_others_wrong.B: A rightward shift with unchanged Emax describes surmountable competitive (reversible) antagonism, whereas here the antagonism is irreversible and the maximum response cannot be restored.
why_others_wrong.D: Increased potency and unchanged Emax is inconsistent with irreversible receptor loss, which tends to reduce, not increase, apparent potency and can also reduce Emax.
why_others_wrong.E: This contradicts the stem, which explicitly states that increasing agonist concentration could not restore the original maximum response.

exam_trap: Competitive reversible antagonism usually changes potency; irreversible antagonism can reduce maximum efficacy.
takeaway: Irreversible antagonist → fewer functional receptors → ↓ Emax.
source: Rang & Dale's Pharmacology, 10th ed.
thinking: Antagonist binds irreversibly to some receptors ↓ those receptors are lost to the agonist however high its concentration ↓ without enough spare receptors the maximum response cannot be reached ↓ antagonism is insurmountable ↓ Reduced Emax
pearl: Phenoxybenzamine, an irreversible alpha-blocker used before phaeochromocytoma surgery, is a classic example; its effect lasts until new receptors are synthesised.

subject: Pharmacology
title: Hepatobiliary surgery: enterohepatic circulation
stem: A drug is conjugated in the liver, excreted in bile and subsequently deconjugated by intestinal bacteria before being reabsorbed. What process is occurring?
why_correct: Enterohepatic circulation occurs when a substance is excreted into bile, enters the intestine and is subsequently reabsorbed and returned to the liver. This can prolong the presence of some drugs or metabolites in the body.

why_others_wrong.A: First-pass metabolism describes presystemic hepatic metabolism of an orally absorbed drug before it reaches the systemic circulation, not the biliary excretion and intestinal reabsorption described here.
why_others_wrong.C: Glomerular filtration is a renal process filtering blood, unrelated to biliary excretion followed by intestinal deconjugation and reabsorption.
why_others_wrong.D: Pulmonary elimination describes exhalation of volatile substances, unrelated to the hepatobiliary-intestinal recycling process described.
why_others_wrong.E: Protein displacement describes competition for plasma protein binding sites, unrelated to biliary excretion and subsequent intestinal reabsorption of a drug.

exam_trap: First-pass metabolism is often chosen because the liver is involved, but that is presystemic loss after oral absorption; biliary excretion followed by gut reabsorption is enterohepatic circulation.
takeaway: Liver → bile → gut → reabsorption → liver = enterohepatic circulation.
source: Rang & Dale's Pharmacology, 10th ed. Goodman & Gilman's The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics, 14th ed.
thinking: Hepatic conjugation then biliary excretion ↓ gut bacteria deconjugate the drug ↓ the free drug is reabsorbed and returns to the liver ↓ Enterohepatic circulation
pearl: Bile acids undergo enterohepatic circulation with reabsorption in the terminal ileum, so ileal resection or Crohn's disease can cause bile acid diarrhoea and predispose to gallstones.

subject: Pharmacology
title: Pharmacology: hepatic enzyme induction
stem: A patient starts a drug that induces hepatic CYP enzymes. The plasma concentration of another drug metabolised predominantly by that enzyme subsequently falls. What is the most likely explanation?
why_correct: Enzyme induction increases the expression or activity of relevant drug-metabolising enzymes. A substrate drug may therefore be metabolised more rapidly, lowering its plasma concentration.

why_others_wrong.A: Reduced metabolism would raise, not lower, the substrate's plasma concentration; induction increases enzyme activity, the opposite of this option.
why_others_wrong.C: The vignette describes a hepatic enzyme effect on a hepatically metabolised drug; renal filtration is not the mechanism being tested and induction does not act on the kidney.
why_others_wrong.D: Enzyme induction changes metabolic clearance, not protein binding; a change in binding alone would not explain a fall driven by an inducer of a metabolising enzyme.
why_others_wrong.E: Induction acts on hepatic metabolism after absorption, not on intestinal absorption itself, so a change confined to absorption does not fit the described mechanism.

exam_trap: Enzyme induction often develops more slowly than direct enzyme inhibition because increased enzyme synthesis may be required.
takeaway: CYP induction → faster substrate metabolism → lower drug concentration.
source: Rang & Dale's Pharmacology, 10th ed. Goodman & Gilman's The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics, 14th ed.
thinking: New drug induces hepatic CYP enzymes ↓ more enzyme is synthesised ↓ the second drug is a substrate of that enzyme ↓ its metabolism speeds up and plasma level falls ↓ Increased hepatic metabolism
pearl: Rifampicin, carbamazepine and phenytoin are potent enzyme inducers that can reduce warfarin effect and the reliability of hormonal contraception, so INR monitoring and contraceptive advice are needed when they are started.

subject: Pharmacology
title: Pharmacology: drug enzyme inhibition
stem: A patient begins a potent inhibitor of a hepatic enzyme responsible for metabolism of a second drug. The concentration of the second drug rises rapidly. What is the most likely mechanism?
why_correct: Enzyme inhibition reduces metabolism of the substrate drug. This can increase plasma concentration and, depending on the drug, increase the risk of adverse effects.

why_others_wrong.A: Increased clearance would lower, not raise, the second drug's concentration; inhibition reduces clearance, the opposite direction.
why_others_wrong.C: Renal filtration is unrelated to inhibition of a hepatic metabolising enzyme, and increased filtration would in any case lower rather than raise drug levels.
why_others_wrong.D: Enzyme inhibition reduces presystemic (first-pass) metabolism, it does not increase it; increased first-pass metabolism would lower, not raise, bioavailability and concentration.
why_others_wrong.E: Receptor downregulation is a pharmacodynamic adaptation to prolonged agonist exposure, not a pharmacokinetic consequence of inhibiting a metabolising enzyme.

exam_trap: Enzyme inhibition can occur rapidly because it does not necessarily require new protein synthesis.
takeaway: Enzyme inhibition → ↓ metabolism → ↓ clearance → ↑ substrate level.
source: Rang & Dale's Pharmacology, 10th ed.
thinking: Potent inhibitor of a hepatic metabolising enzyme started ↓ substrate metabolism slows ↓ rapid rise in substrate concentration ↓ Reduced metabolic clearance
pearl: Clarithromycin inhibits CYP3A4 and can markedly increase simvastatin levels, risking rhabdomyolysis, and can also raise the INR in patients on warfarin.

subject: Pharmacology
title: Hepatobiliary surgery: first-pass extraction
stem: A drug is extensively metabolised by the liver immediately after oral absorption, resulting in substantially less drug reaching the systemic circulation. Which pharmacokinetic concept best describes this?
why_correct: The first-pass effect refers to metabolism of an orally administered drug in the intestinal wall and/or liver before it reaches systemic circulation. Extensive first-pass metabolism reduces oral bioavailability.

why_others_wrong.A: Renal clearance describes elimination via the kidney, not presystemic hepatic/intestinal metabolism of an orally absorbed drug before it reaches the circulation.
why_others_wrong.C: Receptor downregulation is a pharmacodynamic adaptation to repeated agonist exposure and has nothing to do with presystemic drug metabolism.
why_others_wrong.D: Volume of distribution describes how a drug distributes into body compartments once in the circulation, not loss of drug before it ever reaches systemic circulation.
why_others_wrong.E: Protein synthesis is a general cellular process; it does not describe the specific pharmacokinetic phenomenon of presystemic metabolism reducing oral bioavailability.

exam_trap: Volume of distribution is sometimes chosen because less drug appears in plasma, but it describes distribution after the drug reaches the circulation; presystemic hepatic loss is the first-pass effect.
takeaway: Oral drug → gut and liver metabolism before systemic circulation = first pass.
source: Rang & Dale's Pharmacology, 10th ed.
thinking: Oral drug absorbed from the gut ↓ portal blood carries it to the liver first ↓ extensive metabolism before reaching the systemic circulation ↓ reduced oral bioavailability ↓ First-pass effect
pearl: Glyceryl trinitrate has extensive first-pass metabolism, so it is given sublingually or transdermally to enter the systemic circulation directly and bypass the portal system.

subject: Pharmacology
title: Pharmacology: zero-order elimination
stem: A drug is eliminated at a constant amount per unit time because the relevant metabolic pathway is saturated. Which type of elimination is occurring?
why_correct: In zero-order elimination, a constant amount of drug is removed per unit time because the elimination pathway is saturated. In first-order elimination, a constant fraction is eliminated per unit time.

why_others_wrong.A: First-order elimination removes a constant fraction of drug per unit time and requires an unsaturated pathway, which is the opposite of the saturated-pathway scenario described.
why_others_wrong.C: Passive diffusion describes a mechanism of membrane crossing, not a kinetic pattern of elimination over time.
why_others_wrong.D: Receptor-mediated elimination is not the standard term for saturable metabolic/transport elimination kinetics described here; the stem is describing zero-order kinetics from pathway saturation.
why_others_wrong.E: Enterohepatic elimination refers to biliary excretion and intestinal reabsorption of a drug, not the kinetic pattern (constant amount vs constant fraction) being asked about.

exam_trap: First-order elimination is the familiar default and is often chosen, but it removes a constant fraction; removal of a constant amount from a saturated pathway is zero-order elimination.
takeaway: Saturated elimination → constant amount per unit time = zero order.
source: Rang & Dale's Pharmacology, 10th ed.
thinking: Metabolic pathway is saturated ↓ a constant amount, not a constant fraction, is removed per unit time ↓ half-life is no longer constant ↓ Zero-order elimination
pearl: Phenytoin and alcohol show saturable (zero-order) kinetics at higher concentrations, so a small dose increase can produce a disproportionate rise in plasma level and toxicity.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Pharmacology: baroreceptor response to acute hypotension
stem: A patient suddenly loses a significant volume of blood. Arterial pressure falls. Which immediate change is expected from the arterial baroreceptor reflex?
why_correct: Acute hypotension reduces stretch of arterial baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch. This increases sympathetic and reduces parasympathetic activity, producing tachycardia, increased contractility and vasoconstriction.

why_others_wrong.A: A fall in baroreceptor stretch reduces parasympathetic (vagal) outflow to the heart, not increases it, allowing heart rate to rise.
why_others_wrong.B: Sympathetic activity increases, not reduces, when baroreceptor firing falls, driving tachycardia, increased contractility and vasoconstriction.
why_others_wrong.D: Myocardial contractility increases via sympathetic stimulation as part of the compensatory response, rather than falling.
why_others_wrong.E: Systemic vascular resistance rises due to sympathetic-mediated arteriolar vasoconstriction, which helps defend arterial pressure, not lower it.

exam_trap: Candidates may pick increased parasympathetic activity or reduced SVR, but falling baroreceptor firing withdraws vagal tone and increases sympathetic vasoconstriction.
takeaway: Acute BP fall → ↓ baroreceptor firing → ↑ sympathetic activity.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Acute blood loss lowers arterial pressure ↓ carotid sinus and aortic arch baroreceptor stretch falls ↓ vagal tone falls and sympathetic outflow rises ↓ Increased heart rate
pearl: The reflex tachycardia can be blunted by beta-blockers, pacemakers, older age or athletic conditioning, so a normal heart rate does not exclude significant haemorrhage.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Pharmacology: chemoreceptor response
stem: A patient develops severe arterial hypoxaemia. Which peripheral chemoreceptor structure is particularly important in detecting the fall in arterial oxygen tension?
why_correct: Peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies detect changes in arterial oxygen, carbon dioxide and pH. The carotid bodies are particularly important in detecting significant reductions in arterial oxygen tension.

why_others_wrong.B: The hypothalamus is involved in autonomic and thermoregulatory integration, not peripheral chemoreception of arterial oxygen.
why_others_wrong.C: Atrial stretch receptors respond to changes in venous return and atrial volume, not to arterial oxygen tension.
why_others_wrong.D: The carotid sinus contains baroreceptors that sense arterial pressure/stretch, not chemoreceptors sensing oxygen tension.
why_others_wrong.E: The cerebellum coordinates motor function and balance and plays no direct role in detecting arterial oxygen levels.

exam_trap: Candidates choose the carotid sinus because it shares location and nerve supply, but the sinus contains baroreceptors; the oxygen-sensing chemoreceptors lie in the carotid bodies.
takeaway: Carotid body senses O₂; carotid sinus senses pressure.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Severe arterial hypoxaemia ↓ peripheral chemoreceptors sense the fall in PaO2 ↓ the carotid bodies at the carotid bifurcation are the main hypoxic sensors ↓ Carotid bodies
pearl: Central chemoreceptors do not respond to hypoxia, so the ventilatory response to low PaO2 depends on the carotid bodies, and it can be lost after bilateral carotid endarterectomy.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Pharmacology: central chemoreceptors
stem: A rise in arterial carbon dioxide causes increased ventilation. Which mechanism is primarily responsible for detecting the associated change in the central nervous system?

options.A: Direct detection of arterial oxygen by carotid bodies

correct_answer: B. Increased CSF hydrogen ion concentration
why_correct: Carbon dioxide readily crosses the blood-brain barrier and forms carbonic acid in cerebrospinal fluid. The resulting increase in hydrogen ion concentration stimulates central chemoreceptor mechanisms and increases ventilation.

why_others_wrong.A: Carotid bodies are peripheral chemoreceptors that respond mainly to arterial oxygen (and some CO2/pH), not the central CSF-mediated pathway described here.
why_others_wrong.C: Arterial pressure is sensed by baroreceptors, a separate reflex arc unrelated to the central chemoreceptor response to CO2.
why_others_wrong.D: Plasma sodium concentration has no established role in central chemoreceptor stimulation by rising CO2.
why_others_wrong.E: Atrial stretch receptors signal venous return/volume status, not the CSF pH changes that drive central ventilatory responses to CO2.

exam_trap: Central chemoreceptors respond primarily to the CSF consequences of CO2 rather than directly sensing arterial CO2 itself.
takeaway: CO₂ crosses the BBB → CSF H⁺ rises → central ventilatory drive.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Arterial CO2 rises ↓ CO2 crosses the blood-brain barrier freely while H+ does not ↓ CO2 forms carbonic acid in CSF, raising H+ ↓ medullary chemoreceptors increase ventilation ↓ Increased CSF hydrogen ion concentration
pearl: CSF has little protein buffering, so its pH changes sharply with PaCO2; over days bicarbonate adjustment in CSF resets this, which blunts the CO2 drive in chronic hypercapnia.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: renal glucose threshold
stem: A patient develops marked hyperglycaemia. Glucose begins to appear in the urine once the filtered load exceeds the renal tubular transport capacity. Which nephron segment normally reabsorbs the majority of filtered glucose?
why_correct: Filtered glucose is normally reabsorbed almost completely in the proximal tubule through sodium-glucose cotransport mechanisms. When the filtered load exceeds the transport maximum, glucose appears in the urine.

why_others_wrong.B: The thin descending limb is primarily permeable to water for the concentrating mechanism, not the principal site of glucose reabsorption.
why_others_wrong.C: The thick ascending limb reabsorbs sodium, potassium and chloride via the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter and is not the main site of glucose reabsorption.
why_others_wrong.D: The distal convoluted tubule handles sodium chloride reabsorption and calcium regulation, not the bulk of filtered glucose.
why_others_wrong.E: The collecting duct regulates final water and electrolyte balance under ADH and aldosterone control, not glucose reabsorption.

exam_trap: Glucosuria in severe hyperglycaemia reflects saturation of proximal tubular reabsorptive capacity.
takeaway: Filtered glucose → proximal tubule reabsorption.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Glucosuria once filtered load exceeds the transport maximum ↓ glucose is reabsorbed by SGLT2 and SGLT1 ↓ these sit almost entirely in the proximal tubule ↓ Proximal tubule
pearl: SGLT2 inhibitors such as dapagliflozin cause glucosuria and can precipitate euglycaemic diabetic ketoacidosis perioperatively, so they are usually withheld around major surgery.

subject: Physiology
title: Anatomy: renal urea handling
stem: A patient who is water-deprived produces highly concentrated urine. The kidney maintains the medullary concentration gradient partly through recycling of urea. Which nephron structure is particularly permeable to urea under the influence of antidiuretic hormone?
why_correct: ADH increases urea permeability in the inner medullary collecting duct. Urea then contributes to the high osmolarity of the renal medulla, supporting water reabsorption.

why_others_wrong.A: The proximal tubule reabsorbs urea passively alongside water but is not the ADH-regulated segment responsible for the described medullary urea recycling.
why_others_wrong.C: The thick ascending limb is essentially impermeable to water and is not where ADH increases urea permeability; it contributes to the countercurrent multiplier via active NaCl transport instead.
why_others_wrong.D: ADH increases water permeability in the cortical collecting duct, but it is the inner medullary, not cortical, collecting duct where ADH-driven urea permeability is most important.
why_others_wrong.E: The distal convoluted tubule is largely impermeable to urea and is not the site of ADH-regulated urea recycling.

exam_trap: Think of ADH as increasing both water permeability and, in the inner medullary collecting duct, urea permeability.
takeaway: ADH + inner medullary collecting duct → urea recycling.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Water deprivation produces concentrated urine ↓ ADH acts on the collecting duct ↓ in the inner medullary collecting duct it increases urea transporter activity ↓ urea diffuses into the medullary interstitium, adding to its osmolality ↓ Inner medullary collecting duct
pearl: Urea recycling explains why patients on very low protein intake concentrate urine less well, as less urea is available to build the inner medullary gradient.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: phosphate buffering
stem: A patient with chronic metabolic acidosis increases urinary excretion of hydrogen ions buffered by filtered phosphate. What is this form of acid excretion called?
why_correct: Hydrogen ions secreted into the tubular fluid can bind urinary buffers such as phosphate. The amount of hydrogen ion excreted in this buffered form contributes to titratable acid excretion.

why_others_wrong.A: Ammonium trapping refers to hydrogen ion excretion buffered by ammonia as NH4+, a separate acid-excretion pathway from phosphate buffering.
why_others_wrong.C: Bicarbonate secretion by type B intercalated cells removes base during alkalosis; it is not a form of buffered hydrogen ion excretion.
why_others_wrong.D: Chloride secretion is not a recognised renal mechanism of buffered hydrogen ion excretion.
why_others_wrong.E: Potassium filtration relates to potassium handling, not to hydrogen ions buffered by urinary phosphate.

exam_trap: Ammonium trapping (A) tempts because it is the other buffered route of acid excretion, but H+ bound to phosphate is titratable acid, not ammonium.
takeaway: Phosphate-bound urinary H+ = titratable acid.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: H+ secreted into tubular fluid ↓ buffered by filtered phosphate ↓ excreted as dihydrogen phosphate ↓ Titratable acid excretion
pearl: Each H+ excreted as titratable acid or ammonium corresponds to a new bicarbonate added to blood, which is how the kidney regenerates bicarbonate consumed by metabolic acids.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: gfr and afferent arteriole
stem: Constriction of the afferent arteriole supplying a glomerulus occurs. What is the immediate effect on glomerular filtration rate?

options.E: It depends only on plasma oncotic pressure

why_correct: Afferent arteriolar constriction reduces blood flow into the glomerulus and lowers glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure. This reduces GFR.

why_others_wrong.A: Afferent constriction reduces, not raises, glomerular capillary pressure and therefore GFR, the opposite of an increase.
why_others_wrong.C: Afferent arteriolar tone directly affects glomerular capillary pressure, so GFR does change with constriction.
why_others_wrong.D: Constriction produces a sustained decrease in GFR, not a transient increase followed by normalisation.
why_others_wrong.E: GFR depends on multiple Starling forces and vascular resistances, not solely on plasma oncotic pressure; afferent resistance change alone has a direct, predictable effect on GFR.

exam_trap: Candidates who mix up the arterioles choose an increase (A); efferent constriction raises glomerular pressure, whereas afferent constriction lowers both pressure and GFR.
takeaway: Afferent constriction → ↓ glomerular pressure → ↓ GFR.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Afferent arteriole lies upstream of the glomerulus ↓ constriction reduces inflow ↓ glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure falls ↓ Decrease
pearl: NSAIDs block afferent-dilating prostaglandins, so in hypovolaemic or elderly surgical patients they can precipitate acute kidney injury, especially when combined with ACE inhibitors that remove efferent tone.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: efferent arteriole constriction
stem: Moderate constriction of the efferent arteriole occurs while other variables remain relatively stable. What is the immediate expected effect on glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure?

options.E: It becomes equal to Bowman space pressure

why_correct: The efferent arteriole is downstream from the glomerular capillary bed. Moderate efferent constriction increases resistance to blood leaving the glomerulus, tending to increase glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure.

why_others_wrong.A: Increased resistance downstream of the glomerulus raises, rather than lowers, glomerular capillary pressure.
why_others_wrong.C: Efferent resistance directly affects the pressure gradient across the glomerular capillary bed, so pressure does change.
why_others_wrong.D: Efferent constriction raises glomerular capillary pressure; it does not cause the pressure to fall to zero.
why_others_wrong.E: Equalisation with Bowman space pressure would mean zero net filtration pressure, which is not the moderate effect described in the stem.

exam_trap: Efferent constriction can increase glomerular pressure, but severe constriction can ultimately reduce renal blood flow substantially and alter GFR in a more complex way.
takeaway: Moderate efferent constriction → ↑ glomerular capillary pressure.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Efferent arteriole lies downstream of the glomerular capillaries ↓ constriction increases outflow resistance ↓ blood dams back in the glomerulus ↓ Increase
pearl: Angiotensin II preferentially constricts the efferent arteriole to preserve GFR when perfusion is low, so ACE inhibitors can cause a sharp fall in GFR in bilateral renal artery stenosis.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: renal autoregulation
stem: Renal perfusion pressure rises over a moderate physiological range, yet renal blood flow remains relatively stable. Which mechanism contributes directly to this autoregulation?

options.B: Complete paralysis of vascular smooth muscle

why_correct: Renal arterioles respond intrinsically to changes in transmural pressure. Increased pressure stretches the afferent arteriole and promotes smooth-muscle contraction, helping limit excessive increases in renal blood flow and glomerular pressure.

why_others_wrong.B: Paralysis of vascular smooth muscle would abolish, not enable, the myogenic constrictive response that stabilises renal blood flow.
why_others_wrong.C: Increased systemic venous pressure is not the mechanism of intrinsic renal autoregulation, which depends on afferent arteriolar tone responding to perfusion pressure changes.
why_others_wrong.D: Increased lymphatic drainage is unrelated to renal vascular autoregulation.
why_others_wrong.E: A rise in perfusion pressure tends to increase GFR, which autoregulation then limits; a fall in GFR is not the mechanism.

exam_trap: The myogenic mechanism is intrinsic; tubuloglomerular feedback is another major component of renal autoregulation.
takeaway: Renal pressure rise → afferent myogenic constriction.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Perfusion pressure rises but renal blood flow stays stable ↓ an intrinsic renal mechanism ↓ stretch of the afferent arteriolar wall triggers smooth-muscle contraction ↓ Afferent arteriolar myogenic response
pearl: Autoregulation fails when mean arterial pressure falls below its lower limit, so in shock renal blood flow becomes pressure-dependent and sustained hypotension leads to acute kidney injury.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: tubuloglomerular feedback
stem: A rise in sodium chloride delivery to the macula densa causes a local response that reduces glomerular filtration in the associated nephron. Which change contributes to this response?
why_correct: High NaCl delivery to the macula densa promotes tubuloglomerular feedback that constricts the associated afferent arteriole and reduces renin release. This helps stabilise distal tubular delivery and GFR.

why_others_wrong.B: High macula densa NaCl delivery triggers afferent constriction, not maximal dilation.
why_others_wrong.C: High distal NaCl delivery suppresses, rather than increases, renin release from the juxtaglomerular apparatus.
why_others_wrong.D: Increased proximal glucose reabsorption is not part of the tubuloglomerular feedback mechanism, which concerns afferent arteriolar tone and renin release.
why_others_wrong.E: Erythropoietin release is triggered by hypoxia, not by macula densa NaCl sensing.

exam_trap: Increased renin release (C) tempts because the macula densa controls renin, but high NaCl delivery suppresses renin; low distal NaCl is the stimulus for renin release.
takeaway: High macula densa NaCl → afferent constriction + ↓ renin.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Increased NaCl delivery to the macula densa ↓ local signal to the afferent arteriole of the same nephron ↓ afferent constriction lowers glomerular pressure and GFR ↓ renin release is suppressed ↓ Afferent arteriolar constriction
pearl: SGLT2 inhibitors increase distal NaCl delivery and activate tubuloglomerular feedback, causing afferent constriction that lowers intraglomerular pressure; this is thought to contribute to their renoprotective effect.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: anion gap and albumin
stem: A patient with severe hypoalbuminaemia has a measured serum anion gap of 12 mmol/L. How should this result be interpreted?

options.A: Hypoalbuminaemia tends to lower the expected anion gap
options.B: Hypoalbuminaemia always causes a high anion gap
options.C: Albumin does not contribute to the anion gap
options.D: The anion gap is determined only by chloride
options.E: The result proves there is no metabolic acidosis

correct_answer: A. Hypoalbuminaemia tends to lower the expected anion gap
why_correct: Albumin is a major unmeasured plasma anion. When albumin concentration falls, the normal baseline anion gap also falls. Therefore, a seemingly normal measured anion gap can conceal an increased-anion-gap metabolic acidosis in a patient with marked hypoalbuminaemia.

why_others_wrong.B: Hypoalbuminaemia does not always cause a high anion gap; it actually lowers the expected baseline anion gap because albumin is itself a major unmeasured anion.
why_others_wrong.C: Albumin is in fact a major contributor to the normal anion gap, not an irrelevant one.
why_others_wrong.D: The anion gap reflects unmeasured anions overall, including albumin, not chloride alone.
why_others_wrong.E: A seemingly normal measured gap can conceal an underlying high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis when albumin is low, so it does not prove the absence of acidosis.

exam_trap: Option E tempts candidates who accept a normal-looking gap at face value, but low albumin lowers the expected gap and can conceal a high anion gap acidosis.
takeaway: Low albumin → lower expected AG → possible hidden high-AG acidosis.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed. Kraut JA, Madias NE. Serum anion gap: its uses and limitations in clinical medicine. Clinical Journal of the American Society of Nephrology, 2007.
thinking: Severe hypoalbuminaemia ↓ albumin is a major unmeasured anion ↓ the baseline anion gap falls as albumin falls ↓ an apparently normal gap may hide added unmeasured anions ↓ Hypoalbuminaemia tends to lower the expected anion gap
pearl: In critically ill surgical patients the anion gap should be corrected for albumin; otherwise a lactic acidosis from sepsis or ischaemia can be missed behind an apparently normal gap.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Cardiorespiratory physiology: compensation for metabolic alkalosis
stem: A patient develops a primary metabolic alkalosis. Which respiratory response would be expected initially?

options.D: Increased respiratory rate with reduced PaCO2

why_correct: Metabolic alkalosis causes compensatory hypoventilation, which raises arterial carbon dioxide and partially offsets the rise in pH. The compensation is limited because excessive hypoventilation would cause hypoxaemia.

why_others_wrong.A: Increased alveolar ventilation would lower PaCO2 further and worsen the alkalosis; the appropriate compensation is hypoventilation, which raises PaCO2.
why_others_wrong.C: Complete cessation of ventilation is neither physiological nor compatible with survival; compensation is a graded reduction, not total apnoea.
why_others_wrong.D: An increased respiratory rate with a reduced PaCO2 would compound the alkalosis rather than compensate for it, the opposite of what occurs.
why_others_wrong.E: A respiratory response is possible and expected; hypoventilation is the body's mechanism for partially correcting metabolic alkalosis.

exam_trap: Candidates expect hyperventilation as the usual respiratory response, but in metabolic alkalosis the compensation is hypoventilation to retain CO2, limited by the need to stay oxygenated.
takeaway: Metabolic alkalosis → hypoventilation → ↑ PaCO2.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Primary metabolic alkalosis raises pH ↓ chemoreceptor drive falls ↓ alveolar ventilation decreases ↓ PaCO2 rises, partly offsetting the pH, limited by hypoxaemia ↓ Reduced alveolar ventilation
pearl: Surgical causes of metabolic alkalosis include vomiting from gastric outlet obstruction and high nasogastric losses, producing a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic alkalosis treated with 0.9% saline and potassium.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Cardiorespiratory physiology: respiratory alkalosis
stem: A patient is hyperventilating because of acute anxiety. Which primary acid-base abnormality is most likely?

options.E: Mixed respiratory and metabolic alkalosis necessarily

why_correct: Hyperventilation increases alveolar ventilation and lowers arterial PaCO2. The resulting reduction in carbonic acid raises blood pH, producing respiratory alkalosis.

why_others_wrong.A: Respiratory acidosis results from hypoventilation and CO2 retention, which is the opposite of the hyperventilation-driven CO2 washout described here.
why_others_wrong.C: Metabolic acidosis arises from a primary fall in bicarbonate or acid accumulation, not from a ventilatory change; hyperventilation here is the primary event, not a compensation.
why_others_wrong.D: Metabolic alkalosis arises from a primary rise in bicarbonate or loss of acid, not from hyperventilation-driven CO2 loss.
why_others_wrong.E: A mixed disorder is not necessarily present; isolated anxiety-driven hyperventilation produces a straightforward primary respiratory alkalosis.

exam_trap: Candidates choose metabolic acidosis because tachypnoea often signals acidosis, but here hyperventilation is the primary event, lowering PaCO2 and causing alkalosis.
takeaway: Hyperventilation → ↓ PaCO2 → respiratory alkalosis.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Anxiety-driven hyperventilation ↓ alveolar ventilation exceeds CO2 production ↓ PaCO2 falls ↓ pH rises ↓ Respiratory alkalosis
pearl: Before attributing hyperventilation to anxiety, exclude organic causes such as pulmonary embolism, sepsis, metabolic acidosis and salicylate toxicity, which can also present with tachypnoea and a low PaCO2.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: henderson-hasselbalch relationship
stem: The bicarbonate buffer system is described by the relationship between bicarbonate concentration and dissolved carbon dioxide. Which change would increase blood pH, assuming the other component remains unchanged?
why_correct: Blood pH is influenced by the ratio of bicarbonate to dissolved carbon dioxide. An increase in bicarbonate, with CO2 unchanged, increases this ratio and therefore raises pH.

why_others_wrong.A: Raising CO2 with bicarbonate unchanged lowers the bicarbonate-to-CO2 ratio, which lowers pH rather than raising it.
why_others_wrong.B: Decreasing bicarbonate lowers the bicarbonate-to-CO2 ratio, which lowers pH, the opposite of what is asked.
why_others_wrong.D: An increase in hydrogen ion concentration corresponds by definition to a fall, not a rise, in pH.
why_others_wrong.E: A reduced bicarbonate-to-CO2 ratio directly corresponds to a fall in pH, not a rise.

exam_trap: Increased dissolved CO2 (A) tempts those who link CO2 with bicarbonate formation, but raising CO2 lowers the bicarbonate to CO2 ratio and therefore lowers pH.
takeaway: ↑ HCO3− relative to CO2 → ↑ pH.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: pH depends on the bicarbonate to CO2 ratio ↓ CO2 held constant ↓ raising bicarbonate increases the ratio ↓ pH rises ↓ Increased bicarbonate
pearl: Prolonged vomiting or nasogastric drainage, for example from gastric outlet obstruction, raises bicarbonate and produces a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Cardiorespiratory physiology: mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation
stem: A toxin prevents electrons from passing normally through the mitochondrial respiratory chain. Which cellular process is most directly impaired?
why_correct: The mitochondrial electron transport chain establishes a proton gradient used by ATP synthase to generate ATP through oxidative phosphorylation. Blocking electron transport therefore markedly impairs aerobic ATP production.

why_others_wrong.A: Glycolysis occurs in the cytosol and does not require the mitochondrial electron transport chain, so it can continue despite the block.
why_others_wrong.C: Nuclear transcription is an independent process from mitochondrial electron transport and is not directly impaired by this toxin.
why_others_wrong.D: Golgi-mediated protein secretion depends on vesicular trafficking, not directly on the mitochondrial electron transport chain.
why_others_wrong.E: Lysosomal digestion relies on acid hydrolases within lysosomes and is not the process most directly disrupted by blocking electron transport.

exam_trap: Candidates choose glycolysis because it feeds the pathway, but glycolysis is cytosolic and continues, increasingly anaerobically, when the electron transport chain is blocked.
takeaway: Electron transport block → ↓ proton gradient → ↓ oxidative phosphorylation.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed. Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Toxin blocks electron flow along the respiratory chain ↓ no proton gradient forms across the inner mitochondrial membrane ↓ ATP synthase cannot generate ATP ↓ Oxidative phosphorylation
pearl: Cyanide, which can be released in smoke inhalation, inhibits cytochrome c oxidase, causing lactic acidosis with a high venous oxygen saturation because cells cannot use the oxygen delivered.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing: cytochrome c and apoptosis
stem: Mitochondrial membrane injury results in release of cytochrome c into the cytosol. Which process is most directly initiated?
why_correct: Release of cytochrome c from mitochondria is a key event in the intrinsic apoptotic pathway. Cytochrome c contributes to formation of the apoptosome and activation of downstream caspases.

why_others_wrong.B: Complement activation is part of the innate humoral immune response to pathogens or antibody complexes, unrelated to mitochondrial cytochrome c release.
why_others_wrong.C: Coagulation is the clotting cascade responsible for haemostasis, an entirely different process from mitochondrial-triggered apoptosis.
why_others_wrong.D: Necrotic calcification refers to calcium deposition in dead tissue following necrosis, not the regulated apoptotic pathway initiated by cytochrome c release.
why_others_wrong.E: Fibrosis is a chronic tissue response involving collagen deposition, not an immediate consequence of mitochondrial cytochrome c release into the cytosol.

exam_trap: Candidates choose necrotic calcification (D) or fibrosis (E), linking mitochondrial damage with necrosis and scarring, but cytochrome c released into the cytosol forms the apoptosome and initiates intrinsic apoptosis.
takeaway: Mitochondrial cytochrome c release → intrinsic apoptosis.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Mitochondrial membrane injury ↓ cytochrome c released into the cytosol ↓ apoptosome forms and activates caspase-9 ↓ executioner caspases follow ↓ Intrinsic apoptosis
pearl: BCL-2 family proteins control mitochondrial outer-membrane permeability; overexpression of anti-apoptotic BCL-2 in follicular lymphoma allows damaged cells to survive.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing: free radical defence
stem: A reactive oxygen species is converted into hydrogen peroxide by an intracellular antioxidant enzyme. Which enzyme performs this reaction?
why_correct: Superoxide dismutase converts superoxide radicals into hydrogen peroxide and oxygen. Hydrogen peroxide can subsequently be detoxified by enzymes including catalase and glutathione peroxidase.

why_others_wrong.B: Catalase acts downstream of superoxide dismutase, converting hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen, rather than converting superoxide into hydrogen peroxide itself.
why_others_wrong.C: Thrombin is a coagulation cascade enzyme that converts fibrinogen to fibrin and has no role in antioxidant defence.
why_others_wrong.D: Plasmin is a fibrinolytic enzyme that degrades fibrin clots, unrelated to reactive oxygen species detoxification.
why_others_wrong.E: Myeloperoxidase is a neutrophil granule enzyme that generates hypochlorous acid from hydrogen peroxide for microbial killing, not the enzyme that converts superoxide to hydrogen peroxide.

exam_trap: Candidates choose catalase (B) because it is the best-known antioxidant enzyme, but catalase removes hydrogen peroxide; superoxide dismutase is the enzyme that produces it from superoxide.
takeaway: Superoxide → SOD → H2O2.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Reactive oxygen species converted to hydrogen peroxide ↓ the substrate must be superoxide ↓ catalase acts on hydrogen peroxide, the next step ↓ Superoxide dismutase
pearl: Mutations in copper-zinc superoxide dismutase (SOD1) are a recognised cause of familial motor neurone disease, showing the importance of superoxide clearance in long-lived cells.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing: lipid peroxidation
stem: Reactive oxygen species attack membrane polyunsaturated fatty acids. What is the principal type of cellular damage produced?
why_correct: Reactive oxygen species can attack membrane lipids, initiating lipid peroxidation. This damages membrane integrity and can contribute to cellular injury.

why_others_wrong.B: DNA replication is duplication of the genome during the cell cycle, an entirely different process from oxidative damage to membrane lipids.
why_others_wrong.C: Glycogen synthesis is an anabolic carbohydrate storage pathway, unrelated to reactive oxygen species attacking membrane fatty acids.
why_others_wrong.D: Collagen cross-linking is an enzymatic process stabilising extracellular matrix structure, not a consequence of reactive oxygen species attacking membrane lipids.
why_others_wrong.E: Protein glycosylation is the enzymatic or non-enzymatic addition of sugars to proteins, a distinct process from oxidative attack on membrane polyunsaturated fatty acids.

exam_trap: ROS can damage lipids, proteins and DNA; membrane lipid attack is specifically lipid peroxidation.
takeaway: ROS + membrane lipids → lipid peroxidation.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Reactive oxygen species attack membrane lipids ↓ polyunsaturated fatty acids have easily oxidised double bonds ↓ a self-propagating chain reaction damages the membrane ↓ Lipid peroxidation
pearl: Vitamin E is the main lipid-soluble chain-breaking antioxidant in cell membranes, and malondialdehyde is a commonly measured marker of lipid peroxidation.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing: reperfusion injury
stem: A previously ischaemic tissue is reperfused. Paradoxically, additional cellular injury develops after blood flow is restored. Which mechanism contributes substantially to this injury?

options.E: Reduced mitochondrial activity without oxidative stress

why_correct: Reperfusion can generate reactive oxygen species through damaged mitochondria, inflammatory cells and other mechanisms. These reactive species can damage membranes, proteins and DNA.

why_others_wrong.A: Reperfusion by definition restores oxygen delivery to the tissue; it is the restoration of oxygen, together with generation of reactive oxygen species, that paradoxically drives further injury, not reduced oxygen availability.
why_others_wrong.C: Reperfusion injury is actually associated with increased, not inhibited, neutrophil recruitment into the tissue, contributing to further inflammatory damage.
why_others_wrong.D: Ischaemia-reperfusion injury is associated with disrupted, not preserved, ATP homeostasis, as mitochondrial damage impairs oxidative phosphorylation.
why_others_wrong.E: Reperfusion injury is driven by oxidative stress, with reactive oxygen species generated by damaged mitochondria, xanthine oxidase and recruited leukocytes, so absent oxidative stress is incorrect.

exam_trap: Candidates choose reduced oxygen availability (A) by thinking of ischaemia, but reperfusion restores oxygen; that returning oxygen fuels reactive oxygen species and further injury.
takeaway: Ischaemia → reperfusion → ROS + inflammation → additional injury.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Ischaemic tissue is reperfused ↓ injury paradoxically worsens once flow returns ↓ returning oxygen meets damaged mitochondria and recruited leukocytes ↓ burst of free radicals ↓ Reactive oxygen species generation
pearl: Reperfusion after prolonged limb ischaemia can cause compartment syndrome, hyperkalaemia, acidosis and myoglobinuric acute kidney injury, so fasciotomy and close metabolic monitoring are often needed after revascularisation.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing: cell injury and calcium
stem: A cell experiences severe irreversible injury. Which intracellular change contributes directly to activation of destructive enzymes and further cellular damage?
why_correct: Severe cell injury can disrupt calcium homeostasis and increase cytosolic calcium. Increased intracellular calcium activates enzymes including phospholipases, proteases, endonucleases and ATPases, contributing to membrane, protein and DNA damage.

why_others_wrong.A: Severe cell injury increases, rather than reduces, cytosolic calcium as membrane and ion pump function fail, allowing calcium influx into the cell.
why_others_wrong.C: Increased, not reduced, lysosomal enzyme activity contributes to cellular injury, as calcium-activated processes and membrane damage release destructive hydrolases.
why_others_wrong.D: Severe cell injury impairs mitochondrial function and typically depletes, rather than increases, ATP concentration.
why_others_wrong.E: Severe cell injury is associated with loss, not preservation, of membrane integrity, which is part of why calcium can flood into the cytosol.

exam_trap: Candidates choose reduced intracellular calcium (A), forgetting the steep extracellular gradient; failing pumps and damaged membranes let calcium flood in and activate destructive enzymes.
takeaway: Severe cell injury → increased intracellular Ca2+ → destructive enzyme activation.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Severe irreversible cell injury ↓ failing pumps and leaky membranes let calcium flood the cytosol ↓ calcium activates phospholipases, proteases and endonucleases ↓ Increased intracellular calcium
pearl: Calcium overload also opens the mitochondrial permeability transition pore, collapsing the membrane potential and ATP production; calcium entry is a key driver of myocyte death in ischaemia-reperfusion injury.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: GI physiology & metabolism: gastric emptying
stem: A patient eats a meal containing a high proportion of fat. Which gastrointestinal response helps regulate delivery of the meal from the stomach into the duodenum?

options.A: Increased gastric emptying caused by secretin
options.B: Delayed gastric emptying mediated partly by CCK
options.C: Complete inhibition of gastric acid secretion
options.D: Increased gastric emptying caused by bile salts

correct_answer: B. Delayed gastric emptying mediated partly by CCK
why_correct: Fat entering the duodenum stimulates release of cholecystokinin (CCK). CCK contributes to slowing gastric emptying, allowing more time for digestion and absorption of nutrients.

why_others_wrong.A: Secretin is released in response to duodenal acid rather than fat, and it tends to slow rather than accelerate gastric emptying.
why_others_wrong.C: Duodenal fat reduces gastric secretion and motility, but it does not abolish acid secretion completely; the key regulatory response here is slower emptying.
why_others_wrong.D: Bile salts emulsify and solubilise fat in the duodenum; they do not speed gastric emptying, which duodenal fat actually slows.
why_others_wrong.E: Immediate colonic propulsion describes the gastrocolic reflex and mass movements, which do not regulate delivery of chyme from the stomach to the duodenum.

exam_trap: Option A pairs secretin with faster emptying, but secretin responds to acid rather than fat and slows the stomach; duodenal fat delays emptying partly through CCK.
takeaway: Duodenal fat → CCK → slower gastric emptying.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: High-fat meal reaches the duodenum ↓ I cells release CCK and enterogastric reflexes are triggered ↓ gastric motility slows to match delivery to digestive capacity ↓ Delayed gastric emptying mediated partly by CCK
pearl: Gastric emptying is regulated so that nutrient delivery to the duodenum stays fairly steady; loss of this control after gastric surgery allows rapid delivery of hyperosmolar chyme and dumping syndrome.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: GI physiology & metabolism: secretin
stem: Acidic gastric contents enter the duodenum. Which hormone is released in response and promotes pancreatic bicarbonate secretion?
why_correct: Acid entering the duodenum stimulates S cells to release secretin. Secretin promotes pancreatic and biliary bicarbonate secretion, helping neutralise gastric acid.

why_others_wrong.A: Gastrin is released from antral G cells and stimulates gastric acid secretion; acid in the duodenum does not trigger it to drive bicarbonate secretion.
why_others_wrong.C: CCK is released from I cells mainly in response to fat and protein, and chiefly stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion rather than bicarbonate.
why_others_wrong.D: Motilin is associated with the fasting migrating motor complex and is not the hormone released by duodenal acid to stimulate bicarbonate.
why_others_wrong.E: Somatostatin from D cells is broadly inhibitory, suppressing gastrointestinal and pancreatic secretions rather than promoting bicarbonate release.

exam_trap: CCK (option C) is chosen because it also stimulates the pancreas, but CCK drives enzyme secretion in response to fat and protein; acid triggers secretin and bicarbonate secretion.
takeaway: Duodenal acid → secretin → pancreatic HCO3−.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Acidic gastric contents enter the duodenum ↓ low duodenal pH stimulates S cells ↓ secretin drives bicarbonate-rich secretion from pancreatic ducts ↓ Secretin
pearl: Secretin normally suppresses gastrin, but gastrinoma cells paradoxically release more gastrin after secretin injection, which is the basis of the secretin stimulation test.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: GI physiology & metabolism: cck
stem: A fatty meal enters the duodenum. Which combination best describes the major actions of CCK?

options.A: Gallbladder contraction and pancreatic enzyme secretion
options.B: Gastric acid secretion and colonic water absorption
options.C: Pancreatic bicarbonate secretion and gastric acid secretion
options.D: Increased gastric emptying and reduced pancreatic secretion
options.E: Reduced gallbladder contraction and increased gastric emptying

correct_answer: A. Gallbladder contraction and pancreatic enzyme secretion
why_correct: CCK is released from I cells in response particularly to fatty acids and amino acids. It stimulates gallbladder contraction and promotes pancreatic enzyme secretion. It also contributes to slowing gastric emptying.

why_others_wrong.B: Gastric acid secretion is driven mainly by gastrin, histamine and vagal activity, and colonic water absorption is not a recognised CCK action.
why_others_wrong.C: Pancreatic bicarbonate secretion is primarily a secretin effect, and CCK does not act as a major stimulus for gastric acid secretion.
why_others_wrong.D: CCK slows gastric emptying and stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion, so this pairing reverses both of its actions.
why_others_wrong.E: CCK contracts the gallbladder and slows gastric emptying, which is the opposite of both effects described here.

exam_trap: Option C tempts candidates who merge CCK with secretin; pancreatic bicarbonate secretion is secretin’s main action, whereas CCK drives enzymes and gallbladder contraction.
takeaway: Fat/protein → CCK → pancreatic enzymes + gallbladder contraction.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Fatty meal enters the duodenum ↓ I cells release CCK ↓ CCK contracts the gallbladder, relaxes the biliary sphincter and stimulates acinar enzyme release ↓ Gallbladder contraction and pancreatic enzyme secretion
pearl: A CCK analogue is used during hepatobiliary scintigraphy to measure gallbladder ejection fraction when functional gallbladder disease is suspected.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: GI physiology & metabolism: motilin
stem: A fasting patient develops periodic waves of gastrointestinal smooth-muscle activity that clear residual material from the stomach and small intestine. Which hormone is particularly associated with this migrating motor complex?
why_correct: Motilin is associated with the migrating motor complex, a cyclic fasting pattern of gastrointestinal motility that helps clear residual material.

why_others_wrong.A: Gastrin is released after meals from antral G cells and stimulates acid secretion; it is a fed-state hormone rather than the driver of the fasting motor complex.
why_others_wrong.B: Secretin is released when acid enters the duodenum and stimulates pancreatic bicarbonate; it is not associated with fasting clearance waves.
why_others_wrong.D: CCK is released in response to fat and protein after feeding and tends to disrupt, rather than drive, the fasting migrating motor complex.
why_others_wrong.E: Somatostatin is a broadly inhibitory hormone and is not the hormone characteristically linked to initiating the migrating motor complex.

exam_trap: Gastrin and CCK are chosen because they influence motility, but both are fed-state hormones that interrupt the fasting pattern; motilin is linked to the migrating motor complex.
takeaway: Fasting clean-up waves = migrating motor complex → motilin.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Fasting state with periodic waves clearing the stomach and small intestine ↓ this is the migrating motor complex ↓ its intense phase is associated with cyclical motilin release ↓ Motilin
pearl: Erythromycin is a motilin receptor agonist, so low-dose erythromycin is used as a prokinetic in gastroparesis and to clear blood from the stomach before endoscopy for upper GI bleeding.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: GI physiology & metabolism: pancreatic enzyme activation
stem: A pancreatic acinar cell releases trypsinogen into the duodenum. Which enzyme initiates activation of pancreatic protease zymogens?
why_correct: Enteropeptidase, located at the intestinal brush border, converts trypsinogen to trypsin. Trypsin then activates other pancreatic protease zymogens.

why_others_wrong.A: Pepsin is a gastric protease formed from pepsinogen in acid; it does not activate pancreatic zymogens in the duodenum.
why_others_wrong.C: Amylase is a pancreatic enzyme that digests starch and has no role in cleaving trypsinogen to trypsin.
why_others_wrong.D: Lipase hydrolyses dietary triglycerides and does not activate pancreatic protease zymogens.
why_others_wrong.E: Gastrin is a hormone that stimulates gastric acid secretion, not an enzyme that activates trypsinogen.

exam_trap: Pepsin (option A) is chosen as the familiar protease activator, but it works in gastric acid; in the duodenum enteropeptidase starts the cascade and trypsin continues it.
takeaway: Enteropeptidase → trypsin → other pancreatic zymogens.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Trypsinogen is released into the duodenum as an inactive zymogen ↓ a brush-border enzyme cleaves it to trypsin ↓ trypsin then activates the remaining protease zymogens ↓ Enteropeptidase
pearl: Premature activation of trypsinogen within the pancreas is regarded as a key initiating event in acute pancreatitis, leading to autodigestion and a systemic inflammatory cascade.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: Hepatobiliary surgery: bile salts
stem: A patient has markedly reduced delivery of bile salts into the small intestine. Which process is most directly impaired?
why_correct: Bile salts facilitate digestion and absorption of dietary lipids by forming micelles. Reduced bile delivery therefore impairs efficient intestinal absorption of lipids and fat-soluble vitamins.

why_others_wrong.A: Protein denaturation in the stomach depends on gastric acid, which occurs before bile enters the gut and is not bile-dependent.
why_others_wrong.C: Peptides are absorbed mainly in the small intestine rather than the colon, and bile salts are not required for protein absorption.
why_others_wrong.D: Gastric acid secretion is controlled by gastrin, histamine and vagal input, not by bile-salt delivery to the small intestine.
why_others_wrong.E: Intrinsic factor is secreted by gastric parietal cells and is unaffected by reduced bile-salt delivery to the small intestine.

exam_trap: Option E tempts because bile-salt loss and B12 problems both follow ileal disease, but intrinsic factor is gastric; reduced bile delivery impairs micelle formation and fat absorption.
takeaway: Bile salts → micelles → fat absorption.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Markedly reduced bile-salt delivery to the small intestine ↓ bile salts are amphipathic detergents ↓ they form micelles that carry fatty acids, monoglycerides and fat-soluble vitamins to the enterocyte ↓ Formation of micelles
pearl: Biliary obstruction causes pale stools, steatorrhoea and fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption; vitamin K deficiency prolongs the prothrombin time, which intravenous vitamin K corrects before intervention.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: GI physiology & metabolism: b12 absorption
