why_others_wrong.E: Treatment response is assessed after therapy by regression grading or imaging, not by describing differentiation and mitoses in the tumour.

exam_trap: Stage is the commonest wrong choice, but differentiation, atypia and mitoses are histological features; stage needs information about tumour extent, nodes and metastases.
takeaway: Grade = differentiation/aggressive histology. Stage = anatomical extent.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.; Principles and Practice of Surgery, 7th ed.
thinking: Poorly differentiated, marked atypia, numerous mitoses ↓ all are microscopic features of the tumour cells ↓ these define tumour grade ↓ Grade
pearl: Mitotic count is part of formal grading in tumours such as breast carcinoma and soft tissue sarcoma, while the Ki-67 index gives an immunohistochemical estimate of proliferation.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Tumour staging
stem: A patient has a malignant tumour confined to the primary organ with no regional lymph-node or distant metastases. Which aspect of the disease is being described when assessing TNM stage?
why_correct: Cancer staging assesses the anatomical extent of disease, including primary tumour characteristics, regional nodal involvement and distant metastases.

why_others_wrong.A: Cellular differentiation is assessed in histological grading and is not what TNM stage describes.
why_others_wrong.C: Histological subtype classifies the tumour type but does not describe how far the disease has spread.
why_others_wrong.D: Mitotic index is a measure of proliferation used in grading some tumours, not a TNM staging element.
why_others_wrong.E: The molecular driver may guide targeted therapy but does not describe the anatomical extent captured by TNM.

exam_trap: Cellular differentiation is tempting because it appears in every pathology report, but it is a grading feature; TNM stage describes only the anatomical extent of disease.
takeaway: Stage = extent. Grade = histological aggressiveness/differentiation.
source: Principles and Practice of Surgery, 7th ed.; Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Tumour confined to the organ with no nodal or distant spread ↓ a description of where the disease is ↓ TNM records anatomical extent ↓ Anatomical extent
pearl: Staging combines cross-sectional imaging before treatment with pathological staging of the resected specimen; the two can differ, and pathological stage guides adjuvant therapy.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Tumour spread
stem: A malignant epithelial tumour spreads to regional lymph nodes before later producing distant deposits. Which route is most characteristic of carcinoma?
why_correct: Carcinomas commonly spread through lymphatic channels to regional lymph nodes, although haematogenous and other routes can also occur.

why_others_wrong.B: Transplacental spread is a rare curiosity, such as melanoma reaching the fetus, and is not the characteristic route of carcinoma.
why_others_wrong.C: CSF spread occurs mainly with central nervous system tumours or leptomeningeal disease and certainly not in all carcinomas.
why_others_wrong.D: Perineural spread occurs in some carcinomas such as pancreatic and head and neck cancers, but it is not the characteristic route to regional nodes.
why_others_wrong.E: Carcinomas can spread haematogenously, but not exclusively; spread to regional nodes first is characteristic of lymphatic dissemination.

exam_trap: Haematogenous spread exclusively catches candidates out; carcinomas can spread via blood, but sequential involvement of regional nodes first is the hallmark of lymphatic dissemination.
takeaway: Epithelial malignancy → think lymphatics.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Malignant epithelial tumour ↓ regional nodes involved before distant deposits ↓ stepwise spread along draining lymphatics ↓ Lymphatic spread
pearl: Sarcomas, by contrast, typically spread haematogenously, most often to the lungs, so chest CT is part of sarcoma staging and regional nodes are seldom involved.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Cancer cachexia
stem: A patient with advanced cancer develops weight loss, skeletal-muscle wasting and reduced appetite despite an adequate opportunity to eat. Which process contributes importantly to cancer cachexia?
correct_answer: B. Systemic inflammatory and metabolic changes
why_correct: Cancer cachexia is a multifactorial syndrome involving inflammatory mediators, altered metabolism, reduced appetite and increased catabolism, particularly of skeletal muscle.

why_others_wrong.A: Cachexia involves increased, not suppressed, inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-alpha and IL-6.
why_others_wrong.C: Muscle protein synthesis is reduced and breakdown increased in cachexia, not anabolism increased.
why_others_wrong.D: Dehydration alone causes fluid loss but does not explain progressive skeletal-muscle and fat wasting.
why_others_wrong.E: Cancer cachexia is associated with insulin resistance rather than increased insulin sensitivity.

exam_trap: Suppression of inflammatory signalling is the reversed-fact trap; cachexia is driven by increased cytokines such as TNF-alpha and IL-6, with insulin resistance and muscle catabolism.
takeaway: Cancer cachexia = inflammation + altered metabolism + catabolism.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.; Principles and Practice of Surgery, 7th ed.
thinking: Advanced cancer with weight loss and muscle wasting ↓ reduced appetite despite the opportunity to eat ↓ cytokines such as TNF-alpha and IL-6 drive catabolism and insulin resistance ↓ Systemic inflammatory and metabolic changes
pearl: Because cachexia is inflammation-driven, extra calories alone rarely reverse it; management is multimodal, combining nutritional support, exercise and treatment of the underlying cancer.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: Surgical stress and protein metabolism
stem: After major surgery, a patient develops increased urinary nitrogen losses. Which metabolic process most directly contributes?

options.E: Increased collagen storage throughout the body

why_correct: Major surgical stress promotes a catabolic response with increased proteolysis and mobilisation of amino acids. Nitrogen losses therefore increase, particularly after major physiological stress.

why_others_wrong.B: The stress response increases rather than inhibits proteolysis, and blocking protein breakdown would reduce nitrogen losses.
why_others_wrong.C: Nitrogen retention is a feature of the later anabolic phase; increased urinary nitrogen reflects net nitrogen loss.
why_others_wrong.D: Surgical stress increases amino-acid mobilisation from muscle for gluconeogenesis and acute-phase protein synthesis.
why_others_wrong.E: Collagen is not stored throughout the body after surgery, and protein deposition would lower rather than raise nitrogen losses.

exam_trap: Option C is chosen because nitrogen handling is involved, but nitrogen retention is the later anabolic phase; rising urinary nitrogen reflects net loss from muscle protein breakdown.
takeaway: Surgery → proteolysis → nitrogen loss.
source: Principles and Practice of Surgery, 7th ed.; Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Increased urinary nitrogen after major surgery ↓ surgical stress raises cortisol, catecholamines and cytokines ↓ skeletal-muscle protein is broken down and amino acids are deaminated for gluconeogenesis and acute-phase proteins ↓ Increased skeletal-muscle protein breakdown
pearl: Postoperative catabolism cannot be fully reversed by feeding alone; enhanced recovery measures such as minimising fasting, early feeding, early mobilisation and good analgesia help limit muscle loss.

subject: Physiology
title: Fluid compartments
stem: A patient receives an isotonic crystalloid infusion. After equilibration, in which major compartment is most of the administered fluid distributed?
why_correct: Isotonic crystalloid distributes throughout the extracellular fluid compartment. Only a proportion remains intravascular; the remainder enters the interstitial space.

why_others_wrong.A: Isotonic crystalloid creates no osmotic gradient across cell membranes, so it does not preferentially shift into the intracellular compartment.
why_others_wrong.C: CSF is a specialised, tightly regulated compartment and is not where the bulk of administered isotonic fluid distributes.
why_others_wrong.D: Isotonic crystalloid does not remain confined to the intravascular space; a substantial proportion moves into the interstitium as part of the wider extracellular compartment.
why_others_wrong.E: Bone matrix is not a site of fluid distribution for intravenous crystalloid.

exam_trap: Intravascular compartment only (D) tempts those who view crystalloid as a pure volume expander, but after equilibration most of it lies in the interstitium.
takeaway: Isotonic crystalloid → ECF → plasma + interstitium.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.; Principles and Practice of Surgery, 7th ed.
thinking: Isotonic crystalloid infusion ↓ no osmotic gradient into cells ↓ water and sodium cross capillary walls ↓ it equilibrates through plasma and interstitium ↓ Extracellular fluid
pearl: Because most infused isotonic crystalloid moves into the interstitium, large-volume resuscitation causes tissue oedema, so fluid is best given as boluses with reassessment rather than fixed large volumes.

subject: Physiology
title: Fluid resuscitation physiology
stem: A patient with acute intravascular volume depletion receives an isotonic crystalloid bolus. Which immediate physiological effect is most directly intended?
why_correct: The immediate purpose of an isotonic crystalloid bolus in hypovolaemia is to expand the extracellular/intravascular compartment sufficiently to improve venous return, cardiac filling and tissue perfusion.

why_others_wrong.B: The goal of volume resuscitation is to increase, not reduce, venous return in a hypovolaemic patient.
why_others_wrong.C: Cardiac preload is intended to increase with volume expansion, not decrease, to improve stroke volume and perfusion.
why_others_wrong.D: Isotonic crystalloid remains largely extracellular and does not meaningfully raise intracellular sodium concentration.
why_others_wrong.E: Isotonic fluid does not cause intracellular dehydration; that effect is characteristic of hypertonic solutions, not isotonic crystalloid.

exam_trap: Reduce cardiac preload (C) tempts by confusion with treating fluid overload, but the aim of a bolus in hypovolaemia is to increase preload, venous return and perfusion.
takeaway: Volume loss → restore circulating volume → improve perfusion.
source: Principles and Practice of Surgery, 7th ed.; Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Acute intravascular volume depletion ↓ isotonic bolus expands extracellular and intravascular volume ↓ venous return and preload rise ↓ stroke volume and perfusion improve ↓ Increase effective circulating volume
pearl: NICE recommends a 500 mL crystalloid bolus over less than 15 minutes for adults needing fluid resuscitation, with clinical reassessment after each bolus.

subject: Microbiology & surgical infection
title: Surgical-site infection prevention
stem: According to NICE guidance, hair should be removed before surgery only when necessary. If hair removal is required, which method is recommended?

options.A: Razor shaving several days before surgery
options.C: Electric clippers on the day of surgery
options.E: Waxing on the day before surgery

correct_answer: C. Electric clippers on the day of surgery
why_correct: NICE recommends that hair should not be removed routinely to reduce surgical-site infection. If hair removal is necessary, electric clippers with a single-use head should be used on the day of surgery. Razors should be avoided because they can increase SSI risk.

why_others_wrong.A: Razors cause microabrasions that become colonised, and shaving days in advance allows more time for bacterial growth, increasing infection risk.
why_others_wrong.B: NICE advises against razors because they cause skin microtrauma that increases surgical site infection risk, even when used just before surgery.
why_others_wrong.D: Chemical depilation in every patient contradicts the principle of no routine hair removal and risks skin reactions; clippers are the recommended method.
why_others_wrong.E: Waxing traumatises hair follicles and skin and is not a recommended method of preoperative hair removal.

exam_trap: Razor shaving immediately before surgery tempts because timing seems to limit bacterial regrowth, but razors cause microabrasions that increase SSI risk even when used just before incision.
takeaway: No routine hair removal; if necessary → electric clippers → day of surgery.
source: NICE NG125, Surgical site infections: prevention and treatment, current guidance.
thinking: NICE: do not remove hair routinely before surgery ↓ if removal is needed, avoid razors that cause skin microabrasions ↓ use electric clippers with a single-use head on the day of surgery ↓ Electric clippers on the day of surgery
pearl: NICE also recommends a preoperative shower with soap and skin preparation with an antiseptic, preferably alcohol-based chlorhexidine, immediately before incision.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Pulmonary circulation
stem: Which feature distinguishes the pulmonary circulation from the systemic circulation?

options.A: It receives the entire cardiac output
options.B: Pulmonary arterial blood is normally relatively deoxygenated
options.D: Pulmonary arteries have higher pressure than systemic arteries
options.E: Pulmonary capillaries have no endothelial barrier

correct_answer: B. Pulmonary arterial blood is normally relatively deoxygenated
why_correct: The pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. Pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood to the left atrium. The pulmonary circulation is also a relatively low-pressure, low-resistance circulation.

why_others_wrong.A: Both the pulmonary and systemic circulations receive the entire cardiac output in series over each cycle, so this does not distinguish the pulmonary circulation from the systemic one.
why_others_wrong.C: Pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood back to the left atrium, not deoxygenated blood.
why_others_wrong.D: Pulmonary arterial pressure is normally much lower than systemic arterial pressure, not higher.
why_others_wrong.E: Pulmonary capillaries have an intact endothelial barrier essential for gas exchange and fluid regulation; they are not without one.

exam_trap: Candidates may choose 'receives the entire cardiac output', but both circulations are in series and receive the whole output; the deoxygenated arterial blood is what distinguishes the pulmonary circulation.
takeaway: Pulmonary artery = away from heart but deoxygenated.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Vessels are named by direction of flow, not oxygen content ↓ pulmonary arteries carry blood away from the right ventricle ↓ that blood is systemic venous return, so relatively deoxygenated ↓ systemic arteries carry oxygenated blood ↓ Pulmonary arterial blood is normally relatively deoxygenated
pearl: A pulmonary artery catheter samples true mixed venous blood from this circulation, which is why mixed venous oxygen saturation is measured there rather than from a peripheral vein.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Pulmonary vascular resistance
stem: Which physiological change normally causes pulmonary vascular resistance to fall during exercise?

options.A: Recruitment and distension of pulmonary vessels
options.E: Increased pulmonary alveolar pressure in every region

correct_answer: A. Recruitment and distension of pulmonary vessels
why_correct: During increased pulmonary blood flow, previously underperfused pulmonary vessels are recruited and existing vessels distend. This allows increased flow without a proportional rise in pulmonary vascular resistance.

why_others_wrong.B: Widespread vasoconstriction would raise, not lower, pulmonary vascular resistance during exercise.
why_others_wrong.C: Pulmonary arterial (mixed venous) blood does become more deoxygenated during exercise, but hypoxia does not lower pulmonary vascular resistance; alveolar hypoxia, if anything, causes vasoconstriction. The fall in resistance comes from recruitment and distension.
why_others_wrong.D: Capillary closure would reduce the cross-sectional area for flow and raise resistance, the opposite of what happens with recruitment during exercise.
why_others_wrong.E: A uniform rise in alveolar pressure would compress vessels and raise, not lower, pulmonary vascular resistance.

exam_trap: Candidates pick increased pulmonary arterial hypoxia (C), but hypoxia constricts rather than dilates pulmonary vessels; the fall in resistance comes from recruitment and distension.
takeaway: Exercise → pulmonary vascular recruitment + distension → lower effective resistance.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Exercise raises cardiac output and pulmonary blood flow ↓ the pulmonary bed is low-pressure and highly compliant ↓ closed capillaries open (recruitment) and open vessels widen (distension) ↓ total cross-sectional area rises, so resistance falls ↓ Recruitment and distension of pulmonary vessels
pearl: Recruitment and distension let pulmonary arterial pressure rise only modestly as cardiac output increases several-fold; a reduced vascular bed, as after pneumonectomy, loses this reserve and pressure rises more on exertion.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Alveolar gas exchange
stem: A patient develops thickening of the alveolar-capillary membrane due to interstitial lung disease. Which gas-exchange process is most directly impaired?
why_correct: Oxygen and carbon dioxide cross the alveolar-capillary membrane by diffusion. Increasing membrane thickness increases diffusion distance and impairs gas transfer.

why_others_wrong.A: Ventilation (airflow into the alveoli) is not directly impaired by membrane thickening; the diffusion barrier itself is what is affected.
why_others_wrong.C: Perfusion (blood flow through the capillaries) is not the process primarily impaired; it is gas transfer across the membrane that is affected.
why_others_wrong.D: Pulmonary blood flow generation is a cardiac and vascular function, unrelated to alveolar-capillary membrane thickness.
why_others_wrong.E: Haemoglobin synthesis occurs in the bone marrow and is unrelated to alveolar-capillary membrane thickness.

exam_trap: Candidates may choose ventilation or perfusion because both are part of gas exchange, but membrane thickening specifically impairs diffusion across the barrier.
takeaway: Thicker alveolar membrane → longer diffusion distance → impaired gas transfer.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Interstitial lung disease thickens the alveolar-capillary membrane ↓ gases cross this membrane by passive diffusion ↓ greater thickness lengthens the diffusion path ↓ Diffusion
pearl: Carbon dioxide diffuses far more readily than oxygen, so diffusion defects cause hypoxaemia long before hypercapnia, and PaCO2 is often low from compensatory hyperventilation.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Respiratory mechanics
stem: Which change would increase the work required to inflate a stiff lung?
why_correct: Compliance describes the change in lung volume produced by a given change in pressure. A stiff lung has reduced compliance and therefore requires greater pressure generation to achieve a given volume change.

why_others_wrong.A: Increased compliance would make the lung easier, not harder, to inflate, reducing rather than increasing work.
why_others_wrong.C: Reduced elastic recoil is characteristic of a floppy, high-compliance lung (as in emphysema), which is easier, not harder, to inflate.
why_others_wrong.D: Increased surfactant activity reduces surface tension and increases compliance, easing inflation rather than stiffening the lung.
why_others_wrong.E: Reduced surface tension increases compliance and eases inflation, the opposite of what occurs in a stiff lung.

exam_trap: Candidates may choose reduced elastic recoil, but low recoil describes a floppy, high-compliance lung such as in emphysema, which is easier to inflate.
takeaway: Low compliance = more pressure needed for inflation.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Compliance = change in volume ÷ change in pressure ↓ a stiff lung has low compliance ↓ more pressure, and so more work, is needed per unit volume ↓ Reduced compliance
pearl: In ventilated patients with stiff lungs, such as in ARDS, low tidal volumes are used to limit the high airway pressures that cause ventilator-induced lung injury.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Work of breathing
stem: A patient with severe airway narrowing requires substantially greater respiratory effort. Which component of breathing work is primarily increased?
why_correct: Airway obstruction increases resistance to airflow and therefore increases the resistive component of the work of breathing. Elastic work is particularly increased when the respiratory system is stiff, such as in pulmonary fibrosis.

why_others_wrong.A: Airway narrowing chiefly raises resistive work; elastic work rises mainly with stiff lungs or chest wall, so elastic work alone is not the answer.
why_others_wrong.C: Osmotic work is not a recognised component of the mechanical work of breathing.
why_others_wrong.D: Renal work is unrelated to the mechanics of ventilation.
why_others_wrong.E: Metabolic work of erythropoiesis relates to red cell production in bone marrow, not to the mechanical effort of breathing.

exam_trap: Candidates may choose elastic work only, but elastic work rises mainly with stiff lungs or chest wall; airway narrowing chiefly increases resistive work.
takeaway: Obstruction = resistance. Fibrosis = elastic load.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Severe airway narrowing ↓ resistance rises steeply as airway radius falls ↓ more pressure is needed to drive airflow ↓ Resistive work
pearl: Patients with obstructive disease tend to breathe slowly and deeply to minimise resistive work, whereas those with stiff lungs breathe rapidly and shallowly to minimise elastic work.

subject: Anatomy
title: Gastrointestinal motility
stem: Which enteric nerve plexus is located between the circular and longitudinal layers of the muscularis externa?
why_correct: The myenteric, or Auerbach, plexus lies between the circular and longitudinal layers of the muscularis externa and is particularly important in regulating gastrointestinal motility.

why_others_wrong.A: The submucosal (Meissner) plexus lies in the submucosa and mainly regulates secretion and local blood flow.
why_others_wrong.C: The coeliac plexus is a prevertebral autonomic plexus around the coeliac trunk, not an intramural enteric plexus.
why_others_wrong.D: The inferior hypogastric plexus is a pelvic autonomic plexus beside the rectum, not within the gut wall.
why_others_wrong.E: The superior cervical ganglion is a sympathetic ganglion in the neck supplying the head, not an enteric plexus.

exam_trap: The submucosal plexus is the other enteric plexus, but it lies in the submucosa and mainly controls secretion and blood flow rather than motility.
takeaway: Auerbach → muscularis → motility.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.; Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed.
thinking: Enteric plexus between circular and longitudinal muscle layers ↓ intramural plexus within the muscularis externa ↓ controls peristalsis and gut motility ↓ Myenteric plexus
pearl: Absence of ganglion cells in both enteric plexuses of the distal bowel causes congenital aganglionosis, which presents with delayed passage of meconium and is diagnosed by rectal suction biopsy.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: Migrating motor complex
stem: Which gastrointestinal motor pattern is particularly associated with the fasting state?
why_correct: The migrating motor complex occurs during fasting and produces cycles of gastrointestinal motor activity that help move residual material through the upper gastrointestinal tract.

why_others_wrong.B: The defaecation reflex is triggered by rectal distension and relates to faecal evacuation, not to fasting motility of the upper gut.
why_others_wrong.C: The gastrocolic reflex is triggered by food entering the stomach, so it is a postprandial rather than a fasting pattern.
why_others_wrong.D: The swallowing reflex moves a bolus from the pharynx into the oesophagus and is not a fasting motor pattern of the stomach and intestine.
why_others_wrong.E: The accommodation reflex allows the proximal stomach to relax as a meal arrives and is therefore a feeding response.

exam_trap: The accommodation reflex (option E) is chosen because it involves the stomach, but it is triggered by a meal arriving; the fasting pattern is the migrating motor complex.
takeaway: Fasting gut → migrating motor complex.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Question asks for the fasting motor pattern ↓ gastrocolic and accommodation reflexes are meal-triggered ↓ the cyclical interdigestive pattern of stomach and small bowel is the migrating motor complex ↓ Migrating motor complex
pearl: Opioids disrupt the migrating motor complex and propulsive gut motility, contributing to postoperative ileus and constipation.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: Gastric accommodation
stem: A meal enters the stomach and the proximal stomach relaxes so that a substantial volume is stored without a large rise in intragastric pressure. What physiological process is this?
why_correct: Gastric accommodation allows the proximal stomach to relax as food enters, permitting storage of a substantial volume with relatively little increase in intragastric pressure.

why_others_wrong.B: Gastric emptying is the controlled delivery of chyme into the duodenum, not the storage of a meal without a pressure rise.
why_others_wrong.C: Colonic segmentation mixes contents in the large bowel and has no role in gastric storage.
why_others_wrong.D: The migrating motor complex is a fasting housekeeping pattern and is interrupted, not initiated, by eating.
why_others_wrong.E: Intestinal peristaltic inhibition refers to the small bowel, whereas the stem describes relaxation of the proximal stomach.

exam_trap: Candidates choose the migrating motor complex (D), but that is a fasting pattern interrupted by eating; storage without a pressure rise is accommodation.
takeaway: Proximal stomach relaxes during a meal → accommodation.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Meal enters the stomach ↓ the proximal stomach (fundus and upper body) relaxes ↓ vagally mediated receptive relaxation ↓ volume is stored without a large pressure rise ↓ Gastric accommodation
pearl: Accommodation is a vagally mediated reflex, so truncal vagotomy impairs it, causing early satiety and rapid emptying of liquids.

subject: Pharmacology
title: Drug transport
stem: A drug is actively transported from the renal tubular cell into the tubular lumen. Which renal process is occurring?
why_correct: Tubular secretion moves substances from the peritubular blood into the tubular lumen, often through active transport systems in the proximal tubule.

why_others_wrong.A: Glomerular filtration is passive movement of plasma (and unbound drug) across the filtration barrier into Bowman's capsule; it does not involve active transport from the tubular cell into the lumen.
why_others_wrong.C: Tubular reabsorption moves substances from the tubular lumen back into the peritubular blood, the opposite direction to the active secretion into the lumen described here.
why_others_wrong.D: Hepatic extraction refers to removal of drug from blood by the liver; it is unrelated to active transport processes occurring within the renal tubule.
why_others_wrong.E: Passive diffusion into plasma would move substances out of, not into, the tubular lumen, and does not describe an active, energy-dependent transport process.

exam_trap: Tubular reabsorption is chosen by candidates who confuse the direction of transport; reabsorption moves substances out of the tubule, whereas transport into the lumen is secretion.
takeaway: Renal tubule: secretion = into urine; reabsorption = out of urine.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Active transport from tubular cell into the lumen ↓ direction is blood → tubule → urine ↓ this adds drug to the filtrate ↓ Tubular secretion
pearl: Trimethoprim competes with creatinine for tubular secretion, so it can raise serum creatinine without a true fall in GFR, and it can also cause hyperkalaemia.

subject: Pharmacology
title: Drug clearance
stem: A drug is almost completely removed from plasma during a single passage through an organ. Which property does the drug have?
why_correct: The extraction ratio represents the proportion of drug removed from blood during passage through an organ. A high-extraction drug is extensively removed during a single pass.

why_others_wrong.A: A very low extraction ratio describes a drug that is poorly removed during a single pass through an organ, the opposite of the near-complete removal described in the stem.
why_others_wrong.C: Extraction ratio is an organ-perfusion pharmacokinetic concept and is not specific to renal clearance; describing it as 'zero renal clearance' does not match a drug that is efficiently extracted during organ passage.
why_others_wrong.D: A high extraction ratio depends on adequate blood flow delivering drug to the organ; zero hepatic blood flow would prevent, not enable, efficient single-pass removal.
why_others_wrong.E: Near-complete removal during a single pass typically reflects efficient metabolism (or uptake) by the organ; 'no metabolism' is inconsistent with a high-extraction process.

exam_trap: Very low extraction ratio is chosen by candidates who confuse the scale, but a drug almost completely removed in a single organ pass has a high extraction ratio, close to 1.
takeaway: Extraction ratio = fraction removed during one organ passage.
source: Standard pharmacology principles.
thinking: Drug almost completely removed in one pass through an organ ↓ fraction removed per pass defines the extraction ratio ↓ near-complete removal means a ratio approaching 1 ↓ High extraction ratio
pearl: Oral bioavailability of a drug cleared only by the liver is roughly 1 minus its hepatic extraction ratio, so high-extraction drugs such as GTN and lidocaine are given by non-oral routes.

subject: Pharmacology
title: Drug metabolism
stem: A patient takes two medicines. One drug reduces hepatic metabolism of the other, causing the second drug's plasma concentration to rise. Which pharmacokinetic change is most likely?

options.C: Increased renal filtration of every drug
options.E: Increased drug absorption in every case

why_correct: Inhibition of drug-metabolising enzymes can reduce metabolic clearance of a substrate drug. If dosing is unchanged, plasma exposure and concentration may increase.

why_others_wrong.A: Increased metabolic clearance would lower, not raise, the second drug's plasma concentration; the scenario describes the drug's level rising, consistent with reduced, not increased, clearance.
why_others_wrong.C: The scenario describes hepatic enzyme inhibition affecting one specific drug's metabolism, not a generalised increase in renal filtration of every drug in the body.
why_others_wrong.D: Reduced metabolic clearance from enzyme inhibition does not itself alter the drug's distribution into tissues; volume of distribution is a separate pharmacokinetic parameter.
why_others_wrong.E: The interaction described is a metabolic (hepatic enzyme) effect, not an absorptive one; there is no indication that gastrointestinal absorption of either drug is increased.

exam_trap: Reduced volume of distribution is chosen by candidates who link rising levels with less space for the drug, but enzyme inhibition raises levels by reducing metabolic clearance, not distribution.
takeaway: Inhibition = slower metabolism; induction = faster metabolism.
source: Standard pharmacology principles.
thinking: One drug reduces hepatic metabolism of the other ↓ second drug's plasma level rises ↓ less is metabolised per unit time ↓ Reduced metabolic clearance
pearl: Omeprazole inhibits CYP2C19, which reduces activation of the prodrug clopidogrel; this is why the MHRA advises avoiding omeprazole and esomeprazole with clopidogrel.

subject: Pharmacology
title: Receptor regulation
stem: A patient receives prolonged exposure to a receptor agonist. The response to the same concentration of agonist becomes progressively smaller. What is the most appropriate term?
why_correct: Prolonged agonist exposure can produce receptor desensitisation and/or downstream adaptations, reducing the response to the same agonist concentration.

why_others_wrong.B: Potentiation describes an enhanced (typically increased) response to a drug, often from co-administration of another agent; the scenario describes a progressively diminished response, the opposite effect.
why_others_wrong.C: First-pass metabolism describes hepatic metabolism of an orally absorbed drug before systemic circulation; it does not explain a fall in pharmacodynamic response despite unchanged drug concentration.
why_others_wrong.D: Bioavailability describes the fraction of administered drug reaching systemic circulation; the scenario specifies the same concentration is producing a smaller response, indicating a receptor-level, not an absorption-level, change.
why_others_wrong.E: Renal clearance describes drug elimination via the kidneys; it is a pharmacokinetic parameter and does not explain a receptor-level fall in responsiveness at constant drug concentration.

exam_trap: First-pass metabolism and bioavailability are chosen by candidates who look for a pharmacokinetic cause, but the stem fixes the concentration, so the loss of effect is tolerance or desensitisation.
takeaway: Same drug concentration + less effect after repeated exposure → desensitisation/tolerance.
source: Standard pharmacology principles.
thinking: Prolonged agonist exposure ↓ same concentration gives a smaller response ↓ receptor and downstream adaptation ↓ Tolerance/desensitisation
pearl: Patients receiving long sedative or opioid infusions in intensive care develop tolerance and can experience withdrawal if infusions are stopped abruptly, so they are weaned gradually.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Haemostasis
stem: A patient develops a small puncture wound that exposes subendothelial collagen. Which haemostatic event occurs first?
why_correct: Primary haemostasis begins with platelet adhesion to exposed subendothelial structures, followed by platelet activation, secretion and aggregation.

why_others_wrong.B: Fibrin degradation occurs during fibrinolysis once a clot has formed, not as the first response to vessel injury.
why_others_wrong.C: Clot retraction is a later event in which activated platelets contract the formed fibrin meshwork.
why_others_wrong.D: Fibrinolysis breaks down an established clot and follows, rather than begins, haemostasis.
why_others_wrong.E: Plasmin generation is the key step in fibrinolysis, which dissolves clot after haemostasis rather than initiating it.

exam_trap: Clot retraction, fibrinolysis and plasmin generation are genuine haemostatic events, but they occur after the clot has formed; platelet adhesion comes first.
takeaway: Vessel injury → platelet adhesion → activation → aggregation.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.; Principles and Practice of Surgery, 7th ed.
thinking: Puncture wound exposes subendothelial collagen ↓ primary haemostasis begins ↓ platelets bind the exposed collagen ↓ activation and aggregation follow ↓ Platelet adhesion
pearl: Aspirin irreversibly inhibits platelet cyclo-oxygenase, impairing thromboxane A2-dependent activation and aggregation for the lifespan of the platelet, which matters when planning surgery.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Clot retraction
stem: Which cellular component is primarily responsible for clot retraction?
why_correct: Activated platelets contain contractile proteins that generate forces causing the fibrin meshwork to contract, bringing wound edges closer and consolidating the clot.

why_others_wrong.B: Neutrophils are phagocytes involved in acute inflammation and do not provide the contractile force for clot retraction.
why_others_wrong.C: Erythrocytes become trapped within the fibrin mesh but lack the contractile apparatus that drives retraction.
why_others_wrong.D: Endothelial cells regulate haemostasis through factors such as von Willebrand factor and prostacyclin but do not contract the clot.
why_others_wrong.E: Hepatocytes synthesise most coagulation factors but play no direct part in contracting a formed clot.

exam_trap: Erythrocytes are tempting because they make up most of a clot's bulk, but they are passively trapped; the contractile force comes from activated platelets.
takeaway: Clot retraction = platelet contractile activity.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Clot retraction contracts the fibrin meshwork ↓ this needs a contractile apparatus linked to fibrin ↓ activated platelets pull on fibrin via GPIIb/IIIa and actin-myosin ↓ Platelets
pearl: Impaired clot retraction is a classic laboratory feature of inherited GPIIb/IIIa deficiency, showing that retraction depends on platelet integrin binding to fibrin.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Fibrinolysis
stem: Which enzyme directly degrades fibrin within an established thrombus?
why_correct: Plasmin is the principal fibrinolytic enzyme and degrades fibrin into fibrin degradation products.

why_others_wrong.A: Thrombin converts fibrinogen to fibrin, building the clot rather than degrading it.
why_others_wrong.C: Factor XIII cross-links fibrin to stabilise the clot, which makes it more resistant to breakdown.
why_others_wrong.D: Tissue factor initiates the extrinsic coagulation pathway with factor VIIa and does not degrade fibrin.
why_others_wrong.E: Factor V is a cofactor in the prothrombinase complex that promotes thrombin generation, not fibrin breakdown.

exam_trap: Thrombin is the main distractor because it acts directly on fibrinogen, but it builds fibrin; plasmin is the enzyme that degrades established fibrin.
takeaway: Fibrinolysis → plasmin.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: An established thrombus needs fibrin breakdown ↓ the fibrinolytic system generates a serine protease ↓ it cleaves fibrin into degradation products such as D-dimer ↓ Plasmin
pearl: Tranexamic acid blocks the lysine-binding sites on plasminogen so plasmin cannot bind fibrin, and it is used to reduce bleeding in trauma and major surgery.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Fibrinolytic regulation
stem: Which circulating precursor is converted to plasmin by plasminogen activators?
why_correct: Plasminogen is the inactive precursor of plasmin. Tissue-type plasminogen activator and related activators promote its conversion to plasmin.

why_others_wrong.A: Fibrinogen is converted to fibrin by thrombin, not to plasmin by plasminogen activators.
why_others_wrong.C: Prothrombin is converted to thrombin by the prothrombinase complex, not to plasmin.
why_others_wrong.D: Factor XIII is activated by thrombin to cross-link fibrin; it is not a plasmin precursor.
why_others_wrong.E: Protein C is activated by the thrombin-thrombomodulin complex to become an anticoagulant, not converted to plasmin.

exam_trap: Fibrinogen is the name-alike trap; it is converted to fibrin by thrombin, whereas plasminogen activators convert plasminogen into the fibrin-degrading enzyme plasmin.
takeaway: tPA → plasminogen → plasmin → fibrin breakdown.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Plasminogen activators act on an inactive circulating zymogen ↓ tPA cleaves it on the fibrin surface ↓ the product is plasmin ↓ Plasminogen
pearl: Recombinant tPA (alteplase) is used for thrombolysis in ischaemic stroke and massive pulmonary embolism, and recent major surgery is a relative contraindication because of bleeding risk.

subject: Physiology
title: Bone remodelling
stem: Which cell is primarily responsible for synthesising new bone matrix?
why_correct: Osteoblasts synthesise osteoid, the organic component of bone matrix, which subsequently undergoes mineralisation.

why_others_wrong.A: Osteoclasts resorb bone matrix; they do not synthesise it.
why_others_wrong.C: Osteocytes are mature, largely quiescent former osteoblasts embedded in matrix that maintain rather than actively synthesise new bone.
why_others_wrong.D: Chondrocytes synthesise cartilage matrix, not bone matrix.
why_others_wrong.E: Fibroblasts produce general connective tissue collagen but are not the specialised cells responsible for osteoid synthesis in bone.

exam_trap: Osteoclast (A) tempts when the suffixes are confused; osteoclasts resorb bone, whereas osteoblasts synthesise osteoid that then mineralises.
takeaway: Osteoblast = bone formation; osteoclast = bone resorption.
source: Gray’s Basic Anatomy, 3rd ed.; Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Synthesis of new bone matrix ↓ cells lining bone surfaces secrete osteoid ↓ osteoid then mineralises ↓ Osteoblast
pearl: Alkaline phosphatase reflects osteoblast activity, so it is raised in healing fractures, osteomalacia and osteoblastic bone metastases such as those from prostate cancer.

subject: Trauma & orthopaedics
title: Bone healing
stem: Which factor is particularly important for successful fracture healing?

options.E: Complete immobilisation of every fracture for the entire healing period

why_correct: Bone healing requires an adequate vascular supply. Severe local ischaemia compromises cellular activity, matrix formation and mineralisation.

why_others_wrong.A: Persistent severe hypoxia impairs osteoblast function and favours fibrous tissue and non-union rather than bone formation.
why_others_wrong.C: The early inflammatory phase, with its cells and cytokines, is needed to start the healing cascade, so absent inflammation would impair repair.
why_others_wrong.D: Persistent infection destroys bone and soft tissue and is a major cause of non-union rather than an aid to healing.
why_others_wrong.E: Many fractures heal by callus that benefits from controlled micromotion, so rigid immobilisation of every fracture throughout healing is unnecessary and causes stiffness.

exam_trap: Candidates choose complete immobilisation, but many fractures heal by callus that benefits from controlled micromotion; adequate vascular supply is the essential factor.
takeaway: Fracture healing needs blood supply and an appropriate mechanical environment.
source: Gray’s Basic Anatomy, 3rd ed.; Principles and Practice of Surgery, 7th ed.
thinking: Requirements for fracture healing ↓ osteoprogenitor cells need oxygen and nutrients ↓ both delivered by local blood supply ↓ ischaemia, infection and gross instability impair union ↓ Adequate local vascular supply
pearl: Excessive periosteal stripping during open fixation devitalises fracture fragments, which is why biological fixation techniques preserving soft-tissue attachments are favoured.

subject: Anatomy
title: Peripheral nerve regeneration
stem: After a peripheral nerve injury, which cell type provides important support for axonal regeneration?
why_correct: Schwann cells are important in peripheral nerve repair. Following axonal injury, they contribute to the regenerative environment and guide regenerating axons along appropriate pathways.

why_others_wrong.B: Osteoclasts are bone-resorbing cells and play no role in guiding regenerating axons.
why_others_wrong.C: Hepatocytes are liver parenchymal cells with no role in peripheral nerve repair.
why_others_wrong.D: Neutrophils are early inflammatory cells, whereas macrophages and Schwann cells clear debris and support regrowth.
why_others_wrong.E: Platelets contribute to haemostasis and release growth factors but do not form the guiding bands of Büngner.

exam_trap: Neutrophils arrive early after injury and tempt candidates, but debris clearance and axonal guidance are carried out mainly by macrophages and Schwann cells.
takeaway: Peripheral nerve repair → think Schwann cells.
source: Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd ed.; Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Peripheral nerve injury ↓ distal axon and myelin degenerate and are cleared ↓ Schwann cells proliferate and line up as guiding bands ↓ they secrete trophic factors for the regrowing axon ↓ Schwann cell
pearl: Regenerating peripheral axons advance at roughly 1 mm per day, which helps estimate recovery time and explains why distal muscles may waste before reinnervation after proximal injuries.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Wound healing
stem: A healing wound develops abundant new capillaries and a loose extracellular matrix containing fibroblasts. What is this tissue called?
why_correct: Granulation tissue contains newly formed capillaries, proliferating fibroblasts and extracellular matrix. It is characteristic of the proliferative phase of wound healing.

why_others_wrong.B: Necrotic tissue is dead and avascular, the opposite of the actively vascularising repair tissue described.
why_others_wrong.C: Hyaline cartilage is a specialised avascular connective tissue found in joints and the fetal skeleton, not a feature of soft-tissue wound repair.
why_others_wrong.D: Keloid tissue is an abnormal, excessive scar resulting from disordered late collagen deposition, not the early vascular proliferative tissue described.
why_others_wrong.E: A thrombus is an intravascular blood clot, not a soft-tissue repair structure.

exam_trap: Keloid tissue (D) tempts because it is scar-related, but keloid is excessive late collagen; also do not confuse granulation tissue with a granuloma.
takeaway: Granulation = new capillaries + fibroblasts + ECM.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Healing wound ↓ abundant new capillaries ↓ fibroblasts in a loose extracellular matrix ↓ proliferative-phase repair tissue ↓ Granulation tissue
pearl: Healthy granulation tissue is red, moist and bleeds easily; pale or friable granulation suggests poor perfusion or infection, and overgranulation can delay epithelialisation.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Surgical oncology
stem: A surgeon removes a malignant tumour with no macroscopic or microscopic residual tumour at the margins. Which term describes this resection?
why_correct: An R0 resection indicates complete resection with no residual tumour detectable according to the relevant pathological assessment. R1 indicates microscopic residual tumour, while R2 indicates macroscopic residual tumour.

why_others_wrong.B: R1 denotes microscopic residual tumour at the margin, whereas this resection has no microscopic residual disease.
why_others_wrong.C: R2 denotes macroscopic residual tumour left behind, which is the opposite of the complete clearance described.
why_others_wrong.D: A biopsy samples tissue for diagnosis and does not aim to remove the whole tumour with clear margins.
why_others_wrong.E: Debulking without clearance deliberately leaves residual tumour, whereas this resection removed all tumour to clear margins.

exam_trap: R1 is chosen by candidates who confuse microscopic with macroscopic clearance; R1 means microscopic residual tumour at the margin, whereas this resection is complete.
takeaway: R0 = complete. R1 = micro. R2 = macro.
source: Principles and Practice of Surgery, 7th ed.
thinking: Tumour removed completely ↓ no macroscopic or microscopic residual at the margins ↓ residual tumour classification R0 ↓ R0 resection
pearl: R status is a strong predictor of local recurrence after cancer surgery, and in rectal cancer tumour within 1 mm of the circumferential resection margin is generally regarded as an involved margin.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Surgical oncology
stem: A cancer resection leaves microscopic malignant cells at the surgical margin. Which resection category applies?
why_correct: R1 denotes microscopic residual tumour after resection.

why_others_wrong.A: R0 denotes complete resection with no residual tumour, which is not the case when malignant cells lie at the margin.
why_others_wrong.C: R2 denotes macroscopic residual tumour visible to the surgeon, whereas this residual disease is only microscopic.
why_others_wrong.D: R3 is not a category in the residual tumour classification, which runs from R0 to R2 with RX.
why_others_wrong.E: RX is used when residual tumour cannot be assessed, whereas here microscopic tumour has been identified at the margin.

exam_trap: R2 tempts candidates who treat any residual tumour as macroscopic, but R2 means visible residual disease; tumour identified only microscopically at the margin is R1.
takeaway: R1 = microscopic positive margin/residual disease.
source: Principles and Practice of Surgery, 7th ed.
thinking: Malignant cells at the surgical margin ↓ residual disease is only microscopic ↓ R1 denotes microscopic residual tumour ↓ R1
pearl: An R1 resection usually prompts multidisciplinary discussion of re-excision or adjuvant radiotherapy, depending on the tumour type and site.

subject: Statistics & evidence-based medicine
title: Evidence synthesis
stem: A systematic review identifies substantial variation between studies in the magnitude of treatment effect. The investigators quantify the proportion of variability attributable to between-study heterogeneity. Which statistic is most appropriate?
why_correct: I² quantifies the proportion of observed variation across study results that is attributable to heterogeneity rather than sampling error, within the framework of meta-analysis.

why_others_wrong.B: The number needed to treat expresses treatment effect as patients treated per outcome prevented and does not measure between-study variation.
why_others_wrong.C: Sensitivity is a diagnostic test measure of true positives among diseased people, unrelated to heterogeneity in a meta-analysis.
why_others_wrong.D: Specificity is a diagnostic test measure of true negatives among non-diseased people and does not quantify heterogeneity.
why_others_wrong.E: A hazard ratio is an effect measure for time-to-event data and does not describe variability between study results.

exam_trap: Hazard ratio may tempt because it appears in many meta-analyses, but it is an effect measure; I² is the statistic that quantifies between-study heterogeneity.
takeaway: Meta-analysis with between-study variation → think I².
source: Standard evidence-based medicine methodology; Principles and Practice of Surgery, 7th ed.
thinking: Variation in treatment effect between studies ↓ want proportion due to heterogeneity rather than chance ↓ I² ↓ I²
pearl: I² is preferred to the chi-squared (Q) test for heterogeneity because the Q test has low power when few studies are included.

subject: Physiology
title: Renal acid-base physiology
stem: A patient develops a persistent metabolic acidosis. Which renal adaptation is most important for increasing net acid excretion?
why_correct: In chronic metabolic acidosis, the kidney increases net acid excretion, particularly through increased ammonium production and excretion. This allows additional hydrogen ions to be excreted while generating new bicarbonate for the extracellular fluid.

why_others_wrong.A: Ammonium production increases, not decreases, in chronic metabolic acidosis to support enhanced acid excretion.
why_others_wrong.C: Hydrogen-ion secretion increases, not decreases, in chronic acidosis, trapping ammonia as ammonium and buffering with phosphate as titratable acid.
why_others_wrong.D: Bicarbonate reclamation is enhanced, not reduced, as part of the renal compensatory response.
why_others_wrong.E: Increased urinary bicarbonate loss would worsen acidosis; the kidney instead conserves and generates new bicarbonate.

exam_trap: Reduced bicarbonate reclamation (D) tempts as part of acid handling, but the kidney enhances bicarbonate reclamation; net acid excretion rises mainly through ammonium.
takeaway: Chronic acidosis → ↑ NH4+ excretion → ↑ net acid excretion.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Persistent metabolic acidosis ↓ renal glutamine metabolism is upregulated ↓ ammonium is excreted and new bicarbonate generated ↓ Increased ammonium excretion
pearl: Urinary diversion through bowel segments, such as ureterosigmoidostomy or ileal conduits with prolonged urine contact, can cause hyperchloraemic acidosis because the mucosa absorbs ammonium and chloride.

subject: Physiology
title: Urinary acid buffering
stem: Which component of renal net acid excretion consists mainly of hydrogen ions buffered by filtered phosphate?
why_correct: Titratable acid refers principally to urinary buffers such as phosphate that accept secreted hydrogen ions. This permits hydrogen ions to be excreted without requiring an extreme fall in urinary pH.

why_others_wrong.A: Bicarbonate is reabsorbed by the kidney rather than acting as the urinary buffer that constitutes titratable acid.
why_others_wrong.B: Ammonia (forming ammonium) is a distinct renal acid-excretion mechanism from titratable acid, which specifically refers to buffers like phosphate.
why_others_wrong.D: Albumin is not a urinary hydrogen-ion buffer involved in titratable acid excretion.
why_others_wrong.E: Urea is osmotically important in the medulla but does not buffer secreted hydrogen ions as titratable acid.

exam_trap: Ammonia (B) tempts because it is the other buffered acid route, but ammonium excretion is counted separately; phosphate-buffered H+ is titratable acid.
takeaway: Phosphate-buffered H+ → titratable acid.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Component of net acid excretion ↓ secreted H+ buffered by filtered phosphate ↓ quantified by titrating urine back to plasma pH ↓ Titratable acid
pearl: Urinary buffering by phosphate and ammonia lets the kidney excrete large amounts of acid while urine pH stays above its minimum of about 4.5, because free H+ alone could carry very little acid.

subject: Physiology
title: Renal potassium handling
stem: A patient develops hyperkalaemia after a reduction in aldosterone activity. Which renal tubular process is most directly reduced?

options.A: Sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion by principal cells
options.E: Hydrogen secretion by proximal tubular cells only

correct_answer: A. Sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion by principal cells
why_correct: Aldosterone acts mainly on principal cells of the late distal nephron and collecting duct. It promotes sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion. Reduced aldosterone activity therefore predisposes to hyperkalaemia.

why_others_wrong.B: Glucose filtration depends on GFR and plasma glucose concentration and is not regulated by aldosterone.
why_others_wrong.C: Urea filtration is unrelated to aldosterone's action on principal cells.
why_others_wrong.D: Calcium filtration and handling are not directly regulated by aldosterone.
why_others_wrong.E: Aldosterone's key hyperkalaemia-relevant action is on principal cells (Na+ reabsorption/K+ secretion) in the distal nephron and collecting duct, not primarily hydrogen secretion by proximal tubular cells.

exam_trap: Hydrogen secretion by proximal tubular cells only (E) tempts because aldosterone affects acid secretion, but its hyperkalaemia-relevant action is on distal principal cells.
takeaway: Low aldosterone → less K+ secretion → hyperkalaemia.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Reduced aldosterone activity ↓ principal cells express fewer ENaC channels ↓ less sodium reabsorption means a smaller lumen-negative potential ↓ potassium secretion falls and hyperkalaemia follows ↓ Sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion by principal cells
pearl: Hyporeninaemic hypoaldosteronism (type 4 renal tubular acidosis), often in diabetic kidney disease, causes hyperkalaemia with mild acidosis and is worsened by ACE inhibitors, NSAIDs and heparin.

subject: Physiology
title: Phosphate regulation
stem: Which hormone reduces renal phosphate reabsorption and also reduces circulating calcitriol?
why_correct: Fibroblast growth factor 23 promotes renal phosphate excretion and suppresses renal production of calcitriol. It is an important regulator of phosphate homeostasis.

why_others_wrong.B: PTH also promotes phosphate excretion but increases, rather than decreases, circulating calcitriol, distinguishing it from FGF23.
why_others_wrong.C: Aldosterone regulates sodium and potassium handling and has no significant role in phosphate or calcitriol regulation.
why_others_wrong.D: ADH governs water reabsorption via the collecting duct and does not regulate phosphate excretion or calcitriol production.
why_others_wrong.E: Calcitonin primarily lowers serum calcium and is not a major regulator of phosphate reabsorption or calcitriol synthesis.

exam_trap: PTH (B) tempts because it is also phosphaturic, but it raises calcitriol; the hormone lowering both phosphate reabsorption and calcitriol is FGF23.
takeaway: FGF23 → ↓ phosphate reabsorption + ↓ calcitriol.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Reduced renal phosphate reabsorption ↓ PTH and FGF23 both cause phosphaturia ↓ only one of them also lowers calcitriol ↓ FGF23
pearl: After renal transplantation, persistently high FGF23 and PTH can cause marked hypophosphataemia in the early months, often needing phosphate supplementation.

subject: Physiology
title: Endocrine feedback
stem: A patient has primary adrenal failure. Which combination would be expected?

options.E: Normal cortisol and high aldosterone only

correct_answer: C. Low cortisol and high ACTH
why_correct: Primary adrenal failure results from dysfunction of the adrenal cortex. Cortisol production falls, removing negative feedback on the hypothalamic-pituitary axis and causing ACTH to rise.

why_others_wrong.A: High cortisol with low ACTH fits a state of autonomous cortisol excess suppressing the axis (e.g. adrenal adenoma), not adrenal failure.
why_others_wrong.B: Low cortisol with low ACTH is the pattern of secondary (pituitary-driven) adrenal insufficiency, not primary adrenal failure.
why_others_wrong.D: High cortisol with high ACTH suggests ACTH-dependent Cushing's disease, not failure of cortisol production.
why_others_wrong.E: In primary adrenal failure, aldosterone is typically also reduced (given the same gland is failing), so normal cortisol with high aldosterone alone does not fit this picture.

exam_trap: Low cortisol and low ACTH (B) tempts, but that is secondary adrenal insufficiency; primary adrenal failure removes feedback so ACTH rises.
takeaway: Primary adrenal failure → ↓ cortisol + ↑ ACTH.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.; Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Primary adrenal failure ↓ the cortex cannot make cortisol ↓ loss of negative feedback ↓ ACTH rises ↓ Low cortisol and high ACTH
pearl: A short ACTH stimulation test confirms adrenal insufficiency, a high baseline ACTH localises it to the adrenal, and autoimmune adrenalitis is the commonest cause in the UK.

subject: Physiology
title: Thyroid feedback
stem: A patient has primary hypothyroidism due to failure of the thyroid gland. Which pattern is expected?

options.A: High free T4 and high TSH
options.B: Low free T4 and high TSH
options.C: High free T4 and low TSH
options.D: Low free T4 and low TSH
options.E: Normal free T4 and suppressed TSH

correct_answer: B. Low free T4 and high TSH
why_correct: Primary hypothyroidism is thyroid gland failure. Reduced thyroid hormone production removes negative feedback and causes increased TSH secretion.

why_others_wrong.A: High T4 with high TSH suggests a TSH-secreting pituitary tumour or thyroid hormone resistance, not primary gland failure.
why_others_wrong.C: High T4 with low TSH indicates primary hyperthyroidism (excess hormone suppressing TSH), the opposite of failure.
why_others_wrong.D: Low T4 with low TSH is the pattern of secondary (pituitary) hypothyroidism, not primary thyroid gland failure.
why_others_wrong.E: Normal T4 with suppressed TSH suggests subclinical hyperthyroidism, not a hypothyroid state.

exam_trap: Low free T4 with low TSH (D) tempts as a hypothyroid pattern, but it reflects central disease; primary thyroid failure raises TSH.
takeaway: Primary thyroid failure → ↓ T4 + ↑ TSH.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Thyroid gland failure ↓ free T4 falls ↓ hypothalamic-pituitary negative feedback is reduced ↓ TSH rises ↓ Low free T4 and high TSH
pearl: Myxoedema coma can be precipitated by surgery, infection or sedatives in untreated hypothyroidism and is managed with IV thyroid hormone, hydrocortisone and supportive care.

subject: Physiology
title: Pituitary feedback
stem: A patient has secondary adrenal insufficiency caused by pituitary dysfunction. Which biochemical pattern is most likely?

options.C: Low cortisol and low or inappropriately normal ACTH

correct_answer: C. Low cortisol and low or inappropriately normal ACTH
why_correct: Secondary adrenal insufficiency results from inadequate ACTH stimulation of the adrenal cortex. Cortisol is therefore low, while ACTH is low or inappropriately normal for the degree of cortisol deficiency.

why_others_wrong.A: High ACTH with low cortisol is the primary adrenal failure pattern, where the pituitary appropriately drives ACTH up against a failing gland — not the pattern seen when the defect is pituitary in origin.
why_others_wrong.B: High cortisol with high ACTH does not fit a state of insufficiency; it suggests ACTH-driven cortisol excess.
why_others_wrong.D: High cortisol with low ACTH suggests autonomous adrenal cortisol production suppressing the axis, not insufficiency.
why_others_wrong.E: Aldosterone secretion is largely independent of ACTH (driven mainly by the renin-angiotensin system) and is typically preserved in isolated secondary ACTH deficiency, so this combination does not fit.

exam_trap: Low cortisol with high ACTH (A) tempts as the textbook insufficiency pattern, but that is primary failure; a pituitary cause gives low or inappropriately normal ACTH.
takeaway: Secondary failure → low target hormone + low or inappropriately normal trophic hormone.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Secondary adrenal insufficiency from pituitary disease ↓ ACTH drive is deficient ↓ cortisol falls ↓ ACTH is low or inappropriately normal for the low cortisol ↓ Low cortisol and low or inappropriately normal ACTH
pearl: Aldosterone is preserved in secondary adrenal insufficiency, so severe hyperkalaemia is unusual and fludrocortisone is not needed, but glucocorticoid replacement and sick-day rules remain essential.

subject: Genetics
title: Molecular genetics
stem: A mutation occurs in a DNA sequence that normally controls gene transcription by providing a binding site for regulatory proteins near the gene. What type of region has most likely been affected?
why_correct: Promoter and other regulatory DNA regions contain sequences that influence transcription by interacting with transcription factors and associated regulatory proteins.

why_others_wrong.B: Splice sites and the spliceosome act on pre-mRNA after transcription to remove introns, rather than providing the promoter binding site that controls transcription initiation.
why_others_wrong.C: Telomeres are repetitive sequences protecting chromosome ends and do not act as binding sites controlling transcription of a nearby gene.
why_others_wrong.D: The centromere is where sister chromatids join and the kinetochore assembles for segregation, not a gene's transcriptional control region.
why_others_wrong.E: The ribosome is a cytoplasmic RNA-protein complex that translates mRNA, not a DNA sequence, so it cannot be the site of this mutation.

exam_trap: A mutation does not have to alter the protein-coding sequence to alter gene expression.
takeaway: Regulatory DNA mutation → abnormal gene expression without necessarily altering protein sequence.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Mutation in a sequence near the gene ↓ binding site for regulatory proteins ↓ controls transcription ↓ Promoter/regulatory region
pearl: Promoter hypermethylation can silence tumour suppressor genes without any coding mutation, for example MLH1 silencing in sporadic microsatellite-unstable colorectal cancer.

subject: Physiology
title: Protein synthesis
stem: Which cellular structure is directly responsible for translating messenger RNA into protein?
why_correct: Ribosomes translate the nucleotide sequence of mRNA into an amino-acid sequence.

why_others_wrong.A: Lysosomes degrade macromolecules via hydrolytic enzymes; they play no role in translating mRNA.
why_others_wrong.C: Peroxisomes are involved in fatty acid oxidation and detoxification reactions, not protein translation.
why_others_wrong.D: Centrosomes organise microtubules and the mitotic spindle; they have no role in translating mRNA.
why_others_wrong.E: The Golgi apparatus modifies and sorts proteins after synthesis; it does not translate mRNA into protein.

exam_trap: Golgi apparatus (E) tempts because it handles proteins, but it modifies them after synthesis; translation of mRNA into protein occurs on ribosomes.
takeaway: mRNA is read by the ribosome.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: mRNA carries the coded sequence ↓ translation reads codons and links amino acids ↓ performed by rRNA-protein complexes, free or ER-bound ↓ Ribosome
pearl: Many antibiotics target bacterial 70S ribosomes, including aminoglycosides, macrolides, tetracyclines and clindamycin, sparing human cytoplasmic 80S ribosomes.

subject: Physiology
title: Cellular trafficking
stem: A newly synthesised secretory protein is transported through the cell before being released extracellularly. Which organelle is primarily responsible for modifying and sorting this protein after it leaves the rough endoplasmic reticulum?
why_correct: Proteins destined for secretion enter the rough endoplasmic reticulum and are then transported to the Golgi apparatus, where they undergo further modification, sorting and packaging.

why_others_wrong.A: Lysosomes degrade cellular material and are not involved in modifying or sorting secretory proteins in transit.
why_others_wrong.C: Mitochondria generate ATP and are not part of the secretory protein processing pathway.
why_others_wrong.D: Peroxisomes carry out oxidative reactions and detoxification, not modification/sorting of secretory proteins.
why_others_wrong.E: The nucleus is the site of transcription, not of post-endoplasmic-reticulum protein processing.

exam_trap: Lysosome (A) tempts as a membrane-bound processing organelle, but it degrades material; post-ER modification and sorting of secretory proteins occur in the Golgi.
takeaway: Secretory protein pathway: RER → Golgi → vesicle → extracellular space.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Secretory protein leaves the rough ER ↓ needs glycosylation, modification and sorting ↓ packaged into secretory vesicles at the trans face ↓ Golgi apparatus
pearl: Constitutive secretion releases proteins continuously, whereas regulated secretion stores them in granules for stimulus-triggered release, as with insulin from pancreatic beta cells.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Lysosomal storage
stem: A genetic disorder causes accumulation of an undegraded macromolecule within lysosomes. Which broad pathological mechanism is responsible?
why_correct: Lysosomal storage disorders result from inherited deficiencies of lysosomal enzymes or related proteins, leading to accumulation of substrates within cells.

why_others_wrong.B: Increased DNA replication relates to cell proliferation, not accumulation of undegraded macromolecules within lysosomes.
why_others_wrong.C: Excessive glomerular filtration is a renal excretory process unrelated to intracellular lysosomal enzyme deficiency.
why_others_wrong.D: Increased mitochondrial ATP synthesis concerns energy metabolism, not failure of lysosomal substrate degradation.
why_others_wrong.E: Accelerated collagen cross-linking relates to connective tissue/wound remodelling, not lysosomal enzyme deficiency.

exam_trap: The distractors are weak; candidates choosing increased DNA replication (B) confuse cell proliferation with storage, which is failure of lysosomal substrate breakdown.
takeaway: Lysosomal enzyme defect → storage of undegraded material.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Genetic disorder ↓ undegraded macromolecule within lysosomes ↓ missing or defective lysosomal enzyme ↓ substrate cannot be broken down ↓ Failure of lysosomal degradation
pearl: Many lysosomal storage disorders store material in macrophages, causing hepatosplenomegaly, and several are now treated with intravenous enzyme replacement therapy.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Cellular adaptation
stem: A patient develops chronic enlargement of a tissue because individual cells become larger without an increase in cell number. What process is this?
why_correct: Hypertrophy is an increase in cell size resulting in enlargement of the affected tissue or organ.

why_others_wrong.A: Hyperplasia is an increase in cell number, whereas the stem specifies enlargement of individual cells without any increase in cell number.
why_others_wrong.C: Metaplasia is a change from one differentiated cell type to another, not enlargement of existing cells.
why_others_wrong.D: Dysplasia is disordered, atypical cellular growth and differentiation, not simple enlargement of normal cells.
why_others_wrong.E: Atrophy is a decrease, not an increase, in cell size and tissue mass.

exam_trap: Hyperplasia (A) traps candidates who see tissue enlargement and stop reading; the stem specifies bigger cells without any increase in cell number.
takeaway: More cell size → hypertrophy. More cell number → hyperplasia.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Chronic tissue enlargement ↓ individual cells become larger ↓ no increase in cell number ↓ Hypertrophy
pearl: Organs often enlarge by both mechanisms together; the pregnant uterus shows smooth-muscle hypertrophy and hyperplasia, whereas adult skeletal muscle enlarges mainly by hypertrophy.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Cellular death
stem: Which finding is most characteristic of irreversible cell injury?
why_correct: Irreversible cell injury is associated with severe and persistent mitochondrial dysfunction and membrane damage, ultimately leading to necrosis or apoptosis depending on the mechanism.

why_others_wrong.A: Mild cellular swelling reflects failure of ionic pumps and is characteristic of reversible, not irreversible, injury.
why_others_wrong.B: Fatty change alone is typically a reversible metabolic response and does not by itself indicate irreversible injury.
why_others_wrong.D: Increased protein synthesis is not a recognised marker of irreversible cell injury.
why_others_wrong.E: A transient reduction in ATP is characteristic of reversible injury; irreversibility requires severe, sustained mitochondrial and membrane failure.

exam_trap: Mild cellular swelling (A) and a transient fall in ATP (E) are early reversible changes; only severe membrane and mitochondrial damage marks irreversible injury.
takeaway: Membrane failure = think irreversible cell injury.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Irreversible cell injury ↓ swelling, fatty change and transient ATP fall are reversible ↓ point of no return is severe membrane and mitochondrial damage ↓ Severe membrane damage
pearl: Nuclear changes of irreversible injury include pyknosis (shrinkage), karyorrhexis (fragmentation) and karyolysis (fading), seen alongside disrupted plasma and lysosomal membranes.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Vascular pathology
stem: An arterial wall develops a focal permanent dilation due to weakening of its structural layers. What is this lesion?
why_correct: An aneurysm is a localised abnormal dilation of a blood vessel or cardiac chamber due to weakening of the wall.

why_others_wrong.B: A thrombus is a solid mass formed from blood constituents within the vessel lumen, not a dilation of the vessel wall itself.
why_others_wrong.C: An embolus is material travelling through the bloodstream to lodge elsewhere, not a localised wall dilation.
why_others_wrong.D: A haematoma is a localised collection of extravasated blood within tissue, not dilation of an intact vessel wall.
why_others_wrong.E: A varix is an abnormally dilated, tortuous vein, not the arterial wall dilation described.

exam_trap: Varix (E) is the closest distractor as another dilated vessel, but a varix is a dilated tortuous vein, whereas focal arterial wall dilation is an aneurysm.
takeaway: Focal arterial dilation from wall weakness → aneurysm.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Focal permanent dilation ↓ arterial wall ↓ weakening of the structural layers ↓ Aneurysm
pearl: A true aneurysm involves all three layers of the wall, whereas a false aneurysm is a contained leak bounded by surrounding tissue, as after femoral arterial puncture.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Atherosclerosis
stem: Which lipoprotein is most strongly associated with atherogenic cholesterol delivery to peripheral tissues?
why_correct: Low-density lipoprotein is a major carrier of cholesterol to peripheral tissues and plays a central role in atherosclerotic plaque formation when retained and modified within the arterial intima.

why_others_wrong.A: HDL removes cholesterol from peripheral tissues for transport back to the liver (reverse cholesterol transport) and is generally protective against, rather than causative of, atherosclerosis.
why_others_wrong.C: Albumin is a plasma carrier protein for substances such as fatty acids and drugs, not the principal lipoprotein delivering cholesterol to tissues.
why_others_wrong.D: Chylomicron remnants carry dietary lipid remnants but are not the major or most strongly atherogenic cholesterol carrier compared with LDL.
why_others_wrong.E: Fibrinogen is a coagulation factor, not a lipoprotein involved in cholesterol transport.

exam_trap: HDL (A) is chosen by candidates who confuse transport direction; HDL returns cholesterol to the liver and is protective, whereas LDL delivers it to peripheral tissues.
takeaway: Atherosclerosis → LDL retention/modification in arterial intima.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Atherogenic lipoprotein ↓ carries cholesterol to peripheral tissues ↓ retained and modified in the arterial intima ↓ LDL
pearl: Statins lower LDL by inhibiting HMG-CoA reductase and upregulating hepatic LDL receptors, and are recommended for secondary prevention in patients with peripheral arterial disease.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Venous thrombosis
stem: Which factor most directly promotes venous thrombosis in a patient who has been immobile after major surgery?
why_correct: Prolonged immobility reduces the skeletal-muscle pump and venous flow, producing venous stasis. Stasis is one component of Virchow’s triad and strongly promotes venous thrombosis.

why_others_wrong.A: Increased arterial pulsatility concerns arterial, not venous, flow and is not a consequence of postoperative immobility.
why_others_wrong.C: Increased lymphatic drainage would help clear interstitial fluid rather than promote thrombosis, and does not occur with immobility.
why_others_wrong.D: Increased red-cell deformability would ease flow and reduce, not promote, stasis-related thrombosis.
why_others_wrong.E: Reduced platelet adhesion would decrease, not increase, thrombotic tendency.

exam_trap: Reduced platelet adhesion only (E) tempts candidates thinking about clotting, but less platelet adhesion would lower thrombotic risk; immobility promotes thrombosis through venous stasis.
takeaway: Immobility → ↓ venous flow → stasis → VTE risk.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.; Principles and Practice of Surgery, 7th ed.
thinking: Immobile after major surgery ↓ calf muscle pump lost ↓ slow venous flow ↓ one limb of Virchow's triad ↓ Venous stasis
pearl: UK practice combines VTE risk assessment, early mobilisation, mechanical prophylaxis such as anti-embolism stockings or intermittent pneumatic compression, and low-molecular-weight heparin when indicated.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Tumour biology
stem: A malignant tumour develops a population of cells capable of surviving despite reduced oxygen availability. Which adaptive feature is most directly relevant?

options.E: Elimination of mitochondrial function in every cell

why_correct: Tumours can respond to hypoxia by increasing angiogenic signalling, including activation of pathways that promote vascular endothelial growth factor expression and new vessel formation.

why_others_wrong.B: Tumour cells adapt their metabolism to hypoxia, for example by shifting to glycolysis, rather than losing metabolism altogether.
why_others_wrong.C: Permanent cessation of division would halt tumour growth and is not the adaptation that allows hypoxic cells to thrive.
why_others_wrong.D: Hypoxic tumours increase growth-factor signalling such as VEGF rather than losing it.
why_others_wrong.E: Hypoxia may reduce reliance on oxidative phosphorylation, but tumour cells do not eliminate mitochondrial function in every cell.

exam_trap: Complete loss of metabolism or mitochondrial function overstates the hypoxic switch; tumour cells shift towards glycolysis and increase angiogenic signalling rather than shutting metabolism down.
takeaway: Tumour hypoxia → pro-angiogenic signalling → new vessel formation.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Tumour cells survive reduced oxygen availability ↓ hypoxia stabilises HIF ↓ HIF drives VEGF expression and new vessel formation ↓ Increased angiogenic signalling
pearl: Hypoxic tumour regions are relatively resistant to radiotherapy, because oxygen is needed to fix radiation-induced DNA damage.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Tumour differentiation
stem: A pathology report describes a malignant tumour as poorly differentiated. What does this primarily refer to?

options.A: The anatomical stage of the tumour
options.B: The degree to which tumour cells resemble their tissue of origin
options.C: The presence of distant metastases only
options.D: The number of lymph nodes examined

correct_answer: B. The degree to which tumour cells resemble their tissue of origin
why_correct: Tumour differentiation describes the extent to which neoplastic cells resemble the normal cells from which the tumour arose. Poorly differentiated tumours show less resemblance to their tissue of origin.

why_others_wrong.A: The anatomical stage describes the extent of spread, which is separate from the degree of differentiation.
