why_others_wrong.B: Distant metastatic nodes lie beyond the regional drainage basin and are involved later, classed as M1 rather than regional spread.
why_others_wrong.C: Skip nodes are involved nodes that bypass the first echelon, so by definition they are not the first draining nodes.
why_others_wrong.D: Para-aortic nodes are the regional drainage for some organs such as the testis, but not the first draining nodes in every cancer.
why_others_wrong.E: Contralateral nodes are reached only in particular sites or advanced disease, not as the first draining nodes in every cancer.

exam_trap: Skip nodes are tempting because they are a recognised pattern of spread, but by definition they bypass the first echelon; first draining nodes are sentinel or regional nodes.
takeaway: Lymphatic spread follows anatomical drainage pathways.
source: Principles and Practice of Surgery, 7th ed.
thinking: Carcinoma spreads first to nodes directly draining the primary ↓ these form the first echelon of the regional basin ↓ the first node reached is the sentinel node ↓ Sentinel/regional draining nodes
pearl: Sentinel lymph node biopsy, using radioisotope with or without blue dye, is standard axillary staging in clinically node-negative breast cancer and is also used in melanoma.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Surgical oncology: margin assessment
stem: During cancer surgery, the surgeon removes a tumour with a surrounding rim of apparently normal tissue. What is the principal purpose of the surgical margin?

options.A: To allow the lymph nodes to be examined
options.B: To reduce the risk of leaving microscopic tumour at the operative site
options.D: To eliminate the need for pathological examination
options.E: To guarantee cure in every patient

correct_answer: B. To reduce the risk of leaving microscopic tumour at the operative site
why_correct: An adequate oncological margin aims to reduce the likelihood of residual microscopic disease at the resection site.

why_others_wrong.A: Lymph-node assessment depends on removing the draining nodal basin, not on the width of the margin around the primary tumour.
why_others_wrong.C: A clear margin addresses local disease but cannot prevent metastases that may already have occurred through lymphatic or blood spread.
why_others_wrong.D: Pathological examination remains essential to confirm the diagnosis, grade, stage and whether the margins are actually clear.
why_others_wrong.E: A clear margin reduces local recurrence risk but does not guarantee cure, as occult micrometastases may already exist.

exam_trap: Preventing all future metastases or guaranteeing cure overstates the role of a margin; it addresses local residual disease, not micrometastases already present.
takeaway: Surgery removes the primary disease; pathology confirms whether the margin is clear.
source: Principles and Practice of Surgery, 7th ed.
thinking: Tumour excised with a rim of normal tissue ↓ cancer can extend microscopically beyond its visible edge ↓ the margin aims to remove this microscopic spread ↓ reducing residual disease and local recurrence ↓ To reduce the risk of leaving microscopic tumour at the operative site
pearl: Resection status is reported as R0 (no residual tumour), R1 (microscopic residual) or R2 (macroscopic residual), and an involved margin may prompt re-excision or adjuvant therapy.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Surgical oncology: MDT
stem: A patient has a newly diagnosed potentially resectable malignancy. What is the main purpose of multidisciplinary team discussion?

options.B: To integrate surgical, oncological, radiological and pathological information when planning management
options.C: To allow only the surgeon to decide treatment
options.E: To guarantee that surgery will be performed

correct_answer: B. To integrate surgical, oncological, radiological and pathological information when planning management
why_correct: Cancer MDTs integrate information from different specialties to support coordinated, evidence-based treatment planning.

why_others_wrong.A: The MDT relies on histopathology for diagnosis and staging; discussion cannot replace tissue diagnosis.
why_others_wrong.C: The purpose of the MDT is shared decision-making across specialties, not leaving treatment decisions to the surgeon alone.
why_others_wrong.D: MDT discussion should consider the full range of treatment options, including non-surgical and palliative alternatives.
why_others_wrong.E: An MDT may recommend non-operative treatment, so discussion does not guarantee that surgery will be performed.

exam_trap: Option E tempts when a tumour is resectable, but an MDT may recommend non-operative or neoadjuvant treatment, so discussion does not guarantee surgery.
takeaway: Cancer decisions should be informed by the whole clinical picture.
source: Principles and Practice of Surgery, 7th ed.; current UK multidisciplinary cancer-care principles.
thinking: Newly diagnosed potentially resectable cancer ↓ management needs surgical, oncological, radiological and pathological input ↓ MDT integrates these into a shared plan ↓ To integrate surgical, oncological, radiological and pathological information when planning management
pearl: MDT recommendations take account of patient fitness and preferences, and neoadjuvant chemotherapy or radiotherapy may be advised before surgery, as in many rectal and oesophageal cancers.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Surgical principles: postoperative respiratory complication
stem: A patient develops low oxygen saturation and reduced breath sounds at both lung bases after major abdominal surgery. Which postoperative process is particularly likely?
why_correct: Postoperative atelectasis is common after major surgery because of reduced functional residual capacity, shallow breathing, pain and impaired lung expansion.

why_others_wrong.B: Acute appendicitis is an intra-abdominal cause of pain and fever and would not explain bilateral basal chest signs with hypoxia.
why_others_wrong.C: Chronic venous insufficiency causes long-standing leg oedema and skin changes, not acute postoperative hypoxia.
why_others_wrong.D: Renal artery stenosis causes hypertension and renal impairment, with no relation to reduced breath sounds or low saturation.
why_others_wrong.E: Deep-vein thrombosis alone causes leg signs; hypoxia would require pulmonary embolism, which does not typically reduce basal breath sounds bilaterally.

exam_trap: Option E tempts because DVT is a common postoperative complication, but DVT alone causes leg signs; bilateral basal reduced breath sounds with hypoxia indicate atelectasis.
takeaway: Pain + shallow breathing + reduced FRC → atelectasis risk.
source: Principles and Practice of Surgery, 7th ed.
thinking: After major abdominal surgery ↓ low oxygen saturation ↓ reduced breath sounds at both bases ↓ pain and shallow breathing reduce FRC ↓ Atelectasis
pearl: Atelectasis is the commonest early postoperative pulmonary complication; physiotherapy, incentive spirometry, sitting upright and adequate analgesia help re-expand the collapsed lung.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Surgical principles: postoperative delirium
stem: An older patient becomes acutely disorientated and fluctuating several days after surgery. What is the most appropriate initial approach?

options.B: Recognise possible delirium and search for reversible precipitants
options.D: Ignore the change because delirium is inevitable

correct_answer: B. Recognise possible delirium and search for reversible precipitants
why_correct: Delirium is an acute fluctuating disturbance in attention and cognition. Postoperative precipitants include infection, pain, medications, dehydration, hypoxia, metabolic abnormalities and sleep disruption.

why_others_wrong.A: An acute fluctuating change after surgery suggests delirium, whereas dementia is a gradual, persistent decline that should not be assumed.
why_others_wrong.C: Psychosis should not be diagnosed before excluding delirium, which explains acute fluctuating disorientation in an older postoperative patient.
why_others_wrong.D: Delirium is common but not inevitable, and it often has treatable precipitants that require prompt assessment.
why_others_wrong.E: Sedatives given without assessment can worsen delirium and mask its underlying cause.

exam_trap: Option A tempts in an older patient, but acute fluctuating confusion after surgery suggests delirium; dementia is a gradual, persistent decline and should not be assumed.
takeaway: Delirium is a syndrome: find the precipitant.
source: Principles and Practice of Surgery, 7th ed.
thinking: Older patient after surgery ↓ acute disorientation that fluctuates ↓ consistent with delirium ↓ search for infection, drugs, pain, hypoxia, retention and electrolyte disturbance ↓ Recognise possible delirium and search for reversible precipitants
pearl: Non-drug measures such as reorientation, glasses and hearing aids, sleep hygiene, hydration and mobilisation are first line in delirium; sedatives are reserved for distress or risk to safety.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Surgical principles: urinary retention
stem: A patient develops inability to pass urine after pelvic surgery. Which mechanism is most relevant?

options.A: Pelvic autonomic dysfunction affecting bladder emptying

correct_answer: A. Pelvic autonomic dysfunction affecting bladder emptying
why_correct: Pelvic surgery can affect autonomic pathways involved in bladder function, contributing to postoperative urinary retention.

why_others_wrong.B: Gastric acid secretion has no role in bladder emptying and does not explain postoperative urinary retention.
why_others_wrong.C: A visual pathway injury would affect sight, not the pelvic autonomic nerves controlling micturition.
why_others_wrong.D: Pulmonary compliance relates to lung mechanics and has no bearing on the ability to pass urine.
why_others_wrong.E: Splenic enlargement is an upper abdominal finding unrelated to pelvic surgery or bladder function.

exam_trap: Candidates may attribute retention after pelvic surgery only to opioids or pain, but traction or injury to the pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2-S4) can directly impair detrusor contraction and bladder emptying.
takeaway: Postoperative urinary retention has multiple causes; pelvic autonomic injury is one important surgical cause.
source: Principles and Practice of Surgery, 7th ed.
thinking: Pelvic surgery ↓ pelvic splanchnic parasympathetic nerves S2-S4 drive detrusor contraction ↓ operative injury or traction impairs bladder emptying ↓ Pelvic autonomic dysfunction affecting bladder emptying
pearl: The pelvic autonomic nerves are at risk during total mesorectal excision for rectal cancer, which is why nerve-preserving technique is important for postoperative urinary and sexual function.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Surgical principles: pressure injury prevention
stem: A bedbound postoperative patient is at high risk of pressure injury. Which intervention is most appropriate?

options.B: Massage directly over an established pressure ulcer
options.C: Keeping the patient continuously in one position

correct_answer: A. Regular repositioning and pressure redistribution
why_correct: Prevention involves pressure redistribution, regular repositioning according to individual risk, skin assessment and attention to nutrition and moisture.

why_others_wrong.B: Massaging over an established pressure ulcer can cause further tissue damage and is not recommended.
why_others_wrong.C: Keeping the patient in one position sustains pressure on the same areas, which is how pressure injuries develop.
why_others_wrong.D: Good nutrition supports tissue integrity, so reducing intake would increase rather than lower pressure injury risk.
why_others_wrong.E: Regular skin inspection identifies early pressure damage and is a core part of prevention.

exam_trap: Option B may tempt candidates who think massage improves circulation, but massaging pressure-damaged skin causes further tissue injury and is not recommended.
takeaway: Pressure relief is a continuous process, not a single intervention.
source: NICE CG179, Pressure ulcers: prevention and management.
thinking: Bedbound postoperative patient ↓ high pressure injury risk ↓ sustained pressure over bony prominences causes ischaemia ↓ Regular repositioning and pressure redistribution
pearl: Moisture from incontinence or sweat increases skin breakdown, so skin care and barrier products are part of pressure injury prevention along with repositioning and support surfaces.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Surgical principles: informed consent
stem: A competent adult is offered an elective operation and asks about significant risks and reasonable alternative treatments before deciding. What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Withhold risks to avoid causing anxiety
options.B: Provide information about material risks and reasonable alternatives so the patient can make an informed decision
options.C: Obtain consent from a relative instead
options.D: Proceed because the operation is recommended by the surgeon
options.E: Provide only information about the surgeon's preferred option

correct_answer: B. Provide information about material risks and reasonable alternatives so the patient can make an informed decision
why_correct: Valid consent requires appropriate information and voluntary decision-making by a patient with capacity. Material risks and reasonable alternatives should be discussed in a way that supports the patient's decision.

why_others_wrong.A: Withholding material risks prevents an informed decision and is not acceptable simply to avoid anxiety.
why_others_wrong.C: A competent adult makes their own decision; a relative cannot give consent on their behalf.
why_others_wrong.D: A surgeon's recommendation does not replace the patient's informed and voluntary decision.
why_others_wrong.E: Discussing only the preferred option omits reasonable alternatives, including no treatment, that the patient needs to know about.

exam_trap: Option D tempts because surgeons make recommendations, but a recommendation does not replace the patient's informed and voluntary decision about material risks and alternatives.
takeaway: Capacity + information + voluntariness = core elements of valid consent.
source: GMC, Decision making and consent, current guidance.
thinking: Competent adult considering elective surgery ↓ asks about significant risks and alternatives ↓ valid consent needs material risks and reasonable alternatives disclosed ↓ Provide information about material risks and reasonable alternatives so the patient can make an informed decision
pearl: Material risk is judged by what a reasonable person in the patient's position, or this particular patient, would consider significant, and alternatives include the option of no treatment.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Applied Physiology (Respiratory)
stem: A 60-year-old man has a PaO2 of 7.5 kPa and a PaCO2 of 6.5 kPa on arterial blood gas. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
why_correct: Type 2 respiratory failure is defined as PaO2 < 8 kPa with PaCO2 > 6 kPa.

why_others_wrong.A: Type 1 respiratory failure is defined by hypoxaemia with a normal or low PaCO2, but here PaCO2 is elevated at 6.5 kPa, so this pattern does not fit.
why_others_wrong.C: A PaCO2 of 6.5 kPa is above the normal range, so this cannot be interpreted as a normal blood gas.
why_others_wrong.D: A primary metabolic acidosis is a non-respiratory acid-base disturbance and is not what these arterial blood gas values (hypoxaemia with hypercapnia) directly indicate.
why_others_wrong.E: Respiratory alkalosis results from hyperventilation with a low PaCO2, the opposite of the elevated PaCO2 seen here.

exam_trap: Candidates who focus only on the low PaO2 choose type 1 respiratory failure, but the raised PaCO2 of 6.5 kPa makes this type 2 failure.
takeaway: Type 1 = low O2, normal/low CO2. Type 2 = low O2, high CO2.
thinking: PaO2 7.5 kPa is below 8 kPa, so the patient is in respiratory failure ↓ PaCO2 6.5 kPa is above 6 kPa, so there is hypercapnia ↓ hypoxaemia plus hypercapnia indicates ventilatory failure ↓ Type 2 respiratory failure
pearl: In patients at risk of hypercapnic failure, controlled oxygen is titrated to a lower target saturation and non-invasive ventilation is considered if respiratory acidosis persists despite treatment.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Applied Pathology (Lung Cancer)
stem: A 60-year-old smoker has a lung mass. Biopsy shows malignant cells with keratin pearls and intercellular bridges. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Keratin pearls and intercellular bridges are characteristic of squamous cell carcinoma. It is strongly associated with smoking and typically arises centrally in the lung.

why_others_wrong.A: Adenocarcinoma shows glandular differentiation and mucin production, usually in a peripheral mass, not keratin pearls or intercellular bridges.
why_others_wrong.C: Small cell carcinoma consists of small cells with scant cytoplasm, nuclear moulding and neuroendocrine markers, without keratinisation.
why_others_wrong.D: Large cell carcinoma is an undifferentiated diagnosis of exclusion lacking squamous features such as keratin pearls.
why_others_wrong.E: Mesothelioma is a pleural tumour associated with asbestos, not a lung mass showing keratinisation and intercellular bridges.

exam_trap: Adenocarcinoma is chosen because it is the commonest lung cancer overall, but it forms glands and mucin, usually peripherally; keratin pearls and intercellular bridges indicate squamous carcinoma.
takeaway: Keratin pearls + intercellular bridges = squamous cell carcinoma. Central location.
thinking: Smoker with a lung mass ↓ keratin pearls and intercellular bridges on biopsy ↓ these define squamous differentiation ↓ Squamous cell carcinoma
pearl: Lung squamous cell carcinoma tends to arise centrally from large bronchi, may cavitate, and is the lung cancer classically linked to PTHrP-mediated hypercalcaemia.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Perioperative Management (Hypothermia)
stem: A 75-year-old woman undergoes emergency laparotomy. Intraoperatively, her core temperature drops to 34.5°C. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.B: Active warming with forced air blankets and warmed fluids

correct_answer: B. Active warming with forced air blankets and warmed fluids
why_correct: Perioperative hypothermia increases the risk of surgical site infection, coagulopathy, cardiac events, and prolonged recovery. Active warming with forced air blankets and warmed intravenous fluids is standard management.

why_others_wrong.A: Deferring warming allows hypothermia to worsen during surgery, increasing coagulopathy, infection and cardiac risk; it should be corrected intraoperatively.
why_others_wrong.C: Vasopressors support blood pressure but do not treat hypothermia and may worsen peripheral perfusion.
why_others_wrong.D: Deeper anaesthesia increases vasodilatation and impairs thermoregulation, which would worsen heat loss.
why_others_wrong.E: A core temperature of 34.5°C is significant hypothermia requiring active treatment, not observation.

exam_trap: Option A tempts as a way to finish the operation quickly, but deferring warming lets hypothermia worsen intraoperatively, increasing coagulopathy and infection risk.
takeaway: Perioperative hypothermia = active warming. Maintain normothermia throughout surgery.
thinking: Emergency laparotomy in an older woman ↓ core temperature 34.5 degrees Celsius ↓ hypothermia worsens coagulopathy, infection and cardiac risk ↓ warm actively during surgery ↓ Active warming with forced air blankets and warmed fluids
pearl: Emergency laparotomy patients are at particular risk of hypothermia because of open body cavities, cold irrigation and large fluid volumes, so warming should start from induction rather than after a fall in temperature.

subject: Trauma & orthopaedics
title: Trauma Management (Femoral Fracture)
stem: A 30-year-old motorcyclist has an open fracture of the right femur. He is haemodynamically stable. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?

options.B: Application of traction splint, antibiotics, and tetanus prophylaxis

correct_answer: B. Application of traction splint, antibiotics, and tetanus prophylaxis
why_correct: Initial management of an open fracture includes haemorrhage control, traction splinting, antibiotics, and tetanus prophylaxis.

why_others_wrong.A: Immediate nailing is not the first step; antibiotics, splinting and wound care come first, with debridement and fixation planned together in theatre.
why_others_wrong.C: External fixation is a damage-control option applied in theatre after debridement, not the initial emergency management of an open femoral fracture.
why_others_wrong.D: A plaster cast cannot control a femoral shaft fracture and would cover and compress the open wound.
why_others_wrong.E: Observation leaves the wound unprotected and delays antibiotics and tetanus cover, raising the risk of deep infection.

exam_trap: Candidates choose immediate intramedullary nailing as definitive treatment, but initial management is splintage, antibiotics and tetanus cover, with debridement and fixation later in theatre.
takeaway: Open fracture = antibiotics + tetanus + splint. Definitive fixation later.
thinking: Open femoral fracture, stable patient ↓ initial care before theatre ↓ control bleeding, splint to align and relieve pain ↓ IV antibiotics and tetanus prophylaxis early ↓ Application of traction splint, antibiotics, and tetanus prophylaxis
pearl: Closed femoral shaft fractures can lose a litre or more of blood into the thigh, so even a stable patient needs close monitoring; traction splinting reduces bleeding and pain by restoring length.

subject: Pharmacology
title: Pharmacology (Statins)
stem: A 60-year-old man is started on simvastatin for hyperlipidaemia. He presents with muscle pain and weakness. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial investigation?
why_correct: Statin-induced myopathy is a recognised adverse effect, so creatine kinase (CK) should be checked. The BNF advises stopping the statin if CK is more than five times the upper limit of normal or if muscle symptoms are severe.

why_others_wrong.A: Serum calcium is not the relevant investigation for statin-associated muscle symptoms; the recognised biochemical marker of statin myopathy is creatine kinase, reflecting muscle breakdown, not calcium disturbance.
why_others_wrong.C: Hypothyroidism predisposes to statin myopathy and is worth excluding, but creatine kinase is the first test for suspected statin-induced muscle injury.
why_others_wrong.D: Liver function tests are relevant to statin therapy (hepatotoxicity monitoring) but do not investigate muscle pain and weakness, which is assessed with creatine kinase.
why_others_wrong.E: Serum potassium is not the investigation used to assess statin-associated myopathy; muscle breakdown from statin toxicity is detected by measuring creatine kinase, not electrolytes.

exam_trap: Liver function tests are chosen because they are routinely monitored on statins, but they assess hepatotoxicity; muscle pain and weakness on a statin is investigated first with creatine kinase.
takeaway: Statin + muscle pain = check CK. Stop if CK >5x normal (current UK guidance).
thinking: Simvastatin recently started ↓ new muscle pain and weakness ↓ statin-associated myopathy ↓ muscle breakdown releases creatine kinase ↓ Creatine kinase
pearl: Statin myopathy risk rises with high doses and CYP3A4 inhibitors such as clarithromycin; rhabdomyolysis should be suspected if CK is markedly raised with dark urine or acute kidney injury.

subject: Microbiology & surgical infection
title: Microbiology (Necrotising Fasciitis)
stem: A 55-year-old man with diabetes presents with a rapidly spreading, painful, erythematous swelling of the leg, crepitus, and systemic toxicity. What is the most appropriate management?

options.B: Urgent surgical debridement and broad-spectrum antibiotics

correct_answer: B. Urgent surgical debridement and broad-spectrum antibiotics
why_correct: Necrotising fasciitis is a surgical emergency. Urgent surgical debridement is the cornerstone of treatment, along with broad-spectrum antibiotics. Delay increases mortality.

why_others_wrong.A: Antibiotics alone cannot penetrate necrotic, poorly perfused tissue; without urgent debridement mortality from necrotising fasciitis rises.
why_others_wrong.C: Elevation and compression may suit simple cellulitis or oedema but would delay life-saving surgery for necrotising infection.
why_others_wrong.D: Oral antibiotics are inadequate for a systemically toxic patient with necrotising infection, who needs intravenous therapy and surgery.
why_others_wrong.E: Incision and drainage treats a localised abscess, whereas necrotising fasciitis needs wide excision of all necrotic tissue.

exam_trap: Intravenous antibiotics alone is the classic wrong answer; antibiotics cannot reach necrotic, poorly perfused fascia, so delaying debridement for a trial of antibiotics increases mortality.
takeaway: Necrotising fasciitis = urgent debridement + broad-spectrum antibiotics. Time is tissue.
thinking: Diabetic patient with rapidly spreading painful leg swelling ↓ crepitus and systemic toxicity ↓ necrotising fasciitis is a surgical emergency ↓ debridement plus broad-spectrum antibiotics ↓ Urgent surgical debridement and broad-spectrum antibiotics
pearl: A planned return to theatre for a second look is usual, as further debridement is often needed until no necrotic tissue remains.

subject: Acute abdomen & GI surgery
title: Surgical Oncology (Gastric Cancer)
stem: A 65-year-old man has a gastric adenocarcinoma. Staging shows cT2 N0 M0 and he is fit for surgery and chemotherapy. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Perioperative chemotherapy with gastrectomy and D2 lymphadenectomy

correct_answer: A. Perioperative chemotherapy with gastrectomy and D2 lymphadenectomy
why_correct: T2 N0 M0 is not early gastric cancer. Early gastric cancer is confined to the mucosa or submucosa (T1), whatever the nodal status. For resectable cT2 or higher, or node-positive, disease in fit patients, ESMO (2022) guidance and UK practice favour perioperative chemotherapy (FLOT) with gastrectomy, and NICE NG83 advises considering D2 lymphadenectomy at curative gastrectomy. Resection alone is reserved for T1 N0 disease, and selected T1a cancers can be removed endoscopically.

why_others_wrong.B: Gastrectomy alone undertreats resectable cT2 disease; UK and European guidance supports perioperative chemotherapy in fit patients from cT2 upwards.
why_others_wrong.C: Palliative care is inappropriate for a fit patient with non-metastatic, resectable cT2 N0 M0 disease who can be treated with curative intent.
why_others_wrong.D: Radiotherapy alone is not a curative treatment for resectable gastric adenocarcinoma, which requires gastrectomy with perioperative chemotherapy.
why_others_wrong.E: Observation would allow a potentially curable cT2 N0 M0 gastric cancer to progress in a patient fit for treatment.

exam_trap: Do not call T2 disease early gastric cancer: early means T1 (mucosa or submucosa), regardless of nodes. From cT2 upwards, surgery alone undertreats.
takeaway: Gastric adenocarcinoma: T1 = early (endoscopic resection or surgery). Resectable cT2+ or N+ = perioperative chemotherapy (FLOT) plus gastrectomy with D2 lymphadenectomy.
source: ESMO Gastric Cancer Clinical Practice Guideline (2022); NICE NG83 Oesophago-gastric cancer: assessment and management in adults.
thinking: Gastric adenocarcinoma cT2 N0 M0 ↓ T2 is beyond early gastric cancer ↓ resectable and fit for treatment ↓ perioperative chemotherapy plus curative surgery ↓ Perioperative chemotherapy with gastrectomy and D2 lymphadenectomy
pearl: Staging laparoscopy is advised before curative treatment of locally advanced gastric cancer because CT can miss peritoneal metastases, which would change the intent of treatment.

subject: Vascular & fracture complications
title: Vascular Surgery (Acute Limb Ischaemia)
stem: A 70-year-old man presents with acute limb ischaemia. He has a cold, pulseless leg with sensory loss confined to the toes and no muscle weakness. What is the most appropriate classification?
why_correct: Category IIa (marginally threatened) is defined by minimal sensory loss confined to the toes, or none, with no muscle weakness. The limb is salvageable if promptly revascularised.

why_others_wrong.A: Category I limbs are viable with no sensory loss or muscle weakness, whereas this patient already has sensory loss in the toes.
why_others_wrong.C: Category IIb requires sensory loss beyond the toes with rest pain and mild to moderate muscle weakness, and this patient has no weakness.
why_others_wrong.D: Category III involves profound sensory loss with paralysis and inaudible arterial and venous Doppler signals, which is far beyond this presentation.
why_others_wrong.E: Chronic limb-threatening ischaemia describes rest pain or tissue loss from longstanding arterial disease, not an acute presentation graded by the Rutherford acute limb ischaemia categories.

exam_trap: Candidates choose IIb because any sensory loss sounds serious, but IIb requires sensory loss beyond the toes or muscle weakness; toe-only sensory loss without weakness is IIa.
takeaway: Sensory loss confined to toes, no weakness = IIa (urgent). Sensory loss beyond toes or mild to moderate weakness = IIb (immediate). Anaesthesia with paralysis = III (irreversible).
thinking: Acute limb ischaemia ↓ sensory loss confined to the toes ↓ no muscle weakness ↓ Rutherford category IIa definition ↓ Category IIa (marginally threatened)
pearl: Category IIa limbs need prompt revascularisation, whereas IIb limbs need immediate revascularisation; category III limbs with paralysis and profound sensory loss usually require primary amputation.

subject: Paediatric surgery
title: Paediatric Surgery (Hypospadias)
stem: A 1-year-old boy has hypospadias. The urethral meatus is located at the penoscrotal junction. What is the most appropriate management?
why_correct: Hypospadias requires surgical correction (urethroplasty) to bring the meatus to the tip of the glans and correct chordee. Surgery is typically performed between 6 and 18 months of age.

why_others_wrong.A: Circumcision is contraindicated because the foreskin is preserved as tissue for the urethral reconstruction, and it does not relocate the meatus.
why_others_wrong.C: Observation is not appropriate for proximal penoscrotal hypospadias, which causes functional problems with voiding and chordee and needs surgical repair.
why_others_wrong.D: Preoperative androgen stimulation may be used to enlarge a small glans before repair, but it is an adjunct and does not correct the meatal position or chordee.
why_others_wrong.E: Meatotomy widens a stenosed meatus in its existing position and cannot bring a penoscrotal opening to the tip of the glans.

exam_trap: Candidates may choose circumcision (A), but the foreskin is preserved as tissue for the urethral repair, and circumcision does nothing to move the meatus.
takeaway: Hypospadias = urethroplasty; do not circumcise.
thinking: 1-year-old boy with hypospadias ↓ meatus at the penoscrotal junction, a proximal form ↓ causes voiding problems and is often associated with chordee ↓ needs surgical reconstruction, usually in the 6 to 18 month window ↓ Urethroplasty
pearl: Proximal hypospadias combined with an undescended testis should prompt assessment for a disorder of sex development before any surgery is planned.

subject: Anatomy
title: Applied Anatomy (Lower Limb)
stem: A 45-year-old man has a penetrating wound to the popliteal fossa. Of the main neurovascular contents of the popliteal fossa, which lies most superficially?
why_correct: Within the popliteal fossa the main neurovascular contents lie, from superficial to deep: tibial nerve, popliteal vein, popliteal artery. The small saphenous vein is not one of these contents: it runs in the roof, then pierces the deep fascia to drain into the popliteal vein. The common peroneal (common fibular) nerve lies separately along the lateral border, following the biceps femoris tendon.

why_others_wrong.A: The popliteal artery is the deepest of the three central neurovascular structures, lying closest to the femur and knee joint, not the most superficial.
why_others_wrong.B: The popliteal vein lies between the tibial nerve and artery in the superficial-to-deep order, making it intermediate rather than the most superficial structure.
why_others_wrong.D: The common peroneal (fibular) nerve runs along the lateral border of the fossa following biceps femoris, separate from the central superficial-to-deep neurovascular sequence in which the tibial nerve is most superficial.
why_others_wrong.E: The small saphenous vein travels in the roof of the fossa before piercing deep fascia to join the popliteal vein; it is not considered one of the central neurovascular contents at all.

exam_trap: The small saphenous vein lies in the roof, not among the contents, and the common peroneal nerve runs along the lateral border. Of the central contents, the tibial nerve is most superficial and the popliteal artery deepest.
takeaway: Popliteal fossa contents, superficial to deep: tibial nerve, popliteal vein, popliteal artery (nerve, vein, artery). Common peroneal nerve at the lateral border.
thinking: Penetrating wound to the posterior knee ↓ central contents superficial to deep: nerve, vein, artery ↓ small saphenous vein is in the roof and common peroneal nerve at the lateral border ↓ Tibial nerve
pearl: Penetrating popliteal injuries carry a high risk of limb loss from arterial damage; hard signs such as pulsatile bleeding, expanding haematoma or absent distal pulses need immediate surgical exploration.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Applied Pathology (Renal)
stem: A 60-year-old man has haematuria and a rapid decline in renal function over a few weeks. Renal biopsy shows crescents in most glomeruli. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Crescents in the glomeruli are characteristic of crescentic (rapidly progressive) glomerulonephritis. It is a medical emergency and requires urgent immunosuppression.

why_others_wrong.A: Minimal change disease shows essentially normal glomeruli on light microscopy with only foot-process effacement on electron microscopy, not crescent formation.
why_others_wrong.B: Membranous nephropathy is characterised by diffuse capillary wall thickening from subepithelial immune deposits, not crescents.
why_others_wrong.D: Diabetic nephropathy classically shows nodular (Kimmelstiel-Wilson) glomerulosclerosis and basement membrane thickening, not crescent formation.
why_others_wrong.E: Amyloidosis shows glomerular deposition of amorphous, Congo red-positive material, not cellular crescents.

exam_trap: Membranous nephropathy is a common adult glomerular disease, but it causes nephrotic syndrome with capillary wall thickening, not crescents with rapidly falling function.
takeaway: Crescents on biopsy = crescentic (rapidly progressive) GN → urgent immunosuppression.
thinking: Haematuria with renal function falling over weeks ↓ rapidly progressive renal failure ↓ crescents in most glomeruli ↓ Crescentic glomerulonephritis
pearl: Crescentic glomerulonephritis is investigated urgently with anti-GBM antibodies, ANCA and complement, because causes include anti-GBM disease, ANCA vasculitis and immune-complex disease.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Perioperative Management (Nutrition)
stem: A 65-year-old man is malnourished before major surgery and cannot meet his nutritional needs orally despite supplements. His gut is functional. Which of the following is the most appropriate nutritional support?
why_correct: When a malnourished patient cannot meet needs orally and the gut is functional, enteral nutrition is preferred over parenteral nutrition because it maintains gut integrity, has fewer infective complications and costs less.

why_others_wrong.A: An oral diet alone has already failed to prevent malnutrition in this patient, so additional nutritional support is needed before major surgery.
why_others_wrong.C: Parenteral nutrition is reserved for patients whose gut is non-functional or inaccessible and carries line sepsis and metabolic risks.
why_others_wrong.D: Malnutrition increases postoperative complications, so leaving it untreated before major surgery is inappropriate.
why_others_wrong.E: Vitamin supplements alone do not provide the energy and protein needed to correct malnutrition.

exam_trap: Option C tempts as a guaranteed way to deliver nutrition, but parenteral nutrition is reserved for a non-functional or inaccessible gut and carries line sepsis risk.
takeaway: Malnutrition + functional gut = enteral nutrition.
thinking: Malnourished before major surgery ↓ oral supplements insufficient ↓ gut is functioning ↓ use tube feeding into the gut ↓ Enteral nutrition (NG or jejunostomy)
pearl: Preoperative nutritional support for 7-14 days in severely malnourished patients can reduce postoperative complications, and surgery may be scheduled to allow this when safe.

subject: Neurosurgery
title: Trauma Management (Neurotrauma)
stem: A 40-year-old man has a GCS of 6 after a head injury. He is intubated and ventilated. Which of the following is the target PaCO2 to maintain?
why_correct: In severe traumatic brain injury the ventilated patient is kept at a low-normal PaCO2 (4.5–5.0 kPa), avoiding both hypercapnia, which dilates cerebral vessels and raises ICP, and hyperventilation, which causes cerebral ischaemia.

why_others_wrong.A: A PaCO2 of 3.0 to 3.5 kPa is marked hyperventilation, causing cerebral vasoconstriction and ischaemia, reserved only briefly for impending herniation.
why_others_wrong.C: A PaCO2 of 5.5 to 6.0 kPa sits at the upper end of normal, risking cerebral vasodilatation and higher intracranial pressure in a severely injured brain.
why_others_wrong.D: A PaCO2 of 6.5 to 7.0 kPa is hypercapnia, causing cerebral vasodilatation that raises cerebral blood volume and intracranial pressure.
why_others_wrong.E: A PaCO2 of 7.5 to 8.0 kPa is significant hypercapnia, which would markedly increase cerebral blood volume and intracranial pressure after head injury.

exam_trap: Candidates pick 3.0–3.5 kPa (A) believing hyperventilation protects the brain, but sustained hypocapnia causes cerebral ischaemia and is reserved for brief rescue of impending herniation.
takeaway: Ventilated severe head injury → target low-normal PaCO2 (4.5–5.0 kPa); avoid both hypercapnia and sustained hyperventilation.
thinking: Severe head injury, GCS 6, intubated and ventilated ↓ PaCO2 controls cerebral vessel calibre ↓ hypercapnia dilates vessels and raises ICP, while hypocapnia constricts them and risks ischaemia ↓ aim for low-normal PaCO2 ↓ 4.5–5.0 kPa
pearl: Other neuroprotective measures after severe head injury include avoiding hypoxia and hypotension, nursing head-up at about 30 degrees, and avoiding tight endotracheal tube ties that impede jugular venous drainage.

subject: Pharmacology
title: Pharmacology (Antihypertensives)
stem: A 60-year-old man is started on ramipril for hypertension. Which of the following adverse effects is most characteristic?
why_correct: ACE inhibitors such as ramipril characteristically cause a persistent dry cough because ACE also breaks down bradykinin, which accumulates in the airway when ACE is inhibited.

why_others_wrong.B: ACE inhibitors like ramipril do not typically cause bradycardia; this is more characteristic of drugs affecting cardiac conduction such as beta-blockers or certain calcium-channel blockers.
why_others_wrong.C: Peripheral oedema is a recognised adverse effect of calcium-channel blockers such as amlodipine, not a characteristic effect of ACE inhibitors like ramipril.
why_others_wrong.D: ACE inhibitors reduce aldosterone and tend to raise, not lower, serum potassium; hypokalaemia is more typical of thiazide and loop diuretics.
why_others_wrong.E: Gingival hyperplasia is associated with calcium-channel blockers such as nifedipine, and with phenytoin and ciclosporin, not with ACE inhibitors.

exam_trap: Peripheral oedema is chosen by candidates who confuse antihypertensive classes, but ankle oedema is typical of dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers; ACE inhibitors characteristically cause a dry cough.
takeaway: ACE inhibitors = dry cough (most characteristic) + hyperkalaemia + angioedema (rarer, more serious).
thinking: Ramipril is an ACE inhibitor ↓ ACE also breaks down bradykinin ↓ bradykinin accumulates in the airway ↓ a persistent dry cough is the characteristic adverse effect ↓ Dry cough
pearl: If ACE inhibitor cough is intolerable, an angiotensin II receptor blocker is the usual switch because it does not raise bradykinin; check renal function and potassium after starting either drug.

subject: Microbiology & surgical infection
title: Microbiology (Surgical Prophylaxis)
stem: A 55-year-old man is scheduled for elective hip replacement. Which of the following is the most appropriate antibiotic prophylaxis?

options.B: Intravenous flucloxacillin (with gentamicin if high risk)

correct_answer: B. Intravenous flucloxacillin (with gentamicin if high risk)
why_correct: Joint replacement is clean surgery with a prosthesis, so NICE NG125 recommends antibiotic prophylaxis: a single intravenous dose given before the incision (at induction). It should cover Staphylococcus aureus and streptococci. In UK practice, following the BNF and local policy, this is typically intravenous flucloxacillin, with gentamicin added for higher-risk patients. A glycopeptide such as teicoplanin is used in penicillin allergy or known MRSA colonisation.

why_others_wrong.A: Oral amoxicillin does not achieve reliable tissue levels at incision and lacks cover against beta-lactamase-producing Staphylococcus aureus.
why_others_wrong.C: Oral ciprofloxacin has weak staphylococcal and streptococcal activity and is not recommended for arthroplasty prophylaxis.
why_others_wrong.D: Metronidazole covers anaerobes and is used in colorectal surgery, but it has no useful activity against Staphylococcus aureus.
why_others_wrong.E: Joint replacement involves implanting a prosthesis, so NICE recommends prophylaxis even though it is clean surgery.

exam_trap: No prophylaxis tempts because hip replacement is clean surgery, but an implanted prosthesis makes prophylaxis essential; metronidazole is also wrong, as it lacks staphylococcal activity.
takeaway: Joint replacement prophylaxis: single IV dose at induction covering S. aureus, typically flucloxacillin (plus gentamicin if high risk); teicoplanin if penicillin-allergic or MRSA.
thinking: Elective hip replacement ↓ clean surgery but with a prosthetic implant, so prophylaxis is indicated ↓ main pathogens are Staphylococcus aureus and streptococci ↓ single intravenous dose at induction ↓ Intravenous flucloxacillin (with gentamicin if high risk)
pearl: Because prosthetic joint infection is devastating, arthroplasty is also performed in laminar-flow theatres, and known MRSA carriers are decolonised and given glycopeptide prophylaxis.

subject: Hepatobiliary surgery
title: Surgical Oncology (Pancreatic Cancer)
stem: A fit 65-year-old man has a pancreatic head adenocarcinoma with no distant metastases. CT shows encasement of the superior mesenteric artery. What is the most appropriate initial management?
correct_answer: C. Systemic combination chemotherapy with re-staging
why_correct: Superior mesenteric artery encasement without distant metastases indicates locally advanced, unresectable disease. For fit patients NICE NG85 recommends systemic combination chemotherapy (for example FOLFIRINOX), with re-staging to identify the minority who may later become resectable.

why_others_wrong.A: SMA encasement makes the tumour locally advanced and not resectable upfront, so a Whipple procedure at this stage would not achieve clear margins.
why_others_wrong.B: Best supportive care alone would deny a fit patient the systemic combination chemotherapy that NICE recommends for locally advanced disease, which can control the tumour and occasionally allow later resection.
why_others_wrong.D: Radiotherapy alone is not standard first-line treatment for locally advanced pancreatic cancer; systemic combination chemotherapy is the mainstay, with chemoradiation considered afterwards.
why_others_wrong.E: Observation denies a fit patient with non-metastatic disease the systemic chemotherapy that can control disease and occasionally allow later resection.

exam_trap: Arterial encasement means the tumour is not resectable upfront, but with no distant metastases it is locally advanced rather than metastatic; a fit patient should be offered systemic combination chemotherapy with re-staging, not supportive care alone.
takeaway: Pancreatic cancer + arterial encasement + no metastases = locally advanced → systemic combination chemotherapy with re-staging in fit patients.
source: NICE NG85, Pancreatic cancer in adults: diagnosis and management.
thinking: Pancreatic head adenocarcinoma with no distant metastases ↓ SMA encasement means arterial involvement, so not resectable upfront ↓ locally advanced disease in a fit patient ↓ Systemic combination chemotherapy with re-staging
pearl: Involvement of the superior mesenteric or portal vein may still be resectable with venous reconstruction, whereas encasement of the SMA, coeliac axis or common hepatic artery usually defines locally advanced, unresectable disease.

subject: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care
title: Vascular Surgery (Carotid Body Tumour)
stem: A 45-year-old woman has a pulsatile neck mass at the carotid bifurcation. Imaging shows a highly vascular tumour. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Carotid body tumours are highly vascular, pulsatile masses at the carotid bifurcation. They are paragangliomas.

why_others_wrong.A: A carotid aneurysm is an expansile pulsatile mass but not a highly vascular tumour, and imaging shows dilatation of the artery itself.
why_others_wrong.C: A branchial cyst is a fluctuant, non-pulsatile lesion anterior to sternocleidomastoid and appears cystic rather than highly vascular.
why_others_wrong.D: Lymphoma causes rubbery, often multiple, lymphadenopathy and is not a highly vascular mass splaying the carotid bifurcation.
why_others_wrong.E: A thyroid nodule moves with swallowing and lies in the thyroid, not at the carotid bifurcation.

exam_trap: Candidates choose carotid aneurysm because the mass is pulsatile, but imaging shows a vascular tumour at the bifurcation; biopsy of a carotid body tumour risks haemorrhage.
takeaway: Pulsatile neck mass at carotid bifurcation = carotid body tumour. Do NOT biopsy.
thinking: Pulsatile mass at carotid bifurcation ↓ highly vascular tumour ↓ splays the internal and external carotid arteries ↓ paraganglioma of the carotid body ↓ Carotid body tumour
pearl: Carotid body tumours move side to side but not vertically, and excision risks injury to the vagus, hypoglossal and other lower cranial nerves.

subject: Paediatric surgery
title: Paediatric Surgery (Necrotising Enterocolitis)
stem: A 2-week-old premature neonate develops abdominal distension, bilious aspirates, and bloody stools. Abdominal X-ray shows pneumatosis intestinalis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Necrotising enterocolitis (NEC) classically presents in premature neonates with abdominal distension, bilious aspirates, bloody stools, and pneumatosis intestinalis on X-ray.

why_others_wrong.A: Hirschsprung disease presents with delayed meconium and distension, and enterocolitis may complicate it, but pneumatosis in a premature neonate points to NEC.
why_others_wrong.C: Meconium ileus is an obstruction of the terminal ileum by inspissated meconium, typically in cystic fibrosis, presenting in the first days rather than with bloody stools and pneumatosis.
why_others_wrong.D: Intussusception is uncommon in premature neonates and causes colic and redcurrant jelly stool without intramural gas on the radiograph.
why_others_wrong.E: Malrotation with volvulus can cause bilious vomiting and bloody stool, but intramural gas in a premature two-week-old is the hallmark of NEC.

exam_trap: Pneumatosis intestinalis in a sick preterm neonate is the radiological hallmark of NEC, though it is not strictly pathognomonic.
takeaway: Premature neonate + abdominal distension + bloody stools + pneumatosis = NEC.
thinking: Premature neonate aged 2 weeks ↓ abdominal distension, bilious aspirates and bloody stools ↓ pneumatosis intestinalis indicates gas within the bowel wall ↓ Necrotising enterocolitis
pearl: Initial treatment is medical with stopping feeds, gastric decompression, broad-spectrum antibiotics and parenteral nutrition; pneumoperitoneum or clinical deterioration indicates the need for surgery or a peritoneal drain.

subject: Anatomy
title: Applied Anatomy (Cranial Nerves)
stem: A 50-year-old man has a parotid tumour. During parotidectomy, which branch of the facial nerve is most at risk during dissection of the superficial lobe?
why_correct: The marginal mandibular branch is the facial nerve branch most often left weak after parotidectomy: it is thin, runs a long course along the lower border of the mandible and has few anastomoses with other branches, so injury is rarely compensated. It is also at risk during submandibular gland excision. Injury causes weakness of the lower lip.

why_others_wrong.A: The temporal branch is at greater risk during procedures involving the temporal region and temporalis fascia (e.g. temporal artery biopsy, some facelift dissections) rather than during standard superficial lobe parotidectomy dissection.
why_others_wrong.B: The zygomatic branch supplies orbicularis oculi and is at risk in more superior facial dissections, but it is not the branch classically emphasised as most vulnerable in parotidectomy.
why_others_wrong.C: The buccal branch runs across the cheek near the parotid duct and can be at risk, but it is not the branch most classically cited as being injured, unlike the marginal mandibular branch along the mandibular border.
why_others_wrong.E: The cervical branch descends into the neck below the mandible supplying platysma; it is a lesser concern compared with the marginal mandibular branch during superficial lobe dissection.

exam_trap: The temporal and buccal branches can also be injured, but the marginal mandibular branch has few anastomoses with other branches, so its injury most often gives visible weakness.
takeaway: Parotidectomy = marginal mandibular branch most at risk. Lower lip weakness.
thinking: Superficial parotidectomy for a parotid tumour ↓ facial nerve branches are identified and dissected through the gland ↓ the marginal mandibular branch runs along the lower border of the mandible with few cross-connections ↓ Marginal mandibular branch
pearl: The facial nerve trunk is found during parotidectomy using landmarks such as the tragal pointer, posterior belly of digastric and tympanomastoid suture; marginal mandibular weakness shows as lower lip asymmetry on smiling.

subject: Plastic surgery
title: Applied Pathology (Skin Cancer)
stem: A 70-year-old man has a pearly, nodular lesion on his face with telangiectasia and a rolled edge. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Basal cell carcinoma classically presents as a pearly, nodular lesion with telangiectasia and a rolled edge. It is the most common skin cancer and rarely metastasises but causes local tissue destruction.

why_others_wrong.A: Squamous cell carcinoma usually presents as a keratotic, crusted or ulcerated nodule, lacking the pearly rolled edge and telangiectasia described.
why_others_wrong.C: Melanoma is typically a pigmented lesion with irregular shape and colour, not a pearly nodule with telangiectasia and a rolled edge.
why_others_wrong.D: Actinic keratosis is a flat, rough, scaly patch on sun-damaged skin, not a pearly nodule with a rolled edge.
why_others_wrong.E: Keratoacanthoma grows rapidly over weeks into a dome-shaped nodule with a central keratin plug, rather than a pearly lesion with telangiectasia.

exam_trap: Squamous cell carcinoma presents as a keratotic, ulcerated lesion and can metastasise.
takeaway: Pearly nodule + telangiectasia + rolled edge = BCC. Locally invasive, rarely metastatic.
thinking: Older man with a facial (sun-exposed) lesion ↓ pearly nodule with telangiectasia ↓ rolled edge ↓ Basal cell carcinoma
pearl: Although BCC rarely metastasises, neglected lesions near the eye, nose or ear can invade deeply into cartilage, bone and orbit, so periocular lesions merit early specialist excision.

subject: Vascular & fracture complications
title: Perioperative Management (DVT Prophylaxis)
stem: A 60-year-old man undergoes major abdominal surgery. He has a history of DVT. Which of the following is the most appropriate VTE prophylaxis?
correct_answer: B. LMWH and intermittent pneumatic compression
why_correct: Previous DVT plus major abdominal surgery puts him at high VTE risk, so LMWH is indicated, and adding intermittent pneumatic compression gives the most complete protection of the options listed.

why_others_wrong.A: Early mobilisation is encouraged but on its own is inadequate prophylaxis after major abdominal surgery in a patient with previous DVT.
why_others_wrong.C: Aspirin alone is not recommended by NICE for VTE prophylaxis after major abdominal surgery and gives inadequate protection in a high-risk patient.
why_others_wrong.D: Withholding prophylaxis in a patient with previous DVT having major abdominal surgery leaves a high VTE risk untreated and is not appropriate.
why_others_wrong.E: Warfarin is not used for routine perioperative VTE prophylaxis because of slow onset, variable dosing, bleeding risk and INR monitoring needs.

exam_trap: Aspirin alone is not a recommended option after major abdominal surgery; NICE limits its role to elective hip and knee replacement.
takeaway: High VTE risk = LMWH + mechanical prophylaxis.
thinking: Major abdominal surgery ↓ previous DVT gives high VTE risk ↓ pharmacological prophylaxis with LMWH indicated ↓ mechanical prophylaxis adds protection ↓ LMWH and intermittent pneumatic compression
pearl: After major cancer surgery in the abdomen or pelvis, NICE recommends considering extended pharmacological prophylaxis for 28 days after surgery.

subject: Major trauma & fluids
title: Trauma Management (Abdominal Compartment Syndrome)
stem: A 45-year-old man develops abdominal distension and rising airway pressures after massive fluid resuscitation. Intra-abdominal pressure is 25 mmHg. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Abdominal compartment syndrome is a sustained intra-abdominal pressure above 20 mmHg with new organ dysfunction. Management includes urgent medical measures to lower pressure, with decompressive laparotomy for overt or refractory compartment syndrome.

why_others_wrong.A: Bowel obstruction can raise abdominal pressure, but distension with IAP of 25 mmHg and rising airway pressure after massive resuscitation defines compartment syndrome.
why_others_wrong.C: Ileus may cause distension but is not itself a diagnosis of raised pressure with organ dysfunction and does not explain the rising airway pressures.
why_others_wrong.D: Ascites can contribute to intra-abdominal hypertension, but the diagnosis here is the compartment syndrome of IAP above 20 mmHg with new organ dysfunction.
why_others_wrong.E: Peritonitis would present with pain, guarding and sepsis, whereas the stem describes pressure-related organ dysfunction after large-volume resuscitation.

exam_trap: Intra-abdominal hypertension is a sustained intra-abdominal pressure of 12 mmHg or more; abdominal compartment syndrome needs a sustained pressure above 20 mmHg with new organ dysfunction.
takeaway: IAP >20 mmHg + organ dysfunction = abdominal compartment syndrome. Urgent decompression.
thinking: Massive fluid resuscitation ↓ abdominal distension and rising airway pressures ↓ intra-abdominal pressure 25 mmHg ↓ sustained pressure above 20 mmHg with new organ dysfunction ↓ Abdominal compartment syndrome
pearl: Abdominal perfusion pressure is mean arterial pressure minus intra-abdominal pressure; after decompressive laparotomy the abdomen is usually left open with a temporary closure.

subject: Pharmacology
title: Pharmacology (Local Anaesthetics)
stem: A 30-year-old man develops tinnitus, circumoral numbness, and agitation after a large dose of lidocaine. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST) presents with neurological symptoms (tinnitus, circumoral numbness, agitation, seizures) and cardiovascular symptoms (arrhythmias, cardiac arrest). Stop the injection and give supportive care; 20% lipid emulsion (Intralipid) is given for severe toxicity, including cardiovascular compromise.

why_others_wrong.A: Anaphylaxis typically presents with urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm and hypotension from an IgE-mediated hypersensitivity reaction, not the neurological triad of tinnitus, perioral numbness and agitation seen with local anaesthetic toxicity.
why_others_wrong.C: Vasovagal syncope presents with transient hypotension, bradycardia and loss of consciousness triggered by a vagal reflex, not the neurological prodrome of tinnitus, circumoral numbness and agitation described here.
why_others_wrong.D: An adrenaline reaction (from co-administered adrenaline in local anaesthetic solutions) typically causes tachycardia, tremor and anxiety from sympathetic stimulation, not the specific sensory disturbances (tinnitus, perioral numbness) seen with lidocaine toxicity.
why_others_wrong.E: Hypoglycaemia causes autonomic and neuroglycopenic symptoms such as sweating, tremor and confusion, not the specific pattern of tinnitus and circumoral numbness that follows a large dose of a local anaesthetic.

exam_trap: Anaphylaxis is chosen because it is a feared drug reaction, but it causes urticaria, bronchospasm and hypotension, not tinnitus, circumoral numbness and agitation after a large lidocaine dose.
takeaway: LAST = neurological symptoms + cardiovascular instability. Stop injecting, support, and give 20% lipid emulsion for severe toxicity.
thinking: Large dose of lidocaine ↓ tinnitus and circumoral numbness are early CNS features ↓ agitation may progress to seizures and arrhythmias ↓ Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST)
pearl: The maximum safe dose of lidocaine is higher when adrenaline is added because vasoconstriction slows systemic absorption; doses should be calculated by weight before infiltration.

subject: Microbiology & surgical infection
title: Microbiology (Clostridium perfringens)
stem: A 40-year-old man has a deep wound infection with crepitus, rapid progression, and systemic toxicity. Gram stain shows Gram-positive bacilli. What is the most likely organism?
why_correct: Clostridium perfringens is a Gram-positive anaerobic bacillus that causes gas gangrene. It produces alpha toxin (lecithinase), leading to myonecrosis, crepitus, and systemic toxicity.

why_others_wrong.A: Staphylococcus aureus is a Gram-positive coccus in clusters, not a bacillus, and is not the classic cause of gas gangrene.
why_others_wrong.B: Streptococcus pyogenes causes necrotising fasciitis but appears as Gram-positive cocci in chains, not bacilli.
why_others_wrong.D: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a Gram-negative bacillus and is not the classic cause of gas gangrene with crepitus.
why_others_wrong.E: Escherichia coli is a Gram-negative bacillus, which does not match the Gram-positive bacilli seen here.

exam_trap: Streptococcus pyogenes causes necrotising fasciitis but is Gram-positive cocci, not bacilli.
takeaway: Gas gangrene = Clostridium perfringens. Gram-positive bacilli + crepitus. Urgent debridement.
thinking: Deep wound infection with crepitus ↓ rapid progression and systemic toxicity ↓ Gram-positive bacilli on Gram stain ↓ gas-forming anaerobe causing myonecrosis ↓ Clostridium perfringens
pearl: Gas gangrene needs urgent radical debridement, sometimes amputation, with intravenous benzylpenicillin plus clindamycin, the latter also suppressing toxin production.

subject: Plastic surgery
title: Surgical Oncology (Melanoma)
stem: A 55-year-old man has a non-ulcerated melanoma with a Breslow thickness of 1.2 mm and no evidence of spread (stage IB). What is the recommended clinical excision margin according to current UK (NICE) guidance?
why_correct: A non-ulcerated 1.2 mm melanoma with no spread is stage IB, and current NICE guidance recommends a 1 cm clinical excision margin for stage I melanoma.

why_others_wrong.A: A 0.5 cm margin is advised for melanoma in situ; it is too narrow for an invasive melanoma 1.2 mm thick.
why_others_wrong.C: A 2 cm margin is recommended for stage II melanoma, such as an ulcerated or thicker lesion, not for a non-ulcerated 1.2 mm stage I melanoma.
why_others_wrong.D: Current NICE guidance never goes beyond 2 cm, even for stage II melanoma, and a 3 cm margin adds morbidity without improving survival.
why_others_wrong.E: An invasive melanoma needs wide local excision after the diagnostic biopsy to reduce local recurrence, so no further surgery is inappropriate.

exam_trap: Margins follow stage, not thickness alone: ulceration upstages a 1-2 mm melanoma to stage II, which needs a 2 cm margin instead of 1 cm.
takeaway: NICE melanoma margins: in situ 0.5 cm, stage I 1 cm, stage II 2 cm.
thinking: Breslow 1.2 mm, non-ulcerated, no spread ↓ pT2a N0 M0 = stage IB ↓ NICE sets margins by stage: in situ 0.5 cm, stage I 1 cm, stage II 2 cm ↓ 1 cm
pearl: NICE advises considering sentinel lymph node biopsy for stage IB to IIC melanoma as a staging and prognostic procedure rather than a therapeutic one.

subject: Paediatric surgery
title: Paediatric Surgery (Malrotation)
stem: A 3-day-old neonate presents with bilious vomiting and abdominal distension. Contrast study shows a corkscrew appearance of the duodenum. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Malrotation with midgut volvulus presents with bilious vomiting in a neonate. Upper gastrointestinal contrast shows a corkscrew course of the duodenum and proximal jejunum as they twist around the superior mesenteric vessels, often with an abnormally placed duodenojejunal flexure. It is a surgical emergency requiring urgent Ladd's procedure.

why_others_wrong.A: Duodenal atresia gives a double bubble on plain film with no distal gas, not a corkscrew duodenum on contrast study, which indicates a twisted midgut.
why_others_wrong.C: Pyloric stenosis presents at a few weeks with projectile non-bilious vomiting and an olive mass, not bilious vomiting on day three.
why_others_wrong.D: Intussusception usually occurs in older infants with colicky pain and redcurrant jelly stool, and contrast would not show a corkscrew duodenum.
why_others_wrong.E: Hirschsprung disease presents with delayed meconium and distension; a corkscrew duodenojejunal configuration signals volvulus rather than aganglionosis.

exam_trap: Candidates pick duodenal atresia (A) because both cause bilious vomiting, but atresia gives a double bubble on plain film, whereas a corkscrew duodenum on contrast indicates volvulus.
takeaway: Neonate + bilious vomiting + corkscrew sign = malrotation with volvulus. Urgent Ladd's procedure.
thinking: 3-day-old with bilious vomiting and distension ↓ obstruction lies beyond the ampulla ↓ contrast shows a corkscrew duodenum and proximal jejunum ↓ bowel twisted around the superior mesenteric vessels ↓ Malrotation with volvulus
pearl: On ultrasound a whirlpool sign or reversal of the normal relationship, with the superior mesenteric vein lying left of the artery, supports malrotation, but upper GI contrast remains the key investigation.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Applied Physiology (Cardiovascular)
stem: Which of the following is the primary determinant of coronary blood flow?

options.B: Diastolic blood pressure and coronary vascular resistance

correct_answer: B. Diastolic blood pressure and coronary vascular resistance
why_correct: Coronary blood flow occurs predominantly during diastole, when the myocardium is relaxed. It is determined by diastolic blood pressure (perfusion pressure) and coronary vascular resistance. Tachycardia reduces diastolic filling time and coronary perfusion.

why_others_wrong.A: Heart rate affects diastolic filling time and hence the duration available for coronary perfusion, but it is not itself the primary determinant of flow; pressure and resistance are.
why_others_wrong.C: Systolic blood pressure has little influence on coronary flow because the coronary vessels are compressed by myocardial contraction and flow is minimal during systole.
why_others_wrong.D: Right atrial pressure influences systemic venous return and right heart filling, not the determinants of coronary perfusion.
why_others_wrong.E: Pulmonary artery pressure relates to the pulmonary circulation, not the coronary circulation, and does not determine coronary blood flow.

exam_trap: Candidates may choose heart rate because tachycardia worsens ischaemia, but it acts by shortening diastole; the determinants of flow are diastolic pressure and coronary resistance.
takeaway: Coronary flow depends on diastolic perfusion pressure divided by coronary vascular resistance; tachycardia shortens diastole and is harmful in ischaemia.
thinking: Left ventricular contraction compresses intramural coronary vessels ↓ most left coronary flow therefore occurs in diastole ↓ flow = diastolic perfusion pressure ÷ coronary vascular resistance ↓ Diastolic blood pressure and coronary vascular resistance
pearl: Intra-aortic balloon counterpulsation inflates in diastole to augment coronary perfusion, and rate control helps in ischaemia by lengthening diastole.

subject: Breast surgery
title: Applied Pathology (Breast Cancer)
stem: A 55-year-old woman has a breast lump. Biopsy shows malignant cells with loss of E-cadherin expression and single-file arrangement. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Loss of E-cadherin expression with single-file cell arrangement is characteristic of invasive lobular carcinoma.

why_others_wrong.A: DCIS is confined within ducts by an intact basement membrane and typically retains E-cadherin, unlike this infiltrative single-file pattern.
why_others_wrong.B: Invasive ductal carcinoma usually retains E-cadherin expression and grows in sheets, nests or glands rather than single files.
why_others_wrong.D: Medullary-pattern carcinoma shows syncytial sheets of pleomorphic cells with a lymphocytic infiltrate, not single-file E-cadherin-negative cells.
why_others_wrong.E: Tubular carcinoma forms well-differentiated angulated tubules lined by a single cell layer and retains E-cadherin.

exam_trap: Candidates pick invasive ductal carcinoma (B) as the commonest breast cancer, but ductal tumours usually retain E-cadherin; loss of E-cadherin with single-file cells indicates lobular carcinoma.
takeaway: E-cadherin negative + single-file = lobular carcinoma.
thinking: Malignant cells infiltrating in single files ↓ loss of E-cadherin, the cell-adhesion molecule encoded by CDH1 ↓ discohesive cells infiltrate singly rather than forming glands or sheets ↓ Invasive lobular carcinoma
pearl: Invasive lobular carcinoma is more often multifocal and bilateral and is easily underestimated on mammography; germline CDH1 mutations link it with hereditary diffuse gastric cancer.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Perioperative Management (VTE Prophylaxis)
stem: A 72-year-old woman with a BMI of 38 is scheduled for elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy. She has no history of VTE. Which of the following is the most appropriate VTE prophylaxis strategy?
why_correct: Age over 60 and obesity (BMI over 30) place this patient at increased VTE risk, so NICE advises pharmacological prophylaxis with low-molecular-weight heparin for at least 7 days after abdominal surgery, provided her bleeding risk is low.

why_others_wrong.A: Early mobilisation is encouraged but is not sufficient on its own in an older patient with obesity undergoing surgery.
why_others_wrong.B: Aspirin is not recommended for VTE prophylaxis after general surgery; low-molecular-weight heparin is the standard pharmacological agent.
why_others_wrong.D: Intermittent pneumatic compression may be added but alone is insufficient when pharmacological prophylaxis is indicated and not contraindicated.
why_others_wrong.E: Age over 60 and a BMI above 30 increase VTE risk, so this patient does require prophylaxis.

exam_trap: Aspirin is not a recommended agent for VTE prophylaxis after abdominal surgery; its NICE role is limited to selected elective hip and knee replacement patients.
takeaway: Obesity (BMI > 30) + surgery = LMWH.
thinking: Age 72 and BMI 38 ↓ both raise VTE risk ↓ abdominal surgery with low bleeding risk ↓ NICE adds pharmacological prophylaxis to mechanical measures ↓ Low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH)
pearl: Patients undergoing abdominal surgery at increased VTE risk receive mechanical prophylaxis from admission, with LMWH or fondaparinux continued for at least 7 days if VTE risk outweighs bleeding risk.

subject: Major trauma & fluids
title: Trauma Management (Tension Pneumothorax)
stem: A 30-year-old man is intubated after a road traffic accident. Shortly after intubation, he becomes hypotensive with BP 70/40 mmHg, HR 140/min, and absent breath sounds on the right. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.B: Needle decompression in the 4th/5th intercostal space, just anterior to the midaxillary line
options.C: Chest drain insertion in the 5th intercostal space, midaxillary line

correct_answer: B. Needle decompression in the 4th/5th intercostal space, just anterior to the midaxillary line
why_correct: Tension pneumothorax with hypotension and absent breath sounds requires immediate decompression without imaging. ATLS 10th edition recommends needle decompression at the 4th or 5th intercostal space just anterior to the midaxillary line (rather than the older 2nd intercostal space, midclavicular line) because chest-wall thickness there is less likely to defeat the needle; finger thoracostomy is an alternative, followed by a chest drain.

why_others_wrong.A: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis; delaying decompression for a chest X-ray in a hypotensive patient risks cardiac arrest.
why_others_wrong.C: A formal chest drain is the definitive step after decompression, but full tube insertion takes longer than immediate decompression in a peri-arrest patient with tension physiology.
why_others_wrong.D: Sending an unstable patient with a tension pneumothorax to CT delays life-saving decompression and is unsafe.
why_others_wrong.E: Bronchoscopy has no role in the immediate treatment of tension pneumothorax and would delay decompression.

exam_trap: ATLS 10th edition moved the adult needle site from the 2nd intercostal space, midclavicular line, to the 4th or 5th intercostal space just anterior to the midaxillary line; older texts may still cite the 2nd space.
takeaway: Tension pneumothorax with shock: decompress immediately without imaging, needle at the 4th or 5th intercostal space just anterior to the midaxillary line or finger thoracostomy, then chest drain.
thinking: Trauma patient just intubated ↓ sudden hypotension, tachycardia and absent right breath sounds ↓ positive-pressure ventilation converting a pneumothorax to tension ↓ immediate decompression without imaging ↓ Needle decompression in the 4th/5th intercostal space, just anterior to the midaxillary line
pearl: In an intubated patient finger thoracostomy is often preferred, because positive-pressure ventilation keeps the lung expanded and it avoids the failure rate of needle decompression.

subject: Pharmacology
title: Pharmacology (Beta-Blockers)
stem: A 60-year-old man with asthma is started on a medication for angina. Two weeks later, he presents with worsening wheeze. Which drug is most likely responsible?
why_correct: Atenolol is only relatively beta-1 selective, so it can still block airway beta-2 receptors and precipitate bronchospasm in asthma, a risk that rises with dose.

why_others_wrong.A: Amlodipine is a dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker acting on vascular smooth muscle; it does not have bronchoconstrictive effects on beta-2 receptors in the airway.
why_others_wrong.C: Diltiazem is a non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker used in angina; it does not act on beta-2 adrenoceptors and is not associated with precipitating bronchospasm.
why_others_wrong.D: Isosorbide mononitrate is a nitrate vasodilator used in angina; it has no beta-receptor activity and does not cause bronchospasm.
why_others_wrong.E: Ranolazine is a late sodium current inhibitor used in refractory angina; it does not act on airway beta-2 receptors and is not associated with precipitating wheeze in asthma.

exam_trap: Diltiazem may be chosen because it also slows heart rate, but it has no beta-receptor activity; cardioselective beta-blockers such as atenolol can still block airway beta-2 receptors in asthma.
takeaway: Asthma + beta-blocker = wheeze. Avoid beta-blockers in asthma if possible.
thinking: Asthmatic patient started on angina treatment ↓ wheeze worsens two weeks later ↓ atenolol is only relatively beta-1 selective ↓ airway beta-2 blockade causes bronchospasm ↓ Atenolol
pearl: In asthma, rate-limiting calcium-channel blockers such as verapamil or diltiazem are alternatives for angina when a beta-blocker is unsuitable, though they must not be combined with beta-blockers without specialist advice.

subject: Microbiology & surgical infection
title: Microbiology (Clostridium difficile)
stem: A 70-year-old man develops profuse diarrhoea 10 days after a course of broad-spectrum antibiotics. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial investigation?

options.B: Stool toxin assay for Clostridium difficile

correct_answer: B. Stool toxin assay for Clostridium difficile
why_correct: Clostridium difficile infection typically follows antibiotic use and presents with profuse diarrhoea. The initial investigation is stool testing for C. difficile. UK practice uses a two-stage test: a GDH enzyme immunoassay or PCR screen, then a toxin enzyme immunoassay to confirm active infection.

why_others_wrong.A: Routine stool culture does not detect Clostridioides difficile or its toxin, so it is not the right first test.
why_others_wrong.C: Colonoscopy is invasive, carries perforation risk in severe colitis and is not the initial test for suspected C. difficile infection.
why_others_wrong.D: CT abdomen helps assess complications such as toxic megacolon or perforation but does not diagnose C. difficile infection.
why_others_wrong.E: Blood cultures may be sent if the patient is septic but do not identify C. difficile, which is diagnosed on stool testing.

exam_trap: Do not send routine stool culture first. Routine culture does not detect C. difficile or its toxin, and specialist toxigenic culture is too slow for initial diagnosis (although it is more sensitive than toxin assay alone).
takeaway: Post-antibiotic diarrhoea = C. difficile toxin assay. Treatment = oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin.
thinking: Profuse diarrhoea in an older patient ↓ onset 10 days after broad-spectrum antibiotics ↓ suspect Clostridioides difficile infection ↓ diagnose by stool testing for organism and toxin ↓ Stool toxin assay for Clostridium difficile
pearl: Suspected cases should be isolated in a side room with enteric precautions and the causative antibiotic stopped where possible; alcohol gel does not kill C. difficile spores.

subject: Colorectal surgery
title: Surgical Oncology (Colorectal Liver Metastases)
stem: A 60-year-old man has a solitary liver metastasis from colorectal cancer. There is no extrahepatic disease. What is the most appropriate management?
why_correct: Surgical resection of colorectal liver metastases offers the best chance of long-term survival.

why_others_wrong.A: Palliative chemotherapy is used when metastatic disease is unresectable; with a solitary liver metastasis and no extrahepatic disease, resection offers potential cure.
why_others_wrong.C: Ablation is generally reserved for small lesions or patients unsuitable for resection, and resection remains the preferred curative option for a solitary resectable metastasis.
why_others_wrong.D: Observation forgoes a potentially curative treatment in a patient with isolated, resectable liver disease and would allow progression.
why_others_wrong.E: Radiotherapy such as stereotactic ablative radiotherapy is reserved for liver metastases unsuitable for resection or ablation; a fit patient with a solitary resectable lesion should have resection.

exam_trap: Palliative chemotherapy (A) is chosen by candidates who equate metastasis with incurable disease, but isolated resectable colorectal liver metastases can be cured by resection.
takeaway: Resectable colorectal liver metastases = liver resection. Best chance of cure.
thinking: Colorectal cancer with a solitary liver metastasis ↓ no extrahepatic disease ↓ isolated, resectable liver disease is potentially curable ↓ resection offers the best chance of long-term survival ↓ Liver resection
pearl: Resectability depends on leaving an adequate future liver remnant with intact inflow, outflow and biliary drainage rather than on lesion number alone, and decisions are made in a hepatobiliary MDT, often with perioperative chemotherapy.

subject: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care
title: Vascular Surgery (Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm)
stem: A 72-year-old man presents with a pulsatile abdominal mass. CT shows an infrarenal aortic diameter of 5.8 cm. What is the most appropriate management?

options.E: Medical management with statin and aspirin

why_correct: Elective repair is indicated for infrarenal AAA ≥ 5.5 cm in men.

why_others_wrong.A: Annual ultrasound surveillance is for small aneurysms of 3.0 to 4.4 cm, well below this 5.8 cm aneurysm, which has passed the repair threshold.
why_others_wrong.C: Urgent repair is for symptomatic, tender or ruptured aneurysms; this stable asymptomatic AAA warrants prompt referral for planned elective repair.
why_others_wrong.D: Three-monthly surveillance applies to medium aneurysms of 4.5 to 5.4 cm; at 5.8 cm the rupture risk favours repair over continued surveillance.
why_others_wrong.E: Statin and antiplatelet therapy reduce cardiovascular risk but do not prevent rupture of an aneurysm that has reached the repair threshold.

exam_trap: Asymptomatic AAAs below 5.5 cm are usually kept under surveillance, but symptomatic aneurysms and those over 4.0 cm growing more than 1 cm a year should be considered for repair.
takeaway: AAA ≥ 5.5 cm = elective repair. AAA < 5.5 cm = surveillance.
thinking: Infrarenal AAA of 5.8 cm ↓ asymptomatic ↓ above the 5.5 cm repair threshold ↓ planned repair rather than surveillance ↓ Elective surgical repair
pearl: Rupture risk rises steeply with diameter, which is why repair is offered once the aneurysm reaches 5.5 cm, when this risk outweighs operative risk.

subject: Paediatric surgery
title: Paediatric Surgery (Pyloric Stenosis)
