stem: A 6-week-old boy presents with projectile non-bilious vomiting after feeds. Examination reveals a palpable olive-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis classically presents at 4–6 weeks of age with projectile non-bilious vomiting and a palpable olive-shaped mass.

why_others_wrong.A: Duodenal atresia presents in the first day or two of life, usually with bilious vomiting and a double bubble, not at six weeks with an olive mass.
why_others_wrong.C: Gastro-oesophageal reflux causes effortless regurgitation without a palpable pyloric mass, and forceful projectile vomiting is a red flag for pyloric stenosis instead.
why_others_wrong.D: Malrotation with volvulus causes bilious vomiting as the obstruction lies beyond the ampulla, and there is no palpable olive-shaped mass.
why_others_wrong.E: Intussusception produces colicky pain, drawing up of the legs and bloody stool, with a sausage-shaped rather than olive-shaped mass.

exam_trap: Candidates choose gastro-oesophageal reflux (C) because infants commonly vomit, but reflux is effortless with no mass; projectile vomiting with a palpable olive means pyloric stenosis.
takeaway: Projectile non-bilious vomiting + olive mass = pyloric stenosis. Treatment = pyloromyotomy.
thinking: 6-week-old boy ↓ projectile non-bilious vomiting after feeds ↓ olive-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant is the hypertrophied pylorus ↓ Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis
pearl: Ultrasound confirms the diagnosis by showing a thickened, elongated pyloric muscle, and pyloromyotomy follows correction of the hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis.

subject: Anatomy
title: Applied Anatomy (Inguinal Canal)
stem: During open inguinal hernia repair, which structure forms the floor of the inguinal canal?
why_correct: The floor of the inguinal canal is formed by the inguinal ligament.

why_others_wrong.B: Internal oblique and transversus abdominis (with their aponeuroses) form the roof (superior arch) of the inguinal canal, not the floor.
why_others_wrong.C: The external oblique aponeurosis forms the anterior wall of the inguinal canal, not the floor.
why_others_wrong.D: Transversalis fascia forms the posterior wall of the inguinal canal, not the floor.
why_others_wrong.E: The peritoneum lies deep to the transversalis fascia within the abdominal cavity and is not one of the four walls of the inguinal canal.

exam_trap: External oblique aponeurosis is the trap because the inguinal ligament is its rolled lower edge, but the aponeurosis itself forms the anterior wall, not the floor.
takeaway: Inguinal canal: anterior = external oblique, posterior = transversalis fascia, roof = internal oblique + transversus, floor = inguinal ligament.
thinking: Walls of the inguinal canal ↓ anterior: external oblique aponeurosis; posterior: transversalis fascia ↓ roof: arching fibres of internal oblique and transversus abdominis ↓ floor: the inguinal ligament ↓ Inguinal ligament
pearl: In an open tension-free mesh repair the lower edge of the mesh is sutured to the shelving edge of the inguinal ligament, which forms the floor of the canal.

subject: Physiology
title: Applied Physiology (Renal)
stem: Which of the following statements regarding renal blood flow is correct?

options.A: The kidneys receive approximately 10% of cardiac output
options.B: Renal blood flow is autoregulated between mean arterial pressures of 80–180 mmHg
options.C: The medulla receives the majority of renal blood flow
options.D: Angiotensin II increases renal blood flow

correct_answer: B. Renal blood flow is autoregulated between mean arterial pressures of 80–180 mmHg
why_correct: Renal blood flow is autoregulated between MAP of 80–180 mmHg via the myogenic mechanism and tubuloglomerular feedback.

why_others_wrong.A: The kidneys receive approximately 20-25% of cardiac output, not 10%.
why_others_wrong.C: The renal cortex receives the great majority (around 90%) of renal blood flow; the medulla receives only a small fraction.
why_others_wrong.D: Angiotensin II preferentially constricts the efferent arteriole and overall tends to reduce, not increase, total renal blood flow.
why_others_wrong.E: Noradrenaline constricts renal arterioles through alpha-1 adrenoceptors and reduces, rather than increases, renal blood flow.

exam_trap: The cortex receives the majority of renal blood flow (~90%), not the medulla.
takeaway: Kidneys = 20–25% of cardiac output. Autoregulation = MAP 80–180 mmHg.
thinking: Statement question on renal blood flow ↓ kidneys receive 20-25% of cardiac output, mostly to the cortex ↓ angiotensin II and noradrenaline constrict renal arterioles and reduce flow ↓ myogenic and tubuloglomerular feedback mechanisms keep flow stable over a pressure range ↓ Renal blood flow is autoregulated between mean arterial pressures of 80–180 mmHg
pearl: Below the autoregulatory range renal blood flow falls with pressure, and in chronic hypertension the range shifts upwards, so a blood pressure that looks acceptable may still underperfuse the kidneys.

subject: Pharmacology
title: Perioperative Management (Anticoagulation)
stem: A 70-year-old man on warfarin for atrial fibrillation requires emergency surgery. His INR is 4.5. What is the most appropriate management?

options.B: Vitamin K and prothrombin complex concentrate

correct_answer: B. Vitamin K and prothrombin complex concentrate
why_correct: For emergency surgery with a high INR, rapid reversal is required. Prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) combined with intravenous vitamin K is the fastest and most effective method.

why_others_wrong.A: Proceeding with surgery at an INR of 4.5 without reversal carries a very high bleeding risk in emergency surgery and is not appropriate management.
why_others_wrong.C: Fresh frozen plasma alone acts more slowly and provides a less complete, less predictable correction of the INR than prothrombin complex concentrate, making it inferior for emergency reversal.
why_others_wrong.D: Platelet transfusion addresses platelet number or function, not the vitamin K-dependent clotting factor deficiency caused by warfarin, so it does not correct a raised INR.
why_others_wrong.E: Simply stopping warfarin and waiting days for the INR to normalise is far too slow for a patient who requires emergency surgery and does not achieve the rapid reversal needed.

exam_trap: Fresh frozen plasma alone is chosen as a familiar blood product, but it needs large volumes, takes time to thaw and corrects the INR incompletely compared with PCC plus vitamin K.
takeaway: Emergency warfarin reversal = PCC + vitamin K.
thinking: Warfarin with INR 4.5 ↓ surgery cannot be delayed ↓ rapid replacement of vitamin K-dependent factors is needed ↓ PCC acts immediately and IV vitamin K sustains correction ↓ Vitamin K and prothrombin complex concentrate
pearl: Intravenous vitamin K takes several hours to work, so it is given with prothrombin complex concentrate, which corrects the INR within minutes; without vitamin K the INR can rebound as PCC factors are cleared.

subject: Anatomy
title: Applied Anatomy (Abdomen)
stem: A 55-year-old man undergoes laparoscopic cholecystectomy. During dissection of Calot's triangle, the surgeon identifies the cystic artery. From which artery does the cystic artery most commonly arise?
why_correct: The cystic artery typically arises from the right hepatic artery within Calot's triangle. It supplies the gallbladder and cystic duct.

why_others_wrong.A: The common hepatic artery gives rise to the gastroduodenal and proper hepatic arteries; a cystic origin here is uncommon.
why_others_wrong.C: The left hepatic artery supplies the left lobe and is an uncommon origin of the cystic artery.
why_others_wrong.D: The gastroduodenal artery passes behind the first part of the duodenum and only rarely gives the cystic artery.
why_others_wrong.E: The superior mesenteric artery may give a replaced right hepatic artery, but it rarely gives the cystic artery directly.

exam_trap: The common hepatic and gastroduodenal arteries are tempting as named variant origins, but they are uncommon sources; the usual origin is the right hepatic artery.
takeaway: Cystic artery = branch of right hepatic artery. Always identify and confirm before ligation during cholecystectomy.
thinking: Calot's triangle: cystic duct, common hepatic duct and inferior edge of liver ↓ right hepatic artery usually crosses behind the common hepatic duct into the triangle ↓ the cystic artery typically branches from it here ↓ Right hepatic artery
pearl: Before clipping, the critical view of safety should be achieved: only two structures, the cystic duct and cystic artery, entering the gallbladder, with the lower gallbladder freed from the liver bed.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Applied Physiology (Respiratory)
stem: Which of the following statements regarding surfactant is correct?

options.A: It increases surface tension in the alveoli
options.B: It is produced by type I pneumocytes
options.C: It reduces surface tension and prevents alveolar collapse
options.D: It is deficient in adults with emphysema

correct_answer: C. It reduces surface tension and prevents alveolar collapse
why_correct: Surfactant is produced by type II pneumocytes. It reduces surface tension in the alveoli, preventing collapse at end-expiration (atelectasis) and reducing the work of breathing. Deficiency causes respiratory distress syndrome.

why_others_wrong.A: Surfactant reduces, rather than increases, alveolar surface tension.
why_others_wrong.B: Surfactant is produced by type II, not type I, pneumocytes; type I cells form the thin gas-exchange surface.
why_others_wrong.D: Surfactant deficiency is classically associated with neonatal respiratory distress syndrome, not typically described as a feature of adult emphysema.
why_others_wrong.E: By reducing surface tension and preventing alveolar collapse, surfactant decreases, rather than increases, the work of breathing.

exam_trap: Candidates may choose type I pneumocytes because they line most of the alveolar surface, but surfactant is made by type II cells; type I cells are for gas exchange.
takeaway: Surfactant = type II pneumocytes. Reduces surface tension. Deficiency = RDS.
thinking: Surfactant is a phospholipid secreted by type II pneumocytes ↓ it lowers alveolar surface tension ↓ this stabilises small alveoli at end-expiration and eases inflation ↓ It reduces surface tension and prevents alveolar collapse
pearl: Surfactant can be inactivated in adults by aspiration, pneumonia and ARDS, contributing to atelectasis and stiff lungs in critically ill surgical patients.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Applied Pathology (Colorectal Cancer)
stem: A 60-year-old man has a right-sided colon cancer. Which of the following molecular pathways is most commonly associated with right-sided colon cancer?
correct_answer: C. BRAF mutation and microsatellite instability (MSI)
why_correct: Right-sided colon cancers are more commonly associated with BRAF mutations and microsatellite instability (MSI), often through the serrated pathway. Left-sided cancers are more commonly associated with APC and TP53 mutations.

why_others_wrong.A: APC mutation drives the chromosomal instability pathway more typical of left-sided and rectal cancers, not the serrated right-sided pathway.
why_others_wrong.B: KRAS mutations occur on both sides of the colon and are not the defining molecular association of right-sided cancer in this context.
why_others_wrong.D: TP53 mutation is a late event in the chromosomal instability pathway, more typical of left-sided cancers.
why_others_wrong.E: HER2 amplification is uncommon in colorectal cancer, seen in a small minority, and is not characteristic of right-sided tumours.

exam_trap: APC mutation is tempting because it initiates most colorectal cancers, but the APC-led chromosomal instability pathway is more typical of left-sided tumours; right-sided cancers favour BRAF and MSI.
takeaway: Right colon = BRAF + MSI. Left colon = APC + TP53.
thinking: Right-sided colon cancer ↓ often arises through the serrated pathway ↓ serrated lesions carry BRAF mutation and MLH1 methylation causing MSI ↓ BRAF mutation and microsatellite instability (MSI)
pearl: All colorectal cancers in the UK should be tested for mismatch repair deficiency or MSI, which screens for inherited mismatch repair syndromes and predicts response to immune checkpoint inhibitors.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Perioperative Management (Blood Transfusion)
stem: A 65-year-old Jehovah's Witness patient requires major surgery and refuses blood transfusion. Which of the following is the most appropriate preoperative optimisation strategy?
why_correct: For Jehovah's Witness patients refusing blood transfusion, preoperative optimisation with erythropoietin and iron therapy increases red cell mass. Intraoperative cell salvage may also be acceptable if the circuit is continuous.

why_others_wrong.A: Preoperative autologous donation involves storing the patient's blood out of the body, which is generally unacceptable to Jehovah's Witnesses.
why_others_wrong.C: Preoperative transfusion of donated blood is exactly what the patient has refused and cannot be given.
why_others_wrong.D: Optimisation is possible, including iron and erythropoietin to raise haemoglobin before surgery.
why_others_wrong.E: Cell salvage may be acceptable intraoperatively but does not optimise red cell mass before surgery on its own.

exam_trap: Option A tempts as a way of using the patient's own blood, but storing blood outside the body for later return is generally unacceptable to Jehovah's Witnesses.
takeaway: Jehovah's Witness = erythropoietin + iron + cell salvage. Avoid stored blood.
thinking: Jehovah's Witness refusing blood ↓ maximise red cell mass before surgery ↓ iron with erythropoietin raises haemoglobin ↓ Erythropoietin and iron therapy
pearl: Each Jehovah's Witness patient's acceptance of individual blood fractions and techniques should be documented in an advance decision, and a competent adult's refusal of blood must be respected even if life-threatening.

subject: Major trauma & fluids
title: Trauma Management (Thoracic)
stem: A 35-year-old man has a stab wound to the chest. He is haemodynamically stable. Chest X-ray shows a haemothorax. What is the most appropriate initial management?
why_correct: For a haemodynamically stable patient with a haemothorax, chest drain insertion is the initial management. Thoracotomy is indicated if initial drainage is more than 1500 ml, if drainage continues at more than 200 ml per hour for 2 to 4 hours, or if the patient needs persistent blood transfusion.

why_others_wrong.A: Immediate thoracotomy is reserved for massive haemothorax, with more than 1500 ml initial drainage or ongoing loss of about 200 ml per hour, or for instability.
why_others_wrong.C: CT may help define injuries later, but a haemothorax already seen on chest X-ray needs drainage to evacuate blood and allow the lung to re-expand.
why_others_wrong.D: Thoracoscopy has a role in retained haemothorax after drainage, but it is not the first step in a newly diagnosed traumatic haemothorax.
why_others_wrong.E: Observation leaves blood in the pleural space, risking lung collapse, retained clot, empyema and missed ongoing bleeding.

exam_trap: Immediate thoracotomy is tempting after a stab wound, but in a stable haemothorax it is reserved for large initial or persistent drainage; a chest drain comes first.
takeaway: Haemothorax + stable = chest drain. Thoracotomy if massive or ongoing bleeding.
thinking: Stab wound to the chest ↓ haemodynamically stable ↓ haemothorax on chest X-ray ↓ drain to evacuate blood, re-expand the lung and measure loss ↓ Chest drain insertion
pearl: A large-bore drain is placed in the safe triangle, bounded by the lateral border of pectoralis major, the anterior border of latissimus dorsi and a line at the level of the fifth intercostal space; initial and hourly drainage guide the need for thoracotomy.

subject: Pharmacology
title: Pharmacology (Antibiotics)
stem: A 45-year-old man is prescribed gentamicin for a serious infection. Which of the following is the most important adverse effect to monitor?
why_correct: Gentamicin is an aminoglycoside with significant nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity. Renal function and hearing should be monitored. Serum levels guide dosing: a trough or nomogram-timed level for once-daily dosing, and peak and trough levels for multiple-daily dosing.

why_others_wrong.A: Aminoglycosides such as gentamicin are not characteristically hepatotoxic; their major recognised organ toxicities are renal (nephrotoxicity) and cochleovestibular (ototoxicity).
why_others_wrong.C: Cardiotoxicity is not a recognised major adverse effect of gentamicin; aminoglycosides are notable instead for nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity.
why_others_wrong.D: General neurotoxicity is not the principal concern with gentamicin (though it can rarely cause neuromuscular blockade at high doses); the key monitored toxicities are renal and ototoxic, not broadly neurotoxic.
why_others_wrong.E: Pulmonary fibrosis is not associated with aminoglycosides such as gentamicin; it is more characteristic of agents like amiodarone, bleomycin or methotrexate, not this drug class.

exam_trap: Hepatotoxicity is chosen by candidates who assume all drugs need liver monitoring, but gentamicin's key toxicities are renal and ototoxic, guided by serum levels and renal function.
takeaway: Gentamicin = nephrotoxic + ototoxic. Monitor levels and renal function.
thinking: Aminoglycoside prescribed ↓ accumulates in renal tubular cells and inner ear hair cells ↓ dose and level dependent toxicity ↓ Nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity
pearl: Aminoglycosides can potentiate neuromuscular blockade and should be used with caution in myasthenia gravis; ototoxicity may be irreversible and is increased with loop diuretics.

subject: Microbiology & surgical infection
title: Microbiology (Surgical Infection)
stem: A 55-year-old man develops a wound infection 7 days after surgery. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial investigation?

options.B: Wound swab for culture and sensitivity

correct_answer: B. Wound swab for culture and sensitivity
why_correct: A wound swab for culture and sensitivity is the initial investigation for a suspected surgical site infection. It identifies the organism and guides antibiotic therapy.

why_others_wrong.A: Blood cultures are indicated if the patient is systemically unwell or septic, but they are not the first test for a localised wound infection.
why_others_wrong.C: CT is reserved for suspected deep collections or anastomotic leak and is not the initial investigation for a superficial wound infection.
why_others_wrong.D: MRI is not a first-line test for wound infection and is used selectively, for example in suspected osteomyelitis or deep soft-tissue infection.
why_others_wrong.E: Ultrasound can look for a subcutaneous collection but does not identify the organism or its antibiotic sensitivities.

exam_trap: Blood cultures tempt candidates thinking of infection screens, but they are reserved for systemically unwell or septic patients; a localised wound infection is investigated first with a swab.
takeaway: Wound infection = swab for culture and sensitivity. Blood cultures if systemically unwell.
thinking: Wound infection 7 days after surgery ↓ localised surgical site infection ↓ identify the organism and sensitivities to guide therapy ↓ Wound swab for culture and sensitivity
pearl: A superficial SSI with a collection is managed primarily by opening the wound and draining pus; antibiotics are added mainly for spreading cellulitis or systemic features.

subject: Anatomy
title: Applied Anatomy (Thorax)
stem: A 60-year-old man undergoes a right lower lobectomy. During surgery, the surgeon identifies the structures in the hilum. Which of the following structures lies most anteriorly in the right lung hilum?
why_correct: In the right lung hilum, the order from anterior to posterior is: pulmonary vein (most anterior), pulmonary artery (middle), and bronchus (most posterior). This is remembered as "Vein, Artery, Bronchus" (VAB).

why_others_wrong.A: The bronchus lies most posteriorly in the right hilum in the vein-artery-bronchus arrangement, not most anteriorly.
why_others_wrong.B: The pulmonary artery occupies the middle (superior-to-intermediate) position in the right hilum between the vein and bronchus, not the most anterior position.
why_others_wrong.D: Bronchial arteries are small vessels supplying the bronchial walls themselves; they are not among the major structures defining the anteroposterior hilar arrangement.
why_others_wrong.E: Hilar lymph nodes are scattered around the major structures rather than occupying a defined anterior position in the vein-artery-bronchus sequence.

exam_trap: The anteroposterior order is vein, artery, bronchus on both sides; the hila differ superiorly, where the right has an eparterial bronchus and the left has the artery highest.
takeaway: Right hilum = Vein (anterior), Artery (middle), Bronchus (posterior).
thinking: Right lung hilum viewed from the front ↓ anterior to posterior: pulmonary vein, pulmonary artery, bronchus ↓ the pulmonary veins are the most anterior and inferior hilar structures ↓ Pulmonary vein
pearl: Dividing the inferior pulmonary ligament during lower lobectomy leads directly up to the inferior pulmonary vein, the standard way to expose it safely.

subject: Colorectal surgery
title: Applied Pathology (Colorectal Cancer)
stem: A 62-year-old man undergoes colonoscopy for rectal bleeding. Biopsy of a sigmoid polyp shows dysplastic glands extending through the muscularis mucosae into the submucosa. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Invasion through the muscularis mucosae into the submucosa defines adenocarcinoma. Adenomas show dysplasia but remain confined above the muscularis mucosae.

why_others_wrong.A: Hyperplastic polyps show serrated crypts without true dysplasia and do not invade through the muscularis mucosae into the submucosa.
why_others_wrong.B: A tubular adenoma shows dysplasia confined above the muscularis mucosae; invasion into the submucosa means the lesion has become an adenocarcinoma.
why_others_wrong.D: Hamartomatous polyps, such as juvenile or Peutz-Jeghers polyps, are disorganised normal tissue elements and are not defined by dysplastic glands invading the submucosa.
why_others_wrong.E: Inflammatory polyps arise from regenerating mucosa in colitis and lack dysplastic glands invading through the muscularis mucosae.

exam_trap: Tubular adenoma (B) is chosen because dysplastic glands are seen, but invasion through the muscularis mucosae into the submucosa makes the lesion an adenocarcinoma.
takeaway: Dysplasia breaching the muscularis mucosae into submucosa = adenocarcinoma; dysplasia confined above it = adenoma.
thinking: Sigmoid polyp biopsy shows dysplastic glands ↓ the glands extend through the muscularis mucosae into the submucosa ↓ in the colon, submucosal invasion defines carcinoma ↓ dysplasia confined to the mucosa is still an adenoma ↓ Adenocarcinoma
pearl: Colonic mucosa above the muscularis mucosae has few lymphatics, so intramucosal neoplasia rarely metastasises; once a malignant polyp invades the submucosa, depth of invasion, lymphovascular invasion and margin status decide whether resection is needed.

subject: Microbiology & surgical infection
title: Perioperative Management (Antibiotic Prophylaxis)
stem: A 68-year-old man is scheduled for elective colorectal surgery. Which of the following is the most appropriate antibiotic prophylaxis?
why_correct: Colorectal surgery requires broad-spectrum prophylaxis covering Gram-negative organisms and anaerobes. Cefuroxime covers Gram-negatives; metronidazole covers anaerobes.

why_others_wrong.A: Oral vancomycin is used to treat Clostridioides difficile infection and is poorly absorbed, so it gives no systemic surgical prophylaxis.
why_others_wrong.C: Ciprofloxacin alone has negligible anaerobic activity, so it leaves the Bacteroides and other anaerobic bowel flora uncovered during colorectal surgery.
why_others_wrong.D: Flucloxacillin alone covers Gram-positive organisms only and misses the Gram-negative and anaerobic bowel flora.
why_others_wrong.E: Colorectal surgery is clean-contaminated with a high infection risk, so NICE recommends antibiotic prophylaxis.

exam_trap: Flucloxacillin alone tempts as the standard skin-flora agent, but it covers only Gram-positive organisms and misses the Gram-negative and anaerobic bowel flora encountered in colorectal surgery.
takeaway: Colorectal prophylaxis = cephalosporin + metronidazole.
thinking: Elective colorectal surgery ↓ clean-contaminated with exposure to colonic flora ↓ prophylaxis must cover Gram-negative bacilli and anaerobes ↓ Intravenous cefuroxime and metronidazole
pearl: Many UK units use co-amoxiclav or gentamicin with metronidazole instead, limiting cephalosporins because of their association with Clostridioides difficile; the principle of Gram-negative plus anaerobic cover is the same.

subject: Major trauma & fluids
title: Trauma Management (Pelvic Fracture)
stem: A 35-year-old motorcyclist has a pelvic fracture after a high-speed collision. He is hypotensive with BP 80/50 mmHg and HR 130/min and remains hypotensive after an initial 1 litre of crystalloid given pre-hospital. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.B: Pelvic binder application and blood transfusion

correct_answer: B. Pelvic binder application and blood transfusion
why_correct: Unstable pelvic fractures can cause massive retroperitoneal bleeding. A pelvic binder should be applied immediately, and blood transfusion should be initiated.

why_others_wrong.A: CT is unsafe in a patient remaining hypotensive despite resuscitation; the pelvis must first be stabilised and blood given.
why_others_wrong.C: Pelvic bleeding is mostly retroperitoneal venous and bony bleeding, which laparotomy does not control and may worsen by releasing tamponade.
why_others_wrong.D: Angioembolisation may control arterial pelvic bleeding, but a binder and blood transfusion come first to stabilise the patient.
why_others_wrong.E: External fixation is a later definitive or damage-control step; the immediate priority is binder application and blood resuscitation.

exam_trap: Immediate CT or angiographic embolisation are attractive definitive options, but a persistently hypotensive patient needs a pelvic binder and blood first; CT requires haemodynamic stability.
takeaway: Pelvic fracture + shock = pelvic binder + blood transfusion.
thinking: High-speed pelvic fracture ↓ persistent hypotension after 1 litre of crystalloid ↓ ongoing pelvic haemorrhage with shock ↓ close the pelvis and replace blood now ↓ Pelvic binder application and blood transfusion
pearl: A binder should be applied early, ideally before log-rolling, because movement of an unstable pelvic ring can disrupt clot and restart bleeding.

subject: Pharmacology
title: Pharmacology (Heparin)
stem: A 60-year-old man is started on unfractionated heparin for deep vein thrombosis. Seven days later, his platelet count drops from 250 to 80 × 10⁹/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) is an immune-mediated reaction causing a drop in platelet count typically 5–10 days after starting heparin. Paradoxically, it causes thrombosis rather than bleeding.

why_others_wrong.A: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura is not linked temporally to heparin exposure; the timing (around day 5-10 of heparin therapy) and drug context here are classic for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia rather than primary ITP.
why_others_wrong.C: Disseminated intravascular coagulation typically occurs in the context of severe illness, sepsis or trauma with coagulation factor consumption and both bleeding and clotting abnormalities, not as an isolated platelet fall temporally linked to heparin initiation.
why_others_wrong.D: Aplastic anaemia involves pancytopenia from bone marrow failure, not an isolated, immune-mediated platelet fall occurring days after starting heparin.
why_others_wrong.E: General bone marrow suppression would typically affect multiple cell lines and does not have the specific immune-mediated mechanism or characteristic 5-10 day timing after heparin exposure seen in HIT.

exam_trap: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura is chosen because it is an immune platelet disorder, but a fall of more than half in platelets five to ten days after starting heparin indicates HIT, which causes thrombosis rather than bleeding.
takeaway: Heparin + falling platelets = HIT. Stop all heparin. Start a non-heparin anticoagulant such as argatroban or danaparoid (fondaparinux or a DOAC in selected patients).
thinking: Unfractionated heparin started ↓ platelets fall by more than 50% at day 7 ↓ typical 5-10 day timing ↓ immune antibodies to heparin-PF4 complexes ↓ Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia
pearl: HIT is a prothrombotic state, so after stopping heparin a non-heparin anticoagulant is needed; warfarin should not be started until the platelet count has recovered because of the risk of venous limb gangrene.

subject: Microbiology & surgical infection
title: Microbiology (Tetanus)
stem: A 40-year-old man sustains a deep puncture wound to his foot while gardening; the wound is heavily contaminated with soil and manure. He is unsure whether he ever completed a course of tetanus vaccination. What is the most appropriate tetanus management?
why_correct: For a high-risk tetanus-prone wound in a patient whose immunisation is incomplete or unknown, UK guidance (the Green Book) is a dose of tetanus-containing vaccine plus human tetanus immunoglobulin, alongside thorough wound cleaning.

why_others_wrong.A: Toxoid stimulates antibody production over days to weeks, so on its own it may not give immediate protection for a high-risk wound.
why_others_wrong.B: Immunoglobulin gives only temporary passive protection, and without toxoid the patient's long-term immunity is not reinforced.
why_others_wrong.D: Debridement removes devitalised tissue and spores but does not provide immunity against tetanus toxin.
why_others_wrong.E: Antibiotics do not neutralise tetanus toxin or provide immunity, so they cannot replace immunisation.

exam_trap: The number of vaccine doses received and the wound risk decide management, not years since the last dose; toxoid alone gives no immediate protection.
takeaway: High-risk tetanus-prone wound + incomplete or unknown immunisation = vaccine + immunoglobulin.
thinking: Deep puncture wound contaminated with soil and manure ↓ high-risk tetanus-prone wound ↓ immunisation history incomplete or unknown ↓ needs active plus immediate passive protection ↓ Tetanus toxoid and immunoglobulin
pearl: Vaccine and immunoglobulin should be given at different sites, and thorough wound cleaning with removal of devitalised tissue remains essential because spores germinate in anaerobic tissue.

subject: Colorectal surgery
title: Surgical Oncology (Rectal Cancer)
stem: A 60-year-old man has a rectal adenocarcinoma 5 cm from the anal verge. MRI staging shows a T3 tumour with threatened circumferential resection margin and no distant metastases. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
why_correct: MRI shows a threatened circumferential resection margin, which places this tumour in the high-risk group; NICE advises preoperative chemoradiotherapy to shrink the tumour away from the mesorectal fascia before total mesorectal excision, improving the chance of a clear margin and reducing local recurrence.

why_others_wrong.A: Anterior resection without neoadjuvant treatment risks an involved circumferential margin and local recurrence when MRI already shows the margin is threatened.
why_others_wrong.B: Abdominoperineal resection alone still leaves a threatened circumferential margin untreated; downstaging with neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy should come first, whatever operation follows.
why_others_wrong.D: Adjuvant chemotherapy is given after surgery and does not downstage the tumour to secure a clear circumferential margin at resection.
why_others_wrong.E: Local excision is reserved for selected early tumours such as small T1 lesions; it is inadequate for a T3 tumour with a threatened margin.

exam_trap: Anterior resection alone (A) attracts candidates who see a resectable tumour, but a threatened margin on MRI needs neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy first; adjuvant chemotherapy (D) cannot downstage.
takeaway: Threatened or involved circumferential margin on MRI → neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy before TME.
thinking: Rectal adenocarcinoma 5 cm from the anal verge ↓ MRI shows T3 with a threatened circumferential resection margin ↓ immediate surgery risks an involved margin and local recurrence ↓ downstage first, then perform TME ↓ Neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy
pearl: MRI is the key staging test because it shows the tumour's relation to the mesorectal fascia; restaging after neoadjuvant treatment guides surgery, and a complete clinical response may allow a watch-and-wait approach in selected patients.

subject: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care
title: Vascular Surgery (Varicose Veins)
stem: A 50-year-old woman has symptomatic varicose veins affecting the great saphenous vein. Duplex ultrasound confirms saphenofemoral junction incompetence. What is the most appropriate management?
why_correct: NICE recommends endothermal ablation, either endovenous laser ablation or radiofrequency ablation, as first-line treatment for symptomatic varicose veins with confirmed truncal reflux such as great saphenous vein incompetence.

why_others_wrong.A: Compression stockings are offered only if interventional treatment is unsuitable, not as first-line for confirmed truncal reflux.
why_others_wrong.C: Open ligation and stripping is third-line in NICE guidance, after endothermal ablation and foam sclerotherapy.
why_others_wrong.D: Ultrasound-guided foam sclerotherapy is second-line if endothermal ablation is unsuitable.
why_others_wrong.E: Symptomatic varicose veins with confirmed reflux warrant treatment rather than observation.

exam_trap: Candidates choose compression stockings as safe conservative care, but NICE offers them only if intervention is unsuitable; truncal reflux is treated with endothermal ablation.
takeaway: Great saphenous incompetence = endothermal ablation (EVLA or RFA) first-line, then foam sclerotherapy, then surgery.
thinking: Symptomatic varicose veins ↓ saphenofemoral junction incompetence on duplex ↓ truncal reflux ↓ NICE first-line is endothermal ablation ↓ Endovenous laser ablation
pearl: Endothermal ablation carries a small risk of thermal injury to adjacent nerves, such as the saphenous nerve with below-knee great saphenous vein ablation.

subject: Paediatric surgery
title: Paediatric Surgery (Intussusception)
stem: A 9-month-old boy presents with intermittent screaming, drawing his legs up to his abdomen, and passage of redcurrant jelly stool. What is the most appropriate initial investigation?
why_correct: Ultrasound is the diagnostic test of choice for intussusception, showing the classic "target" or "doughnut" sign.

why_others_wrong.A: An abdominal X-ray may show obstruction or a soft-tissue mass but is insensitive and cannot reliably confirm or exclude intussusception.
why_others_wrong.C: CT involves significant radiation and often sedation in an infant, and adds little when ultrasound can confirm the diagnosis quickly.
why_others_wrong.D: Contrast enema is now used mainly as a therapeutic reduction technique, with air enema preferred in UK practice, after ultrasound has made the diagnosis.
why_others_wrong.E: Colonoscopy is invasive, needs anaesthesia and risks perforation of ischaemic bowel, and it has no role in the initial diagnosis of intussusception.

exam_trap: Enema reduction, usually with air, is a treatment rather than the initial diagnostic test; ultrasound comes first.
takeaway: Intussusception = ultrasound (target sign). Treatment = air (pneumatic) enema reduction if no peritonitis; surgery if reduction fails or the child is peritonitic.
thinking: 9-month-old with intermittent screaming and legs drawn up ↓ redcurrant jelly stool from congested, ischaemic mucosa ↓ classic intussusception picture ↓ needs rapid, radiation-free confirmation ↓ Ultrasound abdomen
pearl: Enema reduction is contraindicated with peritonitis, perforation or haemodynamic instability, and because reduction carries a small perforation risk a surgical team should be available.

subject: Anatomy
title: Applied Anatomy (Neck)
stem: A 45-year-old woman undergoes thyroidectomy. During ligation of the inferior thyroid artery, which nerve is at risk?

options.B: External branch of superior laryngeal nerve
options.C: Internal branch of superior laryngeal nerve

why_correct: The recurrent laryngeal nerve ascends in the tracheo-oesophageal groove and crosses the inferior thyroid artery or its branches close to the lower pole, passing in front of, behind or between them, so it is at risk when this artery is ligated.

why_others_wrong.B: The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve is at risk during ligation of the superior thyroid artery/pole, not the inferior thyroid artery.
why_others_wrong.C: The internal laryngeal nerve pierces the thyrohyoid membrane with the superior laryngeal artery to supply supraglottic mucosa, far from the inferior thyroid artery.
why_others_wrong.D: The glossopharyngeal nerve lies higher in the neck, related to the pharynx and carotid sheath structures, with no direct relationship to the inferior thyroid artery during thyroidectomy.
why_others_wrong.E: The hypoglossal nerve runs near the greater cornu of the hyoid and submandibular region, well away from the inferior thyroid artery at the lower pole of the thyroid.

exam_trap: Candidates may pick the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, but it runs with the superior thyroid artery; the inferior thyroid artery is related to the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
takeaway: Inferior thyroid artery = recurrent laryngeal nerve. Superior thyroid artery = external laryngeal nerve.
thinking: Ligation of the inferior thyroid artery near the lower pole ↓ the recurrent laryngeal nerve ascends in the tracheo-oesophageal groove ↓ it crosses close to the artery, passing in front of, behind or between its branches ↓ Recurrent laryngeal nerve
pearl: Because the nerve may pass anterior, posterior or between the branches of the inferior thyroid artery, many surgeons identify the nerve and ligate the arterial branches close to the gland rather than tying the main trunk laterally.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Perioperative Management (ERAS)
stem: Which of the following is a key component of enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS) protocols?
correct_answer: C. Early oral intake and mobilisation
why_correct: ERAS protocols emphasise early oral intake, early mobilisation, and avoidance of unnecessary drains and nasogastric tubes.

why_others_wrong.A: ERAS reduces preoperative fasting and often uses carbohydrate loading, rather than prolonged fasting.
why_others_wrong.B: ERAS avoids routine nasogastric tubes, which delay oral intake and increase pulmonary complications.
why_others_wrong.D: ERAS avoids routine drains, which can impede mobilisation without clear benefit.
why_others_wrong.E: Prolonged bed rest increases VTE, pulmonary complications and muscle loss, so ERAS promotes early mobilisation.

exam_trap: Routine nasogastric tubes or drains may tempt as traditional safety measures, but enhanced recovery avoids them because they delay feeding and mobilisation without clear benefit.
takeaway: ERAS = early feeding, early mobilisation, no routine drains/NG tubes.
thinking: Enhanced recovery aims to reduce the surgical stress response ↓ avoids prolonged fasting, routine tubes and drains, and bed rest ↓ promotes early return to normal function ↓ Early oral intake and mobilisation
pearl: Opioid-sparing multimodal analgesia supports enhanced recovery by reducing nausea, ileus and sedation, allowing earlier eating and mobilisation.

subject: Neurosurgery
title: Trauma Management (Head Injury)
stem: A 25-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department after a fall. GCS is 13. CT head shows a small extradural haematoma with no midline shift. What is the most appropriate management?
correct_answer: B. Conservative management with close observation
why_correct: Small extradural haematomas without mass effect or neurological deterioration can be managed conservatively with close observation and repeat imaging.

why_others_wrong.A: Immediate craniotomy is for large or symptomatic extradural haematomas with mass effect or deterioration, not a small collection without midline shift.
why_others_wrong.C: Burr hole drainage is an emergency measure when neurosurgical craniotomy is unavailable in a deteriorating patient, not for a small stable haematoma.
why_others_wrong.D: Mannitol is a temporising measure for clinical signs of raised intracranial pressure or herniation, such as a falling GCS or unilateral dilated pupil, which this stable patient lacks.
why_others_wrong.E: Lumbar puncture is contraindicated with an intracranial mass lesion because of the risk of herniation, and has no role in managing a haematoma.

exam_trap: Candidates pick immediate craniotomy (A) because any extradural haematoma sounds surgical, but a small collection without shift in a stable patient can be observed closely.
takeaway: Small EDH + no mass effect = conservative with close observation.
thinking: GCS 13 after a fall ↓ small extradural haematoma with no midline shift ↓ no significant mass effect, so no immediate indication for evacuation ↓ neurosurgical advice with close neurological observation and repeat CT ↓ Conservative management with close observation
pearl: Extradural haematomas can enlarge in the first hours after injury, so conservatively managed patients need frequent GCS and pupil checks in a neurosurgical setting and immediate re-imaging if they deteriorate.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Pharmacology (Metformin)
stem: A 65-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and an eGFR of 25 mL/min/1.73m² is scheduled for contrast-enhanced CT. Which medication should be withheld from the time of the scan and for 48 hours afterwards?
why_correct: Current UK (Royal College of Radiologists) guidance recommends withholding metformin from the time of contrast for 48 hours when eGFR is below 30 mL/min/1.73m², unknown, or in acute kidney injury, because contrast-associated kidney injury could precipitate lactic acidosis. With adequate renal function, metformin does not need to be withheld for standard IV contrast-enhanced CT.

why_others_wrong.A: Insulin does not interact with iodinated contrast to cause lactic acidosis and should be continued with glucose monitoring.
why_others_wrong.C: Gliclazide is not associated with contrast-related lactic acidosis and does not need to be withheld for the scan.
why_others_wrong.D: Atorvastatin has no relevant interaction with iodinated contrast and can be continued.
why_others_wrong.E: Amlodipine has no interaction with iodinated contrast and no link to lactic acidosis, so it can be continued.

exam_trap: Metformin is NOT withheld for all contrast studies — only when eGFR <30 (or unknown), or for intra-arterial contrast procedures.
takeaway: Metformin + contrast CT: withhold only if eGFR <30 (or unknown) — not a blanket rule for all patients.
thinking: Type 2 diabetes on oral therapy ↓ eGFR 25, below 30 ↓ iodinated contrast may cause acute kidney injury ↓ metformin accumulation risks lactic acidosis ↓ Metformin
pearl: UK perioperative guidance usually continues once- or twice-daily metformin on the day of surgery, but omits it while a variable-rate insulin infusion is running, when iodinated contrast is given with impaired renal function, or when there is significant risk of acute kidney injury.

subject: Microbiology & surgical infection
title: Microbiology (Hepatitis)
stem: A 40-year-old healthcare worker sustains a needlestick injury from a patient known to have hepatitis B. She is unvaccinated. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
correct_answer: C. Hepatitis B vaccine and immunoglobulin
why_correct: For an unvaccinated individual with a needlestick injury from a hepatitis B positive patient, both hepatitis B immunoglobulin and hepatitis B vaccine should be given.

why_others_wrong.A: Vaccine alone takes weeks to generate protective antibody, so it does not provide immediate protection after a known hepatitis B exposure.
why_others_wrong.B: Immunoglobulin alone gives only short-term passive protection; the vaccine course is needed for lasting immunity.
why_others_wrong.D: Antiviral therapy is used as post-exposure prophylaxis for HIV, not as standard prophylaxis after hepatitis B exposure.
why_others_wrong.E: Observation alone leaves an unvaccinated worker unprotected after a significant exposure to a known hepatitis B source.

exam_trap: Vaccine alone tempts because it is the usual route to immunity, but it takes weeks to produce antibody; an unvaccinated worker also needs immediate hepatitis B immunoglobulin.
takeaway: Needlestick + hepatitis B + unvaccinated = immunoglobulin + vaccine.
thinking: Needlestick from a known hepatitis B positive source ↓ recipient unvaccinated, so no existing immunity ↓ needs immediate passive protection plus active immunisation ↓ Hepatitis B vaccine and immunoglobulin
pearl: After any needlestick, the wound should be encouraged to bleed and washed with soap and water without scrubbing, then the injury reported urgently to occupational health or the emergency department.

subject: Plastic surgery
title: Surgical Oncology (Melanoma)
stem: A 55-year-old man has a pigmented lesion on his back. Excision biopsy shows a melanoma with a Breslow thickness of 2.5 mm. What is the MINIMUM recommended excision margin according to current UK guidance?
why_correct: A melanoma with a Breslow thickness of 2.5 mm is T3 and therefore stage II, for which NICE guidance recommends wide local excision with a clinical margin of at least 2 cm.

why_others_wrong.A: A 0.5 cm margin is advised for melanoma in situ and is far too narrow for an invasive melanoma 2.5 mm thick.
why_others_wrong.B: A 1 cm margin is recommended for stage I melanoma, but a 2.5 mm tumour is at least stage II and needs a 2 cm margin.
why_others_wrong.D: A 3 cm margin exceeds the minimum needed; for a 2-4 mm melanoma 2 cm is sufficient, and wider margins have not improved survival.
why_others_wrong.E: Excision biopsy is diagnostic only; an invasive 2.5 mm melanoma still needs wide local excision to reduce local recurrence.

exam_trap: Do not quote the outdated 2-3 cm range; current NICE guidance sets margins by stage: 0.5 cm in situ, 1 cm for stage I and 2 cm for stage II.
takeaway: Melanoma margins by stage: in situ 0.5 cm, stage I 1 cm, stage II (including Breslow over 2 mm) 2 cm.
thinking: Breslow 2.5 mm ↓ T3, so at least stage II ↓ NICE: stage II needs a 2 cm clinical margin ↓ wider margins add morbidity without survival benefit ↓ 2 cm margins
pearl: Wide local excision margins are measured clinically from the edge of the biopsy scar or residual lesion at operation, and the excision usually extends down to, but not routinely through, the deep fascia.

subject: Anatomy
title: Applied Anatomy (Pelvis)
stem: During a transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP), which structure is at risk of injury if the resection extends too far distally, beyond the prostatic apex?
why_correct: The external urethral sphincter lies distal to the prostate at the apex. Injury during TURP can cause incontinence.

why_others_wrong.A: The internal urethral sphincter lies at the bladder neck, proximal to the prostate, and is not the structure at risk when resection extends distally beyond the prostatic apex.
why_others_wrong.C: The obturator nerve runs along the lateral pelvic wall and can be stimulated during lateral bladder tumour resection (obturator reflex), but it is not related to the prostatic apex or distal TURP margin.
why_others_wrong.D: The rectum lies posterior to the prostate and is at risk during prostatic biopsy or posterior perforation, not specifically from resection extending distal to the apex along the urethra.
why_others_wrong.E: The bladder dome is at the opposite, proximal end of the lower urinary tract from the prostatic apex and is not at risk from over-resection at the distal margin.

exam_trap: Candidates may pick the internal urethral sphincter, but it lies at the bladder neck and is routinely resected in TURP; continence then depends on the external sphincter distal to the apex.
takeaway: TURP = preserve external urethral sphincter. Injury = incontinence.
thinking: TURP resection extending distally beyond the prostatic apex ↓ the membranous urethra lies just distal to the apex ↓ it is encircled by the striated external urethral sphincter ↓ External urethral sphincter
pearl: The verumontanum is the key distal landmark in TURP: resecting beyond it risks the external sphincter, whereas loss of the bladder neck (internal sphincter) commonly causes retrograde ejaculation.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: Applied Physiology (Gastrointestinal)
stem: Which of the following is the primary function of the colon?
correct_answer: B. Absorption of water and electrolytes
why_correct: The primary function of the colon is to absorb water and electrolytes from the remaining indigestible food matter.

why_others_wrong.A: Dietary protein is digested and absorbed as amino acids and small peptides mainly in the small intestine, not the colon.
why_others_wrong.C: Fat digestion depends on pancreatic lipase and bile salts in the small intestine rather than the colon.
why_others_wrong.D: Bile is produced by hepatocytes and stored in the gallbladder; the colon has no role in bile production.
why_others_wrong.E: Iron is absorbed mainly in the duodenum and proximal jejunum, not in the colon.

exam_trap: Absorption of proteins (option A) or iron (option E) is chosen by misplacing small-bowel functions, but nutrients are absorbed proximally; the colon reclaims water and electrolytes.
takeaway: Colon = water and electrolyte absorption. Small bowel = nutrient absorption.
thinking: Question asks the primary function of the colon ↓ nutrients are digested and absorbed in the small intestine ↓ the colon recovers remaining water and electrolytes to form solid faeces ↓ Absorption of water and electrolytes
pearl: Patients with a high-output stoma or short bowel without a colon lose this reserve, so they are prone to dehydration and sodium depletion and benefit from an oral rehydration solution rather than hypotonic drinks.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Applied Pathology (Lymphoma)
stem: A 30-year-old man presents with painless cervical lymphadenopathy, fever, night sweats, and weight loss. Biopsy shows Reed-Sternberg cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Reed-Sternberg cells are the hallmark of Hodgkin lymphoma. It typically presents with painless lymphadenopathy, B symptoms, and has a good prognosis with treatment.

why_others_wrong.A: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma lacks the classic Reed-Sternberg cells in a reactive background and more often involves extranodal sites or non-contiguous nodes.
why_others_wrong.C: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia affects older adults and shows small mature lymphocytes with smear cells, not Reed-Sternberg cells.
why_others_wrong.D: Tuberculous lymphadenitis shows caseating granulomas, and Reed-Sternberg cells are not a feature.
why_others_wrong.E: Sarcoidosis shows non-caseating granulomas, usually with hilar lymphadenopathy, rather than Reed-Sternberg cells.

exam_trap: Tuberculosis also causes cervical lymphadenopathy with fever and night sweats, but it shows caseating granulomas; Reed-Sternberg cells are the defining feature of Hodgkin lymphoma.
takeaway: Reed-Sternberg cells = Hodgkin lymphoma. B symptoms = fever, night sweats, weight loss.
thinking: Young adult with painless cervical lymphadenopathy ↓ fever, night sweats and weight loss are B symptoms ↓ Reed-Sternberg cells on biopsy ↓ Hodgkin lymphoma
pearl: When lymphoma is suspected, an excision or core biopsy is preferred to fine needle aspiration, because diagnosis and subtyping depend on nodal architecture.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Perioperative Management (Diathermy)
stem: A 65-year-old man with a pacemaker is scheduled for surgery using diathermy. Which of the following is the most appropriate precaution?

options.A: Use unipolar diathermy close to the pacemaker
options.D: Place the diathermy pad on the same side as the pacemaker

correct_answer: B. Use bipolar diathermy where possible
why_correct: Bipolar diathermy is preferred in patients with pacemakers because the current is confined to the tips of the forceps, reducing the risk of pacemaker interference.

why_others_wrong.A: Unipolar current near the device is the most likely to cause pacemaker interference, so it should be avoided close to the pacemaker.
why_others_wrong.C: Diathermy can inhibit or reprogramme a pacemaker, so precautions are required.
why_others_wrong.D: The pad should be placed so the current path runs away from the pacemaker, not on the same side as the device.
why_others_wrong.E: A pacemaker should not simply be turned off; any reprogramming, such as to an asynchronous mode, is planned with cardiac physiology support.

exam_trap: Do not place the diathermy pad on the same side as the pacemaker.
takeaway: Pacemaker + diathermy = bipolar preferred. Unipolar if necessary with pad away from device.
thinking: Pacemaker with planned diathermy ↓ monopolar current can be sensed as cardiac activity and inhibit pacing ↓ bipolar current stays between the forceps tips ↓ Use bipolar diathermy where possible
pearl: Implantable cardioverter-defibrillators may interpret diathermy as ventricular fibrillation and deliver shocks, so their tachy-therapies are usually suspended perioperatively with external defibrillation available.

subject: Major trauma & fluids
title: Trauma Management (Abdominal Trauma)
stem: A 30-year-old man falls from his bicycle and strikes his left upper quadrant on the handlebars. He is haemodynamically stable and his abdomen is soft with no peritonism. CT shows an isolated grade III splenic laceration with no active contrast extravasation and no hollow-viscus injury. What is the most appropriate management?
why_correct: A haemodynamically stable patient with a grade III splenic laceration, no active contrast extravasation and no peritonitis can be managed non-operatively with serial examination and repeat haemoglobin, provided associated diaphragmatic or hollow-viscus injury has been excluded.

why_others_wrong.A: Splenectomy is reserved for haemodynamic instability, peritonitis or failed conservative management, none of which is present here.
why_others_wrong.C: Embolisation is used mainly for active contrast extravasation or pseudoaneurysm, and the CT shows no active bleeding.
why_others_wrong.D: Laparotomy is indicated for instability, peritonitis or evidence of hollow-viscus injury, none of which is described in this stable patient with no active bleeding on CT.
why_others_wrong.E: Transfusion is not indicated in a haemodynamically stable patient without active bleeding or significant anaemia.

exam_trap: Splenic artery embolisation tempts with a higher-grade injury, but it is used for active contrast extravasation or pseudoaneurysm, neither of which is present on this CT.
takeaway: Stable splenic injury with no peritonitis and no associated injury = non-operative management with close observation; instability or peritonitis = operate.
thinking: Blunt left upper quadrant injury ↓ haemodynamically stable with a soft abdomen ↓ CT: isolated grade III splenic laceration, no active bleeding or associated injury ↓ criteria for non-operative management are met ↓ Conservative management with observation
pearl: Non-operative management of a splenic injury requires close monitoring in a setting able to proceed to immediate laparotomy, because delayed bleeding can occur after an initially stable course.

subject: Perioperative medicine & nutrition
title: Pharmacology (Insulin)
stem: A 55-year-old man with type 1 diabetes is found unconscious with a blood glucose of 2.1 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
why_correct: For an unconscious patient with hypoglycaemia, intravenous dextrose is the immediate treatment. Oral glucose is contraindicated in unconscious patients due to aspiration risk.

why_others_wrong.A: Oral glucose should not be given to an unconscious patient because of the risk of aspiration.
why_others_wrong.C: Intramuscular glucagon is useful when intravenous access is unavailable, but intravenous dextrose acts faster and is preferred when access is possible.
why_others_wrong.D: Intravenous insulin would lower the blood glucose further and worsen the hypoglycaemia.
why_others_wrong.E: Metformin is an oral glucose-lowering drug that cannot be given to an unconscious patient and would not treat hypoglycaemia.

exam_trap: Intramuscular glucagon tempts as the standard emergency treatment, but it is used when IV access is unavailable; with access, IV glucose works faster.
takeaway: Unconscious hypoglycaemia = IV dextrose. Conscious = oral glucose.
thinking: Unconscious patient ↓ blood glucose 2.1 mmol/L ↓ oral route unsafe because of aspiration risk ↓ IV access allows fastest correction ↓ Intravenous dextrose
pearl: In the UK, 10% or 20% glucose is preferred to 50% for intravenous treatment because concentrated glucose is irritant and can cause tissue necrosis if it extravasates.

subject: Microbiology & surgical infection
title: Microbiology (MRSA)
stem: A 70-year-old man is found to be colonised with MRSA before elective surgery. What is the most appropriate management?

options.B: Decolonisation with chlorhexidine washes and mupirocin nasal ointment

correct_answer: B. Decolonisation with chlorhexidine washes and mupirocin nasal ointment
why_correct: MRSA decolonisation with chlorhexidine body washes and mupirocin nasal ointment reduces the risk of surgical site infection.

why_others_wrong.A: Proceeding without decolonisation leaves the patient at higher risk of MRSA surgical site infection.
why_others_wrong.C: Oral vancomycin is poorly absorbed and is used for Clostridioides difficile infection, not for clearing MRSA carriage.
why_others_wrong.D: Intravenous teicoplanin may be used as surgical prophylaxis in MRSA carriers but does not decolonise skin or nasal carriage.
why_others_wrong.E: MRSA colonisation is not a reason to cancel surgery permanently; decolonisation allows surgery to proceed safely.

exam_trap: Intravenous teicoplanin tempts because it covers MRSA during surgery, but it does not clear skin or nasal carriage; decolonisation requires chlorhexidine washes and nasal mupirocin.
takeaway: MRSA colonisation = chlorhexidine washes + mupirocin nasal ointment.
thinking: MRSA colonisation found before elective surgery ↓ carriage raises the risk of MRSA surgical site infection ↓ eradicate skin and nasal carriage before operating ↓ Decolonisation with chlorhexidine washes and mupirocin nasal ointment
pearl: If an MRSA carrier needs surgery with prophylaxis, a glycopeptide such as teicoplanin is used because flucloxacillin and cephalosporins are ineffective against MRSA.

subject: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care
title: Surgical Oncology (Thyroid Cancer)
stem: A 45-year-old woman has a thyroid nodule. FNA shows medullary thyroid carcinoma. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial investigation?

options.B: Serum calcitonin and RET mutation analysis

correct_answer: B. Serum calcitonin and RET mutation analysis
why_correct: Medullary thyroid carcinoma arises from parafollicular C cells and secretes calcitonin. RET mutation analysis is important because it can be associated with MEN 2A and 2B syndromes.

why_others_wrong.A: Thyroglobulin comes from follicular cells and is a marker for differentiated thyroid cancer, not medullary carcinoma from C cells.
why_others_wrong.C: Medullary carcinoma arises from parafollicular C cells, which do not take up iodine, so a radioiodine scan is unhelpful.
why_others_wrong.D: TSH assesses thyroid function but does not help stage medullary carcinoma or identify hereditary MEN2.
why_others_wrong.E: Anti-thyroid antibodies indicate autoimmune thyroid disease and do not contribute to medullary carcinoma assessment.

exam_trap: Thyroglobulin is a marker for differentiated thyroid cancer, not medullary.
takeaway: Medullary thyroid cancer = calcitonin + RET mutation. Associated with MEN 2.
thinking: FNA shows medullary thyroid carcinoma ↓ arises from parafollicular C cells ↓ calcitonin is the tumour marker ↓ RET testing identifies hereditary MEN2 ↓ Serum calcitonin and RET mutation analysis
pearl: Medullary thyroid cancer does not respond to radioiodine or TSH suppression, so surgery with total thyroidectomy and central neck dissection is the main treatment.

subject: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care
title: Vascular Surgery (Buerger's Disease)
stem: A 35-year-old man presents with painful, cold fingers and toes. He is a heavy smoker. Angiography shows distal small vessel occlusion with corkscrew collaterals. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Buerger's disease (thromboangiitis obliterans) is a non-atherosclerotic inflammatory disease affecting small and medium arteries and veins of the extremities. It is strongly associated with smoking.

why_others_wrong.A: Atherosclerosis affects older patients and larger proximal arteries, whereas this is a young smoker with distal occlusions and corkscrew collaterals.
why_others_wrong.C: Raynaud's phenomenon causes episodic colour changes from vasospasm, with normal angiography between attacks rather than fixed distal occlusions.
why_others_wrong.D: Systemic sclerosis typically affects women with skin thickening and Raynaud's, not a young male heavy smoker with corkscrew collaterals.
why_others_wrong.E: Embolism causes sudden occlusion, often of a single vessel with an abrupt cut-off, rather than multiple distal occlusions with corkscrew collaterals.

exam_trap: Candidates choose atherosclerosis because of smoking, but a young patient with distal small-vessel occlusions and corkscrew collaterals suggests thromboangiitis obliterans.
takeaway: Young smoker + distal ischaemia + corkscrew collaterals = Buerger's disease. Smoking cessation is essential.
thinking: Young heavy smoker ↓ painful cold fingers and toes ↓ distal small vessel occlusion ↓ corkscrew collaterals on angiography ↓ Buerger's disease (thromboangiitis obliterans)
pearl: Complete smoking cessation is the only treatment that reliably halts thromboangiitis obliterans; continued smoking commonly leads to digital or limb amputation.

subject: Paediatric surgery
title: Paediatric Surgery (Oesophageal Atresia)
stem: A newborn has excessive salivation, choking on feeds, and inability to pass a nasogastric tube. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Oesophageal atresia classically presents with excessive salivation, choking on feeds, and inability to pass an NG tube. It is often associated with tracheo-oesophageal fistula (VACTERL association).

why_others_wrong.A: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia presents with respiratory distress, a scaphoid abdomen and displaced heart sounds, and a nasogastric tube can usually be passed.
why_others_wrong.C: Pyloric stenosis develops at a few weeks of age with projectile vomiting, and does not prevent passage of a nasogastric tube into the stomach.
why_others_wrong.D: Duodenal atresia causes bilious vomiting and a double bubble, but a nasogastric tube passes freely into the distended stomach.
why_others_wrong.E: Meconium ileus presents with distension and failure to pass meconium, not drooling and choking with feeds or an obstructed oesophagus.

exam_trap: Candidates may pick duodenal atresia (D) as a neonatal obstruction, but a tube passes easily into its distended stomach; a tube that will not pass means oesophageal atresia.
takeaway: Newborn + excessive salivation + NG tube coiling = oesophageal atresia. Associated with VACTERL.
thinking: Newborn with excessive salivation ↓ choking on feeds ↓ nasogastric tube will not pass and coils in the upper pouch ↓ blind-ending oesophagus ↓ Oesophageal atresia
pearl: A chest X-ray shows the tube coiled in the upper pouch, and gas in the stomach indicates a distal tracheo-oesophageal fistula; maternal polyhydramnios is a common antenatal clue.

subject: Pharmacology
title: Pharmacokinetics: renal clearance
stem: A drug is eliminated predominantly by the kidneys. Its renal function declines substantially, but its volume of distribution remains unchanged. Which pharmacokinetic change is most likely?
correct_answer: B. Reduced clearance and increased half-life
why_correct: If renal clearance falls, total drug clearance decreases. With an unchanged volume of distribution, elimination half-life increases because t½ is proportional to Vd/clearance.

why_others_wrong.A: Clearance falls rather than increases.
why_others_wrong.C: Renal impairment does not necessarily alter Vd.
why_others_wrong.D: First-pass metabolism concerns orally administered drugs and is not increased simply because renal function falls.
why_others_wrong.E: Intravenous administration already bypasses absorption and first-pass metabolism.

exam_trap: Reduced volume of distribution is chosen by candidates who confuse distribution with elimination; renal impairment reduces clearance and prolongs half-life without necessarily changing Vd.
takeaway: Renal impairment → reduced renal clearance → prolonged half-life → potential drug accumulation.
source: British National Formulary (BNF), Principles of Prescribing/Pharmacokinetics, current edition accessed 2026; Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Renal function declines ↓ renal clearance falls ↓ Vd unchanged ↓ t½ ∝ Vd / clearance increases ↓ Reduced clearance and increased half-life
pearl: Vancomycin dosing in renal impairment is guided by trough or AUC-based levels, because reduced clearance prolongs its half-life and increases nephrotoxicity risk.

subject: Pharmacology
title: Drug transporters
stem: A drug is normally secreted from the renal proximal tubule by an organic anion transporter. A second drug inhibits this transporter. What is the most likely immediate pharmacokinetic consequence for the first drug?
why_correct: Inhibition of proximal tubular secretion reduces active renal elimination of the drug, increasing its plasma concentration and potentially prolonging its half-life.

why_others_wrong.A: The transporter is inhibited, so secretion decreases.
why_others_wrong.C: Glomerular filtration depends mainly on filtration of the unbound fraction and is not directly increased by transporter inhibition.
why_others_wrong.D: The interaction occurs in the kidney, not the gastrointestinal tract.
why_others_wrong.E: Renal transporter inhibition does not directly increase hepatic first-pass metabolism.

exam_trap: Increased glomerular filtration is chosen by candidates who assume the kidney compensates, but transporter inhibition does not change filtration; renal clearance simply falls.
takeaway: Renal drug clearance = filtration + secretion − reabsorption.
source: BNF, Principles of Prescribing, current edition accessed 2026; Rang & Dale's Pharmacology, 10th ed.
thinking: Drug secreted by a proximal tubular organic anion transporter ↓ second drug inhibits that transporter ↓ secretion falls ↓ renal clearance falls and plasma level rises ↓ Reduced renal clearance
pearl: Methotrexate toxicity can be precipitated by drugs that compete for its renal tubular secretion, such as NSAIDs and penicillins, so these combinations need caution and monitoring.

subject: Pharmacology
title: Prodrug activation
stem: A medication is administered in an inactive form and converted in the body into an active metabolite. What term best describes this medication?
why_correct: A prodrug is administered in a form that requires metabolic conversion to produce its pharmacological activity.

why_others_wrong.A: A competitive antagonist binds a receptor without producing the full agonist response.
why_others_wrong.B: A partial agonist has intrinsic activity but produces a submaximal response.
why_others_wrong.D: An enzyme inducer increases expression/activity of drug-metabolising enzymes.
why_others_wrong.E: Receptor downregulation reduces receptor availability or responsiveness.

exam_trap: Enzyme inducer is chosen by candidates who link metabolism with induction, but an inducer increases enzyme activity; a medication activated by conversion in the body is a prodrug.
takeaway: Prodrug = inactive or less-active administered compound → active metabolite.
source: Rang & Dale's Pharmacology, 10th ed.; BNF, Principles of Prescribing, current edition accessed 2026.
thinking: Medication given in an inactive form ↓ converted in the body ↓ active metabolite produces the effect ↓ Prodrug
pearl: Cyclophosphamide is a prodrug activated by hepatic CYP enzymes; one metabolite, acrolein, causes haemorrhagic cystitis, which mesna is given to prevent.

subject: Pharmacology
title: Receptor regulation
stem: A patient receives continuous stimulation of a receptor by a high concentration of an agonist. After several days, the same dose produces a smaller physiological response. Which mechanism best explains this?
why_correct: Persistent agonist exposure can cause receptor desensitisation, including receptor phosphorylation, uncoupling from intracellular signalling pathways and, with longer exposure, receptor internalisation/downregulation.

why_others_wrong.B: Increased receptor synthesis would generally increase responsiveness.
why_others_wrong.C: Increased agonist affinity would tend to increase the response.
why_others_wrong.D: Increased receptor reserve would generally increase sensitivity.
why_others_wrong.E: Bioavailability concerns the proportion of an administered drug reaching systemic circulation.

exam_trap: Increased receptor reserve or agonist affinity are chosen as receptor-level answers, but both would increase sensitivity; a shrinking response to the same dose indicates receptor desensitisation.
takeaway: Persistent agonist stimulation can cause receptor desensitisation and reduced responsiveness.
source: Rang & Dale's Pharmacology, 10th ed.; Goodman & Gilman's The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics, 14th ed.
thinking: Continuous high-concentration agonist stimulation ↓ smaller response after several days ↓ receptor phosphorylation and uncoupling, then internalisation ↓ Receptor desensitisation
pearl: In septic shock, prolonged catecholamine infusion and inflammation contribute to adrenoceptor desensitisation, one reason vasopressin, which acts on separate receptors, is used as an adjunct.

subject: Pharmacology
title: Pharmacodynamic synergy
stem: Two drugs are administered together. Their combined effect is substantially greater than the sum of their individual effects, allowing lower doses of each to achieve the desired clinical effect. Which pharmacological concept best describes this?
why_correct: Synergy describes an interaction in which the combined effect is greater than the expected effect of the individual agents.

why_others_wrong.A: Antagonism reduces or opposes the effect of another drug.
why_others_wrong.C: Tachyphylaxis is a rapidly developing reduction in response after repeated exposure.
why_others_wrong.D: Tolerance develops more gradually with continued exposure.
why_others_wrong.E: An idiosyncratic reaction is an unusual, unpredictable drug response.

exam_trap: Do not equate any additive drug effect with synergy. Synergy implies more than the expected combined effect.
takeaway: Synergy = combined pharmacological effect exceeds the expected individual/additive effect.
source: Rang & Dale's Pharmacology, 10th ed.; Goodman & Gilman's Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics, 14th ed.
thinking: Two drugs given together ↓ combined effect substantially greater than the sum of individual effects ↓ more than additive ↓ lower doses of each achieve the desired effect ↓ Synergy
pearl: Combining a cell-wall-active beta-lactam with an aminoglycoside against enterococci is a classic example of synergy, because cell-wall damage increases aminoglycoside uptake into the bacterium.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Cellular adaptation
stem: A patient develops chronic obstruction of a tubular organ. The smooth-muscle cells within the wall become larger, increasing the thickness of the muscular layer. What cellular adaptation has occurred?
why_correct: Hypertrophy is an increase in the size of individual cells, producing enlargement of the affected tissue.

why_others_wrong.A: Hyperplasia is an increase in cell number.
why_others_wrong.C: Metaplasia is replacement of one differentiated cell type by another.
why_others_wrong.D: Dysplasia describes disordered cellular maturation and architecture.
why_others_wrong.E: Atrophy is reduction in cell size and/or tissue mass.

exam_trap: A tissue can undergo both hypertrophy and hyperplasia, but the question specifically describes enlarged individual cells.
takeaway: Hypertrophy = bigger cells. Hyperplasia = more cells.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.; Kumar, Abbas & Aster, Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th ed.
thinking: Chronic obstruction of a tubular organ ↓ increased workload on wall smooth muscle ↓ individual cells become larger ↓ Hypertrophy
pearl: Bladder outflow obstruction from prostatic enlargement produces a thick-walled trabeculated bladder, and diverticula can form between the hypertrophied muscle bundles.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Vascular pathology
stem: An atherosclerotic plaque ruptures, exposing thrombogenic material to circulating blood. What is the immediate pathological consequence most likely to follow?
why_correct: Plaque rupture exposes thrombogenic components, particularly tissue factor and collagen, promoting platelet activation and coagulation with acute thrombus formation.

why_others_wrong.A: Chronic venous insufficiency is a venous disorder.
why_others_wrong.C: Lymphatic obstruction is unrelated to plaque rupture.
why_others_wrong.D: The dominant response is thrombosis rather than sustained vasodilatation.
why_others_wrong.E: Venous valves are anatomical structures and do not form in response to arterial plaque rupture.

exam_trap: Arterial vasodilatation (D) may tempt as a vascular response, but exposure of thrombogenic plaque contents triggers thrombosis, which causes the acute ischaemic event.
takeaway: Plaque rupture → thrombogenic surface exposure → platelet activation + coagulation → acute arterial thrombosis.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.; European Society of Cardiology, Guidelines for the management of chronic coronary syndromes, 2024.
thinking: Atherosclerotic plaque rupture ↓ tissue factor and collagen exposed to blood ↓ platelet activation and coagulation ↓ Acute thrombus formation
pearl: In the carotid territory, plaque rupture with platelet-fibrin embolism causes transient ischaemic attacks, and carotid endarterectomy reduces stroke risk in symptomatic significant stenosis.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Aneurysm pathology
stem: Which mechanism is most directly associated with progressive weakening of an arterial wall in an abdominal aortic aneurysm?

options.A: Increased collagen synthesis with increased wall strength
options.B: Extracellular matrix degradation within the vessel wall
options.C: Increased endothelial nitric oxide production alone
options.D: Complete absence of vascular smooth muscle cells from birth

correct_answer: B. Extracellular matrix degradation within the vessel wall
why_correct: Aneurysm progression is associated with degradation and remodelling of extracellular matrix components, including elastin and collagen, together with inflammatory and proteolytic activity within the aneurysm wall.

why_others_wrong.A: Increased effective collagen synthesis would not explain progressive wall weakening.
why_others_wrong.C: Nitric oxide has multiple vascular effects but is not the primary mechanism described.
why_others_wrong.D: Congenital complete absence of vascular smooth muscle is not the usual mechanism.
why_others_wrong.E: Platelet production does not directly weaken the aortic wall.

exam_trap: Do not reduce aneurysm biology to "high blood pressure". Structural extracellular-matrix degradation is central to wall weakening.
takeaway: Aneurysm progression involves inflammatory/proteolytic remodelling and degradation of vascular extracellular matrix.
source: European Society for Vascular Surgery, Clinical Practice Guidelines on the Management of Abdominal Aorto-iliac Artery Aneurysms, 2024; Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Abdominal aortic aneurysm ↓ progressive weakening of the aortic wall ↓ inflammatory cells release proteolytic enzymes ↓ elastin and collagen degraded ↓ Extracellular matrix degradation within the vessel wall
pearl: In England, men are offered one-off ultrasound aneurysm screening in the year they turn 65, and smoking is the strongest modifiable risk factor for aneurysm development and growth.

subject: Microbiology & surgical infection
title: Fungal biology
stem: Which component is a major structural constituent of the fungal cell wall?
why_correct: Chitin is an important structural component of fungal cell walls, together with glucans and other polysaccharides.

why_others_wrong.A: Peptidoglycan is characteristic of bacterial cell walls.
why_others_wrong.B: Lipopolysaccharide is found in the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria.
why_others_wrong.D: Mycolic acids are characteristic of mycobacterial cell walls.
why_others_wrong.E: Cellulose is the main structural polymer of plant cell walls; true fungal walls are built on chitin and glucans instead.

exam_trap: Peptidoglycan tempts candidates who assume all microbial walls share one polymer, but it is bacterial; cellulose is plant-derived, while fungal walls are chitin and glucans.
takeaway: Fungal cell wall → chitin + glucans.
source: Murray, Rosenthal & Pfaller, Medical Microbiology, 10th ed.; UKHSA, UK Standards for Microbiology Investigations, current resources accessed 2026.
thinking: Fungi are eukaryotes with a cell wall ↓ the wall is built of chitin and glucans ↓ peptidoglycan, LPS and mycolic acid are bacterial; cellulose is plant ↓ Chitin
pearl: Fluorescent stains such as calcofluor white bind chitin in fungal walls, allowing rapid detection of fungal elements in tissue and fluid specimens.

subject: Microbiology & surgical infection
title: Fungal membrane
stem: Which sterol is a characteristic component of the fungal cell membrane and a target of several antifungal agents?
why_correct: Ergosterol is the principal sterol in fungal cell membranes and is targeted directly or indirectly by several antifungal drugs.

why_others_wrong.A: Cholesterol is the major sterol in mammalian cell membranes.
why_others_wrong.C: Cortisol is a human adrenal glucocorticoid hormone, not a structural sterol of the fungal cell membrane.
