exam_trap: Candidates who equate a narrow window with weakness choose an ineffective drug, but the drug is effective; a narrow window means effective and toxic concentrations are close.
takeaway: Narrow therapeutic window = little room between efficacy and toxicity.
source: BNF, Principles of Prescribing, current edition accessed 2026; Rang & Dale's Pharmacology, 10th ed.
thinking: Narrow therapeutic window ↓ effective and toxic concentrations lie close together ↓ small changes in exposure matter ↓ The effective and toxic concentrations are relatively close
pearl: Drugs with a narrow therapeutic window are those in which interactions, renal impairment or dehydration most often cause harm, so levels such as gentamicin, digoxin and lithium are monitored.

subject: Pharmacology
title: Pharmacology: hepatic enzyme induction
stem: A drug induces hepatic cytochrome P450 enzyme activity. What is the most likely effect on another drug that is extensively metabolised by that enzyme?

options.B: Increased metabolism and potentially reduced concentration
options.D: Reduced absorption caused by increased gastric pH

correct_answer: B. Increased metabolism and potentially reduced concentration
why_correct: Enzyme induction increases metabolic capacity. For a conventional active drug metabolised by the induced enzyme, this can reduce plasma concentration and therapeutic effect.

why_others_wrong.A: This describes enzyme inhibition rather than induction.
why_others_wrong.C: Hepatic enzyme induction does not directly stop renal excretion.
why_others_wrong.D: It is not primarily an absorption mechanism.
why_others_wrong.E: Increased metabolism can reduce, rather than increase, drug exposure.

exam_trap: Reduced metabolism with increased concentration is chosen by candidates confusing induction with inhibition; an inducer increases metabolism and can lower substrate concentration.
takeaway: Enzyme induction → metabolism ↑. For an active drug → concentration may ↓.
source: BNF, Principles of Prescribing, current edition accessed 2026; Rang & Dale's Pharmacology, 10th ed.
thinking: Drug induces hepatic CYP activity ↓ more enzyme available ↓ substrate metabolised faster ↓ Increased metabolism and potentially reduced concentration
pearl: Patients on ciclosporin or tacrolimus who start an enzyme inducer such as rifampicin are at risk of subtherapeutic levels and graft rejection, so levels must be monitored closely.

subject: Microbiology & surgical infection
title: Microbiology: bacterial cell wall
stem: Which component is characteristic of Gram-positive bacterial cell walls and contributes substantially to their thick structural layer?
why_correct: Gram-positive bacteria have a thick peptidoglycan cell wall. They do not possess the outer membrane containing lipopolysaccharide characteristic of Gram-negative bacteria.

why_others_wrong.A: Lipopolysaccharide is characteristic of the Gram-negative outer membrane.
why_others_wrong.C: Ergosterol is characteristic of fungal membranes.
why_others_wrong.D: Chitin is an important fungal cell-wall component.
why_others_wrong.E: Myelin is a vertebrate nervous-system structure.

exam_trap: Gram-positive = thick peptidoglycan. Gram-negative = thin peptidoglycan + outer membrane containing LPS.
takeaway: Gram-positive bacteria → thick peptidoglycan.
source: Murray, Rosenthal & Pfaller, Medical Microbiology, 10th ed.; Jawetz, Melnick & Adelberg's Medical Microbiology, 29th ed.
thinking: Gram-positive cell wall ↓ thick peptidoglycan layer retains crystal violet stain ↓ no outer membrane or LPS, which are Gram-negative features ↓ Thick peptidoglycan
pearl: Glycopeptides such as vancomycin act on peptidoglycan precursors but are too large to cross the Gram-negative outer membrane, so they are active only against Gram-positive organisms.

subject: Statistics & evidence-based medicine
title: Evidence: hazard ratio
stem: A survival analysis reports a hazard ratio of 0.60 for treatment compared with control. Which interpretation is most appropriate, assuming the proportional-hazards model is appropriate?

options.A: Treatment reduces absolute risk by exactly 40%
options.B: Treatment is associated with a 40% lower instantaneous hazard
options.C: Treatment increases survival probability by exactly 40 percentage points
options.D: Forty percent of patients are cured
options.E: The median survival is automatically 40% longer

correct_answer: B. Treatment is associated with a 40% lower instantaneous hazard
why_correct: A hazard ratio of 0.60 means the estimated hazard in the treatment group is 60% of that in the comparator group, corresponding to a relative hazard reduction of approximately 40%, under the proportional-hazards interpretation.

why_others_wrong.A: A hazard ratio of 0.60 is a relative comparison of event rates; the absolute risk reduction depends on baseline risk and follow-up, and is not given.
why_others_wrong.C: A 40-percentage-point survival gain is an absolute difference at a set time, which cannot be derived from a relative hazard without baseline survival.
why_others_wrong.D: A hazard ratio compares event rates between the two groups over time and does not describe the proportion of patients who are cured.
why_others_wrong.E: Median survival cannot be read directly from a hazard ratio; the gain in median survival depends on the shape of the baseline survival curve, so a 40% lower hazard does not mean a 40% longer median.

exam_trap: Choosing an exact 40% absolute risk reduction or a 40-point survival gain converts a relative hazard into an absolute effect without the baseline event rate.
takeaway: HR 0.60 → hazard about 40% lower, not absolute risk 40% lower.
source: Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions, current methodology; Steyerberg, Clinical Prediction Models, 2nd ed.
thinking: HR 0.60 under proportional hazards ↓ hazard in treatment group is 60% of control ↓ relative reduction is 1 − 0.60 ↓ Treatment is associated with a 40% lower instantaneous hazard
pearl: The absolute benefit implied by an HR depends on baseline risk: with a high control event rate, an HR of 0.60 represents a large absolute gain.

subject: Statistics & evidence-based medicine
title: Evidence: confidence interval
stem: A randomised trial reports a relative risk of 0.82 with a 95% confidence interval of 0.68–0.99. Which statement is most appropriate?

options.A: The confidence interval includes the null value for relative risk
options.B: The result excludes the null value for relative risk
options.C: The relative risk is definitely 0.82 in every population
options.D: The confidence interval proves absence of bias
options.E: The result establishes clinical importance regardless of effect size

correct_answer: B. The result excludes the null value for relative risk
why_correct: For a relative risk, the null value is 1.00. Because the 95% confidence interval extends from 0.68 to 0.99 and does not include 1, the result is statistically incompatible with the null hypothesis at the conventional two-sided 5% level, assuming the analysis and model are appropriate.

why_others_wrong.A: The interval runs from 0.68 to 0.99 and lies entirely below 1, so it does not include the null value for a relative risk.
why_others_wrong.C: A confidence interval represents uncertainty around the estimated effect; it does not state that the true effect must equal 0.82.
why_others_wrong.D: A confidence interval quantifies random error only and cannot reveal systematic bias from flawed design, conduct or analysis.
why_others_wrong.E: An upper limit of 0.99 is compatible with only a 1% relative reduction, so clinical importance depends on effect size and baseline risk.

exam_trap: Option A tempts because the upper limit of 0.99 is so close to 1, but the interval does not include 1, so the null value is excluded.
takeaway: RR/OR/HR CI crossing 1 → null not excluded. RR/OR/HR CI not crossing 1 → null excluded at that confidence level.
source: Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions, current methodology; Principles and Practice of Surgery, 7th ed.
thinking: Relative risk, null value 1 ↓ 95% CI 0.68 to 0.99 lies below 1 ↓ statistically significant at the 5% level ↓ The result excludes the null value for relative risk
pearl: An upper limit of 0.99 means the effect could be as small as a 1% relative reduction, so the result is significant but the clinical benefit may be small.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: thoracic inlet
stem: Which structure passes between the anterior scalene muscle and middle scalene muscle?
why_correct: The subclavian artery passes posterior to the anterior scalene and between the anterior and middle scalene muscles. The brachial plexus trunks also pass through this interscalene interval.

why_others_wrong.A: The phrenic nerve runs on the anterior surface of the anterior scalene.
why_others_wrong.C: The internal jugular vein lies in the carotid sheath.
why_others_wrong.D: The vagus nerve lies within the carotid sheath.
why_others_wrong.E: The subclavian vein passes anterior to the anterior scalene.

exam_trap: Subclavian artery = between anterior and middle scalene. Subclavian vein = anterior to anterior scalene.
takeaway: Interscalene triangle → subclavian artery + brachial plexus.
source: Gray's Anatomy, 42nd ed.; Gray's Atlas of Anatomy, 3rd ed.
thinking: Interval between anterior and middle scalene ↓ phrenic nerve lies on the front of anterior scalene; subclavian vein passes in front of it ↓ subclavian artery and brachial plexus trunks pass behind anterior scalene ↓ Subclavian artery
pearl: Compression of the subclavian artery and lower trunk in this interval, for example by a cervical rib, causes thoracic outlet syndrome; an interscalene brachial plexus block commonly causes ipsilateral phrenic nerve palsy.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: vagus nerve and lung root
stem: After passing posterior to the root of the lung, the vagus nerve contributes to which structure?
why_correct: The vagus nerve passes posterior to the root of the lung and contributes parasympathetic fibres to the pulmonary plexus. It also contributes to the oesophageal plexus.

why_others_wrong.A: The vagus contributes to the cardiac plexus but the question describes its relationship to the lung root.
why_others_wrong.C: The phrenic nerve is distinct from the vagus.
why_others_wrong.D: The brachial plexus arises from C5–T1 anterior rami.
why_others_wrong.E: The sympathetic chain lies posteriorly along the vertebral column.

exam_trap: Candidates may choose the cardiac plexus, which the vagus also supplies, but behind the lung root its branches form the pulmonary plexus; the phrenic nerve passes in front.
takeaway: Phrenic anterior to root; vagus posterior to root.
source: Gray's Anatomy, 42nd ed.; Gray's Atlas of Anatomy, 3rd ed.
thinking: Vagus nerve passing behind the lung root ↓ phrenic nerve passes in front of the root ↓ vagal branches behind the root form the pulmonary plexus ↓ the nerve then continues to the oesophageal plexus ↓ Pulmonary plexus
pearl: The left vagus gives off the left recurrent laryngeal nerve at the aortic arch before passing behind the lung root, so left hilar or aortopulmonary window tumours can cause hoarseness.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: pulmonary lymphatic drainage
stem: A carcinoma in the peripheral lung is most likely initially to drain to which lymph nodes?
why_correct: Pulmonary lymphatic vessels drain toward pulmonary nodes and then bronchopulmonary (hilar) nodes before continuing toward tracheobronchial and mediastinal nodes.

why_others_wrong.A: Inguinal nodes drain the lower limb and selected superficial pelvic/perineal regions.
why_others_wrong.C: Para-aortic nodes are important for abdominal and gonadal drainage.
why_others_wrong.D: Mesenteric nodes drain the gastrointestinal tract.
why_others_wrong.E: Popliteal nodes drain the lower limb.

exam_trap: Para-aortic nodes are chosen because lung cancer spreads widely, but initial lymphatic spread follows the bronchial tree to intrapulmonary then hilar nodes, not abdominal stations.
takeaway: Peripheral lung → pulmonary nodes → bronchopulmonary/hilar nodes.
source: Gray's Anatomy, 42nd ed.; Gray's Atlas of Anatomy, 3rd ed.
thinking: Peripheral lung carcinoma ↓ lymph flows centrally along the bronchovascular tree ↓ the first stations are intrapulmonary (pulmonary) nodes ↓ then bronchopulmonary hilar and mediastinal nodes ↓ Pulmonary nodes
pearl: Mediastinal nodal involvement is central to lung cancer staging and resectability; it is assessed with PET-CT and sampled by endobronchial ultrasound-guided needle aspiration.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: mediastinal lymphatics
stem: Which lymph-node group is particularly relevant to lymphatic drainage from the trachea and main bronchi?
why_correct: Tracheobronchial lymph nodes lie around the bifurcation and main bronchi and receive lymphatic drainage from the lungs and tracheobronchial tree.

why_others_wrong.B: Inguinal nodes drain the lower limb, perineum and lower abdominal wall, not the airway.
why_others_wrong.C: Mesenteric nodes drain the intestine, not the airway.
why_others_wrong.D: Epitrochlear nodes drain the medial hand and forearm, not the airway.
why_others_wrong.E: Popliteal nodes drain the lateral foot and deep structures of the leg, not the airway.

exam_trap: Candidates may confuse mediastinal with mesenteric nodes, but mesenteric nodes drain the gut; lymph from the trachea and main bronchi passes to the tracheobronchial nodes around the carina.
takeaway: Lung/tracheobronchial drainage → hilar → tracheobronchial → mediastinal pathways.
source: Gray's Anatomy, 42nd ed.
thinking: Lymph from the trachea and main bronchi ↓ drains to nodes clustered around the carina and main bronchi ↓ these are the superior and inferior (subcarinal) tracheobronchial nodes ↓ Tracheobronchial nodes
pearl: Enlarged subcarinal nodes can widen the carinal angle on chest imaging and are accessible for sampling by endobronchial ultrasound or mediastinoscopy.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: neck fascial spaces
stem: An infection originating in the retropharyngeal space can potentially spread inferiorly into which major anatomical region?
why_correct: The retropharyngeal and related deep neck spaces can provide pathways for infection to descend into the mediastinum. This is clinically important because deep neck infection may therefore cause mediastinal infection.

why_others_wrong.B: The femoral canal is part of the groin.
why_others_wrong.C: The inguinal canal is an abdominal-wall passage.
why_others_wrong.D: The lesser sac is an intra-abdominal peritoneal compartment.
why_others_wrong.E: The ischioanal fossa is a perineal space.

exam_trap: Candidates who think only of a local abscess may miss that retropharyngeal pus can descend behind the oesophagus into the posterior mediastinum, a thoracic emergency.
takeaway: Deep cervical spaces can communicate with the mediastinum → potentially life-threatening descending infection.
source: Gray's Anatomy, 42nd ed.; Principles and Practice of Surgery, 7th ed.
thinking: Infection in the retropharyngeal space ↓ space lies between buccopharyngeal and prevertebral fascia behind the pharynx and oesophagus ↓ it continues inferiorly into the thorax ↓ Posterior mediastinum
pearl: Retropharyngeal abscess in children often follows suppurative lymphadenitis and may present with neck stiffness, torticollis and stridor; lateral neck radiograph or CT shows widened prevertebral soft tissue.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: facial nerve
stem: A patient develops weakness of the muscles of facial expression after surgery involving the parotid gland. Which nerve has most likely been injured?
why_correct: The facial nerve traverses the parotid gland and divides within it into its terminal branches supplying the muscles of facial expression.

why_others_wrong.A: Glossopharyngeal nerve supplies the stylopharyngeus and carries posterior tongue sensation/taste.
why_others_wrong.C: The trigeminal nerve supplies facial sensation and muscles of mastication.
why_others_wrong.D: The hypoglossal nerve supplies tongue muscles.
why_others_wrong.E: The accessory nerve supplies sternocleidomastoid and trapezius.

exam_trap: Candidates may choose the glossopharyngeal nerve because it carries the parotid's secretomotor fibres, but it does not supply the muscles of facial expression; the facial nerve traverses the gland and is at risk.
takeaway: Parotid surgery → facial nerve at risk.
source: Gray's Anatomy, 42nd ed.; Gray's Atlas of Anatomy, 3rd ed.
thinking: Weakness of facial expression after parotid surgery ↓ facial nerve leaves the stylomastoid foramen and enters the parotid ↓ it divides within the gland into its terminal branches ↓ Facial nerve
pearl: At parotidectomy the facial nerve trunk is found using landmarks such as the tragal pointer, the posterior belly of digastric and the tympanomastoid suture; the marginal mandibular branch is especially vulnerable.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Physiology: exercise and oxygen consumption
stem: During progressively increasing exercise, which variable generally increases substantially because exercising muscle extracts more oxygen from blood?

options.D: Pulmonary shunt fraction in a healthy person

why_correct: Active skeletal muscle increases oxygen extraction, widening the arterial–venous oxygen difference. This contributes to increased oxygen consumption.

why_others_wrong.B: Dead space as a fraction of tidal volume falls during exercise, and it affects alveolar ventilation rather than muscle oxygen extraction.
why_others_wrong.C: Plasma oncotic pressure governs capillary fluid movement; any slight rise from haemoconcentration does not alter muscle oxygen extraction.
why_others_wrong.D: A major increase in pulmonary shunt is not expected in normal exercise.
why_others_wrong.E: Cerebrospinal fluid is secreted by the choroid plexus at a fairly constant rate and plays no part in muscle oxygen extraction.

exam_trap: Candidates may choose physiological dead space, but its fraction of each breath falls during exercise; increased muscle extraction is reflected in a wider arteriovenous oxygen difference.
takeaway: Exercise → O2 extraction ↑ → a–v O2 difference ↑.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Fick principle: oxygen consumption = cardiac output × arteriovenous oxygen difference ↓ exercising muscle extracts more oxygen ↓ venous oxygen content falls while arterial content is maintained ↓ Arteriovenous oxygen difference
pearl: The Fick principle also underlies the classic measurement of cardiac output, and a falling mixed venous saturation in a critically ill patient reflects a widening arteriovenous oxygen difference.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: heat loss
stem: Which mechanism is the dominant route of heat loss from an exposed person in a cool environment when there is no direct contact with another cold surface?
why_correct: Radiation is an important route of heat loss from the body to surrounding cooler surfaces when there is no direct contact.

why_others_wrong.A: Conduction requires direct contact.
why_others_wrong.C: Sweating is suppressed in a cool environment, so evaporation of sweat is not the dominant route; insensible evaporative loss is smaller than radiant loss.
why_others_wrong.D: Shivering generates heat rather than being a route of heat loss.
why_others_wrong.E: Cutaneous vasoconstriction conserves heat by reducing skin blood flow; it is not a route of heat loss.

exam_trap: Conduction (A) is chosen as a familiar route, but it needs direct contact; shivering and vasoconstriction conserve or generate heat, leaving radiation as the main loss.
takeaway: Radiation = heat transfer without direct contact.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Exposed person in a cool environment ↓ no contact with a cold surface, so conduction is minimal ↓ sweating is suppressed in the cold ↓ infrared emission to cooler surroundings dominates ↓ Radiation
pearl: Radiant loss depends on the temperature difference between the skin and surrounding surfaces, so covering exposed skin and raising ambient temperature are effective ways to limit it.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: fever
stem: During a fever, the hypothalamic temperature set point is increased. What is the expected initial response when the set point rises?
why_correct: When the hypothalamic set point rises, the current body temperature is perceived as too low. The body therefore activates heat-conserving and heat-generating responses such as vasoconstriction and shivering.

why_others_wrong.A: Sweating promotes heat loss and occurs when the body temperature exceeds the elevated set point.
why_others_wrong.C: Heat-loss responses are not the initial response to a newly raised set point.
why_others_wrong.D: Heat production increases.
why_others_wrong.E: Sympathetic activity is not abolished.

exam_trap: Sweating and vasodilatation (A) tempt as features of fever, but they occur when the set point falls as fever breaks; a rising set point first triggers shivering and vasoconstriction.
takeaway: Fever → set point ↑ → shivering/vasoconstriction until temperature catches up.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Fever raises the hypothalamic set point ↓ the current core temperature now reads as too low ↓ heat conservation and heat production are activated ↓ Shivering and cutaneous vasoconstriction
pearl: Antipyretics such as paracetamol lower a raised set point but are ineffective in non-febrile hyperthermia such as heat stroke or malignant hyperthermia, which need active cooling or specific treatment.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: renal free-water handling
stem: A patient produces urine with an osmolality substantially below plasma osmolality. What does this indicate?
why_correct: Urine that is more dilute than plasma represents excretion of water in excess of solute, corresponding to positive free-water clearance.

why_others_wrong.B: A patient must have functioning filtration to produce urine.
why_others_wrong.C: Maximal ADH effect concentrates urine rather than producing very dilute urine.
why_others_wrong.D: Dilute urine does not by itself prove sodium retention.
why_others_wrong.E: Dilute urine requires functioning renal tubular mechanisms.

exam_trap: Maximal ADH effect (C) tempts by confusing the direction; ADH concentrates urine, so urine more dilute than plasma indicates net free-water excretion with low ADH.
takeaway: Urine osmolality < plasma → kidney is excreting free water.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Urine osmolality below plasma ↓ water excreted in excess of solute ↓ free-water clearance is positive ↓ Net free-water excretion
pearl: In hyponatraemia, very dilute urine suggests appropriate ADH suppression as in primary polydipsia, whereas inappropriately concentrated urine points towards SIADH or hypovolaemia.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Pathology: lipofuscin
stem: Which pigment is classically associated with ageing and accumulation of residual lipid-containing material within cells?
why_correct: Lipofuscin is a yellow-brown, granular intracellular pigment associated with ageing and oxidative damage, particularly in long-lived cells.

why_others_wrong.A: Haemosiderin is an iron-storage pigment.
why_others_wrong.C: Bilirubin is a haem catabolite.
why_others_wrong.D: Haemoglobin is the oxygen-carrying protein within RBCs.
why_others_wrong.E: Melanin is a pigment produced by melanocytes.

exam_trap: Haemosiderin (A) is the usual wrong pick for a brown intracellular pigment, but it stores iron after haemorrhage rather than residual lipid from ageing cells.
takeaway: Ageing/oxidative residual pigment → lipofuscin.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Pigment associated with ageing ↓ residual lipid-containing material within cells ↓ indigestible lysosomal residue of lipid peroxidation ↓ Lipofuscin
pearl: Lipofuscin is a residual body, material the lysosome cannot digest, so it is retained rather than cleared and increases steadily with age.

subject: Pharmacology
title: Pharmacology: prodrug
stem: A drug is administered in an inactive form and requires hepatic metabolism to produce its active metabolite. What is this type of drug called?
why_correct: A prodrug is administered in a form that requires metabolic conversion to generate the pharmacologically active compound.

why_others_wrong.A: A competitive antagonist blocks receptor activation competitively.
why_others_wrong.C: A partial agonist activates a receptor but has lower maximal efficacy than a full agonist.
why_others_wrong.D: An enzyme inhibitor reduces enzyme activity.
why_others_wrong.E: An inverse agonist reduces constitutive receptor activity.

exam_trap: Partial agonist or inverse agonist are chosen by candidates who confuse receptor terms with activation, but a drug that needs hepatic conversion to an active metabolite is a prodrug.
takeaway: Prodrug → administered form requires conversion → active metabolite.
source: Rang & Dale's Pharmacology, 10th ed.; BNF, Principles of Prescribing, current edition accessed 2026.
thinking: Drug given in an inactive form ↓ hepatic metabolism produces the active metabolite ↓ effect depends on conversion ↓ Prodrug
pearl: Codeine is converted to morphine by CYP2D6; ultra-rapid metabolisers can develop morphine toxicity, which is why codeine is contraindicated in children under 12 and in breastfeeding mothers.

subject: Pharmacology
title: Pharmacology: receptor desensitisation
stem: A patient receives continuous exposure to a receptor agonist and develops a reduced response despite unchanged drug concentration. Which pharmacodynamic process may explain this?
why_correct: Prolonged agonist exposure can reduce receptor responsiveness through mechanisms including receptor phosphorylation, uncoupling and internalisation.

why_others_wrong.B: Renal filtration is a pharmacokinetic process and does not directly explain receptor-level loss of responsiveness.
why_others_wrong.C: Increased bioavailability increases exposure rather than explaining reduced receptor responsiveness.
why_others_wrong.D: Increased absorption does not explain receptor desensitisation.
why_others_wrong.E: Reduced Vd does not directly produce receptor desensitisation.

exam_trap: Pharmacokinetic distractors such as increased renal filtration may be chosen, but the stem fixes drug concentration, so reduced response reflects receptor desensitisation.
takeaway: Continuous agonist exposure → receptor responsiveness may fall.
source: Rang & Dale's Pharmacology, 10th ed.
thinking: Continuous agonist exposure ↓ drug concentration unchanged ↓ response falls ↓ receptor-level pharmacodynamic adaptation ↓ Receptor desensitisation
pearl: Distinguishing pharmacokinetic from pharmacodynamic causes of lost effect matters clinically: falling levels suggest altered clearance or adherence, whereas stable levels with less effect suggest desensitisation or tolerance.

subject: Pharmacology
title: Pharmacology: drug transporter
stem: A drug given intravenously is recovered largely unchanged in faeces, and its elimination is reduced when a canalicular efflux transporter on hepatocytes is inhibited. Which pharmacokinetic process is responsible for its elimination?
why_correct: Transport of drugs from hepatocytes into bile is part of hepatic excretion. Transport proteins contribute importantly to biliary drug disposition.

why_others_wrong.A: Absorption is movement into the systemic circulation.
why_others_wrong.B: Distribution concerns movement between blood and tissues.
why_others_wrong.D: Receptor binding is pharmacodynamic.
why_others_wrong.E: Renal filtration occurs at the glomerulus.

exam_trap: Renal filtration (E) or absorption (A) are tempting, but recovery of an intravenous drug unchanged in faeces after hepatocyte efflux points to biliary excretion.
takeaway: Hepatocyte → bile → intestinal tract = biliary excretion.
source: Rang & Dale's Pharmacology, 10th ed.
thinking: Intravenous drug recovered unchanged in faeces ↓ it must reach the gut via bile, not through failed absorption ↓ elimination falls when a hepatocyte canalicular efflux transporter is blocked ↓ Hepatic biliary excretion
pearl: P-glycoprotein is an important canalicular efflux transporter; inhibitors such as clarithromycin or verapamil can raise levels of substrates such as digoxin, a common source of drug interactions.

subject: Microbiology & surgical infection
title: Microbiology: mycobacteria
stem: Which cell-envelope component contributes importantly to the characteristic acid-fast property of Mycobacterium species?
why_correct: Mycobacteria contain lipid-rich cell walls with substantial mycolic acid content, contributing to their acid-fast staining characteristics.

why_others_wrong.A: LPS is characteristic of Gram-negative outer membranes.
why_others_wrong.C: Chitin is associated with fungi.
why_others_wrong.D: Peptidoglycan is present but does not explain the distinctive acid-fast property by itself.
why_others_wrong.E: Ergosterol is a fungal membrane sterol.

exam_trap: Peptidoglycan only tempts because mycobacteria do contain peptidoglycan, but it does not explain acid-fastness; the lipid-rich mycolic acid layer is what retains the stain.
takeaway: Mycobacteria → mycolic acids → acid-fastness.
source: Murray, Rosenthal & Pfaller, Medical Microbiology, 10th ed.
thinking: Acid-fast staining of mycobacteria ↓ the cell envelope is unusually lipid-rich ↓ mycolic acids retain the stain despite acid-alcohol decolourisation ↓ Mycolic acids
pearl: Isoniazid inhibits mycolic acid synthesis, which explains its narrow spectrum against mycobacteria, and acid-fast staining of sputum gives a rapid initial result before culture.

subject: Statistics & evidence-based medicine
title: Evidence: multiplicity
stem: A trial tests 20 independent primary hypotheses at the conventional 5% significance level without adjustment. What problem does this create?

options.B: Increased risk of at least one false-positive finding

correct_answer: B. Increased risk of at least one false-positive finding
why_correct: Testing many hypotheses increases the family-wise probability of obtaining at least one statistically significant result by chance, even if all null hypotheses are true.

why_others_wrong.A: Multiple unadjusted testing mainly inflates the risk of false positives; it does not guarantee a type II error in any individual comparison.
why_others_wrong.C: The opposite applies, because 20 unadjusted tests create more opportunities for at least one statistically significant result by chance.
why_others_wrong.D: Running more tests does not reduce random error; it multiplies the opportunities for chance to produce a spuriously significant result.
why_others_wrong.E: External validity depends on how representative the participants and setting are, and testing more hypotheses does nothing to improve it.

exam_trap: "One significant result among many tested outcomes" must be interpreted in the context of multiplicity and prespecified analyses.
takeaway: More hypothesis tests → greater false-positive risk unless appropriately addressed.
source: Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions, current methodology.
thinking: 20 independent primary hypotheses ↓ each at 5% without adjustment ↓ probability of at least one false positive about 64% ↓ Increased risk of at least one false-positive finding
pearl: Trials with several primary hypotheses should use a prespecified multiplicity strategy, such as splitting alpha or testing hypotheses in a fixed hierarchical order.

subject: Research methods & screening
title: Evidence: funnel plot
stem: A systematic review contains a funnel plot showing marked asymmetry. What potential problem should be considered?

options.D: Randomisation failure in every included study

correct_answer: A. Publication bias or small-study effects
why_correct: Funnel-plot asymmetry can indicate publication bias or other small-study effects, although asymmetry is not specific for publication bias.

why_others_wrong.B: Asymmetry does not show absence of heterogeneity; between-study heterogeneity is itself one recognised cause of an asymmetrical funnel plot.
why_others_wrong.C: Funnel-plot asymmetry raises concern about the evidence base and cannot establish that the treatments compared are clinically equivalent.
why_others_wrong.D: A funnel plot shows effect size against precision across studies and cannot show whether randomisation failed within each included trial.
why_others_wrong.E: External validity cannot be established from funnel-plot shape.

exam_trap: Funnel-plot asymmetry is a signal requiring interpretation, not proof of publication bias.
takeaway: Funnel asymmetry → consider publication bias and other small-study effects.
source: Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions, current methodology.
thinking: Marked funnel plot asymmetry ↓ small studies with certain results may be missing ↓ asymmetry not specific to one cause ↓ Publication bias or small-study effects
pearl: Funnel plots are only meaningful when included studies vary in size; if all studies are of similar size, asymmetry cannot be judged.

subject: Anatomy
title: Embryology: thyroid development
stem: The thyroid gland develops embryologically from which structure?
correct_answer: C. Foramen caecum of the tongue
why_correct: The thyroid follicular epithelium develops from an endodermal diverticulum arising at the foramen caecum of the tongue. It subsequently descends in the midline of the neck.

why_others_wrong.A: The first pouch contributes to the auditory tube and middle-ear lining.
why_others_wrong.B: The second pouch contributes to the palatine tonsil epithelium.
why_others_wrong.D: The fourth pouch contributes to the superior parathyroids and other structures.
why_others_wrong.E: The ultimobranchial body contributes parafollicular C cells but is not the origin of the thyroid gland as a whole.

exam_trap: Candidates may choose the ultimobranchial body or the fourth pouch, but these give rise to the parafollicular C cells (and the fourth pouch to the superior parathyroids); the follicular gland itself arises at the foramen caecum.
takeaway: Thyroid follicular tissue → foramen caecum → descends in the midline.
source: Gray's Anatomy, 42nd ed.; Gray's Basic Anatomy, 3rd ed.
thinking: Origin of the thyroid gland ↓ midline endodermal diverticulum from the floor of the primitive pharynx ↓ site marked in the adult tongue by the foramen caecum ↓ gland descends via the thyroglossal duct ↓ Foramen caecum of the tongue
pearl: A thyroglossal cyst moves upward on tongue protrusion and is excised with the central portion of the hyoid bone and the tract to reduce recurrence.

subject: Anatomy
title: Embryology: parathyroids
stem: Which embryological structure gives rise to the inferior parathyroid glands?
why_correct: The inferior parathyroids develop from the dorsal wings of the third pharyngeal pouches and descend with the thymus, accounting for their more variable final position.

why_others_wrong.A: The first pouch contributes to the auditory tube and middle-ear structures.
why_others_wrong.B: The second pouch contributes to the palatine tonsil epithelium.
why_others_wrong.D: The fourth pouch contributes to the superior parathyroids.
why_others_wrong.E: Neural crest cells contribute to several craniofacial structures but are not the principal embryological origin of the parathyroid epithelium.

exam_trap: Inferior parathyroids descend with the thymus; superior parathyroids remain relatively close to their origin.
takeaway: Third pouch → thymus + inferior parathyroids.
source: Gray's Anatomy, 42nd ed.; Gray's Basic Anatomy, 3rd ed.
thinking: Inferior parathyroid glands ↓ arise from the third pharyngeal pouch together with the thymus ↓ descend with the thymus past the fourth-pouch glands ↓ Third pharyngeal pouch
pearl: Because they migrate with the thymus, missing inferior parathyroid adenomas are often found in the thymus or anterior mediastinum, whereas ectopic superior glands tend to lie posteriorly near the tracheo-oesophageal groove.

subject: Anatomy
title: Embryology: superior parathyroids
stem: The superior parathyroid glands are derived from which embryological structure?
why_correct: The superior parathyroids arise from the dorsal wings of the fourth pharyngeal pouches.

why_others_wrong.A: The third pouch gives rise to the thymus and inferior parathyroids.
why_others_wrong.C: The first cleft contributes to the external acoustic meatus.
why_others_wrong.D: The second arch contributes to muscles of facial expression and several associated structures.
why_others_wrong.E: The thyroglossal duct relates to thyroid descent.

exam_trap: Candidates often pick the third pouch, but it forms the inferior parathyroids with the thymus; the superior glands come from the fourth pouch and migrate less.
takeaway: Third pouch → inferior parathyroids. Fourth pouch → superior parathyroids.
source: Gray's Anatomy, 42nd ed.
thinking: Superior parathyroid glands ↓ third-pouch glands travel further down with the thymus and end up inferior ↓ fourth-pouch glands migrate only a short distance and end up superior ↓ Fourth pharyngeal pouch
pearl: Superior parathyroids are more constant in position, typically lying near the cricothyroid junction posterior to the recurrent laryngeal nerve, close to where the nerve enters the larynx.

subject: Anatomy
title: Embryology: adrenal gland
stem: Which component of the adrenal gland is derived from neural crest cells?
why_correct: The adrenal medulla develops from neural crest-derived chromaffin cells and is functionally related to the sympathetic nervous system.

why_others_wrong.A: The zona glomerulosa is a zone of the adrenal cortex, which is derived from mesoderm, not neural crest.
why_others_wrong.B: The zona fasciculata is a zone of the adrenal cortex, which is derived from mesoderm, not neural crest.
why_others_wrong.C: The zona reticularis is a zone of the adrenal cortex, which is derived from mesoderm, not neural crest.
why_others_wrong.E: The adrenal capsule is not the neural crest-derived medulla.

exam_trap: Candidates may choose the zona reticularis because it borders the medulla, but all three cortical zones are mesodermal; only the medulla arises from neural crest.
takeaway: Adrenal cortex → mesoderm. Adrenal medulla → neural crest.
source: Gray's Anatomy, 42nd ed.; Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Neural crest component of the adrenal gland ↓ cortex (glomerulosa, fasciculata, reticularis) arises from coelomic mesoderm ↓ medulla forms from neural crest chromaffin cells, modified postganglionic sympathetic neurons ↓ Adrenal medulla
pearl: Phaeochromocytomas arise from these neural crest chromaffin cells; preoperative alpha-blockade is started before any beta-blockade to avoid unopposed alpha-mediated hypertensive crisis.

subject: Anatomy
title: Embryology: vitelline duct
stem: A persistent vitelline duct most commonly presents clinically as which congenital anomaly?
why_correct: Meckel diverticulum results from persistence of the embryological vitelline duct and is usually found on the antimesenteric border of the ileum.

why_others_wrong.B: Omphalocele results from failure of return of herniated midgut to the abdominal cavity and is membrane-covered.
why_others_wrong.C: Hirschsprung disease results from failure of enteric ganglion-cell migration.
why_others_wrong.D: Pyloric stenosis is a developmental disorder of the pyloric musculature.
why_others_wrong.E: Gastroschisis is a paraumbilical abdominal-wall defect with uncovered bowel.

exam_trap: Candidates may choose omphalocele or gastroschisis because both involve the umbilical region, but those are abdominal wall defects; vitelline duct persistence gives a Meckel diverticulum.
takeaway: Persistent vitelline duct → Meckel diverticulum.
source: Gray's Anatomy, 42nd ed.; Principles and Practice of Surgery, 7th ed.
thinking: Persistent vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct ↓ duct joins the midgut to the yolk sac ↓ partial persistence leaves a blind pouch on the antimesenteric ileum ↓ Meckel diverticulum
pearl: A Meckel diverticulum may contain ectopic gastric mucosa, which causes painless rectal bleeding in children and can be detected with a technetium-99m pertechnetate scan.

subject: Anatomy
title: Embryology: urachus
stem: The urachus is a remnant of which embryological structure?
why_correct: The urachus represents the embryological allantois and extends from the bladder toward the umbilicus. After obliteration it becomes the median umbilical ligament.

why_others_wrong.A: Vitelline duct persistence produces Meckel diverticulum.
why_others_wrong.C: The mesonephric duct contributes to components of the male genital tract.
why_others_wrong.D: The Müllerian duct contributes to the female reproductive tract.
why_others_wrong.E: The ureteric bud gives rise to the collecting system of the kidney.

exam_trap: Candidates often confuse the two umbilical remnants: the vitelline duct gives Meckel diverticulum, whereas the urachus is the obliterated allantois running from bladder dome to umbilicus.
takeaway: Allantois → urachus → median umbilical ligament.
source: Gray's Anatomy, 42nd ed.
thinking: Urachus runs from the bladder dome to the umbilicus ↓ the allantois extends from the cloaca into the umbilical cord ↓ its intra-abdominal part obliterates as the urachus ↓ it becomes the median umbilical ligament ↓ Allantois
pearl: A patent urachus presents with urine leaking from the umbilicus, and urachal remnants can give rise to adenocarcinoma at the bladder dome.

subject: Anatomy
title: Embryology: kidney development
stem: Which embryological structure gives rise to the collecting ducts of the definitive kidney?
why_correct: The ureteric bud forms the ureter, renal pelvis, calyces and collecting ducts. The metanephric mesenchyme forms the nephron components.

why_others_wrong.A: Metanephric mesenchyme forms the nephron.
why_others_wrong.C: The mesonephric duct gives rise to the ureteric bud but does not directly form the mature collecting ducts.
why_others_wrong.D: The pronephros is transient and non-functional in humans.
why_others_wrong.E: The cloacal membrane does not form the collecting system.

exam_trap: Candidates often choose metanephric mesenchyme, but it forms the nephron from glomerulus to distal tubule; the ureteric bud forms the collecting ducts, calyces, pelvis and ureter.
takeaway: UB → ureter + pelvis + calyces + collecting ducts.
source: Gray's Anatomy, 42nd ed.; Gray's Basic Anatomy, 3rd ed.
thinking: Collecting ducts of the definitive kidney ↓ metanephros forms from two components ↓ ureteric bud branches to form ureter, pelvis, calyces and collecting ducts ↓ metanephric mesenchyme forms the nephrons ↓ Ureteric bud
pearl: Early division of the ureteric bud produces a bifid ureter, while a second bud gives a duplex system in which the upper-pole ureter typically inserts lower and more medially and may be ectopic or obstructed.

subject: Anatomy
title: Embryology: oesophagus
stem: The oesophagus develops primarily from which embryological region?
why_correct: The oesophagus develops from the foregut. The respiratory diverticulum also arises from the ventral foregut, requiring separation of the respiratory and digestive pathways.

why_others_wrong.A: Hindgut contributes to the distal gastrointestinal tract.
why_others_wrong.B: Midgut contributes to much of the small bowel and proximal large bowel.
why_others_wrong.D: The neural tube gives rise to the central nervous system.
why_others_wrong.E: The cloaca contributes to distal urogenital and anorectal development.

exam_trap: Candidates may choose the midgut, but the midgut begins in the second part of the duodenum; the oesophagus, like the trachea that buds from it, is foregut.
takeaway: Oesophagus = foregut derivative.
source: Gray's Anatomy, 42nd ed.
thinking: Embryological origin of the oesophagus ↓ foregut runs from the oesophagus to the second part of the duodenum ↓ respiratory diverticulum buds ventrally and is separated by the tracheo-oesophageal septum ↓ Foregut
pearl: Incomplete separation produces oesophageal atresia with tracheo-oesophageal fistula, most often a proximal blind pouch with a distal fistula, suggested by polyhydramnios and a newborn unable to swallow saliva.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: brachial plexus
stem: A lesion affects the posterior cord of the brachial plexus. Which terminal nerve is directly derived from the posterior cord?
why_correct: The posterior cord gives rise directly to the axillary and radial nerves.

why_others_wrong.A: Musculocutaneous nerve arises from the lateral cord.
why_others_wrong.B: Median nerve is formed by contributions from lateral and medial cords.
why_others_wrong.C: Ulnar nerve arises from the medial cord.
why_others_wrong.E: Obturator nerve arises from the lumbar plexus.

exam_trap: Candidates may pick the musculocutaneous or ulnar nerve, but these arise from the lateral and medial cords; the posterior cord ends as the axillary and radial nerves.
takeaway: Posterior cord = terminal axillary and radial nerves.
source: Gray's Anatomy, 42nd ed.; Gray's Atlas of Anatomy, 3rd ed.
thinking: Posterior cord lesion ↓ posterior divisions of all three trunks form the posterior cord ↓ its terminal branches are the axillary and radial nerves ↓ Axillary nerve
pearl: The posterior cord also gives the upper and lower subscapular nerves and the thoracodorsal nerve to latissimus dorsi, which is preserved during axillary clearance whenever possible.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: axillary artery
stem: A surgeon ligates the axillary artery proximal to the subscapular artery. Which arterial collateral network is particularly important in maintaining upper-limb perfusion?
why_correct: The scapular arterial network provides an important collateral route between branches of the subclavian and axillary arteries.

why_others_wrong.A: The genicular network is around the knee.
why_others_wrong.C: The plantar arch is in the foot.
why_others_wrong.D: The Circle of Willis is an intracranial arterial network.
why_others_wrong.E: The palmar venous plexus is venous rather than an arterial collateral network.

exam_trap: Candidates may consider the palmar venous plexus because it lies in the upper limb, but it is venous; the scapular anastomosis bridges subclavian and axillary arterial branches.
takeaway: Scapular anastomoses → collateral upper-limb arterial pathway.
source: Gray's Anatomy, 42nd ed.; Gray's Atlas of Anatomy, 3rd ed.
thinking: Axillary artery ligated proximal to the subscapular artery ↓ suprascapular and dorsal scapular arteries arise from the subclavian system ↓ they anastomose with the subscapular and circumflex scapular branches around the scapula ↓ flow bypasses the ligature ↓ Scapular anastomotic network
pearl: Axillary artery ligation is best tolerated between the thyrocervical trunk and the subscapular artery; ligation distal to the subscapular origin lies beyond the scapular anastomosis, so limb perfusion is less reliably maintained.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: genicular anastomosis
stem: The genicular arterial network is clinically important because it provides collateral circulation around which joint?
why_correct: The genicular arteries and related descending/ascending vessels form an extensive collateral network around the knee.

why_others_wrong.A: The shoulder is served by the scapular anastomosis, not the genicular network.
why_others_wrong.B: The elbow is served by the collateral and recurrent arteries around the elbow, not the genicular network.
why_others_wrong.C: The hip is served by the cruciate and trochanteric anastomoses, not the genicular network.
why_others_wrong.E: The ankle is served by malleolar branches of the tibial and fibular arteries, not the genicular network.

exam_trap: Candidates may pick the hip because of its cruciate and trochanteric anastomoses, but the genicular network surrounds the knee and bypasses popliteal or distal femoral occlusion.
takeaway: Genicular anastomosis = collateral circulation around the knee.
source: Gray's Anatomy, 42nd ed.; Gray's Atlas of Anatomy, 3rd ed.
thinking: Genicular arterial network ↓ genicular branches of the popliteal artery plus descending genicular and lateral circumflex femoral contributions ↓ anastomose with recurrent tibial branches around the joint ↓ Knee
pearl: In knee dislocation the tethered popliteal artery is easily injured and the genicular collaterals cannot sustain the limb, so ankle-brachial pressure index or CT angiography is needed.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: palmar arterial arches
stem: Which artery primarily contributes to the superficial palmar arch?
why_correct: The superficial palmar arch is predominantly formed by the ulnar artery, with contribution from the superficial palmar branch of the radial artery.

why_others_wrong.A: The radial artery contributes importantly to the deep palmar arch.
why_others_wrong.C: The brachial artery is proximal and divides into radial and ulnar arteries.
why_others_wrong.D: The anterior interosseous artery is not the principal contributor.
why_others_wrong.E: The deep brachial artery supplies the posterior arm.

exam_trap: Candidates often choose the radial artery, but it forms mainly the deep palmar arch; the superficial arch is chiefly the continuation of the ulnar artery.
takeaway: Ulnar → superficial palmar arch. Radial → deep palmar arch.
source: Gray's Anatomy, 42nd ed.
thinking: Superficial palmar arch ↓ ulnar artery enters the hand superficial to the flexor retinaculum ↓ it continues as the superficial arch, completed by the superficial palmar branch of the radial artery ↓ Ulnar artery
pearl: The superficial arch lies distal to the deep arch and is often incomplete, which is why collateral hand perfusion is assessed before radial artery cannulation or harvest.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Physiology: cardiac preload
stem: A patient receives a modest intravenous fluid bolus and develops an increase in stroke volume without a major change in contractility. Which physiological mechanism best explains this?
why_correct: An increase in venous return increases ventricular end-diastolic filling. Within the physiological range, increased myocardial fibre stretch increases force of contraction and stroke volume through the Frank-Starling mechanism.

why_others_wrong.B: The Bainbridge reflex concerns heart-rate responses to atrial stretch and does not explain the main change in stroke volume here.
why_others_wrong.C: Baroreceptor failure removes reflex buffering of blood pressure and heart rate but does not explain a preload-driven rise in stroke volume.
why_others_wrong.D: Venous return increases rather than decreases.
why_others_wrong.E: End-diastolic volume increases.

exam_trap: Frank-Starling explains increased stroke volume from increased preload without requiring increased sympathetic stimulation.
takeaway: Preload ↑ → fibre stretch ↑ → stroke volume ↑ within physiological range.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Fluid bolus increases venous return ↓ end-diastolic volume and myocardial fibre stretch rise ↓ contractile force increases without any change in contractility ↓ Frank-Starling mechanism
pearl: A fluid challenge is judged by the change in stroke volume or cardiac output; a patient on the flat part of the Starling curve gains no output and simply accumulates oedema.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Physiology: afterload
stem: A patient develops a sudden increase in systemic arterial pressure. What is the most immediate effect on the left ventricle?
why_correct: The left ventricle must generate a higher pressure to eject blood into the higher-pressure aorta. This increases ventricular afterload.

why_others_wrong.A: Afterload increases.
why_others_wrong.C: Increased afterload tends to impair ejection and can increase end-systolic volume.
why_others_wrong.D: Coronary sinus drainage reflects myocardial venous outflow and is not the immediate mechanical effect of raised aortic pressure on the ventricle.
why_others_wrong.E: By Laplace's law, higher left ventricular systolic pressure increases wall stress, which is a component of afterload, rather than reducing it.

exam_trap: Candidates may choose reduced end-systolic volume, but raised afterload impairs ejection and tends to increase end-systolic volume; the direct effect is increased afterload.
takeaway: Systemic arterial pressure ↑ → LV afterload ↑.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Sudden rise in systemic arterial pressure ↓ the ventricle must generate higher pressure to open the aortic valve and eject ↓ systolic wall stress rises ↓ Increased afterload
pearl: A failing ventricle is highly sensitive to afterload, so a sudden hypertensive surge can precipitate acute pulmonary oedema, which responds to vasodilators such as nitrates.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Physiology: cardiac action potential
stem: Which ion is primarily responsible for phase 0 depolarisation of a normal ventricular myocyte?
why_correct: Rapid phase 0 depolarisation of ventricular myocytes is caused primarily by rapid opening of voltage-gated sodium channels and inward sodium current.

why_others_wrong.A: Phase 1 early repolarisation is driven mainly by a transient outward potassium current, with at most a minor chloride contribution; chloride does not generate the rapid phase 0 upstroke.
why_others_wrong.B: Calcium is particularly important during the plateau phase.
why_others_wrong.C: Potassium currents contribute to repolarisation.
why_others_wrong.E: Magnesium does not carry a significant depolarising current in myocytes; it mainly modulates ion channels and the sodium-potassium pump.

exam_trap: Do not confuse ventricular myocytes with pacemaker cells, whose phase 0 depolarisation depends mainly on calcium influx.
takeaway: Ventricular phase 0 → Na+ influx. Pacemaker phase 0 → Ca2+ influx.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Ventricular myocyte reaches threshold ↓ fast voltage-gated sodium channels open ↓ rapid inward sodium current produces the steep upstroke ↓ Sodium
pearl: Class I antiarrhythmics and local anaesthetics block these sodium channels, which is why local anaesthetic systemic toxicity can cause broad-complex arrhythmias and cardiac arrest, treated with lipid emulsion.

subject: Cardiorespiratory physiology
title: Physiology: cardiac plateau
stem: The prolonged plateau phase of the ventricular action potential is primarily related to:

options.A: Sustained calcium entry through L-type calcium channels
options.E: Complete closure of all ion channels

correct_answer: A. Sustained calcium entry through L-type calcium channels
why_correct: The ventricular plateau results from prolonged calcium influx through L-type calcium channels, balanced by potassium currents. This prolongs the action potential and refractory period.

why_others_wrong.B: Potassium currents continue.
why_others_wrong.C: Sodium moves into, not out of, the myocyte, and the fast sodium current inactivates after phase 0 so it cannot sustain the plateau.
why_others_wrong.D: Chloride is not the principal determinant.
why_others_wrong.E: Ion channels remain active during the plateau.

exam_trap: Candidates may choose complete cessation of potassium movement, but potassium efflux continues and balances calcium entry; the plateau depends on L-type calcium channels.
takeaway: Ventricular plateau → L-type Ca2+ influx balanced by K+ efflux.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Phase 0 sodium upstroke ends ↓ L-type calcium channels allow sustained calcium entry ↓ balanced by outward potassium current, producing the plateau ↓ Sustained calcium entry through L-type calcium channels
pearl: Calcium entering during the plateau triggers calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, so L-type calcium-channel blockers such as verapamil reduce contractility as well as nodal conduction.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: glomerular filtration
stem: Which change would increase glomerular filtration rate, assuming other factors remain constant?

options.A: Increased hydrostatic pressure within Bowman's space
options.E: Ureteric obstruction causing increased Bowman's space pressure

correct_answer: B. Increased glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure
why_correct: Glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure is a major force driving filtration. Increasing it, within physiological limits, increases net filtration pressure and therefore GFR.

why_others_wrong.A: Increased Bowman's space hydrostatic pressure opposes filtration.
why_others_wrong.C: Increased plasma oncotic pressure opposes filtration.
why_others_wrong.D: Marked afferent constriction reduces glomerular capillary pressure.
why_others_wrong.E: Ureteric obstruction can increase hydrostatic pressure upstream and oppose filtration.

exam_trap: Options A and E tempt because raised pressure sounds like more filtration, but pressure in Bowman's space opposes filtration; only glomerular capillary pressure drives GFR.
takeaway: Glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure ↑ → GFR ↑.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.; Boron & Boulpaep, Medical Physiology, 4th ed.
thinking: GFR depends on net filtration pressure ↓ glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure drives filtration ↓ Bowman space pressure and plasma oncotic pressure oppose it ↓ Increased glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure
pearl: Ureteric obstruction raises Bowman space pressure and lowers GFR, so prompt decompression of an obstructed, infected kidney by nephrostomy or stent is a urological emergency.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: renal glucose handling
stem: A patient develops marked hyperglycaemia above the renal transport threshold. What happens when the filtered glucose load exceeds proximal tubular reabsorptive capacity?

options.C: Glucose is converted into urea in the proximal tubule
options.E: Glucose is completely reabsorbed regardless of concentration

why_correct: Glucose is normally reabsorbed predominantly in the proximal tubule. Once the filtered load exceeds the transport maximum, not all filtered glucose can be reabsorbed and glucosuria occurs.

why_others_wrong.A: The kidney does not respond by secreting glucose into the tubular lumen.
why_others_wrong.C: Glucose is not converted into urea in this manner.
why_others_wrong.D: Hyperglycaemia does not stop GFR.
why_others_wrong.E: Reabsorption has a finite transport capacity.

exam_trap: Glucosuria occurs when filtered load exceeds tubular reabsorptive capacity, not simply because glucose is present in plasma.
takeaway: Filtered glucose load > tubular transport capacity → glucosuria.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Marked hyperglycaemia ↓ filtered glucose load rises ↓ proximal SGLT transport maximum is exceeded ↓ excess glucose stays in the tubule ↓ Glucose appears in urine
pearl: The renal threshold for glucose falls in pregnancy, so glucosuria can occur in pregnant women with normal blood glucose.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: Physiology: gastrointestinal pacemaker
stem: Which cells generate the characteristic slow waves that coordinate gastrointestinal smooth-muscle activity?
why_correct: Interstitial cells of Cajal function as pacemaker cells within the gastrointestinal tract and generate slow-wave electrical activity that helps coordinate motility.

why_others_wrong.A: Paneth cells contribute to intestinal antimicrobial defence.
why_others_wrong.C: Goblet cells secrete mucus.
why_others_wrong.D: Chief cells secrete pepsinogen in the stomach.
why_others_wrong.E: Kupffer cells are hepatic macrophages.

exam_trap: Slow waves do not themselves necessarily produce a contraction; action potentials and calcium entry determine effective smooth-muscle contraction.
takeaway: Interstitial cells of Cajal → GI electrical pacemaker activity.
source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.; Gray's Anatomy, 42nd ed.
thinking: Slow waves coordinate GI smooth-muscle activity ↓ they originate in specialised pacemaker cells within the muscularis ↓ these cells form networks around the myenteric plexus ↓ Interstitial cells of Cajal
pearl: Loss of interstitial cells of Cajal is described in diabetic gastroparesis and slow-transit constipation, linking pacemaker failure to clinical dysmotility.

subject: Pharmacology
title: Pharmacology: competitive antagonism
stem: A competitive antagonist is added to a receptor system. Which change is expected for a reversible competitive antagonist?

options.A: Reduced maximal response that cannot be overcome
options.B: Rightward shift of the agonist dose-response curve with preserved maximal response

correct_answer: B. Rightward shift of the agonist dose-response curve with preserved maximal response
why_correct: A reversible competitive antagonist competes with agonist at the same receptor site. Increasing the agonist concentration can overcome the antagonism, producing a rightward shift without reducing the maximal response.

why_others_wrong.A: A reduced Emax is more characteristic of non-competitive/irreversible antagonism.
why_others_wrong.C: Reversible competitive antagonists do not permanently destroy receptors.
why_others_wrong.D: The antagonist does not increase agonist affinity.
why_others_wrong.E: The antagonist itself binds the receptor.

exam_trap: Reduced maximal response is chosen by candidates who confuse competitive with irreversible or non-competitive antagonism; a reversible competitive antagonist shifts the curve right with the maximum preserved.
takeaway: Competitive antagonist → right shift, Emax preserved.
source: Rang & Dale's Pharmacology, 10th ed.
thinking: Reversible competitive antagonist ↓ competes with agonist for the same binding site ↓ more agonist can outcompete it ↓ curve shifts right but the same maximum is reached ↓ Rightward shift of the agonist dose-response curve with preserved maximal response
pearl: Naloxone is a competitive opioid antagonist, so high doses of a potent opioid can overcome it, and its short duration means respiratory depression can recur once it wears off.

subject: Pharmacology
title: Pharmacology: receptor tyrosine kinase
stem: Which endogenous hormone acts through a receptor tyrosine kinase?
why_correct: The insulin receptor is a receptor tyrosine kinase. Ligand binding causes receptor autophosphorylation and downstream intracellular signalling.

why_others_wrong.B: Aldosterone acts through an intracellular mineralocorticoid receptor.
why_others_wrong.C: Cortisol acts through an intracellular glucocorticoid receptor.
why_others_wrong.D: Thyroid hormones act predominantly through nuclear receptors.
why_others_wrong.E: Beta-1 receptors are G-protein-coupled receptors.

exam_trap: Not all hormones act through membrane receptors; steroid and thyroid hormones mainly act intracellularly.
takeaway: Insulin → receptor tyrosine kinase.
source: Rang & Dale's Pharmacology, 10th ed.; Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Receptor tyrosine kinase hormone ↓ steroid and thyroid hormones act on intracellular receptors ↓ adrenaline acts on GPCRs ↓ insulin receptor autophosphorylates ↓ Insulin
pearl: Growth factors such as EGF and VEGF also act through receptor tyrosine kinases, which are targets for cancer drugs including tyrosine kinase inhibitors used in several solid tumours.

subject: Research methods & screening
title: Evidence: intention-to-treat
stem: In a randomised controlled trial, participants assigned to treatment A are analysed in the treatment-A group even if some subsequently stop taking treatment A. What principle is being applied?
why_correct: Intention-to-treat analysis analyses participants according to their original randomised allocation, regardless of subsequent adherence or treatment changes.

why_others_wrong.A: Per-protocol analysis includes only adherent participants, so those who stopped treatment would be excluded rather than kept in their allocated group.
why_others_wrong.C: As-treated analysis groups people by treatment actually received, so those who stopped would be moved out of their allocated group rather than kept in it.
why_others_wrong.D: Case-control is an observational design that selects participants by outcome status and is not a principle for analysing randomised trial participants.
why_others_wrong.E: Crossover describes a design in which each participant receives both treatments in sequence, not a rule for analysing participants who stop their allocated treatment.

exam_trap: ITT preserves much of the benefit of randomisation and is generally preferred for estimating the effect of treatment assignment.
takeaway: ITT → analyse by original randomisation.
source: Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions, current methodology.
thinking: Participants assigned to treatment A stay in group A ↓ even if they stop treatment ↓ analysis follows original allocation ↓ Intention-to-treat analysis
pearl: Intention-to-treat estimates the effect of being assigned to a treatment, which is the policy-relevant question for clinicians deciding what to offer patients.

subject: Research methods & screening
title: Evidence: allocation concealment
stem: Which methodological feature prevents investigators enrolling participants into a particular treatment group based on knowledge of the upcoming randomisation assignment?
why_correct: Allocation concealment prevents those recruiting participants from knowing the upcoming treatment assignment before enrolment. This reduces selection bias at the point of randomisation.

why_others_wrong.A: Blinding of outcome assessors occurs after allocation and concerns assessment of outcomes.
why_others_wrong.C: Intention-to-treat analysis keeps participants in their randomised groups at analysis and cannot stop recruiters foreseeing the next allocation.
why_others_wrong.D: Statistical adjustment is applied after data collection and cannot prevent recruiters selectively enrolling participants who know the next allocation.
why_others_wrong.E: Long-term follow-up concerns outcome ascertainment after enrolment and does nothing to hide the upcoming allocation from recruiters.

exam_trap: Allocation concealment occurs before or at enrolment, whereas blinding of outcome assessors concerns knowledge of treatment after allocation.
takeaway: Allocation concealment → protects randomisation from selection bias.
source: Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions, current methodology; Principles and Practice of Surgery, 7th ed.
thinking: Recruiter could enrol selectively if the next assignment were known ↓ feature that hides the upcoming allocation ↓ acts before enrolment ↓ Allocation concealment
pearl: Unlike blinding, allocation concealment is always possible, for example using central randomisation by telephone or a secure web system after the patient has been enrolled.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Pathology: haemosiderin
stem: A patient has longstanding repeated blood transfusions. Which intracellular pigment would be expected to accumulate as a consequence of increased iron storage?
why_correct: Haemosiderin is an iron-storage pigment formed from aggregates of ferritin and is seen when there is local or systemic iron excess, including repeated transfusion.

why_others_wrong.A: Lipofuscin reflects oxidative injury and ageing.
why_others_wrong.C: Bilirubin derives from haem breakdown and is handled predominantly by the liver and biliary system.
why_others_wrong.D: Melanin is a pigment produced by melanocytes.
why_others_wrong.E: Ceroid is related to oxidised lipid material and is not the characteristic iron-storage pigment.

exam_trap: Ferritin is soluble iron storage; haemosiderin represents aggregated, less readily mobilised iron.
takeaway: Iron excess → ferritin storage → haemosiderin accumulation when storage is substantial.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Longstanding repeated transfusions ↓ each unit adds iron that cannot be excreted ↓ iron stored as ferritin, then aggregated ↓ Haemosiderin
pearl: Transfusion-dependent patients, such as those with thalassaemia major, need monitoring of iron load and chelation therapy to prevent cardiac, hepatic and endocrine damage.

subject: GI physiology & metabolism
title: Pathology: bilirubin
stem: A patient with increased red-cell destruction develops jaundice. Which bilirubin fraction is expected to increase predominantly before hepatic conjugation?

options.E: Direct bilirubin generated in the kidney

why_correct: Haem breakdown produces bilirubin that initially circulates in an unconjugated form bound to albumin. Increased haemolysis therefore predominantly increases unconjugated bilirubin production.

why_others_wrong.A: Conjugation occurs in hepatocytes after uptake of unconjugated bilirubin.
why_others_wrong.C: Bile contains conjugated bilirubin.
why_others_wrong.D: Unconjugated bilirubin is albumin-bound and is not normally filtered into urine.
why_others_wrong.E: Direct bilirubin is conjugated bilirubin formed by hepatic glucuronidation, not in the kidney, and haemolysis mainly raises the unconjugated fraction.

exam_trap: Conjugated bilirubin (option A) is chosen because jaundice is often hepatic or obstructive, but haemolytic bilirubin is produced before the liver and is mainly unconjugated.
takeaway: Haemolysis → increased bilirubin production → predominantly unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.; Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed.
thinking: Increased red-cell destruction with jaundice ↓ haem breakdown in macrophages generates bilirubin ↓ it circulates bound to albumin before hepatic conjugation ↓ Unconjugated bilirubin
pearl: In haemolysis the other liver tests are usually normal, while raised lactate dehydrogenase and reticulocyte count with low haptoglobin support the diagnosis.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Pathology: intracellular glycogen
stem: A child has hepatomegaly and fasting hypoglycaemia. Liver biopsy shows hepatocytes distended by PAS-positive, diastase-sensitive material. Which pathological process is most likely?
why_correct: Defects in glycogen metabolism can lead to excessive intracellular glycogen accumulation in tissues, producing the glycogen storage diseases.

why_others_wrong.B: Iron deficiency does not cause glycogen accumulation.
why_others_wrong.C: Amyloidosis involves extracellular deposition of misfolded proteins.
why_others_wrong.D: Lipofuscin is an oxidised lipid-containing pigment.
why_others_wrong.E: Cholesterol embolisation involves embolisation of cholesterol crystal material from atherosclerotic plaques.

exam_trap: Not all intracellular accumulations are pigments; glycogen is a metabolic storage product.
takeaway: Defective glycogen metabolism → abnormal intracellular glycogen accumulation.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Child with hepatomegaly ↓ fasting hypoglycaemia ↓ PAS-positive, diastase-sensitive material = glycogen ↓ inherited defect of glycogen metabolism ↓ Glycogen storage disease
pearl: PAS stains glycogen, mucin and other carbohydrates; diastase digests glycogen, so diastase sensitivity distinguishes glycogen from mucin, which remains PAS-positive.

subject: Pathology: inflammation & wound healing
title: Pathology: cholesterol accumulation
stem: Foam cells within an atherosclerotic plaque contain abundant intracellular lipid. Which lipid is particularly important in this process?
why_correct: Macrophages within atherosclerotic plaques accumulate modified lipoprotein-derived cholesterol and cholesterol esters, producing the characteristic foamy appearance.

why_others_wrong.B: Triglyceride is not the principal stored lipid defining atherosclerotic foam cells.
why_others_wrong.C: Phospholipids are present in membranes but are not the key accumulated material.
why_others_wrong.D: Bile salts are involved in intestinal lipid digestion.
why_others_wrong.E: Haemoglobin is not responsible for the foam-cell appearance.

exam_trap: Triglyceride only (B) tempts because steatosis stores triglyceride, but plaque foam cells are macrophages loaded with cholesterol and cholesterol esters from modified LDL.
takeaway: Atherosclerotic foam cell → macrophage packed with cholesterol/cholesterol esters.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Foam cells in an atherosclerotic plaque ↓ macrophages take up modified LDL ↓ cholesterol stored as esters in lipid droplets ↓ Cholesterol and cholesterol esters
pearl: Cholesterol crystal embolisation after arterial instrumentation can cause acute kidney injury, livedo reticularis and digital ischaemia.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Pathology: thrombosis
stem: Which feature of Virchow's triad most directly describes abnormal blood flow that promotes thrombosis?
why_correct: Virchow's triad comprises endothelial injury, abnormal blood flow and hypercoagulability. Abnormal flow includes both stasis and turbulence.

why_others_wrong.A: Endothelial injury is the vessel-wall component of the triad, describing damage to the lining rather than abnormal blood flow.
why_others_wrong.B: Hypercoagulability is the blood-composition component of the triad, an increased tendency to clot, not a disturbance of flow.
why_others_wrong.D: Platelet deficiency generally increases bleeding rather than thrombosis.
why_others_wrong.E: Anaemia is not one of the three components.

exam_trap: Hypercoagulability is chosen by candidates who confuse the components; it describes altered blood composition, whereas stasis or turbulence is the abnormal-flow limb of the triad.
takeaway: Virchow triad → endothelial injury + abnormal flow + hypercoagulability.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Virchow's triad: vessel wall, blood flow, blood composition ↓ the question asks about abnormal flow ↓ the flow component is stasis or turbulence ↓ Stasis or turbulence
pearl: Postoperative immobility causes venous stasis, which is why mechanical prophylaxis and early mobilisation are core parts of VTE prevention alongside pharmacological prophylaxis.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Pathology: thrombus organisation
stem: A venous thrombus becomes incorporated into the vessel wall over time, with ingrowth of connective tissue and small vascular channels. What process is occurring?
why_correct: An older thrombus can undergo organisation, with ingrowth of endothelial cells, smooth muscle cells and fibroblasts. New vascular channels may form through the thrombus, producing recanalisation.

why_others_wrong.A: Propagation refers to extension of thrombus formation.
why_others_wrong.C: Fat embolisation involves fat droplets entering the circulation.
why_others_wrong.D: Fibrinolysis can contribute to thrombus resolution but does not describe organised connective-tissue incorporation.
why_others_wrong.E: Vasculitis is inflammation of the vessel wall.

exam_trap: Fibrinolysis only is tempting because thrombi can dissolve, but lysis does not explain connective-tissue ingrowth and new vascular channels, which define organisation and recanalisation.
takeaway: Old thrombus → organisation → possible recanalisation.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Older venous thrombus becomes part of the vessel wall ↓ ingrowth of fibroblasts and connective tissue is organisation ↓ new channels through it restore some flow ↓ Organisation and recanalisation
pearl: Organisation of deep vein thrombus often damages venous valves, leading to chronic venous hypertension and post-thrombotic syndrome with swelling, pigmentation and ulceration.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Pathology: arterial embolism
stem: A fragment of thrombus breaks away from the left atrium. Where is it most likely to produce clinically important embolic occlusion?
why_correct: A thrombus arising in the left side of the heart enters the systemic arterial circulation and may embolise to organs such as the brain, kidneys, spleen or limbs.

why_others_wrong.A: Pulmonary emboli usually arise from venous thrombi entering the right heart.
why_others_wrong.C: The portal vein is a venous system fed by splanchnic capillaries, so an arterial embolus lodges upstream in mesenteric arteries before reaching it.
why_others_wrong.D: The superior vena cava carries venous blood toward the right heart.
why_others_wrong.E: The coronary sinus drains venous blood from the myocardium.

exam_trap: Pulmonary artery is tempting as the most familiar embolism site, but pulmonary emboli arise from venous thrombi; left-sided cardiac thrombi enter the systemic arterial circulation.
takeaway: Left heart thrombus → systemic arterial embolisation.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.; Principles and Practice of Surgery, 7th ed.
thinking: Thrombus fragment from the left atrium ↓ left atrium empties into the left ventricle and aorta ↓ emboli lodge in systemic arteries such as brain, limbs and gut ↓ Systemic arterial circulation
pearl: Atrial fibrillation is the commonest source of left atrial thrombus, and a sudden ischaemic limb in a patient with atrial fibrillation suggests embolism needing urgent revascularisation, often embolectomy.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Pathology: septic embolus
stem: A patient with infective endocarditis develops multiple peripheral infarcts containing microorganisms. What type of embolic phenomenon is occurring?
why_correct: Vegetations in infective endocarditis can fragment and embolise, carrying microorganisms to distant vascular territories and producing septic emboli.

why_others_wrong.A: Fat embolism follows long-bone fracture or orthopaedic trauma and carries fat globules, not microorganisms from infected valve vegetations.
why_others_wrong.B: Air embolism follows venous line procedures, surgery or decompression and causes gas-bubble occlusion, not infarcts containing microorganisms.
why_others_wrong.D: Cholesterol emboli arise from ulcerated atheroma, often after arterial instrumentation, and are sterile rather than carrying organisms from valve vegetations.
why_others_wrong.E: Tumour emboli carry malignant cells, for example from atrial myxoma, whereas endocarditis vegetations carry microorganisms that produce septic infarcts.

exam_trap: Cholesterol embolisation also causes multiple peripheral infarcts, but its emboli are sterile atheroma fragments after instrumentation; organisms within infarcts indicate septic emboli from vegetations.
takeaway: Infective endocarditis + embolic infection → septic emboli.
source: Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed.
thinking: Infective endocarditis with valve vegetations ↓ fragments embolise to peripheral vessels ↓ the infarcts contain microorganisms ↓ Septic embolisation
pearl: Septic emboli can seed infection in their target organ, producing splenic or cerebral abscesses or mycotic aneurysms, so new focal signs in endocarditis need imaging.

subject: Vascular, endocrine surgery & perioperative care
title: Pathology: aneurysm
stem: Which pathological process most directly describes an aneurysm?

options.A: Localised abnormal dilation of a blood vessel or cardiac chamber
