For hydatid liver cysts, the standard management is pre-treatment with albendazole (to sterilise the cyst and reduce the risk of rupture and anaphylaxis), followed by surgical resection or PAIR (puncture, aspiration, injection, reaspiration). Post-operative albendazole is also given to prevent recurrence.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Surgery alone carries a risk of cyst rupture and anaphylaxis. Pre-treatment with albendazole reduces the risk of dissemination.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Hydatid cysts can grow, rupture, and cause complications including anaphylaxis, biliary obstruction, and secondary infection. Treatment is indicated.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Percutaneous drainage alone carries a high risk of cyst rupture, anaphylaxis, and dissemination. It should be combined with albendazole therapy (PAIR technique).
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Praziquantel is used to treat other helminth infections such as schistosomiasis and tapeworm infections. Albendazole, not praziquantel, is the antihelminthic of choice for hydatid disease.

exam_trap: Immediate surgical resection without drug cover is the trap, because intraoperative spillage can cause anaphylaxis and peritoneal seeding; albendazole is given first to reduce this risk.
takeaway: Hydatid liver cyst → albendazole cover + surgery or PAIR; avoid spillage.
thinking: Liver cyst with positive Echinococcus granulosus serology ↓ hydatid disease ↓ cyst spillage risks anaphylaxis and secondary seeding ↓ albendazole cover before (and after) intervention ↓ Albendazole therapy followed by surgical resection
pearl: At operation the field is packed with swabs soaked in a scolicidal agent such as hypertonic saline to limit spillage, and bile staining of the cyst indicates a cystobiliary communication.

subject: Microbiology
title: Microbiology: Microbiology - Specific Organisms
stem: A patient develops severe diarrhoea after a course of clindamycin. Stool test is positive for Clostridium difficile toxin. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in management?

options.A: Stop clindamycin and start oral vancomycin
options.B: Continue clindamycin and add oral metronidazole
options.C: Stop clindamycin and start oral ciprofloxacin
options.D: Stop clindamycin and start intravenous vancomycin
options.E: Stop clindamycin and start faecal microbiota transplantation immediately

correct_answer: A. Stop clindamycin and start oral vancomycin
why_correct: Correct. The first step in managing C. difficile infection is to stop the offending antibiotic (clindamycin). Oral vancomycin is now first-line treatment for C. difficile infection, particularly for severe cases. It is not absorbed systemically, so it acts directly in the colon.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. Continuing clindamycin will perpetuate the C. difficile infection, so the offending antibiotic must be stopped. Metronidazole is no longer recommended by NICE for C. difficile; oral vancomycin is first line.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Ciprofloxacin is a fluoroquinolone that is associated with an increased risk of C. difficile infection. It is not a treatment for C. difficile.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Intravenous vancomycin does not reach the colon in sufficient concentrations to treat C. difficile infection. Oral vancomycin is required.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Faecal microbiota transplantation is reserved for recurrent or refractory C. difficile infection, not as an initial step in a first presentation.

exam_trap: Intravenous vancomycin looks equivalent but is not excreted into the colonic lumen; only oral vancomycin achieves therapeutic concentrations against C. difficile.
takeaway: C. difficile → stop the culprit antibiotic + oral (not IV) vancomycin.
thinking: Severe diarrhoea after clindamycin ↓ C. difficile toxin positive ↓ stop the precipitating antibiotic ↓ start oral therapy that acts in the colon ↓ Stop clindamycin and start oral vancomycin
pearl: Patients with C. difficile need isolation with contact precautions, and hands should be washed with soap and water because alcohol gel does not kill the spores.

subject: Microbiology
title: Microbiology: Microbiology - Specific Organisms
stem: A patient with a history of recurrent urinary tract infections grows an organism that is Gram-negative, lactose-fermenting, and oxidase-negative. Which organism is most likely?
why_correct: Correct. E. coli is the most common cause of urinary tract infections. It is a Gram-negative bacillus that is lactose-fermenting, oxidase-negative, and catalase-positive. It is part of normal gut flora and can ascend the urethra to cause infection.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. Pseudomonas is Gram-negative, lactose-non-fermenting, and oxidase-positive. It is a common cause of hospital-acquired infections, particularly in catheterised patients.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Proteus is Gram-negative, lactose-non-fermenting, and oxidase-negative. It is associated with struvite stones and urease production.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Klebsiella is Gram-negative, lactose-fermenting, and oxidase-negative, but it is less common than E. coli in uncomplicated urinary tract infections. It is more commonly associated with pneumonia, particularly in alcoholics.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Citrobacter freundii can cause urinary tract infections and is Gram-negative and oxidase-negative, but it is a much less common cause of recurrent urinary tract infection than E. coli.

exam_trap: Klebsiella pneumoniae matches every laboratory feature given, so the decision rests on frequency: Escherichia coli causes far more urinary tract infections.
takeaway: Lactose-fermenting, oxidase-negative Gram-negative uropathogen → most likely E. coli.
thinking: Recurrent urinary tract infection isolate ↓ Gram-negative, lactose-fermenting, oxidase-negative = coliform ↓ excludes Pseudomonas (oxidase-positive) and Proteus (non-fermenter) ↓ commonest uropathogen among the lactose fermenters ↓ Escherichia coli
pearl: Proteus produces urease, which alkalinises urine and promotes struvite (staghorn) calculi, so recurrent Proteus infection should prompt imaging for stones.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: Anatomy - Upper Limb
stem: During an anatomical dissection of the cubital fossa, the surgeon identifies the contents. Which structure lies most medially within the cubital fossa?
why_correct: Correct. The cubital fossa contains, from medial to lateral: the median nerve, brachial artery, biceps tendon, and radial nerve (with its superficial and deep branches). The median nerve is the most medial structure within the fossa.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. The biceps tendon lies centrally in the cubital fossa, lateral to the brachial artery; it is not the most medial structure.
why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. The brachial artery lies medial to the biceps tendon but lateral to the median nerve. It is not the most medial structure.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. The radial nerve lies laterally within the cubital fossa, between the brachioradialis and brachialis muscles. It is the most lateral structure.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. The ulnar nerve passes posterior to the medial epicondyle of the humerus (through the cubital tunnel) rather than through the cubital fossa itself.

exam_trap: Ulnar nerve is picked because it is the most medial nerve at the elbow, but it runs behind the medial epicondyle in the cubital tunnel, not within the cubital fossa.
takeaway: Cubital fossa, medial to lateral: median nerve, brachial artery, biceps tendon, radial nerve.
thinking: Contents of the cubital fossa ↓ from lateral to medial: radial nerve, biceps tendon, brachial artery, median nerve ↓ the ulnar nerve passes behind the medial epicondyle, outside the fossa ↓ Median nerve
pearl: The bicipital aponeurosis overlies the brachial artery and median nerve, giving some protection during antecubital venepuncture; a deep needle medial to the biceps tendon risks arterial puncture or median nerve injury.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: Anatomy - Upper Limb
stem: A patient sustains a laceration to the anatomical snuffbox. Which structure is most at risk of injury?
why_correct: Correct. The anatomical snuffbox is bounded by the tendons of abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis laterally, and extensor pollicis longus medially. The floor is formed by the scaphoid and trapezium. The radial artery passes through the floor of the snuffbox, where it is vulnerable to injury from lacerations or fractures of the scaphoid.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. The ulnar artery passes through Guyon's canal at the wrist, on the medial side of the hand. It is not located in the anatomical snuffbox.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. The median nerve passes through the carpal tunnel, which is on the palmar aspect of the wrist. It is not in the anatomical snuffbox.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. The superficial palmar arch is located in the palm of the hand, formed primarily by the ulnar artery. It is not in the anatomical snuffbox.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Extensor pollicis longus forms the medial (ulnar) border of the anatomical snuffbox; it is a boundary of the space rather than the structure within it that is most at risk of injury.

exam_trap: Candidates may choose the extensor pollicis longus tendon, but it forms the ulnar border of the snuffbox; the radial artery crosses its floor.
takeaway: Anatomical snuffbox floor → radial artery over scaphoid and trapezium.
thinking: Laceration of the anatomical snuffbox ↓ borders are APL and EPB laterally, EPL medially ↓ the radial artery crosses its floor over scaphoid and trapezium ↓ Radial artery
pearl: The superficial branch of the radial nerve and the cephalic vein lie in the roof of the snuffbox, so lacerations here may also cause numbness over the dorsoradial hand.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: Anatomy - Lower Limb
stem: During a tarsal tunnel decompression, the surgeon must identify the structures within the tunnel. Which structure lies most anteriorly within the tarsal tunnel?
why_correct: Correct. The tarsal tunnel is located behind the medial malleolus. Its contents, from anterior to posterior, are: tibialis posterior tendon, flexor digitorum longus tendon, posterior tibial artery, tibial nerve, and flexor hallucis longus tendon. The tibialis posterior tendon is the most anterior structure.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. The tibial nerve lies posterior to the tibial artery within the tarsal tunnel. It is not the most anterior structure.
why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. The posterior tibial artery lies between the tibialis posterior tendon and the tibial nerve. It is not the most anterior structure.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. The flexor digitorum longus tendon lies posterior to the tibialis posterior tendon but anterior to the posterior tibial artery. It is not the most anterior structure.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. The flexor hallucis longus tendon is the most posterior structure within the tarsal tunnel, not the most anterior.

exam_trap: Candidates may choose flexor hallucis longus, but it is the most posterior; tibialis posterior lies most anterior, directly behind the medial malleolus.
takeaway: Tarsal tunnel, anterior to posterior: tibialis posterior, FDL, posterior tibial artery, tibial nerve, FHL.
thinking: Tarsal tunnel behind the medial malleolus ↓ order from anterior to posterior: tibialis posterior, FDL, posterior tibial artery, tibial nerve, FHL ↓ tibialis posterior lies directly against the malleolus ↓ Tibialis posterior tendon
pearl: Tarsal tunnel syndrome is entrapment of the tibial nerve beneath the flexor retinaculum, causing burning pain and paraesthesia of the sole, typically worse on standing and walking.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: Anatomy - Lower Limb
stem: A patient presents with a femoral hernia. Which structure forms the anterior boundary of the femoral canal?
why_correct: Correct. The femoral canal has four boundaries: anterior (inguinal ligament), posterior (pectineal ligament), medial (lacunar ligament), and lateral (femoral vein). The inguinal ligament forms the anterior boundary.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. The lacunar ligament forms the medial boundary of the femoral canal. It is a triangular extension of the inguinal ligament.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. The pectineal ligament (of Cooper) forms the posterior boundary of the femoral canal.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. The femoral vein forms the lateral boundary of the femoral canal.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. The iliopsoas muscle lies lateral to the femoral sheath as it passes beneath the inguinal ligament; it does not form a boundary of the femoral canal.

exam_trap: Candidates may choose the lacunar ligament, which is the medial boundary; the anterior boundary of the femoral canal is the inguinal ligament.
takeaway: Femoral canal: anterior inguinal ligament, posterior pectineal ligament, medial lacunar ligament, lateral femoral vein.
thinking: Boundaries of the femoral canal ↓ medially lacunar ligament, posteriorly pectineal ligament, laterally femoral vein ↓ anteriorly the inguinal ligament ↓ Inguinal ligament
pearl: A femoral hernia emerges below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, whereas an inguinal hernia lies above and medial to it, a key bedside distinction.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: Anatomy - Abdomen
stem: During a Whipple procedure, the surgeon must identify the branches of the coeliac trunk. Which of the following is a direct branch of the coeliac trunk?
why_correct: Correct. The coeliac trunk has three direct branches: left gastric artery, common hepatic artery, and splenic artery. The splenic artery runs along the superior border of the pancreas to supply the spleen.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. The superior mesenteric artery arises directly from the abdominal aorta, approximately 1 cm below the coeliac trunk. It is not a branch of the coeliac trunk.
why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. The inferior mesenteric artery arises from the abdominal aorta at the level of L3. It is not a branch of the coeliac trunk.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. The gastroduodenal artery is a branch of the common hepatic artery, which is itself a branch of the coeliac trunk. It is not a direct branch of the coeliac trunk.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. The right gastric artery typically arises from the hepatic artery proper (or common hepatic artery) rather than directly from the coeliac trunk.

exam_trap: Candidates may choose the gastroduodenal artery, but it arises from the common hepatic artery; the coeliac trunk gives only left gastric, common hepatic and splenic arteries.
takeaway: Coeliac trunk branches: left gastric, common hepatic and splenic arteries.
thinking: Direct branches of the coeliac trunk ↓ the coeliac trunk at T12 has three branches ↓ left gastric, common hepatic and splenic arteries ↓ gastroduodenal and right gastric arteries come from the hepatic arteries ↓ Splenic artery
pearl: A replaced right hepatic artery arising from the SMA runs behind the pancreatic head and portal vein and must be identified before pancreatoduodenectomy to avoid inadvertent division.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: Anatomy - Abdomen
stem: A patient presents with a retroperitoneal mass. Which of the following structures is located in the retroperitoneum?
why_correct: Correct. The kidneys are retroperitoneal organs, lying against the posterior abdominal wall. Other retroperitoneal structures include the ureters, adrenal glands, pancreas (except the tail), duodenum (except the first part), ascending colon, descending colon, abdominal aorta, and inferior vena cava.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. The spleen is an intraperitoneal organ located in the left upper quadrant. It is not retroperitoneal.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. The transverse colon is intraperitoneal and has a mesentery. It is not retroperitoneal.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. The stomach is intraperitoneal and is connected to the greater and lesser omenta. It is not retroperitoneal.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. The liver is an intraperitoneal organ (aside from its bare area); it is not a retroperitoneal structure.

exam_trap: Candidates may hesitate over the liver because of its bare area, but it is intraperitoneal; the kidneys lie wholly retroperitoneal on the posterior abdominal wall.
takeaway: Kidneys are retroperitoneal; spleen, stomach, liver and transverse colon are intraperitoneal.
thinking: Retroperitoneal structure ↓ spleen, stomach and transverse colon are suspended by peritoneal folds ↓ the liver is intraperitoneal apart from its bare area ↓ kidneys lie behind the peritoneum in perirenal fat ↓ Kidneys
pearl: Retroperitoneal organs can be approached without entering the peritoneal cavity, for example through a loin incision for kidney surgery, which reduces ileus and intra-abdominal adhesions.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: Anatomy - Head and Neck
stem: During a neck dissection, the surgeon identifies the boundaries of the anterior triangle of the neck. Which structure forms the superior boundary of the anterior triangle?
why_correct: Correct. The anterior triangle of the neck is bounded by: superiorly by the lower border of the mandible, laterally by the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid, and medially by the midline of the neck. It contains the submandibular gland, carotid sheath, and cranial nerves.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. The clavicle forms the inferior boundary of the posterior triangle of the neck, not the anterior triangle.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. The sternocleidomastoid forms the lateral boundary of the anterior triangle and the anterior boundary of the posterior triangle.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. The midline of the neck forms the medial boundary of the anterior triangle, not the superior boundary.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. The hyoid bone lies within the anterior triangle and is used to help subdivide it into smaller triangles, but it does not form the superior boundary of the anterior triangle as a whole.

exam_trap: Candidates may choose the hyoid bone, but it subdivides the anterior triangle; its superior boundary is the lower border of the mandible.
takeaway: Anterior triangle: mandible above, sternocleidomastoid laterally, midline medially.
thinking: Boundaries of the anterior triangle of the neck ↓ medial boundary is the midline of the neck ↓ lateral boundary is the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid ↓ superior boundary is the lower border of the mandible ↓ Mandible
pearl: The hyoid divides the anterior triangle into suprahyoid (submental, submandibular) and infrahyoid (carotid, muscular) triangles, which underlie the nodal levels used in neck dissection.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: Anatomy - Head and Neck
stem: A patient presents with a submandibular gland swelling. Which nerve is at risk of injury during submandibular gland excision, leading to loss of taste sensation from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue?
why_correct: Correct. The lingual nerve is a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V3). It carries general sensation from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and also carries chorda tympani fibres (from the facial nerve) that provide taste sensation. It is at risk during submandibular gland excision, and injury can cause loss of taste and sensation from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. The hypoglossal nerve supplies the intrinsic and extrinsic muscles of the tongue. Injury causes tongue weakness and deviation, not loss of taste.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) supplies taste sensation to the posterior one-third of the tongue. It is not at risk during submandibular gland excision.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. The facial nerve (CN VII) supplies the muscles of facial expression. Its chorda tympani branch carries taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, but the main trunk is not at risk during submandibular gland excision.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. The marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve is also at risk during submandibular gland excision, but it supplies the muscles of the lower lip and does not carry taste fibres from the tongue.

exam_trap: Candidates may choose the marginal mandibular branch, which is also at risk during submandibular gland excision, but it supplies lower lip muscles and carries no taste fibres.
takeaway: Submandibular gland excision: lingual nerve (taste and sensation, anterior two-thirds of tongue), hypoglossal and marginal mandibular nerves are all at risk.
thinking: Submandibular gland excision ↓ nerve looping under the submandibular duct, attached to the submandibular ganglion ↓ carries sensation and chorda tympani taste from anterior two-thirds of tongue ↓ Lingual nerve
pearl: The lingual nerve is identified by its attachment to the submandibular ganglion and must be separated before the gland is freed; the hypoglossal nerve lies deeper and lower, on hyoglossus.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: Anatomy - Thorax
stem: During a thoracic duct injury, chyle leaks into the pleural cavity. Which of the following best describes the anatomical course of the thoracic duct?

options.A: It ascends on the right side of the vertebral column and drains into the right subclavian vein
options.B: It ascends on the left side of the vertebral column and drains into the left brachiocephalic vein
options.C: It descends on the left side of the vertebral column and drains into the left renal vein
options.D: It ascends on the left side of the vertebral column and drains into the superior vena cava
options.E: It ascends on the left side of the vertebral column and drains into the azygos vein

correct_answer: B. It ascends on the left side of the vertebral column and drains into the left brachiocephalic vein
why_correct: Correct. The thoracic duct begins at the cisterna chyli, enters the thorax through the aortic hiatus and ascends in the posterior mediastinum to the right of the midline, between the aorta and azygos vein, before crossing to the left at about T5. It then ascends on the left side of the oesophagus and vertebral column and drains into the junction of the left subclavian and left internal jugular veins (the origin of the left brachiocephalic vein).

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Although the duct lies right of the midline in the lower thorax, it crosses to the left at about T5 and ends at the left venous angle; the right lymphatic duct, not the thoracic duct, drains into the right venous angle.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. The thoracic duct ascends, not descends. It does not drain into the renal vein.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. The thoracic duct drains into the left brachiocephalic vein, not directly into the superior vena cava.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. The azygos vein drains the posterior thoracic wall and mediastinal structures; the thoracic duct instead terminates at the junction of the left subclavian and left internal jugular veins.

exam_trap: Option A is chosen because the duct lies right of the midline in the lower thorax, but it crosses left at about T5 and ends at the left venous angle.
takeaway: Thoracic duct: cisterna chyli → aortic hiatus → crosses left at about T5 → left venous angle.
thinking: Chyle leaking into the pleural cavity ↓ thoracic duct arises from the cisterna chyli and enters through the aortic hiatus ↓ ascends right of the midline, then crosses to the left at about T5 ↓ ends at the junction of the left subclavian and internal jugular veins ↓ It ascends on the left side of the vertebral column and drains into the left brachiocephalic vein
pearl: Chyle is milky and rich in triglycerides and chylomicrons; a persistent postoperative chylothorax that fails conservative treatment may need duct ligation, classically low in the right chest between the aorta and azygos vein.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: Anatomy - Neuroanatomy
stem: A patient presents with a spinal cord injury. Which of the following tracts carries pain and temperature sensation?
why_correct: Correct. The spinothalamic tract carries pain and temperature sensation. It is located in the anterolateral aspect of the spinal cord. Fibres cross the midline within one or two segments of entering the spinal cord and ascend to the thalamus.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. The corticospinal tract carries motor fibres from the motor cortex to the spinal cord. It is responsible for voluntary movement.
why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. The dorsal columns carry proprioception, vibration, and fine touch sensation. They are not responsible for pain and temperature.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. The spinocerebellar tract carries proprioceptive information to the cerebellum for coordination of movement. It is not responsible for pain and temperature.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. The vestibulospinal tract carries information used for postural control and balance; it does not carry pain and temperature sensation.

exam_trap: Candidates pick the dorsal columns (B) because they are the best-known sensory tract, but they carry fine touch, vibration and proprioception, not pain or temperature.
takeaway: Pain and temperature = spinothalamic tract (crosses near entry); fine touch, vibration and proprioception = dorsal columns.
thinking: Pain and temperature modality ↓ carried by the anterolateral system ↓ fibres decussate within one or two segments and ascend contralaterally ↓ Spinothalamic tract
pearl: Because spinothalamic fibres cross near their level of entry while dorsal column fibres ascend ipsilaterally, a cord hemisection gives ipsilateral weakness and proprioceptive loss with contralateral loss of pain and temperature below the lesion.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: Physiology - Cardiovascular
stem: Which of the following best describes the primary determinant of coronary blood flow?
correct_answer: B. Local metabolic factors during diastole
why_correct: Correct. Coronary blood flow is primarily regulated by local metabolic factors, particularly during diastole. When myocardial oxygen demand increases, metabolites such as adenosine, hypoxia, and potassium ions cause coronary vasodilation, increasing blood flow. The left coronary artery flow occurs mainly during diastole.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Coronary blood flow occurs predominantly during diastole, not systole. During systole, the contracting myocardium compresses the coronary vessels, reducing flow.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. While heart rate affects coronary flow indirectly by altering diastolic time, the primary determinant is local metabolic regulation.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Sympathetic stimulation causes coronary vasoconstriction via alpha receptors, but this is overridden by local metabolic vasodilation. Sympathetic stimulation is not the primary determinant of coronary blood flow.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Coronary sinus pressure reflects venous drainage from the myocardium; it is not the primary determinant of coronary blood flow, which is governed mainly by local metabolic autoregulation.

exam_trap: Option A tempts because aortic pressure drives flow, but systolic compression of intramyocardial vessels limits left coronary flow; diastolic perfusion with metabolic autoregulation dominates.
takeaway: Coronary flow: metabolic autoregulation (adenosine); left ventricle perfused mainly in diastole.
thinking: The myocardium extracts most of the delivered oxygen even at rest ↓ so extra demand can only be met by extra flow ↓ metabolites such as adenosine dilate coronary arterioles ↓ left ventricular flow occurs mainly in diastole ↓ Local metabolic factors during diastole
pearl: Because the left ventricle is perfused mainly in diastole, tachycardia shortens diastolic time and reduces subendocardial perfusion, so heart rate control is protective in patients with ischaemic heart disease around surgery.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: Physiology - Cardiovascular
stem: A patient with septic shock has a low systemic vascular resistance. Which of the following best describes the compensatory mechanism that maintains blood pressure?

options.E: Activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system alone

correct_answer: B. Increased sympathetic outflow and tachycardia
why_correct: Correct. In septic shock, low systemic vascular resistance causes hypotension. The body compensates by increasing sympathetic outflow, which causes tachycardia, increased cardiac contractility, and vasoconstriction (though less effective in sepsis due to vasodilation). This helps maintain blood pressure and organ perfusion.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Parasympathetic outflow would decrease heart rate and worsen hypotension. In septic shock, there is decreased parasympathetic tone.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. In septic shock, cardiac output is typically increased (warm shock) due to vasodilation and tachycardia. Decreased cardiac output would worsen hypotension.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Decreased venous return would reduce cardiac output and worsen hypotension, so it cannot be a compensatory mechanism. In septic shock venodilatation and capillary leak actually tend to reduce venous return, which is why fluid resuscitation is required.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. RAAS activation contributes to fluid retention and vasoconstriction over a slower time course; the immediate compensatory response that maintains blood pressure in septic shock is increased sympathetic outflow and tachycardia.

exam_trap: RAAS activation (E) is chosen because it raises blood pressure, but it acts more slowly and not alone; the immediate compensation is sympathetic outflow and tachycardia.
takeaway: Septic shock: low SVR → baroreflex sympathetic drive → tachycardia and raised cardiac output.
thinking: Septic shock with low systemic vascular resistance ↓ falling blood pressure is sensed by baroreceptors ↓ sympathetic outflow rises ↓ tachycardia and increased contractility raise cardiac output to offset low resistance ↓ Increased sympathetic outflow and tachycardia
pearl: Because vasodilatation in sepsis blunts the vasoconstrictor response, hypotension persisting after fluid resuscitation is treated with a vasopressor, with noradrenaline as first-line.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: Physiology - Respiratory
stem: Which of the following best describes the effect of a rightward shift of the oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve?
correct_answer: B. Decreased oxygen affinity for haemoglobin
why_correct: Correct. A rightward shift of the oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve indicates decreased oxygen affinity for haemoglobin, meaning oxygen is released more readily to tissues. This occurs with acidosis (Bohr effect), hyperthermia, increased 2,3-DPG, and increased CO2.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Increased oxygen affinity is represented by a leftward shift of the curve. This occurs with alkalosis, hypothermia, decreased 2,3-DPG, and decreased CO2.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Oxygen carrying capacity is determined by haemoglobin concentration, not by the position of the dissociation curve. The curve shifts affect affinity, not capacity.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Carbon dioxide transport is not directly affected by the oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve. The Haldane effect describes the relationship between oxygenation and CO2 transport.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Haemoglobin concentration determines the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity; it does not describe a shift in the position of the oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve.

exam_trap: Option C is a trap: the position of the curve reflects affinity, not capacity; oxygen-carrying capacity depends on haemoglobin concentration, which a shift does not change.
takeaway: Right shift (raised CO2, acid, 2,3-DPG, exercise, temperature) → reduced affinity and more oxygen unloading.
thinking: Rightward shift = a higher PO2 is needed for the same saturation ↓ the P50 rises ↓ haemoglobin holds oxygen less tightly ↓ more oxygen is unloaded to the tissues ↓ Decreased oxygen affinity for haemoglobin
pearl: Stored blood is depleted of 2,3-DPG, so transfused red cells have a left-shifted curve and unload oxygen less readily at first; levels recover over hours to days after transfusion.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: Physiology - Respiratory
stem: Which of the following best describes the control of breathing?

options.A: The primary respiratory centre is located in the cerebral cortex
options.B: The primary respiratory centre is located in the medulla oblongata
options.C: Breathing is solely controlled by peripheral chemoreceptors
options.D: Breathing is solely controlled by voluntary effort
options.E: The primary respiratory centre is located in the hypothalamus

correct_answer: B. The primary respiratory centre is located in the medulla oblongata
why_correct: Correct. The primary respiratory centre is located in the medulla oblongata. It consists of the dorsal respiratory group (DRG) and ventral respiratory group (VRG). The DRG is mainly inspiratory, while the VRG contains both inspiratory and expiratory neurons, including the main rhythm-generating neurons, and is recruited for active expiration. The pontine respiratory centres (pneumotaxic and apneustic centres) modulate the medullary centres.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. The cerebral cortex can voluntarily control breathing, but the primary automatic respiratory centre is in the medulla oblongata.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Breathing is controlled by central chemoreceptors (in the medulla, responsive to CO2/pH) and peripheral chemoreceptors (in the carotid and aortic bodies, responsive to O2, CO2, and pH). Central chemoreceptors are the primary drivers of breathing.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Breathing is primarily automatic, controlled by the medulla. Voluntary control via the cerebral cortex is possible but not the primary mechanism.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. The hypothalamus regulates autonomic functions such as temperature control and thirst; it is not the site of the primary automatic respiratory centre, which is in the medulla oblongata.

exam_trap: Option A tempts because breathing can be held voluntarily, but cortical control only overrides temporarily; the automatic respiratory rhythm generator lies in the medulla.
takeaway: Respiratory rhythm is generated in the medulla; the pons modulates it and the cortex allows voluntary override.
thinking: Automatic breathing continues in sleep and unconsciousness ↓ its rhythm is generated by brainstem neurons ↓ the dorsal and ventral respiratory groups lie in the medulla, modulated by the pons ↓ The primary respiratory centre is located in the medulla oblongata
pearl: Tonsillar herniation from raised intracranial pressure compresses the medulla, causing irregular breathing and apnoea, a late sign that accompanies the reflex hypertension and bradycardia of brainstem compression.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: Physiology - Renal
stem: Which of the following best describes the primary site of potassium reabsorption in the nephron?

options.E: Thin descending limb of the loop of Henle

why_correct: Correct. Approximately 65-70% of filtered potassium is reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule. This occurs passively, driven by solvent drag and electrochemical gradients. The remaining potassium is reabsorbed in the loop of Henle and distal nephron.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. The loop of Henle reabsorbs approximately 20-25% of filtered potassium, primarily in the thick ascending limb via the Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporter. However, the proximal tubule is the primary site.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. The distal convoluted tubule reabsorbs a small amount of potassium, but it is also a site of potassium secretion under the influence of aldosterone.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. The collecting duct is primarily responsible for potassium secretion (under aldosterone influence) rather than reabsorption. It fine-tunes potassium excretion.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. The thin descending limb of the loop of Henle is primarily permeable to water and is not a major site of potassium reabsorption.

exam_trap: Option D tempts because the collecting duct is central to potassium handling, but it mainly secretes potassium under aldosterone; bulk reabsorption happens in the proximal tubule.
takeaway: Potassium: bulk reabsorption proximally; regulated secretion in the distal nephron and collecting duct.
thinking: Potassium is freely filtered ↓ the proximal tubule reabsorbs roughly two-thirds passively, by solvent drag ↓ the distal nephron mainly adjusts secretion ↓ Proximal convoluted tubule
pearl: Because bulk potassium reabsorption is fixed proximally, day-to-day potassium balance depends on distal secretion, which needs aldosterone and adequate distal sodium delivery; this is why ACE inhibitors and spironolactone cause hyperkalaemia.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: Physiology - Renal
stem: Which of the following best describes the effect of aldosterone on the kidney?

options.A: Increased sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion
options.B: Increased sodium excretion and potassium reabsorption
options.D: Decreased sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion
options.E: Increased calcium reabsorption and phosphate excretion

correct_answer: A. Increased sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion
why_correct: Correct. Aldosterone is secreted by the zona glomerulosa of the adrenal cortex in response to angiotensin II, hyperkalaemia, and ACTH. It acts on the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct to increase sodium reabsorption (via ENaC channels) and potassium secretion. This leads to sodium and water retention and potassium excretion.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. This is the opposite of aldosterone's effect. Aldosterone promotes sodium retention and potassium excretion.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Aldosterone primarily affects sodium and potassium, not water directly. Water follows sodium osmotically.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Aldosterone increases sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion, not decreases them.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. This describes the renal action of parathyroid hormone, not aldosterone, which principally regulates sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion.

exam_trap: Option E describes parathyroid hormone; candidates mixing up steroid and calcium hormones pick it, but aldosterone handles sodium and potassium, not calcium and phosphate.
takeaway: Aldosterone: sodium in, potassium (and H+) out in the distal nephron.
thinking: Aldosterone binds mineralocorticoid receptors in principal cells ↓ more ENaC channels and Na/K-ATPase ↓ sodium is reabsorbed and potassium secreted ↓ Increased sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion
pearl: After adrenalectomy for an aldosterone-producing adenoma the remaining zona glomerulosa may be suppressed, so potassium supplements and spironolactone are stopped and potassium is monitored for hyperkalaemia.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: Physiology - Endocrine
stem: Which of the following best describes the regulation of insulin secretion?

options.A: Increased blood glucose stimulates insulin secretion
options.B: Decreased blood glucose stimulates insulin secretion
options.C: Increased blood glucose inhibits insulin secretion
options.D: Insulin secretion is independent of blood glucose levels

correct_answer: A. Increased blood glucose stimulates insulin secretion
why_correct: Correct. Insulin is secreted by the beta cells of the pancreatic islets of Langerhans. Increased blood glucose is the primary stimulus for insulin secretion. Glucose enters beta cells via GLUT2 transporters, is metabolised to ATP, which closes ATP-sensitive potassium channels, causing depolarisation and calcium influx, leading to insulin release.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. Decreased blood glucose inhibits insulin secretion and stimulates glucagon secretion. This is the opposite of the normal physiological response.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Increased blood glucose stimulates insulin secretion, not inhibits it.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Insulin secretion is highly dependent on blood glucose levels. Glucose is the primary regulator of insulin secretion.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Somatostatin, secreted by pancreatic delta cells, inhibits both insulin and glucagon secretion; it does not stimulate insulin release.

exam_trap: Option E is the trap: somatostatin from delta cells inhibits both insulin and glucagon, which is why somatostatin analogues such as octreotide can disturb glucose control.
takeaway: Glucose → GLUT2 → ATP → K-ATP channel closure → depolarisation → calcium influx → insulin release.
thinking: Rising glucose enters beta cells via GLUT2 ↓ metabolism raises intracellular ATP ↓ ATP-sensitive K+ channels close, the cell depolarises and calcium enters ↓ insulin granules are released ↓ Increased blood glucose stimulates insulin secretion
pearl: Sulphonylureas close the same ATP-sensitive potassium channel independently of glucose, so they can cause hypoglycaemia in patients fasting for surgery and are usually withheld on the day of operation.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: Physiology - Endocrine
stem: Which of the following best describes the action of cortisol?

options.A: It increases blood glucose by promoting gluconeogenesis
options.B: It decreases blood glucose by promoting insulin release
options.C: It decreases blood pressure by causing vasodilation
options.D: It decreases inflammation by inhibiting immune cells
options.E: It increases blood glucose by directly inhibiting glucagon release

correct_answer: A. It increases blood glucose by promoting gluconeogenesis
why_correct: Correct. Cortisol is a glucocorticoid secreted by the zona fasciculata of the adrenal cortex. It increases blood glucose by promoting gluconeogenesis in the liver, increasing protein catabolism (providing amino acids for gluconeogenesis), and increasing lipolysis. It also decreases glucose uptake in peripheral tissues.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. Cortisol increases blood glucose; it does not decrease it. It also does not promote insulin release.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Cortisol increases blood pressure by promoting vasoconstriction and increasing vascular sensitivity to catecholamines. It also causes sodium and water retention.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. While cortisol does have anti-inflammatory effects (by inhibiting immune cells and reducing cytokine production), the question asks about its primary metabolic action. The best answer is its effect on blood glucose.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Cortisol raises blood glucose mainly through gluconeogenesis, protein catabolism, and reduced peripheral glucose uptake; it does not act by suppressing glucagon release.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: Physiology - Gastrointestinal
stem: Which of the following best describes the function of gastrin?

options.A: It stimulates gastric acid secretion by parietal cells
options.B: It inhibits gastric acid secretion by parietal cells
options.E: It stimulates the release of secretin from the duodenum

correct_answer: A. It stimulates gastric acid secretion by parietal cells
why_correct: Correct. Gastrin is secreted by G cells in the gastric antrum in response to food, vagal stimulation, and gastrin-releasing peptide. It stimulates parietal cells to secrete hydrochloric acid, either directly or indirectly via histamine release from enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. Gastrin stimulates acid secretion; it does not inhibit it. Somatostatin inhibits acid secretion.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Secretin stimulates pancreatic bicarbonate secretion. Gastrin primarily affects gastric acid secretion.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Cholecystokinin (CCK) stimulates gallbladder contraction. Gastrin does not have this effect.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Secretin release is triggered by acidic chyme entering the duodenum, not by gastrin.

exam_trap: Option E reverses the physiology: secretin is released by acid entering the duodenum and inhibits gastrin release, rather than being released in response to gastrin.
takeaway: Gastrin (antral G cells) → acid secretion, directly and via ECL-cell histamine.
thinking: Gastrin comes from antral G cells ↓ it is released by food, vagal stimulation and gastrin-releasing peptide ↓ it acts on parietal cells directly and via histamine from ECL cells ↓ It stimulates gastric acid secretion by parietal cells
pearl: A gastrinoma produces severe or multiple peptic ulcers, sometimes beyond the duodenal bulb, often with diarrhoea; a minority occur as part of MEN1.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: Physiology - Gastrointestinal
stem: Which of the following best describes the function of cholecystokinin (CCK)?

options.B: It stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion and gallbladder contraction

correct_answer: B. It stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion and gallbladder contraction
why_correct: Correct. CCK is secreted by I cells in the duodenum and jejunum in response to fatty acids and amino acids. It stimulates pancreatic acinar cells to secrete digestive enzymes and causes gallbladder contraction to release bile. It also inhibits gastric emptying.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. CCK inhibits gastric acid secretion and gastric emptying. Gastrin stimulates acid secretion.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Secretin stimulates pancreatic bicarbonate secretion. CCK primarily stimulates enzyme secretion.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. CCK stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion. It does not inhibit it.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. CCK stimulates, rather than inhibits, gallbladder contraction to release bile.

exam_trap: Option C belongs to secretin; candidates muddle the duodenal hormones, but CCK drives enzyme-rich secretion while secretin drives bicarbonate-rich fluid.
takeaway: CCK (I cells) → gallbladder contraction + pancreatic enzymes; slows gastric emptying.
thinking: Fatty acids and amino acids in the duodenum ↓ I cells release CCK ↓ CCK contracts the gallbladder and relaxes the hepatopancreatic sphincter ↓ it stimulates acinar enzyme secretion ↓ It stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion and gallbladder contraction
pearl: CCK release after fatty meals explains why biliary colic is typically triggered by fatty food, and CCK-stimulated HIDA scanning can measure gallbladder ejection fraction.

subject: Pathology
title: Pathology: Pathology - General
stem: Which of the following best describes the mechanism of amyloidosis?

options.A: Deposition of misfolded proteins in tissues
options.B: Deposition of cholesterol crystals in arteries
options.C: Deposition of calcium salts in soft tissues
options.D: Deposition of urate crystals in joints

correct_answer: A. Deposition of misfolded proteins in tissues
why_correct: Correct. Amyloidosis is characterised by the extracellular deposition of misfolded proteins (amyloid) in tissues and organs. Amyloid is composed of fibrillar proteins arranged in a beta-pleated sheet configuration, which is resistant to degradation. It stains with Congo red and shows apple-green birefringence under polarised light. Common types include AL (primary), AA (secondary), and ATTR (transthyretin).

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. This describes atherosclerosis, not amyloidosis. Cholesterol crystals are deposited in the arterial wall in atherosclerosis.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. This describes metastatic calcification or dystrophic calcification, not amyloidosis.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. This describes gout, not amyloidosis. Urate crystals are deposited in joints and soft tissues.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Lysosomal glycogen accumulation describes glycogen storage diseases such as Pompe disease, not amyloidosis, which involves extracellular deposition of misfolded beta-pleated sheet proteins.

exam_trap: Candidates choose deposition of calcium salts (C) or cholesterol (B) because these also deposit in tissues, but amyloid is misfolded protein staining with Congo red.
takeaway: Amyloid = extracellular misfolded beta-pleated protein; Congo red with apple-green birefringence.
thinking: Amyloidosis ↓ extracellular deposits of misfolded fibrillar proteins ↓ beta-pleated sheet structure resistant to degradation ↓ Deposition of misfolded proteins in tissues
pearl: AA amyloidosis complicates long-standing chronic inflammation such as rheumatoid arthritis or chronic osteomyelitis, and renal involvement commonly presents with nephrotic syndrome.

subject: Pathology
title: Pathology: Pathology - General
stem: Which of the following best describes the difference between dystrophic and metastatic calcification?

options.A: Dystrophic calcification occurs in normal tissues with normal calcium levels; metastatic calcification occurs in damaged tissues with hypercalcaemia
options.B: Dystrophic calcification occurs in damaged tissues with normal calcium levels; metastatic calcification occurs in normal tissues with hypercalcaemia
options.C: Dystrophic calcification occurs in damaged tissues with hypercalcaemia; metastatic calcification occurs in normal tissues with normal calcium levels
options.D: Both occur in damaged tissues with hypercalcaemia
options.E: Dystrophic calcification is reversible with correction of the underlying disorder, while metastatic calcification is permanent

correct_answer: B. Dystrophic calcification occurs in damaged tissues with normal calcium levels; metastatic calcification occurs in normal tissues with hypercalcaemia
why_correct: Correct. Dystrophic calcification occurs in damaged or necrotic tissues (e.g., atherosclerotic plaques, tuberculous lymph nodes) in the presence of normal serum calcium levels. Metastatic calcification occurs in normal tissues (e.g., blood vessels, kidneys, lungs) in the presence of hypercalcaemia (e.g., hyperparathyroidism, malignancy, vitamin D toxicity).

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. This reverses the definitions. Dystrophic calcification occurs in damaged tissues, and metastatic calcification occurs in normal tissues.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Dystrophic calcification occurs with normal calcium levels, and metastatic calcification occurs with hypercalcaemia.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Dystrophic calcification occurs in damaged tissues with normal calcium, while metastatic calcification occurs in normal tissues with hypercalcaemia.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Reversibility is not the distinguishing feature between the two processes; the key difference is that dystrophic calcification occurs in damaged tissue with normal serum calcium, while metastatic calcification occurs in normal tissue with hypercalcaemia.

exam_trap: Candidates choose the reversed pairing (A), mixing up the terms; dystrophic calcification occurs in damaged tissue with normal calcium, metastatic in normal tissue with hypercalcaemia.
takeaway: Dystrophic = damaged tissue, normal calcium; metastatic = normal tissue, high calcium.
thinking: Calcification type ↓ dystrophic: damaged tissue, normal serum calcium ↓ metastatic: normal tissue, hypercalcaemia ↓ Dystrophic calcification occurs in damaged tissues with normal calcium levels; metastatic calcification occurs in normal tissues with hypercalcaemia
pearl: Dystrophic calcification is common in atheroma and damaged heart valves, and is the basis of calcific aortic stenosis.

subject: Pathology
title: Pathology: Pathology - Haematology
stem: A patient presents with fatigue, pallor, and glossitis. Blood tests show a macrocytic anaemia with hypersegmented neutrophils. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Correct. Vitamin B12 deficiency causes macrocytic anaemia with hypersegmented neutrophils (more than 5 lobes). It also causes glossitis (smooth, beefy-red tongue) and neurological symptoms (subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord). It is caused by pernicious anaemia, ileal resection, or strict vegan diet.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Iron deficiency anaemia causes microcytic, hypochromic anaemia with low ferritin and increased transferrin. It does not cause macrocytic anaemia or hypersegmented neutrophils.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Thalassaemia causes microcytic, hypochromic anaemia with target cells and basophilic stippling. It is not macrocytic.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Sickle cell anaemia causes normocytic anaemia with sickle-shaped red blood cells on blood film. It is not macrocytic.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Chronic liver disease can cause macrocytosis, but it does not typically produce the hypersegmented neutrophils and glossitis characteristic of vitamin B12 deficiency.

exam_trap: Candidates choose chronic liver disease (E) because it causes macrocytosis, but it does not give hypersegmented neutrophils, which indicate megaloblastic B12 or folate deficiency.
takeaway: Macrocytosis + hypersegmented neutrophils = megaloblastic anaemia (B12 or folate deficiency).
thinking: Macrocytic anaemia ↓ hypersegmented neutrophils mean megaloblastic change ↓ glossitis ↓ Vitamin B12 deficiency
pearl: Patients who have undergone total gastrectomy or resection of the terminal ileum need lifelong vitamin B12 replacement by intramuscular injection, because intrinsic factor or the absorption site has been removed.

subject: Pathology
title: Pathology: Pathology - Haematology
stem: A patient presents with a bleeding tendency, and blood tests show prolonged prothrombin time (PT) and normal activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Correct. Vitamin K deficiency causes a prolonged PT with normal or mildly prolonged APTT. Vitamin K is required for the gamma-carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX, and X, as well as proteins C and S. Factor VII has the shortest half-life, so PT is prolonged first. Causes include malabsorption, biliary obstruction, and warfarin therapy.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Haemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency) causes a prolonged APTT with normal PT. It is an X-linked recessive disorder.
why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. Haemophilia B (factor IX deficiency) also causes a prolonged APTT with normal PT. It is also X-linked recessive.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Von Willebrand disease causes a prolonged APTT (due to decreased factor VIII) and prolonged bleeding time, but PT is normal.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. DIC classically causes prolongation of both PT and APTT, together with thrombocytopenia and elevated D-dimer, rather than an isolated prolongation of PT.

exam_trap: Candidates choose DIC (E) because it prolongs the PT, but DIC also prolongs the APTT with low platelets; haemophilias (A, B) prolong the APTT, not the PT.
takeaway: Isolated prolonged PT → factor VII first → vitamin K deficiency or warfarin.
thinking: Isolated prolonged PT with normal APTT ↓ extrinsic pathway factor VII affected first ↓ factor VII has the shortest half-life of the vitamin K-dependent factors ↓ Vitamin K deficiency
pearl: In obstructive jaundice fat-soluble vitamin K is poorly absorbed, so a prolonged PT should be corrected with intravenous vitamin K before biliary surgery or ERCP.

subject: Pathology
title: Pathology: Pathology - Endocrine
stem: A patient presents with a thyroid nodule. Fine needle aspiration shows cells with nuclear grooves and psammoma bodies. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Correct. Papillary thyroid carcinoma is characterised by nuclear features including optically clear 'Orphan Annie eye' nuclei, nuclear grooves and intranuclear pseudoinclusions, together with psammoma bodies (calcified concentric laminated bodies) and papillary architecture. It is the most common type of thyroid cancer and typically spreads via lymphatics to cervical lymph nodes.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Follicular adenoma is a benign tumour that shows follicular cells without nuclear grooves or psammoma bodies. It is difficult to distinguish from follicular carcinoma on FNA alone.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Medullary thyroid carcinoma arises from parafollicular C cells and secretes calcitonin. It is associated with MEN 2A and 2B syndromes. It does not typically show nuclear grooves or psammoma bodies.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma is a rapidly growing, undifferentiated tumour with a poor prognosis. It does not typically show nuclear grooves or psammoma bodies.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Hashimoto's thyroiditis shows lymphocytic infiltration and Hurthle cell change on cytology; it does not produce the nuclear grooves or psammoma bodies seen in papillary thyroid carcinoma.

exam_trap: Medullary carcinoma tempts as another thyroid malignancy, but it arises from C cells with amyloid stroma and calcitonin, not nuclear grooves or psammoma bodies.
takeaway: Nuclear grooves, clear nuclei and psammoma bodies = papillary thyroid carcinoma, which spreads to cervical lymph nodes.
thinking: Thyroid nodule sampled by FNA ↓ nuclear grooves ↓ psammoma bodies ↓ diagnostic nuclear features with laminated calcification ↓ Papillary thyroid carcinoma
pearl: Papillary carcinoma can be diagnosed on cytology because its nuclear features are diagnostic, whereas follicular carcinoma needs histology to show capsular or vascular invasion.

subject: Pathology
title: Pathology: Pathology - Endocrine
stem: A patient presents with hypertension, episodic palpitations, sweating, and headache. Urinary metanephrines are elevated. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Correct. Phaeochromocytoma is a catecholamine-secreting tumour of the adrenal medulla. It causes episodic hypertension, palpitations, sweating, headache, and anxiety. Diagnosis is confirmed by elevated urinary metanephrines or plasma free metanephrines. Treatment is surgical resection after alpha-blockade (phenoxybenzamine) followed by beta-blockade.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Conn's syndrome (primary hyperaldosteronism) causes hypertension, hypokalaemia, and metabolic alkalosis. It does not cause episodic palpitations, sweating, or headache.
why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. Cushing's syndrome causes hypertension, weight gain, moon face, buffalo hump, and hyperglycaemia. It does not cause episodic palpitations or sweating.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Addison's disease (primary adrenal insufficiency) causes hypotension, hyperkalaemia, and metabolic acidosis. It is the opposite of phaeochromocytoma.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Carcinoid syndrome causes flushing, diarrhoea, and wheezing due to serotonin release; it is not typically associated with hypertension and elevated urinary metanephrines.

exam_trap: Candidates choose Conn's syndrome (A) because it causes hypertension, but Conn's is continuous with hypokalaemia; episodic symptoms with raised metanephrines indicate phaeochromocytoma.
takeaway: Episodic headache, sweating and palpitations + raised metanephrines = phaeochromocytoma.
thinking: Episodic palpitations, sweating and headache with hypertension ↓ catecholamine excess ↓ raised urinary metanephrines ↓ Phaeochromocytoma
pearl: Before adrenalectomy, alpha-blockade must be established before any beta-blocker is started, because unopposed alpha-adrenergic stimulation can precipitate a hypertensive crisis.

subject: Pathology
title: Pathology: Pathology - Renal
stem: A patient presents with haematuria, hypertension, and oliguria 2 weeks after a streptococcal throat infection. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Correct. Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is a type III hypersensitivity reaction that occurs 1-3 weeks after a streptococcal infection (e.g., pharyngitis or impetigo). It presents with nephritic syndrome: haematuria (cola-coloured urine), hypertension, oliguria, and oedema. It is caused by immune complex deposition in the glomeruli.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Minimal change disease causes nephrotic syndrome (proteinuria, oedema, hypoalbuminaemia, hyperlipidaemia). It does not cause haematuria, hypertension, or oliguria.
why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. Membranous nephropathy causes nephrotic syndrome. It is not typically associated with a recent streptococcal infection.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. IgA nephropathy causes recurrent haematuria, often after upper respiratory infections. However, it typically occurs within 1-2 days of infection, not 2 weeks later. Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis occurs 1-3 weeks after infection.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Goodpasture syndrome causes rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with pulmonary haemorrhage due to anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies, and is not linked to a preceding streptococcal infection.

exam_trap: Candidates choose IgA nephropathy (C) because it follows infection too, but IgA haematuria occurs within days; a latent interval of 1-3 weeks indicates post-streptococcal disease.
takeaway: Nephritic syndrome 1-3 weeks after streptococcal infection = post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis; within days = IgA nephropathy.
thinking: Haematuria, hypertension and oliguria ↓ nephritic syndrome ↓ onset 2 weeks after streptococcal pharyngitis ↓ immune complex deposition ↓ Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis
pearl: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis typically shows a low C3 that recovers within about 8 weeks, and children usually recover fully with supportive management.

subject: Pathology
title: Pathology: Pathology - Renal
stem: A patient with chronic kidney disease develops anaemia. Which of the following is the primary cause of anaemia in chronic kidney disease?
why_correct: Correct. Erythropoietin is produced by the peritubular interstitial cells of the kidney in response to hypoxia. In chronic kidney disease, the damaged kidneys cannot produce sufficient erythropoietin, leading to reduced red blood cell production and anaemia. Treatment includes erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESAs) and iron supplementation.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Iron deficiency can contribute to anaemia in CKD, but it is not the primary cause. The primary cause is decreased erythropoietin production.
why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. Vitamin B12 deficiency can cause anaemia, but it is not the primary cause in CKD. It may occur due to dietary deficiency or malabsorption.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. While red blood cell survival may be slightly reduced in CKD, the primary cause of anaemia is decreased erythropoietin production, not increased destruction.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Bone marrow fibrosis is a feature of myelofibrosis; it is not a typical cause of the anaemia seen in chronic kidney disease, which is primarily due to reduced erythropoietin production.

exam_trap: Candidates choose iron deficiency (A) because it often coexists and must be corrected, but the primary cause of anaemia in CKD is reduced erythropoietin production.
takeaway: Anaemia of CKD = mainly reduced erythropoietin; correct iron before ESAs.
thinking: CKD with anaemia ↓ peritubular interstitial cells of the kidney make erythropoietin ↓ loss of renal mass reduces erythropoietin ↓ Decreased erythropoietin production
pearl: Iron stores should be checked and replaced before starting an erythropoiesis-stimulating agent in CKD, because functional iron deficiency is a common cause of poor response.

subject: Pathology
title: Pathology: Pathology - Gastrointestinal
stem: A patient presents with dysphagia and weight loss. Endoscopy shows a stricture in the lower oesophagus with intestinal metaplasia. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Squamous cell carcinoma of the oesophagus

why_correct: Correct. Adenocarcinoma of the oesophagus typically occurs in the lower third of the oesophagus and is associated with Barrett's oesophagus (intestinal metaplasia due to chronic gastro-oesophageal reflux disease). It presents with dysphagia and weight loss.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Squamous cell carcinoma typically occurs in the upper and middle thirds of the oesophagus. It is associated with smoking, alcohol, and achalasia. It is not associated with intestinal metaplasia.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Oesophageal varices are dilated submucosal veins caused by portal hypertension. They present with haematemesis or melaena, not dysphagia and weight loss.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Achalasia is a motility disorder characterised by failure of the lower oesophageal sphincter to relax. It presents with dysphagia for both solids and liquids, but it is not associated with intestinal metaplasia or a stricture.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Boerhaave syndrome is oesophageal rupture caused by forceful vomiting, presenting acutely with chest pain and mediastinitis, not a chronic stricture with intestinal metaplasia.

exam_trap: Candidates choose squamous cell carcinoma (A) as the classic oesophageal cancer, but it affects the upper and middle oesophagus; Barrett-associated lower third tumours are adenocarcinomas.
takeaway: Lower oesophagus + Barrett's intestinal metaplasia → adenocarcinoma; upper/middle third → squamous cell carcinoma.
thinking: Dysphagia and weight loss ↓ lower oesophageal stricture ↓ intestinal metaplasia means Barrett's oesophagus ↓ Barrett's progresses to adenocarcinoma ↓ Adenocarcinoma of the oesophagus
pearl: In the UK adenocarcinoma has overtaken squamous cell carcinoma as the commonest oesophageal cancer, reflecting reflux and obesity, and progressive dysphagia warrants urgent endoscopy.

subject: Pathology
title: Pathology: Pathology - Gastrointestinal
stem: A patient with cirrhosis develops hepatocellular carcinoma. Which of the following is the most common cause of cirrhosis leading to hepatocellular carcinoma worldwide?
why_correct: Correct. Hepatitis B virus (HBV) is the most common cause of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma worldwide, particularly in Asia and sub-Saharan Africa. HBV can integrate into the host genome and cause direct oncogenic effects, in addition to causing chronic inflammation and cirrhosis.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. Hepatitis C virus (HCV) is a common cause of cirrhosis and HCC, particularly in Western countries. However, worldwide, HBV is more common.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Alcohol abuse is a common cause of cirrhosis in Western countries, but worldwide, HBV is the most common cause.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. NAFLD is an increasingly common cause of cirrhosis and HCC, particularly in developed countries with high rates of obesity and diabetes. However, worldwide, HBV remains the most common cause.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Aflatoxin, a mycotoxin produced by certain Aspergillus species contaminating food, is a co-carcinogen for hepatocellular carcinoma that acts synergistically with hepatitis B, but it is not itself a common cause of cirrhosis.

exam_trap: Candidates choose hepatitis C (B) or alcohol (C) from Western practice, but the stem asks worldwide, where hepatitis B is the leading cause of cirrhosis-related HCC.
takeaway: HCC worldwide = hepatitis B; in the West, hepatitis C, alcohol and fatty liver disease predominate.
thinking: Hepatocellular carcinoma ↓ worldwide (not Western) perspective ↓ endemic chronic hepatitis B in Asia and sub-Saharan Africa ↓ HBV DNA integrates and is directly oncogenic ↓ Hepatitis B virus
pearl: Because HBV is directly oncogenic, HCC can develop in hepatitis B carriers even without established cirrhosis, so surveillance applies to some non-cirrhotic HBV carriers.

subject: Microbiology
title: Microbiology: Microbiology - Specific Organisms
stem: A patient develops a hospital-acquired wound infection with an organism that is Gram-positive, catalase-positive, coagulase-positive and resistant to flucloxacillin. Which organism is most likely?
why_correct: Correct. MRSA is a Gram-positive, catalase-positive, coagulase-positive coccus that is resistant to methicillin and other beta-lactam antibiotics. It is a major cause of hospital-acquired infections, including surgical site infections, pneumonia, and bacteraemia. It is treated with vancomycin, teicoplanin, or linezolid.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. S. epidermidis is a coagulase-negative staphylococcus that is part of normal skin flora. It is often methicillin-resistant, but the coagulase-positive result excludes it.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. S. pyogenes is a Gram-positive coccus in chains, catalase-negative, and bacitracin-sensitive. It is not resistant to methicillin.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Enterococcus is a Gram-positive coccus, catalase-negative, and is intrinsically resistant to many antibiotics but is not typically described as methicillin-resistant.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. VRE is a Gram-positive coccus that is catalase-negative, and its defining resistance is to vancomycin, not methicillin.

exam_trap: Staphylococcus epidermidis is also catalase-positive and often methicillin-resistant, but it is coagulase-negative; a coagulase-positive, flucloxacillin-resistant isolate is MRSA.
takeaway: Coagulase-positive staphylococcus resistant to flucloxacillin = MRSA; treat with a glycopeptide or linezolid.
thinking: Hospital-acquired wound infection ↓ Gram-positive and catalase-positive = staphylococcus ↓ coagulase-positive = Staphylococcus aureus ↓ flucloxacillin resistance indicates a meticillin-resistant strain ↓ Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA)
pearl: Preoperative MRSA screening with decolonisation of carriers, for example nasal mupirocin and chlorhexidine body washes, reduces the risk of MRSA surgical-site infection.

subject: Microbiology
title: Microbiology: Microbiology - Specific Organisms
stem: A patient with a history of intravenous drug use develops infective endocarditis. Blood cultures grow an organism that is Gram-positive, catalase-positive, and coagulase-positive. Which organism is most likely?
why_correct: Correct. S. aureus is a Gram-positive, catalase-positive, coagulase-positive coccus. It is the most common cause of acute infective endocarditis in intravenous drug users, typically affecting the tricuspid valve. It is also a common cause of surgical site infections and bacteraemia.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. S. viridans is a Gram-positive coccus in chains, catalase-negative, and optochin-resistant. It is the most common cause of subacute infective endocarditis on damaged or prosthetic valves, but it is less common in IV drug users.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. S. epidermidis is a coagulase-negative staphylococcus. It is a common cause of prosthetic valve endocarditis but is less common in IV drug users than S. aureus.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Enterococcus is a Gram-positive coccus that is catalase-negative and coagulase-negative. It can cause infective endocarditis, particularly after urinary or gastrointestinal procedures, but is less common in IV drug users.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Streptococcus bovis (gallolyticus) is associated with subacute endocarditis and colorectal malignancy, and is not typically linked to intravenous drug use.

exam_trap: Streptococcus viridans is chosen as the commonest overall cause of endocarditis, but it is catalase-negative, and injecting drug use favours acute S. aureus tricuspid endocarditis.
takeaway: IVDU endocarditis + coagulase-positive coccus → Staphylococcus aureus, often tricuspid.
thinking: Infective endocarditis in an intravenous drug user ↓ Gram-positive, catalase-positive = staphylococcus ↓ coagulase-positive ↓ Staphylococcus aureus
pearl: Endocarditis in people who inject drugs typically affects the tricuspid valve and can cause septic pulmonary emboli, seen as multiple cavitating lung nodules.

subject: Microbiology
title: Microbiology: Microbiology - Viral Infections
stem: A patient with HIV/AIDS has a CD4 count of 80 cells/µL and presents with visual disturbance and floaters. Fundoscopy shows retinal exudates and haemorrhages. Which organism is most likely responsible?
why_correct: Correct. CMV retinitis is a common opportunistic infection in HIV/AIDS patients with CD4 counts below 100 cells/µL. It presents with visual disturbance, floaters, and fundoscopic findings of retinal exudates and haemorrhages (often described as 'pizza pie' or 'cottage cheese and ketchup' appearance). Treatment is with ganciclovir, valganciclovir, or foscarnet.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. HSV can cause retinitis but is much less common than CMV in HIV/AIDS patients. It typically causes mucocutaneous lesions.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. VZV can cause retinitis (acute retinal necrosis) but is less common than CMV in HIV/AIDS patients. It typically causes shingles.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. EBV is associated with oral hairy leukoplakia and lymphomas in HIV/AIDS patients, not typically retinitis.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. JC virus causes progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, a demyelinating brain disease, rather than retinitis.

exam_trap: Varicella-zoster virus is a tempting alternative because it causes acute retinal necrosis, but at a CD4 count below 100 cells/µL CMV retinitis is far more common.
takeaway: HIV + CD4 <100 + haemorrhagic retinitis → CMV.
thinking: HIV with CD4 count of 80 cells/µL ↓ floaters and visual disturbance ↓ retinal exudates and haemorrhages ↓ commonest opportunistic retinitis below 100 cells/µL ↓ Cytomegalovirus (CMV)
pearl: Ganciclovir and valganciclovir cause bone marrow suppression, while foscarnet is nephrotoxic, so blood counts or renal function must be monitored during CMV treatment.

subject: Microbiology
title: Microbiology: Microbiology - Viral Infections
stem: A patient is diagnosed with hepatitis B infection. Which of the following serological markers indicates chronic infection?

options.A: HBsAg positive for more than 6 months

correct_answer: A. HBsAg positive for more than 6 months
why_correct: Correct. Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) is the first marker to appear in acute infection. If HBsAg remains positive for more than 6 months, it indicates chronic infection. Chronic infection can lead to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. Anti-HBs (antibody to HBsAg) indicates immunity to hepatitis B, either from vaccination or resolved infection. It is not a marker of chronic infection.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. IgM anti-HBc indicates acute hepatitis B infection. IgG anti-HBc indicates past or chronic infection.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Anti-HBe indicates a low level of viral replication and is associated with a lower infectivity. It can be seen in chronic infection but is not the primary marker of chronicity.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. HBeAg indicates active viral replication and high infectivity, but it can also be present during acute infection, so it does not by itself define chronicity.

exam_trap: HBeAg positive is chosen because it signals active replication, but it also occurs in acute infection; only HBsAg persisting beyond 6 months defines chronic infection.
takeaway: Chronic HBV = HBsAg positive for more than 6 months; IgM anti-HBc = acute infection.
thinking: Hepatitis B serology ↓ HBsAg indicates current infection ↓ persistence beyond 6 months defines chronicity ↓ HBeAg and anti-HBe reflect replication, not duration ↓ HBsAg positive for more than 6 months
pearl: Isolated anti-HBs indicates vaccination, whereas anti-HBs together with anti-HBc indicates immunity after past natural infection.

subject: Microbiology
title: Microbiology: Microbiology - Fungal Infections
stem: A patient with diabetes develops a severe fungal infection of the nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses that invades blood vessels and causes tissue necrosis. Which organism is most likely?
why_correct: Correct. Mucor is a mould that causes mucormycosis (zygomycosis), a severe opportunistic infection that typically affects diabetic patients in ketoacidosis or immunocompromised patients. It invades blood vessels (angioinvasion), causing thrombosis and tissue necrosis. It commonly affects the nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, and brain (rhinocerebral mucormycosis). Treatment is urgent surgical debridement and amphotericin B.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Candida is a yeast that typically causes mucosal infections (e.g., oral thrush) or candidemia. It does not typically cause rhinocerebral infections.
why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. Aspergillus can cause invasive aspergillosis, particularly in neutropenic patients, but it is less commonly associated with rhinocerebral infection than Mucor.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Cryptococcus is a yeast that causes meningitis, particularly in HIV/AIDS patients. It does not typically cause rhinocerebral infections.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Fusarium species can cause invasive infections such as keratitis and fungaemia in immunocompromised patients, but they are not the classic cause of rhinocerebral angioinvasive disease in diabetic ketoacidosis.

exam_trap: Aspergillus fumigatus is the strong distractor as another angioinvasive mould, but rhinocerebral necrosis in a diabetic patient, especially in ketoacidosis, is classically mucormycosis.
takeaway: Diabetes/DKA + necrotic sinus infection → mucormycosis; urgent debridement + amphotericin B.
thinking: Patient with diabetes ↓ nasal and paranasal sinus infection ↓ angioinvasion with tissue necrosis ↓ rhinocerebral mould disease, classically with ketoacidosis ↓ Mucor species
pearl: A black eschar on the palate or nasal turbinates is the classic sign of rhinocerebral mucormycosis; voriconazole is ineffective, so liposomal amphotericin B with urgent debridement is used.

subject: Microbiology
title: Microbiology: Microbiology - Fungal Infections
stem: A patient with a central venous catheter develops fever and sepsis. Blood cultures grow a yeast that forms pseudohyphae and germ tubes. Which organism is most likely?
why_correct: Correct. Candida albicans is a yeast that can form pseudohyphae and germ tubes. It is a common cause of catheter-related bloodstream infections, particularly in patients with central venous catheters, broad-spectrum antibiotics, or immunosuppression. Treatment is with fluconazole or echinocandins.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. Aspergillus is a mould that causes invasive aspergillosis in neutropenic patients. It does not form pseudohyphae or germ tubes.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Cryptococcus is an encapsulated yeast that causes meningitis in HIV/AIDS patients. It does not form pseudohyphae or germ tubes.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Histoplasma is a dimorphic fungus that causes pulmonary and disseminated infections. It does not form pseudohyphae or germ tubes.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Trichosporon species can rarely cause catheter-related fungaemia, but they do not classically form the pseudohyphae with germ tubes that are characteristic of Candida albicans.

exam_trap: Cryptococcus neoformans is the yeast candidates confuse here, but it is encapsulated and forms neither pseudohyphae nor germ tubes, which are characteristic of Candida albicans.
takeaway: Line sepsis + yeast forming germ tubes → Candida albicans; remove the line.
thinking: Central venous catheter with fever and sepsis ↓ yeast in blood cultures ↓ pseudohyphae and germ tube formation ↓ the germ tube test identifies Candida albicans ↓ Candida albicans
pearl: In candidaemia the central venous catheter should be removed where possible, and ophthalmology review is advised to exclude endophthalmitis.

subject: Microbiology
title: Microbiology: Microbiology - Parasitic Infections
