stem: A patient presents with fever, right upper quadrant pain, and eosinophilia after returning from a trip to the Middle East. Ultrasound shows a liver cyst. Which organism is most likely?
why_correct: Correct. Echinococcus granulosus is a tapeworm that causes hydatid disease. Humans become infected by ingesting eggs from dog faeces. The larvae form cysts, most commonly in the liver (70%) and lungs (20%). It presents with right upper quadrant pain, fever, and eosinophilia. Ultrasound shows a cystic lesion. Treatment is albendazole followed by surgical resection or PAIR.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. E. histolytica causes amoebic liver abscess, which also presents with fever and right upper quadrant pain and appears as a hypoechoic lesion on ultrasound, but as a protozoan it does not typically cause eosinophilia.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. S. mansoni causes schistosomiasis, which can cause liver fibrosis and portal hypertension, but it does not typically cause a liver cyst.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. P. falciparum causes malaria, which presents with fever, chills, and anaemia. It does not cause liver cysts.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Fasciola hepatica causes biliary fascioliasis with eosinophilia and right upper quadrant pain following ingestion of contaminated watercress, but it characteristically involves the biliary tree rather than forming a discrete hydatid cyst.

exam_trap: Entamoeba histolytica is the main distractor, since amoebic liver abscess also causes fever and right upper quadrant pain, but protozoa do not cause eosinophilia, which points to a helminth.
takeaway: Liver cyst + eosinophilia + endemic exposure → hydatid disease (Echinococcus granulosus).
thinking: Travel to the Middle East ↓ right upper quadrant pain with a liver cyst on ultrasound ↓ eosinophilia points to a helminth rather than amoebae ↓ cystic liver helminth endemic in sheep-rearing areas ↓ Echinococcus granulosus
pearl: Suspected hydatid cysts should not be aspirated diagnostically outside a planned PAIR procedure, because spillage can cause anaphylaxis and secondary seeding.

subject: Microbiology
title: Microbiology: Microbiology - Parasitic Infections
stem: A patient presents with haematuria and terminal dysuria after swimming in a freshwater lake in Africa. Which organism is most likely?
why_correct: Correct. S. haematobium is a trematode that causes urinary schistosomiasis. Humans become infected when cercariae penetrate the skin during contact with freshwater. The adult worms live in the vesical venous plexus and lay eggs that cause inflammation and haematuria. It is associated with squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder. Diagnosis is by finding eggs in urine.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. S. mansoni causes intestinal schistosomiasis, which presents with abdominal pain, diarrhoea, and hepatosplenomegaly. It does not typically cause haematuria.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. E. granulosus causes hydatid disease, which presents with liver or lung cysts. It does not cause haematuria.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. E. histolytica causes amoebic dysentery and liver abscess. It does not cause haematuria.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Leptospirosis is also acquired from contaminated freshwater and can involve the kidneys, but it typically presents with fever, myalgia, and jaundice (Weil's disease) rather than terminal haematuria from egg deposition in the bladder wall.

exam_trap: Schistosoma mansoni is the tempting fellow trematode, but it lives in the mesenteric veins and causes intestinal and hepatic disease; terminal haematuria indicates S. haematobium.
takeaway: Freshwater exposure in Africa + terminal haematuria → Schistosoma haematobium; eggs in urine, treat with praziquantel.
thinking: Swimming in a freshwater lake in Africa ↓ cercariae penetrate the skin ↓ haematuria with terminal dysuria = urinary tract involvement ↓ species whose adults live in the vesical venous plexus ↓ Schistosoma haematobium
pearl: Chronic Schistosoma haematobium infection is a recognised risk factor for squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder, and praziquantel is the treatment of choice.

subject: Microbiology
title: Microbiology: Microbiology - Specific Organisms
stem: A patient develops a wound infection after a farm injury. The wound is contaminated with soil, and the patient has not been vaccinated against tetanus. Which organism is of greatest concern?
why_correct: Correct. C. tetani is a Gram-positive, spore-forming anaerobe found in soil and manure. It causes tetanus, a serious infection characterised by muscle spasms and rigidity. It is prevented by vaccination and wound debridement. Unvaccinated patients with contaminated wounds are at high risk.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. C. difficile causes antibiotic-associated colitis, not wound infections. It is not associated with soil contamination.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. C. perfringens causes gas gangrene (clostridial myonecrosis) and food poisoning. It is a concern in contaminated wounds, but tetanus is the greater concern in an unvaccinated patient.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. C. botulinum causes botulism, which is caused by ingestion of preformed toxin in food, not wound contamination. Wound botulism is rare.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Bacillus anthracis typically causes cutaneous anthrax following contact with contaminated animal products or hides, rather than being the organism of greatest concern in a contaminated soil wound in an unvaccinated patient.

exam_trap: Clostridium perfringens is the tempting soil-wound organism because it causes gas gangrene, but absent tetanus vaccination makes Clostridium tetani the greatest concern.
takeaway: Contaminated wound + unvaccinated → tetanus risk: debride, vaccinate and give tetanus immunoglobulin.
thinking: Soil-contaminated farm wound ↓ patient not vaccinated against tetanus ↓ spores of a soil anaerobe germinate in devitalised tissue ↓ toxin-mediated spasms and rigidity ↓ Clostridium tetani
pearl: A tetanus-prone wound in an unimmunised patient needs thorough debridement, a dose of tetanus-containing vaccine and human tetanus immunoglobulin.

subject: Microbiology
title: Microbiology: Microbiology - Specific Organisms
stem: A patient presents with a sore throat, fever, and a greyish-white membrane on the tonsils that bleeds when scraped. Which organism is most likely?
why_correct: Correct. C. diphtheriae is a Gram-positive bacillus that causes diphtheria. It presents with sore throat, fever, and a greyish-white pseudomembrane on the tonsils and pharynx that bleeds when scraped. The toxin can cause myocarditis and neuropathy. Treatment is with antitoxin and antibiotics (penicillin or erythromycin).

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. S. pyogenes causes streptococcal pharyngitis, which presents with sore throat, fever, and exudative tonsillitis. However, the exudate is not typically described as a greyish-white membrane that bleeds when scraped.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. EBV causes infectious mononucleosis, which presents with sore throat, fever, lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly. It can cause exudative tonsillitis but not a bleeding pseudomembrane.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Candida causes oral thrush, which presents with white patches on the tongue and oral mucosa. The patches can be scraped off, but they do not typically bleed and are not associated with a sore throat and fever.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Vincent's angina is caused by fusiform bacteria and spirochaetes in the setting of poor oral hygiene; it is not associated with the exotoxin-mediated systemic effects (such as myocarditis and neuropathy) seen in diphtheria.

exam_trap: Streptococcus pyogenes is the common pick for exudative tonsillitis, but its exudate wipes off easily; an adherent grey membrane that bleeds on removal suggests diphtheria.
takeaway: Grey adherent pharyngeal pseudomembrane that bleeds on scraping → diphtheria.
thinking: Sore throat and fever ↓ grey-white tonsillar membrane ↓ adherent pseudomembrane that bleeds when scraped ↓ toxin-producing Gram-positive bacillus ↓ Corynebacterium diphtheriae
pearl: Diphtheria toxin can cause myocarditis and cranial nerve palsies days to weeks later, and an extensive pseudomembrane with neck swelling ('bull neck') can obstruct the airway.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: Anatomy - Upper Limb
stem: A patient presents with weakness in elbow flexion and sensory loss over the lateral forearm. Which nerve is most likely injured?
why_correct: Correct. The musculocutaneous nerve supplies the coracobrachialis, biceps brachii, and brachialis (elbow flexors). It terminates as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm, which supplies sensation to the lateral forearm. Injury causes weakness in elbow flexion and sensory loss over the lateral forearm.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. The radial nerve supplies the triceps and wrist extensors. Injury causes wrist drop and sensory loss over the posterior arm and forearm, not the lateral forearm.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. The median nerve supplies the forearm flexors and thenar muscles. Injury causes loss of thumb opposition and weakness in forearm pronation. Sensory loss occurs over the lateral palm and digits.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. The ulnar nerve supplies the intrinsic hand muscles. Injury causes claw hand and sensory loss over the medial one and a half fingers.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. The axillary nerve supplies the deltoid and teres minor and provides sensation over the 'regimental badge' area of the shoulder; it does not supply elbow flexors or the lateral forearm.

exam_trap: The radial nerve (A) is chosen because brachioradialis flexes the elbow, but radial injury gives wrist drop and posterior sensory loss, not lateral forearm numbness.
takeaway: Weak elbow flexion + lateral forearm numbness = musculocutaneous nerve.
thinking: Weak elbow flexion ↓ biceps and brachialis affected ↓ lateral forearm numbness = lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm ↓ both supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve ↓ Musculocutaneous nerve
pearl: Elbow flexion is often weakened rather than abolished after musculocutaneous injury, because brachioradialis (radial nerve) and frequently part of brachialis (radial contribution) still flex the elbow.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: Anatomy - Upper Limb
stem: During release of the first dorsal compartment for tenosynovitis, the surgeon divides the extensor retinaculum. Which structures pass through the first extensor compartment of the wrist?

options.B: Abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis
options.E: Extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis

correct_answer: B. Abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis
why_correct: Correct. The first extensor compartment of the wrist contains the tendons of abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis. These tendons are affected in De Quervain's tenosynovitis, which causes pain over the radial styloid.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Extensor pollicis longus runs alone in the third extensor compartment, on the ulnar side of the dorsal radial tubercle.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Extensor digitorum passes through the fourth extensor compartment, along with extensor indicis.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Extensor indicis passes through the fourth extensor compartment, along with extensor digitorum.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. These tendons pass through the second extensor compartment of the wrist, not the first.

exam_trap: Candidates often choose extensor pollicis longus because it is a thumb tendon, but it runs alone in the third compartment, hooking around the dorsal radial tubercle.
takeaway: First extensor compartment = abductor pollicis longus + extensor pollicis brevis; inflamed in De Quervain's tenosynovitis.
thinking: Six dorsal extensor compartments numbered radial to ulnar ↓ first compartment lies over the radial styloid ↓ carries the thumb abductor and short extensor ↓ Abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis
pearl: At surgical release of the first extensor compartment the branches of the superficial radial nerve must be protected, and a separate septum enclosing extensor pollicis brevis is often present and should be released too.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: Anatomy - Lower Limb
stem: A patient presents with pain in the medial arch of the foot. Which bone forms the keystone of the medial longitudinal arch?
why_correct: Correct. The head of the talus sits at the summit of the medial longitudinal arch, between the calcaneus behind and the navicular, cuneiforms and medial three metatarsals in front, and is classically described as its keystone. It is supported from below by the plantar calcaneonavicular (spring) ligament and the tibialis posterior tendon.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. The calcaneus forms the posterior pillar of the medial longitudinal arch. It is not the keystone.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. The navicular lies just in front of the talar head and forms part of the arch, but the head of the talus, not the navicular, is classically described as the keystone.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. The first metatarsal forms the anterior pillar of the medial longitudinal arch. It is not the keystone.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. The cuboid bone is part of the lateral longitudinal arch of the foot, not the medial longitudinal arch.

exam_trap: The navicular (C) tempts because it lies immediately in front of the talar head within the arch, but the head of the talus is classically described as the keystone.
takeaway: Keystone of the medial longitudinal arch = head of the talus, supported by the spring ligament and tibialis posterior.
thinking: Medial longitudinal arch ↓ posterior pillar is the calcaneus, anterior pillar the medial three metatarsals ↓ the head of the talus sits at the summit ↓ supported below by the spring ligament and tibialis posterior ↓ Talus
pearl: Tibialis posterior tendon dysfunction is the commonest cause of acquired adult flatfoot; loss of support under the talar head lets the medial arch collapse, and the patient cannot perform a single-leg heel raise.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: Anatomy - Lower Limb
stem: During an adductor canal block, the anaesthetist targets the saphenous nerve. Which structure forms the roof of the adductor canal?
why_correct: Correct. The adductor canal (subsartorial canal or Hunter's canal) is a fascial tunnel in the middle third of the medial thigh. Its roof is formed by sartorius, with the vastoadductor membrane deep to it; vastus medialis forms the anterolateral wall and adductor longus and magnus form the posterior wall (floor). Contents include the femoral artery, femoral vein, saphenous nerve and nerve to vastus medialis.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. Adductor longus forms part of the posterior boundary of the adductor canal, not the roof.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Adductor magnus forms part of the posterior boundary of the adductor canal, not the roof.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Vastus medialis forms the anterior and lateral boundary of the adductor canal, not the roof.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Gracilis lies medial to the adductor canal but does not form its roof.

exam_trap: Vastus medialis (D) is chosen because it bounds the canal, but it forms the anterolateral wall; sartorius over the vastoadductor membrane forms the roof.
takeaway: Adductor canal: roof sartorius (over vastoadductor membrane), anterolateral wall vastus medialis, floor adductor longus and magnus.
thinking: Adductor (subsartorial) canal in the middle third of the thigh ↓ vastus medialis anterolaterally, adductor longus and magnus posteriorly ↓ roof formed by sartorius overlying the vastoadductor membrane ↓ Sartorius
pearl: An adductor canal block anaesthetises the saphenous nerve while largely sparing quadriceps motor power, so it is often preferred to a femoral nerve block after knee arthroplasty to allow early mobilisation.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: Anatomy - Abdomen
stem: During a right hemicolectomy, the surgeon ligates the main artery supplying the terminal ileum and caecum. Which of the following is a branch of the superior mesenteric artery?
why_correct: Correct. The ileocolic artery is a branch of the superior mesenteric artery (SMA). It supplies the terminal ileum, caecum, and appendix. Other branches of the SMA include the jejunal and ileal arteries, right colic artery, and middle colic artery.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. The inferior mesenteric artery arises directly from the abdominal aorta at L3. It is not a branch of the SMA.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. The left colic artery is a branch of the inferior mesenteric artery, not the SMA.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. The sigmoid arteries are branches of the inferior mesenteric artery, not the SMA.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. The superior rectal artery is the terminal continuation of the inferior mesenteric artery, not a branch of the superior mesenteric artery.

exam_trap: Left colic, sigmoid and superior rectal arteries are all inferior mesenteric branches; candidates choose them when they forget that the midgut ends two-thirds of the way along the transverse colon.
takeaway: Ileocolic artery = SMA branch to the terminal ileum, caecum and appendix.
thinking: Right hemicolectomy ↓ terminal ileum and caecum are midgut structures ↓ the midgut is supplied by the superior mesenteric artery ↓ its terminal branch to the ileocaecal region ↓ Ileocolic artery
pearl: In an oncological right hemicolectomy the ileocolic, right colic (when present) and right branch of the middle colic vessels are divided close to their origins, because the draining lymph nodes follow these arteries.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: Anatomy - Abdomen
stem: A patient presents with an adrenal mass. Which of the following is a characteristic feature of the right adrenal gland compared to the left?

options.C: It lies anterior to the inferior vena cava
options.D: It drains directly into the left renal vein
options.E: It is larger than the left adrenal gland

correct_answer: A. It is triangular in shape
why_correct: Correct. The right adrenal gland is triangular in shape, while the left adrenal gland is semilunar (crescent-shaped). The right gland lies superior to the right kidney and posterior to the inferior vena cava. It drains into the right adrenal vein, which empties directly into the IVC.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. The left adrenal gland is semilunar in shape, not the right.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. The right adrenal gland lies posterior to the inferior vena cava, not anterior to it.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. The right adrenal vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava. The left adrenal vein drains into the left renal vein.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. The right and left adrenal glands are similar in size; the key distinguishing feature described is shape (triangular versus semilunar), not size.

exam_trap: Semilunar shape is chosen through left-right confusion; it describes the left adrenal, while the right gland is triangular and lies posterior, not anterior, to the IVC.
takeaway: Right adrenal: triangular, behind the IVC, short vein into the IVC. Left adrenal: semilunar, vein to the left renal vein.
thinking: Right versus left adrenal gland ↓ the right gland sits on the upper pole of the right kidney, behind the IVC ↓ the right is triangular, the left semilunar ↓ the right adrenal vein drains straight into the IVC ↓ It is triangular in shape
pearl: The short right adrenal vein enters the back of the IVC directly, making its control the most hazardous step of a right adrenalectomy, whereas the longer left adrenal vein drains into the left renal vein.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: Anatomy - Head and Neck
stem: During a parotidectomy, the surgeon identifies the facial nerve and its branches. Which branch of the facial nerve supplies the orbicularis oculi?
why_correct: Correct. The zygomatic branch of the facial nerve supplies the orbicularis oculi, which is responsible for closing the eye. Injury to this branch can cause inability to close the eye and risk of corneal ulceration.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. The temporal branch supplies the frontalis, orbicularis oculi (upper part), and corrugator supercilii. However, the zygomatic branch is the primary supply to orbicularis oculi.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. The buccal branch supplies the buccinator, orbicularis oris, and muscles of the upper lip. It is not the primary supply to orbicularis oculi.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. The marginal mandibular branch supplies the depressor anguli oris, depressor labii inferioris, and mentalis. It is not involved in eye closure.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. The cervical branch of the facial nerve supplies platysma; it does not supply orbicularis oculi.

exam_trap: The temporal branch (A) is tempting because it supplies the upper part of orbicularis oculi, but the zygomatic branch is the principal supply for eye closure.
takeaway: Eye closure (orbicularis oculi) = mainly the zygomatic branch of the facial nerve.
thinking: Orbicularis oculi closes the eye ↓ supplied mainly by the zygomatic branch, with an upper contribution from the temporal branch ↓ zygomatic injury threatens eye closure and corneal protection ↓ Zygomatic branch
pearl: During parotidectomy the facial nerve trunk is usually found using the tragal pointer, the tympanomastoid suture and the posterior belly of digastric as landmarks, before it divides within the gland.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: Anatomy - Head and Neck
stem: A patient presents with a thyroid swelling. Which artery is the first branch of the external carotid artery?
why_correct: Correct. The superior thyroid artery is the first branch of the external carotid artery. It arises just below the greater cornu of the hyoid bone and descends to supply the upper pole of the thyroid gland. It is closely related to the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. The inferior thyroid artery arises from the thyrocervical trunk, which is a branch of the subclavian artery. It is not a branch of the external carotid artery.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. The thyroidea ima artery is an occasional artery that arises from the brachiocephalic trunk or aortic arch. It is not a branch of the external carotid artery.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. The ascending pharyngeal artery is a branch of the external carotid artery, but it is not the first branch. The superior thyroid artery is the first branch.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. The lingual artery is typically the second branch of the external carotid artery, arising above the superior thyroid artery.

exam_trap: The inferior thyroid artery (B) is chosen because it also supplies the thyroid, but it arises from the thyrocervical trunk of the subclavian artery, not the external carotid.
takeaway: First branch of the external carotid artery = superior thyroid artery.
thinking: Branches of the external carotid from below upwards ↓ superior thyroid arises first, near the greater horn of the hyoid ↓ lingual and facial follow ↓ inferior thyroid comes from the thyrocervical trunk instead ↓ Superior thyroid artery
pearl: The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve runs close to the superior thyroid artery, so the upper pole vessels are ligated individually and close to the gland to avoid loss of high-pitched voice.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: Anatomy - Thorax
stem: During a coronary artery bypass graft, the surgeon harvests the left internal mammary artery. From which vessel does the internal mammary artery arise?
why_correct: Correct. The internal mammary artery (internal thoracic artery) arises from the first part of the subclavian artery. It descends behind the upper costal cartilages about 1 cm lateral to the sternal border and gives off branches to the mediastinum, pericardium and anterior chest wall. It is commonly used as a graft in coronary artery bypass surgery because of its excellent long-term patency.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. The internal mammary artery does not arise directly from the aorta. It arises from the subclavian artery.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. The axillary artery is a continuation of the subclavian artery beyond the first rib. The internal mammary artery arises from the subclavian artery before it becomes the axillary artery.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. The brachiocephalic trunk gives rise to the right common carotid artery and right subclavian artery. The internal mammary artery arises from the subclavian artery.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. The vertebral artery is a separate branch that also arises from the subclavian artery, supplying the posterior cerebral circulation; it is not the origin of the internal mammary artery.

exam_trap: Brachiocephalic trunk is chosen for the right side, but it gives only the right subclavian and right common carotid arteries; the internal thoracic artery arises from the subclavian on both sides.
takeaway: Internal thoracic (mammary) artery = branch of the first part of the subclavian artery.
thinking: Left internal mammary artery harvested for coronary bypass ↓ the internal mammary artery is the internal thoracic artery ↓ it arises from the first part of the subclavian artery ↓ it descends behind the costal cartilages lateral to the sternum ↓ Subclavian artery
pearl: The left internal mammary artery grafted to the left anterior descending artery has the best long-term patency of any coronary conduit; harvesting both internal mammary arteries increases the risk of sternal wound complications, particularly in diabetic patients.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: Anatomy - Neuroanatomy
stem: A patient presents with a cerebellar lesion. Which of the following is a characteristic feature of cerebellar dysfunction?
why_correct: Correct. Intention tremor is a characteristic feature of cerebellar dysfunction. It is absent at rest and worsens as the patient approaches a target. Other features include dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, ataxia, and nystagmus.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. Resting tremor is characteristic of Parkinson's disease (basal ganglia dysfunction), not cerebellar lesions.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Spasticity is characteristic of upper motor neuron lesions (e.g., corticospinal tract lesions), not cerebellar lesions.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Hyperreflexia is characteristic of upper motor neuron lesions, not cerebellar lesions. Cerebellar lesions may cause hypotonia and hyporeflexia.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Bradykinesia is a feature of parkinsonism due to basal ganglia dysfunction, not cerebellar disease.

exam_trap: Resting tremor (B) is chosen as the best-known tremor, but it is a basal ganglia (parkinsonian) sign that improves, not worsens, with purposeful movement.
takeaway: Cerebellar lesion = intention tremor, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, ataxia and nystagmus, ipsilateral to the lesion.
thinking: Cerebellar lesion ↓ incoordination of goal-directed movement ↓ tremor absent at rest and worse as the target is approached ↓ Intention tremor
pearl: Cerebellar hemisphere lesions produce signs on the same side as the lesion, so a right cerebellar lesion causes right-sided ataxia, dysmetria and intention tremor.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: Physiology - Cardiovascular
stem: Which of the following best describes the effect of a sudden drop in blood pressure on heart rate?
correct_answer: B. Tachycardia due to sympathetic activation
why_correct: Correct. A sudden drop in blood pressure is detected by baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch. This leads to decreased afferent firing to the medulla, which increases sympathetic outflow and decreases parasympathetic outflow. The result is tachycardia, increased contractility, and vasoconstriction, which help restore blood pressure.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. A sudden drop in blood pressure causes reflex tachycardia, not bradycardia. Parasympathetic activation would slow the heart rate.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. The baroreceptor reflex rapidly adjusts heart rate in response to blood pressure changes. There is always a compensatory change.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Parasympathetic activation slows the heart rate. Tachycardia is due to sympathetic activation.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. A drop in blood pressure reduces baroreceptor firing, which leads to increased, not decreased, sympathetic outflow.

exam_trap: Option D pairs the right heart-rate change with the wrong limb; the tachycardia comes from increased sympathetic and reduced parasympathetic activity, not parasympathetic activation.
takeaway: Fall in blood pressure → reduced baroreceptor firing → sympathetic tachycardia and vasoconstriction.
thinking: Sudden fall in blood pressure ↓ less arterial stretch reduces baroreceptor firing ↓ the medulla increases sympathetic and reduces vagal outflow ↓ heart rate and contractility rise ↓ Tachycardia due to sympathetic activation
pearl: Patients on beta-blockers may not mount a reflex tachycardia, so a normal heart rate does not exclude significant hypovolaemia after trauma or surgery.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: Physiology - Cardiovascular
stem: Which of the following best describes the relationship between preload and cardiac output?

options.C: Preload has no effect on cardiac output

correct_answer: B. Increased preload increases cardiac output
why_correct: Correct. Preload is the end-diastolic volume or end-diastolic pressure. According to the Frank-Starling law, increased preload stretches the myocardial fibres, leading to a more forceful contraction and increased stroke volume, thereby increasing cardiac output.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Increased preload increases cardiac output via the Frank-Starling mechanism. It does not decrease it.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Preload is a major determinant of cardiac output. It directly affects stroke volume via the Frank-Starling mechanism.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Preload does not directly affect heart rate. Heart rate is primarily determined by autonomic tone and other factors.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Increased afterload raises the resistance against which the heart must contract, which generally reduces stroke volume and cardiac output, unlike increased preload.

exam_trap: Option E is the trap: afterload is the resistance to ventricular ejection, and increasing it reduces stroke volume and cardiac output rather than raising them.
takeaway: Increased preload → increased stroke volume → increased cardiac output, until the Starling curve flattens.
thinking: Preload = ventricular end-diastolic volume or stretch ↓ Frank-Starling: more stretch gives a stronger contraction ↓ stroke volume rises ↓ cardiac output (heart rate x stroke volume) rises ↓ Increased preload increases cardiac output
pearl: Passive leg raising transiently increases preload and can predict fluid responsiveness without committing the patient to a fluid bolus, which is useful in critically ill surgical patients.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: Physiology - Respiratory
stem: Which of the following best describes the primary stimulus for breathing in a healthy individual?
why_correct: Correct. Hypercapnia (increased arterial CO2) is the primary stimulus for breathing in healthy individuals. Central chemoreceptors in the medulla respond to changes in pH (which reflects CO2 levels) by adjusting ventilation. Increased CO2 leads to increased ventilation.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Hypoxia is a stimulus for breathing, but it is not the primary stimulus in healthy individuals. It becomes important in chronic respiratory failure (e.g., COPD) where central chemoreceptors become desensitised to CO2.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Alkalosis (increased pH) inhibits breathing. It does not stimulate it.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Hypocapnia (decreased arterial CO2) inhibits breathing. It does not stimulate it.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Metabolic acidosis can stimulate ventilation (e.g., Kussmaul breathing) as a compensatory response, but it is not the primary physiological stimulus for breathing in healthy individuals; that role belongs to arterial CO2 sensed by central chemoreceptors.

exam_trap: Hypoxia (option A) is the tempting choice, but peripheral chemoreceptors respond strongly only when PaO2 falls well below normal; arterial CO2 dominates minute-to-minute control.
takeaway: Normal ventilatory drive = PaCO2, sensed via CSF pH by central chemoreceptors.
thinking: Healthy person at rest ↓ central chemoreceptors in the medulla respond to CSF pH ↓ CO2 crosses the blood-brain barrier and lowers CSF pH ↓ small rises in PaCO2 strongly increase ventilation ↓ Hypercapnia
pearl: Opioids and residual anaesthetic agents blunt the ventilatory response to CO2, so postoperative patients on supplemental oxygen can become hypercapnic and drowsy while their saturations still look acceptable.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: Physiology - Respiratory
stem: Which of the following best describes the effect of surfactant on alveolar surface tension?

options.A: It increases surface tension and promotes alveolar collapse
options.B: It decreases surface tension and prevents alveolar collapse
options.C: It has no effect on surface tension
options.D: It increases surface tension and prevents alveolar collapse
options.E: It is produced by type I pneumocytes

correct_answer: B. It decreases surface tension and prevents alveolar collapse
why_correct: Correct. Surfactant is produced by type II pneumocytes. It reduces alveolar surface tension by forming a monolayer on the alveolar surface. This prevents alveolar collapse at the end of expiration (atelectasis) and reduces the work of breathing. Surfactant deficiency occurs in premature infants (respiratory distress syndrome).

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Surfactant decreases surface tension. Increased surface tension would promote alveolar collapse.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Surfactant has a significant effect on surface tension. It decreases it.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Surfactant decreases surface tension, not increases it.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Surfactant is produced by type II pneumocytes, not type I pneumocytes, which form the thin membrane for gas exchange.

exam_trap: Option E tests the cell type: type I pneumocytes form the gas-exchange surface, whereas surfactant comes from type II pneumocytes, which also regenerate the alveolar epithelium.
takeaway: Surfactant (type II pneumocytes) lowers surface tension, preventing alveolar collapse and increasing compliance.
thinking: Surfactant is produced by type II pneumocytes ↓ its phospholipid layer lowers alveolar surface tension ↓ because collapsing pressure is proportional to surface tension divided by radius, small alveoli then need less pressure to stay open ↓ alveoli resist collapse at end-expiration ↓ It decreases surface tension and prevents alveolar collapse
pearl: Antenatal corticosteroids accelerate fetal surfactant production and reduce neonatal respiratory distress syndrome when preterm delivery is anticipated.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: Physiology - Renal
stem: Which of the following best describes the effect of ADH on the collecting duct?
why_correct: Correct. ADH (antidiuretic hormone, vasopressin) is released from the posterior pituitary in response to increased plasma osmolality or decreased blood volume. It binds to V2 receptors on the basolateral membrane of collecting duct cells, leading to insertion of aquaporin-2 channels into the apical membrane. This increases water permeability, allowing water reabsorption and concentrating urine.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. ADH increases water permeability. Diabetes insipidus (lack of ADH) causes decreased water permeability and dilute urine.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. ADH primarily affects water permeability, not sodium reabsorption. Aldosterone increases sodium reabsorption.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. ADH does not significantly affect sodium reabsorption. It primarily regulates water balance.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Although ADH does enhance urea reabsorption in the inner medullary collecting duct, its principal and defining action is to increase water permeability through insertion of aquaporin-2 channels.

exam_trap: Option E is partly true, since ADH does increase inner medullary urea permeability, but the word 'only' makes it wrong; its defining action is increasing water permeability.
takeaway: ADH → V2 receptor → aquaporin-2 → increased collecting duct water permeability.
thinking: ADH binds V2 receptors on collecting duct principal cells ↓ cAMP signalling inserts aquaporin-2 into the apical membrane ↓ water moves out along the medullary osmotic gradient ↓ It increases water permeability
pearl: Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, classically from lithium or hypercalcaemia, produces dilute urine despite high ADH levels because the collecting duct cannot respond via V2 receptors and aquaporin-2.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: Physiology - Renal
stem: Which of the following best describes the effect of hyperventilation on arterial blood gases?
correct_answer: A. Decreased PaCO2 and increased pH
why_correct: Correct. Hyperventilation causes excessive elimination of CO2, leading to decreased PaCO2 (hypocapnia) and increased pH (respiratory alkalosis). This is seen in anxiety, high altitude, and early salicylate poisoning.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. This describes hypoventilation, which causes respiratory acidosis.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Decreased PaCO2 causes increased pH, not decreased pH.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Increased PaCO2 causes decreased pH, not increased pH.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Hyperventilation typically maintains or increases PaO2 due to enhanced alveolar ventilation, and it causes an increase, not a decrease, in pH.

exam_trap: Option E misleads because hyperventilating patients feel breathless, but increased alveolar ventilation maintains or raises PaO2 and produces alkalosis, not acidosis.
takeaway: Hyperventilation → low PaCO2 → respiratory alkalosis.
thinking: Hyperventilation raises alveolar ventilation ↓ CO2 is eliminated faster than it is produced ↓ PaCO2 falls ↓ less carbonic acid, so pH rises ↓ Decreased PaCO2 and increased pH
pearl: Acute respiratory alkalosis lowers ionised calcium by increasing calcium binding to albumin, which explains perioral tingling and carpopedal spasm in anxiety-related hyperventilation.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: Physiology - Endocrine
stem: Which of the following best describes the action of parathyroid hormone (PTH) on the kidney?

options.A: It increases calcium reabsorption and phosphate excretion
options.B: It decreases calcium reabsorption and phosphate excretion
options.C: It increases calcium reabsorption and phosphate reabsorption
options.D: It decreases calcium reabsorption and phosphate reabsorption
options.E: It decreases plasma calcium by inhibiting osteoclast activity

correct_answer: A. It increases calcium reabsorption and phosphate excretion
why_correct: Correct. PTH acts on the distal convoluted tubule to increase calcium reabsorption. It also inhibits phosphate reabsorption in the proximal convoluted tubule, leading to increased phosphate excretion (phosphaturia). Additionally, PTH stimulates the conversion of vitamin D to its active form in the kidney.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. PTH increases calcium reabsorption. It does not decrease it.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. PTH increases calcium reabsorption but decreases phosphate reabsorption.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. PTH increases calcium reabsorption and decreases phosphate reabsorption.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. This describes the action of calcitonin, secreted by parafollicular (C) cells of the thyroid, which lowers plasma calcium by inhibiting osteoclast activity. Parathyroid hormone raises plasma calcium and does not act this way.

exam_trap: Option C traps candidates who assume PTH conserves both minerals; it retains calcium but causes phosphaturia, which limits calcium-phosphate precipitation.
takeaway: PTH on the kidney: calcium retained, phosphate excreted, calcitriol produced.
thinking: PTH acts to raise calcium and lower phosphate ↓ distal tubule: increased calcium reabsorption ↓ proximal tubule: reduced phosphate reabsorption via sodium-phosphate cotransporters ↓ It increases calcium reabsorption and phosphate excretion
pearl: PTH-related peptide secreted by squamous carcinomas and other tumours mimics these renal actions, producing humoral hypercalcaemia of malignancy with low phosphate and a suppressed native PTH.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: Physiology - Endocrine
stem: Which of the following best describes the effect of thyroid hormones on basal metabolic rate?

options.C: They have no effect on basal metabolic rate
options.D: They increase basal metabolic rate only in children
options.E: They act only on cardiac tissue to increase basal metabolic rate

correct_answer: A. They increase basal metabolic rate
why_correct: Correct. Thyroid hormones (T3 and T4) increase the basal metabolic rate (BMR) by stimulating oxygen consumption and heat production in most tissues. They increase the activity of Na+/K+ ATPase, which consumes ATP and generates heat. Hyperthyroidism causes weight loss, heat intolerance, and increased appetite.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. Thyroid hormones increase BMR. Hypothyroidism causes decreased BMR, weight gain, and cold intolerance.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Thyroid hormones have a significant effect on BMR. They are major regulators of metabolism.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Thyroid hormones increase BMR in both children and adults.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Thyroid hormones increase metabolic rate broadly across most tissues, including muscle, liver, and kidney, not exclusively cardiac tissue.

exam_trap: Option E is wrong because thyroid hormones raise metabolic rate in almost all tissues; the cardiac effects are prominent but the heart is not their sole site of action.
takeaway: Thyroid hormones raise BMR, oxygen consumption and heat production in most tissues.
thinking: T3 acts on nuclear receptors in most tissues ↓ it increases Na/K-ATPase and mitochondrial activity ↓ oxygen consumption and heat production rise ↓ They increase basal metabolic rate
pearl: A thyrotoxic patient must be rendered euthyroid with antithyroid drugs and beta-blockade before thyroidectomy to avoid thyroid storm, which presents with hyperpyrexia, tachyarrhythmia and confusion.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: Physiology - Gastrointestinal
stem: Which of the following best describes the function of secretin?

options.E: It stimulates pepsinogen secretion by gastric chief cells

correct_answer: A. It stimulates pancreatic bicarbonate secretion
why_correct: Correct. Secretin is secreted by S cells in the duodenum in response to acidic chyme. It stimulates pancreatic ductal cells to secrete bicarbonate-rich fluid, which neutralises acid in the duodenum. It also inhibits gastric acid secretion.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. Cholecystokinin (CCK) stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion. Secretin primarily stimulates bicarbonate secretion.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Secretin inhibits gastric acid secretion. Gastrin stimulates acid secretion.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. CCK stimulates gallbladder contraction. Secretin does not have this effect.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Pepsinogen secretion from chief cells is stimulated by gastrin, vagal (acetylcholine) stimulation, and local acid, not by secretin. Secretin's principal action is on pancreatic bicarbonate secretion.

exam_trap: Option B attracts candidates who confuse secretin with CCK; secretin drives watery bicarbonate secretion, while CCK drives enzyme-rich acinar secretion.
takeaway: Secretin = bicarbonate; CCK = enzymes.
thinking: Acid enters the duodenum ↓ S cells release secretin ↓ secretin acts on pancreatic and biliary ductal cells ↓ bicarbonate-rich fluid neutralises the acid ↓ It stimulates pancreatic bicarbonate secretion
pearl: Ductal bicarbonate secretion depends on the CFTR chloride channel, so cystic fibrosis produces viscid pancreatic secretions, duct obstruction and exocrine pancreatic insufficiency.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: Physiology - Gastrointestinal
stem: Which of the following best describes the function of bile salts?

options.A: Emulsification of fats to aid digestion
options.B: Digestion of proteins into amino acids
options.D: Absorption of water in the colon

correct_answer: A. Emulsification of fats to aid digestion
why_correct: Correct. Bile salts are synthesised in the liver from cholesterol and secreted into bile. They emulsify fats in the small intestine, breaking large fat globules into smaller droplets. This increases the surface area for pancreatic lipase to digest triglycerides into fatty acids and monoglycerides. Bile salts also form micelles that facilitate fat absorption.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. Protein digestion is carried out by proteases (e.g., pepsin, trypsin, chymotrypsin). Bile salts do not digest proteins.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Carbohydrate digestion is carried out by amylases and disaccharidases. Bile salts do not digest carbohydrates.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Water absorption occurs in the colon and is not mediated by bile salts. Bile salts are reabsorbed in the terminal ileum.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Pancreatic bicarbonate secretion is stimulated by secretin, not bile salts. Bile salts function to emulsify dietary fats in the small intestine.

exam_trap: Options B and C may be chosen by candidates who think of bile as enzymatic, but bile contains no digestive enzymes; its salts act physically by emulsifying fat.
takeaway: Bile salts emulsify fat and form micelles; they are reabsorbed in the terminal ileum.
thinking: Bile salts are amphipathic molecules made from cholesterol ↓ they break large fat globules into small droplets ↓ this enlarges the surface area for pancreatic lipase ↓ then they form micelles for absorption ↓ Emulsification of fats to aid digestion
pearl: Biliary obstruction removes bile salts from the gut, causing steatorrhoea and vitamin K malabsorption, so a prolonged INR in obstructive jaundice is corrected with intravenous vitamin K before intervention.

subject: Pathology
title: Pathology: Pathology - General
stem: Which of the following best describes the role of p53 in cancer development?

options.A: It is an oncogene that promotes cell proliferation when mutated
options.B: It is a tumour suppressor gene that induces cell cycle arrest and apoptosis in response to DNA damage
options.C: It is a DNA repair gene that is overexpressed in cancer
options.D: It is a cell surface receptor that promotes angiogenesis
options.E: It is a growth factor receptor tyrosine kinase overexpressed in some breast cancers

correct_answer: B. It is a tumour suppressor gene that induces cell cycle arrest and apoptosis in response to DNA damage
why_correct: Correct. p53 is known as the 'guardian of the genome'. In response to DNA damage, it induces cell cycle arrest (via p21) to allow repair, or apoptosis if the damage is irreparable. It is the most commonly mutated gene in human cancers, with loss of function leading to genomic instability and tumour progression.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. p53 is a tumour suppressor gene, not an oncogene. Oncogenes promote cell proliferation when activated by mutation.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. p53 is a tumour suppressor transcription factor that coordinates cell cycle arrest and DNA repair rather than being a DNA repair enzyme itself. In cancer it is inactivated by mutation or loss; mutant p53 protein often accumulates and stains strongly on immunohistochemistry, but this reflects a non-functional protein, not overexpression of a normal repair gene.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. p53 is a nuclear transcription factor. It does not promote angiogenesis; it can actually inhibit angiogenesis.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. This describes HER2/neu, a proto-oncogene product overexpressed in a subset of breast cancers. p53 is a nuclear transcription factor and tumour suppressor, not a cell surface receptor tyrosine kinase.

exam_trap: The oncogene option tempts because mutant p53 accumulates in tumours, but p53 is a tumour suppressor whose loss of function, not activation, drives cancer.
takeaway: p53 = guardian of the genome: DNA damage → p21 → G1 arrest, or apoptosis if irreparable.
thinking: p53 senses DNA damage ↓ it induces p21-mediated cell cycle arrest to allow repair ↓ or triggers apoptosis if damage is irreparable ↓ loss of function removes this brake, so it is a tumour suppressor ↓ It is a tumour suppressor gene that induces cell cycle arrest and apoptosis in response to DNA damage
pearl: Inherited germline TP53 mutations cause a familial cancer syndrome with early-onset sarcomas, breast cancer and brain tumours, illustrating the two-hit model of tumour suppressor genes.

subject: Pathology
title: Pathology: Pathology - General
stem: Which of the following best describes the difference between benign and malignant tumours?

options.A: Benign tumours are encapsulated and do not metastasise; malignant tumours are invasive and can metastasise
options.B: Benign tumours are always larger than malignant tumours
options.C: Benign tumours always recur after excision; malignant tumours never recur
options.D: Benign tumours are poorly differentiated; malignant tumours are well differentiated
options.E: Benign tumours retain normal mitotic activity, while malignant tumours never show mitotic figures

correct_answer: A. Benign tumours are encapsulated and do not metastasise; malignant tumours are invasive and can metastasise
why_correct: Correct. Benign tumours are typically well-circumscribed, encapsulated, and do not invade surrounding tissues or metastasise. Malignant tumours are invasive, infiltrate surrounding tissues, and have the potential to metastasise via lymphatics or blood vessels.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. Size is not a reliable distinguishing feature. Benign tumours can be large, and malignant tumours can be small.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Benign tumours rarely recur after complete excision, while malignant tumours often recur if not completely excised.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Benign tumours are typically well differentiated, while malignant tumours range from well to poorly differentiated. Poor differentiation is associated with worse prognosis.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Malignant tumours typically show increased, often atypical, mitotic activity rather than an absence of mitoses. Mitotic rate is not the defining distinction between benign and malignant tumours.

exam_trap: Candidates may choose differentiation (D) but have it reversed; benign tumours are well differentiated, and only invasion and metastasis reliably define malignancy.
takeaway: Malignancy = invasion and metastatic potential; benign = localised, often encapsulated.
thinking: Benign versus malignant ↓ malignancy is defined by invasion and metastasis ↓ benign tumours are often encapsulated and stay localised ↓ Benign tumours are encapsulated and do not metastasise; malignant tumours are invasive and can metastasise
pearl: Not all benign tumours are encapsulated and some malignant tumours appear well circumscribed, so invasion of surrounding tissue and metastasis remain the definitive criteria of malignancy.

subject: Pathology
title: Pathology: Pathology - Haematology
stem: A patient presents with a white cell count of 50 x 10^9/L, with 90% blast cells on blood film. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Correct. Acute leukaemia is characterised by the presence of blast cells (immature white blood cells) in the blood and bone marrow. It presents with a high white cell count, anaemia, thrombocytopenia, and blast cells on blood film. It is classified as acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) or acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL).

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. CLL is characterised by a lymphocytosis with mature-appearing lymphocytes, not blast cells. It typically affects elderly patients.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. CML is characterised by a marked leucocytosis with a full spectrum of myeloid cells, including mature forms, not predominantly blast cells. It is associated with the Philadelphia chromosome (t(9;22)).
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Lymphoma primarily involves lymph nodes and lymphoid tissues. It can involve the bone marrow and blood (leukaemic phase) but is not primarily diagnosed by blood film showing blast cells.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Myelodysplastic syndrome is characterised by ineffective haematopoiesis and dysplastic changes, with a blast count below 20% by definition; a blast count of 90% far exceeds this and defines acute leukaemia.

exam_trap: Candidates choose myelodysplastic syndrome (E) because it involves blasts, but MDS has fewer than 20% blasts; CML (C) shows a full spectrum of maturing myeloid cells.
takeaway: Blasts 20% or more = acute leukaemia; CML = full myeloid spectrum; CLL = mature lymphocytes.
thinking: Raised white cell count ↓ 90% blast cells on the film ↓ marrow replaced by immature precursors ↓ 20% or more blasts defines acute leukaemia ↓ Acute leukaemia
pearl: Acute leukaemia with a very high white count risks tumour lysis syndrome once treatment starts, so hydration and prophylaxis such as allopurinol or rasburicase are given.

subject: Pathology
title: Pathology: Pathology - Haematology
stem: A patient presents with a lymph node biopsy showing Reed-Sternberg cells. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Correct. Hodgkin lymphoma is characterised by the presence of Reed-Sternberg cells (large, binucleate cells with prominent nucleoli, giving an 'owl-eye' appearance). It typically presents with painless cervical lymphadenopathy, fever, night sweats, and weight loss (B symptoms). It has a good prognosis with treatment.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Non-Hodgkin lymphomas do not typically contain Reed-Sternberg cells. They are classified based on cell type and molecular markers.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. CLL is characterised by lymphocytosis with mature lymphocytes in the blood and bone marrow. It does not typically present with Reed-Sternberg cells.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Multiple myeloma is characterised by plasma cell proliferation in the bone marrow, with monoclonal immunoglobulin in serum or urine. It does not involve Reed-Sternberg cells.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Infectious mononucleosis (EBV infection) causes a reactive lymphocytosis with atypical lymphocytes, which can mimic lymphoma clinically, but it does not produce true Reed-Sternberg cells; these are diagnostic of Hodgkin lymphoma.

exam_trap: Candidates choose infectious mononucleosis (E) because it can produce Reed-Sternberg-like cells and mimic lymphoma, but true Reed-Sternberg cells indicate Hodgkin lymphoma.
takeaway: Reed-Sternberg cells (CD15+, CD30+) = Hodgkin lymphoma.
thinking: Lymph node biopsy ↓ large binucleate owl-eye Reed-Sternberg cells ↓ Hodgkin lymphoma
pearl: Reed-Sternberg cells are typically CD15 and CD30 positive, and classical Hodgkin lymphoma often presents with painless cervical lymphadenopathy in young adults; excision biopsy of a node gives the best tissue for diagnosis.

subject: Pathology
title: Pathology: Pathology - Endocrine
stem: Which of the following is the most common type of pituitary adenoma?
why_correct: Correct. Prolactinoma is the most common type of pituitary adenoma. It causes hyperprolactinaemia, leading to galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea, and infertility in women, and hypogonadism in men. It can also cause visual field defects (bitemporal hemianopia) due to compression of the optic chiasm.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. GH-secreting adenomas cause acromegaly in adults and gigantism in children. They are less common than prolactinomas.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. ACTH-secreting adenomas cause Cushing's disease. They are less common than prolactinomas.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Non-functioning adenomas do not secrete hormones and present with mass effects (headache, visual field defects, hypopituitarism). They are common but less so than prolactinomas.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Craniopharyngioma is a suprasellar tumour arising from remnants of Rathke's pouch, not a pituitary adenoma. It can also cause visual field defects by compressing the optic chiasm but is a distinct entity, more common in children.

subject: Pathology
title: Pathology: Pathology - Endocrine
stem: A patient presents with a thyroid tumour that is composed of parafollicular C cells. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Correct. Medullary thyroid carcinoma arises from parafollicular C cells, which secrete calcitonin. It is associated with MEN 2A and 2B syndromes and can be familial. It is diagnosed by elevated serum calcitonin and treated with total thyroidectomy.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Papillary thyroid carcinoma arises from follicular cells and is characterised by nuclear grooves and psammoma bodies.
why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. Follicular thyroid carcinoma arises from follicular cells and spreads haematogenously to lungs and bones.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma is an undifferentiated tumour with a poor prognosis. It does not arise from C cells.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Hürthle cell carcinoma is a variant of follicular thyroid carcinoma composed of oncocytic follicular cells; it does not arise from parafollicular C cells.

exam_trap: Candidates choose Hürthle cell carcinoma (E) because it is a distinctive cell type, but Hürthle cells are oncocytic follicular cells; only medullary carcinoma arises from C cells.
takeaway: C cells → medullary thyroid carcinoma → calcitonin marker, MEN 2 and RET.
thinking: Thyroid tumour of parafollicular C cells ↓ neural crest-derived calcitonin-secreting cells ↓ Medullary thyroid carcinoma
pearl: Medullary carcinoma is linked to RET proto-oncogene mutations in MEN 2, and phaeochromocytoma must be excluded before thyroidectomy in these patients.

subject: Pathology
title: Pathology: Pathology - Renal
stem: A patient presents with nephrotic syndrome and is found to have a renal biopsy showing spike and dome deposits on electron microscopy. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Correct. Membranous nephropathy is characterised by thickened glomerular basement membrane with spike and dome deposits on electron microscopy (subepithelial immune complex deposits). It is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults. It can be primary (idiopathic) or secondary (e.g., hepatitis B, malignancy, drugs).

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Minimal change disease shows normal glomeruli on light microscopy and effacement of podocyte foot processes on electron microscopy. It does not show spike and dome deposits.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. IgA nephropathy shows mesangial deposition of IgA on immunofluorescence. It presents with nephritic syndrome (haematuria), not nephrotic syndrome.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. FSGS shows segmental sclerosis of some glomeruli on light microscopy. It does not show spike and dome deposits.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis shows mesangial and endocapillary proliferation with a 'tram-track' basement membrane appearance on light microscopy, not spike and dome deposits.

exam_trap: Candidates choose membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (E) because it also thickens the basement membrane, but MPGN gives a tram-track appearance; spike and dome means membranous.
takeaway: Spike and dome subepithelial deposits = membranous nephropathy.
thinking: Nephrotic syndrome ↓ spike and dome pattern on electron microscopy ↓ subepithelial immune deposits with basement membrane spikes between them ↓ Membranous nephropathy
pearl: Patients with membranous nephropathy and heavy proteinuria have a particularly high risk of renal vein thrombosis and other venous thromboembolism, partly due to urinary loss of antithrombin.

subject: Pathology
title: Pathology: Pathology - Renal
stem: A patient is found to have chronic kidney disease on routine blood tests. Which of the following is the most common cause of chronic kidney disease worldwide?
why_correct: Correct. Diabetes mellitus is the most common cause of chronic kidney disease worldwide. Diabetic nephropathy is characterised by proteinuria, declining glomerular filtration rate, and characteristic histological changes (Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules).

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. Hypertension is the second most common cause of CKD. It causes hypertensive nephrosclerosis.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Glomerulonephritis is a less common cause of CKD than diabetes and hypertension.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease is an inherited condition that causes CKD, but it is less common than diabetes and hypertension.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Chronic pyelonephritis, resulting from recurrent infection and vesicoureteric reflux, can cause CKD with renal scarring, but it is a far less common cause worldwide than diabetes mellitus.

exam_trap: Hypertension tempts as a very common cause of CKD, but it ranks second; diabetes mellitus is the commonest cause of CKD worldwide.
takeaway: Commonest cause of CKD worldwide = diabetes mellitus, then hypertension.
thinking: CKD found on routine blood tests ↓ asks for the commonest cause worldwide ↓ diabetic nephropathy leads, with hypertension second ↓ Diabetes mellitus
pearl: Diabetic nephropathy first shows as raised urinary albumin, so albumin:creatinine ratio screening allows early ACE inhibitor or ARB treatment to slow progression.

subject: Pathology
title: Pathology: Pathology - Gastrointestinal
stem: A patient presents with a gastric ulcer. Which of the following is the most common cause of peptic ulcer disease?
why_correct: Correct. H. pylori is the most common cause of peptic ulcer disease, accounting for approximately 70-80% of gastric ulcers and 90% of duodenal ulcers. It is a Gram-negative spiral bacterium that colonises the gastric mucosa, causing chronic inflammation and increased acid secretion.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. NSAIDs are the second most common cause of peptic ulcer disease. They inhibit cyclooxygenase, reducing prostaglandin synthesis and mucosal protection.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Zollinger-Ellison syndrome is a rare cause of peptic ulcer disease caused by a gastrin-secreting tumour (gastrinoma). It causes multiple, refractory ulcers.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Crohn's disease can cause oral and intestinal ulcers but is not a common cause of peptic ulcer disease.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Alcohol can irritate the gastric mucosa and worsen dyspeptic symptoms, but it is not considered a major independent cause of peptic ulcer disease; H. pylori and NSAIDs account for the great majority of cases.

exam_trap: Candidates choose NSAIDs (B) because they are a major cause, especially of gastric ulcers, but H. pylori remains the commonest cause of peptic ulceration overall.
takeaway: Peptic ulcer: H. pylori commonest, NSAIDs second; consider Zollinger-Ellison if multiple refractory ulcers.
thinking: Peptic ulcer disease ↓ Gram-negative spiral organism colonising the gastric mucosa ↓ accounts for most duodenal and gastric ulcers ↓ Helicobacter pylori infection
pearl: After a bleeding peptic ulcer, H. pylori should be tested for and eradicated, as successful eradication markedly reduces the risk of recurrent ulceration and rebleeding.

subject: Pathology
title: Pathology: Pathology - Gastrointestinal
stem: A patient with cirrhosis undergoes endoscopy and is found to have oesophageal varices. Which of the following is the most common cause of cirrhosis in the Western world?
why_correct: Correct. Alcohol abuse is the most common cause of cirrhosis in the Western world. Chronic alcohol consumption leads to fatty liver, alcoholic hepatitis, and eventually cirrhosis. It is associated with portal hypertension, oesophageal varices, and hepatocellular carcinoma.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Hepatitis B is a common cause of cirrhosis worldwide, particularly in Asia and sub-Saharan Africa, but it is less common in the Western world.
why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. Hepatitis C is a common cause of cirrhosis in the Western world, but alcohol abuse is more common.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. NAFLD is an increasingly common cause of cirrhosis in the Western world, particularly in patients with obesity and diabetes. However, alcohol abuse remains the most common cause.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Autoimmune hepatitis is a recognised cause of cirrhosis but is far less common than alcohol-related liver disease in the Western world.

exam_trap: Candidates choose hepatitis C (B) or NAFLD (D) because both are common and rising, but in the Western world alcohol remains the leading cause of cirrhosis.
takeaway: Cirrhosis: Western world = alcohol; worldwide = viral hepatitis (especially hepatitis B).
thinking: Cirrhosis with varices ↓ Western world setting ↓ alcohol-related liver disease leads, despite rising fatty liver disease ↓ Alcohol abuse
pearl: Acute variceal bleeding is treated with resuscitation, terlipressin, prophylactic antibiotics and endoscopic band ligation, with a TIPSS as rescue if bleeding is uncontrolled.

subject: Microbiology
title: Microbiology: Microbiology - Specific Organisms
stem: A patient presents with a petechial rash, fever, and neck stiffness. CSF analysis shows Gram-negative diplococci. Which organism is most likely?
why_correct: Correct. N. meningitidis is a Gram-negative diplococcus that causes meningococcal meningitis. It often presents with a petechial or purpuric rash, fever, neck stiffness, and photophobia. It is spread by respiratory droplets and can cause rapid deterioration and sepsis. Close contacts require prophylaxis with rifampicin or ciprofloxacin.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. S. pneumoniae is a Gram-positive diplococcus. It is a common cause of meningitis in adults and the elderly, but the CSF Gram stain would show Gram-positive organisms.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. H. influenzae is a Gram-negative coccobacillus. It was a common cause of meningitis in children before the introduction of the Hib vaccine.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Listeria is a Gram-positive bacillus. It causes meningitis in neonates, pregnant women, the elderly, and immunocompromised patients.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Group B Streptococcus is a Gram-positive coccus and a leading cause of neonatal meningitis; it is not the organism responsible for the Gram-negative diplococci seen here.

exam_trap: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the commonest adult meningitis cause, but it appears as Gram-positive diplococci; Gram-negative diplococci with a petechial rash indicate meningococcus.
takeaway: Meningitis + petechial rash + Gram-negative diplococci → Neisseria meningitidis.
thinking: Fever, neck stiffness and a petechial rash ↓ bacterial meningitis with septicaemia ↓ CSF shows Gram-negative diplococci ↓ Neisseria meningitidis
pearl: In suspected meningococcal disease, parenteral benzylpenicillin or ceftriaxone should be given without delay and must not wait for lumbar puncture.

subject: Microbiology
title: Microbiology: Microbiology - Specific Organisms
stem: A patient presents with a productive cough, fever, and rust-coloured sputum. Chest X-ray shows lobar consolidation. Which organism is most likely?
why_correct: Correct. S. pneumoniae is the most common cause of community-acquired pneumonia. It classically presents with a productive cough, fever, pleuritic chest pain, and rust-coloured sputum. Chest X-ray shows lobar consolidation. It is a Gram-positive diplococcus and is treated with amoxicillin.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. H. influenzae is a Gram-negative coccobacillus that can cause pneumonia, particularly in patients with chronic lung disease. It is less commonly associated with rust-coloured sputum.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Mycoplasma causes atypical pneumonia, which presents with a dry cough, headache, and malaise. Chest X-ray shows interstitial infiltrates, not lobar consolidation.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Legionella causes Legionnaires' disease, which presents with pneumonia, diarrhoea, hyponatraemia, and neurological symptoms. It is associated with contaminated water systems.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Staphylococcus aureus pneumonia typically follows influenza infection and often causes cavitating or necrotising lung lesions, rather than classical lobar consolidation with rust-coloured sputum.

exam_trap: Staphylococcus aureus pneumonia is tempting in a severe case, but it typically follows influenza and causes cavitation, not classic lobar consolidation with rust-coloured sputum.
takeaway: Rust-coloured sputum + lobar consolidation → Streptococcus pneumoniae.
thinking: Productive cough and fever ↓ rust-coloured sputum ↓ lobar consolidation on chest X-ray ↓ classic typical community-acquired pneumonia ↓ Streptococcus pneumoniae
pearl: The CURB-65 score (confusion, urea, respiratory rate, blood pressure, age 65 or over) guides the decision about hospital admission and antibiotic choice in community-acquired pneumonia.

subject: Microbiology
title: Microbiology: Microbiology - Viral Infections
stem: A patient with HIV/AIDS has a CD4 count of 150 cells/µL and presents with fever, night sweats, weight loss, and a dry cough. Chest X-ray shows bilateral interstitial infiltrates. Which organism is most likely?
why_correct: Correct. Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) is a common opportunistic infection in HIV/AIDS patients with CD4 counts below 200 cells/µL. It presents with fever, night sweats, weight loss, dry cough, and progressive dyspnoea. Chest X-ray shows bilateral interstitial infiltrates. Treatment is co-trimoxazole.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. TB can cause similar constitutional symptoms and occurs at any CD4 count, but a dry cough with diffuse bilateral interstitial infiltrates at a CD4 count below 200 cells/µL is most typical of PCP.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Cryptococcus causes meningitis, not pneumonia. It presents with headache, fever, and neck stiffness.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. CMV causes retinitis, colitis, and oesophagitis in HIV/AIDS patients, not typically pneumonia.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Invasive pulmonary aspergillosis typically occurs in profoundly neutropenic patients and causes nodular or cavitating lesions, not the diffuse bilateral interstitial infiltrates characteristic of PCP.

exam_trap: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is tempting given night sweats and weight loss, but a dry cough with bilateral interstitial infiltrates at a CD4 count below 200 cells/µL is classic PCP.
takeaway: HIV + CD4 <200 + dry cough + bilateral interstitial infiltrates → PCP; treat with co-trimoxazole.
thinking: HIV with CD4 count of 150 cells/µL ↓ dry cough with fever and constitutional symptoms ↓ bilateral interstitial infiltrates ↓ commonest opportunistic pneumonia below 200 cells/µL ↓ Pneumocystis jirovecii
pearl: Exertional desaturation is a sensitive bedside clue to PCP, and adjunctive corticosteroids are given in moderate to severe disease with significant hypoxaemia.

subject: Microbiology
title: Microbiology: Microbiology - Viral Infections
stem: A patient has frequently recurring episodes of painful grouped vesicles on the genitalia. Which virus is most likely responsible?
why_correct: Correct. Herpes simplex virus causes painful grouped genital vesicles that can recur. HSV-1 now causes many first episodes of genital herpes in the UK, but genital HSV-2 recurs far more often, so frequently recurring genital herpes is most likely HSV-2. It is sexually transmitted and can be transmitted to neonates during delivery.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. HSV-1 classically causes oral lesions and now causes many first episodes of genital herpes, but genital HSV-1 recurs much less often than HSV-2.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. VZV causes chickenpox and shingles; shingles produces a painful dermatomal vesicular rash and does not cause frequently recurring genital vesicles.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. HPV causes warts, including genital warts (condylomata acuminata), and is associated with cervical cancer. It does not typically cause vesicular lesions.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Molluscum contagiosum causes painless, pearly umbilicated papules, not painful recurrent vesicles.

exam_trap: Herpes simplex virus type 1 is the strong distractor because it now causes many first episodes of genital herpes, but genital HSV-1 recurs far less often than HSV-2.
takeaway: Frequently recurring genital vesicles → HSV-2; HSV-1 is classically oral and recurs less often genitally.
thinking: Frequently recurring painful grouped genital vesicles ↓ herpes simplex virus ↓ HSV-1 now causes many first genital episodes but rarely recurs genitally ↓ genital HSV-2 recurs far more often ↓ Herpes simplex virus type 2
pearl: A first episode of genital herpes late in pregnancy is an indication for planned caesarean section because the risk of neonatal herpes is high, whereas recurrent episodes at delivery carry a much lower risk.

subject: Microbiology
title: Microbiology: Microbiology - Fungal Infections
stem: A patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and an old lung cavity develops haemoptysis; CT shows a mobile fungus ball within the pre-existing cavity. Which organism is most likely?
why_correct: Correct. Aspergillus fumigatus is a mould that can cause aspergilloma (fungus ball) in pre-existing lung cavities, such as those from tuberculosis or COPD. It presents with haemoptysis and is treated with surgical resection if symptomatic, or observation if asymptomatic.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Candida is a yeast that typically causes mucosal infections or candidemia. It does not typically cause aspergilloma.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Cryptococcus is a yeast that causes meningitis, not aspergilloma.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Pneumocystis causes pneumonia in immunocompromised patients, not aspergilloma.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Mucor species cause mucormycosis, an aggressive angio-invasive infection typically seen in diabetic ketoacidosis or profound immunosuppression, not a fungus ball within a pre-existing lung cavity.

exam_trap: Mucor species tempts as another mould, but mucormycosis is an angio-invasive infection in diabetics or the immunosuppressed, not a ball within an existing cavity.
takeaway: Mobile fungus ball in a pre-existing lung cavity = aspergilloma (Aspergillus fumigatus).
thinking: COPD with an old lung cavity ↓ haemoptysis ↓ mobile fungus ball within the pre-existing cavity ↓ aspergilloma ↓ Aspergillus fumigatus
pearl: Haemoptysis from an aspergilloma can be massive; bronchial artery embolisation is used to control bleeding, with surgical resection considered in fit patients with symptomatic disease.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: Anatomy - Upper Limb
stem: A patient presents with weakness in shoulder abduction and sensory loss over the lateral aspect of the shoulder. Which nerve is most likely injured?
why_correct: Correct. The axillary nerve supplies the deltoid and teres minor muscles and provides sensation over the lateral aspect of the shoulder (regimental badge area). It is at risk with surgical neck fractures of the humerus and anterior shoulder dislocations. Injury causes weakness in shoulder abduction and sensory loss over the lateral shoulder.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. The suprascapular nerve supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus. Injury causes weakness in shoulder abduction (supraspinatus) and external rotation (infraspinatus), but there is no sensory loss because it is a motor nerve.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. The radial nerve supplies the triceps and wrist extensors. Injury causes wrist drop and sensory loss over the posterior arm and forearm.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. The musculocutaneous nerve supplies the coracobrachialis, biceps brachii, and brachialis. It terminates as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm. Injury causes weakness in elbow flexion and sensory loss over the lateral forearm.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. The long thoracic nerve supplies serratus anterior; injury causes winging of the scapula, not weakness in shoulder abduction or sensory loss over the shoulder.

exam_trap: The suprascapular nerve (A) also weakens abduction, but it has no cutaneous territory, so lateral shoulder numbness points to the axillary nerve.
takeaway: Weak abduction + regimental badge numbness = axillary nerve (surgical neck fracture, anterior dislocation).
thinking: Weak shoulder abduction ↓ numbness over the lateral shoulder (regimental badge area) ↓ deltoid plus the upper lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm ↓ Axillary nerve
pearl: Regimental badge sensation should be tested and documented before and after reducing an anterior shoulder dislocation, as the axillary nerve is stretched around the surgical neck and deltoid power is hard to assess in a painful shoulder.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: Anatomy - Upper Limb
stem: During a volar approach to the wrist, the surgeon must identify the flexor retinaculum. Which structure does NOT pass through the carpal tunnel?
why_correct: Correct. Flexor carpi ulnaris does NOT pass through the carpal tunnel. It inserts on the pisiform, hook of hamate, and base of the 5th metacarpal. It is located in the superficial forearm flexor compartment and is supplied by the ulnar nerve. The structures passing through the carpal tunnel are: median nerve, flexor pollicis longus, flexor digitorum superficialis (4 tendons), and flexor digitorum profundus (4 tendons).

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Flexor digitorum superficialis tendons pass through the carpal tunnel to insert on the middle phalanges of fingers 2-5.
why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. Flexor digitorum profundus tendons pass through the carpal tunnel to insert on the distal phalanges of fingers 2-5.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. The median nerve passes through the carpal tunnel and is the most superficial structure. Compression causes carpal tunnel syndrome.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Flexor pollicis longus passes through the carpal tunnel to insert on the distal phalanx of the thumb.

exam_trap: Candidates who assume every forearm flexor tendon crosses the tunnel miss that flexor carpi ulnaris (C) stays superficial and inserts on the pisiform, outside the tunnel.
takeaway: Carpal tunnel = median nerve + FDS (4) + FDP (4) + FPL; FCU and the ulnar nerve lie outside.
thinking: Carpal tunnel contents ↓ median nerve plus nine flexor tendons: FDS x4, FDP x4, FPL ↓ FCU runs superficially on the ulnar side to the pisiform ↓ Flexor carpi ulnaris
pearl: The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum, so sensation over the thenar eminence is typically spared in carpal tunnel syndrome.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: Anatomy - Lower Limb
stem: During a posterior approach to the knee, the surgeon divides the deep fascia over the popliteal fossa. Of the structures in the central neurovascular bundle of the fossa, which lies most superficial?
why_correct: Correct.
