Of the structures in the central neurovascular bundle of the popliteal fossa, the tibial nerve is the most superficial; from superficial to deep the order is tibial nerve, popliteal vein, popliteal artery. The common peroneal nerve leaves the sciatic nerve at the apex of the fossa and runs laterally along the medial border of biceps femoris, outside the central bundle.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. The popliteal artery is the deepest structure in the popliteal fossa, lying directly on the posterior surface of the femur and tibia.
why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. The popliteal vein lies between the popliteal artery and the tibial nerve. It is not the most superficial.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. The common peroneal nerve leaves the sciatic nerve at the apex of the fossa and runs laterally along the medial border of biceps femoris, away from the central neurovascular bundle; of the central structures, the tibial nerve is the most superficial.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Popliteus forms part of the floor of the popliteal fossa, deep to all the neurovascular structures.

exam_trap: Common peroneal nerve is chosen because it is superficial in the fossa, but it runs laterally along biceps femoris outside the central bundle, in which the tibial nerve is most superficial.
takeaway: Popliteal fossa, superficial to deep: tibial nerve, popliteal vein, popliteal artery.
thinking: Deep fascia over the popliteal fossa divided ↓ central neurovascular bundle met from superficial to deep ↓ tibial nerve, then popliteal vein, then popliteal artery on the bone ↓ common peroneal nerve runs laterally outside the central bundle ↓ Tibial nerve
pearl: Because the popliteal artery lies deepest, directly on the posterior femur and tibia, it is at risk in knee dislocation and supracondylar femoral fractures; distal pulses and ankle-brachial pressures should be checked after any knee dislocation.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: Anatomy - Lower Limb
stem: A patient presents with a fracture of the neck of the fibula. Which nerve is most at risk of injury?
why_correct: Correct. The common peroneal nerve winds around the neck of the fibula, where it is superficial and vulnerable to injury. It supplies the anterior and lateral compartments of the leg, which are responsible for dorsiflexion and eversion. Injury causes foot drop and sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot and lateral leg.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. The tibial nerve runs in the posterior compartment of the leg and is not at risk with a fibular neck fracture.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. The sural nerve is a sensory nerve that runs in the posterior leg. It is not at risk with a fibular neck fracture.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. The saphenous nerve is a sensory branch of the femoral nerve. It supplies sensation to the medial aspect of the leg and foot. It is not at risk with a fibular neck fracture.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. The deep peroneal nerve is a terminal branch of the common peroneal nerve, arising only after the common peroneal nerve has already coursed around the fibular neck; it is the common peroneal nerve itself that is directly vulnerable at this level.

exam_trap: The deep peroneal nerve (E) is chosen because it causes foot drop, but it branches only after the common peroneal nerve has wound around the fibular neck.
takeaway: Fibular neck injury = common peroneal nerve: foot drop, weak eversion, dorsum of foot numbness.
thinking: Fibular neck fracture ↓ common peroneal nerve winds superficially around the fibular neck ↓ supplies anterior and lateral leg compartments ↓ foot drop with numbness of the dorsum of the foot ↓ Common peroneal nerve
pearl: Common peroneal palsy can also follow external compression at the fibular neck from a tight cast, prolonged leg crossing or poor positioning in theatre, so this area must be well padded.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: Anatomy - Abdomen
stem: During a gastrectomy, the surgeon ligates the left gastric artery. From which vessel does the left gastric artery arise?
why_correct: Correct. The coeliac trunk has three branches: left gastric artery, common hepatic artery, and splenic artery. The left gastric artery runs along the lesser curvature of the stomach and supplies the stomach and lower oesophagus.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. The left gastric artery does not arise directly from the aorta. It arises from the coeliac trunk.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. The superior mesenteric artery arises from the aorta and supplies the midgut. It does not give rise to the left gastric artery.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. The splenic artery is a branch of the coeliac trunk. It supplies the spleen, pancreas, and short gastric arteries. It does not give rise to the left gastric artery.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. The common hepatic artery is a separate branch of the coeliac trunk; it does not give rise to the left gastric artery.

exam_trap: The aorta (A) is chosen because the left gastric looks like a direct visceral branch, but it is the smallest of the three coeliac trunk branches.
takeaway: Coeliac trunk = left gastric + common hepatic + splenic arteries.
thinking: Coeliac trunk at T12 has three branches ↓ left gastric, common hepatic and splenic arteries ↓ left gastric runs to the oesophagogastric junction, then along the lesser curve ↓ Coeliac trunk
pearl: The left gastric artery supplies the lower oesophagus, and its companion left gastric vein forms a portosystemic anastomosis that dilates into oesophageal varices in portal hypertension.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: Anatomy - Abdomen
stem: A patient presents with a direct inguinal hernia. Through which area of the posterior wall of the inguinal canal does the hernia protrude?
why_correct: Correct. Hesselbach's triangle is bounded by the inguinal ligament (inferiorly), the inferior epigastric vessels (laterally), and the rectus sheath (medially). A direct inguinal hernia protrudes through this triangle, medial to the inferior epigastric vessels.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. The deep inguinal ring lies lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels. It is the site of protrusion for an indirect inguinal hernia.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. The femoral canal is located below and lateral to the pubic tubercle. It is the site of protrusion for a femoral hernia.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. The superficial inguinal ring is the exit point for both indirect and direct inguinal hernias. It is not the site of origin for a direct hernia.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. The conjoint tendon, formed by the fused aponeuroses of internal oblique and transversus abdominis, reinforces the medial inguinal canal but is not itself the triangle bounded by the inguinal ligament, inferior epigastric vessels, and rectus sheath.

exam_trap: Candidates may choose the deep inguinal ring, but it lies lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels and is the entry point of indirect, not direct, inguinal hernias.
takeaway: Direct hernia = medial to the inferior epigastric vessels through Hesselbach's triangle; indirect = lateral, through the deep ring.
thinking: Direct inguinal hernia ↓ protrudes through the posterior wall medial to the inferior epigastric vessels ↓ area bounded by inguinal ligament, inferior epigastric vessels and rectus sheath ↓ Hesselbach's triangle
pearl: At laparoscopic repair the inferior epigastric vessels are the key landmark: a defect medial to them is direct and lateral to them is indirect, a distinction clinical examination cannot make reliably.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: Anatomy - Head and Neck
stem: During a neck dissection, the surgeon identifies the spinal accessory nerve as it crosses the posterior triangle. Injury to the nerve at this point would weaken which muscle?
why_correct: Correct. The spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) supplies the trapezius muscle. It is at risk during neck dissection (e.g., radical neck dissection for head and neck cancer). Injury causes shoulder drop and weakness in shoulder elevation.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. The spinal accessory nerve supplies sternocleidomastoid before it enters the posterior triangle, so an injury within the triangle spares sternocleidomastoid and weakens trapezius.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. The platysma is supplied by the facial nerve (CN VII). It is not supplied by the spinal accessory nerve.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. The digastric muscle is supplied by the trigeminal nerve (anterior belly) and facial nerve (posterior belly). It is not supplied by the spinal accessory nerve.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Levator scapulae is supplied by the dorsal scapular nerve and direct branches from C3-C4, not the spinal accessory nerve.

exam_trap: Sternocleidomastoid (A) is chosen because CN XI supplies it, but that branch arises before the nerve enters the posterior triangle, so it is spared.
takeaway: CN XI injury in the posterior triangle = trapezius weakness (shoulder droop) with sternocleidomastoid spared.
thinking: Spinal accessory nerve crossing the posterior triangle ↓ branch to sternocleidomastoid has already been given off above this point ↓ remaining target is trapezius ↓ Trapezius
pearl: The accessory nerve lies just beneath the investing fascia in the posterior triangle, so it can be injured even during a simple lymph node biopsy there, causing shoulder pain and droop.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: Anatomy - Head and Neck
stem: A patient presents with a parotid gland tumour. Of the major structures that run within the parotid gland, which lies deepest and is at risk during deep-lobe parotidectomy?
why_correct: Correct. Three main structures pass through the parotid gland; from superficial to deep they are the facial nerve, the retromandibular vein and the external carotid artery, which divides within the gland into the maxillary and superficial temporal arteries.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. The facial nerve runs through the parotid gland, dividing it into superficial and deep lobes. It is not deep to the gland.
why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. The internal carotid artery lies deep to the gland, separated from it by the styloid process and its muscles; it does not run within the gland.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. The retromandibular vein runs through the parotid gland, not deep to it. It is formed by the union of the superficial temporal and maxillary veins.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. The great auricular nerve lies superficial to the parotid fascia and is often encountered early in parotidectomy; it is not the structure lying deep to the gland.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: Anatomy - Thorax
stem: During a thoracic surgical procedure, the surgeon identifies the phrenic nerve. Which structure receives its motor supply from the phrenic nerve?
why_correct: Correct. The phrenic nerve arises from C3, C4, and C5 ('C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive'). It provides motor supply to the diaphragm. It also provides sensory supply to the central part of the diaphragm, mediastinal pleura, and pericardium. It is at risk during thoracic surgery and central line insertion.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. The intercostal muscles are supplied by the intercostal nerves (T1-T11). The phrenic nerve does not supply them.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. The phrenic nerve carries sensory fibres from the pericardium, but the pericardium receives no motor supply from it; its motor target is the diaphragm.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. The lungs are supplied by the pulmonary plexus (sympathetic and parasympathetic fibres). The phrenic nerve does not supply the lungs.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. The costal parietal pleura is supplied by the intercostal nerves. The phrenic nerve supplies the central diaphragmatic and mediastinal pleura, not the costal pleura.

exam_trap: Pericardium is chosen because the phrenic nerve does supply it, but that supply is sensory only; the nerve's single motor target is the diaphragm.
takeaway: Phrenic nerve (C3-C5): motor to the diaphragm; sensory to the pericardium and mediastinal and diaphragmatic pleura.
thinking: Phrenic nerve from C3, C4 and C5 ↓ its only motor target is the diaphragm ↓ its other fibres are sensory to the pericardium and mediastinal and central diaphragmatic pleura ↓ Diaphragm
pearl: Phrenic nerve palsy gives a raised hemidiaphragm on chest X-ray and paradoxical movement on sniff testing; the nerve can be injured by topical cooling in cardiac surgery, neck or thoracic surgery, or tumour invasion.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: Anatomy - Neuroanatomy
stem: A patient presents with a lesion in the lateral medulla (Wallenberg syndrome). Which of the following is a characteristic feature of this syndrome?

options.B: Ipsilateral facial sensory loss and contralateral body sensory loss

correct_answer: B. Ipsilateral facial sensory loss and contralateral body sensory loss
why_correct: Correct. Wallenberg syndrome (lateral medullary syndrome) is caused by occlusion of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) or vertebral artery. It affects the spinal trigeminal nucleus and tract (ipsilateral facial sensory loss) and the spinothalamic tract (contralateral body sensory loss). Other features include vertigo, nystagmus, ataxia, dysphagia, hoarseness, and Horner's syndrome.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Contralateral hemiparesis is characteristic of a lesion in the medial medulla (Dejerine syndrome), which affects the corticospinal tract. Wallenberg syndrome (lateral medullary syndrome) typically spares the corticospinal tract.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. This is characteristic of a lesion in the occipital cortex or optic radiation. It is not a feature of Wallenberg syndrome.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Hearing loss is not typically a feature of Wallenberg syndrome. The cochlear nuclei lie at the pontomedullary junction, usually above the territory of lateral medullary infarction; ipsilateral deafness suggests AICA (lateral pontine) infarction.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Ipsilateral tongue weakness from hypoglossal nerve involvement is a feature of medial medullary syndrome, not lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome, which typically spares the hypoglossal nucleus.

exam_trap: Contralateral hemiparesis and ipsilateral tongue weakness are chosen, but they are features of medial medullary syndrome; a lateral medullary lesion spares the corticospinal tract and hypoglossal nucleus.
takeaway: Lateral medulla: ipsilateral face and contralateral body pain and temperature loss, with Horner syndrome, vertigo, ataxia and dysphagia.
thinking: Lateral medullary lesion from PICA or vertebral artery occlusion ↓ spinal trigeminal nucleus and tract involved, giving ipsilateral facial pain and temperature loss ↓ spinothalamic tract already crossed, giving contralateral body loss ↓ corticospinal tract and hypoglossal nucleus lie medially and are spared ↓ Ipsilateral facial sensory loss and contralateral body sensory loss
pearl: Crossed sensory signs, face on one side and body on the other, localise a lesion to the brainstem; nucleus ambiguus involvement in lateral medullary syndrome causes dysphagia, so a formal swallow assessment is needed before oral intake.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: Physiology - Cardiovascular
stem: Which of the following best describes the effect of increased afterload on cardiac output?

options.C: Increased afterload has no effect on cardiac output
options.E: Increased afterload increases stroke volume via the Frank-Starling mechanism

correct_answer: B. Increased afterload decreases cardiac output
why_correct: Correct. Afterload is the resistance against which the ventricle must eject blood. Increased afterload (e.g., systemic hypertension, aortic stenosis) leads to reduced stroke volume and decreased cardiac output. The heart must work harder to overcome the increased resistance, which can lead to hypertrophy and eventually failure.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Increased afterload (e.g., hypertension, aortic stenosis) increases the resistance against which the heart must pump, reducing stroke volume and cardiac output.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Afterload is a major determinant of cardiac output. It directly affects stroke volume.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Afterload does not directly affect heart rate. Heart rate is primarily determined by autonomic tone.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. This describes the effect of increased preload via the Frank-Starling mechanism. Increased afterload instead opposes ventricular ejection and reduces stroke volume for a given contractility.

exam_trap: Option E reattaches Frank-Starling to the wrong variable; increased afterload reduces stroke volume, whereas Frank-Starling links increased preload to increased stroke volume.
takeaway: Increased afterload → reduced stroke volume and cardiac output; chronically, ventricular hypertrophy.
thinking: Afterload = the resistance the ventricle ejects against ↓ more afterload raises wall stress during ejection ↓ fibres shorten less, so stroke volume falls ↓ cardiac output falls ↓ Increased afterload decreases cardiac output
pearl: In aortic stenosis the fixed outflow obstruction makes cardiac output preload- and rate-dependent, so vasodilatation from anaesthesia or tachycardia is poorly tolerated.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: Physiology - Cardiovascular
stem: Which of the following best describes the effect of a left-to-right shunt on pulmonary blood flow?

options.C: No change in pulmonary blood flow

why_correct: Correct. In a left-to-right shunt, blood from the systemic circulation (left side) enters the pulmonary circulation (right side) and passes through the lungs again. This increases pulmonary blood flow and can lead to pulmonary hypertension and right heart failure if uncorrected.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. A left-to-right shunt (e.g., atrial septal defect, ventricular septal defect, patent ductus arteriosus) causes oxygenated blood to recirculate through the lungs, increasing pulmonary blood flow.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. A left-to-right shunt increases pulmonary blood flow by recirculating oxygenated blood through the lungs.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. While a left-to-right shunt can eventually lead to decreased systemic output, the primary effect is increased pulmonary blood flow.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Cyanosis occurs with right-to-left shunts, where deoxygenated blood enters the systemic circulation. Left-to-right shunts are typically acyanotic, at least until Eisenmenger syndrome develops.

exam_trap: Option E catches candidates who equate any shunt with cyanosis; left-to-right shunts are acyanotic until pulmonary hypertension reverses the flow in Eisenmenger syndrome.
takeaway: Left-to-right shunt (ASD, VSD, PDA) → increased pulmonary blood flow; acyanotic.
thinking: Left-sided pressures exceed right-sided pressures ↓ the shunt carries oxygenated blood from left to right ↓ that blood passes through the lungs again ↓ Increased pulmonary blood flow
pearl: Long-standing large left-to-right shunts cause pulmonary vascular remodelling; once pulmonary pressure exceeds systemic pressure the flow reverses (Eisenmenger syndrome) and defect closure becomes contraindicated.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: Physiology - Respiratory
stem: Which of the following best describes the effect of increased airway resistance on ventilation?

options.C: Increased airway resistance has no effect on ventilation
options.D: Increased airway resistance increases lung compliance
options.E: Increased airway resistance shortens expiratory time

correct_answer: B. Increased airway resistance decreases ventilation
why_correct: Correct. Airway resistance is determined by the radius of the airways (Poiseuille's law). Increased resistance (e.g., bronchoconstriction, mucus plugging) reduces airflow and decreases ventilation. This leads to air trapping, hypercapnia, and hypoxaemia.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Increased airway resistance (e.g., asthma, COPD) makes it harder to move air into and out of the lungs, decreasing ventilation.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Airway resistance is a major determinant of ventilation. Increased resistance decreases airflow.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Airway resistance and lung compliance are separate properties; increased airway resistance does not increase compliance. In COPD airway resistance is raised, and in emphysema compliance is also increased, but because of loss of elastic tissue rather than because of the raised resistance.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Increased airway resistance prolongs expiratory time due to slower airflow and can cause air trapping (dynamic hyperinflation) if expiration is incomplete before the next breath; it does not shorten expiratory time.

exam_trap: Shortened expiratory time (E) is chosen, but slower airflow prolongs expiration and can cause air trapping and dynamic hyperinflation.
takeaway: Increased airway resistance → reduced airflow and ventilation, prolonged expiration and air trapping.
thinking: Increased airway resistance, as in bronchoconstriction or mucus plugging ↓ resistance rises steeply as airway radius falls ↓ airflow for a given driving pressure falls ↓ less air moves in and out of the lungs ↓ Increased airway resistance decreases ventilation
pearl: Because resistance varies inversely with the fourth power of radius, halving airway radius increases resistance about sixteen-fold, which is why a narrow endotracheal tube or modest bronchospasm greatly increases work of breathing.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: Physiology - Respiratory
stem: Which of the following best describes the effect of a pneumothorax on lung volume?

options.A: Increased lung volume on the affected side
options.B: Decreased lung volume on the affected side
options.D: Increased lung volume on both sides
options.E: Tracheal deviation towards the affected side

correct_answer: B. Decreased lung volume on the affected side
why_correct: Correct. In a pneumothorax, air enters the pleural space, increasing intrapleural pressure and causing the lung to collapse. This decreases lung volume on the affected side. If tension pneumothorax develops, it can compress the mediastinum and impair venous return, causing cardiovascular collapse.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. A pneumothorax causes air to accumulate in the pleural space, collapsing the lung and decreasing lung volume on the affected side.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. A pneumothorax causes lung collapse and decreased lung volume on the affected side.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. A pneumothorax affects only the affected side, causing decreased lung volume. The contralateral lung may be unaffected or may hyperinflate in compensation.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. In a tension pneumothorax, mediastinal structures, including the trachea, are pushed away from the affected side, not towards it.

exam_trap: Option E reverses the sign: a tension pneumothorax pushes the trachea away from the affected side; deviation towards a side suggests collapse or previous pneumonectomy.
takeaway: Pneumothorax → loss of negative pleural pressure → ipsilateral lung collapse.
thinking: Air enters the pleural space ↓ the negative intrapleural pressure is lost ↓ the lung collapses inwards under its own elastic recoil ↓ Decreased lung volume on the affected side
pearl: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis needing immediate decompression; current ATLS teaching favours the fourth or fifth intercostal space just anterior to the mid-axillary line in adults.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: Physiology - Renal
stem: Which of the following best describes the effect of furosemide (frusemide) on urine output?

options.A: It decreases urine output by increasing sodium reabsorption
options.B: It increases urine output by inhibiting sodium reabsorption in the loop of Henle
options.C: It increases urine output by inhibiting sodium reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule
options.D: It decreases urine output by inhibiting ADH release
options.E: It increases urine output by inhibiting carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule

correct_answer: B. It increases urine output by inhibiting sodium reabsorption in the loop of Henle
why_correct: Correct. Furosemide is a loop diuretic that inhibits the Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle. This reduces sodium reabsorption, leading to increased sodium and water excretion (diuresis). It is used in heart failure, pulmonary oedema, and hypertension.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Furosemide increases urine output. It does not increase sodium reabsorption.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Thiazide diuretics inhibit sodium reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule. Furosemide acts on the loop of Henle.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Furosemide increases urine output. It does not inhibit ADH release.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Inhibition of carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule is the mechanism of acetazolamide, not furosemide, which acts on the Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporter in the loop of Henle.

exam_trap: Option C describes thiazides; both increase urine output, but furosemide acts on the thick ascending limb, which is why it is the more potent diuretic.
takeaway: Furosemide → blocks NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb → potent natriuresis.
thinking: Furosemide is a loop diuretic ↓ it blocks NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb ↓ a large sodium load is delivered distally ↓ natriuresis and diuresis follow ↓ It increases urine output by inhibiting sodium reabsorption in the loop of Henle
pearl: Loop diuretics cause hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia and, at high intravenous doses, ototoxicity, particularly when combined with aminoglycosides.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: Physiology - Renal
stem: Which of the following best describes the effect of angiotensin II on blood pressure?

options.A: It decreases blood pressure by causing vasodilation
options.B: It increases blood pressure by causing vasoconstriction and sodium retention
options.C: It decreases blood pressure by inhibiting aldosterone release
options.D: It has no effect on blood pressure
options.E: It increases blood pressure solely by stimulating ADH release

correct_answer: B. It increases blood pressure by causing vasoconstriction and sodium retention
why_correct: Correct. Angiotensin II is a potent vasoconstrictor that increases systemic vascular resistance. It also stimulates aldosterone release, which increases sodium and water reabsorption in the kidney, increasing blood volume. Both effects increase blood pressure.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Angiotensin II increases blood pressure by causing vasoconstriction, not vasodilation.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Angiotensin II stimulates aldosterone release, not inhibits it.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Angiotensin II is a major regulator of blood pressure. It increases it.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Although angiotensin II can stimulate ADH release, its principal pressor actions are direct vasoconstriction and aldosterone-mediated sodium retention; it does not act solely via ADH.

exam_trap: Option E catches candidates who remember that angiotensin II releases ADH, but 'solely' makes it wrong; its main pressor effects are vasoconstriction and aldosterone release.
takeaway: Angiotensin II → vasoconstriction + aldosterone (+ ADH, thirst) → raised blood pressure.
thinking: Angiotensin II is formed by ACE ↓ it directly constricts arterioles, raising systemic vascular resistance ↓ it stimulates aldosterone for sodium and water retention, plus ADH and thirst ↓ It increases blood pressure by causing vasoconstriction and sodium retention
pearl: ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers are often withheld on the morning of major surgery because they predispose to hypotension after induction of anaesthesia.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: Physiology - Endocrine
stem: Which of the following best describes the effect of insulin on blood glucose?

options.A: It increases blood glucose by promoting glycogenolysis
options.B: It decreases blood glucose by promoting glucose uptake and glycogen synthesis
options.C: It increases blood glucose by promoting gluconeogenesis
options.D: It has no effect on blood glucose
options.E: It increases blood glucose by stimulating lipolysis in adipose tissue

correct_answer: B. It decreases blood glucose by promoting glucose uptake and glycogen synthesis
why_correct: Correct. Insulin is an anabolic hormone secreted by the beta cells of the pancreas. It decreases blood glucose by promoting glucose uptake in muscle and adipose tissue (via GLUT4 translocation), stimulating glycogen synthesis in the liver and muscle, and inhibiting gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Insulin decreases blood glucose. It promotes glycogen synthesis, not glycogenolysis. Glucagon promotes glycogenolysis.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Insulin inhibits gluconeogenesis. Glucagon and cortisol promote gluconeogenesis.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Insulin is the primary hormone responsible for lowering blood glucose.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Insulin inhibits lipolysis in adipose tissue by inhibiting hormone-sensitive lipase; it does not stimulate lipolysis or increase blood glucose in this way. Lipolysis is promoted by glucagon, cortisol, and catecholamines.

exam_trap: Option E is a decoy: insulin inhibits hormone-sensitive lipase and so suppresses lipolysis; uncontrolled lipolysis is what drives ketoacidosis in insulin deficiency.
takeaway: Insulin lowers glucose: GLUT4 uptake, glycogen synthesis, and inhibition of gluconeogenesis and lipolysis.
thinking: Insulin is the anabolic fed-state hormone ↓ GLUT4 moves to the membrane in muscle and fat ↓ glycogen synthesis rises while gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis fall ↓ It decreases blood glucose by promoting glucose uptake and glycogen synthesis
pearl: Perioperative variable-rate intravenous insulin infusions are run with substrate glucose and potassium, because insulin drives potassium into cells and can cause hypokalaemia and hypoglycaemia.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: Physiology - Endocrine
stem: Which of the following best describes the effect of glucagon on blood glucose?

options.A: It increases blood glucose by promoting glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis
options.B: It decreases blood glucose by promoting glycogen synthesis
options.C: It decreases blood glucose by promoting glucose uptake
options.D: It has no effect on blood glucose
options.E: It decreases blood glucose by inhibiting glycogenolysis

correct_answer: A. It increases blood glucose by promoting glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis
why_correct: Correct. Glucagon is secreted by the alpha cells of the pancreas in response to hypoglycaemia. It increases blood glucose by promoting glycogenolysis (breakdown of glycogen to glucose) and gluconeogenesis (synthesis of glucose from amino acids and glycerol) in the liver. It also promotes lipolysis and ketogenesis.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. Glucagon increases blood glucose. It promotes glycogenolysis, not glycogen synthesis. Insulin promotes glycogen synthesis.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Glucagon increases blood glucose. It does not promote glucose uptake. Insulin promotes glucose uptake.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Glucagon is a major regulator of blood glucose. It increases it.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Glucagon promotes, rather than inhibits, glycogenolysis. Inhibition of glycogenolysis is not a recognised action of glucagon.

exam_trap: Options B, C and E each describe insulin-like actions that lower glucose, whereas glucagon is a counter-regulatory hormone that raises it.
takeaway: Glucagon (alpha cells) → hepatic glycogenolysis + gluconeogenesis → raised glucose.
thinking: Low blood glucose ↓ pancreatic alpha cells release glucagon ↓ glucagon acts mainly on the liver ↓ promoting glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis ↓ It increases blood glucose by promoting glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis
pearl: Intramuscular glucagon reverses hypoglycaemia only if liver glycogen is available, so it works poorly in starvation, alcohol excess and advanced liver disease.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: Physiology - Gastrointestinal
stem: Which of the following best describes the function of gastric intrinsic factor?

options.A: It aids in the digestion of proteins
options.B: It aids in the absorption of vitamin B12
options.C: It aids in the absorption of iron
options.D: It aids in the digestion of fats
options.E: It aids in the absorption of folate

correct_answer: B. It aids in the absorption of vitamin B12
why_correct: Correct. Intrinsic factor is secreted by parietal cells in the stomach. It binds to vitamin B12 (cobalamin) in the small intestine, allowing its absorption in the terminal ileum. Loss of intrinsic factor (e.g., pernicious anaemia, gastrectomy) leads to vitamin B12 deficiency and megaloblastic anaemia.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Protein digestion is carried out by pepsin and pancreatic proteases. Intrinsic factor does not digest proteins.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Iron is absorbed in the duodenum via DMT1 and exported into the blood by ferroportin, then carried by transferrin. Intrinsic factor is specific for vitamin B12.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Fat digestion is carried out by lipases and bile salts. Intrinsic factor does not digest fats.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Folate absorption occurs in the jejunum via specific folate transporters and does not require intrinsic factor, which is specific to vitamin B12 absorption in the terminal ileum.

exam_trap: Option E (folate) traps candidates because both deficiencies cause megaloblastic anaemia, but folate is absorbed in the jejunum without intrinsic factor.
takeaway: Intrinsic factor (parietal cells) → vitamin B12 absorption in the terminal ileum.
thinking: Intrinsic factor is secreted by parietal cells ↓ it binds vitamin B12 in the duodenum ↓ the complex is absorbed by receptors in the terminal ileum ↓ It aids in the absorption of vitamin B12
pearl: Terminal ileal resection or disease causes B12 deficiency despite normal intrinsic factor, because the receptors that absorb the intrinsic factor-B12 complex are lost.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: Physiology - Gastrointestinal
stem: Which of the following best describes the function of the migrating motor complex (MMC)?

options.A: It propels food through the gastrointestinal tract during a meal
options.B: It clears residual debris from the gastrointestinal tract between meals
options.E: It is mediated primarily by the parasympathetic nervous system via the vagus nerve

correct_answer: B. It clears residual debris from the gastrointestinal tract between meals
why_correct: Correct. The migrating motor complex (MMC) is a cyclic pattern of electrical and motor activity in the gastrointestinal tract that occurs during fasting (between meals). It consists of four phases and its primary function is to clear residual debris, bacteria, and secretions from the stomach and small intestine, preventing bacterial overgrowth.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. During a meal, peristaltic contractions propel food through the gastrointestinal tract. The MMC occurs between meals.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Gastric acid secretion is regulated by gastrin, histamine, and vagal stimulation. The MMC does not directly regulate acid secretion.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Pancreatic enzyme secretion is stimulated by cholecystokinin (CCK) and vagal stimulation. The MMC is primarily a motility pattern.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. The migrating motor complex persists after vagotomy and is primarily regulated by the hormone motilin, released from enteroendocrine cells in the duodenum, rather than being vagally mediated.

exam_trap: Option E traps candidates because the vagus drives much gut motility, but the MMC persists after vagotomy and is driven mainly by motilin.
takeaway: MMC = fasting housekeeping wave driven by motilin; interrupted by feeding.
thinking: The MMC occurs in the fasting state ↓ cyclical contraction bursts sweep from stomach to terminal ileum ↓ they clear debris, bacteria and secretions ↓ preventing small bowel bacterial overgrowth ↓ It clears residual debris from the gastrointestinal tract between meals
pearl: Erythromycin is a motilin receptor agonist that triggers MMC-like contractions and is used as a prokinetic in gastroparesis and feed intolerance in critical care.

subject: Pathology
title: Pathology: Pathology - General
stem: Which of the following best describes the process of metaplasia?

options.A: Reversible replacement of one differentiated cell type with another
options.E: Programmed cell death of individual cells

correct_answer: A. Reversible replacement of one differentiated cell type with another
why_correct: Correct. Metaplasia is the reversible replacement of one mature cell type with another mature cell type that is better adapted to the environment. For example, squamous metaplasia in the respiratory tract of smokers (columnar to squamous epithelium) and Barrett's oesophagus (squamous to columnar epithelium). It is an adaptive response but can predispose to malignancy.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. This describes anaplasia, which is a feature of malignant tumours. Metaplasia is reversible.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. This describes hyperplasia. Metaplasia involves a change in cell type, not an increase in cell number.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. This describes hypertrophy. Metaplasia involves a change in cell type, not cell size.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. This describes apoptosis, a regulated form of cell death. Metaplasia refers to a change in cell type, not cell death.

exam_trap: Candidates confuse metaplasia with anaplasia (B) or hyperplasia (C), but metaplasia is a reversible change of one mature cell type to another.
takeaway: Metaplasia = reversible mature-to-mature cell type change, e.g. Barrett oesophagus.
thinking: Metaplasia ↓ one mature cell type replaced by another ↓ adaptive and potentially reversible ↓ Reversible replacement of one differentiated cell type with another
pearl: Metaplasia is the soil for neoplasia: Barrett's columnar metaplasia predisposes to oesophageal adenocarcinoma and squamous metaplasia of bronchial epithelium predisposes to squamous cell lung cancer.

subject: Pathology
title: Pathology: Pathology - General
stem: Which of the following best describes the process of dysplasia?

options.A: Reversible replacement of one cell type with another
options.B: Disordered growth and maturation of cells, often a precursor to malignancy

correct_answer: B. Disordered growth and maturation of cells, often a precursor to malignancy
why_correct: Correct. Dysplasia is characterised by disordered growth and maturation of cells, with pleomorphism (variation in size and shape), hyperchromasia (dark nuclei), and increased mitotic activity. It is often a precursor to malignancy, particularly in cervical, oral, and oesophageal epithelium. It is potentially reversible if the stimulus is removed.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. This describes metaplasia. Dysplasia involves disordered growth and maturation, not just a change in cell type.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. This describes hyperplasia. Dysplasia involves disordered growth, not just increased cell number.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. This describes apoptosis. Dysplasia is a pathological change in cell growth and maturation.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. This describes anaplasia, a feature of malignant, undifferentiated tumours. Dysplasia is a lesser, potentially reversible disorder of growth and maturation that may precede, but is distinct from, anaplasia.

exam_trap: Candidates choose metaplasia (A) or anaplasia (E), but dysplasia is disordered growth and maturation, not a simple cell-type switch or established loss of differentiation.
takeaway: Dysplasia = disordered growth and maturation within the basement membrane; a premalignant change.
thinking: Dysplasia ↓ disordered growth and maturation with pleomorphism and hyperchromasia ↓ confined within the basement membrane ↓ potential precursor to malignancy ↓ Disordered growth and maturation of cells, often a precursor to malignancy
pearl: High-grade dysplasia in Barrett's oesophagus is usually treated endoscopically with resection of visible lesions and ablation, because of its high risk of progression to adenocarcinoma.

subject: Pathology
title: Pathology: Pathology - Haematology
stem: A 6-year-old boy presents with recurrent haemarthroses. His maternal uncle has a similar bleeding problem. Blood tests show a prolonged APTT with normal PT and normal platelet count. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Correct. Haemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency) causes a prolonged APTT with normal PT and normal platelet count. It is an X-linked recessive disorder that presents with prolonged bleeding after trauma or surgery, haemarthroses, and muscle haematomas.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. Vitamin K deficiency causes a prolonged PT (and eventually APTT). Factor VII has the shortest half-life, so PT is prolonged first.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Von Willebrand disease causes a prolonged APTT (due to decreased factor VIII) and prolonged bleeding time, but PT is normal. Platelet count is normal.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. ITP causes a low platelet count (thrombocytopenia) with normal PT and APTT. It presents with petechiae and bruising.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. DIC typically causes prolongation of both PT and APTT, together with thrombocytopenia and low fibrinogen, unlike the isolated APTT prolongation with normal platelet count and PT seen here.

exam_trap: Von Willebrand disease can also prolong the APTT, but it is usually autosomal and causes mucocutaneous bleeding rather than recurrent haemarthroses in a boy.
takeaway: Haemarthroses + affected maternal male relative + isolated prolonged APTT = haemophilia A (factor VIII).
thinking: Boy with recurrent haemarthroses ↓ affected maternal uncle suggests X-linked inheritance ↓ isolated prolonged APTT with normal PT and platelets ↓ intrinsic pathway factor deficiency ↓ Haemophilia A
pearl: Haemophilia B (factor IX deficiency) is clinically identical and also X-linked, so specific factor assays are needed; surgery requires factor replacement planned with a haemophilia centre.

subject: Pathology
title: Pathology: Pathology - Haematology
stem: A patient presents with a thrombotic tendency, and blood tests show a prolonged APTT that does not correct with the addition of normal plasma. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Correct. Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) is an autoimmune condition characterised by arterial and venous thrombosis, recurrent fetal loss, and thrombocytopenia. The lupus anticoagulant prolongs the phospholipid-dependent APTT in vitro, and the prolongation does not correct on mixing with normal plasma because it is caused by an inhibitor rather than a factor deficiency. Despite the prolonged APTT, the patient is prothrombotic in vivo.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Factor V Leiden mutation causes activated protein C resistance and a thrombotic tendency. It does not cause a prolonged APTT. PT and APTT are typically normal.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Protein C deficiency causes a thrombotic tendency. It does not cause a prolonged APTT. PT and APTT are typically normal.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Antithrombin deficiency causes a thrombotic tendency. It does not cause a prolonged APTT. PT and APTT are typically normal.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Factor VIII deficiency causes a bleeding tendency, not a thrombotic tendency, so it is inconsistent with the clinical picture described here.

exam_trap: Factor VIII deficiency also prolongs the APTT, but it corrects with normal plasma and causes bleeding, not thrombosis.
takeaway: Prolonged APTT that does not correct on mixing + thrombosis = lupus anticoagulant (antiphospholipid syndrome).
thinking: Thrombotic tendency ↓ prolonged APTT ↓ no correction on mixing with normal plasma, so an inhibitor is present ↓ lupus anticoagulant prolongs clotting tests in vitro but is prothrombotic in vivo ↓ Antiphospholipid syndrome
pearl: Thrombotic antiphospholipid syndrome needs long-term anticoagulation, usually with warfarin; direct oral anticoagulants are not recommended in high-risk, triple-positive disease.

subject: Pathology
title: Pathology: Pathology - Endocrine
stem: A patient presents with hypertension, hypokalaemia, and metabolic alkalosis. Plasma aldosterone is elevated, and plasma renin is suppressed. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Correct. Conn's syndrome is caused by an aldosterone-producing adenoma (or bilateral adrenal hyperplasia). It presents with hypertension, hypokalaemia, and metabolic alkalosis. Plasma aldosterone is elevated, and plasma renin is suppressed (because the excess aldosterone causes sodium and water retention, which suppresses renin release).

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. Secondary hyperaldosteronism (e.g., renal artery stenosis, heart failure, cirrhosis) causes elevated aldosterone and elevated renin. In primary hyperaldosteronism, renin is suppressed.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Cushing's syndrome causes hypertension, weight gain, moon face, and hyperglycaemia. It is not typically associated with hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis unless there is concurrent mineralocorticoid excess.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Phaeochromocytoma causes episodic hypertension, palpitations, sweating, and headache. It is not typically associated with hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Bartter syndrome causes hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis due to a renal tubular defect, but patients are typically normotensive with elevated, not suppressed, renin and aldosterone, unlike Conn's syndrome.

exam_trap: Candidates choose secondary hyperaldosteronism (B) because aldosterone is high, but in secondary disease renin is also high; suppressed renin indicates primary hyperaldosteronism.
takeaway: High aldosterone + low renin = primary hyperaldosteronism; high both = secondary.
thinking: Hypertension with hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis ↓ aldosterone high ↓ renin suppressed means autonomous adrenal secretion ↓ Conn's syndrome (primary hyperaldosteronism)
pearl: The aldosterone-to-renin ratio is the screening test, and adrenal vein sampling is used to distinguish a unilateral adenoma, treated by laparoscopic adrenalectomy, from bilateral hyperplasia, treated with mineralocorticoid antagonists.

subject: Pathology
title: Pathology: Pathology - Endocrine
stem: A patient presents with weight gain, moon face, buffalo hump, and hyperglycaemia. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Correct. Cushing's syndrome is caused by excess cortisol. It presents with weight gain (central obesity), moon face, buffalo hump, purple striae, easy bruising, hyperglycaemia, hypertension, and osteoporosis. Causes include exogenous steroids (most common), pituitary adenoma (Cushing's disease), adrenal adenoma, and ectopic ACTH production.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Conn's syndrome causes hypertension, hypokalaemia, and metabolic alkalosis. It does not cause weight gain, moon face, or buffalo hump.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Addison's disease (primary adrenal insufficiency) causes weight loss, hypotension, hyperkalaemia, and metabolic acidosis. It is the opposite of Cushing's syndrome.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Phaeochromocytoma causes episodic hypertension, palpitations, sweating, and headache. It does not cause weight gain, moon face, or buffalo hump.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Metabolic syndrome features central obesity, hypertension, and hyperglycaemia, but does not produce the moon face, buffalo hump, or purple striae characteristic of cortisol excess in Cushing's syndrome.

exam_trap: Candidates choose metabolic syndrome (E) because it shares obesity and hyperglycaemia, but moon face, buffalo hump and purple striae point to cortisol excess.
takeaway: Moon face, buffalo hump and striae = Cushing's syndrome; exogenous steroids are the commonest cause.
thinking: Weight gain, moon face, buffalo hump ↓ hyperglycaemia ↓ glucocorticoid excess ↓ Cushing's syndrome
pearl: Patients on long-term steroids have a suppressed hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis and need perioperative steroid cover, because abrupt withdrawal can precipitate an adrenal crisis.

subject: Pathology
title: Pathology: Pathology - Renal
stem: A patient presents with haematuria, hypertension, and oliguria. Renal biopsy shows diffuse endocapillary proliferation with subepithelial humps on electron microscopy. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Correct. Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is a type III hypersensitivity reaction that occurs 1-3 weeks after a streptococcal infection. It presents with nephritic syndrome: haematuria (cola-coloured urine), hypertension, oliguria, and oedema. Renal biopsy shows diffuse endocapillary proliferation with subepithelial humps on electron microscopy (immune complex deposits).

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. IgA nephropathy shows mesangial deposition of IgA on immunofluorescence. It presents with recurrent haematuria, often after upper respiratory infections. It does not show subepithelial humps.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Membranous nephropathy causes nephrotic syndrome and shows spike and dome deposits on electron microscopy. It does not present with haematuria, hypertension, and oliguria.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Minimal change disease causes nephrotic syndrome and shows normal glomeruli on light microscopy with effacement of podocyte foot processes on electron microscopy. It does not show subepithelial humps.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis is characterised histologically by crescent formation, not diffuse endocapillary proliferation with subepithelial humps, which is the classic finding in post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.

exam_trap: Candidates choose membranous nephropathy (C) because both have subepithelial deposits, but membranous gives spike and dome with nephrotic syndrome; humps with nephritic syndrome mean post-streptococcal.
takeaway: Subepithelial humps = post-streptococcal GN; spike and dome = membranous nephropathy.
thinking: Nephritic syndrome ↓ diffuse endocapillary proliferation ↓ subepithelial humps on electron microscopy ↓ Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis
pearl: Subepithelial humps are immune complex deposits, and the accompanying low complement (C3) helps separate post-infectious glomerulonephritis from IgA nephropathy, in which complement is usually normal.

subject: Pathology
title: Pathology: Pathology - Gastrointestinal
stem: A patient with chronic gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD) undergoes endoscopy. Biopsy shows columnar epithelium with goblet cells in the lower oesophagus. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Correct. Barrett's oesophagus is a metaplastic change in the lower oesophagus, where the normal squamous epithelium is replaced by columnar epithelium with goblet cells (intestinal metaplasia). It is caused by chronic gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD). It is a premalignant condition that increases the risk of oesophageal adenocarcinoma.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Squamous cell carcinoma is a malignant tumour of the oesophagus. It does not show columnar epithelium with goblet cells.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Achalasia is a motility disorder characterised by failure of the lower oesophageal sphincter to relax. It does not cause columnar metaplasia.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Oesophageal varices are dilated submucosal veins caused by portal hypertension. They do not cause columnar metaplasia.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Reflux oesophagitis shows mucosal inflammation and basal cell hyperplasia in the native squamous epithelium; it does not show columnar epithelium with goblet cells, which defines the intestinal metaplasia of Barrett's oesophagus.

exam_trap: Candidates choose reflux oesophagitis (E) because GORD is the cause, but oesophagitis keeps squamous epithelium; columnar epithelium with goblet cells defines Barrett metaplasia.
takeaway: Columnar epithelium with goblet cells in the lower oesophagus = Barrett's oesophagus (intestinal metaplasia).
thinking: Chronic GORD ↓ columnar epithelium with goblet cells in the lower oesophagus ↓ intestinal metaplasia ↓ Barrett's oesophagus
pearl: Barrett's oesophagus requires endoscopic surveillance with biopsies, and the interval depends on segment length and the presence of dysplasia.

subject: Pathology
title: Pathology: Pathology - Gastrointestinal
stem: A patient presents with a colorectal polyp. Biopsy shows a tubular adenoma with low-grade dysplasia. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
why_correct: Correct. Tubular adenomas with low-grade dysplasia are premalignant lesions that should be removed endoscopically (polypectomy). This prevents progression to colorectal cancer. Surveillance colonoscopy is recommended based on the size, number, and histology of the polyps.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Adenomas are premalignant lesions. They should be removed to prevent progression to colorectal cancer.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Chemotherapy is not indicated for a benign adenoma. It is used for advanced colorectal cancer.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Radiotherapy is not indicated for a benign adenoma. It is used for rectal cancer.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Surgical colectomy is not indicated for a small adenomatous polyp with low-grade dysplasia; endoscopic polypectomy is sufficient, with surgery reserved for polyps not amenable to endoscopic removal or those with invasive malignancy.

exam_trap: Candidates choose observation (A) because low-grade dysplasia sounds harmless, or colectomy (E), but adenomas should be removed endoscopically to interrupt the adenoma-carcinoma sequence.
takeaway: Colorectal adenoma → endoscopic polypectomy plus risk-stratified surveillance.
thinking: Colorectal tubular adenoma ↓ low-grade dysplasia means premalignant but not invasive ↓ adenoma-carcinoma sequence is interrupted by polypectomy ↓ Endoscopic resection
pearl: After complete polypectomy, the need for and timing of surveillance colonoscopy depend on the number, size and histology of the adenomas removed.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: Anatomy - Upper Limb
stem: A patient presents with weakness in elbow extension and sensory loss over the posterior forearm. Which nerve is most likely injured?
why_correct: Correct. The radial nerve supplies the triceps (elbow extension) and the wrist and finger extensors. It provides sensation over the posterior arm, posterior forearm, and dorsal lateral aspect of the hand. Injury causes weakness in elbow extension, wrist drop, and sensory loss over the posterior forearm.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. The musculocutaneous nerve supplies the coracobrachialis, biceps brachii, and brachialis. It is responsible for elbow flexion and sensation over the lateral forearm.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. The median nerve supplies the forearm flexors and thenar muscles. Injury causes loss of thumb opposition and weakness in forearm pronation.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. The ulnar nerve supplies the intrinsic hand muscles. Injury causes claw hand and sensory loss over the medial one and a half fingers.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. The axillary nerve supplies the deltoid and teres minor, producing shoulder abduction and sensation over the lateral shoulder; it does not affect elbow extension or posterior forearm sensation.

exam_trap: The axillary nerve (E) is chosen because it arises from the posterior cord with the radial nerve, but it supplies deltoid and teres minor, not triceps.
takeaway: Weak elbow extension + posterior forearm numbness = radial nerve lesion high in the arm.
thinking: Weak elbow extension = triceps ↓ posterior forearm numbness = posterior cutaneous nerve of the forearm ↓ both are radial nerve branches given off high in the arm ↓ Radial nerve
pearl: In midshaft humeral fractures the radial nerve is injured in the spiral groove below most triceps branches, so elbow extension is usually preserved; weak triceps implies a higher lesion, as in axillary crutch palsy.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: Anatomy - Upper Limb
stem: During a shoulder arthroscopy, the surgeon identifies the rotator cuff muscles. Which muscle is NOT part of the rotator cuff?
why_correct: Correct. Teres major is NOT part of the rotator cuff. The rotator cuff muscles are: supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, and subscapularis (SITS). Teres major is a separate muscle that adducts and internally rotates the shoulder.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Supraspinatus is one of the four rotator cuff muscles. It initiates shoulder abduction (first 15 degrees) and stabilises the glenohumeral joint.
why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. Infraspinatus is one of the four rotator cuff muscles. It is responsible for external rotation of the shoulder.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Subscapularis is one of the four rotator cuff muscles. It is responsible for internal rotation of the shoulder.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Teres minor is one of the four rotator cuff muscles. It externally rotates the shoulder and is supplied by the axillary nerve.

exam_trap: Teres minor is wrongly excluded because of its similar name; teres minor is a cuff muscle supplied by the axillary nerve, whereas teres major is not part of the cuff.
takeaway: Rotator cuff = supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor and subscapularis; teres major is not a cuff muscle.
thinking: Rotator cuff = SITS ↓ supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor and subscapularis blend with the joint capsule ↓ teres major inserts on the medial lip of the intertubercular sulcus and does not reinforce the capsule ↓ Teres major
pearl: Supraspinatus is the cuff tendon most often torn or impinged because it passes beneath the coracoacromial arch, typically producing a painful arc of abduction.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: Anatomy - Lower Limb
stem: A patient presents with weakness in hip abduction and a positive Trendelenburg sign. Which nerve is most likely injured?
why_correct: Correct. The superior gluteal nerve supplies gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, and tensor fasciae latae. These muscles are responsible for hip abduction and stabilisation of the pelvis during walking. Injury causes weakness in hip abduction and a positive Trendelenburg sign (pelvis drops on the contralateral side when standing on the affected leg).

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. The femoral nerve supplies the quadriceps (knee extension) and iliopsoas (hip flexion). Injury causes weakness in knee extension and hip flexion.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. The inferior gluteal nerve supplies gluteus maximus, which is responsible for hip extension (e.g., climbing stairs, standing from a sitting position). Injury causes difficulty in these activities.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. The sciatic nerve supplies the posterior thigh, leg, and foot. Injury causes weakness in knee flexion, foot drop, and sensory loss below the knee.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. The obturator nerve supplies the hip adductors and provides sensation to the medial thigh; it is not involved in hip abduction and would not cause a Trendelenburg sign.

exam_trap: The inferior gluteal nerve (C) is chosen because the two gluteal nerves sound alike, but it supplies gluteus maximus for hip extension, not the abductors.
takeaway: Trendelenburg sign = superior gluteal nerve (gluteus medius and minimus); pelvis drops on the contralateral side.
thinking: Weak hip abduction ↓ positive Trendelenburg sign: pelvis drops to the opposite side on single-leg stance ↓ gluteus medius and minimus failing ↓ Superior gluteal nerve
pearl: The superior gluteal nerve runs between gluteus medius and minimus a short distance above the greater trochanter, so extending the split of gluteus medius too far proximally in the lateral approach to the hip can denervate the abductors.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: Anatomy - Lower Limb
stem: During a knee examination, the surgeon tests the integrity of the posterior cruciate ligament. Which of the following tests is most specific for posterior cruciate ligament injury?
why_correct: Correct. The posterior drawer test is used to assess the posterior cruciate ligament (PCL). It involves pushing the tibia backward with the knee flexed at 90 degrees. A positive test indicates PCL injury.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. The anterior drawer test is used to assess the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL). It involves pulling the tibia forward with the knee flexed at 90 degrees.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. The Lachman test is also used to assess the ACL. It is performed with the knee flexed at 20-30 degrees and is more sensitive than the anterior drawer test.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. The McMurray test is used to assess meniscal tears. It involves rotating the tibia with the knee flexed and extended.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. The valgus stress test assesses the integrity of the medial collateral ligament, not the posterior cruciate ligament.

exam_trap: The anterior drawer (A) can mislead when a sagging PCL-deficient tibia is pulled forward to neutral, mimicking the anterior laxity of an ACL tear.
takeaway: PCL = posterior drawer and posterior sag; ACL = Lachman and anterior drawer.
thinking: PCL resists posterior translation of the tibia ↓ with the knee at 90 degrees, push the tibia backwards ↓ anterior drawer and Lachman tests assess the ACL ↓ Posterior drawer test
pearl: Look for posterior sag of the tibia with both knees flexed to 90 degrees before an anterior drawer, because pulling a sagged PCL-deficient tibia forward to neutral can mimic a positive anterior drawer.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: Anatomy - Abdomen
stem: During a splenectomy, the surgeon ligates the splenic artery. From which vessel does the splenic artery arise?
why_correct: Correct. The coeliac trunk has three branches: left gastric artery, common hepatic artery, and splenic artery. The splenic artery runs along the superior border of the pancreas to supply the spleen. It also gives off the short gastric arteries and the left gastroepiploic artery.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. The splenic artery does not arise directly from the aorta. It arises from the coeliac trunk.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. The superior mesenteric artery arises from the aorta and supplies the midgut. It does not give rise to the splenic artery.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. The left gastric artery is a branch of the coeliac trunk. It supplies the stomach and lower oesophagus. It does not give rise to the splenic artery.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. The common hepatic artery is a separate branch of the coeliac trunk; it does not give rise to the splenic artery.

exam_trap: The left gastric (D) or common hepatic artery (E) is chosen as a parent vessel, but all three are sibling branches arising together from the coeliac trunk.
takeaway: Splenic artery = coeliac trunk branch along the upper border of the pancreas; gives short gastrics and left gastroepiploic.
thinking: Splenic artery ↓ one of the three coeliac trunk branches ↓ runs tortuously along the upper border of the pancreas to the splenic hilum ↓ Coeliac trunk
pearl: Splenic artery aneurysm is the commonest visceral artery aneurysm and carries a particular risk of rupture in pregnancy.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: Anatomy - Abdomen
stem: A patient presents with a femoral hernia. Which structure forms the posterior boundary of the femoral ring?
why_correct: Correct. The femoral ring has four boundaries: anterior (inguinal ligament), posterior (pectineal ligament), medial (lacunar ligament), and lateral (femoral vein). The pectineal ligament (of Cooper) forms the posterior boundary. It is a strong fibrous band along the pectineal line of the pubis.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. The inguinal ligament forms the anterior boundary of the femoral ring.
why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. The lacunar ligament forms the medial boundary of the femoral ring.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. The femoral vein forms the lateral boundary of the femoral ring.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. The iliopsoas muscle and its fascia lie lateral to the femoral sheath and are not part of the femoral ring boundaries.

exam_trap: The lacunar ligament (B) is chosen because it is the sharp edge that strangulates femoral hernias, but it forms the medial, not the posterior, boundary.
takeaway: Femoral ring: anterior inguinal, posterior pectineal, medial lacunar ligament, lateral femoral vein.
thinking: Femoral ring = upper opening of the femoral canal ↓ anterior inguinal ligament, medial lacunar ligament, lateral femoral vein ↓ posterior boundary is the pectineal ligament on the pecten pubis ↓ Pectineal ligament
pearl: In open femoral hernia repair the ring is closed by suturing the inguinal ligament to the pectineal ligament, taking care not to narrow the femoral vein laterally.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: Anatomy - Head and Neck
stem: During a thyroidectomy, the surgeon identifies the recurrent laryngeal nerve. Which structure does the recurrent laryngeal nerve supply?

options.B: Intrinsic muscles of the larynx (except cricothyroid)
options.E: Vocal cord sensation above the vocal folds

correct_answer: B. Intrinsic muscles of the larynx (except cricothyroid)
why_correct: Correct. The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies all intrinsic muscles of the larynx except the cricothyroid. These muscles control vocal cord movement. Injury causes hoarseness due to vocal cord paralysis. Bilateral injury can cause airway obstruction.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. The cricothyroid muscle is supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve. It tenses the vocal cords.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. The pharyngeal constrictors are supplied by the pharyngeal plexus, which receives fibres from the vagus nerve (CN X) and glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX).
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. The tongue muscles are supplied by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII), except the palatoglossus, which is supplied by the vagus nerve.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Sensation above the vocal folds is supplied by the internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve. The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies sensation below the vocal folds and motor supply to the intrinsic laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid.

exam_trap: Cricothyroid (A) is chosen because it is an intrinsic laryngeal muscle, but it is the exception, supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve.
takeaway: RLN = all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid (external laryngeal nerve), plus sensation below the cords.
thinking: Recurrent laryngeal nerve ↓ motor to all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid ↓ also sensory below the vocal folds ↓ Intrinsic muscles of the larynx (except cricothyroid)
pearl: Posterior cricoarytenoid is the only abductor of the vocal folds, so bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy leaves both cords near the midline and can obstruct the airway despite a fair voice.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: Anatomy - Neuroanatomy
stem: A patient presents with a spinal cord injury. Which of the following tracts carries proprioception and vibration sensation?
why_correct: Correct. The dorsal columns (posterior columns) carry proprioception, vibration, and fine touch sensation. They are located in the posterior aspect of the spinal cord. Fibres ascend ipsilaterally to the medulla, where they cross the midline (medial lemniscus) and ascend to the thalamus.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. The corticospinal tract carries motor fibres from the motor cortex to the spinal cord. It is responsible for voluntary movement.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. The spinothalamic tract carries pain and temperature sensation. It is located in the anterolateral aspect of the spinal cord.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. The spinocerebellar tract carries proprioceptive information to the cerebellum for coordination of movement. It is not responsible for conscious proprioception or vibration sensation.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. The anterior spinothalamic tract carries crude touch and pressure sensation, not fine touch, proprioception, or vibration, which are carried by the dorsal columns.

exam_trap: The spinocerebellar tract (D) tempts because it carries proprioception, but this is unconscious proprioception to the cerebellum; conscious proprioception and vibration use the dorsal columns.
takeaway: Vibration and conscious proprioception = dorsal columns (ipsilateral in the cord, cross in the medulla).
thinking: Proprioception and vibration ↓ conscious discriminative sensation ↓ ascends ipsilaterally in the posterior columns and crosses in the medulla as the medial lemniscus ↓ Dorsal columns
pearl: Subacute combined degeneration from vitamin B12 deficiency and tabes dorsalis both damage the dorsal columns, producing sensory ataxia with a positive Romberg test.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: Physiology - Cardiovascular
stem: Which of the following best describes the effect of a sudden increase in blood pressure on heart rate?

options.E: Increased stroke volume via the Bainbridge reflex

correct_answer: B. Bradycardia due to parasympathetic activation
why_correct: Correct. A sudden increase in blood pressure is detected by baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch. This leads to increased afferent firing to the medulla, which increases parasympathetic outflow and decreases sympathetic outflow. The result is bradycardia and vasodilation, which help restore blood pressure.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. A sudden increase in blood pressure causes reflex bradycardia, not tachycardia. Sympathetic activation would increase heart rate.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. The baroreceptor reflex rapidly adjusts heart rate in response to blood pressure changes. There is always a compensatory change.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Sympathetic activation increases heart rate. Bradycardia is due to parasympathetic activation.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. This describes the Bainbridge reflex, triggered by increased venous return and atrial stretch, which causes tachycardia. It is distinct from the baroreceptor reflex triggered by increased arterial blood pressure, which causes reflex bradycardia.

exam_trap: Option E names the Bainbridge reflex, which responds to atrial stretch from increased venous return and causes tachycardia, not to a rise in arterial pressure.
takeaway: Raised arterial pressure → increased baroreceptor firing → vagal bradycardia.
thinking: Sudden rise in blood pressure ↓ more arterial stretch increases baroreceptor firing ↓ the medulla increases vagal and reduces sympathetic outflow ↓ the heart rate slows ↓ Bradycardia due to parasympathetic activation
pearl: Reflex bradycardia follows phenylephrine, a pure alpha-agonist used for hypotension under anaesthesia, which is why it is used cautiously in patients who are already bradycardic.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: Physiology - Cardiovascular
stem: Which of the following best describes the effect of adrenaline on the heart?

options.A: It decreases heart rate and contractility
options.B: It increases heart rate and contractility
options.C: It decreases heart rate and increases contractility
options.D: It has no effect on the heart
options.E: It causes vasoconstriction in all vascular beds via alpha-1 receptors

correct_answer: B. It increases heart rate and contractility
why_correct: Correct. Adrenaline (epinephrine) is a catecholamine that acts on beta-1 adrenergic receptors in the heart. It increases heart rate (positive chronotropy), contractility (positive inotropy), and conduction velocity (positive dromotropy). It also causes vasodilation in skeletal muscle via beta-2 receptors.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Adrenaline increases heart rate and contractility. It does not decrease them.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Adrenaline increases both heart rate and contractility.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Adrenaline has significant effects on the heart. It is a major regulator of cardiac function.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Adrenaline causes vasoconstriction via alpha-1 receptors in most vascular beds, but causes vasodilation in skeletal muscle vasculature via beta-2 receptors; it does not cause universal vasoconstriction.

exam_trap: Option E tempts because adrenaline is a vasopressor, but beta-2 receptors dilate skeletal muscle vessels, so its vasoconstriction is not universal.
takeaway: Adrenaline: beta-1 → faster, stronger heart; beta-2 → muscle vasodilatation; alpha-1 → vasoconstriction elsewhere.
thinking: Adrenaline acts on cardiac beta-1 receptors ↓ positive chronotropy and inotropy ↓ and faster AV conduction ↓ It increases heart rate and contractility
pearl: In anaphylaxis intramuscular adrenaline is first-line because alpha-1 vasoconstriction reverses hypotension and oedema while beta-2 effects relax bronchial smooth muscle.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: Physiology - Respiratory
stem: Which of the following best describes the effect of increased lung compliance on ventilation?

options.A: Increased compliance makes it easier to expand the lungs
options.B: Increased compliance makes it harder to expand the lungs
options.E: Increased compliance is characteristic of pulmonary fibrosis

correct_answer: A. Increased compliance makes it easier to expand the lungs
why_correct: Correct. Compliance is the measure of the lung's ability to stretch and expand. Increased compliance means the lungs are easier to expand for a given change in pressure. This is seen in emphysema (destruction of elastic tissue) and normal ageing. However, increased compliance can lead to reduced elastic recoil and air trapping.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. Decreased compliance (e.g., pulmonary fibrosis, respiratory distress syndrome) makes it harder to expand the lungs.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Increased compliance does not necessarily decrease tidal volume. It makes the lungs easier to expand.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Compliance and airway resistance are separate properties. Increased compliance does not directly increase airway resistance.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Pulmonary fibrosis is characterised by decreased, not increased, lung compliance due to increased collagen deposition and stiffening of lung tissue.

exam_trap: Option E attracts candidates who link fibrosis with abnormal compliance, but fibrosis stiffens the lung and decreases compliance; emphysema is the condition that increases it.
takeaway: Compliance up = emphysema, ageing; compliance down = fibrosis, ARDS, pulmonary oedema.
thinking: Compliance = change in volume per unit change in pressure ↓ high compliance means a given pressure produces more volume ↓ the lungs are easier to inflate ↓ but elastic recoil is reduced, as in emphysema ↓ Increased compliance makes it easier to expand the lungs
pearl: In emphysema high compliance with lost elastic recoil lets small airways collapse on expiration and trap gas, which lung volume reduction surgery aims to relieve by removing hyperinflated lung.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: Physiology - Respiratory
stem: Which of the following best describes the effect of a large pulmonary embolism on ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) matching?
correct_answer: A. Increased dead space (high V/Q ratio)
why_correct: Correct. A pulmonary embolism obstructs pulmonary blood flow to a region of the lung that is still being ventilated. This creates a high V/Q ratio (ventilation without perfusion), which is known as increased dead space. This impairs gas exchange and can cause hypoxaemia and hypercapnia.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. A shunt occurs when there is perfusion without ventilation (V/Q = 0). This is seen in atelectasis, pneumonia, and pulmonary oedema.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. A pulmonary embolism causes a V/Q mismatch by creating areas of high V/Q ratio (dead space).
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. A pulmonary embolism increases dead space (high V/Q ratio), not decreases it.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Pulmonary embolism typically increases the A-a gradient due to impaired gas exchange in the affected, poorly perfused but ventilated lung regions; it does not decrease it.

exam_trap: Option B attracts candidates because PE causes hypoxaemia, but shunt is perfusion without ventilation; the embolised segment is ventilated without perfusion, increasing dead space.
takeaway: PE → high V/Q (dead space); pneumonia or atelectasis → low V/Q or shunt.
thinking: Embolus blocks pulmonary arterial flow ↓ the affected alveoli are still ventilated ↓ ventilation without perfusion pushes V/Q towards infinity ↓ that ventilation is wasted ↓ Increased dead space (high V/Q ratio)
pearl: An intraoperative pulmonary embolism often causes an abrupt fall in end-tidal CO2, because dead-space ventilation dilutes exhaled CO2 and widens the arterial to end-tidal CO2 gradient.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: Physiology - Renal
stem: Which of the following best describes the effect of thiazide diuretics on calcium excretion?

options.C: They have no effect on calcium excretion
options.D: They increase calcium excretion only in hypercalcaemia
options.E: They are the diuretic of choice for calcium-containing renal stones because they increase calcium excretion

why_correct: Correct. Thiazide diuretics inhibit the Na+/Cl- cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule. This lowers intracellular sodium, which enhances basolateral sodium-calcium exchange and increases calcium reabsorption in the distal tubule. This reduces urinary calcium excretion and is useful in treating hypercalciuria and preventing recurrent calcium stones.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Thiazide diuretics decrease calcium excretion. They are used to treat hypercalciuria and prevent calcium kidney stones.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Thiazide diuretics have a significant effect on calcium excretion. They decrease it.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Thiazide diuretics decrease calcium excretion regardless of serum calcium levels.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Thiazides are indeed used to reduce the incidence of calcium-containing renal stones, but this is because they decrease, not increase, urinary calcium excretion by promoting reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule.

exam_trap: Option E is chosen because thiazides are used to prevent calcium stones, but they work by decreasing, not increasing, urinary calcium excretion.
takeaway: Thiazides ↓ urinary calcium; loop diuretics ↑ urinary calcium.
thinking: Thiazides block the Na+/Cl- cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule ↓ intracellular sodium falls ↓ basolateral Na+/Ca2+ exchange increases, enhancing calcium reabsorption ↓ urinary calcium falls ↓ They decrease calcium excretion
pearl: Thiazides can unmask hypercalcaemia, so a raised calcium in a patient on a thiazide should still prompt a PTH measurement to look for primary hyperparathyroidism.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: Physiology - Renal
stem: Which of the following best describes the effect of loop diuretics on calcium excretion?

options.C: They have no effect on calcium excretion
options.D: They decrease calcium excretion only in hypocalcaemia
