options.E: They are used therapeutically to treat hypocalcaemia by reducing renal calcium loss

why_correct: Correct. Loop diuretics (e.g., furosemide) inhibit the Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle. This reduces the positive lumen potential that normally drives calcium reabsorption. As a result, calcium excretion increases (hypercalciuria). This calciuric effect is why loop diuretics were historically used in hypercalcaemia, although they are now reserved for fluid overload after rehydration.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. Loop diuretics increase calcium excretion. Thiazide diuretics decrease calcium excretion.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Loop diuretics have a significant effect on calcium excretion. They increase it.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Loop diuretics increase calcium excretion regardless of serum calcium levels.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Loop diuretics increase, rather than reduce, renal calcium excretion, so they would worsen hypocalcaemia rather than treat it.

exam_trap: Decreased calcium excretion (B) is chosen by confusing loop diuretics with thiazides; loops increase urinary calcium, whereas thiazides reduce it.
takeaway: Loops lose calcium; thiazides keep calcium.
thinking: Loop diuretics block the Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporter in the thick ascending limb ↓ the lumen-positive potential is lost ↓ paracellular calcium and magnesium reabsorption falls ↓ urinary calcium rises ↓ They increase calcium excretion
pearl: The same paracellular mechanism explains loop diuretic-induced hypomagnesaemia, and prolonged use in preterm neonates can cause nephrocalcinosis.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: Physiology - Endocrine
stem: Which of the following best describes the effect of thyroid hormones on heart rate?

options.C: They have no effect on heart rate
options.D: They decrease heart rate only in hypothyroidism

why_correct: Correct. Thyroid hormones (T3 and T4) increase heart rate by up-regulating beta-adrenergic receptors and increasing sensitivity to catecholamines. They also have direct chronotropic effects on the sinoatrial node. Hyperthyroidism causes tachycardia, palpitations, and atrial fibrillation.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Thyroid hormones increase heart rate. Hypothyroidism causes bradycardia.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Thyroid hormones have a significant effect on heart rate. They increase it.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Hypothyroidism decreases heart rate, but the question asks about the effect of thyroid hormones. They increase heart rate.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. By increasing heart rate, contractility, and metabolic rate, thyroid hormones increase myocardial oxygen demand; they do not decrease it.

exam_trap: Option D confuses deficiency with hormone action: hypothyroidism causes bradycardia because hormone is lacking, but thyroid hormones themselves increase heart rate.
takeaway: Thyroid hormones → raised heart rate, contractility and myocardial oxygen demand.
thinking: Thyroid hormone increases beta-adrenergic receptor expression ↓ the heart becomes more sensitive to catecholamines ↓ there are also direct effects on the sinoatrial node ↓ They increase heart rate
pearl: New atrial fibrillation, particularly in an older patient, should prompt thyroid function testing, and beta-blockers such as propranolol control adrenergic symptoms of thyrotoxicosis before surgery.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: Physiology - Endocrine
stem: Which of the following best describes the effect of cortisol on inflammation?

options.C: It has no effect on inflammation
options.D: It increases inflammation only in infection
options.E: It stimulates the proliferation of circulating lymphocytes

why_correct: Correct. Cortisol is a glucocorticoid that has potent anti-inflammatory effects. It inhibits the production of inflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL-1, IL-6, TNF-alpha), reduces the migration of leukocytes to sites of inflammation, and stabilises lysosomal membranes. It also suppresses the immune response.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Cortisol decreases inflammation. It is used therapeutically as an anti-inflammatory agent.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Cortisol has a significant effect on inflammation. It decreases it.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Cortisol decreases inflammation. It does not increase it.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Cortisol causes lymphopenia by promoting apoptosis and redistribution of circulating lymphocytes; it does not stimulate their proliferation.

exam_trap: Option E is the trap: glucocorticoids cause lymphopenia with a neutrophilia, so a raised white cell count on steroids may be a drug effect rather than infection.
takeaway: Cortisol → anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive; lymphopenia with neutrophilia.
thinking: Glucocorticoids act through nuclear receptors ↓ they suppress cytokines such as IL-1, IL-6 and TNF-alpha ↓ they reduce leucocyte migration and cause lymphopenia ↓ It decreases inflammation
pearl: Long-term corticosteroids impair wound healing and can mask peritonitis, so a perforated viscus may present with few abdominal signs in a steroid-treated patient.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: Physiology - Gastrointestinal
stem: Which of the following best describes the function of somatostatin?

options.B: It inhibits gastric acid secretion and gastrointestinal motility
options.E: It stimulates insulin and glucagon secretion from pancreatic islet cells

correct_answer: B. It inhibits gastric acid secretion and gastrointestinal motility
why_correct: Correct. Somatostatin is secreted by D cells in the gastrointestinal tract and pancreas. It inhibits the release of gastrin, secretin, CCK, and other gastrointestinal hormones. It also inhibits gastric acid secretion, pancreatic enzyme secretion, and gastrointestinal motility. It is used therapeutically in acromegaly, carcinoid syndrome, and variceal bleeding.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Somatostatin inhibits gastric acid secretion. Gastrin stimulates it.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Somatostatin inhibits pancreatic enzyme secretion. CCK stimulates it.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Somatostatin inhibits gallbladder contraction. CCK stimulates it.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Somatostatin inhibits, rather than stimulates, the secretion of both insulin and glucagon from pancreatic islet cells, in addition to its inhibitory effects on gastrin, secretin, and CCK.

exam_trap: Option E catches candidates who know somatostatin acts on the islets, but it inhibits both insulin and glucagon secretion rather than stimulating them.
takeaway: Somatostatin (D cells) = broad GI and pancreatic inhibitor; octreotide is its analogue.
thinking: Somatostatin comes from D cells in the stomach, intestine and islets ↓ it acts as a broad inhibitory hormone ↓ it suppresses gastrin, acid, pancreatic secretion and motility ↓ It inhibits gastric acid secretion and gastrointestinal motility
pearl: Octreotide reduces portal inflow by splanchnic vasoconstriction in variceal bleeding and reduces output from high-output enterocutaneous fistulae, although it does not reliably speed fistula closure.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: Physiology - Gastrointestinal
stem: Which of the following best describes the function of the lower oesophageal sphincter?

options.A: It prevents reflux of gastric contents into the oesophagus
options.B: It prevents reflux of bile into the stomach
options.D: It prevents reflux of food into the pharynx
options.E: It relaxes tonically at rest and contracts during swallowing

correct_answer: A. It prevents reflux of gastric contents into the oesophagus
why_correct: Correct. The lower oesophageal sphincter (LOS) is a physiological sphincter located at the gastro-oesophageal junction. It remains contracted to prevent reflux of acidic gastric contents into the oesophagus. It relaxes during swallowing to allow food to enter the stomach. Dysfunction of the LOS causes gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD).

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. The pyloric sphincter prevents reflux of bile into the stomach. The LOS prevents reflux of gastric contents into the oesophagus.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Gastric emptying is regulated by the pyloric sphincter, not the LOS.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. The upper oesophageal sphincter prevents reflux of food into the pharynx. The LOS prevents reflux of gastric contents into the oesophagus.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. The lower oesophageal sphincter is tonically contracted at rest and relaxes transiently during swallowing to permit passage of the food bolus; this option reverses that relationship.

exam_trap: Option E reverses LOS physiology: it is tonically contracted at rest and relaxes during swallowing, and persistent failure to relax is achalasia.
takeaway: LOS: tonically closed, relaxes on swallowing; failure to relax = achalasia, incompetence = GORD.
thinking: The LOS lies at the gastro-oesophageal junction ↓ it is tonically contracted at rest ↓ it relaxes transiently on swallowing ↓ preventing gastric contents refluxing upwards ↓ It prevents reflux of gastric contents into the oesophagus
pearl: In achalasia the LOS fails to relax because inhibitory myenteric neurons are lost; treatment options include pneumatic dilatation, laparoscopic cardiomyotomy and peroral endoscopic myotomy.

subject: Pathology
title: Pathology: Pathology - General
stem: Which of the following best describes the process of apoptosis?

options.A: Programmed cell death that is energy-dependent and does not cause inflammation
options.B: Unregulated cell death that causes inflammation
options.D: Cell death due to direct trauma
options.E: Cell death characterised by karyolysis and release of intracellular contents

correct_answer: A. Programmed cell death that is energy-dependent and does not cause inflammation
why_correct: Correct. Apoptosis is a form of programmed cell death that is energy-dependent (requires ATP) and does not cause inflammation. It is characterised by cell shrinkage, chromatin condensation, and formation of apoptotic bodies, which are phagocytosed by macrophages. It is important in development, tissue homeostasis, and elimination of damaged cells.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. This describes necrosis, which is unregulated, energy-independent, and causes inflammation due to release of cellular contents.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Ischaemia typically causes necrosis, not apoptosis. However, mild ischaemia can trigger apoptosis.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Direct trauma causes necrosis, not apoptosis. Apoptosis is a programmed, regulated process.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Karyolysis and release of intracellular contents are features of necrosis. Apoptosis is characterised by chromatin condensation and formation of membrane-bound apoptotic bodies without release of cellular contents.

exam_trap: Candidates choose karyolysis with release of contents (E), but that is necrosis; apoptosis keeps membranes intact in apoptotic bodies, so there is no inflammation.
takeaway: Apoptosis = energy-dependent, regulated, no inflammation; necrosis = swelling, rupture, inflammation.
thinking: Apoptosis ↓ regulated, energy-dependent programmed cell death ↓ apoptotic bodies phagocytosed with no membrane rupture ↓ no inflammation ↓ Programmed cell death that is energy-dependent and does not cause inflammation
pearl: Apoptosis appears histologically as single shrunken eosinophilic cells with condensed nuclei, whereas necrosis affects contiguous groups of cells and provokes inflammation.

subject: Pathology
title: Pathology: Pathology - General
stem: Which of the following best describes the process of necrosis?

options.A: Programmed cell death that is energy-dependent
options.B: Unregulated cell death that causes inflammation
options.C: Cell death that does not cause inflammation
options.D: Cell death that is always physiological
options.E: Cell death characterised by chromatin condensation and formation of apoptotic bodies

correct_answer: B. Unregulated cell death that causes inflammation
why_correct: Correct. Necrosis is a form of cell death that is unregulated, energy-independent, and causes inflammation due to the release of cellular contents. It is characterised by cell swelling, rupture of the cell membrane, and denaturation of proteins. It is caused by ischaemia, toxins, infections, and trauma.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. This describes apoptosis. Necrosis is unregulated and energy-independent.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Necrosis causes inflammation. Apoptosis does not.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Necrosis is always pathological. Apoptosis can be physiological or pathological.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Chromatin condensation and apoptotic body formation are features of apoptosis. Necrosis is characterised by cell swelling, karyolysis, and rupture of the plasma membrane.

exam_trap: Candidates choose energy-dependent programmed death (A) or chromatin condensation with apoptotic bodies (E), but both describe apoptosis rather than necrosis.
takeaway: Necrosis = unregulated, pathological, inflammatory cell death; apoptosis = programmed, non-inflammatory.
thinking: Necrosis ↓ cell swelling and membrane rupture ↓ release of contents ↓ inflammation ↓ Unregulated cell death that causes inflammation
pearl: Coagulative necrosis is typical of ischaemic infarcts in solid organs such as heart and kidney, whereas liquefactive necrosis occurs in brain infarcts and abscesses, and caseous necrosis in tuberculosis.

subject: Pathology
title: Pathology: Pathology - Haematology
stem: A patient presents with fatigue, pallor, and koilonychia. Blood tests show a microcytic, hypochromic anaemia with low ferritin. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Correct. Iron deficiency anaemia causes a microcytic, hypochromic anaemia with low ferritin (iron stores). It presents with fatigue, pallor, koilonychia (spoon-shaped nails), and pica. It is caused by chronic blood loss, poor dietary intake, or malabsorption.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Vitamin B12 deficiency causes macrocytic anaemia with hypersegmented neutrophils. It does not cause microcytic, hypochromic anaemia.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Thalassaemia causes microcytic, hypochromic anaemia with normal or high ferritin. It is a genetic disorder of haemoglobin synthesis.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Sickle cell anaemia causes normocytic anaemia with sickle-shaped red blood cells. It is not microcytic or hypochromic.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Anaemia of chronic disease is typically normocytic or mildly microcytic with normal or raised ferritin (an acute phase reactant), unlike iron deficiency anaemia, in which ferritin is low.

exam_trap: Candidates choose anaemia of chronic disease (E) or thalassaemia (C), but both have normal or raised ferritin; a low ferritin confirms iron deficiency.
takeaway: Microcytic anaemia + low ferritin = iron deficiency; investigate the cause, especially GI blood loss.
thinking: Microcytic hypochromic anaemia ↓ low ferritin means depleted iron stores ↓ koilonychia ↓ Iron deficiency anaemia
pearl: Unexplained iron deficiency anaemia in men or postmenopausal women warrants investigation for gastrointestinal blood loss, including upper endoscopy and colonoscopy, to exclude malignancy.

subject: Pathology
title: Pathology: Pathology - Haematology
stem: A patient presents with a bleeding tendency, and blood tests show a prolonged bleeding time with normal platelet count, PT, and APTT. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Correct. Von Willebrand disease is the most common inherited bleeding disorder. It causes a prolonged bleeding time (due to defective platelet adhesion) with normal platelet count, PT, and APTT. However, APTT may be prolonged if factor VIII levels are significantly reduced. It is usually autosomal dominant.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Haemophilia A causes a prolonged APTT with normal bleeding time, PT, and platelet count. It is an X-linked recessive disorder.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Vitamin K deficiency causes a prolonged PT with normal bleeding time and platelet count. APTT may also be prolonged.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. ITP causes a low platelet count (thrombocytopenia) with normal PT and APTT. Bleeding time is prolonged due to thrombocytopenia.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Bernard-Soulier syndrome is a disorder of platelet adhesion (glycoprotein Ib deficiency) causing a prolonged bleeding time, but it is typically associated with thrombocytopenia and giant platelets on blood film, unlike von Willebrand disease, in which the platelet count is normal.

exam_trap: Candidates choose Bernard-Soulier syndrome (E), which also impairs platelet adhesion, but it typically has thrombocytopenia with giant platelets; a normal count favours von Willebrand disease.
takeaway: Prolonged bleeding time with normal platelet count and clotting screen = von Willebrand disease.
thinking: Prolonged bleeding time ↓ normal platelet count, PT and APTT ↓ defective platelet adhesion ↓ von Willebrand factor is needed for adhesion ↓ Von Willebrand disease
pearl: Tranexamic acid and desmopressin are commonly used to cover dental extraction or minor surgery in mild von Willebrand disease, while severe types may need von Willebrand factor concentrate.

subject: Microbiology
title: Microbiology: Microbiology - Specific Organisms
stem: A patient presents with a hospital-acquired pneumonia. Sputum culture grows an organism that is Gram-negative, oxidase-positive, and lactose-non-fermenting. Which organism is most likely?
why_correct: Correct. Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a Gram-negative bacillus that is oxidase-positive and lactose-non-fermenting. It is a common cause of hospital-acquired pneumonia, particularly in ventilated patients and those with chronic lung disease. It is intrinsically resistant to many antibiotics and is treated with piperacillin-tazobactam, ceftazidime, or carbapenems.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. E. coli is Gram-negative, lactose-fermenting, and oxidase-negative. It is a common cause of urinary tract infections and intra-abdominal infections, not typically hospital-acquired pneumonia.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Klebsiella is Gram-negative, lactose-fermenting, and oxidase-negative. It can cause hospital-acquired pneumonia, particularly in alcoholics, but it is not oxidase-positive.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Proteus is Gram-negative, lactose-non-fermenting, and oxidase-negative. It is associated with urinary tract infections and struvite stones, not typically hospital-acquired pneumonia.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Acinetobacter baumannii also causes hospital-acquired and ventilator-associated pneumonia, but it is oxidase-negative, distinguishing it from Pseudomonas aeruginosa, which is oxidase-positive.

exam_trap: Acinetobacter baumannii is the strongest distractor as another non-fermenting cause of ventilator-associated pneumonia, but it is oxidase-negative, unlike Pseudomonas.
takeaway: Gram-negative, non-lactose-fermenting, oxidase-positive → Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
thinking: Hospital-acquired pneumonia isolate ↓ Gram-negative, lactose-non-fermenting ↓ oxidase-positive ↓ the classic oxidase-positive non-fermenter ↓ Pseudomonas aeruginosa
pearl: Pseudomonas often produces a blue-green pigment (pyocyanin) and a sweet, grape-like smell in wound and burn infections.

subject: Microbiology
title: Microbiology: Microbiology - Specific Organisms
stem: A child presents with a skin infection around the nose and mouth characterised by golden, honey-coloured crusts. A swab grows beta-haemolytic, catalase-negative Gram-positive cocci in chains. Which organism is most likely?
why_correct: Correct. Honey-coloured crusts are typical of non-bullous impetigo. Catalase-negative, beta-haemolytic Gram-positive cocci in chains identify Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Streptococcus), which causes impetigo alone or together with Staphylococcus aureus. It is also a cause of cellulitis, erysipelas, and necrotising fasciitis.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. S. aureus is the most common cause of impetigo in the UK and also causes bullous impetigo, but it is a catalase-positive coccus that grows in clusters, so it does not match this culture.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Pseudomonas can cause wound infections and ecthyma gangrenosum, but it is not associated with honey-coloured crusts.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. C. perfringens causes gas gangrene, which presents with crepitus, severe pain, and systemic toxicity, not honey-coloured crusts.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Herpes simplex virus causes painful vesicular lesions that ulcerate, not the honey-coloured crusted plaques typical of impetigo.

exam_trap: Staphylococcus aureus is the commonest cause of impetigo in the UK, so it tempts here, but catalase-negative beta-haemolytic cocci in chains identify Streptococcus pyogenes.
takeaway: Honey-coloured crusts = impetigo; S. aureus is commonest in the UK, but catalase-negative chains mean Streptococcus pyogenes.
thinking: Honey-coloured crusts around the nose and mouth ↓ non-bullous impetigo ↓ culture: catalase-negative, beta-haemolytic Gram-positive cocci in chains ↓ group A streptococcus rather than staphylococcus ↓ Streptococcus pyogenes
pearl: Localised non-bullous impetigo is usually treated topically, and children should stay off school until lesions have crusted over or 48 hours after starting antibiotic treatment.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: Anatomy - Upper Limb
stem: A patient presents with weakness in finger abduction and adduction. Which nerve is most likely injured?
why_correct: Correct. The ulnar nerve supplies the dorsal and palmar interossei (which abduct and adduct the fingers), the medial two lumbricals and the hypothenar muscles. Injury causes weakness of finger abduction and adduction, clawing of the ring and little fingers, and sensory loss over the medial one and a half fingers.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. The radial nerve supplies the wrist and finger extensors. Injury causes wrist drop, not weakness in finger abduction and adduction.
why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. The median nerve supplies the thenar muscles and the lateral two lumbricals. Injury causes loss of thumb opposition and weakness in forearm pronation.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. The musculocutaneous nerve supplies the coracobrachialis, biceps brachii, and brachialis. Injury causes weakness in elbow flexion and sensory loss over the lateral forearm.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. The anterior interosseous nerve is a purely motor branch of the median nerve supplying flexor pollicis longus, the lateral half of flexor digitorum profundus, and pronator quadratus; it does not innervate the interossei responsible for finger abduction and adduction.

exam_trap: Median nerve is chosen because it supplies many hand muscles, but its hand territory is the thenar group and lateral two lumbricals; every interosseous muscle is ulnar-supplied.
takeaway: Finger abduction and adduction (interossei) = ulnar nerve.
thinking: Weak finger abduction and adduction ↓ dorsal interossei abduct and palmar interossei adduct ↓ all interossei are supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve ↓ Ulnar nerve
pearl: With ulnar weakness of adductor pollicis, a patient gripping paper between thumb and index finger flexes the thumb interphalangeal joint using the median-supplied flexor pollicis longus, a useful bedside sign.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: Anatomy - Upper Limb
stem: During a supracondylar fracture of the humerus, the median nerve is injured. Which branch of the median nerve is most commonly affected, causing loss of thumb and index finger flexion?

options.E: Palmar digital branch to the index finger

why_correct: Correct. The anterior interosseous nerve is a branch of the median nerve that supplies flexor pollicis longus, the lateral half of flexor digitorum profundus (to the index and middle fingers), and pronator quadratus. It is the most commonly affected branch in supracondylar fractures. Injury causes loss of thumb and index finger flexion (inability to make the 'OK' sign).

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. The recurrent branch of the median nerve supplies the thenar muscles (opponens pollicis, abductor pollicis brevis, and superficial head of flexor pollicis brevis). Injury causes loss of thumb opposition.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve supplies sensation to the thenar eminence. It arises proximal to the carpal tunnel and is not typically affected in supracondylar fractures.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. The posterior interosseous nerve is a branch of the radial nerve. It supplies the wrist and finger extensors. It is not a branch of the median nerve.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. The palmar digital branches are sensory branches arising in the hand; they do not supply flexor pollicis longus or flexor digitorum profundus.

exam_trap: Recurrent branch is chosen because thumb function is affected, but it supplies the thenar muscles for opposition; loss of thumb and index flexion points to the anterior interosseous nerve.
takeaway: Anterior interosseous nerve: FPL, lateral FDP and pronator quadratus; injury abolishes the OK sign without sensory loss.
thinking: Supracondylar fracture with a median nerve branch injury ↓ loss of flexion at the thumb IP and index DIP joints ↓ these are flexor pollicis longus and the lateral flexor digitorum profundus ↓ both are supplied by the purely motor anterior interosseous branch ↓ Anterior interosseous nerve
pearl: Anterior interosseous nerve palsy causes no sensory loss and is easily missed; every child with a supracondylar fracture should be asked to make an OK sign, which collapses into a pinch when the nerve is injured.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: Anatomy - Lower Limb
stem: A patient presents with weakness of plantar flexion and toe flexion and sensory loss over the sole of the foot. Which nerve is most likely injured?
why_correct: Correct. The tibial nerve supplies the posterior compartment of the leg (gastrocnemius, soleus, plantaris, popliteus, flexor hallucis longus, flexor digitorum longus, tibialis posterior) and, via the plantar nerves, the intrinsic foot muscles and the skin of the sole. Injury causes loss of plantar flexion and toe flexion, weakness of inversion and numbness of the sole.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. The femoral nerve supplies the quadriceps (knee extension) and iliopsoas (hip flexion). Injury causes weakness in knee extension and hip flexion.
why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. A sciatic nerve lesion would also weaken the hamstrings and cause foot drop with sensory loss over most of the leg below the knee.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. The common peroneal nerve supplies the anterior and lateral compartments of the leg. Injury causes foot drop and sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot and lateral leg.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. The obturator nerve supplies the hip adductors and the skin of the medial thigh; it does not supply the plantar flexors, the toe flexors or the skin of the sole.

exam_trap: Sciatic nerve is chosen because it carries the tibial fibres, but a sciatic lesion would also weaken the hamstrings and cause foot drop, which are not described.
takeaway: Plantar flexion, toe flexion and sole sensation = tibial nerve.
thinking: Weak plantar flexion and toe flexion ↓ posterior compartment of the leg involved ↓ sensory loss over the sole via the plantar nerves ↓ hamstrings and dorsiflexors not involved, so not the sciatic or common peroneal nerve ↓ Tibial nerve
pearl: The tibial nerve passes behind the medial malleolus beneath the flexor retinaculum, where compression causes tarsal tunnel syndrome with burning pain and paraesthesia of the sole.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: Anatomy - Abdomen
stem: During a Whipple procedure, the surgeon ligates the gastroduodenal artery. From which vessel does the gastroduodenal artery arise?
why_correct: Correct. The common hepatic artery is a branch of the coeliac trunk. It gives rise to the gastroduodenal artery and the proper hepatic artery. The gastroduodenal artery supplies the pylorus, duodenum, and pancreas. It is ligated during a Whipple procedure.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. The left gastric artery is a branch of the coeliac trunk. It supplies the stomach and lower oesophagus. It does not give rise to the gastroduodenal artery.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. The splenic artery is a branch of the coeliac trunk. It supplies the spleen, pancreas, and short gastric arteries. It does not give rise to the gastroduodenal artery.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. The superior mesenteric artery arises from the aorta and supplies the midgut. It does not give rise to the gastroduodenal artery.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. The right gastric artery is a small branch typically arising from the proper hepatic artery (occasionally the common hepatic or left hepatic artery); it does not give rise to the gastroduodenal artery.

exam_trap: The right gastric artery (E) is chosen because it arises nearby, but it usually comes from the proper hepatic artery and is a neighbour, not the parent, of the gastroduodenal artery.
takeaway: Common hepatic artery → proper hepatic + gastroduodenal; the GDA lies behind D1 (bleeding posterior ulcer).
thinking: Gastroduodenal artery runs behind the first part of the duodenum ↓ the common hepatic artery divides into the proper hepatic and gastroduodenal arteries ↓ Common hepatic artery
pearl: The gastroduodenal artery lies directly behind the first part of the duodenum, which is why a posterior duodenal ulcer can erode into it and cause major upper GI haemorrhage.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: Anatomy - Abdomen
stem: A patient presents with an indirect inguinal hernia. Through which anatomical structure does this hernia protrude?
why_correct: Correct. An indirect inguinal hernia protrudes through the deep inguinal ring, which is located lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels. It then travels through the inguinal canal and exits through the superficial inguinal ring. It is the most common type of inguinal hernia and is more common in younger patients.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. The superficial inguinal ring is the exit point for both indirect and direct inguinal hernias. It is not the site of origin for an indirect hernia.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Hesselbach's triangle is the site of protrusion for a direct inguinal hernia. It is bounded by the inguinal ligament, inferior epigastric vessels, and rectus sheath.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. The femoral canal is the site of protrusion for a femoral hernia, which occurs below and lateral to the pubic tubercle.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. The inguinal ligament forms a boundary of the inguinal canal but is not itself an opening through which a hernia protrudes.

exam_trap: The superficial ring (B) is chosen because the hernia emerges there, but both direct and indirect hernias exit it; only indirect hernias enter through the deep ring.
takeaway: Indirect hernia = deep ring, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels; direct = Hesselbach's triangle, medial.
thinking: Indirect inguinal hernia ↓ follows the path of the processus vaginalis ↓ enters the canal at the deep ring, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels ↓ Deep inguinal ring
pearl: The deep ring lies above the midpoint of the inguinal ligament; occluding it while the patient coughs can suggest an indirect hernia, but the test is unreliable and the type is confirmed at operation.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: Anatomy - Head and Neck
stem: During a carotid endarterectomy, the surgeon must identify the carotid body. What is the main function of the carotid body?

options.B: It detects changes in arterial oxygen tension
options.C: It detects changes in arterial carbon dioxide tension
options.E: It detects changes in blood pH exclusively

correct_answer: B. It detects changes in arterial oxygen tension
why_correct: Correct. The carotid body is a chemoreceptor located at the bifurcation of the common carotid artery. It detects changes in arterial oxygen tension (PaO2), and to a lesser extent, carbon dioxide tension (PaCO2) and pH. It signals the medulla to adjust ventilation. It is innervated by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX).

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Blood pressure is regulated by baroreceptors in the carotid sinus, not the carotid body.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. While the carotid body does respond to changes in CO2, its primary function is to detect changes in oxygen tension. Central chemoreceptors in the medulla are more sensitive to CO2.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Heart rate is regulated by the autonomic nervous system and baroreceptors. The carotid body primarily regulates ventilation.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. While the carotid body does respond to changes in pH, this is not its exclusive or primary function; it is most sensitive to changes in arterial oxygen tension, with additional sensitivity to carbon dioxide tension and pH.

exam_trap: Candidates often choose carbon dioxide tension because CO2 is the main drive to breathe, but central medullary chemoreceptors dominate the CO2 response; the carotid body chiefly senses falling PaO2.
takeaway: Carotid body = peripheral chemoreceptor sensing PaO2 (CN IX); carotid sinus = baroreceptor.
thinking: Carotid body at the common carotid bifurcation ↓ peripheral chemoreceptor, not baroreceptor ↓ main stimulus is falling PaO2, lesser CO2 and pH response ↓ glossopharyngeal afferents to the medulla adjust ventilation ↓ Detects changes in arterial oxygen tension
pearl: The adjacent carotid sinus is a baroreceptor, also supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve; handling it during endarterectomy can cause bradycardia and hypotension, which is why local anaesthetic is sometimes infiltrated at the bifurcation.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology: Physiology - Cardiovascular
stem: Which of the following best describes the effect of a right-to-left shunt on arterial oxygen saturation?

options.C: No change in arterial oxygen saturation
options.E: Improvement in oxygen saturation with supplemental oxygen therapy

why_correct: Correct. In a right-to-left shunt (e.g., Tetralogy of Fallot, Eisenmenger syndrome), deoxygenated blood from the right side of the heart enters the left side and is pumped into the systemic circulation. This causes hypoxaemia (decreased arterial oxygen saturation) and cyanosis. Supplemental oxygen does not correct the hypoxaemia because the blood bypasses the lungs.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. A right-to-left shunt causes deoxygenated blood to enter the systemic circulation, decreasing arterial oxygen saturation.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. A right-to-left shunt decreases arterial oxygen saturation by mixing deoxygenated blood with oxygenated blood.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. A right-to-left shunt decreases pulmonary blood flow because blood bypasses the lungs.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. A right-to-left shunt causes hypoxaemia that responds poorly to supplemental oxygen, because the shunted blood bypasses the ventilated alveoli altogether and cannot be oxygenated.

exam_trap: Option E is the trap: shunted blood never meets alveolar gas, so supplemental oxygen corrects shunt hypoxaemia poorly, unlike low V/Q mismatch.
takeaway: Right-to-left shunt → cyanosis that responds poorly to oxygen.
thinking: Right-to-left shunt ↓ deoxygenated venous blood bypasses the lungs ↓ it mixes with oxygenated blood on the left side ↓ systemic arterial saturation falls ↓ Decreased arterial oxygen saturation
pearl: Right-to-left shunts allow venous emboli to reach the systemic circulation (paradoxical embolism), so a patent foramen ovale can explain stroke after DVT or systemic air embolism during surgery.

subject: Pathology
title: Pathology: Pathology - General
stem: Which of the following best describes the process of hyperplasia?

options.C: Change from one cell type to another
options.D: Disordered growth and maturation of cells

why_correct: Correct. Hyperplasia is an increase in the number of cells in a tissue or organ, resulting in an increase in tissue mass. It occurs in tissues capable of cell division (e.g., epidermis, gastrointestinal epithelium, breast, prostate). It can be physiological (e.g., breast during pregnancy) or pathological (e.g., benign prostatic hyperplasia, endometrial hyperplasia).

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. This describes hypertrophy. Hyperplasia involves an increase in cell number.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. This describes metaplasia. Hyperplasia involves an increase in cell number, not a change in cell type.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. This describes dysplasia. Hyperplasia involves an increase in cell number with normal cell maturation.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Hyperplasia can be either physiological (e.g., breast tissue in pregnancy) or pathological (e.g., benign prostatic hyperplasia, endometrial hyperplasia); it is not exclusively physiological.

exam_trap: Candidates confuse hyperplasia with hypertrophy (A), but hypertrophy is an increase in cell size; hyperplasia is an increase in cell number.
takeaway: Hyperplasia = more cells; hypertrophy = bigger cells.
thinking: Hyperplasia ↓ increase in cell number ↓ occurs only in tissues capable of division ↓ Increase in cell number
pearl: Endometrial hyperplasia from unopposed oestrogen can progress to endometrial carcinoma, showing that pathological hyperplasia can be a fertile soil for malignancy.

subject: Pathology
title: Pathology: Pathology - General
stem: Which of the following best describes the process of hypertrophy?

options.C: Change from one cell type to another

why_correct: Correct. Hypertrophy is an increase in the size of cells, resulting in an increase in the size of the organ. It occurs in tissues that cannot divide (e.g., cardiac muscle, skeletal muscle). It can be physiological (e.g., muscle hypertrophy in athletes) or pathological (e.g., left ventricular hypertrophy in hypertension).

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. This describes hyperplasia. Hypertrophy involves an increase in cell size, not cell number.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. This describes metaplasia. Hypertrophy involves an increase in cell size.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. This describes apoptosis. Hypertrophy is an increase in cell size.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. This describes dysplasia, an abnormal pattern of cellular maturation and organisation often seen as a precursor to neoplasia. Hypertrophy is an increase in cell size, not a disordered growth pattern.

exam_trap: Candidates confuse hypertrophy with hyperplasia (B), but hyperplasia is an increase in cell number; hypertrophy is an increase in cell size.
takeaway: Hypertrophy = increased cell size, typical of non-dividing muscle.
thinking: Hypertrophy ↓ increase in cell size ↓ organ enlarges without more cells, as in cardiac and skeletal muscle ↓ Increase in cell size
pearl: Pathological left ventricular hypertrophy from hypertension or aortic stenosis increases myocardial oxygen demand and the risk of ischaemia, arrhythmia and heart failure.

subject: Microbiology
title: Microbiology: Microbiology - Specific Organisms
stem: A patient develops an infected wound over the knuckles after punching someone in the mouth. Which organism, part of normal human oral flora, is characteristically associated with human bite infections?
why_correct: Correct. Eikenella corrodens is a Gram-negative bacillus that is part of the normal human oral flora. It is characteristically associated with human bite and clenched-fist injuries, although these infections are usually polymicrobial, with streptococci and Staphylococcus aureus also commonly isolated. It can cause serious infections, including osteomyelitis and septic arthritis, and treatment typically involves amoxicillin-clavulanate.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. P. multocida is the most common organism isolated from dog and cat bite wounds, not human bites.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Streptococci are frequently isolated from human bite wounds, but Streptococcus pyogenes is not the organism characteristically associated with human bite and clenched-fist injuries.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Pseudomonas is more commonly associated with burns, hospital-acquired infections, and immunocompromised patients. It is not the predominant organism in human bite wounds.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Staphylococcus aureus is commonly isolated from human bite wounds as part of a polymicrobial infection, but it is a skin organism rather than human oral flora and is not the organism characteristically associated with human bites.

exam_trap: Pasteurella multocida is the classic bite organism, but it comes from dog and cat bites; Eikenella corrodens is the characteristic human oral commensal.
takeaway: Human bite or clenched-fist injury → Eikenella corrodens (polymicrobial); dog or cat bite → Pasteurella multocida.
thinking: Infected wound over the knuckles after punching someone in the mouth ↓ clenched-fist (human bite) injury ↓ inoculation of human oral flora ↓ oral commensal characteristic of human bite infections ↓ Eikenella corrodens
pearl: Clenched-fist injuries over the metacarpophalangeal joint should be explored surgically, because a tooth can penetrate the joint capsule and cause septic arthritis even when the skin wound looks trivial.

subject: Microbiology
title: Microbiology: Microbiology - Specific Organisms
stem: A woman who has been using tampons during menstruation presents with high fever, hypotension, and a diffuse erythematous rash followed by desquamation. Which organism is most likely?
why_correct: Correct. Staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome (TSS) is caused by toxic shock syndrome toxin-1 (TSST-1) produced by S. aureus. It presents with high fever, hypotension, a diffuse erythematous rash (sunburn-like), and desquamation of the palms and soles. It is associated with tampon use, surgical wounds, and nasal packing.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. Streptococcal toxic shock syndrome is caused by S. pyogenes and presents with similar symptoms but is often associated with necrotising fasciitis. However, the classic description of TSS with tampon use is staphylococcal.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Pseudomonas can cause sepsis in immunocompromised patients but is not associated with toxic shock syndrome.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. C. perfringens causes gas gangrene, which presents with crepitus, severe pain, and systemic toxicity. It is not associated with toxic shock syndrome.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Neisseria meningitidis causes meningococcal septicaemia with fever, hypotension, and a petechial or purpuric rash, but it does not cause the diffuse erythematous rash with later desquamation seen in toxic shock syndrome, which is caused by toxin-producing Staphylococcus aureus.

exam_trap: Streptococcus pyogenes also causes toxic shock syndrome, but usually with invasive soft-tissue infection; tampon-associated toxic shock with desquamation is classically staphylococcal.
takeaway: Tampon use + fever + hypotension + desquamating rash = staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome (TSST-1).
thinking: Tampon use during menstruation ↓ high fever and hypotension ↓ diffuse erythematous rash followed by desquamation ↓ toxic shock syndrome toxin-1 ↓ Staphylococcus aureus
pearl: TSST-1 is a superantigen that non-specifically activates large numbers of T cells, causing a cytokine storm; management includes removing the source, such as a retained tampon or nasal packing.

subject: Microbiology
title: Microbiology: Microbiology - Viral Infections
stem: A patient presents with a painful vesicular rash that follows a dermatomal distribution on the chest. Which virus is most likely responsible?
why_correct: Correct. Varicella-zoster virus (VZV) causes chickenpox (varicella) as a primary infection and shingles (herpes zoster) on reactivation. Shingles presents with a painful vesicular rash that follows a dermatomal distribution, most commonly on the chest (thoracic dermatomes). Treatment is with aciclovir, valaciclovir, or famciclovir.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. HSV-1 typically causes oral herpes (cold sores) and is not associated with a dermatomal distribution.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. EBV causes infectious mononucleosis, which presents with sore throat, fever, lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly. It is not associated with a dermatomal vesicular rash.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. CMV causes a mononucleosis-like illness and retinitis in immunocompromised patients. It is not associated with a dermatomal vesicular rash.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Coxsackievirus causes hand, foot and mouth disease with vesicular lesions, but these are not confined to a single dermatome. A painful vesicular rash in a dermatomal distribution is characteristic of varicella-zoster virus reactivation (shingles).

exam_trap: Herpes simplex virus type 1 also causes painful vesicles, but it recurs at a localised site, usually the lips, rather than in a dermatomal band.
takeaway: Painful unilateral dermatomal vesicles → shingles (VZV reactivation).
thinking: Painful vesicular rash ↓ confined to a dermatome on the chest ↓ reactivation of latent virus from a dorsal root ganglion ↓ shingles ↓ Varicella-zoster virus
pearl: Antivirals work best when started within 72 hours of rash onset, and post-herpetic neuralgia is the commonest complication, particularly in older patients.

subject: Microbiology
title: Microbiology: Microbiology - Viral Infections
stem: A child presents with fever, cough, coryza and conjunctivitis. Three days later a maculopapular rash appears, starting on the face and behind the ears and spreading to the trunk and extremities. Small white spots are seen on the buccal mucosa. Which virus is most likely responsible?
why_correct: Correct. Measles is a highly contagious viral infection that presents with fever, cough, coryza, conjunctivitis (the three C's), and Koplik spots (white spots on the buccal mucosa). A maculopapular rash appears 3-4 days after the onset of symptoms, starting on the face and spreading to the trunk and extremities. It is prevented by the MMR vaccine.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. Rubella (German measles) causes a milder maculopapular rash that also starts on the face and spreads downwards, but it is accompanied by prominent posterior auricular and suboccipital lymphadenopathy and only a mild prodrome. It does not cause the marked cough, coryza and conjunctivitis or the Koplik spots described here.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Parvovirus B19 causes erythema infectiosum (fifth disease), with a 'slapped cheek' facial rash followed by a lacy reticular rash on the trunk and limbs. It does not cause the cough, coryza, conjunctivitis and Koplik spots of measles.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. VZV causes chickenpox, which presents with a vesicular rash in different stages of healing (crops) on the trunk and extremities. It is not a maculopapular rash.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Human herpesvirus 6 causes roseola infantum, in which the rash classically appears as the fever resolves and starts on the trunk rather than the face. A prodrome of cough, coryza and conjunctivitis with Koplik spots, followed by a rash spreading from the face, is typical of measles.

exam_trap: Rubella also has a rash spreading from the face, but it has a mild prodrome with posterior auricular lymphadenopathy and no Koplik spots.
takeaway: Cough, coryza, conjunctivitis + Koplik spots + rash spreading from the face = measles.
thinking: Fever with cough, coryza and conjunctivitis ↓ white buccal spots = Koplik spots ↓ maculopapular rash a few days later, spreading from the face and behind the ears downwards ↓ Measles virus
pearl: Measles is a notifiable disease in the UK; complications include pneumonia, encephalitis and, rarely, subacute sclerosing panencephalitis years after infection.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: Anatomy - Upper Limb
stem: A patient presents with weakness in thumb opposition and sensory loss over the lateral palm and lateral three and a half fingers. Which nerve is most likely injured?
why_correct: Correct. The median nerve supplies the thenar muscles (including opponens pollicis) and the lateral two lumbricals. It provides sensation to the lateral palm and the palmar aspect of the lateral three and a half fingers. Injury causes loss of thumb opposition and sensory loss in this distribution.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. The radial nerve supplies the wrist and finger extensors. Injury causes wrist drop and sensory loss over the posterior arm and forearm.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. The ulnar nerve supplies the intrinsic hand muscles (interossei, medial two lumbricals, hypothenar muscles). Injury causes claw hand and sensory loss over the medial one and a half fingers.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. The musculocutaneous nerve supplies the coracobrachialis, biceps brachii, and brachialis. Injury causes weakness in elbow flexion and sensory loss over the lateral forearm.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. The anterior interosseous nerve is a purely motor branch of the median nerve supplying flexor pollicis longus, part of flexor digitorum profundus, and pronator quadratus; it causes no sensory loss. The combination of weak thumb opposition with sensory loss over the lateral palm and lateral three and a half fingers points to injury of the main median nerve trunk.

exam_trap: The anterior interosseous nerve (E) is a median branch but is purely motor and spares opposition, so sensory loss in the hand excludes it.
takeaway: Weak opposition + numb lateral palm and lateral three and a half fingers = median nerve.
thinking: Weak thumb opposition ↓ thenar muscles supplied by the median nerve ↓ numbness of the lateral palm and lateral three and a half fingers ↓ palm involvement means the lesion is proximal to the palmar cutaneous branch ↓ Median nerve
pearl: Because the palmar cutaneous branch leaves above the wrist and passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum, numbness of the lateral palm suggests a median nerve lesion proximal to the carpal tunnel.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: Anatomy - Upper Limb
stem: During a shoulder examination, the surgeon tests the integrity of the supraspinatus tendon. Which movement does supraspinatus initiate?
why_correct: Correct. Supraspinatus initiates shoulder abduction for the first 15 degrees. Beyond 15 degrees, the deltoid muscle takes over as the primary abductor. Supraspinatus also stabilises the glenohumeral joint. It is commonly injured in rotator cuff tears.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. External rotation is primarily mediated by infraspinatus and teres minor.
why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. Internal rotation is primarily mediated by subscapularis, teres major, and latissimus dorsi.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Adduction is primarily mediated by pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi, and teres major.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Abduction beyond the initial 15 degrees is driven principally by the deltoid muscle, not supraspinatus. Supraspinatus initiates the first 15 degrees of abduction before deltoid takes over.

exam_trap: Candidates may choose abduction from 30 to 90 degrees because supraspinatus stays active throughout abduction, but its distinctive role is initiating the first 15 degrees, after which deltoid is the main abductor.
takeaway: Supraspinatus initiates the first 15 degrees of abduction; deltoid continues it.
thinking: Supraspinatus tested in shoulder examination ↓ deltoid has poor leverage with the arm at the side ↓ supraspinatus starts abduction ↓ deltoid then becomes the main abductor ↓ Abduction (first 15 degrees)
pearl: The supraspinatus tendon passes beneath the coracoacromial arch to the greater tuberosity, making it the rotator cuff tendon most often involved in impingement and tears; it is tested with the empty can test.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: Anatomy - Lower Limb
stem: A patient presents with weakness in hip extension and difficulty climbing stairs. Which nerve is most likely injured?
why_correct: Correct. The inferior gluteal nerve supplies gluteus maximus, which is responsible for hip extension (e.g., climbing stairs, standing from a sitting position). Injury causes difficulty in these activities and weakness in hip extension.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. The femoral nerve supplies the quadriceps (knee extension) and iliopsoas (hip flexion). Injury causes weakness in knee extension and hip flexion.
why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. The superior gluteal nerve supplies gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, and tensor fasciae latae. Injury causes weakness in hip abduction and a positive Trendelenburg sign.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. The sciatic nerve supplies the posterior thigh, leg, and foot. Injury causes weakness in knee flexion, foot drop, and sensory loss below the knee.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. The obturator nerve supplies the adductor muscles of the thigh, and its injury causes weakness of hip adduction, not extension. Weakness of hip extension with difficulty climbing stairs reflects gluteus maximus dysfunction from an inferior gluteal nerve lesion.

exam_trap: The superior gluteal nerve (B) is chosen by mixing up the two gluteal nerves; its lesion causes a Trendelenburg gait from abductor weakness, not loss of hip extension.
takeaway: Inferior gluteal nerve = gluteus maximus = hip extension (stairs, standing from sitting).
thinking: Weak hip extension ↓ difficulty climbing stairs and rising from sitting ↓ gluteus maximus failing ↓ supplied by the inferior gluteal nerve ↓ Inferior gluteal nerve
pearl: Gluteus maximus contributes little to level walking but is essential for stairs and rising from a chair; the inferior gluteal nerve leaves the pelvis below piriformis and is at risk in the posterior approach to the hip.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy: Anatomy - Lower Limb
stem: During a knee examination, the surgeon tests the integrity of the anterior cruciate ligament. Which of the following tests is most specific for anterior cruciate ligament injury?
why_correct: Correct. The Lachman test is the most sensitive and specific test for anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury. It is performed with the knee flexed at 20-30 degrees, and the tibia is pulled forward. A positive test indicates ACL injury.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. The anterior drawer test is used to assess the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL). It involves pulling the tibia forward with the knee flexed at 90 degrees. It is less sensitive than the Lachman test.
why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. The posterior drawer test is used to assess the posterior cruciate ligament (PCL). It involves pushing the tibia backward with the knee flexed at 90 degrees.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. The McMurray test is used to assess meniscal tears. It involves rotating the tibia with the knee flexed and extended.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. The varus stress test assesses the integrity of the lateral collateral ligament, not the anterior cruciate ligament. The Lachman test is the most sensitive and specific bedside test for anterior cruciate ligament injury.

exam_trap: The anterior drawer test (A) also assesses the ACL, but at 90 degrees hamstring spasm and meniscal blocking make it less reliable than the Lachman test.
takeaway: Best bedside test for the ACL = Lachman (20 to 30 degrees flexion); PCL = posterior drawer.
thinking: ACL resists anterior tibial translation ↓ test at 20 to 30 degrees of flexion ↓ at 90 degrees hamstring guarding and the menisci limit forward movement ↓ Lachman test
pearl: An acute haemarthrosis after a twisting sports injury, often with a felt 'pop', is most commonly due to an ACL tear; MRI confirms it and shows associated meniscal tears and bone bruising.

subject: Clinical Topics
title: Clinical Topics: Clinical - Trauma and Orthopaedics
stem: A patient presents with a tibial shaft fracture and develops severe pain, paraesthesia, and pain on passive stretch of the toes. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.A: Elevate the limb and apply ice
options.E: Remove any constrictive dressing or cast and reassess in 1 hour

why_correct: Correct. The patient has signs of acute compartment syndrome (severe pain, paraesthesia, pain on passive stretch). This is a surgical emergency requiring urgent fasciotomy to release the fascial compartments and restore perfusion. Delay can lead to Volkmann's ischaemic contracture, rhabdomyolysis, and limb loss.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Elevation and ice are inadequate for acute compartment syndrome, and elevation lowers arterial perfusion pressure; the limb should be kept at heart level while urgent fasciotomy is arranged.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Applying a plaster cast may worsen compartment syndrome by increasing external pressure. If a cast is already in place, it should be removed or split.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Antibiotics are not the primary treatment for compartment syndrome. They may be used if there is an associated open fracture, but fasciotomy is the priority.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Releasing external constriction is a reasonable adjunct once compartment syndrome is suspected, but delaying definitive treatment to reassess risks irreversible muscle and nerve ischaemia. Clinically suspected compartment syndrome, as suggested here, requires urgent fasciotomy without delay.

exam_trap: Releasing the dressing and reassessing in an hour (E) delays treatment once compartment syndrome is clinically evident; elevation and ice (A) fail too, and elevation can reduce perfusion.
takeaway: Clinically suspected compartment syndrome → urgent fasciotomy of all compartments.
thinking: Tibial shaft fracture ↓ severe pain with pain on passive stretch of the toes and paraesthesia ↓ acute compartment syndrome ↓ rising compartment pressure threatens muscle and nerve viability ↓ Urgent fasciotomy
pearl: Split all dressings and cast padding down to skin and keep the limb at heart level rather than elevated, which reduces perfusion pressure; leg fasciotomy decompresses all four compartments, usually through two incisions.

subject: Clinical Topics
title: Clinical Topics: Clinical - Trauma and Orthopaedics
stem: A patient sustains a fracture of the distal radius with dorsal displacement of the distal fragment. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Correct. Colles' fracture is a fracture of the distal radius with dorsal displacement of the distal fragment. It is the most common fracture of the wrist and typically occurs after a fall on an outstretched hand (FOOSH). It presents with a 'dinner fork' deformity.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Smith's fracture is a fracture of the distal radius with volar (palmar) displacement of the distal fragment. It is also known as a reverse Colles' fracture.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Barton's fracture is an intra-articular fracture of the distal radius with dislocation of the radiocarpal joint. It can be dorsal or volar.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Scaphoid fracture presents with tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox and is not typically associated with dorsal displacement of the distal radius.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. A Galeazzi fracture is a fracture of the radial shaft with associated dislocation of the distal radioulnar joint, a distinct injury pattern. Dorsal displacement of a distal radius fracture fragment is characteristic of a Colles' fracture.

exam_trap: Smith's fracture (A) is the classic mix-up: it has volar displacement of the distal fragment, the reverse of the dorsal displacement that defines a Colles' fracture.
takeaway: Distal radius with dorsal displacement → Colles'; volar displacement → Smith's.
thinking: Distal radius fracture ↓ distal fragment displaced dorsally ↓ typical after a fall on the outstretched hand ↓ gives a dinner-fork deformity ↓ Colles' fracture
pearl: After any distal radius fracture check median nerve function, because acute carpal tunnel syndrome from swelling or displacement may need urgent reduction and decompression.

subject: Clinical Topics
title: Clinical Topics: Clinical - Trauma and Orthopaedics
stem: A frail 84-year-old patient with a hip fracture is awaiting surgery. Regular paracetamol has been given, and the team want effective analgesia while limiting systemic opioid use. Which of the following is the most appropriate additional analgesia?
why_correct: Correct. A femoral or fascia iliaca nerve block, given by trained staff, provides effective analgesia for hip fracture and reduces systemic opioid requirements and their side effects in older patients. NICE recommends paracetamol, with opioids if needed, and considering a nerve block if these are insufficient or to limit opioid dose; UK anaesthetic guidance supports a block for patients on admission.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Paracetamol alone is insufficient for the severe pain of a hip fracture. It may be used as an adjunct.
why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. Intravenous morphine may still be needed, but it does not limit systemic opioid use and carries a high risk of sedation, nausea and delirium in frail older patients; a nerve block gives better opioid-sparing analgesia.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Oral codeine is insufficient for the severe pain of a hip fracture and is not recommended as first-line analgesia.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Intramuscular pethidine is avoided in older patients because its active metabolite accumulates, particularly in renal impairment, and can precipitate confusion and seizures; a nerve block is the appropriate opioid-sparing option.

exam_trap: Candidates choose intravenous morphine (B), but escalating systemic opioids in a frail patient risks sedation and delirium; a nerve block gives opioid-sparing analgesia.
takeaway: Hip fracture pain → paracetamol plus femoral or fascia iliaca block to spare opioids.
thinking: Frail older patient with hip fracture pain ↓ paracetamol already given and the aim is to limit systemic opioids ↓ a femoral or fascia iliaca block anaesthetises much of the hip and proximal femur ↓ regional block gives opioid-sparing analgesia ↓ Femoral nerve block
pearl: Femoral or fascia iliaca blocks are usually performed in the emergency department, often under ultrasound guidance, and reduce opioid-related delirium, which is common and associated with worse outcomes after hip fracture.

subject: Clinical Topics
title: Clinical Topics: Clinical - Perioperative Care
stem: A patient undergoing major abdominal surgery is at high risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE). Pharmacological prophylaxis is contraindicated because of a high bleeding risk, and the patient has diabetic peripheral neuropathy with reduced sensation in both legs. Which of the following is the most appropriate mechanical VTE prophylaxis?
why_correct: Correct. When pharmacological prophylaxis is contraindicated, NICE guidance supports mechanical prophylaxis, choosing anti-embolism stockings or intermittent pneumatic compression according to the patient's condition. Anti-embolism stockings should not be used in people with peripheral neuropathy or other causes of sensory impairment, so IPC is the appropriate choice, with pharmacological prophylaxis added once the bleeding risk allows.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Early mobilisation is encouraged but is not sufficient as sole prophylaxis in high-risk patients.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Anti-embolism stockings should not be used in patients with peripheral neuropathy or sensory impairment, because pressure damage to the skin may go unnoticed.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. All patients should be assessed for VTE risk, and high-risk patients require prophylaxis.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. LMWH is pharmacological rather than mechanical prophylaxis, and it is contraindicated here by the high bleeding risk.

exam_trap: Candidates choose graduated compression stockings (C), but stockings are contraindicated in peripheral neuropathy because pressure damage may go unnoticed; IPC is preferred.
takeaway: Anticoagulation contraindicated + neuropathy → intermittent pneumatic compression, not stockings.
thinking: High VTE risk with high bleeding risk ↓ pharmacological prophylaxis is contraindicated, so a mechanical method is needed ↓ peripheral neuropathy contraindicates anti-embolism stockings ↓ intermittent pneumatic compression remains suitable ↓ Intermittent pneumatic compression (IPC)
pearl: Other contraindications to anti-embolism stockings include peripheral arterial disease, recent skin grafts, severe leg oedema and fragile skin; pharmacological prophylaxis is added once bleeding risk allows.

subject: Clinical Topics
title: Clinical Topics: Clinical - Perioperative Care
stem: A patient requires an emergency laparotomy within the next few hours. They have no acute coronary syndrome and no major haemorrhage, and their haemoglobin is 68 g/L. According to NICE guidelines, what is the most appropriate transfusion strategy?

options.B: Transfuse to a target haemoglobin of 100 g/L
options.C: Transfuse to a target haemoglobin of 70-90 g/L
options.D: Delay surgery until haemoglobin is above 130 g/L

correct_answer: C. Transfuse to a target haemoglobin of 70-90 g/L
why_correct: Correct. NICE recommends a restrictive red cell transfusion threshold of 70 g/L, with a post-transfusion target of 70-90 g/L, for patients who need transfusion and do not have major haemorrhage or acute coronary syndrome. Haemoglobin should be reassessed after each unit. This avoids the risks of unnecessary transfusion.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. A haemoglobin of 68 g/L is below the restrictive transfusion threshold, and proceeding to emergency surgery without transfusion increases perioperative risk.
why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. NICE recommends a restrictive threshold of 70 g/L with a 70-90 g/L target for most patients; a higher threshold of 80 g/L with a target of 80-100 g/L applies to patients with acute coronary syndrome.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. A target of 130 g/L is unnecessarily high and not supported by guidelines. It would expose the patient to unnecessary transfusion risks.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Intravenous iron takes days to weeks to raise haemoglobin and cannot correct severe anaemia before emergency surgery within hours; it is used to treat iron-deficiency anaemia before planned surgery.

exam_trap: Candidates choose a 100 g/L target (B), but outside acute coronary syndrome NICE uses a restrictive threshold of 70 g/L with a post-transfusion target of 70-90 g/L.
takeaway: No major bleeding or ACS → transfuse below 70 g/L to a target of 70-90 g/L.
thinking: No major haemorrhage or acute coronary syndrome ↓ NICE restrictive threshold applies ↓ Hb 68 g/L is below the 70 g/L threshold ↓ transfuse, reassessing after each unit, to 70-90 g/L ↓ Transfuse to a target haemoglobin of 70-90 g/L
pearl: NICE advises single-unit red cell transfusion in adults without active bleeding, with clinical reassessment and a repeat haemoglobin after each unit before giving more.

subject: Clinical Topics
title: Clinical Topics: Clinical - Perioperative Care
stem: A patient is recovering from surgery and develops a fever on day 2 post-operatively. Which of the following is the most common cause of early post-operative fever?
why_correct: Correct. Atelectasis is classically taught as the most common cause of fever within 48 hours of surgery, although much early fever reflects the systemic inflammatory response to tissue injury. Atelectasis results from reduced lung expansion and mucus plugging; treatment includes physiotherapy, incentive spirometry and early mobilisation.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. Wound infection typically presents later (day 5-7 post-operatively) and is associated with wound erythema, warmth, and discharge.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Urinary tract infection is a common cause of post-operative fever, particularly in catheterised patients, but it is less common than atelectasis in the first 48 hours.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. DVT can cause a low-grade fever but is not the most common cause of early post-operative fever. It typically presents with calf pain and swelling.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Drug fever is a recognised but later cause of post-operative pyrexia, typically arising more than a week after surgery. Atelectasis remains the most common cause of fever in the first 1-2 post-operative days.

exam_trap: Wound infection (B) is chosen because it is common, but it typically appears around days 5-7; fever within 48 hours is usually atelectasis or the inflammatory response.
takeaway: Day 1-2 postoperative fever → atelectasis or inflammatory response; wound infection comes later.
thinking: Fever on postoperative day 2 ↓ within the first 48 hours ↓ wound infection, UTI and DVT usually present later ↓ early fever is classically attributed to atelectasis and the inflammatory response to surgery ↓ Atelectasis
pearl: Fever in the first 48 hours is mostly a non-infective inflammatory response to tissue injury, so blanket cultures are low-yield; fever that persists or appears later after bowel surgery should prompt a search for leak or collection.

subject: Clinical Topics
title: Clinical Topics: Clinical - Perioperative Care
stem: A patient is scheduled for emergency surgery and is assessed for risk of aspiration. Which of the following is the most appropriate action to reduce the risk of aspiration pneumonitis?

options.B: Rapid sequence induction with cricoid pressure
options.E: Nasogastric tube insertion to empty the stomach

correct_answer: B. Rapid sequence induction with cricoid pressure
why_correct: Correct. Rapid sequence induction (RSI) with cricoid pressure is the standard technique to reduce the risk of aspiration during emergency surgery. It involves pre-oxygenation, rapid administration of induction agent and neuromuscular blocker, and intubation with cricoid pressure to prevent passive regurgitation.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Antacids may reduce gastric acidity but do not prevent aspiration. They may be used as an adjunct.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Awake fibreoptic intubation is used for anticipated difficult airways, not primarily for aspiration risk.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Antibiotics do not prevent aspiration. They may be used if aspiration has occurred and infection develops.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Nasogastric decompression does not reliably empty gastric contents and does not protect the airway. Rapid sequence induction with cricoid pressure remains the standard technique for reducing aspiration risk during emergency induction of anaesthesia.

exam_trap: Nasogastric drainage (E) helps but cannot reliably empty the stomach or protect the airway, and awake fibreoptic intubation (C) is for an anticipated difficult airway.
takeaway: Aspiration risk at emergency induction → rapid sequence induction with cricoid pressure.
thinking: Emergency surgery with a possibly full stomach ↓ induction abolishes protective airway reflexes ↓ the airway must be secured quickly with minimal unprotected time ↓ preoxygenation, rapid induction and paralysis, cricoid pressure and a cuffed tube ↓ Rapid sequence induction with cricoid pressure
pearl: Cricoid pressure should be released if it impairs laryngoscopy or if active vomiting occurs; in bowel obstruction a nasogastric tube is aspirated before induction, which reduces but does not eliminate gastric contents.

subject: Clinical Topics
title: Clinical Topics: Clinical - Professional Behaviour
stem: A surgeon is asked to perform a procedure that they are not competent to perform. According to Good Medical Practice (GMC), what is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Perform the procedure anyway to avoid delay
options.B: Decline to perform the procedure and refer to a competent colleague
options.C: Ask a junior colleague to perform the procedure under supervision
options.D: Perform the procedure with telephone advice from a specialist
options.E: Perform the procedure after seeking written consent from the patient

correct_answer: B. Decline to perform the procedure and refer to a competent colleague
why_correct: Correct. According to Good Medical Practice, doctors must recognise and work within the limits of their competence. If asked to perform a procedure they are not competent to perform, they should decline and refer the patient to a colleague who is competent.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Performing a procedure beyond one's competence puts the patient at risk and violates GMC guidance. Doctors must work within the limits of their competence.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. A junior colleague is even less likely to be competent. Supervision does not make an incompetent doctor competent for a procedure they are not trained to perform.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Telephone advice is not sufficient to ensure competence. The doctor should not perform a procedure they are not trained to perform.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Obtaining patient consent addresses the patient's agreement to a procedure but does not confer the competence required to perform it safely. Good Medical Practice requires a surgeon who is not competent to decline the procedure and refer to a colleague who is.

exam_trap: Telephone advice (D) or written consent (E) can seem reassuring, but neither gives the surgeon the competence that GMC guidance requires before performing a procedure.
takeaway: Not competent → do not perform; refer to a competent colleague.
thinking: Asked to perform a procedure beyond one's competence ↓ GMC guidance requires working within the limits of competence ↓ consent, supervising a junior or telephone advice do not create competence ↓ patient safety needs a competent operator ↓ Decline to perform the procedure and refer to a competent colleague
pearl: In a genuine emergency with no competent colleague available, a doctor should still offer help within their abilities while urgently seeking senior support, then document and reflect on the episode.

subject: Clinical Topics
title: Clinical Topics: Clinical - Trauma and Orthopaedics
stem: A patient presents with a suspected scaphoid fracture after a fall on an outstretched hand. Initial X-rays are normal, and MRI is not available at this hospital. What is the most appropriate management?

options.B: Apply a thumb spica cast and repeat X-ray in 2 weeks
options.E: Repeat X-ray immediately in the emergency department

correct_answer: B. Apply a thumb spica cast and repeat X-ray in 2 weeks
why_correct: Correct. Scaphoid fractures can be invisible on initial X-rays, so a clinically suspected fracture is immobilised as if fractured. NICE recommends considering MRI as the further imaging of choice; where MRI is not available, the wrist is immobilised in a thumb spica cast and re-imaged at around 2 weeks, with CT or MRI if suspicion persists.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. A scaphoid fracture can be missed on initial X-rays. Discharging the patient without immobilisation risks non-union and avascular necrosis.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. MRI is the preferred further imaging for a suspected occult scaphoid fracture where it is accessible, but it is not available here, so the wrist is immobilised and re-imaged.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Early mobilisation of a suspected scaphoid fracture can lead to displacement, non-union, and avascular necrosis. Immobilisation is essential.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. An occult scaphoid fracture may not be visible on X-ray until bone resorption at the fracture line occurs, which takes around 10-14 days; repeating imaging immediately will not improve detection. The correct approach is immobilisation in a thumb spica cast with repeat imaging at around 2 weeks.

exam_trap: Candidates discharge with analgesia (A) after normal X-rays, but occult scaphoid fractures are common and missing them risks non-union and avascular necrosis.
takeaway: Suspected scaphoid fracture with normal X-ray → immobilise and re-image (MRI if available).
thinking: Fall on outstretched hand with suspected scaphoid fracture ↓ initial X-rays can miss it ↓ MRI is unavailable ↓ immobilise as if fractured and re-image once bone resorption makes it visible ↓ Apply a thumb spica cast and repeat X-ray in 2 weeks
pearl: The scaphoid's blood supply enters distally and flows retrogradely, so proximal pole fractures carry the highest risk of avascular necrosis and non-union.

subject: Basic Sciences
title: Basic Sciences: Basic Sciences - Statistics
stem: A study reports that a new diagnostic test has a sensitivity of 90% and a specificity of 95%. What does the sensitivity of 90% mean?

options.A: 90% of patients without the disease test negative
options.B: 90% of patients with the disease test positive
options.C: 90% of patients who test positive have the disease
options.D: 90% of patients who test negative do not have the disease
options.E: 90% of the total population will test positive

correct_answer: B. 90% of patients with the disease test positive
why_correct: Correct. Sensitivity is the proportion of patients with the disease who test positive. A sensitivity of 90% means that 90% of patients with the disease will be correctly identified by the test (true positives), while 10% will be missed (false negatives).

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. This describes specificity. Specificity is the proportion of patients without the disease who test negative.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. This describes positive predictive value (PPV). PPV depends on the prevalence of the disease in the population.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. This describes negative predictive value (NPV). NPV also depends on disease prevalence.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. This describes neither sensitivity nor any standard test characteristic and ignores disease prevalence entirely. Sensitivity specifically refers to the proportion of people with the disease who test positive.

exam_trap: Candidates often pick C, but '90% of positives have the disease' is the positive predictive value, which depends on prevalence; sensitivity is anchored to patients who truly have the disease.
takeaway: Sensitivity = true positives / all with disease (TP / (TP + FN)).
thinking: Sensitivity is defined within people who have the disease ↓ true positives divided by all with the disease ↓ 90% means 9 in 10 diseased patients test positive ↓ 90% of patients with the disease test positive
pearl: Sensitivity and specificity are properties of the test and do not change with prevalence, whereas PPV and NPV do; a negative result on a highly sensitive test is most useful for ruling a condition out.

subject: Basic Sciences
title: Basic Sciences: Basic Sciences - Statistics
stem: Which of the following best describes a Type I error in hypothesis testing?

options.E: The predetermined probability of Type II error permitted in a study

correct_answer: A. Rejecting a true null hypothesis
why_correct: Correct. A Type I error occurs when the null hypothesis is true, but we incorrectly reject it (false positive). The probability of a Type I error is denoted by alpha (α), typically set at 0.05 (5%).

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. This describes a Type II error (false negative). The probability of a Type II error is denoted by beta (β).
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. This is a correct decision (true positive). It is not an error.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. This is a correct decision (true negative). It is not an error.
