why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. This confuses the Type I error rate (alpha) with the Type II error rate (beta), which are set and interpreted independently. A Type I error is the rejection of a true null hypothesis.

exam_trap: Candidates mix up A and B; accepting a false null hypothesis is a Type II (false negative) error, whereas a Type I error is wrongly rejecting a true null (false positive).
takeaway: Type I error = false positive = rejecting a true null hypothesis (alpha).
thinking: Null hypothesis states there is no difference ↓ Type I error = false positive conclusion ↓ a true null is wrongly rejected ↓ its probability is alpha, usually set at 0.05 ↓ Rejecting a true null hypothesis
pearl: Running many comparisons inflates the overall chance of a Type I error, so multiple testing needs a stricter significance threshold for each individual test.

subject: Basic Sciences
title: Basic Sciences: Basic Sciences - Statistics
stem: Which of the following best describes the power of a study?

options.A: The probability of rejecting a true null hypothesis
options.B: The probability of detecting a true difference when one exists
options.C: The probability of accepting a false null hypothesis
options.D: The probability of making a Type I error
options.E: The predetermined threshold for statistical significance (alpha)

correct_answer: B. The probability of detecting a true difference when one exists
why_correct: Correct. Power is the probability of correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis (i.e., detecting a true effect or difference when one truly exists). Power is calculated as 1 - beta. A power of 0.80 (80%) is commonly accepted as adequate.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. This describes a Type I error (alpha).
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. This describes a Type II error (beta).
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. This is alpha, not power.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. This describes the significance level, not statistical power. Power is the probability of correctly detecting a true difference when one genuinely exists, and is calculated as 1 minus the Type II error rate.

exam_trap: Option E tempts because alpha is fixed before a study, as power is, but alpha is the significance threshold (Type I error rate); power is 1 minus beta.
takeaway: Power = 1 − beta = probability of detecting a true difference.
thinking: Power concerns finding an effect that really exists ↓ failing to find a real effect is a Type II error (beta) ↓ power = 1 − beta ↓ The probability of detecting a true difference when one exists
pearl: Power rises with larger sample size, larger true effect size, lower variability and a less stringent alpha; underpowered surgical trials risk wrongly concluding that two operations are equivalent.

subject: Basic Sciences
title: Basic Sciences: Basic Sciences - Statistics
stem: A study reports a p-value of 0.03. What is the correct interpretation of this result?

options.A: There is a 3% chance that the null hypothesis is true
options.B: There is a 3% probability of obtaining the observed result (or more extreme) if the null hypothesis is true
options.C: The result is not statistically significant at the 5% level
options.D: There is a 97% chance that the alternative hypothesis is true
options.E: The probability that the results occurred by chance alone

correct_answer: B. There is a 3% probability of obtaining the observed result (or more extreme) if the null hypothesis is true
why_correct: Correct. The p-value is the probability of obtaining a result at least as extreme as the one observed, assuming the null hypothesis is true. A p-value of 0.03 means that, if the null hypothesis were true, a result this extreme or more extreme would be expected 3% of the time.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. The p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true. It is the probability of the data given the null hypothesis.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. A p-value of 0.03 is less than 0.05, so the result is statistically significant at the 5% level.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. This is a common misinterpretation. The p-value does not provide the probability that the alternative hypothesis is true.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. This is a common but inaccurate interpretation of a p-value. The p-value is the probability of obtaining the observed data, or more extreme data, if the null hypothesis were true, not the probability that chance alone explains the result.

exam_trap: Options A and E feel intuitive, but the p-value is neither the probability that the null is true nor that chance caused the result; it is the probability of the data given the null.
takeaway: p-value = probability of data at least this extreme if the null hypothesis is true.
thinking: p-value is calculated assuming the null hypothesis is true ↓ it measures how surprising the data are under that assumption ↓ it is not the probability that either hypothesis is true ↓ 0.03 < 0.05, so significant at the 5% level ↓ There is a 3% probability of obtaining the observed result (or more extreme) if the null hypothesis is true
pearl: A p-value says nothing about the size or clinical importance of an effect; the confidence interval conveys both the precision and the plausible magnitude of the difference.

subject: Basic Sciences
title: Basic Sciences: Basic Sciences - Statistics
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate statistical test to compare the means of two independent groups with normally distributed data?
why_correct: Correct. The unpaired (independent samples) t-test is used to compare the means of two independent groups when the data are normally distributed and variances are approximately equal. It is also known as the Student's t-test.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. The paired t-test is used to compare means of two related groups (e.g., before and after intervention in the same individuals).
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. The chi-squared test is used to compare categorical variables (e.g., proportions), not continuous variables like means.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. The Mann-Whitney U test is a non-parametric test used to compare two independent groups when the data are not normally distributed.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. One-way ANOVA is used to compare the means of three or more independent groups, not two. For two independent groups with normally distributed data, the unpaired (independent samples) t-test is appropriate.

exam_trap: Candidates pick the paired t-test (A) by reflex, but pairing requires related measurements such as before-and-after values in the same patients; independent groups need the unpaired test.
takeaway: Two independent groups + normal continuous data → unpaired t-test.
thinking: Outcome is a mean of continuous data ↓ data are normally distributed, so a parametric test fits ↓ two groups that are independent, not paired ↓ Unpaired t-test
pearl: Check the distribution before choosing a t-test; with skewed data or small samples a rank-based non-parametric test such as the Mann-Whitney U test is preferred for two independent groups.

subject: Basic Sciences
title: Basic Sciences: Basic Sciences - Statistics
stem: Which of the following best describes a confidence interval?

options.A: The range of values within which the true population parameter is likely to lie
options.B: The range of values within which all sample data points lie
options.C: The probability that the null hypothesis is true
options.D: The probability that the alternative hypothesis is true
options.E: The interval within which 95% of individual patient values will fall

correct_answer: A. The range of values within which the true population parameter is likely to lie
why_correct: Correct. A confidence interval (CI) is a range of values that is likely to contain the true population parameter (e.g., mean, proportion) with a specified level of confidence (usually 95%). A 95% CI means that if the study were repeated many times, 95% of the calculated intervals would contain the true parameter.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. This describes the range of the sample data, not a confidence interval.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. The confidence interval does not provide the probability that the null hypothesis is true.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. The confidence interval does not provide the probability that the alternative hypothesis is true.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. This describes a reference range, which reflects the spread of individual values in a population, not a confidence interval. A confidence interval instead expresses the range within which the true population parameter is likely to lie.

exam_trap: Option E is a reference range, describing the spread of individual patients' values; a confidence interval instead describes the uncertainty in an estimated population parameter such as a mean.
takeaway: Confidence interval = plausible range for the true population parameter, not for individual values.
thinking: Confidence interval concerns a population parameter, not individual values ↓ built from the sample estimate and its standard error ↓ 95% CI: repeated sampling would capture the true value 95% of the time ↓ The range of values within which the true population parameter is likely to lie
pearl: For a difference between groups, a 95% CI that crosses zero (or crosses 1 for a ratio such as RR or OR) corresponds to a non-significant result at the 5% level.

subject: Emergency Medicine
title: Emergency Medicine: Emergency Medicine - Sepsis
stem: A patient presents with fever, tachycardia, and hypotension. According to the Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines, what is the most appropriate initial management?

options.B: Administer intravenous fluids and antibiotics within 1 hour
options.C: Obtain blood cultures and await results before starting antibiotics

correct_answer: B. Administer intravenous fluids and antibiotics within 1 hour
why_correct: Correct. Fever, tachycardia and hypotension indicate sepsis with circulatory compromise. Both the Surviving Sepsis Campaign hour-1 bundle and the UK Sepsis Trust Sepsis Six call for broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics within 1 hour of recognition, with intravenous fluid resuscitation started promptly for hypotension, alongside blood cultures (taken without delaying antibiotics), lactate measurement, oxygen titrated to target saturations and urine output monitoring. Antibiotics alone do not correct the hypotension.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. While antibiotics are essential, they should be given alongside intravenous fluids, not alone.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Blood cultures should be taken before antibiotics, but treatment should not be delayed awaiting results. Empiric antibiotics should be started within 1 hour.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Vasopressors are used if hypotension persists despite adequate fluid resuscitation. Fluids are the first-line treatment.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. The Surviving Sepsis Campaign allows up to 3 hours only for possible sepsis without shock while the diagnosis is clarified; with hypotension, broad-spectrum antibiotics should be given within 1 hour of recognition, together with fluid resuscitation.

exam_trap: Candidates choose antibiotics within 1 hour alone (A), but hypotension in sepsis also needs prompt fluid resuscitation; antibiotics do not correct circulatory failure.
takeaway: Sepsis with hypotension → IV antibiotics and fluids within the first hour.
thinking: Fever, tachycardia and hypotension ↓ sepsis with circulatory compromise ↓ hour-1 care: cultures, lactate and IV antibiotics ↓ hypotension also needs prompt IV fluid resuscitation ↓ Administer intravenous fluids and antibiotics within 1 hour
pearl: Hypotension persisting despite fluid resuscitation indicates septic shock needing vasopressors, with noradrenaline first line, and early source control such as drainage of a collection.

subject: Emergency Medicine
title: Emergency Medicine: Emergency Medicine - Trauma
stem: A patient presents with a tension pneumothorax following blunt chest trauma. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.B: Needle decompression in the fourth or fifth intercostal space, just anterior to the mid-axillary line
options.C: Chest drain insertion in the fifth intercostal space, mid-axillary line

correct_answer: B. Needle decompression in the fourth or fifth intercostal space, just anterior to the mid-axillary line
why_correct: Correct. Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis and needs immediate decompression. In adults, ATLS (10th edition) recommends needle decompression in the fourth or fifth intercostal space just anterior to the mid-axillary line, where the chest wall is thinner than at the second intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line (still used in children). Decompression is followed by chest drain insertion.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis and should not be delayed for imaging. Immediate decompression is required.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Chest drain insertion is the definitive treatment, but needle decompression should be performed first to relieve the tension.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Positive pressure ventilation can worsen tension pneumothorax. Decompression must be performed first.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Pericardiocentesis is the treatment for cardiac tamponade, a different life-threatening condition following chest trauma. Tension pneumothorax is treated with immediate needle decompression.

exam_trap: Candidates choose chest drain insertion (C) as definitive care, but in tension pneumothorax immediate needle decompression comes first to relieve the pressure.
takeaway: Tension pneumothorax → immediate decompression in the 4th/5th intercostal space anterior to the mid-axillary line, then chest drain.
thinking: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis ↓ it needs immediate decompression, not imaging ↓ adult ATLS site: 4th or 5th intercostal space just anterior to the mid-axillary line ↓ a chest drain follows ↓ Needle decompression in the fourth or fifth intercostal space, just anterior to the mid-axillary line
pearl: Finger thoracostomy is an alternative decompression in trauma, particularly in ventilated patients, and any decompression must be followed by a formal chest drain.

subject: Emergency Medicine
title: Emergency Medicine: Emergency Medicine - Cardiac
stem: A patient presents 2 hours after the onset of central chest pain, with ST elevation in leads V1 to V4. A primary PCI centre is 30 minutes away. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.A: Administer aspirin and arrange for primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI)
options.B: Administer aspirin and await troponin results
options.C: Administer thrombolysis and await cardiology review
options.E: Administer clopidogrel and arrange elective PCI

correct_answer: A. Administer aspirin and arrange for primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI)
why_correct: Correct. For ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), immediate management is aspirin 300 mg and urgent reperfusion. Primary PCI is the preferred strategy for patients presenting within 12 hours of symptom onset if it can be delivered within 120 minutes of the time fibrinolysis could have been given; otherwise fibrinolysis is offered.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. STEMI is diagnosed on ECG, not troponin. Troponin may be normal early in STEMI. Treatment should not be delayed.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Thrombolysis is an option if PCI is not available within 120 minutes, but PCI is preferred. Awaiting cardiology review may delay treatment.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Morphine provides symptomatic relief but does not treat the underlying coronary occlusion. Reperfusion therapy is essential.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Elective PCI is not appropriate for a patient with ST elevation myocardial infarction, who requires emergency reperfusion. Aspirin should be given immediately and the patient referred for primary (emergency) PCI.

exam_trap: Candidates choose thrombolysis (C), but primary PCI is preferred when it can be delivered within 120 minutes of when fibrinolysis could have been given.
takeaway: STEMI within 12 hours with PCI achievable within 120 minutes → aspirin and primary PCI.
thinking: Central chest pain for 2 hours with ST elevation in V1-V4 ↓ anterior STEMI within 12 hours of onset ↓ PCI centre 30 minutes away, well within the 120-minute window ↓ aspirin plus primary PCI ↓ Administer aspirin and arrange for primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI)
pearl: ST elevation in V1-V4 indicates an anterior infarct, usually from left anterior descending artery occlusion, whereas changes in II, III and aVF point to an inferior infarct, usually from the right coronary artery.

subject: Emergency Medicine
title: Emergency Medicine: Emergency Medicine - Anaphylaxis
stem: An adult develops anaphylaxis after a bee sting. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
why_correct: Correct. Intramuscular adrenaline 0.5 mg (0.5 mL of 1 mg/mL, that is 1:1000) into the anterolateral thigh is the first-line treatment and is repeated after 5 minutes if there is no improvement. It reverses vasodilation, bronchospasm and capillary leak. High-flow oxygen and an intravenous fluid bolus are given for respiratory or circulatory compromise; antihistamines are only for skin symptoms once the patient is stable, and corticosteroids are no longer routinely recommended in the emergency phase.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. Corticosteroids are no longer routinely recommended in the emergency treatment of anaphylaxis, have no proven benefit in preventing biphasic reactions and must never delay intramuscular adrenaline.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. A non-sedating oral antihistamine may be given for skin symptoms after stabilisation, but antihistamines do not treat the life-threatening airway, breathing or circulation features of anaphylaxis.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. IV fluids are important for hypotension but are not sufficient alone. Adrenaline is the first-line treatment.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Intravenous adrenaline at this dose is dangerous and can precipitate arrhythmias; intravenous adrenaline is reserved for specialist use in refractory anaphylaxis at much lower, titrated doses. The correct first-line route and dose is intramuscular adrenaline 0.5 mg.

exam_trap: Candidates choose intravenous adrenaline 0.5 mg (E), but an IV bolus at this dose can cause fatal arrhythmias; first-line treatment is 0.5 mg intramuscularly.
takeaway: Anaphylaxis → IM adrenaline 0.5 mg (1 mg/mL) into the anterolateral thigh, repeated after 5 minutes if needed.
thinking: Anaphylaxis after a bee sting ↓ life-threatening airway, breathing or circulation problem ↓ first-line drug is adrenaline ↓ adult dose 0.5 mg intramuscularly into the anterolateral thigh ↓ Administer intramuscular adrenaline (epinephrine) 0.5 mg
pearl: If features persist after two doses of intramuscular adrenaline and fluids, refractory anaphylaxis needs an expert-led low-dose adrenaline infusion; mast cell tryptase is sent to support the diagnosis.

subject: Emergency Medicine
title: Emergency Medicine: Emergency Medicine - Head Injury
stem: A patient presents with a head injury. The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score is 13 on arrival and is still 13 two hours after the injury. According to NICE guidelines, which of the following is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.E: Skull X-ray to assess for fracture

correct_answer: B. Urgent CT head within 1 hour
why_correct: Correct. NICE (NG232) recommends CT head within 1 hour for adults with a GCS below 13 on initial assessment in the emergency department, a GCS below 15 at 2 hours after the injury, suspected open, depressed or basal skull fracture, post-traumatic seizure, focal neurological deficit or more than one episode of vomiting. A GCS still at 13 two hours after injury meets the 1-hour criterion.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. A GCS that remains below 15 at 2 hours after injury is a high-risk feature, so discharge without imaging is unsafe.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. CT within 8 hours is for patients with no 1-hour indication who have another risk factor, such as taking anticoagulants; a GCS still below 15 at 2 hours requires CT within 1 hour.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Observation alone is insufficient for a patient with a GCS of 13. Imaging is required to rule out intracranial pathology.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Skull X-ray has been superseded by CT in head injury and is not recommended by NICE in this scenario. A GCS still below 15 at 2 hours after injury is an indication for CT head within 1 hour.

exam_trap: Candidates choose CT within 8 hours (C), but a GCS still below 15 two hours after injury is a 1-hour indication under NICE guidance.
takeaway: GCS below 15 at 2 hours after head injury → CT head within 1 hour.
thinking: Head injury with GCS 13 ↓ GCS still below 15 two hours after the injury ↓ NICE high-risk criterion for urgent imaging ↓ discharge, observation alone and skull X-ray are not appropriate ↓ Urgent CT head within 1 hour
pearl: For adults taking anticoagulants with no other indication for CT, NICE advises CT head within 8 hours of the injury; children have separate criteria within the same guideline.

subject: Emergency Medicine
title: Emergency Medicine: Emergency Medicine - Head Injury
stem: A 22-year-old man is struck on the right temple by a cricket ball. He is knocked out briefly, then talks normally for about an hour before becoming increasingly drowsy, and is found to have a fixed dilated right pupil. Which of the following is the most likely underlying pathology?
why_correct: Correct. A fixed dilated pupil (ipsilateral) with contralateral hemiparesis is a classic presentation of an extradural haematoma causing uncal herniation and compression of the oculomotor nerve (CN III). It is often associated with a temporal bone fracture and rupture of the middle meningeal artery.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. Acute subdural haematoma is the commoner traumatic haematoma and can also cause a fixed dilated pupil, but it usually follows a high-energy deceleration injury with reduced consciousness from the outset; a lucid interval after a blow to the temple is characteristic of an extradural haematoma.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Subarachnoid haemorrhage typically presents with a sudden severe headache ('thunderclap'), not a fixed dilated pupil.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Diffuse axonal injury presents with coma without focal neurological signs or pupil abnormalities in the early stages.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. A carotid-cavernous fistula typically presents with proptosis, chemosis, and a cranial bruit following trauma, rather than an acutely evolving fixed dilated pupil. A fixed dilated pupil after head injury is most commonly due to third nerve compression from an expanding extradural haematoma.

exam_trap: Candidates choose subdural haematoma (B), which can also cause a blown pupil, but a lucid interval after a temporal blow is characteristic of extradural bleeding.
takeaway: Temporal blow + lucid interval + ipsilateral fixed dilated pupil → extradural haematoma.
thinking: Blow to the temple with brief loss of consciousness ↓ lucid interval of about an hour ↓ deterioration with a fixed dilated ipsilateral pupil ↓ middle meningeal artery bleed causing uncal herniation and third nerve compression ↓ Extradural haematoma
pearl: The pterion overlies the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery; an extradural haematoma looks lentiform on CT because it is limited by the cranial sutures, and needs urgent evacuation.

subject: Emergency Medicine
title: Emergency Medicine: Emergency Medicine - Chest Trauma
stem: A patient presents with a flail chest following blunt trauma. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?

options.E: High-flow oxygen via non-rebreather mask alone

why_correct: Correct. The initial management of a flail chest is aggressive pain control (e.g., epidural analgesia, intercostal nerve blocks) and physiotherapy to prevent atelectasis and pneumonia. This improves ventilation and avoids the need for mechanical ventilation. Surgery may be considered for severe cases.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Intubation is reserved for patients who fail non-invasive management or have severe respiratory failure. Pain control and physiotherapy are first-line.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. A chest drain is indicated if there is an associated pneumothorax or haemothorax, but it is not the primary treatment for flail chest itself.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Surgical fixation may be considered in selected patients with severe flail chest or failure of conservative management, but it is not the initial management.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Oxygen alone does not address the underlying pain and hypoventilation that drive complications of flail chest. Effective analgesia combined with physiotherapy to support adequate ventilation is the mainstay of initial management.

exam_trap: Option A (immediate intubation) tempts because flail chest looks dramatic, but most patients are managed with analgesia and physiotherapy; ventilation is kept for respiratory failure.
takeaway: Flail chest → analgesia (often regional) and physiotherapy first; ventilate only if failing.
thinking: Flail chest after blunt trauma ↓ paradoxical segment plus underlying lung contusion ↓ pain causes splinting, hypoventilation and atelectasis ↓ effective analgesia and physiotherapy maintain ventilation ↓ Pain control and physiotherapy
pearl: The hypoxia in flail chest is caused mainly by the underlying pulmonary contusion rather than the paradoxical movement itself, so fluid overload should be avoided and respiratory function watched closely.

subject: Emergency Medicine
title: Emergency Medicine: Emergency Medicine - Abdominal Trauma
stem: A patient with blunt abdominal trauma is haemodynamically stable after the primary survey. Which investigation is most appropriate to define the intra-abdominal injuries?

options.B: Focused assessment with sonography for trauma (FAST)
options.C: CT scan of the abdomen with contrast

correct_answer: C. CT scan of the abdomen with contrast
why_correct: Correct. In a haemodynamically stable patient with blunt abdominal trauma, a contrast-enhanced CT scan is the investigation of choice. It can identify solid organ injury, free fluid, and retroperitoneal injuries, and guide non-operative management.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. DPL is rarely used now and has been largely replaced by FAST and CT.
why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. FAST is a rapid bedside adjunct for free fluid, used mainly to guide decisions in unstable patients; it cannot grade solid organ injury or reliably detect retroperitoneal or hollow viscus injury, so CT is needed to define injuries in a stable patient.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Laparotomy is indicated for haemodynamically unstable patients or those with peritonitis. It is not the initial investigation in stable patients.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Serial examination alone is insufficiently sensitive to exclude significant intra-abdominal injury and risks delayed diagnosis. In a haemodynamically stable patient, contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen is the investigation of choice.

exam_trap: Candidates choose FAST (B), but it only detects free fluid and mainly guides unstable patients; it cannot grade organ injury or exclude retroperitoneal injury.
takeaway: Stable blunt abdominal trauma → contrast CT; unstable → FAST and laparotomy.
thinking: Blunt abdominal trauma ↓ haemodynamically stable after the primary survey ↓ there is time to define injuries precisely ↓ contrast CT shows solid organ, retroperitoneal and vascular injury and guides non-operative care ↓ CT scan of the abdomen with contrast
pearl: Most haemodynamically stable liver and spleen injuries are managed non-operatively with close monitoring, with angioembolisation for active contrast extravasation.

subject: Emergency Medicine
title: Emergency Medicine: Emergency Medicine - Cardiac
stem: A patient presents with a narrow complex tachycardia at a rate of 180 bpm. The patient is haemodynamically stable and vagal manoeuvres have failed. What is the most appropriate next management?
why_correct: Correct. For a haemodynamically stable patient with a narrow complex tachycardia (likely supraventricular tachycardia), intravenous adenosine is the first-line treatment. It transiently blocks the AV node, terminating the arrhythmia and helping to diagnose the underlying rhythm.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. Amiodarone is used for ventricular arrhythmias or atrial fibrillation, not typically as first-line for stable narrow complex tachycardia.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. DC cardioversion is indicated for haemodynamically unstable patients with narrow complex tachycardia. This patient is stable.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Beta-blockers may be used for rate control in atrial fibrillation but are not first-line for stable narrow complex tachycardia.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Digoxin has a slow onset of action and is not used for acute termination of a narrow complex tachycardia. Intravenous adenosine is the treatment of choice in a haemodynamically stable patient.

exam_trap: Candidates choose DC cardioversion (C), but synchronised cardioversion is reserved for adverse features such as shock, syncope, myocardial ischaemia or heart failure.
takeaway: Stable narrow complex tachycardia → vagal manoeuvres, then IV adenosine.
thinking: Narrow complex tachycardia at 180 bpm ↓ haemodynamically stable, so no cardioversion ↓ vagal manoeuvres have failed ↓ next, block the AV node transiently ↓ Intravenous adenosine
pearl: Adenosine is given as a rapid IV bolus into a large proximal vein followed by a saline flush; patients should be warned of transient chest discomfort, and it is avoided in severe asthma.

subject: Emergency Medicine
title: Emergency Medicine: Emergency Medicine - Cardiac
stem: A patient presents with a broad complex tachycardia and is haemodynamically unstable. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
why_correct: Correct. For a haemodynamically unstable patient with a broad complex tachycardia (likely ventricular tachycardia), immediate synchronised DC cardioversion is the treatment of choice. If the patient is pulseless, defibrillation (unsynchronised) is required.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Adenosine is used for regular narrow complex tachycardia and occasionally for a stable regular broad complex tachycardia thought to be SVT with aberrant conduction; it is not appropriate in an unstable patient, who needs synchronised DC cardioversion.
why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. Amiodarone is used for stable broad complex tachycardia or after cardioversion in unstable patients. In an unstable patient, cardioversion is the priority.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Beta-blockers are not used for broad complex tachycardia in unstable patients. They may worsen hypotension.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Vagal manoeuvres are used in stable narrow complex tachycardias, not in a haemodynamically unstable patient. An unstable broad complex tachycardia requires immediate synchronised DC cardioversion.

exam_trap: Option B (amiodarone) tempts because it treats ventricular tachycardia, but in an unstable patient drug therapy is too slow; synchronised DC cardioversion comes first.
takeaway: Unstable broad complex tachycardia with a pulse → synchronised DC cardioversion.
thinking: Broad complex tachycardia ↓ haemodynamically unstable ↓ adverse features mean electrical treatment, not drugs ↓ synchronised shock under sedation or anaesthesia ↓ DC cardioversion
pearl: Synchronised cardioversion delivers the shock on the R wave to avoid the vulnerable period of the T wave; if up to three attempts fail, amiodarone is given and cardioversion repeated.

subject: Emergency Medicine
title: Emergency Medicine: Emergency Medicine - Respiratory
stem: A patient with acute severe asthma has received oxygen, nebulised salbutamol, nebulised ipratropium and oral prednisolone but is not improving. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
why_correct: Correct. For acute severe asthma not responding to nebulised bronchodilators and corticosteroids, intravenous magnesium sulphate is recommended. It causes smooth muscle relaxation and bronchodilation. It should be given as a single dose over 20 minutes.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Aminophylline is used for severe or life-threatening asthma not responding to initial treatment, but magnesium sulphate is now preferred as the next step.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Oral prednisolone has already been given; steroids are essential in every acute attack but take hours to act and do not address the failure to respond to bronchodilators.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Antibiotics are not routinely indicated for asthma unless there is evidence of bacterial infection.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Intravenous salbutamol may be considered later in the treatment escalation, but current guidance recommends a single dose of intravenous magnesium sulphate as the next step after nebulised bronchodilators have failed.

exam_trap: Candidates choose intravenous aminophylline (A), but it is considered only after senior review if bronchodilators and magnesium fail; magnesium comes first.
takeaway: Asthma failing nebulisers and steroids → single dose of IV magnesium sulphate.
thinking: Acute severe asthma ↓ already given oxygen, nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium, and steroids ↓ not improving ↓ add a single IV dose of magnesium sulphate ↓ Intravenous magnesium sulphate
pearl: A normal or rising PaCO2 in acute asthma is a life-threatening sign of exhaustion and should prompt early critical care referral.

subject: Emergency Medicine
title: Emergency Medicine: Emergency Medicine - Respiratory
stem: A patient with suspected pulmonary embolism is haemodynamically stable and has a two-level Wells score of 2 (PE unlikely). Which of the following is the most appropriate initial investigation?
why_correct: Correct. For a haemodynamically stable patient with suspected pulmonary embolism, the initial investigation is a D-dimer test. If the D-dimer is negative and clinical probability is low, PE can be excluded. If positive, further imaging (CTPA) is required.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. CTPA is the definitive imaging investigation for PE, but it is not the initial test in stable patients. It is performed after a positive D-dimer or in high-risk patients.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. V/Q scan is an alternative to CTPA, particularly in patients with renal impairment or contrast allergy, but it is not the initial investigation.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Doppler ultrasound is used to detect deep vein thrombosis, which may be the source of PE, but it is not the initial investigation for suspected PE.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. A chest X-ray is often performed to look for alternative explanations for symptoms but does not diagnose or exclude pulmonary embolism. In a haemodynamically stable patient with a low pre-test probability, D-dimer is the appropriate initial investigation.

exam_trap: Candidates go straight to CTPA (B), but with a Wells score of 4 or less PE is unlikely and a D-dimer should come first.
takeaway: Wells ≤4 (PE unlikely) → D-dimer; Wells >4 (PE likely) → CTPA.
thinking: Suspected PE in a haemodynamically stable patient ↓ two-level Wells score 2 = PE unlikely ↓ D-dimer first ↓ a negative D-dimer excludes PE; a positive one leads to CTPA ↓ D-dimer
pearl: D-dimer is sensitive but non-specific, rising after surgery, trauma, pregnancy and malignancy, so it is of limited use in the early postoperative patient.

subject: Emergency Medicine
title: Emergency Medicine: Emergency Medicine - Neurological
stem: A patient presents with a sudden onset of severe headache, neck stiffness, and photophobia. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Correct. A sudden severe ('thunderclap') headache with neck stiffness and photophobia is classic for subarachnoid haemorrhage, most commonly from a ruptured berry (saccular) aneurysm. Non-contrast CT head is the first investigation. If CT performed within 6 hours of onset is normal, lumbar puncture is not routinely needed; if CT is performed more than 6 hours after onset and is normal, lumbar puncture should be considered, at least 12 hours after onset.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. Meningitis presents with fever, headache, neck stiffness, and photophobia, but the onset is usually less abrupt than subarachnoid haemorrhage. A rash may be present in meningococcal meningitis.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Migraine typically presents with a throbbing headache, often unilateral, with nausea, vomiting, and photophobia. The onset is usually gradual, not sudden.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Tension headache presents with a bilateral, pressing headache without neck stiffness or photophobia. It is not sudden in onset.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Cluster headache typically causes unilateral periorbital pain with autonomic features such as lacrimation, but not neck stiffness or photophobia. Sudden severe ('thunderclap') headache with neck stiffness and photophobia is characteristic of subarachnoid haemorrhage.

exam_trap: Candidates pick meningitis (B) because of meningism, but a sudden thunderclap onset points to subarachnoid haemorrhage; meningitis usually develops over hours with fever.
takeaway: Thunderclap headache + meningism → subarachnoid haemorrhage until proven otherwise; non-contrast CT first.
thinking: Sudden severe thunderclap headache ↓ neck stiffness and photophobia = meningism ↓ abrupt onset favours bleeding over infection ↓ most often a ruptured berry aneurysm ↓ Subarachnoid haemorrhage
pearl: After confirmed aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage, oral nimodipine is given to reduce delayed cerebral ischaemia from vasospasm, and the aneurysm is usually secured by endovascular coiling.

subject: Emergency Medicine
title: Emergency Medicine: Emergency Medicine - Toxicology
stem: A 70 kg adult presents 10 hours after taking a single overdose of 20 g of paracetamol. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Start intravenous acetylcysteine immediately, without waiting for the paracetamol level
options.B: Administer N-acetylcysteine only if the paracetamol level is above the treatment line
options.C: Administer activated charcoal if ingestion was within 4 hours
options.D: Administer N-acetylcysteine only if the patient is symptomatic
options.E: Administer intravenous NAC only if the INR is elevated

correct_answer: A. Start intravenous acetylcysteine immediately, without waiting for the paracetamol level
why_correct: Correct. This is a potentially toxic overdose (about 285 mg/kg, well above 150 mg/kg) presenting more than 8 hours after ingestion. Acetylcysteine replenishes hepatic glutathione and detoxifies NAPQI and is most effective within 8 hours, so it is started immediately. Bloods (paracetamol level, liver function, INR, creatinine) are taken at the same time, and the level is interpreted against the UK single treatment line (100 mg/L at 4 hours).

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. Waiting for the level and treating only if it is on or above the treatment line is appropriate for a single ingestion presenting within 8 hours; at 10 hours, waiting would delay treatment further beyond the most effective window.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Activated charcoal is considered only within 1 hour of ingestion; at 10 hours it has no role, and acetylcysteine is the definitive treatment.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Patients with paracetamol overdose may be asymptomatic initially. Treatment is based on the ingested dose and paracetamol levels, not symptoms.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Waiting for deranged liver function or coagulation before starting treatment risks missing the window for effective hepatoprotection. N-acetylcysteine should be started based on ingestion time or paracetamol level, not deranged INR.

exam_trap: Candidates choose to wait for the level (B), which is correct within 8 hours, but at 10 hours waiting delays acetylcysteine beyond its most effective window.
takeaway: Paracetamol over 150 mg/kg presenting after 8 hours → start acetylcysteine immediately.
thinking: 20 g in a 70 kg adult is about 285 mg/kg, above 150 mg/kg ↓ single ingestion presenting 10 hours later ↓ beyond 8 hours, delay reduces acetylcysteine efficacy ↓ start treatment now and review when the level returns ↓ Start intravenous acetylcysteine immediately, without waiting for the paracetamol level
pearl: The treatment line cannot be used for staggered overdoses or an uncertain time of ingestion; these patients are treated on the dose taken and blood results rather than a single plotted level.

subject: Basic Sciences
title: Basic Sciences: Basic Sciences - Statistics
stem: Which of the following best describes a randomised controlled trial (RCT)?

options.A: Participants are allocated to treatment groups based on their preference
options.B: Participants are randomly allocated to treatment groups to minimise bias
options.C: Participants are selected based on their exposure to a risk factor
options.D: Participants are matched based on age and sex
options.E: Participants are followed prospectively without any intervention

correct_answer: B. Participants are randomly allocated to treatment groups to minimise bias
why_correct: Correct. Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) randomly allocate participants to intervention or control groups. This minimises selection bias and confounding, allowing causal inferences to be made. RCTs are the gold standard for clinical trials.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. This describes a non-randomised study, which is prone to selection bias.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. This describes a cohort study, where participants are followed over time based on their exposure status.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Matching is a technique used in case-control studies to reduce confounding, not the defining feature of an RCT.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. This describes an observational cohort study. In a randomised controlled trial, participants are actively allocated at random to receive different interventions.

exam_trap: Option E describes a prospective cohort and D describes matching in case-control studies; neither involves the random allocation of an intervention that defines an RCT.
takeaway: RCT = random allocation to intervention or control to minimise bias and confounding.
thinking: Defining feature asked is how participants are allocated ↓ random allocation balances known and unknown confounders ↓ this minimises selection bias and allows causal inference ↓ Participants are randomly allocated to treatment groups to minimise bias
pearl: Randomisation only protects against bias if allocation is concealed until enrolment, and results should be analysed by intention to treat to preserve the balance it creates.

subject: Basic Sciences
title: Basic Sciences: Basic Sciences - Statistics
stem: Which of the following best describes a cohort study?

options.A: Participants are selected based on the outcome and compared for past exposure
options.B: Participants are followed over time to observe the development of outcomes
options.C: Participants are randomly allocated to treatment groups
options.D: Participants are selected based on their disease status
options.E: Participants are assessed for exposure and outcome at a single point in time

correct_answer: B. Participants are followed over time to observe the development of outcomes
why_correct: Correct. A cohort study follows a group of participants over time to see who develops the outcome of interest. Participants are classified based on their exposure status (exposed vs. unexposed). Cohort studies can be prospective or retrospective.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. This describes a case-control study, where participants are selected based on whether they have the outcome (cases) or not (controls), and their past exposure is compared.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. This describes a randomised controlled trial (RCT).
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. This describes a case-control study.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. This describes a cross-sectional study. A cohort study instead follows participants forward over time to observe whether outcomes develop.

exam_trap: Candidates confuse A and B; selecting by outcome and looking back at exposure is a case-control study, whereas a cohort starts with exposure and follows people forward.
takeaway: Cohort = exposure first, follow over time for outcome → incidence and relative risk.
thinking: Cohort is defined by exposure status at the start ↓ participants are followed forward in time ↓ new outcomes are counted, so incidence and relative risk can be calculated ↓ Participants are followed over time to observe the development of outcomes
pearl: Cohort studies suit rare exposures and can examine several outcomes of one exposure, but they are slow and inefficient for rare diseases, where a case-control design is preferred.

subject: Basic Sciences
title: Basic Sciences: Basic Sciences - Statistics
stem: Which of the following best describes a case-control study?

options.A: Participants are followed over time to observe the development of outcomes
options.B: Participants are randomly allocated to treatment groups
options.C: Participants are selected based on the outcome and compared for past exposure
options.D: Participants are selected based on their exposure status and followed forward
options.E: The incidence of disease can be calculated directly from the study sample

correct_answer: C. Participants are selected based on the outcome and compared for past exposure
why_correct: Correct. In a case-control study, participants are selected based on whether they have the outcome (cases) or not (controls). Their past exposure to risk factors is then compared. Case-control studies are useful for rare diseases and can be conducted retrospectively.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. This describes a cohort study.
why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. This describes a randomised controlled trial (RCT).
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. This describes a cohort study.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Because participants are selected on the basis of outcome status, a case-control study cannot generate a true incidence rate. It instead compares past exposures between cases and controls.

exam_trap: Option E tempts because incidence seems a basic output, but the investigator fixes the numbers of cases and controls, so incidence cannot be calculated; only an odds ratio can be estimated.
takeaway: Case-control = start with outcome, look back at exposure; best for rare diseases.
thinking: Case-control design starts with the outcome ↓ cases with the disease are compared with controls without it ↓ past exposure is measured retrospectively ↓ Participants are selected based on the outcome and compared for past exposure
pearl: Case-control studies are efficient for rare diseases or long latency, but are especially prone to recall bias because exposure is reported after the outcome is known.

subject: Basic Sciences
title: Basic Sciences: Basic Sciences - Statistics
stem: Which of the following measures is used to quantify the strength of association in a case-control study?
why_correct: Correct. In a case-control study, the odds ratio (OR) is used to estimate the strength of association between exposure and outcome. It is the ratio of the odds of exposure in cases to the odds of exposure in controls. An OR of 1 indicates no association.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Relative risk is used in cohort studies and RCTs, where the incidence of the outcome can be calculated in exposed and unexposed groups.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Attributable risk is the difference in incidence between exposed and unexposed groups. It is used in cohort studies.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Absolute risk reduction is the difference in event rates between control and treatment groups. It is used in RCTs.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. The hazard ratio is derived from survival (time-to-event) analysis, typically in cohort studies or trials with follow-up over time. The odds ratio is the appropriate measure of association in a case-control study.

exam_trap: Candidates pick relative risk (A) as the default measure, but relative risk needs incidence, which a case-control design cannot provide because subjects are chosen by outcome.
takeaway: Case-control → odds ratio; cohort or RCT → relative risk.
thinking: Case-control study samples by outcome ↓ investigator chooses the numbers of cases and controls ↓ incidence cannot be calculated, so relative risk is unavailable ↓ odds of exposure are compared between the groups ↓ Odds ratio
pearl: When the outcome is rare, the odds ratio from a case-control study closely approximates the relative risk, which is why it is accepted as an estimate of risk.

subject: Basic Sciences
title: Basic Sciences: Basic Sciences - Statistics
stem: Which of the following measures is used to quantify the strength of association in a cohort study?
why_correct: Correct. Relative risk (RR) is used in cohort studies and RCTs. It is the ratio of the incidence of the outcome in the exposed group to the incidence in the unexposed group. An RR of 1 indicates no association.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Odds ratio is used in case-control studies.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Number needed to treat (NNT) is used in RCTs to describe the number of patients who need to be treated to prevent one additional adverse outcome.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Positive predictive value (PPV) is the probability that a patient with a positive test result actually has the disease. It is not a measure of association.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Attributable risk quantifies the absolute excess risk due to exposure, rather than the relative strength of association. Relative risk is the standard measure of association used in a cohort study.

exam_trap: Attributable risk (E) also comes from cohort data, but it is an absolute excess risk; the relative strength of association is expressed by the relative risk.
takeaway: Cohort study → relative risk = incidence in exposed / incidence in unexposed.
thinking: Cohort follows exposed and unexposed groups forward ↓ incidence is measured in each group ↓ the ratio of incidences gives the strength of association ↓ Relative risk
pearl: Relative risk shows the strength of an association, but absolute measures such as attributable risk and number needed to treat better convey the clinical impact for an individual patient.

subject: Basic Sciences
title: Basic Sciences: Basic Sciences - Genetics
stem: Which of the following best describes an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern?

options.A: The trait appears only in males
options.B: The trait appears in every generation and affects males and females equally
options.C: The trait skips generations and affects males more than females
options.D: The trait is passed only from mother to son
options.E: The trait requires two copies of the mutant allele to manifest

correct_answer: B. The trait appears in every generation and affects males and females equally
why_correct: Correct. Autosomal dominant inheritance means that a single copy of the mutated gene is sufficient to cause the trait. It affects males and females equally, and the trait typically appears in every generation (vertical transmission). Examples include Huntington's disease, Marfan syndrome, and neurofibromatosis type 1.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. A trait seen only in males suggests Y-linked inheritance; X-linked recessive traits affect males predominantly but not exclusively. Autosomal dominant traits affect males and females equally.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. This describes X-linked recessive inheritance.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. No recognised inheritance pattern passes only from mother to son; mitochondrial disorders pass from an affected mother to all her children, and X-linked recessive traits pass from carrier mothers mainly to sons. Autosomal dominant traits pass from either parent to children of either sex.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. This describes an autosomal recessive pattern. An autosomal dominant trait manifests with only one copy of the mutant allele and appears in every generation, affecting males and females equally.

exam_trap: Option E is chosen by confusing dominant with recessive; needing two mutant copies describes autosomal recessive inheritance, whereas one copy suffices in dominant disease.
takeaway: Autosomal dominant: one mutant copy, vertical transmission, males and females equally affected.
thinking: Autosomal dominant ↓ one mutant allele is enough to express the trait ↓ an affected parent passes it to each child with equal chance regardless of sex ↓ vertical transmission through generations ↓ The trait appears in every generation and affects males and females equally
pearl: Male-to-male transmission excludes X-linked inheritance and supports autosomal dominance, while reduced penetrance can make a dominant trait appear to skip a generation.

subject: Basic Sciences
title: Basic Sciences: Basic Sciences - Genetics
stem: Which of the following best describes an X-linked recessive inheritance pattern?

options.A: The trait affects males and females equally
options.B: The trait affects males more than females and is never passed from father to son
options.C: The trait appears in every generation
options.D: The trait is passed only from mother to daughter
options.E: The trait requires only one copy of the mutant allele in females to manifest

correct_answer: B. The trait affects males more than females and is never passed from father to son
why_correct: Correct. X-linked recessive inheritance affects males more than females because males have only one X chromosome. Affected males cannot pass the trait to their sons (they pass their Y chromosome to sons), but they can pass the carrier state to their daughters. Examples include haemophilia A and B, Duchenne muscular dystrophy, and red-green colour blindness.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. This describes autosomal inheritance.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. X-linked recessive traits often skip generations (e.g., an affected male may have unaffected parents if the mother is a carrier).
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. No standard inheritance pattern is transmitted only from mother to daughter; mitochondrial disorders pass from an affected mother to both sons and daughters. X-linked recessive traits are transmitted by carrier mothers to affected sons and carrier daughters.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. This describes an X-linked dominant pattern. In X-linked recessive inheritance, females generally require two copies of the mutant allele to be affected, so the trait affects males more than females and is never passed from father to son.

exam_trap: Option E is chosen by confusing recessive with dominant; disease in females from one mutant copy describes X-linked dominant inheritance, not X-linked recessive.
takeaway: X-linked recessive: males mainly affected, carrier mothers, no father-to-son transmission.
thinking: X-linked recessive ↓ males have one X, so one mutant copy causes disease ↓ females usually need two copies and are mostly carriers ↓ fathers pass their Y, not their X, to sons ↓ The trait affects males more than females and is never passed from father to son
pearl: Haemophilia A and B are X-linked recessive; all daughters of an affected male are obligate carriers, and affected males need haematology input and factor replacement planning before surgery.

subject: Basic Sciences
title: Basic Sciences: Basic Sciences - Genetics
stem: Which of the following is the most common chromosomal abnormality causing Down syndrome?
why_correct: Correct. Down syndrome (trisomy 21) is most commonly caused by non-disjunction during meiosis, resulting in three copies of chromosome 21. This accounts for approximately 95% of cases and is associated with advanced maternal age.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. Robertsonian translocation accounts for approximately 4% of Down syndrome cases. It involves the fusion of chromosome 21 with another acrocentric chromosome (usually 14).
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Mosaicism accounts for approximately 1% of Down syndrome cases. It occurs when some cells have trisomy 21 and others are normal, due to post-zygotic non-disjunction.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Deletion of chromosome 21 does not cause Down syndrome. Down syndrome is caused by an extra copy of chromosome 21.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Isochromosome formation is an extremely rare cause of Down syndrome. The overwhelming majority of cases (around 95%) result from trisomy 21 due to meiotic non-disjunction.

exam_trap: Robertsonian translocation (B) matters for recurrence counselling because it can be inherited, but it causes only a small minority of cases; non-disjunction trisomy accounts for most.
takeaway: Down syndrome → most commonly trisomy 21 from maternal meiotic non-disjunction.
thinking: Down syndrome results from an extra copy of chromosome 21 ↓ most often from meiotic non-disjunction, usually maternal ↓ risk rises with maternal age ↓ translocation and mosaic forms are small minorities ↓ Trisomy 21 due to non-disjunction
pearl: Down syndrome carries surgical associations including duodenal atresia (double-bubble sign on X-ray), aganglionic megacolon and atrioventricular septal defects.

subject: Basic Sciences
title: Basic Sciences: Basic Sciences - Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following is the rate-limiting enzyme in glycolysis?
why_correct: Correct. Phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1) is the rate-limiting enzyme of glycolysis. It catalyses the conversion of fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate. It is allosterically inhibited by ATP and citrate, and activated by AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Hexokinase catalyses the first step of glycolysis (phosphorylation of glucose to glucose-6-phosphate), but it is not the rate-limiting enzyme.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Pyruvate kinase catalyses the final step of glycolysis (conversion of phosphoenolpyruvate to pyruvate), but it is not the rate-limiting enzyme.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Glucose-6-phosphatase is involved in gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis, not glycolysis. It catalyses the conversion of glucose-6-phosphate to glucose.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase is the rate-limiting enzyme of the pentose phosphate pathway, not glycolysis. Phosphofructokinase-1 is the rate-limiting enzyme of glycolysis.

exam_trap: Hexokinase (A) is tempting because it catalyses the first step, but the committed, rate-limiting step of glycolysis is catalysed by phosphofructokinase-1.
takeaway: Glycolysis rate-limiting enzyme = phosphofructokinase-1.
thinking: Rate-limiting step = committed, tightly regulated step ↓ in glycolysis this is fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate ↓ inhibited by ATP and citrate, activated by AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate ↓ Phosphofructokinase-1
pearl: Pyruvate kinase deficiency is the commonest glycolytic enzyme defect causing hereditary haemolytic anaemia, and splenectomy can reduce transfusion needs in severe cases.

subject: Basic Sciences
title: Basic Sciences: Basic Sciences - Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following is the rate-limiting enzyme in the urea cycle?
why_correct: Correct. Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS1) is the rate-limiting enzyme of the urea cycle. It catalyses the formation of carbamoyl phosphate from ammonia and bicarbonate in the mitochondria. It is activated by N-acetylglutamate. Deficiency causes hyperammonaemia.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. Ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) catalyses the second step of the urea cycle, but it is not the rate-limiting enzyme. Deficiency is the most common urea cycle disorder.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Argininosuccinate synthetase catalyses the third step of the urea cycle. Deficiency causes citrullinaemia.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Arginase catalyses the final step of the urea cycle, producing urea and ornithine. Deficiency causes argininaemia.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. N-acetylglutamate synthase produces N-acetylglutamate, the allosteric activator required for carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I activity, but it is not itself the rate-limiting enzyme of the urea cycle. Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I holds that role.

exam_trap: N-acetylglutamate synthase (E) is tempting because it controls the cycle, but it only makes the allosteric activator; the rate-limiting enzyme itself is carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I.
takeaway: Urea cycle rate-limiting enzyme = CPS I (mitochondrial), activated by N-acetylglutamate.
thinking: Urea cycle converts ammonia to urea in the liver ↓ first step is mitochondrial: ammonia + bicarbonate → carbamoyl phosphate ↓ this step is regulated by N-acetylglutamate ↓ Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I
pearl: Urea cycle disorders present with hyperammonaemic encephalopathy; ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency, the commonest, is X-linked, whereas the other urea cycle enzyme defects are autosomal recessive.

subject: Emergency Medicine
title: Emergency Medicine: Emergency Medicine - Burns
stem: A patient presents with a burn covering 30% of their total body surface area (TBSA). According to the Parkland formula, what is the appropriate fluid resuscitation regimen?

options.A: 2 mL/kg/% TBSA of crystalloid in the first 24 hours
options.B: 4 mL/kg/% TBSA of crystalloid in the first 24 hours
options.C: 6 mL/kg/% TBSA of crystalloid in the first 24 hours
options.D: 8 mL/kg/% TBSA of crystalloid in the first 24 hours
options.E: 3 mL/kg/% TBSA of crystalloid in the first 24 hours

correct_answer: B. 4 mL/kg/% TBSA of crystalloid in the first 24 hours
why_correct: Correct. The Parkland formula recommends 4 mL/kg/% TBSA of crystalloid (typically Hartmann's solution) in the first 24 hours. Half of this volume is given in the first 8 hours from the time of injury, and the remaining half is given over the next 16 hours.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. The Parkland formula uses 4 mL/kg/% TBSA, not 2 mL.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. 6 mL/kg/% TBSA exceeds the Parkland estimate and risks over-resuscitation (fluid creep) with compartment syndrome and pulmonary oedema; the Parkland formula uses 4 mL/kg/% TBSA.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. 8 mL/kg/% TBSA is not the Parkland formula.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. This underestimates the recommended volume. The Parkland formula specifies 4 mL/kg/% TBSA of crystalloid in the first 24 hours, with half given in the first 8 hours.

exam_trap: Candidates choose 2 mL/kg/% TBSA (A), the ATLS adult starting volume, but the question asks for the Parkland formula, which uses 4 mL.
takeaway: Parkland = 4 mL x kg x %TBSA; half in the first 8 hours from injury.
thinking: 30% TBSA burn needs formal resuscitation ↓ the question asks for the Parkland formula ↓ 4 mL x kg x %TBSA of crystalloid over 24 hours ↓ half in the first 8 hours from injury ↓ 4 mL/kg/% TBSA of crystalloid in the first 24 hours
pearl: Only partial- and full-thickness burns count towards %TBSA; simple erythema is excluded, and including it overestimates fluid requirements.

subject: Emergency Medicine
title: Emergency Medicine: Emergency Medicine - Burns
stem: A patient presents with a burn to the face and neck. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.B: Secure the airway and consider intubation
options.D: Apply ice to the affected area
options.E: High-flow humidified oxygen via face mask only

correct_answer: B. Secure the airway and consider intubation
why_correct: Correct. Burns to the face and neck can cause rapid airway swelling and obstruction. The airway should be secured early (e.g., endotracheal intubation) before oedema makes intubation difficult. This is a priority over other interventions.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. While dressings are important, airway management takes priority in burns to the face and neck.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Antibiotics are not routinely indicated for burns unless there is evidence of infection. They are not the immediate priority.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Ice should not be applied to burns as it can cause further tissue damage and hypothermia. Cool running water is used for initial cooling.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Oxygen alone does not protect against impending airway obstruction from oedema following facial and neck burns. The airway must be secured early, with a low threshold for intubation, before swelling progresses.

exam_trap: Option E (oxygen via face mask only) appeals because oxygen is always given, but it does not protect against airway obstruction from progressive oedema.
takeaway: Face and neck burns → assess and secure the airway early, before oedema develops.
thinking: Burn to the face and neck ↓ risk of airway burn and rapidly developing oedema ↓ swelling can make later intubation impossible ↓ secure the airway early ↓ Secure the airway and consider intubation
pearl: Features suggesting inhalation injury include singed nasal hairs, soot in the mouth or sputum, hoarseness, stridor and a burn in an enclosed space; carbon monoxide levels should also be checked.

subject: Emergency Medicine
title: Emergency Medicine: Emergency Medicine - Spinal Injury
stem: A patient presents with a suspected cervical spine injury following a fall. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?

options.A: Immediate removal of the cervical collar
options.B: Manual in-line immobilisation and application of a rigid cervical collar
options.C: Flexion and extension views of the cervical spine
options.D: Immediate MRI of the cervical spine
options.E: Log-roll the patient to assess the back before immobilisation

correct_answer: B. Manual in-line immobilisation and application of a rigid cervical collar
why_correct: Correct. For suspected cervical spine injury, manual in-line immobilisation should be maintained, and a rigid cervical collar should be applied. The patient should be log-rolled for examination and transfers. Imaging (CT or MRI) is performed once the patient is stabilised.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. The cervical collar should not be removed until a spinal injury has been excluded.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Flexion and extension views are contraindicated in the acute setting as they can worsen a spinal injury.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. CT is the first-line imaging for suspected cervical spine injury. MRI is used if there is neurological deficit or suspicion of ligamentous injury.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. While log-rolling is later required to examine the back, immobilisation of the cervical spine takes priority as the first step to prevent secondary neurological injury. Manual in-line stabilisation and application of a rigid collar should be performed first.

exam_trap: Option E (log-roll before immobilisation) is chosen by candidates who want to examine the back first, but spinal immobilisation must come before any patient movement.
takeaway: Suspected cervical spine injury → manual in-line stabilisation and immobilisation first.
thinking: Fall with suspected cervical spine injury ↓ prevent secondary cord injury ↓ manual in-line stabilisation then a rigid collar ↓ imaging only after the patient is immobilised and assessed ↓ Manual in-line immobilisation and application of a rigid cervical collar
pearl: CT of the cervical spine is the first-line imaging for adults at high risk of injury, while MRI is added for neurological signs or suspected ligamentous or cord injury.

subject: Emergency Medicine
title: Emergency Medicine: Emergency Medicine - Spinal Injury
stem: A patient presents with a spinal cord injury and develops hypotension and bradycardia. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Correct. Neurogenic shock occurs due to loss of sympathetic tone following a spinal cord injury (typically above T6). It presents with hypotension, bradycardia, and warm peripheries. Treatment includes fluids, vasopressors, and atropine for bradycardia.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Hypovolaemic shock typically presents with tachycardia and hypotension. Bradycardia is not typical.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Septic shock typically presents with fever, tachycardia, and hypotension. Bradycardia is uncommon.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Cardiogenic shock presents with hypotension, tachycardia, and signs of heart failure (e.g., pulmonary oedema). Bradycardia may occur but is not typical.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Anaphylactic shock is typically triggered by an allergen exposure and is associated with urticaria, angioedema, and bronchospasm, not spinal trauma. Hypotension with bradycardia following spinal cord injury is characteristic of neurogenic shock, caused by loss of sympathetic tone.

exam_trap: Option A (hypovolaemic shock) is chosen because trauma patients bleed, but hypovolaemia causes tachycardia; bradycardia with hypotension after cord injury indicates neurogenic shock.
takeaway: Spinal cord injury + hypotension + bradycardia → neurogenic shock, but exclude bleeding first.
thinking: Spinal cord injury ↓ hypotension with bradycardia ↓ loss of sympathetic outflow with unopposed vagal tone ↓ warm, vasodilated peripheries ↓ Neurogenic shock
pearl: Neurogenic shock is different from spinal shock, which is a temporary loss of all reflexes and tone below the level of a cord injury rather than a haemodynamic state.

subject: Emergency Medicine
title: Emergency Medicine: Emergency Medicine - Pelvic Fracture
stem: A patient with a suspected pelvic fracture after high-energy trauma is hypotensive and tachycardic. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?

options.A: Immediate application of a pelvic binder
options.B: Immediate CT scan of the pelvis
options.D: Immediate traction of the lower limbs
options.E: External fixation in the emergency department

correct_answer: A. Immediate application of a pelvic binder
why_correct: Correct. For a suspected pelvic fracture with haemodynamic instability, a pelvic binder should be applied immediately to reduce pelvic volume and tamponade bleeding. This is a life-saving intervention that should be performed before imaging.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. CT scanning is important for diagnosis but should not delay the application of a pelvic binder in an unstable patient.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Laparotomy is indicated for intra-abdominal bleeding, but a pelvic binder should be applied first to control pelvic bleeding.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Traction is not the initial management for a pelvic fracture. A pelvic binder is the priority.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. External fixation may be used later as a definitive or temporising measure but is not the immediate first step. A pelvic binder should be applied immediately to reduce pelvic volume and control haemorrhage.

exam_trap: Candidates choose immediate CT (B), but an unstable patient with suspected pelvic bleeding needs a binder first; imaging must not delay haemorrhage control.
takeaway: Unstable suspected pelvic fracture → pelvic binder over the greater trochanters immediately.
thinking: High-energy trauma with suspected pelvic fracture ↓ hypotension and tachycardia suggest pelvic haemorrhage ↓ a binder reduces pelvic volume and tamponades bleeding ↓ apply it before imaging ↓ Immediate application of a pelvic binder
pearl: The binder is centred over the greater trochanters, not the iliac crests, and persistent instability may need angioembolisation or preperitoneal packing.

subject: Emergency Medicine
title: Emergency Medicine: Emergency Medicine - Cardiac Arrest
stem: A patient in cardiac arrest presents with a shockable rhythm (ventricular fibrillation). What is the most appropriate immediate management?
why_correct: Correct. For ventricular fibrillation (VF) or pulseless ventricular tachycardia (pVT), immediate defibrillation is the priority. The recommended energy for biphasic defibrillation is 150-200 J. Defibrillation should be performed as soon as possible.

why_others_wrong.A: Incorrect. Adrenaline 1 mg is given after the third shock in a shockable rhythm and then every 3-5 minutes; it is never given before defibrillation.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Amiodarone is given after the third shock if the rhythm persists, not as the first intervention.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Intubation should not delay defibrillation. Defibrillation is the priority in shockable rhythms.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. A precordial thump has a very low success rate and is not recommended as standard management of a shockable rhythm. Prompt defibrillation at 150-200 J biphasic is the immediate priority in ventricular fibrillation.

exam_trap: Candidates give adrenaline first (A), but in a shockable rhythm adrenaline and amiodarone come only after the third shock; defibrillation is immediate.
takeaway: VF/pVT → immediate defibrillation; adrenaline and amiodarone after the third shock.
thinking: Cardiac arrest in ventricular fibrillation ↓ shockable rhythm ↓ early defibrillation is the most effective intervention ↓ biphasic 150-200 J, then resume CPR ↓ Defibrillate at 150-200 J (biphasic)
pearl: After each shock, chest compressions resume immediately for 2 minutes without a rhythm or pulse check, to minimise interruptions in CPR.

subject: Emergency Medicine
title: Emergency Medicine: Emergency Medicine - Stroke
stem: A patient presents with sudden onset of right-sided weakness and aphasia. CT head shows no haemorrhage. What is the most appropriate immediate management if the patient presents within 4.5 hours of symptom onset?

options.E: Administer dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin and clopidogrel)

why_correct: Correct. For acute ischaemic stroke presenting within 4.5 hours of symptom onset, intravenous thrombolysis with alteplase is recommended if there are no contraindications. This should be followed by aspirin after 24 hours if haemorrhage is excluded.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. Aspirin is given after thrombolysis (usually after 24 hours) or if thrombolysis is contraindicated. It is not the immediate treatment.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Heparin is not routinely used in acute ischaemic stroke. It may be used in specific circumstances (e.g., atrial fibrillation) but is not first-line.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Thrombolysis is time-critical. Delaying treatment worsens outcomes.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Antiplatelet therapy is not the immediate treatment of choice within the thrombolysis window and, if given before a thrombolysis decision, can increase bleeding risk. Intravenous alteplase is the appropriate immediate treatment within 4.5 hours of onset in the absence of haemorrhage.

exam_trap: Option B (aspirin 300 mg) tempts because aspirin is standard in stroke, but within the thrombolysis window it is delayed until 24 hours after thrombolysis.
takeaway: Ischaemic stroke within 4.5 hours with haemorrhage excluded → intravenous thrombolysis.
thinking: Sudden right-sided weakness and aphasia ↓ CT excludes haemorrhage ↓ acute ischaemic stroke within 4.5 hours ↓ thrombolysis if no contraindications ↓ Administer intravenous thrombolysis (alteplase)
pearl: Patients with a proximal anterior circulation large-vessel occlusion should also be considered for mechanical thrombectomy, so CT angiography is done alongside the plain CT.

subject: Emergency Medicine
title: Emergency Medicine: Emergency Medicine - Seizures
stem: A patient presents with status epilepticus. What is the most appropriate first-line management?
why_correct: Correct. Status epilepticus is a medical emergency. The first-line treatment is a benzodiazepine, such as intravenous lorazepam (or diazepam). If seizures continue, a second dose of benzodiazepine may be given, followed by phenytoin or levetiracetam.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. Phenytoin is a second-line treatment used if benzodiazepines fail to terminate the seizure.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. Oral medication is not appropriate for status epilepticus. Intravenous therapy is required.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Mannitol is used for raised intracranial pressure, not status epilepticus.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Rectal diazepam is a recognised alternative when intravenous access is unavailable, particularly pre-hospital, but it is not first-line when intravenous access is present. Intravenous lorazepam is the first-line benzodiazepine for status epilepticus in hospital.

exam_trap: Option B (phenytoin) tempts because it is used for status epilepticus, but it is second-line after benzodiazepines have failed, not the first drug.
takeaway: Status epilepticus → intravenous benzodiazepine first, then a second-line antiepileptic.
thinking: Status epilepticus ↓ prolonged seizure causing neuronal injury ↓ benzodiazepine terminates seizures quickly ↓ intravenous route available in hospital ↓ Intravenous lorazepam
pearl: If seizures continue after two doses of benzodiazepine, a second-line agent such as levetiracetam, phenytoin or sodium valproate is given, and refractory status needs anaesthesia and intensive care.

subject: Emergency Medicine
title: Emergency Medicine: Emergency Medicine - Toxicology
stem: A patient presents with opioid toxicity. Which of the following is the most appropriate antidote?
why_correct: Correct. Naloxone is a competitive opioid receptor antagonist used to reverse opioid toxicity. It rapidly reverses respiratory depression, sedation, and hypotension. It has a short half-life and may need to be repeated or given as an infusion.

why_others_wrong.B: Incorrect. Flumazenil is a benzodiazepine antagonist. It is not used for opioid toxicity.
why_others_wrong.C: Incorrect. N-acetylcysteine is the antidote for paracetamol overdose. It is not used for opioid toxicity.
why_others_wrong.D: Incorrect. Atropine is used for organophosphate poisoning and symptomatic bradycardia. It is not used for opioid toxicity.
why_others_wrong.E: Incorrect. Activated charcoal is used for gastrointestinal decontamination after certain oral overdoses and does not reverse opioid effects; it also carries an aspiration risk in a patient with reduced consciousness. Naloxone is the specific antidote for opioid toxicity.

exam_trap: Option B (flumazenil) catches candidates confusing antidotes; flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, not opioids, and can trigger seizures in mixed overdoses.
takeaway: Opioid toxicity → naloxone, titrated and repeated as needed.
thinking: Opioid toxicity ↓ respiratory depression and reduced consciousness ↓ competitive opioid receptor antagonist ↓ Naloxone
pearl: Naloxone has a shorter duration of action than many opioids, especially long-acting or slow-release preparations, so patients need monitoring for re-sedation and may need an infusion.

subject: Emergency Medicine
title: Emergency Medicine: Emergency Medicine - Alcohol Withdrawal
stem: A patient with a history of chronic alcohol abuse develops tremors, agitation, and hallucinations 24 hours after admission. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
