exam_trap: Follicular carcinoma is tempting for any thyroid FNA, but it cannot be diagnosed on cytology; it needs capsular or vascular invasion on histology and lacks papillary nuclear features.
takeaway: Orphan Annie eyes = papillary thyroid carcinoma. Best prognosis of thyroid cancers.
thinking: Thyroid swelling sampled by FNA ↓ papillary fragments ↓ nuclear grooves and intranuclear pseudoinclusions are papillary nuclear features ↓ Papillary carcinoma
pearl: Papillary carcinoma spreads to cervical lymph nodes and may first present as a lateral neck lump, whereas follicular carcinoma spreads haematogenously to bone and lung.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Pathology (Colorectal Adenocarcinoma)
stem: A 60-year-old man has a colon biopsy showing glands with stratified, hyperchromatic nuclei and loss of polarity. Malignant glands are seen invading through the muscularis mucosae into the submucosa. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: The features described — stratified hyperchromatic nuclei, loss of polarity, and glandular architecture — indicate adenocarcinoma. Adenomas show dysplasia but not invasion; adenocarcinoma shows invasion through the muscularis mucosae.

why_others_wrong.A: An adenoma shows dysplastic glandular change but, by definition, lacks invasion through the muscularis mucosae, which is present here.
why_others_wrong.C: A hyperplastic polyp shows a serrated, non-dysplastic epithelium without the cytological atypia or invasion described.
why_others_wrong.D: A hamartomatous polyp is a disorganised overgrowth of normal tissue elements without malignant cytological features or invasion.
why_others_wrong.E: Lymphoma would show sheets of lymphoid cells rather than the glandular architecture with stratified, hyperchromatic nuclei described.

exam_trap: Adenoma = dysplasia without invasion. Adenocarcinoma = invasion present.
takeaway: Invasion = carcinoma. No invasion = adenoma.

subject: Pathology
title: Pathology (Fibrocystic Breast Change)
stem: A 35-year-old woman has a breast lump. Biopsy shows increased stromal fibrous tissue and cysts. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Fibrocystic change is characterised by stromal fibrosis and cyst formation. It is a benign condition and the most common cause of breast lumps in women aged 30–50.

why_others_wrong.A: Fibroadenoma presents as a discrete, well-circumscribed, mobile mass of stromal and glandular elements, not diffuse cysts and fibrosis.
why_others_wrong.C: Phyllodes tumour shows a leaf-like stromal overgrowth pattern and can be large and rapidly growing, distinct from diffuse cystic and fibrotic change.
why_others_wrong.D: Ductal carcinoma in situ shows malignant epithelial cells confined within the ductal basement membrane, not benign stromal fibrosis and cysts.
why_others_wrong.E: Invasive ductal carcinoma shows malignant cells breaching the basement membrane into stroma, not the benign picture described here.

exam_trap: Candidates choose fibroadenoma (A) or phyllodes tumour (C) because both contain stroma, but they form discrete masses; stromal fibrosis with cysts indicates fibrocystic change.
takeaway: Fibrocystic change = cysts + fibrosis. Fibroadenoma = discrete firm mass.
thinking: Woman aged 35 with a breast lump ↓ stromal fibrosis and cyst formation ↓ benign hormonally responsive change in the 30-50 age group ↓ Fibrocystic change
pearl: A breast cyst that yields blood-stained fluid on aspiration, or leaves a residual mass, needs triple assessment because it may represent an intracystic carcinoma.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Pathology (Small Cell Lung Carcinoma)
stem: A 50-year-old man has a lung biopsy showing small blue cells with hyperchromatic nuclei and scant cytoplasm. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Small cell carcinoma is characterised by small blue cells with hyperchromatic nuclei, scant cytoplasm, and nuclear moulding. It is strongly associated with smoking and is the most aggressive lung cancer, often metastatic at presentation.

why_others_wrong.A: Adenocarcinoma shows gland-forming or mucin-producing cells, not the small blue cells with scant cytoplasm described.
why_others_wrong.B: Squamous cell carcinoma shows keratinisation and intercellular bridges, not small blue cells with nuclear moulding.
why_others_wrong.D: Large cell carcinoma shows large, pleomorphic cells with abundant cytoplasm, the opposite of the scant-cytoplasm small cells described.
why_others_wrong.E: Mesothelioma arises from mesothelial cells lining the pleura with distinct epithelioid or sarcomatoid patterns, not small blue round cells.

exam_trap: Small cell carcinoma is usually disseminated at presentation and treated with chemotherapy with or without radiotherapy; surgery is only considered for very early (T1-T2a N0 M0) disease.
takeaway: Small blue cells = small cell carcinoma. Chemo, not surgery.
thinking: Lung biopsy ↓ small blue cells with hyperchromatic nuclei ↓ scant cytoplasm indicates neuroendocrine small cell morphology ↓ Small cell carcinoma
pearl: Small cell lung carcinoma stains for neuroendocrine markers such as synaptophysin and chromogranin and is the lung cancer classically associated with SIADH and ectopic ACTH secretion.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Pathology (Seminoma)
stem: A 40-year-old man has a testicular mass. The radical inguinal orchidectomy specimen shows sheets of uniform cells with clear cytoplasm and glycogen. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Seminomas are characterised by uniform cells with clear cytoplasm (glycogen-rich) and a lymphoid stroma. They are the most common testicular germ cell tumour and have an excellent prognosis.

why_others_wrong.B: Non-seminomatous germ cell tumours (e.g. yolk sac, choriocarcinoma, embryonal carcinoma) show more pleomorphic, heterogeneous histology and often raise AFP or beta-hCG, unlike the uniform clear cells described.
why_others_wrong.C: Leydig cell tumours are sex cord-stromal tumours with polygonal, eosinophilic cells (sometimes with Reinke crystals), not glycogen-rich clear cells with lymphoid stroma.
why_others_wrong.D: Sertoli cell tumours are also sex cord-stromal tumours with tubular architecture, distinct from the sheet-like clear cell pattern of seminoma.
why_others_wrong.E: Testicular lymphoma shows sheets of lymphoid cells, typically in older men, and lacks the glycogen-rich clear cytoplasm characteristic of seminoma.

exam_trap: Non-seminomatous germ cell tumours such as yolk sac tumour and embryonal carcinoma tempt, but they show pleomorphic histology and often raise AFP or beta-hCG; pure seminoma does not raise AFP.
takeaway: Seminoma = sheets of uniform clear, glycogen-rich cells; AFP is not raised in pure seminoma.
thinking: Testicular mass ↓ sheets of uniform cells ↓ clear, glycogen-rich cytoplasm ↓ classic germ cell tumour morphology ↓ Seminoma
pearl: Testicular tumours are removed by radical inguinal orchidectomy rather than a scrotal approach, to avoid disturbing scrotal lymphatic drainage and seeding the tumour.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Pathology (Basal Cell Carcinoma)
stem: A 70-year-old man has a skin lesion on his face. Biopsy shows nests of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading and retraction artefact. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Peripheral palisading and retraction artefact are classic histological features of basal cell carcinoma. It is the most common skin cancer and rarely metastasises but causes local tissue destruction.

why_others_wrong.A: Squamous cell carcinoma shows keratinisation and intercellular bridges rather than basaloid nests with peripheral palisading.
why_others_wrong.C: Melanoma shows atypical melanocytes, often pigmented, without the palisading basaloid nest pattern.
why_others_wrong.D: Actinic keratosis is a premalignant lesion with dysplasia confined to the epidermis, not invasive basaloid nests with retraction artefact.
why_others_wrong.E: Keratoacanthoma is a rapidly growing squamous lesion with a central keratin plug, histologically distinct from basaloid palisading nests.

exam_trap: Squamous cell carcinoma is the tempting skin cancer, but it shows keratinisation and intercellular bridges; basaloid nests with peripheral palisading and retraction artefact indicate basal cell carcinoma.
takeaway: Palisading + retraction = BCC. Locally invasive but rarely metastatic.
thinking: Elderly man with a facial skin lesion ↓ nests of basaloid cells ↓ peripheral palisading and retraction artefact ↓ Basal cell carcinoma
pearl: Basal cell carcinoma rarely metastasises, but lesions at high-risk facial sites and morphoeic subtypes recur locally, so margin-controlled micrographic surgery is used for selected lesions.

subject: Pathology
title: Pathology (Hepatitis B - Ground-glass Hepatocytes)
stem: A 55-year-old woman has a liver biopsy showing hepatocytes with ground-glass inclusions. What is the most likely cause?
why_correct: Ground-glass inclusions in hepatocytes represent hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) accumulation in the endoplasmic reticulum. It is a hallmark of chronic hepatitis B infection.

why_others_wrong.A: Alcohol-related liver disease typically shows steatosis, Mallory-Denk bodies and fibrosis, not ground-glass hepatocyte inclusions.
why_others_wrong.C: Hepatitis C classically shows lymphoid follicles in portal tracts and steatosis, not ground-glass inclusions.
why_others_wrong.D: Haemochromatosis shows iron deposition (demonstrated with Perls' stain) within hepatocytes, not ground-glass cytoplasmic inclusions.
why_others_wrong.E: Wilson's disease shows copper accumulation with steatosis and fibrosis, but not the characteristic ground-glass hepatocyte appearance of hepatitis B.

exam_trap: Hepatitis C does not produce ground-glass inclusions. It shows lymphoid follicles and steatosis.
takeaway: Ground-glass hepatocytes = hepatitis B. Lymphoid follicles = hepatitis C.
thinking: Liver biopsy ↓ ground-glass hepatocyte cytoplasm ↓ HBsAg accumulating in the endoplasmic reticulum ↓ Hepatitis B infection
pearl: Orcein staining or immunohistochemistry for HBsAg confirms ground-glass hepatocytes, and HBcAg staining helps assess viral replication in chronic hepatitis B.

subject: Pharmacology
title: Pharmacology (Bisphosphonates - Osteonecrosis of Jaw)
stem: A 50-year-old woman is prescribed a drug for osteoporosis. She develops osteonecrosis of the jaw. Which drug is most likely responsible?
why_correct: Bisphosphonates like alendronate can cause osteonecrosis of the jaw, particularly after dental extraction. They inhibit osteoclast function and reduce bone turnover.

why_others_wrong.B: Calcium carbonate is a simple mineral supplement and is not associated with osteonecrosis of the jaw.
why_others_wrong.C: Vitamin D supplementation is not linked to osteonecrosis of the jaw.
why_others_wrong.D: Raloxifene is a selective oestrogen receptor modulator used for osteoporosis and is not associated with osteonecrosis of the jaw.
why_others_wrong.E: Strontium ranelate works by a different mechanism and is not classically linked to osteonecrosis of the jaw.

exam_trap: Raloxifene or strontium ranelate may be chosen as other osteoporosis drugs, but osteonecrosis of the jaw is classically linked to antiresorptives such as alendronate and denosumab.
takeaway: Bisphosphonates + jaw pain/non-healing extraction = osteonecrosis of the jaw.
thinking: Osteoporosis treatment ↓ osteonecrosis of the jaw ↓ potent antiresorptive suppresses bone turnover and healing ↓ bisphosphonates are the classic cause ↓ Alendronate
pearl: Patients starting bisphosphonates should have a dental review and maintain good oral hygiene; invasive dental work during treatment increases the risk of osteonecrosis of the jaw.

subject: Microbiology & surgical infection
title: Microbiology (Surgical Site Infection)
stem: A 45-year-old man develops a superficial incisional surgical site infection 5 days after a laparotomy in which the bowel was not opened. Which organism is the most likely cause?
why_correct: Staphylococcus aureus is the leading cause of surgical site infection because it commonly colonises the skin and can contaminate surgical wounds. Prophylactic antibiotics targeting this organism are standard practice.

why_others_wrong.A: Streptococcus pneumoniae is a respiratory pathogen causing pneumonia and meningitis, not a typical cause of surgical wound infection.
why_others_wrong.B: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is more associated with hospital-acquired infections in immunocompromised patients or chronic wounds, not the leading cause of routine surgical site infection.
why_others_wrong.C: Escherichia coli is a frequent cause after bowel surgery, but Staphylococcus aureus from skin flora remains the commonest single cause of surgical site infection overall.
why_others_wrong.E: Neisseria meningitidis causes meningococcal disease and is not implicated in surgical wound infections.

exam_trap: Escherichia coli tempts after any laparotomy, but with the bowel unopened the wound is clean and skin-derived Staphylococcus aureus is far more likely.
takeaway: Staphylococcus aureus is the commonest single cause of surgical site infection; after bowel surgery, prophylaxis must also cover Gram-negative and anaerobic gut flora.
thinking: Superficial incisional SSI after laparotomy ↓ bowel not opened, so a clean wound ↓ contamination comes from skin flora ↓ commonest single cause of surgical site infection ↓ Staphylococcus aureus
pearl: Superficial incisional SSI is usually managed by opening and draining the wound, with antibiotics added for spreading cellulitis or systemic features.

subject: Microbiology & surgical infection
title: Microbiology (Surgical Site Infection)
stem: A 60-year-old man has a wound infection with foul-smelling discharge 10 days after colorectal surgery. Which organism is most likely?
why_correct: Bacteroides fragilis is an anaerobic Gram-negative bacillus that is part of the normal colonic flora. It is a common cause of intra-abdominal and wound infections after colorectal surgery.

why_others_wrong.A: Staphylococcus aureus can contribute but is the classic skin-flora cause of clean-wound infection; after colorectal surgery, bowel organisms such as Bacteroides are more characteristic.
why_others_wrong.B: Streptococcus pyogenes causes invasive soft tissue infections (e.g. necrotising fasciitis) but is not the classic organism implicated in colorectal surgical infections.
why_others_wrong.D: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is more associated with hospital-acquired or burn wound infections, not the predominant organism from colonic flora.
why_others_wrong.E: Clostridium perfringens is associated with gas gangrene and severe soft tissue infection, but is not the most likely organism in a routine post-colorectal-surgery wound infection.

exam_trap: S. aureus is more common in clean surgery. Colorectal surgery involves colonic flora.
takeaway: Colorectal surgery infection = anaerobes (Bacteroides) + Gram-negatives (E. coli).
thinking: Wound infection 10 days after colorectal surgery ↓ colonic flora contaminated the operative field ↓ foul-smelling discharge suggests anaerobes ↓ principal colonic anaerobe ↓ Bacteroides fragilis
pearl: Metronidazole covers Bacteroides and other anaerobes, which is why colorectal prophylaxis typically combines it with an agent active against Gram-negative bowel organisms.

subject: Imaging & radiation
title: Imaging (Biliary Tract Imaging)
stem: A 55-year-old man has right upper quadrant pain. Ultrasound shows gallstones and a thickened gallbladder wall. Liver function tests show a mildly elevated bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
why_correct: A mildly deranged LFT picture alongside gallstones raises concern for choledocholithiasis. MRCP is the best non-invasive investigation to assess the biliary tree for stones and obstruction before any intervention, and has largely replaced diagnostic ERCP.

why_others_wrong.A: CT abdomen is less sensitive than MRCP for detecting small common bile duct stones and biliary tree detail.
why_others_wrong.C: ERCP is now primarily a therapeutic rather than diagnostic tool due to its invasive nature and associated risks (e.g. pancreatitis), so it should follow non-invasive imaging.
why_others_wrong.D: A HIDA scan assesses gallbladder function and biliary patency (e.g. for suspected acute cholecystitis), but is not the investigation of choice for suspected choledocholithiasis.
why_others_wrong.E: Plain abdominal X-ray has very limited sensitivity for gallstones (most are radiolucent) and cannot assess the biliary tree.

exam_trap: ERCP is now therapeutic, not diagnostic. Don't use it as a first-line investigation.
takeaway: Suspected bile duct stones = MRCP first. ERCP = therapeutic.
source: NICE CG188, Gallstone disease.
thinking: Gallstones with a thickened gallbladder wall ↓ raised bilirubin and ALP suggest a common bile duct stone ↓ accurate non-invasive duct imaging is needed before any intervention ↓ MRCP
pearl: If MRCP is inconclusive but suspicion of duct stones remains, endoscopic ultrasound is the next option; ERCP is then reserved for therapeutic clearance of confirmed stones.

subject: Physiology
title: Data Interpretation (Arterial Blood Gas)
stem: A 50-year-old man has an arterial blood gas: pH 7.28, PaCO2 4.5 kPa, HCO3- 16 mmol/L, Na+ 140 mmol/L, Cl- 115 mmol/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.B: Metabolic acidosis with high anion gap
options.C: Metabolic acidosis with normal anion gap

correct_answer: C. Metabolic acidosis with normal anion gap
why_correct: The pH is low (acidosis), and the HCO3- is low (metabolic). The anion gap = Na+ - (Cl- + HCO3-) = 140 - (115 + 16) = 9, which is normal (8–12). This suggests a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis, typically from diarrhoea or renal tubular acidosis.

why_others_wrong.A: Respiratory acidosis would show a raised PaCO2, but here PaCO2 is normal/low, so the acidosis is not respiratory in origin.
why_others_wrong.B: The calculated anion gap here is 9, within the normal range (8-12), so this does not represent a high anion gap acidosis.
why_others_wrong.D: Respiratory alkalosis would present with a raised pH, not the low pH (7.28) seen here.
why_others_wrong.E: Metabolic alkalosis would present with a raised, not lowered, pH and bicarbonate.

exam_trap: Candidates pick option B by assuming every acidosis in an unwell patient has a high gap; calculating it gives 9, and the raised chloride indicates a hyperchloraemic acidosis.
takeaway: Normal anion gap = HARDUP (Hyperalimentation, Addison's, Renal tubular acidosis, Diarrhoea, Ureteroenterostomy, Pancreatic fistula).
thinking: pH 7.28 with HCO3- 16 mmol/L = metabolic acidosis ↓ PaCO2 4.5 kPa is low, so respiratory compensation ↓ anion gap = 140 - (115 + 16) = 9 ↓ normal gap with a high chloride ↓ Metabolic acidosis with normal anion gap
pearl: Large volumes of 0.9% saline cause a hyperchloraemic normal anion gap acidosis, one reason balanced crystalloids such as compound sodium lactate are preferred for routine resuscitation.

subject: Physiology
title: Physiology (Diabetes Insipidus)
stem: A 60-year-old man has a serum sodium of 150 mmol/L and a urine osmolality of 150 mOsm/kg. What is the most likely cause?
why_correct: Hypernatraemia with dilute urine (low osmolality) suggests diabetes insipidus. The kidneys are unable to concentrate urine due to lack of ADH (central DI) or resistance to ADH (nephrogenic DI).

why_others_wrong.B: SIADH causes HYPOnatraemia with concentrated (not dilute) urine due to inappropriate water retention, the opposite of the picture described.
why_others_wrong.C: Simple dehydration typically causes the kidneys to appropriately concentrate urine (high osmolality) to conserve water, not produce dilute urine.
why_others_wrong.D: Diuretic use, particularly loop or thiazide diuretics, more commonly causes hyponatraemia or hypokalaemia rather than hypernatraemia with dilute urine.
why_others_wrong.E: Adrenal insufficiency classically causes hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia due to mineralocorticoid deficiency, not hypernatraemia with dilute urine.

exam_trap: Dehydration (option C) is chosen because hypernatraemia suggests water loss, but a dehydrated patient with intact ADH produces concentrated urine, not an osmolality of 150 mOsm/kg.
takeaway: High Na+ + dilute urine = diabetes insipidus. Low Na+ + concentrated urine = SIADH.
thinking: Sodium 150 mmol/L = hypernatraemia ↓ the appropriate response is maximally concentrated urine ↓ urine osmolality 150 mOsm/kg is inappropriately dilute ↓ the kidneys cannot conserve water ↓ Diabetes insipidus
pearl: A water deprivation test followed by desmopressin distinguishes cranial DI, which concentrates urine after desmopressin, from nephrogenic DI, which does not.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy (Deep Inguinal Ring - Medial Relations)
stem: A 45-year-old man is undergoing inguinal hernia repair. Which structure lies immediately medial to the deep inguinal ring?
why_correct: The deep inguinal ring lies lateral to the inferior epigastric artery. This vessel is the key landmark distinguishing indirect (lateral) from direct (medial) inguinal hernias.

why_others_wrong.B: The femoral vein lies inferiorly within the femoral sheath in the thigh, not immediately medial to the deep inguinal ring.
why_others_wrong.C: The lacunar ligament forms the medial boundary of the femoral canal, not a structure adjacent to the deep inguinal ring.
why_others_wrong.D: The pubic tubercle is a bony landmark near the superficial inguinal ring, not immediately medial to the deep ring.
why_others_wrong.E: The spermatic cord passes THROUGH the deep inguinal ring rather than lying medial to it.

exam_trap: Candidates may choose the spermatic cord, but it passes through the deep ring; the inferior epigastric artery lies immediately medial to the ring, and indirect hernias arise lateral to it.
takeaway: Deep ring = lateral to inferior epigastric artery. Direct hernia = medial to it.
thinking: Deep inguinal ring lies above the midpoint of the inguinal ligament ↓ inferior epigastric artery runs up on its medial side ↓ the artery forms the lateral border of Hesselbach's triangle ↓ Inferior epigastric artery
pearl: In laparoscopic repair the inferior epigastric vessels are the central landmark: indirect sacs lie lateral to them, direct defects medial, and the femoral defect lies below the iliopubic tract medial to the femoral vein.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy (Anterior Triangle of Neck - Penetrating Injury)
stem: A 40-year-old man has a penetrating wound to the anterior triangle of the neck. Which structure is most at risk at the level of the cricothyroid membrane?
why_correct: At the level of the cricothyroid membrane the common carotid artery lies medially in the carotid sheath, just lateral to the larynx, and is the major vessel most exposed to an anterior triangle penetrating wound.

why_others_wrong.A: The internal jugular vein is also vulnerable, but it lies lateral within the carotid sheath under cover of sternocleidomastoid, whereas the common carotid artery lies medially beside the larynx and is the structure classically most at risk at this level.
why_others_wrong.C: The vagus nerve lies posteriorly between the internal jugular vein and common carotid artery, relatively protected compared to the more superficial vascular structures.
why_others_wrong.D: The recurrent laryngeal nerve runs in the tracheo-oesophageal groove, more medial and deeper than the structures at immediate risk at this level in the anterior triangle.
why_others_wrong.E: The phrenic nerve lies deep to prevertebral fascia on scalenus anterior, posterolateral to the carotid sheath, so is shielded from an anterior triangle wound.

exam_trap: The internal jugular vein (A) is chosen because it is large and bleeds heavily, but it lies lateral within the sheath, whereas the carotid sits medially beside the larynx.
takeaway: Cricothyroid membrane level = common carotid artery is most at risk.
thinking: Cricothyroid membrane is at about C6 ↓ common carotid artery lies medially in the carotid sheath beside the larynx ↓ it is the major vessel closest to an anterior triangle wound ↓ internal jugular vein lies lateral, vagus behind ↓ Common carotid artery
pearl: Penetrating neck wounds that breach platysma should not be probed in the emergency department; hard signs such as expanding haematoma or pulsatile bleeding mandate surgical exploration.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy (Accessory Nerve - Posterior Triangle)
stem: A 30-year-old man has a stab wound to the lower part of the posterior triangle of the neck. When he pushes against a wall, the medial border of his scapula lifts away from the chest wall. Which nerve is most likely injured?
why_correct: The long thoracic nerve (C5-C7) descends behind the brachial plexus through the lower posterior triangle and then runs on serratus anterior; injury paralyses serratus anterior, causing medial winging of the scapula.

why_others_wrong.A: Accessory nerve injury causes trapezius palsy with shoulder droop and lateral winging on abduction, whereas classic medial winging on pushing reflects serratus anterior palsy.
why_others_wrong.C: The suprascapular nerve supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus (abduction/external rotation); its injury does not cause scapular winging.
why_others_wrong.D: The dorsal scapular nerve supplies the rhomboids and levator scapulae, controlling scapular retraction, not the serratus anterior function responsible for winging.
why_others_wrong.E: The thoracodorsal nerve supplies latissimus dorsi and lies in the axilla; it is not typically injured via posterior triangle trauma and does not cause winging.

exam_trap: The accessory nerve also crosses the posterior triangle, but trapezius palsy gives shoulder droop with lateral winging on abduction; classic medial winging is long thoracic.
takeaway: Winging of scapula = long thoracic nerve (serratus anterior).
thinking: Stab wound in the lower posterior triangle ↓ medial border of the scapula lifts on pushing against a wall ↓ medial winging = serratus anterior failure ↓ Long thoracic nerve
pearl: The long thoracic nerve runs on the surface of serratus anterior on the medial wall of the axilla, so it must be identified and preserved during axillary node clearance.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy (Femoral Canal/Sheath)
stem: A 65-year-old man has a femoral hernia. Which structure lies immediately medial to the femoral canal?
why_correct: The femoral canal is bounded medially by the lacunar ligament, laterally by the femoral vein, anteriorly by the inguinal ligament, and posteriorly by the pectineal ligament. The lacunar ligament is the medial boundary.

why_others_wrong.A: The femoral vein lies LATERAL to the femoral canal, forming its lateral boundary, not medial.
why_others_wrong.B: The femoral artery lies lateral to the femoral vein, even further from the medial aspect of the canal.
why_others_wrong.D: The inguinal ligament forms the ANTERIOR boundary of the femoral canal, not the medial boundary.
why_others_wrong.E: The pectineal (Cooper's) ligament forms the POSTERIOR boundary of the femoral canal, not the medial boundary.

exam_trap: The femoral vein (A) is chosen because it is the canal's immediate neighbour, but it lies lateral to the canal; the lacunar ligament forms the medial boundary.
takeaway: Femoral canal boundaries = lacunar (medial), femoral vein (lateral), inguinal (anterior), pectineal (posterior).
thinking: Femoral canal is the medial compartment of the femoral sheath ↓ femoral vein lies lateral, inguinal ligament in front, pectineal ligament behind ↓ medial boundary is the sharp lacunar ligament ↓ Lacunar ligament
pearl: The lacunar ligament may need to be incised to release a strangulated femoral hernia, and an abnormal obturator artery crossing it (corona mortis) can bleed heavily if cut.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy (Breast Lymphatic Drainage)
stem: A 50-year-old woman has a lump in the upper outer quadrant of the breast. Which lymph node group is the first to receive drainage from this quadrant?
why_correct: The upper outer quadrant drains primarily to the axillary lymph nodes (specifically the anterior/pectoral group). It is the commonest site of breast cancer, and the axilla is the commonest site of nodal spread.

why_others_wrong.A: Internal mammary nodes primarily drain the medial breast quadrants, not the upper outer quadrant.
why_others_wrong.C: Supraclavicular nodes are typically a later drainage site (often indicating more advanced disease), not the first-line nodes for the upper outer quadrant.
why_others_wrong.D: Mediastinal nodes are not a primary or direct drainage pathway from the breast.
why_others_wrong.E: Inguinal nodes drain the lower limb and perineum, not breast tissue.

exam_trap: The internal mammary nodes drain the medial quadrants, not the upper outer.
takeaway: Upper outer quadrant = axillary nodes first.
thinking: Upper outer quadrant lump ↓ lateral breast lymph runs to the anterior (pectoral) axillary group ↓ most breast lymph drains to the axilla ↓ Axillary nodes
pearl: Sentinel lymph node biopsy, using radioisotope with or without blue dye, is the standard way to stage a clinically and ultrasound-negative axilla in early breast cancer.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy (Femoral Canal/Sheath)
stem: A 45-year-old man has a hernia through the femoral canal. Which of the following is the most lateral structure in the femoral sheath?
why_correct: The femoral sheath contains three compartments: lateral = femoral artery, intermediate = femoral vein, medial = femoral canal. The femoral nerve lies OUTSIDE the sheath, lateral to the artery.

why_others_wrong.A: The femoral canal is the most MEDIAL compartment of the femoral sheath, not the most lateral.
why_others_wrong.B: The femoral vein occupies the intermediate compartment, between the artery laterally and the canal medially.
why_others_wrong.D: The femoral nerve lies OUTSIDE the femoral sheath entirely, lateral to it, not within the sheath as the most lateral structure.
why_others_wrong.E: Lymphatics travel within the femoral canal (the medial compartment), not as the most lateral structure in the sheath.

exam_trap: The femoral nerve (D) is chosen as the most lateral structure in the groin, but it lies outside the femoral sheath, leaving the artery most lateral within it.
takeaway: Femoral sheath = artery (lateral), vein (middle), canal (medial). Nerve is outside.
thinking: Femoral sheath has three compartments ↓ lateral artery, intermediate vein, medial canal ↓ femoral nerve lies outside the sheath ↓ Femoral artery
pearl: The femoral artery is palpated at the mid-inguinal point, midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and pubic symphysis, with the vein immediately medial, which guides femoral venous access.

subject: Hand trauma
title: Anatomy (Median Nerve - Palm Laceration)
stem: A 35-year-old man has a laceration to the palm. He cannot oppose his thumb. Which nerve is most likely injured?
why_correct: Opposition of the thumb is performed by opponens pollicis, supplied by the median nerve (via the recurrent branch). Loss of opposition is a classic sign of median nerve injury at the wrist.

why_others_wrong.A: The ulnar nerve supplies adductor pollicis (thumb adduction) and the interossei, not opponens pollicis, so it is not responsible for loss of thumb opposition.
why_others_wrong.C: The radial nerve supplies wrist and finger extensors; its injury causes wrist drop, not loss of thumb opposition.
why_others_wrong.D: The musculocutaneous nerve supplies the anterior arm flexors (biceps, brachialis), unrelated to thumb opposition in the hand.
why_others_wrong.E: The axillary nerve supplies deltoid and teres minor in the shoulder region, with no role in thumb opposition.

exam_trap: Ulnar nerve tempts candidates because it supplies thumb adductor pollicis, but opposition is produced by opponens pollicis, supplied by the median nerve.
takeaway: Thumb opposition = median nerve. Thumb adduction = ulnar nerve.
thinking: Palmar laceration ↓ cannot oppose the thumb ↓ opponens pollicis supplied by the recurrent motor branch ↓ Median nerve
pearl: The recurrent motor branch of the median nerve lies superficially at the thenar eminence and can be divided by apparently minor palmar lacerations.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy (Pancreatic Head - Biliary Obstruction)
stem: A 60-year-old man has a tumour in the head of the pancreas. Which structure is most likely to be compressed, causing jaundice?
why_correct: The common bile duct passes through the head of the pancreas (or just posterior to it). Tumours in this region compress the duct, causing obstructive jaundice.

why_others_wrong.B: Compression of the portal vein by a pancreatic head tumour causes portal hypertension, not jaundice.
why_others_wrong.C: The superior mesenteric artery lies posterior to the pancreatic neck; its compression would cause bowel ischaemia, not jaundice.
why_others_wrong.D: Compression of the inferior vena cava would cause lower limb oedema and venous congestion, not jaundice.
why_others_wrong.E: The left renal vein crosses anterior to the aorta just below the superior mesenteric artery, away from the bile duct, and its compression causes nutcracker syndrome, not jaundice.

exam_trap: The portal vein is also at risk but causes portal hypertension, not jaundice.
takeaway: Pancreatic head tumour = obstructive jaundice (common bile duct compression).
thinking: Pancreatic head tumour with jaundice ↓ distal common bile duct runs in or behind the pancreatic head ↓ compression gives painless obstructive jaundice ↓ Common bile duct
pearl: A palpable, non-tender gallbladder in a patient with painless jaundice suggests malignant distal bile duct obstruction rather than stones, because a gallbladder scarred by chronic stone disease rarely distends.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy (Recurrent Laryngeal Nerve - Thyroidectomy)
stem: A 40-year-old woman has a thyroidectomy. Postoperatively she has hoarseness and weak voice. Which nerve is most likely injured?

options.B: External branch of superior laryngeal nerve
options.C: Internal branch of superior laryngeal nerve

why_correct: The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid. Unilateral injury causes hoarseness and weak voice. Bilateral injury causes stridor and airway obstruction.

why_others_wrong.B: External branch injury paralyses cricothyroid, mainly causing loss of high pitch and voice fatigue; definite hoarseness points to recurrent laryngeal nerve injury.
why_others_wrong.C: The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve is sensory to the larynx above the cords; its injury causes reduced laryngeal sensation and aspiration risk, not motor hoarseness.
why_others_wrong.D: The glossopharyngeal nerve is not involved in thyroidectomy and has no role in voice production via the larynx.
why_others_wrong.E: The hypoglossal nerve controls tongue movement and is unrelated to voice hoarseness from thyroid surgery.

exam_trap: External branch of superior laryngeal nerve injury causes loss of high pitch, not hoarseness.
takeaway: Hoarseness after thyroidectomy = recurrent laryngeal nerve.
thinking: Hoarseness and weak voice after thyroidectomy ↓ vocal fold paralysis ↓ RLN supplies all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid ↓ Recurrent laryngeal nerve
pearl: Vocal cord function should be documented by laryngoscopy before and after thyroid surgery; intraoperative nerve monitoring helps but does not replace careful visual identification of the nerve.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy (Inguinal Hernia - Direct vs Indirect)
stem: A 55-year-old man has a direct inguinal hernia. Which of the following statements is true?

options.A: It passes through the deep inguinal ring
options.B: It is lateral to the inferior epigastric artery
options.D: It is more common than indirect hernias

correct_answer: C. It passes through Hesselbach's triangle
why_correct: Direct inguinal hernias protrude through Hesselbach's triangle, medial to the inferior epigastric artery. They are acquired and less common than indirect hernias. Strangulation is rare because the neck is wide.

why_others_wrong.A: Passing through the deep inguinal ring is characteristic of an INDIRECT hernia, not a direct hernia.
why_others_wrong.B: Direct hernias are MEDIAL to the inferior epigastric artery, not lateral; a lateral position is characteristic of indirect hernias.
why_others_wrong.D: Indirect inguinal hernias are more common overall than direct hernias, so this statement is false.
why_others_wrong.E: Direct hernias have a wide neck and rarely strangulate; it is indirect hernias, with their narrower neck at the deep ring, that are more prone to strangulation.

exam_trap: Indirect hernias are more common and pass through the deep ring, lateral to the inferior epigastric artery.
takeaway: Direct = Hesselbach's triangle, medial to vessels. Indirect = deep ring, lateral to vessels.
thinking: Direct inguinal hernia ↓ bulges through a weak posterior wall of the canal ↓ medial to the inferior epigastric vessels ↓ wide neck, acquired, less common than indirect ↓ It passes through Hesselbach's triangle
pearl: Hesselbach's triangle is bounded by the inferior epigastric vessels, the lateral border of rectus abdominis and the inguinal ligament; weakness of the transversalis fascia here underlies direct herniation in older men.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy (Laparoscopic Inguinal Hernia Anatomy)
stem: A 55-year-old man is undergoing a laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair. The surgeon identifies the "triangle of doom." Which structures form its boundaries?

options.A: Vas deferens medially, gonadal vessels laterally, peritoneal reflection inferiorly
options.B: Inguinal ligament inferiorly, iliopubic tract superiorly, femoral vessels medially
options.C: Inferior epigastric artery medially, deep inguinal ring laterally, inguinal ligament inferiorly
options.D: Rectus sheath medially, psoas laterally, inguinal ligament inferiorly
options.E: Spermatic cord medially, iliac vessels laterally, peritoneum posteriorly

correct_answer: A. Vas deferens medially, gonadal vessels laterally, peritoneal reflection inferiorly
why_correct: The triangle of doom is bounded by the vas deferens medially, the gonadal vessels laterally and the peritoneal reflection inferiorly. It contains the external iliac artery and vein (with the deep circumflex iliac vein and the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve). Staples or tacks placed here can cause catastrophic haemorrhage.

why_others_wrong.B: This description (inguinal ligament, iliopubic tract, femoral vessels) does not correspond to a recognised named triangle relevant to laparoscopic hernia anatomy here.
why_others_wrong.C: Lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels at the deep ring is the site of indirect herniation; it is neither Hesselbach's triangle nor the triangle of doom.
why_others_wrong.D: Rectus sheath and psoas are not the boundaries of the triangle of doom; this combination does not correspond to a recognised landmark used in laparoscopic hernia repair.
why_others_wrong.E: This is not the accepted definition; the triangle of doom is specifically bounded by the vas deferens, gonadal vessels, and peritoneal reflection, not iliac vessels and peritoneum alone.

exam_trap: Do not confuse the triangle of doom with the triangle of pain, which contains the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh and the femoral branch of the genitofemoral nerve.
takeaway: Triangle of doom = vas deferens + gonadal vessels + peritoneum. Contains external iliac vessels.
thinking: Laparoscopic preperitoneal view of the deep ring ↓ vas deferens converges from medial and gonadal vessels from lateral ↓ peritoneal reflection forms the base ↓ external iliac vessels lie within ↓ Vas deferens medially, gonadal vessels laterally, peritoneal reflection inferiorly
pearl: Mesh fixation must avoid both the triangle of doom (external iliac vessels) and the triangle of pain (nerves), so tacks are placed above the iliopubic tract or replaced by glue or self-gripping mesh.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy (Anterior Triangle Neck - Penetrating Injury)
stem: A 60-year-old man has a penetrating wound to the anterior triangle of the neck at the level of the thyroid cartilage. Which structure is most at risk?
why_correct: At the upper border of the thyroid cartilage (C4) the common carotid artery bifurcates within the carotid triangle, where it lies exposed medial to the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid, making it the structure most at risk.

why_others_wrong.A: The internal jugular vein lies lateral to the carotid under cover of sternocleidomastoid, whereas the carotid is exposed medial to that muscle in the anterior triangle.
why_others_wrong.C: The vagus nerve lies posteriorly between the carotid artery and internal jugular vein within the carotid sheath, relatively protected compared to the artery.
why_others_wrong.D: The recurrent laryngeal nerve runs deep in the tracheo-oesophageal groove, more medial and protected than the superficial vascular structures at this level.
why_others_wrong.E: The phrenic nerve runs on scalenus anterior, more posterolateral in the neck, not at immediate risk at the thyroid cartilage level in the anterior triangle.

exam_trap: The internal jugular vein (A) tempts as the largest vessel, but it lies lateral under sternocleidomastoid, while the carotid lies exposed in the carotid triangle.
takeaway: Thyroid cartilage level = common carotid artery bifurcation. Most at risk in penetrating trauma.
thinking: Upper border of the thyroid cartilage is at about C4 ↓ common carotid bifurcates here in the carotid triangle ↓ lies relatively exposed medial to the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid ↓ Common carotid artery
pearl: The carotid sinus at the bifurcation is a baroreceptor supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve, so handling it during surgery can cause bradycardia and hypotension.

subject: ENT: head & neck
title: Anatomy (Recurrent/External Laryngeal Nerve - Thyroid Surgery)
stem: A 45-year-old woman has a thyroid nodule. During thyroidectomy, which nerve is at risk if the superior thyroid vessels are ligated en masse high above the upper pole rather than close to the gland?

options.B: External branch of superior laryngeal nerve
options.C: Internal branch of superior laryngeal nerve

correct_answer: B. External branch of superior laryngeal nerve
why_correct: The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve runs with the superior thyroid artery and is at risk during ligation of the superior pole vessels. Injury causes loss of high-pitched voice (cricothyroid palsy).

why_others_wrong.A: The recurrent laryngeal nerve runs with the inferior thyroid artery near the tracheo-oesophageal groove, not the superior pole vessels, so it is not at risk here.
why_others_wrong.C: The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve is sensory and pierces the thyrohyoid membrane well above the superior pole, so it is rarely injured during pole ligation.
why_others_wrong.D: The glossopharyngeal nerve lies much higher in the neck, supplying the pharynx and posterior tongue, and has no relation to the thyroid vessels.
why_others_wrong.E: The hypoglossal nerve crosses high in the neck near the carotid bifurcation to supply tongue muscles and is not related to the superior thyroid pedicle.

exam_trap: Candidates choose the recurrent laryngeal nerve (A), but it is at risk near the inferior thyroid artery; the superior pole vessels run with the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve.
takeaway: Superior thyroid artery = external laryngeal nerve. Inferior thyroid artery = recurrent laryngeal nerve.
thinking: Superior thyroid vessels ligated en masse high above the upper pole ↓ the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve runs close to the superior thyroid artery ↓ it supplies cricothyroid, which tenses the vocal cord ↓ injury causes loss of high pitch and voice fatigue ↓ External branch of superior laryngeal nerve
pearl: Ligating the superior pole vessels individually and close to the gland capsule protects the external laryngeal nerve; injury is particularly disabling for professional voice users.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy (Carotid Endarterectomy - Nerve Relations)
stem: A 45-year-old man is undergoing a carotid endarterectomy. During dissection, the surgeon identifies the carotid body. Which structure lies immediately posterior to the carotid bifurcation?
why_correct: The vagus nerve lies posterior to the carotid bifurcation, between the internal carotid artery and internal jugular vein. It is at risk during carotid endarterectomy.

why_others_wrong.A: The internal jugular vein lies lateral to the common/internal carotid artery within the carotid sheath, not posterior to the bifurcation.
why_others_wrong.C: The hypoglossal nerve crosses superficial to the carotid vessels higher up, near the angle of the mandible, rather than lying posterior to the bifurcation itself.
why_others_wrong.D: The glossopharyngeal nerve passes between the internal and external carotid arteries more superiorly and is not the structure immediately posterior to the bifurcation.
why_others_wrong.E: The cervical sympathetic chain lies posterior to the carotid sheath as a whole, embedded in prevertebral fascia, rather than being the nerve classically described as posterior to the bifurcation.

exam_trap: The hypoglossal nerve crosses the internal carotid artery more superiorly, not at the bifurcation.
takeaway: Carotid bifurcation = vagus nerve posteriorly. Hypoglossal crosses higher up.
thinking: Carotid sheath arrangement ↓ carotid artery medial, internal jugular vein lateral ↓ vagus lies behind, in the groove between them ↓ at the bifurcation the vagus lies directly posterior ↓ Vagus nerve
pearl: The vagus occasionally lies anterior within the sheath and must be identified before clamping at carotid endarterectomy; injury causes ipsilateral vocal cord palsy because recurrent laryngeal fibres travel within it.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy (Breast - Axillary Tail of Spence)
stem: A 60-year-old woman has a palpable mass in the axillary tail of Spence. Which anatomical structure is this mass most likely related to?

options.B: Tail of breast tissue extending into axilla

correct_answer: B. Tail of breast tissue extending into axilla
why_correct: The axillary tail of Spence is an extension of breast tissue that projects into the axilla through the foramen of Langer. It is a common site for breast pathology and must be examined in all breast assessments.

why_others_wrong.A: Pectoralis major lies deep to the breast and chest wall, not within the axillary tail, and is unrelated to a palpable axillary mass of breast origin.
why_others_wrong.C: Axillary lymph nodes can also produce an axillary mass, but the tail of Spence itself is breast parenchyma extending into the axilla, not lymphoid tissue.
why_others_wrong.D: The brachial plexus lies deep within the axilla near the axillary vessels and is not the structure forming the palpable superficial axillary tail.
why_others_wrong.E: The axillary artery is a deep neurovascular structure of the axilla, not the superficial breast tissue that makes up the tail of Spence.

exam_trap: Do not confuse with axillary lymph nodes. The tail of Spence is breast tissue, not lymphoid.
takeaway: Axillary tail of Spence = breast tissue in axilla. Always examine it.
thinking: Mass in the axillary tail ↓ tail of Spence is breast parenchyma extending through the deep fascia into the axilla ↓ so this is breast pathology rather than a nodal mass ↓ Tail of breast tissue extending into axilla
pearl: Accessory breast tissue can occur anywhere along the embryological milk line from axilla to groin and commonly presents as an axillary lump that enlarges premenstrually or in pregnancy.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy (Obturator Hernia)
stem: A 55-year-old man has a hernia through the obturator canal. Which of the following is the classic clinical sign?
why_correct: Obturator hernia presents with Howship-Romberg sign — pain along the medial thigh due to compression of the obturator nerve. It is more common in elderly women and often presents with intestinal obstruction.

why_others_wrong.A: Obturator hernias classically lack a palpable groin or external swelling because the defect lies deep within the pelvis beneath pectineus.
why_others_wrong.B: Intestinal obstruction is a common presenting feature but is not the classic named clinical SIGN being asked for here; that is Howship-Romberg.
why_others_wrong.D: Haematuria is not a feature of obturator hernia, which affects the obturator canal and nerve rather than the urinary tract.
why_others_wrong.E: Testicular swelling is not associated with obturator hernia; it is more typical of inguinal or scrotal pathology.

exam_trap: Intestinal obstruction (B) is often the actual presentation and tempts candidates, but the question asks for the classic sign, which is medial thigh pain from obturator nerve compression.
takeaway: Obturator hernia = Howship-Romberg sign (medial thigh pain) + intestinal obstruction.
thinking: Obturator hernia ↓ sac compresses the obturator nerve in the obturator canal ↓ pain referred along the medial thigh towards the knee ↓ Thigh pain (Howship-Romberg sign)
pearl: Obturator hernias typically occur in thin, elderly, multiparous women and often present late with small bowel obstruction; CT is the most useful diagnostic test.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy (Retroperitoneal Structures - Flank Trauma)
stem: A 40-year-old man has a penetrating wound to the flank. Which structure lies immediately posterior to the kidney?
why_correct: The kidney lies anterior to quadratus lumborum and psoas major. The 12th rib crosses posteriorly. Posterior relations include quadratus lumborum, psoas major, and the 12th rib.

why_others_wrong.A: The peritoneum lies anterior to the kidney, forming its anterior covering, not a posterior relation.
why_others_wrong.B: Psoas major is a posterior relation but lies medially, related to the medial part of the kidney, whereas quadratus lumborum lies more directly posterior across most of its length.
why_others_wrong.D: The 12th rib crosses the posterior surface of the kidney but is a single bony landmark, not the main muscular structure immediately posterior to it.
why_others_wrong.E: The transversus abdominis aponeurosis lies behind only the lateral border of the kidney, whereas quadratus lumborum lies directly behind most of its posterior surface.

exam_trap: Psoas major (B) is chosen because it is a well-known posterior relation, but it lies medially; quadratus lumborum lies directly behind most of the kidney.
takeaway: Kidney posterior relations = quadratus lumborum, psoas major, 12th rib.
thinking: Posterior relations of the kidney ↓ diaphragm and 12th rib above ↓ psoas medially, quadratus lumborum centrally, transversus abdominis laterally ↓ the muscle behind most of the kidney is quadratus lumborum ↓ Quadratus lumborum
pearl: The subcostal, iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves run across quadratus lumborum behind the kidney, which is why they can be injured in a loin incision, causing abdominal wall numbness or bulging.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy (Recurrent Laryngeal Nerve - Post-Thyroidectomy Stridor)
stem: A 50-year-old woman has a thyroidectomy. Postoperatively she develops stridor. Which nerve is most likely injured bilaterally?

options.B: External branch of superior laryngeal nerve
options.C: Internal branch of superior laryngeal nerve

why_correct: Bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury causes paralysis of both vocal cords, leading to stridor and airway obstruction. This is a surgical emergency requiring immediate re-intubation or tracheostomy.

why_others_wrong.B: Injury to the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve causes loss of the high-pitched voice (cricothyroid weakness), not stridor.
why_others_wrong.C: The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve is sensory and its injury causes reduced laryngeal sensation, not airway obstruction with stridor.
why_others_wrong.D: The glossopharyngeal nerve is not involved in thyroid surgery and its injury does not cause stridor.
why_others_wrong.E: The hypoglossal nerve supplies tongue muscles; its injury causes tongue deviation and dysarthria, not stridor.

exam_trap: The external laryngeal nerve (B) is chosen as another thyroidectomy nerve, but it only weakens cricothyroid and high pitch; bilateral recurrent laryngeal palsy causes stridor.
takeaway: Bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury = stridor. Emergency airway management.
thinking: Stridor after thyroidectomy ↓ both vocal folds paralysed near the midline ↓ loss of posterior cricoarytenoid, the only abductor, on both sides ↓ Recurrent laryngeal nerve
pearl: Stridor soon after thyroidectomy can also be caused by a neck haematoma compressing the airway; the wound should be opened at the bedside to evacuate the clot before definitive airway management.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy (Femoral Canal/Sheath)
stem: A 65-year-old man has a femoral hernia. Which of the following statements is true?

options.A: It is more common in men
options.B: It passes through the femoral canal
options.D: It is lateral to the femoral vein

correct_answer: B. It passes through the femoral canal
why_correct: Femoral hernias pass through the femoral canal, medial to the femoral vein. They are more common in women (due to wider pelvis) and have a high risk of strangulation because of the narrow neck.

why_others_wrong.A: Femoral hernias are more common in women, not men, because of their wider pelvis and femoral canal.
why_others_wrong.C: Femoral hernias are acquired, related to increased intra-abdominal pressure and a widened femoral ring, rather than congenital.
why_others_wrong.D: The femoral canal, and hence a femoral hernia, lies medial to the femoral vein, not lateral to it.
why_others_wrong.E: Femoral hernias have a narrow, rigid neck and therefore a HIGH risk of strangulation, not a low one.

exam_trap: Candidates may choose 'rarely strangulates' by confusing femoral with direct inguinal hernias, but the narrow, rigid femoral ring gives femoral hernias a high risk of strangulation.
takeaway: Femoral hernia = female, femoral canal, high strangulation risk.
thinking: Femoral hernia ↓ descends through the femoral canal, medial to the femoral vein ↓ emerges below and lateral to the pubic tubercle ↓ narrow rigid ring, so strangulation is common ↓ It passes through the femoral canal
pearl: Because of the high strangulation risk, femoral hernias should be repaired promptly once diagnosed rather than managed by watchful waiting.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy (Cystic Artery/Calot's Triangle)
stem: A 45-year-old man is undergoing a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. The surgeon identifies the cystic artery. From which artery does it usually arise?
why_correct: The cystic artery usually arises from the right hepatic artery within Calot's triangle. It supplies the gallbladder and cystic duct.

why_others_wrong.A: The common hepatic artery is the parent vessel from which the right hepatic artery (and hence the cystic artery) arises, but it is not the direct origin of the cystic artery itself.
why_others_wrong.C: The left hepatic artery supplies the left lobe of the liver and does not typically give off the cystic artery, which supplies the gallbladder on the right side.
why_others_wrong.D: The gastroduodenal artery supplies the duodenum, pancreas and stomach via its branches and has no direct relation to the gallbladder.
why_others_wrong.E: The superior mesenteric artery supplies the midgut (distal duodenum to two-thirds of the transverse colon) and does not give rise to the cystic artery.

exam_trap: The common hepatic artery (A) is chosen as the parent trunk, but the cystic artery normally arises from the right hepatic artery within the hepatocystic triangle.
takeaway: Cystic artery = branch of right hepatic artery. Identify before ligation.
thinking: Cystic artery ↓ usually a branch of the right hepatic artery ↓ runs through the hepatocystic (Calot's) triangle to the gallbladder ↓ Right hepatic artery
pearl: The right hepatic artery may loop close to the cystic duct and be mistaken for the cystic artery, which is one reason the critical view of safety must be achieved before anything is clipped.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy (Accessory Nerve - Posterior Triangle)
stem: A 30-year-old man has a stab wound to the posterior triangle of the neck. He develops shoulder droop. Which nerve is most likely injured?
why_correct: The accessory nerve (cranial nerve XI) runs through the posterior triangle and supplies trapezius. Injury causes shoulder droop and difficulty elevating the arm above the horizontal.

why_others_wrong.B: The long thoracic nerve supplies serratus anterior; its injury causes scapular winging, not shoulder droop.
why_others_wrong.C: The suprascapular nerve supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus; its injury impairs initiation of abduction and external rotation, not overall shoulder droop from trapezius loss.
why_others_wrong.D: The dorsal scapular nerve supplies the rhomboids and levator scapulae; injury causes subtle medial scapular winging, not the classic shoulder droop of accessory nerve palsy.
why_others_wrong.E: The thoracodorsal nerve supplies latissimus dorsi and its injury weakens arm adduction/extension, not shoulder droop.

exam_trap: Long thoracic nerve injury causes winging of the scapula, not shoulder droop.
takeaway: Posterior triangle + shoulder droop = accessory nerve (trapezius).
thinking: Posterior triangle stab wound ↓ shoulder droop and weak elevation ↓ trapezius paralysis ↓ spinal accessory nerve is superficial in the triangle ↓ Accessory nerve
pearl: Accessory nerve injury is a recognised complication of lymph node biopsy in the posterior triangle and should be included in consent; shoulder pain and droop may be the first complaint.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy (Breast Lymphatic Drainage)
stem: A 55-year-old woman has a breast lump in the medial quadrant. Which lymph node group is the first to receive drainage from this quadrant?
why_correct: The medial quadrants of the breast drain partly to the internal mammary (parasternal) lymph nodes, which are the characteristic first-echelon nodes for medial lesions, although many medial tumours also drain to the axilla. This is important in breast cancer staging and surgical planning.

why_others_wrong.A: Axillary nodes drain most breast lymph, especially from the lateral quadrants, whereas the medial quadrants characteristically drain to the parasternal internal mammary chain.
why_others_wrong.C: Supraclavicular nodes receive drainage secondarily, after axillary or internal mammary nodes, and are not the first-order nodes for the medial breast.
why_others_wrong.D: Mediastinal nodes may be involved in advanced disease via the internal mammary chain but are not the first echelon of drainage.
why_others_wrong.E: Inguinal nodes have no role in breast lymphatic drainage, which flows cranially via axillary and internal mammary routes.

exam_trap: Axillary nodes (A) are chosen because they receive most breast lymph, but the classic first-echelon drainage of the medial quadrants is the internal mammary chain.
takeaway: Medial quadrants = internal mammary nodes. Upper outer = axillary nodes.
thinking: Medial quadrant breast lump ↓ medial lymphatics pierce the intercostal spaces beside the sternum ↓ drain to the parasternal chain along the internal thoracic vessels ↓ Internal mammary nodes
pearl: Even medial tumours usually also drain to the axilla, so axillary sentinel node biopsy remains the standard staging procedure for medial breast cancers.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy (Pancoast Tumour - Thoracic Inlet)
stem: A 60-year-old man has a tumour at the apex of the lung. Which structure is most likely to be compressed, causing Horner's syndrome?
why_correct: Pancoast tumours at the lung apex compress the sympathetic chain, causing Horner's syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis, enophthalmos). They may also compress the brachial plexus (C8-T1).

why_others_wrong.A: The phrenic nerve, if compressed, causes diaphragmatic paralysis (raised hemidiaphragm), not Horner's syndrome.
why_others_wrong.B: Recurrent laryngeal nerve compression causes hoarseness from vocal cord paralysis, not the ptosis/miosis/anhidrosis triad of Horner's syndrome.
why_others_wrong.D: Brachial plexus (C8-T1) involvement in a Pancoast tumour causes arm pain and weakness in an ulnar nerve distribution, not Horner's syndrome directly.
why_others_wrong.E: Vagus nerve compression can cause hoarseness or cardiovascular effects but does not produce Horner's syndrome, which is a sympathetic chain phenomenon.

exam_trap: The brachial plexus (D) is chosen because Pancoast tumours often invade it, but plexus involvement causes arm pain and hand weakness; Horner's syndrome reflects sympathetic chain involvement.
takeaway: Pancoast tumour = Horner's syndrome + brachial plexus symptoms.
thinking: Apical lung (Pancoast) tumour ↓ invades the cervicothoracic sympathetic chain and stellate ganglion ↓ ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis ↓ Sympathetic chain
pearl: A Pancoast tumour often presents with shoulder and medial arm pain from T1 root and lower brachial plexus invasion before any respiratory symptoms, and can be missed on a plain chest X-ray.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy (Lateral Cutaneous Nerve of Thigh)
stem: A 55-year-old man has a laceration to the anterior thigh. He develops numbness over the lateral thigh. Which nerve is most likely injured?

options.B: Lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh

correct_answer: B. Lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh
why_correct: The lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh (L2, L3) supplies sensation to the lateral thigh. It is at risk during surgery in the inguinal region or from compression (meralgia paraesthetica).

why_others_wrong.A: The femoral nerve supplies the anterior thigh muscles (quadriceps) and its injury causes motor weakness with knee extension loss, not isolated lateral thigh numbness.
why_others_wrong.C: The obturator nerve supplies the medial thigh adductors and skin over the medial thigh, not the lateral aspect.
why_others_wrong.D: The sciatic nerve supplies the posterior thigh and the leg/foot below the knee; injury would cause much more widespread motor and sensory loss than isolated lateral thigh numbness.
why_others_wrong.E: The saphenous nerve is a sensory branch of the femoral nerve supplying the medial leg and ankle, not the lateral thigh.

exam_trap: The femoral nerve supplies the anterior thigh and causes weakness, not just sensory loss.
takeaway: Lateral thigh numbness = lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh.
thinking: Isolated lateral thigh numbness ↓ purely sensory deficit with no weakness ↓ lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh from L2 and L3 ↓ Lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh
pearl: The lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh passes under or through the inguinal ligament near the anterior superior iliac spine, so it can be compressed by tight belts, obesity or pregnancy and injured during iliac crest graft harvest.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy (Ilioinguinal Nerve - Hernia Repair)
stem: A 60-year-old man is undergoing an inguinal hernia repair. The surgeon identifies the ilioinguinal nerve. Which structure does it supply?

options.A: Skin of the upper medial thigh
options.B: Skin of the anterior scrotum and medial thigh

correct_answer: B. Skin of the anterior scrotum and medial thigh
why_correct: The ilioinguinal nerve (L1) supplies sensation to the anterior scrotum (or labia majora) and the upper medial thigh. It is at risk during inguinal hernia repair.

why_others_wrong.A: Upper medial thigh skin is supplied by the ilioinguinal nerve, but this is incomplete because its territory also includes the anterior scrotum or labium majus.
why_others_wrong.C: The lateral thigh is supplied by the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh, not the ilioinguinal nerve.
why_others_wrong.D: The perineum is supplied mainly by the pudendal nerve, not the ilioinguinal nerve.
why_others_wrong.E: The gluteal region is supplied by the superior and inferior cluneal nerves, not the ilioinguinal nerve.

exam_trap: Option A (upper medial thigh) is partly correct and tempts candidates, but it omits the anterior scrotal or labial territory, so B is the complete answer.
takeaway: Ilioinguinal nerve = anterior scrotum + medial thigh.
thinking: Ilioinguinal nerve (L1) ↓ runs through the inguinal canal on the spermatic cord ↓ emerges through the superficial ring ↓ supplies anterior scrotum or labium majus and upper medial thigh ↓ Skin of the anterior scrotum and medial thigh
pearl: Entrapment of the ilioinguinal nerve by mesh or sutures is a recognised cause of chronic groin pain after open hernia repair, so the nerve should be identified and preserved.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy (External Laryngeal Nerve - Thyroidectomy)
stem: A 35-year-old woman has a thyroidectomy. Postoperatively she has loss of high-pitched voice. Which nerve is most likely injured?

options.B: External branch of superior laryngeal nerve
options.C: Internal branch of superior laryngeal nerve

correct_answer: B. External branch of superior laryngeal nerve
why_correct: The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve supplies cricothyroid, which tenses the vocal cords for high-pitched sounds. Injury causes loss of high pitch (singer's voice).

why_others_wrong.A: Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury causes hoarseness from vocal cord paralysis, not isolated loss of high-pitched voice.
why_others_wrong.C: The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve provides sensation to the larynx above the vocal cords and does not control pitch, so its injury does not cause this symptom.
why_others_wrong.D: The glossopharyngeal nerve has no role in laryngeal function and is not at risk during thyroidectomy.
why_others_wrong.E: The hypoglossal nerve controls tongue movement, not vocal cord tension, and its injury would cause tongue weakness, not voice pitch changes.

exam_trap: Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury (A) is chosen as the best-known thyroidectomy complication, but it causes hoarseness from cord paralysis, not isolated loss of high pitch.
takeaway: Loss of high pitch = external branch of superior laryngeal nerve.
thinking: Loss of high-pitched voice ↓ cricothyroid tenses the vocal folds ↓ supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve ↓ this nerve runs with the superior thyroid vessels ↓ External branch of superior laryngeal nerve
pearl: External laryngeal nerve injury is particularly disabling for professional voice users, and the nerve is protected by ligating the superior pole vessels close to the thyroid capsule.

subject: Hepatobiliary surgery
title: Anatomy (Pancreatic Head - Biliary Obstruction)
stem: A 60-year-old man has jaundice and weight loss. CT shows a mass in the head of the pancreas with dilated bile ducts. What is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
why_correct: EUS with FNA is the most accurate method for tissue diagnosis of pancreatic head masses. It allows real-time imaging and fine needle aspiration for cytology.

why_others_wrong.A: ERCP with brush cytology can obtain tissue but has lower sensitivity for malignancy than EUS-FNA and carries risks such as pancreatitis and cholangitis.
why_others_wrong.B: MRCP is excellent for delineating ductal anatomy and the level of obstruction but does not provide tissue for histological/cytological diagnosis.
why_others_wrong.D: CA19-9 is a tumour marker that can support suspicion of malignancy but is neither sensitive nor specific enough to confirm the diagnosis on its own.
why_others_wrong.E: Liver biopsy samples hepatic parenchyma, not the pancreatic mass, and would not confirm a pancreatic head tumour.

exam_trap: CA19-9 is a tumour marker but not diagnostic — it can be elevated in other conditions.
takeaway: Pancreatic mass = EUS + FNA for tissue diagnosis.
source: NICE NG85, Pancreatic cancer in adults: diagnosis and management.
thinking: Jaundice, weight loss, pancreatic head mass with dilated ducts ↓ a tissue diagnosis is needed to confirm malignancy ↓ EUS images the head closely through the duodenum and guides targeted sampling with a better yield than ERCP brushings ↓ Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) with FNA
pearl: EUS sampling of a pancreatic head mass is taken through the duodenal wall, so the needle tract lies within the planned pancreaticoduodenectomy specimen, avoiding the tract-seeding concern of percutaneous biopsy.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy (Carotid Sheath Relations)
stem: During carotid endarterectomy, which structure lies anteromedial to the internal carotid artery?
why_correct: In the carotid triangle, just above the bifurcation, the external carotid artery lies anteromedial to the internal carotid artery. It can be recognised because it gives branches in the neck, whereas the internal carotid has none.

why_others_wrong.A: The internal jugular vein lies lateral to the internal carotid artery within the carotid sheath, not anteromedial.
why_others_wrong.B: The vagus nerve lies posterior between the internal carotid artery and internal jugular vein, not anteromedial.
why_others_wrong.D: The glossopharyngeal nerve passes between the internal and external carotid arteries more superiorly and is not the anteromedial relation described.
why_others_wrong.E: The hypoglossal nerve crosses superficial to both carotid arteries near the angle of the mandible, not anteromedial to the internal carotid at this level.

exam_trap: The internal jugular vein (A) is chosen as a close sheath neighbour, but it lies lateral to the carotid; only the external carotid lies anteromedial to the internal carotid.
takeaway: External carotid = anteromedial to internal carotid.
thinking: Carotid triangle just above the bifurcation ↓ external carotid lies anteromedial and gives branches ↓ internal carotid lies posterolateral and has no neck branches ↓ internal jugular vein lateral, vagus posterior ↓ External carotid artery
pearl: The internal carotid artery has no branches in the neck, which is how it is distinguished from the external carotid at carotid surgery before arteriotomy.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy (Chest Wall - Needle Insertion Landmarks)
stem: An aspiration needle inserted into the 9th intercostal space in the midaxillary line will enter:
why_correct: In the midaxillary line the lung extends only to about the 8th rib in quiet breathing, whereas the parietal pleura reaches the 10th rib. A needle in the 9th intercostal space therefore enters the costodiaphragmatic recess, the most specific description of the part of the pleural cavity entered.

why_others_wrong.A: The cupola (apex) of the pleura lies superiorly at the root of the neck, far from the 9th intercostal space in the midaxillary line.
why_others_wrong.B: The recess is part of the pleural cavity, but the more specific answer is the costodiaphragmatic recess, which contains no lung in quiet breathing.
why_others_wrong.D: Lung parenchyma does not extend down to the costodiaphragmatic recess at this level, since the lung itself is retracted above the recess during expiration.
why_others_wrong.E: The liver lies below the diaphragm on the right side, but a needle at the 9th intercostal space in the midaxillary line first traverses the pleural recess before any solid organ, so this is not the first structure entered.

exam_trap: Pleural cavity (B) is technically true but less specific, and lung (D) is wrong; at this level the needle enters the costodiaphragmatic recess, below the lung edge.
takeaway: Costodiaphragmatic recess = 8th–10th rib at MAL.
thinking: 9th intercostal space in the midaxillary line ↓ lung lower border reaches about the 8th rib here ↓ parietal pleura descends to the 10th rib ↓ needle enters the pleural recess below the lung ↓ Costodiaphragmatic recess
pearl: Pleural aspiration and drains should pass just above a rib, ideally within the safe triangle and under ultrasound guidance, because the intercostal neurovascular bundle runs in the groove beneath each rib.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy (Marginal Mandibular Nerve - Submandibular Gland)
stem: Which nerve is most at risk during submandibular gland excision, causing lower lip weakness?

options.B: Marginal mandibular branch of facial nerve

correct_answer: B. Marginal mandibular branch of facial nerve
why_correct: The marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve runs along, and often loops below, the lower border of the mandible deep to platysma, crossing the facial vessels. It supplies the depressors of the lower lip and is at risk during submandibular gland excision.

why_others_wrong.A: The hypoglossal nerve controls tongue movement; its injury causes tongue deviation and dysarthria, not lower lip weakness.
why_others_wrong.C: The lingual nerve supplies sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and taste fibres via chorda tympani; injury causes tongue numbness, not lip weakness.
why_others_wrong.D: The inferior alveolar nerve supplies sensation to the lower teeth and chin; injury causes numbness, not motor weakness of the lip.
why_others_wrong.E: The glossopharyngeal nerve is not in the operative field of submandibular gland excision and has no role in lower lip movement.

exam_trap: The hypoglossal (A) and lingual (C) nerves are also at risk in this operation, but they cause tongue weakness or numbness; lower lip weakness means the marginal mandibular branch.
takeaway: Marginal mandibular = lower lip weakness.
thinking: Submandibular gland excision ↓ incision placed below the mandible ↓ marginal mandibular branch of VII loops near or below the lower border of the mandible ↓ it supplies the depressors of the lower lip ↓ Marginal mandibular branch of facial nerve
pearl: The incision for submandibular gland excision is placed well below the lower border of the mandible, and ligating the facial vein low and retracting it upwards helps protect the overlying marginal mandibular nerve.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy (Suprascapular Nerve Origin)
stem: The suprascapular nerve receives fibres from which spinal segments?
why_correct: The suprascapular nerve arises from the upper trunk of the brachial plexus, which is formed by the C5 and C6 roots, and supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus.

why_others_wrong.A: C3-C4 fibres mainly contribute to the phrenic nerve and cervical plexus, not the suprascapular nerve.
why_others_wrong.C: The suprascapular nerve arises from the upper trunk and carries C5 and C6 fibres, so C6-C7 misses its principal C5 contribution.
why_others_wrong.D: C7-C8 corresponds more to nerves such as the radial or parts of the posterior cord, not the suprascapular nerve.
why_others_wrong.E: C8-T1 forms the lower trunk of the brachial plexus, giving rise to nerves like the ulnar nerve, not the suprascapular nerve.

exam_trap: C6–C7 (C) is chosen because C6 is involved, but it omits C5, the main root; the upper trunk carries C5 and C6 fibres to the suprascapular nerve.
takeaway: Suprascapular = C5–C6 (upper trunk).
thinking: Suprascapular nerve ↓ arises from the upper trunk of the brachial plexus ↓ upper trunk is formed by the C5 and C6 roots ↓ C5–C6
pearl: The suprascapular nerve passes through the suprascapular notch beneath the superior transverse scapular ligament, while the suprascapular artery usually passes above the ligament.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy (Median Nerve - Cubital Fossa)
stem: A 23-year-old man has a stab wound to the cubital fossa. Which muscle would NOT lose motor innervation from median nerve injury?
why_correct: Adductor pollicis is supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve, so it is spared by a median nerve injury at the cubital fossa, which affects the median forearm flexors (including pronator teres and palmaris longus) and the LOAF thenar muscles.

why_others_wrong.A: Palmaris longus is supplied by the median nerve, so it would lose innervation with a median nerve injury at the cubital fossa.
why_others_wrong.B: Abductor pollicis brevis is one of the median-innervated thenar (LOAF) muscles, so it would be affected by median nerve injury.
why_others_wrong.C: Pronator teres is supplied by the median nerve in the forearm and would lose innervation with a proximal median nerve injury.
why_others_wrong.E: Opponens pollicis is part of the median-innervated LOAF group, so it would also lose motor function with median nerve injury.

exam_trap: Palmaris longus (A) is chosen because it is often absent and seems minor, but when present it is median-innervated; adductor pollicis is the ulnar muscle.
takeaway: Median hand muscles = LOAF. Adductor = ulnar.
thinking: Stab wound at the cubital fossa damages the median nerve proximally ↓ median forearm flexors and LOAF thenar muscles lose supply ↓ adductor pollicis is supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve ↓ Adductor pollicis
pearl: Weak adductor pollicis is shown by asking the patient to grip paper between thumb and index finger; flexion of the thumb IP joint (FPL, median) substitutes for the missing adduction.

subject: Anatomy
title: Anatomy (Suprascapular/Accessory Nerve - Neck Dissection)
stem: After thyroidectomy and radical neck dissection, a patient cannot initiate shoulder abduction. Which nerve is injured?
why_correct: Supraspinatus initiates the first 15 degrees of abduction and is supplied by the suprascapular nerve, which arises from the upper trunk and crosses the posterior triangle, where it can be injured during neck dissection.

why_others_wrong.A: The axillary nerve supplies deltoid, which powers abduction beyond the first 15 degrees, but supraspinatus (suprascapular nerve) is needed to initiate abduction.
why_others_wrong.C: The dorsal scapular nerve supplies the rhomboids and levator scapulae, which retract and elevate the scapula, not initiate arm abduction.
why_others_wrong.D: The lateral pectoral nerve supplies pectoralis major, which adducts and flexes the shoulder, not initiate abduction.
why_others_wrong.E: The thoracodorsal nerve supplies latissimus dorsi, involved in adduction and extension, not initiation of abduction.

exam_trap: The axillary nerve (A) is chosen because deltoid is the main abductor, but deltoid only takes over after supraspinatus has started the movement.
takeaway: Inability to initiate abduction = suprascapular nerve.
thinking: Cannot initiate shoulder abduction ↓ the first part of abduction depends on supraspinatus ↓ supplied by the suprascapular nerve, which crosses the posterior triangle from the upper trunk ↓ Suprascapular nerve
pearl: Shoulder dysfunction after neck dissection is most often due to accessory nerve injury, causing trapezius weakness and difficulty abducting above the horizontal; selective and modified neck dissections aim to preserve it.

subject: Pathology: oncology & haematology
title: Pathology (Breast - Ductal vs Lobular Carcinoma)
stem: A breast lump shows infiltrating malignant cells forming glands and sheets, with retained E-cadherin expression. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Invasive ductal carcinoma (invasive carcinoma of no special type) forms glands, nests and sheets and retains membranous E-cadherin expression. Invasive lobular carcinoma characteristically loses E-cadherin through CDH1 inactivation and infiltrates as discohesive single files.
